en: Ishvara said: O Goddess, listen to the description of the four lingas situated at the four gates, by the mere sight of which a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose. || 1 ||
"O Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, I have been asked by you out of curiosity: 'O Lord, show me a place that is exceedingly beautiful. (2)
It is practiced by many perfected ones (siddhas) who desire non-return [to saṃsāra]; it is secret, pure, and indestructible even at the time of universal dissolution.
That divine sacred site, that grove of asceticism, is peerless and incomparable; endowed with innumerable virtues, it is auspicious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There were palaces with golden pinnacles and various mansions, diverse and wonderful gardens, and many auspicious roads.
Where the attainment of desired fruits is indeed easily obtained, and which resounds with the songs of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras.
"A world of merit, a place of supreme station, an ornament of the triple heaven"—thus was he entreated, O Goddess, on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves.
With a gracious mind, I have declared: listen to the eternal place, the delightful Mahākālavana, which bestows supreme happiness even greater than heaven.
Endowed with incomparable qualities, auspicious, and bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation—no other person so fortunate as he has been seen anywhere in the three worlds.
It is to be resorted to by gods, gandharvas, and siddhas who desire liberation; it was created by me out of curiosity for your pleasure and for the sake of diversion. || 10 ||
Tilaka is the foremost of all sacred fords in the delightful Jambūdvīpa; there, the attainment of the fruits of one's desires and wishes is obtained without effort.

Free from the fears of old age and disease, and devoid of all ailments, it is frequented by Śakra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśa; even the gods, rejoicing in heaven, always long for that place.
But here, the fruit is indeed incalculable and the state of existence is forever inexhaustible; those men on earth who have not cultivated this place are truly cheated.
Even with great effort, it is impossible for gods, dānavas, and humans to describe the qualities of this field, where indeed I myself am personally stationed.
Whatever inauspicious deed has been committed through human action, upon reaching Mahākālavana, all of that shall be reduced to ashes. || 15 ||
That goal which is ordained for men who always dwell in Mahākālavana is not attained at Kurukṣetra, nor at Gaṅgādvāra, nor at Tripuṣkara. (16)
Having gone to the realm of animals and remained in Mahākālavana, they meet their end right there and attain the supreme goal. || 17 ||
Even a heap of sinful karma as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara reaches total destruction upon reaching Mahākālavana. || 18 ||
O beloved, that Mahākālavana is also known as Śmaśāna; there, the gods beginning with Brahmā, led by Nārāyaṇa, reside. (19)
Likewise, the yogins, the Sāṃkhyas, and the perfected ones such as Sanaka and others, worship me with devotion; through devotion to me, they have me as their supreme goal.

Whatever destination belongs to those who practice yoga and austerity, and whatever destination belongs to those who perform sacrifices, that same destination has been ordained by me in the sacred field of Mahākālavana.
And remaining there, I withdraw the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving; therefore, O Goddess, this auspicious Mahākālavana has been fully described.
Having thus heard these various kinds of virtues, O Goddess, you were filled with wonder and set your mind upon departing. (23)
Your mind has become filled with longing to behold the sacred field; having gone together with you to the auspicious Mahākālavana, [you shall see it]. (24)

Behold, O Goddess, that which I have described to you as the place named Vicitra; it rivals the city of Amareśa and is beautiful with increasing bliss. O Goddess, that which I have extolled is the supreme bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (25)
"O large-eyed one, you have spoken; having seen this unsurpassed field, O Mahādeva, let four devoted Gaṇas be appointed for the protection of this place, O Lord, for my satisfaction. (26)
"O Supreme Lord, let four doors be constructed there; likewise, four golden jars, firm and auspicious, should be made. (27)
O Maheśvara, let the fourfold group—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—be assigned according to the sequence beginning with the east. (28)
O Goddess, having heard your words, I have diligently recollected a quartet of Gaṇas for the protection of this sacred field.
Immediately after that, four lords were also installed: Piṅgaleśa, Dhanādhyakṣa, and likewise Kāyāvarohaṇa.
Bilveśvara, the foremost of the Gaṇas, and Durdarśa, the leader of the Gaṇas—these have indeed been appointed by me, for they are capable of protecting the sacred field.
O fair-faced one, for the sake of your pleasure, by your very command and according to the sequence beginning with the east, Piṅgala has been stationed in the eastern direction.
Likewise, O beloved, Kāyāvarohaṇa is in the southern direction; Bilveśvara is in the west, and Durdarśa is likewise in the north.
"O best of the Gaṇas, by my command, you must provide supreme protection for those men who die here within the sacred field. (34)
Listen with diligence to the narrative concerning the origin of Piṅgaleśvara, by the mere hearing of which a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
O Goddess, the maiden Piṅgalā was born in Kānyakubja; she was well-behaved, elegantly attired, and fashioned with supreme beauty. (36)
Her father was highly wise, a knower of the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, devoted to knowledge and meditation, and firmly established in the study of the Vedas.
There was a lord of brahmins named Piṅgala, whose wife was a devoted spouse; she was famous in the world as Piṅgākṣī, and she too has met her death. (38)
Then, due to that sorrow, he became indifferent to the householder stage of life and went to the forest of asceticism, taking his own daughter with him. (39)
Frequented by sages who subsist on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he dwelt there together with those ascetics, devoted to the yoga of meditation.
O Goddess, that righteous-souled one made his dwelling there and protected Piṅgalā; he cherished his daughter, who was like his own heart. 41.
Constantly regarding her alone as virtuous, that great ascetic did not cause her hand to be taken in marriage, reflecting, "She is deprived of a mother."

O illustrious one, although he was detached from worldly existence and fully conversant with all dharmas, that self-controlled man did not properly undertake renunciation while gazing upon his daughter.
Then, while protecting that young, ascetic woman who was bereft of her mother, that brahmin, joined with the law of time, departed for heaven.
Then, O Goddess, that Piṅgalā, wretched, deprived of her father, and deeply distressed, lamented in her affliction, having fallen into an ocean of grief.
Piṅgalā said: "Today, by fate, my father has met the law of time; having abandoned me, he has gone alone, like one who is compassionate and free from desire. (46)
He was equal toward all beings and was exceedingly devoted to my welfare; yet, having utterly abandoned me alone, he has departed from this world to the next.
Afflicted by supreme suffering and overwhelmed by grief for my father, I maintain this wretched body with its futile life. (48)
For even though my father was a knower of Brahman—tranquil, self-controlled, and a master of his senses—he protected me alone, thinking, "She is bereft of her mother."
Separated from that father by whom I was protected in my childhood and by whom I was brought up, I shall never live.
I shall throw myself into a river, or into a kindled fire; or, deprived of my father and without refuge, I shall throw myself from a mountain. (51)
Thus the young woman, afflicted by grief, lamented again and again, even as she was being consoled by those illustrious and most excellent sages together with their wives.

Being embraced repeatedly and pressed hard on all sides by her weeping young female companions, she was deeply distressed; then Dharma, who is devoted to the welfare of others, arrived there filled with compassion.

Then, having become an elderly brahmin, he spoke these words: "Enough, O large-eyed girl, with these most piteous lamentations; your father cannot be recovered, therefore you ought not to grieve. (54)
Youth, beauty, life, the accumulation of wealth, and dwelling together with loved ones are all impermanent; therefore, the wise do not grieve over them.
O beautiful one, that very deed was indeed performed by you in a previous birth, by which there shall be separation from your father in this forest frequented by sages.
"Look, O young girl, at the power of destiny! Having abandoned you, he has gone somewhere. 'This has been done,' 'this must be done,' 'this other thing is half-finished'—[thus he spoke]. (57)
In this way, while one is thus attached to worldly effort, death brings one under its power; therefore, O beautiful lady, casting aside sorrow, you ought to listen.
And by that karma through which you suffered separation from your parents, formerly you were a courtesan named Sundarī, beautiful in form. (59)
Skilled in dancing, singing, and other arts, and proficient with the lute and flute, she was the foremost among courtesans in providing ornaments, clothing, and other such luxuries.
Upon seeing her, endowed with beauty, well-attired, and beautifully adorned, a certain virtuous brahmin became afflicted by passion. (61)
Having recognized that brahmin to be in such a state, afflicted by passion, you were then enjoyed for four years by that lustful man.
Then that foolish Brahmin, devoted to sin and absorbed in sensual objects, was killed by some lustful Śūdra in your house.
Abandoning his auspicious young twelve-year-old wife, he, defiled by contact with a Śūdra woman, went to a terrible hell.
Then his father, though learned, and his mother became exceedingly distressed; afflicted by the separation from their son, they were struck by a terrifying curse.
The mother said: "O woman of wicked conduct, you have employed medicines and other means to bring my son under your control; you have deceived him so that he might be separated from us. (66)
"And because she caused my son to suffer separation from her, may she become wretched and husbandless in another birth. (67)
The father said: "While still in the age of childhood, you will be motherless and deeply distressed; excluded from marriage, you will become fatherless. (68)
Dharma said: "Therefore, O lady of excellent complexion, you, though being a maiden, have encountered this suffering solely because of your previously performed karma. (69)
Piṅgalā said: "O best of the twice-born, you have related to me what occurred in my previous birth; therefore, please provide the certain answer to the question I am asking. (70)
Thus, being one of such terrible sin, of sinful conduct, and so base, how indeed was I born of a Brāhmaṇa who speaks of Brahman? (71)
A wheelwright is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a liquor-seller is equal to ten wheelwrights; a courtesan is equal to ten liquor-sellers; and a king is equal to ten courtesans.
Thus speak the Brahmins, knowers of Dharma and firm in their vows: "How was my birth from this best of the twice-born? (73)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Piṅgalā, although you were devoted to sinful conduct, you were born into the auspicious family of Brāhmaṇas; I shall tell you the reason for that, so listen."
O beautiful one, a certain Brāhmaṇa, addicted to sensual pleasures and greedy for a courtesan, committed the act of theft and was bound by the king's command. (75)
And let him be released by you as well; it has been said that he is neither a thief nor a sinner. Whatever theft has been committed by him would, in fact, have been committed by me alone. (76)
"I shall give you abundant wealth; let this best of the twice-born be released. Having said this, she brought him back home along with that very man.
And a beautiful house was prepared for you, white and perfumed with flowers, incense, and other offerings; and the Brahmin was delighted by you with unsurpassed comfort as he pleased. (78)
By the greatness of that merit, she went to the unsurpassed heaven and was reborn as a daughter in the family of a distinguished Brahmin. (79)
And now, O daughter, you have further experienced separation from me due to that very curse. (80)

Piṅgalā said: In a previous birth, I was born as a prostitute who committed evil deeds; I was wicked, intent on the wealth of others, and devoid of purity and proper conduct. Now I have become miserable due to separation from my father and mother. (81)
"O Lord, I have been deprived of the rite of marriage due to a curse; O Brahmin, show me favor! Tell me, who are you? (82)
"How may birth not be mine again? How may liberation be mine? Freed from the bonds of worldly existence, how shall I go to the auspicious state? (83)

The Brahmin said: "I am Dharma, come here in the form of a twice-born man desiring to test you. O slender-limbed one, through my instruction, by the sight of a single Liṅga, and by the grace of this sacred field (kṣetra), you shall attain supreme liberation."
Piṅgalā said: "In which sacred field is supreme liberation attained, and by the sight of which liṅga is this merit suddenly obtained? This I wish to know. (85)
Dharma said: There is a most secret and auspicious sacred field called Mahākālavana, which is always the cause of liberation for all living beings. (86)

In that meritorious and excellent field, O daughter, at a site extending one yojana, there stands a Liṅga that bestows liberation in the eastern direction; by the mere sight of it, O Piṅgalā, you shall attain liberation.
O illustrious lady, having heard those words of Dharmarāja, Piṅgalā went quickly to where that supreme liṅga was located; she beheld it with supreme devotion and touched it again and again. || 88 ||
Upon seeing that linga, she attained dissolution into that very linga; and at that moment, the gods, remaining right there, spoke.
"In another birth, you, O tawny-eyed one, were most sinful, yet you have been liberated."
Therefore, he shall become renowned in the worlds by the name Piṅgaleśvara; there is no doubt that he will be the destroyer of great sins. || 91 ||
For those who go to the eastern direction and behold Piṅgaleśvara, the performer of a hundred sacrifices (Indra), being pleased, will duly perform their worship.
The gods will become submissive to them, and heaven will undoubtedly belong to them; furthermore, the city of Amarāvatī shall come under their control.

For those whose wealth is accompanied by righteousness, their lineage does not perish; the world shall come under the control of those who practice righteousness, and there is no doubt that their ancestors will attain inexhaustible satisfaction.
Whatever merit is proclaimed to come from a thousand horse-sacrifices, all of that shall be fully attained simply by beholding Piṅgaleśvara. (95)
Whatever lingas exist in this field, whether hidden or manifest, they become worshipped here through the sight of Piṅgaleśvara. || 96 ||
This power of the god Piṅgaleśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Kāyāvarohaṇa. || 97 ||
Mahādeva said: O Pārvatī, listen also to the origin of Kāyāvarohaṇa, by the mere hearing of which a man shall no longer possess a body. || 1 ||
During the Vaivasvata Manvantara, Dakṣa, that lord of progeny, was born from the right thumb of Brahmā, who was desirous of creation.
From the left thumb of that high-souled one was born his wife; in her, that lord himself begot fifty daughters.
Having lost his sons, the Prajāpati established all those blameless, lotus-eyed maidens as his daughters.
O Goddess, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, and twenty-seven to Indra according to the divine rite.
Rohiṇī became forever the beloved of that Moon; however, O Pārvatī, the Moon was cursed by Dakṣa on account of his twenty-six wives.
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, was likewise cursed by Candra and rendered so; he then became the son of Pracetas and performed the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
O Daughter of the Mountain, I was addressed with delusion by Dakṣa regarding the sacrificial portions of all the hosts of gods there, without exception.
Then the bearer of oblations, yoked and impelled by mantras, was seen by you, O large-eyed one, stationed in the supportless sky.
O beloved, remembering our former enmity, I was entreated by you thus: "You are the god of all gods, as well as their refuge and resort. (10)
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, and you alone are the *hotṛ* and the *adhvaryu*. O Lord of all gods, how can the sacrifice proceed without you?
Out of fear, this Agni carries the sacrificial portions for the gods; and Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, is indeed full of pride and arrogance.
Remembering his former enmity, he will certainly not give [it] up unless commanded; therefore, he must be deprived of his body, and the fire must likewise be made skillful.
O Śaṅkara, O destroyer of Tripura, all those gods who have been assembled at the sacrifice of Dakṣa must be rendered bodiless by you.
When you had spoken thus, O goddess of beautiful countenance, I also said: "O lady of pure smiles, in a previous birth, this Dakṣa was your father. (15)
O beloved, Agni is obedient to my command and the gods are mere playthings; yet, O dear one, having heard my words, you have become angry.
Knitting her brows upon her forehead and sighing again and again, she then repeatedly pressed the tip of her nose with her hand out of anger.
While that [nose-tip] was being pressed, O daughter of the mountain, a woman was born with knitted brows, four tusks, and three eyes.
With her leather arm-guards and finger-protectors bound on, with her armor fastened and her girdle secured, she was equipped with a sword, a bow, a quiver, and a banner.
With a thousand faces, a hundred arms, and a thousand feet and bellies, O Goddess, she thus caused the earth to tremble with her discordant footsteps.
"O Goddess, honored by all the worlds, having seen her who is composed of darkness, you named her Bhadrakālī and Māyā. (21)
I then created such a hair-raising person; and he, having joined his palms in reverence, spoke to me again and again: "Command me, O Lord of the Gods, O Sovereign of the World! What shall I do? (22)
Then, O Goddess, having perceived your disposition and having bestowed upon him a pleasing name, he was known as Vīrabhadra. || 23 ||
O Vīrabhadra, by my command, together with this Bhadrakālī, [slay] Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, who is full of pride along with his deities.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, destroy him along with his sacrifice and his followers! I have bestowed a great army upon you, who possess innumerable virtues. (25)
By you as well, Bhadrakālī, a terrifying army was given—a inexhaustible host of Mothers holding skull-bowls and flaying-knives in their hands. || 26 ||
Then, completely surrounded by that great army, the two of them went to the place where Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, was performing a sacrifice.

O Goddess, surrounded by the gods and accompanied by the Brahmins in the assembly hall, those gods were then completely overcome by that army, O Pārvatī, as they drank the Soma purified by mantras with confidence during the sacrifice.
With his three eyes and his trident, the Lord, the sovereign of the thirty gods, suddenly rescued Śakra, who was situated in the midst of the sacrifice along with his host. || 29 ||
By the host known as Yama, and by Yamakalpaprabha, Yama—who was intent on drinking the soma—was drawn away at the sacrifice.
Varuṇa is bound by the noose, and Gaṇapa by the noose; O Supreme Goddess, the heroic lord of the western quarter is bound by the vital breath (prāṇa).

Then, O Goddess, Anila himself was struck down, and Naravāhana, the lord of the northern quarter, accompanied by the treasures (Nidhis), stood at the sacrifice; those men appointed by Vīrabhadra waged a most terrible battle.
Then Bhadrakālī, the terrifying one, waged a fierce battle, along with Vikarālī, Mahākālī, Kālikā, and Kalaśodarī.
With forms like blazing fire, their flesh dried up and exceedingly terrifying; these and hundreds of others were adorned with garlands of human heads. (34)
Then the hosts of gods struck with skull-bowls and flaying knives. Seeing the enraged host of Mothers thus crushing the deities, the Tuṣita gods, eager for battle, then advanced.
Some hurled javelins, others likewise hurled spears; some with sharp lances, and others with swords and battle-axes.
When the host of Mothers was afflicted and the Pramathas were tormented, Bhadrakālī then became enraged with her mace and showers of arrows.
With his sword and other weapons, he afflicted them in battle with six sun-like rays; Bhaga’s eyes and Pūṣan’s teeth were destroyed from his mouth.
The hands of the Sun himself, as well as the feet of Bhāskara—those eight Vasus, skilled in battle, who were struck down by the mace.
Vomiting blood, their heads shattered and their bodies mangled in battle, even those who were proud of their prowess in war were rendered bodiless and destroyed. (40)
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, was bound with a very firm noose, and the remaining gods, filled with fear, went to Brahmā for refuge.
The entire account has been related in detail exactly as it happened; those gods who were originally the Tuṣitas have indeed been made Videhas.

The Vasus and the gods have perished, and the Bhāskaras were afflicted in battle; neither the thousand-eyed Indra, nor Yama, nor the Lord of Wealth is known, and where has Varuṇa, the supreme lord of aquatic creatures, gone? (43)
Everything was destroyed by Bhadrakālī and the host of Vīrabhadra; indeed, the sacrificial post was broken and the water-pot was then shattered.

The great hall was set ablaze and the sacrificial archway was indeed shattered; having heard their words, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, filled with compassion, came to where I was stationed on Mount Mandara.
Having offered praise to me, he then spoke these words: "Those gods who were the primordial Tuṣitas have now been made Videhas."
By Bhadrakālī, O Mahādeva, the Vasus were shattered; the Bhāskaras were oppressed in battle, and the rest perished and fled to the various directions. || 47 ||
"O God, how shall the descent from the Tuṣita heaven come about? Having heard the words of Brahmā, O lady of beautiful countenance, I spoke thus: [48]
Let these Tuṣitas go to the sacred field of Mahākālavana, where Lakuṭīśa has gone to the temple of Kāyāvarohaṇa.
And by my command, the Brāhmaṇas, accompanied by four disciples, [shall remain] when the Dvāpara age has passed and the Kali age has arrived.
There, my disciples, my followers, having reached the earth, shall dwell as blessed ones for the sake of protecting the twice-born. (51)
To the south of that field exists an excellent, divine Liṅga which bestows all prosperity and grants the bodies of the Siddhas. || 52 ||
"By the grace of that Liṅga, these gods shall attain bodies; having heard my words, O beloved, they have gone to the Tuṣita heaven. (53)
Where that supreme Liṅga is, there Muditā was together with Brahmā; by the grace of that Liṅga, she obtained an unsurpassed body.
Once again, they became just like those who had been in Tuṣita; therefore, the gods gave him the name Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara, and he shall become the renowned god who eternally grants all desires.
Those who, having gone to the southern direction, behold the god Kāyāvarohaṇa with supreme devotion—for them, Yama shall become their father.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of births—all that goes to destruction by the mere sight [of this], and not otherwise. (57)
And for those groups of ancestors who have gone to hell due to their own karma, liberation will come about through the sight of that Liṅga.
Those who behold the deity Kāyārohaṇa even by chance shall not return to this world again, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Indeed, even those men who are sinners shall go to the supreme abode, freed from all sins, simply by touching that linga. || 60 ||
If the Lord Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara is worshipped with guile, he bestows a kingdom, enjoyments, and the eternal world of heaven. || 61 ||
Those who, having bathed on the twelfth day, behold Kāyāvarohaṇa, shall pierce through the abode of Brahmā and go to the supreme goal.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of Kāyāvarohaṇeśa has been recounted to you; now listen to that of Bilveśvara.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara. || 82 ||
Śrī Hara said: O beautiful one, listen with reverence to the majesty of Bilveśvara, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
O Great Goddess, in the first aeon, out of compassion for the worlds, the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) were born from Brahmā as he was meditating in ancient times.
In their midst stands a bilva tree, celebrated as the Śrīvṛkṣa; beneath that tree is a man with the luster of gold.
Then, as he sat there, he was seen by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, amidst his various fruits and leaves in constant abundance.
Exceedingly delighted, he devours foods that are both heart-pleasing and soft; likewise, he is an archer equipped with arrows and wearing leather finger-guards and arm-guards.
Wearing a sword, a diadem, and a garland, adorned with earrings and clad in armor, he was broad-chested, possessed of great energy, a youth with the powerful build of a lion.
And Brahmā gave him the name by which he became widely renowned as Bilva; Indra then chose him, saying, "Become the king upon the surface of the earth."
Standing on earth as a friend of Triviṣṭapa, you have been dear to me; I give to you this Vaijayantī garland of unfading lotuses.
"By whose power weapons shall have no effect in battle," he said, "if you grant me the thunderbolt as my weapon. (9)
Therefore, I shall be the king upon this earth; it does not please me otherwise. Thus, by truth, I will protect this earth.
Indra said: "So be it; may prosperity be yours. Become a king for the welfare of your subjects. By my mere remembrance, the thunderbolt shall come into your hand; it shall not be otherwise."
Having been addressed thus, that glorious King Bilva became known as the righteous-souled Kapila, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. || 12 ||
That best of brahmin-sages became a friend to that Bilva; O fair-faced one, having met with him, he sat comfortably with him.
Delighted, he told stories of diverse meanings again and again; likewise, in the course of their conversation, a debate arose between the two of them.
"Charity is the preeminent sacred ford," Bilva declared again and again; however, Kapila stated that Brahman is supreme and austerity is supreme. (15)
Bilva said: "O tiger among the twice-born, through giving one attains a kingdom, happiness, enjoyments, sovereignty, and imperishable heaven; why then do you praise Brahman? (16)
Kapila said: From the Veda the sacrifices proceed; from the Veda the rites for specific desires proceed. Ritual actions proceed from the Veda; this world has the Veda as its root.

Bilva said: "In this world, kings are the best, for they are capable of protecting the world and are like the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) in this realm; why then, O Brahmin, do you praise [the forest]? (18)"

Kapila said: "The Brāhmaṇas are indeed declared to be the foremost, for they possess the power to curse and to bless; they are the ancestors of kings—why then, O Bilva, do you not acknowledge this? (19)
When such curiosity had arisen, Kapila, the best of the twice-born, was struck on the head with a bilva fruit by one who used it like a jointless thunderbolt.
Cut in two by the vajra, Kapila was restored to life through the Brahma-vidyā; having sustained his own body, he approached my presence.
I have been praised with various hymns and indeed properly propitiated; by me, moreover, the state of immortality was granted to the Brāhmaṇa from the thunderbolt.
The twice-born one arrived with a bilva fruit, and friendship was restored between them; yet once again, O Daughter of the Mountain, a similar dispute arose.
And with his left foot, Bilva struck this brahmin; then, taking up a thunderbolt once more, he struck him firmly.
That thunderbolt did not cause him death nor pain; moreover, having realized the invincibility of that great-souled one, Bilva [withdrew].

Then, having approached Nārāyaṇa, he requested his desired boon; and being gratified by Viṣṇu, who said, "I am the giver of boons," that high-minded one, bowing down, spoke thus to Viṣṇu, O Goddess. (26)
Bilva said: "O Hṛṣīkeśa, there is a brahmin-sage named Kapila who is indeed invincible and imperishable; he is my friend, and he has always told me: 'I fear neither god, nor rākṣasa, nor asura. (27)
"You ought to act in such a way that I may say, 'I am afraid neither of a Piśāca, nor of a Yakṣa, nor indeed of anyone else. (28)
Thus addressed by Bilva, that god Puruṣottama said, "So shall it be," and went to the hermitage of Kapila.
Having entered the hermitage and been honored by Kapila, Janārdana addressed Kapila with these conciliatory words: || 30 ||
"O Blessed One, best of brāhmaṇas, master of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches! O lord of sages, I choose one boon today; you ought to grant it. (31)
O great sage, I was propitiated again and again by that lord of kings with a bilva fruit; and when I said, "I am a granter of boons," he chose a boon from me.
"You said, 'I am afraid'; therefore, by your grace, speak so that you may be fearless. Nevertheless, O Lord, speak today for my sake."
Thus addressed with these sweet words by Viṣṇu, Kapila said, "O Janārdana, I do not fear," repeatedly.
"I shall not speak; I am afraid," he said. "Therefore, I will not speak. Having heard these words of Kapila, Janārdana raised his discus and spoke, showing his fear of the brahmin.
"If you do not speak, being afraid, I shall indeed strike you with my discus."
Kapila said: "O Viṣṇu, why do you desire to cause distress here to your beloved discus in vain? Indeed, by the grace of Tryambaka, I am not accessible to your discus."
Then, taking a handful of kusha grass, Kapila approached Vāsudeva and said, "Stop! Stop! (38)
Today I shall destroy all your pride, arrogance, and that wonderful strength of yours; wait now, O Janārdana! (39)
Then a tumultuous battle, hair-raising, took place between Kṛṣṇa and Kapila, lasting for no more than the blink of an eye.
O Goddess, a fierce battle took place in the supportless sky between the divine missiles and the Kuśas; fear entered the hearts of the gods.
In the meantime, Brahmā, surrounded by the gods and deeply distressed, arrived and spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa: || 42 ||
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, remover of the fear of the bonds of worldly existence; O Hṛṣīkeśa, Hṛṣīkeśa, author of creation and dissolution! 43.
Having propitiated the Lord of the World, Indra and the other inhabitants of the triple heaven all dwell there joyfully, endowed with every desire fulfilled.
The three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, have been produced, sustained, and pervaded by the powerful Viṣṇu.
"By that one, pure, all-pervading, and great-souled [Self]," thus indeed were all those sages, the best of munis, addressed. 46.
And Janārdana is declared by the gods, dānavas, daityas, sages, cāraṇas, and pannagas to be the cause of this triple world.
O Garuḍa-bannered one, you are worshipped by the most excellent seekers of boons; O Giver of Cows, why do you yourself fight in vain with those twice-born ones? 48.
And do you not know how this [Kapila], the Brahmin who obtained boons from Hara, attained [his power] through the grace of the Supreme Lord? 49.
For you have indeed attained invincibility and the state of being unconquerable in battle; yet, O Lord, those like you do not act with such hostility toward Brahmins.
"Brahman and the root of Brahman were previously promised by you yourself; therefore, O Lord, consider him a Brāhmaṇa and return at once. (51)
Having thus heard these words falling from the mouth of Brahmā, the Lord of Gods, through his yogic power, understood the strength of Kapila and Śaṅkara.
Being honored by the inhabitants of heaven, he went to the supreme world; once Janārdana had departed, Bilva lamented again and again.
Having heard of the most terrible battle between Kṛṣṇa and Kapila, [he thought: "How shall I conquer Kapila? How may I find peace? To whom shall I go for refuge? Who will be my protector? (54)
"Kapila was not defeated in battle by the all-powerful Viṣṇu; he constantly vies with me—how will he be conquered? (55)
Brahmins are invincible in battle; they are capable of both cursing and bestowing grace. They could reduce the entire universe—including gods, asuras, and humans—to ashes. (56)
"For the supreme Brahmanic splendor is difficult to approach even for the gods. While he was thus lamenting, Vāsava arrived.
Beholding the emaciated Bilva lamenting while holding a thunderbolt in his hand, Purandara, his heart drawn by a sense of possessiveness, replied: || 58 ||
Enough with grief, O protector of the earth; listen to my supreme words. When I was afflicted in battle by the wicked-minded Śambara, who was powerful and arrogant, I then questioned my preceptor.
O King, Bṛhaspati of great splendor was then addressed by him: "Go, O Śakra, at my command to the auspicious Mahākālavana."
Where there exist various most divine lingas, which indeed bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grant all desired objects. || 61 ||
"O Lord of Śacī, worship one Liṅga among them, by the mere sight of which you will become invincible in battle. At his word, Bilva performed the worship perfectly.
At that time, Śambara was indeed conquered by me through my joy for the Liṅga; and that deity attained renown under the name Indreśvara.
Therefore, having gone to that western quarter, you must diligently propitiate the Liṅga worshipped by Varuṇa within that sacred field.

That Liṅga shall attain fame in the three worlds by your name; the Brahmin Kapila, your friend, will say, "I am conquered," and through the majesty of that Liṅga, he will enter into a state of friendship [with you].
When Śakra had spoken thus and departed for the world of the gods, O illustrious lady, he worshipped [him] with devotion using divine, fragrant flowers.
King Bilva went to the auspicious Mahākālavana forest; there, in the western quarter, he beheld a Liṅga worshipped by the gods.
With pearls, gems, garments, and ornaments, Kapila also arrived in that very interval.
He saw King Bilva worshipping again and again; seeing his own supreme form within the body of that Bilva tree and realizing it was Mahādeva, the twice-born one said, "I am conquered. (69)
"I request from you eternal friendship in the presence of Śiva. Thus was Bilva addressed by the high-souled Kapila at that time.
With a serene mind and palms joined in reverence, he said to Kapila, the best of the twice-born: "So be it; may prosperity be yours! I have attained my purpose through this great-souled one."
"Let that very friendship remain forever; so you speak and so you think. Having thus spoken to one another and established that unsurpassed friendship, the two of them— || 72 ||
Having attained supreme joy, they sported for a long time; by virtue of the majesty of that Liṅga, he ruled his kingdom once again.

O Goddess, because that protector of the earth was [honored] with a bilva fruit by Mitra, from that time forward the deity became renowned on earth as Bilveśvara; worshipped with a bilva fruit in this world, he bestows the fruits of all desired objects.
O large-eyed lady, those who behold the supreme deity Bilveśvara shall have their purpose fulfilled and become free from all sins.
O Daughter of the Mountain, those who rejoice at the sight of the God are also liberated from sin and go to my abode.
By the sight of that liṅga, a person swiftly leads ten thousand families of the past and the future to my world. (77)
Having beheld the Liṅga, the ancestors, freed from terrible sins, go joyfully and unwearied to my world. (78)
Even if a man has committed a terrible sin such as the killing of a Brahmin, that evil is dissolved by the sight of Śrī Bilveśvara. (79)
O Goddess, that lunar day which is heard of as the thirteenth of the dark fortnight is declared to be dear to him, destroying all sins. (80)
O beloved, those men who worship the god Bilveśvara on that [day] shall have no return to the terrible abyss of saṃsāra.
Whatever evil has been accumulated through action, mind, or speech—that the Lord washes away when he is duly worshipped on that lunar day.
This power of the god Bilveśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now let the [power of] Uttareśvara be heard.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Bilveśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 83 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Pārvatī, listen to the majesty of Uttarēśvara, which destroys all sins without exception and shatters birth, death, old age, and disease. 1.
In Ayodhyā, there was a highly renowned king born of an illustrious lineage; that wise monarch, named Parīkṣit, went out on a hunt.
Then, as he pursued the deer, the deer fled far away.
Then, exhausted by the journey and overcome by hunger and thirst, he saw a dark forest in a certain part of the wilderness and entered it.
Having seen a lake on the southern side of that forest tract, he plunged into it together with his horse. || 5 ||
Then, having dismounted and placed a lotus stalk before the horse, he sat down by the pond.
Then, while lying down, he heard a song being sung.
Having heard this, he reflected: "I do not perceive any human course of existence here."
"Whose song is this? he wondered, looking about.
Then he saw a maiden of most beautiful appearance gathering flowers, and the king approached her nearby.
The king said to her: "Whose daughter are you, O maiden of most beautiful appearance, who are gathering flowers? (11)
Then, having gone into the presence of the king, she spoke thus: "I am a maiden."
The king said: "I am a petitioner of you."
Then the maiden said: "I can be approached by you only on certain conditions, and not otherwise."
The king asked her, "What is your agreement? (15)
Then the maiden said to him, "Water must not be shown. || 16 ||
The king, having said "So be it," approached her and sat with her. || 17 ||
While the king was still nearby, the army arrived; it remained surrounding the king as he sat there together with them. || 18 ||

Thus honored by Śibī, the king departed with her; then, having quickly reached his own city with her, while sporting with her in secret, he perceived nothing else. Thereupon, the chief minister questioned those women who were in attendance upon him.
"What purpose is served here? those women said; "we have already seen that water; it is not to be relied upon here. || 20 ||

Then Āmātya, having caused a waterless place to be prepared and finding a tree laden with mature flowers and fruit in the autumn, said to the king: "This forest is without water; it would be well for you to take your pleasure here. || 21 ||
At his word, he entered the forest together with that very queen.
In that beautiful forest, he took his pleasure with her alone, free from all fear.
And having entered, the king, together with his beloved, beheld a pond filled with water white as nectar. || 24 ||
And upon seeing that pond filled with frogs, the goddess remained right there on its bank.
Then the king said to that queen: "The water in the pond is even more tranquil."
Having heard those words, she submerged herself into a sacred bathing pool and did not emerge again; though the king searched for her, he did not find her.
Seeing the pond filled with frogs, he commanded his servants, "Let all the frogs be killed! || 28 ||
Whoever seeks me should attend upon me with those gifts of frogs. || 29 ||
Then, while the frogs were being slaughtered, a certain large frog fled in all directions.
Approaching him and perceiving that he had fallen under the sway of anger, he said this: "Be gracious; you ought not to carry out the slaughter of these innocent frogs. (31)
And there is a verse on this point: "O Acyuta, do not crush the frogs; restrain your anger. The great dharma of people who possess discernment is being destroyed. (32)
To him who spoke thus, whose soul was overwhelmed with grief at the separation from his beloved, the king said: "Indeed, even this desire cannot be eradicated by one who is free from desire. (33)
"This woman has not been devoured by these evil-minded ones; rather, these frogs are to be killed in every way. O wise one, you ought not to obstruct us. (34)
Having heard those words, his senses and mind distressed, he said: "Be gracious, O King; I am the monarch named Āyu."
My daughter has been found; that maiden has gone to the world of the nāgas. There dwells the nāga king Nāgacūḍa; when remembered, she will come.
The king said to her, "Remembering her, bring her and give her to me. || 37 ||
Then, having remembered her, he gave her to the king and said: || 38 ||

The great sage Gālava, whose limbs were emaciated by asceticism and who was a master of forgiveness, was provoked to anger by me out of childishness while playing with frogs; he cursed me, saying: "Since you have disregarded me and mocked me out of childishness while playing with frogs, therefore you shall become a frog. (39)
Being thus propitiated, the brahmin replied: || 40 ||

This curse of mine is infallible; therefore, having become the king of frogs in another birth, you shall give your daughter to one born of the Ikṣvāku lineage who is endowed with all virtues. When you go to the Mahākālavana forest and reach its northern quarter, you will then attain liberation through the sight of the Liṅga. || 41 ||
"How deep will my daughter go? And when remembered, she shall return. May it be well with you; I shall now attend to my duties. Having said this, Dardura went to the Mahākāla forest.

To the north of that, he beheld a Liṅga; by the sight of it, he ascended an excellent celestial chariot adorned with many pearls and frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and went to the world of Śakra. || 43 ||
Beholding his majesty, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, spoke these words. || 44 ||
Oh, the majesty of the Liṅga! Oh, the glory of the Liṅga! For even Dardura, fallen by a curse, has attained the world of Vāsava.
For the king named Āyu, having been liberated, attained the state of a frog. || 46 ||
O Pārvatī, having heard these words of the preceptor of the gods, those deities, with joyful minds and composed, gave him a name.
Since King Dardura was liberated from his birth as a frog by the sight of that Liṅga, it shall therefore become renowned [as Dardureśvara].
"Uttaresvara Deva is the dispeller of curses and sins"; having spoken thus, Uttareśvara was indeed worshipped by all the gods.

O Goddess, he who was appointed by me for the protection of the sacred field is the invincible Dardura; he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, destroys great sins, and has indeed attained the status of a Lord.
Furthermore, he who goes to the northern quarter and beholds Uttareśvara shall be endowed with all sovereign powers and proceed to the highest world.
He becomes fortunate, always self-controlled, handsome, and possessed of sons; moreover, for seven births he is born free from disease and endowed with a virtuous character. || 52 ||

Whatever prosperity belongs to Kubera, Śakra, and Yama, and whatever prosperity belongs to Varuṇa—that prosperity arises in ever-increasing measure from beholding the Lord of the North; of this there is no doubt. (53)
O illustrious lady, those who behold the one known as Uttareśvara on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight are successful in their purpose during the Kali Yuga.

What is the use of gifts, what is the use of austerities, and what is the use of sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees? By the mere sight [of him], one obtains a kingdom, and then heaven and liberation in succession.
Whatever sin has been committed since birth, whether it be small or great, all of that goes to destruction by the sight of Uttareśvara. (56)
Thus, these eighty-four lords have been enumerated by you; those whom you were asked about by me in Mahākālavana have now been described.
O Goddess, those men who with devotion perform the pilgrimage of these [deities] in both direct and reverse order shall go to the supreme state.
And whatever man worships the Liṅga there with devotion, he surely delivers a hundred ancestors on his father's side and a hundred on his mother's side.
This power of the eighty-four Liṅgas, which destroys sin, has been told to you, O Goddess. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Eighty-Four Liṅgas, preceded by the Description of the Majesty of the Uttareśvara Liṅga," within the Dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara in the Majesty of the Eighty-Four Liṅgas, in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Chapter 1
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. 1.

Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Puruṣottama. Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Narmadā. Oṃ, salutations to Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations to Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Śuka, and Parāśara; salutations to the gurus, cows, and Brāhmaṇas. May the waters of the Narmadā protect you—waters that intoxicate swarms of bees with the fragrance of the wine-like ichor flowing from the temples of bathing elephants; waters turned tawny by contact with the saffron melting from the breasts of the Siddhas’ maidens during their baths; waters whose banks are lined with trees covered in heaps of flowers offered by sages morning and evening; and waves upon which swans are overtaken by the trunks of elephants and sea-monsters. (2)
May the Narmadā, whose sacred fords on both banks have washed away the flood of the misdeeds of all people, and who is worthy of worship by gods, sages, and men, ever remove our evil. (3)
May she destroy all the misfortunes of living beings—past, future, and present—upon this earth; for you, O sanctifier of all, become the Narmadā, whose waters are merit-bestowing nectar. (4)
May the river Revā, whose sandy banks even ascetics desire for the sake of Śiva, and who is served by hosts of sages, lead to my auspicious welfare.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
In Naimiṣa, the meritorious abode frequented by various ṛṣis, Śaunaka, seated at a sacrificial session, questioned Sūta in detail: (7)
O Sūta, I believe that the perfection of dharma is ever honored in you; for you alone, together with your disciple Vyāsa, are the speaker of meritorious and nectar-like stories.
Therefore, O Sage, I question you, who are the refuge of the ford of Dharma; for many are the sacred fords that exist, and many have been heard by me.
I have heard of the divine river Brāhmī and likewise the Viṣṇunadī; however, I have never anywhere heard of the third, the excellent river Raudrī.
O one of great wisdom, tell me of that renowned [river], which contains the Vedas within, is saluted by hosts of gods, and is adorned by a multitude of sacred fords.
Upon which region does the Revā depend, and how did she originate from Śrī Rudra? Tell me of those sacred fords (tīrthas) that are situated along her course.
Sūta said: Well asked, O lord of the lineage, is this account concerning Narmadā; it is wonderful, purifying, and destructive of faults, O best of men, as has been heard and spoken.
Having brought forth the Vedas, Upavedas, Vedāṅgas, and so forth, he was filled with them; the son of Satyavatī is the speaker of the eighteen Purāṇas.
Having paid homage to him, I shall describe the Purāṇas in their proper order; by the recitation of which there is an increase in merit and longevity.
Revelation (Śruti) and Tradition (Smṛti) are proclaimed to be the two eyes of the Brahmins; one who is deprived of one of them is called "one-eyed," while one who lacks both is declared "blind. (16)
The Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas are the three eyes of the learned; he who perceives through these three eyes is considered a portion of Maheśvara.
The knowledge of the Vedas pertaining to the self was created by the Lord, as were the traditions of Śaunaka, the Purāṇas, and that which consists of the Dharmaśāstras. (18)
These three sciences are primary for the definitive determination of all scriptures; "the Purāṇa is the fifth Veda"—such is the instruction of Brahmā. (19)
He who does not know the Purāṇa indeed knows nothing at all here; for what dharma could that be, or what kind of knowledge could it be? (20)
Or whatever else is not seen here in the Purāṇa, the Vedas were established therein from of old; of this there is no doubt. (21)
"The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me. This was the conclusion reached in ancient times through the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. (22)
The Self is the ancient essence of the Vedas, and those six [limbs] are its distinct parts; indeed, whatever is seen in the Vedas is likewise seen in the Smṛtis.
That which has indeed been seen by both is sung of in the Purāṇas; the Purāṇa is remembered as the first of all scriptures, originating from Brahmā. (24)
And immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths. O Sage, in this current kalpa, there was only one Purāṇa.
Having recalled that meritorious means of accomplishing the three goals of life, which extends over a hundred crores [of verses], the four-faced God spoke to the sages.
From that, the manifestation of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa occurred; then, seeing that the Purāṇa was not being grasped over time, the sage [acted].
Assuming the form of Vyāsa, the All-pervading Lord always withdraws [the Vedas] at the end of every Dvāpara age, when they have reached a measure of eight hundred thousand [verses].
Having divided it into eighteen parts, it is proclaimed here in this world of mortals; even today, in the realm of the gods, its extent is one hundred crore verses.
Thus, four hundred thousand [verses] have been set down here in brief. Now, those eighteen Purāṇas are being mentioned; I shall state them by name—listen, O best of sages. (30)
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manus, and the history of the dynasties—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. (31)
Therein, the ancient Brāhma Purāṇa is the first, adorned with a Saṃhitā consisting of ten thousand verses and filled with various meritorious narratives. (32)
The Pādma is said to consist of fifty-five thousand [verses], and the third, named Vaiṣṇava, has a number of twenty-three thousand.
The fourth is proclaimed by Vāyu and is remembered as the Vāyavīya; through its union with devotion to Śiva, it is called Śaiva by another name.
O Śaunaka, the fifth [purāṇa], the Bhaviṣya, which consists of twenty-four thousand verses, is likewise proclaimed in four sections.
That [Purāṇa] consists of fourteen thousand and five hundred verses; the sixth is proclaimed as the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, consisting of nine thousand verses.
The seventh is declared to be the Āgneya Purāṇa, consisting of sixteen thousand verses; the eighth is declared to be the Nāradīya Purāṇa, consisting of twenty-five thousand verses.
O Blessed One, the ninth name is adorned by two parts; it is said to consist of eighteen thousand verses by way of the count of its textual units.
The tenth is said here to be the Brahmavaivarta, equal in number [to its chapters]; the eleventh is to be known as the Laiṅga, likewise with the number eleven.
O bull among sages, that Liṅga has been composed in two parts; they know the Vārāha Purāṇa to consist of twenty-four thousand verses and as the twelfth [Purāṇa].
O best among the fortunate, the Skanda Purāṇa is divided into seven sections; it is indeed defined by a number of eighty-one thousand verses.
Then, O Kulapati, the fourteenth [Purāṇa] known as the Vāmana is remembered; it was formerly declared to consist of ten thousand verses in number. (42)
They say the fifteenth is the Kaurma Purāṇa, adorned with two parts; formerly it consisted of seventeen thousand verses, O Lord of Sāṃkhya, in the Kali age.
O best among speakers, that which was proclaimed by Matsya to Manu, known as the Mātsya Purāṇa, consists of sixteen sections in sequence and contains fourteen thousand verses in number.
The Gāruḍa is remembered as the seventeenth, and the eighteenth is the Brahmāṇḍa, adorned with two parts; [the nineteenth is] the twenty-first.
And that consists of twelve thousand verses together with one hundred and eight; likewise are the Upapurāṇas which were spoken by the Creator.
This is the easily accessible and excellent Saura [Purāṇa] from the Brahmapurāṇa, consisting of two Saṃhitās, meritorious, and based upon the narratives of Śiva. (47)
The first was spoken by Sanatkumāra and the second was uttered by Sūrya; indeed, O great sage, it is renowned by the name of Sanatkumāra.
The second is the Nārasiṃha, found in the Purāṇa known as the Pādma; and the third is considered to be the Śaukeya in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa. (49)
The Bārhaspatya is the fourth, and the Vāyavya is always esteemed; the Daurvāsasa is remembered as the fifth, and it is always included among the Bhāgavatas.
The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa spoken by Nārada, that which was told of old by the wise, as well as the Kāpila, the Mānava, and likewise that uttered by Uśanas; || 51 ||
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, the two Kālikās, the Māheśvara, the Sāmba, and the Saura, which is a collection of all meaningful topics. || 52 ||
The Pārāśara, Bhāgavata, and Kaurma—the eighteenth in sequence—these Upapurāṇas have been declared by me in their proper order. (53)
Whoever reads or hears this Purāṇa-saṃhitā shall become a partaker of infinite merit; upon death, he shall go to the city of Brahmā.
Chapter 2
Sūta said: || 1 ||
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has proclaimed the majesty of the Narmadā; that which was inquired about by you, I shall now fully relate to you.
O best of sages, who else besides the Lord Brahmā is capable of describing in detail the sacred fords of the Narmadā? (3)
In the past, Janamejaya asked this very same question to the disciple of Dvaipāyana known as Vaiśampāyana.
O Śaunaka, I shall tell you that meritorious account concerning Revātīrtha. Formerly, King Pārīkṣita was initiated for the performance of a sacrifice.
When the sacrificial materials had been gathered and the rites were underway, while the foremost of the twice-born sat and the oblation was being poured into the fire; || 6 ||
Likewise, while discourses on the Dharma were being held everywhere, and while the sounds uttered by people were being heard day and night; (7)
"O noble householder, let it be given! Let it be eaten!"—thus they spoke on the sacrificial ground while the entertainers provided various diversions.
While such a sacrifice, equal to the assembly of the gods in heaven, was being performed, Janamejaya questioned Vaiśampāyana as he sat there.
Janamejaya said: "O Vaiśampāyana, because of the grace of Dvaipāyana, you are considered by me to be possessed of knowledge; therefore, I question you in the presence of these sages."
Tell me the ancient account of the ancestors' resorting to sacred fords; I have heard that they endured various kinds of sufferings for a long time. (11)
O Brahmin, how were my ancestors, the sons of Pṛthā, defeated at dice and forced to wander the earth as far as the ocean out of their longing for sacred fords? (12)
"O dear one, tell me all of that—by whom were those many regions of the earth traversed by you together? For in my opinion, you are omniscient. (13)
Vaiśampāyana said: || 14 ||
O sinless lord of the earth, having paid homage to Virūpākṣa and the great poet Vedavyāsa, I shall relate that which has been asked by you.
But those five grandfathers of yours, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā, having dwelt in the excellent Kāmyaka forest along with the Brāhmaṇas...
O king of kings, there were the high-minded Kaśyapa at Pradhānoddālaka, as well as Vibhāṇḍaka and the great sage Muru. || 17 ||
Pulastya, Lomaśa, and others who had sons and grandsons, having bathed in all the sacred fords without exception, went to the Vindhya mountain.
And there they saw a holy hermitage, crowded with all kinds of trees—campakas, karṇakāras, punnāgas, and nāgakesaras.
It was adorned with *bakula*, *kovidāra*, and pomegranate trees, as well as flowering *arjuna*, *bilva*, *pāṭala*, and *ketaka* trees.
With kadamba, mango, and madhūka trees; with nimba, jambīra, and tinduka; with coconut, wood-apple, date-palm, and jackfruit as well. || 21 ||
It was filled with various trees and creepers, covered by diverse climbing plants, and beautiful with flowers and fruit, like the Caitraratha forest.
It was adorned with vast reservoirs of water embellished by clusters of lotuses, and covered with white, blue, yellow, and reddish-pink water-lilies.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by *cakravāka* birds, frequented by *āḍī*, crows, and cranes, and graced by cuckoos and other birds. || 24 ||
With lions, tigers, boars, and exceedingly fierce elephants, with buffaloes of massive body, and with deer, citraka antelopes, and rabbits; (25)
