Having heard those words of Nārada, which were full of joy, the goddess—the best among the upholders of dharma—questioned the sage with devotion regarding dharma.
The queen said: "O Blessed One, by which vows are the gods pleased in the world of mortals? What gifts are given, and for which would there be great fruit? (90)
And whatever fasts have been prescribed by the wise regarding the duties of women—by performing which virtuous women go to heaven. (91)
O illustrious one, tell me all of that exactly as it is; I wish to hear everything, so speak without hesitation.
Nārada said: Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate lady! This question has been rightly conceived by you; upon hearing it, an increase in righteousness arises for all women. (93)
I shall tell you of those fasts and gifts by which husband and son are brought under one's influence, and by performing which one is constantly honored by one's kinsmen. (94)

By those [means], the unfortunate becomes fortunate, and the fortunate may become unfortunate; likewise, she who has sons becomes sonless, and she who is sonless likewise becomes possessed of sons. (95)
One maiden obtains a husband, while another remains deprived of one; they are born through both performed and unperformed rites—understand this, O beautiful one. (96)
A sesame-cow, gold, silver, cows, and likewise garments; the gift of water, land, perfumes, incense, and ointments. || 97 ||
Wooden sandals, leather shoes, an umbrella, auspicious fans, oil for anointing the feet, oil for anointing the head, bathing, beds, and seats; || 98 ||
Those who give these—honey, beans, milk, clarified butter, salt, molasses, and medicine—do not approach Yama. (99)
On the day of Lalitā, water, a gift of land, as well as rice, sugarcane juice, and two smooth, reddish garments should be given to the couple.
Good fortune indeed arises both in this world and in the next for one who gives to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with good conduct, handsome in form, and possessed of virtues. (101)
O Queen, I shall tell you on which lunar day this should be given: the woman who, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, observes pure vows during the forenoon; (102)

One should offer fuel to the Brāhmaṇa, saying, "May the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) be pleased with me. For thirty-six lifetimes, [the merit of that act] shall reside in the joints of his limbs and sub-limbs. (103)
Neither dust nor even heat arises for one who is dear to the king; moreover, that woman who on the second lunar day offers fresh butter with joy, [attains these benefits]. (104)
He who gives [salt] to an eminent brahmin on the third lunar day shall possess a delicate body; he who bestows salt upon an excellent brahmin on the third day attains this.
May the goddess Gaurī be pleased with me; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof: having obtained a husband, she shall be like Umā together with him. (106)
She who is not widowed shall also sport [in joy] and obtain great fame; having performed the rite at night on the fourth lunar day, she should indeed give sweetmeats (modaka) to a Brahmin.
"May the Lord of Gods, Gaṇanātha Vināyaka, be pleased with me; by that fruit, O beautiful woman, may he [grant success] quickly in all undertakings. (108)
"No obstacle arises anywhere," so said the Grandfather (Brahmā). Then, having reached the fifth lunar day, she who gives sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa— || 109 ||
She shall be endowed with beauty just like Tilottamā herself; moreover, on the sixth day, she shall always be the one who bestows the fruit of the Madhūka tree.
And having dedicated [the offering] to the god born from fire (Agni) through a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, her son shall be like Skanda, the most excellent among the hosts of gods.
O Great King, he who worships the best of the twice-born with gold on the seventh lunar day shall be born as a great king, honored in all the worlds. (112)

Whatever merit has indeed been described by the best of the twice-born regarding him who, for the sake of the world, is the Lord, the God of gods, the Sun; [that merit belongs to the one who performs this act]. 113.
O Queen, I shall explain that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind, O virtuous lady. Ringworm, leucoderma, leprosy, circular patches, and eczema— 114.
Furthermore, even those [defects] acquired through past karma do not exist here in her limbs, for that beautiful woman who bestows a black cow on the eighth lunar day. (115)
If a Brahmin endowed with virtuous conduct is pleased, may Maheśvara be pleased with me; the sins accumulated by her throughout her life shall perish, and she shall be endowed with prosperity. (116)
There is no doubt that this occurs, for such a gift is unsurpassed; whatever woman should cause fragrant incense to be given to a Brahmin with devotion, [she attains this result]. (117)
Listen to the fruit obtained by dedicating [a rite] to Kātyāyanī on the ninth day: her brother, father, son, or husband shall attain the highest battle. (118)
They do not perish, for they are protected by that gift; O Goddess, she who offers the juice of the sugarcane stalk on the tenth day [attains this]. 119.
Having dedicated [the gift] to the world-protectors, she gave it to a Brahmin free from physical defects; by that act of giving, she became eternally beloved by all the world. (120)
"This shall come to pass; there is no doubt about this," Śaṅkara spoke thus. "Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should then offer water on the twelfth day. (121)
Aiming for Nārāyaṇa, she should always cause people to melt away their worldly attachments and cultivate devotion through physical contact and conversation with a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to Viṣṇu.
Because a gift given to a twice-born man with a specific desire for foot-oil or head-anointing becomes indeed infinite in Maharloka and in the waters. (123)
And on the thirteenth day, a woman gives [this] with supreme devotion; in whichever womb she may die and be born again in a future birth, [she shall attain liberation].
On each of those occasions, she was never separated from her husband; nevertheless, on the fourteenth day, one should likewise give a vessel and sandals.
For one who intends to offer dharma to Brahmā, his worlds are indeed free from affliction; and thus, at the end of each fortnight, he should gratify the best of the twice-born with a śrāddha.
O Queen, an uninterrupted lineage is always born upon this earth; thus has the greatness of this lunar day been described to you in connection with the practice of giving. (127)
Likewise, hear now the procedure for the propitiation of the lords of the forest: the Jambu, the Nimba tree, the Tinduka, and likewise the Madhuka. (128)
The mango, the myrobalan, the silk-cotton tree, the banyan and the holy fig; the śamī, the bilva, the āmalī tree, the plantain, and likewise the trumpet-flower tree. || 129 ||
Having approached other most meritorious trees, one shall attain heaven. || 130 ||
Nārada said: Whatever woman performs this unsurpassed vow in the month of Caitra, other vows do not equal even a sixteenth part of that vow.
O fortunate one, by means of that sacred learning through which one no longer perceives misfortune—just as snow, upon encountering the sun, dissolves upon the earth. (132)
Likewise, suffering and misfortune are dissolved through this vow, by which one indeed propitiates the goddess Lalitā known as Madhukā.
O fortunate lady, listen to that procedure being described, which brings happiness: having bathed well on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, with a pure mind, [one should proceed].
Having had an image of Śaṅkara together with Umā made from a Madhūka tree, and having had it consecrated according to the prescribed rites by the best of the twice-born; || 135 ||
The beautiful woman should worship the God according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by fragrant flowers, incense, camphor, and saffron, while reciting the mantra.
"Salutation to Śiva" for the two feet; "to Manmatha" for the penis; "to Kālodara" for the belly; and "to Nīlakaṇṭha" for the throat. (137)
Having worshipped the head for the Universal Soul (Sarvātman), one should thereafter worship Umā; [one should worship] the belly for Kṣāmodarā and the throat for Sukandhā.
One should offer the head [of the vessel] to Saubhāgyadāyinī, and thereafter cause the arghya offering to be presented.

"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Consort of Umā, O Master of the universe! O Lord, destroy all my misfortune with this water offering (arghya). Thus ends the mantra for the water offering. || 140 ||
After offering the *arghya*, he should then present a water-pot filled with water, carried in a *madhūka* vessel, along with gold according to his capacity.

"A water-pot filled with water and endowed with auspiciousness has been given to you, O Lalitā; it increases [your] fortune and other blessings. Thus is the mantra for the gift of the water-pot. || 142 ||
With this mantra, one should offer an excellent water-vessel to a Brahmin; one should avoid salt until the next third lunar day of the bright fortnight. (143)
Having asked forgiveness from the Queen of the Gods, he himself should eat the sacrificial oblation at night; according to this rite, he should proceed month after month.
It is completed on the third day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna; salt should be given in Vaiśākha, and clarified butter is offered in Jyeṣṭha.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, flat beans and milk should be given; in Śrāvaṇa, mung beans should be given; and likewise in Nabhasya and Āśvayuja, śāli rice.
In Kārttika, one should give a vessel of sugar and a water-pot filled with juice; in Mārgaśīrṣa, however, a water-pot made of cotton-wool combined with ghee.
In the month of Pauṣa, saffron should be given; in Māgha, a vessel filled with sesame seeds; and when the month of Phālguna has arrived, a vessel filled with sweetmeats (modakas).
O beloved of the mind, that which is to be given on the third [lunar day] should be avoided on the preceding one; this is the common rule for all of these.
One should worship that very image of the Madhuvṛkṣa tree; all of this is then bestowed upon that brahmin preceptor (ācārya). || 150 ||
Then, at the end of the year, hear the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana): having gone to a honey-tree (madhuvṛkṣa), one should be provided with many ritual materials.
One should bury a Madhūka image in the center of the Madhūka tree; situated there, one should worship the entire [deity] who bears Umā as half of his body.
With abundant offerings for worship, repeatedly with saffron, with smooth flower garlands, and with safflower and filaments.
Having dressed that image in two bright saffron-colored garments resembling the color of linseed flowers, the husband and wife [should do so] eleven times.
With pairs of sandals, parasols, necklaces along with throat-ornaments, bracelets, rings, and beds covered with auspicious spreads; || 155 ||
With their limbs anointed with saffron and worshipped with many flowers, one should feed them with various jewels while they remain in the Madhūka dwelling.
Having risen from the meal and rested upon their beds, one should ask forgiveness; for everything has its root in the Guru, and the Guru is to be known as Maheśvara himself. || 157 ||
When the Guru is pleased, then the entire world, including gods and asuras, is pleased; whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is dear in the home—[all that is attained]. (158)
All that should be given to the teacher by one who desires his own welfare; however, this [following] should be given by the wealthy, while other things should be given as prescribed.

Having duly honored the first couple according to the prescribed rites and auspicious vows, one should honor the second couple—the preceptor and his wife—while avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
Then one should ask forgiveness from the Goddess, the God, the Brahmin, and the Guru: "O Goddess Lalitā, just as you are never separated from Śambhu... (161)
"Likewise, may the non-separation from my husband and sons be granted to me; having performed this third rite known as Madhu according to this procedure. (162)
Indrāṇī attained the status of Indra’s wife and an excellent son, as well as good fortune in all the worlds and the highest happiness of every prosperity. (163)
Whosoever maiden shall observe this vow according to this rule obtains an excellent husband, just as Śatakratu obtained Indrāṇī.
An unfortunate woman attains good fortune, and a fortunate woman becomes possessed of sons; one who has sons attains imperishability and never encounters sorrow anywhere. || 165 ||
The misfortune produced over many births is certainly destroyed; having died, she attains the third heaven and rejoices together with Umā. 166.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures for more than a hundred million eons, she shall again, upon rebirth in the world, obtain a king as her husband.
Fortunate and endowed with beauty, she shall give birth to a son who is a ruler of the earth. || 168 ||
All this has been told to you, the most excellent of all vows. O fortunate one, ask for anything else that resides in your heart as a desire. (169)
Chapter 27
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard the words of Nārada, the queen spoke these words: "O best of Brahmins, show me favor; accept a gift as you desire. (1)
O best of brahmins, I shall give you gold, jewels, gems, and various kinds of garments, as well as whatever else is difficult to obtain.
Having heard the words of the queen, Nārada spoke these words: "O blessed lady, let them be given to others—those twice-born ones whose means of subsistence are exhausted. (3)

"But we, indeed, are endowed with all perfections and are always worthy of being accepted with devotion. Having spoken thus, the queen then [summoned] those who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having summoned indigent Brahmins, he began to bestow whatever Nārada had described as increasing the fortune of giving.
"By this gift, may Hari and Śaṅkara be eternally pleased with me. Then that queen spoke to Nārada, the bull among sages.

The queen said: "O best of the twice-born, you have spoken of giving a gift; indeed, that is centered upon the duty toward one's husband. O most excellent brahmin, may Bāṇa be my husband throughout all my births from birth until death."
"O best of the twice-born, there is indeed no other deity for me, my dear, except Bāṇa; by that truth, may my husband live for a hundred autumns. (8)
Indeed, there can be no other deity for women than their husband; nevertheless, at your word, the gift has been bestowed according to the prescribed rite.
"O giver of honor, O Brahman-sage, we shall perform our own duty toward our husband; you may now depart, and let your blessing be bestowed upon us. (10)
Saying "So be it," Nārada took leave of her, O best of kings; having captivated the minds of them all, his own mind was now fixed elsewhere.
The brahmin departed from sight while being honored by the sky-dwellers; then, O Bhārata, their minds turned toward their husband.
Deprived of their splendor by Nārada, they became pale and utterly bewildered.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In the meantime, Rudra was staying on the bank of the Narmadā, sporting together with Umā; and there Nārada arrived.
Having prostrated before Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, together with Umā, he then informed the God of what had occurred at that time in Tripura.
At my master's command, I went to where that palace of Bāṇa was located; having seen Bāṇa according to protocol, I entered the great inner apartments.
There, having seen the thousands of wives of the wise Bāṇa, he arrived at that city, agitating it according to his desire and as was appropriate.
Having heard Nārada’s words, the Lord of Gods honored them, saying "Excellent! Excellent!", and reflected upon the wandering of Tripura.
Just as the discus released by the powerful Viṣṇu possesses great speed and great extent, so too is it protected by my own splendor.
And that Bāṇa is devoted to me and renowned in the world; moreover, eloquence has been granted by me, especially to the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, for a very long time, Maheśvara, the god of gods and lord of men, reflected upon the matter of complete liberation.
Then, having meditated upon Mount Mandara and placed the earth upon the string of his bow, the three-eyed god meditated upon the eternal deity Viṣṇu as the arrow.
Having visualized the god Hutāśana blazing with faces on all sides at the arrowhead, Suparṇa between the two feathers, and Vāyu in the flight, || 10 ||
Having fashioned a chariot made of earth, he placed both Aśvins at the yoke, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) on the axle, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) on the front pin.
Yama, however, was on the right side, and the most terrible Kāla on the left; Āditya and Candra were on the two wheels, while the Gandharvas were among the spokes and other parts.

Having made the Vedas the excellent horses, he made the eldest of the gods (Brahmā) the charioteer; he fashioned the limbs [of the body] into the bits and so forth, and the Vedic meters into the reins.
Having made the syllable Oṃ his goad to be held in his mouth, Maheśvara placed Dhātṛ in front and Vidhātṛ behind him.
From the wind [direction], from all directions, and likewise from above the machine, [he summoned] the great serpents and piśācas, as well as the siddhas and vidyādharas.
And all the hosts of Gaṇas and multitudes of spirits were in all the joints of his limbs; Mount Meru stood in the middle of his arms, and the great mountain [Himavat] was beneath his arms.
The terrible serpents stationed in the mechanism, as well as Varuṇa and Nairṛta on the two crossbars, and Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, were situated upon those two reins.
Having fashioned a divine chariot with truth as its banner, purity, self-restraint, and protection on all sides, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [mounted it]. || 18 ||
He was armored, wearing a breastplate and a sword, with his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors fastened; having tightly girded his loins and bound up his mass of matted hair.
Having prepared his divine bow and yoked his excellent chariot, the god stood in the midst of the chariot and shone forth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
With the sound of the bowstring, he caused the three worlds to tremble; then Hara, assuming the vaiśākha stance, stood there perfectly still.
Having gazed for a very long time with eyes bloodshot with anger, he meditated upon that supreme mantra and restrained his own self.
He suddenly released an arrow with the desire to slay the city, when the three [cities] had come together and were situated in the intermediate space.
Then, perceiving the convergence of the three cities within half a blink of an eye, he destroyed them with that three-jointed, three-pointed arrow.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the worlds in the three cities were terrified with fear; appearing in the form of Time (Kāla), they were formidable and intent on the destruction of all the asuras.
Then those men of terrible appearance let out loud bursts of laughter, and they even performed the act of blinking their eyes within the paintings.
Mortals with motionless eyes appear as if painted in pictures; the gods dwelling in temples cry out and laugh; and in their dreams they see themselves adorned in red garments. (27)
And falling into a mire-filled pool with their heads adorned with red garlands, they indeed see themselves with their heads anointed with oil.
O best of kings, they saw him mounted upon a vehicle drawn by donkeys, while the great Saṃvartaka wind, resembling that at the end of an eon, blew fiercely.
He uprooted numerous species of trees from their dwellings; there were earthquakes accompanied by thunderclaps, and thousands of falling meteors.
The god rains down blood mixed with many pebbles; the sacrificial fire, properly offered into the fire-pits of the Brahmins, has been extinguished.
It blazes forth, joined with smoke and accompanied by sparks; the elephants have become devoid of rut, and the horses are stripped of their vigor.
Musical instruments were played by the thousands though they had not been struck; banners that were unmoving fell down, as did various kinds of parasols.
Then the trees there blazed up, along with their leaves and branches; everything became utterly agitated, filled with cries of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
The wind-god shattered the various gardens; impelled by him, all the arrows blazed with their tips.
The fire spread everywhere—through trees, shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants, as well as through the houses and all the quarters of the sky.
Everything appeared like the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers and seemed as if it were ablaze; at that time, it was not even possible to go from house to house because of the smoke. || 37 ||
Consumed by the fire of Hara’s wrath, the people in Tripura cry out; the supreme Tripura is burning, set ablaze in every direction. (38)
The shattered peaks fall by the thousands; the fire, mingled with smoke, burns on all sides.
Dancing indeed, pervading all directions and regions, he runs through the forests, in all the temples of the gods, in houses, and in watchtowers.
Incited by Time and provoked by the wrath of Hara, the consumer of oblations (Agni) set out there in that city and burned all the worlds everywhere.
O King, it consumes the world of Tripura together with its children and the elderly, along with its cities, houses, and gates, as well as its vehicles and forests.
Some were addicted to food, others likewise to drink; and other courtesans were devoted to dancing and singing.
Embracing one another, O best of kings, they all go forth unconscious, tormented by the flames of fire and consumed by its heat.

Then other Dānavas there, bewildered by the fire, were being consumed; with their faces overwhelmed by smoke, they were unable to go elsewhere. [They beheld] lotus-pools filled with golden lotuses and crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks.

O Bhārata, various ponds and wells there are being consumed by fire; city gardens and long lakes are seen scorched by the flames, yet they remain covered with unfading lotuses and extend for many yojanas.
There, palaces resembling mountain peaks, adorned with jewels, were seen burnt by fire and shattered upon the surface of the earth. (47)

While men, women, children, and the elderly were being consumed on all sides, the fire blazed mercilessly and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose. O best of kings, one woman was fast asleep in comfort while another remained heedless. (48)

And after sporting, a certain beautiful woman with large eyes, adorned with strings of pearls and resting upon a spacious couch, fell into the fire—distressed and overwhelmed by smoke—as she slept. (49)
In that blazing city, a certain woman, longing out of affection for her son, embraced her son tightly while she herself was being consumed by the fire in Tripura.
A certain woman, possessing a golden complexion and adorned with sapphire ornaments, seeing her husband fallen, collapsed upon him. (51)
O King, one woman, possessing a luster like the color of the sun, lay fast asleep upon her beloved; struck by the flames of fire, she clung tightly to his neck.
Another woman, with a complexion like that of a *medhā* flower, wearing a shimmering golden girdle and a white upper garment, fell upon the surface of the earth. (53)
A certain woman, with a complexion like the jasmine or the moon and adorned with blue gems, joined her palms at her head and addressed the Fire-god.
O Bhārata, the garment of one woman was ablaze, while the hair of another was aflame; and she was joined with golden ornaments that resembled blazing fire.
A certain noble woman, afflicted by intense suffering, lamented upon seeing her husband reduced to ashes, wailing like a female osprey. (56)
Embracing him tightly, another woman, afflicted by great sorrow, suddenly fell upon his head and lamented in her own home. (57)
Seeing [the body] reduced to ashes, one woman wailed like a female osprey; another, seeing her mother and father deprived of consciousness, likewise cried out. || 58 ||
One beautiful woman, tormented by the fire, fell trembling to the ground like an exhausted mare, wandering here and there. 59.
Standing with her face turned away, she did not see the child on her lap; she saw only the house of Kumbhila burnt and fallen to the surface of the earth.
And of Kūṣmāṇḍa and Dhūmra, of Kuhaka and Baka, as well as of Virūpanayana and indeed Virūpākṣa. 61.
Śumbha, Ḍimbha, Raudra, and Prahlāda, the best of asuras; Daṇḍapāṇi, Vipāṇi, and Siṃhavaktra, O sinless one. (62)
Dundubha, Saṃhrāda, Ḍiṇḍi, and likewise Muṇḍi; Bāṇa’s brother and Bāṇa himself, as well as Kravyāda and Vyāghravaktra.

In the same way, O King, in the houses of any other Dānavas who are arrogant because of their strength, fire blazes forth mercilessly; being consumed by the flames, O dear one, the women wail in every house.
O Puruṣa, O Fire, if there is enmity toward a man on the part of the enemy of the gods, then these words of compassion, being without support, have gone to Śiva.
What offense do women commit, these cuckoos in the cage of the household? You are merciless and cruel; why do you harbor such anger toward a woman?
Have you not heard in this world that women are in every way exempt from being slain? Yet, you possess a quality that is indeed fanned by the wind for the purpose of burning.
"You have shown neither compassion nor courtesy toward a woman; for it is barbarians who show mercy upon seeing the words of women. (68)
"Even among the barbarians, a barbarian who is devoid of consciousness is indeed difficult to restrain. Thus they lamented right there, O Bhārata, while the women were wailing.
The fire, abounding in masses of flames, blazed forth intensely; seeing this, Bāṇa, being consumed by the flames, then spoke.
"Having utterly disregarded Hara, I, a sinful soul, am ruined; by me, a wicked fool, those worlds have certainly been destroyed. (71)
Cows and Brahmins have been constantly slain here in this world and in the next; likewise, food and drink have been destroyed, as well as monasteries, groves, and hermitages. (72)
The hermitages of the sages, the groves of the gods, and the abodes of the Gaṇas—all have been destroyed by that sin of mine, as has my ascetic power and my strength. (73)
What shall I do with wealth, or with sovereignty, or with the inner apartments?
"O dull-witted one, it is better that I take refuge at the feet of Śaṅkara; neither mother, nor father, nor kinsman, nor any other person [can save me]. (75)
Having abandoned Maheśāna, the supreme remover of the greatest affliction, one must experience by oneself alone the evil deed committed by oneself.
"I, moreover, shall be burned along with all the virtuous ones. Having spoken thus, he fashioned a Śiva-liṅga upon his head.
Enveloped by fire, he quickly emerged from the house; distressed and with his limbs perspiring, he stumbled again and again. (78)
Praising Hara with a faltering voice, he indeed went for refuge, saying: "O Śaṅkara, if I am to be slain, let me be consumed by the fire of your wrath. (79)
"By your grace, O Mahādeva, let my liṅga not perish; it has been worshipped by me with devotion, O Best of Gods, and meditated upon by me, O All-pervading Lord. (80)
O God, [the body] is dearer than life itself; therefore, you ought to protect it. O best of gods, whether I am worthy of your favor or deserving of death, [you must decide]. (81)

O Mahādeva, may my devotion to you remain unshakable in every birth; even among animals, insects, birds, and those born of the wombs of lower creatures, O Mahādeva, by virtue of my own karma, may my devotion to you remain unshakable. (82)
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, the illustrious Bāṇa, the best among the devoted, sought a boon from the Lord of the gods with this hymn.

Bāṇa said: O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, salutations to the destroyer of all; salutations to the remover of the fear of those afflicted by the dread of worldly existence. O God who brought about the destruction of the body of the flower-armed one (Kāma), and who is beloved by women, salutations to you! 84.

Victory to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, the essence of the supreme truth! Victory to you, who have fashioned a necklace of terrifying serpents! Victory to you, whose body is smeared with pure ashes! Victory to you, the root of all mantras, the sole vessel of the universe! 85.

Victory to you, whose mass of matted hair is tawny like a venomous serpent; victory to you, O Bhairava, who wield the Pināka bow! Victory to you, the odd-eyed one, who has abandoned all attachment; victory to you, O Śaṅkara, who bears the waves of the Ganges! 86.

Victory to you of terrifying form, who hold a skull-topped staff in hand and wear the moon upon your crest! Victory to you, the most praiseworthy among the worlds! Victory to you, the Lord of the mountain of bliss, the essence of the realm of the gods! Victory to you, the essence that has consumed all things! 87.

Victory to you, who are worthy of praise by the worlds and the purifier of the universe; victory to you, whose bull is your emblem and whose deeds are manifold! Victory to you, who fashioned a garland of skeletons from Naraka, and who were the Death to the skeletal corpse of the demon Aghāsura! 88.

Victory to you, O Blue-throated One, whose gait is like that of a noble bull; victory to you, the pacifier of the misfortunes of all the worlds! O Lord of the Earth, that divine holy site (tīrtha) measures five krośas and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon living beings, even those who have committed sinful deeds.
On the southern bank of the Revā is the mountain named Bhṛgu; and upon its summit, that sacred site was established by Śambhu.

Those who fall [into it] go to the abode of Rudra; there is no doubt about this. Whatever creatures on earth, including birds, die right there [in that place], [they likewise attain that state]. || 10 ||

Emerging from Śūlabheda, that other meritorious great river named Gīrvāṇa flows, bringing about the destruction of all sins.
O dear one, in ancient times, Śambhu, having brought forth Sarasvatī, caused her to fall into the midst of the pit where [the skull] had been split by the wielder of the trident.
O King, having fallen there, she became the liberator from ancient sins; it is there that the radiant stone known as Gīrvāṇa exists as a triad.
Among those sacred fords, that particular ford has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again—be they Kedāra, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, or likewise Gayā. || 15 ||
And other excellent holy places do not equal even a sixteenth part of it, nor do those five distinct holy places that exist separately. (16)

Just as the Dharmāraṇya, the well, and Śūlabheda are equal [in merit], so too is the Brahmayūpa and likewise the Devanadī. || 18 ||
Just as Gayāśiras is meritorious, and just as the Śilā of the gods, and as the place Puṣkara and the Mārkaṇḍa lake are [meritorious], so too is this. (19)

Having offered there the funeral cakes and water, which likewise render the cakes inexhaustible, he who performs the *śrāddha* ceremony there drinks that water eternally; he is liberated from all sins, just as a snake is freed from its sloughs. A gift given on the thirteenth day shall possess thirteenfold merit, upon seeing the honored god Gaṇanātha, who has the face of an elephant.

They are liberated from all sins, whether accumulated through ignorance or knowledge; having entered into the midst of the cave, one should mutter the three-syllabled hymn (sūkta). 25.
He shall obtain a sixth part of the merit born of the Nīla mountain; three men dwell there together with the Sun and the Maruts.
This supreme site, consisting of all the gods, contains ten million lingas; just as all rivers and streams reach their end by merging into the ocean.
In the same way, sins are destroyed by the sight of Śūlabheda; O Lord of the Earth, this proof is indeed visible even today.
Sparks quiver within the center of the *liṅga* through the practice of bathing; therein, the second sign of attainment is that a drop of oil does not spread. (29)

O King, he becomes truly purified, both internally and externally; I have not revealed this to anyone, even though I was questioned by the gods themselves.

O Lord of Men, Śūlabheda is a sacred ford that embodies all holy places; by hearing of its power, one is liberated from all sins.

Living in the mortal world, joyful and well-nourished, he is not overcome by the gods; for that sinner’s abode is like a grove of fire.
At that time, O Bhārata, Andhaka reflected: "I shall propitiate Mahādeva so that he may become gracious toward me."
"I request a divine boon that dwells within my mind"; having made this firm resolve, Andhaka departed from his home.
Having reached the bank of the Revā, the Dānava remained engaged in penance; he performed fierce and terrible austerity that caused the hair to stand on end.
Then he remained without food for a thousand divine years; for a second thousand, however, he lived subsisting only on water.
During the third thousand years, he was devoted to inhaling smoke; during the fourth thousand years, he remained steadfast in the practice of yoga.
O Bhārata, no one here has ever performed such extremely severe penance as this man, who remains standing with nothing left but his bones and skin.
Then, O King, a column of smoke issued forth from his head; having passed beyond the world of the gods, it pervaded Kailāsa and remained there.
Then Umā, standing near the God, spoke these words: "Who is this man in the world of mortals who is established in such fierce austerity? (14)
Four thousand years passed, O Supreme Lord; never before has such penance been seen, heard of, or performed by anyone.

Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess, you who are endowed with all auspicious marks! I do not know that lord of the Dānavas who is thus suffering."
"O blessed lady, remaining steadfast in the practice of yoga and meditating upon that supreme state, come there with me to where he is performing his austerities. (19)
Accompanied by Umā, the Lord Maheśvara went there; he saw him remaining as nothing but skin and bone, by the Lord Śambhu.
The Great Lord, Maheśvara, the God of gods, being pleased, replied: "O, alas! A terrible, cruel, and hair-raising deed has been committed! (21)
"And why, my child, have you performed such terrible austerity? I shall grant you a boon, my child, whatever dwells in your mind. (22)
Andhaka said: "If you are pleased with me, O God, and if you are a granter of boons, O Śaṅkara, then by your grace, O Maheśvara, I shall conquer all the gods. (23)

O Goddess of the gods, he attained a height that surpassed even the other gods and asuras.
The Goddess said: "O Maheśvara, by resorting to some means or other, raise him up; grant me this boon: 'Conquer all the gods, with the exception of Viṣṇu.'"
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, there is an excellent means that dwells in my mind; I shall grant him that very boon which was mentioned by you."
Then, sprinkled with nectar, he became healthy at that very moment; thus he was born renewed, with all his limbs beautified.
Listen with a focused mind and accept this supreme boon; with the exception of Viṣṇu, I shall grant you whatever is desired and dear to you.
"May all this be fruitful for you, and may your dharma not be otherwise; O Asura, if you so desire, I grant you this boon. (37)
"You shall conquer all the gods except for Viṣṇu, and even me, were it not for me. (38)

Īśvara said: In ancient times, there was a king of Kāśī known as Citrasena; he was a hero, a donor, a man of excellent character, and possessed of the fulfillment of all desires. || 3 ||
That city, crowded with people and adorned with various jewels, is renowned as Vārāṇasī; it is situated upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Resembling the autumnal moon, adorned by learned men, filled with Indra-poles, and surrounded by cowherds and herds of cattle. || 5 ||
It was crowded with many banners, resounded with the chanting of the Vedas, and was filled with various kinds of merchants engaged in buying and selling.
It was beautifully adorned with mechanical devices, gateways, and other lofty structures; it was filled with divine temples and hermitages situated in dense groves.
It was delightful with various flowers and fruits, adorned with groves of plantain trees, as well as jackfruit, bakula, palmyra, aśoka, and mango trees.
It was adorned with royal fig trees, wood-apple trees, and pomegranates; its auspiciousness was sanctified by the resonant sounds of Vedic recitation.
To the north of that [city] was a most beautiful hermitage, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mandāravana.
Because it is joined with many Mandāra flowers, they know it as Mandāraka; a Brahmin named Dīrghatapas always resides there.
He performs ascetic penance exceedingly; therefore he is known as Dīrghatapas. He dwells there together with his wife, his son, and likewise his daughter-in-law.
His five sons always served him with great diligence; his youngest son, however, was the great ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga.
Perfect in the study of the Vedas, a celibate student endowed with virtues, constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits. || 14 ||
At that time, he would dwell in the form of a deer, moving among the herds of deer; and at the end of each day, he would go into the presence of his mother and father. || 15 ||
The devoted son of the sage always pays his respects and then returns once more to that very forest in the mountain cave.
Playing daily with young deer, that son of the sage, Ṛkṣaśṛṅga, once died by the turn of fate. || 17 ||

Īśvara said: Listen with a focused mind, O lord of the earth, to this divine narrative, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
The king of Kāśī, possessed of great heroism and mighty strength and prowess, was known on earth as that lord of men named Citrasena.
In his kingdom, righteousness always prevailed and unrighteousness was never found anywhere; he constantly delighted in the dharma of the Vedas while protecting his subjects according to dharma.
Devoted to his own duty and always fond of hospitality toward warriors, he, having fully embraced the dharma of the Kṣatriya, enjoys pleasures according to his desire.
There would be no end to his treasury, which abounded in elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; he engaged in scholarly discourse with learned men who were experts in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Speaking thus, the king shone like Śaṅkara on Kailāsa; while protecting his kingdom in this manner, the king spoke to his minister.
"I shall go hunting; you remain for the protection of the kingdom. When the ministers had spoken thus, "Let us go," that lord of the earth departed.
Mounted on horses and galloping along, the kings and provincial lords followed toward the forest, their parasols brushing against one another’s parasols.
The dust raised there from the earth, kicked up by the feet of elephants and horses, completely covered everything, including the cardinal directions and the sun.
There the sun is not seen, nor the cardinal directions, nor the moon; neither trees nor mountain peaks are visible anywhere.
They could not see one another, as if it were midnight during the rainy season; there, that very great herd of deer was observed.
That king ran together with all those princes; there was a great stampede among them, and they quickly fled in the ten directions.
King Citrasena, the lord of the earth, set out alone upon a single path; he went by himself to wherever those deer were.
Then he entered that inaccessible forest, a mountain cave overgrown with creepers and thickets, where one who stands there remains unobserved.
Thinking that the deer had become invisible, the king looked toward the quarters: "In which direction shall I go? Where will my meeting with the army take place? (16)
Thus, having fallen into such distress, King Citrasena, the lord of men, took refuge in the shade of a tree and rested, O King.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, wandering through a difficult forest in a mountain cave, he then beheld a divine lake adorned with clusters of lotuses.
Then, seeing that lake filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and adorned with *cakravāka* birds, that lord of kings was thrilled, his hair standing on end. (19)
Having taken lotuses, he then performed his ablutions; having offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings according to the prescribed rule. (20)
Having covered [the deity] with hundred-petaled lotuses, he worshipped Śaṅkara; then, being properly composed, he went to fetch pure water according to the prescribed rule.
Having emerged from the water and seen a tree nearby on the bank, he placed his upper garment underneath and sat down upon the ground.
Sitting there, he reflected, "What shall I do today? While seated there, he then beheld many deer in that forest region.
Some there were facing the east, and others facing the south; some were facing the direction of Varuṇa (the west), and some were facing the direction of Kubera (the north).
Some were intent on sleep, while others stood with their ears pricked up; in the midst of the deer stood the yogi Ṛkṣaśṛṅga, a man of great asceticism.
Then, seeing the deer, the king thought about food: "Having killed any one of these deer, I shall eat it at my pleasure. (26)
"By eating the flesh of a deer, I shall become healthy; then, having diligently sought out the path, I shall go toward Kāśī. (27)
Having reflected thus, the king then approached the foot of a tree; taking his bow with the tip of his hand, he then fixed an arrow to it.
He discharged an arrow toward where those many deer were; among them, that great ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga was indeed pierced.
Terrified, all those forest-dwellers fled while making a great noise; that sage, having fallen there, cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (30).
"Alas, alas! A grievous wrong has been committed by him who has now slain me. Whose evil intent was it that arose against me, a sinner? (31)
"Standing in the midst of the deer, I do not cause harm to anyone. Hearing those human words, the king was filled with wonder.

Having gone quickly from there, he then beheld a Brahmin endowed with the splendor of Brahman; "Alas! Alas! A grievous deed has been done by me today, by which this twice-born man has been slain. (33)
Citrasena said: "O sinless one, you were slain by me unintentionally, under the delusion that you were a deer. Having gathered much wood, I shall cremate my own body."
Whatever is seen or unseen, nothing is equal to the killing of a Brahmin; otherwise, there will be no purification for me from this Brahmin-slaughter. (35)
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga said: "No success whatsoever shall be yours if I meet my death; there will be many killings upon my current destruction."
"My mother, my aged father, and my ascetic brothers, as well as my brother's wife, will perish when I have met my death. (37)
"These [beings] will become killers; how then can there be purification for you? I shall tell you a means, if you think it right to carry it out. (38)
Citrasena said: "O great sage, let the means that is in your mind be told to me today; I shall perform it all with effort, however difficult. (39)
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga said: "I ask you: how, who, and from where have you come here? Among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, who are you, or are you born of a Śūdra? (40)
Citrasena said: "O dear one, I am not a Śūdra, nor a Vaiśya, nor a Brāhmaṇa; nor am I an Antyaja, O best of Brahmins, but a Kṣatriya, O great sage. (41)
He was a knower of dharma, grateful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings; since this sin arose against his will, how shall purification come about? (42)
Ṛkṣaśṛṅga said: "Take me to the hermitage where my two parents are; there, announce yourself as one distressed by having killed his son. (43)
Seeing me, they will feel compassion for you and will tell you a means by which peace will be attained. (44)
Having heard those words of his, O best of kings, Citrasena placed that brahmin upon his shoulder and went to the vicinity of the hermitage.
When he was unable to carry it, he rested again and again; meanwhile, he saw that brahmin unconscious, with his senses impaired.
Citrasena released him in the shade of a banyan tree; having folded his garment fourfold, he repeatedly fanned it to create a breeze.
O Indra among kings, as he was looking on, the great ascetic Ṛkṣaśṛṅga, a knower of yoga, quickly attained the state of the five elements through the yoga of meditation.
He caused that brahmin to be cremated according to the rites prescribed by rule; having performed his ablutions, he, afflicted with grief, lamented again and again.

"O dear one, I shall tell you an excellent means; listen to it. O lord of men, even Śakra would find it difficult to accomplish that by easy means."

O best of kings, when all those foremost sages had passed away, he summoned the Brahmins who resided there in the hermitage.

"Just as it was described by the sage, so indeed is this holy place; of this there is no doubt. Having witnessed the power arising from the holy site, his hair stood on end with joy.

And at the edge of the forest, he saw women who were passionate, clad in red garments, adorned with the beauty of red garlands, and anointed with red sandalwood paste.

Then some praised her, while others said, "Victory to you, O Goddess! Salutations be unto you! (24)

Homage be to you, who are served by hosts of Siddhas; homage be to you, the most pure and auspicious one for all! Homage be to you, who are served by thousands of Brahmins; homage be to you, O excellent one, born from the body of Rudra! 25.

Homage be to you, the purifier of all that is pure; homage be to you, O Goddess Śivā, the bestower of boons. I bow to you, O most excellent of rivers, who possess cool waters, who grant happiness, who remove sins, and who are wonderfully adorned.

O you whose body is well-frequented by multitudes of various beings, whose limbs are purified by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Uragas, and who are drunk from by great herds of elephants, buffaloes, and boars—O you who possess garlands of great waves of water! 27.
I bow to you, the bestower of all excellence and happiness; release us who are bound by the noose of sin. || 28 ||
Mortals wander in the hells as long as they do not take refuge in your waters; O Goddess, if touched by the rays of the moon or the sun, that [water] bestows the supreme state.

O Goddess, having reached you, rivers become pure and stainless; there is no doubt in this matter. You grant fearlessness to those afflicted by suffering, and you are worshipped by many who are disciplined. (31)
Mortals wander through the hells with their bodies submerged in excrement and urine for as long as they do not touch your water, whose surging waves are shattered by its great power.

O Goddess, even the Mlecchas, Pulindas, and Yātudhānas who drink your holy water are liberated from terrible fear; how much more so, then, the Brahmins here who are afraid of the bonds of worldly existence? (33)
In this terrible age unleashed by Kali, when lakes and rivers have fallen into decay, you shine forth, O Goddess, filled with a flood of water, like the Gaṅgā in the path of the stars in the sky.
O Bestower of Boons, O Distinguished One, by your grace, having protected us until this time, may we attain liberation through your great favor; therefore, grant us your grace. (35)

Those who have taken refuge in you and sought shelter in you—you are their refuge, like a mother or a father to his sons; protected by you, we shall pass through this most terrible time, struck by drought.
Thus praised then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the goddess Narmadā, the best of rivers, appeared in person as that supreme form before the brāhmaṇas. (37)

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O king, those who recite this hymn or listen to it with supreme devotion and tranquility go to Rudra, their limbs adorned with divine garments, by means of a vehicle yoked with a bull. (38)
To those who constantly recite this hymn after bathing in the waters of the Narmadā, this most excellent river shall, at the time of their end, swiftly grant a pure state of existence.
O noble one, he who, having risen at dawn or while still lying down, recites this king of hymns daily, offers his own body as a refuge within his own waters. (40)
Freed from sins and rejoicing in heaven, they indeed become enjoyers of pleasures; it is not otherwise. || 41 ||
O descendant of Bharata, by this hymn of praise, the goddess Narmadā became pleased; flowing toward the southern region, she nourished the brahmins with her waters.
"I grant you immortality, which is not attained even by yogis; that which is difficult for all the gods to obtain, you shall receive through my grace. (43)
Thus, O King, those brahmins, having obtained that unsurpassed boon, set out with joyful hearts and beheld a wonderful and marvelous sight. (44)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Pārtha, those men were seen by them stationed on the bank of the Narmadā; there were exactly five of great strength, intent upon bathing and the worship of the gods.
O great king, having been seen by all those brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, they were questioned by them; listen to how that occurred.

The Brahmins said: "At the edge of the forest, we saw a pair of women who were extremely fierce and terrifying; there were also elderly men there, holding nooses in their hands and inspiring fear. (47)
Difficult to assail and difficult to behold, flickering here and there, and uttering auspicious words—indeed, there is no passage through that place.
"Let all of you look at one another again and again, and let everything that was said by them be recounted. (49)
Five of our most excellent men are stationed there; those illustrious ones must be dispatched with all possible haste.
Then those five men, having heard these auspicious words, looked at one another and spoke again and again.
Where have they gone, whose are they, from where did they come, and what was said by those terrifying ones?
The men said: "Bathing in the holy ford was performed with devotion by all—those from the east, south, west, and north; yet sin was not removed by them. (53)
Then, by the power of this sacred ford, they became free from sin. Listen, all you sages, O twice-born ones who are like fire and time! (54)
And there are terrible sins of embodied beings that are inconceivable; yet by this one most wicked man alone, the wife of his guru was violated. (55)
The property of a friend, as well as gold and wealth, was stolen by another; and a most terrible sin, the killing of a Brahmin, was committed by another. (56)
Furthermore, the drinking of liquor by another occurred unintentionally, and the killing of a cow was committed by a certain sinner out of ignorance. (57)
"O King, even if committed unintentionally, all these are sins. Having heard those words of the Brahmins, they were filled with amazement. (58)
At that very moment, those most sinful ones were born free from defilement, through the power of this sacred ford and by the power of the Narmadā.
"Indeed, no entry for sins whatsoever occurs here. Having reflected thus, all those most wicked ones [spoke] to one another. (60)
Having meditated upon Hari within their hearts, they remembered Citrabhānu; then, having bathed in the holy waters of the Revā, they offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having bowed to the god Bhāskara and meditated upon Janārdana in his heart, he performed a circumambulation with devotion around that blazing Jātavedas (fire).
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of the earth, they have fallen down, agitated by sin; yet, having cultivated a sāttvika disposition, they have abandoned rajas and tamas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, everything that was offered by them into the fire on the northern bank of the Revā was then seen by those Brāhmaṇas stationed upon celestial chariots.
An incomparable marvel was witnessed by the sages on the bank of the Narmadā; from that time forward, they were all entirely freed from passion and hatred.
O twice-born ones, the delighted people frequent Ravitīrtha with a longing for liberation; O lord of men, hear now what the merit of this sacred ford is. 66.
O Lord of Men, oppressed by old age yet pleased by your devotion, I shall describe the location while remaining within a distance of two krośas.
O lord of men, I have heard that Ravitīrtha is as meritorious as Kurukṣetra, as was declared of old by Īśvara to Ṣaṇmukha.
I was present there nearby when all of them heard this from Rudra.
Īśvara said: O Six-faced One, when an eclipse of the sun occurs, those who go to Ravitīrtha at Kurukṣetra obtain a fruit equal to this. || 69 ||
In bathing, giving gifts, as well as in recitation and especially in fire-offerings, the merit is equal to that of Kurukṣetra; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whether in a village or in a forest, the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere; yet at Ravitīrtha, the Revā especially bestows the fruit of merit.

Those who, having conquered their senses, go [to that place] with devotion on the sixth lunar day, on a Sunday, during a Vyatīpāta yoga, on the Dhṛti yoga, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), during an eclipse, or on the new moon day; || 72 ||
And being liberated from lust and anger, as well as from passion and hatred, they fasted before the God with supreme devotion, O lord of men. (73)
Having kept a vigil at night, O Pārtha, one should illuminate the lamp for the Lord, recite the Vaiṣṇava narratives, and likewise practice the study of the Vedas.
Whether it be the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, or the Atharvaveda—one who recites even a single Ṛk verse shall obtain the fruit of the entire Veda. (75)
By means of the Gāyatrī, a human being obtains the fruit of the four Vedas; at dawn, one should honor the Brahmins with gifts of food and gold.
O Pāṇḍava, by the gift of land, clothing, and food according to one's ability, and by the gift of umbrellas, sandals, beds, houses, and so forth; 77.
By the gift of a village-bull, by the gift of an elephant, a maiden, or a horse, and by the gift of a cart for learning, there shall be fearlessness for all.
An enemy becomes a friend, and even poison becomes nectar; the planets become well-pleased, and the Sun himself is gratified with him. (79)
All this, O King, has been told to you regarding the fruit of Ravitīrtha; those men who listen with devotion to the auspicious fruit of Ravitīrtha [attain the same]. (80)
They too, liberated from sin, indeed dwell in the world of the Sun; whatever merit is gained by the gift of a cow, and whatever merit is gained by the sight of Bhṛgu.
By drinking the water of Kedāra, that merit is produced for men; by serving the Aśvattha tree for a year, one becomes a donor of a vessel of sesame seeds.
O Prince, one attains that fruit through the glorification of Ādityeśvara, the power of which, once heard, does not fail to arise [in its effect]. (83)
I shall relate all of that to you with devotion, O lord of the earth; and sins are dissolved just as water in a broken vessel. 84.
One is always born facing toward the sacred ford; of this there is no doubt. O Pāṇḍava, this most secret of all secrets regarding the sacred ford has been told to you.
The wise should always conceal this auspicious narration of the sacred ford from those who are most wicked, ungrateful, and murderers of their masters or friends.

Then, O lord of men, the god who is the consort of Umā was gratified; he granted him the boon of sovereignty over the gods, a kingdom, and the slaughter of the Dānavas.

O son of Pāṇḍu, one is liberated from sins arising from bad dreams, from the occurrence of ill omens, and from those produced by malevolent planets and Śākinīs.

In approaching those who should not be approached, in driving away those who should not be driven away, and in harming one's own master or friends—that which is lost hereof is beyond doubt. (8)
O King, one should perform the auspicious gift of a cow to an eminent Brahmin; or else, one should cause a draft ox, beautiful in all its limbs, to be given to him.

Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should smear it with sandalwood paste; one should then worship with effort using auspicious sprouts and flowers.
Reciting the Bahurūpa mantra while standing facing the southern direction, he should cast [the offering] into water reaching up to his navel according to the prescribed ritual procedure.

Having honored those who were born under unfavorable stars, those intent on the study of the Vedas, and others, with gifts of cattle, gold, betel leaves, and likewise food; || 12 ||
O son of Pāṇḍu, for one who gives ornaments and sandals to Brāhmaṇas, the merit shall be ten millionfold; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O lord of men, listen now to the merit that accrues to whoever casts off their body at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rites.
As long as the bones of a mortal remain in the waters of the Narmadā, for that long the righteous soul dwells in the world of Śiva, which is so difficult to attain. (15)
Then, having passed away from that state, he attains human birth here; he is born as a glorious lord of ten million in wealth, honored by kings. (16)

Furthermore, O best of kings, by going to that sacred ford (tīrtha) and worshipping Karoḍeśvara, one who remembers it attains the supreme goal. || 18 ||
The Lord of the Thirty Gods was installed by Indra, Candra, Yama, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, as well as all the Viśvedevas. || 19 ||
On the northern bank of the Revā, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, whoever—endowed with devotion—should cause a temple to be built; || 20 ||
O best of men, at that sacred ford one shall attain a good state of existence by means of wood, stone, or bricks, using only wealth acquired through righteous means.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and women as well—according to their capacity—those men also go to the world of Śaṅkara, which is honored by the gods.
O King, whoever always listens with devotion to this greatness born of the sacred ford, his sin—whatever has been committed within the span of six months—shall be utterly destroyed.

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Kumāreśvara, renowned among all holy places (tīrthas), located in the vicinity of Agastyeśvara.
O dear one, O lord of men, in ancient times, having propitiated [the deity] with supreme devotion, the six-faced one attained perfection that destroys all sins.
He was born as the commander of the celestial army, the destroyer of all enemies; through his service at sacred fords, this great-souled one became possessed of fierce splendor.
From that time forward, that sacred site was established on the bank of the Narmadā; and whoever goes to that holy place with a single-minded focus and with senses subdued— || 4 ||
On the fourteenth and especially on the eighth day of the month of Kārttika, one should bathe the Lord of Girijā with curd, milk, and clarified butter.

There, O Pārtha, singing should be performed and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) should be made according to the rules by auspicious Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and devoted to the six duties.
O son of Pāṇḍu, whatever is given there becomes inexhaustible; O King, this sacred site, which embodies all holy places, was created by Śikhin.
All this fruit arising from Kumāreśvara has been told to you; O son of Pāṇḍu, merit is obtained simply by the sight of Kumāra.
Upon death, he attains heaven; this is the truth spoken by the Lord.

They shall be filled with bliss until the dissolution of all beings; indeed, no interruption of their lineage occurs for seven births. For they shall possess joy in every birth, O Bhārata. (11)
