Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Immediately following that, O dear one, is the supreme Puṅkhila Tīrtha. In ancient times, O Pārtha, at that Tīrtha, Puṅkha attained perfection.
The lordly son of Jamadagni, possessed of great splendor and the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, performed extensive austerities on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
From that time forth, O lord of men, it became renowned as Puṅkhatīrtha; for whoever bathes in that tīrtha and worships the Supreme Lord, [attains the highest state].
Endowed with strength in this world, he shall attain liberation in the next; by duly worshipping the gods and the ancestors, he becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Whosoever indeed gives up his life at that sacred ford, his destination is undoubtedly the world of Rudra from which there is no return. || 5 ||
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a person obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
O King, whatever man feeds Brahmins at that sacred ford, when one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Whoever worships the Bull-bannered Lord at that sacred site undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 8 ||
Chapter 211.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: I shall relate to you all that was performed by the God of gods—a marvel to the world—for the sake of those dwelling on the banks of the Narmadā.
At the time when the śrāddha ceremony had arrived, the god, having become a leper smeared with red perfumes and ointments, begged from the twice-born who were skilled in performing meritorious rites.
With limbs dripping from blisters, covered by flies and worms, with diseased skin and a foul face, smelling of stench, he stumbles at every step.
Having gone to the brahmin’s residence, he stumbled at the door and said this: "O householder, today there is a meal together with brahmins. (4)
"I wish to perform [the rite] in your house, well-prepared along with these [materials]. Then, having seen that Brahmin, they were accompanied by the patron of the sacrifice.
As it flowed from all his limbs, they cried out, "Fie! Fie! "Depart quickly from this house, O foul-smelling one; hasten away, O lowest of the twice-born! (6)
"Because it has been honored by your sight, this is unfit for consumption by anyone. Having said, "It is even so," Maheśvara, the God of gods, [departed]. || 7 ||
He went into the stainless sky, visible to the best of the twice-born; and when the god had vanished from sight, [the king], having bathed and sprinkled himself all over, [proceeded].
The twice-born and the kṣatriyas ate from their respective plates; and wherever they looked, there were many worms.
Having seen this, they were all struck with wonder and asked, "What is this? Then a certain virtuous and noble Brahmin spoke as follows: || 10 ||
In that assembly of many brahmins, the lord of yogis, out of suspicion, [said]: "He who arrived here first is the yogi, the Supreme Lord. (11)
I consider this to be the playful sport of him who was rebuked; for according to the certainty of the scriptures, such a fruit arises for no one other than that guest. (12)
One should indeed worship the Supreme Self, and especially a guest; for he who does not honor a guest who has arrived at the time of a śrāddha ceremony [incurs sin]. (13)
Piśācas and rākṣasas undoubtedly plunder that [offering] of his—whether it be handsome or ugly, dirty, or clad in soiled garments. (14)

"One should not discriminate between a lord of yogis and even a dog-cooker when they arrive as a guest. Having heard those words of his, the assembly, led by the patron of the sacrifice, [acted accordingly].
The Brahmins ran in every direction to search for the twice-born one; meanwhile, he somehow took refuge in a dense forest by means of someone.
"He has been seen! He has been seen!"—thus it was proclaimed, and they all arrived; then they beheld that brahmin standing motionless like a pillar.
Some cry out but do not move, and some throb but do not see; some wail piteously, while others offer hymns of praise. (18)
O Three-eyed Lord, being constantly praised with pleasing words, you ought to restore once again the lost food of all these brahmins, especially those afflicted by hunger, O Lord of Gods. (19)
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard those words of the brahmins, the Lord, being pleased with supreme compassion, spoke to them.

"Being pleased, I have prepared for you, O beings of great power, that very food as if it were nectar. Let the Brahmins eat together with their kinsmen and servants, and let them worship my mandala constantly. (21)

Thereafter, O Pārtha, is the auspicious abode of the trident-bearing God of gods, renowned as Muṇḍina, which removes all sins; it is especially significant on the full moon of Kārttika and is equal to the sacred site of Gayā.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Now I shall proclaim another great deed of the God, by the mere hearing of which one is quickly liberated from all sins.
Having assumed the supreme form of a monk, Maheśvara, the God of gods, went to a village consisting of a single hall, seeking alms while afflicted by hunger and thirst.
With hands raised holding a rosary, his body smeared with ashes, the Lord of the Universe—adorned with matted hair and earrings—bears a throbbing trident. || 3 ||
Clad in an animal hide, possessing a massive body, and adorned with great serpents, he was indeed sounding a beautiful hand-drum (ḍamaruka) resembling a ḍiṇḍima drum.
The Blessed One, skull in hand, surrounded by many children, was in some places singing and laughing, and in others dancing and speaking.
O Pārtha, in whichever house the Lord might place his drum through his divine play, that house, overwhelmed by the burden, would perish right there.
Thus proceeding, the Lord, surrounded by many people and appearing both visible and invisible in form, went forth.
When people no longer saw him running here and there, they stood in amazement; then, thinking "He will become Śambhu," they offered praise.
While they were thus praising Śaṅkara, the Lord of the worlds with devotion, the Blessed One appeared there in the form of Ḍiṇḍi.
From that time forward, O King, the Lord of Gods is called Diṇḍimeśvara; by seeing him or touching him, one is liberated from all sins.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: I shall further relate another great deed of the Lord, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
O Bhārata, I shall tell you how Śambhu, though not a child, plays with Āmalaka fruits in the form of a child along with the village boys.
O Pāṇḍava, all those stainless stones that were thrown by them were brought back by the god at that very moment; thereafter, Hara threw them down again.
Just as they had gone out to the various quarters and returned from those directions individually, so too did they behold that stainless Being, the Supreme Lord.
And in the third [chapter], the deed of the wise God of gods is told: the supreme among all places, the most excellent Āmaleśvara.
By merely honoring it, the supreme state is attained. || 6 ||
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: I shall now fully proclaim the great deed of the God, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins. (1)
Having become a skull-bearer and wearer of a necklace of bones, he wandered the earth surrounded by Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Ḍākinīs, and Yoginīs. || 2 ||
Assuming a terrifying form and taking his seat upon a corpse, he performed extensive penance after granting fearlessness to the three worlds.
The Āṣāḍhī festival was established there; indeed, it became renowned by the name Āṣāḍhī. Thereafter, the raiment (kanthā) was cast away elsewhere by the Lord Parameṣṭhin.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, he is called Kantheśvara; by the mere sight of him, one indeed obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. || 5 ||
The god wandered there again on the path by chance; seeing him, the seller of meat was addressed by Hara: || 6 ||
"If, O noble one, you do not become angry with me now, then forcibly take my linga; I shall give you much wealth. (7)
Thus addressed by the god, that merchant, deluded by greed, mobilized his superior and mediocre forces at the Linga.
When all that had been well-accumulated over time had finally come to an end, he beheld the lofty linga standing there and was overcome with grief.
Having reduced him to pieces, that supreme lord, the god, seeing him freed from fear, spoke these words with a smile: ||| 10 ||
"And my linga has not been fulfilled; I shall depart if you so intend. However, I will grant you wealth there once the linga is fully completed. (11)
The merchant said: "O Supreme Lord, I am an unfortunate man who has failed to perform meritorious deeds; being unworthy of your favor, I shall grieve for eternal years. (12)
O descendant of Bharata, having heard these words of that merchant's son, Maheśvara remained there after bestowing inexhaustible wealth.
O Indra among kings, from that time forward, the Linga remained there, adorned as if by cranes, for the sake of providing proof and out of a desire to bestow grace upon the world.

O Pārtha, this well-established [place] was created by the God as a sport; it is known as Devamārga and is renowned throughout the three worlds. By seeing or even worshipping it, one is liberated from all sins. || 15 ||
But he who, having gone along the Devamārga, worships Balākeśvara after reaching Pañcāyatana, goes to the world of Rudra. || 16 ||
For those men of purified soul who die on the path of the gods, there shall never again be a return from the world of Rudra.
O best of men, having heard with devotion the majesty of the Devamārga, one is liberated from all sins; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (18)

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, one should go to Śṛṅgītīrtha, which bestows liberation upon all embodied beings; O King of kings, for those who die there, the attainment of liberation is certain, without a doubt.
By offering a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at that very place, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors; purified by that merit, one shall attain the state of Gaṇeśvara. || 2 ||
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, O descendant of the protector of the earth, one should go to the Aṣāḍhī-tīrtha, where Maheśvara stands, having assumed a form according to his will.
This holy ford, O King, which endures through the four ages, is the most excellent among all holy fords; having bathed there, a man shall become an attendant of Rudra.
Whoever gives up their life at that sacred ford attains, without a doubt, a state from which there is no return, from the world of Rudra.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: One should go to the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, which is saluted by gods and demons; that sacred ford is highly meritorious and the destroyer of great sins.
Having become intent on fasting, with senses and mind restrained, one who bathes there according to the prescribed rite is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Whoever, at that sacred ford, should be intent on giving up their life with devotion, will undoubtedly attain a state from which there is no return, from the world of Rudra.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, one should go to the most beautiful holy site known as Jamadagni, where Janārdana attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of the twice-born, how did Vāsudeva, the preceptor of the world, become perfected while assuming a human form out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds?
O sinless one, I desire to hear all this account of the deeds of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, as it is being told by you according to the proper order.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: O great king, in former times there was a great lord of the Haihayas, a king renowned as Kārtavīrya, who possessed a thousand arms.

Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, he was the best among all wielders of weapons; having performed the ceremonial bath after completing his Vedic studies and vows, he granted fearlessness to all living beings.
The illustrious king, the lord of Māhiṣmatī and commander of an akṣauhiṇī, who was possessed of great strength, once went out to hunt deer.
After many days, the highly resplendent Jamadagni reached the unsurpassed Bhṛgukaccha, where the ascetic was staying.
Accompanied by Reṇukā, the illustrious one who grants fearlessness to all beings had a son named Rāma, the Lord who was Nārāyaṇa himself.
Endowed with all the virtues of a kṣatriya, he was the best of brāhmaṇas and a knower of Brahman; he delighted his parents with supreme devotion as if they were the Supreme Reality itself.
Then, seeing Arjuna wandering on a hunt, the powerful Jamadagni approached him and invited him with the rites of hospitality.
Having said, "So be it," that king, together with his servants, troops, and vehicles, went to the holy hermitage of that high-souled sage.
At that very moment, it became endowed with supreme splendor; seeing this, the king was filled with the greatest wonder.

As soon as he had arrived, the king, together with his servants and army, was fed with excellent food by the Siddha Brāhmaṇa through chance; he then asked about the cause and the power [behind] this, saying, "What is this? (13)
Having learned of that power of the wish-fulfilling cow, he then said to the twice-born man: "O Brahmin, give me as my sacrificial fee this excellent, sin-destroying cow."
I give you a hundred times a hundred thousand, ten million, a hundred million, and even a billion cows adorned with ornaments. (15)
Jamadagni said: "O dear one, for ten thousand, a million, or even a hundred crores [of cows], I will not give away this supreme Kāmadhenu; please go back. (16)
O descendant of Bharata, having been addressed thus by that brahmin, the lord of kings, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these words.
"O defiler of the twice-born, since you act with such unrestrained will even toward me, I shall therefore take Surabhi from your house while you look on. (18)
The twice-born said: Who indeed plays fearlessly with a furious great serpent? He who would take away my cow, even though death stands before his eyes! (19)
Having spoken thus, Jamadagni, seized with supreme rage, took up a great staff like another Brahma-staff and spoke.
"O lowest of the Kṣatriya clan! Whatever power or splendor you possess, let that wretch take my cow at once, along with his attendants, for his life is now exhausted. (21)
Having heard these cruel words, the Haihaya king, though surrounded by hundreds [of followers], fled across the surface of the earth and fell down, struck by the staff of Brahmā.
Then, by the sound of the "huṃ" uttered by the cow, thousands of dark-skinned beings with swords, nooses, and axes in their hands were seen emerging.
From the tip of the nostrils and from the tips of the body hairs, the Kirātas and Māgadhas emerged; and from the apertures within, they were born by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Thus, having struck one another and burnt the Haihayas and Ṣṭaṅkaṇas, they met their destruction along with the Brahmin through the fiery splendor of Arjuna.
Having achieved victory in battle and slain that best of the twice-born, Kārtavīrya, deluded by the power of Death, went to his own city rejoicing. || 26 ||
Then, filled with haste, Rāma arrived after his enemy had departed; he saw his mother weeping in the presence of his father.
Rāma said: "By whom has this rash act been committed out of ignorance for his own destruction—he who, desiring to kill my father, seeks to behold Death here? (28)
Then, at Rāma’s words, she became distraught as if her life-force had departed; striking her belly with both hands, she spoke to him.
"By that cruel Arjuna, together with other kṣatriyas, my father was slain here by that one who is powerful in his arms. (30)
"Behold that father of yours, O son, slain, lifeless, and devoid of consciousness; having performed the funeral rites according to the rules, offer him libations as is fitting. (31)
Having heard these words and having saluted his mother, he made a certain vow; listen to it, O lord of men. (32)
Having bathed after purifying the earth of the lineage of kṣatriya families twenty-one times, I shall satiate your husband with their blood.
"Listen to my truth: having severed even the arms of that evil-minded Kārtavīrya with my axe, I shall drink his blood. (34)
Having thus made this vow, that powerful son of Jamadagni, overcome by great anger, then consecrated his father.
Overwhelmed with rage, Rāma went to the city of Māhiṣmatī; having severed that lowest of Kṣatriyas' forest of arms and slain him, [he departed]. (36)
He went forth to destroy the Kṣatriyas, surveying the earth with its seven islands and oceans, along with its mountains, forests, and groves. (37)
From east to west and from south to north, he created five lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka.
Overwhelmed with rage, he offered libations to his ancestors with blood in those lakes of bloody water; so we have heard. (39)
Then Ṛcīka and the others approached the bull among Brahmins and said to him, "Forgive us"; thereupon, he desisted.
The region near those lakes of bloody waters, which is known as Samantapañcaka, is celebrated as a sacred place.
Having turned back from that ritual act, the son of Pāṇḍu, Rāma, whose soul is supremely devoted to dharma, spoke to the ancestors: "This blood which has been shed by me... (42)
"May that which is offered at the five sacred fords become the most excellent of all holy sites. Having said, "So be it," all those ancestors vanished from sight. (43)
Thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, contact with Rāma on the path of the gods destroys all the sins of men through both seeing and touching him. || 44 ||
Even today, for the sake of providing proof to Reṇukā, the ancestral deities are seen stationed upon the path of the gods, effecting the destruction of all sins. (45)
O Indra among kings, at that sacred ford where the Narmadā meets the ocean, men who establish a place of worship according to the prescribed rites are liberated from their sins.
O son of Kuntī, even the great ocean must not be touched with the tip of a blade of kusha grass; O best of kings, one should bathe there while reciting this mantra.
"Salutations to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to you, O Lord of the Waters! O Lord of Gods, be present here in the salt-water ocean. Thus is the mantra for touching [the water]. (48)
"Agni is the radiance and Mṛḍayā is in the body; Viṣṇu is the seed and the navel of immortality. Speaking this truthful word, O Pāṇḍava, one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers. (49)
O King of kings, one should offer the *argha* to the Great Ocean with fruits, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), combined with the five jewels, while reciting this mantra. (50)

"You are the treasury of all jewels, the source of the mine of all jewels; O Lord of the foremost among all immortals, accept this arghya; salutations be unto you. This is the mantra for the arghya. || 51 ||
"O Great Ocean, lift me up from the sins committed since birth! O Treasure of Jewels, go, being honored; O Best of Mountains, [go] on the full-moon day. This is the mantra for dismissal. || 52 ||
Who else besides the god Sāgara is there for the bursting open of the gates of heaven? There, extending as far as the ocean, lies a supreme and unsurpassed great pilgrimage site (mahātīrtha).
There the god was installed by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni; there the gods, along with Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas [reside].
Those men on earth who behold Virūpākṣa, the unsurpassed Jamadagni, and the goddess Reṇukā, worship them.
In that auspicious world, O King, they dwell for as long as they desire; having bathed there, a man, while gratifying the ancestors and the gods, [attains this]. (56)
Having bathed here, having given gifts, and having listened together with devotion, one shall deliver a hundred successive generations of one's lineage from the terrible hell.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the supreme Koṭīśvara Tīrtha, where bathing and giving gifts all become ten-millionfold in merit.
There, the gods along with the gandharvas and those stainless sages attained supreme perfection at Koṭitīrtha—a state difficult to obtain on earth. || 2 ||
And there, O King Koṭīśvara, Mahādeva was installed; by beholding that Lord of the gods of gods, one attains unsurpassed perfection.
O best of kings, whatever is performed at that sacred ford—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious—all of it becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
In that regard, whatever most excellent sages dwell on the southern path, once they have attained perfection and passed away, they certainly go to the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka). || 5 ||
Those foremost of sages who dwell on the northern bank of the Narmadā have previously gone to the world of the gods; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, one should go to the excellent Loṭaṇeśvara on the northern bank of the Narmadā, which destroys all sins.
O King, at that very moment, all that sin accumulated over seven lifetimes perishes simply by the sight of the God of gods.
Whatever sin has been committed since childhood and even that which was done in youth—all of that goes to destruction by the sight of the God of gods. (3)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Brahmin, you have indeed related in its entirety the great and wondrous account of Narmadā’s conduct, which destroys all sins and is marvelous throughout the worlds.
I wish to hear all about that one supreme holy ford which bestows the fruit of all holy fords; having shown compassion, please tell it to me quickly.
O best of beings, whatever difficult questions exist in the three worlds, all of them have been heard by me along with my kinsmen through your grace.
O best among those who know all things, having heard this one supreme question from you through your grace, I shall go [to that place] along with my kinsmen.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! For you whose intellect is such, there is nothing at all that is difficult to attain within the three worlds."
O bull among the Bharatas, that wise man who understands at the proper time and for each occasion duty, wealth, pleasure, and liberation—he alone should act. (9)
Therefore, I shall declare to you the auspicious answer to this question, by hearing which men on earth are liberated from all sins. (10)
The Narmadā is the best of rivers, auspicious and composed of all sacred fords; its special excellence has been described at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
O best of kings, seeing Revā approaching, the great ocean bowed again to the goddess at the confluence with the Revā.
Having reflected in his mind, "Who is this? regarding me, that best of rivers, having known and reflected in his mind upon Revā, the supreme one born from a liṅga; 13.
Rolling along, O dear one, the great ocean came face-to-face with the Revā; there, the great river Narmadā entered the sea.
There, in the ocean, the Linga of the God of gods emerged; from that Linga arose the highly fortunate Narmadā, the best of rivers.

Because she merged into that linga, she is indeed most meritorious. Dwelling eternally on the Narmadā and always drinking the waters of the Narmadā, he is consecrated in all sacrifices and partakes of the soma-drink day after day.
That man who, having bathed at that confluence, worships Loṭaṇeśvara, obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 17 ||
O King, whatever verbal, mental, or physical evil deed has been committed shall all go to dissolution upon reaching Loṭaṇeśvara.
O best of kings, listen to that which was specifically proclaimed by Śaṅkara on the full moon day of Kārttika; it is the remover of all sins.
O best of kings, having seen that the full moon day of Kārttika has arrived, go there and, having fasted on the fourteenth day, indeed bathe in the waters of the Narmadā.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods and performed the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules, one should keep a vigil at night after worshipping Loṭaṇeśvara.
His life is fruitful and his exertion is fruitful; those others are undoubtedly lame, for their birth is useless.
For those by whom Loṭaṇeśvara has not been seen with a one-pointed mind, neither the state of a Piśāca nor birth in a degraded womb shall ever occur in their family.
Having gone there to the confluence and performed his bath according to the prescribed rite, he should likewise awaken [the deity] with meritorious songs and dances.
Then, seeing that the night has turned to dawn, one should bow to the great ocean, take leave of it, and perform the ritual bath there according to the prescribed rules.
Oṃ, salutations to you who possess the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to you, the Lord of the Tīrtha. O God, O Ocean of salt waters, grant me your presence. This is the mantra of invocation. || 26 ||

"Agni is your brilliance and Mṛḍayā is your body; Viṣṇu, the source of immortality, is the depositor of your seed. Speaking these words of truth, O Pāṇḍava, one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers. Thus is the mantra for bathing. || 27 ||
Whatever sin a man has committed throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, he shall cast off that flood of evil by bathing but once in the salt waters.
Otherwise, O best of the Kurus, this powerful lord of divine origin, the great ocean, must not be touched by the gods even with the tip of a blade of kusha grass. (29)

"You are the foremost of all jewels, the source of all mines of jewels; O Lord, sovereign of all the immortals, accept this water-offering (argha); homage be to you! Thus is the mantra for the argha. || 30 ||
Immediately after satisfying the ancestors, gods, and humans, he ascended from that very place onto its bank together with five eminent brahmins.

Having first performed the installation according to the prescribed rite, he should then perform the Śrāddha ceremony with offerings corresponding to the world-protectors (Lokapālas), after having placed the Lokapālas before him.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rule along with the Brahmins, he should afterwards report all his good and evil deeds to them.
Having confessed whatever sin has been committed from childhood through old age and youth, one should invite the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) in their presence.
Whatever inauspicious deed has been committed by me from childhood until my birth, I have confessed it all to the Brahmins while they remain in my presence. (35)
Having spoken thus, he should roll on the ground behind them and then before them, facing them; and having obtained the permission of those five, he should afterwards perform his bath.

And the ancestral rite (śrāddha) must be performed according to the rules for the ancestors, O best of kings; when this is done, O foremost of monarchs, there shall be the destruction of all sins. (37)
But for anyone who, out of a desire to know, wishes to understand the Self and its auspicious and inauspicious karma—listen to this, its final conclusion. (38)
Having bathed there in that great sacred ford, a man who rolls about [in the mud] goes elsewhere as one of sinful deeds, while he who performs righteous deeds proceeds along the river.
Then, realizing "I am an evildoer" and that "evil was accumulated by me in the past," one should bathe in that best of holy places and give gifts according to the prescribed rule.
By worshipping Loṭaneśvara, one is liberated from all sins; by going to Avakragamana, one is freed from all transgressions.
Therefore, O best of kings, having understood this, men should bathe with every effort at that place where Hara is present.
Having bathed in this manner according to the prescribed rite, O protector of the earth, one should honor Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas for the pacification of all sins.
O best of kings, that sacred ford (tīrtha) is indeed distinguished by such qualities; O King, listen with a one-pointed mind to the majesty of that tīrtha.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he who, filled with devotion, performs a śrāddha ceremony there for his forefathers— || 45 ||
He bestows gifts of cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold upon the Brahmins for sixty thousand years and a hundred crores of years.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he is honored in the heavenly world; [he obtains] that fruit which results from bathing and giving gifts at all the sacred fords of the Narmadā. || 47 ||
One obtains that fruit at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean: gold, silver, copper, jewels, pearls, and ornaments. 48.
By giving a bull, land, and grain there at that sacred site, the fruit is inexhaustible; there is no doubt regarding this, whether the act be auspicious or inauspicious. (49)
O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen to the meritorious fruit for that man who, at that sacred ford, gives up his life with devotion according to the prescribed rites. || 50 ||
Having sported for ten million years in the abode of Śiva, he is born as a Brahmin learned in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas into a pure family.
Prosperous with sons and grandsons, endowed with wealth and grain, and liberated from all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Whatever merit is obtained by worshipping Somanātha during twelve pilgrimages under the conjunction of Kṛttikā on the full moon day of Kārttika, that same merit is obtained at Loṭaṇeśvara.
O Pārtha, one obtains that same merit from beholding Loṭaṇeśvara as one does from Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara. || 54 ||
The man who listens with devotion to this auspicious work as it is being recited, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Rudra.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the southern bank of the Revā; within a distance of two krośas is a holy site (tīrtha) unsurpassed even by Mātṛtīrtha.
The meritorious place named Haṃseśvara destroys dejection. A swan born in the lineage of Kaśyapa was the son of a daughter of Dakṣa. || 2 ||
In ancient times, he was born as the vehicle of Brahmā after performing great austerities; once, however, he fell into a state of agitation without following the instructions of the Creator.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, overwhelmed by the hosts of Śiva, he fled in all directions like one terrified during the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, being deprived of Brahmā.
When that bird did not quickly return even though summoned by Brahmā, Brahmā then cursed him and indeed caused him to fall from his position.
Then, realizing that he had been cursed, the swan hurriedly approached the Grandfather (Brahmā), prostrated before him, and spoke as follows: || 6 ||
The swan said: "It does not behove you to curse one born from a womb of animals; for such is the very nature of animals that their minds are devoid of discernment."

Nevertheless, O Lord, I am a sinner in that I have abandoned my master; however, O Grandfather, being suddenly overcome by fear and terrified by the extremely fierce hosts of Śiva rushing toward me, I fled, leaving him behind.
Even now, O Lord, I see only fear before me; for that reason, though remembered by you, I did not come into your presence.

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Even as he was speaking thus before the Creator, the swan—worshipped by the eyes, yet now deeply distressed—gasped for breath: "O Lord, protect me, protect me! I am a sinner, a fool of dull intellect, fallen here before you."

You alone, O God, are indeed the creator of this creation; all these various things have been created by you alone. Since I too have been created by you as such, this fault, O Ordainer, truly belongs to you alone.

No one other than you has the power to either curse or favor; to whom else shall I go for refuge? O Father, protect me, your devotee, who has fallen from the duty of service, who has become like a slave, and who deserves to be struck with slaps. 12.

Knowledge and ignorance have arisen from you alone, as have merit and demerit, existence and non-existence, day and night; you ordain the various states of the world—I indeed take refuge in you, the One. (13)

You are one, yet you possess many forms; through your single activity, you manifest as diverse and manifold. You are both devoid of action and the performer of all actions; therefore, I go to you for refuge.
Homage, homage to the most excellent one; homage, homage to the giver of boons. Homage to the Creator and the Ordainer; homage, homage to the one who is the refuge. || 15 ||
O Lord, how can this speech of mine, devoid of the syllables of training, offer praise? What power or what knowledge do I possess that I have spoken thus? Please forgive me. (16)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: While the swan was speaking thus, Brahmā, with a gracious mind, said: "This very instruction has been given to you; do not fall into despair, O bird. (17)

Purify yourself through austerity so that you may reach the end of the curse. Perform service to the Revā by bathing there and establishing Maheśvara; then, in a very short time, you shall attain your proper state.
And whatever fruit is obtained by performing many sacrifices with excellent sacrificial fees, as well as by gifts of ten million cows and gold, that same fruit is attained when Śiva is installed. 19.
Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a stealer of gold, or a violator of the Guru’s bed—by installing Śiva on the bank of the Revā, one is liberated from all sins.
Therefore, having installed Tryambaka on the bank of the Bharga river, you, freed from all defects, shall go to the supreme state.
Thus addressed by Vidhi, that best of birds, delighted and satisfied, said "So be it" and quickly went to the excellent bank of the Narmadā.
Having performed austerities for some time, he established Śaṅkara.
O best of the Bharatas, having worshipped the unsurpassed Haṃseśvara by his own name, that most excellent of birds attained the supreme abode.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having gone to that Haṃseśvara Tīrtha and bathed there, one should worship the Supreme Lord; he shall be completely liberated from all sins.

Praising the God with a single-minded heart, one shall never fall into a state of wretchedness. O best of kings, by giving a śrāddha, offering lamps, and providing food for the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity, one is glorified in the heavenly world.

O Pārtha, he who worships Śiva with devotion three times a day or even once, and gives a cow that has recently calved to an excellent brahmin, is glorified in the world of Śiva for sixty thousand years.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: From there, one should go a distance of one krośa to the supreme Tīrtha called Tilāda, where Jābāli, by consuming sesame seeds, attained purity.
One who abandons his father or mother, one who lusts after his brother’s wife, one who sells his son, a sinner, and one who acts with deceit toward his guru; || 2 ||
Thus beset by faults, wherever he goes, O Bhārata, there he receives reproach from the virtuous; no one maintains association with him, even in assemblies.
Thus filled with shame, O King, the brahmin did not wait for a long time; for, not knowing any other recourse, he fell into great anxiety regarding his purification.
He visited all the sacred fords and also bathed in the Revā river.
Having reached the Aṇivāpa region on the southern bank of the Narmadā, O Pārtha, the ascetic Jābāli remained there, consuming sesame seeds as his food.

Eating sesame seeds, eating only once a day, likewise eating at intervals of one day, eating every three days, six days, or twelve days, and likewise eating only once a fortnight or once a month; || 7 ||
He also performed vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa with sesame seeds; indeed, he gradually attained the state of a giver of sesame for seventy-two years.
As time passed, the Lord became pleased with him; he granted him purity pertaining to this world and the next, as well as the state of residing in the same realm as the Self (sālokya).
O bull of the Bharatas, that lord was installed by him under his own name; thus the Lord also obtained the designation Tilādeśvara from the world.
From that time forward, that holy place became renowned as a destroyer of sins; having bathed in that tīrtha on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, a man [attains the highest goal].
O Pārtha, likewise devoted to fasting on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī), one should offer oblations of sesame seeds, rub with sesame, bathe with sesame, and offer water with sesame.

Both the giver of sesame seeds and the one who consumes them are liberated from various sins. One who fills a linga with sesame seeds and offers a lamp with sesame oil attains the world of Rudra and purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation. (13)
O best of kings, by the offering of sesame balls at a śrāddha ceremony, even those ancestors who have engaged in improper acts attain their desired destination. (14)
Abiding in the heavenly world, having attained imperishable satisfaction through śrāddha rites and the feeding of brahmins, they rejoice for eternal years. (15)
O King, by uplifting these three lineages—the father’s family, the mother’s family, and likewise the wife’s family—a man indeed leads them to heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, O Pārtha, at a distance of one krośa is the supreme Vāsava-tīrtha, established there by the Vasus after they had stayed for twelve years.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these were the eight Vasus in ancient times.
Afflicted by their father’s curse, O Bhārata, they resorted to the Narmadā tīrtha and, with their senses restrained, performed austerities for the sake of dwelling in a womb.
O King of kings, while they were propitiating the supreme and immutable Lord of Bhavānī for twelve years, Maheśvara then became pleased.
Pratyakṣa bestowed upon them their desired and most excellent boon; then, having established that Maheśvara under his own name, the Vasus, entering the sky, departed once Śaṅkara was pleased.

From that time forward, that sacred site became renowned by the name Vāsava. O great king, whoever worships Śiva with devotion at that sacred site, and diligently offers a lamp along with whatever offerings they may obtain— || 6 ||
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or even every day according to one's ability, he shall dwell in the presence of Śiva for eight thousand years.
Thereafter, he goes to the abode of Śiva and does not experience dwelling in a womb; whether with flowers, or even with sprouts, fruits, or likewise with grains.
One who worships the Lord Īśāna shall never encounter misery; liberated from all sorrow, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
O son of Kuntī, he who dwells even for a single day at Vāsava-Īśvara, having shaken off a heap of sins, rejoices in heaven like the sun.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and give them garments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Beyond that, O Pārtha, at a distance of one krośa, is the supreme Koṭīśvara Tīrtha. Whatever bathing, giving of gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth is performed there by men with devotion, all of it becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
There, indeed, the gods along with the Gandharvas, the Ṛṣis, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas go toward the ocean to behold the Narmadā.
O King, millions gathered at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean, having witnessed the incomparable delight arising from the meeting of the river Revā and the sea.
Having bathed, and having established and worshipped Śiva, the Great Lord known as Koṭīśvara, according to the prescribed rites and with their respective devotion; || 4 ||
At Koṭītīrtha, supreme perfection was attained through the propitiation of Sarvatoṣaṇa; therefore, its merit is incomparable and the most excellent among all sacred fords.
O tiger among kings, whatever is performed at that sacred ford, whether auspicious or inauspicious, all of it becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
At that sacred ford, whatever most excellent sages reside on the path attain the state of perfected immortality as well as the supreme world of the ancestors.
Those who have taken refuge on the northern bank of the Narmadā and those on the southern—my mind is certain that they have gone to the world of the gods.
Having worshipped Maheśvara with bilva and arka flowers, with dhattūra, kuśa, and kāśa blossoms, as well as other seasonal flowers.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having gratified Dhūrjaṭi according to the rules with various services preceded by mantras, and with incense, lamps, offerings, and food, [one should worship].

One attains the world of Śiva for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras; a special merit is recorded for worship performed on the conjunction of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
And always, O best of kings, on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, one should worship Śiva and devotedly feed excellent brahmins.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: From there, one should go a distance of one krośa to the supreme Alikātīrtha. There was a Gandharva woman named Alikā, who was unchaste and of crooked intent.
The granddaughter of Citrasena approached the sage Vidyānanda; she chose him, he accepted her, and she remained in his service for ten years.
For some reason or other, she killed her husband while he was asleep; having gone there, she reported [the matter] to her father, Ratnavallabha.
Abandoned by both father and mother, O King, and reviled by many, she said: "You are a killer of embryos! You are a killer of your husband! Do not show me your face! (4)
"O most wicked woman, slayer of a Brahmin, go! Depart from this house, forsaken! (5)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus, overcome with grief and bewildered, having been rebuked by those two, she reached a certain other sacred ford and set her mind on abandoning her body.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having inquired of the Brāhmaṇas regarding sacred fords, he heard of the sin-destroying tīrtha at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
There, O Pārtha, she performed penance without food, having mastered her vows through the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, Pārāka, Mahāsāṃtapana, and other such austerities.
He indeed emaciated his body through Cāndrāyaṇa and Brahmakūrca fasts; thus, O King, one hundred and fifty years passed in his ascetic penance.

Desiring her purification through the meditation on Śiva, worship, and other such practices, Śiva—having understood her supreme persistence after a few days and being urged by Pārvatī—became well-pleased and spoke. (10)
Īśvara said: "O daughter, do not act rashly; you are now pure of body. I am pleased today by your penance; choose a desired boon."
Alīkā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if I am considered worthy of a boon, grant supreme purification to me, who have been scorched by the fires of various sins. (12)
For you are the protector of me who am without a protector; you alone are the teacher of the worlds. You are the deliverer of the wretched and the helpless, the refuge for all embodied beings. 13.
Īśvara said: "O blessed lady, you are one of pure body; do not grieve at all. Having established me here under your own name, you shall thereafter go to heaven."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished right there; then Alikā also, having bathed with devotion, installed Śaṅkara.
Having given gifts to the brahmins, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he attained a most exalted world, and having approached his father and mother, [he honored them]. 16.
O King, having been affectionately honored by those kinsmen, Sālikā then ascended an excellent celestial chariot, adorned with divine garlands.
Having reached the world of Gaurī, he rejoices even today in her friendship; from that time forth, O son of Pṛthā, it became famous as Alikeśvara.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, whatever woman or man bathes at that sacred ford and worships Mahādeva together with Umā with devotion, [attains the highest goal].
Freed from various sins—whatever mental, vocal, or physical sin was committed in the past—he attains the world of Śaṅkara.
All that [evil] goes to dissolution by always feeding the twice-born and by offering a lamp before the deity; one is never overcome by diseases.
O Indra among kings, by giving an incense burner, a celestial chariot, a bell, and a water-pot to the God, one attains the world of Śakra.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Beyond that, at a distance of one krośa, is the meritorious holy site of Vimaleśvara, where, by means of bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth— || 1 ||
Having propitiated Vimaleśvara, whatever one may desire—whether the attainment of heaven or anything else on earth—one shall obtain it according to one's wish.
Formerly, having slain Tvaṣṭṛ’s son Triśiras, Śatakratu attained supreme purity through the majesty of this sacred bathing place.
There, the brahmin Vedanidhi, having performed great austerities in the past, became stainless like the sun when his various karmic impurities had been exhausted.
In former times, by the grace of Mahādeva, the Sun-god, afflicted by the arrows of Love, [approached] Bhānumatī, his daughter, who was as pleasing to behold as the moon.
Because of that fault he desired [the maiden], and consequently became afflicted with the disease of leprosy; yet, by performing penance here, he attained purity.
Delighted, he returned to his own abode with Mahādeva, who was pleased; and likewise in ancient times, O Pārtha, there was the sage who was the son of Vibhāṇḍaka.

Having encountered the company of yogis in the forest as well as that of a king in the city, the Supreme Self indeed incurs impurity from the defect of association with the passionate (rājasa). || 8 ||
Reflecting thus, he went to the confluence of the Revā and the ocean, and having performed austerities for twelve years together with his wife Śāntā, || 9 ||
Propitiating the three-eyed God with *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, the sage attained purity when Mahādeva was pleased.
O King, in ancient times, Śarva, impelled by Śarvāṇī in the Dāruvana forest, indeed beheld his own stainless form through the delusion of the wives of the sages.
Having deliberated upon the supreme place, the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean, and having stayed there, O great king, he performed austerities together with Umā.
Since he was born from Vimalā, he is Vimaleśvara; by that name he himself remained there, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, having created Tilottamā, and the Lord of Creatures (Viśvakarman) likewise, having created her and beheld that most enchanting woman before them—
Overpowered by the force of his past destiny, he became enamored of her; yet, perceiving her faults, he took refuge on both banks of the Revā.

Wandering among sacred fords, observing silence, bathing three times a day, and constantly remembering Śiva, the royal sage Brahmā attained purity in a short time after bathing at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean and worshipping Śaṅkara. (16)
In this way, many others as well—divine sages and the most excellent of kings—having abandoned the impurity of their defects there, became stainless. (17)
Likewise, O Indra among kings, by bathing there and worshipping Śiva, you too, though already stainless, will attain supreme purity in an even more distinguished manner.
Having bathed there, whether man or woman, and having worshipped Maheśvara, one is liberated from the defects of sin and is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 19 ||
O King, he who observes a fast there and beholds Vimaleśvara on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, as well as on all festival days, [attains the supreme goal].

Having abandoned the sins committed over seven lifetimes, one goes to the abode of Śiva. By performing the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors. One should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 21 ||

Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is beneficial to oneself at home—all that should be given to one possessed of virtue by him who desires that very gift to become inexhaustible. [One should give] gold, grain, garments, an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot. (22)
Having constructed a temple for the God according to one's capacity, one shall become a sovereign on earth; and with songs, dances, and sacred narratives, one should gratify the Supreme Lord.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: These have been described to you in brief according to their importance; O Pāṇḍava, I am not able to state the full number of sacred fords (tīrthas) in detail.
This river Narmadā, the most excellent of all streams and the beloved of Mahādeva, is pure, stainless, and renowned throughout the three worlds.
O King, he who constantly remembers the Narmadā with his mind quickly obtains the supreme fruit of a hundred cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
"Those men who lack faith and those atheists who abide here fall into a terrible hell; thus has the Supreme Lord declared. (4)
The Lord Maheśvara himself constantly resorts to the Narmadā; therefore, this river should be known as meritorious and the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this Gaṅgā of Maheśvara, born from the body of Maheśvara, is called the Southern Gaṅgā of Bhārata.
The Jāhnavī is indeed Vaiṣṇavī Gaṅgā, and the Gaṅgā is Brāhmī Sarasvatī; this [river] is Māheśvarī Gaṅgā, the Revā—of this there is no doubt.

Just as the divine being, having assumed a threefold form within a single person, is designated as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, yet there is truly no distinction therein; even so, O Pārtha, do not conceive of any difference among these three rivers.
For here, O Bhārata, there are crores of sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as hundreds of thousands and thousands, situated on both banks of the Revā.
Who is capable of determining those things situated between trees and in the sky, as well as those found on water and on land—not even Vāgīśa or Maheśvara? (10)
By remembering [Revā], the sin produced in one birth is destroyed; by seeing her, that produced in three births is destroyed; and by bathing in the Revā, the sin committed in seven births perishes.
By him the work of the gods has been accomplished, the sacred fires have been offered according to rule, the four Vedas have been studied, and the Revā river has been plunged into.
Out of their preeminence and for the sake of brevity, these sacred sites have been described to you by me; O Pārtha, it is not possible for me to either hear or speak of them in detail.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me the ritual procedure, as well as the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas). Tell me also what the rule is for undertaking the purpose of expiation (prāyaścitta).

The illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya said: Well asked, O great king, regarding that which is for the highest good in the world beyond; listen with an attentive mind as I speak to you according to my knowledge. 15.
One should perform lasting deeds with this transient body; for the vital breaths will inevitably depart like guests. (16)
One should extract the essence from what is insubstantial: charity from wealth, truthfulness from speech, fame and merit from renown, and service to others from the body. (17)
In this cauldron consisting of great delusion, with the sun as the fire, day and night as the fuel, and the months and seasons as the stirring ladle, Time cooks all beings; such is the report.
Having understood what is declared in the ordinances of the scriptures, you ought to perform action here; for this world is not for the man of doubt, nor the next, nor is there happiness for him. 19.
In respect to a mantra, a sacred ford, a twice-born, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, and a guru—whatever one’s conviction is, such will be the accomplishment.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is said to be "unreal"; it yields no fruit either in this world or after death.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts under the impulse of desire, attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
There are various means here for the purification of the bodies of men; yet there is no purification of one's own body equal to the service of sacred fords (tīrthas). 23.

Or else, the second [type of purification] is through the service of sacred fords (tīrtha) by means of penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa. O King, when a man sets out toward a sacred ford, then the gods and the ancestors, moving through the sky, follow after him.
Having performed the *abhyudayika* śrāddha and taken leave of the deity, his followers depart filled with supreme joy. (25)

Having received the permission of the twice-born and having undertaken the religious observances, he should go to his beloved kinsmen, as well as to Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara together with the lords of the Gaṇas.
Eating at a single sitting, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, speaking the truth, avoiding the food of others, and refraining from accepting gifts. || 27 ||
O best of kings, having avoided malice, deception, and the like, and having assumed the guise of a virtuous man, he should be adorned with humility. (28)
He who is free from hypocrisy and egoism attains the fruit of the sacred ford; he whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained. (29)
O king of kings, he who is free from anger, truthful in character, and firm in his vows, enjoys the fruit of sacred pilgrimage through knowledge, austerity, and fame.
He who treats all beings as himself attains the fruit of the sacred fords; shaving the head and fasting—this is the rule at all sacred fords. (31)
Except for Kurukṣetra, Viśālā, Virajā, and Gayā, [one should perform] bathing, worship of the gods, and indeed the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) during a śrāddha ceremony.

This is the rule for all sacred fords: one should provide food for Brahmins according to one's ability; and this applies to whoever, with a restrained mind, should go there for the purpose of expiation.
I shall also describe its procedure; listen with a concentrated mind, O Pārtha: eating but one meal a day, practicing celibacy, and abstaining from pungent and salty food. (34)
Having bathed, one should visit sacred fords, eat sacrificial food or a single meal, and avoid conversation with the fallen as well as excessive speech. (35)
One should avoid slander, the food of others, and association with the base; one should go about barefoot, wearing two clean garments, and remaining pure. (36)

Having formed a resolution in his mind and obtained the permission of the Brahmins, he should depart; having gone to the sacred ford and bathed there, he should likewise perform the worship of the gods. (37)
If one feels remorse, one shall be liberated from evil karma; [this applies] toward the Veda, the sacred ford, the deity, the astrologer, the medicine, and the preceptor. (38)
Whatever kind of mental cultivation one possesses, such is the success that comes to them; this has been stated in the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis regarding the fruits of visiting sacred fords. (39)

O bull among the Bharatas, having abandoned any doubt regarding the existence of mere explanatory passages (arthavāda), and having reflected upon what is taught in the scriptures, you should determine what is appropriate. (40)

Indeed, for those who are unable to perform difficult penances with the body, one should understand that there is no distinction among sacred sites and perform expiation accordingly for the sake of purification. (41)
Listen to that, O Great King, as it truly is regarding the Narmadā: a man should travel twenty-four yojanas [from there]. || 42 ||
One obtains the auspicious fruit of twenty-four kṛcchra penances; beyond that, for each yojana, a quarter-kṛcchra is prescribed. || 43 ||
And among those, O Great King, for one who should travel with a desire for purification, the wise know that there is an expiation for every yojana.
O Great King, having likewise gone to the place called Praṇava, to the confluence of the Revā and Urī, and to Bhṛgukṣetra, that fruit is remembered as being twofold.
O best of kings, at the confluence of the celestial river and at Śūlabheda, the merit is double; likewise, it is reduced by one-quarter at the confluence of the Karajā.
Likewise at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī and at the confluence of the Kapilā; some say it is tripled at the confluence arising from the Kubjā and Revā.
And at Oṃkāra, O Great King, that too would be appropriate; likewise at the confluences of other rivers with the Revā. (48)
O Yudhiṣṭhira, they say that the fruit previously mentioned is indeed equal to one and a half kṛcchras; however, at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean, one obtains three times that kṛcchra.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is declared that at Śuklatīrtha, a *kṛcchra* penance is fourfold. O best of men, having traveled twenty-four *yojanas*, going from *yojana* to *yojana*, one who should dwell there for a very long time [attains great merit].
One who practices the service of the Revā, endowed with pure intellect, free from hypocrisy and egoism, is liberated for the sake of purification. (51)
Thus, O Pārtha, I have told you the characteristics of the purpose of expiation, as well as the procedure for the pilgrimage to the Revā; this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is a secret.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of sages, tell me the measurement of a yojana; by knowing which, my mind may attain certainty, serving as a cause for its purification. (53)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O Pāṇḍava, I shall describe the measurement of a yojana, as well as the specific hardships encountered during the various stages of the journey.
They say the measure of a finger (aṅgula) is eight horizontal barley-corns or three vertical grains of rice; twelve fingers make a span (vitasti).
Two *vitastis* are a *hasta*; four *hastas* are known as a *dhanus*. That very measure is declared by those who know the distinctions to be a *daṇḍa*, O Yudhiṣṭhira. (56)
Two thousand bows make one *krośa*, and four *krośas* make one *yojana*. This measurement of a *yojana* has been described to you, O bull among the Bharatas. (57)

O best of kings, by means of this one knows the measure of the fruit earned by oneself while traveling on a pilgrimage; thus has been declared the fruit of the *kṛcchra* penance at a sacred site in the form of water. 58.
I shall tell you those specific details as they were previously mentioned in various places; listen to that from me, O protector of the earth, for it is being told to one who possesses faith. (59)
O King, whatever fruit—such as that of the *kṛcchra* penance—is declared for a particular sacred ford, one obtains that fruit of the *kṛcchra*, or even more, by fasting there.
And by reciting [the mantra] there for a day, one obtains according to one's capacity the fruit of a *kṛcchra* penance; having bathed there, seen the renowned Lord of Devas, and worshipped him.

The third [debt] is to be discharged toward the renowned gods through beholding, worshiping, and other such acts; the fourth is to be discharged day and night through the practice of recitation (jāpya) according to one's physical capacity.

O Pārtha, bathing in a great river accompanied by a fast, even if it is within a yojana [of home], bestows upon men the fruit of the Kṛcchra penance.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of sages, O ocean of compassion, tell me this: for one who goes on a pilgrimage for the sake of another, what is the fruit and of what magnitude? Tell me that. (1)

Washed by the waters of the Narmadā and fashioned by Mārkaṇḍeya, it was created here for the adornment of the virtuous and for the welfare of all the worlds.

This dhāraṇī, which pacifies the darkness of calamities, should always be upheld by those seeking the Dharma; by reciting it even once, it swiftly destroys the evil committed during a day and night. (109)

By reciting [the mantra] three times a day for one month before Śiva, the fruit arising from a month is attained; by reciting for three months, that arising from three months; then by reciting for one month, that arising from a year; and by reciting for one year, that arising from a hundred years. || 110 ||
And at the time of the śrāddha, standing before the Brahmins as they eat and reciting the meritorious list of sacred fords (tīrthāvali), one becomes a performer of the Gayā-śrāddha.

The venerable Sūta said: O best of sages, in the same manner, I shall describe the clusters of sacred fords (tīrthas), by which the previously mentioned garland of tīrthas has been woven together as one.

Starting from Oṃkāra-tīrtha as far as the western ocean, there are indeed thirty-five confluences of rivers that destroy all sins.

O best of the twice-born, at the confluence where the two banks of the Revā meet, there are four hundred famous sacred sites (tīrthas) situated together in this manner.
There are three hundred and thirty-three Śiva-tīrthas; O virtuous ones, listen as I describe them to you individually.
O lords of sages, among them there are ten Mārkaṇḍeśvara tīrthas; here there are ten born of Āditya and nine indeed of Kapileśvara.

In all directions for a distance of two *krośas* from Mount Amarakaṇṭaka surrounding the Oṃkāra-tīrtha, three and a half crores [of holy sites] are reckoned.

One hundred [merits] at the confluence of the Sarasvatī, two hundred at Śuklatīrtha, one thousand at the Viṣṇutīrthas, and then ten thousand at Mahiṣmatī.

Thus, O twice-born ones, there are approximately one hundred and one thousand holy sites at Kumbheśvara on the sacred ford; a full lakh of holy sites is situated at the confluence of the Revā.

Renowned throughout the three worlds, honored, and the means for attaining spiritual perfection, there are one hundred and eight sacred sites situated at Bhārabhūti.
At Akrūreśvara Tīrtha, one hundred and fifty tīrthas are situated; and at Vimaleśvara Tīrtha, at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean, the sage declared there to be more than ten million tīrthas.
Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has this supreme majesty of the Revā been narrated to you, exactly as it was formerly taught by Mārkaṇḍeya to the son of Pṛthā.
Likewise, the clusters of holy fords (tīrthakadamba) among them have been declared by me according to their specific characteristics, primarily in their respective numbers and sequence.
This sacred account of Narmadā’s deeds, spoken by the sages, is incomparable, supremely purifying, and removes all sins; it is a meritorious exposition of her majesty.
O lords of sages, for seven kalpas the wise brahmin Mṛkaṇḍu’s son dwelt on the Narmadā; he was the most excellent among those who know the supreme truth.

In the same way, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, having experienced the entire river along with its sacred bathing places step by step, described that purifying stream to the son of Pāṇḍu.

In the region of Ānarta, there is a forest that serves as a refuge for sages; it is pleasing to all beings, with its trees bearing fruit in every season.

By those devoted to ritual bathing and fire-offerings, by those intent on silent recitation and Vedic study, by forest-dwellers, by the triple-staffed ascetics, by the haṃsa-ascetics, and also by the kuṭīcara-ascetics; || 8 ||
Then, after some time had passed, the Blessed Lord, the Destroyer of Tripura, [was attended] by Snātakas, self-controlled ascetics (yatis), and likewise by those who maintain the five fires.

There, mongooses play with great joy alongside serpents; lions with elephants, and cats with mice; and crows with flocks of owls, all entirely free from feelings of enmity.

Thus being gazed upon by the amorous women, Maheśvara wandered along the royal highway, proclaiming, "Give alms! (18)
Then those sages, seeing him thus divested of his garment and causing the arousal of passion in women, spoke with eyes red with anger.
"O wicked one, since this hermitage of ours has been defiled by you, therefore let your own linga fall instantly upon the surface of the earth! (20)

Then, O best of the twice-born, as the Liṅga fell, portending fear for the three worlds, terrible omens appeared everywhere.
Mountain peaks crumble, meteors fall even during the day, and all the oceans gradually overstep their boundaries.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds terrified with fear, led by Śakra and Viṣṇu, went to where the god Pitāmaha was.
And bowing down, they praised him with hymns originating from the sacred scriptures, saying: "He who is the form of creation in the three worlds and is seated upon the lotus-throne. (26)
"O Lord, what is this, what is this that is occurring—a topsy-turvy state by which the entire three worlds have fallen into agitation? (27)
O Lotus-born One, the signs of universal dissolution are visible; will there now be a total destruction even though it is not the appointed time? (28)
The Grandfather of all the worlds is the refuge for all gods, mortals, and Daityas whose bodies are afflicted by fear, for he is skilled in mantras.
Having heard those words of the gods, the four-faced one, having reflected for a long time and having understood through his divine eye, spoke.
"O best of gods, this is not the time for universal dissolution now. Listen to the cause from which these great portents have arisen. (31)
The linga of the trident-bearing God of gods was cast down by the high-souled sages in the land of Anarta for the sake of their wives, through the power of a curse.
Therefore, this triple world, including all that is mobile and immobile, has become utterly confounded; let us go therefore to where the god Maheśvara resides.
"Whoever, at my word, quickly deposits that linga—if not, there will certainly be an untimely destruction even of the entire three worlds; this which I have spoken is the truth. (34)
Then all the hosts of gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu—the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, as well as the two Aśvins—[approached].
They went quickly to that place where the god Maheśvara was, lying asleep in the middle of a pit, overcome with supreme shame.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the lords of gods, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees! Salutations to you, the support of the universe, whose crest is adorned by the moon! (37)

You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call, you are the waters, and you are the great earth, O All-pervading Lord; by you all this triple world, with its mobile and immobile beings, has been created. (38)
O best of gods, you protect and likewise you shall bring about destruction; you are Viṣṇu, you are the four-faced one, you are the moon, and you are the sun. (39)
O Mahādeva, without you nothing exists here; even if a man has committed a great sin on the surface of the earth, O God. (40)
By merely chanting even your name, one goes to the abode of the three heavens; by the proclamation, "Mahādeva, Mahādeva, Mahādeva! [one attains this]. (41)
Tens of millions of killings of Brahmins and tens of millions of instances of forbidden sexual intercourse immediately go to destruction through the chanting of "Mahādeva. (42)
Just as a Brahmin is among men, or as the great ocean is among rivers, so are you established in the sovereignty over all the gods.
Just as the moon is among the stars and the sun is among the luminous bodies, so are you established in the sovereignty over all the gods.
Just as gold is among minerals and Nārada is among the Gandharvas, so you are established in the sovereignty over all the gods.
Just as grain is among herbs and the Golden Mountain is among mountains, so are you established in the sovereignty over all the gods.
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, best among the gods, show us favor and all men; once again, maintain your own linga.
O Lord, if this liṅga were to fall upon the surface of the earth, O Master, the three worlds would surely meet their destruction. (48)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, the Lord whose banner bears the bull, filled with shame, spoke to all those gods who were prostrate before him.
O best of gods, afflicted by the pain of separation from Satī, I have abandoned this linga under the pretext of a curse upon the twice-born.
"Who in these three worlds is capable of toppling this linga of mine? Whether it be a god or even a brahmin—you yourselves know this clearly. (51)
Therefore, I shall certainly not maintain this linga upon the surface of the earth; what use have I for it, being deprived of my wife? (52)
The gods said: O best of gods, that beloved wife of yours named Satī who died previously has been born from Himācala as Gaurī in the womb of Menakā. (53)
"O Destroyer of Tripura, she shall become your wife once again; therefore, taking this linga, bring about the welfare of the dwellers of heaven. (54)
The God of gods said: "From this day forward, if the gods and the twice-born worship my linga with diligence, then I shall sustain it."

Then, having entered Pātāla together with the gods, the Grandfather himself performed worship of that Liṅga with devotion.

Then, being pleased, Mahādeva spoke these words to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and to Vāsudeva, who stood bowed down in humility.
"I am well-pleased with you both; therefore, O illustrious ones, accept from me whatever boon you desire, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (60)
The two of them said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, grant us a refuge consisting of one-third [of yourself] along with the Liṅga, so that there may be a single dwelling place for both. (61)
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," the Lord took the liṅga and installed it in that place, which is worshipped by all the lords of the gods.
Then, taking that gold and fashioning a linga of that same form, the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself joyfully installed it there. || 63 ||
And then, O Brahmins, he spoke with a virtuous voice that made the three worlds resound, while all the inhabitants of heaven were listening. (64)
"For this first *liṅga* has been fashioned by me out of gold; it shall attain renown everywhere as Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla. (65)
Likewise, other men who, out of devotion, fashioned lingas in their entirety from gold and the like, as well as from jewels, pearls, and excellent gems; || 66 ||
Those who worship [the deity] three times a day shall attain the supreme goal, having completely abandoned [images] made of clay as well as those made of base metals.
Having spoken thus, the four-faced one departed for the third heaven along with all the inhabitants of the celestial realm, and the moon-crested Lord also went to Kailāsa.
For this reason, the *liṅga* is worshipped here by gods and demons, especially after they have abandoned the other limbs of Hara. (69)
From that time forward, Brahmā himself remained stationed at that liṅga; and because the Lord Vāsudeva also [resided there], that Śiva is indeed worthy of worship by him.
But he who worships constantly with a mind endowed with faith—by him the triad consisting of Tryambaka, Acyuta, and Brahmā, and the others, are worshipped. (71)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should worship the Śivaliṅga with every effort; one should constantly touch it, gaze upon it, and glorify it.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Liṅga," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 1 ||

Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, when that Liṅga had been uprooted from the surface of the earth, the waters of the Gaṅgā issued forth through that path from Pātāla; they remove all sins of men and grant all desires. || 1 ||
In that regard, O best of the foremost twice-born, listen today as I relate that which occurred there of old, which causes wonder to the world. (2)
The lord of kings named Triśaṅku had fallen into the state of a Caṇḍāla; having bathed there, he regained once more a body befitting a monarch.
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, tell us all this in detail: how did Triśaṅku, that best of kings, attain the state of a Caṇḍāla?"
Sūta said: I shall narrate to you this ancient story concerning King Triśaṅku, which removes all sins and is conducive to purity.
Formerly, there was a tiger among kings born of the solar dynasty, renowned as Triśaṅku, whose prowess was equal to that of a tiger.
The disciple of the sage Vasiṣṭha was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, and a master; by him all the rituals, beginning with the Agniṣṭoma, were constantly performed.
Year after year, all manner of gifts were bestowed by that high-souled one, accompanied by complete sacrificial fees.
To distinguished Brahmins and especially to the destitute, he gave gifts; he fulfilled his religious vows and protected those who sought refuge. || 9 ||

People were cherished like sons, and enemies were utterly destroyed; whatever holy fords and shrines existed upon the earth were visited, while the desired wealth was bestowed according to their wishes upon the ascetics.
Then, after some time, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha was addressed by him while standing in the midst of the assembly, preceded by a salutation.
Triśaṅku said: "O Blessed One, I now wish to perform that sacrifice by which one may go swiftly to heaven with this very body."
Therefore, show me favor and quickly gather the necessary provisions for the success of that sacrifice, as well as the brahmins who are worthy of it.
Vasiṣṭha said: O King, there is no sacrifice by which heaven can be reached with this very body; I tell you this as the truth.
O King, those sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma which were previously proclaimed by the Self-Existent One—by performing them, heaven is attained in another body.
Or perhaps, O protector of the earth, by the power of your sacrifice, whether it be a king, a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, or even someone else—|| 16 ||
Proclaim that person who, having been seen or even heard of here on this earth, has gone to heaven together with his physical body.
Triśaṅku said: "O Brahmin, I know in truth that nothing is impossible for you; therefore, show me favor so that my heart's desire may be fulfilled. (18)
Vasiṣṭha said: "Never before have I uttered a falsehood, even in jest, with my tongue; therefore, there is no sacrifice for you—truly, you wish to perform a sacrifice. (19)
Triśaṅku said: "O tiger among brahmins, O Lord, if you are not capable of performing for me a sacrifice that bestows heaven with this very body," (20)

"O wise one, what can you achieve with the power of your asceticism as a Brahmin? Listen to another word of mine that I speak clearly, O best of the twice-born, while the hosts of sages and others are listening. (21)
"If you do not carry out my word, though I have spoken it repeatedly, then I shall perform that sacrifice by appointing another brahmin as my preceptor."
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the venerable Vasiṣṭha then spoke to him with a loud laugh, "O lord of the earth, do exactly so."

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Triśaṅku and Vasiṣṭha," within the "Legend of Triśaṅku" in the "Māhātmya of the Hāṭakeśvara Region," in the sixth section (Nāgara-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 2 ||
Sūta said: Then, having bowed once more to Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, he went to the place where his hundred daughters were.
Having bowed to them as well, that lord of men spoke to them about that very same matter; he related the entirety of Vasiṣṭha’s words, which had been recounted by them to him.
Then he spoke to them again: "Your father has now been released; being incapable of leading you to heaven while you still possess your bodies, he has departed."
Therefore, if you do not cause me to perform a sacrifice now, I shall immediately abandon you and appoint another as my domestic priest.
"O sons of my preceptor, he who shall lead me, along with this very body, to the abode of the gods by the power of sacrifice—" || 5 ||
Having heard those words of his, all those best of sages were overcome with supreme anger and addressed him in harsh words.
"Since you have abandoned your guru who acted for your welfare, you are now a sinner; therefore, O sinful one, you shall become a Caṇḍāla, despised by the world."
Then, at the conclusion of those words, at that very moment, the lord of the earth assumed the form of an outcaste, bearing a body of deformed appearance.

He was thin-waisted like a barley grain, with a slender neck, tawny eyes, and a crooked nose; his limbs were black, his complexion was like that of a wooden stake, and he was enveloped in a foul odor.
Then, beholding himself transformed into one with the nature of a Caṇḍāla, that lord of men immediately stood with his face cast down in shame.

Being repeatedly reviled by those brahmins with cries of “Go away! Go away! and being tormented on all sides by unrestrained dogs, he—resembling a crow or a cuckoo and shrouded in tattered rags—[proceeded].
Then, overwhelmed by great sorrow, he reflected: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? How will there be peace? (12)
"What was this difficult-to-attain state desired by me, a total fool? By its power, even my own family dharma has been cast away. (13)
"Should I enter the water today, or the blazing fire? Or shall I consume poison? How might my death come about this very day? (14)
"With this body, how shall I look upon those wives with whom I used to sport in such a form? (15)
"How shall I ever again behold my sons, grandsons, friends, relations, and kinsmen, as well as my other servants and people? (16)
All those enemies who were previously conquered by me in battle.
Having heard that I am in such a state today, they will attain joy, free from fear.
Those Brahmins, masters of the Vedas, whom I have gratified with gifts, will today become sorrowful upon hearing that I have come to such a state. (18)
Likewise, what state will those friends who are dear to me and always devoted to my welfare fall into, upon seeing me standing in such a condition? (19)
Who will now employ those noble-bred elephants of mine, sixty years of age and blinded by rut, in mutual combat without me? (20)
Who, other than me, can control with variegated steps those horses—dappled like partridges and well-tamed—along with their firm riders? (21)
Likewise, to whom will those noble servants of mine, who are fierce in battle, go today in my absence, being deeply distressed? (22)
Likewise, this treasury, though lacking in number, possesses many jewels; to whom will it go, protected by me but deprived of my enjoyment? (23)
"In this way, my great wealth of grain, cattle, goats, and sheep will become deficient in number; how can it be that what is protected by me has been diminished by those I hold dear? (24)
Having lamented in this manifold way, the king, filled with sorrow, went on foot toward the vicinity of the city, very slowly.
Then, having reached his own city at night when it was deserted by people, he stood at the gate and summoned his son, who was accompanied by the ministers.
Standing at a distance from the sons of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, he related the entire account concerning the origin of the curse.
Having heard those words of his, which were like a thunderbolt falling, they too, their faces clouded with tears, wept, overcome with grief. (28)
"Alas, O Lord! Alas, O Great King! Alas, you who are ever devoted to Dharma! Bereft of you, how shall we endure today, so deeply afflicted? (29)
Is this appropriate for those evil-minded descendants of Vasiṣṭha, that they should have cast a curse upon their own patron, especially upon Vinata? (30)
O tiger among kings, having abandoned our homes and all else, we shall undoubtedly follow you and attain the status of outcasts. (31)
Triśaṅku said: "If you have unrestrained devotion toward me, then all of you now act as ministers to my son."
