"This Hariścandra is my excellent son, my eldest and most beloved; appoint him without hesitation to my path with all speed. (33)
I, however, shall do that which is established in my mind: either I shall go to death, or I shall go to the abode of the gods in my own body.
Having spoken thus and having abandoned them all, that lord of the earth departed for the forest, proceeding slowly on foot alone.
Then those six ministers quickly installed his highly esteemed son upon the throne amidst the sounding of drums and musical instruments.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Kingdom by Hariścandra," within the Narrative of Triśaṅku, in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 3 ||
Sūta said: Having reflected for a very long time in his mind upon the great sage Viśvāmitra as "Triśaṅku," he then made a firm resolve.
"Except for Viśvāmitra, there is no one else in the three worlds who could provide me protection from this most terrible suffering. (2)
Then, setting out toward Kurukṣetra, he proceeded further on, exhausted, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and intent on asking for directions.
Then, having reached Kurukṣetra in due course, that king diligently searched for the hermitage of Viśvāmitra.
While searching in this manner, the king then beheld from a great distance a cluster of dark-blue trees.
Above, it was surrounded on all sides by cranes and swans wheeling about, as well as by water-fowls such as āṭis and madgus on every side.
Perceiving water there, the lord of the earth, afflicted by thirst, set out in haste, joyful, his fatigue dispelled by the wind from the water.
Then he saw a captivating hermitage situated on the riverbank, frequented by gentle creatures, which destroyed both the mind and sorrow.
It was surrounded on all sides by trees in full bloom and bearing fruit, and it resounded with the various sweet songs of the finest birds.
Where mongooses play with serpents, owls with crows, cats with mice, and leopards with various kinds of deer.

Then, on the bank of the river, he saw Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism, surrounded by a multitude of practitioners of austerity, self-controlled, and devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
Blazing intensely with splendor and ascetic power like a fire, he was clothed in rags and bark garments and had taken refuge beneath a śāla tree.
Then, having gone there, that lord of kings, though standing at a distance, bowed to him with an eight-limbed prostration while proclaiming his own name.
Likewise, with palms joined in reverence, he stood before the other disciples as well, endowed with supreme faith, according to their order and seniority. (14)
But seeing that lord of the earth with his limbs grey with dust, they took him for a Caṇḍāla because of the marks appearing on his body.
Then they indeed reviled him with words of harsh syllables; others likewise shouted cries of "Fie! and repeatedly said, "Go away! Go away! (16).
"Who are you, O sinful one, that have arrived here at this most excellent hermitage of sages, which resounds with the sound of the Vedas and is difficult even for the virtuous to attain? (17)
Therefore, go quickly, before some ascetic, having bestowed a curse upon you, swiftly brings about even the destruction of your life. (18)
Triśaṅku said: "I am a king named Triśaṅku, born of the Solar dynasty; cursed by the sons of Vasiṣṭha, I have been reduced to the state of a Caṇḍāla. (19)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I have sought refuge with Viśvāmitra, the friend of the world, for the sake of liberation from the curse; there is no other higher resort for me.
Viśvāmitra said: You are worthy of being honored by Vasiṣṭha, and especially so by his sons; why then have you been employed by them today in such a sinful act?
O best of kings, what offense have you committed against them? Has there been an attempt on their lives, or perhaps an assault upon their wives? (22)
Triśaṅku said: "I requested from Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, that a sacrifice be performed so that I might go to heaven with this very body. (23)
He said: "O King, there is no sacrifice by which one goes to heaven while not having abandoned this very body for another body. (24)
Having heard that, I said to him: "If he does not lead me to heaven in this very body immediately through the power of the sacrifice," || 25 ||
"Today I shall certainly make another person my guru; of this there is no doubt. Having understood this, the sage said: "Practice that which is for your welfare. (26)
Then, having been abandoned by him, I approached his cruel sons and told them everything that had been recounted by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, O best of sages, I was cursed by them who were tormented by grief; I have been brought to this sinful state and assigned to the condition of a Caṇḍāla.
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, having meditated upon you in my mind and having formed a most profound hope, I have come from very far away to Kurukṣetra.
"O Sage, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that is impossible for you to achieve; therefore, provide a remedy now for me who am suffering. (30)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, standing in the midst of the munis, spoke out of rivalry with Vasiṣṭha. (31)
"O King, I shall cause you to perform that sacrifice by which, as soon as it is completed, you shall go to the third heaven at that very moment. (32)
"O King, you have been thus ordained as an outcaste by those descendants of Vasiṣṭha; however, I shall restore you once more to the status of a king—of this there is no doubt. (33)
Therefore, O protector of the earth, come with me on a pilgrimage to sacred fords; by the power of those sacred fords, you shall become pure once again.
Likewise, one becomes fit for performing sacrifices and is freed from the state of being a Caṇḍāla; there is no sin whatsoever that is not destroyed by bathing in the sacred ford (tīrtha). || 35 ||
Sūta said: Having thus made this resolve, Gādhi’s son, the lord of sages, set out on a pilgrimage, placing Triśaṅku behind him.
At Kurukṣetra on the Sarasvatī, at Prabhāsa and Kurujāṅgala, at Pṛthūdaka, Gayāśīrṣa, Naimiṣa, and the three Puṣkaras; || 37 ||
In Vārāṇasī, at Prayāga, at Kedāra, at the Śravaṇa river, at Citrakūṭa, at Gokarṇa, at Śāligrāma, and at Acaleśvara; || 38 ||
At Śuklatīrtha, at the auspicious river Dṛṣadvatī known as Surājya, and then at other very meritorious tīrthas and sacred abodes.
In this manner, a great length of time passed for that lord of men as he wandered upon the earth together with that high-souled being.
O twice-born ones, even though he bathed separately in such sacred fords, he was not released from his sin or from his state as a Caṇḍāla.
Then, proceeding by stages, he arrived at Mount Arbuda; having ascended it, he beheld Acaleśvara, the destroyer of sins.
As soon as the Lord of Sages emerged from that abode, he beheld Mārkaṇḍa, the best of sages, by name.
Having seen the lord of sages, Viśvāmitra, the friend of the world, he then said: "O lord of sages, from where have you come at this time?"
"O excellent sage, who is this fierce follower of yours who appears to have the form of an outcaste? Explain all of this to me as I ask you. (45)
Viśvāmitra said: "This tiger among kings, renowned as Triśaṅku, has been reduced to the state of a Caṇḍāla by the sons of Vasiṣṭha out of their wrath. (46)
And I have promised him: "I shall wander over the earth consisting of seven islands until you attain the state of being fit for sacrifice."
I have wandered over all the sacred fords and shrines upon the earth, yet this place has not attained purity; I am now utterly exhausted.
Therefore, filled with supreme shame, I shall abandon the entire earth; having left the continents and the great oceans, I will depart from here to another place beyond.
O Brahmin, I speak the truth to you: may I never become an object of derision for the sons of Vasiṣṭha, nor ever be devoid of my vow. 50.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "If it is so, O tiger among sages, then do as I say: do not abandon the earth consisting of seven islands and go anywhere else."
From this mountain, in the south-western direction, there is a sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara in the region called Ānarta.
There, the first Liṅga was established by the supreme gods out of gold; it is celebrated in the world as Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla.
O best of the twice-born, it was there that the water of the Pātālajāhnavī emerged from the netherworld when the Liṅga had been lifted up by Śambhu.
Having entered Pātāla there with effort, O lord of the earth, let him, endowed with faith, perform his ablutions in the waters of the Jāhnavī.
Afterwards, let him behold that Liṅga known as Hāṭakeśvara; thereupon he shall become pure, freed from his status as a Caṇḍāla.
You too shall attain the supreme welfare residing within your heart, as well as whatever else there may be, by remaining steadfast in that very penance.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, then went quickly to that place accompanied by Triśaṅku.
Having entered Pātāla by way of the path of the gods, he bathed Triśaṅku, the best of kings, according to the rites prescribed by rule.
Then, immediately upon bathing and beholding Hāṭakeśvara, that king was liberated from his state as a Caṇḍāla and became resplendent like the sun. || 60 ||
Then that sage spoke to him, who was prostrate and cleansed of sin: "O Indra among kings, by good fortune you are now liberated from the state of a Caṇḍāla."

"By good fortune you have attained supreme splendor; by good fortune you have attained supreme ascetic power. Therefore, perform a sacrificial session according to the rules, accompanied by liberal gifts."
"By means of which you shall attain that perfection which eternally resides in your heart; for your sake, I myself will go and petition the Grandfather."
"Since the foremost of all gods takes his share of the sacrifice at your sacrifice, therefore bring here all the materials arising from the sacrifice even from the world of Brahmā until my return."
"So be it," said that sage of rigid vows; then, approaching his grandfather and bowing down, he spoke these words.
"O Great-grandfather, I shall perform a sacrifice for King Triśaṅku, so that he may go to your abode with his human body. (66)
Therefore, O Grandfather, come there to the sacrificial enclosure together with all the hosts of gods, preceded by Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Accept with your own hand the sacrificial portion as is appropriate, so that by your grace he may go to heaven in his physical body.
Brahmā said: "O Brahmā, heaven is not attained through sacrificial rites with one's own body; rather, it is attained after casting off this body. Therefore, do not speak to me in such a manner."
With Agni as our mouth, we all receive the oblation in the sacrifice, according to the rules prescribed in the Vedas, for the true benefit of the sacrificer.
Therefore, O twice-born one, he shall again offer oblations into the mouth of the fire; through your grace, he will undoubtedly attain heaven. (71)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Viśvāmitra’s Commencement of the Sacrifice for Triśaṅku," within the Legend of Triśaṅku, in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Brahmā, Viśvāmitra, filled with rage, spoke this to the Grandfather: "Behold the power of my asceticism! (1)
"O Grandfather, having caused Triśaṅku to sacrifice according to the rules with proper sacrificial fees, I shall lead him here while you look on."
Having spoken thus, Viśvāmitra went quickly to the earth’s surface and made an effort to perform the sacrificial rites for the great-souled Triśaṅku.
Having summoned Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, he bestowed the initiation at that very auspicious forest, at the time appropriate for the rite.
That wise one himself became the Adhvaryu priest in the sacrificial rite; Śāṇḍilya was the Hotṛ priest therein, and Gautama was the Brahman priest.
The Āgnīdhra was named Cyavana, the Maitrāvaruṇa was Kārmika, the Udgātṛ was Yājñavalkya, and the Pratihartṛ was Jaimini. || 6 ||
Prastotā was Śaṅkuvarṇa, and likewise Unnetā was Gālava; Pulastya was the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, and Garga, the lord of sages, was the Hotṛ.
Neṣṭṛ was Atri, and Bhṛgu himself was the Acchāvāka; Triśaṅku, filled with faith, appointed all of them as his officiating priests.
Having adorned themselves with garments, crowns, and armlets, they performed the ritual shaving of their hair and likewise donned the black antelope skin.
Then, equipped with the horn of a black antelope and devoted to a vow of subsisting on milk alone, he indeed engaged them all in a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra).
When that long sacrificial session had thus commenced in the prescribed manner, divine Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas arrived.
Likewise, other logicians and householders filled with curiosity, as well as the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others such as actors and dancers [were present]. (12)
"Let it be given, let it be given quickly! This alone belongs to them. Let it be eaten, let it be eaten! O people, let favor be shown! (13)
Thus, this great sound was heard constantly there in that sacrificial enclosure at all times, and never anything else whatsoever.
There, mountains composed of grain were seen fashioned there, as well as those made of gold, silver, and especially of jewels. (15)
For the sake of giving, there were also innumerable cows for the foremost of Brahmins, as well as horses and great elephants, tamed yet intoxicated with rut.
In that very extensive and ongoing great sacrifice, mountains were seen arranged all around like so many peaks.
When summoned for their share of the sacrifice, the deities do not approach; they receive that oblation solely through the mouth of the fire.
Thus, as that king performed the sacrifice for twelve years, they passed away, yet the desired fruit of his heart was not attained.

Then, having performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) resulting from the completion of the sacrificial session (*satra*), he gratified those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to their merit.
O best of sages, Triśaṅku then dismissed all his kinsmen, as well as other associates, relatives, and friends.
Then Vinata, filled with shame, spoke to Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, preceded by a prostration.
O Brahmin, through your grace, I have obtained the full fruit arising from the long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra), which is difficult for all human beings to attain. (23)
Likewise, O virtuous sage, although this birth was obtained again and has been lost once more, by your grace, O brahmin-sage, my state as a Caṇḍāla has been destroyed. (24)
But my sole great sorrow is like an arrow fixed in my heart: that by this very body I have not attained the third heaven.
O sage, having heard today that my efforts have been in vain and that I have not reached heaven, the sons of Vasiṣṭha will mock me. (26)
Likewise, those words of Vasiṣṭha remained true: that which he had spoken, namely, that one cannot go to heaven with the body by means of sacrifice.
Therefore, having now taken refuge in the forest, I shall perform penance; I will never again accept a kingdom offered by my son.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Viśvāmitra’s Performance of the Twelve-Year Sacrifice for Triśaṅku’s Ascent to Heaven with His Physical Body," within the *Triśaṅkupākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvarakṣetramāhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgarakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Triśaṅku, Viśvāmitra, the bull among sages, spoke these words while somewhat filled with shame. || 1 ||
Do not despair, O protector of the earth, regarding this matter; with this very body, I shall lead you to heaven.
"O best of kings, I shall perform various deeds for the sake of heaven; I shall do what is desired by you, or else I shall go to my destruction. (3)
Having spoken thus and having directed supreme wrath toward the inhabitants of heaven, he then spoke these terrible words in the very presence of that king.
"Just as I have indeed acquired the status of a twice-born by my own power, so shall I create my own creation; there is no doubt in this. (5)
Then, having beheld that Śaṅkara who bears the moon upon his crest, the great sage prostrated himself according to the rules with devotion and offered a hymn of praise.
Viśvāmitra said: Victory, O God! Victory, O Inconceivable One! Victory, O Beloved of Pārvatī! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, Teacher of the World! (7)

Victory to you, O inconceivable one! Victory to you, O immeasurable one! Victory to you, O infinite one! Victory to you, O infallible one! Victory to you, O immortal one! Victory to you, O unconquerable one! Victory to you, O imperishable one, O Lord of the gods! 8.
Victory to you, the omnipresent Lord of all! Victory to you, the refuge of all the gods! Victory to you, the object of meditation for all people! Victory to you, the destroyer of all sins! 9.
O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, you are the sustainer and the ordainer; you are the creator and the protector of the fourfold multitude of living beings.
Just as oil resides within sesame seeds and ghee within curd, even so the entire world is pervaded and protected by you who remain hidden.
You are Brahmā, you are Hṛṣīkeśa, you are Śakra, and you are Hutāśana; you are the sacrifice, you are the Vaṣaṭkāra, you are the Moon, and you are the Sun. || 12 ||
Or rather, O Lord, what is the use of much speaking with this praise? I shall describe your majesty, as proclaimed by the Vedas, in brief alone.
O All-pervading Lord, whatever exists in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving, all that is pervaded by you, just as wood is pervaded by fire.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am well-pleased; may it be well with you. O excellent sage, ask for a boon. Whatever has long resided in your heart, I shall grant it all without a doubt. (15)
Viśvāmitra said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then by your grace, O Maheśvara, let there be for me the greatness of creation."
Having said to him, "So be it," the Blessed One whose banner is the bull, accompanied by all his attendants, then vanished from sight.
Viśvāmitra also remained right there, intent on meditation, and out of rivalry with him who moves like a swan, he performed the fourfold creation.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Boon by Viśvāmitra," within the Narrative of Triśaṅku, in the Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya of the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: While thus meditating, he entered the water with a specific desire and created the two twilights (saṃdhyā), which are indeed seen even today, O twice-born ones.
Then all the hosts of gods were created by that Great-Souled One, as well as those who travel in celestial chariots, the constellations, and the planets.
Human beings, serpents, and rākṣasas; creepers together with trees; the Seven Sages beginning with Dhruva; and all others who move through the sky. || 3 ||
Having thus created them, the wrathful Viśvāmitra, the Blessed One, then employed them in his own tasks.
At that very time, O twice-born ones, two suns rose simultaneously in the sky, as did two moons; the planets became twofold, and the lunar mansions likewise became twofold along with the Seven Sages.
Thus, all of them, competing with one another in the sky, were seen doubled in number, causing confusion among the people.
In the meantime, Śakra, together with all the inhabitants of heaven, went to that place where the Blessed One, whose seat is the lotus, was staying.
Then, O twice-born ones, having performed a hymn of praise along with the gods using Vedic eulogies, he stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke aloud after bowing down.
O best of gods, a creation has now been made by Viśvāmitra consisting of humans, yakṣas, serpents, gods, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
Therefore, O Grandfather, go yourself and restrain him, before he has pervaded this entire world of moving and non-moving beings through his creation.
Having heard those words of his, Brahmā, accompanied by him alone, went and spoke to Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages and friend of the world.
"O brahmin-sage, desist now at my word, before all the gods, including Indra, are destroyed by the beings you have created. (12)
Viśvāmitra said: "If Triśaṅku, the best of kings, goes to your world with this very body, then I shall not create that world."
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Sages, by your grace, let this king go to the third heaven with me in this very body."
"Cease from creation; no one else shall do this. That deed which has never been performed by anyone in the world has now been accomplished by you. (15)
Viśvāmitra said: "O Lotus-born One, O God, Grandfather of all the worlds, this creation which has been made by me while possessed by anger must be forgiven by you."
"O Lord, by your grace, may my creation thus be inexhaustible; O Lotus-born One, I shall not create another such as this again. (17)
Brahmā said: "O Brahmin, the creation which has been performed by you shall certainly endure; however, among all ritual acts, it shall not be worthy of sacrifice. (18)
Having spoken thus and taking Triśaṅku with him, the great-grandfather, the joyful sage, went to the world of Brahmā and remained right there.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Triśaṅku’s Attainment of Heaven," within the Narrative of Triśaṅku, in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the sixth section (Āgara-khaṇḍa) of the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 7 || || 9 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, when Triśaṅku, that most excellent of kings, had thus attained heaven in his physical body through the exertion of Viśvāmitra.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) attained renown throughout the entire three worlds; from it arose the source that bestows upon people virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
It was untouched by the defects of the Kali age, as well as by other minor sins (upapātaka) and even by such heinous crimes as the killing of a Brahmin, all through the power of the Enemy of Tripura.
Whoever there gives up their life with a mind endowed with faith shall attain liberation, even if that mortal has been a perpetrator of great evil.
Even those who are worms, birds, insects, domestic animals, winged creatures, or wild beasts—whenever they die there, they undoubtedly go to the world of Śiva.
Those who perform their ablutions there with a mind purified by faith—even those who are unrighteous—go to heaven like Triśaṅku.
Those who, afflicted by heat or afflicted by thirst, plunge into that water, they too go to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.
Viśvāmitra, too, having seen that supreme majesty of the sacred ford, abandoned Kurukṣetra and then made his dwelling there.
Likewise, other peaceful sages, having abandoned sacred fords from afar and established hermitages there, have departed for the supreme state.
In the very same way, all men, having come from afar with haste and bathed there, go to heaven even after having committed hundreds of sins.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, by the power of that sacred ford, as the worlds proceeded happily toward the abode of the three gods, || 11 ||
All rituals, such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, have come to an end; no mortal performs a sacrifice, nor does any man observe a vow.
He does not bestow gifts in that manner, nor does he resort to sacred fords; he performs only ritual bathing at Liṅgabhed, being fully concentrated.
Then, having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he proceeds to heaven.
Thereupon, O twice-born ones, all the heavenly realms were filled with men who vied with the supreme gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and the rest. (15)
Then all the hosts of gods, deprived of their sacrificial portions, fell into great distress and consulted one another.
Through the majesty of Hāṭakeśvara, the heavenly world has been filled, crowded on all sides by those with upraised arms who are vying with one another.
Therefore, let that rite be performed by which [this world] shall go to its destruction; [let it be done] at the holy site known as Hāṭakeśvara on the surface of the earth.
Then, O best of the twice-born, by the command of Śakra, the Saṃvartaka wind filled that field on all sides with dust.
When that sacrificial ground had thus met its destruction and the mound of earth had come into being, all the rites originating from sacrifices were once again performed.
Then, after a long time, an anthill arose; in that field, he gradually descended into the netherworld (pātāla).
Then, out of curiosity, the Nāgas from the netherworld (pātāla) come to the world of mortals by that path and wander upon the surface of the earth.
There, having enjoyed human pleasures according to their desire, they depart once again by that very same path to their own abodes.
O best of the twice-born, because of the coming and going of the nāgas, that anthill became famous throughout the entire earth as Nāgabila.
Then, after some time had passed, the Blessed Lord Indra, the subduer of Pāka, became possessed by the sin of Brahman-slaughter and was rendered devoid of splendor.
Then, having obtained the command of his grandfather, he entered by that same path and beheld Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla.
Then, by the mere sight of him, he was instantly liberated from sin; endowed with splendor once more, he returned to heaven.
Having seen that power of the trident-bearing Lord known as Hāṭakeśvara—that Liṅga—he felt fear arising from men.
If some man here, like King Triśaṅku, shall worship that Liṅga with faith and become free from sin; (29)
"He will surely cause me to depart from this abode of the thirty gods; therefore, I shall fill up for him this path leading to Pātāla."
Then, filled with haste, Śatakratu himself hurled that best of mountains, Raktaśṛṅga, into that cave.
The sages said: "O Sūta, how did the sin of Brahmin-slaughter come to pass for the high-souled Lord of the Gods? At what time did it occur? Tell us everything in detail."
What mountain is this Red Peak (Raktaśṛṅga), which was compressed there by him? Of which lord of Śacī does he cause fear among human beings? (33)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, in ancient times Tvaṣṭṛ married the daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, named Ramā, who was endowed with excellent beauty and virtues.
Then a very long time passed for her without a son; consequently, filled with world-weariness, she devoted herself to asceticism for the sake of obtaining a son.
Meditating upon Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods and God of gods, she was endowed with perfect faith through offerings of oblations and worship. (36)
Restrained in her diet and fixed in her observances, she was devoted to ritual bathing and the chanting of prayers; she bestowed various kinds of gifts upon the foremost of the twice-born.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara was pleased with her and said, "I am a granter of boons; choose whatever you desire."
She chose [this boon]: "O Blessed One, by your grace let my son be a hero, invincible by weapons, and one who assumes the forms of both Brahmins and Dānavas. (39)
He was perfected in the study of the Vedas, intent upon the performance of sacrificial rites, and renowned for his splendor and fame among all embodied beings. (40)
The Blessed One said: "There will be no doubt; you shall have a son who is powerful and wise, invulnerable to all weapons, and endowed with great splendor. (41)

A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, a hero, and one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches—he will perform all the rites prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas in their entirety. Moreover, he shall be invincible in battle even by all the gods and demons combined.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished from that place; she too conceived a child from Viśvakarman during her season.
Then, in the tenth month, she gave birth to a beautiful son who resembled twelve suns and was endowed with all auspicious marks.
On the twelfth day after his birth, his father gave him the well-known name Vṛtra, having honored the best of the twice-born.
Then that boy grew like the lord of stars in the bright fortnight, bringing joy to his father and mother and being cherished by his circle of kinsmen.
Then, at the proper time, the twice-born Śukra himself approached the Dānava and bestowed upon him the vow appropriate for Brahmins.
And Vṛtra, who was devoted to his teacher, remained established in the vow of a religious student (brahmacārin) and studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas).
Then, having attained youth, he conquered all the rulers of the earth without exception, brought the world under his control, and immediately thereafter, the netherworld (pātāla) as well.
Then, desiring to conquer Indra, he approached the abode of the gods and turned the deities, headed by the thousand-eyed one, away from the battle.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the wielder of the thunderbolt engaged in eighteen battles with him, yet he did not achieve victory even in a single one.
Then, together with the surviving gods whose limbs were all wounded and mangled, he fled in terror to the world of Brahmā at the time of the day's dissolution.
Vṛtra, having occupied the station of Śakra, enjoyed the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, with every thorn [of opposition] destroyed.
The one of great strength made the Dānavas, who were arrogant in their power, partakers of sacrificial portions in all the divine stations as they had been described.
O best of the twice-born, even when he had thus obtained sovereignty over the three worlds, no contentment arose in him due to his longing for the world of Brahmā.
Then, having summoned Śukra, he spoke these sweet words, bowing low with humility along with his four ministers.
Vṛtra said: O best of those who uphold the lineage of the preceptor, Śakra has gone to the world of Brahmā out of fear; tell me truly, how may there be a way for me to go there as well? (57)
"By means of which I shall destroy Śakra, Viriñci, and likewise everyone else; having given the world of Brahmā to you, I myself shall enjoy the third heaven. (58)
Śukra said: "O best of Dānavas, no way exists for you there; therefore, you ought to find contentment with the sovereignty over the three worlds. (59)
Vṛtra said: "As long as Sutrāman remains, there is no happiness for me; therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall strive for the sake of removing this thorn [from my side]. (60)
O descendant of Bhṛgu, how did Śakra’s movement come to be there? O high-minded one, tell me: why will it not be mine today? (61)
Śukra said: O best of Dānavas, he previously performed penance in Naimiṣa for as long as a thousand years, while meditating upon Śaṅkara.
Indeed, by its power, his movement there has always been possible for him along with his servants and retinue; there is no other cause for this here.
Whoever else performs such penance in the Naimiṣa forest, his departure to the world of Brahmā occurs; of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: Having heard that, he went quickly to the supreme holy site of Naimiṣa and then performed intense penance while meditating upon Maheśvara.
For the sake of protecting the three worlds, he appointed the foremost of the Danavas, who were endowed with great strength and possessed prowess exceeding that of Śakra.
During the rainy season he stayed in the open air; in the winter he took refuge in water; and in the summer, while practicing the penance of the five fires, he remained without food.
Thus, as he remained established in his vow, hundreds of years passed; thereupon, the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, became afraid.
And they constantly muttered mantras solely for his destruction; yet, though they watched for vulnerabilities, they saw none, remaining in their distress. (69)
Then Viṣṇu himself, having reflected for a long time in his mind and having discerned the means for the slaying of Vṛtra, spoke, filled with joy.
Viṣṇu said: "O Śakra, the means for his slaughter has now certainly been known by me; having heard that, act quickly, for there is no other way."
"He has been rendered invulnerable to all weapons by the wielder of the trident; therefore, devise a thunderbolt made of bone for the purpose of slaying him."
Indra said: "O Lord, from the bones of which living being shall the thunderbolt be made? Is it that of an elephant, a śarabha, or something else? Tell me. (73)
Viṣṇu said: "O Lord of the Gods, it should be one hundred cubits in measure and hexagonal; it should be slender in the middle, thick at the two sides, and fierce in appearance. (74)
Indra said: "O Lord of the Gods, no such being is seen even in the three worlds whose bones might be fashioned into a thunderbolt of such a form."
Viṣṇu said: There is a brahmin named Dadhīci who is established in supreme austerity; he is twice as tall as usual and has made his hermitage on the Sarasvatī.
Go to him and request it quickly; he will give you his own bones. For there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given by him when he is entreated.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Śakra went together with the gods to his hermitage at Puṣkara on the banks of the Prācī Sarasvatī.
Then, seeing the gods who had arrived at his own abode, Dadhīci, with a joyful heart, went quickly to meet them face-to-face. (79)
Having prostrated before the thousand-eyed Indra as well as the other [gods], that virtuous sage then performed worship for them with offerings of water for the feet and other honors.
Then, with a joyful heart, standing bowed in humility and prostrating himself again and again before the Thousand-eyed One, he spoke of his own accord.
Dadhīci said: "For what purpose have you gods come? Let your business be announced quickly. I am blessed that you, O slayer of Bala, have come to my house."
Śakra said: "O best of Brahmins, we have all been defeated by Vṛtra; for he cannot be slain by any weapons whatsoever, owing to the fulfillment of his boon. (83)
Hari declared that he would be slayable by a vajra produced from bone; however, there exists no living being of such a size as one measuring a hundred cubits.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, give us your own bones; by this means, the thunderbolt shall become the destroyer of him. (85)
O best of the twice-born, perform the task that destroys the affliction of the gods; otherwise, all the deities will utterly perish.
Sūta said: Having heard that, the venerable sage Dadhīci, his soul filled with joy, gave up his life for the sake of the welfare of those dwellers of heaven.
Then those gods, greatly rejoicing, took all the bones in their entirety and fashioned the great vajra exactly as Viṣṇu had described.
Then Śakra, taking that [weapon], set out toward Naimiṣa; filled with great fear, he was trembling at the onset of night. (89)
There, while Vṛtra remained absorbed in meditation, the Lord of the Thirty-three gods, standing at a distance and intent on flight, struck him with his thunderbolt.
That Vṛtra, the tiger among Dānavas, was likewise reduced to ashes by the blow of the thunderbolt, having encountered the fire like a moth.
Śakra, too, terrified by fear, went and took refuge upon a mountain situated in the midst of the ocean, which was very difficult to ascend and possessed lofty peaks. || 92 ||
He did not know that Vṛtra had been slain by that blow of the thunderbolt; he merely gazed along the path from which Vṛtra’s approach had originated.
In the meantime, the gods, their hair standing on end with joy upon seeing the thread destroyed, praised the lord of the thirty deities.
They did not realize that he had perished out of fear on that mountain in the ocean; after searching for a long time, they finally reached him there with great difficulty.
They beheld him seated in a rugged mountain cave, bereft of luster, miserable, and overwhelmed by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Filling the ten directions with the attachment to the foul odor of his body. || 97 ||
Then the four-faced one, seeing Śakra in such a state, spoke while standing at a distance from all the hosts of gods out of fear of sin: 98.
"O best of gods, this is Śakra, overwhelmed by the sin of Brahman-murder; therefore, he must be avoided from afar, lest you incur sin yourselves. (99)
"Behold all the marks of the slaughter of a Brahmin upon his limbs; they are visible on his body. Therefore, let us go to heaven. (100)

Seeing the gods, headed by his grandfather, who had arrived before him and were suddenly turning away with faces averted, the lord of the gods was filled with wonder. Then, agitated, he said: "O gods, what is this that you are departing? Having seen me, why do you not speak to me? Is all well at my home?"
I hope that Dānava has been slain by my thunderbolt; I hope that wicked-minded one does not seek me out for the sake of battle.
Brahmā said: "O Śakra, that sinful Dānava has been slain by you with that thunderbolt; he has fallen under the power of death. You need not feel any fear."
However, from his slaughter arose the highly censurable sin of killing a Brahmin; O Śakra, because of that, we do not today touch you, who have become untouchable. (105)
Indra said: "Many Dānavas were indeed previously slain by me; yet the sin of killing a Brahmin did not arise for me—how then has this killing occurred for me now? (106)
Brahmā said: "O Vāsava, those Dānavas were slain by you in battle according to the duty of a Kṣatriya; they were all pure, therefore no sin has been incurred."
O Śakra, this one, richly endowed with the sacred thread and especially established in austerity, was slain by you through deceit; therefore, you are possessed of sin.
Indra said: "O Four-faced One, I know my own body to be joined with sin, arising from the signs produced by the murder of a Brahmin; therefore, tell me how I may attain purification. (109)
"O Great-grandfather of all the gods, by this [act] may the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin depart quickly, so that I may become touchable to everyone. (110)
Brahmā said: O best of gods, you ought to undertake a pilgrimage for that purpose; without it, your sin will not be destroyed in its entirety. (111)
Sūta said: Then, at his word, Śakra became intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords; he wandered over the entire earth, performing ritual ablutions at each one individually.
In well-known sacred fords, at the confluences of rivers and streams, in Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Prabhāsa, and Kurujāṅgala; (113)
Likewise, among others, the thousand-eyed one, being free from sin, did not take birth; thereupon, having attained detachment, he reflected in his mind.
"I have bathed in all the sacred fords upon the surface of the earth, yet I am not liberated from sin; what shall I do now? (115)
"Shall I throw myself from the peak of a mountain, or shall I consume poison? Having been deprived of the sovereignty of the three worlds, I have no desire to live. (116)
Having thus attained detachment, Vāsava climbed a mountain and, having resolved upon death, was about to throw himself down. || 117 ||
At that moment, O best of the twice-born, a voice arose from the sky: "O Śakra, do not act rashly now that detachment has arisen in your mind."
"You must exercise sovereignty even now in heaven for eight yugas; therefore, O Śakra, listen with a concentrated mind for the sake of purification from that sin. (119)
"Act quickly upon my words; it must be cultivated and not otherwise, for you previously filled that cavity with dust. (120)
O Lord of the Gods, in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, where Lord Hara himself resides, there arose a serpent-hole from an anthill.
"Go by that path through which the Nāgas emerge and travel upon the surface of the earth; having gone to Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla and bathed in the Pātālagaṅgā, worship Maheśvara."
Then you will be liberated from sin, of this there is no doubt; and you shall once again obtain the kingdom of the gods, free from all thorns.
Sūta said: Then Śakra, having heard that voice arisen from the sky, went quickly to the place where that serpent-hole was located.
Then, having entered Pātāla drenched in the waters of the Gaṅgā, he worshipped that Liṅga known by the name Hāṭakeśvara.
Then, in that very instant, his body became free from impurity; the foul odor vanished, and his vital energy increased.
In the meantime, the gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, arrived and, being greatly delighted, spoke to that king of the gods who was now freed from sin.
"O Śakra, having attained purity and being liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, come then; let us go together to the abode of the thirty gods."
O Śakra, fill this nāga-cavern again with dust; otherwise, humans seeking the means to attain spiritual perfection will come here by this way. (129)
Having bathed in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī and worshipped this Liṅga, even those joined with sin shall go to the supreme goal.
Then all those thirty gods and that lord Śatakratu, having prostrated themselves once more, departed loudly for the abode of the thirty gods.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when Śakra had once again attained the status of Lord of the Devas, a great festival celebrating the slaying of Vṛtra took place there in heaven.
Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, this entire majesty arising from Hāṭakeśvara, which destroys all sins, has been narrated to you.
And whoever shall recite this with devotion, or listen to it with a concentrated mind, he goes to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
Sūta said: Then Śakra, having summoned the Saṃvartaka wind, spoke: "In the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara, there is indeed a great serpent-hole. || 1 ||
Go quickly at my command and fill it with dust, so that no one subject to the law of death may have access there. || 2 ||
Vāyu said: "When the cavity was previously filled by me at your command, a curse originating from the Liṅga was then bestowed upon me by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva)."
"Since this emblem of mine has indeed been covered with dust by you, therefore, O wind-bearer, you shall possess a nature identical to it."
Just as you will surely carry the entire fragrance born of camphor, so too, by my word, will you undoubtedly carry that which is produced from impurity.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, having understood this, show me favor; let someone else be remembered for this task, for I am afraid of the Enemy of Tripura.
Then the lord of the gods reflected upon filling that very serpent-hole, but he did not perceive anything at all [to do so].
Then the preceptor of the gods himself said to Śatakratu: "O Lord of the Thirty-three, why have you become so agitated regarding this task?"
There is here a preeminent mountain renowned by the name Himālaya; three sons were born to him, O Śakra, so listen to that from me.
Maināka is declared to be the first; the second is Nandivardhana; and the mountain celebrated as the third is Raktaśṛṅga.
O Śakra, that Maināka entered the depths of the ocean out of fear of you; even today, he remains stationed right there along with his two wings.
This second one is celebrated as Naṇdivardhana; the breach born from Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage was not entirely filled by him. (12)
By the command of Himācala and the holy sage Vasiṣṭha, he abandoned the land of the gods and went there with all haste.
"The third one, known here as Raktaśṛṅga, still remains even today; bring him, O Thousand-eyed One, and fill the serpent’s hole."
O Lord of the Thirty-three, this pit cannot be filled in any other way; except for that best of mountains, what I have spoken is the truth. (15)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the one worshiped by the gods, the lord of the thirty deities went quickly to that place where Himālaya was staying.
Then, having approached Himavat, the best of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, he spoke these words to him with conciliatory gentleness: || 17 ||
Indra said: "In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, there exists a great serpent-hole. By means of it, men may go to the god Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla."
O best of mountains, whoever shall worship [you], even those devoted to sin, will then engage in competition with me. (19)
Therefore, O Himālaya, send this son of yours, Raktaśṛṅga, there to the cave, by which that opening born of the serpent may be filled.
O Parvata, perform hospitality for me who have arrived at your home by offering your own son; thus you shall attain extraordinary fame.
Saying "So be it," Himālaya honored the god-like one and then spoke to his son Raktaśṛṅga.
"O son, for your sake the thousand-eyed Indra has come into my presence; therefore, go quickly to that place where the serpent-hole is located."
Having fulfilled that entirely for Śakra at my command, may you be happy together with him and the other foremost gods.
Raktaśṛṅga said: "I will not go there by any means, O mortal, to that land where the trees are thorny, harsh, and devoid of fruit. (25)
Neither the Siddhas nor the Gandharvas, neither the gods nor the Kinnaras; neither the delightful sacred fords nor the rivers of pure water [could provide such solace]. (26)
Likewise, those humans who engage in evil conduct, are devoid of virtue, and are always possessed of wicked minds—even if they have entered the animal realm—are all likewise [afflicted]. (27)
"Likewise, O best of mountains, both my wings have been cut off by that Śakra; therefore, we have no power whatsoever to go. (28)
Therefore, let the thousand-eyed one consider some supreme means for his sake, excluding me; this which I have spoken is the truth. (29)
Śakra said: "I myself shall lead you there, torn apart by my own hand; even there, most beautiful trees shall become your refuge. (30)
Likewise, meritorious sacred fords and temples of the deities, as well as the hermitages of sages, shall be situated all around you. (31)
O delight of the mountains, whatever power you possess while staying here shall become ten-millionfold for you while residing there at my word.
Likewise, those men there on earth, even if they are of sinful nature, shall suddenly become free from sin by the sight of you.
Therefore, O son of the mountain, go quickly there with me; otherwise, I shall shatter you into a thousand pieces with a blow from my thunderbolt.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Raktaśṛṅga, filled with fear, suddenly approached and entered that serpent-hole. || 35 ||

O best of Brahmins, he was submerged up to his very nose; at that time, he was accompanied by all his beautiful, lofty horns, which were covered with trees, shrubs, and creepers, and frequented by lovely birds. || 36 ||
Having thus established that mountain, the son of Himācala, Śakra, being delighted, spoke to him: "Accept a boon from me."
Raktaśṛṅga said: "O Lord of the Gods, this alone is the boon for us—that you are pleased. What shall I do with another boon? By your grace, I am happy. (38)
Indra said: "O son of the mountain, even in a dream my sight of you would not be in vain; how much less so when the sight has actually occurred, especially since the task has been accomplished? (39)
Raktaśṛṅga said: "O Lord of all the gods, if a boon must certainly be granted to me, O All-pervading One, may my entire wealth always be at the service of the twice-born."
Indra said: "There shall be a protector of the earth known as Camatkāra; for the sake of the brahmins, he will establish a city upon your head. (41)
There, O tiger among Brahmins, those who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches will, filled with great joy, enjoy your entire wealth without exception.
Likewise, O Son of the Mountain, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, I myself shall come to your most excellent peak.
"I shall worship the Lord of Gods, known as Hāṭakeśvara, together with all the hosts of gods, as well as the Kinnaras and Guhyakas. (44)
And on one day here, Hara himself, being pleased, will take up residence upon your peak together with us.
Therefore, your power shall be preeminent even throughout the three worlds. May it be well with you; I shall now depart for my abode in heaven.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed one (Indra) then departed for heaven; Raktashṛṅga also remained there, pervading that serpent-hole.
Upon it, there arose excellent holy fords (tīrthas) and sacred shrines (āyatanas), as well as the dwellings of sages and their hermitages (āśramas). || 48 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Filling of the Naga-Cavern," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sūta said: There was a king, the lord of Ānarta, known as Camatkāra. In the meantime, he arrived there in the forest to hunt deer. From a distance, he saw a doe beneath a tree with her limbs motionless, confidently and without fear, giving her breast to her fawn.
Then the king, greatly delighted, swiftly struck her in a vital spot with a straight-knotted arrow drawn back to his ear. || 3 ||
Suddenly struck by him with that feathered arrow fletched with vulture plumes, she, afflicted by pain, looked all around in every direction.
Then, seeing the protector of the earth, the wielder of the bow, not far away, she who was devoted to her son spoke with a face drenched in tears.
The doe said: "O protector of the earth, what you have done here is improper; I, whose fawn is still young, have been slain today by this smooth-jointed arrow. (6)
O protector of the earth, I do not grieve for my own death; rather, I grieve for this poor child who is so devoted to the taste of milk. (7)
"Since you have performed such a merciless deed, you shall therefore immediately become afflicted with the disease of leprosy."
The king said: "This is the inherent duty of kings: they cause the destruction of wild animals. Therefore, you ought not to curse me for being engaged in my own duty."
The female deer said: "O protector of the earth, what you have proclaimed is true; deer were created by the Self-existent One for the purpose of being slain by Kṣatriyas. (10)
But listen now with focused attention, O lord of the earth, as I tell you the ritual procedure that was performed by him.
By killing a deer while it is sleeping, engaged in mating, intent on the act of suckling, or absorbed in water, a man is defiled by sin.
For this reason, O King, this curse was pronounced upon you by me; it was neither out of desire nor from death—by truth I touch my own heart. (13)
Having spoken thus, the doe, overcome with agony, gave up her life; and that king, too, became afflicted with the disease of leprosy.
Having seen his own body afflicted with leprosy, the king, deeply distressed, summoned his servants and spoke to them. (15)
"I shall perform penance and worship Śaṅkara until the destruction of my leprosy disease occurs. (16)
Whatever happiness men desire in the three worlds, all that is to be accomplished through austerity; therefore, austerity must be practiced by me.
Now, wandering alone for one day at a time among each individual tree, I shall practice the mendicant's life upon the surface of the earth according to the prescribed rules.
His dwelling was a deserted house covered with dust, or a shelter at the foot of a tree, having abandoned all that is pleasant and unpleasant.
Being impartial toward enemies and friends, and regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, I shall pass my time until the final dissolution of time.
Having thus addressed those servants and dismissed them, that king, intent upon pilgrimage, wandered over the surface of the earth.
Then, after a long time, having received instruction from a Brahmin, the king reached the highly auspicious Śaṅkha-tīrtha.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, there is a place renowned throughout the three worlds for destroying all diseases, filled with clear water. (23)
There, by the mere act of bathing, that best of kings was instantly freed from the disease of leprosy and became possessed of great splendor.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, how was King Camatkāra liberated from leprosy? For how long did that monarch perform penance?
Who indeed were those brahmins shown to Śaṅkhatīrtha by whom [the remedy] was provided for the sake of curing the illness of that afflicted great-souled one? || 2 ||
What is Śaṅkhatīrtha, and in what location is it situated? What is its power? Tell me everything in full detail.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, I shall relate to you this captivating story concerning King Camatkāra, which removes all sins.
Deluded, that ascetic, restricted in diet and subsisting on food obtained as alms, wandered through all the sacred fords in their entirety, beginning with Prabhāsa.
Constantly inquiring after medicines from the foremost physicians and likewise seeking mantras from those who know them for the sake of destroying the disease, he did so again and again.
That tiger among kings did not obtain anything desired—neither a mantra nor a medicine, nor a sacred ford—by which there might be a destruction of his disease.
Thereupon, that best of kings attained supreme detachment; alone, with his mind and self restrained, he remained in that place adorned by all living beings.

He made his dwelling for a long time in that most meritorious field; subsisting on withered leaves and fruits, he always slept upon the ground at night, free from pride and egoism toward one tree or another.
Then, after a few days, while wandering about, that lord of the earth saw many excellent Brahmins engaged in a pilgrimage to sacred fords.

Then, having bowed down to those Brahmins seated upon the ground at the edge of Viśvāmitra’s hermitage, he spoke with humility. The King said: "O best of the twice-born, I am a king named Camatkāra, born of the Solar dynasty and the lord of Ānarta; I have been afflicted by leprosy."
Is there any means here, whether divine or human, whether it be medicine or a mantra, by which this leprosy may be pacified? (13)
O best of the twice-born, show compassion toward me and speak, for my body is seized by leprosy and I have fallen into the utmost distress.
Or else, if you know [the truth], I shall abandon my body here by entering fire, or even water, or by consuming poison. (15)
Having heard those words of his, all those best of the twice-born, filled with compassion, then spoke to that lord of the earth.
O tiger among kings, not far from this place there is a site renowned as Śaṅkhatīrtha, which brings about the destruction of all diseases. (17)
Those men who are seized by disease—those who are one-eyed, blind, or dull-witted; those with missing limbs or extra limbs; those who are misshapen or have deformed faces. || 18 ||
Those who bathe there at the beginning of the dark fortnight of Caitra and do not eat food likewise become free from disease immediately when the moon is situated in the constellation Citrā. || 19 ||
We have seen them hundreds of times, possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns, with forms like that of the god of love, and endowed with splendor and heroism. || 20 ||
The king said: "O best of Brahmins, how is Śaṅkhatīrtha to be known by me? And how did it originate? Tell me in detail. (21)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "Formerly, there was on the surface of the earth an excellent sage named Likhita, the son of the sage Śāṇḍilya, who was endowed with the power of asceticism. (22)
Then his younger brother was born, named Śaṅkha, a knower of the Dharmaśāstras; he always remained established in austerity, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits. || 23 ||
Then, after some time had passed, Śaṅkha, tormented by intense hunger, went to the hermitage of Likhita in search of sweet fruits.
Having reached the empty hermitage of the high-souled Likhita, he then took the fruits, thinking them to be his own.
He ate many ripe and sweet fruits; in the meantime, Likhita arrived accompanied by his disciples.
Seeing that Śaṅkha had taken the fruit, he spoke to him in anger: || 27 ||
"You have taken from me fruits that were not given; why do you, in the form of a thief, pay no heed to the consequences? (28)
Śaṅkha said: "O best of the twice-born, what you have proclaimed is true; the fruits were indeed taken by me here in your secluded hermitage. (29)
Therefore, inflict upon me the punishment appropriate for this act of theft, by which both this world and the next may bring me happiness. (30)
Then, seized by anger, he took Śaṅkha’s hand in his own and instantly cut it off, even though he was being restrained by the ascetics.
Although his hand was severed, Śaṅkha performed most rigorous penance, having returned once again specifically to his own hermitage.
Then, after some time, Mahādeva was pleased with him; appearing before him, he spoke to that lord of sages, Śaṅkha.
Maheśvara said: "O Sage, O being of great fortitude, you have performed a difficult feat; choose from me a boon that is desired by your heart."
Śaṅkha said: "O Lord, O God, if you are pleased with me and if you grant a boon, O Best of Gods, may my hands become as they were before once again. (35)
Likewise, O best of gods, let this sacred ford (tīrtha) bear my name as its mark; let it be renowned in all the worlds as the remover of all sins for human beings. (36)
Whether one has a missing limb or an extra limb, or is even afflicted by disease, if one performs a bath here, one quickly becomes renewed once more.
The Blessed One said: "O best of Brahmins, from this day forward, this sacred ford shall be renowned by your name; it shall be the destroyer of the sins of all embodied beings."

Whether one has deficient limbs or redundant limbs, whoever performs a bath here in the bright fortnight of Caitra while fasting, when the moon is situated in the constellation Citrā, shall become radiant with golden limbs; of this there is no doubt. (39)
O best of Brahmins, whether he possesses desire or is free from desire, by meditating upon her beautiful form, he shall go to the supreme abode whose nature is Śiva.
O Brahmin, when the Śrāddha is performed here on the fourteenth day while the moon is situated in Citrā, the ancestors shall attain supreme satisfaction. (41)
O tiger among brahmins, this very day, at the end of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the afternoon, the Lord of the Night (the Moon) will enter into conjunction with Citrā.
There, for one who has observed the fast and properly bathed, at that very moment his two hands shall become endowed with beautiful form, just as they were before.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished from that place; Śaṅkha, for his part, performed his ablutions there at the time of Kutapa.
And then, at that very moment, his two hands became as they were before—beautiful, resembling red lotuses, and marked with the sign of a fish.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O best of kings, thus was that auspicious holy place (tīrtha) produced upon the surface of the earth through the power of the God of gods, whose mark is the moon. (46)
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should perform a bath there on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, when the moon is situated in the constellation Citrā.
"You shall become free from all diseases, of this there is no doubt; we shall reveal ourselves to you when the time arrives as foretold. (48)
Sūta said: Then, after a few days had passed, on the first day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, when the lord of the night was situated in the constellation Citrā, the fourteenth lunar day arrived.
Then those Brahmins, desiring his welfare, took the king with them and immediately departed toward Śaṅkhatīrtha.
Then, having meditated in his mind upon the complete destruction of the disease of leprosy, he performed his bath according to the prescribed rule, endowed with supreme faith.
Then, freed from leprosy and possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns, he emerged from that water filled with great joy.
Then, having bowed down to all those Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
"O best of Brahmins, it is indeed through your grace that I have been freed from the disease of leprosy, which for a long time has made me an object of contempt among embodied beings. (54)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, I shall not exercise sovereignty; instead, I shall now perform great penance eternally at this very sacred ford.
"O best of the twice-born, let them take this kingdom, this country, the elephants, horses, and so forth—whatever else belongs to me. (56)
Out of great compassion, for the sake of showing grace to me alone—to me who am wretched, endowed with devotion, and especially detached—[please speak].
The Brahmins said: "O best of kings, we are not capable of protecting the kingdom. Therefore, what is the use of accepting it, if by doing so there would be the ruin of the realm? (58)
O best of kings, in former times the earth was given to us by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, after he had cleared it of the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times. (59)
She was seized from us once more by even more powerful Kṣatriyas, who repeatedly treated all the twice-born with contempt as if it were a mere sport.
The king said: "O best of Brahmins, I shall provide protection for you; even though I am engaged in asceticism, you should not entertain any fear whatsoever regarding this matter."
The Brāhmaṇas said: "If you certainly possess faith born of the desire to give, then build and bestow this excellent city even upon this most meritorious field. (62)

For all these eminent Brāhmaṇas, let there be a place provided with walls and moats where we may dwell in comfort after bathing in various sacred fords (tīrthas), all of us following the duties of householders and always devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Sūta said: Having heard that, the protector of the earth, saying "So be it," was filled with great joy and established a most magnificent city in that place.
It was surrounded on all sides by a very high wall and a moat, measuring exactly one *krośa* in both length and breadth, and was truly enchanting.
It was purified at its triple junctions and crossroads, adorned on all sides with banners, and surrounded by lofty, beautiful palaces covered entirely in white plaster.
It was filled with many lands endowed with intoxicated elephants, and with those such as Satyakāma who were praised by the world of the virtuous.
Then that lord of the earth, having filled all his houses with gold, jewels, pearls, and other such articles, [bestowed them].
Endowed with faith, he [should give] especially to Brahmins of noble birth who are knowers of the Vedas, and to those who are learned in the scriptures and self-restrained. (69)
Then, O best of the twice-born, having washed their feet according to seniority and excellence, he offered them [water] according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of the City to the Brāhmaṇas by King Camatkāra," within the "Description of the Origin and Greatness of Śaṅkha-tīrtha" in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 11 ||
Sūta said: Thus that protector of the earth, having constructed a city comparable to the city of Purandara, bestowed it upon the Brāhmaṇas according to his capacity. || 1 ||
It shone with excellent houses variegated with pearls, coral, lapis lazuli, gems, and gold, like the sky with its clusters of stars.
It was surrounded on all sides by divine palaces made of crystal, resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa and adorned with banners.
It was exceedingly beautiful, adorned with thousands of archways that were made of gold, exquisitely variegated, lofty, stainless, and auspicious.

Surrounded on all sides by oblong ponds beautified with jeweled stairways, and provided with gardens, wells, water-lifting machines, and every other requisite, he offered it to the foremost of Brahmins and felt his purpose fulfilled.
Standing constantly at Śaṅkhatīrtha, he then summoned his sons, grandsons, and servants, and spoke these words.
Having constructed this city, I have offered it to the Brahmins; by my command, it must be protected by you with great effort.

"So that all the Brāhmaṇas may be happy and joyful in mind, you must all, with concentrated attention, provide them protection. And whatever king, endowed with devotion, shall protect them—even if he be another—he too shall attain supreme splendor upon the earth. (9)
Through the protection of the Brahmins, he will become invincible to all enemies, majestic, and endowed with prosperity; of this there is no doubt.
"Rich with sons, grandsons, and good servants, long-lived and free from disease, he shall become so through the grace of the Brahmins and by my word. (11)
Furthermore, he who is possessed by hatred and shall bring about distress for these tigers among Brahmins will go to hell.
Likewise, having encountered sufferings and witnessed numerous defeats, he was afflicted by disease and censured due to the separation from beloved kinsmen. (13)

Having encountered the extinction of his lineage, he will go to the abode of Yama; therefore, this city must be protected with every effort, especially at my word, by those who desire their own welfare.
Having thus spoken to them all, that king remained established in austerity; they too did exactly as they were instructed by him.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by King Camatkāra to His Sons and Others for the Purpose of Establishing a City," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having thus entrusted the kingdom to his sons and having personally bestowed that city upon the twice-born, that lord of the earth—
Then, having established a hermitage there, he propitiated Maheśvara, the God of gods, endowed with supreme faith.
That king lived for a hundred years subsisting on fruits, and thereafter, for an equal period of time, he remained composed, feeding upon withered leaves.
After that, he subsisted on water for a hundred years; thereafter, he became one who subsists on air for another hundred years.
Then, when the fourth hundred years had passed while he subsisted on air alone, Mahādeva was pleased and appeared before him for a vision.
He said, "I am well-pleased; ask of me whatever you desire. I shall grant it to you, even if it be difficult for even the gods to attain."
The King said: This most meritorious sacred field, which is the refuge of various holy sites, removes all sins through the greatness of Hāṭakeśvara.
Therefore, by your dwelling here, let this place become even more supremely pure; O Lord, if you are pleased, grant me this which I desire.
O Śarva, Lord of the Immortals, having fashioned this foremost city with a mind purified by faith, I have offered it to the Brāhmaṇas.
By my command, you must always reside there with unwavering constancy, so that it may be endowed with all its divine attributes.
The Blessed One said: "O protector of the earth, I shall remain immovable in this place of yours; I shall become renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Acaleśvara. (11)
Whatever mortal shall behold me while I am stationed here with devotion, his prosperity shall remain forever unshakable.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, whatever man, endowed with supreme faith, performs the *ghṛtakaṃbala* rite for my Liṅga; || 13 ||
Whatever sin has been committed in childhood, in old age, or even in youth, that shall go to destruction for him, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, install my linga right here, so that I may dwell there forever, immovable. (15)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods vanished from sight; and that king also quickly constructed a most beautiful palace.
There, endowed with supreme faith, he installed a linga of the trident-bearing God, characterized by all auspicious marks.
Upon seeing, touching, meditating upon, or even worshipping it, a person is liberated from all sins committed from birth until the end of death.
Then the king reflected: "Will Maheśvara, becoming motionless, establish his presence right here in this very liṅga?"
In the meantime, a voice arose, moving through the sky, gladdening the protector of the earth, Camatkāra, with its beautiful resonance.
O tiger among kings, do not worry about your duties; I shall always make my residence right here at this liṅga forever.
Likewise, O King, I shall tell you another word for the sake of conviction; having heard it, attain peace and observe it with diligence. (22)
"May my shadow always remain fixed upon this linga; let it be situated only behind it, and never positioned in any other direction. (23)
Sūta said: Then he beheld that shadow originating from the Liṅga; it was of the same form as him, eternally motionless, even while the sun remained in that direction.
Then, having attained supreme joy and prostrating himself upon the ground, that best of kings considered himself as one who had accomplished his life's purpose.
O best of Brahmins, even today the shadow of that linga is always seen in such a form that it causes great wonder.
O twice-born ones, he whose death shall occur within six months on this earth does not see that shadow; this is another supreme proof.
Sūta said: Thus the Blessed One remains forever established there, in the form of Acaleśvara, near the city of Camatkārapura.
Because of his immobility, the Lord of Gods resides there as the central one among the sixty-eight sacred fields; by his command, Maheśvara dwells therein.
Therefore, that sacred field is proclaimed here as purifying for all; it becomes the bestower of desires and the bestower of liberation for all embodied beings. (30)
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, I shall fully relate another account that occurred, born of his power; let it be heard.
Due to the greatness of Acaleśvara, all men in that sacred field quickly obtain every fruit they desire in their minds. (32)

Some desire heaven, others liberation, as well as wealth, grain, and sons; whatever desire a mortal contemplates while worshipping Acaleśvara, he obtains that very thing quickly and with little effort.
Then, having seen this, the thousand-eyed Indra [declared]: "All sinful men on earth go to heaven and likewise attain liberation in his very presence. (34)
Then [he abandoned] anger, desire, greed, hatred, fear, attachment, delusion, vice, difficulty, envy, and passion. (35)
Then, O best of the twice-born, the thousand-eyed one himself respectfully summoned all the embodied beings and spoke to them in private.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever on the surface of the earth goes toward Camatkārapura, he must be restrained by you. (37)
Even while residing right there, whoever should go to Acaleśvara, he must be especially restrained by all of you with great effort at my command.
Having promised "So be it," they departed; then, by the command of Śakra, they completely eradicated that [tree's] majesty which had spread upon the earth.
All this narrative, which destroys sins, concerning the god Acaleśvara who dwells in that sacred field, has been recounted to you.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Acaleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Hāṭakeśvara Region" of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim another marvel that occurred there—a secret held within my heart. (1)
In the city of Camatkārapura, there was a certain man born of the Vaiśya caste who was mute and afflicted by poverty.
He who, out of the distress of all people, provides protection for their cattle, and for the sake of maintaining his family, remains content with whatever he obtains; (3)
Once, while he was guarding those cattle in the forest lands, one animal strayed from its herd out of greed for grass.
O best of the twice-born, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra, he was not noticed by him as he was passing by at will.
Then, just as that mute cowherd reached home, the owner of the cow arrived, scolding him.

"Why has that one animal not arrived today as it usually does? Surely he has been killed by you, or sold, or perhaps hidden away. Therefore, bring me the cow quickly; even though I am fasting, I am in haste. (7)
Hearing that, the mute cowherd, terrified with fear, emerged from his house taking his staff, even though he had been fasting.
Then, having reached the forest, he surveyed it on all sides with a keen eye, looking at the difficult terrains and the dense woods.
Then, while wandering through the forest, he clearly saw the footprints of that beast in one place and came to recognize them entirely.
Thereupon, O best of the twice-born, seeking that place, he went from forest to forest all around this city of Camatkārapura.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the circumambulation of that place was performed out of a desire to see the sacrificial animal, both at the site itself and at the place where the animal was tied.
And at the conclusion of the circumambulation, he indeed found that animal; then, having led it home at the end of the night, he presented it to his master.
O gods, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the most meritorious month of Caitra, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) come from every direction to this most meritorious field.
Thus, out of ignorance, that circumambulation was performed by those two—the cowherd and the cow—on that most meritorious day.
Of one who is fasting and mute, and likewise of a beast that is eating. || 16 ||

O best of the foremost twice-born, due to eating without having bathed by chance, after some time had passed, both of them met their death through the exhaustion of their respective lifespans. || 17 ||
And then, by the power of that [merit], the son of the lord of Daśārṇa became a cowherd, remembering his previous birth. (18)
O best of the twice-born, that minister of his was also born as a beast; however, like the king, he remembered his former birth and was always highly esteemed by the monarch.
Then that lord of kings, having arrived together with that very minister on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, performed a circumambulation before her.
At the end of the year, O best of the twice-born, he, endowed with supreme faith, remained without food, observing silence, and traveling on foot.
Once, sages of celebrated vows arrived there at the holy, sin-destroying tirtha originating from Viśvāmitra.
Yājñavalkya, Bharadvāja, Śunaḥśepa, Gālava, Devala, Bhāguri, Dhaumya, Kaśyapa, Cyavana, and Bhṛgu. || 23 ||
Likewise, others of celebrated soul, devoted to the life of celibate studentship, arrived at that sacred field on the occasion of a pilgrimage.
Seeing them, that protector of the earth prostrated with palms joined in reverence and worshipped them with devotion according to their seniority and excellence. || 25 ||
Then that lord of the earth sat down in their midst; that king was like a Tathāgata and was greeted with acclaim by them all.
Then, O lord of the earth, those sages held divine conversations before the king concerning the deeds of the great-souled leaders among sages.
The best of the twice-born, born from the treatises on dharma of the ancient royal sages, produced joy for that royal sage.
Then, at the conclusion of a certain conversation, that king was questioned by those great sages, who were filled with curiosity, after he had offered them blessings prescribed by the Vedas.
The sages said: "O protector of the earth, year after year you come here with effort and, together with your minister, perform the circumambulation of this city. (30)
O best of kings, in this field there are excellent holy places (tīrthas), as well as other famous temples of the deities.
"O King, we do not perceive even the slightest regard for them at any time; this curiosity has arisen in us, so tell us if it is not a secret. (32)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, the king stood bowed down with humility; filled with a touch of shame, he spoke these words. (33)
O best of the twice-born, that which I have been asked by you just now is a secret that has not been revealed by me to anyone on the surface of the earth.
Nevertheless, that which must be done by you is indeed the truth; even if it be most secret, listen, O best of sages. (35)
Sūta said: Thereupon, O best of Brahmins, he related to those lords of sages the account arising from his previous birth.
Just as his lost animal was recovered, and just as the circumambulation of Camatkārapura was accomplished. (37)
Just as the recollection of past births arose through its power, so too did the attainment of a kingdom, prosperity, and the fulfillment of every desire at every step.
Having heard that, all the sages were delighted with the lord of the earth; having bestowed many blessings, they exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (39).
Then, having risen, they all performed a circumambulation of her from the front with supreme faith, according to the prescribed rite. (40)
And by its power, they attained the supreme perfection that is so difficult to obtain even through the recitation of mantras, sacrifices, gifts, and the service of sacred fords.
That king and that minister were both born as gods dwelling in celestial chariots; even today, they are indeed seen in the form of stars in the vault of the sky.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Circumambulation of Camatkārapura," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 14 ||
Fifteenth Chapter. Nārada said: Then the divine Nārāyaṇa, wearing matted hair and bark garments, arrived with a second attendant who carried fruits in his hand.
Seeing them, that fawn-eyed messenger of love lamented; hearing her words, both of them spoke to her.
"Do not fear, O auspicious lady; we two have come to protect you. How have you entered this terrible forest inhabited by the wicked? (3)
Having thus consoled that slender lady, Mādhava said to the Rākṣasa: "O man of base conduct, release this soft-limbed woman of lovely smiles."
O fool of wicked conduct, what have you resolved to do? You are intent on making yourself food for the eyes of the entire world. (5)
O Bhava, by the power of your merit, destroy this ornament of the earth; today let the world be without light and let Kandarpa be stripped of his pride.
"Now, having killed Vṛndārikā in the forest, you shall do so; therefore, release her immediately, for she is a deity of the pleasure-palace."
Having heard these words of Hari, the Rākṣasa, filled with rage, said: "If you are indeed capable, then release him this very day from my hand!"
As soon as these words were spoken by Mādhava, he was glared at with anger and fell down, reduced to ashes, far away from Vṛndā.
