Then, bewildered by the illusory power of the Lord of the Universe, she said: "Who are you, O ocean of compassion, by whom I have been protected here? (10)
O storehouse of austerities, physical and mental suffering along with its torment has been removed by you from that destroyer of Rākṣasas through your sweet speech.
O gentle one, rich in asceticism, I shall perform penance in your hermitage.
The ascetic said: "I am the son of Bharadvāja, known by the name Devaśarman; having abandoned all enjoyments, I have come to this formidable forest. (13)
"With this young brahmin, my disciple, we can go wherever we desire; indeed, I have many other disciples as well who can assume any form at will. (14)
"If you, O auspicious lady, desire to perform penance while staying in my hermitage, come, O Queen; let us go to another forest situated far away."
Having spoken thus to that queen, O lord of men, Hari departed toward the eastern direction with a slow gait through the forest abounding in ghosts and piśācas.
Vṛndārikā, her eyes filled with tears, followed behind him; and Smaradūtī also followed at his back, saying, "Wait for me! (17)
In the meantime, a certain man of wicked conduct and sinful appearance spread a net in the forest; when it was filled with living creatures, [he approached].
Then that leader of sinners contracted that net; having gathered the living beings within the net, he released them.
Seeing the two women, that hunter spoke to Smaradūtī: "O Queen, he is coming to devour me; let my friend seize me by the hand."
Having heard what she said, Vṛndā looked at him with his distorted face; upon seeing him, the beloved of the Ocean-born Goddess was shaken by a gust of fear.
She fled, distressed and pale, together with the messenger of Smara into the forest; running along with her friend, she arrived at the hermitage of an ascetic.
In that forest of ascetics, she beheld an exceedingly wonderful sight: birds with golden bodies, filled with various sounds.
She beheld a pond with golden ground, rich with golden lotuses; rivers flowed with milk, and trees dripped honey.
There were heaps of sugar and piles of sweetmeats, many kinds of delicious foods, and numerous ornaments.
Many divine weapons fell from the sky; the gratified monkeys played, leaping up and falling down.
Then Sundarī Vṛndā beheld that ascetic Maṭha, seated upon a tiger-skin seat, illuminating the three worlds.
He said to him, "O Lord, protect me, protect me from this increase of sin! What is the use of austerity, dharma, silence, or the recitation of prayers? (28)
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, there is no merit greater than the protection of the frightened. Having spoken thus, she, trembling and with limbs languid, addressed the ascetic. (29)
Just then, that wicked-souled one, the binder of all living beings, arrived; terrified by Vṛndādevī, she clung to the neck of Hari.
Embraced by your two arms with a pleasant touch, she will become once again as if she were a creeper of sorrow through the power of your embrace. (31)
"The head of your husband is endowed with all limbs and superior in virtues; therefore, O lady, go now to the picture-gallery for the sake of your husband. (32)
Thus addressed by the sage, she then entered the picture gallery; having taken her beloved’s head, she ascended a divine couch.
O King, as she, with eyes closed in intense longing, drank from his lower lip, his form instantly assumed the appearance of Jālandhara.
At that time, the Lord of the World became identical to his beloved: possessing a form like his, a chest like his, an elevation like his, his very speech, and his very state of mind. (35)
Then, seeing her beloved with his body fully restored, she said: "O Lord, I shall do what is pleasing to you; tell me your desire and my name. (36)
Having heard Vṛndā’s words, the one born from the ocean of Māyā said: "Listen, O Goddess, to how the battle took place between Śambhu and me. (37)
"O beloved, my head was severed by the fierce Rudra with his discus; yet, through the power of your spiritual attainment and because my soul was absorbed in you, [I did not perish]."
That severed [limb] has been brought here along with his life; O dear one, O young girl, you have become sorrowful through separation from me. (39)
"You must forgive my unpleasantness, that I abandoned you and went to the battlefield"—with such words as these, Vṛndā was then reminded by him.
With betel leaves, diversions, and auspicious garments and ornaments, the goddess Vṛndārikā was then endowed with every enjoyment.
Embracing her beloved tightly, she, longing for amorous delight, kissed him; for the bliss arising from the enchantment of Vṛndā is greater even than liberation.
The divine Nārāyaṇa considered Vṛndā to be superior even to the essence of Lakṣmī’s love, as she dispels the sorrow born of separation from Mādhava.
In that royal swan who sported gracefully in the ponds, Kṛṣṇa—due to the influence of her form—lost all desire for Lakṣmī.
In that Vṛndāvana, she appeared in the form of Tulasī; most purifying, she manifested upon the earth from the sweat of Vṛndā’s body. 45.
Having experienced this bliss born from union with Vṛndā’s body, Hari, the Lord of the universe, considered those few days to be the fulfillment of his auspicious purpose.
Once, at the conclusion of their amorous play, Vṛndā beheld the ascetic Puruṣottama, with his two arms, closely embracing her neck.
Seeing him, she released her arm-enclosure from her neck and said: "How have you come here in the form of an ascetic to delude me? (48)
Having heard her words, Hari spoke to her consolingly: "Listen, O Vṛndārikā; know me to be the one who captivates Lakṣmī. (49)
"Your husband has gone to conquer Hara and bring back Gaurī; I am Śiva, and Śiva is I—we do not exist as separate entities. (50)
"Jālandhara has been slain in battle; now, O sinless one, accept me. Nārada said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Vṛndārikā became dejected in countenance; then, O King, she replied in anger.
By him you were bound in battle yet released alive at his father’s word; though you were honored with various jewels, his daughter-in-law was carried off by you.
How can he who is constantly devoted to the wives of others be the lord of dharma? The wise say that even a sovereign must experience the fruits of his own actions.
Just as I was led away by you, a wretched sorcerer, through delusion and magic, so too will some other wretched sorcerer lead away your wife through delusion and magic. (54)
Having been cursed thus, Viṣṇu vanished from sight in an instant; so too did that bedchamber, the couch, and those monkeys.
When Hari had departed for the forest and everything was lost, Vṛndā, seeing the place empty, approached her friend and spoke of the deceitful act committed by Viṣṇu.
"The city has been abandoned, the kingdom lost, and my beloved has fallen into uncertainty; having realized this while in the forest, where shall I go, ordained as I am by fate? (57)
"Beholding my beloved has become the object of my desires," the deeply distressed Queen Vṛndā said, sighing hotly. (58)
"Death has indeed come for me through you, O messenger of Love! When she was addressed thus by her, she replied, "You are the very form of my life. (59)
Having heard what was thus spoken by her, Vṛndā then resolved upon her course of action in the forest; she went there to a great lake.
Having abandoned his suffering, he washed his body with water; then, having bound himself in the lotus posture on the bank and made his mind free from sense-objects, he remained there.
She withered her own body, which had been defiled by association with Viṣṇu, and performed most severe penance without food together with her friend.
Then, a host of Apsarases, having come from the world of the Gandharvas to Vṛndā, said: "Go, O auspicious lady; do not abandon heaven for the sake of this body."

This is the Gandharva weapon, by which the Lord of Śrī attained supreme satisfaction during his conquest of the three worlds; why do you abandon this body here in Vṛnda, which has achieved its desire? Know that your beloved has been struck by the foremost arrow of the wielder of the trident; you are the ornament of heaven, the attainment of merit—O Caṇḍibhadrā, go quickly today and enjoy the forest of the immortals.

Having heard the teaching for women, the beloved of the ocean’s son spoke with a smile: “O daughter of the Lord of the Thirty-three, having been brought from heaven by my most heroic husband, I was first made a vessel of joys; yet, separated from that conqueror of the immortals, I am now bereft of him. Therefore, in this Kali age, may I attain my beloved who has gone to the nectar of immortality, and by whatever means that may be.”
Having spoken thus, Vṛndā, along with her companions, dismissed the hosts of Apsarases; bound by the noose of her affection, they constantly come and go.
Then, having burned away the qualities (guṇas) with the fire of knowledge through the practice of yoga, and having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, Vṛndā attained that which is beyond.
Seeing Vṛndārikā there, the great hosts of Apsaras praised her from the sky in delight and showered her with rains of flowers.
Having prepared a pile of dry wood and placed Vṛndā’s body upon it, Smaradūtī lit the fire and entered it.
Having burned that orb consisting of the globules of the dust from Vṛndā’s limbs and having made it into a mass of ashes, they cast the remainder into the Mandākinī.
There, where Vṛndā abandoned her body and ascended the path of Brahman, that place became Vṛndāvana near Govardhana.

Then the goddesses, having ascended to heaven, spoke of the excellence of the character of the wives of the Lord of the Thirty-three; hearing this from the goddesses, all the immortals and others were delighted in mind. Casting aside their intense fear of the enemy Daitya, they beat their formidable drums. Hearing that, the multitude of attendants seated upon their thrones attained the splendor of auspiciousness.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the State of Brahmā by Vṛndā," in the Jālandhara-episode of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. || 15 ||
Sūta said: Therefore, with every effort and having abandoned all other activities, the proximity of Raktaśṛṅga should be resorted to by the wise. || 1 ||
Of what use are gifts, of what use are ritual performances, of what use are sacrifices, or even vows? One should devotedly serve that sacred field originating from Hāṭakeśvara.
All sacrifices, such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, even when accompanied by complete sacrificial fees, do not equal even a sixteenth part of that sacred field.
Cāndrāyaṇas, Kṛcchras, and Sāntapana penances do not equal even a sixteenth part of that sacred field.
Holy places such as Prabhāsa and rivers such as the Gaṅgā are not worth even a sixteenth part compared to that sacred field.
All gifts of land and all virtues, such as compassion and the like, do not equal even a sixteenth part of that sacred field.
There, in former times, many royal sages attained perfection; as did beasts, birds, serpents, lions, tigers, deer, and other creatures. (7)
There, by the power of time, even those who had perished reached the abode of the gods; this was true even for one there who was devoid of vows or devoted to the work of agriculture.
O Brahmins, one who makes his dwelling there shall go to heaven after death; O best of the twice-born, what is the use of speaking further at length? (9)
Listen to the supreme secret regarding the origin of that sacred field: sacred fields and pilgrimage sites purify human beings here through dwelling and other such means. (10)
The sacred field born of Hāṭakeśvara purifies even by mere remembrance; how much more so, O Brahmins, through sight and especially through touch?

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Excellence of the Fruit of Serving the Presence of Raktaśṛṅga," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: O high-minded one, we have heard from you the origin of Camatkārapura; now proclaim to us the extent of that sacred field (*kṣetra*). Furthermore, proclaim all the meritorious holy sites (*tīrtha*) and shrines (*āyatana*) located there, together with their respective powers.
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, the excellent city of Camatkārapura is a sacred field measuring five krośas in both length and breadth.
To its east is Gayāśīrṣa, to its west the foot of Hari; and to the south and north are those known as Gokarṇeśvara.
O best of the twice-born, that sacred field was formerly known by the name Hāṭakeśvara; it is renowned in the world as the destroyer of all sins.
From the time that place was given by that great-souled Camatkāra to the Brahmins, it consequently attained fame by his name.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O son of a Sūta, tell us in detail that greatness of Gayāśiras which was previously mentioned by you."
Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a lord of the Haihayas named Vidūratha, who was indeed a master of liberality, skillful, and the bringer of destruction to the side of his enemies.
Once, that king, surrounded by his army, went forth to hunt deer into a forest thick with various trees and creepers and teeming with beasts of prey.
There he struck down deer with arrows resembling venomous serpents, as well as buffaloes, boars, hyenas, śambara deer, and ruru deer.
He [encountered] lions, tigers, and rutting elephants by the hundreds and thousands; then, that deer was pierced by him with a straight-knotted arrow.

The arrow, along with its shaft, did not fall upon the surface of the earth but sped away swiftly; then, filled with curiosity, he urged that excellent horse upon its back with great speed, possessing the velocity of the mind and the wind.
Then, leaving his army behind and desiring to catch the deer, the lord of the earth reached another forest region that was fierce and inspiring of fear in the heart.
It abounded with thorny jujube trees, was crowded with groves of silk-cotton trees, and was likewise filled with other harsh trees bristling with thorns.
There, the entire ground was parched, waterless, and enveloped in darkness; it abounded with crows, owls, and vultures, and was devoid of the shade of tree tops. (15)
When the sun had reached the meridian in summer, that king, drawn by the deer, traveled a long distance with a spear in hand and mounted upon an excellent horse.
Consequently, all his followers and servants, their mounts utterly exhausted, distressed by hunger and thirst, and weary, took refuge in various places along the way.
Likewise, others fall down and lose consciousness, being devoured by lions, tigers, and other beasts; while yet others, though still conscious, are unable even to move.
Then that king also, distressed by hunger and thirst, saw that calamity which had befallen himself along with his servants. (19)
Seeking the end of the wilderness, he urged on that horse—a noble steed endowed with every excellence—striking it with lashes of the whip.
Then that king was carried far along a difficult path devoid of all living beings by that horse with the speed of the wind.
Thus, while that king remained undecided and fleeing in all directions, the horse fell upon the surface of the earth, and he too [fell] down from the horse.
Sūta said: Then that king, overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, went deep into the forest on foot and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then, from his position in the sky, he beheld three most dreadful ghosts, with hair standing erect, blood-red eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies.
Seeing them, that king was especially terrified with fear; despairing of his life, he spoke these words with great difficulty: || 3 ||
"Who are you, possessed of such deformed appearances, whom I have never seen before? Such terrifying beings as these have never been encountered by me while wandering here in the world of men."
"I am King Vidūratha, severely afflicted by hunger and thirst; desiring deer, I have arrived here in this forest devoid of living beings. (5)
Then, among them, the eldest, Māṃsāda, having joined his palms in reverence and standing bowed with humility, replied to him.
"O Great King, we are pretas dwelling here in this forest; we are enveloped by great suffering due to the faults produced by our own past actions. (7)
I am named Māṃsādaka; this second one is Vidaivata; and the third is Kṛtaghna—among these three, he is the evildoer.
The king said: "For all living beings, a name arises from their father and mother. What is the cause by which you are all named after yourselves?"
Having heard that, the meat-eater said, "O King, these names of actions were indeed created by us ourselves in private for the sake of mutual designation. (10)
Listen attentively, O protector of the earth, to how the state of being a preta arose for each one of us individually through our respective actions.
"O King, we are indeed Brāhmaṇas by birth; we were born in the city named Vaidiśā in the house of the high-souled Brāhmaṇa Devarāta. (12)
There were atheists who had broken all bounds of propriety and were constantly devoted to the wives of others; they delighted in sinful deeds and were entirely devoid of virtuous actions.
"Due to my addiction to the greed for the tongue, I have always eaten meat; because of that, the name 'meat-eater' (māṃsāda), born of my karma, has been established for me. (14)
"O Great King, this second one who stands before you has always eaten his food without having performed the worship of the deities. (15)
Due to the ripening of that karma, he has taken recourse in the womb of a preta; this second evildoer is known as Vidaivata.
"O best of kings, this most wicked man has always practiced ingratitude; it is for that deed that he is called ungrateful. (17)
The king said: "In this world of men, all living beings subsist upon food. Which among you is it that [subsists] here? Let that be told to me in detail. (18)
Māṃsāda said: "In whatever house, at the time of eating, a quarrel among women breaks out, there indeed the pretas consume even that which is mostly composed of mantras and medicinal herbs. (19)
O protector of the earth, wherever food is eaten by men without performing the Vaiśvadeva rite and without offering the first portion of the cooked food, there the pretas consume it.
O tiger among kings, whatever *śrāddha* or gift is performed at night, excluding the sacred festival days (*parvan*), all of that becomes food for the departed spirits (*preta*s).
In that house where no cleansing is performed, nor any smearing with cow-dung, nor auspicious rites or hospitality, there indeed the departed spirits (pretas) eat.
In that house where broken vessels are not discarded and where the sound of the Vedas is not heard, there indeed the departed spirits feast.
O King, that śrāddha which is devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) or devoid of ritual action, as well as that which is seen by a woman in her menses—such [a śrāddha] accrues to us. (24)
For when twice-born men who are deficient in limbs or have extra limbs, or who have *vṛṣalīs* as their mistresses, eat at that śrāddha, that accrues to us. (25)
If a guest arrives when the time for a śrāddha has come, but departs from the house unhonored, then that śrāddha provides satisfaction only to the departed spirits (pretas).
Or what is the use of much speaking to you? Listen in brief, O King, to that which is our constant food, hearing which you now reproach us. (27)
Whatever food is defiled by hair, threads, bones, phlegm, and the like, or touched by those of low birth—that is what arises for us. (28)
The king said: "By what ripening of karma do men attain the state of a preta? Tell me all of this, O meat-eater, as I ask you. (29)
Māṃsāda said: "That man who is mean, as well as a backbiter and a slanderer, and who is addicted to eating choice meat, is born as a preta. (3)
That man who eats without having performed the rites for the gods and likewise the libations for the ancestors, and without having given to his dependents, is born as a preta.
A man who is devoted to the wives of others, a thief of another's wealth, and one who finds satisfaction in slandering others, is born as a preta.
That man who gives his daughter to an old man, to a low-born person out of a desire for wealth, or to one who is ugly or of bad character, is born as a preta.
That man who abandons a lawful wife—who was born of noble family, well-disciplined, raised in comfort, and free from fault—becomes a preta.
That man who, having taken the property of a deity, a woman, or a teacher, does not restore it—especially the property of a Brahmin—is born as a preta.
A man who finds satisfaction in the misfortunes of others, who is ungrateful, who violates the bed of his guru, and who reviles the gods and Brahmins, is born as a preta.
That man who, being an evildoer, creates an obstacle to wealth being given to Brahmins, is born as a preta. || 37 ||
If a Brāhmaṇa dies with the food of a Śūdra still in his stomach, he is born as a Preta, O King, even if he were a knower of the six Vedāṅgas.
That man who, out of desire or greed, abandons the dharma appropriate to his family and country and practices something else, is born as a preta.
All this has been told by me to you, O best of kings, by which ripening of karma a man is born as a preta.
The king said: "O eater of meat, tell me in detail and with specific particulars that deed by which a man is not born as a *preta*. (41)
Māṃsāda said: "The man who regards the wives of others as his mother, the property of others as a clod of earth, and all living beings as himself, is not born as a preta. (42)
The man who is constantly devoted to the gift of food, who is especially fond of guests, and whose character is defined by the vow of Vedic study, is never born as a preta.
One who is equal toward enemy and friend, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same, and who is the same in honor and dishonor—that man is not born as a preta.
That man who increases the encouragement of those engaged in the practice of giving and those who follow the path of Dharma shall not be born as a preta. (49)
The man who always protects all living beings, including lice, bugs, gadflies, and the like, as if they were his own children, is never reborn as a preta.
A man who is always engaged in sacrificial rites, always devoted to sacred fords, and constantly occupied with hearing the scriptures, is never born as a preta.
A man who constructs ponds, wells, and tanks, and especially groves and water-stations, is not born as a preta.
All of this, our own secret, has been told to you, O lord of the earth; we are despondent because of our state as ghosts, therefore, please become our refuge. (49)
"O protector of the earth, having gone to the meritorious Gayāśiras, perform the śrāddha ceremony with devotion for each of the three of us individually. (50)
"By this [means], through your grace, we shall attain this most terrible state of being a preta; otherwise, our liberation will not happen in any way whatsoever. (51)

The king said: "Since she possesses such recollection of her former births, movement through the air even while in the state of a ghost, and a thorough knowledge of dharma and adharma—for what reason do you revile her?"
Māṃsāda said: "O King, this state of being a ghost is the ninth, designated as divine; it is endowed with the three qualities (guṇas) and possessed of all remaining defects on every side. (53)
In this very [state], the recollection of past births arises correctly; likewise, there is the power of moving through the sky and the certain discernment of dharma and adharma. (54)
O best of kings, these three qualities have been declared regarding the state of being born as a ghost; now I shall tell you of the defects as well, so listen with a concentrated mind. (55)
O King, if we were to depart from this forest for another place, we would surely be struck by blows from unseen mallets. (56)
Likewise, all religious rites have been declared for human beings; they are not for the hungry ghosts, nor for the gods, nor for any others except humans. (57)
O King, we see from afar water-pots filled with water lying on the ground; we are exhausted and distressed by thirst as the sun stands in the constellation of Taurus.
"O best of kings, if we go into their presence, we might then be struck down by blows from hammers that we have not even seen. (59)
Likewise, O King, we see various kinds of delicious foods prepared in the houses of householders while we ourselves remain at a distance, overcome by hunger. (60)
Likewise, we are unable to enjoy those trees which bear excellent fruit, are covered with flocks of birds, are lush, and are endowed with pleasant shade. (61)
What is the use of saying more to you? Whatever action is censurable and brings about suffering, that very thing comes upon us of its own accord. (62)
Without a hole, our very subsistence cannot be maintained; there is neither water, nor shade, nor a vehicle, nor any means of transport. (63)
For this reason, O King, we wander constantly for the sake of finding a flaw, neither at nightfall, nor in the morning, nor during the day. (64)
O lord of the earth, that which you praise for us—our power to move through the sky—that too is useless and not conducive to our welfare; hear the reason for this as well.

What dharma can be accomplished through various determinations for the sake of attaining the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), since liberation, as well as the recollection of past births and so forth, is not thereby achieved? (66)
Therefore, O King, although these qualities have been proclaimed, no spiritual accomplishment whatsoever arises for the hungry ghosts (pretas) by relying upon them. (67)
O lord of men, through these very qualities, despondency arises even more intensely; for they are truly powerless against all auspicious actions due to their connection with the state of a ghost.
The king said:
"If I go again from this great forest to my home, then I shall undoubtedly perform the Śrāddha for all of them at Gayā. (69)
I shall diligently deliver everyone from all sins, even at the cost of giving up my own body; I swear this by my own truth. (70)
Since the doubt residing in my heart has indeed been removed by you today, I shall obtain that [knowledge] and perform a service for you.
Māṃsāda said: "O Great King, not far from this place there is a body of water, endowed with various trees and supremely pleasing to the mind. (72)
Therefore, go northward to where those water-birds are seen traveling in all directions along the path of the sky.
Sūta said: Then that tiger among kings, having risen very slowly and directing himself toward the northern quarter, set out, deeply distressed.
As he was thus proceeding, distressed by hunger and thirst, he beheld from no great distance a dark grove of trees, frequented by wandering cranes, swans, saras cranes, and water-fowls.
Having gone there to the water, the lord of the earth, as if summoned by that cool breeze, proceeded with great haste. (76)
Then he beheld a charming hermitage situated on the bank of a lake, frequented by gentle beings and surrounded on all sides by ascetics.
It was surrounded on all sides by trees in full bloom and laden with fruit, and it resounded with the various sweet songs of the finest birds.
There, at the bottom of the water, he beheld Jaimini, the best of sages, who was devoted to the dharma of Śiva, peaceful, and attended by a multitude of ascetics.
Then, having gone there, that lord of kings prostrated before the lord of sages and likewise before his other disciples, falling upon the surface of the earth.
Having seen him, whom they had never seen before, marked with the characteristics of royalty, yet with limbs greyed by dust like a mountain covered in ashes; || 81 ||
Perceiving him to be a protector of the earth, their eyes wide with wonder, they spoke with sweet words preceded by blessings. (82)
From where have you come to this forest devoid of people, alone, with such delicate limbs, on foot, and overwhelmed by exhaustion? (93)
The signs of a king are seen in you in great abundance; therefore, we do not know for certain—tell us the reason for your arrival. (84)
Then the king said with great difficulty, "Thirst afflicts me; therefore, tell me of some water, having drunk which I may proclaim [your names]. (85)
Then the water was shown to him by them, which was near the king; having drunk it and bathed therein, he became free from thirst.
Then, having gathered the ripe fruits that had fallen from the trees below—well-cleaned—he ate them according to his desire. (87)
Then, having attained supreme satisfaction and gone into the presence of Jaimini, he sat down after bowing deeply to him and likewise to the other sages in due order.
Standing with his palms joined in reverence, he related his own story when questioned by all the ascetics, who were filled with great wonder. (89)
I am King Vidūratha, established in Māhiṣmatī; desiring to hunt deer, I entered a terrible forest together with my soldiers. (90)
Then, as I was wandering about, all my soldiers were lost; others were hidden by the thickets, and I do not know how they remained.
I had a horse beneath me, noble-born and endowed with every excellence; yet, through the ripening of karma, it too met its death. || 92 ||
Wandering about, I have arrived here because my allotted lifespan has come to an end; therefore, tell me, what region is this, and how far is my city from here?
Then those ascetics said: "O King, we do not know that city, nor you, nor this country; what is this place that is being described? (94)
"O King, we have no concern for kings, nor for directions, nor for cities; we are forest-dwellers, eternally devoted to the worship of Śiva. (95)
All the flowers and fruits of the trees have withered; therefore, we shall eat the leaves for the sake of maintaining our bodies. (96)
O lord of men, we do not associate with humans nor do we converse with them; we do not even look at them, but go far away from them.
Let us stay for one day or two days at the foot of each individual tree, so that the sense of "mine-ness" arising from them may not occur.
"O Indra among kings, for this reason we shall spend this night at the tree; we will go elsewhere, for your radiance is [intolerable] in another forest. (99)
O King, seeing you alone, on foot, weaponless, and overwhelmed by fatigue, our compassion has become even greater than before. (18)
"How will this lord of kings pass the night all alone? Having deliberated thus in this forest, they remained right there.
Therefore, let us remain gathered right here for this night; tomorrow morning, we shall all depart as we please.
While they were thus conversing, the Blessed One of piercing rays, resembling powdered saffron, reached the mountain of setting.

Then the king, standing with a bowed head, spoke to those ascetics: "O best of sages, the time for twilight has now arrived; therefore, let the twilight rites be performed by everyone as is appropriate."
Then all those sages, as well as that king and the twice-born ones, performed the evening rites as they had been prescribed by the ancients.
Then the night arrived, longed for by lovers and women, welcomed with endearing words, and especially sought after by unchaste women.
Like the tide of the nectar-ocean and like a creeper on a poison-tree, she is beheld simultaneously by both the owls and the cakravāka birds.
Owls, Rākṣasas, thieves, lustful men, and unchaste women always long for her with eager anticipation, just as farmers long for a good rain. || 108 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for the Evening Rites and Other Duties, Preceded by the Dialogue between Vidūratha and the Sages after He Reached the Hermitage of the Seers Due to the Words of the Flesh-Eaters," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 18 ||
Sūta said: In the meantime, the servants of that king arrived; some, by the turn of fate, had been half-devoured by beasts of prey. || 1 ||
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, wretched and overwhelmed by great suffering, they followed the path of footprints by which that king had gone.
Seeing the king there, they, filled with joy, respectfully exclaimed, "By good fortune! By good fortune! and fell at his feet.
Then they described to that lord of men the calamity involving his army, exactly as it had been seen, experienced, and heard.
Then all those ascetics and that king, together with his attendants, spread leaves upon the ground beneath a tree and fell fast asleep.
Then, while all those high-souled ones were fast asleep there in the forest, that night passed away with ease.
Then, having risen in the morning and performed his morning rites, he prostrated deeply before that sage and took leave of him again and again.
Setting out toward his own city, aiming for Māhiṣmatī, he proceeded slowly along the road together with those personal servants.
Then, having reached his own home and rested for some time, the lord of the earth subsequently proceeded swiftly to the meritorious Gayāśiras.
Having reached that place at the proper time, he bathed, put on clean garments, and, being pure, performed a *śrāddha* for the flesh-eaters with a mind purified by faith.

Then, at the end of his sleep, that protector of the earth beheld him wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot (vimāna), and being praised by kinnaras.
The flesh-eater said: "O protector of the earth, by your grace I am liberated from the womb of a preta. May it be well with you; I shall now depart for the abode of the gods. (12)
Then, having risen in the morning, the lord of the earth, filled with joy, performed the appropriate śrāddha ceremony dedicated to the gods.
He too, in that very same form, appeared before the protector of the earth at the end of his dream; having spoken likewise, he departed for heaven.
Then, on the third day at dawn, the lord of the earth performed the Śrāddha for Kṛtaghna as before, with a mind purified by faith.
Then he too appeared in a dream to that lord of the earth, in that very form of a ghost, overwhelmed by great suffering.
The ungrateful man said: "O Great King, no refuge has been found for me, a doer of evil deeds—a thief of the wealth of a pond and likewise an ungrateful person. (17)
Therefore, O best of kings, act today in such a way that liberation may be born for me; remain devoted to truthful speech. (18)
Truth alone is the supreme Brahman; truth alone is the supreme austerity; truth alone is the supreme knowledge; truth alone is the supreme sacred revelation. || 19 ||
By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun gives heat; by the power of truthful speech the ocean does not overstep its bounds.
Visiting sacred fords, austerity, charity, Vedic study, and service to the guru—all these become useless for one who is devoid of truth. (21)
All phenomena were previously weighed together in one place and elsewhere in truth by the gods out of curiosity; therein, truth was found to be heavier than the scales.
Therefore, O high-minded one, place truth before you and deliver me; this shall be for you the highest good, even greater than ascetic penance. (23)
Vidūratha said: "O deceased one, tell me quickly how liberation arises for you; I shall perform that deed, even if it should be very difficult to accomplish. (24)
The preta said: O King, in Camatkārapura, at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara, Gayāśiras remains covered with dust, out of fear of the Kali age. (25)
Beneath the Plakṣa tree, he [should offer] on all sides with bunches of Darbha grass, as well as many Kālaśāka plants and wild-growing sesame seeds.
"Having gone there, quickly perform a śrāddha with those sesame seeds, those vegetables, and likewise with those kuśa grasses, so that my liberation may be attained. (27)
Having heard those words of that distressed man, he, filled with compassion, went to the place where that tree known as Plakṣa stood.
Having seen those vegetables, sesame seeds, and darbha grass as they had been described by him, he dug a small well in that place for the sake of water.
Then, having invited excellent Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, he performed a Śrāddha ceremony for the sake of the ungrateful man, exactly as prescribed.
Immediately upon the performance of the Śrāddha, a man assuming a divine form and mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot spoke to Vidūratha: || 31 ||
O Lord, by your grace I am liberated from this terrible state of being a ghost; may it be well with you, I shall now depart for the abode of the gods.
Sūta said: From that time forward, that small well became renowned there as the one originating from Gayāśīrṣa, which constantly bestows nourishment upon the ancestors.
O best of Brahmins, he who performs a śrāddha on the new moon day of the fortnight of the ancestors (Pretapakṣa) with black pot-herbs and wild sesame seeds— || 34 ||
Endowed with perfect faith, by likewise using trimmed *darbha* grass, he obtains the entire fruit from the Kṛtaghnapreta Tīrtha. (35)
The groups of ancestors known as the Agniṣvātta-s, as well as those who sit upon the sacrificial grass (Barhiṣad-s), and likewise the Ājyapa-s and Somapa-s, are eternally present there.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the śrāddha ceremony there, whether at the proper time or even at an improper time, for the constant satisfaction of the ancestors.
Sūta said: There, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having been initiated for his forest exile, was wandering upon the surface of the earth accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
O best of the twice-born, having arrived at that place where the Pitṛkūpikā is located, he, afflicted by thirst and exhausted by fatigue, sat down upon the surface of the earth.
In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, the Blessed One, the leader of the day, reached the mountain of setting, resembling a hibiscus flower.
Then, having spread leaves upon the ground beneath the Plakṣa tree and performed the evening rites, the joy of the Raghus lay down to sleep.
Then, in a dream, he beheld King Daśaratha just as before—engrossed in pleasant conversation and joyful in mind.
Then, at the clear dawn when the solar disc had risen, Rāghava summoned the brahmins and related all of that to them.
"O Brahmins, today in a dream I saw my father, intent on pleasant conversation, with a most joyful mind, adorned with white garlands and unguents. (7)
O best of the twice-born, what will be the outcome of this dream? Speak, for my curiosity is great. (8)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O King, we have heard that those ancestors who desire the Śrāddha ceremony, or who behold prosperity, appear in dreams to their sons."
And because Gayā herself was present in this very well, you saw your father in a dream desiring a śrāddha offering.
Therefore, O best of the Raghus, perform here the śrāddha ceremony as prescribed, using wild grains (nīvāra), vegetables, roots, and likewise sesame seeds produced in the forest.
Then the best of the Raghus, endowed with faith, addressed those brahmins, saying, "May your favor be granted regarding these śrāddha rites."
Having said, "So be it," all those best of the twice-born, being greatly delighted, departed toward their own hermitages for the purpose of bathing.
Then, after those brahmins had departed, the best of the Raghus spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who stood at his side bowed in humility.
"Quickly bring vegetables, roots, and fruits for the sake of the śrāddha; O son of Sumitrā, bring Vaidehī, for that beautiful woman is cooking it herself. (15)
Having heard that, Lakṣmaṇa went quickly indeed to the forest itself; for the sake of the śrāddha, he swiftly brought various kinds of fruits.
Dhātrī fruits, mangoes, cucumbers, guḍas, karīras, kapitthas, and likewise many other such fruits in great abundance. || 17 ||
Then, at the command of Rāma, that virtuous lady born of Janaka herself, endowed with humility, prepared it for his sake.
Then, when the Kutapa hour had arrived, those best of the twice-born, having performed their daily rites, came together, filled with devotion for Rāma.
In the meantime, Sītā, standing within the hollow of a Plakṣa tree, concealed herself so that Rāghava would not recognize her.
Calling out "Sītā, Sītā" to her again and again, and perceiving that she was in her menses, he then spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Dear Lakṣmaṇa, you ought to perform properly the service due to the Brahmins arising from this Śrāddha, beginning with the washing of their feet."
Having been addressed with "So be it," Lakṣmaṇa, who possesses auspicious marks, performed all those tasks just as a skilled woman would.
Then, when the Śrāddha ceremony had been concluded and the Brahmins had departed, the virtuous daughter of Janaka appeared at that very moment.
Seeing Sītā, Rāghava, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke harsh words, reproaching her again and again. (25)
"When the twice-born have arrived and the time for the śrāddha has come, tell me, O sinful woman, where you have gone, having abandoned me far behind? (26)
This is not fitting for women of noble family, especially here in this forest; it is improper to roam about in such a desolate and empty place. Therefore, you must be abandoned, O Maithilī.
Having heard those words of his, that daughter of Janaka became terrified; with her limbs trembling, she then spoke in a faltering voice.
O best of the Raghus, you ought not to reproach me in this matter; hear from me why I have departed from this place. (29)
"I have seen your father, Daśaratha himself, in person; and your grandfather, the second [ancestor], residing within the body of a Brahmin. (30)
O best of the Raghus, my father’s grandfather was the son of another; likewise, there were three others similar to kings for those three [grandfathers]. (31)
I have clearly seen those three maternal grandfathers residing within the bodies of the Brahmins, appearing exceedingly joyful; indeed, I consider them to be such. (32)
Then, seeing that my father-in-law had enjoyed various delicious foods many times before, I was overcome with shame and fled from his presence.
Likewise, O Lord, how will your father today eat the foods to be chewed, licked, and especially sucked—bitter and pungent things given by my own hand? (34)
For this reason, O Lord, I have vanished from your presence; even though the time for the śrāddha has arrived, I swear this truth upon my own self. (358)
Having heard that, the lotus-eyed Rāma, his soul filled with joy, embraced her again and again and said to her, "Excellent! Excellent! (36)
Then, having eaten himself, Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, when evening had arrived, performed the twilight rites.
He said to Lakṣmaṇa, "O child, having spread leaves upon the ground, prepare a bed; and bring water for washing the feet. (38)
Then, his soul overcome with anger, the son of Sumitrā said to Rāghava: "I will not prepare a bed, nor will I wash your feet."
Likewise, O Lord, if any other action whatsoever, however slight it may be, causes me intense suffering, I shall abandon you and go elsewhere. (40)

"O best of the Raghus, what I have spoken is the truth regarding my status as a servant. What command can you give Sītā? You do not grant her anything at all. O Rāma, what will you do with me, even though I am so very insignificant? (41)
Having heard those words of his, which were indeed distorted, the wise Rāghava became silent after letting out a slight laugh.
Then, having risen himself and prepared an auspicious bed, he washed his feet with Sītā and immediately thereafter went to sleep.
Lakṣmaṇa also, standing at a distance with eyes bloodshot with anger, took refuge at the foot of a tree and, while sleeping, reflected in his mind: || 44 ||
"Having killed this Raghava while he sleeps and taken Sita as my wife, shall I go to my own abode or even to a distant foreign land? (45)
O Brahmins, as Lakṣmaṇa was thus reflecting in many ways, that night passed for him with great difficulty.
As he lay there, his sleep destroyed by anger and sighing hot breaths repeatedly, no certainty whatsoever arose in him regarding that task.
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed his morning rites, Rāma set out toward the southern direction, taking Sītā with him.
Lakṣmaṇa also, having strung his bow and fixed an arrow upon it, followed behind him, watching for any vulnerability.
Then, having reached Gokarṇa and bowed to Maheśvara, Rāghava set forth just as Saumitri arrived.
With eyes clouded by tears and standing with his face cast down in shame, he bowed his head to Rāma and, deeply distressed, spoke.
O Lord, O best of the Raghus, inflict upon me the punishment arising from my betrayal of my master; for I am an exceedingly sinful, wicked, and ungrateful wretch.
Numerous superior and hostile weapons have been given to you by me; yet, despite my innocence, you have devised a means for my slaughter. (53)
Then, having embraced that kinsman of his, Rāma, his face drenched with tears, said: "My child, I have forgiven you."
"I know clearly that no one else is dear to you except me; therefore come, let us go, for the time may be passing."
Lakṣmaṇa said: "O Lord, if you do not restrain me now, I shall give up my life in the fire for the sake of self-purification. (56)
While Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were speaking thus in that forest, the best of sages known as Mārkaṇḍeya arrived there.
Then Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, bowed down to him and said: "Welcome to you; from where have you come, O noble sage? (58)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O descendant of Raghu, I have now come from Prabhāsa; I shall go to my own hermitage, which is situated right here in this sacred field."
O Rāghava, my great-grandfather was established there by me; his festival today is remembered as bestowing great merit. (60)
Therefore, you too should come quickly with me to that very place; staying at my hermitage, behold the Lord Pitāmaha.

O scion of Raghu, by this [rite], you shall become unassailable by all enemies; for on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon in the month of Jyeṣṭha, you, the eldest son, being composed in mind, [performed it].

For one who performs a bath there, whence can there be fear of death? O Rāma, today is the fifteenth day arising in the month of Jyeṣṭha, conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism; therefore, you ought to bathe.
Then, seeing Rāma about to depart, Lakṣmaṇa said: "O Lord, first grant me permission; then go to the sacred ford."
Rāma said: "O child Lakṣmaṇa, while this tiger among sages stands nearby, it is not appropriate for me to perform an act of atonement; therefore, you must entreat him."
Lakṣmaṇa said: "O Brahmin, if an expiation is prescribed for committing treachery against one's master, grant it clearly to me, so that purification of my body may arise. (66)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Near my hermitage there is an excellent sacred ford called Bālamaṇḍana; those who have committed treachery against their masters are liberated from their sins by bathing there.

In that place, O best of the Kakutsthas, Śakra became free from sin after formerly slaying the embryo of Diti while she was especially trusting; therefore, O high-minded one, go there quickly and perform a ritual bath.
Then you shall be liberated from the sin arising from treachery toward your master; there is no other fault in you, for the transgression was committed only by thought.
"Purification through remorse is the opinion of the wise; for you have committed an act of malice against Rāma with your own mind. (70)
Because of such mental anguish, you are pure, O Lakṣmaṇa; hear another word from me, O sinless one: there is no fault in you.
Such is the power of this sacred field, O Lakṣmaṇa, that even those who dwell here within this five-krośa area are deprived of brotherly affection.
Not even the slightest brotherly affection arises among them anywhere.
A mortal remains devoted to affection and speaks tenderly only so long as he has not touched with his feet this sacred field born of wonder. (74)
Whatever other animals, birds, or wild beasts dwell here as well, they too are devoid of friendship and are full of mutual rivalry.
No one possesses friendship with anyone else; therefore, there is no fault in you for maintaining such a state of fear. (76)
Nevertheless, if some doubt remains established in your mind, then go and perform a bath at that most beautiful sacred ford.
It was there that Śakra became free from sin after having previously committed a most terrible act of treachery by causing the miscarriage of Diti’s fetus while she was trusting him. (78)

O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus, the son of Sumitrā went there and, by bathing in that holy ford frequented by Śakra, became purified. Rāma also went quickly to that excellent hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya.
Having performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rule, he then beheld the Grandfather (Brahmā); thereafter, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he departed toward the southern direction.
By its power, he then slew the foremost of the Rākṣasas, Kharā and the others, as well as the fierce Rāvaṇa together with Meghanāda.
The Brāhmaṇas said: When was the Great-grandfather (Brahmā) established there by Mārkaṇḍeya? In which place did that sage establish his own hermitage? Tell us. || 1 ||
Sūta said: There was a preeminent brahmin named Mṛkaṇḍa, the best among those who know the Vedas, who dwelt in a forest hermitage near the city of Camatkārapura.
With a tranquil soul and endowed with self-restraint, he performed very great austerity while living thus in the hermitage of a forest-dweller.
When he had reached his later years, a most beautiful son was born to him, endowed with all auspicious marks and possessing a splendor like that of the full moon.
Then his father himself gave him the name Mārkaṇḍa; that boy grew up exceedingly in that most excellent hermitage.
Having entered the bright fortnight like the lord of stars in the sky, five years passed for him as he grew, while still engaged in childhood play and remaining upon his father’s lap.
Then, after some time, a certain person arrived there, a knower of the entire science of physiognomy (sāmudrika) and a master of the methods of knowledge.
Beholding that infant from the tips of his nails up to the hair on his head, his eyes wide with wonder, he then broke into a slight smile.
Mṛkaṇḍa, too, beholding the wise one with a smiling countenance, questioned him with humility and a somewhat pleased mind.
Mṛkaṇḍa said: "O tiger among brahmins, why did you, upon seeing this son of mine, remain for a very long time overcome with wonder, your face smiling? (10)
Sūta said: Having been questioned by him repeatedly, that best of Brāhmaṇas then related the very reason for his laughter.
The Brāhmaṇa said: O excellent sage, those marks which are seen on this child’s body—if they be real, then by them the man shall be free from old age and death. (12)
Furthermore, the death of this child will occur from this day forward in six months; there is no doubt, for what I have spoken is the truth. (13)
Knowing this, O best of the twice-born, perform whatever is for the welfare of this boy, both in this world and in the next, at my command. (14)
Having spoken thus, that lord of brahmins departed for his desired destination; Mṛkaṇḍu, for his part, then performed the binding of the sacred girdle (mauñjī-bandhana) for him.
Even though it was not the proper time, he, the knower of causes, reflected for a moment within his own heart and then spoke to his son regarding the reason.
"O son, whichever best of the twice-born you see wandering about, you must certainly address him with humility. (17)
Thus, for that leader of Brahmins who remains steadfast in his vow and is intent on offering salutations, six months pass with three days deducted.
In the meantime, the Seven Sages, devoted to the Agnitīrtha, arrived at the place where Mārkaṇḍa stood, wearing his girdle.
Seeing all those sages, the son of the sage paid homage to them; they all, individually, said to him, "May you be long-lived."
Then, having watched him for a long time out of curiosity because of his childhood, Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, spoke these words to the celibate student.
"All these people have respectfully declared that this child shall be long-lived; yet on the third day, he will undoubtedly cast off his life-breaths. (22)
"O twice-born ones, such a statement as this would not be appropriate for us; therefore, let that action be performed by which he may become long-lived. (23)
Then, having deliberated among themselves, all those bulls among sages said: "There can be no means of livelihood except through the Grandfather."
Therefore, having led this child, whose life is exhausted, before him, let his word be carried out so that he may become a possessor of long life.
Then, taking the religious student with them, they quickly departed for the world of Brahmā, leaving behind their prowess in sacred fords.
Then, having bowed to that god and praised him with hymns declared in the Vedas, the twice-born ones sat down in his presence immediately thereafter.
Immediately after them, he too paid homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā), and the Self-born One himself said to the boy, "May you be long-lived."
Then the Lotus-born One spoke to all the sages who were resting: "From where have you come now, and for what reason? (29)
And let it be told what task must now be performed for you who have come to my house; for who is this boy, though he be but a child, who observes such noble vows? (30)
The sages said: "O Grandfather, while wandering over the surface of the earth in the course of a pilgrimage, we have arrived in the vicinity of Camatkārapura."
"There, O King, we were saluted by this boy; then all of us in turn respectfully addressed him as 'Long-lived One'. (32)
"O best of the wise, only three days remain of his lifespan; for that reason, indeed, we are filled with shame. (33)
Then, having taken him with us, we have arrived in your presence; and you likewise said, "May this boy be long-lived. (34)
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, act in such a way that we may become true to you; for this purpose have we come here. (35)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the sages, the Lotus-born One, taking the boy with him, spoke these words while smiling: || 36 ||
By my grace, this boy shall be free from old age and death; he will become an expert in Vedic knowledge, of this there is no doubt. (37)
Therefore, O best of sages, take this child and go first to his own home on the surface of the earth. || 38 ||
O best of the twice-born, his aged father did not meet his death along with his lawful wife until he had seen his son.
Then all those best of sages arrived at that boy's hermitage, reaching the surface of the earth in its very vicinity.
Without releasing him at Agnitīrtha, they addressed him thereafter and subsequently departed quickly for another place on their pilgrimage.
In the meantime, the brahmin Mṛkaṇḍa, who was deeply affectionate toward his son, did not see his own son; thereafter, he lamented, being exceedingly distressed.
"Alas! My beloved son is not seen today; has he perhaps fallen into a well, or has he been struck down by wild beasts? (43)
Having left me and my mother tormented by grief, my son has set out upon a long journey; fate has acted against us.
Behold, O Brahmin woman, by me, a sinner who has committed evil deeds, the face of my child was not seen as he departed for the abode of Yama. 45.
O high-souled one, that wise man previously told me: "In six months, this son of yours will give up his body."
Therefore, out of grief for my son, I shall offer myself into the fire before this body is consumed by the fire of sorrow, O excellent lady.
The Brāhmaṇī said: "I also agree with what you have proclaimed. Why then do you delay, O Brāhmaṇa? Bring the wood quickly! (48)
So that I, tormented by grief for my son, may enter the fire along with you for the sake of completely pacifying my intense suffering. (49)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, while the couple was thus conversing, that boy, filled with joy, then came into their presence.
Seeing him, the Brahmin, together with his wife, was then filled with joy; with eyes overflowing with tears of bliss, he ran toward him. (51)
Embracing him again and again along with his wife, he then asked: "Where have you been, my child? Why have you returned here after such a long time from your own hermitage? (52)
"Having cast me and my wife, both advanced in years, into an ocean of grief, do not, O dear son, ever again perform such an act."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O dear one, today the sages arrived here; remembering your words, I have saluted them all in due order with humility."
"May you live long," was said by all those best of the twice-born, O Lord, upon seeing me—a child observing a vow—filled with wonder.
Then, O dear one, having observed them, the sage Vasiṣṭha, standing in their midst, spoke to all those sages as if smiling.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O best of sages, that child of whom you spoke as being long-lived will meet his death on the third day."
Then, O dear one, those sages became afraid of that untruth at that very moment; taking [the child] with them, they went to where Brahmā was stationed.
Having been saluted by him, I was addressed by the lotus-born Brahmā: "May you have a long life," and I was asked, "From where have you come here? (59)
Then all those sages recounted his history, declaring that it arose from their blessings, and said, "Therefore, we have come here."
O Grandfather, O Lord, you ought to act in such a way that, through your grace, this child may become long-lived in the world. (61)
Then, O dear one, I was made free from old age and death by Brahmā; together with them, I was quickly dispatched back toward my own home.
But those sages, having bid me farewell right here in the vicinity of the hermitage, all entered this very beautiful lake for the purpose of bathing.
Having heard those words of his, Mṛkaṇḍu, filled with joy, went quickly to the place where those sages were staying.
Having bowed down to all those sages, he stood with his palms joined in reverence and said: "By your grace, my lineage has attained prosperity."
"O best of sages, this which has been spoken by certain teachers is excellent; it relies upon the world of the virtuous and is renowned throughout the three worlds. (66)
Beholding the virtuous is meritorious, for the virtuous are like sacred pilgrimage sites; a pilgrimage site bears fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous yields fruit immediately.
"Therefore, since you have all arrived at my home today as guests, O best of the twice-born, tell me what hospitality I may provide for you."
The sages said: O sage, this alone constitutes for us hospitality equal to ten million-fold: that even your child, though short-lived, has been born free from death. (69)
Mṛkaṇḍa said: "O lords of sages, by protecting our child today who was embraced by Death, you have uplifted our entire lineage. (70)

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for the breaker of vows, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
Therefore, O lords of sages, there shall be no fault of ingratitude on my part; and all of you must undoubtedly act exactly as you have proposed. (72)
The sages said: "O best of the twice-born, if you consider it a way to repay our favor, then by our word, build a house for us according to the command of the Supreme Lord."
"Since this boy of yours has today been rendered free from death by me, therefore establish that god, the Great-grandfather (Brahmā), at a sacred ford."
Together with your son, worship that god Pitāmaha day and night; we ourselves shall do so along with you.

"We shall worship [you] eternally, as will other excellent brahmins, because our friendship is established here with this boy; therefore, it shall be known by the name 'Bālasakhya' (Friendship with the Child)."
This holy ford, known by others as beneficial for children, shall always be [effective] at our word for those afflicted by disease and those afflicted by fear. 77.

O twice-born one, those people who shall bathe a child at this sacred ford—whether that child be afflicted by disease, overcome by fear, or tormented by malevolent planets and the like—[shall obtain great merit]. (78)
O twice-born one, by the grace of the Grandfather and likewise by our word, he shall become free from all defects; of this there is no doubt. (79)
Furthermore, O Brahmin, those humans who are free from desire and endowed with faith, even if they perform only the ritual bath, they go to the supreme goal.
Having spoken thus, all those sages of celebrated vows took leave of that sage and departed quickly for other sacred fords.
Mṛkaṇḍu, together with his son, being greatly delighted, installed the Grandfather (Brahmā) at that place during the month of Jyeṣṭha when the moon was situated in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā.
Thereupon, unwearied by day or night, he propitiated [the deity] together with his son, endowed with faith, and attained the supreme goal.
Sūta said: From that time forward, that holy place has been known as Bālasakhya; it is purifying for all living beings and destroys the diseases of children.
O twice-born ones, that child who performs a ritual bath there during the month of Jyeṣṭha under the Jyeṣṭhā constellation does not suffer from affliction for as long as a year.
He becomes inaccessible to planets, spirits, and piśācas, especially to śākinīs, as well as to all other malevolent beings. || 86 ||

The sages said: Regarding that which was spoken by you concerning the tirtha where Śakra’s ocean flows forth—the place where Lakṣmaṇa was liberated from the sin of committing treason against his master—(1)
O son of a Sūta, how was Śakra formerly liberated from that very sin arising from treachery toward his master, and at what time did this occur?
Why was such a deed committed against Diti by Mahendra, by which the fetus was destroyed? Tell me everything in detail.
Sūta said: From the right thumb of Brahmā was born Dakṣa, the progenitor of beings; and he begot fifty auspicious daughters.
Dakṣa gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, and twenty-seven to Indra according to the divine rite.
O best of the twice-born, Aditi and Diti were the two principal wives of Kaśyapa, who were always dearer to him than even his own life.
Then he procreated the gods, headed by Śakra, from Aditi, and the exceedingly powerful Daityas from Diti.
For the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, a great battle broke out between them; there, those Daityas were struck down in combat by Śakra.
Thereupon, overcome with grief, Diti undertook an unsurpassed vow for the sake of a son; endowed with self-restraint, she remained concentrated in this very sacred field.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara was pleased with her and said, "I am well-pleased; ask for the boon you desire."

She said: "O Moon-crested God, if you are pleased with me, then grant me a son who shall be more powerful than all the gods, the enjoyer of sacrificial portions, and the destroyer of the pride of the gods. (11)
"Unslayable in battle by all the gods of old, including Indra"—having thus promised, Hara vanished from sight.

And Diti conceived a child from Kaśyapa, the bull among sages; then Śakra became afraid upon learning of that conception of a fetus from the great-souled Nārada, the chief of sages, as he was speaking. (13)
Then, having formed a wicked intent toward the destruction of that fetus, he attended upon her day and night without weariness.
O twice-born ones, though he searched for even the most subtle opening, he found none anywhere; nine months passed away.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived and the time for birth was at hand, she, weary from the pregnancy, lay sleeping facing south at the onset of night.
Having fallen under the power of sleep, she became unconscious; rendered motionless by the pleasure in her feet arising from the pressure of Śakra’s hand, she remained still.
Then, seeing her unconscious, Śatakratu abandoned his feet and entered her womb, holding a sharp weapon in his hand; with that weapon, the lord of the gods cut the fetus into seven parts.
Then, in an instant, he saw seven boys with fully formed bodies; thereafter, Hari divided each of those seven into seven parts as well.
Then forty-nine children were born right there; seeing them growing, Śatakratu became afraid and quickly emerged from Diti’s womb before he was noticed.
Then, at the clear dawn when the solar disc had risen, Diti gave birth to seven boys in seven ways.
Then the thousand-eyed Indra, overwhelmed by a foul odor, arrived there; devoid of luster and with a withered face, he stood with his head bowed in shame.
Seeing Śakra in such a state—standing at her side, bowing down with a mind agitated by fear—Diti spoke to him respectfully.
"O Śakra, why are you devoid of energy and luster, and why does such a foul odor emanate from your body? (24)
"Have you slain a brahmin, or a guru, or perhaps a child, or a woman, such that the splendor arising from your body has been destroyed? (25)
Or you were killed by water from the nails, or rubbed by the wind from a winnowing basket, or touched by the dust raised by the sweeping of a goat. (26)
Śakra said: "O highly fortunate lady, what you have just said to me is true; that sinner entered your womb while you were asleep during the night. (27)
O auspicious lady, forty-nine times I cut the embryo; from that, all those boys were born in exactly that same number. (28)
O Goddess, having fled out of fear, you were not noticed by him; for this reason, O blameless one, this loss of luster has occurred.
Diti said: "O Lord of the gods, since you have spoken the truth before me, therefore ask from me whatever boon is desired by your mind. (30)
Śakra said: "O Goddess, these sons of yours, though being cut by me with my sword, were wept for; I have restrained them so that they do not weep repeatedly. (31)
Therefore, let those known by the name Maruts be celebrated throughout the three worlds; freed from their demonic nature, they shall be obedient to me and dear to me.
"All shall become partakers of the sacrificial portions along with me, because this sacred ford has been adorned by you with children. (33)

Because of this, it will attain great renown among many as the "Ornament of Children. Furthermore, whatever woman who is pregnant performs her bath with devotion, no defects whatsoever shall ever arise in her womb.
But when the time for delivery has arrived, she who shall drink the water of this sacred ford will give birth to a son with ease. (35)
Diti said: "O Lord of Gods, Hara was previously entreated by me for the sake of your destruction: 'O God, grant me one son who shall be the annihilator of all the gods. (36)
And you have fashioned it in forty-nine ways; since truth has been spoken by you, therefore this shall come to pass.
Sūta said: From that time forward, by the command of Śakra, those sons of Diti became the Maruts, equal to the gods, and partakers of a share of the sacrifice. 38.
Then the thousand-eyed one said to Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods: "How shall the sin committed through treachery toward his mother go to its destruction? (39)
Bṛhaspati said: "O Lord of the Gods, perform penance right here for the purification of your sin, at this sacred ford which destroys all transgressions and where the sin was committed."

O Purandara, neither by sacrifices, nor by charity, nor by resorting to other sacred sites does the sin committed through treachery toward one's mother go to destruction; rather, it is by abandoning all else and taking refuge at this sacred site of your mother that this occurs. || 4 ||
Sūta said: Thereupon, O best of the twice-born, he himself quickly installed the Liṅga known as Sahasrākṣeśa along with Sākṣa.
He worshipped [him] three times a day with flowers, incense, and unguents, as well as with various other offerings, honors, songs, and diverse dances.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara was pleased with him and said, "I am the giver of boons; O Śakra, pray for whatever you desire."

Śakra said: "O Destroyer of Tripura, may the sin committed by those who betray their mothers go to me; likewise, may it go to other men here who, endowed with faith, shall worship you with true devotion after performing their ablutions with concentrated minds. (45)
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," Hara vanished from sight; Śakra too, freed from his sins, went to the abode of the gods.
Thus, that Tīrtha arose there as an ornament for the ignorant; it is where human beings are liberated from the sin of betraying their master.
All this concerning the origin of Bālamaṇḍana has been narrated to you; now, O best of the twice-born, listen with reverence to its greatness. 48.
Whoever performs a śrāddha there in the bright fortnight of Āśvina, starting from the tenth day in due order until the fifteenth lunar day (49), [attains great merit].
O twice-born ones, he indeed obtains the fruit arising from bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas), and by performing a śrāddha there, he also gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
At that time, the thousand-eyed one (Indra) always comes to the surface of the earth for the sake of partaking in the portions belonging to those born as mortals. 51.
O best of the twice-born, as long as Śakra remains upon the surface of the earth, so indeed do all the sacred fords remain there.
Therefore, with every effort, and especially at that time, one should bathe there in the auspicious holy waters and then worship Śakreśvara.
In this regard, two verses were sung of old by the celestial sage Nārada; let all you sages listen as they are being recited by me. (54)

Having bathed at Bālamaṇḍanaka, one should then behold Śakreśvara. That man who does so when the fifth day of the Śravaṇa constellation arrives in the month of Āśvina, is liberated from all sins on this earth from birth until death.
O best of the twice-born, this is the truth due to the power of that sacred ford.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bālamaṇḍana Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sūta said: To the west of that very place is the unsurpassed Mṛgatīrtha, renowned as the most meritorious on the entire surface of the earth. Those men who, endowed with perfect faith, perform their ablutions at that tīrtha during the sun’s [transit] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra—‖ 2 ‖
While it remains in the center, they do not go to the animal realm by any means, even if they are possessed of sin and endowed with all defects.

Even those who are ungrateful, atheists, thieves, and violators of moral boundaries, if they bathe there at that excellent holy site, they go to the supreme goal, mounted upon a preeminent celestial chariot and being praised by Kinnaras.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, how did Mṛgatīrtha come to be there? Tell us its power, for our curiosity is great. (5)
Sūta said: Formerly, in that great forest, which was filled with various herds of wild animals, resounded with the cries of various birds, and crowded with various trees— (6)
Greatly fierce hunters arrived, bows in hand; with dark complexions, they wandered about like other messengers of Yama.
In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, a herd of deer was seen sitting very confidently beneath a tree.
Then, seeing those hunters even from afar, all the deer, overcome with fear, fled quickly from that place.
Then, seeing a deep pool of water in his presence, all those deer, afflicted by fear and tormented by arrows, entered it.
Then, O best of the twice-born, by the power of that [water], all those deer indeed attained human form within the depths of that water.
Then the hunters questioned those deer who had been turned into humans: "A herd of deer has just now arrived by this path; by which way did they depart? Therefore, tell us without delay."
The humans said: "We were all deer; we have attained this human state, which is so difficult to obtain, through the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha). This is the truth, there is no doubt. (13)
Having heard that, those hunters were overcome with amazement; they quickly cast aside their bows and arrows and performed their ablutions there.
Then, by the mere act of bathing, all those best of kings became possessed of divine garlands and ointments, and all acquired divine bodies.
The sages said: "O Sūta, this which has been proclaimed by you is most wonderful! Merely by bathing, those hunters attained such a body. (16)
Likewise, deer who had attained human form [were purified] by plunging into the water; how then did that sacred site (tīrtha) come to exist upon the surface of the earth? (17)
Sūta said: The water that was previously described to you as arising from the division of the Liṅga was entirely covered with dust by the wind, at the command of Śakra.
O twice-born ones, after reaching the hollow of an anthill, it emerged from there once again; however, in that region, it was indeed very small after a long period of time.
Where in former times the lord of the earth Triśaṅku, having bathed, immediately regained his divine body after having been reduced to the state of a Caṇḍāla. || 20 ||
For this reason, all those deer-hunters who bathed there were completely liberated from sin and attained a supreme form.
Sūta said: There, O best of brahmins, stands another auspicious holy site named Viṣṇupada, which destroys all sins.
When the southern solstice has arrived, he who, being composed, honors that [deity] and offers himself up, endowed with perfect faith; || 2 ||
O best of the twice-born, even if he dies while traveling on the southern path, he attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; there is no doubt in this matter, owing to its power.

And likewise, when the northern [path] has been attained, he who, having worshipped according to the rule, offers himself with devotion and a concentrated mind, shall reach the holy abode of Viṣṇu and become happy.
The sages said: How did the footprint of Viṣṇu, whose birth is unmanifest, come to be there? And how is the Self properly revealed there in the two-fold yoga?
O son of Sūta, tell us all that fruit which is obtained by men when that [place] is seen or touched; for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: When Bali was bound by that powerful Viṣṇu, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were pervaded by his three strides.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, the first step was taken; then, by that great-souled one, the second was taken in Maharloka.
O best of the twice-born, when that wielder of the discus made his third effort, the cosmic egg was split and became light.
Then, when the cosmic egg was pierced by the tip of his foot, the pure water reached the surface of the earth in succession by means of the tip of his big toe.

Then that water, flooding the entire world of Brahmā, was like pure crystal, possessing a luster like that of the kunda flower and the moon; it was crowded with fish and tortoises and teeming with shoals of crocodiles.
From that time forward, she has been known in the world as Gaṅgā Viṣṇupadī; bringing even that sacred field to a state of further purity, she flows on.
Thus, O best of sages, Viṣṇu’s footprint was produced there; it removes all sins for men and is therefore known as Viṣṇupadī.
Whoever, endowed with faith, performs the bath therein as prescribed and touches that foot of Viṣṇu, goes to the supreme abode.
Whoever performs a śrāddha there, endowed with perfect faith after bathing in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī, shall obtain the fruit of a śrāddha performed at Gayā.
That mortal who, having risen early in the morning, constantly performs his ablutions there during the month of Māgha, shall obtain the fruit of Prayāga.
Alternatively, if a man performs a bath there with devotion for even a single moment, or for the duration of a year, he attains liberation.
If the bones of any person are cast into that water, even one who has practiced sinful conduct attains the supreme goal.
Even birds, insects, beasts, worms, and deer who were afflicted by thirst and devoid of devotion entered that water. (19)
They too, liberated from sin, at the end of the body attain that most difficult-to-reach station of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), which is devoid of old age and death.
How much more so, O twice-born ones, those men endowed with faith who, when a sacred festival day has arrived, give gifts to the best of the twice-born who are knowers of the Vedas? (21)
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by the great seer Nārada, having beheld the sin-destroying power of Viṣṇupadī. (22)
What is the use of vows, restraints, various austerities, or sacrifices, now that the waters of the Viṣṇupadī are established upon the surface of the earth? (23)
If one mortal were to perform ablutions at all sacred fords, and another were to bathe in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī, the fruit for both would be equal. (24)
One person bestows all kinds of gifts upon the Brahmins, while another bathes in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī; indeed, those two acts are equal.

In the summer, the practitioner of the five fires remains [exposed]; in the rainy season, he takes refuge under the open sky; and in the winter, he stays in water—such a man alone may truly be said to dwell upon the earth.
One who bathes in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī and touches the station of Viṣṇu—both of these excellent men are declared to be equal.
The merit of one who fasts on alternate days for the duration of his life is equal to the merit of another who bathes once in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī. || 28 ||
The merit gained by one man who fasts for three nights for as long as a hundred years is equal to the merit obtained by another who bathes once in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having spoken thus repeatedly before many sages, Nārada, the most excellent of seers, became silent.
Therefore, one should perform a ritual bath there with every effort; and he who desires his own welfare should touch the foot of Viṣṇu.
The sages said: "Regarding that which was stated by you—that one should offer oneself when the sun has reached the southern or northern solstice of Viṣṇu's station—"
O Sūta, tell us quickly by what rite and with which mantras we may perform all of that, endowed with devotion. (33)
Sūta said: When both the southern and northern solstices have arrived, having worshipped the station of Viṣṇu, one should utter this mantra: || 34 ||
If my death should occur unexpectedly within six months, may your state be my goal; I have entered into the service of you.
Having spoken thus to Hari, one should thereafter worship the Brāhmaṇas; then, together with them, one should eat, and thereby one attains the supreme goal.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Viṣṇupadī Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 24 ||
