Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, I shall relate to you that wonder which occurred there in former times, arising from the majesty of the Gaṅgā.
In the city of Camatkārapura, there was formerly a brahmin of strict vows, renowned by the name Caṇḍaśarman, who was endowed with the qualities of beauty and generosity.
When he reached youth, that Brahmin, though learned in the Vedas, became enamored of courtesans, being tormented by the excesses of his youth.
Then, once at midnight, he rose up afflicted by thirst and requested that courtesan, saying, "I wish to drink water."
Then, mistaking it for water, she took up a vessel containing liquor and gave the drink to him who was overcome by sleep.
When the liquor had reached his mouth, he too, filled with rage, repeatedly reviled that prostitute with shouts of "Fie! Fie! (dhig dhik).
"What is this? What is this, O sinful woman? This despicable deed has been committed by you, in that you have cast loathsome liquor into my mouth! (7)
"Today my Brahminhood has undoubtedly been destroyed by the drinking of liquor; therefore, I shall perform an expiation for the sake of purifying myself. (8)
Having spoken thus and departed from that house filled with sorrow, he then went to a lonely forest and wept piteously.
Then, at the time of dawn, O best of the twice-born, having bathed and provided himself with garments, he shaved all the hairs of his body.
He arrived at the assembly where the foremost of the brahmins were stationed, who were reciting all the scriptures and the Vedāntas in their entirety.
Then, having prostrated himself, he spoke loudly to those best of the twice-born: "Under the delusion that it was water, liquor was drunk by me; inflict punishment upon me."
Then, having deliberated again and again upon the treatises of Dharma, all those brahmins spoke to him as he stood there intent on performing an expiation.
The Brahmins said: "Whether through ignorance or even knowingly, if a Brāhmaṇa should drink liquor, he becomes purified by drinking an amount of fire-colored clarified butter equal to that [liquor]."
If you desire purification, drink ghee the color of fire; for as much liquor as was drunk, that same amount of ghee is required for purification. (15)
Having promised "So be it," O best of the twice-born, he took the ghee and immediately prepared it so that it became like fire for the purpose of drinking.

Just then his father arrived, having heard the news along with his wife; filled with grief, saying "What is this? What is this, my son?", he was dejected, his eyes full of tears, and spoke with a voice faltering with sobs. (17)
Then he related the account of everything that had occurred throughout the night, as well as the appropriate expiation for the brahmins.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he said to all those brahmins, "Let some other expiation be prescribed for me on account of this son."
Having reflected upon the treatises of Dharma and deliberated upon them again and again, I shall undoubtedly give away even my very everything for the sake of my son. (20)
Then all those brahmins, the best of sages, having reflected again and again with reverence upon the treatises of Dharma, spoke to him.
O Brahmin, there is no other atonement for the drinking of liquor for the twice-born than the Mauñjī-homa; therefore, perform that which is prescribed.
Then he said to his son: "You ought not to do this at all; bestow gifts upon the brahmins and undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords."
Then, joined by self-restraint and having performed various vows, you shall gradually attain purity; I tell you this as the truth. (24)
The expiation prescribed by a Brahmin does not lead to purification. || 25 ||
The son said: "O highly fortunate one, since they speak of these vows and so forth, therefore, O father, the Mauñjī-homa must be performed by me; of this there is no doubt. (26)
Whatever I have done in my youth, you ought to forgive it all.
Sūta said: Having understood his resolve, that father, who was devoted to his son, became enraged and, having made up his mind to die, gave away all his possessions.
His virtuous wife, having made the firm resolve to die, looked upon her son, gave him everything including the house and other possessions, and spoke to him.
"O son, once we two have entered the fire, you must then perform the Mauñjī-homa, if you consider me to be your father. (30)
Then, as soon as that couple, filled with joy, had approached the vicinity of the fire for the purpose of death, he was born from them.
At that time, O best of the twice-born, a sage named Śāṇḍilya, who had mastered the Vedas, arrived in that region in the course of his pilgrimage.
Having heard that account, his eyes bloodshot with anger, he spoke to all the brahmins, rebuking them again and again.
"Alas! You are most foolish, since these three Brahmins meet with a futile death when their restraint is so easily accomplished. (34)
In this regard, let all the twice-born listen to the words spoken here by the great-souled Kātyāyana; nevertheless, this man must likewise perform penance.
Cāndrāyaṇa penances, Kṛcchra penances, and likewise Sāntapana penances—as these expiations are prescribed where the Gaṅgā is not present.
O best of the twice-born, the Gaṅgā, known as Viṣṇupadī, is present in that sacred field; let him bathe in her, and he shall thereafter attain purification.
If the Maunji-homa were to be authoritative on the basis of the words of a sage, then this very statement of the sage Kātyāyana is indeed clear [proof]. (38)
Then all those brahmins, filled with great joy, said to him, "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke these words: "O sage, this is indeed the truth. (39)
Then, having awakened that brahmin, those best of the twice-born led him to the place where the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Viṣṇu, is herself established.
There, O best of the twice-born, as soon as that brahmin took a mouthful of water originating from the waters of the Gaṅgā into his mouth, he became pure; all the water then emerged from his belly.
Then, as soon as he had plunged into her most beautiful water, a deep voice arising from the sky spoke these words: ||| 42 ||
"This Brahmin has become truly pure through contact with the foot of Viṣṇu; by merely bathing and sipping water, let him therefore go to his own home. (43)
Then all those Brahmins, including Caṇḍaśarman and the others, exclaiming "By good fortune! By good fortune!", retired to their own mansions.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, such is the power of that Gaṅgā, who flows from the foot of Viṣṇu; she stands at the western boundary of that sacred field as the destroyer of sins.
O best of Brahmins, all this has been narrated to you—the origin and majesty of Viṣṇupadī, which destroys all sins. (46)
Sūta said: That which constitutes its eastern and western boundaries has been fully described by me; I shall now tell you that which extends from south to north.
On the surface of the earth, there is a famous great city named Madhurā, crowded with various brahmins and situated on the bank of the Yamunā.
In that city lived a preeminent brahmin renowned as Gokarṇa, who was perfected in the study of the Vedas and an expert in all the śāstras.
Now, there was another Brahmin of that same name there who was advanced in years; he too was an excellent Brahmin who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge.
Then, after some time, Yama spoke to his own servant, who had hair standing on end, blood-red eyes, black teeth, and a terrifying appearance.
"Go quickly today, O messenger, to the great city named Mathurā; bring from there that best of the twice-born known as Gokarṇa."
The exhaustion of his lifespan occurred at midday on this very day; another such long-lived brahmin was to be abandoned right there.
Sūta said: Then, having gone quickly to that city by the command of Yama, the messenger brought back Vibhrama and the long-lived Gokarṇa.
Then Yama, his soul overcome with anger, spoke to his servant: "This long-lived one has been brought; fie on you, O sinner! What is this that you have done?"
Therefore, lead him to that very place while his body has not yet been consumed by the well-kindled fire of grief caused by his kinsmen.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "I will not go there; by good fortune I have come into your presence, always desiring death and tormented by poverty. (11)
Yama said: "O best of Brahmins, I do not bring a mortal from the surface of the earth even for a moment; nor do I release one whose remaining lifespan is yet full."
For this very reason, my name is remembered as Dharmarāja, because of my equanimity toward all living beings and my avoidance of partiality. (13)
Therefore, O Brahmin, go home while your body has not yet been consumed by fire; you must no longer remain there with your kinsmen who are afflicted by grief. (14)
"O best of Brahmins, request a boon desired by your heart; the sight of me can never be in vain for embodied beings. (15)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Lord, if I must certainly go home again, then tell me that; I ask this, and let it be my boon. (16)
"These fierce hells which have been inhabited by those of evil deeds are now visible; tell me, by what action are they inhabited by people? (17)
Yama said: "O Brahmin, the hells are as numerous as the hosts of living beings on earth; they cannot be described in their entirety even in hundreds of years."
O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim to you those twenty-one [hells] which were created for the sake of sinful people, according to their primary importance.
O best of the twice-born, this first hell is named Raurava, where living beings are cooked in jars of boiling oil.
"O mother! O father! O son! they cry out most piteously—those base men, devoted to cooking for others, who steal the wealth of others. (21)
O best of Brahmins, this second one is known as Mahāraurava; it is constantly inhabited by ungrateful people as well as those who violate the bed of their guru.
They were crying out piteously, tormented by burning, being cooked by the fire-eaters, and being cut into pieces in many ways with sharp weapons.
The third hell, named Andhatamas, is most terrifying; O excellent twice-born one, I shall describe those men who go there.
Those lowest of men who have gazed upon the wives of others with a wicked eye—here, birds with beaks of fine iron pluck out their eyes.
This fourth hell is proclaimed by the name Pratapta; having experienced torment here, they likewise become purified.
The tongues of those who have constantly uttered insults against their gurus, deities, and ascetics shall be repeatedly torn out here, again and again, throughout many births.
This is another, well-known fifth hell named Vidāraka; here those who delight in betraying friends are torn apart with saws.
The sixth, known as Nikumbha, who brings fear to the world, is filled with heated sand and is blown upon by fire.
Those men who formerly inflicted life-ending suffering upon living beings without any fault of theirs are now cooked here amidst heaps of hot sand.
The seventh, known as Bībhatsu, is the lowest of hells; it is filled on all sides with urine and impurities, and is utterly contemptible. (31)
Those wicked-souled lowest of men who have committed slander directed toward the king are held here with their mouths filled with impurity.
This eighth and most base twice-born man is known by the name Kutsita; he is filled with phlegm and urine, as well as foul odors.
Those by whom food was consumed here without first giving it to their guru, the gods, guests, and especially their own servants, have remained in this place.
And this, O best of the twice-born, is the ninth, named Durgama; it is strewn with sharp thorns and teeming with serpents and scorpions.
Those who, while traveling as part of the same caravan, did not give food to one who was perishing, emaciated by hunger, remain here. (36)
This tenth hell, well-known by the name Dussaha, is surrounded on all sides by pillars made of heated iron.
Those sinful men who are attached to the wives of others or to sweet meats and delicacies, embrace here pillars made of heated iron.
O tiger among brahmins, this eleventh other hell is proclaimed as Ākarṣa, which is filled with heated pincers.
Those men who consume the wealth of women, Brahmins, gurus, or deities are dragged there from all sides by means of glowing tongs.
This twelfth [hell] is Sandaṃśa; likewise, those who eat what is forbidden to eat are devoured here by vultures with iron teeth and beaks, O lowest of men. (41)
This is the well-known thirteenth, named Niyantṛka; it is completely pervaded by worms as well as by firm bonds.
O best of the twice-born, the sinful thieves of deposits are bound there with fetters and are devoured by worms, scorpions, insects, and other such creatures. (43)
Likewise, there is a hell named Caturdaśa situated with its face downward; among all the hells, this one possesses the most terrible form. (44)
And here, those men who are slayers of Brahmins are bound with their faces downward, suspended from the branches of trees, and cooked by fire from below.
O best of the twice-born, this great fifteenth hell, crowded with lice, bugs, gadflies, and the like, is known by the name Bhīṣaṇa.
I have provided refuge here for those who delight in false testimony, as well as for those who speak untruths and others who perform evil deeds. (47)
This sixteenth hell, named Kṣudrada, has been described; it is filled on all sides, O best of the twice-born, with men afflicted by the pains of battle.
Those twice-born ones by whom savory meats were eaten through sinful acts, remaining here, devour their own bodies while afflicted by hunger.
Likewise, this seventeenth hell is known as Kṣāra; it is filled with caustic lye and brings terror to all living beings. || 50 ||
Those men who violate their vows and those who are heretics—these worst of evildoers come here and are ground by sharp weapons.
And this eighteenth hell, named Nidāghaka, has been described; it is strewn with glowing embers and is difficult for all embodied beings to endure.
O twice-born one, those men who defile a scripture, a poem, a Brahmin, or a maiden remain here within glowing embers.
And this famous Kūṭaśālmali tree, O best of the twice-born, is twenty-one [yojanas] high and covered on all sides with extremely sharp thorns. || 54 ||
Atheists, those who have transgressed the bounds of propriety, and those who are slayers of Brahmins—all these men here constantly climb up and fall down.
O best of the twice-born, this is the twentieth hell, named Asipatravana, which is difficult for the wicked-minded to endure.
O Brahmin, those men who go here are lookers-out for the faults of others, those who are intent on fraudulent deeds, and those who sell the sacred scriptures. (57)
This is the twenty-first river, named Vaitaraṇī; it must be traversed by all men alike, whether they follow righteousness or sin. (58)
Those men who give a cow when the time of death has arrived, rely upon her tail and are easily delivered across [the ocean of existence].
O best of the twice-born, those mortals who die without having given a cow cross over this [river] by means of their hands and other limbs, even after traversing difficult passages.
O best of the twice-born, all this that I was asked by you—the nature of the hells—has been explained to you in detail out of affection for you. (61)
Therefore, go home quickly before your body is consumed by fire, while your kinsmen, afflicted with grief, take away your desired wealth.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Lord, if I am to go properly to my own home, then tell me by what action a man does not go to hell. (63)
Yama said: A man who is constantly devoted to pilgrimages, who honors the gods and guests, who is devoted to Brahmanas, and who provides refuge, does not go to hell. (64)
O twice-born one, he who is ever intent on helping others, constantly devoted to the recitation of mantras, and dedicated to the study of the Vedas, does not go to hell. 65.
The man who constantly constructs ponds, wells, tanks, and temples for the deities does not behold hell. || 66 ||
He who provides fire in the winter, likewise he who gives water in the summer, and he who provides shelter during the rains—such a person does not behold hell.
A man who is devoted to vows and fasting, whose mind is tranquil, whose senses are conquered, who is always celibate and meditative, does not go to hell. (68)
The man who provides food, especially one who gives sesame seeds, and who is devoted to non-violence, does not behold hell.
One who is perfected in the study of the Vedas, devoted to the scriptures, possessed of refined speech, and constantly intent upon the exposition of dharma—such a person does not behold hell. (70)
The Brāhmaṇa said: Even a fool knows this: a man who performs auspicious deeds does not go to hell, nor does one devoted to sinful actions go to heaven. (71)
Therefore, even a person of impure deeds, by whatever action he destroys his sin—even if it be very slight—goes from there swiftly to heaven.
O best of gods, tell me that vow or indeed that restriction, or the sacred ford, or the recitation and fire-oblation, which brings happiness to all the worlds. (73)
Yama said: O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim to you here a very great secret; it must be guarded with effort at all times according to my word. (74)
By performing which rite, even a man tainted by a great sin (mahāpātaka) does not go to a hell that causes suffering. (75)
In the region of Ānarta, there is the beautiful and auspicious sacred field born of Hāṭakeśvara, which consists of all holy fords and destroys even the greatest of sins.
In that regard, even he who worships Hara with devotion for just half a month, though he be possessed of all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 77 ||
Therefore, go there quickly and propitiate Śaṅkara, so that you may attain liberation along with ten generations of your lineage.
Sūta said: Having heard the instruction, he, filled with joy, set out toward the city of Mathurā for the sake of Dharmarāja. (79)
Just then, a messenger arrived carrying a second cow's ear; seizing it, he quickly showed it before Dharmarāja.
Then, seeing Gokarṇa standing before him as a second messenger set out for home, Dharmarāja spoke to that messenger with great joy: || 81 ||
"Since this Brahmin was brought by you after the appointed time had passed, therefore, quickly abandon him as well along with his companion. (82)
Then, at that very moment, those two Gokarṇa Brahmins were simultaneously liberated; having suddenly regained their respective bodies, they were once again united.
Then that first brahmin, Gokarṇa, who was well-versed in the instructions of Yama, related the matter in detail to the second one.
Then, having abandoned their home, both Gokarṇas remained there; for they had seen that the entire sacred field was pervaded by temples dedicated to the deities.
When the two of them had installed the Liṅga at the northern and southern boundary, they quickly reached the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara to engage in penance.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having propitiated Śiva and performed penance as was appropriate, they both attained heaven in their physical bodies through his power.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a vigil was observed by those two; the man who performs it with devotion goes to the abode of Śiva. (88)
A sonless man obtains sons, and one who desires wealth shall attain wealth; moreover, a man free from desire attains liberation—of this there is no doubt. (89)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, all this has been narrated to you in detail—the extent of this sacred field (kṣetra) and its boundaries in the four directions. (90)

In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, even those men who dwell here and are engaged in agricultural labor attain the supreme goal; how much more so those of self-restrained soul, who are peaceful, self-controlled, and have conquered their senses! (91)
Even insects, moths, beasts, birds, and wild animals that die in that sacred field go to the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt.
How much more so for those men who, having performed the fast unto death there, have renounced the world and are endowed with faith, with Janārdana dwelling within their hearts? (93)
Therefore, with every effort, that sacred field must indeed be resorted to, especially now that the Kali age, shrouded in sin, has arrived. (94)
All sacred fords undoubtedly purify through bathing and giving gifts; moreover, the holy field born of Hāṭakeśvara purifies by the mere act of residing there.
O twice-born ones, wherever there is water in ponds, wells, or tanks, a man who bathes there is liberated from all sins.
Of what use are sacrifices, of what use are futile gifts, what need for vows, or even for recitations? For those desiring heaven, it is better to have made their dwelling in that sacred field.
This greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara field is purifying, life-prolonging, auspicious, and destructive of sins for those who always listen to it. (98)
The sages said: O son of Sūta, tell us in its entirety the nature of the four yugas, their greatness, and their measurement, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, I shall now relate to you exactly what Bṛhaspati spoke in former times when he was questioned by Vāsava regarding this very matter.
In ancient times, while the high-souled Śakra was seated in the assembly hall together with the thirty gods, the deities sat in attendance upon him along with Śacī.
The Gandharvas and Apsaras, as well as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas; the Guhyakas, Kiṃnaras, Daityas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Uragas. || 4 ||
The divisions of time—kalās, kāṣṭhās, and nimeṣas—as well as the lunar mansions and the planets; the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs in embodied form, and likewise the sacred fords and shrines.
In that manner, they recounted various stories concerning the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas, as well as those of the ancient royal sages (rājarṣis) and especially the celestial sages (brahmarṣis).
Then, on a certain occasion, the Lord of the Thirty-three, endowed with humility, questioned Bṛhaspati, the best of Brahmins.
O Blessed One, I desire to hear the measure and the origin of the Yugas; you should explain their majesty and their true nature exactly as they are.
Bṛhaspati said: I shall proclaim to you the majesty arising from the ages; listen with focused attention to its measure and its essential nature.
It is said that the Kṛta age consists of seventeen lakhs and twenty-eight thousand years in its measure, wherein Janārdana is white.

The Dharma was established upon four feet, and the earth was perfectly abundant. The people there were liberated from desire and anger, and devoid of fear and hatred. They were long-lived, peaceful in soul, and had their senses mastered; they were five *tāla* trees in height, radiant, and deeply learned in the scriptures.
In that regard, childhood arises for human beings for sixteen thousand [years], and thereafter youth is said to last for exactly thirty-two thousand. (13)
After that, old age gradually arises for men; it lasts for up to one hundred thousand years at most, though for others it may be longer in some cases.
There, whatever beings there may be—beasts, birds, or wild animals—they speak with divine speech and do not fall into conflict. (15)
Snakes play with mongooses, cats with mice, lions constantly with deer, and even owls with crows.
And even unplowed, the earth produces an abundance of crops—primarily rice, mung beans, and barley—which are delicious and increase strength.
The trees bear fruit in all seasons, possessing both flowers and fruits; they have beautiful leaves, are devoid of thorns, and resemble the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
And cows provide the desired, sweet, and excellent milk; indeed, at all times, they bestow abundant clarified butter upon men. (19)
There, no woman is born as a widow, nor is she unfortunate; no woman is barren, nor deprived of sons, nor is she devoid of virtuous character. (20)
Just as birth occurs, so too does death arise for men in due course; a father never sees his son dead anywhere at any time.
For those people who have died there, rebirth as a preta does not occur; nor is there residence in hell, nor is there the affliction of disease anywhere. (22)
All those twice-born ones were masters of the Vedānta, constantly devoted to the study of their own Vedic texts, delighted by the exposition of the Vedas, and expert in the knowledge of Brahman.
And the Kṣatriyas, having with great devotion appointed a single king as their ruler, always enjoy the earth righteously by his command.
The Vaiśyas performed in abundance those activities worthy of the Vaiśya class, beginning with the tending of cattle as well as those arising from buying and selling.
O best of gods, with the single exception of serving the twice-born, those Śūdras performed no other action there, being endowed with supreme faith. (26)
There, no one was born as an outcaste (cāṇḍāla), nor was there anyone born of mixed castes; neither was there anyone impure, nor was a fifth caste seen upon the earth.
Men perform there sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, as well as vows, observances, and pilgrimages, solely without desire for reward.
O Thousand-eyed One, thus have I described to you this first, meritorious Kṛta Yuga, which brings happiness to all the worlds. (29)
Thereafter, the second age, known as Tretāyuga, proceeds for a duration of twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand years. (30)
He too, the manifest Lord of the World, who dwells in Śvetadvīpa, becomes red there, the Blessed One whose banner bears Garuḍa.
There, Dharma shall consist of three quarters, while sin occupies one quarter; even by that [sin], mutual rivalry arises among the social orders.
Then they desire the fruits arising from pilgrimage to sacred sites, as well as the results of vows and observances, which are the causes for dwelling in heaven and other such rewards. (33)
Then, under the influence of desire, all human beings fall into delusion; from delusion they proceed to malice, and thereafter they commit sin in succession.
Then, O Lord of the Gods, Yama himself prepares twenty-one hells, beginning with Raurava.
Following their karma, those lowest of men frequent those [worlds]; some others frequent the worlds of Mahendra and so forth, while others likewise seek liberation.
In this regard, O Lord of the Gods, there are three kinds of persons—the superior, the inferior, and the middling—and they perform three kinds of actions. (37)
Rising to the height of a palm tree and endowed with splendor and vigor, the Vaiśyas engaged in agricultural work out of a desire for food.
They reap that sown field even once and yet seven times; like trees bearing fruit according to the season, they are endowed with flowers according to the season.
There, trees endowed with foliage according to the season would be most enchanting; and sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others were performed there by the thousands.
O best of gods, these [sacrifices] are performed by the most excellent kings and by Brahmins who desire to attain the heavenly world, through their mutual rivalry with one another.
Desiring the world beyond, men perform pilgrimages, vows, acts of charity, religious observances, and self-restraint there. (42)
In that place, the youth of men lasts for a thousand years; beyond five thousand years, it is said to be old age.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker, as well as the fisherman, the Meda, the Bhilla, the Caṇḍāla, and the Śūdra man—[these are the lowest castes]. || 44 ||
O Lord, in that age there arise men who are censured for their lack of social interaction, as well as others who are devoid of number and inferior to these. (458)
Indra said: O best of the twice-born, how did the birth of these outcastes (antyajas) come about? Tell me this accurately and in its entirety; my curiosity here is great. (46)
Bṛhaspati said: O best of gods, the eightfold creation of these arises from the origin of the outcastes due to defects of the womb; I shall now clearly explain [the classification] by caste.
One born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is called a Sūta; from a Sūta is born a Rajaka, and from a Rajaka, a Carmakṛt.
From a leather-worker was born a dancer known as an outcaste (antyaja). These four were born from the fields of the twice-born. (49)
And so, O best of Maruts, Māgadha was born from a Vaiśya father in the womb of a woman of twice-born origin, through the seed of a Māgadha, becoming a Buruḍa.

The *buruḍa* from a fisherman, and the *medaka* from a fisherman—these four, O best of gods, are born of Vaiśya fathers in the wombs of twice-born men; they are despised in all their occupations. (51)
Likewise, O best of gods, from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, one known as a Bhilla is born; and from a Bhilla [father] and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Caṇḍāla is produced. (52)
O Lord of all the gods, both of these [offenses] occur when a Śūdra acts toward a field produced by the twice-born; this which I have spoken is the truth. (53)
This has been declared by me to you regarding the Tretā Yuga, O best of gods; now listen with diligence to the condition of the Dvāpara age.
That yuga is proclaimed to have a measure of eight hundred thousand years, with a total count of sixty-four thousand years; there, the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa is born as Kapiśa.
Two quarters of dharma and two quarters of sin are established; therein, the youth of men occurs when the entire hundred years have passed. (56)
Beyond that, five hundred others have passed away; there are the worlds of truth and falsehood, as well as gods, kings, and others.
O best of gods, women are also proclaimed to have that same form; they are five cubits in measure, and others are four cubits.
Neither endowed with excessive beauty nor devoid of form, even the beasts, birds, and wild animals speak in indistinct ways. (59)
O Lord of the Asuras, the trees there are not endowed with excessive flowers and fruits; yet, whatever grains are sown by farmers there, they grow abundantly.

The clouds rain as much as desired, and all medicinal herbs flourish; whatever knowledge or scripture exists on the surface of the earth, O best of gods, all that there is characterized by equanimity—neither true nor false. (61)
O best of gods, in the Dvāpara age, the fruit of sacred fords, sacrifices, and gifts arises in accordance with one's inner disposition.
This entire age known as Dvāpara has been fully described to you by me, O Lord of the Gods, exactly as it was seen and heard.
Listen now with an attentive mind as I speak: there is a fierce age called Kali-yuga, wherein Kṛṣṇa Janārdana [dwells].
O Lord, thirty-two thousand years have been described; likewise, [the duration] of the world of the virtuous is four hundred thousand [years], excluding the intermediate periods. 65.
In that regard, dharma is said to consist of one quarter, while sin consists of three; everything beyond the first half [of the age] will result in a downfall.
Sons do not listen to their father, nor do daughters-in-law, brothers, servants, or wives, where there is mutual hatred. (67)
In that place where men possess grey hair at the age of sixteen, there women shall conceive a child at the age of twelve.
O Lord of the Gods, the maximum lifespan for humans, for serpents, and for trees is one hundred years; it does not exceed that number of years. (69)
Thirty-two [mouthfuls] are prescribed for the best of horses, twenty-four for donkeys and camels, sixteen for goats, and twelve by number for dogs. (70)
For other quadrupeds, the number is twenty-five; there, crows, vultures, and long-lived owls dwell.

Likewise, people were devoted to evil and especially ill-situated; likewise, the trees were thorny, harsh, and bereft of flowers and fruit; even when resorted to, they were devoid of shade and frequented by vultures and other such creatures.
O best of gods, where indeed dharma is oppressed by adharma, and truth is likewise [oppressed] by untruth, and kings are always [oppressed] by thieves; 73.
Likewise, teachers [are deceived] by their disciples; the lowest of men by women; masters by their groups of servants; and even those of great learning by fools. (74)
Wherein dwell men who are most righteous, devoted to truth, self-controlled, discerning, tranquil, and likewise intent on the welfare of others. (75)
Mental anxieties, physical ailments, and likewise most extraordinary afflictions are always present there, with the desire to torment the virtuous. (76)
Likewise, mortals born from the intermixture of castes are short-lived; whoever among them do live at all are possessed by suffering. (77)
The cloud does not rain at the proper time, even when the season has arrived; nor does the crop fulfill the farmer's desire, even if there has been good rain. (78)
And even if cows that yield milk are well-nourished, they will not produce much [milk], even if they are carefully protected with great effort. (79)
Likewise, those worlds where the milk of ewes and camels is praised become devoid of splendor, as do those inhabited by thieves.
Likewise, there were Śūdras who were ascetics, Śūdras devoted to dharma, Śūdras who understood the deliberations of the Vedas, and Śūdras intent upon the performance of sacrificial rites. || 81 ||
Śūdras are the recipients of gifts, Śūdras are likewise the givers of charity; Śūdras are also to be honored, and Śūdras are established at sacred pilgrimage sites. 82.
At the time of death, the lowest of men, their consciousness destroyed by delusion, dig five pits with their heads, hands, and feet. (83)
Those Brāhmaṇas who sell the Vedas are devoid of purity.
They will be devoid of Vedic study, constantly intent on the food of Śūdras, generally accepting gifts from the unworthy, and eager for the greed of the tongue. (85)
Where affection arises toward heretics, those engaged in improper acts, and those who live off the wives of others, based on some purpose or motive; || 86 ||
O Thousand-eyed One, by no means whatsoever will all embodied beings—neither the twice-born nor any of the social orders—ever fall into the state of barbarians due to their own inherent nature.
Deprived of festivals and devoid of righteousness, constantly causing intermixture of castes, men will previously have been three and a half cubits tall at the beginning of the Yuga.
From that point they will undergo decline; yet in the Kali age, growth will occur, and at the end of that time, humans will become dwellers in caves.
Due to their smallness and rarity, they will be incapable of performing domestic duties; likewise, sacrifices and Vedic vows will become fruitless.
O Śatakratu, all religious observances, restraints, as well as mantra-practices and sacred fords, have been defiled by contact with barbarians.

Those who are devoid of their own true nature and likewise deficient in water, those practitioners of mantras who are contemptible, and those ascetics who are base—[these are the ones to be avoided]. (92)
There, those contemptible men will arise who, having abandoned even a man of noble birth who is endowed with beauty and youth, [will choose another]. (93)
Out of greed for wealth, men will bestow their daughters upon those who are contemptible; women will give birth to daughters who are eager for sexual pleasure.
Maidens will engage in union with men, and even women of noble birth will deceive their husbands. (95)
In all their undertakings, kings will be immoral; even when guarded with great effort, they will be merciless and will oppress the farmers. (96)
Out of greed for wealth, they will undoubtedly oppress the innocent; and even upon encountering a thief who deserves death, they will [spare him] out of greed for wealth.
In that age, they will abandon even one who acts with malice toward their lives; forsaking the duty of a warrior (kṣatradharma), they will nevertheless engage in battle.
Bṛhaspati said: "O best of gods, I have thus related to you all this without doubt: the characteristics and the measure of all four ages."
And whatever mortal, being always well-composed and devoted, shall proclaim this, he is surely liberated from sin from birth until the end of death. (100)
And whatever man should hear this with a mind purified by faith, he too shall undoubtedly be liberated from the sin born of that day. (101)
Sūta said: And in that assembly of the gods were present all the best of the twice-born, as well as all the sacred fords (tīrthas), beginning with Prabhāsa, in their embodied forms.
Having heard those words of the preceptor of the gods, they felt great fear in their hearts and spoke to the Lord of the Three Worlds: ||| 2 ||
"O Lord of the gods, if such an inauspicious age is to come, we shall meet our destruction and shall not remain in the three worlds. (3)
O Purandara, show us some place now; therefore, O Purandara, tell us of some dwelling place anywhere.

O Lord, O best of gods, relying upon which we shall lead through the terrible Kali age—[those things] untouched by barbarian men, endowed with power, whether in Pātāla, in the heavenly world, or in the mortal realm.
Having heard those words of theirs, Śatakratu, overcome with compassion, spoke once again to Bṛhaspati, the best of Brahmins.
"O Bṛhaspati, if you know of any place in the three worlds untouched by the Kali age, please tell me so that we may take refuge there among the sacred fords."
Having heard those words of Śakra and having meditated for a long time, Vṛhaspati spoke there, gladdening the holy fords that were terrified by fear.
There is a most excellent sacred field called Hāṭakeśvara, which came into being from the falling of the Liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods.
There, at that sacred ford, the wise and high-souled Viśvāmitra formerly performed austerities for the sake of King Triśaṅku.
Staying there, Triśaṅku, together with the king, was freed from sin; having cast off his status as a Caṇḍāla, he went to heaven in his own body.
There, in ancient times, that supreme holy ford was filled with dust by the fierce Saṃvartaka wind at the command of Śakra.
There, he himself as Hāṭakeśvara protects the region below, and in the Kali age, the god Acaleśvara protects the region above.
Indeed, due to the majesty of Hāṭakeśvara and that which arises from Acaleśvara, it is untouched by the Kali age for an extent of five krośas.
Therefore, let all the sacred fords (tīrthas) go there in their own portions; O Śakra, they shall have no fear of the Kali age there, without a doubt. (15)
O best of the twice-born, having heard those words of his, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) went at that very moment to that holy field known as Hāṭakeśvara.
Having prepared their sacred threads and established their own stations, all those best of the twice-born reached that field. || 17 ||
For this reason, that field born [there] is indeed most meritorious; it destroys even the greatest of sins for the sake of the god Hāṭakeśvara. (18)
The sages said: "O Sūta, this which has been recounted by you is most wonderful—that the confluence of all sacred fords (tīrthas) is proclaimed to be in that very field. (19)
O high-minded one, tell me in detail: do those sacred fords (tīrthas) located there possess only that much power? Tell me.
O highly fortunate one, we have a great curiosity regarding all of them—both by name, by location, and likewise by their power. (21)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) are situated, pervading the entire region of Hāṭakeśvara.
It is not possible to recount them even in hundreds of years, such as those belonging to the first Kalpa at the beginning of the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara.
O best of the twice-born, because of the great length of time, many holy fords (tīrthas) have established their residence in that auspicious field.
I shall proclaim to you those heretical doctrines and sacred abodes which lead to annihilation—of which I know the entirety along with their powers; listen with full concentration. (25)
O best of the twice-born, by the mere hearing of which a man is liberated from sin, as well as by meditation, bathing, giving gifts, and touch; (26)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, when all the holy fords (tīrthas) had thus been established, that sacred field attained renown across the entire surface of the earth.
Not far from there, sages of celebrated vows take up residence; likewise, kings accompanied by old age resort to that place for the sake of ascetic penance.
Likewise, those self-controlled ascetics bearing the marks [of their order], desiring spiritual perfection, resort from all sides to that sacred field which is the refuge of all holy fords.
O best of the twice-born, there exists a linga named Siddheśvara, which bestows all perfections upon men and grants perfection itself.
Having become weary of the surface of the earth, Śarva, the all-pervading and eternally auspicious Lord, has himself established himself in this sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara.
The Lord Hara himself has manifested in the form of a *liṅga*; through mere remembrance and sight, he is the eternal bestower of all spiritual perfections.
Because he was propitiated by a Siddha, he is remembered as Siddheśvara; indeed, due to that very boon, Hara remains stationed right here.
The man who beholds it with true devotion or touches it while pure, immediately obtains his desire, even if it be very difficult to attain.
In that place, hundreds of men have previously attained perfection on earth; some through seeing it, others through touching it, and still other men through prostrating before it.
Having approached Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the life span of one who recites his six-syllabled mantra endowed with faith increases.
For as many times as he recites the mantra, for that same number of days shall that mortal live beyond his [natural] lifespan; there is no doubt in this matter. || 11 ||
The sages said: "O Sūta, this which has been narrated by you is most wonderful; for a mortal man would live even longer than his allotted lifespan."
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you what was heard by me directly from the great-souled Vatsa as he was speaking concerning them.
Formerly, while I was living here in my father’s house, that sage named Vatsa, who possessed great splendor, arrived there before me.
Possessing the splendor of twelve suns, he was in the bloom of youth, rich in beauty in all his limbs like another Kāmadeva. || 15 ||
Then he was seen by my father and saluted with devotion; having offered him the guest-offering (arghya), my father, once he had rested, addressed him with humility.
Welcome to you, O best of Brahmins; from where have you come here? Let an instruction be given to me: what may I do for you as is appropriate? (17)
Vatsa said: "O Sūta, I wish to perform the ritual observances arising from the Cāturmāsya in your hermitage, provided that you will grant me your service."
Lomaharṣaṇa said: "O Brahmin, I shall undoubtedly carry out your command. I am blessed and I am graced, since you have come to my home. (19)
O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus, my father then said to me: "Indeed, you must always perform service for your calf."
Then, endowed with humility, I performed all his duties in their entirety, and he, in turn, recounted wonderful stories to me at night.
Having personally seen thousands of ancient royal sages, gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas, as well as islands and mountains.
Once, O best of the twice-born, at the conclusion of our conversation, curiosity having arisen, that brahmin was questioned by me with a mind filled with wonder.
O Blessed One, your body is delicate and you are in the prime of your youth; yet you deliver various and distinct discourses concerning the continents.
O Father, tell me in detail how the entire surface of the earth, together with the oceans, was beheld by you at such a young age.
Those islands, oceans, and mountains that have been described by you cannot be reached by mortals in any way, even in thought.
Curiosity has arisen here upon hearing such incredible words; therefore, you who speak trustworthy speech, proclaim the truth.
O Lord of Sages, is this the power of your asceticism, or is it the efficacy of your mantras, by which the entire surface of the earth has been seen by you?
"Or was it through the grace of the gods, or perhaps brought about by medicinal herbs? O dear one, tell me that most meritorious thing in full detail."
Then that sage, O best of sages, said to me with a smile: "This power of my mantra has truly been understood by you."
Every day, in the presence of Śiva, I recite one thousand and eight repetitions of the six-syllabled Śiva-mantra.

O Sage, because of that, my youth has become firmly established throughout the three periods of time; I possess knowledge of the past and the future, and my life is characterized by the dawning of happiness.
"O illustrious one, many thousands and millions of years have passed for me, yet my youth appears as if it were my very first. (33)
In this regard, O Mahāmati, I shall relate to you in detail how I attained success through the grace of Śaṅkara.
"For I am a Brahmin known by the name Vatsa on the surface of the earth; in former times, I was one who had mastered the Vedas and practiced various scriptures. (35)
At that very time, however, the excellent Apsaras Menakā arrived in the world of mortals by chance during the spring season. (36)
Then, wandering on, she reached that forest named Kāmyaka, which was rich with the songs of intoxicated cuckoos and filled with lovely trees.
There dwells a tiger among sages known as Devarāta, who is perfected in vows and sacred study, and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity. (38)
Seated on the bank of a river in a solitary forest, he was devoted to the worship of the deity, endowed with supreme faith and remaining all alone.
Then, while he was looking on, that woman of excellent complexion, afflicted by the heat and endowed with a divine form, entered the water naked. (40)
Then, at that very moment, the seed of that lord of sages was discharged upon seeing her, whose every limb was beautiful, as she had taken refuge in the midst of the water.
In the meantime, a very thirsty doe arrived; she drank all that semen mixed with water, leaving nothing remaining.
Then she too, by virtue of his power, conceived a human embryo; subsequently, in the tenth month, she gave birth to one whose seed was never in vain.
She gave birth to a daughter with radiant limbs and eyes like lotus petals right there in that holy water, near the hermitage of Devarāta.
Then that sage, having recognized through his own knowledge that she was born of his own power, was overcome with supreme compassion; he took her up and nurtured her.
Endowed with great affection and having performed the auspicious marriage rites, he diligently protected her in the forest from wild beasts.
He himself went a great distance into a forest infested with wild beasts and brought back for his sake fruits that were perfectly pure and excellent.
Remaining there, she grew and became renowned by the name Mṛgāvatī, like a digit of the moon in the sky during the bright fortnight.
Then, while wandering about, I beheld that fawn-eyed woman; at that very moment, I was struck in the heart by the arrow of love.
Having recognized that maiden, who was of the same caste and possessed a lovely smile, the sage went to her home with respect and then made his request.
"O Brahmin, give me this daughter of yours to be my wife, so that I may support her with food, clothing, and other necessities as if she were myself. (51)
Then, at that very moment, Sundarī was bestowed upon me by him according to the rite prescribed in the scriptures, under the lunar mansion presided over by Bhaga.
Then, after a few days had passed, she, having been married, was filled with great wonder; accompanied by her circle of female friends, she went out into the forest for the sake of gathering fruit.
Then, in that well-established forest covered with creepers, she placed her foot upon the head of a serpent hidden by the grass.
Bitten by him, that beautiful woman suddenly fell upon the surface of the earth; afflicted by the poison, she lost her life at that very moment.
Then her friends, having gathered together and being distressed by her sorrow, O son of a Sūta, recounted everything as it had happened while weeping. (56)
Then, having gone quickly and seeing her fallen upon the ground, I, wretched and distressed, uttered lamentations and wept with a piteous voice. || 57 ||
"This beloved of mine, with her large eyes, who was as dear to me as my own mind and life—she has died upon the ground; deprived of her, I have no desire to live. (58)
Therefore, today I shall go to the other world along with her; for one whose palace is bereft of his beloved, what is the fruit of life? (59)
Accompanied by sons, grandsons, daughters-in-law, and groups of servants, the houses of those householders shone; [without their wives], our houses did not shine. (60)
If this slender-limbed woman with sweet voice, whose eyes reach to her ears and whose hips are broad, does not live, I shall undoubtedly die.
O Sūta, descendant of a noble lineage, while I was thus lamenting, all my friends arrived and they too wept in their sorrow.
Having wept there for a very long time together with them, they prepared a great funeral pyre; then, having placed her upon it, the fire was set ablaze.
Then, taking me with great difficulty, they led me toward their own home as I wept, stumbled, and fainted at every step.
Then, at the end of the night, having risen with great haste, my soul overwhelmed by grief for my beloved, I went indeed to that very same forest.
Driven to madness by desire, wandering here and there, lamenting and afflicted by grief, he was in a forest devoid of people.
"O large-eyed one, where have you gone, leaving me in this desolate place? I shall not go home; it would only bring me sorrow, for you are merciless. (67)
At the touch of the rays of the dawn, this moon abandons its own luster, devoid of energy at the end of the night, just as I have been made by Fate.
This slender-bodied Sun, with his crimson orb, approaches; he will surely deliver to me news concerning you. (69)
The sun, pervading the sky, scorches me intensely; externally and internally there is desire—how shall I sustain my life? (70)
The lord of elephants approaches of his own accord, carrying her two breasts; having gone there, I shall ask him if he can describe that beloved to me. (71)
As I was thus lamenting, a great delusion came over me, for I was scorched by the rays of the sun and agitated by passion. (72)
As I wandered through that great forest, whatever tree or living being I saw there, I questioned it out of delusion. (73)
O elephant, if you have seen that young woman whose pair of thighs resembles your own tusks, like maces, then speak of her, having shown compassion toward me. (74)
"O jackal, if you have seen my beloved, whose lower lip resembles the bimba fruit, then tell me; it will bring you great benefit. (75)
Or else, O Bilva tree, tell me if my beloved, who is dear to me as my own life and whose breasts resemble bilva fruits, was seen by you wandering in the forest.
"My high-minded wife has limbs like your flowers; O Campaka, if you know her, tell me quickly. (77)
O Madhūka tree, seeing you, my beloved’s two auspicious cheeks—now pale in hue—have come to my mind as being equal to your flowers. (78)
The thighs of my beloved, who is slender-limbed, are clearly more delicate than even a plantain stalk; by this truth, I touch myself. (79)
"O deer, have you not seen my wife here in this forest? Her eyes are like yours—clear and adorned with kohl. (80)
Even a beast that eats grass, though very old and grown up in the forest—even such a creature does not find delight for a moment when abandoned by its beloved.

Even though born from the womb of a bird, the creator of the *kalāpa* (peacock-feather ornament) constantly displayed his body before his beloved for the sake of increasing the power of the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāmadeva).
This swan that is seen here remembers the female swan; its gait is not like that of my beloved. (83)
Truly, this bird, the cakravāka, is uniquely blessed, for he does not abandon his beloved cakravākī even for a single moment. (84)
This sound that is heard, causing confusion within me—is it produced by a cuckoo, or does it arise from my beloved? (85)
"Seeing me, this male deer flees, and the female deer follows behind him; likewise, my beloved used to follow after me as I ran in the past. (86)
"This elephant, by touching with his trunk my beloved who follows me with affection, causes me to remember my own dear wife. (87)
"Alas, my beloved, with eyes like those of a young deer and a complexion resembling molten gold! Why do you not recognize me as I wander here in this forest? (88)
Where is that devotion? Where is that affection? Where is that contentment? Where is that compassion, since you do not even address me as I speak so piteously? (89)
While I was thus lamenting, my friends arrived there, searching for my whereabouts in the forests and across the rugged terrain.
Then, O son of Sūta, I was addressed by them with eyes red with anger; rebuking me with harsh words, they said, "Fie on you! You are now possessed by lust! (91)
O deluded soul, why do you grieve for human life, which is not to be mourned? For even as you grieve, others will cause you to grieve.
You, we, and others—all living beings born upon this earth—shall all surely die; what cause for lamentation is there in that? (93)
Because she was not seen, your beloved was obtained; again, because she was not seen, she has gone out of sight. She is not yours, nor are you hers; why do you grieve in vain? (94)
There is no absolute cohabitation for anyone with anyone else—not even with one's own body, much less with other people who are in vain. (95)
Whether it be dead or lost, he who grieves for what is past obtains sorrow through sorrow and encounters two misfortunes. (96)
Having thus enlightened me and taken hold of me, they all repeatedly led me from that most dreadful forest to their home by means of the people [there]. 97.
Then, O high-minded one, as I was a householder remembering that beloved wife of mine, a very great anger toward the serpents arose within me.
Then, overcome by anger, I clearly made a vow concerning all serpents; hear that entire terrible declaration. (99)
From this day forward, if I do not kill with a blow of my staff any snake that comes within the range of my sight, then that sin shall certainly be mine. (100)
May the fate that awaits those who steal deposits and those who betray trust be mine, if I do not kill this snake that has come within my sight.

Whatever sin lies in the reviling of the virtuous and whatever in the killing of one's mother or father—may that sin be mine if I do not kill this serpent who has come within the range of my sight. (102)

May that sin which belongs to those who take pleasure in the wives of others and to those who kill living beings be mine, if I do not kill the serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (103)

"And may that sin which is spoken of for those who take pleasure [in harming others] and for those who administer poison be mine, if I do not kill the serpent once it has come within the range of my sight. (104)
May the sin of those who are ungrateful and those who steal the wealth of others be mine, if I do not kill this serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (105)
Whatever sin belongs to those who forge weapons and likewise to those who set fire [to dwellings], may that be mine if I do not kill the serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (106)
"May that sin which comes from breaking a vow, and that which comes from censuring those who observe vows, be mine if I do not kill the serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (107)

Whatever sin there is in the killing of a learned Brahmin, and whatever sin belongs to those who eat forbidden meat—may that sin be mine if I do not kill this serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (108)
May that sin which belongs to those intent on felling trees and those who inflict pain with arrows be mine, if I do not kill this serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (109)
"May the sin of heretics and that which belongs to atheists be mine, if I do not kill the serpent that has come within my sight. (110)
May the sin of those addicted to meat and liquor who feed upon excrement be mine, if I do not kill a serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (111)
"For those who are addicted to falsehood and who look for the weaknesses of others, that merit would be mine if I do not kill a snake that has come within the range of my sight. (112)
Whatever sin belongs to those who give false testimony or to those who hoard grain, may that be mine if I do not kill a snake that has come within the range of my sight. (113)
May that sin which belongs to those who delight in hunting and those who set snares be mine, if I do not kill the serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (114)

May that sin which belongs to those who constantly employ others for their own purposes and to those who live by honey be mine, if I do not kill a serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (115)
May that sin which belongs to those who live by catching fish and have never beheld the face of a god be mine, if I do not kill the serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (116)
When questioned in a dispute by those speaking with partiality—whether out of fear, greed, hatred, or even through desire—(117)
Whatever sin may belong to those merciless and evil-minded ones, may that be mine if I do not kill the serpent who has come within my sight. (118)
May the sin that belongs to those who sell their daughters and to those who associate with evildoers be mine, if I do not kill a serpent that has come within the range of my sight. (119)
"May that sin which is proclaimed for those who sell knowledge be mine, if I do not kill a snake that has come within the range of my sight. (120)
Having made this vow, O son of a Sūta, I was overcome with anger and seized a thick club for the purpose of slaying the wind-eaters (snakes). || 121 ||
From that time forward, having abandoned the livelihood of a Brahmin, I wander upon the earth with a staff as my weapon, searching for serpents.
Overcome by anger, I have slain many serpents—those of virulent poison and massive bodies, as well as others of middling and inferior strength. (123)
Once, having entered a dense forest armed with a staff, I saw there a very old water-snake lying asleep. (124)
Then, raising my staff which resembled the staff of Death in fury, just as I was about to strike him, that serpent spoke to me.
"O best of Brahmins, I have committed no offense against you at all; for what reason, then, do you seek to kill me out of such agitation, even though I am superior to you in age? (126)
Then, overcome by great indignation and remembering my wife Mṛgāvatī, I spoke to that serpent in the water with anger: "In the past, my beloved wife was destroyed by a snake. (127)

Therefore, out of that enmity, I shall slay the great Rākṣasas; today I shall lead even you to the abode of Vaivasvata. Having struck you with a blow of my staff, remember therefore that which is most dear to you.
Then, overwhelmed by great fear, he spoke to me again: "First hear our words, and then do what is appropriate."
"O Brahmin, those who bite humans here are other serpents; we are born of the waters, non-venomous, though appearing in the form of snakes. (130)
Even while he was speaking thus, O Sūta, I struck him with my staff with an unwavering mind for the purpose of slaying him.
Then, from the touch of the staff, at that very moment, the serpent became a great man, resplendent like twelve suns.
Having beheld that marvel, I was then filled with wonder; bowing deeply to him, I spoke aloud and respectfully, saying, "May you forgive me. (133)
"Who are you, O Lord, and what is this form made of serpents? Is this a curse from a Brahmin upon you, or is such play always your delight? (134)
Then that man, joyful and full of humility, spoke to me: "Listen attentively; I shall tell you my own account."
O Brahmin, in former times I was in the most excellent city of Camatkārapura; I was a youth of supreme splendor, wealthy, and possessed of great prosperity.
In that very same beautiful city, there is a meritorious temple of Śiva, adorned with banners, belonging to the god Siddheśvara.
Then, after some time, a festival took place there; the three worlds were made to resound by the sound of musical instruments. (138)
Then, sages of rigid vows arrived there by the hundreds and thousands for the purpose of beholding the god. (139)
The Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, and those who are Kāpālikas, as well as others who observe the Great Vow (mahāvrata) and are devoted solely to the worship of Śiva. || 140 ||
Some eat but once a day, others are without food, while others subsist on air; some drink only water, some eat only fruits, and others likewise feed on withered leaves.
Having saluted Maheśvara, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rule, they sat down before him and engaged in various kinds of conversation.
They were filled with joy for the ancient royal sages and the lords of the gods; likewise, many others as well were endowed with compassion and righteousness. 143.
Some there were dancing, while others were singing; the holy men, filled with devotion, played musical instruments in great abundance.
Other wealthy men, endowed with faith, bestow gifts upon the poor, the blind, the wretched, and especially upon ascetics. || 45 ||
While such a great festival was thus taking place there, full of magnificent splendor, I arrived along with many others, arrogant in my youth. (146)
Hating the vision of Śiva, his heart shrouded in darkness, he was incited by other very wicked men to destroy the festival procession. (147)
Taking up a water-snake of immense length and terrifying form, which was repeatedly licking its tongue and was overcome by extreme old age; (148)
Then, in that great assembly of people, he hurled it; seeing him, all the people fled, tormented by the fear of death.
There lived an ascetic named Suprabha, whose vows were highly praised; he was established in meditative absorption, enriched by excellent disciples, and had burnt away his sins through austerity.
One should hold the neck steady with effort—unwavering, very firm, straight, neither too rigid nor bent—and likewise the entire slender body-frame.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the directions, with the tip of the tongue motionless and placed against the middle of the palate; 152.
Beholding within the center of the whirlpool-lotus an eight-petaled lotus facing downwards, and situated in its central pericarp, the solar disc.
In the center of that [lotus] as well, he saw another man the size of a thumb, resembling twelve suns and possessing an inconceivable form.
Beholding Maheśvara, the Lord of Vaidyanātha, seated upon the lotus throne—whom they call the Imperishable, the all-pervading, and the all-knowing. (155)
Blameless, indivisible, and devoid of old age and death, with his entire body covered in horripilation, he has come under the influence of yogic sleep.
Drenched with tears of joy, his physical form with senses restrained, he retained the fivefold vital winds (vāyu-pañcaka) within his belly through constant practice.
Having joined the thumb and forefinger and placed them against his heart, as he sat there in that manner, that serpent [approached] his body.
He coiled his body around the motionless great-souled one. In the meantime, there was a disciple of his who was endowed with great austerity. || 159 ||
Known by the name Śrīvardhana and having exerted himself in the study of various scriptures, he saw his guru completely encircled by the coils of a serpent.
Perceiving me standing not far away and performing that task, he, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these harsh words.
"If I have ever performed arduous penance or constantly served my gurus, [may it be witnessed] by this pair of quivering lips and by this voice faltering with tears. (162)

"If Maheśvara has been meditated upon by me with a non-conceptual mind, by that truth let this wicked, sinful-souled, and lowest of Brahmins, who has insulted my guru, immediately take on such a body. (163)
Then, even as all the people were looking on and exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!", I attained that terrible state of a serpent at that very moment.
Then, having reached the conclusion of his meditative absorption, the self-restrained sage beheld a serpent of fierce appearance with two tongues situated upon his own body.
Then, seeing me in the form of a serpent, filled with great suffering, standing on the bank and terrified, as was everyone else at that time—
Then, having understood all of that with his eye of wisdom, the sage, overcome with compassion yet filled with indignation, spoke to his disciple Śrīvardhana.
"O disciple, you have not done what is pleasing to me by performing this deed; cursing a wretched Brahmin is not the duty of ascetics. (168)
Equanimous in honor and dishonor, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same, the ascetic—whose appearance is the same toward friend and foe—attains perfection. 169.
Therefore, O child, this Brahmin was cursed by you out of ignorance and due to your childish nature; however, at my command, he is now to be granted favor once again.
Then Śrīvardhana, overcome by indignation, prostrated before his own guru and stood with palms joined in reverence. (171)
Whether spoken by me out of ignorance or out of knowledge, whatever word has been uttered, it is exactly so; there is no doubt. Therefore, O Guru, maintain silence.
"O Guru, not even in jest have I ever spoken a falsehood; how much less so for your sake? Therefore, please observe silence. (173)
The sun rises in the west, the great ocean dries up, and even Mount Meru may crumble—but my word shall never be otherwise.
The teacher spoke again to that disciple with gentle words: "I know that your speech can never be otherwise than the truth."
"A disciple must always be diligently instructed, even if he has reached maturity; how much more so when you are still a child? Therefore, I speak to you repeatedly. (176)
No one can exhaust the merit previously accumulated by sages; for those devoid of the dharma of austerity, no higher destination exists. (177)
Forgiveness alone is declared to be the bestower of success, especially for ascetics.
Therefore, ascetics should conduct themselves by placing forbearance at the forefront.
One should not respond to evil with evil; this is the eternal wisdom. The evil-doer who commits sin is destroyed by his own self. (179)
One who, devoid of right knowledge, commits sin after sin, is burned and burns further; he destroys even that which was already destroyed. (180)
What merit is there in being kind toward those who do one good? Only he who is kind toward those who do him harm is praised by people. (181)
Having spoken thus to that disciple, he then said this to me, being endowed with supreme compassion, firm in his vows, and praised for his observance of those vows.
"O serpent, the word of my disciple shall not be otherwise; therefore, remain in your serpent-form for some time. (183)
The serpent said: "O best of sages, at what time will my curse come to an end? Grant favor to this wretched one, who was ignorant regarding the curse. (184)
Suvrata said: "O auspicious one, it is impossible to calculate the merit of him who performs even for a moment songs and other such acts in the temple of Śiva. (185)
And for him who creates an obstacle even for a moment during a great festival, the measure of that sin cannot indeed be determined by anyone.
Therefore, you wicked brahmin, you shall not attain liberation at all; O evil-minded one, because of your attachment to worldly talk, listen now to my words. (87)
Whoever, endowed with faith, should recite the six-syllabled mantra of Śiva, even the sin born of the killing of a Brāhmaṇa perishes for him. (188)
By the recitation of the six-syllabled mantra, a person washes away the sin born of ten days, as well as that produced over twenty years. (189)
Therefore, standing in the midst of the water, recite that mantra with devotion, by which even the sin committed in another birth goes to destruction. 190.
But when a brahmin named Vatsa strikes you with a staff while you are standing in the midst of the water out of anger, then you shall obtain liberation.
"Therefore, O serpent, go quickly from this place to a body of water. Having been addressed thus by me, that excellent sage became silent. (192)
Then, joined with suffering, I arrived here at this reservoir and remained constantly reciting the six-syllabled mantra. || 193 ||
"O best of Brahmins, by your grace I am liberated from my serpent-form; tell me quickly, therefore, what dear service I may do for you today. (194)
There is no doubt that you are he whom I have described by the name Vatsa; behold, this celestial chariot approaches me because of your excellent vows.
Then that serpent, assuming a divine form, was duly addressed by me: "O Blessed One, grant me some auspicious instruction. (196)
By this, may there arise for us no suffering born from the loss of what is dear, nor poverty, nor disease, nor defeat by enemies. (197)
Then that Supreme Person, full of eagerness, spoke to me again: "O best of the twice-born, the burden of your questions has been fully related by you to me. (198)
And this cannot be told in full detail now that the celestial chariot has arrived; therefore, O twice-born one, I shall speak to you in brief.
O Brahmin, this six-syllabled Śaiva mantra removes the inauspiciousness of men; you should recite it day and night according to your ability. (200)
Then, being liberated from all sins, you will undoubtedly obtain whatever you desire in your heart—whether it be heaven or even liberation.
Indeed, very great sin was committed by me at all times; yet, even so, through the majesty of the mantra, worlds of great prosperity have been attained.
One person, endowed with faith, bestows all kinds of gifts; another recites the six-syllable mantra—the fruit for both of them is equal. (203)
O twice-born one, another man may perform ablutions at all sacred fords, and yet another may chant the six-syllable mantra; the fruit obtained by both is equal. (204)
If another performs a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa penances as prescribed, and another chants the six-syllabled mantra, the fruit for both is equal.

A man who sleeps under the open sky during the rains, dwells in water during the winter, and practices the austerity of the five fires during the summer, [obtains the fruit] for as long as a hundred years.
Another mortal, pure and endowed with faith, who should mutter the six-syllable mantra day and night, is said to obtain a fruit equal to those two.
One person should always perform the Śrāddha rite at Gayā for the sake of the paternal ancestors, while another should mutter the six-syllabled mantra; the fruit obtained by both is equal. (208)
One person may give a thousand cows at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika; another may simply mutter the six-syllable mantra—the fruit for both of them is equal.
If one man bathes in the Saṃnihitī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, and another merely recites the six-syllable mantra, the merit of both is exactly equal.
Another, however, beholds Somanātha during the lunar eclipse; another mutters the six-syllable mantra—the fruit for both of them is equal. || 211 ||
One man may behold Caṇḍīśvara during the northern transit of the sun, while another may mutter the six-syllable mantra; the fruit for both is equal.
One person might cast himself down from a cliff out of devotion upon seeing Kedāra, while another might recite the six-syllable mantra; the fruit for both of them is equal. (213)
One person may accomplish the task by means of dried cow-dung after first offering all his possessions; another may recite the six-syllable mantra—both obtain an equal result.
One person, having renounced all attachments, may attain knowledge alone; another may recite the six-syllable mantra—the fruit for both of them is equal. (215)
O Brahmin, this supreme secret has been proclaimed by me; it must not be given to an atheist, nor indeed to one who is devoid of devotion. (216)
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, I shall speak further out of a desire for your welfare; act upon my words today if you wish for the supreme goal. (217)
Non-violence is the supreme dharma proclaimed in all the Vedas; it is especially so for a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, abandon the killing of snakes. (218)
He who, being utterly merciless, harms living beings that are non-violent, goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
He who grants fearlessness to all beings, both moving and unmoving, becomes enriched with every happiness, both in heaven and here on earth.
There is no god equal to Bharga; there is no river equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no sin equal to violence; and there is no dharma superior to compassion. (221)
Then, hearing those words he had spoken, I—being distressed by the fear of the next world—spoke to him regarding the Dharma characterized by non-violence (ahiṃsā). || 222 ||
"I have heard this saying among the elders: 'There is no fault in a king for the deer slain in the forest. (223)
Likewise, physicians who are experts in the science of medicine declare: "Meat-eaters become endowed with nourishment and live for a long time. (224)
Therefore, in this matter, speak words concerning the supreme highest good; I shall undoubtedly do everything that has issued from your mouth.
Then he spoke to me again: "Do not say so, O best of the twice-born; this is the view of the wicked who are greedy for meat."
"Alas! Most pitiable in this world are those sinful and utterly merciless men, the fools who consume meat, which is a mine of all defects. (227)
Meat is not the cause of longevity, nor of health, nor of strength; all of this would be false. Listen now to an illustration. (228)
Even those who eat meat are seen to be afflicted by disease, weak, and short-lived; realizing this, avoid meat from afar. (229)
Even those on this earth who do not eat meat are seen to be free from disease, long-lived, and possessed of robust limbs; therefore, one should avoid meat.
He who eats the flesh of beings who desire to live goes to a terrible hell, and staying there, he is devoured by them. (231)
For meat does not arise from grass, wood, or even stone; meat comes only when a living being has been killed. Therefore, one should avoid it. (232)
This indeed is the illustration regarding the total avoidance of meat: even a limb of one's own body that has been pierced by a thorn is [treated with care]. (233)
Therefore, all living beings should be viewed by the wise through the analogy of oneself; they must not be harmed, but protected according to one's ability. (234)
The killer, the one who consents, the butcher, the buyer and seller, the preparer, the server, and the eater—these eight are the slayers. (235)
The buyer destroys by means of wealth, the eater destroys by means of consumption, and the slayer destroys by means of killing and binding; thus, there is another threefold destruction. (236)
He who harms nothing by deed, mind, or speech attains the supreme state, which is free from old age and death. || 237 ||
Even if a man subsists on vegetables, roots, and fruits and is devoted to the practice of celibacy, he does not obtain its fruit if he is intent upon violence.
One who practices difficult austerities for more than a full hundred years is surpassed by that other who is devoted to non-violence; the latter, endowed with compassion, is superior to the two.
Whatever desire a person may long for, even if it is difficult to attain, he obtains it without doubt, provided he is endowed with great compassion. (240)
Served by hundreds of celestial women, he rejoices in heaven like a god, traveling in a chariot that moves at his will, bestowing fearlessness upon all beings. (241)
Having spoken thus, O son of a Sūta, that great-souled one, while I was looking on, ascended an excellent celestial chariot and departed for the abode of the gods.
O high-minded one, he was being sung of by the Gandharvas and praised by the Kinnaras on account of the majesty of the six-syllable mantra. (243)
When he had gone to heaven, sorrow then came upon me; remembering the snakes previously slain, my limbs then became broken. || 244 ||
Then, terrified by the fear of my own karma, I uttered many lamentations right there in that great forest. (245)
"Alas! By me, a cruel man, many living beings have been slain; Mahādeva has been reviled, and I shall incur infamy among men. (246)
Therefore, having abandoned violence, I shall perform great austerity; having received initiation from Śiva, I shall worship Maheśvara.
Whatever happiness men in the three worlds desire, all that is to be accomplished through austerity; therefore, austerity must be practiced by me.
"Now, alone, I shall wander through these hermitages as a silent sage, subsisting on alms from each individual tree."
Covered all over with dust, taking shelter in empty dwellings or making his home at the foot of a tree, he has abandoned everything pleasant and unpleasant. (250)
Having lamented thus with effort, O upholder of the Sūta lineage, I then took up the vow of Śiva-initiation, filled with devotion.
Endowed with faith, I recite the six-syllable mantra ten thousand times at the three junctions of the day in the presence of Siddheśvara. (252)
By its power, O son of a Sūta, stability born of youth has arisen within me, as well as knowledge of the worlds beyond and the ability to travel through the air.
When the Dvāpara age has come to an end, I shall go to Siddheśvara; I shall attain Sadāśiva—this which I have spoken is the truth. (254)
All this, O son of Sūta, has been narrated by me to you—the greatness of the six-syllabled mantra, which bestows liberation and destroys all sins. (255)
And that man who should constantly hear this, endowed with perfect faith, shall be liberated from sin from birth until death. (256)
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, you should indeed constantly recite this mantra; you will always attain the supreme desires cherished by your mind.
Sūta said: This greatness of the six-syllabled mantra, which has been proclaimed to you, was previously heard by me from that true guru. (258)
It brings wealth, fame, and long life; it causes the destruction of the enemy faction; and for those who constantly recite or listen to it, it bestows all desires and fearlessness. (259)
The sages said: By which Siddha was the omnipresent Lord Siddheśvara propitiated there? O son of Sūta, explain all of this to us in detail.
Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a lord of the Siddhas known as Haṃsa; because he was childless, much time passed for him.
Then, overcome with anxiety, he went to the divine priest, Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras and the best of Brahmins, and questioned him.
"O Blessed One, old age has come upon me who am childless; therefore, proclaim to me a means for the attainment of offspring. (4)
