"O best of the twice-born, O Bṛhaspati, by what means—whether a pilgrimage to sacred fords, a religious vow, or a rite for peace—may offspring be swiftly obtained through your grace?"
Then Bṛhaspati, having meditated for a long time, spoke to the Siddha: "Go to the sacred field of Camatkārapura and perform penance there."
"Then you shall obtain an auspicious and virtuous son capable of uplifting your lineage; O Lord of Siddhas, I see no other auspicious means for obtaining a son."
Then, having reached that sacred field, that perfected one (siddha), endowed with faith, personally worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rite.
Then, unwearied by day or night, he propitiated [the deity] with offerings of oblations and worship, and with the excellence of songs, instrumental music, and other such rites.
O best of the twice-born, he gratified Śaṅkara with Cāndrāyaṇas, Kṛcchras, Pārākas, and likewise with month-long fasts.
Then, at the end of two thousand years, Maheśvara, being pleased with him, appeared before his eyes and spoke, mounted upon his bull together with Umā.
"O Haṃsa, I am pleased with you today; therefore, ask for whatever you desire. I shall certainly grant it to you, even if it is difficult to attain."
The Haṃsa said: "O Lord, an endeavor for the sake of offspring was previously undertaken by me; therefore, grant me sons who shall uplift my lineage. (13)
"And you, O best of gods, must always remain here in this linga at my word, without doubt, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds. (14)
The Blessed Lord said: "From this day forward, O Siddheśa, by your word, this Liṅga shall be my abode; this which I have spoken is the truth. (5)
Whatever mortal shall worship me with devotion while I am stationed here, I will bestow upon him the entire fruit residing within his heart.
To whoever stands facing the southern direction of my linga and recites the mantra, I shall grant the six-syllabled mantra along with long life and sons. (17)
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva then vanished from sight; and Haṃsa, having gone home, obtained sons of great excellence.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, with every effort, that Liṅga should be diligently touched, worshipped, and saluted with great care. (19)
And it should be recited according to one's ability with the six-syllabled mantra by those desiring the objects of their wish, even those difficult to obtain for the gods themselves. (20)
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another unsurpassed sacred site there called Nāgatīrtha, where for one who has bathed, no fear of serpents arises anywhere.
In that regard, whatever man should perform a ritual bath on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, there shall never be any fear of serpents anywhere even within his family.
There, in former times, Śeṣa and the other Nāgas, tormented by their mother’s curse, performed austerities for the sake of liberation from the fire.
The two nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, likewise renowned upon the surface of the earth, having performed intense penance there, attained supreme perfection.
Ananta, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka of great strength; Karkoṭa the lord of nāgas, and likewise Maṇikaṇṭha as another. || 5 ||
Airāvata, Śaṅkha, Puṇḍarīka, Mahāviṣa, and the others beginning with Śeṣa—these nine Nāgas are remembered here as the leaders.
Their sons and grandsons, along with their countless manifestations, have pervaded this entire surface of the earth.
Then those crooked and wicked ones constantly devour people, both through their great numbers and through mere contact, even without any offense.
Then all these creatures, being oppressed, went for refuge to Brahmā: "O best of gods, we are afflicted; protect us quickly from the serpents! (9)
Until the entire surface of the earth became empty, it was pervaded by all those most terrifying serpents, full of virulent poison.
Then Brahmā spoke to those nine leaders, Śeṣa and the others: "Protect your own progeny while these creatures are being devoured."
Having promised "So be it," all those serpents departed.
Moreover, because of their great number, no protection at all was produced; for even though they were forbidden, they continued to cause the destruction of the subjects. || 13 ||
Then, his soul overcome with anger, Brahmā himself summoned those lords of the clans and spoke to them in the assembly of all the gods.
Since these serpents devour the subjects even without any offense, and despite being restrained, I shall therefore subdue them now.
Janamejaya shall become a protector of the earth on this world; at his sacrifice, the Fire-god will consume the serpents.
Especially due to their mother’s curse, those who have been summoned by mantras by the best of the twice-born shall fall of their own accord into the well-kindled fire.
Having heard that, those nine leaders of the serpents, trembling with fear, immediately prostrated before the Grandfather and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O Blessed One, our kin have been made crooked by you; why then do you show anger toward those who merely follow the nature of their birth? (19)
Brahmā said: "If indeed you were created by me, then by good fortune you are full of poison; why, without any offense, do you devour these creatures?"
The Nāgas said: "O Lord of Gods, establish a boundary between us and human beings; or else, grant us a place entirely devoid of humans. (21)
"In that sacrifice of Parikṣit, devise a means of protection for the serpents who are being consumed on all sides by the fire."
O Great-grandfather, you ought to act in such a way that the continuity of our lineage is not severed throughout all the worlds. (23)
Brahmā said: "There shall be a twice-born man known as Jaratkāru; for the sake of progeny, he will search for a wife upon the earth."
And there shall be a very beautiful young maiden born in your lineage; that woman of excellent complexion should be respectfully given to him for the sake of obtaining a son. (25)
The son who shall be born from them will protect the remaining serpents, who are pure in conduct and established within the bounds of propriety.
Sutala, Nitala, and likewise Vitala—your residence shall be on the fourth level of the earth, situated beneath those.
Since it has been granted by me—extremely beautiful and endowed with every enjoyment—therefore, depart for that very place, leaving the surface of the earth behind.
Go quickly there at my command and enjoy excellent pleasures, together with your sons and grandsons—pleasures that are difficult even for the gods to obtain. (29)

The Nāgas said: "O Lotus-born One, even while enjoying our coils, we are unable to dwell upon this earth; therefore, show us a place where, remaining there, we may live together with human beings according to the established order. (30)
Brahmā said: "This lunar day has been granted by me to you upon the surface of the earth; however, the remaining time, the fifth [tithi], is to be spent there in Rasātala."
Those who have arrived there must not harm men who are free from fault, whose limbs are protected by mantras, and upon whom medicinal herbs have been applied with care.
O best of Nāgas, in the sacred field of Camatkārapura, I have eternally granted a dwelling for the foremost of the Kula-Nāgas upon this earth.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, those leading Nāgas quickly departed for Pātāla, remaining established in that sacred field.
In that regard, the man who worships them on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa attains his desired object through their very grace. || 35 ||
In his lineage as well, there shall be no fear of serpents nor any sin; neither disease, nor calamity, nor fear of spirits shall exist anywhere.
He who, being childless, performs a śrāddha there with the desire for a son, indeed becomes free from his debt to the ancestors upon obtaining an excellent son.

Likewise, even a woman who is barren, if she performs a ritual bath on the fifth lunar day at sunrise during the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa—especially so—she immediately obtains a son capable of uplifting her own lineage. (38)
One who has been deprived of his kingdom, or any man whatsoever, should perform a bath there; he shall become free from all diseases, possess a beautiful form, and be endowed with discipline. (39)
Then, on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, he worships the Nāgas; having destroyed all hosts of enemies, he shall regain his kingdom once more. (40)
For those men whose death occurs from being bitten by a snake, there is no liberation whatsoever from the state of a preta.

O best of the twice-born, as long as the Śrāddha is not performed at that Tīrtha, therefore, with every effort, a Śrāddha must be diligently performed at that Tīrtha where snakes are found, for the sake of one who has died from the bite of a snake.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an auspicious story of the past, concerning the royal sage Indrasena, which destroys all sins. (43)
In former times, there was a protector of the earth named Indrasena, who destroyed the pride of his enemies; that high-souled one performed a thousand horse sacrifices.
Then, by the turn of fate, while sleeping on his auspicious bed, King Indrasena was bitten by a serpent; though he survived the bite, he was suddenly deprived of his life at that very moment.
Then his beloved son performed all the funeral rites for him with devotion, exactly as prescribed in the Smṛtis.
Having cast his bones into the Gaṅgā and performed the sixteen śrāddhas, he then went to Gayā and, endowed with faith, performed the śrāddha ceremony.
Then, having encountered him in a dream, that father, the king, spoke in distress to his son, whose eyes were clouded with tears.
"O son, because of my death by snakebite, the state of a preta has been established for me; therefore, nothing given by you reaches me. (49)
Therefore, my son, go quickly to the sacred field of Camatkārapura; perform a śrāddha rite for the serpents at that holy site on my behalf.
By which my liberation from this dreadful state of a preta might be brought about—he, having risen in the morning and recalled those words of the king, [acted accordingly].
Afflicted by suffering in the form of a preta, he went quickly to that sacred ford and then performed a śrāddha ceremony on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

Having bathed and being endowed with faith, he established a domestic priest; then he was seen once again just as before. Afflicted by grief, he spoke these words in the form of a ghost: "Nothing has been achieved by me for what you have done on my behalf."
Listen, my son, to the fruit of the śrāddha and its cause here: the Brāhmaṇas worthy of the śrāddha here are those born in Camatkārapura. (55)

Even those who are censured for being physically impaired and so forth when performing a *śrāddha* elsewhere are not so here; for whatever gift or even vow is performed here [at this sacred field], [it is highly meritorious]. (56)

Likewise, any other rite worthy of Brahmins originating from sacrifice—even if it is incomplete—shall become entirely perfect through their word; however, if performed in their absence, it clearly becomes futile. || 57 ||
Therefore, having summoned Brahmins from this city, perform thereafter a Śrāddha ceremony in my name, so that liberation may be attained.
Then, having risen in the morning and remembering his father's words, he entered that supreme city, overcome with great sorrow.
Thereupon, the king searched for Brāhmaṇas worthy of the Śrāddha rite; yet, despite his efforts, he did not find any, because the Brāhmaṇas were all wealthy men.
There, no one was suffering, nor was even a poor person distressed; there was neither one devoted to improper action nor one devoted to heresy.
In every place there were great sounds and festivals in every house; likewise, there were the delights of Vedic learning as well as discourses on the Smṛtis.
And it is heard that among the performers of sacrifice, there arise no famines, no diseases, and no untimely death for men; nor does death come to anyone in that city frequented by Brāhmaṇas. (63)
The rain-cloud pours forth rain according to the season, and the crops are of excellent quality; the cows yield abundant milk, as do the goats and sheep. (64)
Whichever Brahmin that lord of the earth invited for the sake of the śrāddha, he would, filled with anger, revile him with harsh words.
"Fie, fie upon you, O performer of sinful deeds, you who are the lowest of Kṣatriyas! Does any Brāhmaṇa ever eat at a funeral śrāddha, especially one for a deceased person? (66)
Therefore, go quickly, O twice-born one, before some [other] brahmin falls [into this state] or, out of great wrath, slays one who obstructs the path to heaven. (67)
Sūta said: Thereupon, that king, distressed and afflicted by fear, departed from that city of Camatkārapura, having fallen into a state of extreme embarrassment.
O Indra among kings, remembering that state of his father, he reflected: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my father attain a favorable destination? (69)
Then, having sent all his ministers toward home, he remained right there in that excellent city alone, in the guise of a mendicant.
Having learned that in that city there was a brahmin of celebrated vows, who was the recipient of the hospitality of all the foremost brahmins; || 71 ||
He was named Devaśarman, compassionate toward those who sought refuge, a maintainer of the sacred fires, learned in the four Vedas, and a follower of the path of the Smṛtis.
Then, having risen in the morning and assumed the body of an outcaste, he cleaned the latrine with great difficulty.
Then, he who was performing the work of cleaning the excrement there approached him and spoke these words, his eyes bloodshot with anger: || 74 ||
"From where have you come here, you who cause an obstruction to my livelihood? Therefore, depart quickly; otherwise, I shall send you to the abode of Yama. (75)
Even as he was speaking thus, that lord of the earth quickly and by force had that place where Devaśarman had arisen cleared out.
Then, at the end of a year, O best of the twice-born, that Caṇḍāla, having prostrated from a distance, spoke to him at the appropriate time.
"O Master, even in your own family there is one who performs such work as cleaning away excrement; therefore, that was neither for us nor for anyone else—why then was another person brought in? (78)
Then, having heard those words, that best of the twice-born said: "No one else has been appointed by me here for the secret task; you must exercise your own authority just as before. (79)
Then, when another day had arrived, that outcaste, filled with rage, took up a weapon and came forth for the purpose of killing that king.
Seeing him with a weapon raised in his hand and determined to strike, he then again struck him effortlessly on the head with his fist.
Then, O twice-born ones, as soon as his eyes had come out, blood flowed forth and he immediately fell down, deprived of life.
Hearing that his own servant, the Caṇḍāla, had been killed by him, Devaśarman approached in great anger for the purpose of slaying him.
Then, accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and other kinsmen, he struck him with clods of earth, rebuking him again and again.
Being thus beaten and reduced to a state of exhaustion by the blows, he then uttered the Vedic chants, displaying his sacred thread.
Then all those brahmins, led by Devaśarman, were filled with wonder as they gazed upon him who was wholly devoted to the chanting of the Vedas.

And he was asked: "What is this work of yours, which is fit for a person of the lowest caste? This speech, consisting of the Vedas, with its clear syllables and melodious sound—is it that you are some excellent Brāhmaṇa who has fallen [from his status] due to a curse? (87)
"Since you perform such a deed that is despised even by the outcastes," he replied with a laugh, "I am a Kṣatriya, a lord of the earth, known as Viṣṇusena, born of the lineage of the Haihayas. (88)
I have come to this place for the purpose of propitiating you; today one year has passed since I took delight in this practice.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, that brāhmaṇa, filled with compassion, joined his palms in reverence and spoke to the lord of the earth.
With what purpose in mind was this censurable deed committed by you? Tell me so that I may quickly accomplish your desire.
"O Lord of the Earth, there is nothing that I have not attained, nor is there anything impossible for me to accomplish; therefore, I shall perform your task, even if it be difficult to achieve. (92)
The king said: "My father was bitten by a serpent and has passed away into the state of a preta. If a śrāddha is performed here at this Nāga-hrada, he may attain liberation. (93)
Therefore, for the sake of crossing over that [state], perform an act of hostility; it was for this purpose that this censurable deed was committed by me against you. (94)
Devasharman said: "Do so, O best of kings; at your father's śrāddha, I myself shall become the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, perform the śrāddha. (95)
Sūta said: Then his friends, sons, grandsons, and kinsmen said, "This śrāddha offered by you is unfit; it is censurable for us to eat."
Therefore, if you are the one who eats at his funeral feast (śrāddha), then we shall all abandon you, as will the other most excellent brahmins.
Devasharman said: "O all of you, and whatever other twice-born ones there may be, abandon me at your pleasure; by me alone has it been promised that I shall eat at this king's śrāddha. (98)
Having spoken thus, that lord of brahmins, accompanied by him, then reached the serpent-lake and partook of food at the śrāddha ceremony.
Immediately after he had finished eating, an unembodied voice spoke, making the entire world resound and gladdening the lord of the earth.
"Delivered from the state of a preta by your power, I am now your son; may it be well with you, I shall now depart for the abode of the gods. (101)
Having performed that, the king, being delighted, bowed to that best of the twice-born and said: "O best of the twice-born, carry out my word, whatever I tell you."
"There is a city named Māhiṣmatī on the bank of the Narmadā; that is our ancestral capital, O Lord. (103)
"O Brahmin, I shall grant you this entire realm with all its objects of enjoyment; remaining there with me as your servant, rule the kingdom free from all thorns."
Devaśarman said: "It is not fitting to say this; a Brahmin does not deserve a kingdom. Therefore, O King, go and protect your own realm. (5)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been thus dismissed by him, that great lord, filled with joy and having accomplished his purpose, went to his own country.
He too was abandoned by all the Brahmins residing in the city, who pointed to Devaśarman as the source of the fault arising from the Śrāddha.
Then, having made his own dwelling in that Nāga lake, he took up residence there, pure and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
O best of the twice-born, those who were the sons of him who was expelled while residing there, their lineages even today are called the Bāhyavāsins.
O best of brahmins, all this has been narrated to you—the majesty arising from the Nāga-tīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Whoever recites this with devotion, or listens to it, when the fifth day has arrived, there shall be no fear arising from serpents even within his lineage.
Likewise, O Brahmins, one is liberated from the sin arising from eating [forbidden food] that was done through ignorance; of this there is no doubt. This which I have spoken is the truth. (112)
Therefore, with every effort, this unsurpassed Nāga-tīrtha should be read about or heard by those who are composed in mind. 113.
When the time for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) has arrived, the twice-born who recites this obtains the entire fruit arising from a śrāddha performed at Gayā. || 114 ||

Likewise, those defects which have been proclaimed regarding the *śrāddha* arising from the materials, as well as those arising from deficiencies in the vows and those arising from the Brahmins; || 115 ||
All those go to destruction when the greatness of Nāgahrada is being recited with concentrated minds at the arrival of the time for the Śrāddha rite. || 116 ||
Likewise, those slain by cows, by Brahmins, or even by beasts of prey, attain the supreme goal when this Śrāddha is recited. (117)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, there is likewise another [place] in that auspicious field, the highly renowned hermitage of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), which grants all desires. || 1 ||
In that place, on the fifteenth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the man who performs his bath with a concentrated mind shall obtain his desired fruit.
Whoever performs a Śrāddha ceremony there with bulbs, roots, fruits, and vegetables, obtains the full fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.

O twice-born ones, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, he who worships them all with devotion using flowers, incense, and ointments according to this rite and in their proper order, O best of Brahmins— (4)

Oṃ, salutation to Atri. Oṃ, salutation to Vasiṣṭha. Oṃ, salutation to Kaśyapa. Oṃ, salutation to Bharadvāja. Oṃ, salutation to Gautama. Oṃ, salutation to Kauśika. Oṃ, salutation to Jamadagni. Oṃ, salutation to Arundhatī. This is the mantra for worship: "O Sages, who grant all desires, whose limbs are purified by the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā), and who hold prayer beads in your hands—accept this *arghya* offered by me. (5)
The sages said: O son of Sūta, at what time was the sacred ford established there by the Seven Sages? Tell us in detail, for our curiosity is great.
Sūta said: In ancient times, a twelve-year drought occurred in the world; all medicinal herbs were destroyed, and consequently, the people were afflicted by ruin.

Reduced to mere skeletons, devoid of energy, and having abandoned their religious duties, vows, and rituals, they were intent on eating what is unfit for food and likewise drinking what is undrinkable.
Mothers abandon their sons, and likewise men abandon their wives; even masters of wealth abandon their own servants—what then to say of those born of others?

O twice-born ones, the agnihotra sacrifices were abandoned by the brahmins and even by the officiating priests; the vows were abandoned by the self-controlled practitioners of vows, even by those who were most venerable among the twice-born.
And wherever grain is seen in any way whatsoever, it is seized by men devoid of shame who are emaciated by hunger. (11)
Thus, when the food supply was exhausted and the surface of the earth was afflicted, the seven sages, overcome by hunger, wandered here and there.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa of great asceticism; Bharadvāja, and another, Gautama of rigid vows; Kauśika, Jamadagni, and likewise the virtuous Arundhatī. (13)
Then Caṇḍābhū became the attendant of all of them, as did Paśuvaktra, who was endowed with humility and served as their servant.
Then those sages, exceedingly emaciated by hunger, reached the territory of King Vṛṣādarbhi in the region known as Ānarta.
There, wandering from house to house for the sake of alms, those best of the twice-born did not obtain even a single mouthful of grain.
Then, seeing the dead boy fallen upon the ground, they consulted among themselves and subsequently seized him for devouring.
While they were cooking him in the fire, being tormented by hunger, King Vṛṣādarbhi arrived upon hearing of their deed.
Vṛṣādarbhi said: "O best of sages, what is this despicable act being performed? This eating of human flesh is the dharma of Rākṣasas. (19)
Therefore, I shall provide you with grain—villages, rice, and even barley. At my word, abandon this dead child without hesitation.
The sages said: "O King, you have prescribed an expiation for the eating of human flesh, but not for accepting gifts even in times of distress, O Ruler. (21)
"Afterwards we shall perform penance arising from [the eating of] human flesh; we shall destroy that sin and then consume it. (22)

Vṛṣādarbhi said: "Acceptance of gifts is declared to be the irreproachable means of livelihood for the twice-born; therefore, all of you should accept it from me—no hesitation should be made in this matter. (23)

The sages said: "O King, accepting gifts from a monarch is terrible; it has the taste of honey but is like poison. It should be avoided from afar by Brahmins, and especially so by those who are wise. (24)
An oil-presser is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a liquor-distiller is equal to ten oil-pressers; a prostitute is equal to ten liquor-distillers; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes. (25)
Accepting a gift from a king is equal to ten thousand slaughterhouses; who would accept such a thing, except for a brahmin overflowing with greed? (26)
He is cooked in all the hells, beginning with Raurava; therefore go home, O King, and may there always be well-being for you. (27)
"We shall go elsewhere; we will not take your wealth. Having spoken thus, all those sages of celebrated vows [departed]. (28)
Having abandoned both that prince and the deceased king, they then departed toward the sacred field of Camatkārapura.
O best of the twice-born, having been thus rebuked by them, that king was filled with great wrath; then, for the sake of testing them, he performed a ritual act.
Then, having filled the udumbara fruits with gold, he scattered them all around on the ground in front of their path.
Sūta said: Then those sages, seeing the udumbara fruits fallen upon the surface of the earth, took them up, being afflicted by hunger.
Then, having observed those heavy objects, O best of sages, Atri broke open one of them; seeing the gold within, he spoke.
Atri said: "O sages, we possess no ignorance, nor do we have the mindset of householders; knowing these to be made of gold, how could we accept these udumbara fruits? (34)
Therefore, having abandoned these figs from afar, though they contain gold within, we shall go toward the *udumbara* fruits, free from all longing.
One is a sovereign ruler of the earth, while the other is desireless; of these two, the desireless one shall always be more fortunate. (36)
Even for the sake of dharma, the accumulation of wealth by Brahmins is censured; for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. (37)
For one who abandons all accumulations, calamities come to an end; indeed, no one possessing all worldly objects is seen to be free from misfortune. (38)
A wise man should weigh poverty against sovereignty on a scale; in my opinion, the state of possessing nothing is superior. (39)
Kaśyapa said: "O Sage, this misfortune has been encountered, namely the acquisition of wealth; for one whose soul is deluded by wealth and power is indeed deprived of the highest good. (40)
The attainment of wealth leads to delusion, and delusion leads to hell; therefore, one who seeks the highest good should diligently abandon wealth from afar.
That dharma which is accomplished through wealth is proclaimed to be perishable; however, that which is accomplished through austerity leads to liberation—this is my conviction. (42)
Bharadvāja said: The hair of an aging man decays; the teeth decay as he ages; likewise, the eyes and ears of a man fail, yet craving alone remains ever youthful. (43)
Just as a seamstress passes thread through cloth with a needle, so too does this self lead the thread of saṃsāra by means of desire.
Just as a horn grows as the body grows, so too does craving grow as wealth increases. (45)
Craving has no end and is difficult to satisfy; it brings forth hundreds of sufferings and abounds in unrighteousness. Therefore, one should utterly abandon it. (46)
Gautama said: By what is one who is contented moved, even when deprived of fruits? O twice-born ones, everyone wanders in distress due to the fickleness of the senses.
For one whose mind is contented, there is prosperity everywhere; for one whose feet are covered by shoes, is not the entire earth as if carpeted with leather? (48)
How can that happiness which belongs to those of peaceful mind, satisfied by the nectar of contentment, belong to those greedy for wealth who run hither and thither? (49)
Discontent is the supreme suffering; contentment is the supreme happiness. Therefore, a person seeking happiness should always remain contented. (50)
Viśvāmitra said: "If the desire of one who longs for it is fulfilled, then another desire is born for that man at that very moment, as if fashioned by destiny. (51)
A person driven by desire is never satisfied even by thousands of objects of desire; like a fire fed with clarified butter, his longing only increases further. 52.
Desiring sensual pleasures out of delusion, a man shall not obtain happiness, just as a partridge running toward the shade of a tree where a hawk dwells. 53.
He who constantly enjoys this earth bounded by the ocean, whether regarding a stone and gold as equal, has achieved his purpose more than that king. (54)
Jamadagni said: "That base Brahmin who, having obtained wealth, rejoices even when he ought to grieve—that dull-witted soul, fearing nothing, does not perceive hell."
For those who are capable of receiving gifts but have desisted from accepting them, the worlds attained by givers are indeed the same as those attained by those who do not accept.
Arundhatī said: Just as an endless lotus fiber remains fixed by reaching its stalk, so too does thirst, which is without beginning or end, reside within the bodies of embodied beings. (57)

That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not age even as one ages, and which is a disease that ends only with life—happiness belongs to him who renounces that craving. (58)
Caṇḍā said: "Since these lords of mine fear wealth and such things as they do snakes and other dangers, for that very reason, why should I not have an even greater fear of them? (56)
Paśumukha said: Whatever wise men, who are ever devoted to dharma, practice—that very same thing should be done by a learned man desiring his own welfare. (60)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and having abandoned those fruits containing gold within them, all the sages of firm vows departed for another place.
Thereafter, they entered the sacred field of Camatkārapura; there they suddenly beheld the wandering mendicant Śunomukha who had arrived.
Accompanied by him alone, they went there into a certain part of the forest and then beheld a charming lake adorned with lotuses.
Then, overcome by hunger, they took many lotus stalks, cast them upon the shore of the lake, and performed their meritorious water-rites.
Then, having all emerged from the water and gathered together with one another, they saw those lotus stalks and spoke these words: || 65 ||
The sages said: "By what merciless-souled being have all our lotus stalks been taken from this place, while we were tormented by hunger? (66)
Suspecting one another, those sages of celebrated vows performed terrible oaths for the sake of their own purification.
Kaśyapa said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks always be an eater of all things, may he harbor greed for deposits, and may he bear false witness. (68)
Let him who steals lotus stalks practice dharma with hypocrisy, serve the king, and always eat honey and meat. (69)

Vasiṣṭha said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks become one who engages in sexual intercourse outside the fertile period, or during the day, or on sacred festival days; may he be a guest to another [in such improper times]. 70.
Bharadvāja said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks be joined with the same sin as that of one who, having acquired a teacher’s scripture, does not provide the fee for it. (71)
May he who steals the lotus stalks be cruel in all things, arrogant because of his prosperity, envious, and a slanderer. (72)
Viśvāmitra said: "Let him eat delicacies all alone, praising himself; let him be a seller of the Vedas, and one who commits the theft of lotus stalks. (73)
Jamadagni said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks give his daughter to an old man; may he become the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) and be a perpetual usurer. (74)
Gautama said: "Let him accept gifts from a butcher, let him engage in the sale of horses, let him utter insults against his guru, and let him commit the theft of lotus stalks. (75)
Atri said: May that evil-minded one who steals the lotus stalks constantly despise his mother and father, and may he consult a Śūdra regarding matters of dharma. (76)
He who, having made a promise, does not give cows or other gifts to a Brāhmaṇa, becomes joined with that same sin as he who commits the theft of lotus stalks. || 77 ||
Arundhatī said: Let that woman of wicked conduct, who committed the theft of the lotus stalks, eat and sleep first, before her husband. (78)
Caṇḍā said: "She who acts contrary to her master, who hates righteousness, who is intent on hating the virtuous, and who commits the theft of lotus stalks—[may she be reborn as me]. (79)
Paśumukha said: "May that man who steals the lotus stalks be constantly devoted to betraying his master and be intent on hating the virtuous. (80)
Śunomukha said: "Let him who steals the lotus stalks study the Vedas according to the rules, let him be a householder fond of guests, and let him speak the truth constantly. (81)
The sages said: "That very oath which you have uttered is pleasing to the twice-born; for you have surely committed the theft of our lotus stalks. (82)
Śunomukha said: "O twice-born ones, these lotus stalks of yours have been taken by me; know me to be Purandara, desiring indeed to hear about dharma. (83)
"O best of the twice-born, I am well-pleased with you because of your lack of greed; therefore, come quickly with me to heaven. || 84 ||
The sages said: "We are intent upon the path of liberation; we do not desire heaven. Therefore, we shall perform penance here at this lake for the sake of final release."

"O best of sages, having wandered over this entire earth bounded by the oceans, you have sustained your life by means of lotus stalks; therefore, go, for your welfare shall come from this meeting with us. (86)
Śakra said: "O you of excellent vows, my sight shall never be in vain; therefore, accept whatever has always been established as your heart's desire. (87)
The sages said:
O Śakra, may this hermitage become renowned upon the surface of the earth by our name, and likewise for men, as the destroyer of all sins. (88)
O best of gods, we shall remain right here forever, with our souls purified for the sake of austerity, until the certain attainment of liberation.
Indra said: "Your hermitage shall become renowned throughout the three worlds; likewise, it shall exist as a granter of all desires for the people. (90)
Whoever, having meditated upon whatever desire, performs a śrāddha here on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, shall obtain all of that.
Furthermore, whatever man, even if free from desire, shall perform a śrāddha or a gift, he will undoubtedly attain liberation.
And those who shall cast off their bodies here in your auspicious hermitage, even if they are possessed of sin, shall attain the supreme goal.
Whoever, with a concentrated mind, shall perform a śrāddha intended for the ancestors using iṅguda, badara, bilva, or even bhallātaka fruits, [shall obtain great merit].
Freed from all sins and praised by the kinnaras, he shall attain the supreme perfection that is difficult even for the gods to reach.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed one was greeted with acclaim by all of them.
He went out of sight, and those best of the twice-born remained there. || 96 ||
Then, as time passed, they too, having performed intense and great penance, attained the supreme state which is free from old age and death.
A linga of the trident-bearing God of gods was installed there by them; by the mere sight of it, a person is liberated from sin.
O best of the twice-born, he who further worships that liṅga with devotion using flowers, incense, and ointments will certainly attain liberation. 99.
This narration of the hermitage of the Seven Sages is sacred, conducive to long life, and the destroyer of all sins. (100)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, there is another hermitage of Agastya located there, where the Lord Maheśvara himself, the soul of the universe, resides. || 1 ||
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, the Sun himself comes and personally worships Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods.
Therefore, anyone else who, having come there with devotion, worships that very Śaṅkara with devotion, goes to the abode of the God.
Whoever performs a Śrāddha ceremony there, endowed with perfect faith, his ancestors are satisfied just as if a Pitṛmedha sacrifice had been performed.
The sages said: "Having reached the hermitage of Agastya, why does the divine Sun-god perform a circumambulation? Tell me this in great detail."
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, listen as I relate this story. There is a mountain on the surface of the earth known as Vindhya.
Upon the tips of the branches of that tree, the rays of the sun cling like clusters of flowers, visible from below by the simple-minded Siddhas.
For him who dwelt on the mountain slopes, even during the nights of the dark fortnight, the darkness of ignorance was dispelled by the radiance of the jewels.
Upon whose ridges the trees, shedding flowers as if driven by the force of the wind, truly shine like clouds pouring down torrents of water.
In which various deer appear running here and there for the sake of nourishing their wives and sons, and for the sake of greed, just like human beings.
There, the trees, their bark scarred by the tusks of elephants, shed tears in the guise of resinous exudations that perfume all directions.
Others, with their long cries like the sound of parchment, seemed as if they were weeping; on whose ridges trees struck down by the trunks of elephants were thought to be lamenting.
Covered by waterfalls flowing here and there, it shone like a man adorned with fine white garments.
He who had previously conceived a rivalry with Sumeru, being overcome by anger, went to the thousand-rayed Sun and spoke to him.
O Bhāskara, why do you perform a circumambulation of Meru, yet how is it that you do not do so for me, even though I am known as a Kulaparvata? (15)
Bhāskara said: "We do not perform the circumambulation of that mountain out of faith; this is the path ordained for me by him by whom this world was created. (16)
Its lofty peaks pervade and reach up into the sky; by that very fact, its circumambulation occurs through the power of that [height] alone. || 17 ||
Having heard this, Mount Vindhya became especially enraged and said, "Behold, O Bhānu, my loftiness today! Then he obstructed the path of the sky by which the sun travels.
Then, beholding the path thus obstructed, the Lord of Day reflected within his own mind: "What shall I do now? (19)
If I were to perform a circumambulation of this mountain, it would cause a displacement of time throughout the three worlds.

Likewise, there will be a reversal of the months, the seasons, and the worlds; all rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others will go to destruction. When the world has lost its sacrifices and festivals, the gods will experience great agony. (21)
Having thus reflected in his mind in many ways, the one of fierce luster, filled with fear, went mentally to Agastya, the bull among sages.
Indeed, there is no one else capable of obstructing this Vindhya except for that Agastya, the best of Brahmins, who was born from Mitra and Varuṇa.
Then, having assumed the form of a twice-born man, that one of piercing rays went to his hermitage in the sacred field of Camatkārapura.
Then, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, he who was devoted to the recitation of the Vedas said: "O best of sages, I have arrived here as your guest. (25)
Then Agastya, filled with joy, said: "Welcome to you, O great sage! You have arrived at the conclusion of the fire-ritual like a long-cherished desire. (26)
"O best of sages, speak the truth; whatever you desire, I shall grant it. At this time, there is nothing that I cannot give to one who makes a request. (27)
Bhāskara said: O excellent sage, I, Bhāskara, have arrived in the form of a brahmin, having considered you alone in the three worlds to be capable of accomplishing every task. (28)
Formerly, for the sake of the gods, you drank up the ocean; likewise, you devoured the Daitya Vātāpi, who was a thorn in the side of the twice-born.
Therefore, O best of sages, you must now be our refuge, since you alone are the protector of the gods and of the social orders here on earth. (30)
Sūta said: O Brahmins, having heard that, the sage was especially delighted; he offered the arghya to the Sun and then spoke respectfully.
"I am blessed and I am graced that you have come to my home; therefore, speak, and I shall carry out your word without fail."
Bhāskara said: "O best of sages, this Vindhya mountain stands here having blocked our path out of rivalry with Sumeru, the foremost of mountains."
Therefore, restrain him by various means such as conciliation and the like; act in such a way that there may be no loss of time and no failure in our mission. (34)
Agastya said: "I shall restrain for you this expanding mountain of the family; therefore, go to your own place and be at peace, O Divākara."
Then, having been sent away by him, that sun of sharp rays departed for his own abode, joyfully taking leave of the lord of sages.
Agastya also went quickly and spoke respectfully to Vindhya: "O best of mountains, by my word, descend immediately to a lower state."
"O Mountain, my mind has today turned toward bathing in the sacred fords of the South; that very intention depends upon you, so act as is appropriate. (38)
Having heard his words, Vindhya, the best of mountains, immediately became humble, endowed with modesty. (39)
O twice-born ones, Agastya also reached his southern boundary and said to him, "Now you must remain standing exactly as you are. (40)
Until my return, there is no need for hesitation here; otherwise, I shall cast a curse by which you will go to your destruction.
Having promised "So be it," that best of mountains, fearing a curse, did not grow further, out of a longing for his return.
O best of Brahmins, even he does not turn back by that very path until this very day, having taken refuge in the southern direction.
Then, having brought Lopāmudrā to that very place, the lord of sages summoned the thousand-rayed sun and spoke to him with respect.
O sharp-rayed one, at your word my own hermitage has been abandoned by me; for your sake, I must not go there again under any circumstances. (45)
Therefore, O Bhānu, at my word, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, you must indeed worship that Liṅga which has been installed by me there.
Bhāskara said: "O sage, I shall do exactly as you have said, without doubt; at the end of the year, I myself shall indeed worship that liṅga."
For whatever other man shall worship the Liṅga on that day, having reached my world, he shall become a partaker of liberation.
Sūta said: For this reason, the Lord of piercing rays always maintains his presence there on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra.
All this that I was asked by you, O best of the twice-born, has been narrated. Speak further if there is any doubt remaining in your hearts.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, regarding that which was spoken by you concerning the sage—that in former times the ocean of milk was drunk up by you for the sake of the gods—[1]
O son of Sūta, O high-minded one, tell us in detail that truth, just as in former times the ocean of milk was drunk by that Sage.
Sūta said: In ancient times, there were excellent Dānavas known as the Kāleyas, who arose as the destroyers of the strength and energy of all the gods.
Then, seeing the three worlds oppressed by them, the powerful Viṣṇu, through the application of his power, addressed the Lord Maheśvara.

O Lord Īśāna, these three worlds have been thoroughly oppressed by the Daityas, the Kālakeyas of great prowess; therefore, O God, you must engage them in a great battle this very day upon reaching the surface of the earth.
Then Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the thousand-eyed Indra, together with the gods, all bearing sharp weapons, arrived upon the surface of the earth.
Then all those Dānavas, having heard that the gods had assembled for the sake of battle, suddenly went forth to face them, filled with wrath.
Then a great battle took place between the gods and the dānavas, by which the entire three worlds were shaken and overwhelmed with fear.

Then a Dānava named Kālaprabha, arrogant in his strength, beheld Śakra standing before him with his hand raised holding the thunderbolt; laughing, he spoke these words with a voice as deep as a cloud.
"Release your thunderbolt, O thousand-eyed one; I shall behold your prowess. After a long time you have come within my sight; by good fortune, you are the lord of the three heavens."
Then, filled with rage, Śatakratu hurled his thunderbolt at him; he too, seizing it with ease, caught it in his left hand.
Then, aiming at Śakra, he released a heavy mace made entirely of iron, fierce like another tongue of Yama.
Struck by her, the thousand-eyed one, unconscious and drenched in blood, leaned against his flagpole and remained seated upon the chariot.
Then Mātali, seeing the slayer of Vala unconscious, turned the chariot toward the east, recollecting the code of conduct for charioteers.
Then, when the chariot of Śakra turned its back in the battle, all the gods, terrified by fear, fled in every direction.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts, having cast aside their shame, were shattered by sharp arrows in their backs. (16)
Then, seeing his army broken by the Dānavas, Madhusūdana quickly mounted Garuḍa and rushed toward Kālaprabha.
Then all those Dānavas, surrounding him and roaring again and again, completely covered him with sharp arrows.
Covered by them on all sides, Viṣṇu shone brilliantly, his limbs fully bristling with joy like another mountain of red chalk.
Then, having cut through the masses of arrows with shafts released from the Śārṅga bow—feathered with heron plumes—he struck down the Daityas.
Then all the hosts of Daityas, being slaughtered by the enemy of the gods, found no protector, like deer tormented by a lion.
In the meantime, a Daitya known as Kālakhañja, overcome by the power of anger, rushed toward Vāsudeva.
Having struck Vāsudeva with five sharp stone-tipped arrows, he, enraged, struck Garuḍa with ten straight-knotted shafts.
Then Mādhava released the Sudarśana discus, encircled by garlands of flames, for the purpose of slaying that Daitya.
He too, beholding that discus fallen from the hand of Vāsudeva, came forward facing it with his mouth wide open to swallow it as it approached.
The preeminent among the great Daityas cried out, "Stay! Stay! and, aiming at Vāsudeva, he then discharged his arrows.
Then the wielder of the discus, struck by the Daitya who had seized his discus, experienced intense agony as he was joined with Suparṇa.
In the meantime, the Lord Tripurāntaka became enraged upon seeing Hari in such a state and Śakra as well with his back turned.
Then, having slain that son of Danu with a blow from his trident, he struck down the others with great force using arrows released from the Pināka bow.
The Blessed Lord Śambhu slew Kālaprabha, Prakāla, Kālāsya, and Kālavigraha, as well as other leaders.
Then all those formidable Dānavas, even the leaders, became intent on flight, devoid of enthusiasm for conquering their enemy.
Then Śakra and Viṣṇu, having regained their senses and grasped their weapons, stood at the forefront of the battle, praising Mahādeva.
In the meantime, seeing the sons of Danu shattered, all the gods, together with Indra, struck them with hundreds of arrows and weapons.
Then those exceedingly powerful Dānavas, for the most part slain, were being struck by the sharp arrows of the gods who appeared radiant with victory.
Inaccessible even to their minds, they entered the abode of Varuṇa; their entire bodies mangled by weapons, their protectors slain, they were deeply distressed.
Sūta said: When they had thus been broken and slain, all those best of gods, with joyful minds, praised the god Maheśvara.
Then, released by him and bowing down again and again, they returned to their respective abodes, led by Śakra and Viṣṇu.
Those tigers among the Dānavas, having been rendered hopeless by the foremost of the gods, all together devised a mantra for the destruction of the inhabitants of heaven.
As they were deliberating, this conclusion was reached by them: "The destruction of the gods does not occur except through the subversion of dharma. (4)
Therefore, those who are ascetics, those who are devoted to sacrifice, and likewise others who are intent on dharma, must be slain at the arrival of night.
Having thus made this resolution and departed from the abode of Varuṇa, they always slaughtered people devoted to dharma during the night.
Wherever there may be a sacrifice, a sacrificial session (sattra), or even a festival, they go there at nightfall and cause the destruction of people.
By them, the sacrifices were destroyed, those initiated were struck down, and likewise the officiating priests as well as other ordinary, most excellent brahmins were slain.
In the hermitage of the high-souled Śāṇḍilya, the foremost of sages, a thousand of the best of Brahmins were devoured by those evil-minded ones.
Hundreds and thousands of twice-borns were slain—five hundred by Viśvāmitra and seven hundred by the wise Atri.
At that very time, however, the entire surface of the earth became devoid of sacrifices and festivals, oppressed by the fear of the Kāleyas.
No one at all lay down to sleep on the surface of the earth during the night; all the people, holding their weapons, remained standing together with the ascetics.
Whosoever sleep at night with confidence, being vessels of righteousness, their bones are seen indeed as soon as morning comes.
Then all the hosts of gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, being deprived of their sacrificial shares, fell into the greatest distress.
Then, having gone to the edge of the ocean for the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods, they were not able to assail those who were situated in a perilous position even with their minds.
Then, deeply distressed, they devised a mantra for the destruction of the ocean; for once it was destroyed, those foremost of Dānavas would surely become vulnerable to slaughter.
"Without Agastya, this ocean will not go to dryness; therefore, let us go and entreat that lord of sages here for this task."
"That virtuous sage resides in the sacred field of Camatkārapura; therefore, let us go to that very place so that we may follow him quickly."
Having thus resolved, all those gods arrived at the hermitage of that preeminent sage, who was born of Mitrā and Varuṇa.
Having beheld all those foremost of gods who had arrived, that excellent sage was delighted and quickly went forward to meet them.
Seeing Brahmā and the other gods, his eyes wide with wonder, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence, his voice faltering with joy.
This sacred field of Camatkārapura, though already pure, has become even more sanctified by your taking refuge here. (22)
Therefore, declare what task must now be accomplished by me; I shall perform it all, even if it should be exceedingly difficult.
The gods said: "Those Daityas known as the Kāleyas, who were left remaining after being slain by the gods, have taken refuge in the ocean and are destroying those who perform auspicious deeds. (24)
When Śubha has met his destruction, the destruction of the dwellers of heaven is certain; therefore, for the sake of slaying them, dry up the great ocean.
By this means, those foremost of Dānavas, having come within the range of his vision, were all slain by the gods, and sacrifices were performed here once again.
Agastya said: "O best of gods, at the end of the year, I shall dry up the ocean by relying on the power of the knowledge of the Yoginīs."
Therefore, go to your palaces, for a year is passing; at the end of the year, you must certainly return once again.
Then, having gone with me and dried up the abode of Varuṇa, those wicked Dānavas who afflict the world must be slain—alas!—by us. (29)
Then all the hosts of gods departed to their respective abodes; Agastya, too, made an effort toward the acquisition of knowledge.
Then, by the power of his mantra, the great sage brought there all the sacred seats (pīṭhas) that exist upon the surface of the earth.
And on the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], having worshipped them with devotion, one should especially honor the assemblies of Yoginīs and young maidens.

The twice-born one propitiated the lore named Viśoṣiṇī; the twice-born one, having worshipped the guardians of the quarters and the guardians of the fields, as well as the deity who moves through the sky, did so with faith.
Then, at the end of a year, the deity became pleased with him and said: "Speak what must be done; O virtuous sage, I have been accomplished for you."
Agastya said: "O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, then enter my mouth quickly, so that, O Goddess, remaining restrained in speech, I may swiftly dry up the ocean."
Having promised "So be it," she quickly entered the mouth of that seer of purified soul as the great vidyā known as Saṃśoṣaṇī.
In the meantime, all the gods, including Indra, arrived; joyful and fully equipped for battle, they held weapons in their hands.
Then that brahmin, focused by all the gods, set out toward the ocean with his face parched at that time.
Then, having gone to the edge of the ocean while being praised by the dwellers of heaven, he, being exceedingly distressed by thirst, spoke to all the gods.
"I shall now immediately dry up this ocean; you must exert yourselves for the destruction of the enemies of the gods."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that sage then effortlessly drank up the entire great ocean, which was teeming with fish and tortoises and filled with crocodiles.
Then, when [the ocean] had become like dry land, those Daityas were slain on all sides with sharp arrows by the best of the gods, who were desirous of victory.
Then, having waged a great and most terrible battle to the best of their power, those who remained as the survivors—most of whom had been slain—pierced the earth and went below.
Then all the gods, having praised that best of sages, said: "Release the water once more for the purpose of filling the great ocean."
O Brahmin, this earth, deprived of the ocean and abandoned by its substance, does not shine, like a woman adorned [with ornaments] but devoid of her husband. 45.
Agastya said: "The knowledge which was propitiated by me for as long as a year—the 'Drier'—by that [knowledge] this water was drunk, and it has likewise reached its final transformation."
This abode of Varuṇa shall indeed reach its full completion once more; having been excavated, it has attained unfathomable depth through the utterly pure waters of the Gaṅgā.
A king named Sagara will appear on the surface of the earth; his sixty thousand sons will undoubtedly excavate [the earth]. (48)
In his very lineage there will be a king named Bhagīratha; for the sake of his kinsmen, he shall bring down the Gaṅgā from the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
By the flow of its waters, the ocean will then become completely filled on all sides; this which I have spoken is the truth.
The gods said: "O best of sages, the task of the gods has indeed been accomplished by you; therefore, O lord of sages, request every boon that resides in your heart. (51)
Agastya said: "O best of gods, by the power of my mantras, all the sacred seats (pīṭhas) have been brought by me to the holy field of Camatkārapura. (52)
Therefore, by virtue of their power, may the residence of all those Yoginīs and especially the Mothers always be right there. (53)
Whoever, endowed with faith, shall worship them on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, for him there shall be everything desired by the mind.
The gods said: "Since variegated seats have been brought by you there, therefore one seat shall exist there known by the name Citreśvara. (55)
Whoever, having meditated upon whichever deity they desire, shall perform worship therein—especially of the Yoginīs, the Vidyās, and the Mothers (Mātṛs). || 56 ||
O great sage, by virtue of our granting this boon, that man shall swiftly attain whatever desire he has, even if he be a perpetrator of great evil. (57)
Having spoken thus and taken leave of that lord of sages, all the gods went joyfully to heaven, and Agastya likewise returned to his own hermitage.
Sūta said: Thus has all this been narrated to you—how, in ancient times, that ocean was drunk by Agastya for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Granting of Boons by the Gods, Following the Naming of the Assembly of Pīṭhas Summoned by Agastya," within the "Account of Agastya’s Drinking of the Ocean" in the "Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Kṣetra," in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 || || 9 ||
The sages said: This seat (pīṭha) is Citreśvara, established by the sage Agastya; proclaim to us its dimensions and its power.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, it is not possible for us to describe the majesty of that sacred seat (pīṭha), even in a thousand years or with ten thousand mouths.
There, hundreds and thousands of yogins who have attained perfection, who are endowed with constant meditation and praised for their vows, reside.
Whatever accomplishment may be attained at other sacred seats through a year of practice, yogis certainly attain that same accomplishment in a single day.
Whoever, endowed with faith, should then recite the mantras there according to the syllables, will certainly obtain the entire fruit arising from their meaning. || 5 ||
A man desiring sons who recites the masculine-mantra forms there shall obtain his desired sons, even if he is already advanced in years.
A man desiring a son should recite the Garbhopaniṣad there; even by the union with a barren woman, he shall be endowed with a son.
If one recites the Śatarudriya for the destruction of the world of enemies, his foes shall immediately go to their utter ruin upon that very seat.
Furthermore, any person who recites the Vāmadevya hymn there for the sake of protection against ghosts, spirits, demons, and the like, shall indeed remain free from affliction.
If a man recites the verse beginning with "ko'dāt" there for the sake of a maiden, while meditating upon whichever maiden he desires, he shall undoubtedly obtain her. (10)
O gods, whoever should recite this [mantra] incessantly for the sake of gaining the favor of a king, the favor bestowed by that monarch shall be unrestrained.
O twice-born ones, he who recites this for the sake of affection toward his sister shall have a wife who becomes virtuous and full of loving devotion to him. (12)
Whoever recites even the mantra "Aditi" for the sake of benefiting the world, shall gain the affection of the world and especially attain great profit.
O twice-born ones, whatever man seeking wealth recites the Śrīsūkta there, his riches shall come from all directions in great abundance.
If a man should chant the Sāman "Bhūmi" for the sake of land, he will certainly become a lord of the earth, even if he is of low birth—this is certain.
Whatever man there is who chants the Rathantara Sāman for the purpose of obtaining vehicles, he indeed obtains swift and auspicious vehicles. || 16 ||
O best of the twice-born, that mortal who recites [the mantra] there seeking elephants shall obtain elephants that drench the ground with their rut.
For that man who recites this mantra for the sake of protection, there shall be protection from all sides, both in times of peace and in times of adversity.
He who, being composed in mind, recites this excellent verse beginning with "The Seven Sages" for the destruction of disease, shall be completely liberated from all ailments. (19)
If a person afflicted by the torment of the planets recites these two [mantras] there, the planets will undoubtedly become favorable to him. || 20 ||
And that man who, afflicted by the torment of spirits, mutters the Bṛhat-sāman, even if that spirit be an Ender (Antaka), it becomes like a father unto him.
And whoever recites the Śākuna Sūkta for the sake of the success of a journey, his journey will be successful even if he is destitute of anything.
If a man recites the Sārpa-sūkta there for the destruction of serpents, serpents shall by no means enter his house.
Whoever, endowed with faith, should recite the mantra "uttiṣṭha" there for the destruction of poison, that poison will immediately go to its destruction.
Whether it be poison from stationary sources, mobile sources, or even artificial poison, it departs by his name, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Whoever, endowed with faith, recites the Vyāghra-sāman there, for him even tigers and other beasts of prey become gentle-minded.
He who recites the plough-mantras for the successful accomplishment of agricultural work—his cultivation shall succeed even in this world when it is bereft of rain. || 27 ||
For the destruction of calamities, a person should recite the Devavrata hymn in that very place; then, through its glorification, O Lord, all calamities go to their destruction.
When the world is afflicted by drought, whoever should recite the Pañcendra-mantra there, for him there shall be the arrival of rain through a hand-performed homa with those mantras.
If a man who is afflicted by thieves should recite there the words "by the two fangs," no calamity arising from thieves shall ever befall him.
Whoever recites the mantra "saṃsṛṣṭam" for the purpose of a dispute shall achieve victory in that dispute, even if he is a sinner. || 31 ||
If a person recites the Rudraśiras for the purpose of exorcising enemies, those enemies of his, due to their own wicked intellect, shall abandon the country and depart. || 32 ||
And for one who recites the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā for the purpose of deluding enemies, those enemies will certainly become overcome by delusion.
The man who recites the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses for the purpose of subjugation brings even his enemies under his control, let alone women and others.

O best of the twice-born, he who, being fully devoted to faith, recites the mantra dedicated to Prajāpati and Varuṇa for the purpose of paralyzing his enemies, all his foes become paralyzed by that mantra.
O twice-born ones, the man who mutters "Kālī Karālī" for the sake of withering away whatever a person holds in his mind, that man causes all of it to wither.
This mantra was then recited by the high-souled Agastya; by its power, the lord of rivers was certainly dried up by him.
I have thus proclaimed to you the power of this sacred seat (pīṭha), which brings about the perfection of mantras and the attainment of worldly fruits. || 38 ||
O best of the twice-born, he who desires heaven again should perform a ritual bath there, as well as acts of charity and especially the ancestral Śrāddha rite. (39)
Alternatively, he who desires liberation and is detached from the ocean of worldly existence, being free from desire and content therein, that wise man should practice austerity.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, regarding the greatness of the recitation of mantras which has been proclaimed by you to us—how indeed does that recitation of mantras attain perfection? (41)
Sūta said: In this regard, I shall relate that which I heard from my father, as he formerly spoke to the eminent Brāhmaṇa, the sage Durvāsas.
O twice-born ones, listen with full concentration to what was previously asked by our father of Durvāsas regarding the practice of mantra-recitation. (43)
Durvāsas said: "I shall practice a certain desired mantra as a practitioner of vows; for the sake of its accomplishment, tell me the procedure prescribed by the scriptures. (44)
Lomaharṣaṇa said: O excellent sage, the accomplishment of mantras is difficult for everyone; it is fraught with obstacles and beset by many pitfalls. (45)
Therefore, O twice-born one, if you desire success in the performance of mantras, you ought to go to that sacred field at Camatkārapura. || 46 ||
Therein lies the Citreśvarī-pīṭha, fashioned by Agastya; it is said to grant immediate success for the mantras residing within the heart. (47)
O twice-born one, no flaw arises there, nor is there any transgression; by the granting of boons by all the inhabitants of heaven, there is no failure whatsoever.

"For that seat (pīṭha) is indeed fourfold, and it declares success for those who abide there according to the respective age (yuga). Therefore, O twice-born one, I shall now describe it to you immediately."
O best of the twice-born, whatever mantra a person desires to accomplish, that man should first recite it one hundred thousand times.

Then that pure man becomes perfected and fit for the mantra; O tiger among Brahmins, he should then recite it four hundred thousand times. Thereafter, an oblation (homa) should be performed with a tenth part of that number in a well-kindled fire.
From that, indeed, arises the accomplishment born of that mantra; therein, for gentle rites, there is an oblation with white mustard seeds.
O best of Brahmins, [the deity] is remembered with *jātī* flowers and the feeding of Brahmins; likewise, in rites for the Rudras, [one should worship] with red flowers and guggulu resin.
And with libations for young maidens, the fire sacrifice shall be fruitful.
O best of the twice-born, this supreme method of mantra accomplishment has been proclaimed by me for all practitioners during the Kṛta Yuga.
This practice of mantra-accomplishment prescribed for the Tretā Yuga is reduced by one quarter; in the Dvāpara Yuga, half of that [half] should be performed, and in the Kali Yuga, only a fourth part.
Thus, having attained there the perfection arising from the mantra, a person may then accomplish his purpose at that sacred seat (pīṭha) according to his own will.
Endowed with the power to both curse and bless, and possessed of splendor, he was unconquerable by all beings and likewise esteemed by the virtuous.
Sūta said: Having heard all those words of my father, that excellent sage then arrived at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Citreśvara. 58.
There, endowed with supreme faith, he accomplished all the mantras in their proper sequence according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. (59)
Thus, O twice-born ones, having perfected his mantra, he went to the city of Camatkāra for the sake of requesting land from the brahmins.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Citreśvarī Pīṭha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, he then beheld a multitude of brahmins resembling gods, seated upon the surface of the earth in a graceful posture. Some among them were knowers of the Vedas, intent upon the exposition of the Vedas; yet others, desiring victory, were disputing with one another in great anger.
There, hundreds of other brāhmaṇas were seen—experts in the science of sacrifice, devoted to the narration of sacrificial rites, and exponents of the Veda.
Other tigers among brahmins, experts in the Vedāṅgas, stood before the assembly and spoke to resolve their doubts.
And other excellent brahmins there, devoted to the study of the Vedas, completely filled the circle of the quarters with the sound of their chanting.
Others, overcome by curiosity, asked one another about the treacherous paths; others laughed upon learning that he was one who travels the right way.
Others were devoted to the exposition of the Smṛtis, while others were reciters of the Śruti; some asked one another about doubts arising from the Smṛtis.
Likewise, other excellent Brahmins, standing there in the midst of the assembly before the elders, recite the Purāṇa.
Then, having seen those brahmins of rigid vows, that sage greeted them and spoke with respect and humility.
"O tigers among brahmins, the thought has arisen in my mind to build a sanctuary for Śambhu; therefore, let a suitable site be shown to me. (10)
"Having constructed an excellent temple for you, O Śambhu, the God of gods, I shall worship that very one whose banner is the bull."
Although he spoke in this manner repeatedly and without weariness, he did not obtain from them any reply, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Then the sage, his soul overcome with anger, cursed those best of the twice-born with a loud voice so that everyone could hear it entirely.

Durvāsas said: The pride of learning, the pride of wealth, and thirdly, that arising from noble birth—these are the intoxications of those who are self-conceited; yet these very same things are the means of self-restraint for the virtuous.
For even those among you who remain intoxicated, because of that, their descendants likewise will be possessed by intoxication. (15)
In this city, even fathers will always be devoid of affection toward their sons; how much more so, then, will relatives and others be? (16)
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, that lord of brahmins immediately turned back after receiving the greatest insult from the brahmins. (17)
Now, in their midst there was a most aged and wise Brahmin, renowned as Suśīla, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Seeing that sage departing in anger and feeling insulted, he quickly pursued him from behind, crying out, "Wait! Wait! (19).
Then, having approached and gone some distance, he prostrated before the sage and said: "O Brahmin, please forgive me at the request of the Brahmins."
Because they were so devoted to their Vedic studies, they did not hear your words, nor was a reply given by them; I tell you this as the truth. (21)
Therefore, this land has been granted by me to you for the sake of a temple for Śambhu; O best of the twice-born, you ought to construct a palace on this site.

O best of Brahmins, having heard those words of his, Durvāsas was filled with joy and performed the *svasti* rite arising from the gift of land; subsequently, abiding by his command, he constructed a palace for him.
Then those brahmins, having learned of this, gave the earth to that ascetic through Suśīla for the purpose of constructing a temple for the deity.
All those twice-born ones were filled with anger toward Suśīla.
Then, having approached him, they said: "We have been cursed by that evil-minded one; you must grant him land for the purpose of building a palace. (26)
Therefore, you too shall be an outsider to us; for even if you are virtuous, you will be designated as "Dus-sila" (Evil-natured) by the wise.
Even this ascetic who builds a temple for Śiva is wicked; he shall not attain success even in hundreds of years.
In the same way, men in this world proclaim the fame of those who have established renown; however, for that evil-minded one, no fame arises even as he watches it being proclaimed.
This palace shall indeed be known as Duḥśīla after your name; it will never be complete in name alone. (30)
"O twice-born ones, because we were rendered devoid of friendship by him, we have become possessed of the three intoxications and endowed with all [evil] lineages. (31)
Therefore, this sinful soul shall also become a partaker of anger; by him, whatever penance has been performed repeatedly shall go to total ruin.
Having spoken thus, those brahmins, their eyes bloodshot with anger, completely abandoned Duḥśīla and then entered their own city.
Although he was of immoral conduct, Devaśarman built his house outside that city; he was abandoned by the city-dwellers just as before.
Those who were born even in his lineage are proclaimed as outsiders; they are excluded from all ritual activities of all the city-dwellers. (35)
Sūta said: When those best of the twice-born had thus departed after pronouncing the curse, Durvāsas, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke to Duḥśīla. || 36 ||
My mantras have attained perfection and are capable of destroying enemies—both those of the Atharvaveda as well as others originating from the three Vedas. (37)
Therefore, today I shall bring this entire city, including its beasts and birds, to destruction, just as a wicked man destroys his enemy.
Duḥśīla said: "O best of men, it is by no means proper for you to perform this deed on behalf of Brahmins, especially that of a Brahmin. (39)
Whether they strike, curse, or speak harshly, Brahmins must always be honored by those who desire the divine worlds. (40)
He who considers himself victorious when Brahmins have been defeated is cooked in the terrible hells, such as Tāmisra and others. (41)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, he who desires an eternal residence in heaven should indeed endure his own defeat at the hands of that brahmin.
Since those mantras have attained perfection in the sacred field of these foremost Brahmins, how will you bring about their destruction? (43)

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for the breaker of vows, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
Therefore, anger should not be displayed by those established in this field; O best of sages, show me mercy and practice forgiveness toward me. 45.
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," he performed penance there and attained the supreme perfection, which is difficult even for the gods to achieve.
That temple on earth, known as Duḥśīla, has also attained great renown; by the mere sight of it, a person is liberated from sin. (47)
The man who, having meditated for a moment, beholds the Liṅga situated in its center on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, never beholds hell.
Sūta said: Right there, King Dhundhumāra established a Liṅga after having constructed a most beautiful temple made entirely of all kinds of jewels.
Having established an excellent hermitage there, he performed most severe penance; by the power of which this god remains stationed within that linga.
A beautiful pond was constructed by that high-souled one near it; filled with perfectly pure water, it was auspicious and comparable to all sacred fords.
Having bathed there, the best of men should behold Dhundhumāreśvara; he shall not encounter difficulties or the hells in the abode of Yama.
The sages said: In which lineage did that protector of the earth, Dhundhumāra, arise? At what time was penance performed here by that great-souled one?
Sūta said: Born of the Solar dynasty, the son of Bṛhadaśva was the powerful one known as Kuvalayāśva; he was likewise called Dhundhumāra.
By him, the great Daitya Dhundhu was slain in the desert of Maru; therefore, he became renowned throughout the three worlds as Dhundhumāra.
Having gone to that great and purifying sacred field of Camatkārapura, he performed austerities at the end of his life, meditating upon Maheśvara.
Having installed that most magnificent liṅga in a temple adorned with jewels, [he worshipped it] with offerings, sacrifices, oblations, and the like, as well as flowers, incense, and unguents.
Then Mahādeva himself, the Great Lord, became manifest before him, mounted upon his bull together with Gaurī and his attendants.
He said, "I am the giver of boons; ask for whatever you desire. I shall grant you everything, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (11)
Dhundhumāra said: "O Lord of all gods, O you whose banner is the bull, if a boon is to be granted by you to us, then you must establish your presence within this linga."
The Blessed Lord said: O best of kings, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, I shall always be present here together with Gaurī; of this there is no doubt.
O King, that man who, having bathed in that pond, shall worship me as I am established in this linga, will go to my world.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the Blessed One then vanished from sight; and that king, with a delighted soul, remained right there, attaining liberation.
Sūta said: To the north of that very Dhundhumāreśvara, an excellent Liṅga was installed by the lord of men, Yayāti. || 1 ||
O twice-born ones, [this was told] by Devayānī, as well as by others, and likewise by Śarmiṣṭhā—the wife of that king—who bestows the fruits of all desires.
O best of the twice-born, when he had attained satisfaction regarding all enjoyments, he then offered his own kingdom and his very body to his son.
Then, having taken that old age from his body, he, accompanied by his two wives, humbly questioned Mārkaṇḍa, the best of sages.
O Blessed One, tell me among all the holy fords and sacred fields which is the most preeminent and purifying; proclaim that to us.
The illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Among all sacred fields here, the field of Camatkārapura, adorned with all holy fords (tīrthas), now appears most preeminent to us. (6)
O best of kings, there the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Viṣṇu who destroys the sins of living beings, resides in person, as do the gods headed by Hara.
Likewise, O best of kings, there are other holy places (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth where their presence is always maintained.
There, a stone measuring fifty-two cubits in dimension was released by the Grandfather for the delight of the twice-born.
O Lord of the Earth, whatever auspicious karma that is accomplished elsewhere in one year attains success there in a single day.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, go there quickly and perform penance, by which you shall attain the worlds residing in your heart together with your wife.
Having heard those words of his, that king, the son of Nahuṣa, went to the sacred field of Camatkārapura accompanied by his two wives.
Then, having installed that liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods, he worshipped it perfectly, endowed with supreme faith.
Then, by the power of that [act], the king, together with his two wives, ascended an excellent celestial chariot and went to the abode of the gods.
Being sung of by the Kinnaras and praised by the Cāraṇas, he vied with the gods, possessing a splendor equal to twelve suns. || 15 ||
The sages said: Regarding that great stone of Brahmā which was described by you as the bestower of liberation upon all living beings and likewise the destroyer of sins— || 1 ||
O son of Sūta, how was she established there, and what is her power? Tell us this in its entirety, for we are not yet satiated.

Sūta said: In ancient times, a great anxiety arose in Brahmā—who is established in the world of Brahmā and whose birth is unmanifest—concerning the undertaking of a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthas).
All the gods indeed have sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth; excluding me, one such ford must be established by me on the face of the earth. (4)

Having reached there at the three periods of the day, I shall perform the rites arising from the junctions (saṃdhyā); thereafter, having returned to the world of mortals, I shall do that very same thing. || 5 ||
Likewise, whatever other righteous action brings about welfare, that I shall perform, just as the gods Śiva and others have done.
Indeed, there is no scope for ritual actions here in heaven; only the fruit of auspicious deeds is enjoyed.
