Therefore, wherever on the surface of the earth this stone shall fall, one must go there at the three junctions of the day for the very purpose of performing religious rites.
Having spoken thus, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) hurled that vast rock born from his seat toward the surface of the earth.
Then that stone, composed of all kinds of jewels, fell upon the ground in the sacred field of Camatkārapura, which is the source of great prosperity for all fields.
Then Lokeśa himself came and beheld that sacred field on the surface of the earth, which was surrounded on all sides by holy fords (tīrthas).
Then, having seen her arrived in that most meritorious region, he attained a state of great joy and immediately spoke as follows: || 12 ||
"Aha! There is no one else in the three worlds more blessed than I, since my residence has been established here in this field which embodies all sacred fords. (3)
Since no ritual action can proceed without water, therefore I must create here a great lake of pure water.
Then he reflected upon his daughter Sarasvatī, who, out of fear of contact with people, flowed toward the depths of the netherworld (Pātāla).
Then, having burst through the surface of the earth, a great river appeared, washing that stone on all sides with its pure waters.
Then, having assumed a physical form, she spoke to the Great-Grandfather: "For what purpose have I been remembered, O God? Let your command be given. (7)
Brahmā said: "You must always remain right here upon this stone in my presence, so that I may perform my rites with your waters during all three junctions of the day."
Likewise, those men who shall perform their ablutions in your waters will attain the supreme perfection that is difficult for gods and humans to obtain. (19)
Sarasvatī said: "O best of gods, I am a maiden who flows through the depths of Pātāla; fearing contact with human beings, I do not come to the surface of the earth. (20)
"Your command must never be carried out by me otherwise; O best of gods, considering this, do whatever is appropriate. (21)
Brahmā said: "For your sake, I shall create a great lake right here in this place, inaccessible to all mortals; it is fitting that you reside there."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods dug a great lake; thereupon, Sarasvatī established her own abode there.
Then the Grandfather commanded the snakes whose venom is in their gaze: "By my command, you must always remain in this lake."
O best of serpents, you must act in such a way that mortals do not touch the Sarasvatī under any circumstances whatsoever.
Sūta said: Having thus established Sarasvatī in that sacred field and having placed that Citraśilā in the center, Brahmā indeed departed for the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka).
Then a great sage named Maṅkaṇaka, firm in his vows and an expert in the science of poisons, arrived at that sacred field.
Wandering there in succession within that place protected by serpents, they surrounded the sage and bound him with nooses.

By the power of his knowledge, he rendered those snakes venomless. Having bathed there, become pure, and performed the libations for the ancestors, he emerged from that water, fulfilled in purpose and filled with joy. (29)
Then, just as the sage was about to properly grasp the blade of kusha grass, the tip of the man's hand was pierced by the point of that darbha grass.
Then, from that wound, a great amount of vegetable juice (śākarasa) emerged; seeing it, he was especially delighted and filled with wonder. (31)
Realizing "I have attained perfection," he then performed a dance after ascending the Brāhmī stone, drenched in tears of joy.
Then, as that high-souled sage was thus dancing, the entire world, both stationary and moving, performed a dance in his likeness.
The entire city of Camatkārapura was shattered and the best of the twice-born were destroyed; with the palaces demolished there, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Then all the hosts of gods, having witnessed that deed of his, spoke to the one whose vehicle is the bull (Śiva) for the purpose of stopping the dance.
"O Lord of Gods, because this dancing [being] causes the entire world, both stationary and moving, to dance, go and restrain him."
"O Lord of the Gods, O Īśāna, no one else is capable of restraining this sage in any way; therefore, act for the welfare of the world. (37)
Then, having heard their words, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull assumed the form of a preeminent brahmin and hastened to his presence.
And he said: "O sage, why is this being danced by you now? Therefore, tell us quickly the purpose; for our curiosity is indeed great. (39)
O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus by Śaṅkara, that lord of brāhmaṇas showed him his hand, which was smeared with the juice of vegetables.
"Do you not see, O Brahmin, that a great amount of vegetable juice has issued from my hand through the opening of my wound? Therefore, success has arrived. (41)
For this reason, O Brahmin, O best of Siddhas, having attained supreme bliss born of spiritual perfection, I perform this dance.
While he was speaking thus, the Blessed One, whose banner bears the bull, instantly struck his own thumb with the tip of his finger.
Then, from the tip of his wound, there suddenly emerged ash resembling snow or crystal, causing great amazement.
Then, O best of the twice-born, that god spoke to that brahmin: "From the tip of whose thumb this pale ash has emerged for me... (45)
Nevertheless, O best of sages, I do not venture to dance; yet you dance even from the mere sight of vegetable juice. (46)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, desist from this censurable dancing; for the ascetic merit of a twice-born man perishes through dance and song. (47)
Then, observing the emission of ashes from his wound, he abandoned his dance and, filled with shame, paid homage to him.
"I consider you to be none other than Maheśvara among the gods; therefore, show me favor so that there may be no loss to my ascetic merit. (49)
The Blessed Lord said: "By my grace, your austerity shall constantly increase and flourish. I shall remain forever in this place together with you. (50)

"O Sage, since I have been requested by you, who are yourself full of bliss (Ānandita), I shall attain renown on the earth by the name Ānandeśvara; and this city of mine shall be known by the name Ānanda. (51)
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva then vanished from sight; and Maṅkaṇaka, that lord of sages, continued to perform penance there.
Then those serpents, having prostrated before the lord of sages, said: "O Blessed One, we have all indeed been rendered free from poison by you."
Therefore, show us favor so that this terrible poison may be neutralized; otherwise, we shall suffer total defeat by all the world.
Maṅkaṇaka said: "I have never spoken an untruth, even in jest; therefore, you shall all become water-snakes of such a kind. (55)
Sūta said: From that time forward, water-snakes were born upon the earth; they possessed that same form and were double-tongued, but were entirely devoid of poison. (56)
Then, having bathed in that auspicious lake of Sarasvatī and having touched that Citraśilā rock, mortals attain the supreme goal. || 57 ||
Then, terrified, the thousand-eyed Indra went to the god Pitāmaha and, accompanied by Yama, quickly spoke these words at that time.
"By your grace, men behold and go to heaven. O Grandfather, as for that great tirtha on earth established by you, known as Sārasvata—having bathed there, men go to the third heaven. (59)
Even those of sinful conduct, excluded from all righteous dharma, attain a good state immediately upon bathing there and touching the stone.
Yama said: O Lord, my office, which consists of the discernment of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of all embodied beings, has been undertaken by me according to what is appropriate. (61)
Therefore, O Lord, abandon me, or else that excellent holy place [by whose power my hells have become devoid of people]. (62)
Having heard those words of Yama, the Great-Grandfather spoke to Śakra, who was standing by his side: "Lead that Tīrtha to its destruction."
Then, O twice-born ones, Śakra went to the lake and filled that Sārasvata lake, as well as that Citraśilā, with dust.
Even today, that man who remains properly established in this place and performs ascetic practice shall quickly attain perfection. (65)
O best of Brahmins, that Maṅkaṇaka also remains there even today together with Lord Śambhu, and it is indeed filled with dust.
There exists a Liṅga established by Maṅkaṇaka that brings great prosperity; by touching it, O best of the twice-born, human beings are liberated from their sins.
The man who worships him on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, even if he is joined with sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Sūta said: To the north of that very deity who reclines upon the waters, there is a highly renowned sacred site that destroys all sins. || 1 ||
He who, being intent on fasting, worships Hari with devotion at His lying down and His awakening, shall go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu.
The second lunar day is named Aśūnyaśayana (the Unempty Bed); it is always the beloved day for the God of Gods when he is asleep during the dark fortnight. (3)
Whoever worships that Lord reclining upon the waters there, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, goes to the abode of Hari.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, how did the one who reclines upon the waters arrive there? By what ritual is he worshipped? Tell us all that in detail.
Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a lord of the Dānavas named Bāṣkali, who possessed great strength and was invincible to all the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Then, having brought the entire earth under his control, that one of great strength went to the abode of the gods together with the hosts of Daityas.
There occurred a great battle between the gods and the dānavas, who were enraged with one another and intent on destroying each other.
For ten thousand years, day after day, that [battle] was terrible; there, a mire of blood arose, and a mountain was formed from bones.
Then, when the tenth thousand-year period had arrived, the thousand-eyed Indra was defeated by him along with his army and his retinue.
Then, abandoning heaven along with all the hosts of gods, he went for refuge to Viṣṇu, whose abode is Śvetadvīpa.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, who has come under the power of yogic sleep; reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa, his feet are massaged by Lakṣmī.
Then all the gods, including Indra, who were true devotees of that deity, performed a hymn of praise from every side with Vedic hymns originating from the Vedas.

Then, having risen, the Lord of the World spoke to the Destroyer of Bala: "O Thousand-eyed One, is all well now in the three worlds, since you have come here in person together with the hosts of gods? (14)
Śakra said: "The lord of the Daityas named Bāṣkali is powerful, having obtained boons from Hara; he is invincible in battle by the gods, and by him I was defeated in the fray."
And now, O slayer of Madhu, O best of gods, he has established himself in heaven; therefore, O supreme deity, he has come here for refuge along with the gods.
In the past, out of fear of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, we gods were all protected by you, as well as others who were evil-minded.
Therefore, protect me also from this even more powerful Dānava Bāṣkali; O Lord of Gods, there is no other supreme refuge for me except you.
The Blessed One said: "When the proper time arrives, I myself shall subdue him. Therefore, O Śakra, perform great penance until that time."
O Vāsava, by means of that ascetic power and vigor, may you be endowed with the strength necessary for the slaying of that powerful Daitya Bāṣkali.
Śakra said: O Lord of the World, tell us which field we should choose to perform great penance for the sake of destroying that Daitya. (21)
Sūta said: Having heard that, the Blessed Viṣṇu, after deliberating for a long time in his mind upon the sacred fields and shrines, then spoke to Purandara.
O Śakra, Camatkārapura is a sacred field that bestows supernatural powers; therefore, go there quickly and perform austerities for the sake of slaying him.
Śakra said: "O Keśava, we shall by no means go elsewhere forsaken by you, being terrified by the fear of Bāṣkali, the lord of the Dānavas. (24)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, come there yourself; protected by you, I shall perform a very great penance.
Sūta said: Then the Blessed Viṣṇu, having said "So be it" along with the gods, came to the sacred field of Camatkārapura together with Śrī.
Then all the hosts of gods, having gone there to those hermitages, joyfully and with firm resolve for the sake of penance, established their respective dwellings. || 27 ||
Vāsudeva, too, having called to mind the ocean Kṣīroda, quickly brought that vast expanse into that ancient lake.
He made his bed there on Śvetadvīpa as before, while being praised from all sides by all the gods who were full of humility.
Then, when the auspicious second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha had arrived, Bṛhaspati himself spoke these gentle words to the thousand-eyed Indra, his eyes clouded with tears.
Bṛhaspati said: O Purandara, today is the second lunar day known as Aśūnyaśayana, which is exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu while he is asleep upon the waters. (31)

When Viṣṇu is duly worshipped during these four months, remaining properly established in the vow according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, he grants all desires whenever he is meditated upon in the mind by one who lies upon the waters.
Thus, having worshipped Hari on the second day of each month for four months, that thousand-eyed one became endowed with splendor.
Seeing him endowed with such splendor, Janārdana was highly pleased and said: "O Śakra, go today for the sake of slaying that Bāṣkali; together with all the hosts of gods, victory shall be yours."
Śakra said: "O Lord, I am afraid of that evil-minded lord of the Dānavas; I will not go there even with all the gods, let alone without you."
The Blessed Lord said: O thousand-eyed one, this Sudarśana discus of mine shall go with you for the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods.
Having spoken thus, Hari then released the Sudarśana discus for the sake of slaying the lords of the Dānavas, accompanied by Śakra.
Śakra also, having gone together with him, completely destroyed all the Dānavas at the forefront of the battle with his discus.
And that Bāṣkali, completely severed by that discus, fell upon the surface of the earth like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. || 39 ||
Likewise, many other heroic Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, having struck down the Sudarśana discus, caused it to return once more to the hand of Hari.
Then those gods, Śakra and the others, being greatly delighted and freed from doubt, approached Viṣṇu once more, bowed down, and thereafter spoke.
O Lord of Gods, by your power all the enemies of the immortals have been slain; and the sovereignty over the three worlds has been regained, with all its thorns removed.
Therefore, O Lotus-eyed One, declare what task must be performed for me that would always be conducive to my welfare and bring fear to my enemies. (43)
The Blessed One said: "O Vāsava, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, I shall always remain right here in this very form within the lake, this meritorious reservoir of water. (44)
Therefore, O Lord of Śacī, having come together with him, you must diligently perform the Aśūnyaśayana vow during the four months of the rainy season.
O Thousand-eyed One, because those who go along that path do not exist, you shall undoubtedly obtain your desired fruit through my grace. (46)
Any other man as well who shall worship me here with devotion will attain those worlds which are difficult even for the gods to reach.

Therefore, O Thousand-eyed One, go and rule the kingdom in Triviṣṭapa. Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, I am to be seen by you right here once again when the time for action has arrived, just as I am in Śvetadvīpa; of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: Then, having seen him and bowed down, Śatakratu departed; Vāsudeva, however, remained right there for the welfare of the world.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, Janārdana, the Supreme Lord, remained there lying upon the waters for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds.
He who worships him with devotion, endowed with supreme faith—especially during the Cāturmāsya period—attains the highest goal. || 51 ||
Likewise, that Dvārakā was established there by all the hosts of gods; indeed, by worshipping it during Cāturmāsya, men go to heaven.

Even at other times, a mortal may obtain his desires by fixing his mind there; therefore, that Dvārakā should be worshipped by men with every effort at all times, and especially during the four months of the rainy season. || 53 ||
All this has been narrated to you, which destroys all sins—the most meritorious narrative of the God of gods who reclines upon the waters.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, another auspicious pool originating from Viśvāmitra is situated there, which grants all desires.
O best of the twice-born, by performing a ritual bath there on the third day of the month of Caitra, a man becomes one who possesses a divine form, like Kāma himself in person.
Or a woman endowed with faith, having bathed there, shall become possessed of offspring, endowed with good fortune, and most desirable on earth. (3)
The sages said: O son of Sūta, tell us at what time did that sage’s holy bathing-place (tīrtha) become established there, and by whom was it made completely stainless? Tell us all of this.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, there was formerly an ordinary waterfall there, which stood upon the surface of the earth as an Avadhūta by virtue of its majesty.
There the celestial river Gaṅgā herself is established; having bathed in her, a man is immediately liberated from all sins.
Whoever, being purified in mind, performs a śrāddha ceremony there for the sake of the ancestors, that śrāddha shall become inexhaustible and provide satisfaction to the ancestors.
O twice-born ones, whatever gift is given at that most excellent sacred ford, as well as burnt offerings, recitations, and so forth, shall yield infinite fruit.
Then, after some time, a doe struck by the arrow of a hunter entered that water and there met her death.
O best of the twice-born, it was at midday on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the constellation presided over by Yama, and on the day of the Sun.
Then, by the power of that water, she became an Apsaras named Menakā, possessing a beautiful smile, belonging to the lord of the gods, and radiant on all sides.

Then, recollecting his power, that woman of excellent complexion came to the holy ford and performed her bath there with true devotion on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the constellation of Yama and on a Sunday.
Once, while wandering during that day, the lord of sages known as Viśvāmitra, endowed with ascetic power, arrived there.
She too, having arrived from heaven for the purpose of beholding the deity, and having worshipped that god, set out toward the celestial realm.
There she saw that sage wandering here and there, established in youth, endowed with great beauty, like another five-arrowed god of love.
He was pervaded by splendors born from the power of his vows, like the sun; his sins had been burnt away by the asceticism he had practiced since childhood.
At the mere sight of him, she was tormented by the arrows of love; full of joy, she rushed toward him for the sake of sexual union. (17)
Having seen her, whom he had never seen before, for the purpose of asking the way, he then quickly went toward her with a joyful inner soul.
He spoke, inquiring about her country and especially about the duties of women: "May you obtain auspiciousness, O blessed lady, in thought, deed, and speech. (19)
"Is your devotion to Vāsudeva always constant and unwavering? O daughter, do you remain devoted to the feet of your husband, endowed with good conduct and humility, and always speaking kindly? (20)
I hope you have always been beloved by your husband through gifts and acts of worship, and likewise by your kinsmen and circle of friends, both in his presence and behind his back. (21)
O woman of excellent complexion, do you fall under the power of sleep at night only when your husband is fast asleep, and do you rise before he has awakened? (22)
O lady of excellent hips, having risen early in the morning, do you yourself perform the sweeping of the house, as well as its decoration and further embellishment? (23)
I hope that, having first paid homage to the gods and immediately thereafter to your guru, you sustain your life by giving food and water according to your capacity. (24)
O radiant lady, I hope that you do not eat food after the sun has set, nor without first giving to your own servants and especially to virtuous people.
Do you drink water purified seven times, protecting the creatures born in the water with your own thick cloth? (26)
Are you endowed with compassion such that you protect even lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and the like—even those who cause distress to your body—just as you would your own children? (27)
O auspicious lady, do you constantly listen with devotion to the Śiva-dharma from the mouths of the virtuous, and do you practice it with respect? (28)
Having heard the meritorious scripture in some places, you perform worship, especially toward the scripture, the reciter, and the commentator. (29)
Do you present to the virtuous the ancient scriptures composed by the lords of men, which are beautiful with well-inscribed letters? (30)
He who, having heard all the scriptures, does not provide the fee for them, should be known as a thief of the scriptures; he does not obtain their fruit at all. (31)
Do you perform, according to your ability, the activities such as dancing, singing, and instrumental music in the temple of Śiva, as well as the offerings, worship, and oblations? (32)
O fortunate lady, do you indeed offer all your upper garments and clothes to virtuous people, preceded by a respectful prostration? (33)
O large-eyed one, I hope you do not constantly wander aimlessly in the houses of others, especially at the onset of night. (34)
I hope, O blessed lady, that you do not eat while your own husband is hungry; I hope you take great care to avoid disobeying his command. (35)
I hope that when your beloved is provoked to anger, you do not offer harsh retorts; and I hope you speak pleasant words for the sake of dispelling his wrath. (36)
I hope that when your beloved has gone abroad, you do not become one who wears soiled garments, and likewise wretched, with a pale face and emaciated? (37)
I hope you do not keep on the roof of your house a broken vessel, or food-remnants discarded by people, even if they might still be of some use. (39)
I trust you go about at night during our vigils and discourses, by the mountain streams, in secluded places, on the riverbanks, and in the forests? (39)
O auspicious one, O beautiful lady, do you not cultivate friendship with unchaste women, with nurses, with female gardeners, and with washerwomen? (40)
Do you always keep your face anointed with saffron, your head strewn with flowers, and your eyes adorned with collyrium? (41)
Menakā said: "O Brahmin, those for whom you have described the dharma are other heroines; we are the courtesans of the gods, who sport according to our own will. (1)
O illustrious one, tell me from which country you have come; for you have captivated my heart at this sacred ford, a refuge for the righteous.
O illustrious one, upon seeing you, who possess the form of Kāmadeva, my entire body is covered with horripilation as I am tormented by the arrows of love. (3)

Therefore, accept me, for I am devoted to you; otherwise, O ascetic, I shall perish before your very eyes, consumed by the arrows of love. Consequently, you will undoubtedly be stained by the sin of killing a woman. || 4 ||
The ascetic said: "O fair-browed one, we are observers of vows, devoted to celibacy; O blessed lady, though we are fools regarding the ways of desire, we are intent upon the teaching of Śiva."
Celibacy is declared to be the root of all those who observe vows; especially for the devotees of Śiva, you shall establish this even more firmly.
Even the ascetic merit that a practitioner of vows accumulates over more than a hundred years is destroyed by a single instance of sexual union with a woman; such is the case for a Pāśupata as well.
"And why, O timid one, do you speak of me as a Pāśupata hunter? Such a most sinful deed is censured in the teaching of Śiva. (8)
That evil-souled man who pursues a woman while falsely observing the Pāśupata vow shall, after passing through ten successive births, be cooked in hell.
"O fair-faced one, let alone physical union or touch; even conversation with women leads to sin for a Pāśupata. (10)
Therefore, O beautiful woman, go very quickly from this place; you ought to go to that place where you shall obtain what you desire.
Menakā said: "O you of great splendor, you are surely not skilled in the ways of passion; for that reason, you seek to dissuade me, a woman full of desire, with such words."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, Viśvāmitra, filled with great anger yet indifferent to her acceptance, then spoke this once more.
Viśvāmitra said: "Live or go to death; I shall not carry out your word. For the sin that arises from the destruction of a vow is greater than the killing of a woman. (3)

The wise have declared that an expiation exists for those observing vows when the killing of a woman has been committed; however, there is no such expiation for associating with them again. Therefore, you ought not to go [with them].
Not only do those endowed with vows incur sin from association with women; even men outside of vows who are attached to women fall downward.
At their very first union, a woman displays the wandering of saṃsāra under the pretext of circumambulating the sacred fire.
Therefore, a wise man should avoid even conversation with women; let alone physical association, for one who desires his own welfare.
A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter; through lack of touch he remains firm, but by contact with her he melts away.
Women are the root of all misfortunes for every living being on earth; therefore, they should be abandoned from afar, for they are the obstructors of heaven.
Even women who are of noble birth, possessed of wealth, and have protectors, develop passion for a single man; these women are exceedingly fickle.

Indeed, there exists nothing else on earth more conducive to sin than women, by whose association a person wanders through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). Even one who is base performs service for them in secluded places; indeed, those women serve him whether he be deformed or lowly.
Because of the lack of purpose among men and out of fear of their attendants, women—who are themselves beyond restraint—remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands. (13)
Sūta said: Thus rebuked by him, Menakā, filled with anger and her lips quivering, cursed that best of sages.
"Since I have been abandoned by you while still full of desire, O evil-minded one, and since you have cast aside the duty born of passion, therefore accept this curse from me. (15)
O evil-minded one, become this very day possessed of wrinkles and grey hair; let your limbs be worn out by old age, your vision dimmed, and your body trembling. (16)
Sūta said: As soon as these words were spoken, O best of sages, that very moment he instantly became exactly as she had described.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, he too prepared to curse her; taking water from his water-pot, his eyes were red with indignation.
"O lowest of courtesans, since I, though faultless, have been cursed by you, therefore you too shall quickly become one whose limbs are decayed by old age. (19)
By his word, she too immediately assumed such a form as that best of sages, possessing a body marked by wrinkles and grey hair.
Then, having bathed there in that reservoir of water with her former nature, she became once again exactly as she had been before.
Seeing that supreme wonder, filled with extreme haste, he too performed his ablutions there and became as he was before.

Then, endowed with the qualities of beauty and magnanimity due to the greatness of that sacred site (tīrtha), the two of them, having joyfully taken leave of one another, went to their desired destination.
Having thus understood the greatness of the sacred ford, the venerable sage installed a linga of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Then, at that most excellent tirtha, the powerful lord performed very great austerity; with a clump of kusha grass, he made that lake vast.
Having bathed there, the man who worships the supreme Liṅga known as Viśvāmitreśvara shall go to the abode of Śiva.
Even today, water equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā is seen there; it is meritorious, removing all sins, and bestowing all desires. || 27 ||
He who performs a bath there with a mind purified by faith, having reached the world of the gods, rejoices together with his ancestors.
From that time forward, that holy place attained renown upon the earth, as well as in the netherworld and the heavenly realm, bestowing beauty and magnanimity upon men. (29)
O best of the twice-born, all this that I was asked by you has been narrated—the majesty of Viśvāmitreśa, which destroys all sins.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Viśvāmitra-kuṇḍa and the Majesty of Viśvāmitreśvara," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 44 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, right there is the highly meritorious Puṣkara-traya, where in former times penance was performed by the king who was the lord of Ānarta.
He who performs a bath there at midday during the month of Kārttika when the moon is situated in the constellation Kṛttikā attains the supreme goal.
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, tell us how the highly meritorious triad of Puṣkara came to be there; in what location is it to be recognized, and by what signs? Speak."
Sūta said: I shall proclaim to you by what marks the three Puṣkaras were formerly seen there by the wise sage Viśvāmitra.
Formerly, while that great sage Viśvāmitra was dwelling there, the auspicious Kārttikī festival arrived, conjoined with the lunar conjunction of Kṛttikā.
Having realized that this sacred field consists of all holy fords, Gādhi’s son, a treasure-house of asceticism, then reflected thus within his own mind: || 6 ||

Today is this auspicious Kārttikī day, joined with the conjunction of the Kṛttikās; on this day, men obtain the highest good by bathing in the waters of Puṣkara. However, the primary Puṣkara is far away and cannot be reached at present.
"Therefore, whatever is situated here, in that very place I shall perform my bath. Having made this resolution with a mind purified by faith, [he proceeded]. (8)
Thereupon, he searched for lotuses everywhere; however, because of the great number of sacred sites there, he could not arrive at a certain conclusion.
Having seen and then lost sight of the body of water, he then performed his ablutions; wandering here and there, he subsequently became exhausted.

Then, having taken refuge at the foot of a tree and seated himself upon the ground, he became pure and, with faith, praised Tripuṣkara. "From the middle [pool], heaven is one yojana away; from the smallest, half a yojana; and from the greatest pool, it is known by those of auspicious nature to be as close as the reach of a hand."
For holy fords undoubtedly purify through bathing and giving; indeed, by the mere sight of Puṣkara, a man is liberated from sin. (13)
By resorting to the Puṣkara forest, even with only vegetables, roots, and fruits, when a single Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.
At Puṣkara, bathing is difficult to perform; at Puṣkara, austerity is difficult to practice; at Puṣkara, dwelling is difficult; everything at Puṣkara is difficult. (15)
The man who bathes at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation is instantly liberated from the sins accumulated from birth until death.
The man who bathes once at dawn during Jyeṣṭha, at midday during Madhyama, and when the sun has set during Kaniṣṭha, shall attain heaven.
The sin of all embodied beings remains within their bodies for as long as men do not perform their ablutions with the waters of Puṣkara. 18.
Just as darkness perishes when touched by the rays of the sun, so too does sin quickly depart through contact with the water of Puṣkara. || 19 ||
Even after committing a sin such as the killing of a Brahmin on this earth, a person attains freedom from fault by bathing at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika.
What is the use of gifts, what use of vows and burnt offerings, and what use of extensive sacrifices? The fruit of all these is obtained by bathing at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika.
If these words, which I have uttered with perfect sincerity, are true, then let me quickly behold the one born from Puṣkara this very moment.
O best of the twice-born, while the wise Viśvāmitra was speaking thus, an incorporeal voice arose from the sky.
O Viśvāmitra, best of sages, my stay in the sky is constant, except for the single day of Kārttikī when it is joined with the conjunction of the Kṛttikās. || 24 ||
Therefore, my stay on the surface of the earth for this day shall certainly be here; perform your ritual bath in this very sacred forest. (25)
Viśvāmitra said: It is heard that you are the refuge of all holy places (tīrthas); how then, O Lord of Tīrthas, do I know you to be established right here?
Then, O best of the twice-born, a voice arose from Tārā, who ranges the sky, gladdening Viśvāmitra, the foremost of sages.
Not far from this forest there are bodies of water; in one of them, a lotus is found situated with its face turned downwards. (28)
In the second [lotus] the face is upward-facing, and in the third it is horizontal; there, by means of the upward-facing lotuses, the Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara is to be known.
O best of the twice-born, that which has side-facing openings is proclaimed as the middling; likewise, the lotus on the earth with downward-facing openings should be known as the smallest.
"O best of sages, having recognized [the time] by these signs, perform your bath. Having heard that, the sage rose quickly and departed from there.
Those reservoirs of water were filled with such lotuses; having seen them, one endowed with faith should perform the ritual bath in the prescribed order.
And then, he duly performed the libation for the ancestors according to the prescribed rite.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he performed the Śrāddha ceremony right there according to the prescribed rite, using potherbs, roots, wild grains (nīvāra), and fruits.
There, standing on the bank, he gazed with a concentrated mind; on the full moon day of Kārttika, during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation, he was eager to see the omen.
The Brāhmaṇas said: What kind of sign appears at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika when the conjunction with the Kṛttikās occurs? Tell us all of that quickly. (36)
Sūta said: When the moon enters the conjunction of Kṛttikā on the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, then the most excellent lotus emerges from the midst of the water.
In its center, a person the size of a thumb is seen by people who have bathed well and are endowed with faith; from that, one obtains the fruit of the sacred ford (tīrtha). || 38 ||
For this reason, having bathed, the great sage Viśvāmitra, exerting himself with great effort, gazed upon that sign. (39)
While the wise Viśvāmitra was thus observing, King Bṛhadbala, the lord of Ānarta, arrived there.
Exhausted from excessive hunting, he had killed many herds of deer, as well as bears, boars, sāranga antelopes, and sambara deer.
He encountered lions, tigers, wolves, and other such violent forest-dwelling creatures on that path at midday.
Then, at the foot of a tree, he saw Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, seated after having performed his ablutions, gazing upon the body of water.
Then, having descended from his horse and prostrated deeply before him, that best of kings, afflicted by fatigue, entered into that water.
In the meantime, a lotus emerged from the water, endowed with a thousand petals and possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns.
Seeing that great and most wonderful lotus, the protector of the earth, overcome with curiosity, himself took it up with his left hand.
O best of the twice-born, as soon as he touched that lotus, a very great sound arose, by which the entire universe was filled.
Upon hearing that sound, the protector of the earth fell into a swoon; having fallen, he sank into that water, and the lotus vanished from sight.
Then, with great difficulty, he was dragged out from the water by his servants, who were afflicted by pain and grief and cried out, "Alas! Alas! in lamentation.
Then, having reached the shore and regained consciousness with great difficulty, as soon as he looked at his own body, he saw that leprosy had set in.
Then, seeing his own body in such a state—with his nose, feet, and hands withered, and his voice reduced to a gurgling sound—he fell into despair. (51)
Then, having gone to the side of the sage Viśvāmitra, the king spoke these piteous words in a voice faltering with tears.
"O Blessed One, behold my body as it has become; indeed, while submerged here in the water, it has suddenly turned loathsome. (53)
"O Lord of Sages, was it a defect in the water, or was it the earth, by which my body has so suddenly undergone such a transformation? (54)
Viśvāmitra said: "O lord of the earth, this very lotus which you have touched while impure is the Sāvitra lotus, in the center of which the Sun himself is established. (55)
O King, when the conjunction with Kṛttikā occurs for the Moon in the month of Kārttika, then this [phenomenon] arises in the water of Puṣkara.
This is that Puṣkara, the eldest, where you, afflicted by fatigue, have entered; and today is the full moon of Kārttika, conjoined with the asterism Kṛttikā.
Having seen this, a person should indeed perform a bath here in the reservoir of water; endowed with supreme faith, he goes to the highest goal.
"O King, this lotus was touched by you merely for the sake of plucking it while you were still impure; therefore, such has been the result. (59)
Bṛhadbala said: "O best of sages, how might the destruction of my leprosy come about—whether through austerity, religious observance, or indeed by the performance of a vow?"
Viśvāmitra said: "O lord of the earth, propitiate the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) in this sacred field; from that, you shall attain perfection arising from the destruction of your leprosy."
Having heard those words of the sage, King Bṛhadbala immediately installed an image of the Sun at that very moment.
Endowed with supreme faith, he worshipped according to the prescribed rites with flowers, incense, and unguents, especially on Sundays.
Devoted to fasting, and endowed with supreme faith, he should worship with red sandalwood and red flowers.
Then, at the end of a year, that lord of the earth became completely free from the disease of leprosy, possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns.
Then, having regained his own kingdom and enjoyed manifold pleasures, at the end of his body he likewise attained the abode of the Lord of Day.
Sūta said: Thus, O best of the twice-born, the wise Viśvāmitra manifested the triad of Puṣkara there before the eyes of all the world.
The man who performs his ritual bath there during the month of Kārttika, on the full moon day of Kārttika, and under the Kṛttikā constellation, goes to the world of Brahmā.

Likewise, that man who beholds Bhāskara established with great strength, having performed this for a year on Sundays until it becomes a moment [of perfection], is liberated from diseases even if he be afflicted by them. (69)
A healthy man immediately obtains what his heart desires; one free from desire attains liberation through the grace of the one with the piercing rays.

He who performs the rite of releasing a bull at the full moon of Kārttika when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation, at the most meritorious Puṣkaras, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should desire many sons, so that even one of them might go to Gayā, or perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), or set free a dark-colored bull.
On one side are all the sacred fords and on the other all gifts; but on yet another side is the release of a bull at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārtika.
Whoever should constantly hear this or recite it, endowed with faith, having indeed attained all desires, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The sages said: O high-minded one, proclaim all those other holy places that exist there; for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: There is another very beautiful sacred site there called Sārasvata, where even one who is utterly mute becomes eloquent in speech after bathing.
O best of the twice-born, he obtains his desired objects, both human and divine, as well as the worlds extending up to the realm of Brahmā.
Formerly there was a king renowned by the name Balavardhana, who enjoyed the earth girt by the oceans, which he had acquired through the strength of his own arms.
A son endowed with all auspicious marks was born to him; when the twelfth day had arrived, his father summoned the best of the twice-born and clearly gave him the name Ambuvīci.
Then that boy grew up, being pampered by the king; yet he remained mute and was unable to speak.
Then, when his seventh year had arrived, Balavardhana met his death, having been slain by his enemies in battle.
Then, because no other son existed, that prince—though mute and though a child—was installed in the kingdom by the ministers.
Thus, while that dull-witted monarch remained in his kingdom and was still in the state of childhood, the realm fell into ruin.

Then the principle of the aquatic creatures was set in motion upon the surface of the earth; all people were oppressed by those who were stronger, while the weak were tormented by the more powerful. (10)
Then those ministers spoke to Vasiṣṭha, their own family priest: "O great sage, devise a means for this king to obtain a son who is handsome."
Behold, the entire surface of the earth has become desolate; because this king is dull-witted, do what is appropriate.
Then, having meditated for a very long time, he spoke to all his dejected ministers, who were filled with distress, while that king was listening.
There is a sacred ford called Sārasvata, which grants all desires to men; let this king bathe there in the region of Hāṭakeśvara.
Then, at his word, he went there immediately and quickly; by bathing in that holy place (tīrtha), he instantly became whole-bodied once more.
Having understood that power of Sarasvatī, the lord of the earth, endowed with supreme faith, meditated upon Sarasvatī.
Then, quickly taking earth from the riverbank, he himself fashioned the goddess Bhāratī as four-armed. (17)
Holding a most beautiful lotus in her right hand, and likewise a rosary of beads possessing a splendor that has surpassed the stars in her other hand.
Likewise, in another [hand] he holds a water-pot filled with divine water, and in his left hand a book from which all branches of knowledge arise.
Then, having carefully seated her upon the surface of a pure stone slab, he worshipped her with true devotion using incense, garlands, and ointments.
And thereafter, having become composed in his presence, the king offered praise with a loud voice and a mind purified by faith. (21)
O Goddess, whatever state there may be, whether existent or non-existent, consisting of bondage or liberation—all that is pervaded by you through your secret power, just as wood is pervaded by fire.
You abide in the heart of every person in the form of accomplishment; you abide on the tongue in the form of speech, and in the eye in the form of light.
O Queen of Gods, you alone in the three worlds are to be grasped through devotion; you are solely intent on protecting the wretched and the distressed who have come to you for refuge.
You are fame, you are fortitude, you are intelligence; you are known as devotion and splendor. You are sleep, you are hunger, and you are the glory dwelling within all beings. (25)
Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Vapuḥ, Prīti, Svadhā, Svāhā, Vibhāvarī, Rati, Prīti, Kṣiti, Gaṅgā, Satya, Dharma, and Manasvinī. (26)
Lajjā, Śānti, Smṛti, Dakṣā, Kṣamā, Gaurī, Rohiṇī, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, Devamātā, and likewise Diti. (27)
Brahmāṇī, Vinatā, Lakṣmī, Kadrū, Dākṣāyaṇī, Śivā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Kṛṣi, Vṛṣṭi, Śruti, and Kalā. (28)
Balā, Nāḍī, Tuṣṭikā, Kāṣṭhā, Rasanā, and Sarasvatī; whatever else exists in the three worlds that has not been mentioned here due to its great number—[all these are within her]. (29)
O Goddess of the gods, that very form of yours is both moving and unmoving; [therein dwell] the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Devas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
Yakṣas, guhyakas, bhūtas, daityas, and those who are vināyakas—all of them have attained supreme perfection through your grace. (31)

Likewise, there are many others whom I have not mentioned; let those deities, who have been propitiated with difficulty and worshipped with extensive rites, as well as you who have been praised here, remove my sin.
Thus praised by that king, Bhāratī, the goddess of the gods, quickly became manifest before his eyes and, being well-pleased, spoke this: 33.
Sarasvatī said: "O protector of the earth, I am well-pleased by this hymn of yours, performed with constant and steadfast devotion; therefore, quickly choose a boon as you desire. (34)
The king said: "From this day forward, by my command, you must remain here in this image without doubt, for as long as my fame remains firm within these three worlds. (35)
"Whoever should properly propitiate you while you are stationed here on my account, you must indeed quickly grant him that which corresponds to his devotion. (36)
Sarasvatī said: "The man who, having bathed here in these auspicious waters, shall constantly worship me while I am stationed here on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days," || 37 ||
"O King, I shall grant him all his desired wishes. Sūta said: "Thus the goddess Sarasvatī herself remained there. (38)
From that time forward, for the welfare of the worlds, the Supreme Goddess [was worshipped], and one devoted to fasting on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days [attains her grace].
The mortal who worships her with white flowers and unguents shall be eloquent and highly intelligent in every birth, throughout all his lives. (40)
By the grace of Sarasvatī, though he may be born again and again, not even one among his descendants will ever be born dull-witted.
The man who listens to the Dharma in her presence will surely dwell in heaven for three yugas by her power.
And that man who, endowed with faith, always performs the gift of knowledge in her sanctuary, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. (43)
He who bestows upon a preeminent brahmin a book originating from the Dharmaśāstras shall obtain the complete fruit of a horse sacrifice.
He who, standing before her, performs the study of the Vedas, shall obtain the entire fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 458 ||
The sages said: O Sūta’s son, O one of great intelligence, tell us in detail the majesty of Mahākāla; for you know everything.
Sūta said: O protector of the earth, in former times there was a king, the delight of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, renowned as Rudrasena, the destroyer of all enemies.
He was like the ocean in profundity, resembling the moon in gentleness; he was like the thousand-eyed Indra in valor, and comparable to Kandarpa in beauty.
His capital was the preeminent city known as Kāntī, endowed with every excellence, featuring lofty ramparts and arched gateways.
In that same way, he had a beloved wife who was highly esteemed; she was renowned by the name Padmavatī, endowed with beauty, magnanimity, and virtuous qualities.
Accompanied by her, the king always arrives from his own abode on the day of Vaiśākha, surrounded by a small army.

O best of the twice-born, in that sacred field and seat (pīṭha) at Camatkārapura, that lord of the earth, joined with faith and accompanied by his wife, performed a night vigil before the god Mahākāla.

Devoted to fasting and meditating upon Maheśvara, O best of the twice-born, [he worshipped him] with pleasing song and instrumental music, with dance, with the recitation of dharma among the brahmins, and with extensive studies of the Vedas. || 8 ||
Then, having risen at dawn, bathed, and put on clean garments, he, being pure, gave gifts to the Brahmins, especially to those devoted to asceticism.

Every year, that lord of the earth would always come there and perform a vigil before that deity on the full moon day of Vaiśākha for the sake of the poor, the blind, the wretched, and thousands of others.
In whatever manner that protector of the earth performs his vigil at night before Mahākāla, in that same manner his prosperity increases.
Enemies go to destruction and prosperity increases; at that time, the lord of the earth arrived there.
On that very day, he saw excellent brahmins who had arrived from various directions standing before Mahākāla.
There, some of the best of Brahmins, accomplished in the study of the Vedas and devoted to the perfection of their vows, engaged in most meritorious discourses.

There were others belonging to the ancient royal sages and divine sages; others still to the sacred fords, and yet others to the celestial rishis; as well as enchanting representations of sacrifices, oceans, and islands. (15)
Then that protector of the earth, having bowed to them in due order, sat down in the midst of the assembly and was greeted with salutations by all of them.
Then, when a certain conclusion of the discourse had been reached, those lords of sages, filled with curiosity, questioned the protector of the earth.
O King, on the day of Vaiśākhī, you should always come from afar and perform a night vigil before this deity year after year.
You exert yourself with great effort, having abandoned all other activities, such as bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, which have been prescribed by those who contemplate the scriptures. (19)
If it is not a secret, then proclaim it in its entirety; surely you know all that which is the fruit of the night vigil.
The King said: "O best of the twice-born, although I have been asked about a supreme secret by you, I shall nevertheless proclaim it in its entirety."
Formerly, indeed, I was born into the merchant caste in the city of Vaidiśa; I was destitute, abandoned by my kinsmen, and humiliated at every step.
Then, after some time, the Blessed Lord Indra did not send rain upon Vaidiśa for twelve years—seven and five.
Then, due to the cessation of rain, all people were afflicted by hunger; for lack of food, some died and others departed to other lands.
Then, taking my own wife, whose limbs were emaciated by hunger, her face filled with tears, wretched and stumbling at every step, I departed. (25)
O best of the twice-born, having heard from the people that Saurāṣṭra was well-supplied with food, he set out immediately after meditating upon it in his mind for the sake of his livelihood.
Then, traveling by stages and subsisting on food obtained through alms, he reached the region of Ānarta near the city of Camatkārapura.
There I beheld a beautiful lake, adorned with clusters of lotuses, filled with clear water, and surrounded by aquatic birds.
Then, having reached that place, I bathed in the cool water; for I was afflicted by hunger, afflicted by thirst, and especially afflicted by exhaustion.
Then I was told by my wife: "O Master, take lotuses from the pond for the sake of sale, so that there may be food today. (30)
"Yonder city, resembling the city of Indra, is visible from afar; having reached this best of cities, you ought to make your sale. (3)
Then, O best of the twice-born, I took many lotuses for the purpose of selling them, desiring food. (32)
O best of the twice-born, having reached Camatkārapura, I then wandered through all the triple-junctions, crossroads, and houses.
No man accepts those lotuses; by the power of my own misfortune, people have become averse to purchasing them. (34)
Then, while my throat was parched with hunger and I was exhausted, the sun reached the mountain of setting, and the time of twilight arrived. (35)
Then, having attained dispassion, I slept in that ruined temple; together with my wife, I laid those lotuses upon the surface of the earth.
Then, when midnight had arrived, the sound of singing was heard by me; thereupon, I thought in my mind: "This is undoubtedly a wakeful vigil. (37)
Therefore, I shall go; if some man should accept these lotuses from me for a price, from that my food will arise. (38)
Having made this resolution, he quickly took lotuses and set out with his wife toward the place where the sound of singing was heard.

Then, O best of sages, having arrived at that sacred site, I beheld Mahākāla, the Lord of the gods of gods, being worshipped by the foremost of the twice-born standing before him, who were devoted to the practice of japa and song.
O best of the twice-born, some performed dance, others song, and still others recitation; some performed fire-offerings, while others engaged in the narration of dharma.
Then I asked someone there: "Is a vigil being observed here? Who are these people so intent on the vigil? Tell me quickly. (42)
He said: "This vigil for the god Mahākāla is being performed with devotion by Brahmins who are dedicated to fasting. (43)
Today is the supreme, merit-bestowing Vaiśākhī, known as a sacred lunar day; on this day, a man who performs a vigil before this deity Mahākāla with devotion undoubtedly attains happiness.
"O good man, give me these lotuses; taking their price, I shall give you three palas of gold for the sake of food. (45)
Then, O best of brahmins, it was resolved in my mind: "I shall worship Mahākāla, the lord of the gods, with these lotuses."
"No meritorious deed whatsoever was performed by me in another body; surely because of that, I have become thus, fallen into such misery. (47)
Moreover, this wife of mine, who speaks so sweetly, has her throat parched with hunger; due to the lack of food, she will undoubtedly perish by morning. (48)
While I was reflecting thus, my beloved, standing there bowed in humility, spoke these sweet words to me.
O Lord, do not sell lotuses out of greed for wealth; rather, act upon the beneficial words that I shall now speak to you. (50)
"Without a doubt, our fasting has arisen from force due to the lack of grain; and our keeping of the vigil as well will be caused by hunger. (51)
There, during the day, both of them—afflicted by the heat and exhausted by fatigue—performed their ablutions in the beautiful lake and likewise offered worship to the deity.
Therefore, let us now worship the god Mahākāla with these lotuses, by which the highest welfare may arise for both of us. (53)

The King said: Then, O best of the twice-born, having established himself in the quality of goodness (sattva) and performed worship with those lotuses, Maheśvara was honored by both of them who were filled with joy.
Due to the torment of hunger, not even the slightest sleep came to us in any way, even though we remained here in the temple in the presence of Hara.
Then, at the time of dawn when the orb of the sun had risen, O best of the twice-born, I died right here in this very place, overcome by hunger.
Then my beloved, taking that body with her, entered the fire, filled with great joy.
By its power, I was born as the lord of Kāntī, a sovereign of the earth; and she too, the virtuous daughter of the lord of Daśārṇa, became one who remembers her former births.
Then, having recognized me as her own husband when I arrived at the svayaṃvara, she was likewise recognized by me and brought back as my former wife.
For this reason, O best of the twice-born, I perform the vigil for this Mahākāla every year on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
Having worshipped Mahākāla together with this beloved wife using flowers, incense, and ointments—this which I have spoken is the truth. (61)
O Brahmins, this vigil throughout the night was indeed performed by me at that time; yet this fruit has arisen through the power of this very deity.
Now, endowed with faith, according to the prescribed rule, I do not know what fruit this action of mine will bestow upon me.
All this has been truly recounted to you by me, O best of the twice-born; by that truth, may this Mahākāla be propitiated. (64)
Sūta said: Having heard this, O best of the twice-born, their eyes blossomed with wonder, and they repeatedly offered words of praise to that reciter of prayers.
The Brahmins said: "O protector of the earth, all these words spoken by you are true; by the grace of Mahākāla, nothing on earth is difficult to obtain."
Therefore, O King, we shall specifically perform a night vigil for this deity with faith every single year.
Then that king and all those twice-born ones performed a vigil in the presence of Mahākāla.

Filled with exceptional joy through various songs and instrumental music, religious narrations, dances, and diverse Vedic recitations, all the kings from that time forward performed [the rites] imbued with wonder. (69)
Then, at the clear dawn, that king arose, worshipped Mahākāla and all those best of the twice-born, and having taken leave of them, departed joyfully with his army toward his own city.
Then, in the course of time, having reached the end of his body, that lord of the earth attained the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
O best of Brahmins, all this greatness arising from Mahākāla, which destroys every sin, has been narrated to you. (72)

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Mahākāleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Holy Field of Hāṭakeśvara" in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: In that very region, there is the highly renowned hermitage of King Hariścandra, surrounded by various kinds of trees.
There he performed austerities after establishing Umā and Maheśvara, while bestowing various desired gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas.
In ancient times, there was a king named Hariścandra, the son of Triśaṅku; he was the illustrious lord of Ayodhyā, born of the Solar dynasty.
While he ruled according to the Dharma, there was certainly no famine, nor disease, nor untimely death; nor was there any fear caused by thieves.
The clouds always rain at the proper time, the crops are abundant, the waters are full of flavor, and the trees bear fruit in all seasons. || 5 || || 2 ||
In that dwelling, there was punishment; in the gambling with dice, there was the besieging of the house. The moon is the sole source of faults, and owls are fond of darkness.

In the case of lamps, there is the exhaustion of oil; in marriage, the taking of the hand; likewise, in prose, there is a break in the meter; and in the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), there is the arising of the impulse to give.
For that universal monarch, though endowed with such virtues, there was only one great defect: he was destitute of a son.
Then, having gone for the sake of his son, he performed very great penance after installing a Liṅga with devotion in the sacred field of Camatkārapura.
Practicing the five-fire austerity in the summer, staying under the open sky during the rains, and taking refuge in water during the winter, he meditates upon Maheśvara.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara, being pleased with him, appeared before his eyes, accompanied by Gaurī and surrounded by hosts of attendants.
He said, "I am the giver of boons; ask for whatever you desire. I shall grant it to you, even if it be very difficult to obtain."
Then, having prostrated before him and praised him loudly with well-known hymns, he stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke with humility.
"O best of gods, by your grace, whatever exists upon the surface of the earth—all that which is desired by my own mind—is present in my home. (14)
Beautiful wives, a kingdom with its thorns removed, a body free from disease, and likewise wealth beyond measure.
"One great sorrow is mine, that no offspring exists; therefore, O Lord Śaṅkara, if you are pleased, grant me a son. (6)
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of kings, by my grace, a son shall be born to you before long; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, go home at once."
Sūta said: In the meantime, Gaurī, her eyes bloodshot with anger, having rebuked Mahādeva, then spoke to that king.
"O great fool, because you did not offer me a salutation immediately after Hara, I shall therefore bestow a curse upon you. (19)
A son shall be born to you, just as was foretold by the wielder of the trident; however, even in infancy, you shall experience that supreme suffering born of death.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lady, together with the god Śambhu and likewise with her other attendants, thereafter vanished from sight.
Having received both the boon and the curse immediately thereafter, that king did not return home, but instead performed very great penance once more.
Having seated Gaurī and Maheśvara together upon a single seat, she then worshipped them both with flowers and unguents.
The lord of the earth gave gifts especially to the Brahmins; sleeping on the ground, with a tranquil mind, he took food only at every sixth mealtime.
Then, at the end of a year, the Lord whose banner bears the bull appeared once more before him, accompanied by Pārvatī.
Then that king, having simultaneously offered salutations to both according to the prescribed rite, spoke these words with humility: || 26 ||
O Goddess, formerly, with my mind overwhelmed by a flood of bliss, I did not bow to you; therefore, you ought not to be angry with me. (27)
O Goddess, you always occupy half the body of the wielder of the trident; why then, when he is bent, are you not also bent? Tell me this. (28)
He who bows to that Lord of Gods, by him you are always bowed to; it is my conviction that when you are bowed to, the Lord of Gods is likewise bowed to. (529)
Nevertheless, O Goddess, you were worshipped by me as distinct from him, yet seated upon the same throne and honored equally with him.
Therefore, grant me your grace; let that boon which was previously mentioned by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) for the sake of obtaining a son become fruitful for me this very moment.
O Goddess, you ought to act in such a way that, through your grace, there may be for me a son who upholds the lineage, long-lived, and of firm prowess. (32)
The Goddess said: "O King, my word can never be otherwise in this matter; therefore, even though he is but a child, your son shall meet his death. (33)
Having experienced that suffering arising from near-death, he shall regain his life-breaths once more before long through my grace. (34)
And from him shall arise a long-lived victor who sustains the lineage, a preeminent sovereign of the whole earth, a donor, a performer of sacrifices, and a knower of dharma. (35)
Therefore, O King, go home and rule the kingdom you desire; you shall obtain an excellent son just as I have described.
Furthermore, whatever other human being worships me here, established in this form, shall do so together with the divine Śambhu.
To him I shall grant sons desired by his heart, as well as whatever else he may wish for; there is no doubt about this, and it shall happen before long.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O best of kings, request again from me whatever you desire; the sight of me shall not be in vain—I tell you this truth.

Hariścandra said: "O Lord of Gods, I have accomplished my purpose; everything is present in my home. Having been abandoned by you, even that son has been granted to me—victorious and the upholder of my lineage."
Nevertheless, your command must not be rendered futile in any way; for this reason, O Lord, I shall request that which I desire.
Our minds were always inclined toward performing the Rājasūya sacrifice; however, at that time, all my ministers and friends sought to dissuade me.
A sacrifice is performed by all those kings who have been made to pay tribute; yet, O Lord, they do not offer tribute without war. (43)
Therefore, those who desire my welfare restrain me, who am intent on war and eager to achieve the sacrifice, as they abide by the path of policy.
Therefore, through your grace, may the Rājasūya sacrifice take place; may it reach completion without obstacle. I choose nothing else for myself. (45)
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," Hara vanished from sight; and that king, having obtained the boon, returned to his own palace.
Thus, Umā and Maheśvara were first fashioned there by that lord of men, and afterwards they were fashioned by others as well.

O twice-born ones, he who performs worship of those two with fruits on all his limbs when the fifth day arrives, shall obtain his desired son, capable of uplifting his own lineage, for as long as a year.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Umā and Maheśvara," in the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Right there, situated upon the bank of the lake, is the highly meritorious site known as Kalaśeśvara, which destroys all sins. || 1 ||
Upon seeing Kalaśeśvara, a person is liberated from sin.
Formerly, there was one named Kalaśa, born of the Yadu lineage; he was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all the worlds.
Then, after some time, Durvāsas, the best of sages, having completed his four-month vow, arrived at that house.
Then the king, rising quickly, went forward to meet him with joy, respectfully saying, "Welcome, welcome to you! (5)
Then, having bowed to him with devotion and having personally washed his feet, he offered the arghya and spoke as follows, his eyes clouded with tears of joy.
"This kingdom, these sons, these women, and this wealth—tell me everything, O sage, and I shall grant whatever you require. (7)
Durvāsas said: "O great king, it is fitting for you to speak thus regarding such a task for a brahmin like me, who has come to your home and observes vows."
"O best of kings, I have no need for wealth nor for a kingdom; therefore, as one observing the Cāturmāsya vow, I am now eager to perform the concluding feast (pāraṇa)."
Therefore, O King, whatever food has been prepared for you in your house, give that to me for my meal; my hunger is increasing exceedingly. (10)
Sūta said: Thereupon, that protector of the earth himself presented him with well-prepared food, as was available, for the purpose of his meal.

Various condiments and many kinds of cooked foods—drinks, things to be sucked, things to be chewed, and foods of many kinds to be licked—as well as various meats well-prepared with salt and other seasonings. (12)
Then that brahmin, emaciated by hunger and filled with haste, ate; though full of joy, he did not perceive the taste of the food due to his large morsels. || 13 ||
Then, O brahmins, having tasted the flavor of the meat and being satisfied by it, that lord of sages, his soul overcome with anger, cursed him.
"Since you have caused a breach of my vow by giving me meat, therefore you shall become a fierce tiger that feeds on raw flesh. (15)
Then that king, terrified, bowed down to the lord of sages and spoke with a dejected face, trembling and deeply distressed.
O sage, since I have offered hospitality with prepared food to you whose throat is parched by hunger, why are you intent on cursing me? (17)
Therefore, O best of brahmins, show favor to me, your devotee and humble servant; quickly grant relief from this curse through your grace.
Durvāsas said: A twice-born man should not eat meat except at a śrāddha or a sacrifice, especially at the conclusion of a vow or during the Cāturmāsya period. (19)
If a twice-born man, having set himself to observe a fast, nevertheless eats meat, his vow certainly becomes futile, for he has consumed meat in vain. (20)
Therefore, my vow arising from the Cāturmāsya has been ruined; for that reason, O Indra among kings, you have now been cursed by me in anger.
The king said: "Nevertheless, O Brahmin, bring about for me the end of this curse as you desire, especially since I am devoted, wretched, and particularly innocent. (22)
Durvāsas said: When your cow Nandinī shows you the Liṅga formerly worshipped by Bāṇa, then your liberation will swiftly come to pass.
Having spoken thus, that best of Brahmins departed for his own hermitage; and that king also became a tiger of most fierce appearance.
Then, having lost his memory and seeing creatures standing before him, he was driven away by others who struck him, and he entered the great forest.
Then those ministers, desiring that kingdom for the king who was awaiting the end of his curse, indeed made it well-protected.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of King Kalaśa’s Attainment of the State of a Tiger through the Curse of Durvāsas," within the Narrative of Kalaśeśvara, in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya of the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 49 ||
In this manner, O twice-born one, a very long time passed as that lord of men, in the form of a tiger, was slaying various creatures in the forest.
Then, after some time, O best of the twice-born, a beautiful cowherd settlement (gokula), crowded with cowherds and cowherdesses, arrived in that region.
There is a cow there named Nandinī, with full udders, a broad expanse of hips, the color of a swan, and yielding milk from her udders like jars. (3)
Then, wandering at the edge of a grove in search of grass for her own herd, she came upon the linga of the trident-bearing God.
He beheld him endowed with splendor, established there of his own accord, resembling twelve suns, supreme, and bringing delight to the mind.
Then, O twice-born ones, standing upon it and endowed with supreme faith, she poured forth a great quantity of water for the purpose of his ablution.
Thus, no person in that forest thick with trees knew that she was constantly performing the ritual bathing of that liṅga.
On another day, a tiger arrived at that place—one with sharp fangs and a massive body, bringing fear to all living beings.
Then, O best of the twice-born, by the turn of fate, that Nandinī arrived there and fell within the range of vision of that tiger.
Then, remembering her own small calf tied up in Gokula—one that did not eat grass and subsisted only on milk—she lamented piteously.
Today, having abandoned my young son—who was being kept confined by the cowherds in the cow-pen—I have arrived alone in this forest devoid of people. (11)
By that truth through which I have come today out of devotion to bathe Śiva, by that truth may I be reunited with my son.
While Nandinī was thus lamenting piteously at length, the tiger smiled and spoke these harsh words. (13)

The tiger said: "O cow, why do you utter these vain lamentations while remaining under my power? Therefore, O auspicious one, for the sake of attaining heaven, remember the God who is most dear to you. (14)
The cow said: "O tiger, I do not lament for my own sake in this state of great misery; rather, death, which brings auspiciousness, has occurred for me on account of the worship of Śiva. (15)
"My calf is tied in the cow-pen, remembering my arrival; subsisting on milk, how will it endure without me? (16)
For this reason, O tiger, I lament in great distress; I swear by the truth that it is not for the sake of my own life that I do so. (17)
Therefore, O great tiger, release me immediately, for I am devoted to my son; having delivered him to my circle of friends, I shall return to your presence.
The tiger said: "How is it that having once entered the jaws of death and somehow escaped, you emerge from it only to enter it again? Therefore, I shall devour you. (19)
Nandinī said: "O tiger, hear from my mouth those oaths by which I shall return to your presence; then do what is appropriate. (20)
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin which lies in the murder of a Brahmin and in the deception of one's mother and father. 21.
May I be tainted by the sin of those who bathe naked and of those who engage in sexual intercourse during the day, if I do not return again. 22.
"May I be tainted by that sin which belongs to those who follow women during their menses and to those who sleep naked, if I do not return again. (23)
If I do not come again, may I be tainted by that same sin which belongs to those who betray trust and to those who are ungrateful. 24.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin which belongs to those who defile cows, maidens, and Brahmins. 25.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin of those who perform useless cooking and those who eat meat in vain. (26)
"May I be tainted by that sin of those who break their vows and those who approach women outside the proper season, if I do not return again. (27)
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin which belongs to those who slander, those who inform on others, and those who practice with weapons. 28.
Sūta said: Then, having heard those oaths, that tiger was filled with wonder; considering them to be true, he spoke again to Nandinī, who was devoted to her calf. (1)
"If this is so, then go to that house and look for your own son; having entrusted him to his friends, then return once more. (2)
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Vyāghra, Suśīlā Nandinī then departed toward her home, where her young son was staying.
Then, seeing his mother arrived at an improper time with a terrified heart and observing her lamenting, the son spoke out of astonishment: || 4 ||
Why have you arrived at an improper time? Why is your mind so bewildered? Why is your face drenched with tears? O Mother, tell me quickly.
Nandinī said: "If you ask me, my son, then suckle at my breast; once you are satiated by that, I shall tell you the entire account."
Sūta said: Having heard her words, having drunk the milk as was appropriate, and having been smelled on the head by her, he then spoke quickly.
"O Mother, tell me today the entire account arising from the forest, by hearing which from your mouth, O Mother, my own composure shall be restored."
Nandinī said: "O son, today I went at my will into the great forest; while wandering here and there, I was encountered there by a tiger."
O son, having been entreated by me while devouring that claw-armed beast, he said, "I shall come to Gokula after seeing my own offspring, provided I am bound by oaths."
Having been released by him through the many oaths he has made, I shall go back to that very place once you have been seen and spoken with. (11)
Vatsa said: "I shall go to that very place where you are going; for now, death in the presence of my mother would indeed be praiseworthy for me. (12)
"You must indeed die alone, deprived of me; even without the drinking of milk, in a very short time. (13)
O mother, if a tiger should kill me while I am with you, surely that same destination which belongs to those devoted to their mothers shall be mine. (14)
Or rather, O auspicious lady, let those oaths which were made by you to him be mine; therefore, remain right here in this Gokula.
There is no kinsman equal to a mother for children who live on milk; there is no protector equal to a mother, and there is no refuge equal to a mother. (16)
There is no one as worthy of worship as a mother; there is no friend equal to a mother; there is no deity equal to a mother, both in this world and in the next. (17)
Thinking thus, the best of men should always practice devotion toward their mother. Those sons who follow this supreme duty ordained by Prajāpati attain the highest goal. || 18 ||
Therefore, I shall depart, while you remain here in Gokula; I will undoubtedly protect your life with my own life. (19)
Nandinī said: "Death was ordained for me alone, not for you, my son, on this day. So how can you protect my life with your own vital breaths? (20)
"O son, this is the final and supreme instruction from your mother; you must carry it out with diligence, following my word. (21)
"O son, while wandering in the forest, you must not succumb to negligence; for from greed arises destruction, both in this world and in the next. (22)
Deluded by greed, men enter the ocean, the forest, and battle; there is nothing in this world that men will not do out of greed. (23)
A person is destroyed by three things: greed, negligence, and misplaced trust; therefore, one should not be greedy, nor negligent, nor should one place trust [in others]. 24.
"O son, you must always protect yourself with great effort from all predatory beasts as you wander through the dense forest. (25)
"My son, you must never go anywhere alone, abandoning your own herd, even if you find grass and food in a precarious place. (26)
Having spoken thus and repeatedly licking that calf, she was overcome with great grief, her eyes clouded with tears. (27)
Then, O best of the twice-born, she went to see all her female companions, her body tormented by grief for her son and utterly distraught.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having gone to the forest where they were wandering at their pleasure, joyfully eating the grass they desired, he spoke to them all.
In Bahula, Campaka, Dāma, Vasudhāra, Ghaṭasrava, Haṃsanāda, Priyānanda, Śubhakṣīra, and Mahodaya; || 30 ||
Likewise, other cows that are stationed near the cow-pen, let them hear my words and act accordingly thereafter: "Today, while wandering not very far from my own herd," (31)
Then, having entered a dense forest devoid of human beings, she was encountered there by a tiger while she was wandering in search of grass.
"I have arrived for the sake of seeing you and conversing with your son, having gained the trust of that claw-weaponed one through difficult oaths. (33)
Indeed, that son was seen, spoken to, and disciplined by me; now he has been given to you all like a little son.
O auspicious ladies, whatever wrong I have done to you, whether out of ignorance or intentionally, that must be forgiven by you through your grace. (35)
For this child of mine is helpless, weak, and miserable; being a nursing infant tormented by grief for his mother, he must be protected by all of you. (36)
Wandering through uneven places, going to other cowherd settlements, and being attached to improper activities—he must always be restrained with earnest care. (37)
I shall go there where that tiger resides; this is my final salutation made to all of you. (38)
The cows said: "O Nandini, you must not go there under any circumstances; surely you do not understand the duty in times of distress, since you are departing. (39)
