A word spoken in jest does no harm; nor does it harm when addressed to women, at the time of marriage, during a life-threatening emergency, or when all one's wealth is being seized. These five instances of untruth, they say, do not constitute a sin.
Therefore, you must not go there; there is no fault in this for you, O auspicious one. Protect your own son and come with us to our own home.

Nandinī said: "O auspicious ones, it is fitting for virtuous people to perform such an act for the sake of sustaining the lives of others; however, doing so for the sake of one's own life is not praised by the righteous."
The world is established in truth; Dharma is established in truth. By virtue of his truthful speech, the ocean does not overstep its boundaries. (43)
Having given the earth to Viṣṇu, Bali took refuge in the netherworld; relying upon his word of truth, the lord of the Daityas does not emerge.
What sin has not been committed by that man of unrefined intellect, who, having made his own word a vow, does not act according to what was spoken? (45)

The friends said: "O Nandini, you are worthy of being saluted by all the gods and asuras alike—you who, for the sake of establishing truth, are casting away your life-breaths, which are so difficult to abandon."
But what shall we say to you, O auspicious lady, who yourself speak of dharma and artha, who are endowed with all virtues even from childhood, and who are ever established in truth? (47)
Therefore go, O illustrious lady; your little son is not to be grieved for. Whatever we have been told by you, that indeed we shall do. (48)
Furthermore, we know this well: for men who are always truthful, the undertaking of an action never becomes fruitless in any way whatsoever. (49)
Sūta said: Having thus addressed all her companions, Nandinī, afflicted by grief for her son, set out toward the tiger.
Tormented by the fire of grief and despairing of seeing her son, she was like a cakravākī bird separated from her mate, or like a creeper fallen from a tree.
Like a blind woman deprived of sight, stumbling at every step, she prayed to all the presiding deities of the forest for the sake of her son.
May all the presiding deities of the forest protect my young son, whether he be asleep or wandering about, at my command. (53)
Having thus lamented in her mind, she arrived at that place where he sat—his mouth agape, possessing sharp fangs, and inspiring terror.
And a tiger, its throat emaciated by hunger, was watching her path, filled with impetuous agitation and licking the corners of its mouth. (55)
Nandinī said: "I have come, O great tiger, abiding by my truthful oath; satisfy yourself now with my flesh as you desire. (56)
Upon seeing her, that evil-minded one also attained supreme detachment; Satyāśayā, for her part, returned, having cast aside the fear of death. (57)
The tiger said: "Welcome to you, O auspicious one, O excellent cow, O speaker of truth! Indeed, nothing inauspicious ever befalls those who possess truth. (58)
"O blessed lady, you said with oaths that you would return again; because of that, curiosity has arisen in me as to what she will do. (59)
Therefore, O blessed lady, I am one of evil conduct, cruel, and a slayer of living beings; by this deed, I shall forever go to a terrible hell.
Therefore, O highly fortunate lady, you ought to show favor to me, a sinner and one of most wicked soul, by granting me instruction.
"By what means may I attain the highest good in this world and the next? Nothing remains unknown to you; such is my conviction regarding your truthful conduct. (62)
Therefore, proclaim to me in brief the entire essence of Dharma, by which the complete fruit of association with the virtuous may arise for me. (63)

Nandinī said: "They praise austerity in the Kṛta age, and meditation alone in the Tretā; in the Dvāpara they praise sacrifice and yoga, but in the Kali age, charity alone. Among all forms of giving, there is no gift superior to this. (64)
He who grants fearlessness to all beings, both moving and unmoving, becomes liberated from all fears and attains the Supreme Brahman. || 65 ||
The tiger said: "O auspicious lady, that gift is appropriate for other beings as well, for whom the maintenance of life depends upon non-violence and food."

"Since our sustenance of life cannot occur without violence, therefore, O highly fortunate lady, tell me some instruction that brings happiness even to me, who am a violator of embodied beings, so that it may lead toward true dharma. (67)
Nandinī said: "In this place there is a very great liṅga, formerly installed by Bāṇa; by its power, I have certainly been liberated by you from this thicket. (68)
Rising early in the morning, you should always perform circumambulation and prostration to it; then you will attain your desired success. (69)
"O you whose weapons are your claws, no power exists in any other action of yours, such as worship and the like, because of the deficiency of your two hands; this is my opinion. (70)
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, that cow then stood before the tiger at the edge of the forest and showed him that linga.
By the mere sight of him, he too attained liberation at that very moment; he became a king once again, just as before, released from his state as a tiger.
Then that best of kings, remembering the curse given by Durvāsas and his own kingdom along with his sons, spoke to Nandinī.
"I am a king named Kalaśa, born of the Haihaya lineage; formerly, for a certain reason, I was cursed by Durvāsas. (74)
Then, having been propitiated, he said to me: "When Nandinī reveals that liṅga, then liberation will occur. (75)
Surely you are that very Nandinī; I have recognized you through the end of my curse. Therefore, tell me the truth, O excellent cow: what region is this?
O illustrious lady, having seen a human being on the road, I shall quickly find a way to return once more to my own home. (77)
Nandinī said: "O King, this sacred field of Camatkārapura destroys all sins; it comprises all holy fords and bestows all desires. (78)
Whatever merit ascetics might gain elsewhere in a year, that is perfectly attained here in a single day; of this there is no doubt. (79)
Thinking thus, I have always bathed the Liṅga with milk, having abandoned this herd with a heart purified by devotion. (80)
The King said: "Go, Nandini; may it be well with you. Return to your own child, to Gokula, to your friends, to your own people, and likewise to your other kinsmen. (81)
I previously heard about this sacred field from the mouths of Brahmins; though I always desired to inquire further, I was never able to see it for myself. || 82 ||
O Nandini, being occupied with the duties of kingship and attached to enjoyments, I have now obtained this for myself; I do not wish to abandon it.
"By good fortune, that curse was bestowed upon me by the high-souled sage; for how else, O beautiful one, could the attainment of this sacred field have been possible? (84)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and dismissed Nandinī, the protector of the earth remained right there, meditating upon that Liṅga day and night.
Having constructed for his sake a preeminent palace of wondrous appearance, shaped like the peak of Mount Kailāsa, he performed austerities in front of it.
Then, O twice-born ones, by its power, within just a few days he attained the supreme perfection that is difficult even for performers of sacrifice to reach.
In that regard, he who offers a lamp during the month of Kārttika is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 88 ||
When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, the man who performs singing, dancing, and so forth before him with devotion, goes to the supreme goal. (89)
O best of the twice-born, this entire majesty of Kalaśeśvara, which destroys all sins, has been narrated to you in detail.
And whoever recites this with devotion, endowed with supreme faith, he too, being liberated from sin, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 91 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kalaśeśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 51 ||
Sūta said: There, that king established Umā and Maheśvara after constructing a supreme temple that bestows happiness upon the sight of the virtuous.
In front of him, a beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) was likewise constructed there; it was filled with clear water and adorned with clusters of lotuses.
The man who, having bathed there with devotion on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, beholds those two with a concentrated mind, is not born here again.
In the eastern direction of that very place, near the Agastya-kuṇḍa, there is a highly meritorious step-well (vāpī) which destroys all sins.
The man who performs a bath in that [tirtha] during the month of Phālguna, fasting on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, obtains his heart's desire.
In its southern region there is the river Kapilā, where Kapila attained the perfection arising from Sāṃkhya.
To the east of Kapilā, the Siddhakṣetra is celebrated, where in former times hundreds of thousands of Siddhas attained perfection.
Whatever desire a person contemplates while performing austerity for that purpose, he shall certainly attain it within six months.
O Brahmins, beneath that there exists an auspicious Vaiṣṇavī stone; it is square, revolving, and the destroyer of all sins.
The Sarasvatī, which flows between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, is always washed by the waters of the great river and bestows liberation upon men.
The Triveṇī flows before it, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; especially for those Brāhmaṇas who have been cremated upon it.
"Surely liberation will come to them; a cow's footprint is seen there in the ashes of the funeral pyre. Knowing this, O Brāhmaṇas, those who have died there should be consecrated. (12)
O best of the twice-born, to the north of that very place is Rudrakoṭi, which is worshipped by high-souled Brahmins from the south.
In the form of great yogis, the best of the twice-born from the south, having heard [of him] for themselves, went to the field of Camatkārapura to see Umāpati.
Then, filled with curiosity and endowed with supreme faith, those numbering ten million went swiftly, desiring a vision of him.
"I shall see that Hara first! I shall see him first!"—thus, filled with such faith, they went and made this oath.
Among these, whoever should look upon that great yogi, the Lord, as the final deity, he shall become a doer of evil.
Then, having understood their intention, the Lord Maheśvara, pleased by their devotion, assumed ten million forms for their benefit.
O best of the twice-born, he attained a vision [of the Lord] with ease; from that time forth, that place has become renowned as Rudrakoṭi.
O best of the twice-born, for that purpose a verse was recited long ago by Nārada, who was filled with joy upon beholding Rudrāvarta.
"Blessed are those on earth who shall obtain the fourteenth day of the Rudrāvarta on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, Māgha, and likewise Caitra. (21)
Having committed sin on this earth for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, a man, upon beholding Rudrāvarta, attains freedom from sin.
Having gone to Rudrāvarta and beheld Hara, the Lord of Yoga, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, a man certainly becomes free from sin. || 23 ||
O twice-born ones, he who performs a śrāddha there in Mahāyogipura, at Rudrāvarta, obtains the fruit arising from a hundred sacrifices.
That man who, being intent on fasting, performs a night vigil, goes to heaven by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will. || 25 ||
In that regard, he who gives a tawny cow to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires shall become a member of Gaṇa; of this there is no doubt, and he likewise becomes beloved of Hara.
For one who stands before a great yogi and recites the six-syllable mantra, that mantra shall yield a merit six times greater than that of a Rājasūya sacrifice.
Whoever should recite the Śatarudriya before him with devotion shall obtain the fruit of all four Vedas that have been studied. || 28 ||
Whether it be song or dance that a man performs before him, he shall attain the merit of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. (29)
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, that sage born of Brahmā ceased speaking; then, delighted, he quickly departed on his pilgrimage.
Sūta said: Right there is the Ujjayinī-pīṭha, which grants the desires of men, endowed with many wonders, and frequented by numerous perfected beings (siddhas). || 1 ||
O best of the twice-born, Maheśvara himself always resides within its center in the form of Mahākāla.

O best of the twice-born, that man who, being composed, performs a śrāddha there on the full moon day of Vaiśākha and then beholds the Lord of Gods known as Mahākāla, should worship Him by taking refuge in His southern form.
O best of the twice-born, having rescued ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself—these twenty-one persons—he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having meditated upon whichever desire one has in mind, one should worship the *pīṭha* there; and having worshipped the assembly of Yoginīs as well as the assembly of maidens. (5)
He attains all of that, even what may be very difficult to obtain, provided he is composed on the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha.
Any man endowed with faith, who is pure and devoted to fasting, and who performs a vigil before him filled with devotion—he goes to the supreme abode, free from old age and death.
Of what use are vows, or useless gifts, or recitations, or religious observances? All of these are not worth even a sixteenth part of your [devotion to] Mahākāla.
Sūta said: Right there is the highly fortunate pit known as Bhrūṇagartā; it is vast in form and destroys all sins.
Where King Saudāsa was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, and King Suṣeṇa was liberated from the sin of killing a woman. || 10 ||
The sages said: "How did the murder of a Brahmin come to pass for that king Saudāsa, even though he was devoted to the Brahmins? Tell us that. (11)
It is heard that he was a protector of the earth devoted to the welfare of the Brahmins; how then did he become a slayer of Brahmins in deed, thought, and speech? (12)
And how did one who was liberated again resort to the pit of the embryo? How did that pit come into being? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, when the fall of the phallus of the trident-bearing God of gods occurred, he was then overcome with shame due to the absence of that phallus.
Having dug an exceedingly vast pit, the wielder of the trident then entered it; he did not reveal himself to anyone at that time.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, that pit was formed there; I shall now relate how that servant became free from sin within it.
There was a king named Mitrasaha, most righteous; his son was Saudāsa, who was born directly from the solar dynasty.
By him, the high-souled one, vast sacrifices were performed with gold as the excellent sacrificial fees, and innumerable gifts were bestowed. (18)
Then, after some time, while a twelve-year sacrificial session was being conducted according to rule and by means of rites prescribed by ordinance, (19)
At the onset of night, two exceedingly powerful Rākṣasas, Krūrākṣa and Krūrabuddhi, arrived to create obstacles for the sacrifice.
Together with many rākṣasas, as well as others known as bhūtas, and with invincible piśācas who were intent on the destruction of sacrifices. || 21 ||
Then all those Rākṣasas, having observed some slight opening, entered that sacrificial enclosure, crawling about on all sides.
Slaying the best of Brahmins and devouring the sacrificial offerings, as well as those various things prepared for the sake of the sacrifice. || 23 ||
In the meantime, a great cry of "Alas! arose there as the brahmins were being devoured by the exceedingly powerful rākṣasas.
Then King Maitrāvaruṇa, becoming enraged and abandoning his initiatory vows, took up his bow along with an arrow and, seeing them, began to destroy them.
Having performed the protective rites himself under the guidance of his own family priest Vasiṣṭha, he slew Krūrākṣa along with many Rākṣasas.
Then, seeing that his excellent brother had been killed and that tiger among kings was unassailable due to his Brahmanic splendor, he became cruel-minded.
Taking with him the surviving Rākṣasas, he, whose body was wounded by his arrows, fled in fear accompanied by his army.
Then, relying on that enmity toward his elder brother, the Rākṣasa sought a vulnerability day and night for the purpose of killing him.
O brahmins, while that high-souled one was thus observing for a flaw, his twelve-year sacrificial session reached its conclusion.
Not even the slightest vulnerability was found by that evil-minded one, for the protection ordained by Vasiṣṭha remained intact during that sacrifice of the lord of the earth.
Then, having dismissed all the Brahmins to whom he had given sacrificial fees, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke this to Vasiṣṭha: || 32 ||
"O Guru, today I am eager to feed you with my own hand; please grant me this favor by eating at my residence today. (33)
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, had his feet washed by him and sat down for the meal.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Kūrabbuddhi beheld that auspicious meat, which had been well-prepared according to the prescribed rules by the cooks.
Having fashioned a sacrificial cauldron (ukhā) of such a kind and according to that same measure, unexpectedly, he filled it with human flesh and carried it away laden with meat.
Then that tiger among sages, while eating, realized it was indeed human flesh; enraged, he spoke there with indignation: || 37 ||
"Since you, O lowest of men, have caused me to eat human flesh like a Rakshasa, therefore you shall become a Rakshasa this very day. (38)
Then, having observed those cooks individually, the king skillfully investigated the source of that meat. (39)
They said, "O protector of the earth, such meat as this was not cooked by us; believe it, for it was not prepared by any other human being. (40)
"O Lord, O Protector, having ascertained whether this is a Rākṣasa, a Piśāca, or a Dānava—apart from these—then do whatever is appropriate. (41)
In the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived and told him everything regarding the activities of that Rākṣasa.

Having heard that, King Saudāsa became enraged and prepared to cast a curse upon Vasiṣṭha; taking water in his hand, the lord of the earth was about to pronounce the curse when Nārada, seeing him thus intent on cursing, spoke these words.

O protector of the earth, even if twice-born ones are slaying, cursing, or hating you, they must nevertheless be honored by one who desires his own welfare; moreover, O best of kings, this preceptor is to be revered by you. (44)
Therefore, you ought not to curse the holy sage with a counter-curse. Thus forbidden, the king released all that water from his hand onto his own feet instead. (45)
Then, O best of the twice-born, those two feet of his, drenched by the water of that burning curse, were consumed and turned black at that very moment.
O tigers among the twice-born, from that time forward that king on earth became especially known by the name Kalmāṣapāda.
Sūta said: In the meantime, the brahmin Vasiṣṭha, filled with shame, realized that he had then bestowed a curse upon that king in vain.
He said: "O King, this curse given by me to you is rendered futile; yet my word can never, under any circumstances, become untrue. (49)
Therefore, O best of kings, having become a Rākṣasa for some time, you shall regain your own form; listen now to the time at which that shall occur. (50)
When you slay that Rākṣasa of cruel intellect, then you shall obtain liberation from this most dreadful state of being a Rākṣasa. || 51 ||
Sūta said: In the meantime, that king became a Yātudhāna—tall-bodied, with hair standing erect, black teeth, and terrifying.
Then, having assumed the nature of a rākṣasa, he slew the foremost of brahmins and destroyed the sacrifices as well as the hermitages of the sages.
Then, after some time, that Rākṣasa of cruel intellect, having learned one day that he had become a Rākṣasī and was deprived of his weapons, [acted].
Thereafter, remembering the enmity caused by the killing of his brother, he arrived there surrounded by many Rākṣasas for the purpose of slaying him.
Then, having surrounded the king on all sides, the Rākṣasa, filling the quarters with his roar, spoke these words in anger.
O evil-minded one, reap today the fruit of that which you did by force during Vasiṣṭha’s sacrifice: our eldest brother, who was slain by you.
The king said: "O man of evil conduct, perform that very deed of which you speak! Your thundering is as fruitless as that of an autumnal cloud."
Having spoken thus and then seizing a tree, that king rushed toward him, roaring like a thundercloud.
He too, uprooting a tree with eyes bloodshot with rage and knitting his brows into a triple-furrowed frown, advanced toward him.
Thus, those two heroes of great strength engaged in a battle with trees.
In that forest, they both performed [deeds] that brought about the destruction of many trees.
Then, seeing that Kūrabuddhi was exhausted, the lord of the earth seized him by the feet and whirled him with force in the air.
Then, filled with rage, he slapped his arms upon the ground; and having pounded it again and again, he made it into pieces of flesh.
When that heroic Rākṣasa was slain, the lord of the earth, being liberated from his state as a Rākṣasa, regained a body born of a king.
Then those remaining Rākṣasas, having surrounded that lord of the earth on all sides with massive trees, struck him with showers of stones.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the king, with trees in his hands, struck them down as if laughing, acting with confidence and ease.
Then, having slain the Rākṣasas and regained his former body, he reached his own city with the hair on his body standing on end in joy. (67)
Then he [saw him] bereft of luster, enveloped in a foul odor, and marked by the signs arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin, as well as various other distinct characteristics. || 68 ||
Having seen him, his ministers, as well as his sons, grandsons, and others, did not approach the king, being filled with fear of contact with sin.
And they said, "O best of kings, you ought not to enter into association with us here, since you are possessed by the sin of killing a brahmin. (70)
Therefore, having summoned Vasiṣṭha, perform an expiation by which this body of yours, being impure, may attain purity. (71)
Then that king, standing at a distance and filled with humility, quickly summoned Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, and spoke these words.
O Brahmin, by your grace that Rākṣasa has been slain by me; I have been freed from the curse. Now, O Sage, listen to my further words.
A foul odor emanates from all parts of my body; all my limbs are weighed down by a burden and have become as motionless as mountains.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, why is it that this great loss of my splendor has occurred, since even my ministers and sons do not touch me today? (75)

Vasiṣṭha said: "O best of kings, while you were in the state of a Rākṣasa, many Brāhmaṇas were destroyed by you and likewise many sacrifices were ruined. Therefore, O foremost of monarchs, you have been touched by the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa."
The king said: "Therefore, O Brahmin, grant me an expiation for the sake of purification, by which, freed from sin, I may regain my own kingdom. (77)
Vasiṣṭha said: "In this matter, O best of kings, undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords; being free from possessiveness and free from egoism, you will thereby attain perfection."
Then that best of kings, with his mind restrained and his senses conquered, performed ablutions at Prayāga and other sacred fords with a concentrated mind.
That foul odor does not vanish, nor does his vigor increase; his body does not attain lightness, nor is he freed from laziness. || 80 ||
Then, O best of the twice-born, wandering about, he once arrived at the sacred field of Camatkārapura for the purpose of bathing.
Exhausted, afflicted by hunger and thirst, at midnight enveloped in darkness, the king suddenly fell into a pit filled with water, O King. (82)
Then, having emerged from that sacred bathing place with great difficulty, the lord of the earth beheld himself possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns.
Seeing that he was free from foul odor, possessed of effort, and had attained lightness, he thought: "Surely I am liberated from sin. (84)
At that very moment, however, an incorporeal voice spoke, gladdening the protector of the earth who had been liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"O Great King, you are now liberated from your former sins by the power of this sacred ford; therefore, go to your own home. (86)
O Lord of the Earth, Śaṅkara is eternally present here in the form of an embryo, especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
When the *liṅga* of the trident-bearing God of gods fell due to the curse of a twice-born, this pit was then created by him.
Filled with shame, burdened by great sorrow, separated from his virtuous wife, and having reached the state of being an embryo, he [spoke]. (89)
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, this pit is the remover of all sins; it became renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Bhrūṇagarta.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that voice dwelling in the sky then ceased; and that tiger among kings, filled with joy, departed for his own city.
Then, seeing him freed from sin and resembling the sun in splendor, his sons as well as mortals bowed down to him, filled with satisfaction.
Then that tiger among brahmins, Vasiṣṭha, approached the lord of the earth and spoke to him with a voice faltering with joy.

"By good fortune you have been liberated from the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin, O Indra among kings; by good fortune, endowed with splendor once more, you have reached your own city. (94)
Therefore, O protector of the earth, tell me at which holy place you arrived, so that you were liberated from the terrible sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin.
Then he related exactly as it had happened the account of that brahmin-sage’s experience arising from the pit of the fetus.
Then those aged ministers and that king, the lord of sages, immediately installed their son named Pratardana upon the throne.
O best of the twice-born, having reached that very Bhrūṇagartā, they performed austerities while meditating upon Mahādeva day and night. (98)
And having worshipped Maheśvara, the God who assumes the form of a fetus, they attained the supreme perfection that is difficult to obtain within a short time. (99)
From that time forward, O best of Brahmins, that pit became famous on the surface of the earth as Bhrūṇagartā, the destroyer of all sins.
In that place, the man who performs a śrāddha on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight will surely deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, one should perform a śrāddha ceremony there with every effort, as well as a ritual bath and gifts according to one's own capacity. (102)

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhrūṇagartā," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 53 ||
Sūta said: Likewise, the goddess Carmamuṇḍā is established in that place; she was formerly installed by the high-souled Nala himself. || 1 ||
He who worships her with devotion on the day of Mahānavamī, having obtained his desired wishes, attains the eternal state.
Formerly, there was a lord of the earth named Nala, the son of Vīrasena, who was endowed with all virtues and brought about the destruction of all his enemies. || 3 ||
He had a virtuous wife, dearer to him than his own life, known as Damayantī, the daughter of the lord of Vidarbha.
Then, O Brahmins, possessed by Kali, that lord of the earth played at dice day and night with his kinsman Puṣkara.
Then, addicted to that vice, even though being restrained by virtuous people, he lost his seven-limbed kingdom and abandoned his beloved wife.
Then, taking her with him, he entered the dense forest—devoid of water, overcome with shame, and his senses agitated by grief.
Then he reflected: "If she goes to Bhīma’s palace, then she will be released from the hardship arising from dwelling in the forest."
"I, being full of pride, must not go there under any circumstances; therefore, having abandoned her, I shall depart far away during the night."

"By whom that virtuous woman was abandoned, he shall go to that city of Kuṇḍina. Having made this resolve, he left her while she slept peacefully and departed for the formidable forest, teeming with wild beasts.
And having risen at dawn, as soon as she looked toward the radiant direction, she saw that her own side where Nala had been standing was empty.
Then, having lamented piteously there in the forest, afflicted by grief, she set out upon the path and slowly made her way toward her father’s palace.
And Nala, the lord of the earth, wandering alone in that forest, constantly took refuge in the thickets of trees.
Then, leaving that forest, he went to another great forest, which was filled with various kinds of trees and teeming with many beasts of prey.
Thus wandering from forest to forest, that protector of the earth eventually reached the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
In the meantime, that great ninth day arrived, on which kings especially worship the Goddess of the Gods.
Then, having fashioned an image out of clay wearing a skin and a skull, the king subsequently gratified it with fruits and roots due to his lack of wealth.
Then, having offered praise to her and standing before her with palms joined in reverence, the Lord of Niṣadha himself, endowed with supreme faith, [spoke].
Victory, O omnipresent Goddess, O excellent bearer of the skin and the skull! Victory, O auspicious daughter of Dakṣa, who are skilled in the destruction of the race of Daityas! 19.
Victory to you, O Kālarātri, inconceivable one, beloved of the ninth and eighth lunar days; victory to you, O Goddess, three-eyed one, desired by Tryambaka, worshipped by the gods! 20.
O Goddess of terrible form and beautiful form, O Great Knowledge, O Great Power, O Great Prosperity, O Great Body, O Victorious Goddess, O You of Great Vows! 21.
O eternal one, O sustainer of the world, O you who delight in wine, meat, and fat; O Vikarālī, O Mahākālī, victory to you, O follower of the departed spirits!
Delighting in corpses and vehicles, beautiful, adorned with ornaments of serpents, holding a noose in her hand, possessing great hands, and having made her abode in a flood of blood.
O you who are resplendent with the sound of the *phetkāra*, adorned with song and instrumental music; O primordial Jaya, O object of meditation, you who take refuge in half the body of Bharga! 24.
You are delight, you are fortitude, you are contentment; you are Gaurī, you are the sovereign of the gods. You are Lakṣmī, you are Sāvitrī, and you are undoubtedly Gāyatrī. (25)
Whatever form of woman is seen in the three worlds, O Goddess, all that consists of you; there is no doubt in me regarding this at any time.
By that truth, O you who are worshipped by gods and demons, quickly take up residence here; being pleased by devotion, grant your presence. (27)
Sūta said: Thus praised by Nala, the lord of the earth, that Goddess, who is affectionate toward her devotees, appeared before him and spoke to the king.
The illustrious Goddess said: "I am well-pleased with you now, my child, by this hymn of praise; therefore, receive from me the boon that resides in your heart. (29)
Nala said: "Damayantī is my wife, dearer to me than my own life. She was abandoned by me in a lonely forest filled with swarms of predatory beasts."
O Goddess, by your grace, act quickly so that I may once again obtain that very same faultless and unbroken virtue. (31)
O Goddess, whoever should offer praise to you with this hymn before you, on that very day, whatever is desired in their heart should be granted by you to them.
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," she then vanished from sight; and that tiger among kings obtained everything she had declared.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Carmamuṇḍā Constructed by Nala," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having seen Naleśvara, the God of gods, situated right beside that very [shrine], which was established by King Nala and by beholding which one is liberated from sin; || 1 ||
O twice-born ones, that man who beholds him with devotion on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha becomes liberated from all diseases and attains the supreme state.
Itching, scabies, ringworm, circular skin lesions, and eczema—all these perish for beings of purified soul upon merely seeing him. (3)
In front of him was a pond, well-filled with clear water, teeming with fish and tortoises, and adorned with clusters of lotuses.
Whoever performs a bath there at dawn on a Monday shall be freed even from the disease of leprosy and become renewed once more.
When Śambhu was thus established by King Nala, the Lord, being pleased, said to him: "Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
Nala said: "O Lord Śaṅkara, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds and for the destruction of disease, you must remain here, always present."
Śaṅkara said: "O King, at your word, when Monday arrives, I shall dwell in this temple at dawn; of this there is no doubt."
O Lord of the Earth, for the entire day and night on the eighth day of the month of Māgha.
For the destruction of diseases of living beings, especially during the bright fortnight.
Whoever, having bathed in the perfectly pure pool, shall behold me stationed here on that day, being endowed with right faith—for him, the diseases arising in the body shall go to their destruction.
Any person who, at the end of night on a Monday, applies even the clay produced from this pit to their own body, shall become free from diseases and endowed with physical vigor.

Furthermore, O best of kings, he who is free from desire and shall worship me at that time with true devotion using flowers, incense, and ointments, being liberated from all sins, will go to my world.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, O brahmins, the Blessed Lord Hara, the illuminator of the three worlds, vanished at that very moment, just like a lamp here.
King Nala, having attained satisfaction and having propitiated him for a long time, then summoned all the Brahmins born in Camatkārapura.
This Śambhu has been installed by me in your presence, by the mere sight of whom the destruction of all diseases is brought about. (15)
"Now, O twice-born ones, I shall depart for the sake of my own kingdom and for the city of Niṣadhā; he is to be honored by all of you with composed minds. (16)

The Brahmins said: "O tiger among kings, we shall do so with concentrated minds; we shall exert ourselves for your sake in the rites concerning the gods and in the ceremonies such as processions. (17)

Thus, endowed with supreme faith, we shall perform worship; and those who will be our sons and grandsons, as well as others born in our lineage, shall likewise perform worship of this [deity] with great devotion. (18)
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by those brahmins, the king, filled with satisfaction, set out after bowing deeply to them and being highly honored by them all.
Thus the Blessed Lord Śambhu remained established in that place, bringing about the destruction of all diseases for the welfare of all the worlds.
Therefore, he should indeed always be visited with every effort, especially on Mondays by one who desires eternal welfare. (21)

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Naleśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having beheld the Lord of the Gods, Sāmbāditya, situated not far from that [place], a mortal attains all the desires residing within his heart. || 1 ||
But that mortal who, with devotion, beholds [the deity] on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, falling on a Sunday, shall not behold the hells.
Formerly, there was a twice-born man named Gālava, a great sage who was constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and had mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences.
Devoted to pure vows, peaceful, dedicated to the gods and the twice-born, grateful, of excellent character, and skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
As he was living in this manner, O best of the twice-born, his final years arrived; since he was childless, great sorrow then arose within him.
Then, having completely abandoned all household duties, that devoted man, with a concentrated mind, worshipped the Sun in this very sacred field.
Taking refuge at a banyan tree, endowed with supreme faith, he established an image of the Sun according to the rites prescribed in the Pañcarātra.

During the rainy season he slept under the open sky, and in the winter he took refuge in the water; in the summer he practiced the austerity of the five fires, remaining without food and with his senses subdued.
Then, when the fifteenth year had arrived, the blessed Sun, taking recourse in a banyan tree, spoke to him who was standing nearby.

The illustrious Sūrya said: "I am the giver of boons today; may it be well with you, O Gālava, request a boon. Even that which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, I shall surely grant to you immediately."
Gālava said: "O best of gods, I am childless and have reached the final stage of my life; therefore, grant me a supreme son who will cause the increase of my lineage. (11)
The illustrious Sūrya said: "O Brahmin, a son shall be born to you who will cause the lineage to increase; he will be radiant, famous, a knower of the scriptures, and one who has mastered the Vedas."
"This worship of mine which has been performed by you in the presence of Sāmbasūrya—this [deity] shall be known by the name Sāmbasūrya upon the surface of the earth. (3)
Furthermore, anyone endowed with faith who shall worship this on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, continuing for twelve such solar days; || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, he who observes these seven seventh days with devotion while remaining without food shall, without a doubt, obtain a son who increases his lineage.
Having spoken thus, the seven-horsed Sun ceased; Gālava too, with a joyful heart, went to his own abode.
Not long thereafter, a son was born to him, endowed with all the auspicious marks, just as that god had described.
Then his father himself gave him the name Vaṭeśvara, because he had been granted [the boon] by the delighted Aṃśumālin while residing in the banyan tree (vaṭa).
O best of the twice-born, having seen the sons of Vaṭeśvara as his grandsons, Galava performed very extensive penance and approached the Sun.
Vaṭeśvara, too, having recognized that the Sun had been established by his father, caused a most beautiful temple to be built for him.
From that time forward, he became known in the world as Vaṭāditya; indeed, as the bestower of sons to those who are childless, he became famous throughout the three worlds.

He who, devoted to fasting on a Sunday falling on the seventh lunar day, worships him with devotion for seven or twelve years in succession, obtains an excellent son who increases his own lineage. || 22 ||
But that man who worships him, whether he be free from desire or not, shall surely attain liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Now, there is a verse sung of old by the celestial sage Nārada, upon seeing the god Vaṭāditya, the lord of the gods, who bestows sons. (24)
Even a woman who has been barren for a hundred years, or one who is unfortunate, shall immediately become pregnant through the grace of Sāmbasūrya. (25)

What is the use of gifts, what use of vows, what use of meditations, or what use of recitations accompanied by fasts, when the Lord of the Gods, Sāmbasūrya, is present for the sake of obtaining a son? (26)
The man who, having found leisure, beholds [the deity] here with devotion on a Sunday for one year, O son, obtains an excellent son and supreme happiness.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, for the sake of one's own welfare and for the increase of one's lineage, one should behold that God with all effort and with great care. (28)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, in that sacred field, the Sun-god was thus installed by Bhīṣma, with the approval of the foremost of Brahmins and by his own will. || 1 ||
In ancient times, there was a beloved son of Śantanu, renowned as Gāṅgeya; he was a most famous man of excellent character who remained a celibate ascetic (ūrdhvaretas).

Thereafter, for the sake of his mother, he engaged in a great and tumultuous battle with the descendant of Bhṛgu for twenty-three days, resembling the war between the gods and the asuras, using sharp weapons and missiles.

Then Brahmā and the other gods established themselves there personally for the sake of restraining those two and for the peace of all embodied beings; and having raised them up, they returned once again to heaven.
Ambā also, having suffered this supreme humiliation arising from the son of Gaṅgā, entered a well-kindled fire with her eyes reddened by rage.
Having rebuked the son of the River with eyes clouded by tears, she then spoke from her position between the fires to the grandfather of the Kurus: || 6 ||
"O Bhīṣma, O evil-minded one, since I have been abandoned by you while afflicted by desire, I shall therefore quickly return to the earth for your destruction. (7)
"You shall certainly be joined with the sin of killing a woman, if dharma arising from the Smṛti scriptures is indeed the authority in this matter. (8)
Then Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, overcome with compassion and filled with humility, questioned Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages.
"O Blessed One, that which was spoken by the daughter of the King of Kāśī—that all my sinful deeds which cause my death shall belong to you. (10)
O best of Brahmins, would that [result] come about by mere words, or not? I have a doubt in this matter; you should explain the truth to me exactly as it is. (11)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Whether one is insulted or even beaten, if a woman or a twice-born man should give up his life on account of that person, the sin of that act shall belong to him.
Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, one should never provoke a woman or even a Brahmin, whether they are striking or cursing. (13)
But you, moreover, neglected that wretched woman when she was afflicted by desire; having previously won her at the svayaṃvara, how could you not be a partaker of sin?
Bhīṣma said: "For that purpose, O Brāhmaṇa, tell me an expiation for the sake of purification—whether it be austerity, or charity, or a vow, or even a religious observance. (15)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O bull of the Bharatas, the entire sin that is traditionally held to result from the slaughter of ten eminent Brāhmaṇas arises from the killing of a woman.
Therefore, in this matter, there is neither gift-giving, nor austerity, nor vows and the like; setting aside pilgrimage to sacred sites, you should therefore practice that [devotion]. || 17 ||
Sūta said: Having heard his words, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, became intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords and wandered over the circle of the earth.
Then, wandering upon the surface of the earth, he arrived in due course at the sacred field of Camatkārapura, which is filled with various holy pilgrimage sites.
Then that great-souled one beheld the highly meritorious Gayāśiras; and filled with faith, he bathed and performed the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules.
Just then, a voice from the sky spoke these words: "O Bhīṣma, Bhīṣma, O mighty-armed one! You ought not to perform this rite for the ancestors."
Since you are joined with the sin of killing a woman, therefore listen to my words: there is a place renowned as Śarmiṣṭhātīrtha, which destroys all evil deeds.
From this place, in the western direction (vāruṇī), a meritorious man who performs a bath on the sixth lunar day when the moon is in conjunction with Kṛṣṇāṅgāraka shall [attain great merit]. || 23 ||
He is liberated from the sin incurred by killing a woman; there is no doubt in this matter. Therefore, O son, on this very day, which is joined with Tuesday—
That very sixth lunar day is meritorious; therefore, go there quickly. O son, I am your father, Śantanu, the lord of the earth.
Knowing that he was tainted by the murder of a woman, Bhīṣma then quickly came here; having gone swiftly to that place, he remained there with a concentrated mind.
Having performed his ablutions, he then performed the śrāddha ceremony endowed with faith; thereafter, having returned once more, that Śatānanda spoke to him.
O best of the Kurus, you have undoubtedly become free from sin; therefore, go to your own home and attend to the affairs of the kingdom.
Then, filled with wonder and having recognized that unsurpassed sacred site, that best of the Kurus likewise [recognized] the image consisting of Vāsudeva and the other one. (29)
With a mind purified by faith, [one should fashion] an image of the Sun made of *pārijāta* wood, characterized by the proper marks, well-proportioned, and beautiful in form. (30)
Likewise, filled with devotion, he installed another linga of the trident-bearing God and Durga, according to the rites prescribed by the rules.
Then, having summoned all those Brahmins born in the city, Bhīṣma of the Kuru lineage, standing bowed in humility, spoke to them.
"O Brahmins, out of compassion for me, I have constructed these four temples for you in this sacred field. (33)
"Protect [them]; I shall depart quickly toward my own home, impelled by my divine ancestors who have taken their place upon the path to heaven. (34)

No person on earth, whether by force or by wisdom, is capable of altering an action performed in another body. (20)
Otherwise, the wise man is exalted by an intellect pregnant with the scriptures; like a master, he performs his previously accumulated karma in a different manner.
The happiness and suffering of embodied beings attend upon their own actions; for he who is the cause of these is bound by egoism.
One's own karma runs after one who is running very swiftly; it lies down with one who is lying down and stands by one who is standing.
Just as shadow and light are always perfectly connected to one another, so too are action and the agent; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (29)
To whatever place a man must go to experience pleasure or even pain, he is led there by force, as if bound by a rope.
It is the authority for the production of pleasure and pain among living beings, whether they are awake and attentive or even asleep.

That which is unprotected remains by divine protection, while that which is well-guarded perishes when struck by fate. Even one abandoned in the forest without a protector lives, whereas one who exerts every effort at home does not survive.

O auspicious lady, whatever maiden performs her bath there with devotion on that day shall obtain an excellent husband; of this there is no doubt. (87)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Gaurī then touched her with her hand; and at that very moment, she became possessed of a body of divine form.
Abandoned because of her old age, though she was adorned with divine garlands and unguents, possessed full and elevated breasts, and walked with the gait of an elephant in rut. (89)
Then, having taken her and appointed her as her own servant, she went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, accompanied by Hara.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been called Śarmiṣṭhātīrtha; it is renowned throughout the three worlds as the destroyer of all sins.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should perform a bath there with every effort on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, according to the prescribed rules.
This greatness of the Strītīrtha, which I have described, is purifying, life-prolonging, and the destroyer of all sins for men. (93)
And that person who, having risen early in the morning, always recites this, shall always obtain all the desires cherished by the mind. (94)
Likewise, when a festival day has arrived, that man who recites this, or he who hears it with devotion, quickly goes to the abode of Śiva. (95)

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śarmiṣṭhā-tīrtha," in the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Now, there is a most beautiful Liṅga there known as Someśvara, famous throughout the three worlds, which was fashioned by Soma himself.
He who worships there for an entire year on every Monday, even by taking but a moment, is liberated from even a terrible disease.
There is no doubt that [he is cured] even of consumption, let alone of diseases such as leprosy; therefore, one afflicted by disease should worship him with every effort. (3)
In ancient times, Soma, afflicted by the disease of consumption, propitiated him and became free from illness, just as King Pāṇḍya did. || 4 ||
The sages said: O son of Sūta, how did the wasting disease (kṣayavyādhi) formerly arise in Soma, the lord of medicinal herbs, and how did he attain its alleviation?
O Mahāmati, tell us all this in detail, as well as the auspicious story of that king, the Pāṇḍya.
Sūta said: Formerly, the Lord of the Night (the Moon) married the twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa in the presence of the gods, Agni, and Bṛhaspati.
Those known in the world as constellations, beginning with Aśvinī, which are praised by the best of the twice-born and by astrologers, are endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtuous qualities.
Then, among all of them together, Rohiṇī became the beloved of that Lord of Night, dearer to him even than his own life.
Then, having abandoned all those daughters of Dakṣa equally, he remained united with Rohiṇī day and night.
Then, tormented by desire and afflicted by misfortune, they went to Dakṣa and, filled with grief and their faces bathed in tears, spoke.
O father, that sinner to whom you have affectionately given us as wives has not granted us even our fertile seasons. (12)
Therefore, O illustrious one, we shall enter the fire and give up our lives without delay; we speak the truth before you.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, Dakṣa, overcome with grief, took them all himself and went into the presence of the Moon.
Then the wise Prajāpati Dakṣa spoke directly to them, repeatedly rebuking the Lord of the Night with harsh words.
"O lowest of night-stalkers, what is this that you intend to do? O fool, excluded from the company of the virtuous, this deed is condemned by the treatises on dharma. (16)
"Even though the fertile season has arrived, my daughter, why do you not speak with affection to me? Do you not know the treatises on dharma? (17)
He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt in this matter. (18)
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of the Night (the Moon), feeling ashamed, spoke with his face cast downward: "I shall carry out your command, O Dakṣa."
Then Dakṣa, with a joyful mind, having presented all his daughters to Him of the Cold Radiance (Śiva) and taken leave of him, subsequently departed for his own abode. || 20 || || 3 ||
Candra also, as before, abandoned all those daughters of Dakṣa and, out of passion, engaged in union with Rohiṇī alone. || 21 ||
Then, even more distressed, they went to where their father was staying; with eyes full of tears, they spoke words appropriate for that occasion.
"O father, this great sorrow dwells within our hearts: that misfortune has arisen which is censured by all women. (23)
Furthermore, you yourself have been rendered one whose efforts are in vain and who is like one without authority by that wicked, lustful man, having gone [to him] on our behalf. (24)
We are not able to bear that sorrow in our hearts in any way; for that Moon rejoices constantly in the company of Rohiṇī.

"Especially because of your word, the Lord of the Night has been forbidden [to us]. Therefore, grant us your permission now; for we are tormented by the sorrow of misfortune and shall give up our lives. (26)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, Dakṣa, filled with rage, went into the presence of the Lord of the Night (the Moon) and then cursed him.
"Since you have not acted in accordance with my words, which were endowed with righteousness, therefore a terrible wasting disease shall consume you. (28)
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, Dakṣa departed; and at that very moment, the Moon was seized by consumption and began to wane day by day.
Then, having become emaciated and being unable to indulge his desire, he abandoned Rohiṇī and wandered upon the surface of the earth.
Seeking physicians for the sake of destroying his wasting disease, he, having conquered his senses, applied various medicines.
Nevertheless, that Lord of Night was not at all released from consumption; due to Dakṣa’s terrible curse, he continued to waste away day by day.
Thereupon, having attained detachment and being devoted to pilgrimage, he became endowed with faith, having abandoned even that most excellent medicine.
Then, O best of Brahmins, while wandering among sacred fords and shrines, he arrived at the supreme field of Prabhāsa.
Having bathed there and become pure, the Lord of Night (the Moon), upon beholding Prabhāsa, was about to depart elsewhere when he saw [something] standing before him.
He saw a sage named Romaka, firm in his vows, endowed with the power of asceticism, and compassionate toward all living beings.
Having seen him, O best of the twice-born, the Moon, afflicted by the disease of consumption, bowed down and spoke aloud with great respect out of despondency: || 37 ||
"O best of Brahmins, I am utterly exhausted by the power of this wasting disease; therefore, provide a remedy, for I have come to you for refuge. (38)
I questioned physicians, and they prepared medicines for me in many ways, O illustrious one; yet day by day I have become utterly emaciated. (39)
"If you do not impart some instruction to me for the destruction of this disease, then by that means I shall cast off my body this very day. (40)
Romaka said: "O Lord of the Night, even for another person a curse cannot be made otherwise; how much less so for that Dakṣa of immeasurable splendor? (41)
Therefore, I shall give you this highly esteemed instruction here, by which the destruction of your wasting disease will become certain.
"There is nothing in this world that cannot be granted by the trident-bearing God of gods when he is well-pleased; therefore, propitiate him according to his word. (43)
"O night-walker, truth always resides on earth in the sixty-eight sacred fords; having installed that liṅga in them, it serves for his destruction."
Therefore, worship [him] constantly with a mind purified by faith; you will undoubtedly attain the complete destruction of decay and disease.

Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the Lord of Night (the Moon) was greatly delighted; having installed divine liṅgas of the Trident-bearer (Śiva) in that sacred field of Prabhāsa, he worshipped them with devotion, marking each with his own name.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, appeared before him and said, "I am the granter of boons; ask for whatever you desire. (47)
Candra said: "O Lord of Gods, I am utterly emaciated by consumption; therefore, I have come to your feet—save me! I pray for nothing else. (48)
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull summoned Dakṣa right there and then spoke to him with respect.
"This Candra, your son-in-law, has been cursed by you; you have not done what was auspicious. Therefore, at my word, show him favor. (50)
Dakṣa said: Although I spoke words consistent with dharma, this man of evil intellect did not act upon them before me; having falsely promised "I will do it," he remains a liar.
O Bull-bannered Lord, he was cursed by me in anger on account of my son; yet what was spoken by me even in jest shall not turn out otherwise.
The God of gods said: "From this day forward, by my word, this maker of night shall undoubtedly look upon all those daughters with equal regard at all times."
Therefore, let one side meet with destruction and the other side attain prosperity, so that your word may become true, endowed with my grace. (54)
Then Dakṣa, having said "So be it," went to his own abode; and Lord Śaṅkara also spoke again to the moon-crested one.
O Moon, request yet another desired boon from me, so that I may grant it all, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (56)

Candra said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, you must always maintain your presence within all the Lingas installed by me. (57)
The God said: "O Lord, when the sixty-eight Liṅgas have been installed by you, I shall grant my presence on Mondays at your request. (58)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished from that place; then Candra, filled with joy, beheld them all together.
O best of Brahmins, remembering the words of Śaṅkara, the sons of Dakṣa were thereafter filled with great joy.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, there were lords of Soma (Someśvaras) in those sixty-eight sacred fords (tīrthas), and likewise in others thereafter. (61)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, the goddess Camatkārī was formerly present right there; she was established in ancient times by King Camatkāra with great faith.
By her, that buffalo-demon, who possessed hundreds of thousands of illusions, was formerly slain in battle while she maintained her vow of virginity.
O twice-born ones, when that city had been created there by that Great-Souled One, she was then established for the purpose of its protection.
For the sake of protecting that city, as well as its inhabitants and all those foremost of Brahmins whose minds were purified by devotion; || 4 ||
Whoever properly worships her on the day of Mahānavamī, for him no fear arises anywhere throughout the entire year.
From ghosts, spirits, and piśācas, and especially from enemies; from diseases, thieves, and other wicked beings as well.
Whatever desire a pure man contemplates while worshipping her with true devotion on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, he attains that without a doubt.
One who is free from desire attains happiness and liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. By the grace of that Goddess, this which I have spoken is the truth. (8)
Having propitiated that Supreme Goddess, numerous kings, brahmins, and other yogins attained perfection in former times.
He who, endowed with faith, performs circumambulation of her constantly for the duration of a year shall not go to the womb of an animal.
In her abode, a great marvel occurred in the past; that which I shall proclaim to you, listen with well-concentrated minds. (11)
In former times, there was an excellent king named Citraratha, renowned as the lord of the Daśārṇas and the destroyer of all enemies.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, always with devotion and endowed with faith toward her, he performed one hundred and eight circumambulations.
Then, having bowed down to that goddess, he returns home again, surrounded on all sides by his fourfold army.
In this manner, a very long time passed for that lord of men, who was devoted to circumambulation, as well as for the queen, who was devoted to her religious observances.
Then, after some time, that king, having gathered there, saw the best of Brahmins seated within the queen's chamber.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of that goddess, the lord of the earth—
With a concentrated mind, he paid homage to all those twice-born ones standing before him.
Then, seated there together with them, he engaged in auspicious conversations concerning the ancient royal sages and the brahminical sages.
Then, at the conclusion of a certain conversation, he was questioned by those best of the twice-born, who were filled with curiosity and stood bowed in humility.
"O King, we all ask you out of curiosity; therefore, tell us if this secret is not something that should remain hidden from you. (20)
"Every month, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, you come from very far away and perform circumambulations of the deity. (21)
Having diligently abandoned all other rites such as worship and the like, you surely know the entire fruit that arises from circumambulation.
The king said: "O best of the twice-born, what has been uttered by you is true; even a secret must now be told to you by me. (23)
Formerly, I was a parrot in this auspicious sanctuary, taking refuge in a nest built on the western side of the goddess.
O best of the twice-born, as he was constantly going out and entering there, it became a perpetual circumambulation of the Goddess.
Then, in the course of time, my death occurred right here in this very palace; by its power, I was indeed born here as a king with the memory of my former birth.
For this reason, O best of the twice-born, having approached from afar with a concentrated mind, I perform a circumambulation of this deity.
"Formerly, while dwelling in a nest devoid of devotion, I performed a circumambulation of the Goddess; by that act, I have become a lord of the earth. (28)
"Now, endowed with faith, I perform this circumambulation; O best of the twice-born, I do not know what spiritual merit will accrue to me from it. (29)
Sūta said: Having heard that, those brahmins, their eyes wide with wonder, joyfully offered words of praise to that king.
Then that king, having bowed down to all those best of the twice-born and having taken his leave, departed quickly for his own home with his army.
Now, he who performs circumambulation endowed with faith, being liberated from all sins, obtains his desired fruit. || 32 ||
From that time forward, all those Brahmins, led by devotion, as well as others, performed circumambulations of her for the sake of liberation.
And by its power, they attained the supreme perfection desired, which is difficult to obtain even for the gods, both in this world and in the next. (34)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge here in that Goddess who, established in that sacred field, bestows all desires upon men. (35)
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another lake there, fashioned by the gods, where King Anarta, known by the name Suhaya, attained perfection.
By that very king, an auspicious Liṅga was installed there, known as Ānarteśvara, which bestows all spiritual perfections upon men.
In that regard, whatever man should perform a ritual bath in the lake on a Saturday (Aṅgāraka-ṣaṣṭhī), he attains spiritual perfection just as the Lord of Anarta did.
The sages said: "How was perfection attained by the high-souled Ānarta? O Sūta, tell us all of that; you know everything, there is no doubt."

Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a lord of the earth named Ānarta Suhaya. Having been defeated in battle by all his enemies, he became intent on flight; left alone and surrounded by many, he was defiled by Mlecchas and remained like one who has consumed the remnants of a meal.
Then, knowing him to be born of a hero, one who was devoted to the Kāpālika vow took his skull-bowl for the sake of his own ritual practice.
Dwelling in the vicinity of Ānarteśvara and remaining in the forest, he [performed his rites] at night with that water which embodies all the gods.

Having filled it at night with water drawn from a pond, he would release it. Formerly, there was a merchant known by the name Siddhasena, who was wealthy, possessed of servants, and always devoted to merit. (8)
Then, after some time had passed, O best of the twice-born, he set out toward the northern direction accompanied by a caravan, with the intention of trading.
Then, traveling in due course with all of them, he reached a desert region devoid of trees and water, abandoned by all living beings.
Having reached that place at night, the weary travelers, having sought out various spots on all sides, fell asleep and thus came under the power of slumber.
Then, having reached dawn and rising quickly, they set out toward the northern direction, leaving behind only one servant of the Śūdra.
Exhausted by the journey, he fell deeply under the sway of sleep and did not wake even when the departure had begun and a great clamor arose.
He was not remembered by those caravans with whom he had set out from home, nor was he seen by anyone as he stood upon the riverbank.
When the caravan had thus departed and the orb of the sun had risen, he then awoke, touched by the intense heat.
As long as he looked, that caravan leader saw nothing at all in that place; nor was any trail of footprints visible for them in that desert.
Then, his soul overwhelmed by suffering, running hither and thither, he fell upon the surface of the earth at midday, afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Thus, while he remained fallen upon the surface of the earth, afflicted by thirst and barely clinging to life, the sun reached the mountain of setting with great difficulty.
Then, as the sun grew dim, he regained consciousness slightly and reflected in his mind: "Where shall I go now? (19)
No path is perceived anywhere, nor is any human being seen; there is neither water here nor shade. Surely my death has arrived. (20)
While that Śūdra was thus immersed in thought in that desolate wilderness, night thereafter arrived.
Then, in an instant, he heard the sweet-sounding song and likewise the enchanting sound of the Nandis and Vṛddhas as they recited.
Then, in an instant, he saw the assembly filled with hosts of pretas, and one preta established in the sovereignty over them all.
Then those hungry ghosts (pretas) standing at his side—some began to dance, others sang before him, and still others offered hymns of praise.
Then he said to that Śūdra, "O guest, take your meal; drink water at your pleasure, so that there may be merit for me. (25)
Then, having cast off his fear by the command of the King of the Dead, he ate his meal and drank water with complete confidence. || 26 ||
Then all those pretas, endowed with their state as pretas, performed the act of eating according to seniority and in due order.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the entire night passed for them as they played with all the diversions appropriate for kings.
Then, when the dawn was clear and the solar disc had risen, as soon as that Śūdra looked, he saw nothing there at all.
And then he reflected: "Is this a vision in a dream, or a delusion of our minds, or perhaps even a magical illusion?"
Or rather, this is indeed true, since this supreme satisfaction has arisen within me, who was afflicted by hunger and distressed by thirst. (3)
While he was reflecting thus, the sun ascended the courtyard of the sky, scorching the surface of the earth with its heat.
Then, afflicted by hunger and thirst, he reached the end of the day after taking refuge under a certain tree that offered little shade.
Then, when the onset of night had arrived, he beheld once again the King of the Pretas in that same form, accompanied by those very same pretas.
In that very manner, the Śūdra, freed from fear and filled with great joy, partook of the meal arising from that hospitality. (35)
In this manner, at the onset of night, that king would always come and likewise offer him hospitality.
Then, when the next day had arrived, that Śūdra asked the king: "What is this wonder that is seen at the onset of night?"

"O illustrious one, your power perishes at the end of the night. Proclaim this secret to me, O Lord of the Dead, if it is not concealed; for curiosity has arisen in me upon seeing this extraordinary feat. (38)
The preta said: There is a meritorious great sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara, and there the Gaṅgā and Yamunā are situated at their confluence.
Very near to those two is the auspicious temple of Śiva; there, one who observes the great vow, a steadfast celibate, performs penance.
Having performed his own rites there, he always placed my skull, filled with water, by his bed for the purpose of purification at night. (41)
Indeed, O high-minded one, it is through its power that this prosperity of mine arises at night; when it is emptied during the day, it returns once again.
Therefore, show me favor; go there and, having reduced that skull of mine to powder, cast it into those waters.
By which my liberation from this most dreadful state of a preta may arise. || 44 ||
Likewise, there in that place, in the eastern direction, is that supreme sacred site (tīrtha) known as Gayāśiras, which grants liberation from the state of being a preta.
"Go there, O high-minded one, and perform the śrāddha for all of them; O auspicious one, a beautiful casket is seen standing by your side."
"Inscribe here the names of all of them according to their seniority; then, having shown great compassion, perform the śrāddha ceremony immediately. (47)
"O auspicious one, we shall lead you there by an easy means; and we shall show you a most magnificent treasure for the purpose of your funeral rites. (48)
When that Śūdra had thus agreed, they quickly placed him upon their shoulders and carried him to the field as instructed.
They showed him a treasure consisting of abundant wealth; taking that, he went to the place where that lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) was staying.
Then, having bowed to him with devotion, he, full of humility, related in detail the entire account of that Lord of Beings.
Then, having obtained that skull and ground it to powder, he, being composed and filled with joy, cast it into the middle of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
In the meantime, the deceased, assuming a body of divine form and seated in a celestial chariot, spoke these words to that Śūdra, filled with joy: || 53 ||
"By your grace, I am now liberated from this dreadful state of a preta; may it be well with you, for I shall now depart for the abode of the gods. (54)
Now, perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for all of these very persons by going to the meritorious Gayāśiras, whereby liberation shall be attained. || 55 ||
Then, filled with wonder, he performed the Śrāddha rite individually for each of those beings every day with a concentrated mind.
By the power of that [act], all those pretas also went to heaven; filled with joy, they granted him a vision in his dream.
Then that Śūdra, having recognized that field as a multiplier of merit, did not go home again but remained right there engaged in austerity.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, he installed a Liṅga known as Śūdrakeśvara, which destroys all sins.
The man who, endowed with faith, performs the ritual bath for those two and worships the Liṅga known as Śūdrakeśvara according to the prescribed rules, [attains the highest goal].
Freed from all sins, he proceeds to the abode of Śiva, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and being praised by Gandharvas.
That person who gives up his life there after performing the fast unto death (prāyopaveśana) shall not obtain birth again in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 62 ||
Even he who, while residing there, drinks but a mouthful of water from that [lake] is liberated from all sins committed from birth until the end of death.
He who provides food there for the foremost of Brahmins, his ancestors remain satisfied for as long as three hundred kalpas.
And he who, with a concentrated mind, gives even a mere trifle of gold there, obtains the entire fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 65 ||
Therefore, O twice-born ones, a man who desires eternal heaven should, with every effort, resort to that most excellent sacred ford at all times. (66)
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by the great seer Gautama, out of wonder upon beholding the power of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. (67)
A man who, being composed in mind, bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā and beholds Śūdreśvara, shall immediately attain heaven.
O best of Brahmins, I have thus related to you all this majesty of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, which destroys every sin.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ānartakeśvara and Śūdrakeśvara," within the *Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya* of the *Nāgara-Khaṇḍa*, the sixth section of the *Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Likewise, there is a famous place there known as Rāmahrada, where his ancestors were gratified by that blood.
In that month of Bhādrapada, whoever reaches the new moon day and gratifies the ancestors with devotion shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
The sages said: "O Sūta of great intelligence, this which you speak is most wonderful—that by him the ancestors were there gratified with blood."
Pure substances have been declared by the wise for the purpose of satiating the ancestors; blood is said to be the substance for the complete gratification of the Rākṣasas.
And why was that action, which is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti and censured by the virtuous, performed by the son of Jamadagni? O Sūta, tell us that.
Sūta said: Out of the power of his anger, while fulfilling his vow, he performed that deed by which his ancestors were gratified with blood.
O best of the twice-born, his father Jamadagni, who was established in his own duty and free from fault, was formerly struck down by a Kṣatriya, O brahmins.
Then, overcome with anger, that great-souled one declared: "My ancestors must be satiated by the blood of a Kṣatriya. (8)
For this reason, by that noble-souled one, the ancestors were properly gratified with devotion using that blood mixed with sesame seeds.
The sages said: "Why was the great sage Jamadagni killed by a Kṣatriya? What was the name of that king? O Sūta, tell us that in detail."
Sūta said: Formerly, the son of Ṛcīka known as Jamadagni dwelt there in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, his sins having been burnt away.
He had four sons endowed with virtues; among them, Rāma, though the youngest, was the eldest by virtue of his qualities.
Once, while Jamadagni was dwelling in the great forest, his sons had gone out from the woods in search of roots and tubers. (13)
In the meantime, the powerful lord of the Haihayas arrived—he who was renowned on the surface of the earth as Sahasrārjuna.
Desirous of deer, he wandered here and there in that forest, afflicted by fatigue, while the sun stood at midday in the zodiac sign of Taurus.
Then, having seen that hermitage filled with various trees, he entered it accompanied by his fourfold army.
Then he saw the great sage Jamadagni staying there, seated after having performed his ablutions, devoted to the worship of the gods.
Then, upon seeing that king, the sage was filled with joy; having offered him the guest-offering (arghya) according to the rules and having greeted him with a welcome, he honored him.
He too, having prostrated before him with great humility, addressed him in return and inquired after his welfare.
The king said: "O Brahmin, is all well with you, along with your sons and disciples, your sacred fires, your wife, and your entire retinue? (20)
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life as well; for you, a treasury of asceticism who are honored by all the worlds, have been seen by me.
Having spoken thus and rested for a very long time, that royal sage, having drunk water, bowed down to the great muni and said this to him.
"Grant me leave, O Brahmin; I shall go to my own home. You must command what task is to be performed by me for your sake. (23)
Jamadagni said: At the time of worshipping the deities, you have come to my house like a cherished desire; you are a guest embodying all the gods. || 24 ||
Therefore, O best of kings, I have supreme joy and devotion; so please accept this food given by me with my own hand. (25)
Whether he be a king, a Brahmin, a Shudra, or even one of the lowest caste—whoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is a guest who serves as a bridge to heaven.
The king said: "O Brahmin, these soldiers of mine number in the hundreds and thousands. How is it fitting for me to eat while they have not eaten? Tell me. (27)
Jamadagni said: "I shall provide food for all your soldiers; you need have no anxiety in this matter, for I am a sage who possesses nothing."
O Indra among kings, this cow which you see tied near me always grants whatever is desired by the mind when she is entreated. (29)
Sūta said: Then, O best of the twice-born, that king, filled with curiosity, replied, "So be it," and remained in that very hermitage.
Then, having satiated the gods and the ancestors immediately thereafter, he next worshipped Agni, the bearer of oblations, and the brahmins.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he sat down together with all his hungry servants, who were afflicted by fatigue and filled with wonder, once they had prepared for him.
Then that best of sages requested that cow: "O auspicious one, give to whomever requests anything for the sake of food whatever it may be."
Then that cow gave birth to various kinds of auspicious food, and especially to cooked food that was supremely pleasing to the mind.

Then there was food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, food to be licked, and likewise food to be sucked; various side dishes that were astringent and pungent, as well as sour, sweet, and bitter, all possessing excellent qualities. || 35 ||
Having thus attained supreme satisfaction through that cow, the king, together with his servants and his army, partook of foods produced from nectar.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, the king, filled with wonder, requested that cow from the great sage Jamadagni.
"O Brahmin, this Kāmadhenu is not fit for sages dwelling in the forest whose minds are tranquil; therefore, give her to me yourself. (38)
By her power, I shall today make the worlds mine, and I shall subdue my enemies, though they be stationed in fortresses and endowed with vast armies. (39)
If this is done, there will be welfare and immediate fame for you, both in this world and in the next; therefore, do what I have said.
Jamadagni said: "O King, this sacrificial cow is my only one, as dear to me as my own life. She must never be given away and is always to be honored; therefore, you ought not to ask for her. (41)
The king said: || 1 ||
"O twice-born one, for her sake I shall give you a hundred thousand cows, or whatever other wealth you desire. (42)
Jamadagni said: "O great king, it is traditionally held that even an ordinary cow must not be sold; how much more so a sacrificial cow endowed with such powers as these? (43)
That Brahmin who, out of delusion and desire for wealth, sells a cow, undoubtedly sells his own mother in this world. (44)
