Having drunk liquor or having killed a twice-born man, an expiation for the twice-born is prescribed; however, for those who sell cows, no atonement is found. (45)
The king said: "O Brahmin, if you give me this cow of mine peacefully, I shall take it even by force; therefore, let it be given peacefully. (46)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having heard that, Jamadagni, filled with rage, rose from the floor of the assembly hall, crying out, "Weapon! Weapon! (astraṃ astram).
Then those servants of that king, who were skilled in reading his mind, struck that brahmin—who had not yet reached for his weapon—with their sharpened weapons. || 48 ||
As that high-souled Jamadagni was being thus struck, his beloved wife named Reṇukā, overcome with grief, threw herself upon him. 49.
Though that woman of excellent complexion was mangled by various kinds of sharp weapons, she was not deprived of her life in any way, owing to the remainder of her lifespan.
Having thus slain Jamadagni, the best of Brahmins, the lord of the earth drove that cow to where the city of Māhiṣmatī was located.
Then that cow, being driven away and filled with anger upon seeing Jamadagni slain, lowed piteously again and again.
As she was becoming enraged, fierce Pulindas and Medas issued forth from her mouth by the hundreds and thousands.
All of them, bearing various weapons like another host of Yama’s messengers, spoke respectfully to the cow: "Give us your command at once! (54)

She said, "This is indeed the power of the lord of the Haihayas. Then, by those fierce Mleccha tribes filled with rage, he was begun to be destroyed with sharp weapons without restraint. || 55 || || 1 ||
Not a single man stood even before them in battle, much less dared to fight them suddenly, being overcome by great fear.
Then, seeing their army broken and being slaughtered on all sides by the Pulindas of fierce appearance, the ministers spoke to the king: || 57 ||
"O Lord, a supreme loss of luster has arisen in you today due to the slaughter of a Brahmin; therefore, abandoning this cow, please go to your own abode. (58)
Until his powerful son named Rāma arrives—if he does not slay you right here along with your army, you shall meet your death. (59)
This most exalted Kāmadhenu cannot be taken away by force; for she is the very embodiment of power, and it is she herself who creates this world.
Then that king, terrified especially by their words, abandoned that cow and departed for his own abode, having lost his servants.
Sūta said: In the meantime, Rāma arrived at the front of the hermitage accompanied by his brothers, having taken fruits, tubers, and roots.
He saw his hermitage devastated and surrounded by many Pulindas, and that cow mangled by blows from clubs and stones.
He asked, "What is this that has come to such a state of turmoil? The hermitage grounds are surrounded by Ābhīras and Pulindas. (3)
"By whom has this cow of mine been reduced to such a state, shattered by blows? And why are all these female and male ascetics weeping? (4)
Where is my aged father today, and where is my mother, who is so fond of her son? Why does she not come before me with affection as she used to do in the past?
Then all the ascetics, afflicted with great sorrow, related to him the entire account of Sahasrārjuna’s deeds exactly as they had witnessed them.
Then all those brothers, having heard those words which were like the fall of a thunderbolt, and having seen their own father mangled by weapons, [were overcome with grief].
Leaving behind the mighty Rāma, they wept, tormented by grief for their mother, whose every limb was wounded, who was reduced to mere breath, and who was filled with agony.
Then, having wept for a long time and lamented again and again, they performed his funeral rites according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Then, at the conclusion of the cremation, having prepared a suitable pit, the sons released Rāma and offered water mixed with sesame seeds to their father.
Then Rāma, the best among those who bear arms, was addressed by other ascetics: "Why do you not offer a handful of water to the father of the deceased? (11)
Then, as he was being addressed in many ways by the ascetics, that son of Jamadagni counted the wounds inflicted upon his mother by sharp weapons.
Then Rāma, sighing deeply, spoke to those lords of sages: "Listen to the prohibition of giving water which was enacted by me."
"My father was slain by a Kṣatriya without any fault; twenty-one wounds remain upon my mother's body. (14)
Therefore, O Brahmins, if I do not indeed rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas according to the number of my blows, may all sins be mine. (15)
Whatever sin was committed here by that base Kṣatriya born of the murder of his father and mother, as well as other loathsome acts, [was done by him].
Then, having filled this pit, which is worthy of water for the ancestors, with the blood of that very man and of other evil-minded kṣatriyas, I shall satisfy my father with blood, not with water.
Sūta said: Having heard his terrible vow, those best of ascetics were struck with great astonishment; they said nothing further after that.
Then, having reached the end of the period of impurity, Rāma, filled with wrath, took up a sharp axe and set out toward Māhiṣmatī.
Together with all those Śabaras, as well as the Pulindas and Medakas, who had bound their arm-guards and finger-protectors and were wielding excellent arrows and bows.
Likewise, Arjuna also, having heard that the best of the Bhrigus had arrived accompanied by a great army and likewise upholding his vow, [prepared himself].
Then, seeing him face-to-face, he went forth for battle together with all kinds of warriors, all of whom were like gods and asuras.
Then, O best of the twice-born, a great battle took place between the Pulindas and the warriors of the lord of the Haihayas, who were like unto gods and asuras. (23)
Then all those Haihayas were slain in battle by the Śabaras with arrows resembling venomous serpents, as they roared again and again.
And because of that sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin, you have all become devoid of luster and are falling to the surface of the earth.
No one there was capable of displaying manliness; all, intent on flight, were being slain by sharp arrows. || 26 ||

Then, seeing his army broken, the lord of the Haihayas, filled with rage and acting with haste, desired to make his own bow strung; yet, despite applying great effort, he was unable to string it. (27)
Then he drew his stainless sword from its scabbard; however, he was unable to draw it out and fell into a state of extreme embarrassment.
Rāvaṇa, the fierce one who makes the worlds cry out, was defeated by the mace; that very mace also fell from his hand onto the surface of the earth at that moment.
By those auspicious hands, numbering a thousand, who supported the flow of the Narmadā, they all became overwhelmed with trembling.
By the power of destiny, they were unable to draw their weapons in any way whatsoever; likewise, all the mantras of the divine missiles had fallen into oblivion.
In the meantime, Rāma arrived, overwhelmed with rage; raising his sharp axe, he then spoke harshly to him.
O sinful lord of the Haihayas, show me now quickly those hands by which my father was slain by you! 33.
Struck by the splendor of his Brahmanic power, he too was addressed very harshly by him; yet he did not utter any reply, remaining as if depicted in a painting.
Then Rāma, the best among those who bear arms, repeatedly rebuking his forest-like arm, slowly and steadily cut it off.
Then, O twice-born ones, having severed his head with an axe, that scion of Bhṛgu's lineage himself carefully caught the blood from the blows.
Then, having filled large jars, he gave them to the Śabaras; thereafter, he spoke respectfully to the Mlecchas and the hunters.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, a pit was dug by my brothers and filled with water for the purpose of satiating the ancestors.
"Go quickly and, by my command, undoubtedly pour this great quantity of blood into her for the sake of this sinful rival. (39)
By which means, having gratified my own father with devotion according to the prescribed rite, there may be for me liberation from that paternal debt? (40)
Sūta said: Then those Śabaras, with great effort, carried that blood born of the Haihaya to the place where that pit originating from his father was located.
And Bhārgava, having slain him and taken all that blood, then dispatched it to where his paternal pit was located.
That descendant of Bhṛgu does not abandon anyone—neither the child nor the aged; he especially spares a Kṣatriya, whether he be in the prime of youth or even still in the womb.
He himself slew the kings, as well as others at their sides; enraged, he caused destruction on all sides through his soldiers.
In that very manner, he himself eagerly took up their blood and caused it to be taken; then, from their sides, he quickly dispatched them to that place.
Having thus rid the entire earth of Kṣatriyas, the descendant of Bhṛgu then proceeded to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Then, having bathed with those bloods and taken up many sesame seeds, he arranged them counter-clockwise and performed the libation for the ancestors.
In the presence of all the brahmins as well as other ascetics, he fulfilled his vow and became free from sorrow.
Then, having performed the horse sacrifice when the world was devoid of Kṣatriyas, he bestowed the entire earth as a sacrificial fee upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Then the Brahmins, having obtained their boon, said to that best of the Bhṛgus: "You must not remain on our land, for it is traditionally held that there can be only one king."

He too, saying "So be it," was filled with great joy; then, having reached the edge of the earth and having mounted his massive bow and discharged the Āgneya weapon, he knit his brows into three furrows and, overcome with great wrath, spoke to the Lord of Rivers.
Rāma said: "The earth, together with its mountains and forests, was cleared of Kṣatriyas by me and then bestowed upon the Brāhmaṇas at the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha)."
Therefore, give me a place by making a retreat for yourself; for once I have given the earth to the Brahmins, I shall not take it back again.
Or if you do not obey my word today, O Lord of Rivers, I shall turn you into dry land, parched by the fire-weapon.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the ocean, overwhelmed with fear, then made way for him as much as he desired.
Then that scion of Bhrigu’s lineage, intent upon the practice of asceticism and remembering the slaughter of his father, made his dwelling right there.
Then that descendant of Bhṛgu established all the Pulindas and Śabaras, together with the Medas, upon the mountains at the edge of the earth.

Sūta said: Then, when the world was devoid of Kṣatriyas, the Kṣatriya women, for the sake of continuing their lineage, bore excellent sons begotten upon Brāhmaṇas. Having attained growth, those sons born of the wives (kṣetrajas), who were equal to Kṣatriyas, seized the earth by their prowess, having cast down the best of the twice-born.
Then all those brahmins, having fallen into a state of humiliation and filled with great sorrow, approached Bhārgava and spoke.

O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! That earth which was given by you to us at the horse-sacrifice has been forcibly seized by the Kṣatriyas. Therefore, give it back to us after slaying those lowest of Kṣatriyas; perform that increase of our welfare if you possess any manliness.
Then Rāma, overcome with wrath, once again set out for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas along with those Śabaras, Pulindas, and Medakas.
Having slain the kṣatriyas right there and taking their abundant blood, he filled that pit and performed the libation for his ancestors.
And in the horse-sacrifice, he gave the earth back to the Brāhmaṇas; then, banished from there by them, he went to the vicinity of the ocean.
In this manner, O best of Brahmins, he cleared the earth of all Kṣatriyas twenty-one times and offered it back to the twice-born.
The ancestors were indeed gratified by the blood of that high-souled one; thus his vow was fulfilled, and he became free from anger.
Then, when the twenty-first libation for the ancestors was reached, an incorporeal voice arose from the sky, originating from the ancestors.
O Rāma, Rāma, O highly fortunate one, abandon this censurable deed; we have attained satisfaction because of your fulfillment of your own word.
This deed which has been performed by you, another will not perform; it was never done by anyone before, arising as it does from enmity toward your father.
"Therefore, O child, we are pleased; we shall grant you whatever your heart desires. Therefore, quickly request that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (14)

Rāma said: "O ancestors, if you are pleased with me, and if you grant my desire, then let this meritorious holy place (tīrtha) become world-renowned by my name, free from the defect of blood, and frequented by excellent ascetics. || 15 ||
The Pitṛs said: "This pit which has been fashioned by you for the libation of the ancestors shall attain fame throughout the three worlds as 'Rāmahrada'. (16)
Wherever people endowed with devotion offer libations to the ancestors, they shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and attain the supreme goal. || 17 ||
And on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, whatever man shall perform a śrāddha with devotion for one slain by a weapon; || 18 ||
Even if he has fallen into the state of a preta or is dwelling in hell, he shall deliver that preta, even one possessed of sin.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to Rāma, they then ceased; and Rāma, free from anger, performed penance in that very place.
Therefore, with every effort, those endowed with faith should perform a Śrāddha ceremony for one slain by a weapon on that very day. (21)
And for those who have died through misfortunes such as [death by] serpents, fire, poison, or imprisonment, it is declared that the Śrāddha performed on that day bestows liberation.

Whoever offers libations of water even with those waters there during the fortnight of the departed ancestors, having become free from debt to them, is glorified in the world of the ancestors. || 23 ||
O best of Brahmins, all this majesty arising from the Rāmahrada has been narrated to you; it is the destroyer of all sins. (24)
The man who himself recites this with devotion at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony undoubtedly obtains the entire fruit born of a *śrāddha* performed at Gayā. (25)
Or, when a festival day has arrived, he who recites this in the presence of Brāhmaṇas obtains the entire fruit of the Pitṛmedha sacrifice. || 26 ||
Or even that man who listens with devotion while this is being recited, undoubtedly obtains the entire fruit of having performed the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice. || 27 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another Śakti there that destroys sins, which was released by Kārttikeya after he had indeed slain Tāraka in battle.

Likewise, there is a very great pool filled with clear water, created by him himself; whoever bathes therein and worships her shall be instantly liberated from all sins committed from birth until death.
The sages said: Tell us, at what time was that Śakti released by him? For what purpose was she sent by her Lord? And what is her power? Tell us yourself.
Sūta said: Formerly there was a Dānava named Tāraka, endowed with exceeding strength, the heir of Hiraṇyākṣa, who brought fear to the three worlds.
Having learned that Janaka had been destroyed by the powerful Viṣṇu, he then performed intense penance after reaching the Gokarṇa mountain.
For as long as a thousand years, he remained subsisting on withered leaves, meditating upon Mahādeva with body, mind, and speech.
Then, with various offerings for the worship of Varuṇa and diverse food oblations, that Daitya, filled with sorrow, [remained] at the end of a thousand years.
Perceiving that Rudra was not satisfied, she then performed fierce austerity; cutting off her own flesh, she offered it as oblations into the sacrificial fire.
Then Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, mounted upon his bull, being pleased, went to grant him a vision along with all his attendants.
Thereupon, Mahādeva, filled with joy, made all the directions resound with a piercing cry, speaking with a voice faltering from rapture.
"O Tāraka, I am pleased; perform such a feat of daring! Ask for whatever your heart desires, so that I may grant it to you. (11)
Tāraka said: "O Lord, by your grace, act in such a way that I may become invincible to all the gods in battle, with the sole exception of you. (12)
The Blessed One said: "By my grace, all this shall undoubtedly come to pass. O Daitya, that which you have requested—that you alone shall be powerful here [shall be granted]."
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva went to his own abode, and Tāraka likewise, greatly rejoiced, returned to his own palace.
Then, surrounded by a vast army of Dānavas, he went to fight against the famous city of Śakra, Amarāvatī.
Then a great battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas, lasting until the end of a thousand years, with death as the only means of withdrawal.
There, at the front of the battle, there was constant destruction of the gods and victory for the Dānavas, by the grace of the wielder of the trident.
Then those dwellers of heaven made preparations for victory: they constructed various kinds of armor, mechanical engines, and moats.
O best of the twice-born, other [measures] as well were diligently employed for the protection of the body, and likewise especially for the chief warriors.
Those lords of the gods showered [gifts] upon the Dānavas day and night.

At that time, mallets, slings, shataghnis, excellent arrows, darts, spears, and crescent-headed shafts were fashioned, as well as the various methods for arranging battle formations suited to specific engagements.
Likewise, they performed many other various forms of treacherous warfare, numerous terrifying displays, deceptions, and the entirety of Indra’s magical illusions.
Yet those best of the twice-born did not achieve victory; for in that great battle, they were shattered by the blows of the Dānavas.
Then the thousand-eyed one, terrified with fear, said to Bṛhaspati: "O best of the twice-born, day after day we are being defeated by the Daityas."
In whatever manner I employ effective means for the sake of battle, in that very same manner my defeat occurs in the great conflict. (25)
Therefore, O preceptor of the gods, reflect with your own wisdom upon a means by which I may achieve victory in battle and your own fame remains irreproachable. (26)
Sūta said: Then Bṛhaspati, having meditated for a long time and having perceived the means of victory in the great battle, spoke to the Lord of Śacī with a joyful countenance.
O Śakra, I have understood that means for the great battle, by which enemies are conquered repeatedly as if in mere play. (28)
When Tripurāntaka was requested for his desired boon by him, he then spoke these words after bowing down repeatedly. (29)
O Lord, by your grace, act in such a way that I may become invincible to all the gods in battle, with the sole exception of yourself. (30)
Mahādeva himself will not slay his own disciple; for who, having planted even a poisonous tree, would then cut it down himself? (31)
"He who is the father may indeed become the son"—this is recorded as a Vedic statement. Therefore, let Hara quickly procreate a son who will bring about his destruction.
Having appointed him to the command of the army, let us wage a great battle with the Daityas using our weapons, and thereby attain victory.
This very means has been proclaimed by me here to you for the sake of victory, O Thousand-eyed One; there is no other in the three worlds. (34)
Then Pākaśāsana, accompanied by all the hosts of gods, stood bowed in humility and spoke of that matter to Śambhu.
O Bull-bannered One, exert yourself for the sake of producing a son, so that I may appoint him to the command of the celestial armies.
And by your grace, I shall attain victory in battle after slaying all the Dānavas together with Tāraka.
"Otherwise, I shall have no victory in battle with the Dānavas. Thus spoke the high-minded preceptor of the gods to me, having understood the situation correctly.
Then Śaṅkara, laughing loudly, said to the lord of the gods: "O Śakra, I shall swiftly carry out your word; of this there is no doubt. (39)
"I shall procreate a son who will be the destroyer of all the Daityas; by making him your commander-in-chief, you shall attain victory at all times. (40)
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva went to Mount Kailāsa and, together with Gaurī, engaged in the appropriate acts of love as was fitting.
Endowed with gestures (hāva) and expressions (bhāva), as well as with laughter and other such states, he remained for a thousand divine years as if it were but a single blink of an eye.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds terrified with fear and oppressed by Tāraka, held a consultation for that purpose.
A thousand years passed for the wielder of the trident while he was absorbed in pleasure; yet he did not perform any duty toward the gods.
Therefore, let us go to that place where the god Maheśvara dwells together with Gaurī on the secluded Kailāsa.
Then, all the gods, together with Indra, gathered at that very place, bearing the supreme agony arising from the enemy of Tāraka.
Then, having reached Kailāsa, as they were approaching the presence of Bhava, they were stopped by Nandin with the words: "You must not go further than this."
"In this secret place, the Blessed One is stationed together with Pārvatī; it is inaccessible even to us, therefore let us not go there yet."
Then, all those gods dispatched Vāyu there with the instruction: "Let it be quickly ascertained what Mahādeva is doing."
Then Vāyu went to that place where the blessed Śiva was staying, absorbed in pleasure with Gaurī and having attained supreme bliss.
Then, as Śukra had moved from his place but had not yet reached the womb, the god beheld Vāyu stationed not far away.
Then, overcome with shame, he rose at that very moment, abandoning his beloved who was attached to him and saying, "Do not get up."
Then he spoke to that Vāyu, who stood bowed in humility: "For what purpose have you come here? Is all well with the dwellers of heaven? (53)
Vāyu said: These gods, Śakra and the others, have been turned back by Nandin; with their enthusiasm destroyed by Tāraka, they remain on the mountain slope.
Therefore, having addressed them and comforted them with respect, dispatch them quickly to that place where those Dānavas reside.
Then, at that very moment, the Destroyer of Tripura summoned them; with a dejected face, he spoke to those who stood before him with their palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One said: "The undertaking which I made for your sake and for the purpose of obtaining a son has today been rendered fruitless by Vāyu, once Śukra had departed from his own place."
"This semen of mine, held within the center of the linga through fortitude, remains entirely unfailing; tell me, where shall I deposit it? (58)
By which [rite] a son shall be born, a supreme destroyer of the Dānavas, who will be the commander of your armies and invincible by enemies in battle. (59)
No one other than Vaiśvānara is able to sustain this [world], which resembles the fire at the end of an aeon; therefore, let him uphold it eternally.
By means of which I release [this] there for the sake of my daughter and for victory—this vigor is exceedingly intense, possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns. (61)
Then all the gods, having praised Agni with reverence, said: "O Agni, hold this seed born of Bhava within the interior of your mouth."
Then Pāvaka quickly extended his own mouth, carrying out Śakra’s command with a mind free from hesitation.
Śaṅkara also, afflicted by the arrows of Kāma, cast his gaze there; meditating upon the divine Gaurī, he attained supreme bliss.
The Fire-god also, being intensely scorched by him who resembled the fire of universal destruction, cast himself upon the ground into a very extensive thicket of reeds.
In the meantime, the six auspicious Kṛttikās arrived there as the wives of the six sages, wandering here and there.
Śatakratu himself gave them this instruction: "This seed of the Three-eyed One must be protected with great effort. (67)
"Here a son shall be born, possessing a splendor equal to twelve suns; he will, for the most part, become a son to you as well. (68)
Sūta said: Having assented with "So be it," they carried out that command of Śakra; they performed in every respect all that pertains to the duties of a lying-in chamber.
Then, on another day, by that very power, a beautiful child was born with two arms and one face, possessing a splendor equal to twelve suns.
As soon as he was born, he wept in great distress; hearing that crying, all the Kṛttikās approached him.
And Mahāsena, beholding those Mothers who had approached him, became filled with longing; he then became six-faced and likewise possessed of twelve eyes and arms.
With self-restraint, he drank from each breast individually, and with two arms, he embraced them both with affection.
In the meantime, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all the gods, along with Indra, as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases, arrived there.
Then a great, unrestrained festival broke out in that place, the sound of its songs and musical instruments filling the entire universe.
Rambhā and other graceful celestial nymphs danced for him, while the preeminent Gandharvas, headed by Citrāṅgada, sang.
Then all the deities respectfully gave him the name Skanda, because he had spilled his seed upon the ground.
Then, at that time and place, the consecration of that prince was performed by Śambhu himself as the commander-in-chief of the gods.
To him, a spear of wondrous appearance was given by Brahmā himself; it was unfailing, intended for victory and for the destruction of the faction of the Daityas.
The peacock was provided very swiftly by Tryambaka for the purpose of a vehicle; likewise, the divine weapons were given by Mahendra and the high-souled Viṣṇu.
Then, all the gods, being individually satisfied, as well as the hosts of Mothers, bestowed their desired weapons upon him.
Then, placing that commander-in-chief at their head, the lords of the gods went with their armies to where Tāraka was stationed.
Tāraka, too, seeing the gods who had come to him of their own accord for the sake of battle, went quickly forward to meet them, filled with joy. (15)
Then there occurred a very great battle between the gods and the Dānavas, whose eyes were bloodshot with rage, making death their point of no return.
Then Skanda, having observed Tāraka standing at a distance in the battle, challenged him and thereafter released that spear for his death.
Then that terrible spear, having pierced the heart of that Daitya, fell at the outskirts of the city of Camatkārapura, drenched in blood.
Tāraka, however, perished and was deprived of his life-breaths at that very moment; then all the hosts of gods were filled with joy toward that one of great strength.
Having praised him with various kinds of hymns, they spoke when he had been slain; and, being fearless, they quickly went to heaven together with Śakra.
Skanda, too, taking up that spear, established it there in that best of cities, by which very means Raktaśṛṅga became firm.
The sages said: "O high-minded one, tell us in detail: how was Raktaśṛṅga made firm by him, even though he was already steady? By whose word did this happen?"
Sūta said: When indeed that most terrible earthquake occurred, Raktaśṛṅga was shaken from his own place with extreme velocity. || 23 ||
Then, by the fall of that Daitya, all the palaces in Camatkārapura were shattered, just like other excellent mountain peaks.
When that mountain shook, the birds were distressed; most met their death, while others were afflicted by fainting.
Then the remaining Brahmins, filled with wrath, went to Skanda and said: "O sinner, what is this that has been done by you, lacking in intelligence? (26)
"We have all been brought to ruin, along with our sons, cattle, and kinsmen; therefore, afflicted by this sorrow, we shall pronounce a curse. (27)
Skanda said: "O best of the twice-born, this was performed by me for the benefit of all the worlds; that the fierce Dānava was slain was not otherwise. (28)
Therefore, please grant me your favor; the Brahmins are always worthy of my respect. Even all those twice-born ones who have died, I shall restore to life through this refuge of immortality.
"Furthermore, I shall restore them to life, of this there is no doubt; likewise, by my own power, I shall make this mountain perfectly immovable. (30)
Having spoken thus and taking up that spear drenched in blood, he planted it upon the summit of Raktaśṛṅga.
Then, filled with joy, he spoke to the four goddesses: Āmavṛddhā, likewise Āmrā, Māhitthī, and Camatkarī.
"You must ensure that this best of mountains remains motionless, so that even at the time of universal dissolution, its blood-red peak does not waver from its place. (33)
May this excellent city always become renowned by my name. || 32 ||
All the brahmins will always offer worship to you. || 34 ||

Saying "So be it," they then, delighted by Skanda’s words, firmly impaled him from the four directions with the points of their spears. Then Skanda, devoted to his service to the twice-born, took up the nectar of immortality and restored even those best of the twice-born who had died back to life.
Then those Brahmins, being greatly delighted there, granted him an excellent boon; and he said: "May this best of cities always attain renown by my name; this is the desire in my heart. (37)
The sages said: "O best of gods, this city shall henceforth be known by your name as Skandapura; likewise, it is currently called Camatkārapura. (38)
"We shall perform worship for you after having constructed a magnificent temple; likewise, all four deities who were supported by you [shall be honored]. (39)
"We shall worship all of them with reverence in all our rites; and this power of yours, O best of the foremost gods, we shall especially worship on the sixth lunar day, endowed with faith. (40)
Sūta said: Thus addressed by the Brahmins, the mighty Mahāsena remained right there, having recognized that field as supreme because of their words. (41)
He who worships him with devotion and pure intent on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra—him the one whose vehicle is peacock (Skanda) grants satisfaction.

O twice-born ones, whatever man, endowed with perfect faith, should rub his back against that stone after worshipping it with flowers and other offerings, he shall not be afflicted by disease for as long as a year.
Thus was power established there by that wise Skanda for the protection of Raktaśṛṅga, and especially for that city.
Sūta said: A Liṅga was installed right there by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; by beholding it, one is liberated from all sins along with Duryodhana. || 1 ||
The sages said: O Romaharṣaṇa, tell us at what time was that Liṅga installed there by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men?
Sūta said: In former times, there was a daughter of Balabhadra named Bhānumatī, who was endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed beauty, generosity, and virtuous qualities.
Then, after consulting with Viṣṇu, the Yādava gave her as a wife to the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana.
Then all the Kauravas, headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, set out quickly from Nāgapura toward the city of Dvāravatī.
Likewise, the five sons of Pāṇḍu, accompanied by their retinues and considering themselves brothers to Duryodhana, went joyfully to Dvāravatī, joined by a great army.
Then, proceeding by degrees, all those Kurus and Pāṇḍavas reached the region of Ānarta, which was abundant with wealth and grain.
That supreme sacred field, which removes all sins and bestows merit, is renowned throughout the three worlds as that of the god Hāṭakeśvara.
Then the pure-souled elder, the grandfather of the Kurus, spoke as if smiling to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons.
Bhīṣma said: "O child, this unsurpassed sacred field of the god Hāṭakeśvara, which destroys all sins, was seen by me in the past. (10)
"Here I have been liberated from the sin arising from the murder of a woman; therefore, O Indra among kings, we shall remain right here for five days."
By which we may behold all the sacred fords and shrines, whatever meritorious sites exist here belonging to the sages of purified souls.
Then, at those words, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, filled with curiosity, set out together with his hundred sons.
He went quickly to that place where that supreme sacred field was located, crowded with hosts of ascetics and endowed with auspicious hermitages.

All directions were resounded by a great, divine voice; the surface of the earth was clouded by the smoke arising from the worship of the sacrificial fire; and it was likewise crowded with many sporting deer running about.
Then, out of fear of the calamity, the king withdrew his own army and [remained] together with the five Pāṇḍavas as well as his hundred sons.
Accompanied by Bhīṣma, Somadatta, and Bāhlīka, as well as by the heroic preceptor Droṇa and his son Kṛpa. || 17 ||
Accompanied by the son of Subala, Karṇa, and other kings who had been abandoned by their retinues, he wandered in that sacred field.
All those high-souled kṣatriyas who were assembled there performed all religious rites with minds purified by faith.

Having wandered repeatedly among the most meritorious sacred fords and having heard the teachings of the twice-born again and again, those best of the twice-born performed their ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
Others gave distinguished gifts and desired things, especially to the wretched, the miserable, and the ascetics.
Others performed śrāddha rites with devotion for the sake of their ancestors, while others offered libations (tarpaṇa) to the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Some kings performed fire-sacrifices, others recited mantras without restraint, and others, being peaceful and endowed with perfect faith, engaged in the study of the Vedas. || 23 ||
Others, having heard of the shrines of the deities endowed with greatness and those belonging to former kings, worship them especially.
By means of offerings of oblations, fine garments, perfumes, flowers, and unguents; by means of cleansing, the offering of banners, and likewise by means of auspicious spectacles. || 25 ||

O best of the twice-born, all the brahmins there were made successful through his devotion by means of ornaments, flower garlands on all sides, and gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, cows, garments, and gold.
Having thus bathed and likewise worshipped the gods and the brahmins, O best of kings, they, together with Dhṛtarāṣṭra, then departed for their own camp.
Filled with wonder, they praised the sacred fords and shrines, as well as the twice-born and the ascetics of rigid vows in that holy field.
Sūta said: Thus all those Kauravas and the illustrious sons of Pāṇḍu departed from that place for the city of Dvāravatī.
Having gone there with joyful hearts, they then performed the marriage of King Duryodhana with Bhānumatī.
With the sound of various musical instruments accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, and with thousands of bards singing enchanting songs and recitations.
Thus a great festival took place there for eight days, as the Yādavas and Kurus gathered together with one another.
There, the charioteers, panegyrists, bards, wandering minstrels, eminent Brahmins, and likewise other logicians became fulfilled in their purpose.
Then, when the ninth day had arrived, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, headed by Bhīṣma, spoke these words with affection to the lotus-eyed Lord.
O lotus-eyed one, bound by the fetters of affection, we do not wish to abandon our reliance upon you and Rāma under any circumstances.
Nevertheless, O Mādhava, you must proceed toward your own city together with Balabhadra; therefore, grant us liberation.
Viṣṇu said: Not even a year has passed for you who are stationed here, nor a month, nor even a fortnight; why then has this eagerness come upon you?
Therefore, let us Kurus and Pāṇḍavas remain together right here, you and we, for diversion through hunting and gambling.
If you have affection for me through the practice of training in weapons, the taming of elephants, and likewise through other desired things, [then let it be so]. (11)
Bhīṣma said: "O Viṣṇu, these words which have been spoken by you are appropriate. Now hear my further speech, for the sake of which we are indeed eager. (12)

While we were traveling toward your presence in the region of Ānarta, we beheld the great and most wonderful sacred field born of Hāṭakeśvara; there, the Liṅgas of high-souled kings were seen by us. (13)
Of those born from the lineage of the Sun and the Moon, and of other great-souled ones as well. || 14 ||
For the gods, the dānavas, and especially for the sages, there were forms endowed with great splendor, enjoying various palaces.
And then, O Mādhava, the minds of the leaders of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas became firmly resolved upon the purpose of establishing a Liṅga there.
Having gone there quickly, we shall each, according to our ability and as we desire, install our own respective lingas separately. (17)
For this reason, O Acyuta, we have departed quickly; we do not reach satiety in your company even in hundreds of years.
Therefore, O Lord, having made your mind firm, give us your command today; we shall come here once more, longing for a vision of you. (19)
The Blessed Lord said: I know that most meritorious field which destroys all sins, which is constantly praised by ascetics and by others who travel on pilgrimages.
Therefore, we shall go there together with you, for the purpose of installing the Liṅga and out of a desire to see the sacred field.
Sūta said: Having heard that, all the Kauravas attained supreme joy, as did the sons of Pāṇḍu and whatever other kings were there. || 22 ||
Then all those Kurus and Pāṇḍavas set out together, shaking the earth with the trampling of their elephants and horses.
Then, having reached that sacred field and established their camp at a distance, the Kauravas and the leading Yādavas went to Camatkārapura.
There, having summoned all the Brāhmaṇas and bestowed upon them various ornaments and garments, they spoke with great humility.
"We all desire here to perform the rite of establishing the liṅgas, each according to our own capacity, by constructing separate temples for the principal deities. (26)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, having shown us favor and compassion, please command us quickly so that the ritual may proceed.
"You shall become the officiating priests in all rituals; no other Brahmin, even if he were Bṛhaspati himself, shall be external to this task. (28)
For we have heard the ancient account being proclaimed concerning that royal sage, which arose from the funeral śrāddha performed for him by Viṣṇu.

O twice-born ones, just as he diligently performed the śrāddha for his deceased father in the presence of the brahmins and others who had been mentioned, so too [did he perform it] for the rest. || 30 ||
Although he performed the rite at a sacred ford on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa according to the prescribed method for the Nāgas, his father was nevertheless not liberated.

O best of the twice-born, due to his state as a preta and the fault of a serpent, he remained there until that śrāddha was performed with devotion in the presence of Devaśarman; at that moment, O brahmins, his father was liberated from that terrible state of a preta.
O best of the twice-born, whatever righteous deed is performed here [without this], it becomes external and fruitless; this we know clearly. (33)
We especially entreat you, having fallen into this state of wretchedness; therefore, let favor be shown, and grant us your command without delay.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, those Brāhmaṇas consulted with one another regarding that matter, deliberating on what deed would constitute a meritorious act. (35)
Some said, "We will not give away the earth for the sake of the temple; therefore, let them go quickly to one of these [other kings]. (36)
This sacred field is established with an extent of five krośas, and it is completely surrounded by the palaces of the gods of former times.
Others said: "Intoxicated by wealth, you live in comfort; you do not know the pain of poverty, and therefore you speak such harsh words. (38)
Therefore, we shall indeed bestow the earth upon them, so that their purpose may be accomplished and the ornamentation of this place may come to pass. (39)
Likewise, others who were moderate said: "Since Janārdana himself is personally requesting the land, why is it not given? (40)
Therefore, let the Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Yādavas who have assembled there construct palaces primarily themselves, and others as well.
Where the son of Gaṅgā himself, as well as others—Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his sons and the mighty Pāṇḍavas—make a request, a refusal there is not appropriate for the purpose of establishing a Liṅga. (42)
Having heard those words of theirs, the best of the twice-born—both the impoverished and the wealthy, as well as those with desire and those free from desire—agreed.
Then, having come together and reached a firm decision through consultation, all those brahmins spoke to the best of the Kurus, the Yādavas, and the Pāṇḍavas.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "This field is the smallest of all those belonging to kings; it is pervaded on all sides by palaces. What, then, can we say now? (45)

Therefore, sirs, please construct, according to your own inclination, most beautiful temples right here in this sacred field, facing [the deity], established separately according to seniority and excellence. (46)
Then, filled with joy, those led by Dhṛtarāṣṭra constructed a series of palaces in due order, according to their importance and excellence.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Effort Made by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Others to Establish the Temple," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, accompanied by his hundred sons, installed one hundred and one Liṅgas there.
And likewise, five lingas were installed by all the Pāṇḍavas—by Draupadī, Kuntī, and Gāndhārī, as well as by chance.
And Bhānumatī established four [images] of Gaurī; then Vidura, Śalya, Kaliṅga, and Yuyutsu [established others].
Then by Bāhlīka with his son, by Karṇa with his son, as well as by Śakuni there, and by Droṇa and Kṛpa.
By Aśvatthāman, each of these excellent individual lingas was installed with supreme devotion, situated within a magnificent temple.
There, the powerful Viṣṇu established that Liṅga after constructing a temple endowed with lofty spires.
Also by the wise Sāmba, who is of the Sātvata lineage, by Balabhadra, by Pradyumna, by Aniruddha, and likewise by other principal Yādavas.
By his sons, Cārudeṣṇa and the others—the ten sons of Rukmiṇī—endowed with faith, a principal group of ten Liṅgas was installed.
Having thus established the lingas, all those Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Yādavas were then exceedingly joyful and felt they had accomplished their purpose.
Having stayed there for a long time and having given gifts many times, he made the Brahmins born in Camatkārapura wealthy.
Having given them excellent elephants of various breeds many times over, as well as diverse and beautiful villages, fields, and fine cows.
Large bulls, fine garments, lands, dwellings, as well as female and male slaves, servants, and various kinds of gifts.
Then, having taken leave of them all and prostrating themselves again and again, they all departed for their own abodes, filled with joy.
Sūta said: Thus has all this been narrated to you—how that sin-destroying Liṅga was installed by that king, as well as by Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Likewise, by other kings who were preeminent, as well as by the Pāṇḍavas and the Yādavas, each established separately. || 5 ||
The person who, permeated by devotion, properly worships them, shall obtain all the desires wished for by his own mind.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Installation of Liṅgas by the Kauravas, Pāṇḍavas, and Yādavas," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Āgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, in a former kalpa, this unsurpassed sacred field was given to Brahmā by the blessed Rudra when he was pleased.
When, however, the Liṅga known as Hāṭakeśvara had been installed, it was given back to Brahmā by Rudra, who was pleased with the gods.
Then this field was indeed granted by Śambhu to Ṣaṇmukha for the protection of the Brahmins from the defects of the Kali age and other such evils. (3)
Requested by Brahmā, this first and most excellent [place] was established; then, commanded by his father, the son of Gaṅgā took up residence there.
He who beholds the Lord on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation shall become a wealthy Brāhmaṇa, a master of the Vedas, for seven births.
The palace of the god Mahāsena was exceedingly beautiful, standing high above all the worlds as if desiring to drink the very sky.
Having heard that, all the gods came quickly out of curiosity; having gone there, they looked about and beheld that most sacred city.
O twice-born ones, in the northern and eastern regions of the palace, they commenced the sacrificial rites as prescribed by the Brahmins.
And having performed the sacrifice and given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them, all the gods, joyful and having obtained the fruit born of that place, went to the celestial realm (triviṣṭapa).

Consequently, that place of his came to be known as Devayajana; for whatever fruit one might obtain by performing a hundred sacrifices elsewhere, one obtains that here by means of a single sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Sūta said: Likewise, there is another auspicious triad of suns located there; when these three are pleased, a human being shall attain liberation within the three worlds.
There, Muṇḍīra is the first, and likewise Kālapriya is the next; Mūlasthāna is the third, which destroys all diseases.
There the sun transits at Muṇḍīra at the end of night, at Kālapriya at midday, and at Mūlasthāna at the arrival of night.
At that time, even if a man beholds it with devotion for but a single moment, that man who has found the opportunity attains liberation; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
The sages said: It is heard, indeed, that Muṇḍīra is in the eastern quarter of the earth; in the middle is the god Kālapriya, and between them is Mūlasthāna.
How was it that those three suns were born there, O Sūta, in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: On the shore of the ocean, there is an excellent city named Viṭaṅkapura, adorned with lofty ramparts kissed by the waves of the sea.
There was a certain brahmin there who, due to the ripening of his past karma, was afflicted with the disease of leprosy when his youth had arrived.
He had a virtuous wife, of noble birth and adorned with good character; though he was such [a man], she generally regarded him as if he were the god of love himself.
I also took various medicines, even those of great value, as well as ointments for that purpose and diverse kinds of wholesome foods.
Likewise, he constantly and respectfully summoned the best of physicians; yet, for that purpose, no remedy for his bodily ailment could be found. (11)
O best of the twice-born, in whatever manner he took those medicines, in that very same manner his leprosy spread throughout all his limbs.
Now, while that best of brahmins was living in this manner, a certain traveler, weary with fatigue, arrived as a guest at his house. (13)
Then, seeing that the brahmin had arrived at his house, his virtuous and beloved wife, out of true devotion even though he was unknown to her, gratified him with excellent hospitality.
Then, when that best of the twice-born had bathed, sipped water for purification, finished his meal, and rested upon his bed, the brahmin householder spoke to him.
He was endowed with splendor like the sun, possessed of the qualities of beauty and nobility, and appearing like another god of love incarnate in the prime of youth.
The leper said: "O Brahmin, from where have you come and where will you go? Tell me now. Though endowed with such beauty, why are you alone like one who suffers from affliction? (17)
The traveler said: There is a city named Kāntīpura, which is like the city of Indra, constantly inhabited by well-established people devoted to the vows of dharma. (18)
Having established my residence there, I was leading the life of a householder when I was seized by a terrible form of leprosy, just as you are now, O best of the twice-born. (19)
Then I heard from the Purāṇa known as the Skānda that there is a triad of suns on earth that destroys all diseases.
Then, having fallen into despair after being tormented for a long time by medicines—by alkaline, sour, astringent, pungent, and bitter [substances]—(21)
Then, having made a firm resolve in his mind and taking great wealth, he went to the lord Muṇḍīra and stood in his very presence.
Then, having risen in the morning, I would daily behold that all-pervading Lord; I would worship Him according to my ability and thereafter offer my prostrations. (23)
Especially on Sundays, fasting and with my senses restrained, I shall keep a vigil at night to the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
Then, at the end of the year, having bowed to that Lord of Day (the Sun), he thereafter approached Kālapriya, endowed with supreme faith.
O Brahmin, by that very same rite, I perform the worship of that Lord of Day as well at midday, with a mind purified by faith.
Then, at the end of that year, having bowed to him according to his ability, he went to the god located in the western direction at Mūlasthāna.
O best of the twice-born, I performed worship for him according to that very same rite during the twilight hour, remaining there for a full year.
Then, at the end of the year, Bhāskara approached me in a dream and, smiling with a joyful heart, spoke to me, O Brahmin.
"O Brahmin, I am well-pleased with you because of this act performed with devotion; therefore, let your leprosy depart as a result of my propitiation alone. (30)
Go quickly to your own home, O best of the twice-born; you are weary. Behold all your kinsmen standing there in longing for your sake.
In the past, you stole the gold of a high-souled Brahmin; by the ripening of that karma, this disease of leprosy has befallen you.
"O twice-born one, I have now joyfully destroyed that [sin] for you; knowing this, you must never again commit the theft of gold. (33)
Those men who are seen in the world afflicted by the disease of leprosy have all committed the sinful act of stealing gold. (34)
Therefore, those who desire the supreme and eternal happiness of their own bodies should, according to their ability, give gold and not steal it. (35)
Having spoken thus, the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) then vanished from sight; and I, overcome with wonder, rose quickly from my bed.
O twice-born one, I beheld my own body, though afflicted by the disease of leprosy, as divine and possessing the luster of twelve suns, just as you see it now.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too should behold those three suns with devotion according to this procedure, by which your leprosy shall be pacified.
What is the use of medicines, or of diets even when combined with pungent substances, while these three suns remain present as the lords who destroy all diseases? (39)
"May it be well with you; I shall now depart for that city. Today, I have rested in your house just as if in my own home, O Brahmin. (40)
Thus addressed by that traveler, the Brahmin afflicted with leprosy, filled with sorrow, then looked toward the face of his wife.
She said, "O beloved, what has been spoken by this traveler is fitting; therefore, go quickly to that place where those three suns are. (42)
"I shall go there with you, devoted to serving you; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, depart quickly, O Lord. (43)
Thus addressed by her, he then took a great deal of wealth and set out together with his beloved toward the lord of Muṇḍīra.
On my solemn promise, I shall go to behold those three deities: Muṇḍīra, Kālanātha, and Bhāskara of Mūlasthāna.
Then, O best of the twice-born, afflicted by the disease of leprosy, he arrived with great difficulty at the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Having seen that great sacred field frequented by multitudes of ascetics, he, weary from the disease of leprosy and exhausted on the road, spoke to his beloved wife.
"I have fallen into despair because of this illness and hunger; I am unable to move forward until I reach Lord Muṇḍīra. (48)
Therefore, I shall undoubtedly cast off my own body right here; go to your own home, O beloved, having found a splendid caravan.
The wife said: "O beloved, never have I eaten while you had not yet eaten; nor, O illustrious one, have I ever slept even in private while you were awake. (50)
Therefore, having reached this great field where you are established, how can I go home, abandoning you for the sake of the next world? (51)
"How shall I show my face to them—to my kinsmen, my elders, and others who are so very dear—bereft as I am of you? (52)
Therefore, O Lord, bound as I am by the fetters of affection, I shall enter the fire along with you; I swear this truly upon my own soul. (53)
"O Mahāmati, as many fasts as you have observed, so many have we as well; how then can I go to that house? (54)
Having thus understood her resolve, that brahmin then prepared a funeral pyre for the purpose of cremation and entered it together with her.
Having meditated upon the Sun in his mind, as soon as he took up the fire, he beheld three brilliantly shining persons standing before him.
Seeing that, he was overcome with wonder: "Who are these three men? Never before have I seen anyone endowed with such splendor. (57)
The men said: "O twice-born one, do not go upon the path of death, distressed by your renunciation; turn back and go to your own home together with your wife."
The Brāhmaṇa said: Since I previously made a vow that my own home would be abandoned upon seeing Muṇḍīrasvāmin as well as another, Kālavallabha. (59)
"The primary place must be established; therefore, let me eat the grain. Having looked upon them, how can I go to my own abode? I shall eat the grain, and by that means, I shall give up my life. (60)
The men said: "O Brahmin, we are the three Bhāskaras who have come together right here; our minds are drawn by devotion to you—tell us, what shall we do? (61)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "If you three have come here to me in person, then let this leprosy go to its destruction like three suns. (62)
Likewise, you yourselves must always remain in this very field, and your presence must be maintained throughout the three worlds just as before.
The Bhāskaras said: "O Brahmin, we shall do exactly so; we will remain here forever. And you too, freed from disease, shall attain unsurpassed happiness. (64)
"Therefore, O twice-born one, designate for our sake three palaces, so that having approached them at the three times of day, we may come into your presence. (65)
Having spoken thus, they all then departed from his sight; he too beheld his own body, freed from disease.
Resembling twelve suns and endowed with all auspicious marks, he then spoke to his wife, who stood before him bowed down in humility.
Behold, O fair-browed one, my body as it stands once more in its true form, through the grace of the God of gods, the Sun-god garlanded with rays.
Therefore, remaining here eternally, I shall worship the Sun; I will not go back to my home again—this which I have spoken is the truth. (69)
Having spoken thus, that best of Brahmins, filled with devotion, constructed three beautiful palaces in that most splendid sacred field.
One belongs to Muṇḍīrasvāmin, another to Kālapriya, and yet another to Mūlasthāna, adorned with an excellent banner.
He established the virtuous images of all three of those Suns, as indicated by the scriptures, at Hastārka on a Sunday.

Then, having worshipped them for a long time with flowers, incense, and other offerings, the twice-born man, having reached [the deity] at the three junctions of the day in due order, attained the abode of the Sun at the end of his body.
Sūta said: Thus those three best of the twice-born became Bhāskaras there, the destroyers of all diseases for the world of devotees. (74)
He who beholds them at their own proper time, as previously described, on a Sunday, shall obtain his desired objects, even those difficult for men to attain. || 75 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, regarding that which has been stated by you—that Umā and Maheśvara, those two Supreme Lords, were [worshipped] there by King Hariścandra— || 1 ||
"Do you say that [the two] are established thus in the middle of the altar, or are they two others placed there near the city of Camatkārapura? (2)

O Sūta, it is heard that Pārvatī and Parameśvara always reside in the center of the sacrificial altar; previously, their marriage took place after they had reached Oṣadhiprastha, the beloved city of Himavat.

In this matter, a doubt has arisen within us regarding even your words, though they are worthy of faith; having heard them, tell us: is this a delusion on your part, or is it something we have misperceived? (4)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, no delusion has arisen on our part, but rather on yours; however, listen as I explain the entire reason for this. || 5 ||
This beautiful wedding of Umā and the Three-eyed One, which took place previously on Mount Oṣadhiprastha, brought joy to all the gods.
O best of the twice-born, he was previously born in the Vaivasvata interval—he who is well-known as the seventh among you and is known here to you.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, that marriage which took place between those two occurred in great detail during the first Manvantara of Svāyambhuva Manu.
The sages said: O Sūta, we have heard in detail that marriage which took place long ago between Pārvatī and Hara at Oṣadhiprastha.
In the past, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the marriage of Vṛṣayāna took place at the enchanting Dakṣa-sacrifice in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Therefore, O upholder of the Sūta lineage, you must recount this to us in detail exactly as it happened; this is a matter of the greatest curiosity.
Sūta said: In this regard, I shall fully proclaim to you the marriage ceremony of the trident-bearing God of gods, which destroys all sins.
From the right thumb of Brahmā, Dakṣa Prācetasa was born; and five hundred daughters were born to him, O twice-born ones. (13)
Among them, the eldest was a virtuous and chaste woman named Satī, possessed of a pure smile; she was a maiden endowed with all virtues and had long, wide eyes.
Neither among the goddesses, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, nor those born of the Nagas, was there any other woman of such form as that slender-waisted lady. (15)
Then Dakṣa, having been repeatedly entreated with great effort, gave her—who was herself full of longing—to the trident-bearing Śiva, who was likewise filled with desire for her as his wife.
Then, having reflected upon that most meritorious field which is worthy of the gift of a daughter, he presented himself there accompanied by his sons, ministers, and servants.
Then he brought forth various kinds of abundant wealth suitable for marriage, especially those items that are auspicious.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the sun under the constellation presided over by Bhaga during the bright fortnight of Caitra, Maheśvara arrived.
Together with all the hosts of gods, led by the god Viṣṇu, as well as the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and others.
By the Siddhas, the hosts of Sādhyas, the Bhūtas, the Pretas, and likewise the Vaināyakas; by the Gandharvas, the throngs of Cāraṇas, the Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. || 21 ||
In the meantime, Dakṣa, his hair standing on end with joy, went out to meet him accompanied by all his circles of friends.
With great musical instruments being played, and with numerous sūtas, māgadhas, and bards reciting on all sides, as well as with singers singing likewise; (23)
Then all the gods, personally honored there by Dakṣa, sat down in due order according to their rank and seniority, surrounding the entire sacrificial altar situated within the pavilion.
Then Dakṣa, having prostrated before the Grandfather (Brahmā), spoke with affection: "O Lord, you must perform the marriage rites for the Master."
May she herself become our daughter, so that she may be fortunate, virtuous, possessed of sons and grandsons, ever well-behaved, and beloved by her husband. (26)
Saying "So be it," with a heart full of joy, he rose up and then performed the rites, beginning with the offering of hospitality.

Having performed the ritual of giving away [the bride] there according to the prescribed rules, the Creator then caused Satī and Śiva to take each other’s hands in marriage in due order, in the presence of the Mothers, as was appropriate.
Then, having approached the altar, he performed the entire fire-rite in full detail, exactly as prescribed, according to the rules stated in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
The more he gazed with curiosity at Satyā’s beautiful limbs, the more her grandfather, filled with joy, became afflicted by desire.
Leaving aside one face, he—afflicted by intense passion—beheld her covered with a garment in such a way that no one would have noticed.
Out of shame, he did not look directly at Śambhu’s face, nor did she, overcome with bashfulness, reveal her face openly.
Then, for the sake of seeing him, he sought a means; thereafter, afflicted by desire, he proceeded by way of smoke.
Having cast many moist fuels into the fire repeatedly, [the smoke] likewise arises from those moist substances due to the offering of only a small amount of clarified butter.
In the meantime, smoke appeared on all sides, such that the base of the altar was rendered as if enveloped in darkness.
Then the Blessed One, the Destroyer of Tripura, covered with both hands the eyes of those others who were stationed there, which were clouded by smoke.
Then, having lifted the garment, the Grandfather, afflicted by desire, gazed upon the face of Satī with a delighted inner soul.
His semen was discharged; then, immediately upon seeing that, it fell rapidly onto the surface of the earth, resembling a mass of snow.
Then, at that very moment, Padmasambhava covered that semen with a mass of sand so that no one would perceive it.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, having perceived this with his divine eye, spoke these words out of anger because of that emission of semen.
"O sinful one, what is this despicable deed that has been committed by you? It is not at all fitting for my beloved to look upon me with affection. (41)

"You know this web of karma, which has not been perceived even by Śaṅkara; O Creator, how could that remain hidden even from me throughout the three worlds? Whatever exists in the three worlds, whether moving or stationary, I am situated within it, O fool, just as oil is inherent within sesame seeds. (43)

"Therefore, O Brahman, touch your own head; this is beyond doubt. As soon as Brahmā, things having thus transpired, touched his head with his hand, there stood manifest before him the one who has the bull as his vehicle, in that very form.
Then, O twice-born ones, his body overwhelmed with shame, he stood with his face cast downwards, surrounded on all sides by Indra and all the other immortals.
Then, overcome with shame, he prostrated before Maheśvara and, having offered praise, said: "Forgive me, forgive me! || 46 ||
O Lord, tell me the expiation for the purification of this sin, and the punishment according to justice, by which my sin may pass away. (47)
The Blessed Lord said: "Therefore, with this very form situated upon your head, perform penance while established in meditative concentration and intent upon my worship."
It shall become renowned everywhere on earth by the name Rudraśiras; it is the performer of all rites for the twice-born who possess splendor. (49)
"Since this deed of mortals has now been performed by you, therefore, having become a mortal, you shall wander upon the surface of the earth. (50)
But whoever, seeing you in this form, shall ask: "What is this, O Blessed One, Tripurantaka, upon the head of Brahmā? (51)
Furthermore, whoever hears all of their deeds out of curiosity shall attain liberation from the sin committed through another's wife.
To the extent that people shall proclaim this deed of yours, to that same extent shall your purification from this sin come to pass. (53)
O Brahmin, this alone is proclaimed as your atonement: that which causes people to laugh in the world and brings you supreme reproach. (54)
Moreover, this semen of yours, which has fallen into the middle of the sacrificial altar, was seen by me while you were afflicted by desire; it shall not be in vain.
To whatever extent this place is touched by the dust of its sands, to that same extent shall there be sages of firm vows.
Those known as the Vālakhilyas were all the size of a thumb; endowed with the power of asceticism, they were capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.
In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, at that very moment, eighty-eight thousand sages of purified souls, each the size of a thumb, emerged from the center of that sacrificial altar.
Then, having prostrated themselves, they spoke loudly to the god Pitāmaha: "O Father, show us a place for the sake of penance that is free from the Kali age."
The Grandfather said: "O sons, perform penance in this sacred field together with me; by this, you shall attain the supreme perfection that is very difficult to obtain in this world. (60)
Having agreed, saying "So be it," and having established a beautiful hermitage there, the Vālakhilyas performed austerities and attained supreme perfection.
Then Brahmā also brought all those marriage rites to completion in due order, as they had been prescribed by him himself in the Śruti.
As showers of flowers fell from all sides from the courtyard of the sky, while musical instruments were being played and songs were being sung; (63)
While the foremost of the Brahmins were reciting and Rambhā and other celestial women were dancing with passion, it was enchanting to the eyes and minds of the gods.
Thus a great festival arose, with songs being sung by Tumburu and others, just as they had been performed of old in the celestial realm.
Then, at the conclusion of the ritual, the Blessed Lord, the Destroyer of Tripura, spoke with devotion to the Lotus-born Brahmā: "What sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall I give to you?"
"O best of gods, even if the marriage rite should be very difficult to obtain, speak quickly, O illustrious one; there is nothing that I cannot give. (67)
The Grandfather said: "O Lord of the Gods, you must always remain here upon this altar in this very form for the purification of the sins of men. (68)
O Moon-crested One, by staying in your presence, I shall perform the most intense penance in my own hermitage for the destruction of this great sin. (69)

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the constellation presided over by Bhaga, if a person with devotion gazes [upon it] on a Sunday, at that very moment his sins shall go to utter destruction.

Any woman who is unfortunate, barren, one-eyed, or devoid of beauty—even she shall assume a beautiful form simply by the sight of you; she will become blessed with offspring, enriched with great enjoyments, and fortunate—of this there is no doubt. (71)
Maheśvara said: "For the welfare of all the worlds, I shall remain established upon this altar together with my wife, O Creator, because of your truthful word."
Sūta said: Thus that Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, remains there together with his wife in the middle of the altar, the destroyer of the sins of the worlds.
O twice-born ones, all this has been narrated to you regarding how the marriage of Vṛṣanātha formerly took place during the era of Svāyambhuva Manu.

Whoever, when the time for marriage has arrived or at its commencement, listens to this narrative with an undistracted mind after worshipping the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), for him every matrimonial rite shall be free from obstacles. (79)
And the daughter shall be endowed with happiness, good fortune, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities; likewise, she shall be a mother of sons, chaste, and devoted to her husband.
The sages said: O Sūta, in which place there did Brahmā perform his penance, along with all those Vālakhilyas and the sages of celebrated vows? || 1 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, on the northwestern side of that Haravedī, Brahmā performed penance with perfect faith and effort.

In the west, there were the Vālakhilyas, devoted to recitation and ritual bathing; O best of Brahmins, I shall now relate to you that wonder which occurred there formerly in the hermitage of the Four-faced One.
There, a certain woman of ill-conduct born of a Brāhmaṇa lineage would always take pleasure with her lover Devadatta at night.
Unknown to her husband, her mother, and other relatives, she approached the dark fortnight with a joyful heart in a secluded place.
Then, after some time, O twice-born ones, she was seen by someone staying there in the company of her lover, and she was reported to her own husband.
Then her husband, filled with anger, reviled her with extremely harsh words and struck her with blows.
Then, having summoned her courage yet resorting to her feminine nature, she spoke with eyes filled with tears, standing with her palms joined in a gesture of supplication.
O Lord, why do you strike me—who am free from fault and prostrate at your feet—with cruel blows based on the words of wicked people? (9)
Having made a solemn oath to you, or else having consumed poison, or having entered the sacrificial fire, I shall act so as to provide proof.
Then the brahmin said to her: "If you are free from sin, perform the divine ordeal yourself before the gods and the brahmins."
Having promised "So be it," that virtuous woman, filled with daring, then performed the divine ordeal according to the prescribed rite.
And that evildoer attained purification in the presence of all his kinsmen, the twice-born, his gurus, and even the gods.
In the meantime, a great cry of "Well done! arose for her, while a highly censurable sound of "Fie! was uttered by everyone toward her husband.
"Alas! This wicked and lowest of Brahmins is of sinful conduct, he who would falsely accuse his own sinless lawful wife. (15)
O best of the twice-born, being thus censured by all the world, he then became deeply distressed and directed his anger toward the fire.
Then, deeply distressed, he resolved to utter a curse; censuring him again and again, he spoke these harsh words to Agni.
"I have seen with my own eyes this woman united with a paramour; O Fire, why was this great sinner not reduced to ashes by you? (18)
Therefore, I shall now undoubtedly curse you, a doer of evil deeds who sides with the untruthful, with a terrible curse.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the enraged twice-born man, the seven-rayed one (Agni), terrified with fear, spoke to him with palms joined in reverence.
Agni said: "O Brahmin, this is not my fault that your beloved was not burned; even though I have committed an offense, listen here to my words as they are clearly spoken. (21)
O best of the twice-born, you have learned today that she has been united with her lover for a long time. (22)
But because this [woman] has been purified by me and not burnt, O twice-born one, I shall tell you the reason for that; listen with a focused mind. (23)
O twice-born one, in that very temple where she formed a union with another's beloved, Brahmā remained stationed with the head of Rudra.
Having then engaged in various amorous sports equal to those of another's beloved, she then beheld Rudra stationed upon the head of Brahmā.
Then, she washes her limbs in that pond situated before her; even though she has committed sins, this woman of pure smiles attains purification through that act. (26)
In this place, the Grandfather of the worlds, Brahmā, was formerly free from sin; yet, upon beholding the face of Satī, even he became a doer of evil, afflicted by desire.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, there is not even the slightest fault in me here; this is the power of the Rudraśīrṣa and of the water of that pool.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, take her—who is completely purified and freed from sin—and go home; this which I have spoken is the truth. (29)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Fire-god, that woman who was seen by me suddenly in the company of another's lover—I shall not take her home today, even though she is pure. (30)
Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born, firm in his pure vows, abandoned her and went to his own home; afterwards, the people likewise departed for their homes.
She too, having been abandoned by her husband, was delighted in heart upon learning the greatness of that sacred ford as described by the mouth of Vaiśvānara.
In that very temple, with that same supreme lover, she performed acts of love and immersed herself in the water of the pool.
Then others, being exceedingly steadfast out of fear of the next world, turned their faces away from the wives of others; and women likewise were devoted to their husbands.
Having approached from afar, they all gathered in that temple and celebrated a festival of love known as the Rudraśīrṣa.
Then they immerse themselves in that pool which destroys all sins; by beholding the head of Rudra, they become liberated from evil.
In the meantime, the dharma arising from one's wife was lost among men; thereafter, it arose for women from their own husbands.
O best of the twice-born, whoever sees a woman, even one of noble birth, who is rich in beauty, brings her there and, being greatly delighted, enjoys her company.
Likewise, whatever handsome man a woman sees anywhere, she too brings him there and celebrates the festival of sexual union. (39)
Neither by sin nor by anything performed with deceit is one defiled, whether it be a man or a woman, by the power of that sacred ford. (40)
Then, after some time, King Vidūratha was born in the region of Ānarta, and in due course, he reached old age.
He had a wife who was slender, youthful, and possessed of excellent beauty; she was dearer to him than his own life when he had reached the latter stage of his life.
That king, seized by old age, does not dwell in her heart; having arrived at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha), a man enjoys his desired object. || 43 ||
The king, having also learned of her conduct, was overcome with anger; he then went to that most beautiful sacred field.
He quickly filled that pit with heaps of dust, demolished that temple, and then spoke these terrible words.
And whoever shall fill up this pit that has been filled with earth and bury it, and shall again make this temple new once more; || 46 ||
Whatever sin men, deluded by desire, shall commit here, all of that will accrue to him who committed the offense against another's wife. (47)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and taking his beloved with him, that king then departed for his own home with a deeply joyful heart.
Then, perceiving that his beloved had ceased her efforts and was distracted by other thoughts, the king guarded her with great care and did not place any trust in her at all.
On another day, having placed a fine weapon within her braid, that woman of excellent complexion went to his bed for the purpose of killing him.
Then, having shared laughter with him born of his kṣatriya nature, she engaged in amorous play with charming gestures and many amorous expressions.
Then, while the king had fallen under the power of sleep, that beloved of the king took a weapon from her own braid and struck him mercilessly.
Thus was born for him that terrible fruit, arising immediately from the destruction of the sacred ford—an act censured by all the world—of the lord of Ānarta.
Even today, O best of the twice-born, that Lord of Gods, Rudraśīrṣa, remains there; for fear of breaking the linga, he was not shattered by him.
He who, having stood before it on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having worshipped with garlands and other offerings, should recite the Rudraśiras while pure; || 55 ||
And by the power of that Lord, one obtains their desire quickly, provided they stand before Him and recite [the mantra] up to one hundred and eight times.
Without a doubt, that man who recites it before him even once, O twice-born one, attains the supreme goal; indeed, he becomes Rudra himself. || 57 ||
O best of the twice-born, one is constantly liberated from the sin committed during the day; all this concerning the origin of the Rudraśīrṣa has been narrated to you.

This majesty of the Rudraśīrṣa brings about the immediate destruction of all sins; it is indeed the supreme auspiciousness, bestowing long life and increasing fame. Therefore, it should be heard with great reverence. (59)
Sūta said: To the south of that very place, there is a highly renowned Liṅga established by the Vālakhilyas, which destroys all sins. || 1 ||
Having propitiated him in the past, those [gods], filled with indignation toward Śakra, generated the bird Garuḍa, who is here renowned as the vehicle of Viṣṇu.
The sages said: O son of a Sūta, how did the anger of those Vālakhilyas arise toward Śakra, and how was Garuḍa born?
Sūta said: In ancient times, the Prajāpati Dakṣa performed a sacrifice according to the prescribed rites in that most beautiful field, providing complete and excellent sacrificial fees.
Then Śakra and the other gods were invited by Dakṣa for the sake of assistance, as were the sages and the stainless royal seers.
Likewise, there were Brahmins learned in the Vedas and skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites, as well as those in the householder stage of life and those dwelling in the forest.

Then those sages known as the Vālakhilyas, firm in their vows, took up a single fuel-stick for the sake of assisting Prajāpati; yet, burdened by its weight, they set out for that sacrificial enclosure filled with distress.
Then, on the path of them all, there appeared a puddle the size of a cow's hoofprint, filled with water, appearing at the arrival of an unseasonable cloud.
Then, desiring to cross over and being distressed as they wandered here and there, exhausted by the labor of carrying their sacrificial fuel, they were beheld by the King of the Gods.

While traveling along that path toward the sacrifice of the Prajāpati Dakṣa, he looked back for a long time, and then, having smiled out of curiosity, he proceeded on, overstepping [the way] and intoxicated with the pride of his own sovereignty.
Then, filled with anger after witnessing their defeat at the hands of Śakra, they returned to their own hermitage and held a firm and decisive consultation.
