"Since this wicked one has surpassed us all by attaining the station of Śakra, he must therefore be cast down from that true state."
Another Śakra must be fashioned, born from the power of mantras, by means of the great sūktas of the Atharvaveda that originate in the rites of sorcery (ābhicārika).

By this [weapon] with which he is struck down, this Śakra—who is intoxicated by pride, endowed with the greatness of his sacrifice, and whose prowess is limited by small intelligence—[shall be slain]. (14)
Then, having become pure, they diligently offered oblations into the fire day and night with the Skanda-sūkta and the Kṣurikā-mantra.
O best of the twice-born, [one should perform this] with the Garbhopaniṣad, the Nīlarudras, the optional Rudraśīrṣa, and together with the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Having placed a water-pot filled with water in the center of the mandala, they performed a ritual touch there with its auspicious waters at the conclusion of the fire-oblation.
In the meantime, Śakra beheld extremely terrible portents arising on all sides, foreboding his own destruction.
His left arm and eye indeed throb repeatedly; furthermore, he cannot see the tip of his nose, the tip of his tongue, nor his jaw.
He did not see a shadow devoid of a head, nor two suns in the sky, nor Arundhatī, nor Dhruva, nor the footsteps of Viṣṇu.
And Hari, while sleeping, does not see the slow-moving celestial river situated in the sky, nor the dark-limbed woman who constantly holds a weapon.
Seeing those great portents—a woman with disheveled hair, naked, with black teeth, and terrifying—the king of the gods spoke to Bṛhaspati.
Terrified by fear, he asked, "O Guru, what is this? Such very great portents and various ill omens are indeed arising. (23)
"O wise one, tell me now: what will be my destruction? Is it that of the sovereignty over the three worlds, or rather that of my wealth and such? (24)
Bṛhaspati said: "Those great ṛṣis, the Vālakhilyas, who were standing on the path like a cow’s footprint, wishing to cross over, were transgressed by you while you were intoxicated with pride. (25)
O Lord of Śacī, although it was not performed by them, the fire-oblation has been completed with those very Atharvaṇa mantras, and the water-pot has been consecrated.
For your utter destruction, Hari, the supreme leader of all the gods, will appear through the Atharvan mantras; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of his, the thousand-eyed one, overcome with fear, approached Dakṣa and, with a dejected face, spoke immediately thereafter.
O Prajāpati, for the sake of our destruction, the sages known as the Vālakhilyas have properly undertaken an effort directed against Śakra or someone else. (29)
Go there yourself and restrain them before another [rival] is born; for Śakra has come for the purpose of destroying us, and there is nothing they cannot accomplish. (30)
Then Dakṣa, having gone quickly surrounded by Śakra and the other immortals, spoke this to them with a smile, endowed with humility: || 31 ||
"O Brahmins, what is this great and most terrible deed being performed, by which all these three worlds that are established have been thrown into such turmoil? (32)
Then, seeing Dakṣa arrive at their own abode, they quickly went out to meet him, holding vessels for the arghya offering in their hands.
Having offered the *arghya* according to the rule and performed worship with devotion, they bowed down and said, "Welcome to you, O Prajāpati! (34)
"Let an order be given quickly as to the purpose for which you have come here; we shall do what is pleasing to you, even at the cost of our own lives. (35)
Dakṣa said: "This most terrible deed, which brings fear to all the gods, must be abandoned by you without agitation; it is for this purpose that I have come here."
The sages said: "We had come to your sacrifice with great devotion by the command of Śakra; yet, out of an excess of pride, he insulted us, laughing at us again and again. (37)
For the sake of destroying Śakra, we have begun, through fierce mantras of power, to create another Śakra; and we have reached the conclusion of the fire-oblation. || 38 ||
How then is the potency of mantras rendered fruitless? Alas! This is especially so regarding that which is declared in the Vedas; therefore, O Lord, explain this to me. (39)
If you alone were indeed capable of acting otherwise, then do so yourself, O Lord; for we possess no such power. (40)
Dakṣa said: "O highly fortunate ones, what you have proclaimed is true; the power arising from Vedic mantras cannot be made otherwise. (41)
Thus, this oblation which has been performed by you with focused minds according to the Vedic mantras for the sake of the King of the Gods, as well as the consecrated water-pot; || 42 ||
By my word, this king shall become the sovereign of the birds, endowed with splendor and heroism, and possessing even greater valor than Śakra.
"By my word, this king of the gods must be forgiven for that which was done by him through his deluded nature and whatever he has thus performed. (44)
Having spoken thus, Dakṣa then revealed himself to them as the thousand-eyed one, who stood bowed in humility and overcome with fear.
Seeing the thousand-eyed one trembling with palms joined in reverence, they said: "O Śakra, do not commit an offense against the Brahmins."

Furthermore, if you desire sovereignty over the dwellers of heaven, then even a dull-witted, foolish, or ritual-deficient twice-born man must never be disregarded by the wise who aspire to both worlds. (47)
Indra said: "Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, whatever ill deed has been committed by me, that must be forgiven by all the twice-born, especially at the word of Dakṣa. (48)
"Choose a boon from us that always dwells in your heart; I shall grant it without a doubt, for there is nothing that I cannot give. (49)
The sages said: "May whatever is desired in the heart be attained by that man who, endowed with faith, performs a fire-sacrifice (homa) in this pool after having worshipped this Linga. (50)
Indra said: "Whoever, having worshipped this Liṅga here, shall perform a fire-oblation (homa) in this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), shall indeed immediately obtain his desired object made fruitful. (51)
Or, even one free from desire, having fully worshipped this auspicious liṅga, shall attain supreme perfection, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (52)
Sūta said: Having thus spoken to the Vālakhilyas, the lords of sages, the thousand-eyed Indra mounted Airāvata and then departed for the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
O best of the twice-born, Dakṣa also performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites, with those Vālakhilyas seated nearby, full of joy.

Now follows the future account of the majesty of the one named Suparṇa. The sages said: "As for that which was stated by you—that Garuḍa, endowed with splendor and heroism, was born from the sacrificial rite of the sages—" || 1 ||
Tell us in detail how he was born there; for such is the traditional report heard: that he was born from Vinatā.
Sūta said: That water-pot which had been consecrated with the Atharvaṇa mantras—those mantras [recited] by the Vālakhilyas who were filled with great indignation—[was brought forth]. || 3 ||
When the lord of birds had been pointed out by Dakṣa while being warded off, Kaśyapa took the jar and departed for his home.
Then, greatly rejoiced, he spoke to his own beloved Vinatā: "O blessed lady, drink this most excellent water, purified by mantras."
By this [rite], you shall give birth to a son who is stronger than the thousand-eyed Indra, radiant, illustrious, and invincible by all the Dānavas.
Having heard those words of his, that woman of beautiful hips drank that water at that very moment; she then immediately conceived a child.
Thus, by drinking that water, Garuḍa was born from Kaśyapa, endowed with fiery vigor and bringing fear to all serpents.
By him, who was filled with devotion to his mother, the nectar was taken away through his prowess after overcoming Purandara, and it was presented to the serpents.
He who was born as the beloved of Viṣṇu and attained the state of being his vehicle, and who always remains stationed at the top of the chariot’s banner.
By that high-souled and wise one, who had previously performed austerities in this very field and whose wings had been lost, the Three-eyed Lord was brought to a state of satisfaction.
By whose favor she attained the status of a partisan, and by the grace of the God of gods, she was further made even more distinguished than before. (12)

The sages said: "How did the two wings of that high-souled Garuḍa grow back? How were they regained by him, and how was Maheśvara pleased? O son of Sūta, tell us this in detail and exactly as it happened. (13)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, in former times there was a Brāhmaṇa named Mitra, a scion of the lineage of the Bhṛgu clan, who was a friend of Garuḍa even from his childhood, O Lord.
In former times, a daughter was born to him named Mādhavī, who was highly esteemed, endowed with beauty and generosity, and marked by all auspicious characteristics.
Neither among the goddesses, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, nor the Pannagas, is there any woman of such great fortune and beauty as that slender-waisted lady.
Then, standing bowed in humility, he spoke to Garuḍa, the lord of birds and his supreme friend, for the sake of obtaining that boon.
"O Lord of Birds, look today for a suitable bridegroom for this daughter of mine, so that I may give her to him. (18)
Garuḍa said: "O best of the twice-born, mount my back and wander over the entire circle of the earth, taking this maiden with you."
"Therefore, you yourself must find for this maiden a husband who is worthy and endowed with good qualities; from this, my friendship with you shall arise. (20)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus by the maiden, that brāhmaṇa immediately mounted the back of Garuḍa for the sake of obtaining the boon.
Whichever young boy of youthful form the brahmin saw, he remained in no way within the range of his mind.
For some, the form is exceedingly fierce and the lineage is not pure; for another, though both lineage and form may be excellent, there is no accumulation of virtues. (23)
Or rather, for him who possesses a multitude of virtues, there is supreme beauty, partiality [toward the virtuous], wealth, and other such excellent characteristics. (24)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, at the end of a thousand years, that lord of birds, the Brahmin, wandered over the surface of the earth for the sake of obtaining a boon.
Then, at one time, those two, wandering here and there and becoming exhausted, arrived at this very field with the desire to see Vāsudeva. (26)
Having beheld Śvetadvīpa as well as the auspicious Badarī, the Ocean of Milk together with Vaikuṇṭha, and another refuge of his; || 27 ||
Then the sage Nārada, born of Brahmā, was seen by them; he was then questioned with conciliatory words regarding Viṣṇu, the eternal Brahman.
"O sage, where does the lotus-eyed Lord reside at present? All the abodes of Viṣṇu have been searched by us both everywhere with great joy, yet that Keśava has not been seen."
Nārada said: In the form of the one reclining upon the waters, he always remains for four months in the sacred field born of Hāṭakeśvara.
Therefore, go there without delay for the sake of seeing him, so that the Wielder of the Discus may come into the sight of both of you.
I too was set out for that very same place in order to see him; and as I was departing, I was joined by you for some divine purpose.
Then those two—the lord of birds and the lord of sages—and that sage, the son of Brahmā, all arrived at the place where Janārdana lay upon the waters.
Then, having seen from afar that great Vaiṣṇava splendor, Garuḍa and the lord of sages, Nārada, spoke to the Brāhmaṇa.
O best of the twice-born, stay right here, even at a distance from this splendor which, accompanied by your son, is like the fire at the end of an aeon. || 35 ||
If you do not succeed, you will turn to ashes like a moth encountering fire, having approached me at nightfall while resorting to a foolish disposition.
By his grace, we have endured this which is otherwise most difficult to bear; it causes no pain to our bodies, nor does it produce any other loathsome effect. (37)
Having thus left that brahmin there at a distance along with his sons, the two of them went to the place where Janārdana was fast asleep in the water.
Intent on divine praise, with their hands joined in añjali at their heads, their entire bodies covered in horripilation and their faces bathed in tears of joy. || 39 ||
Having circumambulated that god Hari three times, they prostrated themselves with eight limbs; and at his feet, they beheld the daughter of the ocean seated there.
Another woman was intent on massaging his feet, her gaze fixed upon the face of Viṣṇu; she was advanced in age and draped in white garments. || 41 ||
Seated nearby, fully intent on perfect meditation, she possessed the radiance of twelve suns; her limbs were slender, yet her body was covered in horripilation.
Then both of them were delighted by Viṣṇu out of joy; they were addressed and questioned regarding the purpose for which they had come together.
Śrī Nārada said: "O Keśava, it is indeed for the sake of the gods' mission that I have come here into your presence; this is why Garuḍa questioned me regarding the Brahmin."
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of sages, is all well with all the inhabitants of heaven? Has no fear arising from the Dānavas befallen Indra?"
Did the gods, together with Indra, receive their sacrificial portions? And was no arrogant Dānava present upon the surface of the earth? (46)

Śrī Nārada said: Now the Earth, having arrived in the presence of the Four-faced One, crying out repeatedly, afflicted by her burden and severely oppressed by the Dānavas, spoke there to the Lotus-born Lord while filled with great sorrow. (47)
Dharaṇī said: That great asura Kālanemi, who was slain by the all-powerful Viṣṇu, has been born as Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena.
Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, Keśin, and another named Pralamba; likewise, there was another most terrible Rākṣasī named Pūtanā. (49)
"By these very Dānavas running hither and thither, as well as by other fierce ones, my suffering is being produced in vain. (50)
Thus born with his arms raised in the world of mortals, the people could not at all contain him above me because of their great number. (51)
O Lord, if you do not quickly effect the removal of this burden, then I shall go to the subterranean realm (rasātala); of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of hers, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, consulted with the gods and sent me to your presence.
The Blessed Lord Janārdana, the God, should be addressed by you with these words: "How may he descend upon the surface of the earth and destroy its burden? (54)
Therefore, O Lord, having taken birth yourself upon the surface of the earth, O All-pervading One, you have come here for this purpose: to destroy the burden of the world.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Sage, having consulted with Brahmā, I shall thus act for the removal of the earth's burden, together with the gods including Indra. (56)
Having spoken thus to Nārada, that bull among sages, Viṣṇu then said to Garuḍa: "For what purpose have you come here? (57)
Śrī Garuḍa said: I have a beloved friend, a Brāhmaṇa born of the lineage of Bhṛgu; he has a lotus-eyed daughter named Mādhavī.
A husband worthy of her has not been found by that high-souled one; therefore, I have been commanded: "O best of the twice-born, if I am esteemed by you, bring a husband for her who is suitable."
Then, for the sake of that boon, I searched the entire earth; yet, for that purpose, no one was found who possessed all the required qualities.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, you are established in my heart; you are a suitable husband for her, endowed with all virtues.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, urged by my words, accept the hand of her who is endowed with exceeding beauty.
The Blessed One said: "O best of the twice-born, bring that lotus-eyed maiden here, so that having seen her myself, I may afterwards do as has been declared."
Garuḍa said: "Out of fear of your splendor alone, I released that maiden along with her father far away; how then can I bring her here?"
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of the twice-born, my splendor there shall not burn her because she is accompanied by her father; therefore, you must bring her here quickly."
Thus addressed by that powerful Viṣṇu, he then honored that maiden and that brahmin, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then that brahmin, having prostrated deeply before Madhusūdana, sat down beside Garuḍa like Lakṣmī herself.
That faultless maiden of excellent form, due to her childhood nature, sat upon a single bed to the right of the enemy of Mura.
Then Lakṣmī, her limbs overcome with anger, having reflected that she was a co-wife, cursed that maiden who had resorted to unrighteousness.
"O sinful woman, since you have cast shame far away and, filled with joy, have mounted my bed in front of my beloved, therefore you shall surely become a deformed horse-faced creature. (13)
When the curse had been thus pronounced by Śrī, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from all those present there, as did the indignation of the twice-born one.
The Brāhmaṇa said: A thousand may be asked for a maiden, yet only one performs the taking of her hand; by mere words alone, she can never become his wife. (19)

As long as it has not been given by the people themselves, with a formal vow, in the presence of the fire and the twice-born, and in the presence of the guru, according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras; || 16 ||
Therefore, O sinful woman, since this rival wife has been made equal to you and freed from those defects, she shall have the face of a horse, while you shall become elephant-faced.

Having spoken thus, that lord of brahmins then said to Keśava: "Hospitality has indeed been rendered to you by your wife in a fitting manner; therefore, I shall go to where such a daughter may be found. (18)
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of the twice-born, you should not feel any distress regarding this matter; for those who have come into my presence, nothing inauspicious ever occurs."
Therefore, she shall not indeed become horse-faced in this birth; take her, go home, and bestow her upon him who desires her.
In a bed, the left side is prescribed for one's wives, while the right side is for kinsmen who are sleeping at that time.
O Brahmin, this daughter of yours, having taken refuge in the abode of Bandhu, shall therefore become my younger sister in another birth.
"If this woman, who bears the face of a horse, was told by my beloved that she had descended to the surface of the earth for some divine purpose," || 23 ||
Therefore, O twice-born one, having performed very great austerities together with her, I shall likewise attain Śubhāsyā and even Lakṣmī.
Having thus gratified that brahmin with his speech, the Blessed One then engaged in various delightful conversations with Garuḍa.
Then, at the conclusion of that conversation, Garuḍa, seeing that aged woman endowed with splendor, spoke to Puruṣottama.
"O best of gods, this woman who stands by your side is unprecedented; she is old. For what purpose is she here? Tell me, O Janārdana, who is she and from where has she come? (27)
The Blessed Lord said: O best of birds, she who is renowned in this world as Vṛddhakanyakā is named Śāṇḍilī; she is all-knowing and devoted to the life of celibacy.
"O Lord of Birds, endowed with the power of asceticism and saluted by all the gods, there is indeed no woman such as this in the three worlds. (29)
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having heard those words of his, the lord of birds laughed and, looking at her for a long time, spoke to Vāsudeva.

Garuḍa said: "It is not surprising that such very great austerity is performed, nor is it surprising that such gifts are bestowed; however, it is truly wonderful how battle is waged in combat by those skilled in war. (31)
O Supreme Person, this celibacy is not surprising nor is it a marvel; yet it is truly wonderful, especially since it is undertaken after reaching the stage of youth. (32)
And especially regarding women in this matter, I have no faith; for one who is in the prime of youth and has entered the state of an animal must necessarily [act thus]. (33)
Indeed, youth must be transformed for the sake of spiritual authority; for if these women do not occasionally obtain a man, [they will fall into corruption].

Afflicted by the arrows of desire, they engaged in sexual union with one another; even toward one who was leprous, diseased, aged, or maimed, they regarded him as the five-arrowed god of love in the absence of a man. (35)
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor is a beautiful-eyed woman ever satiated with men.
These women did not establish such boundaries out of fear of others, except perhaps out of fear of the king or fear of their elders. (37)
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his, Śāṇḍilī, though a celibate student observing a vow of silence, harbored anger in her heart.
In that interval, at that very moment, both wings of that lord of birds were destroyed, and he became a mere torso here.
He was a fierce mass of flesh, free from all diseases, yet unable to move even a single step anywhere. (40)
Sūta said: Having witnessed that behavior of Garuḍa, the lotus-eyed Lord was amazed and reflected: "What is this that has occurred just now? || 1 ||
Even by a blow from a thunderbolt, not even a single hair of his would have fallen; how then did those two wings suddenly fall to the ground? (2)
Surely, by this high-souled one, the censure of women that was made—having gazed upon Śāṇḍilī—has defiled his lifelong celibacy.
By the power of her ascetic merit, her two wings have been brought down; no one else in the three worlds possesses such power.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the one whose banner is Garuḍa, filled with humility for her sake, smiled and sought to propitiate Śāṇḍilī.
The Blessed Lord said: "Indeed, by this [statement], general words have been spoken regarding all women; for what reason, O highly fortunate one, was such a thing done by you?"
Śāṇḍilya said: O Janārdana, O Teacher of the World, having beheld my face, he smiled; yet even by his own will, he uttered this censure of women.
For this reason, O Keśava, this restraint has been placed upon him by me—not through thought, nor through speech, nor through action.
The Blessed Lord said: "Nevertheless, O sinless one, show him favor at my request, if you consider this appropriate, O auspicious lady. (9)
Śāṇḍilī said: "O Lord, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whatever has been meditated upon even by my mind does not turn out otherwise, especially when [the mind] is possessed by anger."
Therefore, at my command, let him propitiate Śaṅkara; for no one else has the power established to grant him the acquisition of a companion.
Or rather, O lotus-eyed one, established in such a form as this, he shall remain in the world; I tell you this truth.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of hers, Janārdana spoke to Garuḍa, who stood there filled with dejection, resembling a mass of ashes.
O best of the twice-born, this alone is the boon for her, who is like unto a human being: that which was spoken by you for the sake of regaining your wings—the propitiation of Śambhu.
Therefore, with a steady mind and without weariness, propitiate the moon-crested God swiftly, day and night.
O Kāśyapa, by the power of that deity, through his majesty, your body shall once again become such as it was, even before long.
Having heard that, Garuḍa, who had swiftly undertaken the Pāśupata vow, installed the Lord Īśāna and then brought him satisfaction.
Then, in his presence, he performed Cāndrāyaṇa, Kṛcchra, Sāntapana, Prājāpatya, and Pārāka penances.
Having bathed at the three periods of the day, he thereafter devoted himself to the ash-bath, reciting the Rudra-śiras, the Rudras, the Nīlarudras, and other such mantras.
Having bathed him according to the prescribed rite, he himself performed worship for him and offered oblations, honors, and gifts in accordance with the injunctions.

Thus, while he remained established in his vow, devoted to recitation and worship, Maheśvara became pleased at the end of a thousand years and said: "I am the giver of boons; choose what you desire, O best of the twice-born. (21)
Garuḍa said: "O Lord, behold my condition brought about by Śāṇḍilī; she has shown partiality toward us, and indeed, I entreat you regarding that."
"O Hara, you must remain right here at this linga forever from now on, provided that you wish to grant my desire; do so without doubt at my word. (23)
The Blessed One said: "From this day forward, my residence shall be here in this linga; and you, endowed with that same form, shall possess especially great strength and speed."
"You shall become so, O bird, there is no doubt, through my grace. Having spoken thus to him, the Lord then personally touched him with his hand.
Then, at that very moment, beautiful wings grew upon him, as well as divine feathers resembling gold.
Then, having bowed to that god, the bird, being greatly delighted, departed for his own abode after taking leave of Maheśvara.
At his word, Lord Hara also always made his full residence in that linga whenever the three junctions of the day arrived.
If one should renounce one's life through yoga at that holy shrine after performing the fast unto death (prāyopaveśana), one is not born again. || 29 ||
Even one of evil conduct, or a follower of the Kaula path, or even one who is merciless; whether a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or even a killer of an embryo—(30)
He who worships three times a day with a mind purified by faith shall dwell for a year in the world of Śiva and be glorified there. || 31 ||
Or else, O twice-born ones, that man who beholds it with great devotion for even a moment on a Monday, [obtains the merit] for as long as a year.
That man also goes, without a doubt, to the abode of Śiva, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and served by hosts of apsarases.
Therefore, with every effort, and especially in the Kali age, the god named Suparṇa should indeed be visited by those endowed with faith.

Likewise, those who have resorted to the practice of fasting unto death (prāyopaveśana) at its conclusion should renounce even their vital breaths; desiring the proximity of Śiva, this which I have spoken is the truth. (35)
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, I shall relate to you that wonder which occurred there in the past, as it has been recounted in the Purāṇa.
In former times, there was a protector of the earth named Veṇu, born of the Solar dynasty; he was always joined with evil, dull-witted, and tormented by lust. || 2 ||
Edicts were issued by high-souled Brahmins, but those were completely seized by other tigers among kings. (3)
Many women were destroyed, and widows especially so.
And there were beautiful maidens born of their own lineage. || 4 ||
That evildoer does not permit the worship or the adoration of the deities; nor does he perform sacrifice, nor oblation, nor the private recitation of sacred texts.
Then he spoke to all the people: "Worship me always; there is no one superior to me, whether a god or even a brahmin. (6)
When I am pleased, whatever resides in the hearts of all—whether auspicious or inauspicious—shall undoubtedly be fulfilled in these worlds.
By him was committed the slaughter of those who were unarmed and trusting; men who had sought refuge were abandoned and left overwhelmed by fear.
Having seen the great battle and the hosts of enemies arrayed before him, he fled, abandoning the duty of a warrior solely for the sake of preserving his life. (9)
The non-thieves were seized, while the thieves were always protected; the virtuous were constantly tormented by him as he confiscated their wealth.
No vow was performed by him with a mind purified by faith; nothing was given to the Brahmins, nor was any sacrifice ever offered. (11)
Thus, O virtuous twice-born ones, for that king who was constantly addicted to evil, there arose a severe case of leprosy as well as the extinction of his lineage.
Thereafter, when he was seized by disease and deprived of sons and grandsons, his kinsmen arrived suddenly and seized the kingdom. (13)
And they banished him from that country on foot, alone and abandoned by all his circles of friends.
He too was abandoned by everyone, even by his own wives, because of that sinful deed, as they recalled his former conduct.
Then, wandering alone and fallen into a state of misery, utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst, he arrived at this very field. (16)
Then, having reached the palace known as Suparṇa, he arrived there only to find that he had been abandoned; at that moment, he gave up his life through fasting.
Then, having assumed a divine body and ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he went to the world of Śiva, which is difficult to attain even for the righteous.
Served by celestial nymphs, praised by kinnaras, and sung to by gandharvas, he remained at the side of Śiva.

Then, seeing him in her presence, Gaurī asked with respect: "O Lord, who is this virtuous man who has arrived at your abode? What deed was performed by him that he has come here bearing such splendor? (20)
The Blessed Lord said: This lord of the earth, known by the name Veṇu, was always of sinful conduct; he was afflicted with leprosy upon the surface of the earth. (21)
Abandoned by his own wives and overcome by a host of enemies, he arrived at the palace of the one named Suparṇa while wandering about.
Exhausted by fasting, he was abandoned by all his vital breaths in that auspicious sanctuary where my presence resides.

It is by its power that I have arrived here; this which I have spoken is the truth. Furthermore, anyone else who, having undertaken a fast, should there relinquish their life-breaths [shall attain the same].
O lady of excellent complexion, he shall attain a prosperity that surpasses all else—namely, those hosts whom you see standing by my side, O Goddess. (25)

O Goddess, all of them performed the vow of fasting unto death there. Even the insects, moths, beasts, birds, and wild animals that were released from that palace go to my presence when they lose their lives. (26)
Sūta said: Having heard those words spoken by Lord Śambhu, Pārvatī, her heart filled with wonder, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (27).
From that time forward, men in this world who desired liberation came from afar and surrendered their very lives there.
Having undertaken the vow of fasting unto death, even those devoted to sin, when endowed with supreme faith, attain the highest perfection.
All this has been narrated to you, which destroys all sins—the majesty of the one named Suparṇa, as I heard it from my own father. (30)

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the One Named Suparṇā," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya of the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 83 ||
The sages said: "That which has been spoken by you regarding Viṣṇu, the God of gods—concerning his obtaining Mādhavī as his sister when she had arrived at another birth—" (1)

"I shall make her horse-faced with a most beautiful countenance through ascetic penance. How was she fashioned by him, and how was that penance performed? Tell us everything in detail, for our curiosity is great. (2)
Sūta said: Having heard that message from Nārada concerning the gods, Viṣṇu went together with the deities and held a consultation to reach a decision.
Then, at the end of the Dvāpara age, the glorious Hari was born in the house of Vasudeva for the purpose of removing the burden [of the earth] and for the slaying of the Dānavas.
The Lord, the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas, was born from the womb of Devakī; likewise, he had another wife named Rohiṇī.
From her was born the powerful Balabhadra, named Hali; and the third was she named Suprabhā, who was dear to Vasudeva.

In her, that Mādhavī was born, assuming the form of a horse-faced being. Seeing that daughter born with such a deformed appearance, Suprabhā, accompanied by Vāsudeva, fell into a state of extreme despondency.
Then all those Yādavas, having performed rites for peace and prosperity, spoke in great alarm, "May there be well-being, may there be well-being! May it be so within this family of ours."
Thus, although she was endowed with youth and yet possessed by such suffering, no one chose her as a bride upon beholding that horse-faced woman.
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu, having learned that his sister was in such a state, as well as her mother and father who were likewise overwhelmed with grief; ||| 10 ||
Taking her with him, he then departed quickly accompanied by Baladeva to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara in order to perform penance thereafter.
Devoted to the performance of sacrifice, he fully gratified Brahmā through various vows, gifts, and the propitiation of the brāhmaṇas.
Then, at the end of that year, Brahmā became pleased with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and said, "I am a granter of boons; ask for whatever you desire."
Viṣṇu said: "O Lord, this sister of mine was indeed born with the face of a horse; by your grace, may she possess a beautiful face—this is my desire. (14)
The illustrious Brahmā said: "By my grace, this virtuous woman of auspicious countenance shall become renowned by the name Subhadrā—a mother of heroes and beloved of her husband. (15)
O Viṣṇu, whatever man here shall worship her in this form with devotion, together with you and likewise with this wielder of the plow (Balarāma), [he shall attain his desires]. || 16 ||
On the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, by means of perfumes, flowers, and ointments, he too shall obtain whatever resides in his heart; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Keśava, whatever woman has been abandoned by her husband or is barren, if she worships this [deity] on the third day while endowed with devotion, [she shall obtain her desire].
She will be rich with excellent sons, fortunate, and endowed with happiness; she will always possess sovereignty and be graced with all virtues. (19)
Having spoken thus, the four-faced one then ceased; Vāsudeva too, with a joyful soul, went to the city of Dvāravatī.
Having taken that large-eyed woman, whose face was like the orb of the moon, and having obtained the permission of the Grandfather (Brahmā), he departed accompanied by Baladeva.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, thus that Mādhavī, afflicted by the curse of Lakṣmī, descended to the surface of the earth, assuming a beautiful form.
The son of Pāṇḍu, the descendant of Pṛthā, married that woman of lovely smiles; from her was born a heroic son, renowned as Abhimanyu.
O best of the twice-born, all this concerning the birth of Mādhavī has been narrated to you in connection with the story of the god named Suparṇa.
And whatever mortal recites this, or listens to it endowed with devotion, that person is liberated from the sin produced on that very day. (25)
The sages said: "We have today heard all that is the fruit arising from the maturation of that curse which was given by Padmā to Mādhavī."
How was it that Kamalā, who had been cursed by that high-souled brāhmaṇa, was born again with an auspicious face instead of having the face of an elephant? || 2 ||
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, by the curse of that brāhmaṇa, at that very moment she was transformed into one with the face of an elephant, causing great amazement.
She was addressed by Hari: "Stay for some time, O auspicious one, in this very form until the end of the Dvāpara age. (4)
Then, O daughter of the ocean, having descended to the surface of the earth, I shall once again perform penance by the power of asceticism for the sake of you, O lady of auspicious countenance.
Then, disregarding those words of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, she, being greatly delighted, performed intense penance for the sake of obtaining a beautiful face and skin.
Having reached this sacred field, she performed her ablutions three times a day and, remaining untiring by day and night, she gratified Brahmā.
Then, at the end of the year, Brahmā, having attained satisfaction, said to her: "O beloved of Keśava, choose a boon; I am pleased with you."
Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, I have been turned into an elephant-faced one by a Brahmin who, being greatly enraged for some reason or other, pronounced a most terrible curse. (9)
Therefore, O Grandfather, make me once again possess that very form; if you have attained satisfaction with me, I choose nothing else.
Brahmā said: "O blessed lady, by my grace your face will undoubtedly become auspicious, especially so; therefore, go to your own home."
"O beautiful one, from this day forward, greatness has been granted to you by me; therefore, your name here shall be Mahālakṣmī. (12)
The man who worships you with devotion, O elephant-faced one, shall become a sovereign lord of elephants upon the earth.
O Goddess, on the second day and thereafter, whoever shall worship you with great devotion while addressing you as Mahālakṣmī and reciting the Śrīsūkta— || 14 ||
"He shall not remain destitute for even seven future births. Having spoken thus, the four-faced one then ceased.
She too, being delighted, went to where Keśava was staying. || 16 ||
Sūta said: Now, there is also another [form] there, the twenty-seventh, the Goddess established by the constellations (nakṣatras), who bestows all that is desired.
O best of Brahmins, in former times Soma indeed married twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa.
Among them, one named Rohiṇī became his beloved; he was always more attached to her than even to his own life, and he remained with her.
Then all those daughters of Dakṣa, tormented by misfortune, attained a state of supreme detachment and remained in this sacred field engaged in ascetic penance.
Having installed the goddess Durgā, they, endowed with supreme faith, worship that sovereign of the gods with offerings, honors, and gifts.
Then, after a long time, she attained satisfaction with them and said, "O daughters, I am well-pleased; I shall grant you a boon."
Therefore, let that which is established in your minds be requested; I shall undoubtedly grant everything that resides in your hearts.
Then they all said: "O Goddess, by your grace, whatever is desired by us exists within the three worlds."
O Caṇḍikā, if you are pleased, grant us that one happiness of a husband which arises from good fortune, setting aside all else.
Due to the fault of our misfortune, we have all fallen into supreme suffering; we are unable by any means to sustain our dear lives within our bodies.
The Goddess said: "From this day forward, by my grace, your good fortune arising from your husband shall undoubtedly result in the dawning of happiness. (11)
Furthermore, any other woman who has been abandoned by her husband, having fasted on the fourteenth day, shall always worship me while staying here with true devotion.
She shall become endowed with good fortune and possessed of sons; for as long as a year, she remains devoted to eating but a single meal a day.
That woman who worships me while abstaining from pungent foods and salt shall experience neither the suffering born of a husband nor misfortune. (14)
When the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina arrives, she who is intent on fasting and worships me at midnight shall indeed always possess exceedingly great good fortune.
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, that goddess ceased speaking; and they all, greatly rejoiced, went to the palace of Dakṣa.

In the meantime, Dakṣa was summoned by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) and addressed: "O Dakṣa, why have you afflicted the Moon with consumption? This was an improper act, since he is your son-in-law. (17)

Dakṣa said: "By me, my daughters—numbering twenty-eight, possessed of unblemished conduct and free from fault—were married off; yet, O Lord, with the exception of Rohiṇī alone, they were abandoned by me despite being repeatedly forbidden."
Then, out of great anger, I afflicted that dull-witted man, who spoke untruths and was under the sway of Kāmadeva, with consumption. (19)
The Blessed Lord said: "From this day forward, He shall move about equally with all of you; by my word, there is no doubt in this matter. This which I have spoken is the truth. (20)
"Even the word spoken by you shall never be false; therefore, this [moon] will undergo waning for one fortnight and waxing for the other. (21)
Dakṣa, having said "So be it" to that, went home; but Candra always looked upon those daughters of Dakṣa with equal regard.

O excellent twice-born ones, as she wanes during one fortnight and waxes during another, that goddess is therefore called Saptaviṃśatikā on earth; she remains established in that sacred field, bestowing all prosperity upon women.
And whoever, having become pure, should recite this with devotion before her on the arrival of the eighth lunar day, shall obtain good fortune.
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, there likewise exists that auspicious sanctuary of Soma, by the mere sight of which a man is liberated from his sins.
When Monday arrives during a lunar eclipse, even a sinful man who beholds it does not see hell.
The sages said: "The abodes of all the gods are seen here; how is it that there is this one unique abode belonging to the Moon?"
"This most wonderful matter remains in our minds regarding the son of the Sūta; therefore, O illustrious one, tell us everything, for you know it in its entirety. (4)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, this entire world is traditionally held to consist of Soma; therefore, when he is established, the three worlds become established.
And all these medicinal herbs, as well as the crops and other plants here on the surface of the earth—all of them consist of Soma, by which living beings subsist.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, having obtained the Soma, the gods beginning with Brahmā attain supreme satisfaction and rejoice in succession; for that reason, he is the most excellent here.
Sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others are likewise established in Soma; for by drinking it, the best of the twice-born attain satisfaction therein.
For this reason, Soma is remembered as superior to all; indeed, he is remembered as the most worthy of worship among both gods and dānavas. || 9 ||
Just as palaces are built for other lords of the gods upon the surface of the earth, so do human beings construct them for the Lord of Night (the Moon). || 10 ||
Those men by whom a temple for the Lord of Night was constructed on earth have attained the state of liberation after having accumulated a store of merit.
The auspicious merit that would be obtained by a thousand palaces of Maheśvara, men obtain that same auspicious merit by means of a single [palace] of Candra.

Then, O best of the twice-born, having learned of the majesty of that palace atop the moon, the gods led by Brahmā, their minds terrified with fear, took refuge on the summit of Mount Meru and spoke these words for the purpose of obstructing it: || 13 ||

When the gentle lunar mansion was present, on a Monday during the month of Saumya (Mārgaśīrṣa), when the lunar day presided over by Soma had arrived, and likewise during a lunar eclipse—at that time, endowed with the five 'sa' sounds, he entered the temple of Soma.
He who, having completed it in a single day, shall establish a palace, obtains the true fruit of a mansion rising above all the gods, like the moon.
He who shall otherwise construct a temple for Candra with a mind purified by perfect faith will obtain a thousandfold [merit]. (16)
Having encountered the extinction of his lineage, he shall go to hell; for this reason, men on earth do not [commit such acts], being afraid of it.
O virtuous twice-born ones, this palace of the Lord of Night (the Moon), which is exceedingly meritorious, is situated right here in the field of the Lord of Night.
That palace was constructed by King Ambarīṣa after he had somehow obtained the opportunity, as prescribed by those who contemplate the scriptures.
To the north of that very place, another second [image] was installed; likewise, Candramas was installed by Dhaṃdhumāra. (20)
And then, O twice-born ones, by the power of that [rite], both those two protectors of the earth attained supreme perfection, which is free from birth and death.
Furthermore, there is another third palace in the Prābhāsika field, which was constructed by King Ikṣvāku, who was endowed with faith.

Indeed, having excluded these three palaces on this surface of the earth, there is no other [palace] belonging to Candra; this which I have spoken is the truth. There is one [other] on the bank of the Narmadā at the meritorious confluence of the Revā and the Ūri.
Thus has this entire supreme majesty of the Moon been narrated to you; it destroys all sins for those who read or even hear it.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Temple of Soma," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, in the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 87 ||
The sages said: O son of Sūta, those four deities whom you have mentioned—Camatkārī, Mahitthā, Mahālakṣmī, and another—[1]
Ambāvṛddhā and Caturthī—these three among them are proclaimed; however, the Caturthī has been described in detail, while Ambāvṛddhā has not.
O son of Sūta, tell me everything regarding her power; by whom was this pilgrimage instituted? Tell me all of it in detail. (3)
Sūta said: This Ambā, the ancient sovereign of the gods, is the power consisting of asceticism (tapas). Listen to me as I relate everything concerning how she was previously established here.
When this city was founded by King Camatkāra, then, for its protection, these four deities were created by that pure-souled king with the approval of the twice-born.
Then that monarch had a daughter named Ambā, and another known as Vṛddhā, both endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility.
O best of the twice-born, both of them were married by the King of Kāśī according to the rites prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, in the presence of the gods, the brahmins, and the sacred fire.
Then, after some time, a great battle took place between the king of Kāśī, the lord of the earth, and those Kālayavanas.
Then, in that battle, the powerful King of Kāśī was slain by those fierce beings who had obtained boons from Hara, along with his servants, troops, and mounts.
Then both the mother and the aged woman, having encountered the sorrow-bringing state of widowhood, went to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, which bestows all that is desired.
Thereafter, they exerted themselves in the worship of the Goddess and undertook auspicious vows for the purpose of destroying their husband's enemies.
Even after a full hundred years had passed, the Queen of the Gods was not satisfied; thereupon, having attained detachment, they both desired the destruction of their own bodies.
The Brahmins, having repeatedly cut their own flesh with Atharvan mantras originating from the Kṣurikā-sūkta, purified it with mantras out of devotion.
Then, having performed the fire-oblation in the well-kindled sacrificial fire, from that very fire-pit there emerged a woman with four arms and a beautiful countenance.
A woman dressed in white garments, resembling the rising sun, emerged; likewise, another with beautiful eyes and face was like molten gold.
Emerging from that pit, holding a sword and inspiring fear, there was another Śakti of similar form, exceedingly terrible.
"You two have requested a boon; let that which resides in your hearts be asked for, even if it be difficult to obtain. || 17 ||
They both said: "Our beloved husband, the powerful King of Kāśī, has been slain in battle by the enraged Yavanas, led by Kāla. (18)
O two Great Goddesses, by your grace, you must undoubtedly act in such a way that their destruction may come to pass. (19)
Both of us must likewise remain here with reverence; for this task is considered by us both to be for the sake of protecting our own city. (20)
Having heard those words of theirs, both those deities then replied, "So be it," and established themselves in that sacrificial pit.
In the meantime, from that sacrificial pit, there emerged hundreds of thousands—indeed, beyond count—the Mothers of manifold forms.
There, one had the face of an elephant, another likewise the face of a horse; others had the faces of dogs, while still others had the faces of birds and goats. (23)
Others had the bodies of animals with faces born of humans; some had three heads, five heads, and others had ten heads. (24)
Some stand with faces situated in the secret place, others with faces situated in the heart; some stand with faces positioned at the sides, and others with faces turned toward the back.
Some have one hand, some two hands, and others likewise five hands; others have twenty hands, and still others are handless. || 26 ||
Some had many feet, some were footless, and others had but one; likewise, there were others with only half-feet, with faces turned downward, and terrifying to behold.
Some had one eye, some two eyes, and others likewise had three; some were mounted upon elephants, and others were mounted upon horses.
Others are mounted upon bulls, monkeys, lions, goats, tigers, and serpents; likewise, some are mounted on iguanas, horses, and donkeys, while others are seated upon birds.
Riding upon thousands of tortoises, cocks, serpents, and other creatures, some weeping, others singing, still others dancing and laughing, they were intent on playing with one another.

There were many with hair standing erect, with disheveled hair, and with hair on their limbs; likewise, there were those with long hair, those with disheveled hair, and those with hair like that of horses.

Some had short teeth, others had long teeth, and some were terrifying with their large teeth; likewise, there were others with tusks like elephants, and those with iron teeth who brought both fortune and misfortune.
Some had hanging ears, some distorted ears, and others had ears like winnowing baskets; some had spike-like ears, some deformed ears, some many ears, and some possessed beautiful earlobes.
Some were dressed in a single garment, some were naked, and others were clad in many garments; some wore skins as coverings, while others were provided with coverings made of stories.

Terrifying, some held swords in their hands, others arrows, and still others spears; likewise, some held nooses, while others carried javelins and bows; some held tridents and mallets, and others were adorned with holding *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons.
Then, having heard this from them, they all, filled with joy, set out for that place where those Kālayavanas were stationed.
Then, having beheld that army emerging from the Goddess—fierce in form, intense, deformed, and possessing distorted faces—they [were struck with awe]. (37)
With dejected faces and terrified on all sides, they were all being run down and mercilessly devoured by those goddesses.
The kingdom of those evil-minded men, together with its children and the elderly, and accompanied by those women, was utterly devoured by those goddesses.
Having thus expelled that kingdom, all those best of the twice-born, filled with joy, returned once more to their own abode.
Then, having bowed down with great humility to the two of them, they spoke aloud: "Those Yavanas have been slain, O Kṛṣṇas, along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen."
"Thus, that entire great land of theirs has been abandoned. Now, let some food be given for the sake of satisfaction, and furthermore, let some place be pointed out for our residence. (42)
The two goddesses said: "May the embryos of those women who sleep here in the mortal world during the light of the twilight hour quickly become yours. (43)
"Those women who go forth weeping at the crossroads and the triple-junctions—their embryos have been bestowed upon you; enjoy them! (44)
"Of all those who creep about while impure from food remnants, and who sport and sleep [there], their offspring shall indeed be for your nourishment. (45)
That child who is born in the lying-in chamber while food remains uneaten shall be prepared for your meal. (46)
That boy for whom there shall be no keeping of the sixth-night vigil will become food for you; of this there is no doubt. (47)
Or, wherever the fire shall meet its destruction in the maternity chamber, he, assuming the form of a child, will become your food. (48)
The child who stays in that lying-in chamber which is entirely bereft of auspicious things—that one has been assigned to you. (49)
Those children who sleep in the open air during the twilight—all of them have been offered to you for your meal.
If one does not perform an auspicious rite on the anniversary of their birth at the end of the year, that very body of theirs has been assigned to you. (51)
That man who, having performed an oil massage, does not bathe, is offered to you for the sake of food; of this there is no doubt. (52)
Any man who stands as one who has eaten the remnants (ucchiṣṭa), or who is situated in the middle of a crossroads, is to be devoured by all [the goddesses] with an unwavering mind. 53.
Any man who, deluded by lust, approaches a woman in her menses, or sleeps naked, or bathes naked, must be eaten immediately. 54.
He who, being of deluded intellect, bathes facing the south at night, and he who sleeps upon his bed—he too shall be swiftly devoured. (55)
He who voids urine or excrement at night facing north, or during the day facing south, is indeed fit for consumption.
He who, at the onset of night, should consume curd and barley meal, or engage in sexual intercourse with an outcaste woman—he indeed must quickly be eaten [by the dogs]. (57)
Sūta said: Thus addressed by the two of them, those deities then stood surrounding them on all sides with hearts full of joy.
In the meantime, the powerful King Camatkāra constructed for the two of them a palace resembling the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
From that time forward, they remained in that famous and highly prosperous field known as Ambāvṛddha, always intent upon the protection of the city.
That man who, having risen in the morning, beholds their faces, for him no deficiency shall arise for the duration of a year.
Whether one performs worship at the beginning of the Vṛddhi rites or at their conclusion, no flaw whatsoever shall arise for that person on this earth.
And whatever man should perform worship to those two at the time of his journey, having obtained his desired fruit, he shall quickly reach his own home. || 63 ||
Whoever offers an oblation to them on the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight shall obtain his desired objects in this world and a good state of existence after death.
He who, endowed with faith, performs worship on those two days known as Mahānavamī shall always be free from thorns [obstacles].

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Ambāvṛddhā," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, while that host of Mothers remained thus perpetually there, a decline of children occurred in the house after house of the Brāhmaṇas.
Especially among the young people in the excellent city of Camatkāra, all those deities wander about, searching for a vulnerability.
Then all those brahmins, having understood that the destruction of the boys had been brought about by the deities through the emergence of a vulnerability, [proceeded]. || 3 ||
Having approached and diligently honored the elder Ambā, they stood bowed in humility and, tormented by grief, spoke.
For the protection of all the Brahmins, this excellent and enchanting temple has been constructed by you both through the king’s miraculous power.
"Thousands of children are carried off at night by these deities of yours from all sides, having found a vulnerability."
Therefore, let favor be shown to these high-souled brāhmaṇas; otherwise, we shall abandon this city and go elsewhere upon the earth.
Having heard those words of theirs, Ambā was then filled with compassion; she struck the ground with a kick of her foot and thereby created a cave.
Having placed his own sandals upon her, he then spoke to all those deities, who stood with all their limbs bowed in humility.
"These two divine sandals of mine are always to be kept within the cave; they must be served by all [of you], and you must never go outside anywhere. (10)
Whosoever, out of delusion, shall go forth having resorted to greed, she, being deprived of her divine nature, shall become a jackal.
The deities said: "O Great Goddess, who will perform our worship in this place? Or what shall be our food here? Therefore, tell us, O Sovereign of the Gods. (12)
Ambā said: "Having come here, the yogins who contemplate in meditation shall perform worship properly for all [the goddesses], endowed with devotion. (13)
Having first worshipped my two sandals with meat, wine, and other offerings in due order, they shall attain a perfection that is difficult even for the immortals to achieve.
Then, saying "So be it," they remained within the cave, surrounding her auspicious sandals which bestow liberation.
Then, having arrived there, even men who have come from afar, after properly worshipping the sandals and those Mothers, thereafter attain supreme perfection, free from birth and death.
In the meantime, the rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice were lost, as were pilgrimages, vows, restraints, and observances.
And even those Brahmins who are peaceful and always condemn intoxicants with their own hands, they too [are seen] with various kinds of liquors. || 18 ||
Having abandoned all sacrificial rites, they gratify me with meats, and likewise with incense and ointments, honoring the sandals cherished by the Mothers.
In the meantime, all the gods, including Indra, became terrified upon seeing the cessation of sacrificial rites, being overwhelmed by hunger and thirst.
Having approached the Great Lord Maheśvara, they stood bowed down with humility, praising him with various hymns spoken in the Vedas and with the Śatarudriya prayers. || 21 ||
The gods said: "In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, the two sandals are situated there, well-concealed within a cave together with Ambā and the Mothers."
O Lord of Gods, even Brāhmaṇas, through devotion, perform worship with wine and meat; by means of those two, they attain the supreme goal. || 23 ||
"O Lord, all religious rites have now perished here in the world of mortals; our very existence has come to an end, deprived as we are of our share of the sacrifice. (24)
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, act so that there may be an end to our sandals; let sacrifices flourish upon the earth, and let us have supreme joy. (25)
The Blessed Lord said: That power who is renowned as Ambā is the Supreme Goddess; she is the Mother of the Universe, imperishable, and she is also my own mother.
Therefore, O illustrious ones, how could anyone be able to bring about its destruction, even with their mind, let alone by means of sandals? (27)
However, O lords of the gods, I shall provide a means for your happiness there, by which greatness shall arise for you both and for the sandals.
Having spoken thus, the god Maheśvara then performed meditation, withdrawing the eight-petaled lotus with its pericarp situated within his heart.
Within that [lotus], he beheld his own auspicious self, seated, measuring only the tip of a thumb, subtle, and possessing the brilliance of twelve suns.
As he was meditating in this manner, from that third eye there emerged a beautiful, auspicious maiden, white and clad in white garments.
Then, having prostrated before that god Maheśvara, she said to him: "For what purpose, O God, have I been created? Let my command be given. (32)
The Blessed Lord said: "In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, two auspicious sandals are established; perform worship with them for the sake of Śrīmātā, the foremost among the mothers of the worlds."
"He who, having utterly abandoned his own daughter born of your lineage, shall perform worship to her [image], shall become food for his mothers. (34)
You too, through lifelong celibacy and with great devotion, must perform worship to those two; otherwise, you shall meet with destruction.
Those men who, intent on devotion, shall perform your worship, shall be esteemed by the Mothers and shall always be endowed with happiness.
Having spoken thus, he then explained to her, in detail and according to what was appropriate, the path of mantra as well as the specific path of worship.
Then Mahādeva, having bestowed upon them ornaments such as the parasol and other gifts, dismissed all those lords of the gods with due honor.
The maiden said: "O Lord, as you have described, the maidens born of your lineage shall worship these two most beautiful sandals of yours. (39)
"How will my lineage continue through lifelong celibacy from childhood? You ought to explain all of this to me in detail and exactly as it is. (40)
The Blessed Lord said: Whichever maiden you shall address with this entire collection of mantras, she will become perfectly possessed of your own disposition.
And in this manner, O highly fortunate one, all other maidens born in your lineage shall, through the power of the mantra, arise in succession.
Then, having reached that cave where the sandals were located, she performed worship according to the prescribed rules, just as instructed by the Enemy of Tripura.

Sūta said: That man who, with a concentrated mind, performs worship with the sandals using the hand of a maiden born of that lineage, shall obtain happiness in this world and, after death, be endowed with bliss.
Therefore, with every effort, the sandals should be worshipped especially with the hand of a maiden; and that maiden, too, should be honored.
"To men who desire eternal happiness both in this world and in the next, and who are endowed with devotion," Maheśvara spoke thus.
O best of the twice-born, all this majesty arising from the sandals has been narrated to you, along with the account of the illustrious Mother, the goddess Ambā.
And whoever listens to this with devotion on the fourteenth day, being composed in mind, and especially on the eighth day, shall attain the supreme state. || 48 ||

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Holy Mother’s Sandals," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 89 ||
The sages said: "O high-minded one, you have previously mentioned Agnitīrtha and Brahmatīrtha; however, their origin and their greatness have not been told."
Therefore, speak in detail, explaining each one separately; we have not yet reached satiety while listening to the nectar of your words.
Sūta said: In this regard, I shall narrate to you the auspicious story that destroys all sins, which originated at Agnitīrtha and brings about every form of happiness.
In ancient times, there was a king named Pratīpa, born of the lunar dynasty, who was endowed with heroism and proficient in the knowledge of Brahman.
To him were born two sons endowed with all auspicious marks: Devāpi was the first among them, O twice-born ones, and Śaṃtanu was the second.
Then, when that best of kings had turned away and attained the state of Śiva, Devāpi abandoned his kingdom for the sake of asceticism and departed for the forest.
Thereupon, all the ministers swiftly installed Śantanu and his younger brother in their ancestral kingdom.
In the meantime, Śakra, filled with wrath, did not send rain for twelve years while he was ruling that kingdom.
Therefore, the entire world has fallen into hardship, tormented by hunger; everyone has become like Cāmuṇḍā, except for those who have come under the power of death.
Women have been abandoned by their husbands, sons by their own fathers, and likewise mothers by their sons; what then can be said of other worlds?
If, by the turn of fate, anything whatsoever belonging to anyone is seen anywhere—whether the crop be ripe or unripe—it is seized by others through force.
All the trees were withered, as were all the reservoirs of water; even the rivers, including the Gaṅgā and others, remained with only meager amounts of water.
Thus, when the rain has ceased and the path of dharma has likewise perished, this world will be filled with heaps of bones and covered in ashes. (13)
No one performed sacrifices, nor Vedic study, nor observed vows; thus the sky was gazed upon by those distressed by hunger in search of rain.
At that very time, however, the great sage Viśvāmitra, his entire body reduced to nothing but skin and bone, tormented by hunger, wandered here and there.
Wandering from there, he reached a certain desolate village, which was filled on all sides with heaps of bones produced by dead mortals.
Then, while wandering there, he arrived at the dwelling of a Caṇḍāla—a desolate place strewn with cow-bones and enveloped in a foul stench.
Then he saw there a dog that had been dead for a long time, completely dried up and devoid of scent, lying at the edge of the house. (19)
Then, having taken it up and being intent on the duties for times of distress, the sage subsequently washed it in water and then cut it into pieces.
Then, emaciated by hunger, he cooked the very first portion of the food in a well-kindled fire for the sake of a meal.
While he was taking up [the water], satiating the ancestors, and offering it into the fire, the Fire-god abandoned the entire surface of the earth.
Having harbored intense anger in his heart toward Śakra, he immediately vanished from the sight of all the inhabitants of the earth. (22)
In the meantime, when the fire had departed from the mortal world, those remaining on the surface of the earth were especially afflicted.
In the meantime, the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, wandered over the surface of the earth in search of Agni.
Then, as they were wandering about, they beheld a great elephant fallen upon the ground, sighing and tormented by the heat of the fire.
Then the gods, seeing the elephant, asked him with great haste: "O elephant, have you seen that fire here in the forest?"
The elephant said: "The fire has entered this dense thicket of bamboo; having been scorched by it, I have now come here with great difficulty. (27)
Then, having been enveloped by them in that bamboo thicket, the Fire-god emerged afterwards after the gods had bestowed a curse upon the lordly elephant.
"O lowest of elephants, since I have been commanded by you, O god, therefore your tongue shall become reversed in your mouth. (29)
Having thus cursed the elephant, Vaiśvānara quickly vanished once more; and the gods likewise clung to his back, desiring to see him.
Then, while wandering through the great forest, they saw Śuka; they said, "O Śuka! If fire has been seen by you, please inform us."
Śuka said: "O best of gods, this Pippala tree which is seen from afar within the womb of the Śamī—within this Aśvattha tree resides the Fire."
The nest which was mine here, together with my young ones, was completely consumed by his splendor; I have emerged from that calamity with great difficulty.
Having heard that, all those gods immediately surrounded Śamīgarbha; and Pāvaka, having swiftly cursed Śuka, emerged.
"O wicked one, because you have reported me to the gods, therefore, O Śuka, your speech shall no longer be clear. (35)
Having spoken thus, Jātavedas, desiring a vision of the God, went to the field of Hāṭakeśvara belonging to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Having seen a very deep reservoir situated in the northeast direction, he entered it and remained there, concealed.
In the meantime, hundreds of fish, turtles, and frogs were seen there, scorched by the heat of the fire and dead.
Then, a single frog, half-burnt, emerged from that water due to the remainder of its lifespan; it was seen from afar by the gods.
And being asked, O frog, tell us if you have seen the consumer of oblations; for that purpose all the gods, including Indra, have arrived here. (40)
The frog said: "A fire is currently situated within this reservoir of water; because of it, these many aquatic creatures dwelling in the midst of the water have perished. (41)
"O best of gods, our family has met its destruction; I have emerged from this watery refuge with great difficulty."
Having heard that, all those gods surrounded that body of water on every side and stood there; then Agni cursed the frog.
"O foolish frog, since I have been reported to the gods by you, you shall surely become tongueless here upon this earth. (44)
Having spoken thus, the Fire then emerged from that place; at that moment, he was addressed by the high-souled Brahmā himself.
"O Agni, for what reason do you depart upon seeing the gods? You are indeed the primordial mouth through which all of these [gods] are established. (46)
An oblation properly offered into you reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Therefore, you alone abide as the sustainer and the ordainer of the universe; when you are satisfied, the world is maintained, but when you are angry, it shall perish.
All sacrifices, such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, are established in you; furthermore, all living beings live by taking refuge in you. (49)
O Agni, you always move within all living beings; by that very power, you thoroughly digest both food and drink situated within the stomach.
Therefore, show favor to all the inhabitants of heaven; tell us the cause of your anger, because of which you depart, having abandoned us.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the Lord Parameṣṭhin, he bowed to the Lotus-born One and, suppressing his anger out of affection, spoke.
Agni said: "O Lotus-born One, listen to the reason why I, having harbored anger toward Śakra, vanished after abandoning the world. (53)
Due to a drought caused by Mahendra, there was a depletion of medicinal herbs; consequently, I was joined with dog-meat by Viśvāmitra. (54)
For this reason, I did not perish out of desire nor from agitation; I was afraid of eating what should not be eaten—this truth has been spoken by me. (55)
Having heard that, the four-faced one then said to Śakra: "What Agni has said is indeed appropriate; why do you not rain? (56)
Śakra said: "O Grandfather, Śantanu, the lord of the earth, bypassed his elder brother and established himself in the ancestral kingdom of his father and grandfather."
For this reason, O Lord, the rain has been withheld by me. Therefore, tell me what I should do now; you are the authority, O Grandfather. (58)
The Grandfather said: "The sin resulting from that transgression has been incurred by that king; it has been experienced as drought and so forth. Therefore, bring forth rain quickly."
O Lord of the Gods, as long as these three worlds do not perish due to my word, there shall be no destruction even out of season, nor from hunger caused by the failure of crops.
In the meantime, Śakra, filled with haste, commanded the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds to bring rain upon the surface of the earth.
At Śakra’s command, they too instantly filled the entire surface of the earth, roaring and accompanied by lightning.
Then Brahmā spoke again to the Fire-god along with the gods: "O Purifier, become manifest in the Agnihotra sacrifices of the Brahmins. Now, request from me whatever boon you desire."
Agni said: "O Four-faced One, let this sacred reservoir on the surface of the earth become famous by my name; it shall be known as Vahnitīrtha."
O Lord, whoever rises here at dawn, bathes, and endowed with faith, recites the Agni-sūkta and beholds you with reverence—his satisfaction must be swiftly granted by you at my word. (65)
The illustrious Brahmā said: "In this place, whichever twice-born man learned in the Vedas rises early in the morning, bathes, and having recited the Agni-sūkta, shall then gaze upon me;"
O Purifier, he shall obtain the entire fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, and the sins accumulated over many lifetimes shall go to destruction.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the blessed Grandfather ceased; and Pāvaka also remained present within the agnihotra sacrifices of the brahmins.
Thus, the most wonderful Vahni-tīrtha arose there; a man who bathes there in the morning is liberated from all sins. (69)
Agni said: "O Lord of the World, while I remained unsatiated for twelve years, no sacrificial oblation was obtained anywhere among mortals who were overwhelmed by the affliction of hunger."
O Lord, after a long time, sacrifices will once again take place on earth with animals born there, as well as with other things such as grain.
Śrī Brahmā said: O Consumer of Oblations (Agni), whatever Brāhmaṇas dwell here shall always, day and night, gratify you with the offering of the Vasordhārā.
They will satisfy you with true devotion, and through that you shall obtain nourishment; they too shall be endowed with the fulfillment of their heart's desires and their cherished goals.

O Fire, O Anala, at the time of the transition [of the sun], if those who offer the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) should happen to sneeze while you are being invoked with oblations, [the following shall occur].
Whatever sin they have committed, whether knowingly or unknowingly, all of it—from birth until the end of death—shall go to destruction. (75)
When you have attained satisfaction, there will afterwards be a king named Śibi, renowned and born from the lineage of Uśīnara. (76)

Endowed with faith, he will perform a twelve-year sacrificial session (sattra) and shall gratify you for a year by pouring a continuous stream of "wealth" (vasordhārā), day and night, from the mouth of a jar without interruption.
Then, having attained supreme satisfaction, you shall obtain supreme nourishment, being honored upon the surface of the earth by all the best among the knowers of the Vedas. (78)

From this day forward, whatever rite shall take place here—whether for peace (śāntika) or for prosperity (pauṣṭika)—accompanied by the Vasordhārā, all of that will become supremely gratifying to you. (79)
Furthermore, whatever rite pertaining to the Viśvedevas may be performed by the twice-born, if it is devoid of the Vasordhārā, it will become fruitless.
Because it causes that ritual action, such as a sacrifice, to become complete—namely the *śāntika* and *vaiśvadeva* rites—it is here called the *pūrṇāhuti* (the full oblation).
He who, endowed with right faith, shall offer the stream of wealth (vasordhārā), will obtain in its entirety whatever desire he has meditated upon in his mind.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having thus spoken and having himself pacified the enraged Pāvaka, the blessed Grandfather ceased speaking.
Then, together with all the gods, including Śakra, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, he went to the world of Brahmā, and those gods returned to their own abodes.
Pāvaka, who resides within the agnihotra sacrifices of the best of the twice-born, likewise accepted the oblation produced from the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) according to the prescribed rites.
Thus, the unsurpassed Agnitīrtha arose there; bathing there in the morning, a man is liberated from the sins committed during that day.
Then, seeing those gods departing toward their own hermitage, the lordly elephant, the parrot, and the frog spoke to them, filled with sorrow.
"O lords of the gods, we have been cursed by Pāvaka on your account; therefore, let some means also be devised for the sake of our tongues."
The gods said: "O best of elephants, even though your tongue is reversed, it will undoubtedly be capable of performing its function, especially compared to those of others. (7)
Likewise, established in the palaces of kings, you shall eat choice food, endowed with great honor.
And just as your tongue, O Śuka, has been made dull by the consumer of oblations, nevertheless it shall be worthy of praise among the protectors of the earth.
And for the illustrious ones as well as others, by our grace, O frog, because you have been rendered tongueless by that fire, your voice shall travel far even though you are tongueless.
Having spoken thus, those gods then departed for their own abodes, after she had bestowed her favor upon them, filled with supreme compassion.
Sūta said: This majesty of Agnitīrtha has been proclaimed to you; now, O twice-born ones, let the origin of Brahmakuṇḍa be heard.
When Brahmā was established there by the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, a sacrificial pit filled with pure water was then constructed at that spot.
And it has been declared that in the month of Kārttika, when the moon is situated in the asterism Kṛttikā, one should properly perform the Bhīṣma-vrata after bathing here in these auspicious waters.
Whoever thereafter worships the god born from the lotus, even if he is a Śūdra, shall cast off his body and go to the womb of Brahmā.
If even a Brāhmaṇa performs a bath there in that pool after properly observing the Bhīṣma-vow, he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
As the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya was speaking thus, every word of his was heard by a certain cowherd.
Then, impelled by faith, he duly and correctly performed that Bhīṣma-pañcaka when the month of Kārtika had arrived.
Then, on the full moon day during the conjunction with the Kṛttikās, having worshipped the Lotus-born [Brahmā] according to the prescribed rite, Puruṣottama was subsequently worshipped.

Then, through the ripening of time, he passed away and was born in the house of a Brāhmaṇa in this very city, O best of the twice-born; remembering his former birth, endowed with splendor, and bringing great joy to his father and mother.
As he was thus proceeding toward growth in that excellent city, the affection arising from his father and mother remained just as it had been established.
Even when another body arises for him, that twice-born man, established among Śūdras, always makes him endowed with wealth.
And whatever gift of assistance was considered appropriate for him, on another day, that father from his previous birth—a Śūdra—met his death when the exhaustion of his lifespan arrived. (12)
Then, having experienced great sorrow for him, he immediately thereafter performed all the funeral rites with complete devotion.
Then, having observed such behavior of his, he was questioned by his father, mother, sons, and others who were filled with curiosity.
Tell us why you are always so filled with excessive affection for this lowly cowherd, even though he is devoid of desire. (15)
"Do you also perform the funeral rites for him who is dead? Tell us all this, unless it remains a secret. (16)
Having heard those words of theirs, he was somewhat filled with shame and said to them: "Listen, and I shall tell you without any doubt. (17)
"In another body, I was her highly esteemed son; skilled in the work of tending cattle, I was always dearer to her than her own life. (18)
Then, after some time had passed, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya heard the words concerning the origin of Brahmakuṇḍa as they were being proclaimed.
