On the full moon day of Kārttika, during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā nakṣatra, the man who performs the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow and, having conceived perfect faith, shall perform a ritual bath here; || 20 ||
Having seen the god Pitāmaha and having worshipped Janārdana, even a Śūdra shall become a Brāhmaṇa in another birth.
Therefore, having bathed properly there in that auspicious, excellent pool during the month of Kārttika, I have been born as a true twice-born.

"In the lineage of the brahmin-sage Candrodaya, which is renowned on earth, I have maintained an affection for him because I remember our former birth; toward him, even though he is a Śūdra, I always feel a great and unrestrained love. (23)
Therefore, on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation, knowing this, I shall perform with devotion the excellent Pañcaka vow of Bhīṣma.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his, those and other best of the twice-born, endowed with perfect faith, performed the Pañcaka rite for Bhīṣma. || 25 ||
From that time forward, that pool became famous upon the surface of the earth; situated in the northern direction, it is known as Brahmakuṇḍa.
The Brāhmaṇa who indeed always performs his ablutions there becomes a preeminent lord of Brāhmaṇas as he is born again and again. (27)

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Brahmakuṇḍa," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Now there is another very beautiful place there called Gomukha, which was obtained in ancient times from the mouth of a cow and destroys all sins.
O Brahmin, formerly there lived here in Camatkārapura a certain cowherd who was afflicted with leprosy and had become exceedingly emaciated. || 2 ||
Then, after some time, at the hour of midday, Gokula arrived on that path while the moon was conjoined with the constellation Citrā. || 3 ||

On the eleventh lunar day, while the sun was situated in Taurus, she was afflicted by thirst; nevertheless, having approached from afar, she beheld a single blade of grass, intensely blue, and was filled with great joy.
O twice-born ones, as soon as he had swiftly uprooted it with his tusks and began to pull it out, a stream of water issued forth from its base.
Then, having tasted a blade of grass from it, she who was afflicted by thirst drank the very sweet water, which resembled milk, with great confidence and very slowly.
By the force of her drinking that water there on the surface of the earth, a very extensive pit was formed, filled with water.
Then, O best of the twice-born, hundreds of other cows, afflicted by thirst, drank that pure water which was like the essence of nectar.
In whatever manner the cows went there to drink water, that pit increased in size in that very same manner through the contact of their mouths.
Then, when the entire Gokula had become free from thirst, the cowherd, though himself afflicted by thirst, entered that water.
Having washed his limbs and drunk water, as soon as he quickly emerges, he beholds his own body possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns.
Then, filled with wonder, he went to his own home and related the entire account before the people.
Just as a cow might uproot a clump of grass there according to its strength, just as water has flowed out from it, and just as he has plunged into it; || 13 ||
Having seen that, all those men went to that divine water; especially those afflicted by disease, they performed their ablutions with concentrated minds.
And at that very moment, they become liberated from diseases and sins; being free from sin, they immediately go to the abode of the gods.
From that time forward, O best of the twice-born, that holy place became renowned by the name Gomukha, because it was produced on the surface of the earth from Gomukha.
Then, seeing that which bestows heaven upon men without effort, the thousand-eyed Indra became afraid and filled it with dust.
The sages said: "O son of a Sūta, tell us what was that cause ordained by which such water issued forth from that place?"
Sūta said: In this place, in former times, King Ambarīṣa performed penance; overcome by grief for his son, he gratified the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
O best of the twice-born, he had one son, widely renowned and celebrated as Suvarcā, who was born to him when he was advanced in years.
Due to the ripening of past karma, even that child, his son, was afflicted with the disease of leprosy, causing great suffering to his father and mother.
Then, having gone to that field which grants one's desires, the lord of the earth performed great penance for the sake of his son and for the destruction of disease.
Then, having become pleased with him, Janārdana himself granted him a vision and spoke these words with respect: || 23 ||
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; therefore, ask for whatever is desired in your heart. I shall grant you that boon, my son, without a doubt. (24)
The king said: "O Keśava, this son of mine, though but a child, is afflicted by leprosy; he is my beloved. Therefore, bring about the complete destruction of his disease. (25)

The Blessed Lord said: "In former times, there was a king known by the name Meghavāhana; he was devoted to Brahmanas, grateful, and had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures. (26)
Then, after some time, a Brahmin was killed by him; having entered the inner apartments at night, he committed the act of an adulterer.
Then he saw that as soon as the sun had risen at dawn, he had assumed the form of a twice-born brahmin, equipped with a sacred thread.
Then, realizing him to be a Brahmin, he was overcome with remorse and deeply distressed; having gone to the city of Kāśī, he thereafter performed penance with a concentrated mind. || 29 ||
Having entrusted his son with the kingdom and attained supreme detachment, he became self-controlled, restricted in diet, and subsisted on food obtained through alms.
Then, in the course of time, that lord of the earth arrived at the abode of Yama, even though he was free from sin, yet marked by this sign.

"By the very fact that this [suffering] arose from the killing of a Brahmin, even while they were still in their childhood, those men who are seen here on earth afflicted with leprosy have surely committed the slaughter of a Brahmin in another birth. (32)
He who goes to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara and performs a Śrāddha ceremony becomes free from his debt to all his ancestors. || 33 ||
"O King, know this as the truth from me as I speak: leprosy does not arise from anything other than the killing of a Brahmin. (34)
Ambarīṣa said: "For this very purpose, O Lord of the gods, have you been worshipped by me, O Master. When you, the Lord of Devas, are pleased, nothing on earth remains unattainable. (35)
Thus addressed by him, the Blessed One Madhusūdana then, through meditative concentration, called to mind the waters of the Ganges located in Pātāla.
She was meditated upon by that powerful Viṣṇu; having created a subtle opening, she then emerged from it at that very moment.
Then the four-armed Lord spoke these words to Ambarīṣa: "Let your son immerse himself here in the most meritorious waters of the Jāhnavī."
By which one becomes free from leprosy at that very moment; likewise [one is freed] from the sins and minor offenses arising from the murder of a Brahmin. (39)
At that very moment, the king, having summoned his son, bathed him with those waters in the direct presence of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then, O best of the twice-born, as soon as that boy had bathed, he was instantly freed from the disease of leprosy and became radiant like the rising sun.
Then, having bowed down to that god, filled with great joy, he went to his own abode together with his father, O twice-born ones. (42)
When that protector of the earth had departed with his son, Hari instantly filled that opening so that no one would know of it.
For this reason, that water which was previously the remover of all sins has once again been manifested upon the surface of the earth by means of the mouth of a cow.

Even today, one who becomes highly purified on this earth by the touch of its water and performs a bath at sunrise on a Sunday finds that ailments such as goiter and the like are swiftly destroyed here. (49)
There are also most terrible diseases arising from ringworm and scabies, as well as those born of contagion, such as eruptive boils and eczema.
Furthermore, a mortal who, being free from desire, performs a ritual bath there with devotion, goes to the world of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
On the very day that Gaṅgā was brought there by Viṣṇu, the Sun was situated in Taurus and the Moon was in Citrā. || 48 ||

The lunar day was indeed the eleventh (Ekādaśī) of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; and on that very day, a clump of grass was pulled out by the mouth of a cow—such was the specific conjunction established there.
Likewise, if others also obtain water on that day and perform their bath with true devotion, they too shall obtain that same fruit. (50)

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Gomukha Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Likewise, there is another most beautiful iron pillar in that sacred field, which was left behind by Paraśurāma after he had broken his own axe.
O best of the twice-born, upon seeing her, a man who is fully devoted to fasting is indeed liberated from his own sins at that very moment.
The sages said: Why did Paraśurāma break his own axe and fashion that iron staff? And why was it cast away there? (3)
Sūta said: When Rāma, having created a lake and offered libations to his own ancestors, had his anger subsided after bestowing the earth upon the foremost of the twice-born at the sacrifice. || 4 ||
Then, having taken that axe which possessed the brilliance of the sun, he set out joyfully with his heart fixed upon the ocean in order to bathe there.
Then he was addressed by all the sages dwelling in that sacred field, who were ever devoted to tranquility and desired his welfare.
O Rāma, O Rāma, O highly fortunate one! Although you have fulfilled your vow, it is not fitting for you to hold a weapon in your hand. (7)
"By this [hand] being held in your hand, your anger will by no means leave your body; therefore, abandon it."
Having heard those words of theirs, Rāma then, with palms joined in reverence and full of humility, spoke to those best of the twice-born while smiling.
And that axe, O best of Brahmins, was fashioned long ago from indestructible iron produced by the splendor of Rudra by Viśvakarman.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, how could I completely abandon him? || 9 ||
"Even though I am devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, I shall nevertheless depart for another region."
O best of the twice-born, if anyone else should seize this axe when it has been released by me, he shall become my victim. (12)
"I am not able to endure this offense in any way; even against a preeminent Brāhmaṇa, how much less so against any other person? (13)
Nevertheless, O best of the twice-born, there is no peace for you even if this is released, nor even if it is taken by you; therefore, it must be guarded with great effort.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O highly fortunate one, if it is so that you grant [this] for our protection, then quickly break off a portion there, form it into a *piṇḍa*, and offer it to us. (15)
By means of which we all provide protection, having resorted to the supreme barley, and no one at all can seize it even after the passage of time. (16)
Having heard those words of theirs, Rāma, the best among wielders of weapons, fashioned an iron staff and shattered that axe.
Then, standing bowed with humility, that best of the Bhārgavas respectfully entrusted him to the care of the foremost of Brahmins for their protection.
The Brahmins said: "O Rāma, we shall indeed preserve and worship this iron staff produced from your axe. (19)
Just as Skanda’s fame is established here consisting of power, so too, O Rāma, shall yours consist of iron pillars.
But that king who, having been deprived of his kingdom, shall propitiate her, will recover his own kingdom before long and become powerful. (21)
Or whatever twice-born man, for the sake of knowledge, shall always worship her, he, having attained supreme knowledge, will reach omniscience. || 22 ||
"Whether it be a man or a woman who is childless, whoever shall worship this staff of yours, he or she will become possessed of a son. (23)
Whoever, being intent on fasting, shall worship her—especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina—[shall obtain great merit].
He shall always obtain his desired wishes, even those dwelling in his mind. || 24 ||
Having heard this, Rāma then bowed to those very twice-born ones and departed swiftly toward the abode of the ocean.
Then those brahmins constructed an excellent temple for her; having installed her there, they performed worship with concentrated minds.
And from his presence, they obtain exactly those desires residing in their hearts, which would otherwise be difficult even for the gods to attain in a very short time. (27)

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Lohayaṣṭi," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 94 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another [liṅga] there that grants the desires of men according to their place; it was established by King Ajāpāla and is the destroyer of sins.

And on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, the man who indeed worships Ajāpāleśvarī with devotion using incense, flowers, and ointments, attains his desired objects, which are difficult for all human beings to obtain.
By the grace of that Goddess, this which I have spoken is the truth: in former times there was a king named Ajāpāla, who was highly esteemed by the virtuous. (3)
He who acts for the welfare of the whole world like a mother and like a father—having obtained by him that auspicious kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather. (4)
Then the Great-Souled One himself reflected in his mind: "I must perform that deed which has not been done by other kings here on earth, nor will those who come after me ever do it. (5)
This alone is declared to be the supreme duty of kings: the constant protection of their subjects and the establishment of their well-being.
In whatever manner those greedy kings seize me by force, in that very same way, agitation of the mind arises within my heart.
Without elephants, O King, rulers are unable to protect their forces of horses and so forth, and especially their infantry.
Without that [protection], he would be easily accessible even to the lowly; for this reason, kings collect taxes from the people.
Therefore, even without me, as well as by the Nāgas and men, the kingdom must be swiftly governed with its thorns removed through the power of asceticism.
By him, who always delighted the worlds by collecting taxes, [the conduct] of other kings—especially that of the high-souled ones—was surpassed. || 11 ||
Having thus composed his mind, he summoned Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages and his family priest, and then spoke to him with reverence.
O Brahmin, tell me quickly: on this earth, which is the supreme holy site where Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, or Brahmā attains satisfaction in a short time? (13)
O best of brahmins, by that truth I swear to you: I undertook this asceticism for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, not for my own sake. 14.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O tiger among kings, there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) on this earth, all endowed with supernatural power."
Likewise, O King, there are sixty-eight sacred fields upon the earth, in whose presence Maheśvara is ever present.
Likewise, O lord of the earth, all the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others—are pleased; it swiftly bestows supreme perfection upon human beings. (17)
The sacred field of the god Hāṭakeśvara destroys all sins; furthermore, Caṇḍikā attains satisfaction with all the gods as well.

She is quickly propitiated on earth by men endowed with right faith; therefore, having reached that sacred field, O illustrious one, worship that Goddess with faith, and you shall swiftly attain perfection. 19.
Having been addressed thus by him, he then went to that supreme field, installed that goddess, and worshipped her with devotion.
Devoted to the life of celibacy, pure, and dedicated to his vows, he remained self-controlled, restricted in diet, and performed his ablutions three times a day.
Thus propitiated there with perfumes, flowers, and ointments, that goddess then attained satisfaction toward him who was intent on worship.
The Goddess said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child, by virtue of this constant vow and by this performance of the ritual of offerings and worship which you have yourself undertaken."
Therefore, speak, O protector of the earth, so that I may immediately fulfill everything residing in your heart, even that which is difficult for the gods themselves to attain. (24)
The King said: "Desiring the welfare of the worlds, I have undertaken this vow, so that by my grace they may attain unsurpassed happiness. (25)
Therefore, O illustrious lady, grant me in abundance various weapons endowed with knowledge, which may move at will in every direction. (26)
Even those who stand by my side on the surface of the earth know whatever offense has been committed in the world, such as adultery with another's wife and so forth. (27)
Then they inflict upon him a mutual punishment corresponding to that sin, so that there may be no confusion among them.
O Goddess, likewise grant me a diverse collection of mantras by which I may swiftly effect the subjugation of diseases and sentient beings. (29)
By this means, may all men in my kingdom be endowed with happiness—free from disease, possessed of nourishment, and devoid of fear and sorrow. (30)

"O Queen, I shall not carry out the recruitment of elephants, horses, and chariots, for their nourishment would come from wealth, and that wealth would arise from taxes taken from all the people; therefore, that is not my desire. (31)
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the Earth, this most wonderful deed has been undertaken by you, which has never been performed by anyone before, nor will anyone ever perform it. (32)
Nevertheless, I shall act in this way and will give you in their entirety weapons endowed with knowledge and a corresponding collection of mantras.
By this [means], even all those most dreadful diseases are seized; however, they must always be protected by my mantras as well.
If they go far away from your sight, they will afflict human beings, and after a long time, they will obtain even more [suffering] than that.
O protector of the earth, when you depart from this world for heaven, then that which is established here before me shall be placed within these waters. (36)
By my word, all mantras as well as weapons will undoubtedly be restored, so that every worldly activity of the king may proceed as it did before. (37)
Sūta said: "O best of the twice-born, as soon as he had replied, 'So be it,' many divine weapons manifested themselves for him at that very moment."
Whatever [remedies] were employed by that Great-Souled One through his perfection of knowledge, and likewise the spells for diseases which he himself requested—[all these were present]. (39)
And those by whom diseases are seized are always released at their own will; remaining within the range of vision, they are easily protected.
Then, having obtained that entire favor arising from Caṇḍikā, the king gave all of that, including the elephants and other gifts, to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having diligently restrained all those diseases with mantras, he left behind only his own wife and his one son, Daśaratha.
Taking up a staff himself, he later protects those who have the form of goats; such was the conduct of that lord of men as he dwelt upon the earth. (43)
Even a secret offense would not belong to anyone, much less one that is manifest; for if someone in this world of mortals should commit a sin through negligence, [it would not be his]. (44)
A defeat corresponding to that [offense] arises for him at that very moment—either death, or imprisonment, or suffering born from enemies. (45)

Even weapons that have not been seen before manifest themselves at that very moment; and those men, having hidden them in many ways within the kingdoms of other monarchs, cause Vaivasvata to seize their wheel.
One should not commit a sinful act there out of fear; especially so after having directly perceived that danger from weapons. (47)
Then those people, freed from sin and with their bodies completely purified, attained unsurpassed happiness as the diseases were subdued. || 48 ||
While the worlds remained thus, free from sin and disease, all the hells within the abode of Yama became empty.
No man goes to hell, nor does any man enter the path of death; as it was in the Kṛta age, so too did it remain established in the Tretā age.
Then, when worldly activity arising from the realm of Yama had perished, and beings became free from death, they attained a state equal to that of heaven. (51)
Then Vaivasvata, having gone to the abode of Brahmā, bowed down to the Grandfather and spoke, overwhelmed with grief.
"O Lord, in the past, desiring to observe dharma and adharma among human beings, I was appointed by you for the purpose of restraining and favoring them."
O best of gods, King Ajāpāla rendered all that fruitless by propitiating the goddess Caṇḍikā through the power of his asceticism.
O Lord, neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor any evils arise for anyone on that earth, just as it was in the Kṛta Yuga.
Therefore, O best of gods, act once again as before, so that all worldly affairs may take place within my abode. (56)
Having heard those words of his, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, gazed upon the face of Śiva who was seated nearby.
Then, having heard that most extraordinary news concerning Yama, the three-eyed Lord laughed loudly and spoke to the four-faced one: (58)
Maheśvara said: "O King, how is one who has set out upon the path of dharma and possesses virtuous conduct restrained there, and what punishment is meted out?"
Therefore, because that path was shown by that great-souled monarch, an unprecedented path born of dharma was perfectly established by him.
Therefore, O best of gods, I too must act so that his favor may be unprecedented, and yet so that dharma is not violated.
Having spoken thus to the four-faced one, Śiva then said to Yama: "Tell me what remains of the lifespan of this King Ajāpāla, so that when that time has arrived, I may lead him to my own abode."
Yama said: Five thousand years of his lifespan have already passed; fifty-five remain. How then can I wait for him? (63)
O best of gods, as long as your own abode remains empty, you must therefore quickly devise some means for its destruction.
When Yama had spoken thus, he dismissed him toward his home; then, assuming the form of a tiger himself, he went into his presence.
Established there, that king, devoted to the protection of his subjects, roared repeatedly with a sound as deep as a thundercloud.
Seeing that tiger, who bore a fierce form, those goats, terrified, sought refuge with the goat-herd. || 67 ||
Even as that king was guarding them with great effort, those goats were devoured by Śaṅkara in the form of a tiger.
Then, having witnessed that slaughter and being unaware of the situation, that lord of the earth cast away his staff from his hand and seized a sharpened weapon. (69)

The weapon that had been given to him by her out of satisfaction, which was equal to the fierce flame of fire, as well as other weapons bestowed by the Goddess, Maheśvara Śaṅkara gradually grasped with his own mouth.
Then, due to the absence of weapons, even though he was being held back by his beloved, the king engaged that tiger in a duel.
Then, by the touch of her body, he cast off that tiger's skin and assumed a form adorned with the moon and dappled with ashes.
Seeing her, who was divine, wearing a garland of severed heads, holding a khaṭvāṅga staff, and accompanied by serpents, that protector of the earth, together with his wife, then bowed down.
Then, having offered praise, he stood bowed down with humility, his eyes drenched with tears of joy, and spoke with a voice faltering with delight. (74)
The king said: "O Lord, whatever blows were dealt by me to you out of ignorance, as well as the insults offered—O All-pervading One, may all that be forgiven. (75)
The Blessed Lord said: "O son, this entire defeat of yours has been forgiven by me, for I am well-pleased having witnessed your superhuman deed. (76)
O King, just as you have ruled the kingdom and protected the subjects, no other monarch has ever done so, nor will any do so in the future. (77)
Therefore, O best of kings, go with me to Pātāla, together with this very body and with this lawful wife of yours.
Henceforth, you must not remain in the mortal world by any means, since the action arising from you is contrary to all the gods.
The king said: "O Lord, I shall do exactly so; having gone to the great city of Ayodhyā, I will establish my son in the kingdom and inform the ministers. (80)
Thus was I addressed by the Goddess in the past, O King, when she was well-pleased; she bestowed upon me a collection of mantras and various weapons.
O wise one, when you abandon this mortal world so difficult to leave behind, then all [your remains] must be cast entirely here into my pool.
O Lord of the Gods, grant those [gifts] to me once again, so that by your grace I may now attain freedom from debt to that goddess. (83)
Having been addressed thus by him, the Blessed Lord, the Destroyer of Tripura, commanded all those [attendants] and, having gone there quickly, bestowed [the boon].
And there the son himself declared, "He shall become the king, endowed with heroism and generosity, capable of uplifting our lineage. (85)
And you, come with me this very day to my palace; having entered here into the holy water arising from the Devī-kuṇḍa.
Furthermore, whoever on this fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha worships this goddess with devotion while in these waters— || 87 ||
O best of kings, by entering [the fire], he will give up his life and go to where Hāṭakeśvara resides in Pātāla.
O best of kings, that man who shall perform a bath [there] will not suffer from more than one hundred and eight diseases. (89)
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord took the king together with his wife, and with those goats and those weapons, entered that water arising from the Devīkuṇḍa.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he was led to his own temple by that very same human body, accompanied by his wife.
Even today he remains there, free from old age and death, worshipping that god Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla.
Thus, that goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, having manifested there, was installed by that king with a mind purified by faith. (93)

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Ajāpāleśvarī," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya, within the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 95 ||
Sūta said: When King Ajāpāla had thus departed for the netherworld (rasātala), his son became king, honored by his ministers.
He who always goes to heaven and constantly delights Vāsava, by whom Śanaiścara was conquered while he was piercing Rohiṇī.
In whose house Viṣṇu himself, having become fourfold, joyfully took birth for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa. || 3 ||
Having come here to this excellent field, he gratified Madhusūdana; and after constructing a beautiful temple, he then installed [the deity] therein.
He himself also constructed a famous step-well for him, which attained supreme renown in this world as the "Rājavāpī" (the King’s Step-well).
He who performs a śrāddha on that [tithi], especially when the fifth day of the fortnight of the deceased (pretapakṣa) has arrived, shall become dear to the virtuous.
The sages said: "How was the son of Sūrya conquered by him, and how did he pierce the cart of Rohiṇī? Tell us how Nārāyaṇa was propitiated by him. (7)
Sūta said: While that knower of dharma was ruling the earth according to his own duty, the world was always filled with supreme happiness.
The cows yield abundant milk, the crops are full of quality, the rain-god pours down rain according to desire, and the trees bear fruit in their proper seasons.
Then, after some time, the astrologers told that king: "The son of the Sun will cause the destruction of Rohiṇī."
Immediately after that, a famine will swiftly arise; there shall be a terrible twelve-year drought, by which the entire surface of the earth will be deprived of human beings.
Having heard those words of theirs, the king became enraged and set out; mounting his celestial chariot, he proceeded toward Śanaiścara.
In former times, a celestial chariot that travels at will was granted to him by Śakra out of satisfaction; while stationed there, he pursued Śanaiścara.
Then, O King, having left the path of the sun and thereafter the path of the moon, he reached the course of the constellations and strung his great bow.
Having fixed an arrow there, he rushed toward Śanaiścara; standing before him, he spoke to the son of the Sun, who was looking downward.
"O Śanaiścara, leave this path of Rohiṇī immediately at my command; otherwise, I shall send you to the abode of Yama. (16)
By this arrow with its sharpened point and smooth joints, empowered by the mantras of divine weapons—I speak this truth to you. (17)
Having heard those exceedingly fierce and great words of his, Manda was struck with amazement and then spoke as follows: || 18 ||
"Who are you? Tell me, O illustrious one, for you block my path, which is inaccessible to anyone in the world, even to all the gods and asuras. (19)
The king said: "I am a king named Daśaratha, born of the solar dynasty and the son of Aja; I have arrived here out of anger to restrain Kāma."
Maṇḍa said: O lord of the earth, there is no connection whatsoever between you and me, such that you, full of wrath, desire to destroy my path. (21)
The king said: "Indeed, you shall break the cart born of Rohiṇī; this is the statement currently uttered by my astrologers. (22)
"When that [mountain] has been split by you, O dull-witted one, Śatakratu will no longer rain," so say the astrologers who are experts in the science of luminaries (jyotiḥśāstra). || 23 ||
Then, when the cessation of rain occurs, food is no longer produced upon the earth; due to the lack of food, the people on the surface of the earth consequently go to their destruction.

Then, when the destruction of people has occurred, rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others no longer take place upon the surface of the earth; consequently, universal dissolution (saṃkṣaya) shall indeed ensue.
For this reason, O son of the Sun, your path has been obstructed; that you desire to go to Rohiṇī—this which I have spoken is the truth. (26)
Śani said: "Go, my son, to your own home; you are pleasing to me as well. O lord of the earth, I am satisfied by your valor, and not by any other."
This action which has been performed by you was not created by anyone else; nor will anyone else—whether a god or a human—ever perform it. (28)
O protector of the earth, I do not see anything at all above me, since everything that comes within my sight is reduced to ashes by my burning gaze. (29)
As soon as I was born as an infant, I suddenly gazed upon my father's feet; thereupon, I was restrained by my mother.
"O son, you must not look at anything whatsoever under any circumstances, if dharma arising from your mother’s word is authoritative for you. (31)
Therefore, O best of kings, you have performed such a great and most difficult deed for the sake of the subjects, having cast my fear far away. (32)
Therefore, O protector of the earth, for your sake I shall not separate Rohiṇī under any circumstances, even throughout hundreds of other world-ages.
Therefore, choose a boon from us today; it shall be granted, O King, even that which resides within the heart and is difficult for all embodied beings here to attain.
The king said: "When the day arrives for you to receive an oil massage, you must not cause him any pain until the following day."
He who offers you gifts of sesame seeds and likewise gifts of iron, according to his ability each day for the duration of a year, indeed [attains this] through you. (36)
For he must always be protected during times of great hardship and distress, O son of the Sun, even when you are situated in the affliction of your field of vision.
Whoever, when your day has arrived, should properly perform a propitiatory rite with devotion, offering oblations of sesame seeds along with sacrificial fuel-sticks and unbroken grains; || 38 ||
O illustrious one, if you would grant me a boon, you must diligently provide protection for him for seven and a half years. (39)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having thus spoken "So be it," Śanaiścara then ceased speaking at the word of the king.
All this that I was asked by you has been related in great detail—the conversation that took place between the Sun’s son and King Daśaratha when the occasion for the piercing of Rohiṇī had arisen.
Whoever recites this constantly, and especially whoever listens to it, the affliction caused by Śanaiścara shall go to destruction for them. (42)
Sūta said: From that time forward, O twice-born ones, the slow-moving [planet] Mars did not pierce the cart of Rohiṇī, by virtue of the command of that King Daśaratha.
Having heard that account, Śakra was greatly delighted; he approached that king and then spoke to him respectfully.
O Lord of the Earth, this most wonderful deed has been accomplished by you, which cannot even be conceived by another in their mind. (3)
For this very reason, satisfaction has arisen within you today; therefore, accept from me now whatever boon resides in your heart as your desire.
The King said: O best of gods, I pray for eternal and supreme friendship with you in all undertakings, established for the welfare of the world.
Indra said: "So be it, O lord of kings! My friendship with you shall always endure, eternal like that of Vasiṣṭha."
"You must always come to my side in the assembly in the presence of the gods, especially so that our friendship may flourish. (7)
Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed one departed for his abode in the third heaven; the king also returned to his own palace filled with joy.
Having protected the entire world from the fear caused by Śanaiścara, and having attained an unsurpassed renown while being praised by bards, [he departed]. || 9 ||
From that time forward, whenever the time of twilight arrived, he would always perform his evening rites and then proceed to the palace of Śakra.
Having stayed there for a long time, he heard the enchanting song of the Gandharvas and beheld their auspicious dance performed according to the rhythmic measures (tāna) and other technical rules.
Having heard various meaningful stories falling from the mouths of the celestial sages, and having himself recounted them as well, he then proceeds to his own abode.
Having ascended a supreme celestial chariot, resounding with the cries of swans and peacocks, and adorned on all sides with enchanting banners; || 13 ||
Whenever he departs from the abode of Śakra for his own residence, at that very moment, his seat is always consecrated with sprinkling.
At that time, by Śakra’s command, the king did not understand it at all; however, on another day, Nārada, the best of sages, explained to him everything arising from the sprinkling.
He came to the very house of that royal sage to hear his account, under the pretext of a pilgrimage to holy places, in order to increase his enmity.
Having heard what was spoken by Nārada, which was indeed worthy of faith, the king did not take it to heart, reflecting upon his own unrighteousness.
Nevertheless, overcome by curiosity, he went to the abode of Śakra; having stayed there for a long time on another day, he departed.
Standing at a distance from his own seat, he gazed upon that which was unobservable; having reached a certain interior of the house, he was filled with curiosity.
Then, at the command of Śakra, a celestial servant rose up and sprinkled the king’s throne with water.
Seeing that, the king, filled with anger, approached Vāsava and said: "O Śakra, what is this? Why is my throne being sprinkled? (21)
Have I slain brahmins, or have I violated some teaching originating from the brahmins, or have I reviled the brahmins? (22)
Or have I been lost in battle upon seeing the assembled enemies, or have I uttered words of wretchedness with a mind terrified by fear? (23)
Or else, O Śakra, in my kingdom, the weak are oppressed by those who are stronger, or they are robbed by thieves and the like, as well as by deceivers. (24)
Or has some confusion of wombs occurred within my kingdom, or a mixture of castes (*varṇa-saṃkara*) arisen through the abandonment of the prescribed order of ritual? (25)
Or rather, O Lord of the Thirty-three, is anyone who is free from fault ever punished in my kingdom because they have been defamed by the words of a wicked person? (26)
Or whether it be a thief, or a sinner, or one who has committed an offense himself, or another person who is contemptible—does such a person escape by means of bribes? (27)
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, have I perhaps abandoned someone who had come here for refuge, trembling with fear and terrified for his life? (28)
Or on whose back-flesh have I ever eaten anywhere? And especially, O Lord of the Thirty-three, have I ever [eaten the flesh] of a Brahmin? (29)
Or what gift did I give to that high-souled Brahmin such that I later felt regret? Was it given afterwards and then neglected, or was it perhaps disregarded from the start? (30)
Or rather, why is it that in my kingdom the tears of the wretched and the suffering fall everywhere, day and night? (31)
O Lord of the Gods, does my ancestral rite or my domestic ritual fall into neglect, or is it being performed in violation of the prescribed rules? (32)
As for that constant sprinkling of my seat with water which you perform, speak quickly regarding whatever sin has been committed by me. (33)
Indra said: "O great king, no sin exists within your body, nor in your kingdom, your lineage, your household, or especially among your circle of servants. (34)
But listen further, I shall declare what sin will befall you; by that very [sin], the seat itself shall indeed be sprinkled at all times.
O King, for one who is always seized by the ancestral debt, there is no refuge, nor does he attain heaven. (36)
O King, when a man beholds the face of his son, he becomes an object of hatred for the gods and especially for the ancestors.
Then he certainly attains freedom from debt toward his ancestors; yet you, O King, have not attained that freedom from debt which I have described.
By that act, you have constantly performed the ritual sprinkling upon the seats of the ancestors; therefore, strive for the sake of a son, if you desire the supreme goal. (39)
"O King, likewise, one must protect oneself from hell and from the notion of being a 'man'. Having been addressed thus by Śakra, King Daśaratha then—

Overwhelmed by great sorrow and standing with his face cast down in shame, he then took leave of the Thousand-eyed One, went to his own city of Ayodhyā, and quickly entrusted his kingdom to his ministers.
Then he said to them all: "I must now perform penance until my son is obtained; of this there is no doubt."
This kingdom must be protected with diligent effort according to the prescribed rules by you all, at my command, until my return. 43.
The ministers said: "O Great King, this exertion you undertake for the sake of a son is indeed appropriate; for one who is childless, what is the use of a kingdom or wealth? (44)
"We shall provide protection for your kingdom on all sides; you, however, remaining established in tranquility, perform penance for the sake of your son. (45)
Having gone to Kārtikeyapura, where in former times your father performed austerities and obtained the success he desired in his heart. (46)

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Daśaratha’s Exertion in Performing Austerities," within the *Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya* of the *Nāgara-Khaṇḍa*, the sixth part of the *Śrī-Skānda-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 97 ||
Sūta said: Then King Daśaratha, dismissed by those ministers, arrived at the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara filled with joy. || 1 ||
Having arrived there, he then worshipped with true devotion the Goddess who had been established there by his father in the past, after bathing in the auspicious waters of the pool.
Then, having seen other principal sacred sites and having bathed in numerous holy waters and given gifts many times, he [proceeded].
He caused a palace to be built for the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, and there he installed an auspicious image of Viṣṇu.
In front of him, he caused a pond filled with clear water to be constructed, provided with rows of steps and praised by virtuous men.
Then, intent on propitiating the gods, he performed intense and very great penance by means of many methods while subsisting only on water.
Then, when a hundred years had passed, Janārdana was pleased with him, having observed the intense austerity performed by that king.
Having gone to the assembly and taken his place upon the king of birds, he, surrounded by many hosts of gods, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. Even that which is difficult for you to obtain, I shall grant you in its entirety."
The king said: "O Lord, this entire undertaking of penance has been performed by me for the sake of a son; therefore, grant me sons who shall ensure the increase of my lineage. (10)
O Lord of the Gods, everything else remains certainly in my house; whatever prosperity I possess exists solely through your grace. (11)
Viṣṇu said: O King, I myself shall undoubtedly take incarnation in your house, having assumed a fourfold form.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, having gone home for the sake of the gods' work, rule your great ancestral kingdom according to what is right.
Likewise, this pond of pure water which has been constructed by you shall become famous in the world as the Rājavāpī (the King’s Pond). || 14 ||
Having bathed in this [tirtha] with devotion, the man who shall worship it on the arrival of the fifth day, endowed with supreme faith— || 15 ||
Then, O King, as long as he performs the Śrāddha for a year, that sonless man shall indeed obtain sons who cause the increase of his lineage.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished from that place; and the king, with a joyful countenance, returned home.
Then, in a short time, four sons were born to him from his three wives, who became famous throughout the world.
He had a very beautiful and renowned wife named Kauśalyā; from her was born his eldest son, the first-born, known by the name Rāma. (19)
Likewise, he had another wife, the youngest, named Kaikeyī; her son was this famous Bharata.
Likewise, there was another wife named Sumitrā who stood in the middle; from her were born two sons of great strength, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa.
Likewise, there was another maiden of excellent complexion, whom he gave to King Lomapāda, who was childless. (22)
O twice-born ones, having thus attained freedom from his debt to his ancestors, King Daśaratha, having fulfilled his purpose, then departed for heaven.
Thereafter, Rāma became the sovereign emperor (sārvabhauma), by whom the invincible Rāvaṇa, that thorn in the side of the gods, was slain. || 24 ||
By whom Rāmeśvara and Lakṣmaṇeśvara were fashioned here, and by whom the goddess Sītā was likewise established here in embodied form. (25)

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Rājasvāmī and Rājavāpī," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: Regarding that which was spoken by you—that Rāmeśvara was established there by Rāma, and likewise Sītā was established there by him— 1. Regarding that which was spoken by you—that Rāmeśvara was established there by Rāma, and likewise Sītā was established there by him—
And likewise, that refuge was constructed by him for the sake of Lakṣmaṇa; all these words of yours appear to me as being entirely contradictory to this great fact.
"O Sūta, you previously stated that Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and joined by Sītā, arrived at this sacred field and set out for the forest. (3)
Having performed the ancestral rites at Gayāśīrṣa and having encountered Lakṣmaṇa, he set out once more for the forest, filled with rage toward him.
"O son of Sūta, explain all of this and resolve our doubt regarding what you said: that Maheśvara was then manifested here by him."

Sūta said: "In this matter, I have no doubt, yet it remains with you as well. Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall speak of it in its entirety; listen. This sacred field is primordial and never undergoes decay anywhere."
When another day had arrived, that joy of the Raghus then fell into a conflict with the son of Sumitrā.
Furthermore, this day was another one on which Rāmeśvara himself was installed with devotion by that high-souled man who was afflicted with grief.
The sages said: On another day, at what time did that best of the Raghus arrive there? What sorrow befell him? Please narrate that.
Sūta said: Having abandoned Sītā, the lotus-eyed Rāma, terrified by public scandal, thereafter ruled the kingdom.
Having fashioned a golden Sītā as his wife for the successful completion of the sacrifice, that illustrious man did not by any means take another wife.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years, he ruled a kingdom free from all thorns, observing the vow of celibacy.
Then, O twice-born ones, when ten thousand years had passed and the eleventh was reached, a messenger of the gods arrived at the residence of Rāma.
The King of the Gods said to him: "I have been sent into your presence by the King of the Gods; therefore, perform the ritual union with me in a secluded place. (14)
Thus addressed by that messenger at that time, the joy of the Raghus withdrew to a secluded place and thereafter held a consultation.
As that great-souled one sat thus in the place of counsel, because of the vast number of people in his desired assembly, no secret could be maintained.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, the messenger spoke respectfully, laughing even though he was situated in a secluded place amidst a gathering of people.
Just as a snake that has lost its fangs or an elephant deprived of its rut is disregarded by men, so too is a king who lacks authority treated with contempt by his subjects.
O best of the Raghus, this is not my command; I am merely informing you. Furthermore, you ought not to hear even the conversation with Śakra in private. (19)
Having heard those words of his, his eyes bloodshot with anger, he knit his brows into three furrows and then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, if any man should come here out of delusion while I am seated here conversing with him, I shall undoubtedly slay him instantly with my own hand. (21)
If I do not kill him when he has come here within the range of my vision, then may I not attain that supreme destiny which is reached by the righteous. (22)
Knowing this, you must undoubtedly exert yourself with effort, so that no one may be executed by me now at the king's gate. (23)
Having said "So be it," Lakṣmaṇa, who possesses auspicious marks, approached the palace gate and cleared the area of people.
Thereafter, the divine messenger also held counsel with Rāma, as directed by Śakra and likewise by other inhabitants of heaven.
The divine messenger said: "You have descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa; and that wicked, sinful thorn of the three worlds has been slain."
"O illustrious Lord, everything that was to be done has now been accomplished by you; therefore, let the gods, led by Śakra, have a protector."
If this pleases your mind and does not cause you present distress, then show favor to the gods and therefore come quickly, abandoning the heavenly realm for the highly censured world of mortals.
Sūta said: In the meantime, Durvāsas, the best of sages, arrived; overcome by hunger, he then cried out, "Where is he? Where is that best of the Raghus? (29)
Lakṣmaṇa said: "That best of kings is occupied with some matter concerning the affairs of the gods; therefore, O chief of brahmins, wait here for a moment. (30)
Rāma consoled the messenger born of Śakra, showing compassion toward him as he was bowed down in humility. (31)
Durvāsas said: "If that best of the Raghus does not come within my sight quickly, I shall utter a curse and consume his entire lineage; of this there is no doubt. (32)
O Lakṣmaṇa, there exists nothing greater than my own vision; what other task remains for you, O fool, that you boast so? (33)
Hearing that, the sorrowful Lakṣmaṇa reflected in his mind: "Death for me alone would be better than the destruction of the entire lineage. (34)
Having thus made his resolve, he then rushed toward Rāma; prostrating himself on the ground like a staff with palms joined in reverence, he spoke.
"O Lord, Durvāsas, that tiger among sages, stands at your door seeking an audience; overcome by hunger, what shall I do? Please instruct me. (36)
Having heard those words of his, he then spoke to that messenger: "Go and tell the Lord of Gods, without any doubt, in my name: 'I shall come into your presence at the end of the year.'"
Having spoken thus and dismissed that messenger, he then said to Lakṣmaṇa: "O child, quickly usher in that sage Durvāsas."
Then, having taken the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the water for washing the feet (pādya), Lord Rāma, with a joyful heart and surrounded by his ministers, went forward to meet him. (39)
Having offered him the arghya according to the rules and prostrating before him again and again, Rāmadeva then spoke with a voice faltering with joy.
Welcome to you, O best of sages; once again, a very hearty welcome to you! This kingdom, these sons, and this wealth are yours, O Lord. (41)

"O best of sages, having shown me your favor, please accept [this]; I am blessed and graced that you have come to my home—you who are worthy of worship even by the three worlds and a treasury of all asceticism without exception. (42)
The sage said: "O best of the Raghus, having observed the Cāturmāsya vow while fasting, I have arrived at your abode today, hungry for the sake of food. (43)
Therefore, O delighter of the Raghus, quickly grant me food; there is no other reason for this than my having renounced wealth and such things.
Then, standing before him himself, he fed him with various kinds of pure, delicious foods, with a mind purified by faith. (45)
With various kinds of foods to be licked, sucked, chewed, and eaten, as well as with diverse other types of food, he provided for that sage according to his every desire.
Sūta said: Having thus eaten at the desire of Rāma’s palace, that brahmin-sage, after bestowing his blessing, subsequently departed after taking leave of the joy of the Raghus.
Then, after that sage Durvāsas had departed from his presence, Lakṣmaṇa took up his sword and spoke to the divine Rāma.
O Lord, take this sword and quickly strike me down, so that your word may become true and the promise you made long ago be fulfilled.
Then Rāma, after reflecting for a long time upon that vow he had himself made, [approached] the man who had entered nearby for the purpose of slaughter.
Then, with his inner self deeply agitated, he reflected intensely, his eyes clouded with tears and sighing like a serpent.
Seeing him with a dejected face, sighing again and again, the son of Sumitrā, standing bowed in humility, spoke once more.
This indeed is the supreme duty for kings in particular: that their own word be made true and acted upon without hesitation.
Therefore, O Lord, you yourself have declared before me that very celestial messenger, with a loud cry of anger. (9)
O Saumitri, if I were to kill with my own hand anyone who comes here into the presence of my messenger, then I would not be a doer of great evil.
Therefore, O father, I have come here out of fear of the sage Durvāsas; though I was strictly forbidden by you, quickly kill him!
Then, having deliberated for a very long time together with his ministers, as well as with Brāhmaṇas learned in the Dharmaśāstras and others who had mastered the Vedas, the king—
Then Rāma, his face drenched with tears and sighing repeatedly with a faltering voice, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who stood before him bowed in humility. (12)
Go, Lakṣmaṇa; you are released by me to go quickly to another land. For the abandonment or even the killing of the virtuous—both are equal.
I must not see you again under any circumstances, nor should you remain even in this region, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me. (14)
Having heard those words of his and having prostrated himself thereafter, Lakṣmaṇa departed from that city at that very moment.
Even without engaging in conversation with anyone in his own home—whether with his mother, his wife, his son, or a friend—(he remained thus).
Then, having gone to the Sarayū and plunged into its waters, he became pure and sat down on its secluded and auspicious bank.
Then, having assumed the lotus posture and likewise having established himself within the Self, he subsequently emitted that [Self] in the form of light through the aperture of Brahma.
Then, having seen that great splendor moving through the sky, Rāghava was filled with wonder and thought, "What could this be? || 19 ||
Then, O best of the twice-born, at that very moment, the mortal portion was abandoned by that Vaiṣṇava energy consisting of the fourth part.
His body, its splendor departed, quickly fell upon the auspicious sandbank of the Sarayū like a piece of wood or a clod of earth. 21.
Then Rāghava, hearing that Lakṣmaṇa had lost his life and was fallen upon the bank of the river, lamented, deeply afflicted by grief.
Having gone to that place himself, accompanied by his ministers and friends, he beheld Lakṣmaṇa fallen and lamented piteously.
Alas, my child! Why have you departed for heaven, leaving me behind—leaving your most beloved brother, the best of men, who has always remained steadfast in your will?
Even as I was traveling through that great forest from the city, I was followed by you at that time, even though you were being restrained.
Even when the exceedingly powerful rakshasa named Kabandha arrived at the terrible onset of night, I was protected by you along with my wife.
By whom that night-stalker of such a form was slain in battle—Indrajit—he now lies fallen upon the surface of the earth, his life departed.
By whom that fierce Rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā was destroyed even as a mere sport at my command—he stands here in such a state. (28)
Relying upon the strength of whose arms I destroyed the night-stalkers, that very brother of mine now lies fallen here like one who is helpless. || 29 ||
Alas, my child! Where have you gone, abandoning me and your own brother, your eldest, who is as dear to you as your own life? Has your affection for us perhaps vanished somewhere? (30)
Sūta said: Having thus uttered many kinds of lamentations, the descendant of Raghu, together with his mothers, was dejected and overwhelmed by great sorrow.
Then those ministers, seeing that best of the Raghus together with the women, lamenting and distressed, spoke to him.
The ministers said: "O Indra among kings, do not grieve like an ordinary man; rather, perform now those funeral rites for the deceased that ought to be done. (33)
Those of evil intellect grieve for what is lost, dead, or past; but for the wise, O King, that which was lost long ago is simply lost, and the dead are simply dead. (34)
Having spoken thus to him, those ministers then lamented loudly over Lakṣmaṇa’s body, anointing it with sandalwood, uśīra, and saffron.
Having wrapped it with auspicious cloths mixed with camphor, agallochum, and other highly fragrant substances, and having adorned it with beautiful flowers, || 36 ||
Having constructed a very extensive funeral pyre with sandalwood and agalloch wood, they placed his body upon it, facing the southern direction.
In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, a marvel occurred there; listen as I relate it all in its entirety, O brahmins. (38)
Just as they were placing his body upon the funeral pyre and offering it to the consumer of oblations (the fire), the body vanished. || 39 ||
In the meantime, after a shower of flowers, a voice issued forth from the expanse of the sky, making all the directions resound.
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, do not be overcome by grief; it is by no means proper for you to offer fire to him in any way whatsoever. (41)
For one who is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman and has renounced the world, especially for all such yogis, setting fire [to the body] is not appropriate. || 42 ||
"O Rāma, this kinsman of yours has gone to the abode of Brahmā; having emerged from himself through the door of Brahman, he of great renown has departed. (43)

Then those ministers, having heard that voice coming from the sky, said: "O Great King, he who has attained supreme perfection is beyond grief; therefore, O Lord, let us go quickly to our own abode. (44)
Let the affairs of state be considered, as well as those pertaining to the funeral rites; perform what is appropriate out of affection for him, after consulting the most excellent of Brahmins.
Rāma said: "I will not go home now without Lakṣmaṇa; I shall abandon my life here just as I did with that high-souled one."
"This son named Kuśa, who is dear to me, has been given by me; if it pleases you, let him be established in my kingdom. (47)
Having spoken thus, Rāma, desiring then to go to the abode of the gods, reflected once more, remembering his friend Vibhīṣaṇa.
Then, being well-pleased by his great devotion, I granted him an imperishable kingdom in Laṅkā for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. (49)
The race of Rākṣasas is remembered as being exceedingly cruel, especially those nourished by boons who are born here upon this earth. 50.
If that great-souled Vibhīṣaṇa, due to his nature as a Rākṣasa, should enter into hostility with the gods just as Rāvaṇa did; || 51 ||
The gods will subdue him by means of stratagems preceded by conciliation, just as they did with his brother Daśānana, who was a thorn in the side of the three worlds.
"Otherwise my word would become false; therefore, having gone into his presence, I shall give him instruction so that he does not offend the gods. (53)
Likewise, my supreme friend, a second monkey, stands here—the highly fortunate Sugrīva—and another, Jāmbavān. (54)
The son of Vāyu (Hanumān) together with his attendants, accompanied by the son of Vālin, as well as the one named Kumuda, Tāra, and other monkeys too. || 55 ||
Therefore, having conversed with them and having respectfully taken leave of all of them, I shall then go toward my home, having fulfilled my duty to the gods.
Having reflected thus for a long time, he summoned the Puṣpaka chariot; mounting it there, he went swiftly toward the city named Kiṣkindhā.
Then those monkeys, seeing the brilliant radiance arising from the Puṣpaka chariot and realizing that Rāghava had arrived, went quickly to meet him face to face.
Then, having bowed from afar, they fell upon the ground on their knees, repeatedly uttering the cry of "Victory! here and there.
Then, joined by him alone, they entered that great city of Kiṣkindhā, which was adorned on all sides with excellent banners.
Then, having descended from that foremost of celestial chariots, Rāma quickly entered the auspicious palace of Sugrīva, which was adorned on every side.
There, seeing Rāma settled and rested, those monkeys honored him with offerings such as the *arghya* and then questioned him immediately thereafter.
The monkeys said: "O descendant of Raghu, you appear bereft of your usual luster; you are exceedingly emaciated and distressed. Is all well at your home?"
Or has your younger brother Lakṣmaṇa, who is ever devoted to you, not been seen by you today standing near you, O Rāghava? (64)
Likewise, O Lord, Sītā, who is as dear to you as your own life-breath, is seen standing by your side; this is our greatest wonder. (65)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, Rāghava sighed deeply for a long time; with his eyes filled with tears, he reported everything to them.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Sītā was abandoned, as was her brother Lakṣmaṇa, for whose sake he had himself arrived there. || 67 ||
Having heard that, all the monkeys, headed by Sugrīva, were then overcome with great sorrow; they wept and thereafter embraced him closely.
Having lamented thus loudly for a long time, they then spoke to the best of the Raghus: "O King, let a command be given; whatever may be accomplished by us here [is at your disposal]. (69)
"We are blessed on the surface of the earth, O best of the Raghus, that you come to our home endowed with such affection. (70)
Rāma said: "O Sugrīva, having stayed one night in your palace, I shall depart for Laṅkā in the morning, where that Vibhīṣaṇa resides."
O best of monkeys, you too, accompanied by the chief minister, must come with me to the residence of Vibhīṣaṇa.
Sūta said: Having thus spent that night there, the best of the Raghus was attended with true devotion by all those foremost of monkeys.
Then, when the morning was bright and the orb of the sun had risen, having performed his morning rites, he summoned the Puṣpaka chariot.
By Sugrīva, Suṣeṇa, Tāra, and Kumuda; and by Aṅgada, Kuṇḍa, and the wise son of the Wind (Hanumān). || 3 ||
Together with Gavākṣa, Nala, and likewise Jāmbavān, as well as ten other monkeys, he ascended the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then, at the proper time, Rāghava set out toward Laṅkā by means of that very same resplendent aerial chariot, which moved with the speed of thought.
At that very moment, he reached the great city named Laṅkā and beheld those regions where the battle had formerly taken place.

Then Vibhīṣaṇa, seeing the brilliant radiance arising from the Puṣpaka chariot and recognizing that Rāma had arrived, went forward to meet him with great joy, accompanied by all his ministers, as well as his servants and sons.
Then, seeing Lord Rāma from afar, Vibhīṣaṇa prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, uttering the cry of "Victory! (Jaya).
Having respectfully embraced the Tathāgata, Vibhīṣaṇa subsequently entered that city of Laṅkā together with him alone.
Having reached the palace of Vibhīṣaṇa, he sat upon a splendid throne there, surrounded on all sides by those monkeys.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa offered everything to him—the kingdom, his sons, his wife, and whatever else he possessed. || 11 ||
Then, standing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke with humility: "O Lord, let an instruction be given; tell me, what task shall I perform? (12)
"O Lord, tell me why you have arrived here so suddenly; why has that son of Sumitrā not come with you, nor Jānakī?"
Sūta said: Having reported everything to him with a voice faltering with emotion, Rāghava, his face covered by a flood of tears, sighed again and again.
Then the joy of the Raghus spoke words of truth for the benefit of Vibhīṣaṇa, having consoled him who was tormented by grief.
O best of Rākṣasas, having now renounced the kingdom, I shall go quickly to the third heaven where Lakṣmaṇa resides.
O tiger among Rākṣasas, I do not have the strength to remain even for a moment in the world of mortals deprived of that high-souled kinsman.
"O Vibhīṣaṇa, I have come to you for the purpose of instruction; therefore, listen with an undistracted mind and act accordingly. (18)
This prosperity arising from sovereignty produces intoxication in men, just as wine does for those of small intellect; therefore, you must not indulge in it.
Indeed, all the immortals, beginning with Śakra, must always be honored and revered by you, so that your kingdom may remain eternal forever. (20)
"Let my word come true: for this reason I have come here, even though your immensely powerful brother has already attained his established sovereignty. (21)

Therefore, the gods are always to be honored, for [otherwise] one would meet with sudden destruction. If any human should somehow arrive here, he must be regarded as my own body by all the night-stalkers.
Likewise, O Vibhīṣaṇa, you must restrain all the night-stalkers; having crossed my bridge, they must not go down to the surface of the earth.
Vibhīṣaṇa said: "O Lord, I shall undoubtedly carry out your command in this way; however, my life would depart if the mortal world were abandoned by you."
Therefore, O Lord, you ought to take me as well to that very place where Lakṣmaṇa, who went before you, now dwells together with yourself.
Śrī Rāma said: "O best of Rākṣasas, I have ordained an imperishable kingdom for you; therefore, you ought not to make me act falsely in any way whatsoever."
"On my own bridge, I shall establish three auspicious forms of Śaṅkara for the sake of fame; they should always be worshipped by you with devotion, as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. (27)
Having spoken thus to Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, that best of the Raghus remained there in Laṅkā for ten nights together with the monkeys.
He recounted various wonderful stories of battle that had indeed been fought before, and he observed all the diverse positions and maneuvers of combat.
Praising those exceedingly powerful rākṣasa heroes—Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit, and the others—who had come forward to face him in battle.
Then, when the eleventh day arrived, the joy of the Raghus ascended that Puṣpaka chariot and set out toward his own city.
Accompanied by those monkeys and preceded by Vibhīṣaṇa, he then installed Maheśvara at the edge of the bridge.
Having thus established the three Rāmeśvaras there—with a mind purified by faith—at the center as well as at the beginning, Rāma himself [performed the rites]. (33)
Having thus reached Setubandha, he set out toward his own home; at that moment, Vibhīṣaṇa, having prostrated himself again and again, spoke to him.
Vibhīṣaṇa said: "By this path of the bridge, men will come with a desire to behold Rāmeśvara, filled with curiosity and faith. (35)
O Great King, the race of Rākṣasas is considered the most cruel; upon seeing a human approaching, a desire for flesh arises within them. (36)
When some rākṣasa shall devour some person, a certain violation of my command will surely occur, even for one devoted to me. (37)
In the Kali age, the men who are kings will become impoverished; out of greed for gold and for the sake of seeing the deity, they will come here. (38)
They will come constantly, having abandoned the fear caused by the Rākṣasa; yet, if anyone should cause their slaughter at the hands of a Rākṣasa, [that person shall suffer]. (39)
"O Lord, there will be a fault for me arising from treachery toward my master; therefore, O Guru, devise some means so that the sin caused by the violation of your command may never arise for me."
Having heard those words of his, that best of the Raghus then said, "So be it," and prepared his bow.
Then, in the Middle Country, the best of the Raghus cut down that [cloud] which was ten yojanas wide and possessed the form of fame, using sharpened arrows.
The peak where Śaṅkara himself was established by him, along with that liṅga, fell into the waters of the ocean. || 43 ||
Having thus established that bridge as an impassable path, he then set out for his home together with the monkeys and the rākṣasas.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Installation of Rāmeśvara by Śrī Rāma in the Middle of the Setu," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 101 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, listen to that wonder which occurred on the road as Rāma was setting out toward his own abode.
O twice-born ones, as that Puṣpaka chariot was traveling through the path of the sky, it suddenly became motionless, causing wonder among men.
Then, seeing that Puṣpaka remained motionless in the courtyard of the sky, Rāma spoke these words to the son of the Wind out of wonder: || 3 ||
"O Māruti, go quickly to the earth and find out the cause: why has this Puṣpaka come to a standstill in the sky? || 4 ||
Sometimes the movement of this great-souled Puṣpaka, born from the vision of Brahman, is not perceived by anyone anywhere.
Having said, "So be it," Hanumān went quickly to the surface of the earth and, having returned, spoke again after prostrating before the best of the Raghus.
Below this place is an auspicious field known as Hāṭakeśvara, where Brahmā himself, the creator of the universe, is personally established.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two divine physicians, and the Aśvins—all of them stay there, as do other Siddhas and Kinnaras. || 8 ||
For this reason, the Puṣpaka does not pass beyond that field; it has become motionless. This which I have spoken is the truth.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Rāghava, filled with curiosity, directed the Puṣpaka chariot toward that sacred field.
Then, together with all those monkeys and various kinds of rākṣasas, he joyfully descended into that sacred field on all sides.
He beheld the sacred fords and holy shrines; then he gazed upon Cāmuṇḍā, who was fashioned by the Grandfather (Brahmā), and having bathed there in the pool that grants all desires.
Then Rāma beheld the four-armed god fashioned by his father, looking like the Lord of Gods himself.
Having become pure and bathed in the royal step-well, and having offered libations to his own ancestors, he then reflected upon that field which bestows great merit.
Just as my father established the Liṅga of Keśava, so too has my beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa, who has ascended to heaven, [established it]. || 15 ||

I shall establish his designated emblem (liṅga) here in this most sacred field, as well as that auspicious form endowed with a physical body together with Sītā, and likewise myself in the form of stone.
Having thus made this resolve, Rāma, the best among those who bear arms, established five palaces with true devotion. (17)
Then all those monkeys, and especially the Rākṣasas, each separately installed their own respective Liṅgas.
Having remained in that very place for a very long time, endowed with faith, they then departed for Ayodhyā, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
All this has been narrated to you regarding how the great Rāmeśvara, together with Lakṣmaṇeśvara, is situated in that most beautiful sacred ford (tīrtha).
The person who, having risen early in the morning, always beholds these two, obtains the entire fruit that is found here in the hearing of the Rāmāyaṇa.
Furthermore, whoever recites the life-story of Rāma on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day obtains before him the entire fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Construction and Consecration of the Five Temples of Lakṣmaṇa and Others by Śrī Rāmacandra in the Holy Region of Hāṭakeśvara," in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: "O son of a Sūta, it is indeed a marvel that you have related this, namely, that even by Rākṣasas and Vānaras, Liṅgas were installed. (1)
Therefore, O son of Sūta, tell us in detail, in each respective place and in whatever manner, the lingas that were installed by them in those various locations.
Sūta said: Then Sugrīva, having searched the entire field without exception, reached Bālamaṇḍanaka; there, being composed, he bathed.

Then he installed a face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga) there for the wielder of the trident (Śiva). Likewise, O best of the twice-born, all the other monkeys installed face-liṅgas for the wielder of the trident according to their desire, for the sake of their own identification.
He who offers a "butter-blanket" (ghṛtakambala) to those lingas of the faces [of Śiva] when the sun is situated in Capricorn goes to the world of Śiva. || 5 ||
Then, O twice-born ones, in the western quarter of that field, lingas with four faces were installed by the Rākṣasas.
In the eastern quarter, Rāma, filled with devotion, established five palaces that destroy all sins.
Likewise, he constructed a small well in the southern quarter, near the Ānarttīya lake; it is the destroyer of sins.
Whoever performs a Śrāddha ceremony there when the southern solstice has arrived, having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
O twice-born ones, he who offers a lamp there during the month of Kārttika does not see those twenty-one terrible hells; nor is he ever born blind, wherever he may be reborn.
The sages said: "O son of a Sūta, by whom was that Ānartīya tank constructed there? And what is its power? Proclaim it to us in its entirety."
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, the greatness of the Ānarttīya lake cannot be fully described by even a single voice, even in hundreds of years.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, being composed in mind, one should bathe and offer libations to the gods and the ancestors according to the prescribed rites.

Then, on the day of the festival of lights (Dīpotsava), having performed the ancestral rite (śrāddha) with a concentrated mind and having worshipped Dāmodara and Yama, one should offer a lamp with one's own devotion.
The King of Dharma should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unguents; and black gram and sesame seeds should be offered with the words, "May Govinda be pleased. (15)
By the gift of sesame and mung beans, and by the satiation of the twice-born, the Supreme Person, the God, together with Yama, is pleased. (16)
O Brahmins, he who performs such an act at the sacred ford known as Ānarta obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 17 ||
On the day that Rāma arrived there filled with great joy, he was approached by all the best of the twice-born and addressed with respect.
O descendant of Raghu, the best of sages, Agastya, resides here; go and behold him, O lord of brahmins, who was born from Mitra and Varuṇa.
Then, having heard their words, the lotus-eyed Rāma, delighted, went quickly along with the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
Having prostrated before him with the eight-limbed salutation, that best of the Raghus was firmly embraced by that joyful, high-souled one.
Not very far from him, endowed with humility, he sat upon the surface of the earth, standing with his palms joined in reverence.
Then, questioned by the sage, he related in detail his entire account regarding his journey to heaven.
Just as Sītā was abandoned, and just as the abandonment of his own [son] was carried out by the high-souled Saumitri after he himself had been forsaken; 24.
Likewise, having approached Sugrīva and similarly Vibhīṣaṇa, and having conversed with them, you returned here; thereafter followed the arrival of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then the sage Agastya related various wonderful stories before him, illustrating them with many examples of ancient royal sages.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversation, seeing that the best of the Raghus was fickle-minded, she presented him with an excellent jewel-ornament.
What is not found among the gods, yakṣas, siddhas, and vidyādharas; nor among the nāgas and lords of the rākṣasas—what need is there to mention human beings? (28)
From it, thousands of rainbows emerge even at night during the dark fortnight, appearing with a brilliance like that of the sun.
Then Rāma, having taken it, his eyes wide with wonder and filled with curiosity, asked: "O Sage, from where did this [come] to you? (30)
"Tell me of this neck-ornament, fashioned from jewels, which produces great wonder and dispels darkness; such a thing does not exist in the three worlds. (31)
Agastya said: "O best of the Raghus, this excellent lake which you see situated near my hermitage was created by the God of gods."
On its bank, I beheld a wonder unsurpassed; I shall relate that to you, so listen, O delighter of the Raghus. (33)
Once, O best of the Raghavas, having risen at midnight, I beheld a radiance like the sun along the path of the sky.
To that extent, that celestial chariot was resplendent with throngs of apsarases; and in its center sat a certain young man, blind, yet mounted there, being praised by the kinnaras, O King.
Wearing this exceedingly pure jewel-ornament upon his neck, which shone like twelve suns, he was like a second God of Love.
Then, descending from that foremost of celestial chariots, O scion of Raghu’s line, he clung to the shoulder of one divine messenger and reached the edge of the waters.
Then, having dragged the corpse out from that water, he quickly began to devour the dead man's body with his teeth.
In whatever manner that descendant of Raghu consumed the great flesh, in that very same manner his body was produced again with that same form. (39)
Then, having finally attained satisfaction after a long time, becoming pure and filled with great joy, he emerged from the water and ascended his celestial chariot.
Then, having gone quickly, I asked that king out of curiosity, even as he was being attended on all sides by Gandharvas who were intent upon his welfare.
"O best of the celestial beings, wait for a moment! I am a brahmin named Agastya, born from Mitra and Varuṇa. (42)
Having heard that, he then stood face-to-face and offered his salutation, together with all those inhabitants of celestial chariots and the kinnaras and others.

"This king, having prostrated before me, stands here with folded hands and asks: 'Who are you, possessing such a form and splendor, seated upon this excellent celestial chariot, and being served by Apsarases, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras? (44)
Having come here to the edge of the pond, you have consumed human flesh; why has this aberration arisen in your vision? (45)
The celestial being said: "Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, that you have come into my presence! Surely destiny has been favorable to me, since you have arrived."
The sight of the virtuous is meritorious, for the virtuous are like sacred pilgrimage sites; a pilgrimage site bears fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous bears fruit immediately. (47)
Therefore, O great sage, I shall relate your entire narrative to you, by which my food has become censurable and my prosperity has likewise come to such a state. (48)
O great sage, in former times I was a king named Śveta, the sinful ruler of Ānarta who oppressed all the world. (49)
