Having spoken thus, the lord of the earth thereafter performed all their duties himself, day and night, without weariness.
Then, O best of the twice-born, all those wives of the eminent brahmins, full of affection and tenderness, approached Damayantī’s palace.
With saffron, agallochum, camphor, flowers, and various kinds of perfumes, they worshipped that image, and the king did so day after day.
Then, O best of the twice-born, those female ascetics standing before him spoke to one another, bringing satisfaction to that king.
"When prosperity shall ever arise in our home, we shall undoubtedly perform the worship of Damayantī both before and after it, at all times and in all rites. (24)
Whichever maiden, upon seeing her, shall go to the middle of the altar, she will undoubtedly always be as dear to her husband as his own life. (25)
Therefore, with every effort, when the sacrifice for a maiden has arrived, Damayantī should be beheld and worshipped with great diligence. (26)
Sūta said: Thus, in that city, by that high-souled king, sixty-eight [families] were established, and peace was brought to the clans.

And due to fear of the serpent king, four lineages of those twice-born ones also went there, where their ancestors had previously resided; sixty-four of the remaining twice-born remained in that city.
The sages said: "O Lord, what kind of fear of the nāgas did they have, by which they departed, abandoning their own abodes? Tell us this in detail. (29)
Sūta said: Formerly, there was a lord of Ānarta named Prabhañjana; he was a knower of dharma, possessed of great prowess, and the bringer of destruction to the factions of his enemies.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when his son was born in his later years while the planets were situated in unfavorable positions, [the following occurred].
Then, having summoned astrologers who were experts in the scriptures, he informed them of everything regarding the time of his birth.

The astrologers said: "O protector of the earth, this son born to you is most contemptible, for he was born at an inauspicious and fierce time, arising from the three-fold junction known as Gaṇḍānta."
If this king should somehow bring him back to life, he will destroy the countries for the sake of his father, mother, and city.
The king said: "Is there any means here, whether divine or even human, by which the welfare of my son and of the realm may be secured? (35)

The Brāhmaṇas said: "Just as a machine that has arisen is countered by another machine, and just as armor serves as a defense against the strikes of arrows, so too does propitiatory pacification serve as a warding off against the afflictions caused by the planets. (36)
Therefore, O King, always remain free from agitation and perform rites for peace, so that all the planets may become gentle and bring about auspiciousness. (37)
When the planets were situated in unfavorable positions and in odd signs, the king then departed for the city of Camatkārapura.
Having summoned all the Brahmins there, he spoke to them respectfully: "Indeed, it is by your grace that we always govern the kingdom. (39)
Those who have passed away and those who will arise in our lineage—of them you are the refuge, just as a rain-cloud is for crops. (40)

Since my son was born here under the influence of planets situated in malefic positions, this rite for pacification has been prescribed by the astrologers to bring peace to that inauspiciousness. (41)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, perform for me the propitiatory rite as prescribed; otherwise, neither my sons, nor my kingdom, nor my prosperity will increase.
Then those brahmins, having consulted with one another, said: "O Lord of the Earth, for your well-being we shall perform a propitiatory rite here."

O King, those sixteen twice-born ones—who are virtuous, self-restrained, and peaceful—should always be sent by you with devotion as offerings; and at the end of each month, the consecration originating from the Rudra-pitcher should be received.
By acting in this manner, your son shall attain growth, as will the kingdom, the treasury, and whatever else there may be.
Then, having bowed to them with joy and returned to his own dwelling, he was always urged by them to celebrate the festival arising from the birth of his son.
Then he dispatched the necessary materials to Camatkārapura, [instructing] that the consecration must indeed be received according to the prescribed rites at the end of the month.
Those tigers among Brahmins, born of the four Vedic lineages and devoted to the practice of celibacy, performed the propitiatory rite in due order.
Month after month, those twice-born ones remained ever peaceful, self-controlled, and masters of their senses; then, at the conclusion of that month, others performed that rite for pacification.
Then, at the end of the month, that king also arrived with great devotion; having received the consecration and having honored the best of the twice-born, [he departed].
Having fully gratified other Brahmins with garments, crowns, and the gift of cattle and land, the lord of the earth then proceeds to his own abode. (51)
While this propitiatory rite was thus proceeding for the king, a very long time passed in peace, health, and the arrival of wealth.
Then, after some time had passed, even at the beginning of a month for the king, while that propitiatory rite was being commenced, a great disease arose.
There will be a particularly great destruction of his son, as well as of the inner apartments, the entire kingdom, and the mounts.
Thereupon, for the sake of pacification, he dispatched there to that excellent city abundant materials and especially distinguished sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). || 55 ||
In whatever manner the twice-born performed the oblation there in the fire, in that same manner all diseases increased everywhere in an especially severe way.
His great horses and likewise his mighty elephants perish; his enemies, having assembled from all directions for the sake of conflict, are destroyed. || 57 ||
Then that king, overwhelmed and seized by disease, reached Camatkārapura and spoke to all the brahmins.

"O lords, now that you have passed away, calamities overwhelm me. Therefore, O illustrious ones, why is it that my prosperity is wasting away, while diseases increase, accompanied by hosts of enemies? (59)
Therefore, a specific oblation must be performed for the pacification of disease; and I shall bestow distinguished gifts upon the twice-born.
Then all those brahmins, becoming composed, performed a propitiatory rite (śāntika) in the presence of that king for his welfare.
In whatever manner those well-composed [sages] performed the rites at the conclusion of the oblations, in that very same manner the disease of this king continued to increase.
In the meantime, all those best of the twice-born became enraged; they resolved to cast a curse upon the planets, beginning with the Sun.

The Brahmins said: "Even though the planets have been worshipped with true devotion and according to the prescribed rites, they continue to afflict the king's city along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen. (69)
Having thus made their resolve, purified themselves, and become composed, they, overcome with anger, pronounced whatever curse they intended upon the planets.
Then Agni, having assumed a physical form, spoke thus to the best of the twice-born: "O lords of brahmins, do not by any means bestow a curse out of anger."
"Listen to my words regarding the planets from whom the fault has been removed: those sixteen twice-born ones perform a fire-oblation every month. (67)
And standing in their midst was one born three times, the lowest of Brahmins; by him, all that sacrificial substance was defiled. (68)
Those planets, beginning with the Sun, do not accept what is given by me; therefore, they inflict this even greater suffering upon the king. (69)
Therefore, abandon him and perform the fire-oblation without delay, so that all the planets, headed by the Sun, may attain supreme satisfaction. (70)
The king shall become healthy, free from enemies, and endowed with sons; he shall constantly attain happiness through the power of my peace-rite. (71)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One and the Fire vanished from sight; those Brahmins, too, were dejected in countenance and overcome with great shame.
Then, remaining there and praising that Purifier once more, they said to Vaiśvānara: "Tell us who the twice-born man is here who has been born thrice."
By means of which, having completely abandoned that [king], we may perform an act for the sake of the pacification of all the faults of this high-souled monarch. (74)
Vahni said: "O best of the twice-born, even though I know their fault, I shall not speak of it in any way; all Brāhmaṇas on the surface of the earth are worthy of my worship."
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O Fire, if you do not proclaim that Brāhmaṇa to us, we shall pronounce a curse upon you; therefore, tell us quickly. (76)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, Vahni (the Fire-god), filled with fear, reflected for a long time: "What shall I do from now on that will bring about auspiciousness?"
If I defile a Brahmin, there will undoubtedly be a sin, as well as the resulting curse. (78)
I shall either proclaim that best of the twice-born as being present, or he will undoubtedly curse me; for when enraged, they are like venomous serpents.
As he was reflecting thus, a great sweat arose on his body, by which that sacrificial pit intended for the oblation was filled.
Then, having emerged from the sacrificial pit, the Fire-god stood with palms joined in reverence, trembling and terrified with fear, and spoke to those brahmins.
I shall not, by any means, proclaim with my own tongue the fault arising from this Brāhmaṇa; therefore, listen, O twice-born ones! (92)
O Brahmins, let those sixteen twice-born ones who are situated here in the water of sweat perform their bath today for the sake of their own complete purification.
Whosoever among these shall be born of three [mothers], his body, even after bathing, will be covered with boils.
Then all those brahmins performed their ritual immersion there in due order and attained purification, with the exception of one brahmin at that time.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there from the people, upon seeing that best of the twice-born suddenly covered with boils.
Then that brahmin, filled with shame, cast his face downward and departed from the midst of the assembly, from the place where the brahmins had gathered.
Vahni said: "O best of the twice-born, this task has been accomplished by me for you previously; therefore, having been brought to the further shore by you, I shall go to my own abode."
"O best of the twice-born, even in a dream my sight shall not be in vain; therefore, let whatever is desired and dwells in your hearts be requested. (89)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O Fire, let this water of yours, which is always born of perspiration, remain right here for the sake of the purification of the twice-born. (90)
"Any man born of another [caste] who performs an immersion here—you must mark him with the appearance of erupting boils. (91)
Having said, "So be it," he indeed vanished from sight; O twice-born ones, all those fires then conferred with one another regarding a mantra.
From this day forward, the origin of all Brāhmaṇas must be established here through the purity of their paternal and maternal descent. (93)
Whosoever is proclaimed as a brahmin originating from Camatkārapura, he should be known as a pure son of noble family once he has bathed here. || 94 ||
To him a daughter should be given; he shall become worthy of the śrāddha rite.
For he alone is indeed to be employed in all religious duties.
When the sixty-eight lineages have been assembled in their proper order, he who is pure through direct perception of them is the pure one who sanctifies the assembly. 96.
And whatever censures exist, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, as well as others uttered by wicked people that cause doubt regarding dharma; (97)
All those noble sons (kulaputrakas) here shall be known as purified; likewise, all other censurers shall meet their destruction.
As long as the bath has not been performed here in the presence of all the twice-born, that person clearly shall not become a Brahmin. 99.
Sūta said: Having thus made this agreement, the Brāhmaṇas born in Camatkārapura performed a rite for peace (śāntika) for the benefit of that king. 100.
Then, in that pool, a bath was performed by all those great-souled ones, and even by the remaining great-souled ones who were terrified with fear, for the sake of purification.
Then, O twice-born ones, that king attained freedom from disease at that very moment; even today, O best of the twice-born, whoever performs a bath there [obtains the same].
On the full moon day of Kārttika, he shall be liberated from the sins arising from adultery with another's wife; for the twice-born there, purification occurred during those three ages.

Considering the terrible Kali age to be filled with those devoid of noble lineage and conduct, as well as other sinners who take pleasure in the wives of others, all the brahmins there then performed a verbal rite of purification.
O best of the twice-born, before the God of gods, Brahmā, those who are unwearied [should act] for the sake of purifying their paternal and maternal lineages.
O best of the twice-born, even today, whoever performs a ritual bath there, that Trijāta is undoubtedly consumed by fire. (106)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Fire-Pit for the Purification of the Trijātaka," within the *Damayantī-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 113 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, that brāhmaṇa, overwhelmed by eruptive boils and filled with supreme shame, went into a certain part of the forest.
Then, having attained detachment, he remained established in fierce austerity, abandoning his entire household and all affection arising from wife and children.
Emaciating his own body through observances and restraints, he went to a certain place near water and established Maheśvara there.
Then, after a long time, Maheśvara was pleased with him; appearing before him, he said, "Ask for whatever you desire."
Trijāta said: "O Lord, due to the fault of my mother, I have fallen into extreme embarrassment in the midst of the foremost Brahmins as well as the sovereign of Ānarta. (5)
"O Lord, even though I am possessed of great knowledge, I am unable to speak of or show myself to anyone, knowing that I have been born thrice. (6)
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, let such a policy be ordained so that I may become the most excellent among all those twice-born ones. (7)
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of the twice-born, among those Brāhmaṇas who dwell in Camatkārapura, you shall surely become the most excellent of all by my grace."
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, wait for some time; when the proper moment has arrived, I shall indeed lead you there.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished from that place; the Brāhmaṇa also performed penance, worshipping Hara in that manner.
Then, after some time, O twice-born ones, there was a brahmin named Devarāta in Mākandīpura, born of the lineage of Maudgalya.
His son was named Kratha, whose body was arrogant with youth; he was always filled with pride and established in his own prowess.
O twice-born ones, once that brahmin went toward Nāgatīrtha while wandering in the forest on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Then he beheld the son of the lord of the Nāgas, possessed of great splendor, known as Rudramāla, who was in the company of his mother.
Then, having observed that very small serpent-son and recognizing it as a water-snake, he crushed it with a club. || 15 ||
As he was being struck, a great cry was then uttered by him: "Alas, mother! Father! Father! I am perishing, though I am innocent! (16)
Having heard that sound produced by a human being, the Brahmin, terrified by fear of the serpent, went quickly to his own home.
Then his mother, having emerged from her watery abode, saw as soon as she reached the shore that her son had been struck down.
Then, seeing her son in such a state—pierced by the blows of the staff and with all his limbs drenched in blood—she fell into a swoon.
Then, having regained consciousness once more, she uttered many lamentations, tormented by grief and compassion, her eyes clouded with tears.
"Alas, alas! O son, having abandoned me, where have you gone? Have you departed to a place from which there is no return? Do you have no affection for me? (21)
"By what sinful and evil-souled one have you been slain, my son? Even though you are sinless, my son, with whom is Yama angry today? (22)
[This is] for that evil-minded one, together with his city, his kingdom, and his family, by whom you were slain today on the fifth day and yet not worshipped.
Having played with the dust today and returned after a long time, the sky will now come into her lap out of desire and bring about exhaustion.
Who will speak before me today words that are faltering, charming, and yet cause people to laugh, if not you? (25)
"O son, who today, apart from you, will take delight while resting upon his father's lap and pulling at his beard? (26)
"You are forbidden by me, my child; you have followed after me to this world of mortals, O dear one, which is crowded with many defects. (27)
Having lamented thus, the Nāga woman, enraged and emaciated by grief, took her dead son and went into the presence of Ananta.
Then, having cast that dead son of hers before him, she, separated from him, uttered piteous lamentations like a distressed osprey.
The Naga king also, seeing his son struck down, fell into a swoon, tormented by grief for his son. || 30 ||
Then, having regained consciousness with difficulty after being sprinkled with cold water, he uttered piteous lamentations like an ordinary man.
In the meantime, all the nāgas gathered there and wept in their distress, their eyes overwhelmed with tears.
Vāsuki, Padmaja, Śaṅkha, and the highly venomous Takṣaka; Śaṅkhacūḍa, Sacūḍa, and the terrible Puṇḍarīka. || 33 ||
Añjana and Vāmana, as well as Kumuda; the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, and likewise the Nāga Karkoṭaka. || 34 ||
Puṣpadanta, Sudanta, Mūṣaka, Mūṣakādana, Elāpatra, Supatra, Dīrghāsya, and Puṣpavāhana. || 35 ||
These and other nāgas likewise arrived there by the thousands, having learned that the lord of the pannagas was tormented by grief for his son.
Then, having awakened that lord who subsists on air, they all [instructed him] by means of various illustrations and the unfolding of stories concerning past events.
Thus exhorted by them after a long time, that best of serpents, being deeply distressed, then made his son subject to burning by fire.
And at the time for the offering of water, he addressed all the serpents—all the nāgas who had assembled for the purpose of receiving the water. (39)
"I will not give water to my own son under any circumstances, even if urged by you and likewise by other kinsmen. (40)
As long as the destruction of that wicked man—who brought about the end of my son, along with his wife, children, and servants—has not been ordained, [I shall remain here].
Having spoken thus, Śeṣa then purified that twice-born man by means of the sinful wooden staff with which his son had been slain.
Then the lord of the serpents spoke to those nāgas standing at his side: "Let my best friends go to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara."
Having swiftly slain that slayer of his son along with his family and retinue, the entire city of Camatkārapura must thereafter be consumed.
All the foremost of the serpents must take up residence right there; furthermore, that city must be constructed in such a way that they never dwell there again.
Having been addressed thus by him, the prominent Nāgas who had been mentioned went there in haste and first approached that best of the twice-born.
Having devoured the sleeping son of Devarāta, they thereafter, filled with great wrath, consumed his entire family as well. (47)
Then all those beings, even though they were of animal birth, became enraged and devoured others as well—young, old, and children. 48.
In the meantime, a most terrible outcry arose in that city among the foremost of Brahmins, caused by the devouring of serpents.
On that ground, whatever else was seen there, all of it was pervaded by fierce serpents bearing black bodies. (50)
In the meantime, some who arrived fell under the power of death; some, reeling from the poison, collapsed upon the surface of the earth.
Others, having abandoned their homes and everything else, including their children, flee in terror toward the distant forest.
Other Brahmins, experts in mantras, exert themselves on all sides; others, seized with fear, run slowly away while carrying medicinal herbs.
Thus, with that city as their objective, all those foremost of serpents moved about in such a way that no Brāhmaṇa might dwell there.
Then, having made the city empty, all those best of serpents roamed at will there among the sacred fords and shrines.
No serpent at all emerged from the field to go outside, nor did any other human being enter into that field. (56)
In this manner, the established order between serpents and humans arose, characterized by mutual killing and devouring, occurring both externally and internally. (57)
In the meantime, Śeṣa, having abandoned the sorrow arising from his son, was filled with joy; accompanied by those of his own kind, he offered water for him.
Then some of those brahmins, overwhelmed by fear of the serpents and filled with grief, quickly gathered together in secret and looked toward the various quarters of the sky. (59)
Then they went to the forest where Trijāta was staying; having obtained boons from Hara, he remained there joyfully, established in a very great austerity.
Having seen all those people thus overwhelmed by suffering, he remembered his sons, wife, and others, who were weeping piteously and profusely.
He too, filled with sorrow upon seeing those eminent Brahmins born in his own city, then spoke with eyes clouded by tears: ||| 62 ||
"Let all the Brahmins listen now to my words: while I was departing from that city, Hara was propitiated by me. (63)
O best of the twice-born, a desired boon was granted to me by him; it has not yet been accepted by me, and I shall now request it.
So that there may be the complete destruction of those evil-natured Nāgas, by whom—those of sinful deeds—all our city has been flooded. (65)
Having spoken thus, that brahmin Trijāta then entreated the Supreme Lord: "O God, grant me that boon now."
Then the Lord of Gods said: "O twice-born one, request quickly that which I shall grant as your desired boon, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (67)
Trijāta said: "O Bull-vehicled One, our entire city has been rendered devoid of people by the Nāgas; therefore, let them all go to their destruction."
O best of gods, by which it may be filled once again by the brahmins, my own fame shall also arise from the restoration of my own abode. (69)
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, nothing improper was done by those high-souled serpents, even though their son here was blameless and yet slain by the Brahmin."
Especially, O best of the twice-born, when the fifth day arrives—on that very day in the month of Śrāvaṇa, where the serpents are worshipped.
Therefore, I shall proclaim to you this unsurpassed perfected mantra, by the mere utterance of which the poison of serpents is destroyed. (72)
O highly fortunate one, having gone there surrounded by all those brahmins, cause that mantra to be proclaimed everywhere with a loud voice.
Upon hearing that, those lowest of serpents who do not go to Pātāla will become free from poison by your word; of this there is no doubt.
Trijāta said: "Tell me that great mantra which destroys all venomous creatures, by means of which, having gone to my own place, I may exterminate the serpents. (75)
The Blessed Lord said: "What is called 'gara' is poison; it does not exist there at present. By my grace, O best of Brahmins, this [mantra] should indeed be uttered by you. (76)
"Having heard this, those lowest of serpents who remain there—neither poison nor non-poison shall avail them—they shall be slain at will."
From this day forward, that place on the surface of the earth shall become widely renowned by the name "Nagara," increasing your fame. (78)
Likewise, any other Brahmin who is a Nāgara born of a pure lineage should consecrate the water three times with the mantra called "Nagara."
Even a living being bitten by Time and fallen under the power of death, he himself will cast into his own mouth and restore it, endowed with life. (80)
Even if situated elsewhere, that mortal who shall remember this three-syllabled mantra while fast asleep shall not be harmed by a serpent. (81)
Whether it be stationary, moving, or even artificial poison (gara), once touched by this mantra, it becomes like nectar.
Diseases arising from indigestion and whatever other ailments originate in the stomach—all these go quickly to destruction through the power of this mantra. || 83 ||
Having spoken thus to that brahmin, the Lord whose banner bears the bull then vanished from sight, like a lamp devoid of oil.
Although he was born three times, Trijāta, with a joyful heart, quickly went toward Camatkārapura together with those remaining Brāhmaṇas who had survived the slaughter. 85.
Thus all those Brahmins, endowed with the three births, arrived while loudly crying out, "Not poison! Not poison! (na garaṃ na garam). || 86 ||
The sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, which extends on all sides, was pervaded by fierce and cruel venomous serpents who had come under the command of Śeṣa.
Then, having heard that mantra originating from Śiva which had been perfected, those serpents, rendered devoid of poison and stripped of their splendor, fled in every direction.
Some, having reached anthills from which various openings emerge, and others too, those serpents entered the netherworld (pātāla).
Whosoever are terrified by fear, oppressed by old age, or likewise others due to childhood, they are unable to move about. (90)
All those serpents there were slain by the thousands with wooden staffs by those lords of brahmins who sought to retaliate for what had been done to them.
Having thus exterminated all those Brāhmaṇas, they were freed from their distress; placing Trijāta at their head, they performed the duties pertaining to their respective stations.
O best of the twice-born, by the grace of Bharga, the God of gods, that city came into existence immediately after that time.
Whoever constantly recites this narrative concerning the city shall never experience any fear arising from serpents, in any place or in any way. (94)

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Name Nagar," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 114.
O high-minded one, tell me: who is that three-born Brāhmaṇa there? What is his name, from whom did he originate, what is his lineage, and what is his designation?

What is the use of those who are well-born, rich in virtues, or distinguished by their brilliance and learning? Better even than they is one born of the three [low castes] who has rescued his own station. (2)
Sūta said: That best of the twice-born was born in the lineage of the sage Sāṃkṛtya; he was renowned as Prabhāva, the son of Nimi known by the name Datta. || 3 ||
Having thus cleared the site, he established a beautiful sanctuary for the trident-bearing God of gods, known by the name Trijāteśvara.
Having propitiated him day and night, endowed with perfect faith, he went to heaven in his own body after some time had passed. (5)
Whoever beholds it with true devotion and always bathes it during the equinoxes, in his lineage no one born of the three [lower] castes shall ever be born by any means.
The sages said: O Sūtanaṇdana, tell us by name those lineages that have perished and those that have been established, as well as that city.
Sūta said: Among them, those belonging to the Upamanyu lineage, those born of the Krauñca lineage, and those born of the Kaiśorya lineage were the best of the twice-born, known as Traivaṇeyas.
They did not regain even those four lineages as they were before—namely, those of Śuka and the others—which had previously been lost due to the fear of the Nāga.
I shall now fully declare to you the remaining Brāhmaṇas born of various lineages; those born of the Kauśika lineage are recorded as being twenty-six.
Seventy-seven of the best of the twice-born were born of the lineage of Kaśyapa; twenty-one were born of the lineage of Lakṣmaṇa and arrived there.
There, those who had perished were regained once more in that place, though they remained deeply distressed; three Bhāradvājas arrived, and fourteen Kauṇḍanīyas.
Likewise, there are twenty of the Raitikas, eight of the Pārāśaryas, twenty-two of the Gargas, and twenty of the Hārītas. (13)
Twenty-five lineages of the Aurva-Bhārgava gotra have been proclaimed; those of the Gautamas are twenty-six, and the Ālūbhāyanas are twenty.
There are twenty-three branches of the Māṇḍavyas and twenty-three of the Bahvṛcas; however, those of the distinguished Sāṃkṛtyas are exactly ten in number separately.
Likewise, five of the Aṅgirasas are proclaimed; ten Ātreyas are enumerated, as well as the Śuklātreyas. (16)
The Vātsyas are declared to be five; the Kautsas are nine and seven; the Śāṇḍilyas and Bhārgavas are five; and the Maudgalyas are recorded as twenty.
The Baudhāyanas and Kauśalas are proclaimed to be thirty in number; the Atharvans are fifty-five, and the Maunas are seventy-seven. || 8 ||
The Yājuṣas are known as thirty; the Cyāvanas are twenty-seven; the Āgastyas are thirty-three; and the Jaimineyas are ten. (19)
The Naivṛtas are fifty-five, the Pāṭhīnas seventy, and the Gobhilas as well as the Kākvas are recorded as five each of the twice-born. || 2 ||
The descendants of Uśanas and Daśārha are said to be three each; likewise, there are sixty of the Lokākhyas and seventy-two of the Aiṇiśas. (21)
The Kāpiṣṭhalas, those called Śārkaras, and those called Dattas are seventy-seven; one hundred Śārkavas are proclaimed, and the Dārjyas are seventy-seven. || 22 ||
Three are remembered as the Kātyāyanas, three as the Vaidiśas; likewise, there are five Kṛṣṇātreyas and likewise five Dattātreyas. (23)
The Nārāyaṇas, Śaunakeyas, Jābālas numbering in the hundreds, Gopālas, Jāmadagnyas, Śālihotras, and Karṇikas; || 24 ||
The Bhāgurāyaṇas, as well as the Mātṛkas and the Traiṇavas—all these, O best of the twice-born, were excellent Brāhmaṇas in their respective order. || 25 ||
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of honoring all these very [deities], forty-eight [tīrthas] were formerly proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself. (26)

All these were individually described by the Lotus-born One: the rites of twilight libations, those arising from the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the Śrāddhas, the fortnightly rites, and likewise the funeral rice-balls for the ancestors.

The sacred threads (yajñopavīta) together with their lineages (pravara) have been described in their entirety, as well as the specific types of girdles (mauñjī) and the various distinctions of the topknots (śikhā). || 28 ||
Having propitiated the Grandfather, the God of gods, with the trijāta [sandalwood paste], he then performed this for the sake of his own fame among those best of the twice-born.
The sages said: How was Brahmā propitiated by the high-souled Trijāta? How was the Karmakāṇḍa divided by that great-souled one? Tell us everything in detail, for our curiosity is indeed great. (30)
Sūta said: For his sake, all the brahmins propitiated the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā), saying, "O All-pervading Lord, our entire abode has been uplifted by him alone. (31)
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, grant him unsurpassed knowledge of the Vedas, by which the specific ritual acts may be performed here in this supreme city.
O Lotus-born One, O Lord of Gods, let such a policy be enacted by you through your grace, so that his gravity may be restored. (33)
Then Brahmā gave him that unsurpassed collection of mantras, by which everything—the meaning of the Vedas and the performance of sacrificial rites—is understood.
Then, with a heart full of joy, he spoke to them all: "This one shall become possessed of the meaning of the Vedas and attain great renown. (35)
Known as Bhartṛyajña, he was an expert in sacrificial rites; whatever he tells you regarding the section on rituals, perform it without hesitation.
"Awakened by my word, you shall perform that task for the sake of heaven and liberation; he will connect all of you with the meanings of the Vedas. (37)
And those others who have gone to other countries and places anywhere—having abandoned this very place, O best of the twice-born, this is the truth. (38)
And this [Buddha] shall perform his activities in place of the Vedas for the sake of the intellect; neither in falsehood nor in evil shall his speech ever dwell. (39)
Having spoken thus, the Grandfather, the Lord of Gods, ceased; Bhartṛyajña also performed all those auspicious sacrificial rites.
For the benefit of the Brāhmaṇas, the meaning of that Śruti alone has been proclaimed through ten authorities; all of them are the most excellent of Brāhmaṇas. (41)
Indeed, those best of Brahmins from the sixty-four lineages were thus brought there by that high-souled one born of the three [fires].
Fifteen hundred of them were born together in one place, and by him they were made to share in common both worldly enjoyments and liberation.
Divided into sixty-eight parts, it arose from the previous expenditure of life-span; therein, according to the enumeration of men, there was [the following] within the lineage.
From that time forward, it was established as a general rule for all that, by the word of one born of the three [castes], [the matter] would be resolved swiftly even from afar.
The best of Brahmins gathered there, and the prosperity of the city increased; O twice-born ones, no one left for elsewhere out of distress.
Then it was further filled abundantly by their sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, daughters' sons, and nephews by the thousands.
O twice-born ones, that city flourishes like blades of durva grass, growing in countless and manifold ways from stalk to stalk.
Sūta said: Thus has this entire auspicious enumeration of lineages been told to you, as well as the glorification of the sages, which destroys all sins.
Whoever constantly recites this or listens to it with great devotion, for him there shall never be a break in his lineage on this earth.
Thus he is liberated from the sins arising from birth and death, and he never experiences separation from that which is dear to him.
Sūta said: Likewise, there is another highly renowned goddess there named Ambarevatī, who bestows desires upon men and grants happiness to children. (1)
Having seen and worshipped her, especially on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a mortal shall never encounter misfortune for his family.
The sages said: By whom was that goddess Ambarevatī established there? O son of a Sūta, tell us what her power is and what her nature is.

Sūta said: When the various Nāgas, fierce with poison and their eyes bloodshot with rage, were commanded by Śeṣa for the destruction of this city, then his beloved wife was also afflicted by grief for her son.
Having gone forward himself, he devoured that brahmin along with his family, by whom his son had been struck down.
Now, that lord of the twice-born had a younger sister who, having been joined with widowhood from childhood, was devoted to austerity and dedicated herself to the vow of celibacy.
Seeing that her entire family, including the one called Bhaṭṭikā, had been devoured, she then spoke to the Naga's wife while holding water in her hand: || 7 ||
"O double-tongued one, since you have brought my family to ruin and have shown me great suffering arising from my kinsmen."
In the same way, you too, having attained this most despised human state, and having obtained a human husband and acquired sons and grandsons— || 9 ||

"You shall not experience the suffering born of their destruction while remaining in the human state; however, I hereby pronounce this curse upon you for your conduct toward one who exists in the state of a nāga. (10)
Having heard that curse originating from Bhaṭṭikā, Revatī was then possessed by great anger and quickly bit her.
Then, having reached her body, the serpent’s fang, fierce with poison, shattered into a hundred pieces; it did not pierce the skin anywhere.
Then, overcome with shame, her face drenched in her own blood, she sat down dejectedly upon the surface of the earth.
In the meantime, the Nāgas and others who had assembled there, beholding Revatī in such a state and filled with fear, said: "O Goddess, what is this source of pain upon your face? (14)
Or rather, is this the power of some excellence of blood? (15)
Revatī said: "O best of serpents, this transformation has arisen in my mouth because of that most wicked female ascetic who is seen there. (16)
Therefore, [kill] this most wicked sister of that evil-minded man, by whom my son has now been slain by a son of a twice-born.
"O best of serpents, let it be eaten, let it be eaten quickly—this blood now present in my mouth for the sake of my destruction. (18)
Then those enraged serpents bit that ascetic woman all over her limbs simultaneously, as if she were an ordinary woman.
Then, in the same manner as with Śeṣa’s wife, fangs emerged from the mouths of those others as well, and blood was produced therefrom.
Then, having seen that power of hers, those best of nāgas, the remaining ones, terrified with fear, fled in the ten directions.
Bhaṭṭikā also went quickly toward her own hermitage, distressed, while being watched on all sides by great serpents trembling with fear.
Then, seeing that entire place being scorched by great serpents and abandoned by its own people who were filled with immense suffering, [he reflected].
That virtuous woman, fully devoted to her vows, departed elsewhere; performing a pilgrimage to sacred fords, she wandered across the earth.
When that place had been thus vacated, Revatī then remembered the curse of Bhaṭṭikā and was overcome with great sorrow.
"How shall my dwelling in the womb of a human woman come to pass through a curse, and how shall there be union with a human lover? (26)
This sorrow arising from the birth of a son does not afflict my heart as much as this dwelling within a human womb for the sake of a human being.
Likewise, having been abandoned by my husband's teeth, how shall I show my own face to him again? Here, salt remains upon my wound. (28)
Therefore, remaining right here in this sacred field, I shall serve [the Lord]; for what shall I do, deprived of my son, even if I reach home? (29)
Then, having installed that goddess Ambika, the sovereign of the gods, she propitiated her perfectly, endowed with right faith.
With offerings of perfumes and flowers, as well as various kinds of food oblations, and with captivating songs, dances, and instrumental music; (31)
Then, after a few days had passed, the Goddess of the Gods, being pleased, said: "I am a granter of boons; ask for whatever resides in your heart."
Revatī said: "O Goddess, in former times I was cursed by a Brāhmaṇī for a certain reason, because you, having yourself become human, would resort to a human being. (33)
Then, afflicted by my curse, you shall obtain the fruit arising from their destruction—a great suffering born of your own sons. (34)
Likewise, O Goddess of the Suras, my fangs have been extracted; how then, through your power, may their restoration come to pass? (35)
"O Goddess, may we have sons who likewise increase our lineage; this is my desire, O Goddess, and I pray for nothing else. (36)
The Goddess said: "O beautiful one, you must not dwell here under any circumstances; for you shall dwell within a human womb, and your husband shall be a man. (37)
Therefore, O lady of excellent complexion, listen now to my words which I shall speak to you—words that bring about the destruction of your suffering and are true. (38)
Without a doubt, he will be born in this triple world, assuming a human form, as your husband for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose. (39)
Likewise, O auspicious lady, the Naga named Takṣaka, under the influence of a Brahmin’s curse, will become a king named Raivata in the region of Saurāṣṭra.
His wife will be named Kṣemakarī, born of a distinguished lineage; there is no doubt that she will arise from the curse of a Brahmin.
Having entered her womb, you shall take birth; you will become once again the wife of Śeṣa, who exists in the form of Rāma.
Therefore, O auspicious goddess, do not grieve over this matter; by that means, your birth shall take place in a womb born of a human being.
In that regard, whatever destruction you see arising from your own family will undoubtedly lead to the welfare of that very situation. (44)
After that, O timid one, a sinful age will arise; following that, barbarians possessing the nature of mortals will prevail everywhere.
Therefore, for the sake of dwelling in heaven, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, will undoubtedly destroy his entire lineage by himself. (46)
Furthermore, beautiful fangs will grow upon your face; therefore, go to Pātāla where your husband resides.
Moreover, O auspicious lady, declare whatever else is desired by you that resides in your heart; great joy has arisen within me.

Revatī said: "O Sovereign of the Gods, it is fitting that you always remain right here under my name, so that my fame may arise throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (49)
Likewise, from the world of the Nagas, I shall always worship you on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, and especially on the ninth day.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, accompanied by all the nāgas and endowed with supreme faith, I shall perform worship for you. (51)
On that day, whatever other men also offer worship, by your grace, let those men not behold the destruction of their beloved ones.

The Goddess said: "So be it, O blessed lady; my residence shall be here. I will always grant prosperity to those who worship me under your name, especially on the day of Mahānavamī, O lady of pure smiles. (53)
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by her, Revatī, the beloved of Śeṣa, then departed for her own home, filled with great joy.
From that time forward, that goddess remained established in that sacred field; by her name, she grants the desires of men and destroys all calamities.
She is celebrated as Ambā, Durgā, and Revatī, the beloved of the serpent; therefore, she is proclaimed in the world upon the earth and in the sky as Ambarevatī.

He who, endowed with faith and having become pure, worships her with a concentrated mind on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina, shall not experience any calamity arising within his own family for the duration of a year.
Having seen a hole in front of him occupied by a serpent, one is liberated from defects arising from planets, spirits, and piśācas, as well as from other calamities. (58)
The sages said: O son of Sūta, why did the fangs originating from serpents emerge from the body of that woman named Bhaṭṭikā who was previously described by you?
O son of a Sūta, has the power of our asceticism failed, or is it the power of the mantra? This is a matter of great curiosity to us. (2)
Since those [poisons] are especially fierce even in a human body, let alone in that of the Nāgas; therefore, describe them all.
Sūta said: Formerly, while she was still in her childhood living in her father’s house, that Brahmin woman became afflicted with widowhood as a result of the ripening of her past karma.
Then, even in her childhood, she studied various scriptures; she performed pilgrimages to deities and bathed at sacred fords with a concentrated mind.
Having gone there to Kedāradeva, she remained constantly composed; rising every morning, she performed a song with devotion before him.
Then, drawn by the lure of that song, both Takṣaka and Vāsuki emerged from Pātāla, having assumed the forms of brahmins.
There too, she heard a great song, adorned with all the musical scales (tāna), endowed with melodic modulations (mūrcchanā), and resplendent with the seven notes (svara).
It was likewise filled with ascetics, villages, and various classes of settlements; and it consisted of stringed instruments, wind instruments, solid percussion instruments, and hollow instruments.

Although that brahmin lady was unskilled in the technicalities of rhythm, tempo, measure, the *vardhamāna* scale, and so forth—those very limbs of song—she nevertheless brought satisfaction to those two by means of the pure clarity of her voice alone.

Then, out of greed for that song, all the inhabitants of that city would rise at dawn and come to Kedāra out of curiosity. Then, after some time, those two Nāgas, lifting [the people] up, forcibly carried them toward their own city while the whole world looked on.
Assuming a fierce form that terrifies people, and having encircled it with their foremost coils, they went to the depths of Pātāla.

Then, having led her to their own home, they, afflicted by desire, said to her: "O large-eyed one, become our wife, devoted to dharma; for this purpose you have been brought from the surface of the earth to Pātāla."
Bhaṭṭikā said: "O Takṣaka, since you have quickly abducted me—though I am peaceful and indifferent to the festival of love—and brought me here, I am one born of the Brāhmaṇa lineage. (15)
"In the past, you took recourse to me while assuming a human form, with your mind and self captivated by desire; therefore, you shall become a mortal. (16)
"O man of evil conduct, if you shall assail me by force, this head of yours shall instantly split into a hundred pieces. (17)
Having heard that most terrible curse, he was overwhelmed with fear; then, standing with his palms joined in reverence, he sought to appease her.
"Out of great delusion, while attached to desire, I brought you here; therefore, show me favor so that there may be an end to my curse. (19)
Sūta said: Thus propitiated by Takṣaka, the daughter of the twice-born then spoke to that serpent, her eyes clouded with tears.
"O Takṣaka, if you do not come back to me in the world of mortals, I shall bring this curse to its conclusion there; of this there is no doubt. (21)
In the meantime, Takṣaka, his mind afflicted by lust, learned that a human woman had been brought to his own home.
Then his wives, possessed by great jealousy and with eyes reddened by anger, arrived for the purpose of destroying her.
Then Takṣaka, having understood their intention and desiring to reach the end of his curse, departed from their side filled with fear.
Then he remembered the vidyā named Vajrā; she then joined her body to his for the sake of protection, and the serpent-woman arrived.
Then, enraged, she bit that virtuous daughter of a Brahmin; thinking her to be a rival wife, she was born with her fangs shattered.
Then she, born of a twice-born family, seeing her behaving with feelings born of rivalry toward co-wives and filled with jealousy, became angry and cursed her as well. (27)
"Since you regard me, who am free from fault, as if I were possessed of fault, therefore, O sinful woman, quickly become a human being who partakes in suffering. (28)
Then, having seized her, Takṣaka, the best of the Nāgas, released her at midnight in that temple of Kedāra.
Then, standing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to that goddess: "O virtuous lady, grant me an end to my curse, so that I may go to my own home."
Bhaṭṭika said: "O serpent, you shall become a king in the region of Saurāṣṭra; on earth, you will be known by the name Raivataka, always a vessel for enjoyments. (31)
And then, having cast off this body in the sacred fields within the midst of the hermitages, you shall attain your own abode through the power of that field. (32)
Takṣaka said: "This beloved wife of mine has been joined with a curse by you; let her remain my wife even while we exist in human form. (33)
Do this for me, who am wretched and imploring you; let there be no union of hers with any other man. (34)
Bhaṭṭika said: "This auspicious girl shall become the daughter of the lord of Ānarta; then, having received his hand in marriage, she will become your wife. (35)

Renowned as Kṣemaṅkarī and endowed with beauty and youth, she will enjoy many pleasures with you upon the surface of the earth; thereafter, that beautiful woman will indeed follow you to the other world.
Sūta said: Thus addressed by her with the respectful words, "May it be forgiven," he prostrated himself and then departed for his own abode, filled with great joy.
When the remainder of the night had arrived, she stood before Kedāra and once again performed that supreme song which brings delight to the ears.
Then, hundreds of other Brāhmaṇas, exceedingly rich in devotion to Kedāra, arrived there, desiring to behold that Kedāra once again. 39.
Seeing that Bhaṭṭikā, born of a Brahmin, had arrived, they were filled with wonder and immediately questioned her.
"O beautiful one, who was that nāga who arrived in the form of a brahmin? Where were you taken by him, and for what purpose? Tell us. (4)
Why, moreover, have you been liberated? Tell us everything exactly as it is; a very great curiosity has arisen in us on account of you. (42)
Sūta said: Thereupon she related the entire account concerning Takṣaka, as well as the events arising from the Nāgas, born of both curses and favors.
In the meantime, her entire family arrived; hearing that she had come there, they wailed loudly, afflicted with grief.
Then her mother, her eyes clouded with tears, embraced her; and the other friends likewise embraced her with affectionate hearts.
Then, their minds overcome by wonder as they repeatedly heard the news arising from the world of the Nāgas, they were led back to their own home.
Then, in that city, all the citizens said to one another: "An improper act has been committed by this evil-minded Brāhmaṇa."
When she brought back that very young woman who had been living in another's house, [he replied: "Indeed, there are many women belonging to other brahmins as well. (48)
"Even those who are young and beautiful shall be joined with widowhood; this same rule shall apply to all of them. Since they will surely cause a confusion of castes, let them be banished. (49)
Then all those best of the twice-born, having come together, spoke these words, originating from the scriptures, to that Brāhmaṇa with conciliatory gestures. (50)
"O Brahmin, this daughter of yours is young and endowed with beauty; she has been carried away to Pātāla by a passionate Nāga. (51)
He will say this: "I have been released by that lustful man; I am faultless. Yet this world does not place its trust in her, even though she has declared herself pure. (52)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, grant purification to the foremost of the twice-born, so that, O wise one, the women of others also shall not perish. (53)
Having said, "So be it," he then questioned his daughter in private: "If you have any grievance, speak of it."
If not, grant purification for the satisfaction of the Brahmins.

Bhaṭṭika said: "O father, what you have said is correct, as is what has been said by other twice-born men; the purification of a woman would indeed be appropriate even through the transgression of the door. (56)
How much more so, then, having gone to another country with a passionate man? Therefore, I have no doubt that tomorrow morning, after bathing, I shall enter the fire.

"Having entered, I shall undoubtedly provide purification for all the Brahmins; and having obtained purification from the fire, I myself shall consume the food, the drink, and whatever else there may be here. (58)
Having been addressed thus by her, he, filled with great joy, rose at dawn and had wood brought from outside the city.
Then Bhaṭṭikā also, having bathed, pure and wearing white garments, together with all her attendants as well as her own family members, [proceeded]. (60)
With a serene face and full of joy, intent upon meditation on Viṣṇu, she went to that place where the great mountain of wood stood.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having kindled the fire there himself and performed three circumambulations, he spoke with palms joined in reverence: || 62 ||
If there exists in my body even the slightest fault born of passion, or if it has been inflicted by force by that evil-minded Takṣaka, [then let him burn me].
Furthermore, another person might come along; therefore, let this kindled fire burn [him] quickly. (64)
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman then entered her own palace; the well-kindled sacrificial fire was instantly transformed into water.
And that auspicious woman saw herself situated in the midst of the water.
Then a great rain of flowers fell from the sky.
The divine messenger, stationed upon his celestial chariot, spoke these words: "O highly fortunate lady, you are pure by virtue of the conduct born from your own limbs."
No other woman shall ever be equal to you; for in all her limbs, O illustrious lady, there are always three and a half crores of hairs present.
"O virtuous lady, among them not even a single one has ever committed a sin. Therefore, go quickly to your own home accompanied by your kinsmen. (69)
Perform meritorious deeds and propitiate Keśava; this very spot of the funeral pyre belonging to you shall be filled with water.
"A holy ford (tīrtha) shall become renowned in the world by your name; those who perform their ablutions here during the sleeping and waking festivals of Hari [shall attain great merit]. (71)
"They shall attain the supreme perfection that is difficult even for the immortals to reach. Having spoken thus, the voice arising from the divine messenger ceased.
Then Bhaṭṭikā, filled with joy, bowed to her own father and said: "I will not go home; what shall I do at home? (73)
Right here, in my own sacred ford, I shall always worship Acyuta; likewise, subsisting on food obtained as alms, I shall perform penance.
Therefore, my dear father, go home; I shall remain here, taking refuge at the front.
Then Janaka, as well as those citizens, went to their respective homes greatly rejoicing, praising her individually.
By her, the image of the Three-Striding Lord (Viṣṇu) was first fashioned there; afterwards, having constructed a Māheśvara Liṅga, she built an excellent temple.
Thereafter, she performed penance, subsisting on food obtained as alms, while being praised by all the people born in the city of Camatkārapura.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I have related all this to you that I was asked, concerning how her body remained forever firm and impenetrable.

O twice-born ones, for those who constantly recite this excellent narrative called the Bhaṭṭikā—whether regarding serpents, other beings, or even weapons—no ill-repute resulting from evil deeds shall accrue to them, O best of the twice-born. (80)
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, as for what you have stated—that Takṣaka will be born as a very powerful king named Raivata in the region of Saurāṣṭra—" || 1 ||
Likewise, his beloved wife, named Kṣemaṃkarī, will be born as a beautiful woman in the palace of the lord of Ānarta.
"O son of a Sūta, relate the entire account to them both; curiosity has arisen in us as we listen to your wonderful narration. (3)
O son of a Sūta, we have heard that Kedāra is on the Himālaya; how did it come to be there? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, O twice-born ones, I shall here proclaim all of this to you exactly as it was previously heard by me from the mouth of my own father.
Formerly, due to the fault of that curse, Takṣaka was born on the surface of the earth as one named Raivata in the palace of the lord of Saurāṣṭra.
A daughter was also born in the house of the lord of Ānarta, and her name became very famous throughout the earth.
O best of Brahmins, her name Kṣemaṅkarī was made manifest through her deed. Formerly, there was a king named Prabhañjana, the lord of Ānarta.

Hostility arose for him with many kings; consequently, O best of the twice-born, the country was depopulated and cattle were forcibly carried away. Battles broke out with his enemies by day and by night.
Then, after a few days had passed, his wife Priyaṃvadā, having bathed after her menses, conceived a meritorious embryo within her own womb.

From the moment that embryo took refuge within her womb, from that time forth security was established for the kingdom as well as for the city. By him, some enemies who were exceedingly difficult to conquer were defeated in battle; likewise, others were slain, while still others entered into a state of friendship.
Then a beautiful daughter was born to her, with eyes as long as lotus petals; by her presence, the lying-in chamber was illuminated even in the darkness of night.
Then that king, filled with satisfaction, celebrated a magnificent festival for her like that for a son, amidst the sounds of singing, instrumental music, and other performances.
O twice-born ones, when the thirteenth day arrived, that king performed for her a fitting naming ceremony in the presence of the Brahmins.
O twice-born ones, because security has arisen through her very presence even while she remains in the womb, she shall therefore be known by the name Kṣemaṅkarī.
Thus well-established, she is said to increase day by day, just as the digit of the moon grows in the courtyard of the sky during the bright fortnight.
Then, at an auspicious time for marriage, the lord of the earth gave her, who had reached the bloom of youth, to Raivata, the sovereign of Saurāṣṭra.
Then a daughter was born to them, renowned by the name Revatī; due to the fault of Bhaṭṭikā’s curse, she became the illustrious wife of Śeṣa.
She who was wedded by the wise Nāga king in the form of Rāma became possessed of sons and grandsons, and grew proud with the intoxication of her good fortune.
Yet, despite their efforts, no son was born from them to perpetuate the lineage in any way; O best of Brahmins, because of this, great sorrow arose even at the end of their lives.
Then, having entrusted the entire kingdom without exception to the group of ministers for the sake of their sons, they have come here for the purpose of performing ascetic penance.
Then, having returned to their own hermitage, they remained there with concentrated minds, having installed the goddess Kātyāyanī and becoming intent upon her worship.
By her, who observes the vow of a maiden, the fierce great asura named Mahiṣa was slain on that great mountain Vindhya.
Then, being pleased, she gave them a son who increased their lineage, known by the name Kṣemajit, who was capable of destroying the opposing side.
Then, having regained his own kingdom, that lord of the earth once again caused his son to prosper, filled with great joy.
When that son of Kṣemajit had reached youth, he installed him in the kingdom and then returned once more to his own abode.
O best of the twice-born, this is that very field of Hāṭakeśvara; having abandoned everything else as well as his other attendants, he remained there together with his wife.
There he established a linga of the trident-bearing God, and then, with a concentrated mind, he constructed a captivating temple.
O best of the twice-born, it is called Raivateśvara; by the mere sight of it, all embodied beings are freed from every sin.
In that field where Durgā had previously been installed by the king, she, endowed with faith, constructed a temple for her, bestowing security.
From that time forth, she too is celebrated by the name Kṣemaṃkarī; she who was also called Kātyāyanī is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
O best of the twice-born, whoever beholds her on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra shall always attain their desired success.
All this has been narrated to you—the description of Raivateśvara and the power of Kṣemaṅkarī, which destroys all sins. (34)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Kṣemaṃkarī and Raivateśvara Origin Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 118.

The sages said: "O son of Sūta, you have mentioned that the goddess Kātyāyanī became the destroyer of Mahiṣa. Tell me how that came to pass. Of what nature was that foremost of Dānavas who assumed the form of a buffalo? Why was he slain by the goddess? Tell me that in detail. (2)
Sūta said: In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the supreme majesty of the Goddess, by the mere hearing of which the destruction of enemies occurs for mortals. (3)
Formerly, there was a Dānava named Mahiṣa, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, who, in the form of a buffalo, had enjoyed the three worlds.
The sages said: O son of a Sūta, was he born with the actual form of a buffalo, or tell us, was he produced by the fault of some curse?

Sūta said: He was indeed born endowed with a beautiful form, with a face like a hundred-petaled lotus, long-armed, broad-necked, and marked with all the auspicious signs; he was named Citrasama and was possessed of splendor and valor.
From his very childhood, he has generally awakened the buffaloes, completely abandoning all other mounts such as horses and the like. (7)
Once, mounted upon a buffalo, that son of Danu set forth; having reached the bank of the Jahnavī, he began slaughtering the water-birds.
Then Durvāsas, the best of sages, established himself in profound meditative absorption on the bank of the Gaṅgā, having arranged an exceedingly high and unsurpassed lotus-seat.
With his mind fixed on the bird, that lord of sages was empty-minded; thus, O twice-born one, he did not see the buffalo trampling him with its hooves due to the force of its speed.

Then, his limbs smeared with blood, he saw the Dānava before him; seeing that he was devoid of even a prostration, he was overcome with anger. Then, taking water in his hand, he spoke to him in fury: "O sinner, because my body has been wounded by the hooves of Mahiṣa..."
"Because you have caused the destruction of my concentration, therefore, O evil-minded one, become a buffalo for as long as you live, endowed with perfect knowledge. (13)
Then that great buffalo was born, possessing a black body, with exceedingly long horns, like another mountain of collyrium.
Then, filled with humility, he sought to propitiate that sage: "O Brahmin, grant me release from this curse; I was ignorant due to my state of childhood. (15)
Then that sage said to him: "My word shall not be in vain; therefore, as long as my life-breaths remain, it shall be so. (16)

"O evil-minded one, you who have reviled me in the form of a buffalo! Having thus abandoned him, that lord of sages went elsewhere to the bank of the Gaṅgā; he too, having quickly departed, spoke to Śukra. || 17 ||
"I have been cursed by Durvāsas for a certain reason and brought to the state of a buffalo; therefore, you must be my refuge. (18)
O best of Brahmins, please devise a plan by your grace so that this former body may be restored and its state as an animal may perish. (19)
Śukra said: His curse cannot be altered in any way by anyone, except by abandoning the one god, Maheśvara.
Therefore, go quickly and propitiate that unsurpassed Liṅga in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
In that regard, O best of Dānavas, success is swiftly attained; even when the Age of Sin has arrived, how much more so in the first age?
Having been addressed thus by Śukra, that Dānava went quickly to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara and thereafter performed penance there.
Having installed the great Liṅga with devotion for the trident-bearing God, he then constructed a temple resembling the peak of Kailāsa.
As that great-souled one remained thus engaged in asceticism, a very long time passed while he persisted in his arduous penance.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, went within the range of his vision and said, "O Dānava, I am well-pleased; choose a boon."
Mahiṣa said: "I have been cursed by Durvāsas and consigned to the state of a buffalo; therefore, by your grace, let this animal condition come to an end for me. (27)
The Blessed Lord said: "His word cannot be made otherwise in any way whatsoever; therefore, I shall provide you with an easy means—listen to it."
Whatever human enjoyments there are, as well as those belonging to the gods and the asuras—all of these shall come and find refuge here within your body. (29)
Since gods and asuras desire a mortal body for the sake of enjoyment, you shall therefore obtain all of them through this physical frame of yours. (37)
Mahiṣa said: "If it be so, O Lord of the gods, that I may obtain enjoyment [of life], then let this body of mine be indeed unslayable, O Master. (31)
O best of gods, [this applies] specifically to the ten classes of divine beings, to humans, to animals, to nāgas, and to birds.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Dānava, there is no embodied being on the surface of the earth who is not subject to death. Therefore, O Lord of Daityas, setting aside one person, choose the rest."
Then, having meditated for a very long time, he spoke to the Bull-bannered Lord: "Except for one woman, there shall be no killing of me by others."
Likewise, in this sacred ford of mine, whatever man performs his bath with faith and without distraction shall thereafter behold you.
O Śaṅkara, by your grace, may he attain complete success that fulfills all desires, as well as the destruction of all calamities and the increase of his splendor. (36)
The Blessed Lord said: "On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having bathed here at your holy ford, he shall thereafter behold my Liṅga with affection."
At that very moment, the afflictions arising from spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and the like, as well as diseases such as fevers and others, shall go to their destruction. || 38 ||
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods then vanished from sight; thereafter, Mahiṣa also departed for his own abode.
Having gone there and summoned all the Dānavas, he then spoke, filled with indignation, while standing in the midst of the assembly.
My father, my paternal uncle, and whatever other ancestors of mine there were—all those Dānavas were slain by the gods, led by Vāsudeva. || 41 ||
Therefore, I shall destroy them, even the gods, in a great battle; for after that, I will indeed seize the sovereignty of the three worlds.
Then those Dānavas said, "This is most appropriate and unsurpassed: this kingdom which Śakra exercises in heaven is ours."
Therefore, go this very day and quickly slay Indra at the head of the battle; then, enjoying celestial pleasures, we shall dwell happily in heaven.
Thus all those Dānavas, having reached a firm decision through counsel, went to the peak of Mount Meru together with their servants, armies, and vehicles.

Then Śakra and the other gods, seeing that force arising from the Dānavas—equipped with various weapons and missiles—arrived suddenly at the gate of their own city, immediately marched out for the sake of battle.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Nāsatyas, the best of physicians; as well as the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, and those who are Siddhas and Vidyādharas. || 47 ||
Then a battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas, who, threatening one another, made death their only point of retreat. 48.
Thus the battle continued in heaven for three years; there, exceedingly vast rivers of blood flowed forth.
On another day, he saw Śakra seated upon Airāvata, with a white parasol being held over his head, surrounded by gods who held divine weapons in their hands.
Then Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, his soul overcome with anger, attained great speed and rushed directly toward him.
Then, with his two extremely sharp horns, he pierced the elephant Airāvaṇa in the heart; thereupon, the elephant let out a most dreadful cry.
Then, turning his face away and intent on flight, he rushed with speed toward the city where Amarāvatī is located.
Though his frontal globes were repeatedly wounded by blows from the elephant goad and though he was restrained by the mahout, he did not stop in any way whatsoever.
Then the thousand-eyed one, beholding the arrogant Mahisha and the Daityas roaring with shouts, slapping their arms, and other such gestures, spoke: || 55 ||
"O Daitya, do not think that the lord of the thirty gods has perished; this serpent, rendered helpless by my power, is fleeing from the battlefield. (56)
Therefore, wait for a moment while I mount my excellent chariot and destroy your pride by striking you down with sharpened arrows. (57)
In the meantime, Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, arrived with a chariot yoked to ten thousand horses possessing the speed of the wind.
Then those horses, struck by Mātali with the goad, galloped forward as if leaping into the sky. || 59 ||
Then, having quickly strung his bow, the subduer of Pāka covered the Dānava with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, regaining his momentum and once again overwhelmed by rage, he rushed with speed toward where the lord of the gods was located.
Then, becoming enraged, he repeatedly brandished his horns and, employing great speed, tore apart those fine horses of his.
Then those horses, terrified and with wounded chests, their entire bodies drenched in blood, followed the path of Airāvaṇa.
Then, seeing Śakra’s chariot turned back, all those best of gods fled in fear, taking to his path.
Then all the Dānavas, seeing the gods broken in battle, released a shower of weapons while roaring like clouds.
In the meantime, night arrived, shrouded in darkness; nothing there came within the range of anyone's vision.
Then all the Dānavas, having withdrawn from the battle on all sides, took refuge on a peak of Mount Meru and established a pleasant dwelling there.
Endowed with victory and having attained supreme satisfaction, they recounted stories arising from the battle, describing exactly how that combat had occurred.
The gods also, their enthusiasm crushed and their bodies mangled by blows, gathered together with Bṛhaspati at their head and held a consultation among themselves.
Now our army has been turned away by the Dānavas; it is shattered, utterly dispirited, and incapable of the work of battle. (70)
Therefore, having abandoned this, we shall enter the city Amarāvatī, where there is no fear born of Dānavas, even in the abode of Brahmā.
Having thus made this resolution, all the gods, together with Indra, then departed for the world of Brahmā, leaving the city of Śakra empty.
Then, having risen in the morning, those Dānavas, filled with great joy, saw that Śakra’s city was empty and entered it immediately thereafter.
Then, having installed the Daitya Mahiṣa in the position of Śakra, they bowed down filled with satisfaction and held a great festival.
They took the sacrificial portions of all the inhabitants of heaven, as well as those deities who were favored by the gods in all their respective abodes.
Sūta said: Thus were Śakra and the other gods defeated by Mahiṣa on the field of battle; thereafter, he ruled the kingdom even over the three worlds.
Whatever essence he perceives within the three worlds—elephants, horses, chariots, steeds, and so forth—that asura seizes it all.
As he was thus proceeding, the gods, together with Indra, assembled for the purpose of slaying him and held a discussion filled with distress.
In the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived; he witnessed that entire, most formidable legal proceeding concerning Mahiṣa.
Then he related to them in full detail everything concerning his extensive activities and the great oppression he had caused to the three worlds.
Then, upon hearing those words of Nārada arising from such talk of the world, their great anger increased even further.
The heat born of their anger issued forth through the portals of their mouths, by which the entire circle of the quarters was instantly rendered turbid.

In the meantime, Kārttikeya arrived there and asked: "O Sage, what indeed is this cause of the gods' anger, by which the entire circle of the quarters has fallen into such turbidity? Nārada said: "O Skanda, I have just now related to you the news of how the three worlds have been brought under control by all these Dānavas, who are intoxicated with pride."

Neither a jewel of a woman nor a jewel of a horse remained in anyone's house; seeing them, those irresistible ones, fierce with intoxication, would seize them and release them [only after taking what they desired].
Having heard that, a special indignation arose within Kārttikeya, just as anger had previously come upon the gods through their mouths. || 11 ||
In the meantime, at the conclusion of his anger, a beautiful maiden was born, endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of divine luster.
Because that girl was born here from the mingling of Kārttikeya’s anger with the anger of the gods, she is therefore known as Kātyāyanī.
Then the Lord of the Thirty-three gave her the thunderbolt as a weapon; Skanda gave her a spear with an exceedingly sharp point, and the god Janārdana gave her a bow.
Mahādeva took the trident, Varuṇa himself took the noose, Āditya took white arrows, and Candramas took an excellent shield.
Nirṛti, being pleased, [gave] a sword, and Hutāśana a firebrand; Vāyu gave a sharp dagger, and likewise Dhanada a mace.
O best of the twice-born, having thus beheld those twelve weapons, the fierce Lord of the Pretas took up his staff for the slaughter of the enemies of the gods.
Then Kātyāyanī assumed twelve arms and swiftly seized those divine weapons of the gods.
Then, with the hair on his body bristling with joy, he spoke to them all: "O best of the gods, tell me without delay the purpose for which you have been created."
"I shall perform every task for you; there is no doubt in this. The gods said: "The fierce Dānava Mahiṣa has now arisen here. (20)
"You are invulnerable to all beings, especially to humans; with the exception of one woman, you were created by us for that reason. (21)
Therefore, go now to that best of mountains called Vindhya; perform there fierce penance, by which your splendor shall increase.
"Therefore, once we recognize you as one endowed with splendor, we ourselves shall take the lead and wage war against that evil-minded one. (23)
Then, consumed by your weapon, he shall go to his death; and we, having slain our enemy, shall attain the sovereignty of the gods.

Sūta said: Having heard those words of the gods, that Supreme Goddess then spoke: "O gods, quickly provide me with some vehicle. Thereupon Gaurī gave a lion with a distorted face for the purpose of transport; mounting it, she then set out toward the Vindhya mountain.
Having ascended one of its peaks, which was delightful, endowed with the finest trees, strewn with fruits and flowers, and adorned with bowers of creepers; || 3 ||
Then that virtuous woman, devoted to rigorous vows, performed austerities, restraining her own group of senses while meditating upon Maheśvara.
O twice-born ones, in whatever measure her asceticism increased, in that same measure her beauty and luster grew within her body.

In the meantime, the servants of the lord of the Daityas arrived there; seeing her endowed with the vow and possessing an exceedingly wonderful form, they went and spoke to their wicked master, Mahiṣa.

The spies said: "While wandering upon the surface of the earth, we have today seen on the Vindhya mountain an unprecedented young maiden, endowed with twelve arms, bearing various radiant weapons, and with her limbs covered by a shield."
Neither among goddesses, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor Naga maidens have we ever before seen a woman of such form and shapely hips.
O Lord, we do not know for what purpose that illustrious woman performed her penance—whether out of a desire for heaven, a desire for wealth, or a desire for a husband.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, fell under the power of Kāmadeva at that very moment, even from merely hearing them.
Then, placing them at his front and accompanied by a great army, he went, filled with curiosity, to where that maiden was staying.
Just as a foolish jackal, seeking his own death, [approached] a lioness who was sleeping in the forest, fully trusting and entirely free from fear.
O excellent twice-born ones, from the mere sight of her, that foremost of Dānavas was struck by the arrows of Kāma at that very moment.
Then, standing alone before her and having drawn his army to a great distance, he, infatuated by her beauty, spoke these pleasing words: (14)
"O lady of lovely smiles, this vow of yours is contrary to youth; therefore, abandon it and become the mistress of the three worlds. (15)
For I am the lord of the Dānavas named Mahiṣa, as you have likely heard, by whom the thousand-eyed Indra was utterly defeated in single combat.
The entire three worlds are now under my control; therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, become my most beloved wife.
I have another thousand very beautiful wives; all of them shall now serve you today.
And I too, O lady of beautiful hips, having bestowed all my wealth upon you, shall remain entirely devoted to the state of your servant.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the Supreme Goddess then spoke to him, rebuking him with eyes bloodshot with anger.
"Shame, shame on you, O man of sinful conduct! Why do you speak thus to me, whose mind and soul are struck by lust, while I am observing the vow of a maiden? (2)
I have been created by the supreme gods for the purpose of slaying you; therefore, I shall destroy you, remembering that which is cherished in your heart.
Mahiṣa said: "If it be so, O lady of beautiful hips, then the maiden would be fit [for this], since she should be sought after by all living beings here. (23)
O lady of excellent complexion, dharma and austerity are practiced for the sake of heaven, so that one may enjoy those pleasures which are both divine and human. (24)
Therefore, O beautiful one, give yourself to me by the Gāndharva rite of marriage, since that is proclaimed to be the foremost among all others. (25)
As he was speaking thus, that goddess, overcome with rage, instantly discharged an arrow toward the interior of his mouth.
He entered his mouth like a serpent entering an anthill; then, pierced by those arrows from every direction, he roared from within the cavity of the mouth.
He shed copious blood like a mountain of red chalk; then, his soul overcome with anger, he slowly turned back.

Hurriedly taking refuge in his own army, and brought under the sway of passion, he said to all the soldiers: "Let this wicked woman be seized, so that she does not give up her life, though shattered by blows. (29)
"She will undoubtedly become my beloved wife, provided she does not meet her death by the falling of a weapon. (30)
Thus addressed by him, the Dānavas, intoxicated with the frenzy of battle, rushed toward her, discharging sharpened arrows.
