In the meantime, the goddess saw them standing there, having resolved to fight and threatening her again and again. || 32 ||
Then, with ease, the goddess released sharp, great arrows and instantly struck them all in their vital organs.
Then the Daityas and Dānavas were struck down by sharp arrows; some met their death, while others fled hither and thither.
Then, beholding his army broken by her in battle, the Daitya, overcome with rage, personally rushed toward her.
Dealing hundreds of thousands of blows with his horns and repeatedly letting out a fierce roar like an autumnal cloud, he [attacked]. (36)
In the meantime, the Goddess let out a loud, boisterous laugh; the entire expanse of the three worlds was filled with that sound.
Thus, as she was laughing, Pulindas, Śabaras, Mlecchas, and other forest-dwellers emerged from the interior of her mouth. (38)
Śakas and Yavanas by the hundreds, assuming human forms, with their bodies covered in armor like other messengers of Yama. (39)
"O Goddess, tell us who created us on this earth; by what purpose, O fair-faced one, is everything being accomplished so swiftly? (4)
The Goddess said: "By my command, slay these very wicked soldiers who are arrogant in their strength, swiftly and according to your desire."
Then, having heard those words, they—brandishing their swords and bows and leaping with joy—rushed toward the army of the Daityas, assuming great speed.
Then a great and most terrible battle broke out among them; there, no one anywhere could distinguish between their own side and the enemy.
Then all those Dānavas were broken by the warriors born of the Goddess; others were slain, while still others were rendered mangled by their blows.
Then, seeing his army broken, Mahiṣa, overwhelmed with rage, spoke to the Goddess in words of harsh syllables out of anger.
"O sinful woman, thinking that you were a female, I did not slay you in battle today; therefore, behold my blow, for you shall understand the truth and not otherwise. (46)
Having spoken thus, he of great speed hurled especially fierce blows with his two tusks, threatening him again and again.
Then, seeing that Dānava who had come close to her, the goddess swiftly mounted him on his back out of anger.
Then that Daitya, having taken to the path of the sky, pierced by the palm of the back [of the hand] and drenched in a flood of blood, cried out. (49)
In the meantime, that lion born of Jyotis seized her by the hindquarters with his sharpened tips of fangs out of rage.
Then the Dānava, having become motionless and being trampled by the foot, let out terrible cries, unable to move even a single step.
In the meantime, all the gods, including Indra, arrived and, remaining in the sky, spoke to the goddess while filled with joy.
"O Goddess of the Gods, quickly sever the head of this [demon] with this sharp sword before he escapes elsewhere. (53)
Hearing their words, the queen, filled with rage, drew her sword and struck at his exceedingly thick neck.
By that stroke of the sword, the demon's neck, though thick and tough, was split in two, thereby bestowing satisfaction upon the inhabitants of heaven.

Resembling twelve suns, holding a shield and a sword within his mouth, he then threatened that great goddess as she raised her sword; brandishing that sword, which was like the rising sun, against her body.
Then, having seized him by the hair, just as he was about to hurl a blow that would have destroyed his body, that Dānava spoke: || 57 ||
The Dānava said: Victory, O Goddess! Victory, O inconceivable one! Victory, O Sovereign of all the gods! Victory, O omnipresent Goddess! Victory, O beloved of all people! || 58 ||
Victory to you, O eternal bestower of desires! Victory to you, O beauty of the three worlds! Victory to you, who are intent on protecting the three worlds and are truly fearless from any quarter! 59.

Victory to you, O Goddess who brings joy; victory to you, O destroyer of the Daityas! Victory to you, O beloved who cuts away affliction; victory to you, who bestows delusion upon those devoid of devotion!
You are creation; you are the supreme goddess; you are Lakṣmī; you are Sarasvatī; you are Svāhā; you are Svadhā; you are contentment, nourishment, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.
Therefore, show me favor; protect my life and have compassion for me, who am bowed down before you, utterly wretched, and especially destitute. (62)
"I, the powerful son of Hiraṇyākṣa, was cursed by Durvāsas and reduced to the state of a buffalo; I have been liberated by you, O Goddess. (63)
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, the pride born of being a Dānava has been released by me today; I shall now enter into the state of your servant.
Victory to you, O omnipresent Goddess, destroyer of all that is evil! 65.
Having heard those piteous words of his, that queen of the gods, overcome with compassion, then spoke these words to the deities stationed in the sky.
"What shall I do? O gods, compassion has arisen within me toward him; therefore, I will not kill this Dānava who speaks so piteously. (67)
Even if he turns his back, or wields a sword as a weapon, or cries out "I am yours," or even if he is the slayer of my father—I would not kill such an enemy in battle. (68)
The gods said: "O Goddess of the gods, if you do not destroy this lowest of Dānavas, he will annihilate the entire triple world, including all that is mobile and immobile. (69)
All this exertion of ours will likewise be in vain; so too will all your own suffering, born from your very birth. (70)
The Goddess said: "O immortals, I will not kill him, nor will I abandon him; having seized him by the hair, I shall hold him for all time. (71)
The gods said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! The words spoken by you are fitting. Indeed, this is what ought to be done at such a time, O Goddess of the thirty deities."
Now, in the world of mortals, you have assumed this form—fierce, with a weapon raised in hand, seated upon a buffalo. (73)
He who shall worship you while you are established in this form will obtain supreme honor, which is difficult even for the immortals to attain. (74)
Through union with him, you shall become renowned as Vindhyavāsinī; what is the use of speaking much to you? Listen to my words in brief.
O Goddess, our supreme truth, which brings welfare to all the worlds, shall become the power of the kings dependent upon you.
When the time for battle has arisen, there is no doubt that whichever man shall undertake either departure or entry [into this place] will become a devotee. (77)

Having remembered you, prostrated before you, and especially having worshipped you, success shall always be attained by him in all undertakings; this is true even for a coward, let alone for a brave warrior. 78.
On the ninth day or the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, whichever mortal, endowed with true devotion, shall worship you; || 79 ||
O beautiful goddess, for as long as a full year, he shall indeed have no disease, no fear, and no defeat; nor shall there be untimely death, nor any calamity arising from thieves and the like.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to that goddess, those gods, filled with joy and permitted by her, departed for their own city, Amarāvatī.
Having gone there and after a long time regained his own kingdom, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, joyfully protected the three worlds, whose hosts of enemies had been destroyed.
Thereafter, all the worlds became endowed with happiness; furthermore, the gods in the three worlds once again became partakers of their sacrificial shares.
Thereafter, that goddess attained renown throughout the three worlds, especially in all sacred fields, holy fords, and shrines.
In the meantime, a king named Suratha was born; by him, with true devotion, this very sacred field (kṣetra) was established. || 85 ||
The man who beholds her with true devotion on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra shall, for the duration of a year, have his purpose fulfilled; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Kātyāyanī and the Defeat of Mahiṣāsura," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 121.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, all this that I was asked by you has been narrated—how that foremost of the Danus, named Mahiṣa, was slain by the Goddess.
Now I shall proclaim a meritorious narrative originating from Kedāra that destroys all sins; listen to it with concentrated minds.
The sages said: "O Sūta, it is heard that Kedāra is located at Gaṅgādvāra on the Himālaya; how did he come to be here? Tell us everything in detail."
Sūta said: This is true; the Lord Svayambhū himself resides on that mountain. However, O twice-born ones, the deity dwells there for only eight months.
The Lord should reside there as long as the summer and the rainy seasons last; however, during the cold season, he always remains in this sacred field.
The sages said: O son of a Sūta, tell us what that deed is by which one may dwell for four months in the Himālaya region, just as one does for eight [months] elsewhere? 6.
Sūta said: Formerly, at the beginning of the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, there was a Daitya of great strength, Hiraṇyākṣa, who possessed great splendor and was endowed with the power of asceticism.
Indeed, this entire world was pervaded by them after they had ousted the lord of the gods; and by their power and prowess, the sacrificial portions of the deities were seized.
Then Śakra, together with the gods, took refuge at Gaṅgādvāra; deprived of the glory of his kingdom and afflicted by great sorrow, he performed penance.
As that great-souled one was thus performing intense austerity, [the Earth], assuming the form of a buffalo, emerged from the surface of the earth.
Then Mahādeva himself spoke to Śakra: "O best of gods, tell me everything quickly; O Vāsava, by means of this form, [I shall act] against all the Daityas."

Indra said: "O Lord, destroy these five: the great Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, Subāhu, Vakra, Kandhara, and Triśṛṅga, as well as Lohitākṣa. When these are slain, all the Dānavas will undoubtedly be destroyed."

"What is the use of other wretched, ruined ones, by whom nothing at all can be accomplished here? Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One quickly went to where that chief of the Dānavas, the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa, was located.
Then, seeing from afar that buffalo, who resembled a mountain and was approaching with a fierce form, all those Dānavas [prepared for battle] on every side.
Then others struck them with stones and clubs, while still others, arrogant in their strength, let out lion-roars and slapped their arms.
Then, disregarding them, the Lord effortlessly delivered a blow where that lord of the Dānavas resided together with his four ministers.
Then, as he rushed forward brandishing a weapon, [the boar] sent him to the abode of Yama with a blow of his tusk.
Having slain those ministers, headed by Subāhu, he then struck them down even while being assailed on all sides by his enemies, the Dānavas.
Not even a weapon discharged with great effort by skilled strikers ever struck his body in any way. (19)
Having thus slain those five principal Daityas, Maheśvara went once more to that place where Śakra was stationed; then, with a joyful soul, he spoke to Śakra, who was endowed with ascetic merit.
The five Dānavas whom you mentioned have been slain by me; therefore, once again exercise your sovereignty over the three worlds.
O Lord of Gods, ask for another desired boon from me, so that I may go to the peak of Kailāsa with all haste.
Indra said: "O Śaṅkara, remain here in this very form for the sake of protecting the three worlds, and for the sake of dharma and auspiciousness. (23)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Śakra, this form was indeed assumed by me for the sake of slaying him; since he was incapable of being slain by any other living beings, he has been killed by me."
Therefore, O best of gods, I shall remain right here according to your word; in this very form, I shall be the bestower of liberation upon all embodied beings.
Having spoken thus, Virūpākṣa then fashioned a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that resembled pure crystal and was as pleasing as delicious milk.
Then the Blessed One, the destroyer of Tripura, spoke to the Lord of the Gods in a voice as deep as a thundercloud, while all the gods were listening.
Whoever, having become pure upon seeing me, beholds this pool, and then drinks the water three times—first with the left hand, then with the right, and finally with both hands.
With his two hands, that man shall surely deliver three generations of his lineage—even those of sinful conduct who are situated in hell. (294)
With the left hand [support] the maternal side, and with the right the paternal side; then, with both hands, support yourself according to my word.
Indra said: "O Bull-vehicled One, I shall come daily from heaven to worship you while you remain here, and likewise I shall drink the water. (31)
"What shall I maintain that has been spoken by you in the form of a buffalo? Therefore, you shall become famous by the name Kedāra. (32)
The Blessed Lord said: "If you do this, O Śakra, then there shall be no fear of the Daityas for you; moreover, all supreme splendor shall be established within your body. (33)
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed one then had an excellent palace constructed for that purpose—a beautiful, well-lit, and enchanting edifice.
Then, having bowed to that god and taken leave of him, he departed for his own abode situated upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Then, having come daily from heaven, he, being composed and filled with great devotion, performed worship for the trident-bearing Lord Kedāra.
Having drunk the mantra-water three times, O best of Brahmins, he departed; then, after some time, he arrived there once more. (37)
In that time, the entire mountain peak was filled with snow; so too were that pool and the deity, together with his temple.
Then, his soul overwhelmed with sorrow yet endowed with supreme devotion, he prostrated himself toward that direction and returned to his own home.
Thus, as he was coming along, four months passed for him, whose mind was filled with the desire to see Mahādeva and who had not yet beheld Him.
Then, O brahmins, when the summer season had arrived again at the Himalaya, that god appeared within the range of vision, established in that very form.
Then, having performed the worship arising from the Cāturmāsya period with great devotion, he engaged in singing, instrumental music, and other such offerings before him.
Then the Lord, the Blessed One, the Destroyer of Tripura, having appeared before him, beheld that faith of the cowherd and spoke.
"I am well-pleased, O Lord of Gods, by this exclusive devotion of yours; therefore, ask for whatever desire resides in your heart, and I shall grant it. (44)
Śakra said: "By your grace, this unsurpassed sovereignty has been attained by me; whatever exists in the three worlds, all that is situated within my home. (45)
Therefore, O Bull-bannered One, if you grant me your favor, or if you are pleased and wish to bestow a boon, then fulfill this request of mine. (46)
"O Lord of the Gods, I have heard that this mountain remains accessible for eight months, as long as the sun remains situated in Pisces. (47)
Thereafter, it becomes inaccessible, shrouded by a flood of snow, for as long as four months until the sun enters Aquarius.
O Destroyer of Tripura, O Lord of the Gods, he is born as one who is unapproachable even for me; how much more so for humans and others of feeble strength? (49)

Therefore, O Lord of the Thirty-three, whether in heaven, in the netherworld, or in the mortal realm, remain in this form for four months, so that there may be no violation of my vow, O Lord of the Gods.
Sūta said: Then the God, having meditated for a long time, attained supreme satisfaction and spoke to the slayer of Bala with a voice like the roar of clouds.
"O Thousand-eyed One, there exists upon the surface of the earth a field belonging to us in the region of Ānarta, known by the name Hāṭakeśvara. (52)
There, O Vāsava, at your word, I shall undoubtedly remain for all time from the sun being in Scorpio until the end of Aquarius. (53)
Therefore, go there quickly, construct an excellent palace, and having installed my image, perform worship as is appropriate, so that I may maintain my own splendor there for your sake.
Sūta said: Having heard this from the trident-bearing God of gods, the thousand-eyed Indra went there and performed that which had been spoken by the Lord.
Then, having constructed a palace and installed the form of the Trident-bearer, he fashioned a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of the same shape, filled with clear water.
Then, having bathed in the pool, he worshipped [the deity] with flowers, incense, and unguents, and drank the water three times as he had done before.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, that Blessed One, having been propitiated there by Śakra in the past, arrived here from the most beautiful Himālaya mountain.
That mortal who would properly worship Him for four months during the onset of snowfall attains Śiva. (59)
Even at other times, the wise person who performs worship with true devotion shall wash away their sins from birth until the end of death.
In that regard, the wise, who are experts in all the scriptures, praise song and various kinds of dance before the God. (61)
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by Nārada, the celestial sage; that I shall proclaim to you, O best of Brahmins—let it be heard.
Having drunk the water at Kedāra and offered the funeral cake at Gayā, and then having attained the knowledge of Brahman, there is no rebirth.
O best of Brahmins, this entire account of the origin of Kedāra has been narrated to you—a narrative that destroys all sins.

O Brahmins, that man who hears this correctly, or recites it, or causes it to be heard before him—it is the destroyer of all sins; at that very moment, he is liberated from the multitude of his misdeeds against Kedāra.
Sūta said: Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, there is another unsurpassed holy site there called Śuklatīrtha, which even today is indicated by white Darbha grass.
Formerly, in the city of Camatkārapura, there was a certain washerman named Śuddhaka, skilled in extracting splinters, who was accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
He was established as the foremost among all washermen, and he performed the cleaning of garments for the most eminent Brahmins. (3)
Then, after some time, being absorbed in meditation, he cast the garment of the foremost of Brahmins into a vat of indigo; only after a long while did he become aware of it.
Then, with a dejected mind and overwhelmed by fear, he summoned his wife and sons and spoke these words to them in private.
Many priceless, fine garments belonging to the high-souled Brahmins were, out of delusion, thrown into the midst of indigo dye.
"They will undoubtedly carry out acts such as killing and binding; therefore, let us depart for another place, taking this night with us."
O best of the twice-born, having thus made his resolve and taking what was essential from his home, he set out together with his wife, fleeing in all directions.
Then his daughter went to her own friend, the daughter of a fisherman, and said: "O blessed lady, may you forgive whatever ill deed I have committed."
Whether out of ignorance or knowledge, while playing with you—whether out of affection, the nature of childhood, anger, or great jealousy—(10)
Then, having heard this suddenly, her eyes clouded with tears, she said: "What is this, O blessed lady, that you speak to me in such a manner?"
The friend said: "O fair-eyed one, my father has, through a lapse of memory, cast into the Nīlā river the highly precious garments belonging to the brahmins. (12)
"Having learned of this at dawn, they will inflict a terrible punishment. Having resolved his mind thus, my father has now set out. (13)
"O blameless one, I have come into your presence for the sake of seeing you; having been permitted by you, I shall depart, so please release me. (14)
Then, having heard those words, she, with a cheerful countenance, said: "If it be so, O lotus-eyed one, you shall not go anywhere. (15)
"Go quickly and restrain our father, saying, 'Do not go. To the northeast of this place, there is a body of water. (16)
Once, my father cast into it a net made of extremely black hair, which immediately turned white.
Then, filled with wonder, he himself bathed out of curiosity; as soon as he attained whiteness, he became one who bore such a black body.
With his hair suddenly turned pure white, he instantly caused detachment in women; from that time forward, no one has gone there without first learning of it.
Therefore, O auspicious one, let him quickly wash his garments right there; thus, O beautiful lady, your father shall attain supreme purification.
Then, having gone quickly, that virtuous woman, with a joyful countenance, related those words of her father to him in haste.
"My friend has instructed me that not far away there is a body of water; everything else than white turns to whiteness when thrown therein. (22)
Therefore, having gone there to that body of water at dawn, wash these garments; they will undoubtedly attain whiteness. (23)
The washerman said: "O daughter, this will not come to pass—that the destruction of the indigo clinging to the cloth should occur; for so it has been declared by the ancients. (24)
The fool, the woman, and the crab are bound by the same single fetter as diamond-paste; likewise, the fish, the indigo-dyer, and the drunkard are held by that same bond. (25)
The maiden said: "First, you must come there, taking care to bring the garments; for they shall attain purification from the water, and only then should you indeed return."
Furthermore, it is firmly established in my heart that everyone must either go back to the temple or depart from that place to some other region.
Having heard those words of hers, her kinsmen and servants repeatedly exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and departed that very night.
Placing the daughter of the fisherman at their head, those best of the twice-born, endowed with their own wealth, fell into a state of great uncertainty. (29)
Then that fisherman’s daughter showed him a body of water, overgrown with many creepers and difficult for embodied beings to enter.
Then, O twice-born ones, that washerman, having taken all the garments there, entered that water and indeed began to wash them.
Then, at that very moment, those garments which had been dark-blue in luster became entirely crystal-clear in luster at that very same instant.
Then, filled with satisfaction, he exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and having embraced his daughter, he spoke respectfully to the fisherman's daughter.
We present fine garments to the best of the twice-born in due order.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having gone to his own home, he joyfully bestowed all those garments in their proper order.
Then those brahmins, seeing that purification brought about by the garment and seeing the washerman thus turned white, were filled with wonder.
They asked: "What is this wonderful phenomenon, arising from the garments and hair, that has come into being so beyond compare? Tell us, if you deem it right. (37)
The washerman said: "O Brahmins, these fine garments were cast by me into the indigo vat out of delusion, and they have been completely ruined. (38)
Then, O best of Brahmins, accompanied by his family, he set out at the onset of night toward the edge of the horizon, overcome by a great fear.
Then this daughter of ours, afflicted by great sorrow and longing to see her again, went to her own friend, the daughter of the fisherman. (40)
Having understood through her all my intention, which was caused by my suffering, she then showed me her own lake as she stood before me.
As soon as these garments were thrown into it, they instantly acquired such a color; indeed, this is a cause for wonder.
Likewise, as soon as I had bathed there, my black hair instantly attained a state of supreme whiteness; this has been clearly explained by me. (43)
Having heard this, those brahmins, filled with curiosity, immediately scattered that grain and went there for the purpose of testing him.
The many black substances, such as hair and so forth, by the thousands—all of them attain whiteness, having abandoned their dark color. (45)
Then those who were aged, distinguished by their white hair, bathed with faith, as did the righteous youths. (46)
Then, having attained purity and being endowed with splendor and vigor, they come to exist through its power and proceed to the supreme goal. || 47 ||
Then Vāsava, having seen that Śuklatīrtha which grants liberation, filled it with dust out of fear arising from human beings.
Even today, whatever grows there, even grass and the like, all of it attains whiteness through the power of that water.
There, one who is endowed with faith performs a śrāddha ceremony using kuśa grass grown on that spot.
With those very white [flowers], one may cause all the ancestors, even those who have gone to hell, to cross over.
Having applied the clay arising from that sacred ford to his body, that best of men performs a bath and obtains the fruit of all sacred fords.
O Brahmins, the man who with devotion performs the libation (tarpaṇa) using those darbha grasses and wild sesame seeds pleases his ancestors.
O best of the twice-born, the fruit that is obtained through the horse sacrifice is likewise attained here by performing the Gayā-śrāddha and by the release of a cow known as Nīla.
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, how did Śuklatīrtha come to be there? Describe it to us in detail, for our curiosity is great. (54)
Sūta said: Śvetadvīpa was brought by the all-powerful Viṣṇu to that sacred field, out of fear of the Kali age, so that its whiteness might not be lost.
O best of the twice-born, even Śvetadvīpa does not turn dark when touched by the Kali age; therefore, he was established there.

Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another excellent holy place there called Mukhāra, where those preeminent sages and brahmins came together with the thief. It was by its power that the thief attained perfection and became renowned as Vālmīki, the author of the Rāmāyaṇa.
Formerly, in Camatkārapura, there was a Brahmin named Lohajaṅgha, born of the lineage of Māṇḍavya, who was devoted to his father and mother.
He had one wife who was dearer to him than his own life; she was devoted to her husband, her very life was her husband, and she delighted in what was pleasing and beneficial to him.
Then, as he remained there, devoted to the practice of Brahman, a very long time passed while he was intent upon his father and mother.
Once, the blessed Śakra did not send rain upon the surface of the earth for as long as twelve years throughout the entire region of Ānarta.
Thereupon, O best of the twice-born, Lohajaṅgha fell into great distress; he obtained no alms anywhere, nor did he receive anything by way of a gift.
Then, seeing both his parents afflicted by hunger, he was overcome with great sorrow and thought of his wife.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How might I obtain a vision of these two elders, and especially of my wife? (9)
Then, filled with sorrow, he went into the forest for the sake of fruit; yet he obtained nothing at all, for all the trees were withered.

Then he saw an old woman accompanied by a small amount of grain, traveling along while overcome by great exhaustion. Thereupon, taking that grain and her clothes, that merciless man went home delighted and presented it to his parents.
Although he had thus acquired his mark [of skill] in the work of bandits, he nevertheless constantly committed theft and thereby sustained his own family.
Even when a time of plenty arrived, he performed no other work; having abandoned the livelihood of a Brahmin, he practiced the act of theft.
Then, after some time had passed, on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, the seven seers—Marīci and the other twice-born ones—arrived there.
Then, seeing them in a secluded place, filled with malice and anger, he raised his staff and said with force, "Stay! (16)
Baring his three-pronged frown, he rushed forward with haste, threatening them with harsh words as if striking them.
Then those sages, seeing him resembling a messenger of Yama yet endowed with a sacred thread, spoke to him, filled with compassion.
The sages said: "Aha! You are a Brāhmaṇa; why then do you perform this most despicable deed? Indeed, O fool, this action is the work of a Mleccha."
We are peaceful sages who have renounced all possessions; we do not accept even the slightest thing from you that stands near us.
Lohajaṅgha said: "O twice-born ones, please quickly give me these white rags, as well as bark garments, antelope skins, and sandals. (21)
If not, then by striking down his existence with the vajra-like mace, you will undoubtedly cause him to reach the abode of the King of Dharma.
The sages said: "O thief, we shall give you everything; however, tell us the report about which we ask out of curiosity. (23)
"For what purpose do you commit theft? You are a Brahmin, yet you are utterly merciless. Have you been overcome by terrible vices, or are you perhaps a hunter disguised as a twice-born? (24)
Lohajaṅgha said: "This act arising from theft was not done for my own pleasure; know that it was for the sake of my family. This is dharma, there is no doubt. (25)
My parents are established in old age, as is my devoted wife, who is skilled in the duties of the household. (26)
Whatever I acquire by means of this work, all of that is surely for his sake; I swear this truly upon my own soul. (27)
Therefore, abandon all your wealth before it is too late; what is the use of these vain words? For this hand of mine is throbbing only to strike you down.
The sages said: "If it is so, O thief, then go and ask your family: 'Will you become a sharer in my portion of sin, or not? (29)
If even a portion of your sin goes to me through this sharing, then do it; otherwise, O wicked one, it will become unbearable for you.
"O evil-minded one, for you who have fallen into this terrible Raurava hell, we speak these words without doubt, regarding you as a Brāhmaṇa. (31)
Filled with compassion, they stayed with us even though Sudarśana had been born; for from the sight of sages whose minds are restrained, auspiciousness surely arises. (32)
One person commits the sins, while the multitude enjoys the fruit; those who enjoy are liberated, but the doer is smeared with the fault.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, the thief was somewhat filled with fear: "What these men have spoken is true; there is no doubt about it. (34)
Therefore, having gone there, I shall ask my own family; if they should grant me a share, I will indeed take on a portion of the sin.
"If they do not accept this task, or if I must abandon it, a great fear has now arisen in my mind. (36)
O lords of sages, if you do not go elsewhere, but instead become intent on flight and return to your own homes; || 37 ||
I ask my circle of dependents, and especially your word: if my family will take upon themselves a share of that sin, then I shall accept whatever is at your disposal. (38)
Or else, he will forbid this sin of mine; then I shall undoubtedly abandon all of you along with your retinues.
Then, having made oaths for the sake of providing him with assurance, and having shown compassion toward him, they released him to go home.
He too, having gone there, approached his own father and asked: "Listen, O father, to our words, and then give us your reply. (41)
Having committed thousands of forbidden acts such as theft and the like, I constantly nourish you; do you have a share in that, or not? (42)
Tell me, who am a sinner and am asking you, the truth regarding this matter; for a doubt has arisen within me, so explain it quickly. (43)
The father said: "O son, in my childhood, I brought you up with an agitated mind; performing both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, I nurtured you with an affectionate heart. (44)
For this reason, moreover, when old age has arrived, you again tend the cow, performing both auspicious and inauspicious deeds. (45)
"O son, not even the slightest portion of either merit or sin belongs to you now, nor does it belong to me. (46)
The action performed by oneself alone is experienced by oneself; whether it be auspicious or sinful, other people are recorded as the experiencers. (47)
Whether you bring food by means of honest labor, by theft, by agriculture, or by trade, no concern arises in me. (48)
Therefore, do not keep this in your heart: "I shall perform a censurable act," for you are the one who partakes of its portion, while we are all merely those who enjoy it. 49.
Sūta said: Having heard these words, with his inner self deeply agitated, he went to his mother and questioned her about that very matter with great earnestness.
Then she also repeated that which had been spoken by his father; O best of the twice-born, it was extraordinary regarding both his auspicious and sinful deeds.
Then, overcome with grief, he went and questioned his wife; she too then spoke of that similar sin committed against her elders.
Then, tormented by grief and filled with remorse, he went to where those ascetics were, even as he continued to reproach himself.
Then, having bowed down to them all and standing with palms joined in reverence, he said: "Depart, depart, O Brahmins; may you forgive me, may you forgive me."
"Since I, having resorted to folly and being utterly deluded by great evil, have reviled you, you should therefore grant me forgiveness today. (55)
"O best of the twice-born, your entire speech was spoken by my two gurus and by my wife; because of that, grief has come upon me. (56)
Therefore, may all you best of sages show me favor by granting instruction, so that I may destroy my sin. (57)
"O best of the twice-born, I have always committed blameworthy deeds—especially against women, the lords of the twice-born, and ascetics. (58)
Whosoever among people are most wretched and incapable of being awakened, all of them have been robbed by me; they shall never be capable [of awakening]. (59)
"By me, who was deluded for the sake of my family and deprived of the company of the virtuous, the very scripture I was studying has today fallen [into place] within my heart. (60)
O best of beings, if I were not to have this audience with you today, I would undoubtedly commit other sins as well. (61)
And among them was a virtuous sage named Pulaha; being of a humorous disposition, he spoke to that best of the twice-born for the sake of causing confusion.
I shall proclaim to you a single, most beautiful mantra; by meditating upon it while reciting it, you will attain eternal perfection.
This mantra, beginning with "jāṭaghoṭa," bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Therefore, O Brahmin, recite this day and night without weariness.
Then you will attain perfection, which is difficult even for the gods to achieve.
Having spoken thus, those brahmins then departed on their pilgrimage; that thief, however, remained right there, devoted to the recitation of prayers.
With a mind focused on nothing else, he then began that recitation; he became established in samādhi, by which means he attained the supreme state.
As that brahmin was thus recollecting that mantra, his body became motionless and he remained steady in his task.
Then, after a long time, O best of Brahmins, that high-souled one, who remained absorbed in meditation, became completely covered by an anthill on all sides.
His mother and father, as well as his wise wife, all fell under the power of death after searching for him with great effort.
And remaining there, that man of great vows was not recognized as having renounced the world; he was liberated from the impressions of saṃsāra through that encounter with the sage. (71)
Then, after some time, those sages arrived again by that same path on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
And the twice-born ones said this: "Tell us that place where there was a meeting with the thief, that fierce robber who wore the disguise of a Brāhmaṇa. (73)
Then they heard from within the anthill the sound of that very same great-souled one reciting the mantra beginning with "jāṭaghoṭe."
Then those blows echoed in every direction upon the ground; thereafter, they saw an anthill, and within it, that thief.
O best of the twice-born, Pulaha informed him of that mantra which he was reciting, as well as its accomplishment, in the form of a joke. (76)

Or rather, this truth has been declared by the teachers who possess the vision of the scriptures: that even a small amount [of practice] brings about accomplishment, because from it, accomplishment is attained. (77)
In regard to a mantra, a sacred ford, a twice-born, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, or a guru—whatever one's conception is, such is the success that comes to pass. (78)
Then, seeing that thief successfully accomplished even by means of a wicked mantra, those brahmins were filled with wonder and especially overcome with compassion.
Then, with substances suitable for concentration, as well as oils and medicinal herbs for that purpose.

O twice-born ones, they crushed his body while he remained long established in samādhi; then, having regained consciousness and looking at them again and again, he, filled with wonder, spoke thus to those sages who were present.

Lohajaṅgha said: "O best of the twice-born, why did you not go away when released by me? I shall not take anything whatsoever belonging to you under any circumstances; since it was for the sake of my family, therefore depart now as you please. (82)

The sages said: "After wandering here in this forest for a long time, we have returned; yet, because you were absorbed in meditative concentration, much time has passed by without being noticed by you. (83)
Those two aged parents of yours, having been released by you, have gone to their destruction; and you, through our grace, have attained supreme perfection. (84)
"Since you have attained supreme perfection while staying within an anthill, you shall therefore become famous in the world by the name Valmīki."
"O twice-born one, because the worlds were formerly robbed by you while stationed here, this sacred site shall thereafter attain fame by the name Mukhāra."
Those twice-born ones who shall perform their ablutions here with faith on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa will wash away the sin arising from acts of theft.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, those brahmins then took leave of the sage; having bowed down to him, they thereafter departed for their desired destination.
He too remained right there, established in austerity, and is remembered as Vālmīki.
Thereafter, he became the most excellent and preeminent among sages; even today, that lord of sages remains there in embodied form.
Whoever worships him with devotion, especially on the eighth day, being fully endowed with right faith, becomes a poet upon this earth.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Mukhārī Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 124.
Sūta said: Thereafter, there is the beautiful and renowned Karṇotpalatīrtha, where a man who bathes properly shall never again suffer separation.
In every way, he was distinguished by his beloved wealth and kinsmen, as well as by his prowess, his righteousness, and especially by his wife.
In former times, there was a lord of the earth known as Satyasandha; born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, he was endowed with every form and virtue.
To that Bahuputra was born a daughter named Karṇotpalā, who was exceedingly beautiful and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 4 ||
Then, on the twelfth day, her father, having consulted repeatedly with the Brahmins, as well as his servants and ministers, gave her a name.
Since this daughter of mine was born from an utpala lotus upon my ear, therefore this most beautiful girl has become known by the name Karṇotpalā.
She was the only one among his many sons, endowed with all auspicious marks; therefore, O best of the twice-born, let her be known by the name Karṇotpalā.
Then, having been given a name, that girl grew day by day, constantly bringing delight like a digit of the moon.
Then, O best of the twice-born, cherished by her kinsmen, she gradually attained youth, passing from hand to hand among them all.
Then, seeing her endowed with youth, that lord of the earth reflected in his mind: "To whom shall I give her?"
"There is no suitor equal to her here upon the surface of the earth, nor in heaven, nor in the netherworld; what should I do now? (11)
Having reflected thus in many ways on that matter, the lord of the earth reached a firm conclusion in his mind: "In this case, the Grandfather (Brahmā) must be consulted."
"Today, that god will impel me toward this suitor; I shall bestow my daughter upon him and certainly not upon anyone else. (13)
Having thus made this resolution, he then took her with him and went to the world of Brahmā to ask for a boon on her behalf.
Then, O best of Brahmins, just as that lord of men reached the world of Brahmā, the twilight belonging to Brahmā arose.
In the meantime, Brahmā, eager for his evening rites, sat down and at that moment entered into a state of meditative absorption.
Satyasandha, too, seeing his grandfather established in meditative absorption, sat down nearby, waiting for the conclusion of that meditation.
Then, having beheld himself within himself, the Great-Grandfather [Brahmā] saw that the eight-petaled lotus had been properly manifested, situated within his heart.
Situated in the center of the pericarp, radiant, multicolored, and exceedingly stable; with his face bathed in tears of bliss and his body marked by horripilation. (19)
Then, having sipped water and washed his feet, he looked in every direction, bowing down before all the inhabitants of the world of Brahmā.
In the meantime, the king, having taken that fair-faced woman and having paid homage together with her, then spoke respectfully: ||| 21 ||
"O King, I have arrived from the mortal world into your presence; I am the king Satyasandha, renowned throughout the land of Ānarta. (22)
"This is my daughter, named Karṇotpalā, who is most beautiful; on this earth, I have not found anywhere a husband equal to her. (23)
"O best of gods, he has come to your side because he resembles him; therefore, tell me of her husband, so that I may give him [to her]. (24)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having heard those words of his, the Lotus-born One then spoke with a smile in the assembly of all the gods.
O King, if you ask me regarding the husband for this maiden according to dharma, she must not be given to anyone at present; hear now the reason why.
O Lord of the Earth, a daughter should be given to one born of her own lineage, who is senior in age, for the sake of dharma, fame, and the increase of the family. (27)
This daughter of yours in the mortal world has attained the status of the eldest; hear now the true reason for this among all the rulers of the earth. (28)
Three ages have passed while you have remained near me; O King, those mortals on the surface of the earth whom you previously beheld have all gone by.
Another creation has now arisen upon the surface of the earth; you do not know this because of the greatness arising from my world.
The gods do not, under any circumstances, take a human woman as their wife, for she is a contemptible receptacle for phlegm, urine, and excrement. (31)
Therefore, O King, remain right here together with your daughter; for whatever you possessed, such as elephants, horses, and so forth, has all gone to ruin.
Your sons, grandsons, servants, and whatever other kinsmen you have—all of them have met their end, as well as others who were looked after by you. (33)
Having promised "So be it," that best of kings remained standing; meanwhile, his daughter, afflicted by great sorrow and weeping, spoke.
"O father, I shall not dwell in this place born of Brahmā, having been abandoned by my circle of friends and separated from my kinsmen. (35)
Therefore, I shall go right there, where my mother is, and where those friends who brought me joy used to play with me.
"Separated from my husband, I shall not endure for the duration of time; therefore, go quickly to where my mother resides. (37)
Having heard those words of hers, that best of kings, with a heart melting with affection, took her and then arrived at his own country.
As far as he looked, he saw that where there were dry lands there were now bodies of water, and where there were bodies of water there had arisen impassable masses of dry land. (39)
Other worlds and likewise other dharmas are situated among them; even while questioning, one does not know the connection with anything whatsoever. (40)
Likewise, at that very moment, as soon as they were touched by the mortal wind, that lord of the earth and that maiden became seized by old age, their hair turned white.
O best of the twice-born, her limbs were covered with wrinkles, her teeth were decayed, and her breasts had sagged; she was unpleasant to behold, deformed in body, and had sunken eyes.
The king, likewise overcome and trembling at every step, asked: "What country is this, and what city is this? (43)
Then the people said to him: "This country is called Ānarta; here is the renowned king Bṛhadbala, who is well-versed in the true dharma. (44)
This is the city named Prāptipur; this is that river Sābhramatī; and this is celebrated as its meritorious Garta-tīrtha.
There dwell these sages, peaceful and self-controlled, devoted to the eightfold qualities; they are highly fortunate, intent on austerity, and dedicated to ritual bathing and the chanting of prayers.
Then, having heard that, he wept aloud; filled with pain and grief, he embraced his daughter.
Seeing those two most elderly ones weeping, all the people, moved by compassion, gathered together and, being deeply distressed, questioned them.
"O old man, why do you weep so unrestrainedly, afflicted by great sorrow? Tell us the reason for this, along with this elderly woman. (49)
Has some beloved person been lost to you, or has there been a loss of wealth? Or have you been humiliated by someone? Tell me, do not delay. (50)
King Bṛhadbala, who knows the Dharma, is a slayer of the wicked, and is devoted to protecting the virtuous; by him, he provides you with happiness. (51)

Satyasandha said: "I am the lord of Ānarta, known as Satyasandha. This is my beloved daughter, named Karṇotpala. Desiring to give her away, I went from here to the world of Brahmā to consult the divine Grandfather; I remained there for what seemed like a mere moment."
Then I returned once more until I beheld the surface of the earth; by that time everything had become contrary, and I understood nothing at all.
Having heard that, those people went away with eyes wide open in wonder and, filled with satisfaction, related everything to Bṛhadbala.
Having heard all of that, he also departed from there with even greater speed, traveling on foot to where King Satyasandha was stationed.
Then, having prostrated before him, he stood with his palms joined in reverence, saying: "Welcome to you, O protector of the earth; once again, a very hearty welcome to you. (57)
"Take back this kingdom of yours once more; as my devoted servant, rule it according to your own will and bestow various kinds of gifts. (58)
Then, having embraced him and repeatedly placed his head upon his own, he spoke with words faltering from emotion, his face drenched with tears. (59)
"O child, I have ruled the kingdom; various kinds of gifts have been given by me; and sacrifices headed by the horse-sacrifice have been performed with full sacrificial fees. (6)
Therefore, I shall practice austerities together with this daughter of mine, so that she may regain her former auspicious youth.
Bṛhadbala said: "O Indra among kings, I have heard all this through tradition: that the king Satyasandha departed, taking his daughter with him. (62)
He did not return again to that excellent city; thereafter, O King, his ministers protected the kingdom for a long time, and then his son, renowned by the name Suhaya, was consecrated.
O Lord, I was born as his seventy-seventh descendant in succession; I am the great lord, a man arisen from your lineage. (64)
Therefore, O Lord, perform penance here in this very auspicious place that has become sacred, at Gartātīrtha, together with her.
"By bowing daily at your feet at the three junctions of the day, may I undoubtedly attain the highest good; therefore, please grant me your favor. (66)
Satyasandha said: "O good son, in the past I established a Liṅga of Vṛṣabhanātha in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara; it still exists there."
"I shall perform his worship constantly, day and night; therefore, lead me there along with this daughter of mine. (68)

While those two kings were thus conversing with one another, Brahmins arrived from Gartātīrtha, filled with curiosity upon hearing that the auspicious and ancient preceptor had reached the lord of the earth.
Then that king, having offered them the arghya water, stood with palms joined in reverence and respectfully spoke of the events in heaven, saying, "Please be seated."

Then all those Brahmins, filled with great wonder, sat down comfortably according to their seniority on the four sides of the lord of men; and they questioned that protector of the earth regarding the news originating from the house of Brahmā.
Just as he had previously departed from and returned to that place, and just as numerous conversations with the Lotus-born One took place.
Then, having reached the end of the conversation, the king, who was true to his word, approached Bṛhadbala who was standing nearby and said something to him.
I have performed various and numerous sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, and I have given diverse gifts whose number is not known. (74)
"O son, once I went to the excellent city of Camatkārapura; I saw that city surrounded on all sides by Brāhmaṇas. (75)
By those perfected in recitation and self-study, devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice, endowed with the duties of householders, and possessed of the fruits of both worlds; || 76 ||
And then he thought in his mind: "That forest-dweller is my elder brother, by whom this eternal and imperishable fame has been acquired. (77)
Therefore, I too shall establish a city of such great height and bestow it upon the Brahmins for the sake of increasing my fame. (78)
O lord of the earth, as I was constantly reflecting in this manner, my departure for the world of Brahmā occurred in the interim.
For this alone remains in my mind as a source of regret, O protector of the earth, and nothing else, since I have accomplished all that was to be done in every respect. (80)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, request some among these high-souled ones, so that by your command I may grant them a good abode after having prepared it for them.
Then he entreated the best of Brahmins for that purpose: "O sirs, having shown compassion toward me, please accept [this] as a gift. (82)
"Because this king has offered you an excellent city with true devotion, I shall protect you all, and they shall all be born of my own lineage. (83)
Then, having with great difficulty brought some [of them] together, Bṛhadbala reported to the king, "Let these be given to them. || 84 ||
Then, having washed the feet of them all, that lord of the earth, true to his promise, granted them excellent land for the sake of a city.
As he himself was about to depart, he gave this command to Bṛhadbala: "O conqueror of enemy cities, you must bring this city to a state of readiness."
And having gone together with her to that field of Hāṭakeśvara, he reached that liṅga and, filled with joy, performed austerities there for a long time.
Having reached a certain sacred reservoir of water, Karṇotpalā also, having installed an image of Gaurī, performed austerities endowed with faith.
In the meantime, the king, the lord of Ānarta, met his end through the law of time, having been slain in battle along with his sons.
Then all those brahmins born at Gartatirtha, filled with distress, approached Satyasandha and spoke.
"O Lord of the Earth, we have merely taken possession [of this land], yet no fruit whatsoever has arisen for us from our livelihood or from what originates in the city. (91)
Therefore, O best of kings, establish yourself in your own duty so that the means for our sustenance may be secured. (92)
"O best of kings, King Bṛhadbala, who was shown to us by you for the sake of our livelihood, has met his end in battle. (93)

Satyasandha said: "O best of the twice-born, I have renounced the world and am no longer capable of maintaining a livelihood; yet, there is no doubt that some man shall still exist within my lineage. (94)
Therefore, go to your own palace; let favor be shown to me. By your misfortunes, King Bṛhadbala has been slain.
Thus addressed, those brahmins, considering his words to be true, went quickly to their own abodes; he, too, performed penance for a long time.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of King Satyasandha," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya, within the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 125.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, while he was thus engaged in penance together with his daughter, all the Brāhmaṇas originating from Camatkārapura arrived.
The brahmins said: "In all matters of doubt, and especially in disputes, because of the absence of the lord of kings, utter defeat has arisen. (2)

Then that lord of the earth was consecrated by the best of the twice-born; he was questioned and entreated to protect his own kingdom. On another day, standing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke.
The king said: "O best of the twice-born, I am unworthy even to dispel your doubt, especially since I have now laid down my weapons for the sake of providing protection."
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O Great King, since we are all superior even to a monarch, we have taken refuge in our own place with pride and arrogance. (5)
O Great King, for no one at any time or in any way is there ever any doubt regarding their conduct, even while established in their specific duties.
In the past, an incalculable commentary was composed for us by that Great-Souled One; thereafter, it was brought to growth by the best of kings who were devoted to it.
And especially by you, as long as King Bṛhadbala remains—whatever king there may be in the realm of Ānarta, he shall bestow [these gifts]. || 8 ||
We shall diligently describe all the modes of livelihood for householders as they appropriately apply; yet what need is there for us to speak before you, since you already know everything? (9)
"O Indra among kings, consider a place where a livelihood may be obtained, and a means by which that established way of life may continue with ease."
Then, having meditated for a very long time, he summoned those born at Gartatirtha who were descendants of the lineage of Upamanyu and were masters of the Vedas.
Then, having performed a prostration, he spoke with reverence, especially regarding the Brahmins residing in my domain: || 12 ||
All duties and tasks must be performed by you with humility, like servants; and my every word must be constantly observed.
These shall maintain the supreme form of the boundary in all matters of doubt, and especially in disputes. (14)
And in other royal affairs, they will deliver a verdict after hearing your words, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. (15)
These should be protected through grace and brought to nourishment according to one's ability, having abandoned all envy for the sake of the increase of my own abode. (16)
Having been told "So be it" by them, that king spoke again with respect to those most excellent Brahmins born in the city of Camatkāra.
"For the sake of your livelihood, in all matters and at all times, these Brahmins born of Gartātīrtha have been given by me to you. (18)
By their word, may everything pertaining to you be brought forth; indeed, the establishment [of the rite] shall surely arise as indicated by the four branches of Vedic study. (19)
O best of brahmins, it is not otherwise; whether it be very little or much, that which was spoken by others numbering one hundred thousand born in your city [is the truth]. (20)
Sūta said: Then those Brahmins, being delighted, took those best of the twice-born and performed all their duties at all times according to their counsel.
Then, in that city, a code of conduct was established that increased righteousness; likewise, there was prosperity for everyone in all their undertakings and for the city itself.
By their grace, those twice-born ones born at Garta-tīrtha, having attained supreme prosperity, rejoice endowed with happiness. || 23 ||
Then, after some time had passed, that king approached that excellent city and spoke with respect to all the brahmins.
"O best of the twice-born, by your grace I have performed very great penance in this sacred field; I shall now depart for heaven. (25)
"O best of the twice-born, there is currently no king remaining in our lineage; I shall indeed show you this very linga of his. (26)

For the sake of worship, for the sake of livelihood, and especially for the sake of enjoyment; therefore, you yourselves must perform his worship with great effort, particularly by means of a chariot procession, out of compassion for me.
The Brāhmaṇas said: Twenty-seven Liṅgas on the surface of the earth are as desired; they are always worshipped by the sons of Camatkāra. || 28 ||
"Likewise, we shall always worship this twenty-eighth liṅga originating from you; be free from anxiety, O King. (29)
"We shall always perform his festival procession during the month of Kārttika, along with offerings, worship, oblations, songs, and instrumental music according to our ability. (30)
Thus addressed by them, he was delighted; having gone to his own hermitage, he then bathed that liṅga and performed worship with great devotion.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, when the lineage of all those eminent Brāhmaṇas was thus on the verge of extinction, that Liṅga born of Hara was installed by him.
The mortal who, endowed with faith, bathes and worships throughout the entire month of Kārttika, shall surely attain liberation.

When the day of Soma arrives, one who has found the opportunity should perform its worship in this manner, having bathed it according to the prescribed rite; that mortal shall likewise attain liberation—this, O Father, I have heard.

The sages said: "That woman named Karṇotpalā whom you have mentioned to us—having reached a certain reservoir of water, she remains performing austerities. Tell us everything concerning her, how she is established in her penance."
Sūta said: Having established herself at the feet of Gaurī and being endowed with supreme faith, the goddess Girijā, the beloved of Śaṅkara, then attained satisfaction.
Then she said to her, "O daughter, I am pleased; state your desire, so that I may grant it without doubt, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (3)
Karṇotpalā said: "O Goddess, for the sake of my husband, my father is deeply distressed; he has been deprived of his kingdom and his happiness, and is abandoned by his family. (4)
Thereupon, having attained supreme detachment, he performed penance; meanwhile, I reached old age while still remaining in my maidenhood.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Suras, by your grace, let there be some husband for me who is renowned for his preeminent beauty among all gods and mortals. (6)
"By your grace, may I possess such supreme beauty and youth that even my father, though an ascetic, may experience happiness. (7)
The Goddess said: On the third day of the month of Māgha, on an auspicious Saturday, under the constellation presided over by the Vasus, one should meditate upon her youthful form.

"You must perform your bath here in this most meritorious reservoir; then, having assumed a divine body, you will be endowed with youth—of this there is no doubt. This which I have spoken is the truth. (9)
O highly fortunate lady, whatever other woman shall perform her ablutions on that day, she too will likewise become endowed with such beauty.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that goddess then vanished from sight; she, moreover, searched for the third [goddess] together with Śani.
With great effort, under the very constellation whose essence is Vasudeva, she meditated upon that Goddess who grants all desires.
Then, O brahmins, after a few days had passed, that third lunar day arrived, endowed with yoga, just as it had been previously described by the Goddess.
Then, meditating upon beauty, fortune, youth, and a desired husband, she entered that water at midnight.
Then, having assumed a divine form and endowed with youth, she emerged from that water, causing amazement among the people.

In the meantime, awakened by the words of Gaurī, the blessed Kāma arrived for that purpose, filled with affection for his wife, and said: "O highly fortunate lady, I am Kāma himself who has come here."
Therefore, become my wife, as directed by Pārvatī; do not delay.
"O auspicious one, because I have come into your presence out of affection (prīti), you shall become my wife, known by the name Prīti."
Karṇotpalā said: "If it is so, O Smara, go and request my father yourself; for a maiden should act according to her own will, as she has never been directed by anyone else."
"This beautiful palace which is seen not far away—our father stands within it, established in ascetic penance. (20)
Having gone there first, I shall stand near him; then you, arriving afterwards, will entreat me for her.
Saying "So be it" at Kama's word, she went into his presence; having prostrated herself, she then said: "By good fortune, O father, I have once again... (22)
"Having propitiated the beloved of Hara, you have attained lovely youth; therefore, perform my marriage and obtain the happiness residing in your heart."
O dear one, that exceedingly handsome god of the flowery bow, sent by that goddess for my sake, has himself arrived in your presence.
Then, beholding his own daughter endowed with youth, filled with great joy, and especially united with her beloved, he said: "O daughter, today the fruit of my asceticism has been realized."
And it is a blessing for your life, O auspicious lady, that you have attained this fresh youth, and that you have obtained such a beloved husband, granted by the Goddess, born of the mind.
In the meantime, Kāma approached him and said: "O King, give me your daughter of lovely smiles. (27)
O best of kings, I have been personally commanded by Gaurī for her sake; I am known as Kāmadeva, by whom the three worlds have been infatuated. (28)
Then, O best of the twice-born, that lord of the earth, having made the fire a witness according to the word of the Brahmins, bestowed that maiden upon him.
And because that beautiful-eyed woman became the object of his affection, she—being inseparable from Rati—became the auspicious one named Prīti (Affection).
Thus she performed penance there in that reservoir; therefore, it attained renown by her name throughout this entire earth.
Any woman or man who, having risen early in the morning, performs the ritual bath throughout the entire month of Māgha, shall obtain the fruit of Prayāga.
He is born handsome and capable in birth after birth; he never at any time suffers separation from his kinsmen.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Karṇotpalā Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 127.
Sūta said: Satyasandha too, his heart gladdened upon seeing the virtuous woman endowed with happiness and united with her beloved husband, felt that he had accomplished all his purposes.
Then, resorting to the southern form of that very Liṅga, he assumed a firm lotus posture and became fully intent upon right meditation.
Then, established at the gateway of Brahman, he drew himself out by means of his own self, filled with horripilation.
Then those Brahmins from Camatkārapura, having arrived for the purpose of seeing the deity, beheld the corpse.
Unpleasant, devoid of luster, and having become untouchable due to death, he lay not far from the linga; they exerted themselves for the purpose of cremating him. || 5 ||
When they had prepared a massive funeral pyre and were ready to search for him, the corpse had vanished and was no longer to be found anywhere.
Then, filled with wonder, they praised him repeatedly with words full of commendation, speaking of him again and again many times.
Then, from among those twenty-seven, they all examined everything regarding that arisen liṅga, including its worship and other rites.
For that king who is true to his word, those lingas shall be eternal, granting the desires of devoted beings and destroying all sins.
The sages said: O high-minded one, when the lineage of King Camatkāra had become extinct, who else became the sovereign of Ānarta and the king there?
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, when King Bṛhadbala had been slain in battle, all the people, accompanied by their sons and kinsmen, assembled together.
Wherever that protector of the earth, who was true to his word and endowed with austerity, was staying, they, agitated by grief, spoke to that king while he was situated in private.
"Your lineage has now come to an end, for no one remains; how then shall this earth become yours as an heir? (13)
O best of kings, in a state of anarchy, the law of the fish prevails—specifically within the kingdom, the city, and especially the village. (14)
O King, those who are devoted to the wives of others and those whose livelihood is that of thieves—all of them indeed maintain the bounds of propriety out of fear of the king. (15)
Therefore, casting aside your asceticism, rule the kingdom that has come down through your ancestral line; likewise, having obtained a wife, do not delay in seeking a son for the sake of the lineage.
The king said: "O best of the twice-born, I have renounced; I do not desire to rule a kingdom, nor do I wish to maintain a collection of sons or wives in any way whatsoever. (17)
I shall declare for your sake, for the purpose of obtaining a son for your master, a means by which King Ānarta may become a protector of the world. || 18 ||
When the Kṣatriyas were completely struck down by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, whose mind was overcome by anger, even those who were still in the womb.
Then the wives of the Kṣatriyas arrived before their ritual bathing after menstruation; they approached the Brāhmaṇas for the sake of obtaining sons, and never for the sake of sexual pleasure.
Then sons endowed with splendor and valor were born; they became the kṣetraja offspring of the protectors of the earth and were established as rulers of the world.
Therefore, these women who are the wives of Bṛhadbala remain here; having approached the Brāhmaṇas as is appropriate when they have bathed after their menses, those people [should act]. || 22 ||
And they shall obtain sons who will be bulls among Kṣatriyas; those who will protect the earth and protect the subjects.

Likewise, there is here the auspicious Vāsiṣṭha pool, which bestows the birth of sons; having bathed there during her season, a woman immediately becomes pregnant, and from bathing here, a beloved wife is born with unfailing seed.
Those who were previously born as Kṣatriyas from Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriya women—all of them were born by its power; there is no doubt in this matter. || 25 ||
Whichever twice-born man had been chosen by whichever Kṣatriya woman in the past, he approached her and bathed together with her, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
From that single instance of sexual union, and by the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha), sons were born to all of them, but never a daughter.
Whatever mantras there are that grant sons and originate from the four Vedas, all of those were employed here by Vasiṣṭha, desiring a Kṣatriya lineage.
By the mere act of bathing here, a couple shall obtain a virtuous son; therefore, this pool is called "Suputrada" (the Bestower of a Virtuous Son).
Therefore, let all those wives born of Bṛhadbala perform their ablutions here according to the prescribed injunctions.
There shall be nothing at all that is untrue, nor likewise anything that causes reproach; for a verse cited by the ancient teachers is heard as follows: || 31 ||
Fire from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone—these have arisen in excellence; yet their all-pervading heat is extinguished within their own respective sources.
Having heard all those words of the ministers, all the people went quickly and reported it to King Satyasandha.
Then all those wives of the king, having bathed after their menses, approached the most handsome Brahmins with great joy.
Having bathed there at that holy ford (tīrtha) created by Vasiṣṭha, which bestows sons, and having once encountered contact with the offspring of a twice-born man, [one attains the desired fruit].
O best of the twice-born, all of them became possessed of sons; that lord of men had one hundred and five [sons].
O Brahmins, there were one hundred and five of them.
For each of the excellent sons, it was supremely conducive to the increase of their lineage and rightly produced joy for all the inhabitants of the kingdom. (38)
Among them, the eldest son became the lord of Ānarta on earth; he was widely renowned by the name Aṭa, the destroyer of all enemies. (39)
He is renowned as Aṭeśvara, by whom this deity was established here; by seeing him with pure devotion, the extinction of one's lineage does not occur.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, why was his name "Aṭa" established? It is devoid of any [etymological] derivation; therefore, please explain it.
Was this name given to him by his ministers, or even by the Brahmins, or perhaps by his mother? Tell us that, for our curiosity is great. (42)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, that name was not given by his mother, nor by the brahmins, nor by his ministers, O King; it was given by a messenger of the gods stationed in the sky.
I shall relate it exactly as it happened; you must listen with well-composed minds, for how that king was born from the daughter of the lord of Daśārṇa. 49.
Endowed with beauty and youth, that fawn-eyed woman, having approached an excellent brahmin rich in form, then set out, desiring to bathe at the Putratīrtha.
Together with that brahmin, who was like Kandarpa himself, a great friendship then arose between the two of them from their mutual sight.
Having reached that very rare holy place which bestows sons with great difficulty, those two, desiring happiness, bathed in its waters and emerged.
And as they proceeded along the path, they succumbed to the dharma of desire; out of intense longing and great joy, they cast shame far behind them.
Then, while the world was censuring him with words of reproach, when his exertion had failed and he was about to rise, the twice-born one stood up. (49)
At that moment, a voice created by the gods suddenly arose from the sky, saying: "Because this Brahmin is indeed wandering along the royal highway. (50)
This son was indeed begotten by the Brāhmaṇa out of longing; therefore, he shall become famous in the world as King Aṭa.
He was long-lived, possessed many sons, and brought about the destruction of the enemy faction; for these reasons, O Brahmins, he became known as Aṭa.

O best of Brahmins, here is the Moon who uplifts his own lineage and grants the desired objects to those who seek them; having reached this sacred field, he established this supreme Liṅga named after himself, which bestows all things desired by men.
Whoever, endowed with faith, should worship him on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, for that person no suffering whatsoever arising from the lack of progeny shall occur.
Even a woman of a hundred years, having bathed in the Kuṇḍa that bestows sons, should then behold Aṭeśvara, being fully devoted to Śiva.
One immediately obtains a son who is supreme in increasing the lineage; by his grace, there is no doubt, just as Kārttikeya has said. 56.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Aṣṭeśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 128.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another hermitage there, originating from Yājñavalkya, which is world-renowned and bestows spiritual perfection even upon the ignorant.
There, the wise Yājñavalkya, having performed intense austerities, obtained all the Vedas that had been taken away by his preceptor.
The sages said: Who was that preceptor of the wise Yājñavalkya, by whom—after having taught him—the Vedas were subsequently taken away by that high-souled one?
And for what purpose did it occur? O son of a Sūta, explain this to us in detail; a supreme curiosity has arisen in all of us twice-born ones.
Sūta said: There was a tiger among Brāhmaṇas, renowned as Śākalya, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Long ago, O Brahmins, in the city of Vardhamāna during the Bṛhatkalpa, there lived one devoted to the study of the Vedas, accompanied by many disciples.
O best of the twice-born, rising every morning, he would out of grace bestow the gift of knowledge upon his worthy disciples.
O brahmins, he then performed the office of domestic priest for that high-souled and very beloved king, who was born of the Solar dynasty.
Having performed all his religious duties for him day after day, he would return to his own home, honored by that king.
Having appointed one disciple for the sake of that king’s peace, he explained the authoritative measure and the procedure pertaining to the fire-oblation (homa).
The disciple, having performed all those rites with great concentration, bestowed his blessing upon the king and returned to his own home.
O best of the twice-born, as that high-souled Śākalya was acting in this manner, some time passed while he served as the royal priest.
Then, at the time of the wedding, having seen that most censurable deformity of his as he stood upon the sacrificial altar, Śambhu himself uttered a curse.
Then Śākalya, having approached Yājñavalkya who had arrived at that time, engaged him in the royal palace for the purpose of performing propitiatory rites.
He too, out of pride in his youth, with all his limbs completely exposed and utterly shameless, went forth with his body scarred by the nails of courtesans. || 15 ||
Then, having performed the rite for pacification, at the conclusion of his recitation, he went—laughed at by the people—to present the water of peace to that king.
And the king, seeing that brahmin who was such a lecherous man in form, did not accept the blessing uttered by him, but instead spoke these words: || 17 ||
"O best of the twice-born, I am impure and currently reclining upon my bed; therefore, pour this water upon this pillar born of the Śāla tree. (18)
Having perceived that king with contempt, his face clouded with anger, he directed his attention toward that pillar and meditated upon that eternal Brahman.
Having spoken thus, "You, having painted the sky," he recited the Yajurvedic mantra.
He quickly sprinkled the water for pacification upon his head.
Then, as soon as the water had fallen, that pillar instantly became adorned with sprouts and shone forth, resplendent with flowers and fruits.
Upon seeing him, the king’s eyes then blossomed with wonder; having felt remorse, he then spoke these words.
O best of the twice-born, please grant the consecration to me as well; by this very mantra, my state of purity shall be established. (23)
Yājñavalkya said: "O King, you are unworthy of my consecration and gift; therefore, I shall depart this very moment for the place where that teacher of mine resides. (24)
The king said: "I shall give you garments, vehicles, and wealth; therefore, perform my consecration now with this mantra."

Yājñavalkya said: "O best of kings, a mantra does not manifest its power without the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), as was previously declared by the Lotus-born One in the rite of consecration. Therefore, I shall not perform that which resides in your heart."
Having spoken these words to the king, that twice-born Yājñavalkya, having resorted to a state of desirelessness, departed quickly for his own home. || 27 ||
Then, on the following day, when Śākalya had arrived, the king, standing bowed in humility with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him.
"O best of Brahmins, that disciple who was sent by you this morning must be sent once again to my house for the sake of performing propitiatory rites. (29)
Having said "So be it," he then went to his own home, summoned Yājñavalkya, and spoke to him with respect.
Even now, go to the palace for the sake of the king’s peace; especially, my son, you have been summoned by the lord of kings.
Yājñavalkya said: "O dear one, I will not go to the house of that man who is possessed by arrogance and devoid of purity, even for the sake of bringing peace."
The water that I had raised for his consecration—that water was instead directed by that evil-minded man toward a piece of wood.
Then, at that very moment, I also poured water upon that wood right there, and it immediately attained growth.
Śākalya said: "For this very reason, my dear son, you have been specially summoned; therefore, go there quickly, for kings are not to be disregarded. (35)
Pride undoubtedly arises in kings from being insulted; he who displays pride in return will not be beloved. (36)
Those servants who always discern here the causes for anger and favor gradually ascend even upon a king who shakes them off. (37)
He for whom honor and dishonor are equal, who understands the minds [of others] and likewise knows the proper time, who is all-enduring, patient, and wise—he shall be beloved by the king. (38)
Therefore, disregarding any insult, go to the king's palace; my command must not be transgressed by you, for this is the eternal dharma. (39)
Yājñavalkya said: "If you act thus toward the disciples whom you have appointed there, a violation of the established order will certainly result in the breaking of my command. (40)
Therefore, if you should compel me against my will toward him, I shall abandon you and go elsewhere; for so it has been declared by the great seers: ||| 41 ||
Even a guru, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, and treading upon a wrong path, is ordained to be abandoned. (42)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Śākalya, overcome with anger, then spoke to him again, reviling him repeatedly.
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple, there is no object on earth by giving which he would truly become free from his debt. (44)
Therefore, go quickly to my place of study after returning the knowledge given by me; otherwise, I shall curse you.
