Having spoken thus and consecrated it, he then offered water for drinking with Atharvaṇa mantras arising from the Nāda and Bindu.
He drank that water at that very moment; having drunk it, his senses became agitated, and he vomited up, according to the nature of vomiting, that which was mixed with the knowledge of reality.
Then, with a face flushed with anger, he spoke again to Śākalya: "Not even a single syllable of yours exists within my belly."
Therefore, I am not your disciple, nor do you stand as my guru. Now, I shall go elsewhere according to my own will; what can you do?
Having spoken thus, he then departed from that ancient place and repeatedly questioned the people once more about the sites of spiritual accomplishment (siddhikṣetra).
Therefore, this field has been ordained for him by the wise; it grants success to all living beings and shall never be in vain.
Let alone the performance of penance, or even the observance of vows and restraints; success is attained even for one who merely dwells in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
In whatever state a person dwells in that field, their accomplishment will be of a corresponding nature, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (53)
O best of the twice-born, having heard that and quickly reached this sacred field, he installed [the deity] and thereafter propitiated the Sun.
Restrained, restricted in diet, and devoted to the holy life, having attained the Gāyatra-nyāsa with a mind free from conceptual construction, || 55 ||
Then, at the end of the year, the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke to him, having restrained his fierce splendor while remaining visible to him.
"Yājñavalkya, choose a boon, whatever pleases your mind; I shall grant it all to you, for there is nothing that should not be given to you. (57)
Yājñavalkya said: "O best of gods, if you are pleased regarding my mastery of Vedic study, become my preceptor this very day; this is the desire within my heart. (58)
Bhāskara said: "Pervaded by compassion for you, I withdrew that supreme splendor and then returned here; therefore, O twice-born one, you are not consumed by it."
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I myself shall cast into this very pit the auspicious mantras dedicated to Sarasvatī as proclaimed in the Vedas. (50)
Having bathed there and become pure, whatever originates from the Veda that you shall recite even once will remain fixed within your throat [your memory].
The entire true meaning shall become manifest and known to you through my grace; of this there is no doubt. This which I have spoken is the truth. 62.

O twice-born one, from this day forward, whatever human being bathes here in this lake at dawn and recites the Sāvitra hymn after beholding me, for him that shall undoubtedly come to pass which has been spoken by me, O brahmin.
Yājñavalkya said: "O Lord of Gods, let it be so; all the words that you have spoken are accepted. However, listen to another word of mine which I shall speak to you. (64)
"O Lord of the World, I will by no means accept a human teacher; have compassion for me. (65)
Then, with a deeply satisfied inner soul, Sūrya bestowed upon her a beautiful lore named Laghimā for the sake of its power.
Then, having entered into his ear, he said to him: "Enter into my horses and practice the mastery of the sciences; perform the study of the Vedas."
O best of Brahmins, if this is what you desire from my mouth, then let there be no fault for you regarding this defect of mine arising from my rays.
Thus addressed by him, he then took refuge at Vājikarṇa; having become light, he then studied the Vedas from the mouth of Bhāskara.
O best of the twice-born, having thus attained perfection, Yājñavalkya composed a beautiful Upaniṣad endowed with the entire meaning of the Vedas.
After explaining this to the king Janaka, he then approached his son Kātyāyana, the author of the Vedic Sūtras.
Having cast off his body there at the Brahmadvāra that had been constructed, he joined his splendor to the body of Brahmā according to his power.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and beheld that Sun-god, and having recited the *Nādabindu* [Upaniṣad] before him, a man shall attain liberation.
The sages said: O Sūta, regarding that son of Yājñavalkya who has been mentioned by you—whose mother was she? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: He had two excellent wives endowed with all virtues; one of them was his wife Guṇavatī, who is celebrated by the name Maitreyī. || 2 ||
Another, the eldest and auspicious one, was known as Kātyāyanī; her son was Kātyāyana, the expounder of the meanings of the Vedas.
Between those two, two very beautiful sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are situated there, where men who have bathed go to those worlds of great prosperity.
There is the holy ford of Kātyāyanī, and the excellent holy ford of Śāṇḍilī, who was endowed with devotion to her husband; likewise, another [holy ford] is situated there.
There, Kātyāyanī, having been enlightened by Śāṇḍilī, attained supreme detachment, though she was previously distressed by the suffering caused by her co-wife.

In that place, O best of the twice-born, whatever woman, being composed in mind, performs her bath on the third lunar day during the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, she shall become endowed with good fortune. Furthermore, even one who is unfortunate, or one-eyed, old, or a dwarf, becomes beloved through the power of that [act], O best of the twice-born.
The sages said: "O Sūta, of what nature was the suffering caused by her rival that befell Kātyāyanī? And how was the instruction from Śāṇḍilī obtained; of what kind was it?"
"O Kātyāyanī, explain to us the established mystery; this instruction uttered by her will not be common. (10)
Sūta said: Having seen Yājñavalkya closely engaged with Maitreyī, Kātyāyanī then became afflicted with great sorrow due to jealousy.
She neither bathed nor ate, nor did she ever indulge in laughter; with eyes filled with tears, she became entirely consumed by heavy sighs.
Then, on one occasion, having gone outside for the sake of gathering fruit, she saw a woman named Śāṇḍilī standing by her husband's side.
To that virtuous woman, who stood with her palms joined in reverence and bowed down in humility, he too—his gaze fixed upon her face, full of passion and with a gracious look—[spoke]. (14)
Having inquired about news concerning the emergence of virtues and faults, she spoke accordingly; and seeing that couple, she was delighted by their mutual regard for one another.

She reflected within her own mind: "How truly blessed is this ascetic woman, whose husband is devoted to her face, who speaks of both her virtues and faults, who is full of passion and very affectionate, and who does not maintain another wife. (16)
Having reflected thus, O best of the twice-born, that virtuous woman went back to her own hermitage again and again, while censuring her own body.
Then once, O twice-born ones, while her husband had gone out on some business, Śāṇḍilī was staying alone in a secluded place.
Then Kātyāyanī, having approached him, respectfully asked: "O auspicious lady, tell me some instruction that brings great prosperity. (19)
By this [rite], a husband is born who always looks to the face of his wives and never treats them with contempt through harsh words. (20)

She does not approach another woman even in her thoughts in any way. I am exceedingly tormented by the sufferings inflicted by my husband, especially those caused by my co-wives; therefore, please tell me [the remedy]. (21)
Just as your husband has become subject to your will and always grants your desires, he shall never, under any circumstances, even in his mind, take another woman to himself.
Śāṇḍilī said: Listen, O virtuous lady, I shall tell you this supreme secret, how my husband became submissive to me and looked only to my face. (23)
"My father, Śāṇḍilya, the best of sages, remained at Kurukṣetra in the stage of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) during the earlier part of his life. (24)
There, a daughter was born to that great-souled one; she then grew up in due course in that very forest of asceticism.
There I perform the appropriate service at the time of the fire-oblation; and I constantly bring wild rice and other grains. (26)
Then, after some time, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived at my father’s hermitage, greatly fatigued.
Then, at my father’s command, I provided him with rest there by performing services such as washing his feet, as well as bathing and other such duties.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, as he sat with his face turned toward me, O lady of excellent complexion, he was questioned by my mother with humility.
"O tiger among sages, when we had reached old age, this one daughter was born to us; she is dearer to us than our own lives. (30)
Therefore, quickly proclaim for her an easy means that results in happiness—a vow, or a religious observance, or a fire-oblation, or even a mantra.
By performing which [rite], one shall have a husband who is very gentle, endowed with excellent virtues, pleasant-spoken, attentive to her face, and averse to the wives of others. (32)
Having heard those words of hers, that sage then meditated for a long time and, with a serene countenance, spoke these words.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, the five Piṇḍas are established; there, the supreme goddess Gaurī was herself installed by Gaurī.
Let her, endowed with supreme faith, always worship her with affection for the duration of a year, especially on the third lunar day. || 35 ||
Then, having reached the end of the rainy season, she will obtain a husband as is fitting—of such a form and as is appropriate; of this there is no doubt. (36)
There, O illustrious lady, Gaurī previously went, having abandoned Maheśvara out of jealousy toward Gaṅgā, after she had recognized that the sacred field bestows excellent spiritual accomplishments.
Then she reflected: "Which goddess should I worship for the sake of good fortune, since other celestial women worship her? (38)
Therefore, rich in supreme devotion and having stirred up my own enthusiasm by myself, I shall worship both [the deity] and myself for the sake of spiritual perfection. (39)
Then, having concentrated her mind, she prepared five lumps of clay in one place, while reciting auspicious Atharvan mantras arising from the Prāṇāgnihotra.
Having placed them within the lumps of clay, she united earth, water, fire, air, and space with them.
These five great elements are goddesses of firm vows; therefore, she worshipped them with flowers, incense, and unguents.
Then, having learned that Girijā was there established in asceticism, Bhava, his heart drawn by her mantra, arrived there with great haste.
And with a joyful soul, he said: "Why have you come here, leaving me—who am free from fault, ever devoted, and who looks only to your face? (44)
Therefore, come with me to Kailāsa, mounted upon my bull; or else, tell me the reason if there is some fault in me anywhere. (45)
The Goddess said: "You bear upon your head the personified Jāhnavī, whose essence is the water from your feet; therefore, I shall by no means go to your abode."
O you whose banner is the bull, as long as you do not abandon her—who has clearly become my co-wife—you continue to offer her constant salutations.
Even though this is manifest before my very eyes, you feel no shame regarding the twilight ritual; therefore, abandon this most shameful deed.
"O God, if it is your will, you must command me; otherwise, I shall not go to your palace by any means. Having heard this, O Bull-bannered One, do what is pleasing to you. (49)
The god said:
O Goddess of the gods, I do not sustain that Gaṅgā out of a desire for my own pleasure.
Requested by King Bhagīratha for the sake of his kinsmen, he performed a most severe penance for a thousand divine years.
"O Lord, since the Gaṅgā, having descended from heaven, does not go to Pātāla by that path, therefore, at my word, carry the Jāhnavī upon your own head."
"I have given him my promise; I shall undoubtedly uphold it, even if the force of the Ganges were to fall from the sky onto the surface of the earth. (53)
If you do not go to the netherworld, then listen here with a one-pointed mind as I shall fully explain that which exists within the objects of the senses. 54.
O lady of excellent hips, this Gaṅgā emerged from my head; thereafter, having pierced the Himavat mountain, she became divided into two streams.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, that river named Sindhu, having gathered nine hundred other rivers, went to the western ocean.
Likewise, O daughter of the mountain, that very river named Gaṅgā, having taken up as many other rivers, flows toward the eastern ocean.
Thus, O daughter of the mountain, these eighteen hundred rivers flow into the ocean; by that means, it remains eternally full.
Although the waters of the ocean are constantly being dried up day and night by the submarine fire (Vāḍava), the clouds nevertheless take up water from it. || 59 ||

Then they rain down upon the world of mortals, and from that the crops are produced; by means of the crops the world lives, and likewise sacrifices become possible. Through their share in the sacrifices, all the gods thereafter attain satisfaction.
For this reason, O Goddess, I bear Gaṅgā upon my head; it is not out of affection nor from desire, but because by her the world is sustained.
Or else, if I should somehow abandon her from my head, she would pierce the earth from afar with great speed and go to the netherworld (rasātala). || 62 ||

Then the ocean, the lord of rivers, would quickly dry up while being drunk by Aurva; consequently, no rain would arise. Due to the absence of rain, the destruction of the world would follow—this which I have spoken is the truth.
Thus has it been told to you by me for the sake of Gaṅgā, O Goddess of the gods; now hear another [account] regarding Sandhyā, by which I bow down to her.
The God said: O Goddess of the Suras, this night has been ordained for the Dānavas, and especially for the Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Rākṣasas. || 1 ||
Whatever auspicious rite, such as bathing and the like, is performed there, all of that accrues to them; this was ordained of old by the Self-born One himself.
By him, when he established the boundaries for them together with the gods, as well as for the eldest sons of Kaśyapa who were entitled to shares in the sacrifice.
For that purpose, ten thousand Dānavas, intoxicated by the pride of battle, with spears and javelins in their hands and bows drawn aloft, obstructed the sun.
Whatever water is sprinkled with reference to that thousand-rayed one (the Sun) while reciting the Sāvitra mantra, that becomes the fruit for them.
Slain by that water which was like a thunderbolt, they instantly released the thousand-rayed sun at all times, O Goddess of the Suras.
For this reason, O Pārvatī, I am casting this water in the form of a weapon, directed toward the time of twilight and the Sun, but not toward the Twilight itself.
Whatever the best person practices, that is followed by those standing behind him; even as the sun moves toward its rising, cruel men seek to obstruct it.
O Goddess, those too were struck down by the best of Brahmins with the waters of the twilight prayers; and even as they were being released by me, they fell down unconscious.
For this reason, O Goddess, both at the two twilights, I and other brahmins bow down to the Sun.
Therefore, O daughter of the mountain, abandon your jealousy and come home; having cast you aside, who is praiseworthy, there is no other woman in my heart.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, whether you are free from desire or possessed of desire, that you bow down to this Sandhyā, who is designated as a woman, produces pain for me."
Therefore, O Lord, as long as you do not abandon the Gaṅgā and especially the Sandhyā prayers, I shall have no satisfaction. (13)
Having spoken thus, that goddess then undertook a special vow, disregarding even Mahādeva himself as he was personally entreating her.
Then he reflected: "What is this cause that persists, by which she, though detached, does not manifest longing for me? (19)
Nor could Pārvatī, the goddess who was blinded by feigned jealousy, be satisfied in any way by conciliation; for this was certainly no small cause.
Then, having recognized that power of the mantra, the Supreme Lord himself, maintaining meditative absorption, [perceived it] through his most subtle knowledge.
He properly propitiated that very mantra by means of the mantra and especially by means of the ritual placement (nyāsa), worshipping the Self by the self.
Just as the five elements, which constitute the very self of the Goddess, were worshipped separately, so too did the God enter into the midst of them all.
Having withdrawn those very [deities] from his meditative absorption (samādhi) and separated them, he worshipped them; then, having again stationed them externally, he performed the worship.
Therefore, there is no other whatsoever who is more worthy of worship than he; and by his sovereign power over all the gods, Īśāna was created by him.
In this manner, while that lord Īśāna was thus propitiating the Master, the Goddess arrived, drawn by his mantra, to the place where he was.
Then, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to that god: "O Lord, everything has been understood by me; do not abandon me, your beloved. (23)
Therefore, come, O Lord; let us go wherever you desire. O God, may all that I have failed to do according to your word be forgiven me.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, embraced her who possessed a pure smile, and laughing loudly, spoke these words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud: 25.
"Whosoever among women shall worship with devotion this supreme body created by you from your own self, according to this very rite, she shall have you as her husband. (26)
Especially on the third lunar day, O auspicious one, for as long as a year, she shall obtain a truly excellent husband who grants sons and fulfills all desires.
Likewise, for those men who [worship] this form of mine called Īśāna, even their wicked wife shall become gentle. (28)
Furthermore, those who worship with devotion for the sake of a maiden shall, without doubt, obtain that very maiden whom they have kept in their minds. || 29 ||
And those mortals who, being free from desire, shall always worship [it], they shall attain supreme perfection, which is devoid of old age and death.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva placed his beloved upon the bull, and mounting it himself, he subsequently departed for Mount Kailāsa.
Nārada said:
Therefore, let this daughter of yours quickly worship the auspicious Gaurī, consisting of five lumps (*pañcapiṇḍa*), for the duration of one year.
On the third day, she will especially obtain a virtuous husband who looks to her face with great affection and is endowed with beauty and other such qualities.
Śāṇḍilya said: Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best of sages, departed from there for a pilgrimage, having been affectionately dismissed by my mother.
And by my own command, even while remaining in the state of maidenhood, she was worshipped for one year with offerings out of a desire for a husband.
On the third [lunar day], having specifically attained the auspicious path through various food offerings, gifts, perfumes, garlands, and ointments; || 36 ||
By her power, this excellent twice-born man named Jaimini has attained [this state], just as you have seen him, O Kātyāyanī; what is the use of praising others? (37)
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too should worship her with a concentrated mind; O beautiful lady, you will attain a great fortune equal to that of Maitreyī.
"Even while you were still in your maidenhood, this Gaurī was not worshipped by you for a full year on the third lunar day, nor for longer. (39)
Because of him, rivalry arose even though his good fortune was unrestrained; O Goddess, this which I have spoken is the truth according to the prescribed rule. (40)
Sūta said: Having heard everything that was proclaimed by Śāṇḍilī, Kātyāyanī then bowed to her, took leave of her, and went to her own abode. || 41 ||
Then, when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa had arrived, on the third day of the bright fortnight, she worshipped that goddess for a year, subsisting on barley-meal.
He caused the married women to be fed with delicious foods and flavorful dishes, prepared without oil or alkaline salts, and scented with fragrances such as saffron and others.
Then, when the year was complete, Yājñavalkya went into her presence and said: "O lady of pure smiles, why do you undergo such hardship?"
"By me, who am beloved, devoted, and ever-granting of desires; therefore come, O auspicious one, let us go to our own abode."
Having spoken thus, he took her by the right hand as she stood joyful, her limbs covered in horripilation, and went toward his abode.
Thereafter, with a joyful countenance, he dwelt together with her, just as he always did without distinction alongside Maitreyī. (47)
Then he begot upon her a son endowed with virtues, named Kātyāyana, who was highly proficient in the science of sacrifice.
He whose son was Vararuci, an ocean of virtues, omniscient in all matters, and one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (49)
It was installed here in this auspicious field for the sake of those seeking knowledge, having been especially propitiated on the fourth lunar day falling on a Thursday.
O Brahmins, he who, with devotion, performs the recitation of peace-mantras (śāntipāṭha) according to the prescribed rite before Mahāgaṇapati, the bestower of all knowledge— || 51 ||
O best of the twice-born, he who takes up this garland of flowers and recites it according to his ability shall become a knower of the Vedānta, such a Brahmin, in birth after birth forever. (52)
Furthermore, he who, due to incapacity, acquires [the Veda] through the payment of wealth shall especially become a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
He shall always obtain birth in the house of learned men who perform sacrifices; never, under any circumstances, in the homes of fools or those who are censured.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Gaṇapati Installed by Vararuci, and the Greatness of Gaurī and the Five Piṇḍikās in the Origin of Īśāna," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 131 ||
The sages said:
O son of a Sūta, you have described to us the holy site of Yājñavalkya located there, as well as that of Vararuci; and the Vaināyakya tīrtha is also known to exist. || 1 ||
O Mahāmati, nothing was spoken there by Kātyāyana; what indeed has he done, or what has been forgotten by you? (2)
Therefore, tell us quickly if there is any sacred site (tīrtha) created here in this field by that Great-Souled One which bestows all spiritual perfections (siddhi). || 3 ||
Sūta said: By that brahmin Kātyāyana, the sacred site named Vāstupada was established there, which grants all desires to men.
Where forty-three deities and five others are worshipped, and having been worshipped, they bestow accomplishment (siddhi) at that very moment. || 5 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, why are those deities worshipped while stationed there? Proclaim their names individually, according to their respective divisions.
Sūta said: Formerly, a certain great being emerged from the surface of the earth—unprecedented, fierce, extremely violent, black-toothed, and terrifying.

With spike-like ears, a thin face, and hair standing erect, he was terrifying; for the purpose of destroying the gods, and especially human beings, he had been summoned by the lord of the Dānavas through mantras revealed by Śukra. He was incapable of being slain by any weapons, and especially by missiles.
Then the gods, beholding that which was so terrifying, filled with great wrath, struck him with various sharp weapons.
Though they exerted every effort, they were utterly unable to strike his limbs; instead, they were devoured by him by the hundreds and thousands.
Then all those gods, together with Indra, exerting their effort and placing Brahmā at their head, rushed toward that being.
Then, having seized it with effort on all sides and in every limb, that [mountain] was cast down upon the surface of the earth by the gods who possessed fivefold qualities.
Then, having all sat down around him on every side, they dealt him blows, yet they did not strike him.
That being, born from the *Atharvaṇa* hymn and the *Amṛtabindu*, was sent by the Daityas along with Muṇḍa into his presence.
Thus it remained exactly so until the end of a thousand years; out of fear they did not release them, nor were they able to kill them.

Within his belly resided Brahmā and those immortals headed by Śakra; stationed in the four directions, they remained there in great effort, filled with wrath. Then all those Dānavas held a consultation among themselves.
For this being, who is fierce and created from semen, there is at that very moment only one prescribed means for the destruction of the gods.
Then those mighty Dānavas, discharging sharp weapons and uttering various cries, advanced by the thousands.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu arrived there at that very moment; then Viṣṇu spoke to the Bhūta, as if gladdening him with his words.
Whichever deity is established in whichever limb produced from you, having performed worship there, he shall thereby gratify you.
But no such worship as this, which has been offered by me to you today, has ever existed for a deity anywhere in this world. (22)
Then he made this promise with an unwavering mind: "I shall do exactly as you have said; now hear my further words. (23)
"If any man should ever fail to offer me worship in any way whatsoever, he shall become my food. (24)
Sūta said: When the Discus-wielding Lord replied, "So be it," that being became motionless, filled with great joy.

Then the gods, rising up and discarding that [armor], with weapons in hand, struck with sharpened arms those who were eager to flee, devoid of shame, overcome by indignation, and uttering piteous cries. || 26 ||
Then, having become composed once the Daityas had been struck down, Hari said to the Lotus-born One: "O Lord, please bestow a name upon this being."
Brahmā said: "O Hari, since this word has been spoken by you in response to my word, and because [the word] 'vāstu' was uttered, therefore it shall be called Vāstu."
Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa summoned Viśvakarman and explained to him the detailed procedure for the purpose of worship.
In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, the wise son of Yājñavalkya first summoned Viśvakarman and spoke to him.
O high-minded one, establish my hermitage in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara according to this very procedure that has been described.
"Therefore, having understood everything, I shall cause it to flourish upon the earth for the sake of enlightening the ignorant; come therefore with all haste. (32)
Then Brahmā, intent on the welfare of his son, summoned Viśvakarman and dispatched him to that place.
Then Viśvakarman also went there and performed the complete worship of the site (vāstupūjā) exactly as it had been described and as it was ordained by Brahmā.
Kātyāyana also, having seen all of that, then performed it by the thousands for the benefit of the world, beginning with the rite of the sacrificial peg (śālākarma).
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the site of the sacred ground (vāstupada) was established in that field; in this field, a man touched by sin shall be liberated from his karma.
In that way, one shall not incur any defect whatsoever arising from being born in the house, nor from [defects] originating in the craft, the site, or even the construction of the dwelling.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, under the asterism Rohiṇī, that supreme station was established there by that high-souled Vāstu.
And that man who properly performs worship toward him according to that very same rite shall attain the status of a sovereign ruler. (39)
Having reached a house that is beset by defects and afflicted by artisans and the like, upon entering it, one attains prosperity on that very day.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Origin of the Vāstu-padas," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, there is also another deity there known as Ajāgṛhī, who brings about the destruction of all diseases. || 1 ||

O twice-born ones, when King Ajāpāla was devoted to the welfare of all the world, all diseases departed in the form of goats; at that time, he would bring them there at night and place them in that spot.
Therefore, because it is situated there, that place is known as Ajāgraha; by seeing it on the surface of the earth, all people experience the destruction of their diseases. (3)
O best of Brahmins, I shall relate to you that sovereignty which existed there in former times; it should be heard by you with well-composed minds. (4)
A certain twice-born man, assuming the form of an ascetic, arrived there at night while traveling on a pilgrimage; having reached the field, he was overcome with fatigue. || 5 ||
Then, beholding the herd of goats settled there, filled with great happiness, engaged in the act of chewing their cud, trusting, and free from fear from any quarter; || 6 ||
Having realized that this must undoubtedly be a human being, he thought: "Animals do not remain in the deserted forest at night without being empty."
Then, blowing "phūtkṛtya" and "phūkṛtya" as far as the heavens, he did not utter a word; meanwhile, another remained there fast asleep, lost in thought.
"Someone must certainly come here quickly from somewhere for the protection of these animals; therefore, I remain here without fear."
Thus, as he lay fast asleep, that night passed away; then, O best of the twice-born, it departed quickly for him who was so exhausted.
Then, as soon as he beheld his own body at dawn, he saw it completely surrounded on all sides by diseases such as leprosy and others.
Unable to move even a single step from his place anywhere, and though deprived of his splendor by the fierce one, he then indeed reflected.
What is this cause by which my body has become thus? This disease has arisen quite suddenly, and I am not even able to move. (13)
While that brahmin was reflecting thus, at that very moment, a person appeared who shone like twelve suns.
Then, holding a staff in his left hand, he drove that herd away, calling them by name and gathering them individually.
Then he saw that brahmin surrounded on all sides by diseases, unable to move anywhere; thereupon, he spoke to him with respect.
"Who are you, O best of the twice-born, who have arrived here in such a state? Clearly, there is no illness of anyone anywhere in my kingdom. (17)
I am a king named Aja, if my name has reached your ears; for the sake of protecting people, I guard against diseases in the form of a goat. (18)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, tell me what specific disease resides within your body, so that I may effect its suppression. (19)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "Devoted to pilgrimage, I wander over the circle of the earth; in due course, I have arrived here at this sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara. (20)
O best of kings, I intended to stay for the duration of the night; however, O monarch, seeing these animals, it is certain that there will be human beings here as well. (21)
And then, O King, I fell asleep here in the vicinity of the cattle.
Then, as soon as I looked at my own body at dawn, I saw it completely surrounded on all sides by diseases such as leprosy and others.

"O best of kings, I do not know any other cause in truth. What is the use of speaking about this again and again, O best of kings? Therefore, act so that my body may become free from disease, for it is [afflicted] by much [suffering]. (24)
Then those diseases were addressed by King Ajāpāla: "By whom has my command been violated today? Who is to be executed by me now? (25)
The Diseases said: "O King, do not be angry in any way regarding this matter; for this twice-born man is currently afflicted by three diseases. (26)
Consumption, leprosy, and scabies, O best of the twice-born—these three defects born of contagion are proclaimed even today. (27)
Of these, the first two are known to be incurable; the remaining ones, however, go to their destruction through medicines and mantras.
And from these two comes the power of Brahmā, by which there is no turning back; therefore, O best of kings, do here what may be appropriate for you. (29)
O King, because these three were touched by this Brāhmaṇa, they undoubtedly entered his body for that duration.
Furthermore, O protector of the earth, hear the words falling from our mouths, which are for the benefit of all living beings and for the increase of your own welfare. (3)
O King, because he remained there for a long time, his excrement was deposited upon the earth; by that, this [region] quickly became known as Medinī.
Even those mortals who, at a later time, shall come together upon this earth and touch the ground, they too shall become like this.
O Great King, we remaining diseases that are established here shall become subject to the power of mantras and medicines once you have departed. (34)
But these two, born from the curse of a Brahmin, cannot be seized again.
Having heard that, the king remained stationed in that very place and spoke again to that Brāhmaṇa: "O twice-born one, you must not be afraid."
"I shall protect you from this most terrible disease; therefore, wait here for some time at my command. (37)
Having spoken thus, he then performed very great penance for that purpose, propitiating that deity of the sacred field with perfect devotion.
O twice-born ones, day and night, without weariness, he [should worship] with the Muṇḍaka, the Atharvaśīrṣa, the hymn arising from Kṣetrapāla, and the Vāstusūkta.
Having performed the fire-oblation with *siddhārtha* seeds, red flowers, and well-incensed *guggulu*, the king should thereafter especially recite the *Nīlarudra* mantras.
Then, at the conclusion of the night and that oblation, the Goddess, drawn forth by the mantra, rose up and emerged, having pierced through the surface of the earth.
Then the deity of that field spoke to that king.
"O protector of the earth, by the power of this sacrifice of yours, I have emerged from the surface of the earth today; I am known as the presiding deity of this sacred field. (43)
Therefore, O illustrious one, tell me what task I may perform for you; having attained supreme satisfaction, speak whatever you desire. (44)
The King said: "O Goddess, you must especially remain in this place forever, so that the defect of this ground arising from contact with disease may depart. (45)
O Goddess of gods, from this day forward, let such a policy be established; otherwise, by association with her, human beings will become overbearing.

"Just as this brahmin seen here before us is seized by disease, so too shall there be fault for me, O Goddess, because I have allowed diseases to remain here for a long time; of this there is no doubt. (47)
Likewise, O Goddess of the Suras, may this Brāhmaṇa be freed from disease through your grace; you should always remain here upon this earth.
The deity of the field said: "I have made this entire place free from the defects of disease; I shall remain here forever. (49)
"Whoever comes here to this place of mine now afflicted by disease and worships me with devotion, he shall become free from illness. (50)
Therefore, let this best of the twice-born worship me today with reverence, being endowed with supreme devotion, purified, and composed in mind. (51)
In this sacred field, there is another famous place known as Candrakūpikā.
O lord of the earth, bathe in it daily according to the prescribed rule. (52)
And that which was formerly performed by the high-souled Candra, who was afflicted by the wasting disease and cursed by Dakṣa, for the purpose of his own purification. || 53 ||
Likewise, a deity named Khaṇḍaśilā resides here; having bathed in the Saubhāgyakūpikā, one should behold her as well. (54)
It was formerly fashioned with devotion by Kāmadeva, who was afflicted with leprosy, for the purpose of bathing [the deity] and for the destruction of his leprosy.
Likewise, O best of kings, there is a pool of Apsarases here; having bathed there during the day of the Sun, one's scabies is then cured. (96)

Sūta said: Then that Brāhmaṇa, having reached the highly meritorious Candrakūpikā, performed his ablutions and worshipped that Goddess with devotion. Thereafter, within a month, he was swiftly liberated from consumption (rājayakṣman).
Then, having seen that well of good fortune fashioned by Kāma, and having performed his bath there, he beheld that Khaṇḍaśilā stone.
In that same way, O best of the twice-born, he was freed from leprosy within a month through the power of that goddess, especially by means of the small well.
Then, having bathed for one day on a Sunday in the pool of the Apsarases, he was completely abandoned by disease, just as a sensualist is abandoned by his intellect.
Then that Brāhmaṇa was born, possessing a splendor equal to twelve suns; filled with great satisfaction, he bestowed his blessing upon that king.
Having been granted permission by the king, he departed for his desired destination, having offered repeated salutations to the deity and to those two.
And that king, seeing those who had the appearance of goats yet were full of faults, and beholding his own Brāhmaṇa likewise, was greatly delighted.
And he himself went to that place where Hāṭakeśvara was situated, accompanied by his own beloved wife and in that very same body.
O best of the twice-born, because that goddess, the deity of the sacred field, remained in Ajāgraha, she became renowned everywhere as Ajāgṛhā.
Even today, that man who is seized by consumption (yakṣman) who worships her according to that very same ritual correctly shall quickly become free from disease. || 66 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Ajāgruha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: "When the Moon was formerly cursed by the enraged Dakṣa, you have related all of that—the narrative concerning Somanātha."
Now tell me how Kama became afflicted with leprosy in ancient times, and by what fault he was subjected to that curse.
Tell us how the goddess Śilākhaṇḍā and likewise Saubhāgyakūpikā came into existence there.
Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a brāhmaṇa renowned by the name Hārīta; dwelling in the vānaprastha stage of life, he performed austerities there.
He had a virtuous wife, endowed with beauty and nobility; she was like the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, belonging to the slayer of Madhu.
She was renowned by the name Pūrṇakalā, endowed with all excellent qualities; upon seeing her, even the Lotus-born Brahmā quickly fell under the sway of desire.
Once, that Mind-born One arrived at that sacred field together with Rati and Prīti, desiring to behold the Lord of Love.
In the meantime, she too arrived there for the purpose of bathing; having discarded her garments, she entered the body of water.
Then Kāmadeva, beholding that lady of auspicious countenance, was himself pierced in his heart by his own flower-arrows.
Then, having abandoned both pleasure and joy, tormented by the arrow, he reached a certain secluded spot and fell fast asleep beneath a tree.
With all his limbs bristling with horripilation, sighing repeatedly with very long, fire-colored breaths, and his eyes filled with tears; || 11 ||
Standing within her sight, he gazed at her with a fixed gaze, like a yogi established in perfect samādhi, meditating upon that Brahman which is firmly established.
She too, beholding Kāma standing before her with passion, his face distorted by a yawn and his body trembling—
Pierced by his arrow, she too became filled with longing, especially toward Kāma, being utterly infatuated by his beauty.
Then, having emerged from that difficult water, she of the pure smile reached the edge of the bank and stood within the range of his vision.
Then Kāma, having risen, slowly approached his presence; with palms joined in reverence, he then spoke respectfully.
"Who are you, O large-eyed one, who has come here to bathe in this reservoir for my destruction, O lovely-limbed lady? Therefore, listen to my words. (17)
"O lady of lovely smiles, I am renowned in the world as the one whose arrows are flowers; even the gods have been brought to humiliation by me with my own shafts. (18)
Struck by my arrow, Rudra cast shame far away and bore a woman upon half of his own body.
Then Brahmā, pierced by envy, lusted after his own daughter; from her he begot those sages, the Vālakhilyas, who were of such a nature.
Afflicted exceedingly by my arrows, Śakra came from heaven to the surface of the earth and lusted after Ahalyā, the virtuous and beloved wife of Gautama. (21)
Thus, even the gods who are more exalted are crushed by my arrows; how much more so, O fair-browed one, are humans, who are mostly like worms and exceedingly fickle? (22)
O lady of beautiful smiles, from the lowest insect up to Brahmā, the entire world has been subjected to the utmost mockery by my arrows.
But I, O timid one, have been brought to this state by you, O auspicious lady. (24)
Therefore, O illustrious lady, grant me today the fee for sexual union, before my life-breaths depart from this body. (25)
Sūta said: Having heard those words, she, who was devoted to her husband, was struck especially hard in the heart by his arrows.
That virtuous woman was entirely ignorant of the ways of love; having grown up among ascetics, she knew nothing else at all. (27)
And whatever is said regarding that subject by those afflicted by desire—to speak of that—she remained for a long time with her face cast down, scratching the ground with her big toe.
In the meantime, the sun reached the mountain of setting; it was the time for recreation when the one who maintains the sacred fires arrived at his dwelling.
Hārīta also, having watched her path for a long time without taking food, then reflected: "Why has she not come here?"
Having bathed in that best of holy fords and having beheld that Moon-well (Candrakūpikā), as well as Kāmeśvara, the Lord of Gods, who grants desires and bestows happiness upon men.
Then, accompanied by his disciples and looking here and there, he arrived at that place where both of them were standing.
Kāma addressed her in many ways while being struck by his own arrows; she too stood with her face cast down in particular shame.
Hidden behind a thicket, he overheard all that amorous chatter; then, perceiving her state of mind directed toward him, he spoke out of anger.

"O wicked one, because you have thus afflicted my wife with arrows—she who was unaware, virtuous, and devoted to her husband's duty—you shall therefore be afflicted with the disease of leprosy and become loathsome to behold. (35)
"O evil-souled one, you shall be liberated even from your own wife; and she too, standing with her face cast down in particular shame, shall likewise be freed. (36)
Moreover, she will become like a stone, devoid of consciousness; for upon seeing you, she became filled with passion, thereby being cast out from her own duty.
Then Kama prostrated himself before him and sought his favor, saying: "O Brahmin, I did not recognize that this beautiful woman was your wife."
Therefore, various contradictory statements have been uttered by him; she is not at fault here, for she has been severely tormented by my arrows. (39)
She has become intensely full of passion, yet not a single word was spoken by you, O Sage; therefore, you ought not to grant her a curse under any circumstances.
"This offense is mine in this matter; therefore, O best of Brahmins, inflict punishment upon me for the arising of her curse once again. (41)
O best of the twice-born, even the gods beginning with Rudra are not capable of withstanding my arrows; since that is so, how could this stone possibly endure them?
Likewise, O Lord of Sages, the wise declare that sin here is threefold: mental, verbal, and the third, born of action. That [sin] has become twofold for us, while for her, O Muni, it is but one. (43)
Therefore, you shall carry out the complete punishment of your beautiful wife; O daughter of another, you have nothing to fear.
Through remorse, one may be freed from whatever sin has been committed mentally or verbally; indeed, by simply propitiating the person against whom those words were spoken, one is purified.
O great sage, since it has been proclaimed by all the treatises on Dharma, one may expiate for a sin born of action through the prescribed penances.
Hārīta said: O deity of love, her sin lies elsewhere; the primacy of this dharma of yours is recorded as residing in the mind. (47)
Therefore, this [state] shall remain forever as it is, O lowest of men; what more can you do? I shall not say anything further regarding your duty.
First, everything is conceived by the mind; immediately after that, it is spoken by speech, and then it is performed through action.
For the mind is indeed the authority in all actions at all times; for this reason, I have completely brought it under control.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Hārīta, the best of sages, went to his own hermitage; and she too, Pūrṇakalā, instantly became a stone-form.
O twice-born ones, even Kāmadeva was seized by a terrible leprosy; with his nose, feet, and hands withered away, he became loathsome to behold.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when enthusiasm for desire had vanished and this world was seized by disease, a cessation of creation occurred.
The world merely wastes away and does not undergo growth; even those living beings born from sweat have gone to total destruction. (54)
In the meantime, all the gods were overwhelmed with anxiety: "What is this? Why is the world, along with those dwelling in the water and those dwelling on land, perishing? (55)
Not a single fool is seen anywhere, nor is there any woman pregnant; is all well with you, Smara? (56)
Then, knowing that he who was residing in this sacred field had been seized by disease, they all arrived in haste with their inner selves filled with agitation.
And having seen that Kusumāyudha standing before Kāmeśvara, who was contemplating Maheśvara with an exceedingly deformed appearance, [she was struck with wonder]. || 58 ||
Then, afflicted by great sorrow, they said: "O Flower-armed One, what is this? Why has despondency arisen in you, overwhelmed as you are by the disease of leprosy? (59)
Then, overcome with supreme shame, he became downcast and related everything regarding Hārīta’s conduct that had resulted from the curse.
Then those gods said, "Whatever sin has been committed by our speech," || 3 ||
Through the propitiation of that [deity], everything undoubtedly goes to complete destruction. || 61 ||
Therefore, O mind-born one, propitiate this goddess in the form of a stone, so that your leprosy may perish and your splendor may increase.
In this world, there would be a great creation and the duty of the gods would be fulfilled; for you have no sin born of the body, except for that which arises from speech.
In this sacrificial pit of yours, whatever other man, endowed with faith, bathes and touches this stone which is indeed liberated from sin. (64)
Even one afflicted with the disease of leprosy due to the karma arising from his own body shall become free from that illness and relieved of his fever.
And this reservoir of water shall become famous in the world as Saubhāgyakūpa; there is no doubt that it will bring about the destruction of all diseases.
Dandruff, difficult eruptions, and likewise other types of scabies shall indeed vanish instantly for one who bathes here upon seeing this [image].
Having spoken thus, those gods then departed for the abode of the thirty deities; Kāmadeva, remaining there, then performed her worship.
And then, O best of the twice-born, when just one month had passed, he became possessed of such a form as Smara himself had been in the past.
Then, having established a dwelling place for her, he, endowed with faith and exerting effort for the sake of creation, went to his desired region. || 70 ||
She too, with her face bowed down, was cursed by him in that very same manner; she became shaped like a fragment, and for that reason she is known as Khaṇḍaśilā.
Whoever worships her with devotion on that [day] and likewise on the thirteenth day, for him there shall be no censure arising from the wives of others.
O best of the twice-born, Kārttikeya, the son of Śaṅkara, has specifically declared this regarding a lustful woman; what I have spoken is the truth. (73)
Likewise, by worshipping the god Kāmeśvara, who is established as the deity of desire, on the thirteenth lunar day, one shall obtain all desires.
O tigers among brahmins, Smara likewise remained there, endowed with passion and delight, having taken up residence in that excellent palace in embodied form.
Whatever man, being deformed or unfortunate, remains composed on the thirteenth lunar day and worships him with flowers produced from saffron; || 76 ||
That woman who has been abandoned by her husband and is surrounded by co-wives is born endowed with good fortune and beautiful form. (77)
O best of the twice-born, on the thirteenth day, one should likewise worship that god, who is enriched by a beautiful wife, with saffron filaments produced from saffron.

O Brahmins, she is born fortunate and possessed of offspring; she is enriched with wealth and grain, freed from suffering and grief, liberated from all defects, and highly praised upon the surface of the earth. (79)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Greatness of the Khaṇḍaśilā and Saubhāgyakūpikā," in the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 134.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another very beautiful lake there known as Dīrghikā, which is world-renowned and the destroyer of all sins.
A man who bathes properly at sunrise on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is liberated from all sins.
Formerly, there was a very famous brahmin named Vīraśarman in the excellent city of Vardhamāna; he had completed his studies of the Vedas and was purified by the performance of his vows.
A daughter was born to him who, by some lapse from her good fortune, was exceedingly tall in stature and a source of laughter for the people.
Then, although that maiden had attained youth and possessed such beauty, no one chose her as a bride, mindful of the words of the scriptures.
A man who, deluded by lust, marries a girl whose hair is excessively sparse, or who is overly tall or overly short, [commits a fault]. (6)
Within six months, that man will certainly meet his death; for this reason, everyone abandons such a girl.
Seeing her from all sides to be possessed of extreme length, the men were overcome with world-weariness and performed most rigorous penance.
She performed Cāndrāyaṇa penances and Kṛcchra penances many times, as well as Pārāka penances and Sāntapana penances exactly as prescribed.
Whatever vow existed, whatever restraint or self-control, and whatever other auspicious deed there was—all that was performed by her.
Thus, while she remained steadfast in her vow, old age duly approached; nevertheless, the increase of her splendor brought about by her asceticism continued to grow.
And she constantly goes to the assembly hall of Mahendra out of great curiosity, specifically to hear the opinions of the celestial sages and the gods.
When she left her seat and set out toward her own home, at that very moment Indra’s servants performed a ritual sprinkling there.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, on another day she was seen by her performing the ritual sprinkling upon her own seat. (14)
Then, her body overcome with anger, that young maiden knitted her brows into three furrows and spoke to Purandara.
"O Śakra, seeing what fault has my seat been sprinkled by you? Has this fault ever been committed by me, or was it done by another? (16)
Therefore, tell me my transgression; otherwise, I shall undoubtedly cast a most terrible curse upon you. I swear this by my own truth. (17)
Indra said: "O auspicious lady, there is no fault regarding your long nails here, with one exception; it is for that reason that this consecration upon the throne is being performed."
Although you were still a maiden, you arrived during the censured period of menstruation; it is because of that fault that you have met with this misfortune, and there is no other cause for it here.
Therefore, even now, some ascetic shall marry you; choose him as your husband, by whom you may attain purity.
Then, overcome with shame, that long-haired maiden quickly went down to the ground in the excellent city of Vardhamāna.
Then, raising her right hand and wandering here and there, she began to shriek at the crossroads and the triple-junctions.
If any twice-born man by birth should now take my hand in marriage, I shall grant him half of my ascetic merit as a blessing.
Hearing her prattling thus day and night, the people, thinking her to be mad, laughed among themselves.
Then, after a few days, while she was performing her ablutions in the pond, she was observed by a Brāhmaṇa afflicted with the disease of leprosy.
Then, having summoned her who was deeply distressed, he spoke softly.
"I shall marry you today, having performed the grasping of your hand, provided that you always carry out my every word. (27)
The maiden said: "O lord of the twice-born, I shall carry out your word without a doubt; perform my marriage today according to the rites prescribed by the sacred law."
Sūta said: Then he took the right hand of that maiden according to the procedure prescribed in the Grhya texts, in the presence of the gods, the fire, and the preceptor.
Then she, having again performed the auspicious marriage rites, said: "O Lord, give me your command; what may I do for you now? (30)
The husband said: "O beautiful one, I wish to bathe in the sixty-eight sacred fords; if you are able, perform this with your assistance. (31)
Saying "So be it," that devoted wife then quickly made firm that measurement and constructed a beautiful hut of bamboo.
Then, having joined her palms in reverence, she spoke to her own husband with a joyful inner soul, [offering him] a seat made of soft cotton.

"For your sake, this beautiful bamboo hut has been constructed; O my lord, climb up quickly so that, having placed you upon my head, I may carry you to all the sacred fords and most auspicious holy fields. (34)
Then the leper, his soul filled with joy, slowly rose from the ground; having been lifted up by her, he was like one who had been sleeping in a bamboo hut.
Then, placing him upon her head, she wandered at her pleasure through all sacred fords and all holy fields, bathing her own husband.
In whatever manner that leper performed his ablutions in the sacred fords, in that very manner the luster in his limbs began to increase. || 37 ||
Then, wandering gradually over the surface of the earth, that virtuous woman arrived at the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara at the onset of night.
Exhausted, fallen into a state of distress, and weighed down by her burden, the devoted wife was blinded by sleep, sighing and stumbling at every step. (39)
Then, in that very place, Māṇḍavya, the bull among sages, remained there in great suffering with his body impaled upon a stake.
Then, having approached that stake at night, that devoted wife, a great satī, went along burdened by the weight upon her own body. || 41 ||
Then, moved by her, that bull among sages, Māṇḍavya, having experienced extreme agony, spoke, being deeply distressed.
"By whom has this sinful dart been driven into my heart, by which I, though already possessed of suffering, have been made a vessel for further misery? (43)
Dīrghikā said: "O illustrious one, you were not seen by me with eyes impaired by sleep; therefore, though touched, you are untouchable, for you are the greatest of evildoers."
There is no other person like you on the face of the earth so evil-minded, that even with a spear risen upon his head, he does not meet his death.
"O fool, I am a devoted wife; for the sake of a pilgrimage, I carry upon my head my beloved husband, though his limbs are impaired. (46)
Why do you, being of dull intellect, offer such harsh contempt toward her—especially since she is human and you do not know her? (47)
Māṇḍavya said: "I am exactly as you have described me, without a doubt: a sinful soul, of deluded intellect, and untouchable for all embodied beings. (48)
If this cruel husband of yours is still alive at dawn—he by whom I was subjected to such intense suffering that it nearly brought an end to my life—[then what can be said? (49)
Therefore, this one who is dear to you, having been touched by my rays and cursed by me, shall bring about the abandonment of his life. (50)
Dīrghikā said: "If my husband's death will thus occur at dawn, then the sun shall not rise tomorrow morning."
Having spoken thus, she then sat down upon the ground, having set aside her bamboo hut along with her husband on the earth.
Then that leper said to her: "Thirst is setting in for me; therefore, bring some very cold water for the purpose of drinking. (53)
Having heard her husband’s command in that very way, she wandered here and there in eager anticipation for water, yet she saw none; nor did she go far away, leaving him in such a state in the forest.
Filling her heart with fear arising from the wild beasts and her husband, Dīrghikā then sat upon the ground, touched the feet of her lord, and spoke these words in a loud voice, distressed by grief.
"If it is true that you have been a devoted wife and that I have behaved rightly toward you, by that truth let auspicious water well up from the surface of the earth. (56)
Having spoken thus, she then struck the earth with a kick, honoring her devotion to her beloved and desiring his life.
In the meantime, as Māṇḍavya looked on, water—pure and sweet—emerged immediately upon the striking of his foot.
Then he bathed him, who was afflicted by fatigue, in that water; after that, having bathed himself, he gave the water to him to drink and then drank it himself.
In the meantime, out of fear caused by her devotion to her husband, the sun did not rise; consequently, a great lapse of time occurred.
Then, observing that the night was long, all those people who were lustful, as well as the women of good family, attained great satisfaction.
The Kauśikas, the Rākṣasas, the thieves, and those men who were paramours—all of them, being greatly delighted, spoke while embracing one another. (62)
Today Fate has been pleased with us, as has the Lord Manmatha, by whom the night has been made long and the sun has been brought to destruction. (63)
Furthermore, those brahmins who were peaceful and intent upon sacrificial rites—all of them fell into distress when deprived of the rising sun. || 64 ||
No one performed a sacrifice, nor did any virtuous twice-born man act as a priest; there was no ancestral rite (śrāddha), no formal resolve (saṃkalpa), and no Vedic study whatsoever.
There was no bathing, nor charity, nor especially the worldly course of life; there was no legal transaction, nor any duty arising from dharma.
In the meantime, all the gods, led by Śakra, fell into a state of extreme distress, being deprived of their shares of the sacrifice.
Then, having approached Bhāskara, they spoke, filled with sorrow: "O God, O Divākara, why do you not rise? (68)
Without you, this entire world has fallen into a state of agitation. || 69 ||
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world, rise up as you did before, so that sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma may proceed upon the earth.
Sūrya said:
"By the command of my devoted wife, all worldly prosperity has been renounced by me; therefore, O gods, all of you go and speak on my behalf. (71)
"By means of which, having obtained that speech, I may proceed according to my pleasure; otherwise, that devoted wife will surely curse me in her anger. (72)
Thus, O best of gods, endowed with such austerity, she attained preeminence; likewise, she established another great quality: devotion to her husband.
Who would be able to act contrary to her word? For this reason, I am afraid and do not emerge at all.
Even those performing a thousand sacrifices would not obtain that fruit which a woman attains solely by being devoted to her husband. (79)
Then all those gods, having gone to that supreme sacred field, stood before her and addressed that Dīrghikā with gentle words.
O devoted wife, it was not well done by you that the sun was obstructed; for by that, all auspicious rites on the surface of the earth have been destroyed. (77)
Therefore, O wise lady, let the sharp-rayed sun rise by your word, so that the specific sacrificial rites may proceed upon the earth. (78)
The devoted wife said: "O gods, this husband of mine, who is dearer to me than my very life, is meeting his death this very day as the solar disc rises. (79)
"I have been cursed by this wicked and most sinful Māṇḍavya, who has accused me of a crime even though I am innocent; how then can I speak to Bhāskara? (80)
I have no need for sacrifices for the sake of prosperity, nor for any other rites such as ancestral offerings (śrāddha) and gifts, unless they are performed with humility.
Sūta said: Then all those gods, having looked at one another for a long time and being afflicted by great sorrow, spoke to her with humility. (82)
"O auspicious lady, let this beloved husband of yours rise as the sun; let him go to his death this very instant, and may he become a lord of sages. (83)
"O you who are devoted to your husband, we shall quickly restore even him to life, though he has entered the path of death, for your sake."
"You shall behold him, twenty-five years of age, like another Kāmadeva, with limbs brilliantly radiant and endowed with all auspicious marks. (85)
Having become a fifteen-year-old girl with eyes as broad as lotus petals, you shall attain happiness in the world of mortals through the perfect realization of your desire.
O auspicious one, this tiger among sages, now free from sin and liberated from the piercing of the stake, has become a partaker of happiness; O weary one, [be at peace]. (87)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, as soon as she had replied, "So be it," the blessed Sun rose with great speed at that very moment.
Then, touched by the rays of the sun, he died and was afflicted with severe leprosy; yet, touched by the hands of the gods, he rose up once again.
Twenty-five years of age, like another Kāmadeva, he was filled with joy as he recollected his entire former birth.
The Dīrghikā pond also, having been touched by Lord Śambhu himself, became endowed with youth and marked by divine characteristics.
With eyes like lotus petals, she was lovely, her face resembling the orb of the moon; she was slender-waisted, with very fair limbs and full, elevated breasts. || 92 ||
Then, having lowered that tiger among sages from the tip of the trident, the best of the gods, filled with joy, spoke to him respectfully.
O Sage, these words spoken by you have been proven true; even though he was a leper, the Brahmin died having been touched by the rays of the sun.
We have raised you up again and made you young once more; therefore, go to your own hermitage together with this wife of yours.
Our vision never becomes fruitless in any way whatsoever; therefore, ask for that which has always resided within your heart. (96)
Māṇḍavya said: "O best of gods, I shall accept a boon arising from you; however, let Dharmarāja declare one final decision for me. (1)
O best of gods, for all living beings in this world, the performed action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—attends them and nowhere else; this is the truth.
"What sin have I committed here, or even elsewhere, that I have come to such agony and yet cannot die by any means? (3)
The King of Dharma said: "O Brahmin, while you were living in another body during your childhood, you pierced a crane in the earth with a very sharp spear."
"O twice-born one, not even the slightest other sin has been committed by me; for this very reason, I have undergone this suffering. (5)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Māṇḍavya, filled with intense anger, then spoke to Dharmarāja who stood before him.
"O evil-minded one, since you have inflicted such a severe punishment upon this person for a very minor offense, therefore accept a curse from me. (7)
Having obtained a human body, you will remain situated in the womb of a Śūdra and shall experience abundant suffering born of the loss of caste.

Thus, this rule has been established by me today for all embodied beings: from the eighth year onwards, whether it be a male or a female creature, they shall indeed be seized on account of their reprehensible conduct.
Having spoken thus to Dharmarāja, O twice-born ones, Māṇḍavya then departed, freed from his anger, toward his desired destination.
Then, seeing him set out, all the inhabitants of heaven, who had been anxious on account of Dharmarāja upon hearing such a curse, spoke.
The gods said: "O Blessed One, you ought not by any means to turn Dharmarāja—who is merely attached to sin—into a Śūdra by means of a curse."
Therefore, O twice-born one, show favor to this lord of dharma; at our request, immediately ask for a boon as you wish.
Māṇḍavya said: "O best of gods, the word spoken by me cannot be otherwise; this Dharmarāja shall inevitably go into a Śūdra womb."
Furthermore, his lineage shall not continue in that womb; he will once again attain the supreme sovereignty of Dharmarāja.
And let him, undistracted, worship Trilocana in this very field; by the grace of that deity, he shall swiftly meet his death.
"O guardians of heaven, if you would grant me a boon, then let this stake become a bestower of true dharma through our touch. (17)
The gods said: "Whoever, having risen in the morning, shall touch this stake, he shall indeed be liberated from sin in this world. (18)
Having spoken thus to that sage, those gods, led by Śakra, then addressed that devoted wife respectfully along with her husband.
O lady of excellent complexion, you too should request a desired boon from us; whatever has long resided in your heart, there is nothing here that we cannot grant.
The devoted wife said: "O lords of the gods, let this pit which has been dug by me in this place attain fame throughout the three worlds by my name as 'Dīrghikā'. (21)
The gods said: "From this day forward, O beautiful one, this pit of yours shall become renowned throughout the three worlds in this world as the 'Dīrghikā' (the Long Pond)."
Those men who, having risen early in the morning, shall perform their ablutions in this [river], will be liberated from all sins at that very moment.
When the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo and the fifth day has arrived, those men who perform their ablutions here endowed with faith—|| 24 ||
"Those who are childless shall have sons who increase their lineage. Having spoken thus to her, O best of the twice-born, the gods then departed for heaven.
The virtuous Sundarī, though devoted to her husband, enjoyed unsurpassed amorous pleasures with that very same lover.
Upon the most delightful mountains, on the sandy banks of rivers, in various gardens, and in forests and groves; (27)
Then, when he had reached old age at the end of his life's course, he devotedly resorted once again to that very same sacred site of his own.
Then, having cast off her body and seeing her own husband dead there in the water, that devoted wife went to the world of Brahmā.
Thus has this entire, supreme narrative of Dīrghikā been recounted to you; by merely hearing it, a person is liberated from sin.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Origin of the Dīrghikā," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 136 ||
The sages said: "By whom was that tiger among sages, Māṇḍavya of great asceticism, impaled upon a stake? And for what reason? Tell us."
Sūta said: Formerly, that sage Māṇḍavya, while performing a pilgrimage, arrived at this sacred field endowed with supreme faith.
Having reached that great, purifying, and excellent holy site belonging to Viśvāmitra, he, observing his vow, performed the libation for the ancestors facing the sun.
The hymn beginning with "Vibhrāṭ" is the most excellent and is dear to the Sun-god; meanwhile, a thief took someone's stolen property.
O twice-born ones, someone arrived there pursued by people following behind him; then the thief, seeing that best of sages standing in silence, [fled].
Then, having dropped the stolen goods before him, he entered deep into the cave; in the meantime, those men arrived for the sake of the plunder.

Seeing that stolen property lying before him, they said to that bull among sages: "A thief has come along this path with the stolen goods in his hand; tell us quickly, O illustrious one, by which way he departed. (7)
And although he was wise and knew that the thief was staying within the cave, he said nothing at all, being entirely devoted to his vow of silence.
Although addressed repeatedly, he remained preoccupied with thoughts of another; thus, protecting the life of the thief, he did not say anything at all.
Then they all deliberated: "This is surely a robber who has arrived from behind us and assumed the form of a sage. (10)
Then, without any deliberation, all those wicked Ābhīras led him into a certain part of the forest and immediately impaled him upon a stake.
Thus, at that time, the wise Śūlin was struck with a terrible spear by that faultless sage, as a result of the ripening of his own past karma.
The sages said: "What dharma, austerity, meditation, or other practices were performed by Dharmarāja for the sake of destroying the curse of Māṇḍavya? Proclaim that to us. (1)
Sūta said: Having incurred the curse of Māṇḍavya, Dharmarāja became deeply distressed; O best of the twice-born, he performed penance while remaining established in that sacred field.
Having constructed a palace for the God of gods, the one with matted hair (Kapardin), he worshipped him undisturbed with flowers, incense, and unguents.
Then, after a long time, Maheśvara was pleased with him and said, "I am a granter of boons; ask for whatever you desire."
The King of Dharma said: "O Lord, in former times I was cursed by the high-souled Māṇḍavya, even though I was abiding in my own duty and free from all faults."
And by him, being enraged, it was said: "You shall be born from a Śūdra womb."
And even there, you will immediately experience great suffering arising from the destruction of your kinsmen, born of my curse, and resulting from your birth.
Therefore, O best of gods, protect me from that womb; for how could I, having become such as I am, take birth within it? (8)
And even there, there is great suffering arising from the destruction of kinsmen; for this reason, O best of gods, you have been propitiated by me.
The Blessed Lord said: "The word of that holy sage cannot be made otherwise. Therefore, even though you are a Śūdra, you shall not obtain offspring."
Even upon seeing the destruction of your kinsmen, you will not experience sorrow, because even though they are being forbidden, they will not follow your word.
For this reason, O King of Dharma, no sorrow arising from your kinsmen shall arise in your mind; this which I have spoken is indeed the truth. (12)

O wise one, having remained for a hundred years as a Śūdra devoted to dharma, you have given many instructions out of a desire for the welfare of your kinsmen—even to those who were always devoid of faith and possessed of sinful natures. (13)
Then, when a hundred years have passed, having properly cast off the self through the gate of Brahman alone, you shall proceed to liberation itself.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One then vanished from sight; Dharmarāja likewise incurred that curse originating from Māṇḍavya.
Then, having descended to the surface of the earth in the form of Vidura, that high-minded one made the words of Māṇḍavya come true.
He was born directly from the Blessed One Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, the brahmin son of Parāśara, having emerged from the womb of a maidservant.
All this has been narrated to you concerning the origin of Dharmarāja—the narrative about which I was asked, and which destroys all sins. (18)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Dharmarājeśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, this is the meritorious majesty arising from Dharmarājeśvara, which I formerly heard from the presence of my own father.
Therefore, I shall proclaim it; listen with well-composed minds. It is renowned throughout the three worlds and is the destroyer of all sins.
In that field, formerly there was a brahmin born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, known as Upādhyāya, who was devoted to the knowledge of the Vedas.
When he had reached his later years, a son was born to him, who was devoted to the rules of Vedic study and possessed abundant wealth.
When his son was born at only five years of age, he fell under the power of death, causing great sorrow to his father and mother.
Then that brahmin became enraged at Vaivasvata, seeing his own son arrived at the abode of Dharmarāja.
Taking water in his hand, having become pure and composed, he, being distressed, pronounced a terrible curse upon Dharmarāja.
"Since I have been made sonless today by that evil-minded one, therefore that wicked-souled Yama shall also become sonless."
Likewise, people on this earth shall not offer him worship, nor shall they proclaim his name, as they do for other inhabitants of heaven.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, shall utter his name, for that person there shall be no obstacle in the performance of auspicious rites. || 10 ||
Having heard that most terrible curse from the brahmin, Yama, though remaining steadfast in his own duty, became filled with sorrow.
In the meantime, having gone to the abode of Brahmā, Yama, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Grandfather.
Behold, O Lord of Gods, how I, though faultless and abiding in my own duty, have been cursed by the twice-born as if I were some other ordinary person. (13)
Therefore, O Grandfather, I shall relinquish your command; terrified by the fear of a Brahmin's curse, I have spoken this truth.
O best of beings, formerly cast down into a Śūdra womb by the curse of Māṇḍavya, you have now been rendered childless and unworthy of honor.
Sūta said: Having heard those piteous words of Vaivasvata, Śatakratu himself spoke this at that appropriate time.
"O Lotus-born one, O Lord of the Gods, this which has been spoken by this King of Dharma is appropriate, as he abides in your command. (17)

O Grandfather, those mortals who abide by their appointed time must inevitably be withdrawn—whether in childhood, youth, or old age; of this there is no doubt, nor can it ever be done before the time. (18)
This very thing has been accomplished by you for the sake of the high-souled Samitra, who was equal in friendship and equal in weapons, and it is known as the supreme title of Dharmarāja. (19)
Therefore, having reflected upon this today, let some faultless means be devised by which he may carry out your command.
Brahmā said: "O Lord of the Gods, I am not able to undo the curse of Brahmā; however, I shall now employ a remedy."
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, performed meditation for that purpose, being perfectly composed in the presence of all the gods.

As he was thus absorbed in meditation, there appeared all around him one hundred and eight formidable diseases in embodied form, consisting of wind, abdominal tumors, and phlegm; they addressed him with great respect.
The diseases said: "O Lord of the gods of gods, O All-pervading One, for what purpose have we been created by you? Let an instruction be given quickly; let your favor be bestowed. (24)
Brahmā said: "Go quickly to the surface of the earth at my command, without doubt; by the command of Yama, you must go among human beings without hesitation. (25)
Having spoken thus to those diseases, the Grandfather then addressed Dharmarāja, who was standing nearby, deeply dejected and with his face cast downwards.
"All these diseases have been appointed by me for you, O Yama; they shall always provide assistance in all your undertakings."
Whosoever among mortals now meets his end, you must always diligently dispatch your messengers for his execution. (28)
Because of that, slander arises among these people on the surface of the earth, born from the fear of birth; but such slander does not arise for you. (29)
Therefore, go to your own place and be intent upon your own duty; by my command, you shall undoubtedly not incur such fault.
Then, having taken all those diseases and reached the realm of Yama, the son of the Sun spoke to him respectfully: || 31 ||
Having repeatedly questioned Citragupta on this earth, one must depart when the time for the destruction of birth has arrived. (32)
Furthermore, I have established there an excellent Liṅga in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, which destroys all sins.
That man who, having risen early in the morning, beholds him with true devotion—he must always be avoided by you from afar, according to my word. (34)
Having spoken thus to those hunters, Vaivasvata himself then took that son of the brahmin and departed quickly, assuming the form of a twice-born man, to that very beautiful palace.
Then that brahmin, seeing his own son returned home accompanied by the wise Dharmarāja in the form of a brahmin, [was filled with joy]. (36)
Then, with a joyful heart, accompanied by his own wife, he went quickly toward him, crying out, "My son! My son! (37)
Then, having embraced him once more with eyes clouded by tears, and having smelled the crown of his head, he spoke these words.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O son, how have you returned from that abode of Yama? No one returns again after having gone there, even if he be possessed of great prowess. (39)
What is this magical illusion that has arisen before me? Is this a dream, or is it a delusion of my vision? (4)
"O son, who is this Brahmin standing by your side, endowed with divine splendor? O my child, I pay homage to him. (41)
The son said: "This is Yama himself who has arrived in the form of a brahmin; filled with compassion and knowing that you were joined with sorrow, he has come to take me away. (42)
Therefore, O father, grant him the grace of a curse today; for if I am dear to you, do so out of great affection for one who has come to your home. (43)
Then, having offered his salutation to him, that best of Brahmins, with his face cast down in shame, spoke respectfully.
