The Brāhmaṇa said: Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived, since I have obtained the sight of my son who had gone to the abode of Yama. (45)
And you, O father, have attained supreme satisfaction for the sake of a son; therefore, act in such a way that he may be united with a son. (46)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O son, my word has never been false at any time, even when spoken in jest; how much less so when uttered by one who is suffering? (47)
Therefore, O wise one, by the power of my curse, he shall certainly have no son born of divine origin under any circumstances whatsoever. (48)
"And there shall be another son born from a human womb who will deliver him by means of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. (49)
What is the purpose of a son being born who is not capable of delivering his paternal lineage by performing auspicious deeds that are supreme on earth? (50)
Likewise, listen to my words as I speak, O dear son, regarding that curse which was indeed formerly pronounced upon him for the sake of performing worship. (51)
O son, that worship of his which was established through various mantras declared in the Vedas shall not exist in this world in any way whatsoever.
His worship shall be performed with mantras originating from human beings; this will be more distinguished than that of all the gods—this truth has been spoken by me. (53)
The son said: "O best of the twice-born, having established him upon the surface of the earth, I shall worship him perfectly; what need have I for other gods? (54)
Therefore, O elder brother, by your grace, I shall proclaim the mantras originating from humans, as well as the ritual procedure for worship.
Then, having performed the ritual with the mantra "tataḥ sugaṃ naḥ panthā," he, with a joyful heart, carried it out while Dharmarāja was listening.
Having heard that, Yama, with a very gracious mind, spoke thus to that brahmin in a voice faltering with joy: (97)
Yama said: "O best of Brahmins, my sight can never be in vain for anyone; this is true even for other gods. Therefore, request whatever you desire."
The Brāhmaṇa said: "This son of mine shall install your image here; whatever twice-born man worships it with this very mantra," (59)
For as long as a year until the arrival of the fifth day, may he never experience grief for his son in this world by any means. (60)
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," Yama, with a highly delighted mind, then went to the realm of Yama and became intent upon his own office.

That heir of the Brāhmaṇa, having constructed an excellent temple, worshipped Yama with devotion by installing him in its center, using that very mantra taught by his father according to the prescribed rites.
And then, having gradually obtained numerous sons and grandsons and having remained upon the earth for a long time, he eventually succumbed to the law of time.

All this has been narrated to you, as much as was heard in the Purāṇa of old. Whoever recites this with devotion when the fifth day arrives, for him there shall be no untimely death, nor any grief arising from his children.
The sages said: "Regarding that which was stated by you—that a son in human form will be born here to Yama—who is he, O son of a Sūta, from whom he has arisen?"
Sūta said: A son was born to him upon the surface of the earth in the womb of Pāṇḍu, renowned as Yudhiṣṭhira, the preeminent among all Kṣatriyas.
He by whom the Rājasūya sacrifice was performed with complete sacrificial fees, having compelled all the lords of the earth to pay tribute through his prowess.
He performed five horse-sacrifices with complete sacrificial fees; having caused the horse to roam over the earth, he subsequently attained the supreme goal.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā, or performs the horse sacrifice, or sets free a dark-colored bull.
That this high-souled one has chosen from me the status of being my daughter—his son shall indeed be the performer of great horse-sacrifices.
By whichever son the protector of dharma considers his purpose fulfilled, what is the use of hundreds of other sons who do not effect the upliftment of the lineage? (7)
Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, this entire narrative concerning the birth of the son of Dharmarāja has been recounted to you; it is a supreme account that increases righteousness.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Dharmarāja’s Son," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya of the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another deity there who bestows sweet food; by the mere sight of whom a man obtains sweet food. || 1 ||
O best of the twice-born, in a former time, during the Bṛhatkalpa, there was a king known by the name Vasusena, renowned as the lord of Ānarta.
Endowed with supreme sovereignty, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots, he was a radiant conqueror of enemy factions, a donor, an enjoyer of pleasures, and one who had mastered his senses.

At the time of the sun's passage into a new sign, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at lunar and solar eclipses, on other festival days, and on various other occasions, he [performed his rites] with great devotion.
He bestows various kinds of jewels upon the twice-born, such as sapphire, emerald, coral, crystal, and the like.
Rubies, pearls, and especially corals, as well as elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and various kinds of garments.
O best of Brahmins, he should not give grain to anyone, considering it to be exceedingly easy to obtain; this is especially true of water.
Then, having ruled the kingdom for a long time and having seen his sons born as grandsons, he met the law of time after the lapse of some period.
Then his ministers consecrated his son, who was endowed with heroism and nobility, in the kingdom, and he was known as Satyasena.
Vasusena also, having attained heaven through the power of his charity, became adorned with divine garments and embellished with celestial jewels.
Served by celestial nymphs and seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, he wandered through all the worlds at his own will, yet remained overcome by hunger.
With his mind agitated by thirst and his mouth parched, he did not see anyone else there in heaven who was eating.
Nor [should one drink] water attached to a drinking vessel, nor water containing grain.
Then, having gone there, O best of the twice-born, he spoke to the Thousand-eyed One; his body overcome by hunger and thirst, he stood with his face cast down in shame.
"O best of the gods, no one here is seen to be afflicted by hunger or thirst, with the exception of myself; therefore, tell me what this is. (15)
This hell has presented itself to me in the form of heaven; what is the use of these ornaments, garments, celestial chariots, and the like? (16)
O Lord of Śacī, for one who is tormented by hunger, even this heaven is declared to be like fire; this thought dwells within my mind as well. (17)
Therefore, show me favor so that hunger does not afflict me; otherwise, O best of gods, cast me quickly into the Raurava hell.
Indra said: "O protector of the earth, you yourself are indeed unworthy of hell; for by you, gifts have been given at all times beyond counting. (19)
But furthermore, O King, in some places neither food nor water was given; yet, having reflected upon nothing at all, [the merit arose], for it is indeed easily obtained.
One who desires eternal satisfaction both in this world and in the next should always give water with food, and food accompanied by a sacrificial fee.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, though you are possessed by hunger even in heaven, you are adorned with the finest ornaments and have taken refuge in an excellent celestial chariot.
The king said: "Is there some means here, whether divine or even human, by which my exceedingly intense hunger and thirst may come to an end? (23)
Indra said: "If some son of yours constantly gives water to the Brahmins and always [gives] grain, then satisfaction will arise for you. (24)
"O best of kings, it is not otherwise; even on a single day, there is no acquisition for you of what has not been given. This which I have spoken is the truth. (25)
Even that son of the lord of the earth, while following your path, does not give water nor grain to the twice-born. (26)
In the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived from the world of Brahmā at the place where those two—the king and the lord of the gods—were stationed.
Then Śakra, rising up filled with satisfaction, offered him the arghya according to the prescribed rite and spoke these words with great respect: || 28 ||
"O best of Brahmins, from where have you come, and where are you currently bound? For what purpose have you arrived? If it is not a secret, tell me now. (29)
Nārada said: O Śakra, I have arrived from the world of Brahmā and am now setting out for the surface of the earth for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites; there is no other reason for this.
Sūta said: Having heard that, the king was delighted and spoke to that lord of sages: "O bull among sages, let your grace be bestowed upon me, a wretched man."
"O Lord, you must say on the surface of the earth: 'My son, the lord of the earth, the renowned ruler of Ānarta, is Satyasena. (32)
I saw your father in the abode of Śakra, his body overcome by hunger and thirst, dejected in spirit, standing in the midst of the gods.
Therefore, if you are my son and you truly protect the truth, then offer the crops and the waters aloud in my name.
Having promised "So be it," Nārada, the best of sages, took leave of the thousand-eyed Indra and set out toward the surface of the earth.
Then, wandering through sacred fords (tīrthas) in due order, that virtuous twice-born man reached the region of Ānarta and approached Satyasena.
Then, having been duly honored by that king, the sage respectfully related his father’s message to him in private.
Having heard that, King Satyasena, tormented by grief, dismissed that best of sages after honoring him according to the prescribed rites.
Then, with great devotion, he daily fed a thousand eminent Brahmins with sweet foods, intending them for Janaka.
Likewise, he performed the act of providing water-stations, especially during the summer season, having abandoned all other activities arising from dharma. (40)
While that king was thus ruling, O twice-born ones, a terrible drought occurred, bringing about the destruction of all crops.
For as long as twelve years, the Lord of the Thirty-three did not release water upon the surface of the earth; all the worlds were afflicted by hunger.
Because of the absence [of merit] here, it no longer yields grain as abundantly as before for the sake of the Brahmins, directed toward his own father. (43)
Then, his body overcome by hunger and wearing extremely soiled garments, the father of that king spoke to his son in a dream.

"O son, because of you as my son, I remain afflicted by hunger and thirst even though I dwell in heaven; therefore, indeed, grant me food. If you are truly born from me, then offer water mixed with food in my name. (45)
Then, overcome with grief because of that dream-vision, the king held a consultation with his ministers regarding the lack of food.
"I shall propitiate the bull-bannered god for the sake of the harvest; you must always provide protection for the kingdom with due respect. (47)
Then, having arrived at that very place and established Maheśvara, he propitiated him perfectly with vows and religious observances.
Then, at the end of a year, when he had attained satisfaction, the Blessed Lord Śiva said, "I am a granter of boons; ask for whatever you desire. (49)
The king said: "O Lord of the gods, this ritual was performed by me for the sake of food; therefore, O you who have the bull as your vehicle, grant me immeasurable [food] quickly."
In this manner, let rain fall upon the entire surface of the earth, so that crops may now grow and waters may abound.
O best of gods, by your grace, may there be eternal satisfaction for my high-souled father who dwells in heaven. (52)
The Blessed Lord said: "Before long, abundant rain will fall upon the surface of the earth; likewise, whatever kinds of food exist upon the earth shall come to be."
Therefore, O Indra among kings, go now toward your own home at my word; this shall undoubtedly come to pass.
And this Liṅga of mine, O King, which has been installed by you—whosoever, having risen in the morning, shall behold it properly; || 55 ||
O best of kings, by my word, he shall surely obtain sweet food as delicious as nectar in every birth, forevermore.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished from that place. The king also, filled with great joy, returned to his own abode and thereafter ruled a kingdom from which all thorns had been removed.
Sūta said: Even now, when this terrible Kali age has arrived, whoever rises at dawn and beholds that giver of sweet food with devotion—
O twice-born ones, if he so desires, he obtains delicious food; or, if free from desire, he attains the abode of the trident-bearing God.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Miṣṭānnadeśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sūta said: Furthermore, there exists another meritorious triad of Gaṇapatis there; one bestows heaven, another bestows the mortal world, and yet another is meritorious in that it removes the suffering of hell.
It is indeed the destroyer of all obstacles, worshipped by gods and dānavas; it bestows all desires and increases both knowledge and fame.
The sages said: O Sūta, three kinds of persons are born here upon the surface of the earth; there are the superior, the middling, and others who remain as the inferior.
Indeed, the most excellent ones seek only liberation alone, having gone where they do not return to the surface of the earth by any means whatsoever.

Those of middling capacity [attain] the path to heaven and delightful divine enjoyments, as well as sport together with celestial nymphs (apsaras), all brought about by such actions as sacrifices and other rites. || 5 ||
The base ones, whose souls are devoted to sense-objects, take delight here in the world of mortals; having formed an exceedingly great attachment there, they are like insects in poison.
Having abandoned both heaven and liberation, why is this mortal state desired? For what reason do mortals pray to this leader of the Gaṇas, who bestows only mortal [rewards]?
By whom were those elephant-faced deities established in that field, and at what time are they to be seen? Tell me everything in detail.

Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having previously performed severe penance in the world of mortals, they then go joyfully to heaven according to their own will; likewise, others follow the path of liberation with minds manifested through meditation.
Then, once, while heaven was crowded with the best of men and the gods were being scattered in every direction by his power, [he spoke].
Having gone there himself, the thousand-eyed Indra, accompanied by all the hosts of gods, spoke to Śaṅkara, who was seated on a single throne together with Gaurī.
Indra said: O Supreme Lord, by men who have attained perfection through the power of austerity, our entire majesty—including our homes and all else—is pervaded. (12)
Therefore, having shown us some favor, please consider now some means by which we may remain here in this abode of Śiva in happiness.
Then, O twice-born ones, having heard those words of theirs, Virūpākṣa gazed upon the moon-like face of Pārvatī as she sat by his side.
Then the Goddess, having rubbed her own body repeatedly and extracted all that impurity, fashioned from it the face of a serpent. || 15 ||
He had four arms and a massive body, endowed with a large protruding belly, and he caused great wonder among all those inhabitants of heaven.
Then, with humility, he said to the goddess Śikharavāsinī: "O Mother, tell me without delay the purpose for which I have been created; let that task be performed. (17)
"By your grace, there is nothing in the three worlds that is unattainable for me. (18)
The Goddess said: "O Śrī, you must create obstacles for those men in the mortal world who are always intent upon heaven and liberation, even in their auspicious undertakings. (19)
Thirty *saritāṃ-patayas*, seventy-seven *śaṅkus*, sixty *mahāsarojas*, and twenty *nikharvas*. (20)
There are ninety-five crores, fifty-five lakhs, twenty-five thousand, nine hundred and sixty, along with other groups, stationed here together with ten thousand Arbudas. || 21 ||
May all those foremost of the Gaṇas, among whom Nandī is remembered as the first and Mahākāla as the next, come under your control and prosper for you.
"I have granted you sovereignty, my child; exercise that authority. You shall be established in the leadership over all the hosts of Gaṇas. (23)
Having spoken thus, that goddess then had brought golden jars filled with water from excellent holy fords, containing medicinal herbs and bringing great prosperity.
The Queen of the Gods herself performed his consecration, accompanied by the entertainment of song and instrumental music, and the sounds arising from dances and auspicious rites. (25)
Thirty-three crores of gods who reside in heaven all came there and performed auspicious rites for him.
Then the Lord whose banner is the bull, being pleased, gave him a sharp axe in his hand, which was indeed always his most excellent weapon.
The highly fortunate Pārvatī, devoted to maternal affection, [offered] a vessel completely filled with sweetmeats that was indeed inexhaustible for the purpose of his meal.
Kārttikeya, filled with great joy and moved by the affection of a kinsman, regarded the mouse as his brother and took it as his vehicle. (29)
With a joyful heart, Brahmā bestowed upon him divine knowledge regarding the past, the future, and whatever exists in the present. (30)
Viṣṇu, the thousand-eyed one, bestows wisdom and great, supreme good fortune; Kāmadeva bestows good fortune, while Kubera bestows wealth and other such blessings.
The Lord Sun [bestows] majesty, and the Moon [bestows] foremost splendor.
Likewise, all the other gods gave many desired things for the sake of pleasing the Goddess and the Lord God. (33)
O best of the twice-born, having thus obtained the boon, that Lord of the Gaṇas thereafter constantly devoted himself to the service of the gods while creating obstacles upon the earth.
Then, for those striving for the sake of Dharma, for liberation, and for the performance of meritorious deeds, Gaṇeśa—whoever is remembered there—descends upon the surface of the earth.

O twice-born ones, having approached there, he was installed by the celestial beings (vaimānikas), so that people desiring heaven performed his worship at the very beginning of all undertakings, being intent on the destruction of obstacles.

At that very time, the Brāhmaṇas born in Camatkārapura—who were devoted to the knowledge of Brahman and seeking the cause of liberation—installed there the Lord known as Mokṣada (the Giver of Liberation).
Furthermore, by others desiring heaven, Heraṃba was installed there as the opener of the gate to heaven, established with his true name exactly as it has been proclaimed.

Likewise, there resides another group of attendants named Martyada; by them, those who have fallen from heaven never again go to hell or similar realms, nor to the state of an animal, a worm, or even an immobile being. || 39 ||
For this reason, O best of the twice-born, Heramba was born in that meritorious field as the giver of death to mortals, yet always the giver of heaven to those who have attained it.
All this meritorious narrative concerning the origin of Heraṃba has been told to you; when heard by men, it destroys all obstacles.
The man who worships on this fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha will not encounter any obstacle whatsoever for the duration of that year. (42)
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, there is also another deity there, Citreśvara, who resides in the center of Citrapīṭha and bestows wonderful happiness upon men.
Having seen, worshipped, or bathed [this image], a person is liberated from the major and minor sins arising from adultery with another's wife. || 2 ||
Having violated the wife of his guru, or a maiden born of his own lineage, or a woman of low birth, or one engaged in a vow, with a mind addicted to lust; || 3 ||
The man who worships him on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra quickly destroys that sin and thereafter proceeds to the heavenly world.
Likewise, King Citrāṅgada remained there together with Jābāli and the maiden born of him who was naked, standing before him after having been cursed by Jābāli in the past.
Whosoever among those three should perform the oblation on that day, he obtains a desired woman and the success that resides in his mind.
The sages said: Why was the youth Citrāṅgada cursed by Jābāli in the past, and why was his daughter, while still a maiden, deprived of her garments?
Even today she remains there, assuming a contradictory form that constantly causes people to laugh; therefore, O Sūta, tell us about it.
Sūta said: In former times, there was a sage renowned by the name Jābāli, who always practiced ascetic penance through lifelong celibacy from his youth.
Having reached the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, O excellent twice-born ones, he began a great penance even while still in his childhood.
By performing the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, Pārāka, and other penances gradually and steadily, he brought those gods within the range of his fear.
Then Śakra and the other gods, terrified on the summit of Mount Meru, assembled and held a consultation among themselves for the purpose of creating obstacles for him.
If the increase of this asceticism continues in this manner perpetually, it will surely displace Indra from his sovereignty over heaven.
Therefore, let Rambhā, the most excellent of the Apsarases, go to the side of that seer of purified soul to obstruct his vow of celibacy.
Since celibacy has been proclaimed by the twice-born as the root of austerity, in its absence, there is only hardship in a vow and no fruit whatsoever.
Having thus made their decision, all the gods then respectfully summoned Rambhā and spoke to her with great reverence by the command of Mahendra.
"Go quickly, O illustrious lady, to where Jābāli resides in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, in order to create an obstacle to his penance. (17)
Those various states and those various captivating stories should be employed, so as to increase his unrestrained passion within his mind. (18)
Rambhā said: "O Lord of the Gods, that sage does not understand the nature of desire. O God, how shall I make one who is ignorant of passion fall under the sway of love? (19)
Indra said: "At my command, this Vasanta shall go into his presence; by the mere sight of him, he will be restored to his memory."
Therefore, O fair-faced one, go there quickly with him, so that success may be achieved and the task of the gods may be swiftly accomplished. (21)
Then, having bowed to him, she set out quickly toward the earth’s surface, accompanied by Vasanta, to where Jābāli was staying.
Then, suddenly, a profusion of flowers appeared upon the Aśoka tree, and clusters of blossoms emerged on the Tilaka and the mango trees.
Indeed, in the cool season, the lotuses attained full bloom, and a fragrant southern breeze blew, granting all desires.
In the meantime, the excellent Apsaras Rambhā arrived there at the bank of the lake where Jābāli was staying.
Holding a rosary in his hand, he recited mantras many times with devotion, having performed the libations for the ancestors as desired.
Then, as he was looking on, she released her garment.
Then that excellent Apsaras entered that water for the purpose of bathing.
Beholding her, who was radiant with youth, standing there unclothed and touched by the southern breeze, he too fell under the sway of desire.
Then, O excellent sage, at that very moment a tremor came over him, and the rosary fell from the tip of his hand onto the surface of the earth.
A most intense horripilation arose over all his limbs; warm tears fell, drenching the surface of the earth. (30)
Then, perceiving him to be agitated, that excellent Apsaras, who knew the mind, emerged from that water and took hold of her garment.
Then, having approached him and prostrated with great respect, she spoke these sweet words, further strengthening his resolve.
"O Brahmin, O sage, is all well with you in the hermitage? O wise one, is it well with your Vedic study, your asceticism, your disciples, and the deer and birds? (33)
The sage said: || 9 ||
"O lady of beautiful hips, my welfare is now established everywhere; especially so since you, endowed with all auspicious marks, have arrived here. (34)
"Tell me, O illustrious lady, who are you, you who increase my passion? Are you a goddess, or a daughter of the asuras, or a serpent-nymph, or perhaps a human woman? (35)
Declare it! Do you not see the trembling in my body, this unrestrained horripilation, and this flood of tears born from my eyes? (36)
Rambhā said: Is this the natural state of your limbs, or has it arisen from some other disease? I do not perceive any health arising from your body.
The sage said: "O fair-eyed one, this is neither my natural bodily state nor caused by diseases; listen to the full reason why my body has become thus."
For as long as the time required for your vision to arise lasts, for that long shall this form produced from my body remain. (30)
Therefore, O beautiful one, upon seeing you, I have become possessed by the god of love, even though I am devoted to celibacy and uphold this great vow.
Rambhā said:
"If it is so, O best of Brahmins, enjoy me as you please; there would be no fault in this, for I am a courtesan. (41)
"O Brahmin, we are common to all since we were created by the Self-born One; indeed, for all the worlds, and especially for the twice-born. (42)
And I too, O sage, having beheld you who resemble the god of love, have been struck by the sharp arrows of desire; thus, I do not venture to depart. (43)
In the past, I have seen gods, as well as yakṣas, vidyādharas, siddhas, kinnaras, nāgas, and guhyakas; what then to say of humans?
"O tiger among Brahmins, the form of your body has not been seen even by a single one of them; therefore, O best of Brahmins, accept me as your devotee. (45)
He who would reject a woman who has come to him of her own accord and is tormented by desire—that fool is cooked in a terrible hell for eternal years. (46)
Having spoken thus, she then embraced that great sage; though he was unwilling in word, he was full of longing in his heart.
Then, having led that lord of sages into a bower of creepers, she dallied with the sage through artificial gestures described in the treatises on love.
Thus he remained there with her until the end of the day, attached to the nature of desire and having abandoned all other activities.
Then, having become free from desire and overcome with shame, he dismissed Rambhā and thereafter performed his purification.
Released by him, that playful woman, having accomplished her purpose, departed full of joy to where the gods together with Indra were.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Agitation of Jābāli," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 143 ||
Sūta said: Having gone thereafter to heaven, she spoke to the thousand-eyed Indra, who was accompanied by the gods: "O Blessed One, by good fortune, that great sage has been provoked. (1)
All the ascetic merit that you have accumulated with great hardship has been destroyed; likewise, you have been rendered devoid of luster—may you now become a partaker of happiness.
Having spoken thus, Rambhā, praised by all the gods, conceived a fetus in her own womb from him whose seed is never in vain.
Jābāli, too, having felt remorse in many ways, remained once more established in austerity at that very same hermitage.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived, she gave birth to an auspicious daughter with eyes like lotus petals, marked by divine characteristics.
Then, perceiving her to be of human origin, he went to that very hermitage and released her in the presence of the ṛṣi, speaking as follows: || 6 ||
O tiger among sages, protect this girl now, who was conceived through your own vigor and has been dwelling within my womb.
"O Brahmin, there is no dwelling for humans in heaven by any means; for this reason, she has been entrusted to you by me. (8)
Having spoken thus, Rambhā departed quickly for the abode of the gods; and Jābāli, upon seeing that maiden, was filled with affection.
Then, having placed that girl in a well-concealed bower of creepers, he nourished her day and night with juices produced from sweet fruits.
That maiden also gradually attained great growth day by day, just as the digit of the moon in the sky does upon reaching the bright fortnight.
In whatever measure that lotus-eyed woman grew, in that same measure Jābāli’s deep affection for her also increased.
In her childhood, that most beautiful girl played with the deer and birds who were completely trusting of her, increasing the joy of the sage.
Then, having abandoned her childhood, with her body covered in bark garments, she rendered assistance to that ṛṣi in all his duties.
He brought from the forest whatever sacrificial fuel, kusha grass, and other items were needed, along with fruits and flowers; thus he increased his [the sage's] delight.
Then, after a few days, during the summer season, that fawn-eyed woman went far from her own hermitage for the sake of gathering fruit.
In the meantime, a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, one of the celestial dwellers, arrived there, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
There, in that secluded place, he beheld that young woman, whose face resembled the full moon, like a digit of the moon fallen upon the surface of the earth. (18)
Then, his limbs overwhelmed by passion, he descended from the celestial chariot to the surface of the earth and, with palms joined in reverence, addressed her with sweet words.
Who are you, O girl with eyes as beautiful as lotus-petals, who, radiant like the interior of a lotus, wanders alone in this desolate great forest in the midst of the woods? (20)
The maiden said: "O sage, I am named Phalavatī, the daughter of Jābāli; I have come here to this forest for the sake of gathering fruits and flowers."
Citrāṅgada said: "That best of sages is heard to have been a celibate from his youth; how then, O lady of beautiful thighs, were you born as his wife without [having had] a husband?"
The maiden said: "O highly fortunate one, it is true that this sage has no wife; however, listen to me as to how [this child] was born to him."
In former times, he beheld a celestial nymph named Rambhā; thereafter, overcome by desire, he enjoyed her company at his pleasure.
Then, born from her womb in the most exalted world of the gods, she was once again dispatched by her to this world for that very sage.
In this way, that Jābāli, the best of sages, became my father; I was nourished by him with the juices produced from various fruits.
Therefore, it was named Phalavatī by that great-souled one: "For this which you ask of me is indeed appropriate for me. (27)
Citrāṅgada said: "Having beheld your form, I have fallen under the power of desire; therefore, accept me, O timid one, for otherwise I shall perish. (28)
"I am a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, who has arrived at this sacred field, endowed with faith, for the purpose of a pilgrimage to the holy sites of the celestial dwellers. (29)
The maiden said: "I am still under the authority of my father, observing the conduct of a young girl; O Citrāṅgada, I do not know anything at all of the ways of love."
Therefore, request my father; he will give me, a wise woman, to you—a youth who is suitable and worthy.
This auspicious speech of yours is pleasing to my heart as well; I am blessed if I may embrace your neck according to my desire. (32)
Citrāṅgada said: "O illustrious lady, I am unable to wait for such a length of time; this great fire of passion arising within my limbs is consuming me. (33)
Therefore, O beautiful one, show me favor by granting me pleasure; for who knows what the state of that mind will become, or what its form will be? (34)
The maiden said: "If you behave in this manner, my father will undoubtedly burn you with a most terrible curse out of his wrath. (35)
Citrāṅgada said: "O giver of honor, in time your father will consume me; furthermore, this fire of passion will immediately reduce me to ashes. (36)
Having spoken thus, he then took that young girl by her right hand as she was trembling and filled with shame, and entered the abode of the gods.
There, afflicted by desire, he took his pleasure with her, who at that moment had become blinded by passion and had abandoned all sense of shame. (38)
Thus, as she remained there with him, the day passed; O best of sages, the sun then set as quickly as a blink of an eye.
In the meantime, the brahmin Jābāli, overcome with grief upon learning that his daughter had not returned, wandered everywhere.
"Alas! Has that daughter of mine been devoured by wild beasts? Or has she climbed some tree and fallen to the surface of the earth? (41)
Or perhaps, having reached some body of water and not knowing its depth, that young woman, seeking water, entered and sank there? (42)
Thus lamenting, that brahmin wandered through the dense forest, his body pierced by kusha grass and thorns, and distressed by hunger and thirst. (43)
Whatever sound arising from beasts or birds he hears during the night, he goes forth there, considering that [direction] to be fruitful.
Then, in due course, that excellent sage arrived at the palace of Hara, where that maiden, accompanied by Citrāṅgada, was staying.
Speaking without hesitation and repeatedly uttering words of passion—words that were utterly unworthy of young maidens, and especially those born of Brahmins. (46)
Then, having listened for a very long time from a distance, he was filled with amazement; and seeing the maiden's conduct, his eyes became bloodshot with anger.
Then, seizing a bundle of wood, he rushed forward with speed toward the two of them alone for their destruction, reviling them again and again.
"Fie, fie upon you of sinful conduct! You have defiled your maidenhood and brought a stain upon me even throughout the three worlds. (49)
Having obtained such a husband through this most base deed, I shall therefore destroy you, who are joined with this sin. (50)
Having spoken thus, just as that excellent sage was about to hurl his blow, Citrāṅgada vanished quickly along the path of the sky.
Naked there as well, her limbs exhausted by the pursuit of passion, she was unable to rise from the ground and go anywhere.
Then, having struck her down to the ground with a torrent of blows from wooden clubs and perceiving that she was dead, he was overcome with rage.
Then, seeing Citrāṅgada traveling through the path of the sky, overcome with fear, he pronounced a most terrible curse upon him as well.
"May that wicked man, who flies away after violating my daughter, fall down before long like a bird with its wings clipped. (55)
Afflicted with the disease of leprosy and unable to move at all, in that interval he fell from the sky onto the earth.
And that youth Citrāṅgada was afflicted with the disease of leprosy; then the sage, with a piece of wood raised in his hand, spoke to him in anger.
"Who are you, O evildoer, by whom this maiden has been forcibly violated? I shall now send you to the abode of Yama. (58)
Citrāṅgada said: "I am a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, a dweller of the third heaven; I have arrived at this sacred field on the occasion of a pilgrimage. (59)
Then, upon seeing the maiden, he fell under the sway of the god of love.
Therefore, I have resorted here to this bower of creepers, secluded from people; for that reason, grant forgiveness to me, who am wretched and prostrate before you.
Just as there might be the destruction of a disease, or just as there might be movement in the sky, so too, by your grace, let my anger toward the virtuous be but slight. (62)
Jābāli said: "By my word, you shall indeed assume such a form; and this wicked daughter of mine shall likewise always remain thus, stripped of her garment."
There is no doubt that she will come to life if she should ever place a garment anywhere upon her own body. (64)
"Surely her head too will burst apart; of this there is no doubt. Having spoken thus, he departed for his own hermitage in a state of great anger. (65)
Citrāṅgada also remained right there with her in that same manner; then, after some time had passed, [a certain person] arrived at that sacred field.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, at the onset of night, the Lord who bears the moon upon his crest, surrounded by fierce Gaṇas and accompanied by the formidable Yoginīs, set out for the sacred seat of Citreśvara.
Then, when midnight had arrived, those most dreadful yoginīs cried out, "Human flesh! Human flesh! for the purpose of eating it.
Dancing before that God of gods, the wielder of the trident, they vied with those leaders of the Gaṇas who were dancing all around them.
Whoever at that time offers them great flesh purified by mantras shall attain his desired accomplishment.
Whether it be liquor, meat, or other offerings such as fruits, his success is ordained to be exactly as it resides within his own heart.
In the meantime, that maiden born of Jābāli and Citrāṅgada went there and spoke respectfully.
"O Yoginīs, may you, filled with joy, eat this flesh of mine, which I have offered myself for your pleasure. (73)
Then, having seen that man covered with the disease of leprosy and that naked maiden, they were all filled with wonder.
All those fierce hosts and that three-eyed god, the Lord, filled with curiosity, questioned Citrāṅgada there.
Who are you, endowed with such fortitude and established in great courage, that you offer even your own life, so dearly cherished, to a mere insect? (76)
And who is this woman, devoid of garments yet free from distress, who, together with you, offers her own body—something that ought not to be given to anyone? (77)
Sūta said: Then he related everything regarding his own conduct—how he had consorted with a maiden and how the curse of the great sage was incurred.
Then, seeing Citrāṅgada, that Gandharva of the gods, to be in such a state, Śaṅkara was overcome with compassion and spoke as follows.
Having obtained my sight, death shall never occur; this sight is not in vain, therefore pray with reverence.

Citrāṅgada said: "O Śaṅkara, I am utterly despondent because of this disease; therefore, O Lord, I have come here so that the destruction of the disease may occur through the destruction of the body. (81)
Therefore, bring about the destruction of my disease if you would grant me a boon; furthermore, bestow upon me the power of moving through the air, so that I may go to heaven.
Śrī Śaṅkara said: "O best of Gandharvas, install my liṅga here upon this pedestal; then worship it with devotion for as long as the year lasts. (83)
In whatever manner you perform excellent worship of my liṅga, day by day, in that same manner the destruction of your disease shall occur. || 84 ||
Then, having attained movement through the sky, you shall go again to heaven by my grace; there is no doubt, for this which I have spoken is the truth. (85)
Since this maiden has entered into the center of the sacred seat (pīṭha), she shall become a yoginī named Phalavatī.

Established in this very form as one who is naked, she shall receive the primary worship and grant whatever is desired; at that time, it will exist in the minds of the worshippers with a hundredfold increase in merit.
A mortal should worship this [goddess], and thereafter this seat (pīṭha). For him who shall worship it, his desired success will thus come to pass.
Having spoken thus, she was then filled with great joy and, standing in the midst of the assembly of yoginīs, performed a dance thereafter.
Thus that yoginī and excellent woman became there; she performed such a supreme dance that Maheśvara was pleased.
Then, delighted, he spoke to her in the presence of all the yoginīs: "By this dance of yours, and especially by this song," (91)
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; therefore, listen to my words. When this very day reaches midnight, whoever performs worship for you,"
Through the honoring of liquor, meat, and food, and by means of mantras originating from the Āgamas, he will at that time become possessed of the power to both curse and grant grace.
It will undoubtedly effect the binding and deluding of the enemy, as well as their eradication and even their subjugation. (94)
Having established a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should worship the guardians of the directions, as well as Kṣetrapāla and all those deities associated with the act of traveling. 95.

Likewise, having first performed the worship at the crossroads according to the prescribed ritual, and having subsequently worshipped you, whoever shall perform the fire-oblation (homa), [shall attain success]. || 96 ||
Or, by means of dust raised from the left foot of an enemy, or with guggulu incense, one will effect a paralysis that lasts for a thousand [years].
And he who, fixing his enemy in his heart, shall apply with emblic myrobalans the powder produced from the rubbing of that enemy, will bring about his delusion. (98)
He who takes the water used for an enemy's bath as well as their mud, and offers it into the fire together with the remains of Śiva’s offerings (śivanirmālya), [shall achieve his goal]. || 99 ||
In your presence, that man will surely cause his enemy to vanish; moreover, through association with you, your beloved Citrāṅgada shall also obtain true honor as a consequence arising from you.
Phalavatī said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, then grant me yet another excellent boon. (101)
"Abide in my heart and grant me that happiness by which everything is produced; may this Jābāli, my father, always remain clothed. (102)
"May I remain right here day and night, in whatever manner it may be, so that he shall experience torment upon seeing my rival. (103)

She who indulges in the pleasures of the brahmin lineage arising from liquor and meat—she who constantly smells the scent of liquor and sees prepared meat, and who is always devoted to her own desires—goes to misery day by day. (104)
The Blessed Lord said: "O auspicious one, what has been spoken shall come to pass, and it has already been fulfilled now. I shall go to Kailāsa; you remain here as previously instructed."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the Lord Hara vanished from sight; and all those Yoginīs likewise settled in their respective places.
Citrāṅgada also, having constructed an excellent temple right there, installed a liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Thereupon, he propitiated [him] day and night without weariness. || 108 ||

Then, at the end of a year, freed from disease and assuming a beautiful form, he ascended an excellent celestial chariot and went to the abode of the gods. And that man named Jābāli likewise became naked.
Always remaining right there in that world, he became an object of ridicule for people; yet, beholding those transformations arising from his own son, he was filled with sorrow.
Then, having reached that very seat, the great sage, overcome by intense sorrow, censured the birth of women.
"Alas! Women will arise from sinful men, whose conduct is such even though they are born of the lineage of the twice-born. (112)
"Only once have I associated with a woman; yet from birth until death, I have incurred such sin as this. (113)
But as for those lowest of men who are ever attached to them, I do not know what their destination will be in this world, even though I reflect upon it.
While he was speaking thus, those yoginīs, filled with rage, spoke there to that brāhmaṇa who was surrounded by compassion.
The Yoginīs said: "O fool, do not revile women, for you have resorted to their yoga; since this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, is sustained by women. (116)
By whom Śeṣa was produced, and after him the Tortoise; by whom the earth is supported, upon which the entire universe is established. || 117 ||
"Blessed is this daughter of yours, O fool, who has attained supreme yoga and reached the highest state in just a few days here. (118)
But you, having fallen into folly and resorted to the path of the Vedas, being joined with ignorance, shall wander here in this cycle of worldly existence.
The sage said: "All women are most censurable; they cause suffering in all conditions, both in this world and in the next, and no happiness is obtained from them. (120)
For whose sake Śumbha and the great asura Niśumbha were slain, as well as Rāvaṇa, King Daṇḍa, and thousands of others. || 121 ||
Having obtained such a beloved Brahmin as Gautama, Ahalyā—devoid of virtuous character due to her feminine nature—approached Śakra and desired him.
The maiden said: "O deluded soul, as for what you say—that women are objects of reproach—tell me that so that I may enlighten you. (123)
O sage, there is no wisdom in your heart, nor shame, nor compassion; for even an outcaste would not perform that deed which has been done by you.
"O base one, I have been slain by you with a blow; yet no concern for the sin arising from the murder of a woman has been held in your heart. (125)
Especially when committed with a mind possessed by anger toward one's daughter, sins depart from this place through various kinds of expiations.
If you proclaim the truth regarding that which arises from the killing of a woman, then this sorrow of mine would not exist, since I have been slain by you, O lowest of the twice-born! (127)
O evil-minded one, that sin of yours—by which you were cursed and reduced to a state of nakedness—shall not depart anywhere, even at the end of a kalpa.
Therefore, afflicted by great suffering, eat while staying right here with me; you will likely no longer revile [me], nor will you seek to kill me. (129)
All women are beyond reproach; they are never to be found fault with. For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds. (130)
The Sage said: Women are of sinful conduct; they are never purified. For those whose delight is in another's husband, it bestows the state of an outcaste.
The maiden said: "Do not speak thus, O fool-souled one, that women are impure. In this regard, a verse was sung of old by Manu; listen to it from me. (132)
Brahmins are pure from their feet; cows are pure from their backs; goats and horses are pure from their mouths; and women are pure in every respect. || 133 ||
The sage said: Brāhmaṇas are pure in every respect, and cows are pure in every respect; goats and horses are pure in their mouths, but women are never pure [in their mouths]. 134.
The maiden said: "The wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is in his hand, the desire-tree (kalpadruma) is in his house, and Kubera is his servant—he who has a beloved woman in his home. (135)
The sage said: All calamities are his suffering, and all that is in his house is suffering for him—for whomsoever there is a lustful woman in his home, for him there is hell in every respect. (136)
The maiden said: "Whatever pleasures exist here, and whatever objects of enjoyment there may be—whether arising from dharma, artha, or kāma—they indeed originate from women. (137)
The sage said: Whatever great sufferings and whatever afflictions belong to embodied beings, [all those arise from the mind].
Whatever hardships and undesirable things there may be, they all arise from women.
The maiden said: "A woman may demonstrate all four—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—by means of the four circumambulations of the fire, even during her marriage. (139)
The sage said: Even at their first union, a woman displays the wandering of worldly existence under the very pretext of performing circumambulations of the sacred fire. (140)
The maiden said: "What men, even those rich in wisdom, would not become dispassionate upon seeing her with full breasts and eyes reaching to the tips of her ears? (141)
The sage said: Who indeed do not perish—those of deluded intellect who, with the notion that she is delightful, approach a woman with broad hips, like moths approaching flames? (142)
The maiden said: "Blessed is he who enjoys the breasts of women—smooth, firm, elevated, and beautiful—especially when accompanied by honey and meat. (143)
The sage said: "It would be better to touch two venomous serpents—swollen, hooded, and having just shed their skins—than to touch the breasts of one's wife."

The maiden said: "It is not merely their physical arrangement that is beautiful to the embodied; even the embrace of these lovely women leads to happiness and the bristling of one's hair with joy. (145)

The sage said: "It is not merely their physical arrangement that is charming; it brings sin to the sight, and the body of women, when touched, leads to destruction in this life and to hell after death. (146)
The maiden said: Who in this world is not happy? Who indeed is not virtuous? And who is not most desirable, to whom women are attracted? (147)
The sage said: Who would not attain liberation there? Who would not become most praiseworthy? Who would not be endowed with well-being—he who is not attached to women? (148)
The maiden said: "Even for a worm sleeping within the cycle of worldly existence, a woman's body is desirable here; how much more so, then, for a man who possesses discernment? (149)
The sage said: Just as that which is born of impurity is pleasing to a worm, so too is the body of a woman pleasing to a lustful man who is born of the cycle of worldly existence.
The maiden said: "Having reflected upon what might be an eternal place of happiness for men, the Creator, seeing nothing else, brought forth this jewel among women. (151)
The Sage said: Seeing no other means whatsoever for the bondage of the world, the Creator then fashioned this snare consisting of women, composed of the very form of woman. (152)
Sūta said: Thus, while that tiger among sages was rendered speechless by her in that encounter, he then spoke to his own daughter.
The sage said: "I must not engage in conversation with you now at any time, you who, though but a child, thus forbid me on all sides. (154)
Therefore, I consider myself truly more blessed today, since you, my daughter, are such as this—so expert in the sacred scriptures.
Therefore, O illustrious lady, not even the slightest anger exists within me; thus, play as you desire, staying in the midst of the yoginīs.
Then, seeing her father who was so affectionate and kind, she was filled with shame; bowing down while standing in the midst of the yoginīs, she spoke again. (157)
O Lord, whether out of ignorance or knowledge you have been forbidden by me, everything must be forgiven by me today, especially for the sake of Vālikā. (158)

Having arrived at this sacred seat (pīṭha), all those best of the twice-born and men devoted to devotion shall first perform worship; thereafter, they shall attain the supreme goal of all sacred seats. || 159 ||
Thus she was born there, originating from the sage Jābāli; and so too were the eminent sage Jābāli and Citrāṅgadeśvara. || 160 ||
Whatever mortal should perform worship of those three every single day, he shall attain perfection therein. || 161 ||
There is nothing whatsoever on this earth that cannot be accomplished; one shall be honored by kings and others, and likewise obtain divine enjoyments. (162)
Therefore, with every effort, that sage and that maiden should be especially honored, as well as that god Maheśvara. || 163 ||
All this narrative, which grants all desires, has been recounted to you; it brings benefit both in this world and in the next for those who read or hear it.
The sages said: "O Sūta, that which you have related—that the maiden did not die even though struck by the fierce blows—is a matter of great wonder."
Furthermore, since this Yoginī has arisen, bestowing satisfaction upon Hara, tell me everything regarding your purpose and that wonderful cause.

Sūta said: She entered that most meritorious Amareśvara together with him on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, where death does not exist (3). Moreover, O twice-born ones, when even at the end of one's natural lifespan death is absent, how much more so before its time? Therefore, although she was struck down very violently at that time, she did not meet her destruction (4).
The sages said: "Tell us of the deity who is called Amareśvara, the bestower of immortality—who established him here, what is his power, and how is he renowned?"
Sūta said: In former times, the high-souled Kaśyapa united with two auspicious daughters of Prajāpati, Aditi and Diti, both of whom were exceedingly beautiful.

The gods were born of Aditi, and the lords of the Daityas from Diti. Due to their status as half-siblings, a great enmity arose between them. Then the gods were struck down by the Daityas, while others were forced to turn their backs in retreat; still others, terrified with fear and with mangled limbs, fled in all directions.
Then the mother of the gods, afflicted by suffering, remained there and performed penance day and night, devoted solely to meditation upon Śiva.
Thus, while she remained engaged in penance, after four yugas had passed, a Śiva-liṅga emerged, piercing through the surface of the earth.
Then, filled with joy, she praised him with various hymns and, with a concentrated mind, paid homage by prostrating herself with the eight limbs of her body.
In the meantime, a divine voice, bodiless and with a resonance as deep as a thundercloud, arose in the expanse of the sky.
"Choose a boon, O auspicious lady, whatever resides in your heart; I, the moon-crested Lord, being pleased, shall grant it to you today. (13)
Aditi said: "O best of gods, my sons are being slain in battle by the Dānavas; therefore, make them invulnerable at the forefront of the fray so that they may be free from exhaustion. (14)
The Blessed Lord said: "O auspicious lady, those who, having touched this my liṅga, shall go forth into battle, shall be unslayable for the duration of one year."
Furthermore, any other person here who, being composed in mind, shall perform a vigil on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha; (16)
He too shall remain free from disease for a full year, even if the day of his death has arrived, provided he stays in this auspicious sanctuary.
"Death will come and will bypass him from afar. Having spoken thus, that voice then ceased thereafter.

Then Aditi, being well-pleased, gathered together her remaining sons who had survived the slaughter and showed them that very liṅga; she recounted all of its majesty, including the boons that had been proclaimed.
Then all those gods, having prostrated before that liṅga, returned toward them, taking up their weapons and filled with satisfaction.
There those Dānavas remained joyfully in the auspicious position of Śakra, endowed with the enjoyments of heaven and situated within the Nandana grove.
Then those Dānavas, seeing the many inhabitants of the triple heaven arrive suddenly for the sake of battle, bearing various weapons, [were struck with fear].
Having mounted excellent chariots and equipped with weapons, missiles, and armor, they advanced toward the enemy for battle, roaring like clouds.
Then a battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas, whose minds were impelled by wrath and who made death their only means of retreat.
Then all those gods, having obtained boons from Hara, struck down the innumerable Daityas in many ways with sharpened weapons.
And those among them who remained after the slaughter, abandoning the abode of the thirty gods and intent on flight, entered the ocean, the dwelling place of sea-monsters.
Then Śakra regained his own kingdom, which had been seized by the Dānavas; it was entirely restored to its former state, with all thorns removed.
Then those remaining Dānavas, having learned of that greatness arising from the Liṅga, as well as the majesty of Vṛṣanātha and the origin of this sacred field (kṣetra), [acted accordingly].

Śukra related all this: "Whoever, having become pure, worships that Liṅga on the fourteenth day at the onset of night during the dark fortnight of Māgha, that man shall never, even if seized by Time (Death), be deprived of his life-breaths. (29)
Therefore, O highly fortunate ones, having approached that Linga on that day at night, you should worship it, so that you may be freed from death. || 30 ||
This truth has been declared by me until the end of the year; that the hosts of gods [attained their state] through its power is beyond doubt. (31)
Then, having learned that counsel of the lords of the Dānavas from his son Nārada, the Lord of the Gods, a Brāhmaṇa, became terrified in his mind.
There, for the protection of the god, he made a pact with the gods so that there might always be a full effort on that day.

Then, thirty-three crores of gods, equipped with weapons, stationed themselves in that sacred field for the protection of that Liṅga; on the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month of Māgha, they remain well-armored and ready to strike.
Then those Dānavas, seeing the gods stationed there, fled in every direction with their minds terrified by fear.
Then, when the dawn had brightened and the orb of the sun had risen, all the gods once again held counsel with one another.
If we abandon this field and go to the abode of the gods, the Dānavas will approach this Liṅga and worship it.
"Then they too will all become incapable of being slain, just as we are; therefore, let us thirty-three leaders remain right here. (38)
"Let all the remaining ones among these very millions go there as well, joined with the Thousand-eyed One (Indra), as protectors of themselves and others in heaven. || 39 ||
Then the eight Vasus were there, as well as the twelve Ādityas, the eleven other Rudras, and the two beautiful Nāsatyas.
These remained in that sacred field for the protection of its emblems; the others, together with Śakra, departed for the abode of the gods.
Sūta said: Thus has been described the power of the Liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods, which was formerly established by Aditi and about which you have inquired.
Since death does not exist for embodied beings when that [liṅga] is seen, it is therefore renowned throughout the three worlds as the Liṅga called Amara. || 43 ||
In that very place where that maiden was slain by that twice-born Jābāli, who was greatly enraged, in the temple of that god—|| 44 ||
On that day, it was the fourteenth of the month of Māgha; therefore, although the poor woman was well struck, she did not meet her death.
O best of Brahmins, all this has been narrated to you—the origin of that Linga and its majesty, which destroys all sins. (46)
And for whoever recites this with devotion in the presence of that Liṅga, the fear of untimely death shall never arise in any way.
In front of it is an auspicious pool filled with clear water, constructed by the goddess Aditi for her own ablutions.
Having bathed there, the man who beholds that Liṅga and keeps a vigil at night on that very day after day, shall not meet with untimely death for a full year from that time.
The sages said: O high-minded one, please tell us the names of all the Ādityas, as well as those of the Vasus, Rudras, and the Aśvins, individually.
Sūta said: Vṛṣadhvaja, Śarva, and Mṛgavyādha as the third; Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Pinākin is indeed the sixth.
Dahana, Īśvara, and Kapālī as the ninth; Vṛṣākapi is the tenth, and Tryambaka is indeed Rudra.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Makha, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. || 4 ||
Varuṇa, as well as Sūrya, Bhānu, Khyāta, and Tāpana; Indra, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, and likewise Bhaga.
Gabhasti, Dharmarāja, Svarṇaretas, Divākara, Mitra, and Vāsudeva—these twelve are the Bhāskaras.
Nāsatya and Dasra—these two are known as the Aśvins, the highly fortunate physicians of the gods, born from the womb of Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter.
These thirty-three who are renowned as the leaders of the gods are eternally stationed in this very field for the sake of slaying the Dānavas.
The man who, with his senses restrained, worships them with devotion when the prescribed day arrives, shall not meet with untimely death.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, the Rudras should be worshipped by the wise, especially in that sacred field, by those desiring the supreme state.
On the tenth day the Vasus are to be worshipped, and especially on the eighth day by those desiring heaven, with various kinds of diversions.
Furthermore, on the seventh and the sixth [lunar days], those men who desire strength free from adversaries should worship the suns.

Likewise, those mortals who always desire the destruction of disease and the attainment of freedom from illness should worship the two physicians of the gods on the twelfth day; they shall become free from ailment.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Amareśvara Kuṇḍa," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, in the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another deity there who bestows sons upon men; he is Hara, named Vaṭikeśvara, the destroyer of all sins.
O best of the twice-born, it was there that Vaṭikā formerly performed penance; after Śuka had gone to the forest, she obtained from Vyāsa a son named Kapiñjala.
The sages said: Whose daughter was that girl there, and how did she perform penance? And why did Śuka, having abandoned his home, take refuge in the forest? (3)
How did she of the pure smile obtain Kapiñjala as a son from Vyāsa? (4)
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, there once arose in Vyāsa—a great soul who was free from desire, tranquil, and omniscient—a certain thought regarding the matter of a wife.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when the lineage born of the Kurus had reached its end, they approached King Vicitravīrya.
Thereafter, by the command of Satyavatī, he begot three heroic sons in her womb, the eldest of whom was Pāṇḍu.
While remaining in the vow of a forest-dweller, he became intent on sexual union once; thus, through sons born of his wife, the lineage of Kuru was established.
Then he reflected: "Today I shall take a wife; through the dharma of the householder's life, I shall attain an auspicious goal."
Then he requested Jābāli for his auspicious daughter; he quickly gave him that beautiful maiden named Vaṭikā.
Then, united with her, he took up residence in the forest; remaining in the stage of life of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he was intent upon sexual union.
Then, at her side, Piñjalā became pregnant; having encountered delusion during her season, she conceived from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
Then, that embryo situated there in the womb of Vyāsa’s wife reached supreme growth, like the moon in the bright fortnight.
As he remained thus united with her, twelve years passed while the fetus grew constantly, yet birth did not occur.
Whatever words he heard there at any time while staying in the womb, he, endowed with wisdom, retained them all within his heart.
Even while dwelling in the womb, he had thoroughly studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, as well as the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the entire body of scriptures concerning liberation.
Even while staying there, he performs his private recitation (svādhyāya) by day and by night; and he should not, under any circumstances, contemplate the intellect born of his previous birth.
That mother also, being thus distressed, constantly undergoes great suffering; for as he, having taken refuge in her womb, grows larger and larger, so too does she suffer.
Then, overcome with wonder, Vyāsa spoke these words: "Who are you that have entered the womb of my wife, assuming the form of an embryo? (19)
"Why do you not come out? What will you do with this? The embryo replied: "I am a Rākṣasa, I am a Piśāca, I am a god, and likewise a human. (2)
"I was an elephant, and also a horse, a cock, and even a goat; indeed, there were eighty-four thousand species of wombs in number. (21)
I am deluded regarding all of them; so who am I that I should speak anything now, having become a human being and taken refuge in a womb? (22)
I shall not perform any human rite, nor shall I ever act out of desire; for I have become weary from wandering here in this dreadful cycle of existence. (23)
Remaining here, liberated from worldly existence and always devoted to the practice of yoga, I shall proceed upon the path to liberation; from this place, I shall attain liberation without a doubt.
O best of the twice-born, every living being remains possessed of knowledge, detachment, and the memory of previous births for as long as it stays within the womb. (25)
When one has emerged from the womb and is touched by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, then it perishes instantly; this is the truth, without a doubt. || 26 ||
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall not emerge by any means whatsoever; from this womb I shall go to liberation from that place without a doubt.
Vyāsa said: That Vaiṣṇava Māyā shall not prevail over you in any way; depart from this most terrible and contemptible hell.

"Therefore, resorting to yoga after this dwelling in the womb, go to Śiva. For that reason, show me your own face, so that by the sight of your face, I may be freed from my debt to the world of the ancestors. (29)
The Embryo said: "O twice-born one, if you grant me Vāsudeva as my surety, then my birth shall take place now by your own hand; it cannot be otherwise."
Sūta said: Then Vyāsa, having gone quickly toward Dvārakā in great sorrow, related the account in detail to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Accompanied by him alone, Vyāsa subsequently returned to his own home; he intended to give Viṣṇu, the stainless one, as a surety for him.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "I am the guarantor for the destruction of your Māyā upon your departure. Having emerged at my word, go to the unsurpassed liberation. (33)
Then, O twice-born ones, he quickly emerged at the word of Viṣṇu, having reached the age of twelve years and being close to youth.
Then, having bowed down to the enemy of the Daityas, as well as to Vyāsa and his mother, the son of Vyāsa set out for forest-dwelling at that very moment.
Then that sage said to him: "Stay, my son, in your own home; so that I may perform for you the purificatory rites, such as the birth ceremony and others."
The child said: "In birth after birth, hundreds of purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been performed upon me—those rites consisting of bonds by which I am cast into the ocean of worldly existence."
The Blessed Lord said: "O Sage, because this little son of yours prattles like a parrot (śuka), let him therefore be known by the name Śuka, he who is an expert in the science of Yoga. (38)
Free from delusion and illusion, he will not remain in his own palace; therefore, let him go, and do not harbor affection for him.
"I shall go home; you are now freed from your father's debt. This which I have spoken is the truth, simply by the sight of my son. (40)
Having spoken thus and taking leave of Vyāsa, Hṛṣīkeśa quickly mounted the king of birds and set out toward Dvārakā.
Then, after Hṛṣīkeśa had departed, Vyāsa spoke to his son, who was setting out for the forest dwelling and was indifferent toward his own home.

Vyāsa said: For those devoid of the duties of a householder, the word of the father perishes. He who, out of delusion, does not properly carry out the father's command goes to hell; therefore, my son, do not go against my word. (43)
Śuka said: "O best of sages, just as I have been born by you today, and as you were born by me in another birth, so too am I your father."
Therefore, you must grant me leave, for this is the established order of dharma; I am not to be forbidden from departing for the forest of asceticism.
Vyāsa said: Birth in the house of a Brāhmaṇa is attained by men through meritorious deeds; having received there the sacraments prescribed in the Vedas, one becomes a sage.
Śuka said: If liberation were attained through purificatory rites (saṃskāras) without auspicious action (karma), then even heretics who observe vows would attain that liberation.

Vyāsa said: One should first be a student (brahmacārī), and after that a householder (gṛhastha); then a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and an ascetic (yati), and thereby one shall attain liberation (mokṣa). || 48 ||

Śuka said: If liberation were attained through celibacy alone, then it would belong eternally to eunuchs; if it belonged to those in the householder stage of life, then the entire world would be liberated.
Or else, it arises for those deer who are attached to the forest.
Alternatively, if liberation were to result for men through the duties of ascetics, then that liberation would first belong to all those who are poor. (51)
Vyāsa said: For those men who are devoted to the duties of a householder and who walk upon the path of the righteous, both this world and the next have been fully proclaimed by Manu.
Śrī Śuka said: For those who are well-concealed within the house by the bonds of kinship, how can there be a journey upon the path of the righteous due to the onset of delusion and passion? (53)

Vyāsa said: For a man dwelling here in the forest, there is not only hardship arising from his own body; all rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors do not flourish there. Therefore, one should consider what is for one's own welfare while living in the home.

Śrī Śukadeva said: For those sages whose great austerities are purified by their devotion, all the fruits of their penance remain as long as they take refuge at your feet; for such men never behold the faces of the wicked, which is indeed their true happiness.
Vyāsa said: For men who follow the duties of the householder stage of life, the household and its possessions bestow eternal happiness both in this world and in the next. (56)

Śrī Śuka said: By the turn of fate, cold may arise even from fire, and heat even from the moon; in this world of mortals, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a birth of happiness resulting from worldly attachment.

Vyāsa said: Human birth, which is difficult to obtain on earth, is acquired with great merit and hardship. Once it is obtained, what has not been gained if one becomes a knower of the duties of the household?
Śrī Śukadeva said: If a human being here were endowed with knowledge at the time of birth, that knowledge would indeed dissolve upon perceiving his own [true] state. (59)
Vyāsa said: Even for a joyful son, for a young donkey, and for people eager for ashes, even the sound of one crying out brings delight.
Śrī Śuka said: O Sage, in this world, people find satisfaction in a child who has long been covered in filth, crawling about and smeared with dust; such a person is truly childish.
Vyāsa said: There is a most terrible hell named Punnāman in the abode of Yama; one who is childless would go there, and for that reason a son is highly praised.
Śrī Śuka said: O great sage, if heaven were attained through a son, then it would belong to all—especially to pigs, dogs, and even locusts.

Vyāsa said: A mortal becomes free from debt to the ancestors by seeing a son; likewise, he becomes free from debt to the gods through a grandson, and finds refuge in heaven through a great-grandson. (64)
Śuka said: "The vulture lives for a long time and beholds his own progeny; why does he not, through that continuous succession, attain liberation? (65)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, he abandoned his father—who was afflicted by great sorrow and lamenting in many ways—and departed for the forest.
Seeing him, Vyāsa became distressed and despaired of seeing his son; tormented by grief for his son, he remained together with his wife.
Sūta said: Having thus recognized her own son to be indifferent toward home, Piṅgalā, overcome with grief, spoke these words to Vyāsa.

"O best of the twice-born, I shall practice penance for the sake of a son; grant me permission so that I may propitiate Maheśvara, by means of which there may be born to me a supreme son who will cause the increase of my lineage. (2)
Having thus made her resolve and obtained the permission of the sage, that devoted wife reached this sacred field and performed austerities.
Having installed the god Śaṅkara, he constructed before him a very extensive tank of pure water that destroys sins through bathing.
Then the Blessed Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, having attained satisfaction with her, spoke to her with a joyful inner soul, saying, "I am the giver of boons."
The illustrious Mahādeva said: "I am well-pleased with you, O blessed lady; choose a boon, O lady of virtuous vows. Whatever resides eternally within my heart, there is nothing that I cannot grant."
Vaṭikā said: "O best of gods, grant me a son who shall increase my lineage, who always delights the heart, and who is possessed of good character and humility. (7)
Śrī Mahādeva said: "O most auspicious one, there is no doubt that you shall have a son, O highly fortunate lady, exactly as you have specifically requested."

Furthermore, any other human woman who, being composed, bathes here in this pond and worships my liṅga—which was installed by you today—on the fifth day for the duration of a year when the bright fortnight has arrived, [shall obtain the same fruit].
And she who is afflicted by misfortune, having given [this gift] on the third day here, shall indeed obtain an excellent son as the supreme fruit.
After bathing here in the water, she shall worship my liṅga; at the end of the year, she will become endowed with good fortune.
Furthermore, whatever man bathes here and worships me, if he has desires he shall obtain his desires, and if he is free from desire, he shall obtain liberation itself.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished from that place; she, for her part, obtained a son from Vyāsa, who was known as Kapiñjala.

In whatever manner she was previously described by the trident-bearing God of gods, and by whom the goddess Kelīvarī was formerly established here—she who bestows all perfections in the world and was worshipped there in the past.
The sages said: O son of Sūta, it is heard that there is a goddess named Kelīśvarī; tell us her greatness and her origin in great detail.
At what time did the Mistress of the Gods arise, and for what purpose? What benefit arises from her worship and salutation? (2)
You have spoken of Kātyāyanī and Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the gods; and how did Śrīmātā come into being, and for what purpose is she the sovereign of the gods? (3)
Śrīmātā, as well as Tārā and the goddess Śatruvināśinī, have been mentioned; however, Kelīśvarī has not yet been spoken of—therefore, tell of her now.
O son of a Sūta, curiosity has arisen in us regarding this matter.
Sūta said: From the beginning, there is one primordial deity established in the world in many forms, for the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the destruction of the faction of the Daityas.
Whenever and wherever a calamity befell the gods here, at that very time, that supreme power which exists pervading all things [intervened].
This entire mother of the world took birth upon the surface of the earth; she is Kātyāyanī on this earth for the sake of destroying the demon Mahiṣāsura.
When the supreme form had descended and entered these three worlds, there were two Dānavas, Śumbha and Niśumbha, who were arrogant because of their strength.
Then she herself, having assumed the form of Cāmuṇḍā, descended when Kālayavana had risen up, bringing fear to all the gods.

That very goddess Śrīmātārūpiṇī was born upon the surface of the earth; she was created by Śambhu, whose mind was intent on the destruction of the demon Andha, as the playful goddess by whom this entire world is pervaded. (11)
Then, by her power, having slain the Daityas without exception, Andhaka—who brought calamity to the three worlds—was subsequently killed.
The sages said: Whose son was this Andhaka? What was his power, and how was he slain? Why was he killed in battle? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: Dakṣa had a daughter named Diti, the abode of all virtues; Hiraṇyakaśipu was born as her son.
By whom all the gods, beginning with Śakra, were conquered on the field of battle; by that very high-souled one, sovereignty over heaven was established extensively. 15.
Out of fear of whom all the gods fashioned numerous most excellent weapons, along with armor and shields.
And he who was himself torn open by the powerful Viṣṇu out of wrath, having placed his hands upon the knee and the back. (107)
To him were born two sons endowed with the qualities of heroism and magnanimity: the elder was called Prahlāda, and the second was Andhaka.
When Hiraṇyakaśipu had reached the world of death, Prahlāda was then addressed by his circles of friends and by ministers endowed with humility.
Now govern this ancestral kingdom of your father and grandfather; bear the burden arising from sovereignty and strike down the gods in battle.
Prahlāda said: "I shall not rule the kingdom on this earth under any circumstances; therefore, listen now to my words. (21)
The gods, led by Śakra, do not desire the kingdom of the Daityas; Viṣṇu himself, the Blessed One, is their eternal protector.
I would undoubtedly sacrifice my life or even all my possessions; yet, alas, I am not capable of engaging in battle with Hari.
"I shall by no means engage in battle with him who has been constantly worshipped and bowed to by me, O Lord of the Gods. (24)
Sūta said: When the kingdom inherited from his father had been relinquished by Prahlāda, Andhaka was installed there after the ministers had consulted among themselves.
The son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, who destroyed the pride of gods and dānavas, also, immediately thereafter, entrusted the kingdom to his ministers.
Having abandoned desire, as well as anger, hypocrisy, and envy, he performed austerities for a long time while meditating upon the Grandfather (Brahmā).
With his senses conquered and his mind perfectly tranquil, equanimous toward all living beings, taking refuge at the foot of a tree, he remained peaceful with a contented inner self.
For as long as a thousand years he subsisted on fruits, and for another thousand years his food consisted of withered leaves.
O best of the twice-born, meditating day and night upon the Grandfather, the God of gods, he then subsisted on air for that length of time.
Then, when the fourth thousand-year period had arrived, Brahmā himself, having approached him in person, spoke to him joyfully: || 31 ||

Brahmā said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. Being pleased with you, I shall grant it even if it be very difficult to obtain. Andhaka said: "If you grant me a boon, O Brahmā, as desired in my mind, then let that which destroys old age and death be given to me, O best of gods. (33)
