The venerable Brahmā said: No one at all exists here on the surface of the earth who is free from old age; nor indeed does anyone exist on this earth whose birth would not be followed by death.
Nevertheless, I shall grant it to you, who are so devoted to many dharmas; therefore, O illustrious one, go to your own home and rule the kingdom.
His kingdom would yield little fruit, like a cremation ground serving as a dwelling, crowded with many thorns and filled with those of cruel deeds. (36)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the four-faced one then vanished from sight. After some time, impelled by the law of Time and remembering the enmity toward his father, he then spoke to his ministers.
Andhaka said: "Our father has been slain by the gods, as has our uncle of great strength, through deceit and not through valor; therefore, I shall destroy them. (38)
What is the purpose of a son being born who does not attain renown everywhere through well-performed deeds, like a banner at the forefront of a lineage? (39)
The ministers said: "O illustrious one, these words which have been spoken by you are fitting; all the gods who are our adversaries should indeed be slain. (4)
"These worlds indeed belong to us; who are the gods and who are the twice-born? We shall seize the sacrificial portions by slaying the gods headed by Śakra. (41)
Having thus made this agreement, accompanied by a vast army, they went swiftly to that place where Śakra was stationed.
Śakra, too, seeing the army of the Dānavas suddenly approaching, then mounted the elephant Airāvaṇa and went forth for battle.
Together with all the hosts of gods, headed by the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas; in the meantime, Śakra took up his most terrible thunderbolt.
Aiming at Andhaka, the slayer of enemy heroes released it at him; that best of Danujas, laughing, was struck by that thunderbolt.
In the battle, filled with joy, he addressed Śakra with a piercing cry: "O Śakra, today at long last I have beheld the strength of your arms. (46)
Now, O slayer of Bala, you yourself behold us! 47.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, he then whirled his heavy mace and released it—fashioned by Viśvakarman and resounding with the great noise of a hundred bells.
It was made entirely of iron, heavy, resembling the tongue of Yama, another [form of] destruction, measuring a hundred cubits in size, and increasing the fear of living beings.
Struck by her, Śakra, his senses overwhelmed by a swoon, leaned against the flagpole and sat down upon the head of the elephant.
Then, seeing Śakra unconscious, the enraged Skanda released his own spear, which was infallible and like a thunderbolt.
Beholding her approaching, the exceedingly powerful Dānava, with sharp arrows, effortlessly turned her back in an instant.
Then Skanda also, taking up his bow, discharged arrows resembling venomous serpents toward him, displaying his swiftness in weaponry.
In the meantime, all the gods completely covered the army of the Dānavas from every side with showers of weapons.
Then all the Dānavas afflicted the army of the gods with their blows, and those inhabitants of heaven fled.
Then, seeing the gods broken, the bull-vehicled Lord, accompanied by his retinue, revealed himself to the gods as if to comfort them. (59)
"Do not fear, O all you deities; behold my exertion! Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu then [acted] with Atharvan mantras.
He invoked the supreme, unsurpassed power of the Lord of the Universe; thus invoked, that supreme power went into the presence of Hara. (58)
Seeing her arrived before him, accompanied by all the gods, he bowed down and praised her with devotion through this hymn: || 59 ||

The Blessed Lord said: Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods; salutations to you, O beloved of devotion. O omnipresent one, O goddess of all deities, salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe.
Salutations to you who, in the form of Śakti, bring about creation and dissolution; salutations to you who are endowed with radiance, with earrings blazing like lightning.
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, O Goddess; you are creation, you are purity, and steadfastness. You are Arundhatī as well as Indrāṇī; you are Lakṣmī and you are Pārvatī.
Whatever form of woman exists throughout the three worlds, all of that is your own form; such is the certainty established in the scriptures. (63)
The Goddess said: For what purpose have I been summoned by you, O Bull-vehicled One? Proclaim all that to me regarding those fierce Atharvaṇa mantras.
By means of which I shall perform your entire task exactly as it was described.
The Blessed Lord said: "O illustrious lady, all these gods, headed by Śakra, have been expelled from heaven by Andhaka, the sovereign of the Daityas."
Therefore, listen to me as I go forth for the purpose of slaying him; quickly provide me with assistance so that I may destroy him on the field of battle.
"All these groups of Mothers have now been given by me to you; they will destroy the Dānavas who stand before you, emaciated as they are with hunger. (68)
For you, having assumed a playful form in a thousand ways, were summoned from the midst of the fire by means of many transformed appearances.
Therefore, you shall be known by the name Kelīśvarī throughout the three worlds; and whoever shall worship you with devotion in this very form, [shall attain success]. (70)
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, his desire shall be fulfilled; moreover, when the time for battle has arrived, he shall offer praise to you with this hymn.
Whichever king shall perform this, victory will be his in battle, even if his own army is small and his horses are few.
"Victory will surely come through your grace; of this there is no doubt. Thus was Kelīśvarī addressed by the God of gods at that time.
Delighted, she set out at the head of that army of existence, together with all the hosts of Mothers, who were uttering fierce and most terrifying cries. (74)
Then those Dānavas—fierce, devoted to the zeal for battle, and striking with various weapons—beheld that army of women which had arrived. (75)
Deformed, with a distorted appearance and a distorted voice, he held a weapon raised in his hand and was wholly intent on the desire for battle. || 76 ||
Some laughed with melodious voices, while others reviled him; other Dānavas, recognizing her as a woman, did not strike her.
Even while being struck down, they felt shame and remained steadfast in their own manliness; in the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived.
He related the entire account to Andhaka: "O best of the Danus, these women have not arrived for the purpose of battle. (79)
This *kṛtyā*, mounted upon a lion and standing with hands marked by discs, was created by Rudra for the purpose of slaying you. (80)
This one named Kelīśvarī has emerged from the fire-pit; together with these fierce women, she has come by resorting to the power of mantras.
When the oblation was performed by Śambhu, the God of gods, who was passionately devoted to his own [nature], that very Lord, becoming enraged, approaches you in person.
Having stationed those best of gods in his own palace for battle, he vowed their slaughter before the Supreme Lord (Brahmā).
Having understood this, O illustrious one, perform whatever is appropriate.
Andhaka said: "I am not afraid of Rudra, nor of anyone else; I shall not strike women, upholding the vow of a man. (85)
Sūta said: As that high-souled Dānava was speaking thus, a great cry arose from all sides in that region.
Some Dānavas were devoured, while others were slain; and still others, with their limbs half-eaten, perished.
Likewise, other powerful Dānavas who were fighting there were devoured by the Mothers, along with their weapons and their mounts.
Hearing that, Andhaka, fainting with rage, took up his sword and rose up, crying out, "What is this? What is this? (89)
Then he saw the dānavas, who were arrogant in their strength, utterly shattered; some were being devoured, while others were intent on flight.
And he sees other beloved wives standing nearby their slain husbands, weeping and lamenting in extreme distress.
Then, seeing that slaughter, Andhaka, overcome with rage, rebuked all those yoginīs who were prepared for battle.
And they did not feel any fear of that Daitya in any way; they simply continued to slaughter and devour the Dānavas.
Then that Dānava, seeing their conduct, became overwhelmed with fear and, out of anger, protected his own body. (94)
At that very moment, uttering a roar, he released the fierce weapon of darkness (tamas); in the meantime, the entire three worlds were enveloped in gloom.
Nothing at all is perceived there, whether even or uneven; only the lord of the Dānavas sees everything, and no one else.
Then he destroyed those yoginīs with sharp arrows, in such a way that other women would come to possess forms exactly like theirs.
Then, seeing that supreme success of the yoginīs, that Dānava, overwhelmed by fear, brought about the withdrawal of that weapon.
Then, having approached Śukra, the dejected one spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Behold, O best of the Bhārgavas, the destruction wrought upon me by women. (99)

By the power of the mantras of my weapons, which are incapable of being countered, the hosts of the enemies of the gods have arisen in great numbers and my army has been destroyed on all sides. || 1 ||
Therefore, O high-minded one, you too must acquire that knowledge if you desire my welfare; otherwise, there is no victory in battle.
Sūta said: Having heard his words and having conceived compassion in his heart, Śukra then went to the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara, which bestows spiritual perfection.
Having fashioned a triangular sacrificial pit, he performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rites with his own flesh, using fierce Atharvan mantras.
As he was thus offering oblations according to that very rite at that time, the goddess Kelīśvarī became as well-pleased as she had been with Rudra.
Having quickly approached Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, he said to him: "O tiger among the Bhārgavas, do not bring about the depletion of my flesh. (4)
I have been meditated upon by the Three-eyed One; so tell me, what shall I do for you?
Śukra said: "O auspicious one, just as assistance was rendered by you here for Rudra, so too must it be done for Andhaka; this is my boon."
Whatever dānavas have been devoured or destroyed in battle, let them all quickly come back to life within this army.
The Goddess said: "O Brahmin, I shall restore to life all those Dānavas slain in battle who have not yet been consumed by me, once they have entered the mouth of the Yoginī."
Having spoken thus, that goddess, with a joyful countenance, gave him the lore named Amṛtavatī, by which those who have died are restored to life.
Then Śukra, with a joyful heart, went and said to Andhaka: "The goddess Kelīśvarī has been accomplished; she belongs to me just as she belongs to Śambhu."
"O Daityas, that auspicious lore was granted to me by her; by its power, I shall restore all those who have died to life."
"O best of Dānavas, you must always show devotion to her, especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days at all times. (12)
This is that supreme power by which this entire world is pervaded; she is to be accomplished solely through devotion, and never by means of force.
Thus addressed by Śukra, the lord of the Dānavas then worshipped that goddess, endowed with heartfelt devotion.
Having praised them with various hymns, he then spoke respectfully to all the other mothers as well, according to their seniority and in due order.
O Goddess, whatever anger I have shown toward you out of ignorance and the like, that must now be forgiven by you, for I am wretched and prostrate before you. (16)
The illustrious Goddess said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child, and by the power of Bhārgava; therefore, choose a boon, for my appearance is never in vain."

Andhaka said: "To those embodied beings who meditate upon you in this very form and worship you with true devotion after having installed an image of you, you must grant the success they desire in their hearts. (18)
The Goddess said: "Whatever man shall establish me in this form, I will grant him liberation, even if he be a sinner; of this there is no doubt. (19)
O best of the Danus, to whoever shall perform my worship on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, I shall grant heaven, even if that person is a sinner.
"To whoever shall perform for me even a single vision or a meditation, I shall grant a kingdom and all enjoyments that arise from the human world. (21)
Having spoken thus, that goddess then vanished from sight at that very moment, along with those hosts of Mothers, even as he was watching.
Then Śakra, by means of that perfected [mantra], restored all the Dānavas—the Daityas who had been eaten—to life once they were dead.
Having met with them, that lord of the Daityas, with a joyful inner soul, reached the city of Śakra and ruled the kingdom day and night.
Meditating upon that goddess and worshipping her day and night, the mighty one did so especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
Then, having recognized that power of hers, the son of Vyāsa, who had attained supreme perfection, installed her in this place. || 26 ||
Sūta said:
Thus the goddess Kelīśvarī became the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī); therefore, she should especially be installed, worshipped, and meditated upon. || 27 ||
In this way, the man who either recites or hears [this] from the Goddess shall be liberated from even the most grievous calamity while it is being spoken.
Or, a king who has been deprived of his kingdom, if he listens on the eighth day, shall regain his entire kingdom once more, with all thorns removed. (29)
And when the time of battle has arrived, the man who hears this shall slay the hosts of his enemies and attain victory. (30)
Sūta said: Andhaka, having then acquired the supreme knowledge obtained by Śukra, as well as the grace of Kelīśvarī born of devotion which increases one's strength, [proceeded]. || 1 ||
Then, after considering his own invincibility arising from the boon of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and with Maheśvara in mind, he gave way to anger.
And he dispatched a messenger toward Mount Kailāsa, saying: "Go, messenger, and now speak to Hara on my behalf."
Abandoning this Śakra, remain here on this mountain in happiness; otherwise, [he will] quickly arrive along with Kailāsa and his wife.
Having slain you along with your hosts in battle, I shall dwell happily in the Nandana grove; I shall destroy you—I swear this by my own soul in truth.
Having been addressed thus by the Daitya, that messenger went quickly from there and spoke to Śaṅkara with particularly harsh words.
Then the Lord whose banner is the bull, his soul overcome with anger, dispatched his attendants for the sake of slaying that evil-minded one.
Vīrabhadra, Mahākāla, Nandi, and likewise Hastimukha; Aghora, Ghoranāda, and the mighty Ghoraghaṇṭa.
Each of these had ten million other followers; he dispatched them all for the sake of slaying that evil-minded one.
Then, dispatched by him, those hosts with deformed faces, filled with great joy, roared like clouds.
Armed with weapons, they all went for the sake of battle to where that city was located; it was reached by that powerful Dānava, who had encountered Śakra.
Then, seeing that the hosts had arrived, those Dānavas, wielding their weapons and exceedingly arrogant, suddenly sallied forth for the sake of battle.
Then a battle took place between the Gaṇas and the Dānavas, mutually most fierce, with death as the only means of turning back.
Then all the hosts of Hara, defeated by those Dānavas on the field of battle, fled in fear toward the various directions, intent on seeking the gaze of Hara.
Hara, too, seeing those hosts broken, rushed forth in anger; then, upon seeing Hara, the Daityas fled in the ten directions.

Andhaka, too, having seen Hara, went forward to face him for battle. Then a great battle took place between Andhaka and Hara, just as the great battle had occurred in the past between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
With discuses, hollow arrows, iron shafts, javelins, swords, and mallets—in this way, the Dānava cannot be slain by various weapons.
Abandoning their combat with missiles, they engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle; grasping hand with hand, they then struck one another with their fists.
Then the Lord of the Gods, having been assailed and oppressed by the bond of the Dānava, became motionless and subsequently fell into a swoon.
Knowing him to have fallen into a swoon, Andhaka indeed went out from his house; meanwhile, Sthāṇu regained consciousness in an instant and took up his bow.
Taking up an iron club that was heavy to bear, the Lord then reached the lord of the Dānavas and struck him on the head.
He too struck the Lord of the Gods with great force using his sword; then, in that great battle, the God also invoked the Kaubera weapon.
With that weapon, he struck the Dānava in the heart; then, being struck by it, he vomited forth a stream of blood.
Having fallen face downwards and then pierced by the trident, that sinner remains fixed upon the tip of the trident and thereafter revolves like a wheel.
Andhaka, too, beholding himself in such a state, then praised the god Maheśvara with well-composed words.
Andhaka said: Salutations to you, the creator of the worlds, to Śarva whose self consists of the three qualities, who is seated upon the bull-throne, and who is adorned by the moon. 26.
Salutations to the one who holds a skull-topped staff in his hand; salutations to the bearer of the trident; salutations to the wielder of the hand-drum, the bow, the skull-bowl, and fire. || 27 ||
Salutations to you whose body is the destruction of the form of Smara, who consist of the eightfold forms, whose body is your own essential nature, and who, though formless, possess manifold forms.
Salutations always to the one who dwells in the cremation ground, who has the form of Bhairava, and who brought about the destruction of the head of Viriñci, the creator.
You are all-pervading and the creator of all; indeed, you alone are the destroyer and none other. You are the earth, you are passion (rajas), you are light, and likewise you are darkness.
"O Maheśvara, you are the body of all beings, the very soul of life. Thus did the lord of the Dānavas praise the God while stationed upon the tip of the divine trident.
Sūta said: Having heard his praise in this manner, Maheśvara was thoroughly pleased; then, out of joy, he spoke to that best of the Danus who stood upon the tip of his trident.
The Blessed Lord said: O Daitya, this is not the vow of a hero that one utters words of conciliation because of being oppressed by the hand of an enemy—especially by one born of the Daitya race.
Andhaka said: "O best of gods, I am despondent while leaning against the tip of your trident; therefore, slay me, so that my agony may quickly come to an end. (34)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Daitya, death does not exist for you; this was merely considered by me. Therefore, having pierced your chest with my trident, you have been held thus in the sky. (35)
Therefore, now go among the Gaṇas, freed from sin; having abandoned your demonic disposition, be endowed with supreme faith.
Andhaka said: "My nature as a Dānava has now departed; I shall be your servant, of this there is no doubt. I swear this by my own truth. (37)
Śaṅkara said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child; tell me what you desire. Ask for it, and I shall grant it, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (38)
Andhaka said: "That mortal who, having fashioned an image of you in this very form with my body fixed upon the tip of a trident, shall install it upon the earth—" (39)

"O best of gods, his liberation must be granted by you at my word. Having said "So be it," Maheśa released him from the tip of the trident; he was reduced to mere bones, emaciated in limb, and resembling Cāmuṇḍā, O twice-born ones.
Then, having attained the status of a Gaṇa, he sang a captivating song before the God of gods and especially before Pārvatī. (41)
Because his humming was like that of a bee and brought pleasure to the ears, he was therefore called Bhṛṅgiriṭi by the Enemy of Tripura.
Thus he attained the status of an attendant of the trident-bearing God of gods; trusted in all affairs, he thereafter became entirely devoted to them.
From that time forward, Maheśvara, the God of gods, has been installed on the surface of the earth by people in that very same form in this world. || 44 ||
Here, the supreme and extraordinary perfection is attained through his grace. Then, after some time, the lord of the earth was deprived of his kingdom.
There was a renowned man named Suratha, born of the Solar dynasty; having approached his own domestic priest Vasiṣṭha, he spoke with humility, his eyes clouded with tears. (46)
O Brahman, although you, my protector, are present, my kingdom has now been forcibly seized by enemies from me, a man of wretched fortune. (47)
Therefore, show me favor so that my sovereignty may be established; by your grace alone, there is no other recourse for me. (48)
Vasiṣṭha said: "If it is so, O Great King, go quickly at my word to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, which bestows all spiritual perfections."
There, having established Maheśvara in the form of Bhairava, whose fierce trident-tip was raised in his hand and which had pierced the body of Andhaka; (50)
Then, O King, worship Him with the Nārasiṃha mantra, using red flowers, incense, and red ointments.
Then, having attained true vigor and being endowed with splendor and heroism, you will undoubtedly slay all your enemies through his grace.
The Blessed One must be worshipped by you with supreme purity; otherwise, you will encounter obstacles—this which I have spoken is the truth. (53)
Then, having heard his words, that king went quickly; he then installed the god Bhairava in that sacred field.
Then, having become self-restrained and devoted to celibacy, he worshipped with devotion by means of the Nārasiṃha mantra.
Then, at the conclusion of ten thousand recitations of that mantra, Bhairava attained satisfaction and immediately spoke as follows.
The illustrious Bhairava said: "I am well-pleased with you, O King, having been worshipped with this mantra. Therefore, ask for whatever you desire, so that I may grant it all to you."
Suratha said: "O Lord of the Gods, my kingdom was seized by my enemies; through your grace, may it be restored to me once more, entirely freed from those enemies. (58)
O Lord, whatever other man should likewise come here and worship you with this very mantra, you must grant him success. (59)
"O God, O Lord of the Suras, let it be granted to me at the end of a thousand divine ages. Having promised him "So be it," Hara vanished from sight.
Suratha also regained his own kingdom after slaying his enemies in battle.

The sages said: "O son of Sūta, you have described here innumerable sacred fords (tīrthas) originating from gods and humans, as well as temples of deities, and likewise those originating from monkeys and established by Rākṣasas. (1)
O son of a charioteer, tell us by whom it has been seen or even touched, so that everyone may obtain here the full and desired fruit. || 2 ||
Sūta said: "O highly fortunate ones, this is true; there is no counting them—neither of the sacred fords (tīrthas), nor of the lingas, nor likewise of the hermitages (āśramas)."
In that regard, he who performs a bath at Śaṅkhatīrtha with a concentrated mind, especially on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), obtains the fruit of all [such acts]. || 4 ||
The man who beholds the eleven Rudras there with devotion has, by that act, seen all the Great Lords (Maheśvaras) as equal to Siddheśvara.
He who beholds Vaṭāditya, especially on the sixth day of the month of Caitra, has seen the Sun-god in his entirety; for all [the deities] stationed there have been seen by him.
Likewise, those who behold the goddess Māhitthā with unwavering faith—by that, all those difficult-to-traverse [realms] have been seen by them; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever beholds Gaṇeśa, who bestows the gateway to heaven upon men, has thereby seen all the Vināyakas; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, he who beholds Gaurī, the eldest, installed there by Śarmiṣṭhā, has thereby beheld all those Gaurīs.
The man who, having risen in the morning, beholds Cakrapāṇi, has thereby beheld all the Vāsudevas there.

The sages said: "By you, he who was born as such and who stands as Cakrapāṇi for us was not mentioned; why was he not told? Was he forgotten? Tell us! At what specific time should he be beheld by the wise?"

Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, this [Liṅga] was installed by Arjuna in this very sacred field. A person who rises early in the morning [should visit it] both at the time of its sleep and its awakening. || 12 ||
Having bathed with great devotion, whoever beholds the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), his sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed at that very moment.
O Brahmins, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were incarnated by Brahmā for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth and for the establishment of Dharma.

O best of the twice-born, at that time, at the end of the Dvāpara age, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna descended upon the surface of the earth in the mortal world; following their mutual affection, these two—Nara and Nārāyaṇa themselves—were established there. (15)
Just as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, descended upon the surface of the earth for the destruction of the Rākṣasas, so too did Kṛṣṇa descend as another [incarnation]. || 16 ||
O twice-born ones, when Pārtha set out on a pilgrimage from Śakraprastha, that most excellent of cities, by the command of Yudhiṣṭhira; || 17 ||
Seeing his brother, the twice-born one, together with Draupadī in private, Arjuna bowed down and, prostrating himself with humility, spoke.
Arjuna said: "O best of kings, I have now arrived for the sake of weapons; O monarch, grant me permission to release the brahmin’s cow. (19)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Go quickly, O Arjuna, to that place where the cows of the best of the twice-born are being led away by thieves; release them, O Dhanañjaya! (20)
"Then go on a pilgrimage for twelve years; thereafter, liberated from sin, you shall come into my presence. (21)
If a wise man should see a person with his wife standing in a secluded place—even if that person were an extreme sinner—how much more so if it be one's own kinsman? (22)
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should not look upon anyone staying in private with his wife, especially a kinsman. (23)
Having promised "So be it," he quickly mounted his chariot, took up his bow and arrows, and departed immediately thereafter.
O twice-born ones, by whichever path those cows were being led away by force by the thieves—having set aside all the brahmins who were bearing sharpened weapons—[by that same path they went]. (25)
Then, having slain the thieves in an instant, he personally brought back all their limbs and presented them to the high-souled Brāhmaṇas.
Then, having seen many sacred fords and shrines, that son of Pāṇḍu arrived at this very field for the purpose of bathing.
Therefore, he had previously observed that field for the most part when he arrived there accompanied by Duryodhana. (28)
Then he worshipped that liṅga which had been established in ancient times, known by the name Arjuneśvara, with flowers, incense, and unguents.
Especially for the other lords of the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas. || 30 ||
Then the son of Pāṇḍu reflected in his mind: "I am Nara himself, and Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa himself."
Therefore, I shall establish here Cakrapāṇi, the Lord of the Gods, and a temple such as which does not exist anywhere else on the surface of the earth.
"Even at the end of a kalpa, there shall never be the destruction of this sacred field; likewise, the temple here in this field shall remain exactly as it is. (33)
O best of the twice-born, having thus made this resolution in his own mind, the younger brother of the Pāṇḍavas subsequently constructed a Vaiṣṇava temple.
Then, having summoned Brahmins born in Camatkārapura, he caused the consecration to be performed, relying upon their doctrine.
Having bestowed many gifts and numerous edicts, he subsequently gave them yet another thing that would bring them satisfaction.
Then, standing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to them all: "I am Nara, born from a Brāhmaṇa, who has come to the earth for the sake of Pāṇḍu. (37)
Having abandoned that auspicious Badarī in my human form, I have built this temple here for the sake of its renown; it is named after me as "Nara," with a mind purified by faith. (38)
Therefore, O twice-born ones, he should always be glorified by you as Cakrapāṇi, by whom my name has been made manifest.
The sound reaches the world of Viṣṇu as long as the moon and sun endure.
Likewise, a great festival should be celebrated at the sleeping and waking of Hari, especially when the day of Viṣṇu arrives in the month of Caitra.
O best of the twice-born, having abandoned these three worlds, I myself shall perform worship of this Viṣṇu here at Badarī.
Whatever mortal shall perform his worship on that day, being liberated from all sins, he shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, for those who reside in the field of Vāsudeva, a vision of Him is beneficial; by seeing Him constantly, one shall attain [the highest good].

Sūta said: Having been told "So be it" by them, the descendant of Daśārha, the joy of the Pāṇḍus, entrusted that burden to them and, with a tranquil inner self, thereafter went to other sacred fords, having accomplished his purpose.
Thus stationed there, the Lord himself, Hṛṣīkeśa, bearing the form of Cakrapāṇi, is the destroyer of the sins of living beings.

And even today, when the three Ekādaśīs have arrived, Viṣṇu’s portion [should be offered]; therefore, by those endowed with faith, he should always be worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure, and especially saluted. (47)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Cakrapāṇi," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 152 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another unsurpassed holy site there called Rūpatīrtha, where a man who bathes properly becomes beautiful even if he was previously deformed.
Formerly, after that Brahmā, the creator of the world, had performed an extensive creation of the fourfold kind as described, the Blessed One [spoke].
Then he thought: "I shall create a single divine celestial nymph, endowed with a collection of all beautiful forms, through my divine power of illusion."
Then, taking a single sesame seed from each of all the gods, he subsequently fashioned her form, which was truly marvelous.
Upon seeing her, the Grandfather himself became agitated.
Then the Lotus-born One sent her toward Kailāsa, saying: "Go, O Goddess of pure smiles, and pay homage to Mahādeva."
Then, having gone quickly to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, she saw Śaṅkara there seated together with Pārvatī.

And Śaṅkara, having seen her, was struck with the utmost wonder; yet, seeing Pārvatī standing by his side, he did not look at her well out of fear. Then she circumambulated Maheśvara, bowed down, and stood with palms joined in reverence, endowed with supreme faith.
As long as he remained on the right side, Mahādeva, with his eyes drawn toward him, made his face turn to the right.
When that auspicious [face] was positioned in the west by virtue of its circumambulation, the western face was therefore created for that purpose. || 11 ||
Thus, O twice-born ones, while she was positioned facing north, the god Śambhu, with a mind fearful of Gaurī, fashioned his northern face; yet he did not move his neck in any way whatsoever.
In the meantime, Nārada, the bull among sages, having prostrated before Maheśvara, spoke to Pārvatī thereafter.
Nārada said: Behold, O Pārvatī, the censurable conduct of your husband; upon seeing a beautiful woman, he has produced four faces.
"I know this: there is no woman anywhere equal to you, nor does anyone else know it so, O Goddess of the Gods. (19)
O Pārvatī, today you will become an object of ridicule among all the wives of the gods, having learned that the Lord is attached to another woman.
O Goddess, you know what kind of mind has arisen toward this prostitute, who is censured by the wise, even though it originates from Śiva. (17)
Having taken her, he will establish her in his own palace; yet, overcome by extreme shame, O auspicious lady, he does not speak a word.
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Nārada and seeing the four-faced one, she was overcome with great anger upon beholding Hara in that deformed state.
Then that daughter of the mountain, having adopted the conduct of a queen, quickly closed all the eyes of the god.
In the meantime, the mountains crumbled on all sides, and all the oceans transgressed their boundaries.
O best of the twice-born, when the emergence of the dissolution had occurred, then the supreme day of Brahmā, characterized by creation, arrived.
Furthermore, that night of the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, at the time of dissolution, is said to be equal to his own twinkling of an eye; at that time, everything becomes composed of water.
Then all the hosts there, led by Bhṛgu and Nandin, as well as that divine sage, being afraid, spoke to that queen of the gods.
"Release, release them now, O eldest of the gods; otherwise, the destruction of this entire world will come to pass. (25)
Even though she was addressed in this manner, as long as that goddess did not release him, the Lord discharged a supreme eye from his forehead.
He who, filled with compassion for the worlds, provides their protection, is not able to restrain the Goddess, who is dearer to him than his own life. 27.
O twice-born ones, because the gods call Ambikā "the three-eyed one" (tryambakāṇi), the Lord of the Gods is therefore celebrated in the world as Tryambaka.
Then, having abandoned that god, the goddess who was the daughter of the mountain, her eyes reddened with anger, spoke to Tilottamā who stood before her.
"O sinful woman, because my beloved has been mocked by you with your beauty and turned into four-faced [Brahmā], therefore, become deformed immediately! (30)
Then, in that very instant, she suddenly became one with a broken nose, shorn hair, large teeth, sunken eyes, and a protruding belly.
Then, seeing her own body in such a state, that excellent Apsaras stood with her palms joined in reverence and, trembling, spoke.
"O Goddess, I have been sent by Brahmā to pay homage to the wielder of the trident; and for that reason, I have come especially to you as well. (33)
Therefore, it would not be fitting for you to give a curse to one who is faultless and free from passion; instead, you ought to show me your favor.
Having heard those words of hers—both humble and truthful—Pārvatī, filled with remorse, then spoke these very kind words.
"This anger toward you has arisen swiftly from the very nature of women; therefore, come, let us go together to the surface of the earth. (36)
There is a holy ford named Rūpada, which was created by me myself, with its pure waters for the purpose of bathing on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Any woman who, having risen early in the morning, performs her bath there while the solar disc is still invisible, shall surely become possessed of great beauty.
"I always perform my bath there on the third day of the month of Māgha; today I shall go there for the bath, having made a firm resolve. (39)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and taking Tilottamā with her, that goddess went to Rūpatīrtha in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
There, the Queen of the Gods herself performed her bath according to the prescribed rite; immediately after her, Tilottamā also did so, filled with devotion.
Then, at that very moment, the beautiful woman became radiant; she became even more distinguished than the form she had previously possessed.
Then, filled with contentment and overcome with wonder, she bowed down to that Queen of the Gods and spoke with a voice faltering with joy.
O Great Goddess, by your grace I have attained my ancient form; I shall go to the world of Brahmā, so you should grant me permission.
Gaurī said: "I shall grant you a boon, my daughter, whatever resides in your heart; therefore, ask with confidence, for the sight of me is never in vain."
Tilottamā said: "O auspicious goddess, by your grace I shall establish my own sacred site (tīrtha) here in this field; let it attain fame upon the surface of the earth. (46)
Even there, you must certainly perform a ritual bath at the end of the rainy season; for it is for the welfare of all women and bestows beauty and good fortune. (47)
Gaurī said: "O auspicious one, for your sake, I shall always perform my bath there on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra when midday has arrived. (48)
For the benefit of all women, according to your word, there is no doubt that whichever woman performs [this rite] at that sacred site on that day, [shall obtain the fruit]. (49)
That bath will bring her union with happiness, and she shall be endowed with joy; she will be envied by all women upon the surface of the earth. (50)
Any man who performs a bath there with great devotion shall become endowed with beauty and good fortune for seven births.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been thus addressed by the goddess at that time, the Apsaras created a very extensive pool filled with pure water.
Then she placed Pārvatī near him; thereafter, Tilottamā departed for the world of Brahmā, filled with joy.
From that time onwards, O twice-born ones, the pool created by the Apsarā came into being, wherein men obtain good fortune merely by bathing.
Especially for women, the attainment of a son is unsurpassed; likewise, whatever else may be desired that dwells within the heart [shall be granted]. (55)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Origin of the Apsaras Kuṇḍa," in the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 153.
Sūta said: Whatever woman, having bathed there in that excellent pool and having beheld Pārvatī, then bathes in that auspicious tīrtha consisting of beauty, [attains her desire]. || 1 ||
Furthermore, if one should behold Pārvatī endowed with supreme faith, one is immediately liberated from all [sins] committed from birth until the end of death. || 2 ||
O twice-born ones, there indeed resides a female attendant of Pārvatī named Jayā; by her, a pool was constructed there in the vicinity of Gaurīkuṇḍa.
The woman who performs her ablutions there on the third day and subsequent days shall become endowed with sons and good fortune, and beloved by her husband.
Likewise, there is another excellent Vijayā-kuṇḍa there; even a barren woman who bathes there becomes endowed with sons.
O twice-born ones, he never saw any calamity befall his sons, nor separation from them, nor any suffering, even in his dreams.
Even a woman who has borne only one child, or one who is barren, should perform a bath there; having obtained various sons, she is honored in the heavenly world. || 7 ||
The sages said: "O Sūta, among these holy fords (tīrthas), is there one that bestows excellent success? Is there perhaps some place where, by bathing, bodily perfection might be attained?"
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, among those twenty-seven liṅgas that exist, O brahmins, all spiritual perfection (siddhi) was attained in one of them.
O best of the twice-born, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, [the rite was performed] for one endowed with sattva and joined to the vow of a hero.

He who performs their worship according to the prescribed rite at midnight, while reciting the previously mentioned mantra with devotion, shall in due course become the most excellent of practitioners.
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), he should loudly recite the Kṣurikā-sūkta; then, having properly worshipped Śaṅkara once more in their presence.
One should indeed worship the lords of the directions individually and separately with devotion.
Then Gaṇeśa indeed arrived—deformed, terrifying, pot-bellied, naked, and possessing black teeth. || 14 ||
With sword in hand, he said: "Engage in battle with me, casting aside this deceit on the ground, if you are a hero of virtuous nature. (15)
Furthermore, by that very act of drawing [the bow], he who is swiftly struck by it is led by that very body to that state.
In that place where there is never old age, death, or sorrow—likewise, in the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Citreśvarī, the attainment of perfection for a single person is proclaimed. || 17 ||
He who, endowed with perfect faith, worships the Pīṭha there on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha according to the procedure prescribed in the Āgamas; || 19 ||
Afterwards, taking a skull-bowl filled with human flesh, I shall today make a sale of this great meat. (19)
O excellent twice-born ones, if there is anyone of virtuous nature who does not accept the price for the accomplishment, and if someone then requests it and accepts it, [the merit remains]. (20)
Taking that with him, he went forth to where the god Maheśvara is located—the Liṅga born of Hāṭakeśvara, which was installed by Citraśarman.

The man who, standing in the midst of that place, worships it with devotion at midnight on Śivarātri using a hundred thousand flowers, shall quickly attain perfect success in his very body at that very moment.
O best of the twice-born, all the seats of spiritual accomplishment (siddhisthāna) are indeed situated in that sacred field for those men who are engaged in the vow of heroes (vīravrata).

The sages said: O high-minded one, that path to perfection which has been described by you as characterized by darkness (tāmasa) is unworthy for the foremost of Brahmins, and especially for those well-versed in the Vedas (śrotriya).
O Sūta, tell me how liberation is attained even after a very long time by Brāhmaṇas whose internal organs are pure and who have abandoned all injury to living beings. || 25 ||
O illustrious one, tell us the truth regarding the means of liberation for the twice-born.
Sūta said: Having likewise bathed in the Kuṇḍa in front of Ānandeśvara, which is joined with ten Rudras, according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures, || 27 ||
A mortal man, having bathed in the Viśvāmitra lake during the month of Māgha, shall attain perfection that is difficult even for the gods to achieve.
At dawn, one should present a vessel of sesame seeds to a Brahmin; liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 29 ||
Even if one should be of wicked conduct, eating all things and selling all things, provided he is endowed with faith before the deity named Suparṇa; || 30 ||
A man who, having undertaken the vow of fasting unto death, gives up his life while devoted to abstinence, is not born again. || 31 ||
Thus, the threefold accomplishment (siddhi) conducive to the welfare of Brāhmaṇas has been declared; O best of Brāhmaṇas, it is sattvic and praised even by the gods. (32)
The sages of celebrated vows declare that whatever other sacred fords and shrines of deities exist there, they bestow the attainment of heaven.
Thus has this entire, supreme majesty of the sacred field (kṣetra) of the god Hāṭakeśvara been narrated to you, which destroys all sins.
Whoever bathes here in all these sacred fords and beholds them with devotion—even if he is a sinner—is liberated from all [sins]. || 35 ||
This first section of the Purāṇa composed by Kārtikeya has been proclaimed; it is auspicious and removes all sins. (36)
Whoever recites this with devotion or listens to it with a concentrated mind, having enjoyed vast pleasures here in this world, goes to the third heaven.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit results from all acts of charity, one who listens with faith obtains that very fruit. (38)
Indeed, by hearing this Purāṇa, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births and shall uplift a hundred generations of one's lineage. (39)
Then Vyāsa should be honored with gifts of clothing and ornaments, as well as with cows, land, gold, food offerings, and various other kinds of gifts.
Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who is Manu himself and the son of Satyavatī, was fully honored by him; he by whom Vyāsa was so well worshipped. || 41 ||
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple, there is no object on earth that, by giving it, one could become free from debt.
This is a great purifier, conducive to long life, auspicious, and a source of well-being; having heard it, one is liberated from all sufferings—of this there is no doubt. (43)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Citreśvarī Pīṭha-kṣetra," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, likewise the eight Vasus remain there, having taken up a single station and being worshipped at all times.
Likewise, there are eleven Rudras and twelve Ādityas; furthermore, the two physicians of the gods, the Aśvins, are stationed there.
Deities stand there, numbering in the tens of millions of leaders; each one is a preeminent Brāhmaṇa, agitated by fear of the Kali age.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, for the sake of always obtaining a share of the sacrifice, when the month of Madhu has arrived on the eighth day of the bright fortnight— || 4 ||
Having become pure and bathed, a man wearing washed garments should satisfy those Vasus and then worship them, O best of the twice-born.
Then, with devotion, one should offer the food offering (naivedya) using this mantra, "vasavastvā kṛṇvan," and [the following mantra], "vasavaśchaṃdasā."
Then, one who is composed and offers fragrant incense should utter this mantra: "May the Vasus conquer you. (7)
O best of the twice-born, listen now to the fruit that belongs to him who performs the ārārtika rite once again: "May the Vasus conquer you! (8)
Whatever fruit may come from worshipping ten million maidens, all that is obtained by worshipping those eight Vasus.

Likewise, having installed and worshipped those twelve Ādityas who are stationed in that sacred field on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, one endowed with perfect faith should honor them with flowers, perfumes, and unguents.
Thereafter, in their presence, he performed all twenty-one vows known as the Ādityavrata; hear now the fruit of his merit.
Whatever fruit a man may obtain by worshipping twelve crores of suns, he shall obtain that entire fruit by worshipping this [liṅga]; of this there is no doubt. || 12 ||
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, regarding those eleven Rudras who are situated in a single location within that sacred field—listen to the fruit obtained by their worship.
He who, having installed those lords of the gods, worships them with devotion on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, and recites the Śatarudriya; || 14 ||
By that [measure], eleven crores have been worshipped; there is no doubt about this. This which I have spoken is the truth. (15)
Just as the two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, are established there, so too [they are present] in the month of Āśvina, on the lunar day of the full moon in the asterism of Aśvinī.
He who, having worshipped those two, recites the Aśvinī-sūkta, fully attains merit multiplied twenty million times. || 17 ||
O best of the twice-born, all this majesty arising from the Vasus, as well as that of the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins, has been narrated to you.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another [liṅga] established there by Yājñavalkya, renowned as Puṣpāditya, which grants all desires to men. || 19 ||
Whatever desire a person contemplates and then worships, he obtains that entirely, even if it be very difficult to attain. (20)
One without a son obtains sons; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth; one with many enemies shall achieve their destruction; and one seeking knowledge shall become a knower of the scriptures.
O best of the twice-born, that man who beholds it on a Sunday falling on the seventh lunar day shall be liberated from even great sins committed during that day.
For through worship, the sin accumulated over a year is destroyed; it goes to its destruction without a doubt, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (23)
He who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations with fruit in hand shall indeed be liberated from all sins committed from birth until death.
Whoever performs a circumambulation while desiring whatever object of desire, obtains that without doubt; one who is free from desire shall attain liberation.
If one performs the rite of bathing during a solar transit on a Sunday—whether it occurs while the sun is in Aries or in Libra—his desired goal shall be accomplished.
In that regard, by those desiring their cherished fruit with every effort, that deity should be beheld and especially worshipped. (27)
Whatever fruit is obtained by all the gods born in Camatkārapura when they behold [it], one shall obtain that same fruit by beholding it. 28.
The sages said: "If that deity was indeed installed by Yājñavalkya, how is it called Puṣpāditya? You ought to tell us this. (29)
Sūta said: In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history concerning how Puṣpāditya was born and established by Yājñavalkya.
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and excellent city named Vaidiśa; it is filled with various palaces and adorned with magnificent ramparts.
There, in a place filled with hundreds of gardens and adorned with lakes, there lived a preeminent king renowned as Citravarma.
While that knower of Dharma, who was ever devoted to righteousness, was ruling, there was neither famine nor disease, nor any fear caused by thieves. (33)
In that city, there was a man known by birth as a Kṣatriya named Maṇibhadra; he was indeed endowed with wealth inherited from his father and grandfather.
That entire city, along with the king and his ministers, subsisted on wealth acquired through usury whenever a need arose.
And he shall be hunchbacked in body and likewise pervaded by old age; his limbs shall be wrinkled and grey-haired, and he shall bear an exceedingly deformed appearance. (36)

And likewise, Kukīnāśa, though possessing abundant wealth, that sinful-souled man gave nothing at all to anyone; yet, afflicted by thirst for more, he did not consume anything himself under any circumstances. (37)
Even though he was of such a nature, exceedingly deformed and very wicked-minded, he nevertheless sought a maiden of his own caste who was beautiful to behold.

She had lips like the bimba fruit, a beautiful body, and a slender waist that could be grasped by a single fist; her large eyes were like lotus petals, her ankles were well-concealed, and she possessed lovely hair. (39)
She was red in color, deep in the seven parts of her body, and likewise possessed of all auspicious marks; she was of noble birth and exceedingly beautiful.
O tigers among the twice-born, [he was born] from a Kṣatriya who was afflicted by poverty; he then reported that entire account to his wife.
Having heard that, she fainted from grief; then she was revived by him with words drawn from illustrative examples.
The Kṣatriya said: There is no science, no craft, no task, and no art, nor is there any knowledge, that is not offered by the wealthy to those who seek their wealth. (43)
In this world, even a stranger acts as a kinsman to the wealthy; yet even one's own kin act like wicked men toward the poor when it comes to their own interests.
For from wealth that has increased and been gathered from here and there, all activities proceed, just as rivers flow from mountains. (45)

That even one unworthy of worship is worshipped, that even one who should not be approached is approached, and that even one who is not to be saluted is saluted—that indeed is the binding power of wealth.
Just as the sense organs depend upon food and so forth, all activities here likewise depend on wealth; for this reason, wealth is said to be the means for accomplishing everything.
This world of living beings, seeking wealth, frequents even the cremation ground; having abandoned even its own progenitor, it goes far away when destitute. (48)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kṣatriya’s Address to His Own Wife for the Purpose of Giving His Daughter to Maṇibhadra," within the Narrative of Maṇibhadra at the Great Abode of Puṣpāditya, in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 155 ||
Sūta said: Thus enlightened by him, that wife went to a secluded place, and immediately thereafter, a desire arose in her to give away her daughter.
Then, having quickly washed the feet of Maṇibhadra, he placed water along with unbroken grains (akṣata) in his hand for the purpose of giving the daughter in marriage.
He too, while the water was held in his hand, said to that Kṣatriya: "Perform my marriage with the maiden this very day, quickly! (3)
"Since I desire to remain [here], for that reason I have come to your house. The Kṣatriya said: "There is no lunar mansion (nakṣatra) here suitable for you, nor any presiding deity (bhagadaivata)."
There is no auspicious time for marriage while Madhusūdana is asleep; yet, when this very time has arrived, whatever girl is married— || 5 ||
And she will certainly attain widowhood in the middle of that year; such was what I heard from the foremost of astrologers as they were speaking.

Therefore, when an auspicious lunar mansion presided over by Bhaga has arrived, and while Madhusūdana is awake, you must marry my daughter, so that she may bring you prosperity and grant you sons and grandsons.
Maṇibhadra said: "The lunar mansion has Agni as its presiding deity, and Madhusūdana is fast asleep. (8)
"Now that this year has come to an end and the marriage has been settled, the fire of passion has arisen within my body and now afflicts me. (9)
Therefore, show me favor by means of marrying your daughter; I shall give you wealth so that you will become happy.
Sūta said: Therefore, O best of the twice-born, out of greed for wealth, that Kṣatriya had the marriage performed at that very moment, O Brāhmaṇas.
He gave his daughter, who stood there afflicted with great sorrow and her eyes filled with tears; she was then married by him in the presence of the fire and the Brahmins.
Having led her to his own home, he thereafter sought to engage her in the practice of desire; though she was virtuous and unwilling, he was exceedingly unrestrained toward her.
He too, having attained a state of desirelessness and having repeatedly rebuked her with many sarcastic remarks, tormented that beautiful woman.
Then, when dawn had arrived, he brought peace [to the situation] and expelled the entire circle of servants from the house.
O best of the twice-born, having adopted a supreme disposition of envy, he appointed only one person as gatekeeper, a eunuch.
And it was said by you: "Entrance here into my house must not be granted to a servant, nor to a beggar, nor to an old man, nor likewise to one observing a vow. (17)
Having thus performed the ritual procedure, he then engaged in all legal transactions together with the people, involving thousands of lakhs of wealth.
Not even a trifle was given by that evil-minded man to our father-in-law; nothing at all, except for some white garments for his wife.
When two watches of the day had passed, he returned home; she then gave him a limited amount of food for his meal.
He himself would eat only as much as was necessary, accompanied by a single Brahmin; and having finished his meal, he would then go outside for the sake of business.
When the time of twilight had arrived, he would return to the palace; his wife, that woman of evil character, remained there staying upon the palace roof.
Having attained supreme detachment, yet still possessed by suffering and grief, she was like a fish fallen from the water onto another dry land. || 23 ||
Like a female cakravāka bird when day is spent, like a female swan separated from her mate, or like a doe deprived of her deer; (24)
O twice-born ones, he too gave food daily to a single Brāhmaṇa, having first addressed that Brāhmaṇa with these words preceded by conciliation.
"O Brahmin, you must always eat with your face turned downward in my house; if you look at my wife, you will suffer humiliation. (26)
Thus mocked by him, those who look upward with faces turned upwards, as well as others terrified by fear, do not go to his abode.
Then, after some time, an excellent brahmin named Puṣpa arrived at that city in the course of a pilgrimage.
Though he was in the prime of his youth and possessed an exceedingly handsome form, he was emaciated by hunger and utterly exhausted when midday had arrived.
He indeed wanders everywhere through the houses of men; he has been commanded by someone that Maṇibhadra shall provide him with food.
Then, O twice-born ones, he went and requested food from him; and that best of the twice-born was addressed by him at that time, O excellent brahmins.
"You must eat with your face turned downward; my beloved must not be seen by you. Otherwise, O Brahmin, you will undoubtedly suffer humiliation."
Knowing this, O illustrious one, perform that which is for your welfare.
Puṣpa said: "For me, who am emaciated by hunger, there is no purpose in looking upon the wives of others; for I am devoted to the study of the Vedas and intent on pilgrimage to sacred fords. (34)
Maṇibhadra said: "Therefore, come now with me to my residence; there I shall especially provide you with food accompanied by a sacrificial fee."
Having thus made this agreement, O best of Brahmins, those two went along the market road to where the eunuch was stationed.
Having detained a Brahmin by his side, he entered the middle of the house; then, with his wife, he had grain measured out and cooked.
Then, having performed the worship of the deities up to the Vaiśvadeva offering, he should summon Puṣpa, wash his feet, and seat him.
Having performed the rite of worship for him and offered well-prepared food, the twice-born then sat down for their meal; meanwhile, Puṣpa gazed upon her feet, which resembled lotuses. (39)
Just as he, established in youth, gazed out of curiosity, so too was her face beheld by him out of that same curiosity. (40)
Then Maṇibhadra, out of great anger, caused him to take on that form and said to the eunuch, "You must mock this man."
Then, O best of the twice-born, he struck that Puṣpa on the head.
Having dragged with his two feet that messenger who had fallen down upon the ground and was drenched in blood, he set out upon the path. || 43 ||
When he was led as far as the crossroads where the people frequented, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose then in that excellent city.
Seeing him in that state, all the citizens then sprinkled him with cool water, moved by compassion.
Having been administered fanning with air, he was restored to consciousness; having regained his senses with great difficulty from that water, he then spoke to them. (46)
"I have committed no theft, nor have I pursued another's wife; behold, O people, how I am being tormented by Maṇibhadra! (47)
A Brahmin devoted to visiting sacred fords and dedicated to the practice of celibacy was invited for a meal and subsequently brought to this state. (48)
"Is there no king here, O great people, by which this injustice—especially toward a blameless Brahmin—is being permitted? (49)
The people said: "In former times, many brahmins were tormented by that sinful embodied being, who, endowed with royal favor, was filled with envy. (50)
"Because of the king's favor, no one says anything in his presence; therefore, arise, let us go, and we shall provide you with food. (51)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Maṇibhadra’s Mockery of the Brāhmaṇa Puṣpa," within the "Greatness of Puṣpāditya" section of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 156 ||
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having been thus addressed by those people, Puṣpa then spoke to them in anger: "I will not eat! || 1 ||
"Until I have performed an atonement for this sin, speak, O highly fortunate ones, whether you be a god or a deity. (2)
Likewise, others whose mantras are perfected produce immediate conviction; when propitiated, they immediately grant boons to human beings.
The people said: "One deity stands here who provides immediate proof; likewise, one deity is heard of here on the surface of the earth."
Puṣpa said: "Who is that god? How far away is he, and in what place is he situated? O deities, show me compassion and tell me. (5)
The people said: "O Brahmin, we have heard that in Camatkārapura there is a Sun-god installed by Yājñavalkya, who produces immediate proof [of his power]."

O twice-born one, that man who, on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, performs a circumambulation while holding fruit in his hand, [attains the merit of] one hundred and eight [circumambulations].
Bestowing success upon him, she grants whatever is desired with a focused mind; likewise, there is another goddess named Śāradā, who resides in Kāśmīra.
"Even that [rite] bestows success only upon one who has performed the fast. Having heard those words of the people, O best of the twice-born, he—
Then, having set out from that place toward Camatkāra, he reached Camatkārapura on the seventh day, which was a Sunday.
Having arrived there and bathed, becoming pure and composed, he went to where the Sun, established by Yājñavalkya, remains.
Then, having performed one hundred and eight circumambulations and taking coconuts, he was endowed with supreme faith.
Then, his throat parched with hunger and utterly exhausted, he sat down before him, performing recitations and offering hymns of praise to the Sun-god.

And with the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa and other hymns, resorting to the high-pitched tone (tāra-svara), and with the seven musical instruments, he [worshipped] with devotion, saying "Agnireva" (Agni alone). || 14 ||
Possessing firm devotion, he [worshipped] with Sāman chants known as the Ādityavrata and others, as well as with the Kṣurikā-mantras originating from the Atharvaveda.
When another Sunday arrived, the Sun-god was still not satisfied; having reached the full moon day, he attained a state of supreme detachment.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Puṣpa, having performed his bath and being pure in washed garments, consecrated the ground with the mantra "Bhūḥ" for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial altar.
He prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, and having established the fire upon that mound with the mantra "Agnim īḷe," he then placed the fire there.
Having performed the under-spreading with the formula "I spread around with grass," he should then offer the seat for the Brahman priest with the mantra beginning "O Brahman. (19)
Having recited "sutrāmāṇam," he performed the placement of the fuel-sticks (samidh), and then, having set down the vessel for sprinkling water (prokṣaṇīpātra), he performed the sprinkling.
Then, in due order, he assigned his own body to the place of the oblation for all the vessels, beginning with the *sruva* ladle.

But according to the rule for the placement of the deity, he [should perform] the taking up and the sprinkling by means of the procedure prescribed for the teacher, and the subsequent [mantra] is "To Sūrya, indeed... (sūryāya tvā). || 22 ||
Having recited, "This fuel is your self," he should then offer a piece of wood and subsequently two oblations of clarified butter with the two mantras beginning with "Agni-Soma."
O twice-born ones, having performed the *vyāhṛti-homa* with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," and having offered oblations right there with the fierce mantra beginning with "ye te śataṃ... (24).
And he invoked the Fire-god, saying: "O God, become manifest before my eyes. Having thus brought the blazing deity face-to-face by means of this mantra, he then—

Having performed the invocation of Kālī, Karālikā, and the others who are remembered as the seven tongues of flame, [he should offer oblations] then into the blazing consumer of the sacrificial offering.

And having cut his own flesh with a blade, he offered it as oblations; then, after offering to the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions with the words "Svāhā to the body hairs," he proceeded further.
As soon as he utters "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," he is seized by the Sun with his own hand from all sides, right up to his very self.

The means for his destruction have been fully proclaimed therein; I shall declare them to you—listen, O best of kings. (28)
Whatever mental sin arises here among men, it perishes at that very moment once remorse has been felt for it. || 29 ||
Whatever verbal sin there may be does not perish without being experienced; this which I have spoken is the truth regarding that which is outside of the *puraścaraṇa* rite. (30)
Having informed the foremost of Brahmins, one should perform what they prescribe; by performing the expiation exactly as stated, one shall thereafter attain purification.
Alternatively, if the king, having learned of it, inflicts punishment upon him, he attains purification by that means, even if he were indeed a sinner.

If one does not speak at all out of shame before the foremost of Brahmins, or if one dies while the king is unaware of it, Yama, the son of Vivasvat himself, shall be the one to inflict punishment upon him. (33)
Therefore, having committed a sin with all effort, a wise person should perform the expiation as it has been declared and prescribed by the Brahmins. (34)

Rohitāśva said: O Lord of Sages, for all those sins that have been committed, please describe some vow, or a gift, or even a fire-oblation, by which one becomes free from sin without the need for purificatory rites (puraścaraṇa). (35)
A man constantly commits subtle sins in every way; how could there be the capacity to perform expiations for them all? (36)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, there is a meritorious vow known as Puraścaraṇa; indeed, the seventh [lunar day] beloved of the Sun is designated as Puraścaraṇa.
O King, by performing this [vow], even one who has become a servant of Yama shall cleanse away the various sins committed and accumulated throughout his life. 38.
Therefore, O Great King, quickly carry out my word, so that you may be liberated from all sin arising from the body. (39)
Rohitāśva said: O best of sages, regarding that which is known as the *puraścaraṇa* on the seventh [lunar day], by what rite should it be performed and at what time? Tell me this. (40)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, when the sun is situated in Capricorn, one should observe this vow on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday.

On that day, O best of kings, one should not speak with heretics or those who have fallen from their caste. After eating and performing the cleansing of the teeth at dawn, O King, the religious observance (niyama) should then be undertaken with this mantra: 42. [Mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [The mantra continues: "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya, namo nārāyaṇāya, namo viṣṇave, namo jaganmayāya, namo jagatpitre, namo jagadgurave, namo 'nantāya, namo 'vyaktāya, namaḥ puruṣottamāya, namo viśvamūrtaye, namo viśvātmane, namo viśveśvarāya, namo viśvaprabhave, namo viśvasaṃhartre, namo viśvabhāvanāya, namo viśvabhuje, namo viśvaga, namo viśvahṛdayāya, namo viśvaprakāśāya, namo viśvapratiṣṭhitāya, namo viśvādhārāya, namo viśvatomukhāya, namo viśvavyāpine, namo viśvavidhātre, namo viśvabandhave, namo viśvabhojine, namo viśvavibhave, namo viśvavibhāvāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo viśvavibhāvanāya, namo vi
O Lord of the Day, on this seventh day for the performance of the *puraścaraṇa* rite, I shall observe a fast; today, you are my refuge. (43)
Then, at the time of afternoon, having bathed and being pure with washed garments, one should worship with devotion the image originating from the Lord of Day.
Then, O Mahāvīra, one should worship the feet and other limbs with red flowers: "Salutation to Pataṅga" for the two feet; "Salutation to Mārtaṇḍa" for the two knees. || 45 ||
I offer my secret parts to the Lord of Day; my navel to the one of twelve forms; my arms to the lotus-handed one; and my heart to the one of sharp rays. 46.

Having thus worshipped according to the rules the throat with [the mantra] "to the one resembling a lotus petal" and the head with "to the one consisting of splendor," one should take camphor for the incense.
O King, the food offering (naivedya) should consist of rice mixed with jaggery, wrapped in red cloth; likewise, the lamp and the waving of lights (ārārtika) should be performed with a red thread.
Having taken water in a conch shell mixed with red sandalwood, and having then added fruit, one should thereafter offer the *arghya*.
Whatever ill deed has been committed by me, whether through ignorance or even knowingly, O Lord, let expiation be performed and let my offering be accepted. (50)

Then he should worship the brahmin with perfumes, flowers, and unguents; having given him food and a sacrificial fee according to his own means, he should perform the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the sake of bodily purification.
Having joined his palms in reverence and gazed up at the sun, he, having approached the sun, should recite this mantra.
"O God, this vow has been undertaken by me in your presence; may it reach fulfillment without obstacle through your grace, O Bhāskara! (53)
Then, O best of sages, when the month of Phālguna has arrived, one should worship the God with a Kunda flower according to that very same rite.
One should offer incense of guggulu and an offering of cooked rice; cow dung is prescribed as the substance for consumption for the purification of all sins. (55)
When the month of Caitra has arrived, one should worship Hari with fragrant offerings; the food offering is said to be *guṇikā*, and the incense is derived from resin (*sarjarasa*).

By consuming water infused with *kuśa* grass, one attains purification of the body; and in the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform worship with *kiṃśuka* flowers while subsisting on ghee according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer as an oblation liquor and meat, and present incense; here, the consumption of curd must be performed for the purification of the body.

O King, worship with *pāṭala* flowers should be performed for the Sun; roasted barley flour (*saktu*) is prescribed as the food offering, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is remembered as the substance for consumption. (59)
O Great Hero, O King, for the purification of all sins, one should worship the Sun with *kapilā* flowers and *munipuṣpa* blossoms in the month of Āṣāḍha.
Ghārikā is prescribed as the food offering; one should partake of honey and clarified butter, and, endowed with supreme faith, offer agallochum (agaru) as incense.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, there is worship of the sharp-rayed Sun with the kadamba flower; one should offer sweetmeat balls (modaka) as the food offering and use tagara as incense.
By taking water from a cow's horn, one is immediately liberated from sin; on the full moon day of Bhādrapada, one should perform worship and offer milk as a food offering.
Incense produced from the nakha tree, the consumption of milk alone, worship with lotuses in the month of Āśvina, and fried cakes (pūrikā) with ghee as the food offering. 64.
Incense made from saffron is prescribed, and the consumption of camphor is traditionally taught.
O King, the worship of the Sun-god with Tulasī is prescribed for the month of Kārttika; as an offering, one should provide the confection known as *khaṇḍa* and safflower incense.
One should perform the consumption of that which is called *lavaṅga*, which purifies all sins, and worship with *bhṛṅgarāja* during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. (67)
For the food offering, pheṇikā cakes should be given, and incense made from molasses; likewise, the consumption of kaṅkola is for the complete satisfaction of Bhāskara.
In the month of Pauṣa, worship with a hundred-petaled lotus is prescribed for the Sun; natural incense is enjoined, and likewise, dried dates (śuṣkalī) are offered as the food offering.
At the time of consumption, one should perform all those rites previously mentioned; and upon completion, one should then give a sixth part of what was produced in the house.
O best of kings, O supreme ruler, for the purification of all sins, one should then provide a Brahmin with his desired food according to one's own capacity. (71)
He who performs this Saptamī rite dedicated to the Sun in this manner becomes liberated from all sins and attains stainless purity.
The Brahmins said: "O highly fortunate one, this was indeed told in former times by Mārkaṇḍeya to the wise Rohitāśva; therefore, you too should perform it."
By which your preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) is truly accomplished. || 74 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having heard those words of his, Puṣpa also joyfully performed that Saptamī exactly as it had been described by him.
He gave a sixth part of his own wealth—consisting entirely of both base and non-base metals—to that high-souled Brāhmaṇa, as befits a householder.
With a joyful inner soul, he too took that wealth—gold, gems, and jewels beyond all counting.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Puraścaraṇa Saptamī Vow," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 162 ||
Sūta said: Then all those citizens, having seen that vessel of wealth, cast aside all desires and resolved that it should not be taken by anyone.
Then, having made an agreement and having brought a mediator, they, established in the place of Brahmā, spoke through his mouth.
Having disregarded the best of the twice-born through this greed-driven act and having taken flowers and wealth, the expiation is proclaimed as follows.
And likewise, a sixth part of his wealth was taken from him; therefore, he shall become an outcast among all. || 4 ||
Among the citizens and the foremost of the twice-born, he was like any other ordinary man.
And from this day forward, whoever shall establish a connection with him, he too shall become an outcaste to all the Nāgaras. || 6 ||
Furthermore, whoever shall ever provide him with food or drink in his house, he too shall likewise become fallen.
Having spoken thus, O twice-born ones, he then gave three claps of his hands; O best of the twice-born, he placed him, equal to a flower, in the station of Brahmā.
Then all those brahmins went to their respective homes; but Caṇḍaśarman, being greatly distressed, then went to the side of Puṣpa.
With the consent of all these very people, I then granted you that penance; nevertheless, you were rendered fallen.
Therefore, I shall fall into the well-kindled fire; I have no desire to live, having been abandoned by my own kinsmen.
Puṣpa said: "O best of the twice-born, you should not despair regarding this matter, for you have been defiled by the most excellent of brahmins on account of wealth."
I shall satisfy the citizens with various kinds of wealth; they will beg from me whatever is required for the purification of your body.
"I shall indeed give them only that much for your sake. Having spoken thus, he returned to the abode of Brahmā with great haste.
Having brought the four-footed animal, he spoke with a mouth situated in the middle: "That brahmin Caṇḍaśarman, who was made to fall for my sake—" || 15 ||
"Out of greed for wealth, you have [stolen] that property; I shall give all that wealth back to you, as well as whatever else is in my house. Let the word of the twice-born be done. (16)
Then all those best of the twice-born, their eyes bloodshot with rage, uttered various hisses and spoke in anger.
"Fie, fie upon you, O practitioner of evil deeds! Why does your tongue not split into a hundred pieces, since you prattle such a contemptible thing? (18)
"We have not cast this man out for the sake of wealth, because an expiation has been performed by even one among us who was of evil intent. (19)
By him, the Smṛtis—and especially the Purāṇas—were corrupted, as he established his own position and performed this very action.
The expiation should be administered together with four others; O best of the twice-born, this very thing was declared by Manu after consultation. (21)
"Your sin has now been transferred to his body; because it was given by him alone, he remains fallen. (22)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, O twice-born ones, all the brahmins went to their respective abodes; Puṣpa also, deeply agitated, fell into a state of extreme embarrassment.
Then he went to his own abode, sighing like a serpent.
Then he reflected: "As long as no act of daring is performed, success for human beings will not arise in any way whatsoever. (25)
Therefore, for the sake of Caṇḍaśarman, I shall perform a great deed so that ingratitude does not occur, as it has been declared by the wise. (26)

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
Having thus resolved in his mind, O best of the twice-born, when the seventh lunar day fell on a Sunday, he then [performed] one hundred and eight [recitations].

Having performed circumambulations of Puṣpāditya, that wise man should then take up a sharp weapon and, according to the previously mentioned procedure, repeatedly cut off his own limbs and offer them as oblations into the fire.
Then, as he offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the remainder of his body, the Radiant One himself appeared before him in person and spoke.
