"O Puṣpa, do not act rashly; I am well-pleased with you, O sinless one. Speak further, O illustrious one, what may I give to you? (31)
Puṣpa said: "O Lord, this Caṇḍaśarman, the best of the twice-born, has been brought low for my sake by all the Nāgaras; restore him to his former status."
Having consulted the scriptures, a great-souled one prescribed an expiation for me; nevertheless, I was reviled by all those base and intolerant people.
The Blessed One said: "O best of the twice-born, it is not possible to act otherwise even regarding the word of a single citizen; how much less so, then, for all of them?"
This supreme twice-born Caṇḍaśarman shall become purified; he will be renowned throughout the entire surface of the earth as a Brāhma Nāgara.
And those who shall be his sons upon the surface of the earth will also attain renown; they shall be honored and worshiped by kings. (36)
And those kinsmen and friends who shall come together with him, they too will become most auspicious.
And you, too, by my grace, shall have your limbs restored in their entirety.
Having spoken thus, the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) then vanished from sight; and Puṣpa also, at that very moment, attained the state of having his limbs uninjured.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Origin of the Brāhmaṇas and Nāgaras," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 163.
Sūta said: In the meantime, Puṣpa, with a delighted heart, went to the house of Caṇḍaśarman and exclaimed, "By good fortune! By good fortune! (1)
Then, seeing him with a pale face and eyes filled with tears, accompanied by all his kinsmen, wives, servants, and sons; || 2 ||
Puṣpa said: "For your sake, I have propitiated the Sun by the sacrifice of my body; by his grace, there shall be no falling of flesh upon your body."
Your sons, grandsons, and all those born in your lineage shall all be superior in virtue to the Nāgaras. || 4 ||
Therefore arise, O twice-born one; let us go to the holy river Sarasvatī and establish a hermitage upon its bank for our residence.
"I shall dwell with you alone; of this there is no doubt. I possess abundant wealth, as do those others who are your followers. (6)
"I shall support them all; let the fever of your mind be cast aside. Having heard that, Caṇḍaśarman, accompanied by his sons and kinsmen, [acted accordingly].
Then, with Sarasvatī in mind, he departed from the city; having circumambulated the sacred site and offered salutations, he was deeply distressed.
With eyes filled with tears and dejected, he went facing north; accompanied by Puṣpa, he was repeatedly consoled.
Then, having reached the holy river Sarasvatī, which possesses cool waters, is frequented by hosts of sages, and is garlanded with rolling waves; || 10 ||
Then, relying upon the counsel of Puṣpa, he made his dwelling on its southern bank, surrounded by all his kinsmen.
While residing in the city, Caṇḍaśarman made this vow: "I shall always eat only after twenty-seven liṅgas have been seen."
O best of the twice-born, as he repeatedly recalled that previously made vow, his heart burned day and night.
Having bathed in the Sarasvatī and become pure, he, with a concentrated mind, performed the recitation of the six-syllabled mantra separately for each.
Having uttered the name of the Liṅga, O best of the twice-born, he performed a prostration ending with the word "namas," using five hundred finger-breadths of clay.
Having established [the image], one should worship it with devotion using flowers, incense, and ointments; thereafter, endowed with supreme faith, one should recite the Prāṇarudra mantras.
"One should not move a Śivaliṅga, whether it be poorly situated or well-situated. Thinking thus, that lord of the twice-born did not at all remove them.
O best of the twice-born, he constantly fashioned twenty-seven lingas out of mud, one above the other.
Then, after a long time, Kardamaparvata was born.
Then Mahādeva, pleased by the excess of his devotion, pierced through the surface of the earth and revealed his *liṅga* to him.
And he spoke respectfully to him with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: "O Caṇḍaśarman, O twice-born one, I am well-pleased by this devotion of yours."
Therefore, worship this Linga constantly with great devotion, for by doing so you shall obtain the fruit of twenty-seven Lingas.
Furthermore, any other man who shall worship this with devotion will also obtain the spiritual merit of the twenty-seven Liṅgas. (23)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished from that place; and Caṇḍaśarman, filled with joy, worshipped him according to the true principle.
He caused a beautiful temple to be built for that Liṅga; then, after reflecting upon it again and again, he bestowed a name upon it.
"Because he remains present through the constant remembrance of the Liṅgas situated in the city, therefore he shall be known by the name Nāgareśvara. (26)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having thus installed that liṅga, Caṇḍaśarman then worshipped it with flowers, incense, and unguents.
O best of the twice-born, one likewise obtains the fruit of worshipping those twenty-seven liṅgas that are located in the city.
Then, after a long time, being pleased by Nāgareśvara, he went directly to the world of Śiva, seated within a celestial vehicle.
Puṣpa also established another deity, Puṣpāditya, on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī, and thereafter became intent upon its worship.
Having gone to see him as well, he spoke these words with affection: "O Puṣpa, I am pleased; may it be well with you. O observer of noble vows, choose a boon."
"I shall give even that which is not to be given; therefore, ask me without delay."
Puṣpa said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then grant that which resides in my heart to me who am entreating you. (33)
O Lord, those twelve forms of yours that reside in Camatkārapura are to be worshipped by all the inhabitants of heaven according to their measure.
May that man on earth obtain the entire fruit of their worship who worships this image of yours which has been installed by me. (35)
"May this [image] known as Nāgarāditya become famous on the surface of the earth, she who has been installed by me in the temple on the bank of the Sarasvatī. (36)
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," the Sun vanished from sight, O best of Brāhmaṇas; like a lamp, that was truly wonderful.
Then, after a long time, O best of the twice-born, Puṣpa also reached the world of the Sun by means of a brilliantly shining celestial chariot.
You were the wife of Caṇḍaśarman, renowned by the name Śākambharī; by you, O auspicious one, Durgā was installed on the beautiful bank of the Sarasvatī.
Then, O best of the twice-born, she was propitiated with true devotion day and night; thereupon, O most excellent of the twice-born, she, being pleased, granted her a boon.
"O daughter, I am pleased; may it be well with you! O Śākambharī, accept this: by my grace, whatever boon you desire shall undoubtedly be yours forever. (41)
Śākambharī said: "O Goddess, those sixty-four groups of Mothers who are established in Camatkārapura and who become pleased through laughter are well-known there. (42)

Whatever merit arises from the offering of the *bali* at night, and whatever merit arises thereafter through the increase [of the ritual], may all that merit belong to whoever worships your form. (43)
Having come here to the riverbank, this [image] was installed by me. || 44 ||
The Goddess said: "In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, on the day known as Mahānavamī, whoever shall come before me and worship with devotion," (45)
The entire fruit thereof shall accrue to him immediately; of this there is no doubt. This which I have spoken is the truth, especially for a citizen. (46)
Having spoken thus, that goddess then vanished from sight; and because of her name, that goddess is called Śākambharī on earth.
O best of the twice-born, for that man who performs worship immediately after a prosperity-rite (vṛddhi), there shall never be any obstacle to his prosperity.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Nāgareśvara, Nāgarāditya, and Śākambharī," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya of the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 164.
Sūta said: From that time forward, on the auspicious and holy bank of the Sarasvatī, a very great settlement was established for both the Bāhyas and the Nāgaras. || 1 ||
O best of the twice-born, that which was known through learning and wealth by the sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and daughters' sons of Camatkārapura before [the city]: || 2 ||
Then, after some time, the wise Viśvāmitra, out of anger, cursed the Sarasvatī and caused her to flow with blood.
Then that [place] was frequented day and night by joyful Rākṣasas, and by other Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas intent on song and dance.
Then those citizens and outsiders, abandoning her, stood at a distance; terrified and pursued by the Rākṣasas, they fled to the holy bank of the Narmadā, in the vicinity of Mārkaṇḍa’s hermitage.
The sages said: Why was Sarasvatī cursed by the wise Viśvāmitra? What offense was committed against him by that great river?

Sūta said: O Brahmins, in ancient times there was a great enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha, a profound conflict that threatened their very lives for the sake of Brāhmaṇahood. Then the great sage Viśvāmitra was addressed by all the Brahmins: ||| 7 ||
Even the Kṣatriya, having placed the Grandfather, the God of gods, at his head, did not provoke this enmity with Vasiṣṭha alone. (8)
The sages said: O high-minded one, how did Viśvāmitra, though a Kṣatriya, become a Brahmin? Why was he not addressed as such by Vasiṣṭha, even though he had been proclaimed so by Brahmā himself?
Tell us all of this; a great curiosity has arisen within us.
Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a great sage named Ṛcīka, the son of Bhṛgu, who was perfected in vows and study, a great ascetic of immense renown. (11)

Once, in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, that lord of sages arrived at the place named Bhojakaṭa, belonging to King Gādhi, where the river named Kauśikī flows, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed therein, that best of the twice-born remained on the bank, established in meditative absorption, performing recitations and offering libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Just then, a most beautiful princess arrived there, endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of every virtue.
As he gazed upon her, beautiful in every limb, he was so overwhelmed by the arrows of desire that he did not know what to do.
Then, having regained consciousness with great difficulty, he questioned the people: "Whose daughter is this virtuous maiden, and for what purpose has she come here? (16)
"O people, tell me everything: where will that woman of beautiful limbs go? (17)
The people said: "This is the daughter of Gādhi, renowned as the most beautiful woman in the three worlds; she has come from the inner apartments, eager to worship Gaurī. (18)
Desiring a good husband endowed with all excellent qualities, she saw this very large palace standing here on the riverbank.
And here Umā is established, worshipped by all the gods; and having bathed her and worshipped her according to the prescribed order, [one obtains the fruit]. || 20 ||
Having offered various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), he will thereafter perform a simple musical entertainment with the lute (vīṇā) that brings delight to the path of the senses.
Then, when the sun had grown dim, he would go to his own palace; and Ṛcīka, having heard those words of the people, [acted accordingly].

Afflicted by the arrows of desire, he went quickly to the house of Gādhi. Seeing that Ṛcīka, the best of the Bhṛgus, suddenly arrived, Gādhi, the most excellent of kings, went forward to meet him in haste. (23)
Then, having performed the honoring according to the ritual prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
O Brahmin, even though you are free from desire, what is the reason for your arrival? Tell me all of that, so that I may grant you everything.

Ṛcīka said: "O best of Brahmins, you have a daughter who is worthy of a bridegroom and possesses an excellent complexion; O lord of the earth, give her to me according to the Brāhma form of marriage. (26)
It is for this purpose that I have come to your house, tormented by love; O King, she was seen by me as she had arrived to perform worship to Gaurī.

Sūta said: Having heard that, Gādhi, the best of kings, was terrified with fear; considering him to be of a different caste, poor, and moreover old, and fearing a curse for not giving him [the girl], he then spoke a pretext.
"O best of the twice-born, there is a bride-price for the giving of our daughter; if you offer that, I shall give her to you without a doubt. (29)
Ṛcīka said: "Speak quickly, O tiger among kings, regarding the bride-price for my daughter; I shall give you everything, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (30)
Gādhi said: "O best of Brahmins, there are seven hundred horses, swift as the wind, all white except for one black ear."
"To him who shall bring [it] and give it to me, I shall give my daughter. || 32 ||
Sūta said: Having promised "So be it," Ṛcīka, the best of sages, reached Kānyakubja and entered [the city] on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Thereafter, he performed the recitation of the hymn beginning with "Aśvo voḍhā," which consists of sixty-four verses and is endowed with its specific meters, seers, and deities.
O twice-born ones, because Gādhi proclaimed that method for making [the horse] swift, those horses emerged from the water on account of that.
All white, swift-moving, and with one ear black, there were seven hundred of them, accompanied by an equal number of men.

From that time forth, the Aśvatīrtha became renowned upon the earth—situated on the auspicious and meritorious bank of the Gaṅgā near Kānyakubja—at which, when a bath is performed, a mortal obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. || 37 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Aśvatīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 165 ||
Sūta said: Then Ṛcīka, taking those horses with trustworthy men, departed for the place where Gādhi was staying.
He presented those excellent horses for the sake of the maiden; Gādhi, having then accepted them as suitable for the horse-sacrifice, [proceeded].
Then the king approached each one of them individually; subsequently, he gave that maiden, the most beautiful in the three worlds, to him.
Then, once the marriage had been completed according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, Ṛcīka, the best of sages, performed the rite witnessed by the Brahmins and the fire.
Upon entering her bedchamber, the sage became free from desire; then, established in that state of dispassion, he spoke to his own wife.
"I shall go to the forest for the sake of asceticism, O lady of beautiful hips; you should ask for some boon, so that I may grant you what you desire. (6)
Having heard those words spoken by him who was free from desire, she, distressed and with eyes filled with tears, went toward her mother.
O best of the twice-born, she then spoke these words to her husband who was free from desire, regarding the granting of the boon exactly as it had been stated by him.
Then, O best of Brahmins, as soon as she heard what her daughter had spoken, that mother spoke these words to her.
"If this husband of yours, my daughter, grants you a desired boon, then request from him a son endowed with Brahmanical status."
"O auspicious lady, for my sake, ask for this only son who is endowed with the complete splendor of a kshatriya; for I remain here without a son. (11)
O twice-born ones, having heard her mother’s words, that woman of virtuous vows approached Ṛcīka and related her mother’s speech to him in its entirety and in detail.

Having heard her words, he then prepared two portions of sacrificial porridge (caru); having performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice according to the rules, he paid homage to the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū).
O best of the twice-born, he placed the entire spiritual power (brāhmya-tejas) into one [son], and likewise the entire kṣatriya power (kṣātra-tejas) into the other.
He first gave his excellent brahmin sacrificial oblation (caru) to his wife; having caused her to eat it, he said, "Perform the embrace of the aśvattha tree. (15)
"Then you shall obtain a virtuous son endowed with Brahmanic splendor; as for the second *caru*, offer that to your mother. (16)
Then Ṛcīka, the best of sages, said to her: "Having eaten this sacrificial porridge (caru), you must embrace a banyan tree."
"Thereafter, O highly fortunate lady, you shall obtain a virtuous son endowed with the splendor of a Kṣatriya; my word shall not be in vain. (18)
Having spoken thus and released those two splendors, Ṛcīka, the best of Brahmins, being well-pleased, himself became honored.
Having gone home with their hearts full of joy, they said to one another, "This shall indeed come to pass."
Then the mother said to her daughter: "Every person exerts special effort for their own sake when a task is undertaken, even when it is a common one. (21)

O lady of beautiful eyes, the *caru* which has been prepared by him for the sake of the true goal (*tattvārtha*), and the collection of mantras which he has employed therein—O highly fortunate one, this which I have spoken will come to pass with special efficacy; this is the truth. (22)

Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, accept this sacrificial porridge (caru) from me; give me your own. And let an exchange be made between the two trees, O highly fortunate one, so that I may have an excellent son. (23)
Skilled in the affairs of state, heroic, and a crusher of enemy forces, even one who is merely a brahmin on your side will bring you satisfaction. (24)
Then, O best of the twice-born, when she was addressed by her illustrious mother in a secluded place, she made a transposition between the tree and the sacrificial porridge.
Then, after the two auspicious and beautiful-eyed women had bathed in the Puṃsavana forest, they immediately conceived a child from union with their husband.

Then, having conceived that embryo, she who was the most beautiful woman in the three worlds immediately became endowed with the splendor of a Kṣatriya; thereafter, her mind turned toward sovereignty, arising from the mastery of elephants and horses.

He likewise engaged in accounts of battles arising from the hosts of gods and asuras; he listened to them constantly and set his mind upon amusements. Thereafter, he carried out the performance of his kingdom according to his desires.
Having brought from his father’s house thoroughbred horses as well as elephants, red garments, and unguents such as saffron from Kashmir; || 29 || || 1 ||
Having observed her conduct—which was worthy of sovereignty and characterized by manifold enjoyments, yet entirely devoid of the practices befitting Brahmins—he [reflected]. (30)
And then, filled with rage, he said: "Fie upon you, O sinful woman! What is this that has been done? Surely a reversal has been made between the sacrificial pap (caru) and the mountain! (31)
O sinful woman, I perceive through you that such is your conduct.
It was worthy of a Kṣatriya, yet entirely devoid of the practices of the twice-born.
He had cast aside his bark garments and was devoid of ritual bathing and recitation; yet he was anointed with various fragrances, foremost among them musk.
Your mother is established in tranquility; she is devoted to the chanting of prayers and burnt offerings, intent upon pilgrimages, and eager to hear the Vedas.
Therefore, he will undoubtedly become a Kṣatriya son. || 35 ||

And the mother shall give birth to a son who will be the best of Brahmins, devoted to discourse on the holy life (brahmacarya), as indicated by the signs arising from the characteristics of the womb. (36)
For this reason, this verse was previously uttered by those who contemplate the scriptures: "Whatever longings pregnant women may have... (37)
"In this world, a son will be born to them with a nature exactly like that. Having been told this, she, trembling with fear and with palms joined in reverence, [spoke]. (38)
With eyes filled with tears and feeling dejected, she spoke these words: "O Lord, this statement which has been uttered by you is indeed true. (39)

"O Bhava, you know the past and the future here even without signs; therefore, show me favor so that there may be a son who is a Brāhmaṇa. You are by no means fit to be the father of a Kṣatriya son. (40)

Ṛcīka said: "Whatever Brahmanic luster there may be, that has been placed by me in your sacrificial porridge. And I shall never effect a reversal of your Kṣatriya luster and that of your mother; otherwise, I would be the lowest man in the world and a transgressor of the scriptures. (41)
The wife said: "O tiger among the Bhṛgus, if it be so, then whatever grandson may be born here to me, let all the Kṣatriya splendor brought by you be infused into his body. (42)
"May your son, however, be an excellent Brāhmaṇa who is even more distinguished than you. (43)

Ṛcīka said: "So be it; by my word, O auspicious lady, your son shall be a Brāhmaṇa, while your grandson shall be exceedingly difficult to withstand in battle, endowed with the splendor of a Kṣatriya. (44)
Then, having obtained the boon of truth and possessing a serene countenance, she reported all that her beloved had spoken to her mother.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived under the constellation presided over by Bṛhaspati, she gave birth to a son who resembled the rising sun.

Endowed with Brahmanic splendor, a pure treasury of ascetic powers, there was one renowned as Jamadagni, famous throughout the three worlds; his son was the highly illustrious one known by the name Rāma. (47)
By him, through the power of Kṣatriya splendor and by the grace of his grandfather, the earth was cleared of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Paraśurāma," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 166 ||
Sūta said: Then Gādhi’s wife, having indeed consumed the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the mantra on that auspicious day, conceived a child there.
O best of the twice-born, when she was born with the fetus already within her, that virtuous woman became devoted to pilgrimage and dedicated to the performance of vows.
Wherever the sound of the Vedas arose, she would always listen to it with great joy, her entire body covered in horripilation; she did so even after renouncing all royal ornaments and pleasures.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived, that best of twice-born women also gave birth to a son of great luster, endowed with Brahmanic splendor.
Thus celebrated throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, that illustrious one grew ever superior to all other men.
O best of the twice-born, when he had reached the bright fortnight like the moon in the sky, he became endowed with youth.
Then, although he was unwilling to accept his own great ancestral kingdom, he was appointed to the sovereignty by Gādhi, as he was capable of ruling the realm.
For he was perfected in the study of the Vedas and recited them constantly, traveling day and night along the path appropriate for a Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having installed his son in the kingdom, that illustrious one, accompanied by his wife, became a forest-dweller, devoted to the stage of life of a forest hermit (vānaprastha).
Viśvāmitra, established in his kingdom, was devoted to honoring the twice-born; then, together with all the brahmins, he practiced while intent upon ritual bathing and the chanting of prayers.
Then, after some time, having attained great wealth through hunting, he entered a fierce forest teeming with various wild animals.
There in the forest, he slew boars, śambaras, elephants, hyenas, ruru deer, rhinoceroses, and likewise wild buffaloes.
O best of the twice-born, with his mind intent on the hunt, he wandered through the great forest, [encountering] lions, tigers, great serpents, and śarabhas.
O best of the twice-born, when midday had arrived and the sun was situated in Taurus, Viśvāmitra became exhausted by hunger and thirst.
He reached the holy hermitage of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha; and Vasiṣṭha, too, beheld Viśvāmitra, that best of kings.
When the king arrived at his own hermitage, he went forward to meet him with joy; having offered the arghya and madhuparka to that monarch, [he welcomed him]. (16)
Then he spoke these words: "Welcome to you, O lord of the earth! Speak what must be done; I shall surely perform whatever task you have upon coming to my home."
Viśvāmitra said: "O Lord of Sages, exhausted from hunting and with my senses distressed by thirst, I have arrived here at your hermitage for the sake of a drink."
Having drunk that cool water, I have become free from thirst and am now established in peace; O Brahmin, grant me permission so that I may go to my home. (19)

Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, it is the fierce hour of midday and the sun is exceedingly scorching. Therefore, having taken your meal in my hermitage, you shall go to your own abode once the afternoon has arrived."
The king said: "I have come for the hunt with a fourfold army."
My army is stationed at the gate of your hermitage; for what master eats while his servants remain hungry? (22)
He goes to a terrible hell and is swiftly abandoned by all virtues; therefore, O Sage, command me quickly to go to my own home.
Vasiṣṭha said: "If you have servants who are hungry at the gateway, bring them all here quickly; I shall bring them supreme satisfaction."
"O best of kings, I possess a most beautiful wish-fulfilling cow named Nandinī; through her ascetic power, she grants every desire. (25)
"O best of kings, it will bring complete satisfaction to your entire army; therefore, let it be brought quickly—behold the fruit born of my cow! (26)
Having heard that, the lord of the earth summoned his entire army; he then bathed, performed his prayers, and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having caused the Brahmins to recite the benedictions and having taken his seat upon the lion-throne, in the meantime, the cow Nandini was summoned.
Summoned by Vasiṣṭha and standing before Viśvāmitra, she then spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
"Let an instruction be given to me; what shall I do? Command me. (30)
Vasiṣṭha said: "At my word, perform the washing of the feet and other rites for the royal sage Viśvāmitra until the meal is concluded. (31)

"With all kinds of foods—solid, lickable, suckable, and drinkable—of various sorts, provide for the satisfaction of the lord of the earth along with his army, as well as for the horses and elephants, with fodder and other provisions in due order. (32)
Sūta said: Having replied, "So be it," she then created in an instant that which had been described by the sage, as well as ten thousand servants.
Then those servants, taking all that food, gave it to each one individually, preceded by respectful hospitality.
Thus, in that very moment, the lord of the earth, together with his army, his retinue, and his elephants, camels, horses, and bulls, was brought to satisfaction by her. (35)
Then, O twice-born ones, having witnessed that marvel, King Viśvāmitra, together with his ministers, was overcome with astonishment and held counsel.
"Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how wonderful! By her, this army of ours, which was distressed by hunger and thirst, has been suddenly brought to satisfaction. (37)
Therefore, let this excellent cow be led back to her own home; what will this brahmin do, being without servants and dwelling in the forest? (38)
Then, having summoned Vasiṣṭha, he spoke these words: "Let Nandinī be given to me; what will you do with her? (39)

"You alone, dwelling in the forest, are free from dualities and without possessions; nevertheless, O best of sages, I shall grant you excellent villages, elephants, horses, and whatever else you desire for your expenses. (40)
Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, this sacrificial cow of ours yields all desires; O Great King, even though she belongs to ordinary twice-born men, this cow must not be given away. (41)
How much more so this Nandinī, who grants all desires? Listen further, O Indra among kings, to an unsurpassed statement from the Smṛti: || 42 ||
For regarding the sale of cows, that which was stated by Manu himself: "That best of the twice-born who accepts wealth produced from the sale of cows... (43)
He who sells his mother should be known as an outcaste; therefore, O lord of the earth, I will not give that Nandinī to you.
Neither by conciliation, nor by sowing dissension, nor by gifts in any way, nor by force, O Great King, can he be overcome; therefore, go to your own abode.
Viśvāmitra said: "O twice-born one, those who understand the nature of wealth know that whatever jewel exists on the earth belonging to a king, all of that must be considered royal property. (46)
Therefore, this cow Nandinī, who is like a jewel, remains mine; I shall seize her even by force with a staff if you do not grant her to me through peaceful means.
Having spoken thus to Vasiṣṭha, King Viśvāmitra then commanded his servants: "Let food fit for a king be prepared."
Then that Nandinī, being led away by the group of servants, was struck with blows using stones and even clubs.
Her eyes filled with tears, miserable and mangled by blows, she approached with great difficulty and spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
"O best of sages, have I been given by you to this king, that his men are driving me away as if I were his own mistress? (51)
Vasiṣṭha said: "O cow, even though my life is at its end, I shall not give you away; therefore, O cow, protect yourself by your own power through my grace. (52)
Thus addressed then by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the cow, overcome with anger, let out fierce "huṃ" sounds.
And by her utterances of the sound "huṃ," men emerged, bearing weapons—Śabaras, Pulindas, and Mlecchas, beyond all counting.
And by them, all the servants of King Viśvāmitra were slain; thereupon, that lord of the earth, Viśvāmitra, was overcome with anger.
Having prepared his fourfold army with fury, he waged war against them, having resolved upon death.
Then all those soldiers, as well as those elephants and horses, were seen being slain by men born of cows while they looked on. (57)
Having abandoned Viśvāmitra, everyone else was struck down; seeing that lord of the earth surrounded by Mlecchas and fighting, [he rushed to his aid]. (58)
Having shown compassion, Vasiṣṭha spoke thus to Nandinī: "O Nandinī, protect the king who is surrounded by these Mlecchas. (59)
For the king must be protected with great effort; by his grace this entire world abides on the path of the righteous and does not proceed upon the wrong path. (60)
Then, as Nandinī approached to restrain him, Viśvāmitra raised his sword and prepared to strike her.
Vasiṣṭha, observing her being struck at that moment, paralyzed both the arm and the sword of that king.
Then King Viśvāmitra, overcome with embarrassment and filled with shame, spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
"O best of sages, protect me as I am being slaughtered by these most cruel barbarians; make my arm free from paralysis. (64)
"Because of my transgression, my entire infinite army has been destroyed; therefore, I shall go to my palace, for there is no further purpose in battle."
Having attained fortune, knowledge, and even sovereignty, one who is ill-behaved and intoxicated by pride does not remain long in battle, just as I have been. (66)
Sūta said: Thus addressed by King Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha made that arm of his free from the defect of stiffness.
Having performed an auspicious rite, he spoke these words while smiling: "Go, O King; you have been released by me from the fault of arrogance."
"Do not, moreover, engage in conflict with the Brahmins. Having been thus permitted by him, King Viśvāmitra then [departed]. (69)
O best of the twice-born, filled with shame, she proceeded on foot to her palace; having reached the gate of her city at the very beginning of the night, when it was well-guarded.
There, with eyes clouded by tears, he uttered this lamentation: "Fie on the strength of the Kṣatriyas! Fie on their heroism! Fie on their very life! (71)
Praiseworthy is the singular power of Brahman, and absolute is the splendor of Brahman.

"This deed must be performed by me so that the power born of Brahman may arise; having renounced my own kingdom, I shall practice great austerity. Having made this resolution and established his son, renowned by the name Viśvasaha, upon the throne, he departed for the forest of penance.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Viśvāmitra’s Renunciation of the Kingdom," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 167.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having thus renounced his kingdom, Viśvāmitra reached the Himavat mountain and performed most rigorous austerities.
During the rainy season he slept under the open sky, in the winter he dwelt in the water, and during the summer he practiced the penance of the five fires; thus he remained for three hundred years.

O best of Brahmins, he then remained for three hundred years subsisting on fruits and roots while meditating upon the Supreme Brahman; thereafter, he remained for an equal period of time subsisting on withered leaves.

Thereafter, he remained subsisting on water for that same duration, and then for ten thousand years he subsisted only on air. Sūta said: Then, having witnessed the power of his asceticism, the Lord of the Gods thought, "This best of kings will surely cast me down from my position."
Then, overcome by great fear, he approached Viśvāmitra, the best of kings, and spoke with exceedingly beautiful and gentle words.
Indra said: "O Viśvāmitra, O King, I am well-pleased with this austerity of yours. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever is desired and dwells in your heart. (7)
Viśvāmitra said: "O Śakra, if you are now pleased with me, grant me the status of a Brāhmaṇa; O Purandara, know that for this purpose I have performed ascetic penance."

Indra said: "How can one become a Kṣatriya with this very body, O twice-born? One is born as such through the twenty-four purificatory rites (saṃskāras) doubled [to forty-eight]. Therefore, quickly ask for something else that remains more desired by you."
Viśvāmitra said: "O Lord of the Gods, I do not seek anything higher than the status of a Brāhmaṇa."
Even the sovereignty over the three worlds would be yours; what need is there to mention other objects? Therefore, O best of gods, go and protect your own kingdom.
"Either I shall cast off this body, or I shall attain the state of being twice-born. Having heard those words of his, the King of the Gods departed for heaven.
Knowing his resolve, Viśvāmitra, surrounded by all the gods, also performed that same kind of difficult penance.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when another thousand years had passed for King Viśvāmitra, who subsisted on air alone.
Brahmā himself arrived, accompanied by the meritorious celestial sages; he spoke to that protector of the earth, whose sins had been consumed by austerity.

The illustrious Brahmā said: "O Viśvāmitra, O best of beings, I am well-pleased with this penance. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—and I shall grant it to you, even if it be difficult to obtain. (16)
Viśvāmitra said: "O God, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then grant me Brahminhood, O God; there is nothing else more greatly desired by me. (17)
Brahmā said: "How can the status of the twice-born arise for one born of a Kṣatriya? Indeed, why do you speak such a desired thing that contradicts both Śruti and Smṛti? (189)
That which has not been born upon the surface of the earth shall never come to be at any time.
Viśvāmitra said: "Go, O Lord of the gods, to the unsurpassed world of Brahmā; I shall either cast off my life-breaths or attain the status of the twice-born."
Then Ṛcīka, standing in the midst of the celestial sages, spoke these words: "O Lord, for the sake of his birth, I have prepared this sacrificial oblation (caru) with Vedic mantras."
On all sides, the entire essence of Brahman was placed there by me; by that very means, O four-faced one, this person of kṣatriya birth has become a brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, O Great-grandfather, proclaim him as a Brahmarṣi; for even while established in kingship, he performed honors worthy of the twice-born with due respect.
By the power of the Brahma-mantra, summon that Brahman-sage, so that we may all together praise Viśvāmitra, the best of the twice-born.
Then Brahmā, having meditated for a long time with Vedic mantras and his own splendor, spoke to him as he was thus born: "I have created you as a Brāhmaṇa."
"Abandon this difficult and terrible asceticism immediately at my word; for when you were addressed by Brahmā, it was said without doubt: 'You are a Brahmarṣi. (26)
Then he was addressed by all those beginning with Ṛcīka, as well as by the celestial sages.
Then, standing in their midst, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, spoke filled with anger: "I shall never speak [thus] again."
O Grandfather, although you know that he was born from a Kṣatriya father, O Lord, you speak thus out of courtesy toward Ṛcīka. (29)

Although he was addressed in many ways by his grandfather and in numerous ways by the sages headed by Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, then departed, leaving behind all those most excellent of the twice-born.
And that best of sages, having arrived at the region known as Ānarta, stayed in the field of Hāṭakeśvara near Śaṅkha-tīrtha.
There, the meritorious Brahma-śilā is situated together with Śvetadvīpa; there also stands the auspicious river Sarasvatī, which removes all sins.
Having established a hermitage there, he performed extensive austerities; meanwhile, Viśvāmitra, filled with indignation, arrived there for the purpose of slaying him.
At a distance from that hermitage, situated in the southern direction, he established a hermitage for himself there, contemplating his [the sage's] vulnerabilities.
Having remained there for a very long time, he did not see anything at all; then, he began a rite of sorcery directed against him.

As it is stated in the Sāmaveda according to the ritual rules of the Sāman—that which is of the nature of slaughter—by him who was offering oblations into the fire with those terrible mantras, || 36 ||
A fierce, dreadful spear emerged, with disheveled hair and terrifying in appearance; it mounted the shoulder of a monkey while uttering a loud, tumultuous roar.
Equipped with various weapons like another Yamajihvā, she said: "Speak, O best of Brahmins; what task shall I perform for you? (38)
And by your command, I shall even destroy the entire three worlds.
Viśvāmitra said: "My enemy, the base-minded Vasiṣṭha, remains here; go quickly and slay him, for his sake I have made this effort."
Thus addressed by the wise Viśvāmitra, she set out toward the north, heading for the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
At that very time, O twice-born ones, many great and portentous omens appeared in the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
A great meteor fell, striking the solar disc, and likewise a rain of blood mixed with bones broke forth. (43)
Having reached the blazing quarter of the sky, the jackal likewise howled; seeing those great portents, Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, [was moved].
As long as he beholds forms filled with garlands of flames, he then thoroughly understands everything by means of his divine eye.
"This Śakti, employed by Viśvāmitra for my destruction, has been fashioned in the form of a Kṛtyā through excellent mantras originating from the Sāmaveda. (46)
"Stay! Stay!"—thus addressed by him, she then became motionless; she was paralyzed by him with his own mantras originating from the Atharvaveda.
Then, assuming the form of a woman, she spoke to the bull among sages: "Among the Vedas, the Sāmaveda stands preeminent. (48)
"Joined with that rite by the wise Viśvāmitra, do not disregard my blow, O Sage; I shall protect your life-breaths with but a slight touch, O Sage. (49)
Vasiṣṭha said: "If it be so, O auspicious one, grant me your touch, but not a touch that pierces my vital organs; for out of compassion for you, I have withdrawn the Atharvan mantras."
Then that terrible spear, discharged by Viśvāmitra, having touched his body, fell upon the surface of the earth.

Then Vasiṣṭha, being pleased, spoke these sweet words to her: "O highly fortunate one, from this day forward, all people, composed in mind and endowed with supreme devotion, shall perform worship unto you. (52)
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, those who perform worship endowed with supreme faith— || 53 ||
They shall all remain free from disease for as long as a year; therefore, by my command, you must always remain right here.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by that high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the goddess remained right there at that very moment by his word.
She receives supreme worship, especially that performed by the Nāgaras; she is renowned by the name Dhārā, bestowing happiness upon the world of devotees. (56)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Origin of Dhārā," in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, within the sixth section of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: Why is she declared to be the giver of satisfaction especially to the Nāgas? And why is she renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Dhārā? (1)

Sūta said: Formerly, in the city of Camatkāra, there was a virtuous ascetic woman named Dhārā, renowned as a noble Nāgarī Brāhmaṇa. In the past, she had been a close friend of the highly intelligent Arundhatī. || 2 ||
When Arundhatī arrived at the auspicious city of Camatkārapura, she came together with Vasiṣṭha to bathe in the Śaṅkha-tīrtha.
Then she was seen there by her, standing on the tip of her big toe, subsisting on air, taking no food, and endowed with a divine body.
And being questioned by her, that virtuous woman said: "Who are you, whose daughter are you, O auspicious one? For what purpose do you remain in this severe penance? Tell me, O beautiful lady. (5)
Dhārā said: "I am the daughter of a Nāgara Brahmin named Devaśarman; while I was still in my childhood, widowhood befell me."
Having heard the greatness of Śaṅkhatīrtha and of Śaṅkheśvara, I have therefore remained established here, intent upon his worship alone.
Arundhatī said: "A great affection for you has arisen from the very sight of you; therefore, come, let us go to my auspicious hermitage."
On the bright bank of the Sarasvatī, which destroys all sins, stay there with me, always delighting in scholarly discussions of the scriptures.
Then that ascetic woman set out together with her, having been granted permission by her father, her mother, and likewise by her kinsmen.
She had been her friend for a long time; then, after some period of time, that Śakti arrived there.

Released by Viśvāmitra for the purpose of slaying Vasiṣṭha, she was paralyzed by Vasiṣṭha and transformed into the form of a goddess; auspicious, she is worthy of worship by gods and mortals alike, bestowing all forms of protection.
Then, O brahmins, by means of that stream, a palace was constructed resembling the peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Then he offered a hymn of praise to her, and that ascetic woman [did the same].
Salutations to you, O Supreme Brahmanī; salutations again and again to the yoga of concentration. Salutations be to you, the supreme half-measure, the void, and that which is half of its half. 15.
Salutations to you, O support of the universe; salutations to you, O sustainer of all beings. Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; salutations to you, O you of golden luster.
Salutations to you, who are richly endowed with the lion-vehicle; salutations to you, O goddess of mighty arms! Salutations to you, desired by the gods; salutations to you, the slayer of the Daityas.
Salutations to you whose head is severed while your body is trampled by a buffalo; salutations to you who delight in the Vindhya mountains and are fond of offerings of wine and meat.
You are Lakṣmī, you are Śacī, you are Gaurī; you are Siddhi, you are Vibhāvarī; you are Svāhā, you are Svadhā; you are Tuṣṭi, you are Puṣṭi, you are Sureśvarī. || 19 ||
O Goddess, you are the embodiment of power, the agent of creation and destruction; this entire triple world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, is seen within you. 20.
Just as oil resides in sesame seeds and ghee resides in curd, and fire resides within wood—though well-concealed, it is not perceived. (21)
In the same way, O Goddess of gods, although you are omnipresent, you are not perceived.
Sūta said: By means of this foremost hymn, that Supreme Goddess was remembered by her as she worshipped her day after day for many groups of years.
Then, after some time had passed, on the bright eighth day of the month of Caitra, on that very day, the goddess was bathed and worshipped in the river.
Then, having offered the bali-oblation and praised her with this hymn, she appeared before her eyes and spoke to that ascetic woman.
"O daughter, I am pleased; may it be well with you, O sinless one, because of this hymn of praise. Choose a boon—may it be well with you—and I shall grant you whatever you desire. (26)
Dhārā said: "O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then let my name alone belong to you here in this temple. (27)
Furthermore, whatever city-dweller on this day, having performed three circumambulations and having offered three fruits to you, [shall obtain the fruit]. || 28 ||
Having praised you with this hymn and performed a prostration, for as long as a year, every disease of that person must be guarded against by you. (29)

May any woman who is barren become endowed with sons; may the unfortunate become possessed of good fortune, the ugly become beautiful, and the diseased be freed from disease and filled with every happiness. (30)
The Goddess said: "I shall be known as Dhārā in this temple built by you; I will remain here forever for the sake of your fame, of this there is no doubt. (31)
In this place, O ascetic woman, whatever city-dweller comes with devotion and performs three circumambulations after offering me three fruits—
"He too shall remain free from disease for the duration of one year. Having spoken thus, the goddess then vanished from sight.
The stream also remained there together with Arundhatī; even today it is seen in the sky, situated close to her.
O best of the twice-born, whoever shall here proclaim or hear this account arising from the descent of the stream shall be liberated from the sins committed during that day. (35)
Therefore, with every effort, this should especially be recited; and it should especially be heard with great devotion by the people of Nāgara. || 36 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Dhārādevī and the Account of the Origin of the Dhārā [Spring]," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 169.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, another marvel also occurred; that Śakti was released by Viśvāmitra against Vasiṣṭha.
And by the wise Vasiṣṭha, for the sake of slaying that brahmin-sage, [the demon's power] was paralyzed with Atharvan mantras, and perspiration broke out upon him.
From his perspiration, water was produced; it became cool. Water emerged from his two feet, and it appeared right here. || 3 ||

Having split the earth, a stream of very cool water emerged, as pure, purifying, and clear as the waters of the Gaṅgā. The Gaṅgā herself became manifest, accompanied by all the sacred fords (tīrthas); the pool was filled with water that was stainless, cool, and auspicious.
O best of the twice-born, whatever woman who is barren performs a bath in that [tirtha], she shall immediately become possessed of a son, O brahmins, even in this fierce Kali age.
Anyone else who performs a bath shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords.
That man who, having bathed there, beholds the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, shall obtain wealth, grain, as well as sons, and the happiness arising from sovereignty.

Any woman who is unfortunate or barren shall also become possessed of sons; on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, endowed with the yoga of devotion, she should offer an oblation of food, a bali-offering, and rice-balls right there during the deep of night.
Furthermore, the woman who herself performs [the rite] with a pure maiden, or the woman who indeed receives the *piṇḍikā* together with the *bali* offering; || 10 ||
O twice-born ones, even a woman who is a hundred years old—if she should eat the *piṇḍikā*—she too shall possess sons, even if she be most advanced in age.
How much more so, then, for a woman endowed with youth, possessed of good fortune, and blessed with the happiness of sons, through the sight of the Goddess herself? || 12 ||
The deity born of the disposition of all the city-dwellers is traditionally known as their family deity; she is the lineage deity of fifty-eight and a half clans.
For this reason, the procession should be well-performed by the citizens; for without the citizens, the Goddess of the Suras does not attain satisfaction through the procession. (14)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Greatness of Dhārā Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: At that very time, the great sage Viśvāmitra, perceiving that the spear had been rendered useless, was overcome with anger.
He discharged the Brahma-weapon, consecrated with mantras, for the purpose of slaying him; as soon as it was aimed, a tremendous roar arose. || 2 ||
Then numerous meteors fall from the vault of the sky; thereafter, spears, javelins, lances, and iron clubs likewise descend.
Bhindipālas, maces, swords, and battle-axes; arrows, spears, and śataghnīs by the hundreds and thousands. || 4 ||
Vasiṣṭha, having recognized that the Brahmā weapon had been dispatched by the son of Gādhi for his own death, thereafter purified himself.
Taking up a blade of grass and invoking the Brahmāstra upon it, he said to the son of Gādhi: "May it be well with you from my side."
"By my word, let this weapon be destroyed without a doubt. Then, that Brahmāstra, which had arisen from him, was destroyed by him.
Then the Vajrāstra was released and destroyed by [the other] Vajrāstra; whatever weapon this Viśvāmitra, filled with rage, discharged— 8.
But Vasiṣṭha destroyed each of those by the power of his mantra; at that very moment, however, the ocean was agitated.
Mountain peaks are crumbling, a great rain of blood has fallen, and the signs of a dissolution have appeared upon the earth; will this great dissolution come to pass before its time?
Then all the gods, together with Indra, went to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and spoke of those signs of universal dissolution that were appearing upon the surface of the earth.
Then Brahmā, having meditated for a long time, spoke to those inhabitants of heaven: "This battle has been set in motion between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha."
Because of him, this world has become agitated by the manifestation of divine weapons.
Therefore, let us go there before the destruction of all beings occurs through the power of these divine weapons. 14.
Then they went to that place where those two best of sages, Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha, were fighting with one another.
Then Brahmā spoke to the two of them in a voice that was exceedingly sweet and gentle: "Let this battle, born of divine weapons, be desisted, before the dissolution of the entire earth occurs."
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Lord, I am not employing this weapon with the desire to slay Viśvāmitra; rather, for the sake of self-protection, I am neutralizing his weapon with my own weapon."
"O Brahmin, this merciless one is discharging his weapons solely for my destruction; restrain him now! (18)
Brahmā said: O Viśvāmitra, best of sages, by my word, you must protect Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent of Brahmins, as well as this entire world. (19)
O Brahman-sage, cease the discharge of your weapons immediately.
Viśvāmitra said: "O Great-grandfather, he does not address me as a twice-born in any way; therefore, this anger has arisen in me regarding his execution. (21)
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, let this Brāhmaṇa speak to me quickly, so that I may ward off the missile which has been aimed at him.
Brahmā said: "O Vasiṣṭha, speak now to Viśvāmitra at my command; by that he shall become a Brāhmaṇa, and thus there will be protection for your life."
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Lotus-born One, I do not call one born of a Kṣatriya a Brāhmaṇa; this man, though born of a Kṣatriya, is in no way capable of killing me. (24)
The splendor of Brahman is not destroyed by the splendor of the Kṣatriya; knowing this, O Four-faced One, do that which is appropriate. (25)
Brahmā said: "O Viśvāmitra, best of the twice-born, abandon this [fight] born of divine weapons; engage in battle with Vasiṣṭha, otherwise I shall curse you."
Viśvāmitra said: "Having cast aside my divine weapons, that evil-minded one must be slain by me; finding some vulnerability, you go back to your own refuge. (27)
Sūta said: Having replied, "So be it," Brahmā went to the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), while Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha remained on the bank of the Sarasvatī.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Withdrawal of Divine Weapons in the Battle between Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: From that time forward, O best of the twice-born, Viśvāmitra remained intent on seeking out vulnerabilities for the purpose of slaying Vasiṣṭha.
By the power of his own spiritual strength, just as an elephant [overcomes] a mosquito, that river was [subdued] by Viśvāmitra when another day arrived.
Summoned, she arrived quickly in the form of a woman; with palms joined in reverence, she said, "Let my command be given: O Brahman-sage, for what purpose have I been summoned now? (3)
Viśvāmitra said: "O great river, whenever you perform your immersion in my waters, then, assuming your supreme speed, bring me to your side."
With his ears filled with water and his limbs motionless, he stands there; I shall slay him quickly, for I perceive no other vulnerability.
Thus addressed by Viśvāmitra at that time, the river, terrified and filled with fear, spoke these words out of dread of the curse: || 6 ||
"I shall not commit an act of hostility against the high-souled Vasiṣṭha; O Brahmarṣi, it is certainly not fitting for you to bring about the death of a Brāhmaṇa."
If you have indeed been declared by Brahmā himself to be a Brahmarṣi, then this Vasiṣṭha is not subject to desire; therefore, abandon your anger.
He who even in his mind contemplates the killing of a Brāhmaṇa shall be liberated by the Taptakṛcchra penance; so said Manu, the son of Svayambhū.
If a man should utter with his speech the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the Lord has declared that his purification shall be through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Therefore, I will not carry out your command under any circumstances; however, do whatever you please regarding that which was said for the sake of Vasiṣṭha.
O best of the twice-born, having heard that, Viśvāmitra became enraged at her; listen as I relate what curse he pronounced upon that excellent river.
"O Kunadī, because my word was not heeded by you regarding this sin, therefore this water-born flow of yours shall become a stream of blood. (13)
Having spoken thus, with eyes bloodshot with anger, he then threw water from his hand—consecrated with mantras seven times—into her.
And then, O twice-born ones, at that very moment, that water became blood—the highly meritorious Sarasvata water—which turned the color of a conch shell.
In the meantime, bhūtas, pretas, and night-stalkers arrived; drinking again and again, they danced, sang, and laughed.
Whatever ascetics were stationed there on its bank, they all abandoned it and took refuge in a distant land. || 17 ||
And those citizens who were stationed there outside the city, beginning with Caṇḍaśarman, they too departed to a great distance. (18)
Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, went to Mount Arbuda; Viśvāmitra, the brahmin-sage, went to Camatkārapura.
Having established a hermitage in that region of the Hāṭakeśvara field which was crowded with Brahmins, he performed most rigorous penance.
By which he became capable of creation and rivals even with Brahmā; all this has been narrated to you regarding how the water of Sarasvatī [came to be]. || 21 ||
Having reached the state of blood due to the curse of Viśvāmitra, the brahmins headed by Caṇḍaśarman departed for other lands.
The sages said: "Oh, how truly marvelous is the power of the great sage Viśvāmitra, by whom that water was turned into blood through the potency of his mantra!"
From that time onwards, O illustrious one, tell me how the water was obtained; relate everything concerning the Sarasvatī in detail.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, for a long time that great flow of the Sarasvatī became filled with blood and was frequented by spirits and Rākṣasas.
Then, after some time, while Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was staying at Arbuda, he was addressed by her, who was distressed and filled with grief.
O Sage, for your sake she was cursed by Viśvāmitra out of anger; she has become a river carrying floods of blood, devoid of the company of ascetics.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, show me favor so that there may be water once again, and the blood in my stream may come to an end.
O Brahmin, O lord of all sages, there is no power whatsoever that you lack, whether in the creation, destruction, or maintenance of the three worlds.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O blessed lady, I shall act in such a way that water will once again flow forth from your stream and all the blood will come to an end."
Having spoken thus, that brahmin-sage descended to the surface of the earth and went to the Plakṣa tree from which the Sarasvatī river flows down.
Intent upon meditative absorption there, he sat upon the surface of the earth, having fallen into a state of extreme agitation toward Viśvāmitra.
While gazing at the surface of the earth with a Vāruṇa mantra, a great quantity of water then burst forth from the ground after piercing through it.
O best of Brahmins, by looking with his two eyes through the two apertures, water quickly issued forth from one of them, where the Sarasvatī was born.
Then, at the foot of that Plakṣa tree, that blood was forcibly carried away by his speed; it filled [the area] completely, and from that, a great river was formed.
But that second stream which issued forth from him in agitation became the river named Sābhramatī upon the surface of the earth.
Thus Sarasvatī returned to her natural state; O highly blessed twice-born ones, this is what I have related to you in response to your question concerning Sarasvatī. (15)

This exposition, named Sārasvata, bestows supreme intelligence. Whoever reads it or even hears it, their intellect shall increase; by the grace of Sarasvatī, this which I have spoken is the truth. (16)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Liberation from Sarasvatī’s Curse and the Origin of the Sābhramatī," within the *Sarasvaty-upākhyāna* of the *Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 173 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, I shall tell you of another Liṅga situated there, which was installed by Pippalāda and is known as Kaṃsāreśvara—how wonderful!

"When it is seen, the sins of people arising from the day pass away; when bowed to, those of six months; and when worshipped, those accumulated over a year. The sages said: "O son of Sūta, tell us why that Liṅga which was established by Pippalāda is called Kaṃsāreśvara."
Who is this Pippalāda? Tell us whose son he is, and for what purpose was the Liṅga installed in that sacred field by that high-souled one?
Sūta said: This burden of questions has been set forth by you; nevertheless, having paid homage to the Self-Existent One (Brahmā), I shall speak.
Yājñavalkya’s sister, renowned as Kaṃsārī, performed most severe penance while observing celibacy from her youth.
O twice-born ones, after some time had passed, she was accompanied by her kinsman in the meritorious hermitage of Yājñavalkya.
O virtuous twice-born ones, having seen a certain beautiful apsaras at the end of a dream, his semen was discharged while he was established in a state of youthfulness and engaged in ascetic penance.
His great garment was completely soaked with semen; and that was cast away by him when morning had arrived.
Then Kaṃsārikā took up that garment for the sake of bathing, O best of the twice-born, unaware that it was moistened by the semen of one whose seed is never in vain.
While she was performing a sacrifice, water infused with virility entered the middle of her womb when her fertile period had arrived.
Then a fetus formed within her, situated in the middle of her womb; and it grew constantly, like the lord of stars in the bright fortnight.
Having taken that embryo situated within her own womb, that ascetic woman was then joined with great sorrow and overcome by shame.
Filled with wonder, she reflected for a very long time; concealing herself, she thought, "I do not come into the sight of men. (14)

Having made the performance of her vows her bait, she remained always in seclusion; when the tenth month had arrived and midnight was at hand, a young son was born to her, possessing a radiance like that of the rising sun.
Then, taking him and wrapping him in a fine cloth, she went to a forest devoid of people; with eyes full of tears, miserable and weeping, she departed in secret. (16)
Then, having gone to a very large *aśvattha* tree in a secluded place, she unfastened [it] beneath it and spoke these words. (17)
O Aśvattha, you are the form of Viṣṇu; you are established among the gods. Therefore, O Lord of the Forest, protect my son from all sides. 18.
This young son of mine has come to you for refuge; therefore, grant protection to him from that sinful and merciless woman.
Having spoken thus and having wept for a very long time, that ascetic woman, her eyes clouded with tears, subsequently departed for her own hermitage.
While that mother was weeping beneath that lordly tree, a voice born from the sky arose, sounding like the roar of a thundercloud.

"Do not grieve for the sake of this boy, O auspicious lady; he is Bṛhaspati, who has descended to the surface of the earth due to the curse of his elder brother Utathya, and he shall attain his full fitness."
And he will divide the Atharvaṇa Veda—which consists of a hundred kalpas and is very extensive—into a hundred branches, and further arrange it into nine divisions and five kalpas.
"He shall consume the essence of the pippala tree; therefore, he will become famous in the world as Pippalāda. (24)
Since you have become filled with wonder that this child was born to me tall and without a father, therefore hear the reason for that. (25)
O auspicious one, you wore as a garment during your fertile period that bathing cloth of your brother which had been drenched with his semen.
At the time of bathing, however, the waters touched his seminal fluid; by that unerring seed, this son of yours was conceived.
Knowing this, O illustrious lady, perform whatever is appropriate.
Sūta said: Having heard those words from the world of the gods, which were like a thunderbolt strike, she broke out into cries of "Alas! Alas! and fell to the surface of the earth.
Like a creeper whose tree has been cut down, that poor woman fell.
When she was delayed, that great sage Yājñavalkya, seeing the hermitage empty, questioned the other lords of sages.
"Where has my sister, the daughter of Kaṃsa’s enemy and a great ascetic, gone? Without her, this entire circle of my hermitage is empty today. (32)
A certain ascetic declared: "Your younger sister has fallen motionless upon the ground near an aśvattha tree. (33)
"I have seen her, O best of sages; meditate upon her without delay. Then, filled with haste and agitation, he ran forth. (34)
Where that ascetic woman was described by that ascetic, she remained standing there, sighing, as he looked upon her.
Then, having sprinkled her again and again with cold water and fanned her once more until she regained consciousness, at that moment Kātyāyanī and Maitreyī arrived in great agitation.
"What is this? What has happened? Speak, O brother; do not delay! (37)
Or have you been bitten by a snake, or afflicted by a disorder of the humors? (1)
Or have you been seized by a spirit, or are you afflicted by a fever of Mahendra? || 38 ||
Then, having regained consciousness and seeing Yājñavalkya standing before her together with his wife, she released her life-breaths out of shame.

Then, O twice-born ones, having seen her dead and having wept for a long time, Yājñavalkya—bearing his grief, accompanied by his wife, and having offered the fire and the water-libation—departed for his own hermitage. (40)
Then that boy also grew, sustained by the nourishment from tasting the *pippala* fruit; he gradually attained growth at the foot of that *aśvattha* tree. (41)
Then, after some time, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived by that path on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā). || 42 ||
Seeing there a boy who possessed a splendor equal to twelve suns, alone in the empty forest and intent on tasting the pippala fruit, he, overcome with wonder, asked: "Who are you here all alone? (43)
In this empty, most terrible forest, crowded with lions and tigers, where are your mother and father, and for what purpose do you stand here? (44)
And how do you dwell? Tell me everything in detail.
Pippalāda said: "I do not know my father, nor my mother, nor any kinsman; nor do I know you—who has come here to my side at this moment? (46)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his and having meditated for a long time, the lord of sages, perceiving the truth with his divine eye, spoke to him while smiling.
Nārada said: "O child, you have been recognized by me as being born from the seed of Yājñavalkya, produced by the power of destiny in the womb of your sister during her season."
Due to the fault of Utathya’s curse, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, [acted]; listen now to the reason for that, which was for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (49)
And this Atharvaveda, which has been composed with a hundred branches and a hundred ritual manuals (kalpas) of hidden meaning, is for the accomplishment of the purposes of kings.
"You must perform the rite with nine branches and five kalpas, which shall bring about happiness."
O highly fortunate one, that garment of Yājñavalkya which was worn by you and which became drenched with semen has been put on as your lower robe. (52)
By his sister, who was performing great penance and not out of desire, that semen, having issued from her womb, became mixed with the water. || 53 ||
"Because it was not in vain, you have been born here upon the surface of the earth; for your mother, knowing this, has indeed met her death out of shame. (54)
O highly fortunate one, your maternal uncle as well as your father reside in Camatkārapura; go from here to their side.
"Now is the time for your vow, and the eighth year has indeed arrived. Having heard those words of his, he stood with his face cast down in shame.
Then, after a long time, he spoke these words to him in distress: "Tell me, what sin was committed by me in a previous life? (57)
O virtuous sage, because of this censurable birth resulting from separation from my mother, I shall abandon my own life through this suffering.
Nārada said: No evil deed whatsoever was committed by you in a previous life; however, hear the reason why this calamity has arisen for you.
"You were born with Saturn as your natal lord; of this there is no doubt. It is because of him that you have reached this condition, for there is indeed no other cause. (60)
Having heard those words of his, with eyes bloodshot with anger, he looked upward toward Śanaiścara.
At the mere fall of his glance, he instantly fell from his own celestial chariot, just as Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and descendant of the Sun, once did.
O best of the twice-born, having received his father’s command, he stood with his face turned downwards; even in his childhood, the feet of the Sun were then scorched by him alone.
Then Nārada spoke to him as he was falling face downwards: "O Śanaiścara, you have been cast down by this [child] due to his state of childhood. (64)
Therefore, do not look at him, lest he become enraged; likewise, do not fall to the ground by force, in accordance with my word.
Having thus paralyzed Śanaiścara while he remained in the sky, the lord of sages then spoke to that boy Pippalāda.
"Do not be angry, O child; this is the planet [Rāhu], the son of the Sun. When situated in the eighth house, he causes affliction even to the gods. (67)
The one situated in the birth-sign is especially significant, as is the second; for if this one should ever look upon you with anger, [all would be lost].
"He will undoubtedly reduce me to a heap of ashes before him; for as soon as he was born, my two feet were gazed upon by this son of the Sun. (69)
But when he had arrived and was filled with joy by his longing to see his son, the garment was made to vanish; and [the mother], perceiving him to have eyes of fierce aspect, [was struck with fear].
Then both of them, though burnt, remained wrapped in skin; even today those two forms are seen upon the solidified surface of the earth. (71)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Nārada, that boy, overcome with great fear, then questioned the sage.
"O excellent sage, tell me how my satisfaction shall be attained: he was cast down from the sky through ignorance, by me who did not recognize his power. (73)
Nārada said: Planets, cows, kings, and especially Brahmins, when honored, honor in return; when treated with disrespect, they consume [the offender] with fire.
Therefore, O Lord, offer praise to this Sun with all your power, so that he may become gracious and abandon the wrath born of his fall. (75)
Then, with palms joined in reverence, that boy, filled with great fear, offered a hymn of praise after questioning the sage.
O best of the twice-born, Pippalāda, bowing down again and again, said: "Salutations to you who abide in wrath; salutations be to you, O Piṅgala! (77)
Salutations to you who possess the form of Vasu, and let there be salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa; salutations to you whose body is fierce, and salutations to you, the Ender.

Salutations to you who are known as Yama; salutations to you, O all-pervading Lord, who are the son of the Sun; salutations to you who are known as Mandā; O Śanaiścara, let there be salutations to you.
O Lord of Gods, show favor to me, who am wretched and prostrate before you.
Śanaiścara said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child, by this hymn of praise now. Choose a boon—may it be auspicious for you—so that I may grant it to you at once."
Pippalāda said: "O son of the Sun, O highly fortunate one, from this day forward you must never in any way cause suffering to our children. (82)
O son of the Sun, by my word, let it be so until his eighth year: whoever shall praise you here with this hymn upon rising in the morning, [shall obtain his desire].
O son of the Sun, you must not cause him any affliction, for he who performs an oil massage on the day of your lunar mansion (Sunday) [is protected]. || 84 ||
For eight days, no harm whatsoever should be done to him; for he who, having fashioned you out of iron, places you face-down in the midst of oil— || 85 ||
One should retain that oil and then perform a bath; one must not cause him pain, but rather grant a profit to the king.
When the conjunction of Adhyardhāṣṭamī has arrived during your watch, O Man, and when your own day (Tava-vāra) has come, he who [offers] sesame seeds combined with iron— || 97 ||
O Lord, you should not cause distress to him who, according to his own ability, gives a black cow to a Brahmin for your sake. (88)

O Lord, you should not cause any affliction to one who offers a sacrifice with fuel-sticks of śamī wood for your sake, even if he is born under the constellation Aṣṭamā (Mūla), which consists of one and a half stars. || 99 ||

Likewise, whoever worships you with black sesame seeds, black flowers, and ointments, and burns guggulu incense, you must abandon all suffering for that person who has wrapped [the image] in a black cloth. (90)
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by him, Śani replied, "So be it," and taking leave of Nārada, he departed for his own abode.
Nārada also, filled with compassion, took that child and, having gone to Camatkārapura, presented him to Yājñavalkya.
He related the account of his birth and origin; he reported everything that had been seen by means of the lamp of knowledge. || 93 ||
"This infant son of your sister, born of your own prowess, was found by me in the forest at the foot of an Ashvattha tree, in the vicinity of an Ashvattha. (94)

"Perform the initiation ceremony for him now, as he has reached eight years of age. O best of Brahmins, there is no fault in this, nor for your sister. Therefore, accept your own son, especially since he is your nephew. (95)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that divine sage then vanished from sight; and Yājñavalkya, having heard that, fell into a state of supreme despondency.
Even while merely contemplating that evil, he finds no peace; constantly reproaching himself, he grieves by day and by night. (97)
Having recognized him as his son by those various inherent marks that remained with him, he then nourished him and initiated him into the vow.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Pippalāda," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: While he was thus lamenting and censuring himself, O twice-born ones, Brahmā himself approached him and spoke.
O twice-born one, you should not entertain any doubt regarding this son; this boy was born to you through the power of destiny, solely out of ignorance.
Yājñavalkya said: "Nevertheless, O Lord, purity of my heart does not arise. Therefore, O best of gods, tell me the expiation for the sake of purification. (3)
Brahmā said: "O highly fortunate one, if the purification of your mind does not proceed by any means, then install a liṅga of the trident-bearing God."
Whatever sin a man commits, whether through ignorance or even through knowledge—including the killing of a Brahmin or that which arises from the slaying of a woman—[he is purified]. || 5 ||
Even for one who constructs a temple of Hara made of five types of bricks, that [sin] perishes just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Especially, O highly fortunate one, in that most pure field born of Hāṭakeśvara, which destroys all sins.
"O best of the twice-born, now that this Kali age has arrived, wherein no sin exists, I too desire to perform a sacrifice here."
"I shall bring that holy site, Puṣkara, which is dear to me, so that it does not fall into futility through fear of the Kali age. (9)
But when the Kali age has arrived, O Brahmin, all sacred fords (tīrthas) shall become useless, with the exception of this supreme field.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the four-faced one then vanished from sight; and Yājñavalkya, having heard all those words of the Grandfather (Brahmā), [acted accordingly].
Having recognized this field as unsurpassed, he installed the Liṅga; then he spoke these words with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Whoever bathes this Liṅga of mine with true devotion on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, his sin shall depart.
Whatever sin has been committed through another's wife, or even that which was done together with one's mother—that evil shall be washed away when [the image] is bathed and honored by others. (14)
When this day has arrived, whatever sin was committed by him arising from his faction, having been produced through ignorance, shall pass away.
From that time forward, O best of the twice-born, he became celebrated as the auspicious Yājñavalkyeśvara in that sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Yājñavalkyeśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 175.
Sūta said: Having seen that the Liṅga had been installed by the wise Yājñavalkya for the sake of his mother’s purification, he [established] that excellent Liṅga under her name.

O best of Brahmins, filled with supreme faith, he established him there; then, having brought a preeminent Brahmin born of the Nāgara lineage from the Garta-tīrtha—one who maintained the sacred fires and performed sacrifices—he said: "Just as this site of the city is, so too are you consecrated. (3)
O best of the twice-born, by your word, all the sixty-eight clans have been established under your leadership.
They shall carry out their duties as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist; O Govardhana, you must concern yourself with his well-being.
The citizens should be urged for the sake of worshipping the Liṅga; through the worship of that Liṅga, your lineage shall attain prosperity.
Without worship, he will meet with destruction; of this there is no doubt. And those born of your lineage who worship [him] with great devotion— || 7 ||
O initiated one, whatever various rites they shall perform using this liṅga will attain success through its grace. (8)

Govardhana said: "O twice-born one, I shall always perform the worship of this linga; I shall practice devotion for its sake, O twice-born one, and likewise those others who shall arise in my lineage for the purpose of its worship. (9)
Pippalāda said: "O Brāhmaṇas, quickly bring the Nāgara sages there; with their consent, I shall perform the mere naming ceremony for the deity. (10)
