Then he summoned wise brahmins who were perfected in sacred learning and study, and devoted to the performance of sacrificial rites.
The great sage Pippalāda, having bowed to them, spoke aloud: "My mother died previously; her name was Kaṃsārī."
O best of the twice-born, I have now established this definition of her characteristics in brief; by your word, let it attain renown.
Whoever bathes this [image] arising from Yājñavalkyeśvara on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days shall indeed attain supreme welfare.
Sūta said: Then, out of reverence for that virtuous sage, all those brahmins established his name as Kaṃsārīśvara.
O best of the twice-born, all this that I was asked by you has been narrated; how the destroyer of sins, known as Kaṃsārīśvara, was born and installed by the high-souled Pippalāda himself.
And whoever, endowed with full capacity, should properly recite or listen to this meritorious narrative in the presence of that deity, [attains the fruit]. || 17 ||
Whatever sin has been conceived in the mind, including that committed with another's wife, that very sin goes to destruction, according to the word of Pippalāda.
Whoever should always recite the Nīlarudra hymns with devotion before him—especially the Prāṇarudras accompanied by the Bhavarudras—[attains the highest state]. 19.
Even the sin arising from the killing of a Brahmin perishes for him; likewise, when fear of a foreign army arises, or when there is fear of drought. (20)
When the Atharvaveda is recited at its conclusion in his presence, the enemy goes to destruction and rain is swiftly produced.
When a state of royal distress arises, the king becomes righteous; freed from all diseases, he is devoted to the protection of his subjects. || 22 ||
When the fear of calamities arises, his affliction is pacified gradually and without doubt, just as Pippalāda had said. (23)
What is the use of speaking much to you? Whatever great calamity there may be, that very calamity is somewhat mitigated by the recitation of the Atharvaṇa.
In the presence of this god, it indeed quickly goes to destruction. || 25 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Greatness of Kaṃsāreśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another Gaurī there known as Pañcapiṇḍikā, who was indeed installed by Lakṣmī while she was abiding in a human state.
Merely by the sight of her, a woman shall obtain good fortune in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the sun is situated in Taurus.
Upon it is a woman who indeed holds a water-fountain; by bathing in it day and night, one shall obtain supreme good fortune.

Whatever fruit a woman obtains from all the prescribed vows, from gifts originating with Gaurī, and from those offerings born of her desires—she obtains all that fruit by means of constructing a water-wheel.
Therefore, with every effort, for the sake of securing good fortune, women should diligently construct a water-machine (jalayantra) for Gaurī during the month of Jyeṣṭha. || 5 ||
O best of Brahmins, what is the use for women of vows or observances, or of other such acts as recitations and fire-offerings that cause great hardship? (6)
O tigers among brahmins, when the water-mechanism was held by the women over Gaurī with true devotion, while the sun stood in the constellation of Vṛṣabha.
She is never born as a barren woman, nor as one who bears only a single child; for seven successive births, she shall not be possessed by misfortune.
The sages said: Gaurī is described as four-armed, yet the Supreme Goddess is seen with five lumps (piṇḍas). How did this come to be? Tell us, for this is our doubt. (9)
Sūta said: And when the dissolution is about to occur, O brahmins, he then makes himself; he assumes an excellent form consisting of five lumps (piṇḍas).
This is that supreme Śakti, the sovereign of the gods, who pervades everything; by her this entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded. 11.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space itself—one should preserve these for the sake of creation; therefore, this constitutes the five-fold aggregate (pañcapiṇḍikā).
Whatever merit is produced when this [Liṅga] is worshipped while it is visibly present, that same merit is increased three-thousandfold where there is a five-piṇḍika [Liṅga].
Especially in the month of Jyeṣṭha, by means of the worship of water-machines (jalayantra), I shall here relate to you an ancient legend.
O best of the twice-born, this is the account of what occurred concerning the wife of the King of Kāśī, and that which was formerly spoken by Lakṣmī when she was questioned by Viṣṇu.
Lakṣmī said: In ancient times, there was a king of Kāśī known as Jayasena; he had a thousand wives who were endowed with great beauty.
Then he obtained another beloved and most beautiful wife, who was indeed a portion of my own essence while I existed in human form—the daughter of the wise Viṣvaksena, the sovereign king of Madra.
Having gone there, she then rose at dawn and, on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā, fashioned an image of Gaurī made of clay consisting of five lumps.
Then he worshipped him with the five mantras, and thereafter with excellent perfumes, garlands, incense, and most beautiful garments.
Then, having honored that Goddess with food offerings, supreme rice-dishes, songs, dances, and instrumental music, he should bid her farewell, dedicating those acts to her.
Having given abundant gifts to the twice-born who have come for brides, he then returns home amidst the sounds of many musical instruments.
And in whatever manner she performs that worship of Gaurī, in that same manner her own good fortune shall increase even further. (22)
And her good fortune shall be greater than that of all her co-wives. || 23 ||
Then her co-wives, all of whom were filled with sorrow, saw that very increase in her good fortune day after day.
Some said: "This is her constant practice; having taken up clay, she worships five lumps of earth. (25)
The great seers declare that her perfection is achieved through mantras; others say it is due to the meritorious deeds she performed in previous lives. (26)
In this manner, a great length of time passed for them in extreme suffering. Then, after some time, they all consulted with one another. (27)
They came into her presence at that very same reservoir, where she was worshipping Gaurī after having fashioned those five *piṇḍikās*.
Then, having observed them all and abandoned the worship of Gaurī, she quickly went forward to meet them and stood with her palms joined in reverence.
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones; once again, a very hearty welcome to you! Let your purpose be declared quickly, so that I may carry it out at once. (30)
The co-wives said: "We have all come into your presence out of curiosity, having been consumed by the fire of misfortune produced by your own good fortune. (31)
Therefore, O highly fortunate lady, tell me: why do you daily worship a five-lump image made of clay? What is it that increases one's good fortune?
What indeed is the cause of this for you, or is it born from a mantra? O highly fortunate one, if this power is a secret, do not fail to tell us.
Padmāvatī said: "O fair-faced ones, although that which I have been asked is a supreme secret and a profound mystery—something that ought not to be spoken—I shall nevertheless tell it to you."
"Since you have all come together at the time of Gaurī’s worship, you are all my sisters; I harbor no feeling of envy toward you. (35)
Formerly, I was a maiden in the city named Kusuma; I was given by that high-souled and wise merchant’s son, the Śūdra Vīrasena, according to the sacred law for the purpose of marriage.

Then, at the time of my marriage, five excellent syllables were bestowed upon me for my spiritual growth, along with the initiation of a woman; furthermore, I was thereafter instructed in the worship of Gaurī.
"O daughter, as long as you worship yourself with these syllables, you must by no means drink water at all. (38)
"By its power, you shall attain whatever desired object you seek. And I said to her, "So be it," O fair-faced one. (39)
Then, when the wedding was completed, I went with my husband to where my father-in-law resided, as well as my most cruel mother-in-law.

She always forbids me from performing the worship of Gaurī; consequently, terrified by fear and devoted to the worship of Gaurī, whenever I go to a body of water for the sake of water, [she obstructs me] right there at that reservoir. (41)
Then, taking clay and with those very five mantras, I, devoted to her with supreme faith, worship Gaurī.
"I cast it into the water and then I went to my home. After some time had passed, my auspicious husband set out for another country on business as a merchant; he too took that same path. (43)
Taking me with him out of affection, he traveled along a desert path and reached a waterless region, a most terrifying expanse of sand.
Likewise, during that most terrible time, while the lord of the day (the Sun) was situated in Taurus, the entire caravan rested in the middle of the land.
At that very time, I saw nearby a single deep well resembling a cloud; however, the desert region appeared as if it were water, and this was what occurred to my mind. (46)

And that water which is seen nearby in such abundance—having bathed here and become pure, and having worshipped Gaurī with devotion, I shall afterwards drink the very sweet water born of this lake. (47)
Then, having set out, as I moved step by step, the further I went, the more that mirage receded. (48)
In the meantime, O fair-faced one, the sun reached the middle of the sky, situated in Taurus, by which I am scorched from above.
With burning sands all around in the region below, I was then distressed and tormented by thirst in that desert land.
Then she fell upon the ground, covered with boils; thereupon, the story originating from the Mahābhārata was remembered by me within my mind.
Just as the sacrifice was performed by Nṛga with grains of sand while he was being cast into a well devoid of grass, clods of earth, and water; (52)
Therefore, the gods are to be grasped through devotion; being pleased with that high-souled one, I worship Harapriyā with grains of sand.
Pleased by that, the goddess grants me my kingdom today, once another body has been attained, which shall fulfill my heart's infinite desires.
Then, with those same five mantras that had come to her memory, the Goddess was worshipped with five handfuls of sand.
Then, O excellent women, at that time I met my death and was born in the world-renowned palace of the lord of Daśārṇa.
"By the grace of that Goddess, I am endowed with the memory of my past births; though I am the youngest among you, I stand as the eldest by virtue of my good fortune. (57)
For this reason, having fashioned these five lumps out of clay instead of Gaurī, I worship them day after day.
This secret has been declared by me to you without doubt; by this truth, may Gaurī grant me my heart’s desire. (59)
Lakṣmī said: Then all those co-wives stood with their palms joined in reverence; bowing down again and again, they spoke to me with humble words.
"Show us favor and let the fivefold mantra be given, by which alone that supreme Goddess, the Queen, will be pleased with you. (61)
"I have spoken thus to all of you: 'Ask for whatever you desire; I shall grant it all. This is my true word."
Then, O Lord, I spoke that fivefold mantra to them, who had been made disciples through their actions of speech, mind, and body. (63)
Viṣṇu said: O Goddess of gods, tell me also what that fivefold mantra is like, which was formerly practiced by you and then communicated by you to them.

Lakṣmī said: Salutations to the Earth, O Mistress of Forbearance; salutations to you who are composed of water, O Auspicious One; salutations to you, O Radiant One; salutations to you who have the form of wind.
Salutations again and again to the one endowed with the form of space, who possesses the five forms.
By these mantras, the Supreme Goddess was worshipped by me in the past; therefore, I have obtained a kingdom that is very difficult for all women to attain. (67)
And so, O Lord of the Gods, having fashioned a beautiful image made of jewels, the Goddess was installed there by me in that sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Any woman who worships her becomes beloved by her husband immediately; she is freed from all sins—of this there is no doubt. (69)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Greatness of Pañcapiṇḍikā," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 177.
Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, it was by worshipping Gaurī that this kingdom was obtained by me, as well as supreme good fortune, which is difficult for all women to attain. (1)
Yet, O Supreme Lord, I have not obtained offspring, even though such good fortune exists and such youth remains. (2)
"I am consumed by that suffering; I find no peace by day or night. Then, after some time, Durvāsas, the best of sages, [arrived].
He arrived at the palace of the lord of Ānarta out of respect, both for the purpose of the Cāturmāsya festival and to collect the sacred earth.
Then, having been honored by King Ānarta in due order, and having offered the arghya and madhuparka, he was addressed after bowing down.
Welcome to you, O best of sages; a most hearty welcome to you! There is no one else in the world more blessed than I, nor anyone equal to me.
"O Sage, those two feet of yours which were soiled with dust have been cleansed by my hair; tell me, what may I do for you now that you have come to my home? (7)
I would even grant you my kingdom; what need is there to mention other things? (8)
Durvāsas said: "O King, I shall perform the Cāturmāsī rites in your palace; meanwhile, please attend to me and fetch the earth. Having agreed, saying "So be it," that best of kings spoke to me.
O lady of excellent countenance, service to him must be performed at all times, preceded by the worship of the deity, until the conclusion of the Cāturmāsya vow.
Having said, "So be it," I then performed everything that was worthy of service, just as a daughter does for her father.
When the four-month period had passed and the sage was about to depart, he spoke to me with satisfaction: "Daughter, what may I do for you? (12)
Then, having prostrated before the Blessed One again and again, I said to him: "O Brahman, I have no offspring; because of that, I burn day and night. (13)
"Such being the case, O best of sages, and while the king is still in the prime of his youth, tell me the truth so that I may have offspring. (14)
Then, through vows, observances, gifts, and burnt offerings, he meditated upon me for a very long time and spoke as if smiling: || 15 ||
"O daughter, in another body you worshipped Gaurī with heated sands when the time of death had arrived."
Although you obtained the kingdom through devotion to her, you are now afflicted by this burning, because Gaurī was joined with heat by you when she was fashioned from sands.
The deity is not found in wood, nor in stone, nor in earthen materials; the deity is found within all things when joined with the application of mantra. || 18 ||
Endowed with devotion in thought and joined by the application of mantra, the Goddess, having arrived through the power of the mantra, was worshipped by you with sand.

"Because of that, this constant torment remains within your body; therefore, O lady of auspicious countenance, fashion Gaurī out of jewels in five forms and install her in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara."
When the sun is situated in Taurus, you must diligently maintain a water-machine that pours over her from above, day and night.
Then, in whatever measure her state of coldness shall come to be, in that same measure your burning shall find relief day and night. (22)
"At the end of the burning, you will conceive a fetus; from that, you shall obtain a son who is capable of bearing the burden of the kingdom, heroic, and renowned throughout the three worlds. (23)
Any other amorous woman who shall worship her in this manner during the month of Jyeṣṭha will likewise become as powerful as you.
Lakṣmī said: Then I spoke again to that blessed lord of sages: "I have no attachment to human existence; a great dispassion remains within me. (25)
Seeing that the life of all embodied beings is like the current of a river, tell me, O illustrious one, what supreme vow there may be. (26)
"O excellent twice-born one, there is nothing that has been properly performed by which human status might not be attained. Then, having meditated for a very long time, that Supreme Lord said to me:
"Daughter, there is a meritorious vow that brings supreme satisfaction to Gaurī; by performing it correctly, a woman indeed attains the status of a goddess. (28)
The Great Goddess, known as Gomayā, was indeed made from cow dung; consequently, O woman of excellent complexion, they all attained Goloka. (29)
"O auspicious lady, perform that by which you shall attain divinity. Then, O best of gods, that sage was addressed by me once again.
O virtuous sage, at what time and by what rite should it be performed? Tell me everything in detail so that I may carry it out. (31)
Durvāsas said: On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, having risen in the morning, one should thereafter clean one's teeth with a tooth-stick.
Then, having undertaken the vow consisting of fasting, one should utter the name of Gaurī with a mind purified by faith. (33)
Then, when night had arrived, having fashioned four images of Gaurī out of clay exactly as they are described here, listen now with a focused mind.

One Gaurī should be fashioned with five lumps (piṇḍas) as previously described; when each watch of the day arrives, one should perform worship upon them. Learn from me the mantras for each of them individually.
O Goddess, beloved of Śaṅkara, you were born in the home of Himācala; having emerged from the womb of Menā, accept this worship—salutations to you! (36)
Then one should offer incense and camphor with faith; one should also provide a lamp fed with ghee, using a red thread. || 37 ||

Having worshipped with jasmine flowers (jāti), one should place sweetmeats (modaka) as the food offering (naivedya); then, having covered [the deity] with a red cloth and offered the water of honor (arghya), thereafter— || 38 ||
Whatever tree provides the flower, its wood shall serve as the tooth-stick; let it be used with devotion and this mantra, using a citron (mātuliṅga). || 39 ||

One should diligently offer the *arghya* accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). "O beloved goddess of Śaṅkara, O auspicious daughter of Himācala! Accept this *arghya* offered by me; salutations unto you. (40)
One should perform that very same consumption for the purification of the body; then, at the end of the watch (prahara), one should worship Ardhanārīśvara.

O Pārvatī, one should worship with devotion using fragrant offerings and this mantra: "May she who is established as the left half of Hara’s body accept my worship; salutations to you, that Goddess. (42)
Then, with devotion, one should likewise offer auspicious incense made of agarwood; as for the food offering, one should offer grains, and the arghya-water with a coconut.

With this mantra, that very same [substance] should be given; it is traditionally taught as the consecrated food (prāśana). As for the two Supreme Lords who abide as Ardhanārīśvara, [one should worship them]. || 44 ||
"O two gods, may this water of honor (arghya) be accepted by you; may you both be the bestowers of all happiness. When the third watch has arrived, one should worship with a hundred-petaled lotus.
One should worship the two deities Umā and Maheśvara with this mantra.
May the two deities Umā and Maheśvara, who are endowed with the powers of creation and dissolution, accept this worship offered by me with great devotion. (47)
Then, incense made from guggulu, an offering consisting of ghārikā, and an arghya with nutmeg are prescribed; that same [nutmeg] is also known as the substance for consumption.
Then, the *arghya* should be offered with devotion using this mantra, along with incense made from powdered knots (*granthicūrṇa*), and the *arghya* consisting of the fruit of the *madana* tree. (49)
That very [substance] should be consumed for the sake of purifying the body. || 50 ||
O gods Umā and Maheśvara, who bestow all desires and happiness, please show me the greatest compassion and accept this arghya from me. (91)
When the fourth watch has arrived, one should worship that Gaurī of five lumps with devotion using the *bhṛṅgarāja* plant and this mantra: || 52 ||
O Goddess of gods, the five elements beginning with earth which have been described—accept this worship in your five forms; salutations be unto you! (53)

One should offer cakes fried in ghee to the Goddess with great devotion; likewise, one should offer incense made from *granthi* powder and an *arghya* consisting of the fruit of the *madana* tree. That same fruit should be used for the ritual consumption (*prāśana*), and this is remembered as the *arghya* mantra: 54. [The mantra follows: "O Goddess, accept this *arghya* offered by me with devotion. [End of verse 54]
May the Goddess, composed of the five elements and established in fivefold forms, the Sovereign of the Gods, accept this water offering given by me. 55.
In this manner, that entire night should be passed in the presence of those [goddesses] with the sounds of singing, instrumental music, and so forth; one must never succumb to sleep.
Then, at the clear dawn when the solar disc has risen, having bathed, he should worship a Brahmin together with his wife with great devotion.
O daughter of a king, O lady of pure smiles, one should give garments and ornaments according to one's ability, and food consisting of sweet delicacies should be offered to Gaurī.
Then, O slender-waisted one, having brought either a female elephant or a mare, and having likewise placed those four Gaurīs upon it; 59.
Accompanied by the sound of singing and instrumental music as well as the resonance of the Vedas, one should cast it into a river, a pond, or a large well.
O beautiful one, I speak this to you with true devotion using this mantra.
"O Goddess, you have been summoned by me; O auspicious one, you have been worshipped by me. For the sake of bestowing good fortune upon me, please depart as you wish. (62)
Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, O All-pervading One, when the month of Nabhasya had arrived, that third [day] was observed by me with supreme devotion, exactly as it has been described. (63)
When the second [day] had likewise arrived, and especially on the third, at dawn as I looked, I saw that the fourfold Gaurī, made of jewels, which I had worshipped, had come to life.
And as I was setting out toward the riverbank for my departure, she said, "I shall perform the ritual dismissal," and thus the Goddess of the Gods became manifest. (65)
"O daughter, contemplate my fourfold form here within the water; having heard my words, let it be done accordingly. (66)
Establish it in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara and do not cast it away, so that it may become inexhaustible for the benefit of all women.
"Request any boon; being worshipped here, I shall grant it all. Thus addressed by me, the daughter of the mountain, the sovereign of the gods, was honored. 68.
"If you, O Goddess, Queen of the Gods, are pleased and grant me a boon, then may I never again be born in a human womb. (69)
"May Viṣṇu, the eternal bestower of desired boons, always be my husband; I have no other desire, not even sovereignty over the splendors of heaven. (70)
And any other woman who, with a concentrated mind, performs this vow, O Goddess, produces as much satisfaction for [the deity] as is produced by all other vows combined. (71)
"O Pārvatī, it must be performed by me in such a manner; so shall it be," Gaurī said to me, and then she vanished from sight. (72)
And that goddess, O Lord, as well as that group of four Gaurīs, was installed by me there in the auspicious field of Hāṭakeśvara.
O Supreme Lord, it is by your power that I have obtained you as my husband—you who are eternal, imperishable, and one who always looks upon my face. (74)
"O Lord of the Gods, all this that I was asked has been told; by this truth, O Lord of Devas, I touch your feet. (75)

Sūta said: Having heard those words of hers, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, being greatly delighted, laughed and then spoke to Mahālakṣmī, who was standing upon his chest, embracing her again and again. || 76 ||
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! This which you have spoken is the truth. Although I already knew it, O lady of excellent complexion, I questioned you."
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, all this that I was asked by you has been narrated—how Gaurī became four-armed and how she became Pañcapiṇḍikā.
And that person who, having risen in the morning, recites this with devotion, shall never be deprived of fortune nor shall he encounter misfortune. (79)
Therefore, O Brahmins, this auspicious narrative concerning Gauri, which has been proclaimed by me, should be recited with every effort. (80)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Pañcapiṇḍikā-Gaurī," in the Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya of the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 178 || || 9 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another auspicious triad of Puṣkaras located in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, which destroys all sins.
O best of the twice-born, when he is seen, touched, or even glorified, sin goes to destruction just as darkness does before the sun.
All sacred fords are undoubtedly purified by bathing and giving gifts; however, by the mere sight of Puṣkara, one is liberated from all sins.
The sages said: It is heard that there is a sacred ford named Puṣkara, renowned throughout the three worlds, which was created by Brahmā and measures one yojana in extent.
To the north of the river Candrabhāgā as far as the Sarasvatī, and to the south of the Karatoyā—this is the boundary of the three Puṣkara lakes.

"O Sūta, you previously told us that [the Lord] was stationed in the sky; this is a source of curiosity for us, O Sūta—how did He come to Hāṭakeśvara? You ought to tell us how He arrived at that sacred field. (6)
Sūta said: O highly fortunate ones, what has been stated by you is true; O best of the twice-born, listen with concentrated minds to that which pertains to that sacred field.
Having paid homage to the Self-Existent One, I shall speak of it in its entirety and in detail.
While Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, was dwelling in the world of Brahmā, the divine sage Nārada, a muni who had wandered through the three worlds, arrived there.
Having bowed his head at [his] feet, he sat down before him.
Brahmā said: "O child, why have you not been seen for so long? From where have you come now? Where have you wandered? Tell me, my child, explain the reason for this."
Nārada said: O Lord, I have now arrived from the world of mortals with great haste for the purpose of worshipping your feet; I swear this by my own soul. (12)

Brahmā said: Tell me the rumors arising from the world of mortals; what kind of kings are there, and what kind of best of the twice-born? And what sort of legal proceedings are currently taking place there? (13)
Nārada said: O best of gods, the Kali age has now arisen in the world of mortals.
Kings, having abandoned the path of the righteous and being thus devoted to greed, mercilessly oppress the people for the sake of wealth. || 15 ||
Devoid of the spirit of heroism and violators of others' wives, they do not honor brahmins, nor the gods, nor even their teachers.
Those Brāhmaṇas who sell the Vedas, who are devoid of purity, who are addicted to accepting sinful gifts, who neglect the twilight prayers, and who are utterly merciless; || 17 ||
Constantly engaged in agricultural work like Vaiśyas, the cattle-herders—all the Vaiśyas on the surface of the earth—went to their total destruction.
Śūdras who are constantly desirous of dharma and even śūdras who are ascetics—all these perform worldly activities while laughing and devoid of shame. (19)
On this earth, men form friendships with whoever possesses wealth and young women in their home. (20)
In the hearts of widows, of those observing vows, and of all who bear sectarian marks, great desire resides; they remain outwardly engaged in the practice of their vows.
The sacred fords (tīrthas) fall into ruin, as do those resorted to by sinful people; terrified by the Kali age, they all flee in the ten directions.
O Grandfather, it is because I am stationed there during the Kali age.

Especially in this Kali age, women become wanton and full of desire for pleasure; quarreling with their husbands and intent on magical spells, they perform vows in vain, having abandoned all talk of their own husband. (24)
Kali has been made exceedingly powerful by your granting of a boon; whenever a battle occurs among mortals, an itching arises in his heart.
In heaven or on the summit [of Mount Meru], in the netherworld or at the feet, and now in the world of mortals, it has been seen by me many times.
And likewise between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law, as well as between father and son; especially between kinsmen, and similarly between master and servant. (27)
For thieves, for kings, and especially for husbands and wives, the clouds will contain little water and the earth will yield little grain. (28)
Likewise, cows with very little milk contain no clarified butter in their milk; even so, he beheld their battles day and night.
Having wandered for a long time among mortals, I have finally met with him; I shall go back to that very place again, for a great itching remains. (30)
Having heard those words of Nārada, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became agitated in his senses with anxiety on account of Puṣkara. || 31 ||
And my sacred ford on earth, renowned by the name Puṣkara, will surely go to destruction, overwhelmed by the Kali age. (32)
Therefore, I shall not desire any other place where strife does not exist, so that there I may release my own sacred site, Puṣkara.
And when the Kali age has arrived, which brings fear to all living beings, let all the sacred fords (tīrthas) go there in particular.
When the Kali age has arrived, they will undoubtedly depart for their own abode. || 35 ||
Having thus resolved in his mind, the Grandfather (Brahmā), after meditating upon it himself, then spoke with reverence to the lotus held in his hand.
"O Lotus, descend upon the surface of the earth where the Kali age does not exist, so that I may bring my own sacred site, Puṣkara, to that very place. (37)
Then that lotus, sent by him, having wandered across the entire surface of the earth, fell upon the sacred field (kṣetra) originating from Hāṭakeśvara.
Having seen the pure Brahmins, learned in the Vedas and devoted to their private recitation, [he saw them] on all sides with their sacrificial rites and the concluding ceremonies of those sacrifices.
The courtyard of the sky was pervaded on all sides by sacrificial posts and the like, as well as by the resonance of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas.
When the entire circle of the quarters was thus pervaded, no other sound could be heard; and likewise during the great debates of the logicians.
When the entire Vedānta has been explained in many ways, those sages are seen there, established in their religious observances.
Some take food only once a day, some abstain from food entirely, and others eat only every other day; some fast for three nights, while others are devoted to the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Others were observers of the Mahāpārāka vow, as well as those who fasted for a month; some were eaters of food ground with stones, and others used their teeth as mortars.
Some great sages there subsisted on withered leaves, while others fed on fruits; having seen that field endowed with such various qualities, [they were amazed].
Then, realizing that it had fallen there upon the surface of the earth, it moved again from the place where it had previously fallen.
O best of the twice-born, in another place from that, in the second, and likewise in the third from that, there is a beneficial third lotus.
Then three pits were formed, and in those three places, within the pits, water appeared, clear and resembling crystal.
In the meantime, O best of the twice-born, the Grandfather himself arrived at that place for the successful accomplishment of the sacrificial rite.
Having seen the field known as Hāṭakeśvara on all sides, crowded with various Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, as well as many ascetics devoted to the practice of vows. || 50 ||
"Oh, what a field! Oh, what a field! It is meritorious, delightful, and dear to the twice-born. Therefore, I shall perform a sacrifice in this field which is a refuge for the twice-born. (51)
I shall also bring those three auspicious Puṣkara lakes—the eldest, the middle, and the youngest—into these meritorious pits.
And when the Kali age has arrived, so that [the teaching] does not go to ruin, one should sit upon the surface of the earth, having personally determined it with the mind.
Having meditated for a very long time, he brought there the three excellent Puṣkara lakes: the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Then, with a joyful heart, he said: "Indeed, these three Puṣkaras have been properly brought by me out of fear of the Kali age. (55)
Those who shall perform their ablutions here, endowed with supreme faith, will attain the highest, imperishable perfection through my grace.
And those who, being well-composed, shall perform the ancestral rites on the full moon day of Kārttika at Gayāśīrṣa, for them there shall be the greatest merit.
There, they shall obtain more than a hundredfold merit from the first Puṣkara; for I performed a sacrifice there at the previous Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārtika.
And on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, I shall perform [the rite] here, and again on the second [lunar day].
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then commanded Sadāgati: "O Vāyu, by my command, quickly bring Purandara here."
Together with the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts, as well as the Gandharvas, the world-protectors, the Siddhas, and the Vidyādharas. || 61 ||
"By whom may I have assistance in the entirety of the sacrificial rite? Having heard all of that, Vāyu went to the abode of Śakra and related everything that had been said by Parameṣṭhin.
He proceeded there quickly together with all the hosts of gods; then, having prostrated before Brahmā, he spoke these words.
"O Lord, let a command be given; for I have been summoned by you. Whatever the purpose may be, I shall accomplish it; therefore, announce it quickly. (64)
Brahmā said: "O Śakra, I have brought here these three most meritorious Puṣkaras; out of fear of the Kali age, I shall make them permanent."
"Having performed three Agniṣṭoma sacrifices on the full moon day of Vaiśākha according to the rites, quickly gather all the necessary materials for that purpose."

Having heard that, Śakra, with humility, said "So be it," and in great haste brought together the necessary materials and the most excellent of the twice-born who were worthy of them and proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. (67)
Then that great-grandfather performed the sacrifice according to the rules; everything was done exactly as prescribed by the injunctions, with full sacrificial fees.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Manner of Bringing Requisites and Summoning Brāhmaṇas for the Commencement of the Sacrifice, Preceded by the Origin of the Three Puṣkaras," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 179 ||
The sages said: "O Sūta, this which has been narrated by you is most wonderful—namely, that the sacrifice was performed in that sacred field by the high-souled Brahmā."
Whatever sacrifices, such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, take place upon the surface of the earth, it is indeed that Lord of the Gods who is to be worshipped in those sacrifices.

Tell us, who was the one sacrificed there by that very sacrificer? Who were the officiating priests present there by whom that entire sacrificial rite was performed in his presence? This is our supreme curiosity.
And what sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) was given by him to those twice-born ones? Who was appointed as the Adhvaryu there, by whom that sacrifice was performed? || 4 ||
Who was the Hotṛ and who was the Agnīdhra? Who was established there as the Brahman? And who was the Udgātṛ stationed there as the preceptor in the sacrificial rite?
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I shall narrate to you everything concerning the origin of the sacrifice, as well as the account of the wonders that occurred there.
The members who were present there, as well as the officiating priests, the best of the twice-born—to them, sacrificial fees were bestowed by that high-souled one.
While the god Brahmā of immeasurable splendor was performing a sacrifice, the god Śatakratu, recognizing that the four-faced one desired to perform a sacrifice, [acted accordingly]. || 8 ||
He arrived together with all the hosts of gods for the sake of providing assistance; likewise did the Blessed Lord Śambhu come along with all the hosts of deities.
Seeing them arrived and assuming the nature of mortals, Brahmā, standing with palms joined in reverence, spoke with humility.
Welcome to you, O best of gods; please show me your favor. Pray, take your seats as is fitting in these beautiful places.
I am blessed and I am graced that you have come here of your own accord, just as those summoned by mantras go to all the sacrificial sessions to relieve their distress.
The gods said: "O Lotus-born One, tell us quickly what must be done here and by whom; O highly fortunate one, instruct us in the true nature of that sacrifice of yours."
Brahmā said: O Viśvakarman, go quickly for the sake of preparing the sacrificial pavilion, as well as the wife’s hall and the sacrificial altars.
Have all the sacrificial pits constructed in their proper places, as well as all the sacrificial vessels, the ladles, and the cups.

The sacrificial posts, together with their sockets, should be made according to a specific measurement; likewise, the pits for the purpose of cooking should be made according to that same measurement. || 16 ||
"Ten thousand and eight hundred bricks must be prepared by you quickly; the sacrificial altars (cayanāni) are to be constructed with haste. (17)
"In that same way, the golden person must indeed be fashioned. Having been told "So be it," Tvaṣṭṛ then departed even more swiftly than before.
Then the Lotus-born One said to Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods: "O Bṛhaspati, you must summon all the officiating priests worthy of the sacrifice."
This number, up to sixteen, is not appropriate for anyone else; therefore, O Śakra, you must always perform service to the twice-born.

O Treasurer, you must provide for those who are weary the massage of hands and feet, as well as the rubbing of their backs; these are the rewards appropriate to the occasion that should be granted by you.
O Viṣṇu, you must always provide fine garments, gold, and whatever else is desired; furthermore, you must constantly examine what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

Whatever has been done, whether properly or not, let it all be rendered effective by one who is ever vigilant. May all the world-protectors guard every direction, and may they prevent the entry of spirits, ghosts, and demons, as well as the arising of Rākṣasas. (23)
Whatever desire anyone may have—whether it be some garment or wealth—that should be given to them after due consideration by the lord of all sacrifices.
May the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts be the servers for the people who desire to eat. || 25 ||
In the meantime, Viśvakarman arrived in great haste and said to the Lotus-born One: "The sacrificial pavilion is fully prepared. (26)
O Four-faced One, everything else that has been commanded and spoken by you [is as it should be].
Then Bṛhaspati, having approached the Grandfather, said: "O Lord, the Brāhmaṇas have been assembled by me for the sacrificial rite."
O Lord of Gods, having yourself examined them, appoint sixteen Brahmins to the office of officiating priests for the successful accomplishment of the sacrificial rite. (29)
Then Brahmā, having seen them in person and examined them with great care, appointed them to the office of officiating priests and thereafter performed the honoring due to them.
The sages said: O Sūta, proclaim the names of all the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and tell us, O Sūta, which specific ritual function was assigned to each therein.
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, Bhṛgu was then chosen by him as the Hotṛ priest, and likewise the sage Cyavana was appointed as the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Acchāvāka was Marīci, Grāvastut was the sage Gālava, Pulastya was the Adhvaryu, and Atri stood as the Prasthātṛ. || 33 ||
There, the sage Raibhya was the Neṣṭṛ; Sanātana was the Unnetṛ; Nārada, Garga, and Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin were the Brahmans. || 34 ||
Bharadvāja was the Āgnīdhra, Pārāśara was the Hotṛ, and likewise, in that sacred field, the sage Gobhila was the Udgātṛ. (35)
In the same way, Kauthuma was born as the Prastotṛ priest in the sacrificial rite; Śāṇḍilya was the Pratihartṛ, and likewise Aṅgiras was the Subrahmaṇya. || 36 ||
For the successful accomplishment of that sacrifice, these sixteen officiating priests were appointed with humility, adorned with garments and ornaments.
Then Brahmā himself, having performed the rites of honoring for all [the gods] according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, spoke respectfully: (38)
"O best of the twice-born, I have come to you for refuge; may you all favor me by initiating me for the performance of the sacrifice. (39)

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Sacrificial Rite, Preceded by the Honoring of the Brāhmaṇas who Attained the Sacrificial Ground and the Assignment of Positions to the Priests and Others," in the Brahma-yajña episode of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: In the meantime, the Madhyaga born at Gartātīrtha was dispatched there by all the Nāgaras and the best of Brāhmaṇas.
Go once more to the presence of Madhyaga and speak to that angry grandfather, who destroys the livelihood of Brahmins and has strayed from the path of righteous conduct.
This field was granted by the gratified Maheśvara to us and to our ancestors, the twice-born, when the hole produced by the serpent had been filled.
O Grandfather, since that was given, five hundred and five generations have passed away today without a doubt, while you remain angry.
No one has ever treated us with such contempt as you do now—you, a man of sinful deeds who has strayed from the path of justice.
Whoever performs a sacrifice or a śrāddha ceremony here outside the city, along with the Nāgaras and Brāhmaṇas, shall indeed be liable to execution by all the twice-born.
No prosperity arising from that [deed] shall ever accrue to him; this was declared by him at the time when he indeed granted us our place.
Therefore, perform the sacrifice with the Brahmins of the city; otherwise, you will not be permitted to perform it while the Brahmin citizens are alive.
Having been addressed thus, he then went to where the Lotus-born One was situated in the center, standing at a distance from the sacrificial pavilion and surrounded by Brahmins.

Having heard all that was specifically said by all the Nāgaras at that time, the Lotus-born One spoke these words with conciliation: yatproktaṃ nāgaraiḥ sarvaiḥ saviśeṣaṃ tadā hi saḥ | tacchrutvā padmajaḥ prāha sāṃtvapūrvamidaṃ vacaḥ || 10 ||
"O best among those who dwell within, you have spoken this entire truth while having assumed a human form and being surrounded by officiating priests."
"What shall I do? All those priests, headed by the Adhvaryu, have been chosen by me for the sacrificial rite through negligence, not out of desire. (12)
Therefore, bring all those best of the twice-born to this place; permitted by them, I shall go to the sacrificial pavilion.
The mediator said: "Having renounced your divinity and assumed a human state, how is it that those best of the twice-born have come into your presence?"
O Lotus-born One, just as cows are the most excellent among animals, so indeed are the Nāgaras the most excellent among all Brahmins here on earth. (15)
Therefore, O Grandfather, if you desire to attain this state born of sacrifice, then propitiate all the Nāgas with devotion.
Sūta said: Having heard that, the Lotus-born One (Brahmā), surrounded by his officiating priests, went in fear to the place where the angry Nāgara brahmins were stationed.
Then, having prostrated before them all with humility, he spoke these words, standing with his palms joined in reverence after listening [to their speech].
O best of the twice-born, I know that in this sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, any Śrāddha or sacrificial rite performed outside of you is in vain.
Out of fear of the Kali age, I have brought my own Puṣkara to this place; this sacred ford belonging to you has been offered as a trust.
O best of the twice-born, these officiating priests have been brought by the Guru for the successful completion of the sacrifice; they were unaware of the superiority inherent in the Nāgara lineage.
Therefore, let forgiveness be granted to me for the reason that this choice was made by me regarding these very brahmins for the sake of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And this sacred ford of mine shall be the destroyer of your sins, even when the Kali age has arrived; of this there is no doubt. (23)

The Brāhmaṇas said: "If you perform a sacrifice here that is excluded from the city-dwellers, then all the other gods will become followers of your path, as will the kings; therefore, this sacrifice must not be performed by you."
"O Lord of Gods, even if you perform the sacrificial rite in this manner, yet disregarding all the twice-born, depart quickly from our presence. (25)
Brahmā said: "From this day forward, whatever sacrifice or Śrāddha rite anyone shall perform here, whether by those born of Nāgas or by outsiders, it shall become fruitless."
Furthermore, if any other person, even a city-dweller, should perform a sacrifice elsewhere while abandoning this sacred field, that [sacrifice] will come to naught.

"O Brahmins, this boundary has now been established by me for the sake of the Nāgaras. Having shown us favor, you ought to grant permission for the sake of the sacrifice; O Brahmins, grant me your formal consent so that I may perform the sacrifice. (28)
Sūta said: Then, permitted by those gratified Brāhmaṇas, the Grandfather performed the sacrifice according to the rules, as did the Brāhmaṇas who had been chosen by them.
O best of Brahmins, Viśvakarman, abiding by the counsel of the Nāgas, arrived there and fashioned the crest-jewel for his head. (30)
Brahmā, having attained supreme satisfaction, said to Nārada: "Bring Sāvitrī here quickly, so that I may go to the pavilion."

While musical instruments were being played by the Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas; while the Gandharvas were absorbed in song and the twice-born brahmins were intent on the chanting of the Vedas; Pulastya, having taken up the fire-drill (araṇi), spoke these words.
"Patnī! Patnī!"—thus the best of Brahmins stood there, crying out loudly. || 33 ||
In the meantime, Brahmā dispatched Nārada, the best of sages, with a sign, saying, "Let the wife be brought here."
He too, approaching slowly, spoke playfully to Sāvitrī, desiring an opportunity for a fight with Sāvitrī while Brahmā looked on.
"O Goddess of the Suras, I have been sent to your side by my father; come, for I have now bathed and am setting out for the sacrificial pavilion. (36)
O Goddess of the Gods, as you proceed there all alone, what kind of form do you appear to have in that assembly, looking truly like one who is without a protector?
Therefore, let all the celestial women who exist be brought here; surrounded by them, O Goddess, you shall go to the great sacrifice.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best of sages and the most excellent of ascetics, went to his father and said, "Father, Mother has been summoned by me. (39)
However, her firm disposition was slightly perceived by me; having heard those words of his, I was then filled with indignation.

Then he dispatched Pulastya into the presence of Sāvitrī, saying: "Go, my child, and bring her back to this place; she has become lax in spirit. Behold me, exhausted by the burden of the moon, standing upright. (41)
This present time for the sacrificial rite will soon pass away; this auspicious moment for the journey to the sacrifice remains with only a short portion left.
Having heard those words of his, Pulastya went quickly to where Sāvitrī was staying, occupied with singing and dancing.
Then he said: "O Goddess, why do you remain unperturbed? This is the time appropriate for the commencement of the sacrifice; only a small portion remains. (44)
Therefore, come; let us go, for our father stands in great distress, afflicted by the weight of the Soma and surrounded by all the gods. || 45 ||
Sāvitrī said: "O father, your father is established there, surrounded by all the gods; how can I go there alone, like one who is without a protector? (46)
Therefore, go to your father and say: "Please wait for a moment. || 47 ||
Until Śakrāṇī, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and other divine maidens arrive at this assembly, I shall come here quickly with them.
I have sent Vāyu to invite them all; you must tell your father that they will arrive very soon.
Sūta said: He too, having gone quickly, spoke to Brahmā, who was oppressed by the weight of the moon: "O Lord of the World, she does not come; she is absorbed in her domestic duties. (50)
She said to me: "Accompanied by the wives of the gods at the sacrifice, I shall go; yet not one of them has appeared even now. (51)

Knowing this, O best of gods, do whatever pleases you. This time for the undertaking of the sacrifice is passing away; moreover, that woman remains preoccupied with her household duties and is lax in her resolve. (52)
O twice-born ones, having heard those words of Pulastya, the Grandfather then spoke these words to Śakra, who was standing nearby.
Brahmā said: "O Śakra, Sāvitrī does not come; she too is a woman of lax character. Nevertheless, this very sacrifice must be performed by me with this wife."
"Go, Śakra, and bring some maiden with all haste, before the time for the commencement of the sacrificial journey arrives. (55)
O twice-born ones, having heard the words of the Grandfather, Śakra quickly approached that maiden while she was wandering nearby for that very purpose.
Then she beheld a slender maiden born of a cowherd, with a face like the moon and eyes like lotuses, her head occupied by a jar of buttermilk.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and having reached the bloom of youth, she was then questioned by Śakra: "Who are you, O lotus-eyed one? (58)
Tell us, is she a maiden or one who has a protector; whose daughter is she? (59)
The maiden said: "I am a cowherd's daughter; may you be blessed! I have come to sell buttermilk. If you will take it from me, give me the price quickly; do not delay. (60)
Having heard that and realizing she was a cowherd girl, the lord of the three heavens, filled with haste, took her up and cast the buttermilk upon the ground.
Then Śakra, taking her as she was weeping, quickly entered through the mouth of the bull and drew her out through his private part.
O best of brahmins, having thus rendered it most pure and bathed it with auspicious waters, they clothed it in two fine garments at the Jyeṣṭhakuṇḍa.
Then, filled with joy, he went quickly before the four-faced one in the assembly of all the gods and spoke, having taken hold [of him].
O best of gods, this maiden has now been brought by me for your sake; she is beautiful of limb and endowed with all auspicious marks.
O Four-faced One, having recognized her, the cowherd girl was made to enter through the mouth of a cow and was drawn out through the secret organ for the sake of purification.

Śrī Vāsudeva said: The lineage of cows and that of Brāhmaṇas constitute a single family divided into two parts; on one side reside the mantras, and on the other resides the sacrificial oblation (havis). || 67 ||
"Born from the womb of a cow, she is the offspring of the twice-born; O Lord, perform her marriage for the successful completion of the sacrifice."
As long as the time arising from the vehicle of sacrifice does not waver. || 69 ||
Rudra said: "Since she entered through the mouth of the cow and emerged by the downward breath (apāna), this wife of yours shall therefore be named Gāyatrī."
Brahmā said: "Let all the Brahmins speak, so that even this cowherd girl, having become an excellent Brahmin woman, may become my wife. (71)
The Brahmins said: "O Caturvaktra, let her be the most excellent of Brahmins, though born of the cow-caste; at our word, perform the marriage ceremony quickly. (72)
Sūta said: Then, O twice-born ones, the divine Grandfather performed the taking of her hand in marriage, having placed Soma upon her head according to the ritual prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
And the great goddess Supāvanī remains established there; even today she is renowned in the world as the bestower of wealth and good fortune. (74)
Whatever mortal, with a concentrated mind, performs the gift of a daughter in marriage there, obtains the entire fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 79 ||
The maiden who there obtains the grasping of the hand with her husband shall be virtuous, possessed of sons, and endowed with happiness and good fortune. (76)
O best of the twice-born, the ancestors of that man who offers the piṇḍa-oblation on that day become satisfied and gratified, as if at a sacred ford for the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha).

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gāyatrī-tīrtha during the Marriage of Gāyatrī," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 181.
Sūta said: Having thus obtained Gāyatrī as his wife, the four-faced one (Brahmā), with a heart full of joy, set out for the sacrificial pavilion.
Gāyatrī also, joyfully taking that fire-drill upon her head, set forth, completely abandoning her contemptible state as a cowherd girl. || 2 ||
While musical instruments were being played and the sound of the Vedas reached the heavens, the Gandharvas sang melodiously on all sides.
Accompanied by all the gods and the twice-born, Brahmā, having assumed a human form, arrived at the sacrificial pavilion together with Gāyatrī.
In the meantime, Viśvakarman performed the shaving of the hair for the Creator (Brahmā), and immediately thereafter, that of the fingernails for Gāyatrī.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Pulastya gave him a staff made of udumbara wood, along with a hide provided with the horn of an ena deer, accompanied by mantras.
Having taken hold of the wife’s hall and the silent Gāyatrī, he placed another auspicious girdle made of muñja grass around his waist.
Then the Creator, accompanied by the officiating priests and honoring the words of the Vedas, performed the supreme rite as prescribed in the sacrificial pavilion.
And while the Pravargya ceremony was being performed, a great marvel occurred there: a certain person appeared, naked, with a deformed face, assuming the form of a rogue.

"Come with a skull in hand; let food be given! Though he was being forbidden by them, he entered the sacrificial assembly hall. Having committed that improper wandering, he was even threatened by the ascetics. (10)
The members of the assembly said: "Why have you, joined with sin, entered the sacrificial pavilion—you who are a skull-bearer, naked in form, and devoid of the performance of sacrificial rites? (11)
Therefore, O fool, depart quickly before Brahmā becomes enraged, as well as the other foremost brahmins and the gods together with Indra. (12)
The rogue said: "O best of the twice-born, having heard of this sacrifice of Brahmā, I have come here from afar while hungry; why then do you revile me? (13)
A sacrifice is said to be successful when the poor, the blind, and all the wretched have been satisfied; otherwise, it leads to destruction, according to the words spoken by the Brahmins.

One deficient in food burns the kingdom; one deficient in mantras, however, burns the officiating priests; and one deficient in sacrificial fees burns the sacrifice itself. There is no enemy equal to a sacrifice [performed] without these. (15)

The Brahmins said: "If you have come desiring to eat, go quickly to this hall of sacrifice where the ascetics, the wretched, the blind, and the miserable—who are emaciated by hunger and parched with thirst—eat. (16)
"Or else, O ascetic, if you desire wealth or desire clothing, go where the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) has taken refuge in this hall of charity. (17)
"O great fool, this sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is beyond reproach; since it is honored on all sides as meritorious, why do you, O evil-minded one, revile it? (18)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus, he cast his skull upon the surface of the earth and immediately vanished from sight like a lamp.
The officiating priests said: "How should the sacrificial rite be performed while the skull remains in the assembly hall? Therefore, you must remove it," so spoke those best of the twice-born.
Then, one [of them], addressed in many ways by the members of the assembly and the best of the twice-born, raised a wooden staff and likewise hurled it outside.
Then another skull of that same kind appeared there; when that too was thrown in, yet another arose once more. || 22 ||
In this way, hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and even millions were born there; by them, the sacrificial enclosure was filled on all sides.
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the entire sacrificial pavilion upon seeing those multitudes of skulls that were defiling the sacrificial rites.
Then, having entered into meditation, the Grandfather reflected; and perceiving that entire misfortune caused by Hara, he assumed a joyful appearance.
Then, having approached Maheśvara who was stationed at the sacrificial enclosure, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke respectfully.
"O Lord, what is this? Is it fitting that there should be a deficiency in the ritual of this sacrifice? Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, withdraw all these skull-bowls. (27)
"Let there not be a disruption of this sacrificial rite now that you have arrived. (28)
Then the Lord whose crest is the moon, filled with rage, said: "He is my most beloved vessel, always present for my meal. (29)
"O Grandfather, why do these lowest of the twice-born hate me? For they did not likewise offer oblations into the fire for my sake."

O Vidhi, just as other deities [receive offerings], so let this oblation purified by mantras be offered to you. Therefore, O Vidhi, if the completion of the sacrificial rite is to be achieved, [let it be done thus].
All this sacrificial offering (havya) must be placed upon that skull; likewise, it should especially be offered to me within the fire.
"The oblation must indeed be offered here; only then will the sacrifice reach completion. Not otherwise. This is the truth spoken before you, O Four-faced One. (33)
The Grandfather said: O Lord of Gods, your forms are manifold and distinct; they are beyond numbering, and all of them are to be meditated upon as possessing all attributes.
O Three-eyed One, this form has been described to you as the Great Vow (Mahāvrata); yet such would not be the nature of a sacrificial rite, nor would it be appropriate for that very purpose.
O Three-eyed One, although I cannot by any means perform this deed today which is outside the Vedas, I do not venture to act contrary to your word either. (36)

O Lord of the Gods, the sacrificial oblation is to be cooked in earthen potsherds; from this day forward, in sacrifices, the Śatarudriya, consisting of the *puroḍāśa* cake, is to be offered by the twice-born for your sake, O Lord of Devas. (37)
Especially among all sacrifices, this [mantra] must be recited with particular care; for through the gateway of the skull-bowls, you have assumed your own true form.
And you shall be manifest, O best of gods, known by the name Kapāleśvara; therefore, O Rudra, you will become another twelfth [linga] in this sacred field (kṣetra). 39.
Whoever, having commenced a sacrifice here, shall worship you first, his sacrifice will proceed to completion without obstacle. (40)
When this was said, O best of the twice-born, all those skull-bowls then vanished and became beyond counting.
Then, being delighted, the four-faced one immediately established there a Liṅga of Maheśvara known by the name Kapāleśvara.
And then he spoke these words: "Whoever shall honor this [account], having bathed in my three pools, shall attain the supreme goal. (43)

Furthermore, whoever shall perform a vigil for this Liṅga with a well-composed mind on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, shall obtain liberation from the sins accumulated since birth. (44)
When this was said by Vidhi, Tripurāntaka was greatly delighted; having reached the sacrificial pavilion, he proceeded to the vicinity of the altar.
Then, having paid homage to Maheśvara with eyes wide open in wonder, the brahmins commenced the ritual for the sake of the sacrifice.
Sūta said: And while the four-faced one was thus performing the sacrifice there, ten million sages dwelling in the southern region arrived.
Having heard of the sacrifice of the Grandfather, they were filled with curiosity: "What kind of sacrifice will it be, in which the Lotus-born One is consecrated? (488)
And what kind of field is that meritorious place known as Hāṭakeśvara? And of what nature are those lords of brahmins who stand there as officiating priests? (49)
Then, when the sun had reached the meridian, they were utterly exhausted; it was the day of the Sun (Sunday), and the moon was situated in the constellation of the Aśvins.
On the lunar day belonging to Vaivasvata, being oppressed by the heat, they reached a certain reservoir and entered the auspicious water.
Some had ears like spikes, others had enormous ears; some had crooked noses, while others had large bellies, huge teeth, long lips, and thick heads.
Others had flattened eyes, while still others had long necks; they were black-limbed, with cracked feet and long, protruding claws.
Then, as soon as they emerged and looked at one another, they were freed from their deformed appearance and became like the god of love himself.

Then, filled with wonder and greatly delighted upon seeing the transformation of their forms and recognizing that supreme sacred site, they said to one another: "By bathing here, this excellent form has been attained by us. (55)
Therefore, this sacred ford shall become known as Rūpatīrtha; it will be famous throughout the entire three worlds as the destroyer of all sins.
Those who perform their ablutions here, endowed with supreme faith, shall possess beautiful forms always, birth after birth.
Those endowed with faith who offer libations to the ancestors even with water at Gayā-śrāddha shall obtain a far greater reward than that.
Those men who shall perform the gift of jewels here will undoubtedly become kings in birth after birth. (59)
Having made this firm resolve, we shall remain right here for now; we will not go to any other sacred ford, even if it be most beautiful.
Having spoken thus, those sages then divided all of that; they each made their own sacred fords (tīrthas) out of mere sacrificial threads (yajñopavītas).
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, even today the Teacher of the World first touches the water at that sacred site; it is eternally beloved and auspicious.
Furthermore, that mortal who, free from desire, performs a bath there with faith shall attain the supreme good characterized by spiritual perfection.
Thus all those sages, having divided that great lake and having performed their extensive evening rites right there, [remained].
Then, at the onset of night, they arrived where the divine Grandfather was present, having been initiated and observing silence, seated within the sacrificial pavilion.
Having bowed down to him, they all then went to where the officiating priests were staying, seated and exhausted from the sacrificial rites performed during the day.
With their feet being massaged with devotion by the gods headed by Indra, they remained standing; then, having saluted them all, they sat down before them.
Then they engaged in various discourses arising from the sacrificial rites, concerning the drinking of Soma, its transposition, and its origin.
They declared the origin of the Udgātṛ and likewise of the Adhvaryu to one another, relying on the truth; yet others disparage that. (69)
Other Mīmāṃsakas there, their eyes bloodshot with anger, being experts in speech, resort to debate and strike down their [opponents'] doctrine. (70)
And other excellent brahmins, who were experts in the supplementary sciences and remained impartial, abandoned their debate and spoke with intentional meaning as had been declared. (71)
Likewise, others, each relying on their own respective positions, engaged in disputes concerning the Mahāvīra-puroḍāśa, the piling of the altar (cayana), and other such matters.
In this manner, that night passed for those twice-born ones.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Events on the First Day of the Sacrifice Preceded by the Origin of Rūpatīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 182 ||

Sūta said: When the second day arrived for the commencement of the sacrificial rites, O best of the twice-born, listen to that account of all the gods which occurred on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and caused great wonder. || 1 ||
When the sacrificial rite had commenced by the officiating priests who were masters of the Vedas, a certain mischievous young student took hold of a water-snake.
Then, having entered the assembly hall there, he laughed and threw that serpent—which was terrifying with all manner of miseries—into the presence of the Brahmin.
Then the Dundubha, wandering quickly here and there, [approached] the brahmins who were seated in the assembly hall and engaged in the sacrificial rites.
Alas! While the invocation for the long sacrificial session remained unissued, that serpent coiled itself all around his body.
Out of fear of the penance, he did not move from his own place, nor did he utter a word there, with his eyes fixed upon the sacrificial altar.
In the meantime, O twice-born ones, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in that assembly of brahmins, filled with despair due to the fear of a serpent.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose upon seeing him enveloped by the serpent; his son, humble-souled, was engaged in the ritual of Mitra and Varuṇa.

Standing there, he saw his father enveloped by a serpent; having recognized his son's behavior regarding the danger arising from the snake, the sage, filled with wrath, then cursed that young student.
"O wicked-minded one, since you have thrown a serpent into the assembly, therefore, by my word, become a serpent immediately and without doubt. (10)
The boy said: "This water-snake was released here by me in jest as a mere play; it was not aimed at your father. Why then do you curse me, O twice-born one? (11)
In the meantime, having released his body, that serpent went elsewhere, and he too attained the state of a serpent.
That young brahmin, the son of Sanātana, having attained the state of a serpent, was overcome with pain and grief and surrounded by other brahmins.
Then, having gone to Bhṛgu with eyes clouded by tears, he prostrated himself before him and spoke these words in a faltering voice.
I am the son of Sanātana and the grandson of Parameṣṭhin; I have been cursed by your son, the high-souled Cyavana.
"O best of Brahmins, I am faultless; therefore, protect me from that curse. Hearing this, Bhṛgu himself, overcome with compassion, spoke to Cyavana.
"O dear one, what you have done is improper, that this young student has been cursed by you; even a serpent full of poison would not be able to overpower me. (17)

"Is this, then, a water-snake, devoid of venom and resembling a rope? This snake was not released by this twice-born man with me in mind. Therefore, quickly grant this twice-born man release from his curse. (19)
Cyavana said: "If the ocean should overstep its bounds, if the sun should turn cold, and if the lord of the night should become hot, then let my word prove false. (19)
Having heard those words of his, the Grandfather himself came there and stood where his grandson was, assuming the form of a serpent.
He said: "O son, you must not feel despondency in any way; listen now to these words of mine regarding how you have attained the state of a serpent. (21)
Formerly, desiring to create a ninth race of Nāgas, I intended that it should arise from your side upon the surface of the earth, established within its proper bounds.
He shall not cause suffering to those men who employ mantras and medicinal herbs; rather, he shall receive supreme honor throughout the entire surface of the earth. (23)
"In this place, within the sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara, there is most auspicious water; O son, you must always make your residence there."
While you remain there engaged in ascetic penance, the Naga Karkoṭaka will give his own virtuous daughter to you; from that, progeny shall arise.
On this earth, when the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived for the ninth Kula, which is bounded by the sea; || 26 ||
The ninth lineage shall receive supreme honor upon the earth; from this day forward, that water is known as Nāgatīrtha.
It shall attain renown upon the surface of the earth as the destroyer of all sins for those who perform their ablutions here when the fifth day arrives. (28)
For them, there shall be no fear arising from snakes for as long as a year; moreover, whatever mortal afflicted by poison bathes there [in that place], [shall be freed].
At that very moment, having become free from poison, he shall attain supreme bliss; and whatever woman desires a son, on the fifth lunar day at sunrise, [should act likewise].
If she performs the bath in that manner with fruits in her hand and with great devotion, she shall quickly become a mother of virtuous sons, even if she is currently barren.
Sūta said: While Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, was speaking thus, other nāgas who had been invited to that sacrifice arrived there.
Vāsuki and Takṣaka, Puṇḍarīka and Kṛśodara, the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, as well as Śeṣa and Kāliya. || 33 ||
Having bowed down, they spoke these words loudly to the god Pitāmaha: "O Prapitāmaha, we have arrived here at this sacrifice by your command. (34)
O Great-grandfather, let an order be given for our assistance, so that we, established in the kingdom of the Nāgas, may act swiftly. (35)
Brahmā said: "O great serpents, this assistance of yours is for us; go quickly with this king of the Nāgas and remain there."
Therefore, everyone stationed there should remain at the Nāga-tīrtha. || 37 ||
Whoever, harboring a wicked intent, comes here to my sacrifice to cause an obstacle, he must be restrained immediately. (38)
Whether it be a Rākṣasa, a Piśāca, a Bhūta, or even a human, O Nāgas, this is my most important task: the protection of my sacrifice. (39)
Likewise, when the month of Bhādrapada arrives, you too shall receive worship there on the fifth day of the dark fortnight.
Sūta said: Having replied "So be it" to him and having prostrated before the Grandfather (Brahmā), they, accompanied by the son of Sanātana, resorted to the Nāga-tīrtha.
From that time forward, that sacred ford has been known as Nāgatīrtha; it grants all desires to those men who perform their ablutions there with devotion.
Whoever performs a bath there even once, endowed with devotion, no fear arising from serpents shall ever arise within his lineage.
There, having honored the lords of the Nāgas led by Sanātana, he offers sweet food to the twice-born together with virtuous people. (44)

Until the end of seven births, he shall not encounter misfortune; nor shall there be any vulnerability from spirits, ghosts, or piśācas, especially from śākinīs, nor any diseases, mental anxieties, or fear of enemies. (45)
And whoever, O best of the twice-born, shall hear this being recited with devotion, he too shall not be afflicted by serpents for the duration of a year.
If this greatness of Nāgatīrtha is recited repeatedly before one who has been bitten by a serpent, he shall live even if bitten at the time of death.
This greatness arising from Āgatīrtha, which is written in this book, remains wherever it stays; there no serpent dwells.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Greatness of Nāgatīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 183.

Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, when the third day arrived, on the thirteenth lunar day, all those officiating priests (ṛtvijas) took up the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) and became engaged in their respective duties arising from the sacrificial rites.
Then the great sacrifice of the Grandfather proceeded; it was enriched with the fulfillment of all desires and endowed with every excellence.
"Let it be given, let it be given! Let it be eaten, let it be eaten!"—thus one sound was heard, while the second arose from the twice-born.
In that auspicious sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā), there was no third person present who could desire any wish arising from gold or jewels.
He undoubtedly obtains that which he desires, increased fourfold; there, auspicious mountains of cooked food are seen to have been prepared. || 5 ||
There were great rivers of ghee and milk, and heaps of wealth for the purpose of giving; in the meantime, O best of the twice-born, a certain wise man arrived there.
He who always knows the past, the future, and the present—having paid homage to Brahmā and seated himself before him—(spoke).
O best of the twice-born, he related in its entirety everything that had happened from his childhood onwards to all the brahmins during their various ritual activities.
Then all those officiating priests, their minds possessed by curiosity and their eyes wide with wonder, questioned that man of knowledge.
Then, remembering their own duties which had been forgotten, they indeed recalled the innumerable censurable acts they had committed in every respect.
Then they questioned that wise man once again: "O twice-born one, how has this world-transcending knowledge been established within you?"
"Who is your guru? Tell us, for our curiosity is indeed great. Oh, what knowledge! Oh, what knowledge! This has never been seen nor heard before. (12)
O best of the twice-born, such as this form of yours seen stationed upon Pārtha—is it that you have been thus enlightened by Brahmā himself, O Brahmin? (13)
What indeed could be gained by Hara being pleased, or what by the Lord who wields the discus? For such clear knowledge does not arise for one who has not been awakened by another. (14)
The guest said: "Piṅgalā, the osprey, the serpent, and the deer in the forest, the arrow-maker, and the maiden—these six are my gurus. (15)
Having observed their conduct, knowledge has arisen within me. || 16 ||
The Brahmins said: "O illustrious one, tell us how your gurus were situated, and what kind of conduct you observed in them. (17)
"In which country were you born, and in which place? Tell us. What is your name and what is your lineage? Tell us everything in detail. (18)
The guest said: "In this city there were four Brahmins who had been exiled: Śunaḥśepa, Śākreya, the Buddhist, and Dānta as the fourth. (19)
Among them, however, was one who was a Buddhist, known as Śānta Dānta; he was renowned for belonging to the Chandoga lineage and had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Born among the Nāgaras and now standing in my final years, I am his first son, dearer to him than even his own life.
Then, O best among the foremost of the twice-born, when I attained youth, I—
At that time, my beloved father met his death.
In the meantime, O twice-born ones, King Sutapas, the lord of Ānarta, appointed me to the office of chamberlain.
Having observed him to be peaceful and self-controlled, the high-souled king became confident; for in his inner apartments there was a chief consort named Piṅgalā.
Endowed with beauty yet possessed of misfortune, there were then hundreds of other wives of his residing in the inner apartments.
At the onset of night, they all become agitated; they fetch other fragrances, incenses, and flowers. (26)
In front [of him] were excellent, fragrant ointments, various kinds of flowers, and other fine garments. (27)
This continued until the time for retiring to bed arrived; they were filled with the ardor of passion and covered in horripilation.
"One knows me while I am asleep and will surely call out; the other likewise knows me, and thus they are mutually intolerant of one another. (29)
They vie with one another, they fight, and they speak harsh words; then, from among them, one proceeds into the presence of the king. (30)
The rest, having reached their targets, sighed and fell asleep; yet, afflicted by grief due to their defeat, they could not find sleep.
With their limbs tormented by desire and their eyes filled with tears, they stood there.
For hope is the supreme suffering, and hopelessness is the supreme happiness; having turned hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.
She never indulges in amorous display nor does she ever engage in rivalry; Piṅgalā never falls into agitation, but sleeps in comfort.
Then, having seen that supreme conduct of hers, I too abandoned all hopes and slept here happily from then on.
For those who sleep comfortably at night, the digestive fire of their bodies is kindled; it then receives food that is supremely nourishing.
That cause was born for the increase of my splendor; therefore, O best of the twice-born, Piṅgalā became my guru.
Those men whose limbs are ensnared by the fetters of hope and who are thus afflicted do not sleep at night at all, due to their constant anxiety over failing to attain that [object of desire]. (38)
