Thereafter, neither the external fire nor their digestive fire blazes; they have no desire for food at all, and that [fire] does not increase their vital energy. (39)
An end exists for everything, but for desire, it does not exist in any way whatsoever.
In whatever measure gain accrues here to men who have made their request, in that same measure it increases, like a fire fed with oblations.
Just as the horn of a ruru deer grows as its body grows, so too does craving increase through one’s own efforts. (42)
Knowing this, a fortunate man of discernment should perform that work by day by which he may sleep happily at night. (43)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Piṅgalā on the Third Day of the Brahma-sacrifice," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The guest said: "All this has been related to you—how Piṅgalā became my teacher, and how the osprey was born; now I shall tell you that as well. || 1 ||
"I possessed abundant wealth, a great inheritance from my father and grandfather. (2)
Furthermore, those sons, heirs, and even kinsmen—all of them constantly oppress me for the sake of wealth and grain. (3)
"He whom I do not give [to] him oppresses me as well, being himself greatly distressed and displaying the exhaustion of his life-force. (4)
O twice-born ones, some beg for wealth with conciliation, others through sowing dissension, others by instilling fear, and still others by means of force.
Thus, O friend, I find no happiness anywhere from their presence; day and night I contemplate the complete destruction of my afflictions, yet I see no means by which peace may arise. (6)
On another day, a kurara bird was seen in the sky traveling with great speed, carrying a piece of meat in its beak.
Being struck from all sides by various birds for the sake of his flesh, he then surrounded that meat on account of the fear of the flocks of birds.
For as long as they were there, they all became happy; likewise, even while I was suffering, my own kinsmen were happy.
Seeing the kurara bird with meat in its beak being killed by those without meat, the kurara thrives in happiness through the renunciation of that meat.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he summoned all his kinsmen—his sons and grandsons—and then made this announcement in their presence.
"Having made a threefold oath of truth that there is nothing else in my house, O kinsmen, divide the wealth according to what is right and take it. (12)
From that time forward, O twice-born ones, I have remained in happiness, released by them; for this reason, that osprey became my preceptor.
The attainment of wealth leads to delusion, and delusion leads to hell; therefore, one who seeks liberation should abandon that which is wealth as if it were a calamity from afar.
Just as meat is devoured by fish in the water, by beasts of prey on the earth, and by birds in the sky, so too is one who possesses wealth preyed upon everywhere.
Even one who is free from fault is tormented by kings and others if he possesses wealth; whereas a poor man, even if he has committed a transgression, remains untroubled everywhere.
Supported by others, the wealthy go along, stumbling at every step and speaking with faltering voices like drunkards. (17)

Hatred toward food, outward affection, and a constant bitterness in the mouth—regardless of whether it is heavy or light—are the characteristics of the wealthy, just like those of people suffering from fever. 18.

There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired; there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure—fie on wealth, the vessel of misery! (19)
This world of living beings, driven by the pursuit of wealth, frequents even the cremation ground; sons, too, abandon their own progenitor if he is destitute. (20)

A father is dear to his son, and a son is indeed dear to his father, only so long as there is no connection between them involving wealth; once a relationship born of riches has arisen, mutual enmity is produced. (21)
For this reason, O ascetics whose wealth is penance, I have renounced my riches; by that happiness, I abide according to the instruction of the osprey.
And listen, O highly fortunate ones, to how my serpent remained as my preceptor. || 23 ||
Just as I abandoned my home upon seeing the behavior of the serpent, so too the undertaking of a house leads only to great suffering and never to happiness. (24)
A snake, having entered a dwelling built by another, prospers in comfort; after living there happily, it shall again go to another such place. (25)
"He does not think, 'You belong to me,' nor 'This house is mine'; for him, the house does not truly arise as his own, since it was not created by himself. (26)
Furthermore, for one who builds a palace through various kinds of personal afflictions, that [palace] does not follow him even when the time of death has arrived.
From the home, a wife is born, and from her, a son and a daughter; for their sake, he thereafter performs what ought and ought not to be done.
Enveloping himself like a silkworm in its cocoon, he does not realize it.
Beings attached to sons, wives, homes, and fields sink down, submerged in the ocean-mud of greed like aged wild elephants.
One person commits the sins, while the multitude enjoys the fruit; those who enjoy are liberated from guilt, but the perpetrator is smeared with the fault.
For this reason, O best of the twice-born, I have abandoned that which pertains to dharma, seeing it to be like the movement of a snake—an obstacle on the path to liberation.
One should stay for one night in a village and three nights in a town; he who acts thus is called a *yati*, while any other is a mere hypocrite of yoga.

That ascetic who, when the smoke has ceased and the fire is extinguished, practices the "madhukarī" (honey-gathering) mode of begging at the houses of the foremost Brahmins, is known as a true *yati*, and no other.
If one carries a staff and begs for alms, yet remains thus without having overcome his worldly calamities, and neither abides [in truth] nor attains dispassion, he is certainly not a renunciant.
Sleeping during the day, eating food in vain, talk of women, looking at improper things, white clothing, and gold—these are the six causes of downfall for ascetics.

He who is equal toward enemy and friend, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same, and who is impartial toward friend, son, and stranger—he is known as a true ascetic (yati), and no other.
He for whom honor and dishonor are equal, whether in his own country or abroad, who neither rejoices nor feels aversion—he is known as a *yati*, and no other. (38)
He who does not go again to that house where he especially obtained alms or shelter is considered a true ascetic (yati), and no other. || 39 ||
Having understood this, O Brahmin, and having observed the behavior of the serpent, I have resolved to renounce all attachments for the sake of liberation.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, this serpent became my preceptor; through his power, great splendor was produced within my body. (41)
Just as the bee became my teacher, so do I speak; on which tree was that certain bee seen by me in union? (42)
Having relied upon the Śākha [branch], they established their former bond; and when the spring season arrived, those trees became laden with flowers.
Having taken the essence—the most excellent and most supreme—of those fragrant fruits and flowers, as well as those endowed with fragrant petals.
For he always perches upon the tip of this tree's branch; being joyful due to his lack of despondency, he is then clearly observed. (45)
Then, after a long period of time, a great honeycomb was produced, by which hundreds of thousands of others attained satisfaction through the honey.

Having observed that activity of his and many other scriptures extensively, I then extracted the essential core from each of them individually; thus, numerous treatises and the entirety of the Vedāntas were composed by me.
Just as bees do, the twice-born depend upon those [trees] for their livelihood.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, Madhu was born as my son; endowed with that splendor, I am so, and there is no other cause for it here. (49)
Those exponents of Vedānta who prevail here, endowed with vows, free from greed, and devoid of craving, become possessed of great splendor.
Those of evil intellect who are deficient even by one [of these] become possessed of greed and delusion; being sinful, they are born as those deprived of consciousness.
Having seen and deliberated upon the very numerous Vedānta texts, I have composed works of equal form, seeking the welfare of the mortal world. (52)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, Madhupa attained the status of my preceptor; I shall tell you exactly how he became an arrow-maker. (53)
For the sake of self-realization, thousands of yogins endowed with wisdom have been seen by me, and they have each spoken according to their own capacity. (54)
Just as the vision of the Self will arise for a worthy disciple, so too [it arises] through the eighty-four doors born of meditative absorption (samādhi).

Through innumerable postures beginning with the lotus posture (padmāsana), through various means of measurement, and likewise through the study of spiritual sciences (adhyātma), I have still not perceived the Self in any way whatsoever.
Then, having attained dispassion, I wandered over the surface of the earth; yet for the sake of a guru, I did not find a teacher for the realization of the Self.
When another day arrived, as I was traveling along the royal highway, I saw the protector of the earth surrounded by a great army.
Then, leaving the path and approaching the front of the king, I took my place at the door of the hermitage, standing slightly raised up.
And standing there was a certain man, an arrow-maker, engaged in the straightening of arrows with curved joints.
When the king had gone far away, another servant approached him in that same manner. || 61 ||
O twice-born ones, while I was listening, he, being intent on the task of splitting the reed and standing upright at that time, questioned him with great haste.
"How much time has passed since the lord of the earth departed? Tell me by which path he went, so that I may follow behind him. (63)
Then that man, standing with his face cast downwards, said to him, O Brahmins: "The lord of the earth is passing along this royal road. (64)
"I have not seen any royal servant here at present; ask someone else, for if you have business with him, let him speak."
"I am stationed here, fully occupied with the task of preparing arrows. Having heard those words of his, I reflected thus within my own mind: || 66 ||

"Yoga, which gives rise to the knowledge of Brahman, occurs through one-pointedness of mind; it cannot happen otherwise for me. Therefore, I shall practice the cessation of the mind for the sake of the perfect realization of Brahman, and thus that [knowledge] will be mine. (67)
From that time forward, I have always maintained within my own mind the Universal Form as well as the Sun residing in the lotus of the heart.
Then, O best of the twice-born, in all directions, at the ends of the quarters, in the sky, and upon the surface of the earth, I saw only him alone and nothing else whatsoever. (69)
And I, endowed with splendor, remain established by its power.
In this way, O best of the twice-born, that arrow-maker became my guru; now listen how, in former times, a girl likewise became my preceptor.
When I, having renounced all attachments, departed from my home, my wife followed right after me.
Taking my infant son and a single beautiful daughter, I was then addressed by my wife as I remained in the stage of life of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha). || 73 ||

Follow my word, for liberation will indeed occur right here: whether one be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic, if he is self-restrained, he shall surely attain liberation. (74)
Or else, if you abandon me and go elsewhere, then I shall die; this is the truth, without a doubt. (75)
"When I am dead, these two children—the girl and the boy—will follow me in death; therefore, O Lord, have mercy. (76)
Do not go to another holy site, even though you know it yourself; this field born of Hāṭakeśvara is remembered as most meritorious.
"O Lord, I have heard this regarding all sacred fords from the foremost of Brahmins as they speak, as well as from other ascetics. (78)
O Lord, O All-pervading One, this verse has been recited by me in many ways from the mouth of the truthful and excellent sage Viśvāmitra. (79)
All sacred fords are undoubtedly purified by bathing and giving gifts; however, the holy field born of Hāṭakeśvara purifies even through mere remembrance.
Then, with great difficulty, I promised to dwell in a hermitage; whether it be the life of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) or otherwise, I have accordingly established myself there.
For while I was staying there, a maiden standing nearby was playing with her forearms, which were adorned with bracelets, moving them here and there. (82)
In whatever measure she subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits, her body likewise became thinner day by day.
Then sorrow arises within me at the thought of their impending fall. After some time, however, three bracelets appeared upon her hand; thereafter, a conversation arose between those two.
Then, after a long time, one [of them] became established by those two; for him who remained there, neither conflict nor noise arose. (85)
Having reflected upon that, I indeed abandoned that hermitage as well; and having made this firm resolve, I thought thus in my mind: || 86 ||
There is constant quarreling with many, and likewise rivalry with two; I shall wander alone, like a maiden’s bracelet. (87)
Then, having abandoned my wife who was sleeping there with the infant, I traveled a long distance to a place where she would not know me.
Having abandoned the bonds of worldly existence, I wander upon the surface of the earth, sleeping wherever the sun sets and eating whatever I happen to obtain. (89)
Then, O Brahmins, knowledge gradually dawned upon me in this way: concerning the past, the future, and especially the present. (90)
"Thus, O best of the twice-born, this daughter was born to me for the sake of a heavy burden. (91)
All this that I have been asked regarding my preceptor has been told to you; I do not speak anything false before you in any way. (92)
Thus has this knowledge arisen in me through these very six modes; by means of these, this supramundane knowledge has been brought about through your confidence.

Sūta said: Then all those excellent brahmins questioned him: "Having abandoned the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) along with your wife and child, where have you gone? Tell us that; and for how long did you remain there?"
The guest said: "O best of the twice-born, being afraid, I have slept wherever the sun set for hundreds and thousands of villages, and indeed for hundreds of years beyond all counting. (95)
The principal sacred fords (tīrthas) have been seen, as well as the shrines (āyatanas); and the most excellent mountains and rivers with pure waters have also been seen. (96)
And while staying in Vārāṇasī, I myself realized that a sacrifice to my grandfather was to take place in this place of mine. 97.
Then, O best of the twice-born, I arrived there in haste out of curiosity to see what kind of sacrifice that would be in which the Grandfather himself was the sacrificer.
Sūta said: In the meantime, all the gods, including Indra, arrived, placing Vāsudeva and likewise Maheśvara at their head.
Having arrived at another place, Pulastya and the other officiating priests likewise came, and Brahmā himself also arrived, wearing a deer-skin.
Then, having attained satisfaction through that knowledge of his, all the inhabitants of heaven, being givers of boons, said to him: "We grant you a boon. (101)
Therefore, choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—and ask for whatever you desire; we shall certainly grant it to you, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (102)
The guest said: "If the gods are pleased with me and grant me a boon, I pray for divinity even with this very body. (103)
It was endowed with sacrificial portions for the other inhabitants of heaven as well, and especially, O best of gods, it was situated in a position above them.
The gods said: "Surely, having become a celestial being, you shall dwell in the world of the gods with this very body, though deprived of a share in the sacrifice. (105)
"O Brahmin, if we were to grant you a share of the sacrifice for a human being, then the Veda would become invalid because of that which was given by you. (106)
The guest said: "I have no need for divinity, nor for that which is devoid of a share in the sacrifice. Therefore, I shall accomplish that by which liberation will come to pass. (107)
Having heard that, the Lotus-born one, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to all the gods: "May all the deities listen to the beneficial words that I speak. (109)
"This brahmin has come from afar for my sacrifice; he is especially a worthy recipient born of knowledge. (109)
"Since a boon has been promised to him by all the gods, therefore, O best of deities, let that which he desires be granted to him."
Maheśvara said: "I shall explain how his satisfaction may always arise, exceeding even his share of the sacrifice; listen, O best of the gods. (111)
Hari is remembered as the lord of this sacrifice that is being performed; for this reason, that deity is called Yajñapuruṣa (the Person of Sacrifice). || 112 ||
From this day forward, whatever śrāddha shall take place among mortals—whether for the gods or for the ancestors—you shall be established at its conclusion. (113)
O best of the twice-born, having recited his name and subsequently having recited the name of Yajñapuruṣa, food should be given to the Brāhmaṇa.
By that, his satisfaction shall always be even greater than at the conclusion of a sacrifice; for whatever Śrāddha has been performed without offering to him, it will become as if nothing were done.
All that will go to waste, just like an oblation poured into ashes, for whoever shall worship him only after reaching the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Accompanied by the name of Viṣṇu, that gift will become inexhaustible; for even if it is very small, it is generally offered with a mind purified by faith. (117)
Whether at a Śrāddha ceremony or a Vaiśvadeva rite, whoever does not honor him, all that [offering] of his will become useless once he has arrived. || 118 ||
When he has attained satisfaction, all the gods will go to great joy; and the ancestors likewise come to him when he is turned away, as well as when he is facing toward them.
Having heard those words of Maheśvara, all the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, then joyfully said, "So be it."

From that time forward, the honoring of guests came into being. Therefore, one should always honor a guest with every effort; [this] is the sacrifice of the Supreme Person (puruṣayajña), and never merely that of a single individual.
The guest said: "O best of the twice-born, there is my own sacred site here, where penance was performed by me in the region of Hāṭakeśvara during the Puru-kāla."
When the lunar day (tithi) of the fourth falls conjoined with Mars (Aṅgāraka), on that day the presence of all the gods must be invoked.
May he who performs his bath on that very day when it has concluded obtain the fruit of all holy fords through your grace. 124.
"So be it," the supreme gods then said to the guest. In the meantime, the sage Pulastya spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Pulastya said: All the officiating priests and the gods are assembled, filled with curiosity; let them rise quickly for the successful accomplishment of the sacrificial rite. 126.

In the meantime, all those officiating priests (ṛtvij), impelled by his words, arose and returned to their respective places. Then, O best of the twice-born, the sacrifice proceeded once more, as they performed the sacrificial rites beginning with the oblations (homa).
The sages said: O highly fortunate one, son of Sūta, tell us once more in detail the supreme majesty of the guest and our duty toward him.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to this supreme majesty, by the mere hearing of which the sin produced during the day shall perish.
And that auspicious account which I previously heard from my father.
For householders, there is no higher duty than the honoring of guests; nor is there any fault in a guest for failing to honor him. (4)
If a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated, he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that person and taking away their merit. (5)
Truthfulness, purity, austerity, study, charity, and sacrifice performed for a hundred years—all of this is lost for him who does not honor a guest.
He from whose house guests arrive from afar feeling at ease is called a true householder; all others are merely guardians of a dwelling.
For those men on this earth who have performed meritorious deeds in the past, these three are never thwarted: the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the act of giving (dāna), and auspicious speech.
When the guest is satisfied, all the deities are satisfied with the householder; when he turns his face away, they all turn their faces away as well—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a householder should always satisfy a guest, even by the gift of his own self, if he desires merit for himself. (10)
O best of the twice-born, three kinds of guests are declared for householders; I shall tell you their proper time, so listen with full concentration.

The one worthy of ancestral rites (śrāddhīya), the one belonging to the Vaiśvadeva offering (vaiśvadevīya), and the third, the one brought by the sun (sūryoḍha); and others who seek food—these are proclaimed as the common [guests]. || 12 ||
When the Śrāddha has been performed according to the resolve, arising for the feeding of the ancestors, whoever arrives at that very time is indeed a partaker of that Śrāddha. (13)
One who has traveled a long distance, who is weary on the road, and arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering—him one should recognize as a guest; one who arrives earlier is not a guest.
Whether he be dear or hateful, a fool or even a scholar, one who arrives during the Vaiśvadeva rite is a guest who leads to heaven.
One should not inquire about his lineage, conduct, status, or even his Veda; rather, having seen his sacred thread, one should feed him with great devotion.
If a guest does not arrive during a *śrāddha* or a *vaiśvadeva* rite, one should then offer an oblation of clarified butter to the Fire-god (*Havirbhuj*), addressing him by that [guest's] name.
If one lacks the capacity to provide a full meal, then one should give according to one's devotion; even a small amount of that person's food is sufficient for [the recipient] to attain satisfaction.

Likewise, there is another third type called the "guest carried by the sun" (sūryoḍha), who arrives either after the meal has been finished or during the night; the householder should provide him with food according to his ability.
If one whose turn has arrived at sunrise departs from the house without having received worship, he departs after transferring his own sin to that person and leaving him disappointed.
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, pleasant speech—these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous. (21)
By a welcome, the fires attain satisfaction for the householder; by a seat, the Self-born Grandfather himself attains contentment.

Through the offering of *arghya* one pleases Śambhu; through the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), all the gods including Indra; and through the gift of food, Viṣṇu—the guest who embodies all the gods—is pleased. (23)
Therefore, O Brahmins, he should always be honored and especially fed; indeed, another Brahmin who is a householder should be fed by him even after merely uttering his name.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Guest," in the Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara-Kṣetra-Māhātmya, within the Nāgara-Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 186 ||
Sūta said: When the fourth day of that sacrifice had arrived, the sacrificial rites were thereafter commenced by the officiating priests.
All the rituals, beginning with the drinking of soma as well as the slaughter of the animal, were performed; and having taken the animal's rectum, the Prasthātṛ priest held it.
O best of the twice-born, while the assembly was in the midst of its deliberations in a secluded spot for the sake of the fire sacrifice, a certain Brāhmaṇa arrived as that place became crowded.
Having entered there, the youth, eager for the taste of meat, saw the anus of the animal and began to eat it with great longing.
In the meantime, the traveler arrived in his presence; seeing him eating, he then uttered a curse.
"Fie, fie upon you of sinful conduct! That anus which was held for the sake of the *homa* has been defiled by you through greed, and you have thereby caused an obstacle to the sacrifice. (6)
"I must certainly not perform the fire-oblation now with what remains of my food; this which you have performed is the work of Rākṣasas. (7)
Therefore, by my word, become a Rākṣasa without delay.
At that very time, however, he indeed became one with hair standing erect, red eyes, spike-like ears, black teeth, and was exceedingly terrifying.
With long lips and a terrifying face, devoid of flesh and fat, with only skin, bones, and sinews remaining, he indeed had the form of Cāmuṇḍā.
And that sage named Viśvāvasu, the son of Pulastya, arrived for the purpose of eating meat purified by mantras. (11)
The grandson of Parameṣṭhin was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; seeing him in the form of a Rākṣasa, all the twice-born trembled on every side.
Others likewise muttered hymns that destroy demons, while some sought refuge in Viṣṇu and others in Rudra.
Others, however, sought refuge with the Grandfather and with Gāyatrī, crying out, "Protect! Protect! with their minds terrified by fear.
O twice-born ones, having then seen himself freed from the state of a Rākṣasa, he, distressed and with eyes filled with tears, rushed toward his grandfather.
Having bowed down, he then spoke these words to him with palms joined in reverence.
"O Lord of Gods, I am your grandson, a twice-born son of Pulastya; today, O All-pervading One, I have been reduced to the state of a Rākṣasa by my father out of anger. (17)
"O Lord of Gods, out of greed for the tongue and not knowing the goat's anus, O God, that which was prepared for the sake of the fire-oblation was eaten by me. (18)
Therefore, show compassion toward my body so that I may attain human status; let a policy be devised by which my state as a Rākṣasa may pass away. (19)
Having heard his speech, the Grandfather (Brahmā) took pity on him and spoke these words of the Sāman to the Pratiprasthātṛ priest.
"This child, my grandson, does not know what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; therefore, O best of the twice-born, remove this demonic nature from him. (21)
Having heard that, the sage said: "O Lord, O All-pervading One, this expiation must be performed for your sacrifice, which has been defiled by this [act] committed by Guda."
Therefore, this one who has caused an obstacle to my sacrifice has been cursed by me; I shall not, under any circumstances, take away his state as a Rākṣasa.
"Even in jest, I have never spoken a word that was untrue."

Brahmā said: "I shall perform an expiation for the successful completion of this sacrifice. Having performed the fire-oblation according to the rules with Gaurī as the prescribed sacrificial fee, you must, at my word, remove the demonic nature from her."
He said: "O Great-grandfather, if fire were cold and the moon were hot, then my word spoken would be otherwise. (26)
Having heard those words of his and having ascertained them to be certain, Brahmā then spoke to Viśvāvasu, who was in the form of a Rākṣasa.
"O child, remain for now in this form at my word; perform [this rite] and I shall grant you an unsurpassed station. (28)
There are other Rākṣasas dwelling in the western region of this Camatkārapura, who remain established within the bounds of propriety.
In Laṅkā, the Rākṣasas, seeking a virtuous state here, have come to that region and perform austerities with firm vows. || 3 ||
Establish yourself there as their sovereign, remaining devoted to the welfare of the city-dwellers; for there are many Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Piśācas.
And whatever other rākṣasas there may be who have resorted to evil dispositions, they all go there and are subdued at that very moment.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and especially kūṣmāṇḍas, upon seeing Nāgara before them, flee far away out of fear of him.
Therefore go there, my son, and become the sovereign of them all; the kingdom of the Rākṣasas is now granted to you by me.
The Rākṣasa said: O Grandfather, for me who am thus established in the sovereignty over the Rākṣasas, tell me what I should eat there and what should be given to them. (35)
O Lord, tell me, O Ruler of Gods, having shown compassion toward me, how it is that the king must provide food for his servants. (36)
And that king who does not provide sustenance for his circle of servants goes to the Raurava hell; indeed, this is what I have heard. (37)

Brahmā said: Whatever śrāddha has been devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and bereft of sesame seeds and darbha grass—all that has been given by me to you, even if it were performed at a most sacred pilgrimage site.
Whatever śrāddha a pig might see, or a woman in her menses, or a dog, or even a rat—that shall all become yours. (39)
But whatever śrāddha is performed devoid of the prescribed rules, or with darbha grass that is rootless or longer than a span—that shall all be yours. (40)
Whether it be sesame, or food cooked in oil, or even awned grain—if these are not given at the śrāddha, that [offering] shall become your śrāddha.
Whatever Śrāddha is performed by those who have not bathed, by those who have not washed their garments, and by those who are smeared with oil, all of that shall become so for you.
Or if a buffalo-breeder eats it, or one with white leprosy, or even one with deformed nails, or a twice-born man afflicted with leprosy eats it—that shall become your śrāddha.

Whether it be one with a missing limb, or one with an extra limb, or one who is censured; whether he be afflicted by a great disease, or a thief, or even a usurer—wherever such a person eats at a Śrāddha, that Śrāddha shall become [fruitless] for you.
Whatever one with black teeth eats, whatever the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) eats, or whatever one who is naked eats—that shall become your śrāddha.
Whatever sacrifice is devoid of sacrificial fees, whatever is performed by those who are impure, and whatever is lacking in celibacy—the fruit of that shall be yours. (46)
That for which no guest is to be honored, whether at a *śrāddha* or in a sacrificial rite performed at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* offering—all that shall be yours. (47)
Where one who performs the śrāddha, a Brāhmaṇa, or even the eater does not observe silence after the invocation, that shall be considered a valid śrāddha for you. (48)
Whatever man performs a śrāddha in earthen vessels, or in vessels that are cracked, all of that shall become so [ineffective]. || 49 ||
Wherever there is visibly salty water or where buttermilk has become spoiled, the offering of *jātī* flowers shall serve for all of that. || 50 ||
Whether the sacrificer is a twice-born man or one devoid of celibacy, that śrāddha has been offered by me to you, free from the three vessels.
But that śrāddha at which food is served in an iron vessel—that has been offered by me to you; likewise, any other [offering] is lost. (52)
Whatever is given or offered in sacrifice at night through mantras or ritual actions—except during the solstices and lunar festivals—is indeed contemptible.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, immediately ceased; that Rākṣasa also obtained a Rākṣasa station right there.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrāddha Attainable by Rākṣasas," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 187 ||
Sūta said: Then, when the fifth day had arrived, those best of the twice-born, all having bathed well and being pure, stood there dressed in white, washed garments.
Instructed by Pulastya, they performed all the ritual acts; having entered the sacrificial assembly, they first proceeded with the selection of the officiating priests.
The priests, being highly composed, uttered the *praiṣas* (directions) as instructed by the *adhvaryu* in their proper sequence for the purpose of the oblation into the blazing fire. || 3 ||
At that very time, however, the ritual duty was undertaken by the Udgātṛ priest; and the Sāman, which is indicated by singing, is performed with wooden stakes (śaṅku). || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, he who has performed seven circumambulations while standing in the midst of the assembly hall—there all those gods come, longing for their shares of the sacrifice.
And they were especially filled with joy for the sake of drinking the soma; then, when the consumption of the soma had begun, a song was sung composed by the Udgātṛ priest.
And a certain wise maiden arrived, eager for the chanting of the Sāman hymns and desiring the wonderful birthplace of Śaṅkukarṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin and Greatness of the Yakṣmatīrtha at the Concluding Bath of the Brahma-sacrifice," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 190 ||
The sages said: "O son of a Sūta, you have stated why Sāvitrī did not come—how she was summoned with deceitful words by Pulastya, and how she remained intent upon her household duties. (1)
Then, out of anger, Brahmā withdrew Gāyatrī; however, she was highly praised by the gods and the foremost of Brahmins, and thus became his wife. || 2 ||
And how was Sāvitrī born? Having learned of her, tell us everything in detail—how she entered the sacrificial pavilion and the wife’s chamber.
Sūta said: Knowing her beloved to be under her control, Sāvitrī became confident; having become steady, she then brought together all the wives of the gods.
Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Medhā, as well as Arundhatī; Svadhā, Svāhā, Kīrti, Buddhi, Puṣṭi, Kṣamā, Dhṛti, and many others likewise accompanied by Apsarases. || 5 ||
O best of the twice-born, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, Tilottamā, and all the hosts of Apsarases arrived there.
Accompanied by those women whose hands were filled with offerings for the goddess and whose minds were full of joy, she set out toward the pavilion.
While musical instruments were being played, accompanied by the sound of singing, especially those of the foremost Gandharvas and Kinnaras.
As that illustrious lady was proceeding toward that sacrificial pavilion, her right eye throbbed repeatedly at that moment.
The deer moved counter-clockwise, as did other birds and creatures; they traveled in reverse order and repeatedly uttered discordant cries.
Furthermore, her right limbs throbbing repeatedly produced an unrestrained agitation in her mind. (11)
And all those celestial women, stationed by her side, danced and laughed and sang according to their enthusiasm. || 12 ||
And they did not perceive the agitation arising from the omen in their hearts; all were intent on singing and dancing out of mutual rivalry.
"I shall enter first, I shall enter first into this great sacrifice"—thus, filled with eagerness, they proceeded along the path at that time. (14)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Occurrence of Ill Omens and Portents at the Time of Sāvitrī’s Arrival at the Sacrifice," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 191 ||
Sūta said: Then, hearing the great sound of musical instruments that had arisen, Nārada, having recognized his own mother, went forward to meet her.
Having prostrated himself, becoming dejected in spirit and overwhelmed with tears, he spoke with a faltering voice, his throat choked with sobs.
Then, for the sake of protecting himself from the curse and to further increase her anger, the Brahmin, who delights in strife, stood before the celestial women.
O Goddess, you were then summoned by me with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, faltering at every step, and thereafter by Pulastya.
Relying on her feminine nature, she did not come even at the time of initiation.
Then, by the command of Vidhi, Śakra brought another maiden born of a cowherd, who possessed a divine form.
Then, having been introduced by Govaktra through the secret path, O illustrious lady, she was instantly drawn forth and brought back at that very moment.
Then she was approved by Viṣṇu for the purpose of marriage; and the name Gāyatrī was bestowed upon her by Īśvara as your follower.
"All the Brahmins said, 'O Brahmin, let her be called Brāhmaṇī; O Lord, at our word, take her hand in marriage. (9)
Then, having been addressed by all the gods, he quickly united that fair-faced woman with her husband according to the dharma arising from matrimony.
Or what is the use of saying much more to you? O Goddess of the Gods, the girdle was fastened around the waist of that Gopī as she entered the wife’s chamber.
Having seen that censurable act, he departed from the sacrificial pavilion; overcome by indignation, he was unable even to look at her.
Having understood this, O highly fortunate lady, do what is appropriate. Go or stay there in that pavilion devoid of dharma. (13)
O best of the twice-born, having heard that, the goddess Sāvitrī then became dejected in countenance, like a lotus pond at the onset of winter.
Like a creeper whose roots have been severed, like a female cakravāka bird separated from her beloved, or like a lake whose waters have vanished at the arrival of the bright, white season; (15)
She was like the crescent moon when it has waned, like a doe deprived of her stag, like an army whose king has been slain, and like a virtuous wife whose husband has departed.

Like a withered garland of flowers, or like a cow whose calf has died, she had fallen into a state of supreme despondency and remained motionless; seeing her thus, the wives of the gods then spoke to Nārada.
"Fie, fie upon you, O lover of the Kali age, who creates detachment through passion! All this has been done by you; such is the intervention of that Ordainer."
Gaurī said: "O Goddess, this one who is fond of strife speaks words that are both true and false; by means of this very activity, this sage always sustains his life. (19)
"O Sāvitrī, I was told repeatedly by the Three-eyed One in the past: 'O beloved Pārvatī, if you desire my happiness, you must not place trust in the words of the sage Nārada. (20)
From that time forth, I have never placed any faith in his words; therefore, let us go to where your husband resides.
Having personally witnessed the situation, one should then do whatever is appropriate; one should not remain here today merely because of his word—let us go there.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Gaurī, Sāvitrī, deprived of joy, headed toward the sacrificial pavilion, stumbling at every step.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he departed with a vacant mind; yet even so, her sweet song continued to appear before him. 24.

O best of the twice-born, just as earache has repeatedly occurred, and just as there is the playing of a drum accompanied by the mṛdaṅga and ānaka drums, yet it is a performance that yields no fruit; || 25 ||
Just as one cannot see a ghost, that great satī was unable to look upon the mortal as he was departing for the sacrifice at that time.
Perceiving that very body of hers as both a source of aesthetic delight and a burning coal, the great chaste lady, miserable and with eyes filled with tears, departed.

Then, having reached that sacrificial pavilion with great difficulty—as if it were a prison cell that had come within the range of her sight, difficult even to behold—she approached it in this manner.
Then, seeing Sāvitrī arrived at the sacrificial pavilion, the four-faced one immediately stood with his face cast down in shame.
Likewise, Śambhu, Śakra, and Vāsudeva, as well as whatever other deities were present there in the sacrificial pavilion.
Then those tigers among brahmins, having abandoned the sound of the Vedas, all became mute, their minds terrified with fear.
Then, beholding her husband together with his co-wife, Sāvitrī, her eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these harsh words: || 32 ||
Sāvitrī said: "How is it fitting for you, who are of such advanced age, to do this—to have married this wife born of a cowherd? (33)
Of both these groups, those women who have beloved husbands as they desire, yet are devoid of purity and proper conduct and are averse to religious duties; || 34 ||
In whose lineage all people take delight in the practice of bestiality, abandoning their own uterine sister as well as another's mother. (35)
In her family, all people regard every woman as supreme, just as cattle eat grass while going to drink water.
They did nothing but excrete feces and urine, and merely carry heavy loads.
In the same way, her entire family consumes nothing but whey. || 37 ||
Having discharged urine and feces, and being freed from the experience of rebirth, he knows no other duty than to attend to his own belly for the sake of dharma. (38)
Even the lowest-born (antyajas) perform that work which is censured; the Ābhīras do that as well—so why was this done by you? (39)
If you must have another wife for the sacrifice, or if you desire some famous Brāhmaṇī woman renowned throughout the three worlds, [then act accordingly]. (40)

O Creator, you are surely a vain shaveling; in my opinion, you are certainly a rogue, since you have caused this girl—who has abandoned her purity and whose virginity is defiled—to be taken [in marriage]. (41)
This girl, who was previously enjoyed by many, has now arrived as a cowherd’s daughter; she is exceedingly sinful and surpasses hundreds of common prostitutes. (42)

Likewise, a maiden born of the lowest caste (antyaja) who has lost her virginity gives birth [to such a child]; similarly, a certain cowherd’s daughter also gives birth to one of that same kind. || 43 ||
He shall cause the lineage of his mother, his father, and his wife’s father to fall; therefore, by this despicable deed upon the surface of the earth, [he brings ruin]. 44.
"Neither you nor the other foremost gods shall receive that worship, provided that there is any truth whatsoever in my words regarding this deed. (44)
"And those who shall perform worship [to you] will become destitute; how are you not ashamed to do this which is so contemptible? (46)
"Since you have performed this which is unfit for your sons, your grandsons, other inhabitants of heaven, and especially for the brahmins. (47)

Or rather, this is not a fault; for men are not subject to the power of desire; they feel shame and discern what ought and ought not to be done, as well as what is auspicious and inauspicious. || 48 ||
One who has fallen under the sway of desire considers what should not be done as what ought to be done; he regards a friend as an enemy and an enemy as a friend. (49)
Just as there is no truth in a gambler, nor friendship in a thief, nor a friend for a king, so too is there no sense of shame in lustful men. 50.
Fire might indeed become cold, and the moon might become fiery; even the salt ocean might become sweet—but a lustful man certainly never feels shame.
This co-wifely rivalry that has arisen would not cause me such pain as it would for even a thousand women or men. (52)
If you have fallen under the sway of desire, then act toward those who are of noble birth, pure, and especially of your own kind, as well as toward others. 53.
Moreover, this is a great misery: that you have married an Ābhīrī woman who is despised, like a courtesan whose virtue is lost and who has many husbands. (54)
Therefore, O Creator, I shall go to that place where your name is not heard—that of one who is greedy for sensual pleasure and devoid of shame.

"O Creator, since I have been brought here by you and humiliated before the wives of the gods, the gods themselves, and the twice-born, therefore no one shall perform worship for you from now on. (56)
From this day forward, whatever mortal upon the surface of the earth shall perform worship with mantras, just as others do for the dwellers of heaven, [he shall obtain the fruit]. (57)
And his lineage shall become impoverished and beset by suffering—whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra—in his household. (58)
"Since this daughter of an Ābhīra has been censured by me in my very presence, there shall indeed be no progeny for her because of my word alone. (59)
She shall not receive worship in the world as do other celestial women. || 60 ||
And whatever woman should perform worship of it anywhere, she shall become full of suffering, barren, and possessed of misfortune.
"Just as this most wicked woman, who has lost her character and has five husbands, shall attain fame in the world, so too shall she [attain it]."
O night-stalker, her lineage shall become wicked; they will be abandoned by truth and purity, and deprived of the company of the virtuous.
"In this lineage, there shall be those who live by tending cattle and have no fixed dwellings. Having thus cursed Brahmā, the virtuous woman then cursed Gāyatrī as well.
Then Satī cursed all the hosts of gods: "O Śakra! Since you have brought her here, she who has five husbands! (65)
Therefore, having performed this service for your guru, obtain the full auspicious fruit; you have been defeated by your enemies in battle and shall fall into captivity.
"O Vāsudeva, because she has indeed had five husbands through you, she will undoubtedly remain in prison for a long time. (67)
Since you previously approved of this ritual act, I shall therefore curse you without a doubt; and you too, O evil-minded one, shall fall into the state of being another's servant.
O Rudra, although you are standing nearby, you neglect this deed; O fool, you do not restrain us—therefore, listen to my words.
"While your beloved husband is still alive, I have experienced the suffering born of separation from him; once you are dead, that same suffering shall befall me. (70)
In this sacrifice, this woman who has had five husbands has entered, which is contemptible; and you too, O Fire, accept the oblation out of greed. (71)
Likewise, in other sacrifices as well, you shall be perfectly free from doubt; therefore, O one of wicked conduct, you shall become an eater of all things.
Always accompanied by Svadhā and Svāhā, you shall never attain supreme happiness at any time, just as you did before.
And all these Brāhmaṇas, their minds afflicted by greed, perform the fire-oblation even in a sacrificial rite that is censurable. (74)
Wherever this woman, who has five husbands, is settled through greed for wealth, there the speech uttered shall be considered Brahmanical. (75)
Therefore, you shall be afflicted by poverty, as well as husbands of low-caste women (vṛṣalī), and sellers of the Vedas; of this there is no doubt. (76)
"O Lord of Wealth, you bestow wealth upon the failure of a sacrifice; therefore, all that wealth of yours shall become unusable. (77)
Likewise, all the hosts of gods who have sought refuge in providing assistance here, in this sacrifice which is full of faults and has five husbands, [will surely suffer]. (78)
They will now be abandoned by their lineage; defeated by the Dānavas, they shall experience nothing but suffering. (79)
And on her sides, the other four who are stationed there are called Ābhīrī and Sapatnī; they are delighted by meditation.
Those who are constantly intent on hatred toward me, led by Śivadūtī and her like—will they ever have any mutual association with one another? (81)

Not even by another man on this earth shall there be even a mere sight of him; nor shall there ever be a dwelling for embodied beings upon mountain peaks, in inaccessible places, or in difficult terrains, being forever deprived of all enjoyments.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Sāvitrī, her mind overcome with anger, dismissed all those wives of the gods who were standing by her side.
And she set out facing north, even though she was being restrained on all sides by all the wives of the gods, headed by Lakṣmī herself.
"I shall go there where even the name of this lustful man is not heard; indeed, I will go there quickly. (85)
One left foot was placed upon the slope of the mountain, while with the second she likewise ascended onto the head of that Aṅgiras.
Even today, that beautiful footprint of hers is visible there; it is meritorious, a destroyer of all sins, and remains upon the mountain slope.
Even a man of evil conduct who worships him is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme state. || 88 ||
Whatever desire a person meditates upon, he worships that; he will certainly attain it, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (89)
Sūta said: Thus the goddess Sāvitrī remained there, taking refuge on the mountain, having then suffered great humiliation from the presence of her own husband.
He who worships her properly, especially on the full moon day, shall then attain all desires cherished by his mind.
Listen to the fruit obtained by that woman who, with devotion, offers a lamp before him using red threads and clarified butter.
As many threads as are consumed by that lamp, and for as many moments as the ghee lamp remains burning, for that many thousands of births shall she be a partaker of good fortune.
Accompanied by sons and grandsons, she shall be wealthy and adorned with virtuous character.
She is neither unfortunate nor barren, nor is she one-eyed or deformed. || 94 ||
Listen to the fruit that accrues to that woman who performs a dance or a song there before him, even if she is a widow. (95)
In whatever manner she shakes her own limbs while dancing, in that very same way she surely shakes off whatever sin was committed in the past.
As many living beings as hear her song there, for that many thousands of years shall she dwell in heaven.
She who makes a gift of fruit dedicated to Sāvitrī rejoices in heaven for as many Yugas as there are fruits in that offering. || 98 ||

O best of the twice-born, he who gives sweet food, especially to women, and to those wives blessed with good husbands at the Dakṣiṇāmūrti shrine, rejoices in heaven for as many yugas as there are grains of rice in that offering.

O best of the twice-born, whoever performs a śrāddha there, endowed with perfect faith, even with a single grain or a single plant, for him too arises the merit that comes from a śrāddha at Gayā. || 100 ||
The twice-born man who performs even a single twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) using water spat out by his own wife while facing the southern direction [incurs great sin]. 101.
And when the evening time has arrived, O best of Brahmins, by him the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) for twelve full years has been properly saluted.
O Brahmins, listen as I describe to you the fruit that belongs to that Brāhmaṇa who, standing before her, recites the Sāvitrī mantra. || 103 ||
By ten [recitations], the sin produced in this life is destroyed; by a hundred, that committed in the past; and by a thousand, the transgression of three ages perishes. (104)
Therefore, with every effort, one should go toward Camatkārapura and worship that Goddess; she should especially be praised with hymns. || 105 ||
Whoever reads or hears this narrative of Sāvitrī shall be liberated from all sins and become a partaker of happiness in this world. || 106 ||
All this that I was asked by you, O best of the twice-born, has been related; the entire majesty of Sāvitrī has been told. What more shall I speak?

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Sāvitrī," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 192 ||
The sages said: O son of a Sūta, when Sāvitrī had departed in such a state of anger, what was done there by Gāyatrī and by the gods, beginning with Brahmā?
Explain all of this to us, for our curiosity is indeed great: how did the gods, though possessed by a curse, remain there in that pavilion?
Sūta said: Then, O best of the twice-born, when Sāvitrī had departed after having uttered the curse, Gāyatrī suddenly rose and spoke these words. (3)
The word spoken by Sāvitrī cannot be made otherwise by any means, even by all the gods and asuras combined.
The highly virtuous and illustrious Sāvitrī, devoted to her husband, is worthy of worship by all the gods; she is the eldest and most excellent among the assembly of the virtuous.
But this, O best of gods, is the nature of all women: even the fall of a thunderbolt might be endured, but never talk of a co-wife.
"Those Brahmins and gods who have been cursed here on my account by Sāvitrī—I myself shall personally provide for them in common, according to my power."
"O best of gods, this method preceded by mantras has been declared as one that is not to be honored by any of the castes, beginning with the Brahmins."
In all the abodes of Brahmā and at all times upon the surface of the earth, no rite whatsoever shall attain success without Brahmā.

Whatever merit is found in the worship of Kṛṣṇa, and whatever merit is found in the worship of a Liṅga—that fruit shall indeed always be multiplied ten millionfold by the sight of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt, especially on all sacred festival days (parvan).
And you, O Viṣṇu, were told by her: "When you attain birth as a mortal, even there you shall be in the service of others. (11)

Having assumed those two forms, you shall take birth there; for this lineage of mine called the Gopas was described by her, and therein you shall attain growth for a long time for the sake of purification.
One shall be named Kṛṣṇa, and the second shall be designated Arjuna; you shall perform the role of charioteer for that one of yours who is called Arjuna. (13)
Therefore, even though they have committed an improper act, those cowherds shall attain praise from all people and especially from the gods. (14)
And wherever men born of my lineage shall dwell, there, even in the forest, the abode of Śrī shall prevail.
"O Śakra, you have been told by her, filled with anger: 'Having suffered defeat at the hands of his enemy, he shall fall into prison. (16)
Brahmā himself shall effect your liberation according to my word.
Then, having entered into battle, you shall not suffer defeat; for you, O Agni, were called "the consumer of all" by her when she was enraged.
Therefore, even that which is impure will, when touched by your rays from the front, quickly attain purity; thereafter, you shall receive worship.
And my wife named Svāhā shall satisfy the gods, and Svadhā likewise shall satisfy all the ancestors, by my word, without a doubt.

"O Rudra, regarding that separation from your beloved which was mentioned by her, you shall have another wife even more excellent than she; she is the auspicious daughter of Himācala, renowned by the name Gaurī. (21)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Gāyatrī," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Āgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 193.
Sūta said: Having thus granted those boons to all who were subject to her curse, she then became intent upon a vow of silence and sat down upon the surface of the earth.
Then all the hosts of gods, the ascetics, and the great seers, having exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent! to her, spoke these words: || 2 ||
By the grace of the Goddess, all people here in the mortal world, being composed in mind, will especially worship this [image] of the Brāhmaṇas. || 3 ||
But those mortals who, after worshipping Brahmā, subsequently worship this Goddess of the Suras, attain the supreme goal.

That maiden who, having attained union with her husband in this world, remains composed and then performs prostrations at his feet as well as those to Gāyatrī, will undoubtedly become a Prajāpati upon reaching her husband. || 5 ||
Endowed with all the pleasures of the senses and possessed of wealth and grain, that woman who is unfortunate or barren shall become beautiful.
The sages said: Regarding that which was stated by you—"When one hundred and five [ages] had passed, Hara bestowed this unsurpassed [gift] upon the lotus-born"—how did this come to be? (7)
He is content with the Brahmins; or is there another Maheśvara? You ought to explain this doubt of ours to us again, exactly as it is. (8)
Tell us also the measure of the lifespan of Śaṅkara, as well as that of Hari and Brahmā; for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I shall describe to you in detail the established measure of the lifespan for all three [ages].
A fourth part of a nimeṣa is a truṭi; two of those make a lava. Two lavas are said to be a kalā, while fifteen [lavas] make a kāṣṭhā.
They say thirty *kāṣṭhās* make a *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* are considered a *kṣaṇa*. Those skilled in time-measurement (*mauhūrtas*) state that twelve *kṣaṇas* constitute the measure of a *muhūrta*.
A day and night is declared by the wise to consist of thirty muhūrtas; a month consists of thirty days and nights, and two months are designated as a season (ṛtu).
Three seasons constitute an *ayana*, and two *ayanās* make a year; O best of the twice-born, that is indeed one day and night of the gods.
There, the northern course is the day and the other is the night, consisting of seventeen lakh years of human beings. (15)
O virtuous twice-born ones, that first age, the Kṛtayuga, will likewise consist of twenty-eight thousand years.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the second age, the Tretā Yuga, is declared to consist of twelve lakhs and sixteen thousand years. (17)
The third age, Dvāpara, is proclaimed to consist of eight hundred thousand years, along with sixty-four thousand years, according to the correct calculation.
The Yuga arising from Kali is declared to consist of four hundred thousand years; the wise know that fourth [Yuga] to be thirty-two thousand years less.
A thousand cycles of the four yugas constitutes one day of Brahmā; thirty such days make a month for him, and twelve months constitute a year. (2)
Brahmā, their grandfather, lives for as long as a hundred of them; at present, he has remained for eight years and six months.
On this first day of the month, during the second watch of the night while Friday was current, [the vision of] the Great-Souled Tathāgata occurred. || 22 ||
A single day of Viṣṇu is said to consist of one full year of Brahmā.
He too lives for a hundred years according to his own measure; fifty-five years are prescribed for him from the time of his birth.
When five lunar days (tithis) coincide with half a watch (yāmārddha) on a Monday, that day becomes a "Māheśvara" day by the Vaiṣṇava calculation of years.
Śiva remained in that form for a hundred years, until his mouth, from which Sadāśiva had emerged, exhaled.
Afterwards, one attains power until there is exhalation; for all embodied beings, this applies to every inhalation and exhalation. (27)
And for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, as well as for the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, there were twenty-one thousand six hundred and one hundred [verses]. (28)
O best of the twice-born, the measures for day and night have been declared; one *pala* proceeds from six inhalations and exhalations. (29)

A nāḍī is said to consist of sixty palas; sixty of those constitute a day and a night. There is no end to the count of the inhalations and exhalations arising from Sadāśiva; therefore, he is remembered as imperishable.
Others as well who go forth endowed with the knowledge of Brahman become imperishable; this which I have spoken is the truth.
The sages said: "If it is thus, O son of a Sūta, then here Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara undoubtedly go to their destruction when a full hundred of their own years has passed. (32)
O son of Sūta, how then do those who are wise speak of liberation for humans, whose lives in this mortal world are so short? Please explain this.
Surely their discourse regarding the arising of the path to liberation is false.
Sūta said: Time is without beginning or end and is devoid of numerical measure; countless Brahmās, Viṣṇūs, and Maheśvaras have attained liberation.

When their own hundred years have passed, like grains of sand in a river, if those humans possess faith arising from the knowledge of Brahman according to their own measure, they shall undoubtedly attain liberation. (36)

Just as these gadflies, mosquitoes, and insects of humans are born and die, and are not counted anywhere at all, so too are mortals considered in comparison to Indra and the other gods upon the surface of the earth. (37)
Just as mortals stand in the place of insects in relation to the gods, so too should the gods be understood in relation to Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
Just as the gods are situated in the place of a worm for Brahmā, so too is Brahmā situated in the place of a worm for Viṣṇu. || 39 ||
O best of the twice-born, just as the Grandfather [Brahmā] is situated in the place of a worm for Viṣṇu, so too is that [Lord] to be known through Śiva and Śakti. 40.
Just as Viṣṇu is to be known as a worm by those two [names], O best of the twice-born, so too are those two to be understood as having the form of worms for Sadāśiva. (41)
And thus, through various sacrifices with a mind purified by faith, they go from the knowledge of Brahman to that which arises from Sadāśiva. 42.
By performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), they go to heaven for that purpose after having enjoyed various kinds of pleasures.

Furthermore, upon the exhaustion [of their merit], they return to the surface of the earth due to their good deeds; however, having attained that which is superior to the knowledge of Brahman, rebirth no longer exists for them.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice there; thereafter, through many births, one will gradually attain liberation. || 45 ||
In that first birth, he attains a mere fraction of that knowledge; in the second, it becomes twofold, and in the third, it becomes threefold.
In this way, it shall increase by one in each successive birth. || 47 ||
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, if you know it, explain all this to us: how does the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman come about for mortals? (48)
Sūta said: What power do I have to speak regarding this knowledge arising from mortals? How can one who does not know it himself speak of it to another? (49)
O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim to you that supreme instruction which was given to me by my father, arising from the knowledge of Brahman. (50)
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, there are indeed two auspicious holy sites established by two young maidens, which bestow the knowledge of Brahman upon men. (51)
It was fashioned by two maidens, one a Brāhmaṇī and the other a Śūdrī; whoever performs a ritual bath in them on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day [attains merit].
Afterwards, one should worship with devotion the two famous sandals of accomplishment, which are well-concealed, situated within a pit, and have been worshipped by a virgin.
At the end of that year, the knowledge of Brahman arises; and those two, having been deposited by Śakti, are for the sake of increasing one's own vision.
My father went there, which brings the bliss of the knowledge of Brahman to the worlds desiring liberation; and having gone there, he remained possessed of that knowledge. || 55 ||
At his command, I went there and remained for a year; I worshipped the sandals, and thereafter knowledge was firmly established within me.
"Whatever has been heard in the world, whether established in the foremost Purāṇas, or that which is present and that which is yet to come—all that I know, O twice-born ones. (57)
By his grace, the authority of this [work] is established here beyond doubt; for, setting aside the single act of reciting the Vedas, the status of being a Sūta resides in me.
I know his every purpose just as the sage Bhartṛyajña does; therefore, go to him right here if you have a need for liberation.

"What is the use of these sacrifices that grant heaven but cause one to return again? Go and worship those sandals which bestow perfection upon men, by means of which, at the end of a year, the knowledge of Brahman arises. (60)
The sages said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! A great instruction has indeed been given; by it, we have all been delivered from the ocean of saṃsāra. (61)
"We too shall go there to that twelve-year sacrificial session when it is completed; of this there is no doubt, for we are all resolved. (62)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sandals Situated in the Garta-kṣetra at the Two Kumārikā Tīrthas for the Purpose of Attaining the Knowledge of Brahman," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 194 ||
The sages said: "The Śūdrī and the Brāhmaṇī whom you have mentioned—these two unsurpassed holy sites (tīrtha) are located in the field of Hāṭakeśvara."
How did that arise there, or by whom was it created? O Mahāmati, explain all of this in detail.
We have previously heard of the origin of your sandals; tell us also of their majesty and how they came into being.
Sūta said: In former times there was a Brahmin of the Nāgara lineage, renowned as Chāndogya; even in his lineage, O best of Brahmins, there were those renowned as the Chāndogyas.
To him, a knower of the Sāmaveda who lived according to the duties of the householder stage of life, a most beautiful daughter was born when he had reached his later years.
Endowed with all virtues and marked by all the auspicious characteristics, she has seven parts that are red, three that are deep, five that are subtle, and a waist that is not large.
She had large eyes like lotus petals, long hair, and was most beautiful; she had lips like the bimba fruit, fine body hair, and a radiance equal to the full moon.
O best of the twice-born, her father gave her the name Brāhmaṇī, because she was bestowed by the well-honored Brāhmaṇas at the edge of the sacrificial pavilion.
When he had reached his later years and remained childless, that slender-limbed woman grew like the crescent of the moon.

When the bright fortnight had arrived, bringing delight to the eyes of the people, on the very day that [the birth of] the high-souled Chāndogya occurred, a daughter of such form was born to the lord of Ānarta.

By the flood of light from her body, that entire lying-in chamber became brilliantly radiant, as if filled with heaps of jewels, even though it was the onset of night; therefore, her father gave her the name Ratnavatī.
Then that beautiful woman entered into friendship with the brahmin lady, and no separation ever occurred between them.
O best of the twice-born, when she reached her eighth year, her father [provided for her] a single meal, a single bed, and food consisting of a single grain.
He reflected upon her marriage and the selection of a bridegroom; she, for her part, perceiving her father’s intention, was filled with sorrow. (14)
Then Ratnavatī, fearing separation from her friend, spoke, distressed with eyes full of tears and in a voice faltering with sobs. (15)
"Friend, my father will perform my marriage ceremony now; and once I am married, there will never again be friendship between us. (16)
Hearing her words, which were like a thunderbolt falling, that female friend wept, embracing her neck, her senses overwhelmed by affection.
Then, having heard that crying, her mother Mṛgāvatī came in great agitation and spoke these words.
"Why do you weep, my daughter? Who has done you an injury? I shall punish that evil-minded person this very day. (19)
Ratnavatī said: "Listen to me, O most beloved Brāhmaṇī, who is as dear to me as my own life; having obtained marriage, this auspicious woman will depart for her husband's home."
"Deprived of her, I cannot live by any means; for this reason, O Goddess, I weep, being deeply distressed. (21)
Mṛgāvatī said: "If it is so, daughter, then wherever you shall go to the house of your husband, there is a brahmin who is established as the domestic priest (paurohitya) of that king."
I shall give this dear friend of yours to his son; there too, you will have union with her.
Having spoken thus, the queen then summoned Chādogya, the best of the twice-born, and standing bowed with humility, addressed him.
"O Brahmin, this daughter of yours is very dear to my daughter; this passionate woman cannot endure separation from her for even a moment. (258)
Likewise, this daughter of mine is very dear to you and to your daughter; therefore, O observer of noble vows, do as I say and carry out my word.
Whenever this maiden is given by me to a king, my own daughter must be given to that Brahmin who serves as his priest. || 27 ||
O best among the foremost of the twice-born, O virtuous one, by your grace, may there be no mutual division between those two as they remain in one place. (28)
The son of Chāndogya said: "He who, being a Nāgara, gives away his daughter to someone other than a Nāgara, or he who accepts her for the purpose of marriage in any manner whatsoever—" (29)
"That corrupter of the assembly is not a true Nāgara here on earth; therefore, I shall by no means give my daughter to anyone other than a Nāgara—this is the resolve I have made. (30)
The Brahmin woman said: "I shall not go to my husband; I am a maiden living in celibacy. I shall go wherever my dear friend is to be given away."
"O father, if you force me into marriage against my will, I shall either consume poison or enter the fire. (32)
"Or else, my dear father, I shall certainly kill myself with a weapon; knowing this, O father, do whatever is appropriate. (33)
Sūta said: Having learned of her resolve, that brahmin, overcome with grief and fearing the sin of killing a woman, abandoned her and went to his own home. || 34 ||
O best of the twice-born, she too took delight with Ratnavatī, her heart always filled with joy, having completely abandoned her affection for her father.
She attained youth, being peerless in beauty upon the earth.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Daughter of the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 195.
Sūta said: Then, beholding his daughter endowed with youth, possessed of incomparable beauty, and of excellent complexion, the king of Ānarta reflected: "To whom shall I give this maiden? || 1 ||
And he who gives his own daughter to an unworthy suitor out of greed for gain or some ulterior motive goes to hell. (2)
As he was reflecting in this manner, a great length of time passed; yet he did not see any suitable and unsurpassed bridegroom.
Then he dispatched those men who were renowned as painters, skilled in the art of painting, to all the abodes of living beings.
"Go, by my command, to all the kings upon the surface of the earth; having inscribed [their names] within a scroll, show it thereafter. (5)
"Since my daughter, upon seeing that king, has become desirous of him as a husband, there will be no fault on my part, for she is virtuous. (6)
Having heard those words of his, all the painters then set out across the surface of the earth to the houses of the kings.
Having had them drawn, those kings—youthful, of noble lineage, and endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue—were presented before him in due order by that monarch at the command of Ratnavatī.
Then, from among all of them, the noble King Vṛhadbala, the lord of Daśārṇa, was chosen by her as her husband.
Then the delighted lord of Ānarta, having understood well [the situation], sent him [to the bridegroom] for the sake of the marriage and spoke these words.
"Go, in my name, to the lord of Daśārṇa; having approached him with humility, he should be told that he must come into my presence for the sake of my marriage."
Come to your own daughter, so that I may give her to you—she who is renowned by the name Ratnavatī and is the most beautiful even in the three worlds.
Having gone quickly to where King Bṛhadbala was, he clearly related the entire message of the Lord of Ānarta.
Having suddenly heard those most excellent words of theirs, that king attained supreme satisfaction and set out toward that city, accompanied by a great fourfold army.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Return of Bṛhadbala, Lord of Daśārṇa, to the City of the King of Ānarta," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 196 ||
Sūta said: At that very time, O best of the twice-born, there was a Nāgara known as Viśvāvasu, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
When he had reached his later years, a son was born to him, known as Parāvasu, who was always as dear to him as his own life.
When his youth had arrived, he devoted himself to the study of the Vedas, together with esteemed companions who were constantly intent on jesting.
Then, after some time had passed, when the month of Māgha had arrived, he went to the house of his preceptor and engaged in study during the night.
Rising at midnight, protected by all his friends, he reached the house of the courtesan and fell asleep together with her.
Having placed a water vessel filled with water nearby, suitable for his own ritual sipping (ācamana) as well as for drinking.
When the remainder of the night had arrived, he, overwhelmed by thirst and overcome by sleep and lethargy, rose up and left his bed.
The cup of liquor belonging to the prostitute was placed right beneath him; as soon as he took it, he drank the liquor, mistaking it for water.
Then, having fully realized the nature of liquor and abandoned his vessel, he became deeply distressed; having attained supreme detachment, he uttered many lamentations.
"Alas! What a transgression have I committed today while overcome by sleep, that I have drunk this despicable liquor, mistaking it for water? (10)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my purification come about? I shall perform an expiation, even if it be extremely difficult. (11)
Having thus resolved in his mind, when morning had arrived, he reached Śaṅkhatīrtha and performed an excellent ablution there.
Having hurriedly caused his hair, including the top-knot, to be shaved, he went to where [the sage] was staying, devoted to the chanting of the Vedas. || 13 ||
The preceptor, together with his disciples, took refuge in the place of Brahmā; having gone there, he stood at a distance and settled down like an outcaste.
When he was seen by his friends devoid of both beard and hair, he was then struck repeatedly on the head with the tips of their hands out of laughter. (15)
But the preceptor, seeing him dejected, overwhelmed with tears, and shorn of his beard and hair, then spoke to him with affection: ||| 16 ||
"My child, why are you sitting so far away today, bearing such dejection? Come into my presence and tell me: by whom have you been defeated?"
Parāvasu said: "O Guru, having stayed in the house of a prostitute and having recognized my own water-pot [as being used for her], I have now become unworthy of your service. (18)
"O Lord, having taken from her a vessel of liquor filled with wine, grant me a means of purification for the sake of my complete cleansing. (19)
Whatever has been proclaimed in the Dharma-Drōṇas, that I shall perform without doubt. || 20 ||
Then his friends, the young students who were standing there, laughed loudly and spoke to him in the presence of the courtesan as if she were their teacher.
"O King, this maiden known among the people as Ratnāvatī—having grasped her breasts, you shall quickly drink from her lower lip; then your purification will be achieved, and not otherwise. (22)

Parāvasu said: "This is no time for jesting, my friend, now that I am in such a dire state. If you have any affection for me arising from our long-standing friendship, then bring other brahmins and tell them the means of my atonement."
Then, casting aside their jesting and being pained by that sorrow, they approached Viśvāvasu and related the account of what had occurred.
Having heard those words of theirs, which were harsh to the ear, he too, accompanied by his wife, went to the place where his son was staying.
Joined with great suffering, stumbling at every step due to old age as well as grief arising from his son's misconduct. (26)
Then the couple, afflicted by great grief, spoke to their son with voices choked with tears: "Alas, son! What is this that has been done? He too related the entire account of his own deeds to them.

"Therefore, I shall perform an expiation for the sake of self-purification. Then Viśvāvasu summoned brahmins who were learned in the Smṛtis, endowed with knowledge of the Śrutis, and experts in Vedic lore for that purpose.
Then Parāvastu, standing before them with palms joined in reverence, said: "I consumed wine at night without knowing it; having taken up a courtesan’s vessel, I mistook it for my own water-pot."
Having understood this, O best of the twice-born, let such an expiation be granted as is appropriate, by which my purification may arise through your grace.
Having been addressed thus by him, those brahmins who were versed in the Smṛtis consulted the Dharmaśāstra and then spoke to that twice-born man.
If one grants an unworthy penance out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or fear, he partakes in that very sin. || 32 ||
"Therefore, we shall grant you an expiation; if you are able to perform it, then do so with a concentrated mind. (33)
Parāvasu said: "O twice-born ones, if I do not follow your word, then I ask you this: why was I not seen by anyone while I was practicing the drinking of wine? (34)
Therefore, speak what is appropriate for my purification; prescribe an expiation for me, even if it be fierce and life-threatening, otherwise you shall incur sin.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "A twice-born man who, being conscious, should consume liquor, becomes purified by drinking that same amount of molten gold. (36)
