And for those slain by weapons who have certainly attained the heavenly realm, he who does not perform the śrāddha on that specific day when they have passed away [will suffer].
"And his ancestors, their bodies afflicted by hunger and thirst, shall remain in a state of suffering for as long as a year; so said the Grandfather (Brahmā). (34)
Therefore, with every effort, one should have all that performed on that day; if it is done for anyone else, it accrues here to the departed spirits (pretas). || 35 ||
Then the Blessed One granted them that very lunar day for the performance of the śrāddha rite, provided it was performed without a person killed by a weapon. || 36 ||
Even for an embodied being fighting face-to-face in battle, struck by sharp weapons, the mind sometimes wavers.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Śrāddha for the Departed," in the Dialogue between Indra and Viṣṇu, within the *Māhātmya* of the Holy Region of Hāṭakeśvara, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 204 ||
Viṣṇu said: "O thousand-eyed one, knowing this, act according to my word; if those who were slain at the head of the battle are dear to you."
And while fighting in your presence, satisfy them with a śrāddha at Gayā, so that they may all attain liberation from their state as ghosts. || 2 ||
And those who were intent on flight, slain and killed in the back. || 3 ||
Indra said: "Year after year, the Grandfather (Brahmā) then performs a Śrāddha ceremony at Gayā on that day for the ancestors who possess divine forms."

Therefore, O Lord, how may I go there for the sake of accomplishing my faith? For that reason, tell me of something on this earth for the sake of my faith, which grants liberation, so that by your word, O Janārdana, I may go there.
Viśvāmitra said: Then, having meditated for a very long time, Janārdana spoke to him: "There is a great and meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) which is even superior to that."

O Lord of the Gods, on the day of the new moon and on the fourteenth day, Gayā, accompanied by all the holy fords (tīrthas), perfectly migrates there into the center of the small well within the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
The man who performs a Śrāddha ceremony there while the sun is situated in Virgo shall deliver his own ancestors through Brahmins born of eight lineages.
Even those who have fallen into the state of hungry ghosts [are saved], how much more so those residing in heaven; for the Brahmins born in that field originate from eight lineages.
Having undertaken fierce austerities, they dwell on the Himalayan mountains; having come there out of fear of the gifts bestowed by the lord of Ānarta.
Taking them, go there quickly and, out of respect, awaken them; employ those means beginning with conciliation and act before them.
And by performing the ancestral rite (śrāddha) according to the proper rule, you shall thereafter obtain your desire; and all those who have assembled there shall also become happy.
"Indeed, they are to be worshipped by us along with you for the sake of the śrāddha. Upon hearing that, Śakra immediately attained supreme satisfaction.
O Indra among kings, Vāsudeva also then set out with haste toward Himavat and went to the Ocean of Milk.
Even Śakra, having taken refuge on the Himavat mountain, beheld those twice-born ones who were born of the eight lineages and proclaimed by Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Fruit of the Gayā Śrāddha," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth section of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śakra and Viṣṇu. || 205 ||
Viśvāmitra said: Indra also, at the word of Viṣṇu, arrived at the Himavat mountain, having mounted Airāvata, the lord of serpents, who resembled a mountain.

There he saw those sages born of Camatkāra, endowed with restraints and self-discipline, devoted to virtuous conduct, established in the stage of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha), and free from desire and anger.
Some of those Brahmins remained there eating at intervals of one day, others ate only at every sixth meal-time, and still others were devoted to the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

Some remained as stone-grinders, while others used their teeth as mortars; some subsisted on withered leaves, and others likewise lived on water; still others, subsisting only on air, performed most rigorous austerities.
Then, O best of the twice-born, they beheld Śakra arriving there, honored by the Cāraṇas and Siddhas, whom they had never seen before.
All those Brāhmaṇas were addressed by those staying near the hermitage.
"O twice-born ones, this Śakra has arrived at your hermitage; let hospitality be offered to him as prescribed by those who contemplate the scriptures."
Then all those brahmins, their eyes wide with wonder, quickly went forward to face him and stood with their palms joined in reverence.
With their hair standing on end with joy, they all addressed him according to the rites prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, and with humility asked: "What is the reason for your arrival? (9)
O Lord of the Gods, even though he is devoid of effort, our curiosity has been aroused.

Indra said: "Is it well with you, O best of the twice-born, in your performance of the agnihotra sacrifices in their entirety, in all your ascetic practices, as well as in your study and hearing of the Vedas? (11)
"Having abandoned the auspicious holy field of Hāṭakeśvara, which is full of sacred fords, why have you come here to this mountain that causes suffering from the cold?"
Therefore, let all these excellent brahmins come together with me to the meritorious city of Camatkārapura, which is crowded with many sages.
"O best of the twice-born, having gone there now at the command of Vāsudeva, I shall perform a śrāddha with devotion at Gayākūpa."
In your presence, on the fourteenth day when the fortnight of the departed has arrived, the state of moving through the sky has clearly been attained by all of you. (15)
"Accompanied by your children, the elderly, and your wives, and together with your sacred fires, go with me; may prosperity be yours, for there you shall find a dwelling place. (16)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "We shall not go there to Camatkārapura again; for there are other Brāhmaṇas there who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (17)

"There are citizens who are performers of sacrifices, followers of the Smṛtis, and devoted to the Śrutis; perform the Śrāddha ceremony in their presence, if you possess the faith born of the Śrāddha."
Indra said: "Those Brāhmaṇas who have been mentioned by you there—all such as they are—are masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (19)
They were all endowed with learning and Vedic study, especially those who performed sacrifices; yet they were all exceedingly devoted to hatred and spoke harsh words.
Possessed by egoism, desiring to conquer one another, and devoid of austerity, they are attached to sensual enjoyments day and night.
"You have all been praised by Viṣṇu as being endowed with every virtue; therefore, you must all come together with me."
The Brahmins said: "Because of that fault, we have indeed abandoned our own abode, which was endowed with many sacred fords and showed the way to heaven. (23)
If we go there together with you, O Purandara, all our kinsmen will be devoted solely to passion and hatred.
Endowed with envy and unrighteousness, they will constantly commit offenses at every step, speaking with harsh words. (25)
"From that, anger will arise; from anger comes the destruction of ascetic merit (tapas); and because of that, liberation is not attained. Therefore, O Lord, how shall we proceed? (26)
Furthermore, there was a king in that land who was always devoted to charity; he was renowned throughout the entire earth as the lord of Ānarta. (27)
He gives various gifts, such as elephants, horses, gold, and so forth; if we do not accept them there, he becomes angry. (28)
"When the king became enraged and our own kinsmen turned hostile, our success in asceticism was lost; therefore, we abandoned our own city. (29)
"O Lord of Gods, if we accept the gift of that king, there will be a complete destruction of his ascetic merit, for so it was declared by the Self-born One himself. (30)
An oil-presser is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a liquor-seller is equal to ten oil-pressers; a prostitute is equal to ten liquor-sellers; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes. (31)
How then can we accept a gift from him, who is devoted to evil, while all the other citizens are possessed of great greed? (32)
Indra said: "O best of the twice-born, this power belongs to that sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara; it has remained established there for all time. (33)
Of the ancestors and sons, and especially of kinsmen; of mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law, and of sisters and brothers' wives. (34)
Beneath that city resides the Lord himself, known as Hāṭakeśvara; by his majesty, all people [are protected].
Thereupon they are tormented and give rise to mutual hatred. Have you not heard how Rāma, along with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, fell into the greatest conflict? (36)
Filled with rage, O brahmins, he spoke unspeakable words to Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa in their presence; and they, at that time, [responded] to him in the same way.
If one should dwell there for even a month, free from anger, then one attains liberation; by staying for five nights, one becomes a partaker of heaven.
Therefore, you must go there along with me; the citizens will not treat you with the conduct of envy.
"And there shall be no anger on your part toward those residing there; by my grace, O best of Brahmins, this which I have spoken is the truth. (40)
King Ānarta will not employ anyone at all for the purpose of giving gifts, even among your sons and grandsons who shall give away their daughters.
On the new moon day, when the sun is situated in Virgo, the performance of a śrāddha for them will yield a fruit a thousandfold greater. (42)
O best of the twice-born, whoever shall perform [this rite] at Gayākūpī in your presence, the fruit that will accrue to him shall be equal to a hundred thousandfold.
"There is no doubt regarding the *śrāddha* at Gayā; this which I have spoken is the truth. O best of the twice-born, if you do not come there for the sake of performing the *śrāddha*," (44)
"Then I shall indeed bestow upon you a curse that will cause obstacles to your asceticism; knowing this, come there quickly with me. (45)
Having been addressed thus by him, all of them—Kaśyapa, Kauṇḍinya, Ukṣṇāśa, Śārkava, and Dviṣ—in that very moment [departed] together with Śakra.
Baijavāpa was the sixth, and likewise Kāpiṣṭhala Dvika; O King, this group of eight lineages was obtained along with Indra.
Having summoned all the ancestors, beginning with the Agniṣvātta group, as well as the Viśvedevas in their entirety, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) set forth.
Pervaded by right faith toward Camatkārapura, at that very moment, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [arrived]. 49.
On that day, he too set out for Gayā for the sake of performing a śrāddha; meanwhile, the Viśvedevas, having made their promise, set out for Gayā according to the prescribed rite.
Śakra, abandoning his ancestral rites, went to where the Grandfather was; Śakra, having reached that city, arrived at Gayākūpī.
Then, having bathed and filled with faith, he invited the Viśvedevas and the ancestors for the sake of the śrāddha at the time known as Kutapa.
In the meantime, those ancestors who had been summoned by him arrived—both those who were of divine form and likewise those who were of the form of spirits (pretas). || 53 ||
All the Viśvedevas, who had previously gone to Gayā, were then present there in person, having taken their place near the twice-born.
For that reason, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) then made a delay, because the Viśvedevas are to be honored first at a śrāddha ceremony.
In the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived; having approached Śakra, who was longing for the Viśvedevas, he spoke to him.
Nārada said: O Śakra, the Viśvedevas have now gone to the ancestral śrāddha at Gayā; I saw them proceeding there with great joy.
Having heard that, he became enraged at them instantly and, standing before the brahmins, spoke these harsh words.
"O sirs, today I shall perform the śrāddha rite excluding the Viśvedevas; likewise, all other men on this earth shall do so. (59)
Whoever performs a śrāddha here after first placing the Viśvedevas before him, his effort will go to waste, like rain falling upon barren soil.
Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed Indra performed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites in their entirety for all the gods who had been slain at the forefront of the battle.
At that very moment, O best of kings, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O best of kings, [this is for] those for whose sake that śrāddha has been performed."
O Śakra, O Śakra, O mighty-armed one, those for whom you have performed the śrāddha, though they were established in the state of a preta, are now freed from that state of being a preta. (63)
By the grace of heaven, they have gone there assuming divine forms and bodies—those who had previously gone to heaven while fighting in the great battle.
"And they have all attained liberation through your grace, O Vāsava. Hearing those words, Vāsava was filled with great joy.
"Aha! A holy ford! A holy ford!"—praising it again and again, in the meantime, the Viśvedevas arrived, full of eagerness. (66)
O King, having performed the śrāddha for Brahmā at Gayā, they then said to the slayer of Vṛtra: "O Śatakratu, perform the śrāddha here. (67)
Furthermore, the fruit born of a śrāddha cannot be obtained without us; we have come from afar for the sake of your śrāddha, having been previously invited by you to perform the śrāddha for Brahmā.
Having heard those words of theirs, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) became enraged and spoke harsh words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
From this day forward, whatever śrāddha anyone else performs in the world of mortals before you, it shall be in vain for them. (70)
"All people here shall now perform the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha rites; this boundary has been established by me in this world of mortals. (71)
The bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and whoever else are stealers of the śrāddha—those who are protected by the Viśvedevas, I shall protect them as well.
Having diligently joined the power of faith with the body of the sacrificer, all those slain by me shall quickly depart to a distant place.
Having spoken thus to the Viśvedevas, the Thousand-eyed One then addressed all the Brāhmaṇas: "The Śrāddha rite must be performed by you and by other men, even without the Viśvedevas. (74)
When the lords of the twice-born said, "So be it," the Viśvedevas, deeply distressed, wept with a flood of tears that inundated the earth.
O King, by that warm tear of theirs, the earth was flooded, along with numerous beings and countless eggs.
Then, from those eggs, beings of fierce appearance emerged—black-toothed, spike-eared, with hair standing erect, and terrifying; they had red eyes, O King, and then they spoke to the Viśvedevas.
"We are all hungry; let food certainly be given. Since we have been sent by you, we ask for nothing else. (78)
The Viśvedevas said: "Whatever śrāddha may be performed on earth even in our absence, and whatever food shall be yours through supreme faith," (79)
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, all those Viśvedevas, filled with great sorrow, went to the world of Brahmā; and bowing down to the Grandfather, they spoke with piteous voices. (80)
"O Lord, we have been made outsiders by the enemies of Bali, because we went to your śrāddha at Gayā, having been invited there previously. (81)
Because of that, the Thousand-eyed One became enraged; therefore, come to our presence and show us favor, so that we may indeed become worthy of the śrāddha.
Having heard that, Brahmā, filled with supreme compassion, quickly took the Viśvedevas along with those Kūṣmāṇḍas.
Śakra, too, having performed the funeral rites for those celestial beings, remained devoted to pilgrimage to sacred sites and established himself in that very state.
At that very time, Brahmā arrived there, accompanied by the Viśvedevas and mounted upon his swan-vehicle.
Śakra, too, seeing that the Lotus-Seated One had suddenly arrived, took the water for honoring (arghya) and the water for washing the feet (pādya), and quickly went forward to meet him.
Then, bowing his head with all eight limbs in humility, he spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Welcome to you, O Grandfather! (87)
"By the mere sight of you, my three births have been known by me; quickly, I shall perform auspicious deeds as I do now. (88)
I shall accomplish this clearly and without doubt in the next world. || 89 ||
O Lord, though you are free from desire, tell me very quickly the reason for your arrival, so that I may do everything for you. (90)
Brahmā said: O best of gods, those without whom even my own Śrāddha would not take place—those Viśvedevas have today been excluded from the Śrāddha by you.
No good has been done by you, O auspicious one, by performing that action through which the Vedas and likewise the Smṛtis have been rendered invalid.
"O Śakra, these were previously invited by me for the sake of the śrāddha; there is no fault on your part regarding these great-souled ones. (93)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, strive for the sake of their liberation from the curse, so that all these who are now deeply distressed may become worthy of the śrāddha rite.
For this was previously declared by me to all the twice-born: that this aforementioned śrāddha shall indeed be fruitful.
How then do you make my word untrue? || 96 ||
Indra said: "O Grandfather, these have been cursed by me as well while I was filled with anger; therefore, act in such a way that I may remain true to my word."
Brahmā said: "O Vāsava, I shall so arrange it that your word shall come true, specifically for the sake of the Viśvedevas."
All men on the surface of the earth shall perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, which you have described as being performed without the Viśvedevas. (99)
O Lord of the Gods, on that day of the fourteenth of the fortnight of the departed, you ordained for one slain by a weapon— 100.
"Even when the anniversary of his death has arrived, by my word, the auspicious Śrāddha of Nāgara shall be performed without the Viśvedevas. (101)
But whoever shall perform a śrāddha at any other time without them, it will undoubtedly become fruitless for him by my word. (102)

"Excepting one man slain by weapons on that day, whatever person performs a *śrāddha* in that manner, it shall become a feast for all beings. Viśvāmitra said: When Śakra had thus spoken "So be it," Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, was then addressed by the Viśvedevas, who stood before him bowed in humility. (104)
"These sons have arisen from my very tears; O Lord, food has been given by me to them who were afflicted by hunger. (105)
"May this *śrāddha* rite be devoid of us, because of our anger toward Vāsava, so that the word uttered by us may come true. (106)
O Grandfather, act likewise for us and for Vāsava; determine an auspicious meal by which there may be supreme satisfaction.
O Lotus-born One, it is solely through the grace of all these that [this has come to pass].
Padmaja said: At the time of the śrāddha, whatever is placed in the eating vessels of the brāhmaṇas should indeed be discarded by those who draw a line of ashes across them in their entirety.
Wherever any śrāddha shall take place without the protection of ashes—whether it be the ekoddiṣṭa, the pārvaṇa, or even the vṛddhi-śrāddha— [it will be fruitless]. (11)
"And to these very ones, that was now granted by me, being pleased. Having spoken thus, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) then bestowed names upon them.

Since this ground was remembered by the word *ku* and moistened by tears (*aśru*), eggs were produced from it, and from those these thick beings were born; they shall become renowned as *kūṣmāṇḍas* throughout the three worlds. (112)
Then, having divided them into three parts, he assigned them in due order to Agni, Vāyu, and Arka, and spoke these words.
That triad of verses concerning the deities which is renowned in the Yajurveda—by means of that, a portion should be offered to these through a devotional oblation (bhakti-homa). || 114 ||
And from the performance of the *koṭihoma*, by means of [the offering] from the midst of their own respective portions, they shall undoubtedly attain satisfaction through my word. (115)
Having spoken thus, the four-faced one then vanished from sight; likewise, the Viśvedevas were delighted, as were the Kūṣmāṇḍas especially.

For this reason, protection consisting of ashes is placed upon the eating vessels of the Brahmins during a Śrāddha, out of fear of the Kūṣmāṇḍas. Listen, for the Nāgaras do not desire any flaw in their Śrāddha. || 117 ||
Since they were born in their place endowed with courtesy, the protection consisting of ashes was forbidden by them through the splendor of Bhartṛyajña.
For that reason, all the citizens never perform [the rite] at any time; and even Indra, when that four-faced one had departed for his own abode, [did not perform it]. || 119 ||
Standing with palms joined in reverence and bowed down in humility, he spoke to all the brahmins born in Camatkārapura.
"Listen to my words, O Brahmins; thereafter you shall act accordingly. I shall install the Linga of the trident-bearing God of gods. (121)
Then those brahmins showed him that supreme place; he too, having installed the linga, went to heaven filled with joy. || 122 ||
Viśvāmitra said: O lord of men, I have related all this to you that I was asked, as well as the majesty of Gayākūpī, which bestows all desires. || 123 ||
Ānarta said: You have proclaimed to me the greatness of Gayākūpī; now you should also speak concerning that which arises from Bālamaṇḍana. 124.
In what place was that liṅga installed by Śakra? Tell us, O highly fortunate one; for what is the fruit when it is seen? (215)
Viśvāmitra said: "O brahmins, when the Thousand-eyed One was requested by you for the sake of a liṅga—a site that is auspicious, pure, and situated in the center of all sacred fields—" || 126 ||
Then they showed him that most meritorious Liṅga, the ornament of Bāla, where in ancient times the sons of Diti known as the Maruts were born.
By that very [power] they were formerly destroyed, yet they did not meet death; for they recognized that place as most pure, which had been seen by them in the past.
Seeing that supreme place where Diti had performed penance, desiring a noble son, the Lord of the Gods spoke to Jīva.

"O Guru, tell me quickly which auspicious moment is now appropriate, and on which day I may install the excellent *liṅga* born of Hara, which does not suffer destruction even when the dissolution of the universe occurs. (130)
Then, having meditated for a long time, he spoke to that lord of Śacī: "In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, under the Puṣya asterism on a Sunday... (131)
"O Lord, on the thirteenth day, when a desired and auspicious rising of the stars has occurred, install the Liṅga now at my word. (132)
"That divine [object] shall remain firm for you until the end of the kalpa. Having heard that, the king of the gods was filled with great joy. (133)
Then, amidst the chanting of the *puṇyāha* by the Brahmins and the sounds of songs and musical instruments, he installed it in the presence of Bālamaṇḍana. || 134 ||
Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, having gratified the best of the twice-born, he gave them as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) an excellent place called Āghāṭa.
O best of kings, that which is situated on Mount Māṅkūla and adorned with a divine rampart belongs in common to all the Brahmins. (136)
Then, having summoned the Brahmins of the eight lineages, he spoke this to them: "You must always maintain concern for the welfare of the Liṅga. (137)
Since I have granted him a livelihood lasting as long as the moon and sun, that [income] arising from twelve villages must be accepted for his sake. 138.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O best of the gods, we shall not carry out your word. Listen now to the reason arising from our concern regarding the Liṅga. (139)
The property of a Brahmin, the property of a deity, and especially that which arises from a tank—if even a small portion of these is consumed here, it shall destroy all one's ancestors. (140)
If someone born in our lineage should eat it, he will cause us all to fall; therefore, we have great fear of this.
Then that best of the twice-born, standing in their midst, spoke with palms joined in reverence, seeing that Śakra, who had previously rendered him assistance, was distracted in mind.
"I, Devaśarman by name, renowned for my three ancestral lineages, shall perform the rites concerning the origin of your linga. (143)
"O Vāsava, if you grant me a son, for I am childless—one from whom a lineage shall arise until the dissolution of all beings. (144)
"He who knows the Dharma, who is grateful, and who avoids the property of the gods"—having heard this, Vāsava was delighted and spoke to that best of the twice-born.
Indra said: "A most auspicious son shall be born to you, one who will uphold your lineage, righteous in soul, truthful in speech, and a renouncer of the property of the gods. (146)
Furthermore, whatever sons shall be born in the lineage of that great-souled one, they shall all here be like him, masters of the Vedas.
Furthermore, O virtuous twice-born one, hear my words which I shall speak to you; likewise, let all these lords of brahmins who have assembled here listen. (148)
O Four-faced One, at the Bālamaṇḍanaka Tīrtha, this excellent Liṅga was installed by me facing the Four-faced One (Brahmā) according to his command.

Whoever performs the ritual bath here and offers libations to the ancestors at this sacred ford (tīrtha), by him his ancestors will be satisfied as if gratified from the very beginning of their birth.

"O sirs, these twelve villages which have been given by me to this deity—those Brahmins who shall reside there when the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is at hand, having first performed his *śrāddha*, shall thereafter perform [their own] *śrāddha*. (151)
They will perform their duties, being freed from obstacles; prosperity will accrue to them, unless some hindrance should arise. (152)
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, those people residing in that village who had come here with composed minds— || 153 ||
Having bathed at Bālamaṇḍanaka, those who worship this Liṅga with concentrated minds and true devotion shall attain the supreme goal. || 154 ||
Those who shall cause harm to my linga within the villages will, even after a long interval of time, meet their destruction upon arriving here. (155)
Whatever holy places exist on earth, including the oceans and lakes, shall all come to the Bālamaṇḍanaka Tīrtha on that day.
Viśvāmitra said: Having spoken this, the thousand-eyed one, filled with anger, then addressed these words to the twice-born of the Aṣṭakula lineage standing before him. (157)
Whatever words were spoken by these seven brahmin families, I shall crush them, for they are ungrateful; because of their ingratitude, there is no doubt. 158.
For this was previously declared by the truthful Svāyambhuva Manu, pointing it out to all people who are ungrateful.

For the slayer of a Brahmin, for the drinker of liquor, for a thief, for one who has broken his vows, and for a rogue, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
"Brahmins, cows, women, children, and ascetics are not to be slain; therefore, I do not kill these, even though a great opportunity for their destruction exists. (161)
Then, taking water along with darbha grass in his own hand, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, cursed those ungrateful best of the twice-born.
Even after obtaining prosperity through my word, these best of the twice-born shall become destitute, having taken away everything from my gateway.
And the twice-born born in their lineage shall, without a doubt, carry out the abandonment of these devotees; they will be as utterly cruel as I am, all devoid of courtesy, and always gluttonous.
Having spoken thus to those brahmins born of the seven lineages, he then spoke again to the remaining brahmins who resided in the city.
"O best of the twice-born, let a place be given to me right here; so that at the end of the year, I may dwell for five nights in this very spot. (166)
For the sake of the full worship of this deity, for the happiness of the world of mortals, and for the honor of all you Brahmins here. (167)
Viśvāmitra said: Then all those brahmins, being greatly delighted, showed him that excellent place for that purpose and spoke immediately thereafter.
O Śakra, having arrived at the station of Brahmā, you must remain there for five nights; O Lord, may the world of mortals enjoy happiness.

In this place, indeed before you, we shall perform a great festival with the sounds of song and musical instruments, with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, and with the satiation of the twice-born—a festival that grants the fulfillment of all desires. (170)
Viśvāmitra said: Having heard those words of theirs, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) was delighted; having honored all the twice-born ones, he then departed for his abode in the third heaven. || 171 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bālamaṇḍana Tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 206 ||
Viśvāmitra said: O lord of men, I have related all this to you that I was asked, namely the greatness of Bālamaṇḍana, which destroys all sins. || 1 ||

O best of kings, when even a single bath is performed there on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, the merit arising from bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas) is obtained. || 2 ||
Ānarta said: Why is it that on the surface of the earth, the abode of Śakra and the Pañcarātra do not arise for them in a manner superior to that of other inhabitants of heaven?
At the end of the rainy season, on which days does Śakra descend to the surface of the earth? In which month? Tell me all of this.
Viśvāmitra said: Listen, O lord of the earth, I shall relate this story to you—how, after five nights, Śakra was no longer present upon the surface of the earth.
Formerly, in the Bṛhatkalpa, there was Jayatsena, the lord of the gods, the master of the entire three worlds, who destroyed the pride of the Dānavas.
Indeed, she was always receiving worship throughout the entire three worlds; then, after some time, [there was] the beloved wife of the sage Gautama.
He had a wife named Ahalyā, who was peerless on earth in her beauty; seeing her, Śakra fell under the sway of the god of love and desired her.

O King, whenever Gautama had gone out for the sake of sacrificial fuel, grass, fruits, or roots—indeed, whenever he was away—that enjoyer of desires would always come from the heavenly world in person, accompanied by those great-souled ones.
Then Nārada, the best of sages, related to him all the deeds of Śakra as well as that which had arisen concerning Ahalyā.
Having heard that, Gautama went quickly and immediately to his home, where he saw the Lord of the Gods arrived together with his wife.
Śakra too, upon seeing Gautama, became intent on flight; agitated by fear, he departed from that hermitage even though he was naked.
Ahalyā too, seeing her husband arrived, stood with her face cast down, O King, trembling with fear and her senses overwhelmed. (13)
And Gautama, O great king, having witnessed that conduct of his wife, gave her a curse with eyes bloodshot with anger.
"O Śakra, because you have committed such a despicable evil deed—corrupting my virtuous wife—therefore, become one who is without testicles. (15)
"And let there be a thousand vulvas upon your face without delay, by which you shall bring about the ruin of the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile. (16)
Furthermore, O Vāsava, if you come here to this mortal world for the sake of worship, then your head shall shatter into a hundred pieces.
Having thus cursed Śakra, he then spoke to Ahalyā, his eyes bloodshot with anger, rebuking her again and again. (18)
"Since this despicable deed was committed by you out of wickedness, therefore, having become made of stone, remain upon the surface of the earth. (19)
Then, at that very moment, she became his wife in the form of stone; and Indra likewise became deprived of his two testicles.
Indeed, there appeared on the region of his face the mark of a thousand lotuses.
Then, having reached a secluded cave on Mount Meru, Hari, filled with shame, constantly resorted to it and did not return to his own city.
Then all the hosts of gods, filled with anxiety and deprived by him, did not know his location there, though they remained intent on searching the caves. || 23 ||
When Virājaka was born in heaven, the world was oppressed by fierce Dānavas.
In the meantime, Jīva was questioned with agitation by Śakrāṇī, who was terrified with fear: "Where has Purandara gone? (25)
Then Jīva, having meditated for a long time and beheld him with the eye of knowledge, went forth accompanied by the gods and spoke very harshly.
"Why have you abandoned the enjoyments of sovereignty in this way and taken refuge in solitude? What meditation have you practiced, or what fierce austerity have you undertaken? (27)
Having heard the words of Bṛhaspati, Indra, his face covered with shame, spoke dejectedly, overwhelmed with tears.
"I shall not rule even over the three worlds under any circumstances; behold how my condition has become such because of the sage Gautama. (29)
With a face marked by a thousand sexual organs, how shall I present myself before those gods, as well as Paulomī and Śiva?
O Bṛhaspati, my worship arising from the mortal world has perished due to the curse of the sage Gautama for some particular reason.
Having heard that from the king of the gods, Bṛhaspati, overcome with great sorrow and surrounded by all the deities, went into the presence of Gautama and spoke to him himself.
O Brahmin, now that Śakra has abandoned it, even this entire triple world is being oppressed by the Dānavas, and its sacrificial rites and festivals have perished.

"Filled with profound shame, he does not desire his own kingdom; therefore, O best of the twice-born, you ought to grant him favor according to the rules. By my word, O most excellent of brahmins, you should revoke the curse through your grace. (34)
Having heard that, Gautama said: "My word shall not be false; I will not violate the word that was spoken by you yourself. (35)
Then Viṣṇu himself and Maheśvara spoke to them, as did all the hosts of gods who stood there bowed in humility.
Otherwise, the word of Brahmā cannot be made to prevail by you. Therefore, O best of Brahmins, grant the grace of a mitigation for the curse of Hari.
Seeing the firmness of his mind, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, approached Brahmā and reported everything to him.
Thus, the curse of Śakra arose from that great sage.
Just as this contemptible mockery was perpetrated against the king of the gods, so too has the entire triple world been thrown into turmoil by the Dānavas. (40)
Having heard how that husband of Śacī was ashamed and did not exercise his sovereignty, the Lotus-born One (Brahmā), accompanied by Hari and Śambhu, quickly [departed].
He went to the place where the sorrowful Indra resided; and the Grandfather (Brahmā), having summoned Gautama, remained right there.
Then he spoke in the presence of the gods and Vāsava: "O best of sages, that which has been done by the king of the gods is improper."

Since your wife was corrupted by you whose mind was struck by lust, there is no fault in you; that Purandara was cursed because of this vulnerability. Indeed, supreme forbearance is always praised as the highest virtue among sages.
Just as Śatakratu himself exercises sovereignty over the three worlds, so too should policy be carried out by you through your own grace. (45)
"Having given him testicles and having further destroyed these vulvas, act in such a way that his destination shall be in the world of mortals. (46)
Having heard those words of theirs, out of reverence for the gods, that sage then joined his two testicles, which had been produced from rams.
Having touched those parts with his hand, the excellent sage created eyes; then Gautama, of great asceticism, spoke to those gods.
"O best of gods, this thousand-eyed Śakra has been created by me; he shall possess the testicles of a ram and rule his own kingdom. A beautiful splendor born of eyes shall appear upon his face. (49)
"And his masculinity shall be restored by means of two testicles produced through medicine; furthermore, there shall be no opportunity for him to receive worship while among mortals. (50)
In the meantime, the thousand-eyed Purandara was born, endowed with supreme splendor through the power of that sage.
Then, having grasped the feet of the high-souled Gautama in the assembly of all the gods, Śakra spoke these words: || 52 ||
O best of Brahmins, worship arising from the mortal world is difficult to obtain; act in such a way that it may be mine through your grace. (53)
"O twice-born one, let not this consciousness born of the Lord of the Three Worlds go to destruction; by your grace, let it be so ordained that it may remain eternal. (54)
Having heard that, the excellent sage, overcome with shame and compassion, spoke to Indra, the subduer of Pāka, in the presence of all the gods.
And for five nights, your worship shall take place in the mortal world; you shall attain a satisfaction that is no different from what you would experience over an entire year.
In whatever country, city, or village there is a great festival for five nights, the people there shall remain free from disease for the duration of a year.
There shall be neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor any famine whatsoever; there shall be no destruction of the king, nor any unhappiness anywhere in the world. (58)
O Purandara, in that place where your great festival shall take place, there the cows will abound in milk; the people will have plenty of food, they will be happy, and free from all calamities.
Indra said: "If this is so, then when autumn has arrived—charming to all living beings, strewn with *saptacchada* trees, and beautifully adorned with *bandhūka* flowers—" (60)
In a place permeated with the fragrance of jasmine, abounding in fresh crops, illuminated by the light of the moon's rays, and filled with the humming of bees.
In that place filled with white and blue lotuses, there shall be a great festival; therefore, perform it so that everyone, whether young or old, may be filled with joy. 62.
Gautama said: Today, under the Śravaṇa asterism—a meritorious lunar mansion belonging to Viṣṇu, free from all sins—this great festival has been granted to you.
"My wife was violated by you under the lunar mansion named Pūṣan; therefore, O Purandara, your fall will clearly come to pass under that very one. (64)
By means of this, let my fame and your deed of speaking thus become renowned in this world, so that no one might commit sin. (55)
The five asterisms beginning with Śravaṇa shall each individually be equal to five sacrifices for the sake of your worship; there is no doubt that they will embody all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Whoever, having meditated upon whatever desire, shall perform worship to you especially with fruits and flowers, shall obtain all of that in its entirety. || 67 ||
Furthermore, your image shall never be worshipped anywhere; you have defiled my wife, a Brahmin woman who is as dear to me as my own life. (68)
Therefore, Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas will, according to their ability, install a staff made from that tree using all of your mantras.

"O Thousand-eyed One, according to the ritual procedure of the Pañcarātra as practiced by other celestial dwellers, you must then perform the transition and accept worship originating from mortals; in this way, you will find satisfaction. (70)
O Vāsava, whoever shall awaken this sleeping staff exactly as it is, for that person alone will there be superior success.
He who is devoted to the Pañcarātra vow and dedicated to celibacy shall perform your worship with fruits and flowers as prescribed.
He shall attain complete liberation from all sins committed through another's wife.
Homage to Śakra, the god; homage to you, Śunāsīra! Homage to you whose hand holds the thunderbolt; homage to you whose hand wields the vajra! || 74 ||
O Śakra, whoever shall offer you this arghya with this mantra, all the sin committed through another's wife shall depart from him. (785)
O Purandara, whoever shall proclaim this dialogue of yours with me with true devotion, and likewise listen to it, [shall attain the highest goal]. (76)
"For him, no disease shall arise for as long as a year. Having heard that, all the gods, saying "So be it," were filled with great joy.
Taking Śakra with them, they returned once more to Amarāvatī; Gautama, however, went to his own dwelling, overcome with anger.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Great Festival of Indra," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 207 ||
Viśvāmitra said: When Śakra had thus reached heaven and all the gods were present, Gautama returned to his own hermitage, blazing with great anger.
Then he related everything regarding the deeds of the gods and the granting of the boon to Śakra in the presence of Śatānanda.
Having heard that, standing bowed in humility, he said to his father: "Father, why do you not show me favor toward my mother? (3)
O All-pervading Lord, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by you in raising [the dead]; therefore, grant me your grace so that it may come to pass for me and my mother.

O best of sages, this is a meeting for one who is wretched and full of longing. Therefore, quickly rouse her and then prescribe the procedure for expiation; therefore, instruct me swiftly so that purification may arise.
Gautama said: "If purification occurs for a vessel smeared with liquor, then purification occurs for women through the sprinkling of semen into the womb."
A Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor is purified by the Mauñjī-homa; likewise, having performed the Tiṅginī rite, he is cleansed, but this does not apply to a woman who has violated her dharma.
Just as a liquor vessel is generally purified when properly cleansed by fire, so too a woman is purified when burnt by fire—even she into whose womb the semen of another has entered. (8)
For this reason, O son, that stone was fashioned by me as your mother; for there can be no purification of it whatsoever.
Śatānanda said: "If this is so, for his sake I shall enter the fire, or I shall consume poison, or I shall throw myself into the water."
O dear one, because of separation from my mother, this which I have spoken is the truth; likewise, other sages such as Manu and others remain as repositories of dharma.
"O father, having reflected upon all the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and many Vedāntas, grant that same purity to me as well; otherwise, I shall bring about the destruction of my mother's life. (12)
Viśvāmitra said: Having heard that and meditated for a very long time, Gautama embraced his son with both arms, smelled the crown of his head, and then spoke to him.
"If it is so, my child, do not commit this rash act that gives rise to sin; listen to my words regarding the destruction of your own body. (14)
I have previously known the purity regarding your mother's fitness for sacrifice; by that, she will undoubtedly become worthy of my palace. (15)

"In the lineage of the Sun, Janārdana will be born in the form of Rāma, having assumed a human body for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa. By the touch of his foot, you shall become pure once again. Therefore, my dear son, wait for that time and do not fall into anxiety. This I have fully known, my child, through my divine vision. (18)
Having heard this and saying "So be it," Śatānanda, who was devoted to his mother, stood there filled with great joy, awaiting that time.
Then, after a long time, Janārdana in the form of Rāma was born in the household of Daśaratha for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa.

That Blessed Viṣṇu, who was present in the form of a child, was brought by me to my own hermitage for the protection of my sacrifice and for the destruction of the Rākṣasas who were destroying the sacrificial rites. (21)
My sacrifice was completed by those fierce Rākṣasas who were slain; that descendant of Raghu was brought here to me from Ayodhyā. || 22 ||
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of Sītā’s marriage, he heard of her svayaṃvara and the gathering of kings.
Then, on the way, I saw Ahalyā in Gautama’s auspicious hermitage; she was in the form of a stone, exceedingly large in size.

Then I said to Rāma, "O child, touch this with your hand, so that she may regain her human state; for due to the fault of a curse from the sage Gautama, this beloved wife of that noble sage has become a stone. (25)
Then, O best of kings, Rāma, filled with curiosity, touched that stone without hesitation at my word. (26)
Then, as soon as she was touched by Rāma, O Sage, that woman, though born of human origin, shone forth, assuming a divine form and body.
Then, overcome with shame, she prostrated before Gautama, remembering her own deed that had been instigated by Śakra.
"O my lord, grant me the expiation for everything without exception—that which Prajāpati has declared for a man's union with another's wife. (29)
"I shall perform even this difficult task, of this there is no doubt, so that through the practice of *puraścaraṇa* my purification may be attained. (30)
Then, having reflected for a very long time, Gautama spoke at that time: "Perform a hundred *cāndrāyaṇa* penances and a thousand *kṛcchra* penances. (31)
Devoted to pilgrimage for ten thousand years, you will attain complete purification by properly beholding those sixty-eight sacred sites that exist upon the earth.
Having promised "So be it," she remained constantly devoted to her vows, visiting in succession the sixty-eight sacred fords, beginning with Vārāṇasī.
Wandering about, she worshipped those lingas with great devotion, and in due course, she arrived at the place of origin of Hāṭakeśvara.
As soon as that virtuous woman looked, she saw that the great serpent-hole, the path leading to the netherworld, was filled with serpents.
The great sages, devoted to pilgrimages, used to go there first for the purpose of beholding the god Hāṭakeśvara. || 36 ||
Then she reflected: "If the Lord of the Gods, the deity Hāṭakeśvara, is not seen, one will certainly not obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage."
Therefore, I shall perform austerities, remaining steadfast even in what is most difficult to do, so that by their power I may behold that Lord of the Gods.
Having thus made her resolve, she performed most difficult austerities for the sake of beholding the god who dwells in the netherworld.
That ascetic woman practiced the penance of the five fires in the summer, stayed in water during the winter, and slept in the open air during the rainy season.
Having then installed a mobile liṅga in his own name near that [fixed one], he worshipped it three times a day with perfumes, flowers, and unguents.
While she remained thus established in austerity, a great length of time passed, yet no vision of the one born of Hāṭakeśvara occurred.
Then, after some time, her son Śatānanda, his soul overwhelmed by maternal affection and intent on visiting sacred fords, arrived at that field while searching for her. (43)
Then, having beheld her there established in that severe asceticism, he bowed down and stood before her in a wretched state, and, filled with sorrow, spoke these words.
Why is this body being tormented here by performing such extremely severe penance at the sixty-seven sacred fords and at those lingas located there? (45)
Those Liṅgas of Maheśvara have been seen by you; this one, situated in Pātāla, is known as Hāṭakeśvara.
No man saw her in the field, nor was she seen by anyone; therefore, the purity that had been established by her own husband was indeed maintained. 47.
Therefore, come, let us go to our father’s auspicious hermitage; our father watches for your path, just as a farmer watches for rain.
Ahalyā said: "O Lord, as long as I do not see the deity known as Hāṭakeśvara, I shall not go to my home; only when I see that Hara will I return. (49)
"Then, my son, I shall go home; this is the resolve I have made. (50)
Having heard that, he also said to her: "If this is indeed your resolve, then I too must go to my father's presence along with you."
Having spoken thus, he then installed that Śāmbhava Liṅga and, remaining established in austerity, worshipped it three times a day.
The royal sage Śatānanda, however, gratified him with perfumes, flowers, ointments, various food offerings, and Vedic hymns.

O Sage, as he remained thus—observing the vow of eating only at every sixth mealtime and devoted to the practice of his religious observances—a great deal of time passed; yet the Lord of Gods was not satisfied with those two in any way whatsoever.
Then, after a long time, the great sage Gautama himself arrived there, longing for the sight of his son.
Seeing his son established in asceticism along with his wife, he was first pleased, but afterwards he was filled with sorrow.
"Alas! What great misery; my son has become emaciated. By the power of my asceticism, how shall I lead him to my own home? And likewise, this wife of mine stands before me pale and wasted. (57)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he addressed them both: "Return to your own home, having brought your ascetic penance to an end."
Śatānanda said: "O father, mother, you have been entreated in many ways to desist from your penance; yet she does not go to the palace as long as Hāṭakeśvara has not been seen."
"But deprived of you, I shall certainly not go; knowing this, O illustrious one, do what is appropriate. (60)
Gautama said: "If such is the firm resolve, my child, both yours and that of your mother, I shall show you Hāṭakeśvara through the power of asceticism."
Having spoken thus, that great sage then performed penance; for a hundred years the sage remained fasting on alternate days, and during that time he subsisted on food only at every sixth meal-time.

Thereafter, that lord of sages became one who eats only once every three nights; for that duration he subsisted on fruits, for that duration he lived on water, and thereafter the sage remained for a further period subsisting only on air.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, when [the time] had reached its ultimate limit, that supreme Liṅga emerged, bursting through the surface of the earth.
Resembling twelve suns and endowed with all auspicious marks, in that very interval, the Lord Śambhu became manifest.
At that very moment, the Lord who bears the moon upon his crest came within the range of his vision and spoke these words.
"O Gautama, O you of noble vows, I am well-pleased with this austerity of yours."
And this Linga of mine, known by the name Hāṭakeśvara, has emerged from the netherworld (Pātāla) because of your devotion, O great sage. (68)
Indeed, for this very purpose you, together with your wife and your son, performed that penance; and its entire fruit has now been realized exactly as desired. (69)
"Let your wife Ahalyā behold this, so that she may obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage resulting from the sixty-eighth [year]. (70)
And you too, choose a boon, so that I may grant it all to you.

Gautama said: Whatever fruit arises for men from seeing the place known as Hāṭakeśvara even once, and whatever merit arises from being situated in Pātāla—that same merit is obtained by seeing this [liṅga], and especially by worshipping it.
Furthermore, whatever other people worship that [liṅga] with great devotion on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, may they go to heaven.
Men desiring spiritual perfection do not recognize this Liṅga; therefore, they enter the cave out of a longing for Hāṭakeśvara.
Even those endowed with sins, by the power of this Linga, [are freed] from the sin arising from another's wife through the sight of Ahalyeshvara. (79)
In that same manner, human beings are also liberated by means of the worship performed by those two on that very day at Śatānandeśvara.
Viśvāmitra said: At that very time, O King, the entire heaven was overrun by men who were rich in sin and devoid of all righteousness.
No one performs a sacrifice, nor a pilgrimage to sacred fords, nor any other [rite]; neither a vow nor a religious observance, nor even a word of discourse regarding charity. (78)
And having seen those three marks, touched them, and worshipped them with devotion, || 79 ||
Then all the gods, filled with fear and surrounded by rivaling humans, went to Purandara and spoke to him, overcome with distress.
O Thousand-eyed One, in the world of mortals all dharmas have gone to ruin; even men of sinful conduct come here. (81)
Filled with pride, they always compete with us. In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, there are three unsurpassed Liṅgas. (82)
That which was established and installed there by the high-souled Gautama, together with his son and his wife, [endures] through the power of its worship. (83)
Even all those of evil conduct come here; consequently, all the hells of Yama have now become empty. (84)
Having propitiated the Lord of the Gods at that very spot through austerity, Gautama brought Hāṭakeśvara from Pātāla. || 85 ||
Through its power, this worldly convention has arisen upon the surface of the earth.
Knowing this, act in such a way that the sacrifices proceed; without them, there can be no satisfaction for us whatsoever.
Having heard that, Vāsava summoned Manmatha there, as well as Wrath, Greed, Hypocrisy, and Envy joined with Hatred. (98)
Then, having gone quickly to the surface of the earth at my command, all of you must, by your own power, restrain those who worship Gautameśvara. 89.
Having received the command of Śakra, they went to the surface of the earth to [the shrines of] Ahilyeśvara-deva and Śatānandeśvara.
Kāmādika and others took possession of those men who worshiped Gautameśvara, as well as Ahilyeśvara and Śatānandeśvara. || 91 ||
Then, once again, sacrifices were performed throughout the entire surface of the earth; all of them were accompanied by complete sacrificial fees, as were the vows and religious observances. (92)
Pilgrimage to sacred fords, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and whatever other virtuous deeds there may be—all this has been declared by me, O Lord of the Earth, as you asked. (93)
In connection with Gayākūpī, [this describes] the deeds of Śakra and Gautama, the majesty of Bālamaṇḍana, together with that of Śakreśvara.
The establishment of Indra among mortals, the narrative of Ahalyā, the majesty of Gautameśvara, and likewise that of Ahalyeśvara; || 95 ||
And whoever should constantly hear this, endowed with supreme faith, shall be instantly liberated from the sin arising from another's wife.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gautameśvara, Ahalyeśvara, and Śatānandeśvara," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 208 ||
Ānarta said: O tiger among sages, tell me now the complete majesty arising from Śaṅkha-tīrtha; great faith has arisen within me.
"Oh, what a sacred ford! Oh, what a sacred ford is this known as Hāṭakeśvara! It is a field upon the surface of the earth, auspicious and filled with every wonder. (2)
O best of the twice-born, I do not attain satisfaction in any way while listening to the great majesty and the origin of this sacred field.
Viśvāmitra said: In this regard, I shall relate to you another ancient narrative concerning the greatness of Śaṅkha-tīrtha, exactly as it occurred upon the surface of the earth.
Formerly there was another lord of the earth, the sovereign of Ānarta, just as you are now on this earth, the protector of all people.
Suddenly, that best of kings became afflicted with leprosy and his limbs became deformed; he was childless, beset by enemies, and filled with fear.
Harassed on all sides by all the rulers of the earth and having suffered the loss of his kingdom, he reached Mount Raivataka.
Even there, he is constantly oppressed on all sides by thieves.
When he became deprived of elephants, horses, and chariots, and was likewise destitute of treasury, he then reflected: "What shall I do now? (9)
Even all their wives are forcibly carried away by thieves.
Thinking thus, O tiger among kings, he went indeed to see the omnipresent Nārada when the day sacred to Viṣṇu had arrived.
There he beheld Nārada, the best of sages, who had arrived in the course of his pilgrimage with the desire to see Dāmodara.
Then, having bowed to him with his head and standing with palms joined in reverence, he sat down before him and spoke these words in a piteous manner.
The king said: "O best of sages, I have been utterly defeated by my enemies; consequently, due to the loss of my kingdom, I have arrived here upon this great mountain. (14)
"In this forest, I am being tormented on all sides by wicked thieves; whatever horses, elephants, and so forth have come along with me—" || 15 ||
All of that—treasuries, wives, and wealth—has been carried off by thieves. Therefore, O best of sages, speak to me, for great detachment has taken hold within me. (16)
O best of sages, whatever extremely terrible sin of mine has arisen from any other birth, by which I have suddenly reached this state—[may it be destroyed]. (17)
Having heard those words of his and having meditated for a long time, the lord of sages, perceiving the king’s distress with his divine eye, then spoke to him.
Nārada said: "O great king, nothing censurable was ever done by you in a previous body; I have known all this through my divine vision. (19)
Formerly, you were a king of the Lunar dynasty in the city known as Siddhapannaga, the destroyer of all enemies.
By you, great sacrifices were performed with complete sacrificial fees; great gifts were bestowed, and the most excellent brahmins were honored. (21)
By the ripening of that karma, he again attained the status of a king.
Ānarta said: "O Lord, I do not recall any duty performed by me in this birth; why then has this sudden fall from my kingdom arisen? (23)
O tiger among sages, I have now realized that for a person devoid of fortune, life in this world becomes utterly futile. (24)
A man who has lost his fortune is as good as dead; a kingdom without a king is dead; a gift given to one who lacks Vedic learning is dead; and a sacrifice without sacrificial fees is dead. (25)
Even a kinsman becomes an enemy to a mortal man who is bereft of fortune; seeing him, he will surely beg from me, and having seen that [other], he will go elsewhere. (26)
"Just as those whom I have already gratified depart even further away upon seeing me now, so too will he seek me out. (27)
Abandoning a man who is devoid of wealth, even if he be of noble birth and most excellent, one's own kinsmen go elsewhere, just as birds desert a withered tree.
If a poor man approaches the house for the sake of that cause and effect, the wealthy scold him and do not come near him.
Even if a miser is wealthy, when he comes to beg, the thought arises in men's minds: "He will give me something. (30)
"You belong to my former lineage, and your father was always devoted to affection for my father; yet you yourself have been devoid of affection. (31)
Speaking thus, even those of noble birth are seen standing before the wealthy in this world out of a desire for riches; yet they would rather see a poor man exercising sovereignty on earth.

O great sage, there will be nothing but the withering of the heart. These two are sharp thorns that cause the body to wither: he who, being poor, desires [wealth], and he who, being powerless, becomes angry. (33)
Greedy for wealth, they frequent even cremation grounds at the onset of night; having abandoned even their own progenitor, they always go very far away.
Even one who is utterly foolish may become a scholar, and even one of low birth may belong to a noble family, provided he possesses wealth that is righteous; otherwise, it is the reverse. (35)
"O best of sages, I am now weary of life; therefore, tell me why this poverty has come upon me. (36)
"You have seen with your divine eye another previous birth of mine, in which I was afflicted by leprosy and suffered defeat at the hands of enemies. (37)
"O best of sages, you tell me that I am not touched by even the slightest evil deed; I remember having seen this [state] in a previous birth. (38)
"O virtuous sage, I have never at any time committed any evil deed; why then has this loss of my kingdom occurred? (39)
In this matter, curiosity has arisen within me; therefore, grant me a definitive conclusion: does the karma that has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, exist or not? (40)
Viśvāmitra said: Having heard those words of his and having meditated for a long time, Nārada, overcome with supreme compassion, then spoke respectfully. (41)
Listen, O King, I shall explain how purification comes about, and how the recovery of your kingdom may once again be achieved. (42)
Upon your land lies a field of great merit, renowned throughout the three worlds; there exists a beautiful holy site known as Hāṭakeśvara, celebrated as Śaṅkhatīrtha, which destroys all sins. (43)
Whoever performs a bath there, endowed with supreme faith, when the eighth day of the bright fortnight has arrived in the month of Mādhava; || 44 ||
When Sunday arrives at the time of the sun's rising, one becomes free from all leprosy and becomes like the sun itself.
Whatever desire one may contemplate, even if it be difficult for all to attain, one obtains that without doubt upon beholding the auspicious Śaṅkheśvara. (46)
O King, have you not heard of the majesty of that sacred site while residing in your own country, such that you have come here?
Siddhasena said: O virtuous sage, tell me how the god Śaṅkheśvara came to be manifested.
Nārada said: O King, I shall relate to you this ancient narrative of how Śaṅkheśvara and Śaṅkhatīrtha came into being.
Formerly, there were two Brāhmaṇas, Likhita and Śaṅkha; they were brothers, learned in the Vedas, and established in severe austerity.
Then, after some time had passed, O King, he arrived at the hermitage of his elder brother, who was engaged in writing, in order to offer his salutations.
He saw the hermitage empty, devoid of any written record.
Then, seeing ripe fruits in that forest, he took them out of affection, thinking it was his brother’s royal hermitage.
In the meantime, Likhita arrived at that hermitage; there he saw Śaṅkha holding a large fruit.
"What is this evil deed you have committed, an act of wickedness censured by the virtuous? This despicable work of theft, that the fruits were taken by you! (55)
By this deed, the ascetic merit of you—who have engaged in the act of theft and are censured by the Brahmins—will go to complete destruction.
Śaṅkha said: "It is a well-known and universally established Vedic tradition in the world that a brother born from the same womb is like a father to his elder brother. (57)
O best of Brahmins, O Lord, does a son then have no right to his father’s wealth, that you thus revile me with such harsh words? (58)
Likhita said: "In this matter, no fault whatsoever arises for the son who takes [the property]; for the father's wealth is undoubtedly situated in one place [within him]. (59)
But when a son or a brother who has already been partitioned should take away wealth, he incurs the fault arising from theft; this is my settled opinion. (60)
Furthermore, the father always takes back the wealth of his son; there is never any fault in this, even if [the son] has already been divided [from the estate]. (61)
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by Manu, the author of the Smṛti; that speech arising from the Dharmaśāstra I shall now proclaim to you. (62)
Only three have been declared [to be non-independent]: the wife, the slave, and likewise the son; whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. 63.
Śaṅkha said: "If, O father, such a great fault of theft exists in me, then punish me quickly so that there may be no loss of my ascetic merit."

Viśvāmitra said: Having learned of his resolve, the pitiless brother took up a stainless weapon and then severed the arms of his brother; even though his hands were cut off, that brahmin was nonetheless filled with agony. (65)
O King, he considered that to be the favor of his eldest brother.
Then, considering that field named Hāṭakeśvara to be the granter of desires, he reached it and, having found a certain body of water, performed penance.
During the rainy season he slept under the open sky, in the winter he resorted to water, in the summer he practiced the penance of the five fires, and he took food only at every sixth mealtime.

Having bathed the Sun and Sthāṇu (Śiva) before them, while reciting the Śatarudriya and the Rudras as declared in the Sāma Veda, likewise reciting the Bhava-rudras, the Prāṇa-rudras, the Nīlas, together with the Skanda-sūkta; || 69 ||
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara was pleased with him; having appeared before his eyes, he spoke together with Sūrya and Vṛṣeśvara.
Maheśvara said: "O Śaṅkha, O child of noble vows, I am pleased with this austerity of yours; therefore, tell me quickly what I shall grant to you now."
Śaṅkha said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, let my hands become as they were before."
"O Lord of the foremost gods, having shown me the greatest compassion, O God, you must always make your residence right here in this Liṅga. (73)
"O Lord, let this reservoir of water become famous on the surface of the earth under my name for as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars endure. (74)
O Lord, whoever performs a bath here while holding in their mind some rare object, that entire thing shall be accomplished for them. (75)
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of brāhmaṇas, since I have obtained your vision today on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava."
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall undoubtedly perform my transition into this Linga of yours for one full day; of this there is no doubt.
And whoever, when this day has arrived, performs a bath right here at this sacred ford (tīrtha) originating from Bhava, as the rising of the Sun approaches on a Sunday; || 78 ||
"O twice-born one, he who shall worship my image installed by you will be liberated from the disease of leprosy and go to my world. (79)
O best of Brahmins, even at other times, he will undoubtedly attain liberation from the sin committed through ignorance by my word, O most excellent of the twice-born. (80)
Likewise, these two hands of yours that have been severed shall both become just as they were before through the consecration in that yoga. (81)
O Brahmin, this shall now be my proof for you: having performed your bath once more, you must then worship my image.
Others as well who have attained deformity shall, while you remain in this conjunction, bathe and worship me; O twice-born one, they shall attain liberation. (83)
Having spoken thus, the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) then vanished from sight; Śaṅkha also, having bathed at that very moment, worshipped the Maker of Day.
As soon as he saw himself, he saw that he was endowed with hands; beholding himself thus, he was struck with the utmost wonder. (85)
From that time forward, O King, that best of the twice-born established his hermitage in that very place and performed austerities; he then attained the supreme goal.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, having attained this conjunction in its true essence, you too should bathe according to that very same rite and worship the Sun.
Whoever should constantly hear this or recite it before the Sun, not even a single person in their lineage shall ever be born with leprosy.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Origin of Śaṅkhāditya and Śaṅkhatīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 209 ||
Viśvāmitra said: Having heard those words of the celestial sage Nārada, King Siddhasena attained that supreme yoga.
When the month of Mādhava has arrived, on the eighth lunar day falling on a Sunday, at the moment of sunrise, one should bathe and worship the Sun.
At that moment, he was suddenly freed from leprosy; then, having assumed a divine body, he attained supreme satisfaction. || 3 ||
Then he performed an expiation for the chewing of betel leaf, which had been done unknowingly along with its lime and leaf.
Thereupon, having attained supreme prosperity, that lord of the earth governed his ancestral kingdom just as he had done before.
O best of kings, all this majesty arising from Śaṅkhatīrtha has been recounted to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Ānarta said: "O Brahmin, this which has been proclaimed by you is most wonderful—that Lakṣmī was utterly destroyed for him because of eating powdered leaves."
By what kind of person was his expiation performed for the sake of purification? And by what kind of person was that kingdom restored to its former state? (8)

Viśvāmitra said: "O lord of men, this most meritorious and pure betel vine, if used improperly in the mouth, brings about many defects; therefore, it should be consumed with care and given away according to one's ability. (9)
Ānarta said: How did the betel vine originate, and why is it considered to have such great defects? You should explain to me here how its consumption becomes improper. (10)

Viśvāmitra said: "This burden of questions you have proclaimed to me is indeed great; nevertheless, O King, I shall speak if you have such curiosity, regarding that from which the fault of consuming powdered leaves arises. (11)
In ancient times, for the sake of the nectar of immortality, the gods churned the ocean with the mountain Mandara as the churning stick and Vāsuki as the rope.
With Bali clinging to the region of his mouth and all the gods at the region of his tail, the Tortoise then supported [the mountain] according to the counsel of Vāsudeva.
O best of kings, even before Mount Mandara began to revolve, the three jewels suddenly appeared in Ānarta.

Clad in blue garments, the man was dark-complexioned with a crooked nose; he had black teeth, a thick head, a long neck, and a large belly; his feet were shaped like winnowing baskets, his eyes were flat, and he was terrifying to behold. || 15 ||
Likewise, his wicked wife was like a Rākṣasī in form; devoted to the pains of pregnancy, she held a child by its finger.
Then all the hosts of gods, and especially the Dānavas, abandoned that churning-stick and rushed forward to seize them. (17)
Then, O Indra among kings, seeing them transformed, everyone was filled with apprehension; they did not accept [the gifts] at all, but laughed among themselves.
Then Bali, the Daitya, standing with his palms joined in reverence, said: "Whatever Brahmā and the others may obtain, and whatever arises before them—all that [is yours]."
Therefore, let the lotus-born one accept these three jewels, by the offering of which to whomsoever may success be attained in this churning.
That speech was praised by Viṣṇu, as well as by Śaṅkara, by all the gods beginning with Indra, and especially by the Dānavas.

In the meantime, O King, Brahmā took back those three [jewels] out of courtesy toward all the gods, even though he did not desire them himself. O Monarch, they once again applied themselves with effort and churned the ocean.
Then Vāruṇī was born, endowed with a divine fragrance; she was seized by Bali in the very presence of the enemy of Bali (Viṣṇu).
And when another whirlpool arose, the Kaustubha gem emerged; it was seized, O great king, by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Then, while another great whirlpool remained there, the Lord of Night (the Moon) appeared; he was seized by the Bull-bannered One (Śiva) at that very moment.
From that, the Pārijāta tree was born, endowed with divine fragrance; it was taken by all the gods and established in the Nandana grove.
Immediately after that, Surabhi, accompanied by her calf, departed by way of the sky and established herself in Goloka.
Then, O King, Dhanvantari was born, holding in his hand a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) filled with nectar, accompanied by the gods and the dānavas.
Seized simultaneously by the gods and the Daityas, who were both enraged and desirous of conquering one another, the physician Kamaṇḍalu fell into the hands of the gods.
Then, O King, those possessed by greed churned that ocean; from it was born Lakṣmī, white-robed and holding a lotus in her hand.
O best of kings, Viṣṇu was chosen by her himself when the ocean was being churned excessively by the gods and the dānavas.
The Kālakūṭa poison arose, by which all the gods and demons encountered supreme suffering and were scattered in the ten directions.
Seeing him, O lord of kings, the Blessed Śambhu, who possesses fierce prowess, devoured him; consequently, he became blue-throated (Nīlakaṇṭha).
Then, having abandoned the churning-stick Mandara as well as Vāsuki, a battle broke out between the Daityas and the gods for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Then Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a woman, spoke to those Daityas; thereupon, Balī, being delighted, gave that very nectar to her.
Having placed his supreme trust [in him], he waged war against the gods; then Viṣṇu, abandoning his female form, assumed a male appearance.
Taking that very nectar, he went to where the dwellers of heaven were; with a joyful heart, he said to them, "O gods, drink the nectar! (37)
"By means of which, having attained immortality, you may slay the Dānavas"; having promised "So be it," they drank the supreme nectar.
Thereupon they became immortals and slew the great asuras in battle.
O Lord of the Earth, while their ritual of drinking was underway there, Rāhu, assuming the form of a god, eagerly drank the nectar.
O King, at that very moment, that great Daitya was noticed by both the Moon and the Sun, who reported to Hari: "This is not a god; he is a great Asura."
O best of kings, having heard that, Vāsudeva released his Sudarśana discus, which possessed a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt, for the sake of his slaughter.
O lord of the earth, his body was pervaded by that nectar for as long as it existed; therefore, even though it was severed by that unfailing [weapon], that head [remained alive].
Then, as soon as that son of Siṃhikā had attained immortality, he was addressed by Acyuta with words that were exceedingly sweet and gentle.
"O highly fortunate one, abandon the Daityas and become esteemed by the gods; you shall always receive supreme worship within the circle of the planets. (45)
Having promised "So be it" and abandoned those foremost of Daityas, he receives worship from mortals as he remains stationed within the circle of the planets.
In the meantime, the Daityas, defeated by the best of the gods, fled in all directions in utter terror; some even met their death.
And the nectar remaining from what had been drunk was placed in the Nandana grove, right where the tethering post of the king of the nāgas stood.
Even that lordly elephant, who used to flow with rut day and night, stood still; by its power, that pitcher of nectar was split open.
Then a creeper sprang forth from that very water-pot; it climbed upon a hitching post there and attained supreme growth.
Taking those leaves produced from it, which were unprecedented and fragrant, those best of gods considered them to be such and ate them.
O King, they were especially delighted for the sake of purifying their mouths.

Then, O Lord of the Earth, the physician Dhanvantari, by means of his own intelligence, [concluded] that since the betel vine (nāgavallī) was born at the elephant-stable (nāgālāna), it would become [the remedy]. || 53 ||
"By my word, the abode of Smara shall always exist; thereafter, he gave her the name 'Nāgavallī'. (54)
And then he brought about a combination, O King, such that betel was produced from areca nut, lime powder, and catechu.
Then, after some time, King Vāṇīvatsaraka brought Śakra to a state of satisfaction by means of his stainless austerity.
Then Indra, pleased by that asceticism, spoke these words: || 57 ||
Indra said: "O King, I am now pleased by this asceticism; tell me what boon I shall grant you, which has always been desired by your mind. (58)

He said: "If you are pleased with me, if a boon is to be granted to me, O Lord, give me a celestial chariot that travels through the sky, by which I may come to your abode every day from the surface of the earth for the sake of saluting you."
Having promised "So be it," he gave him a celestial chariot that moved with the speed of thought and wind, resounding with the cries of swans and peacocks.
Having ascended there constantly, he goes to the abode of the thirty gods, endowed with supreme devotion, in order to pay homage to the Thousand-eyed One.
Śakra himself presented betel to him with his own hand, and he consumed it with a joyful inner soul.
O Lord of the Earth, even when old age had arrived, his passion increased greatly through the power of betel.
Then that king, endowed with humility, spoke thus to Śakra: "May you show me favor by granting me a betel vine. (64)
"So that he may go forth to spread [the teaching] and bring it to the world of mortals," he replied, "So be it," and then gave it to him. (65)
Having gone to his own city, he then established her in his garden; thereafter, after a long time, she became widely known throughout the earth.
From tasting her, the world became possessed by lust; no one performed sacrifices, nor especially the officiating of sacrifices, and all other religious acts born of dharma perished.
Then all the hosts of gods, deprived of their sacrificial shares and afflicted by anger, went and spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).

O best of gods, in the world of mortals the performance of dharma has greatly perished, because the people are excessively attached to desire due to the consumption of betel-leaf. Therefore, show us favor so that our religious rites may be restored.
At that very time, O King, the impoverished man saw the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrive at Puṣkara for the purpose of performing a sacrifice.
Then, bowing down and standing with humility, he said: "O best of gods, I am weary while living in the house of a Brahmin. (71)
Therefore, O Lord, proclaim to me that most excellent place belonging to those possessed of wealth, wherein an abundant and eternal satisfaction arises. (72)
Having heard those words of his and reflected for a long time, the Grandfather spoke to that poor man regarding the means for the wealthy man to find a vulnerability here.
