"O poor man, you must always place your residence upon the powdered leaf; and by my word, the tip of the leaf for the betel should be placed by my wife. (74)
And upon the stalks of all the leaves, as well as within the heartwood of the khadira tree at night, you shall always dwell with those two, your son.
These four positions are said to create vulnerabilities for the wealthy; especially for kings, go quickly according to my word. (76)
Nārada said: O lord of men, all that I was asked by you has been related to you.

O King, just as there are holes caused by betel leaves among the wealthy in this world, all of those have been committed by you unknowingly, O Monarch; therefore, indeed, the sudden destruction of your prosperity has occurred. (78)
The king said: O Lord of Sages, tell me also the expiation for that purpose; it may happen that I sometimes consume betel-leaf in such a manner. (79)
By which purity arises from the consumption of betel? || 80 ||
Viśvāmitra said: Listen, O King, I shall declare the expiation that one should perform for the sake of purification from the consumption of improper betel-leaf, by means of consolation. 81.
O King, on a sacred festival day, one endowed with perfect faith should invite a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

Having washed his feet, one should have him put on two garments; then, having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should have a golden leaf fashioned according to one's means and place a pearl upon it within the powder.
One should likewise offer a betel nut, lapis lazuli, khadira wood, and silver to the Brahmin with this mantra. (84)
Whatever stalks arising from leaves I previously ate, as well as powdered leaves and other things, and even the khadira wood at night—[all that has been consumed]. (85)
"For the sake of purifying that sin, please accept this betel leaf. Then, O King, the Brāhmaṇa should recite this mantra: (86)
For the sake of the sacrificer's welfare and for the purification of all sins, whatever betel-leaf was consumed either unknowingly or intentionally [is hereby offered]. (87)
And whatever else you may eat at any time through my favor, no fault shall accrue to you for that by my word; of this there is no doubt. (88)
By giving betel-leaf according to this rite, one attains purity; O King, a man is not seized by the defect of improper betel. (89)
Therefore, O Great King, you should indeed observe this vow; for it is most meritorious and increases great enjoyments. (90)
O Indra among kings, he who bestows [this] with devotion according to this rite shall never again be deprived of betel-leaf throughout his various future births.
He who, having consumed betel, does not offer it as a gift, shall be deprived of betel in every birth throughout this world.
O Lord of the Earth, that mouth which is devoid of betel-leaf belongs to a miser or a pauper; it is indeed a hole, not a mouth.
He who, having first given betel-leaf to the best of Brahmins, should consume it himself, shall be handsome, fortunate, and skillful in birth after birth. (94)
O Lord of the Earth, all this has been told regarding the fruit that arises for men from eating bad betel-leaf, as well as [the fruit] that arises from its gift.
O King, regarding the consumption of betel-leaf in connection with the Śaṅkhāditya festival, I shall describe both the faults and the merits, as well as the rules for its gift and its eating. (96)

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Betel and the Greatness of Betel," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 210 ||
Viśvāmitra said: Having explained the cause of the king’s misfortune of poverty and his disease of leprosy, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke again. (1)
Nārada said: O King, I have related all this to you—the cause of leprosy and of poverty—having understood it correctly with my divine eye.
Now I shall fully explain how your defeat has arisen here from enemies, due to the insult of the twice-born.
Whosoever is consecrated here as the sovereign of Ānarta, he first goes to the village of the Nāgaras out of devotion.
O King, that which was intended by you was not given at all due to negligence; those twice-born ones were thus defeated, even as they begged again and again. (5)
Likewise, by the power of your anger, you have abolished other edicts of the twice-born, as well as those inherited from your father and grandfather.
Therefore, this defeat arising from your enemies has occurred here; knowing this, O sirs, issue commands to the best of the twice-born.
"Perform the liberation of those very ones who have been seized. Having heard that, the king then, with great devotion, at the Śaṅkha-tīrtha—
Having bathed and invited the Brahmins together with the mediator, O King, he washed their feet in front of Śaṅkhāditya.
Then, having washed his feet, the king bestowed one hundred and twenty-six edicts upon the high-souled Nāgaras.
In the meantime, all those enemies who were stationed there met their death through the grace of the Brāhmaṇas. || 11 ||
Viśvāmitra said: "O best of kings, all this has been narrated to you regarding the origin and power of Śaṅkha-tīrtha; what more do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śaṅkha-tīrtha," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 211 ||
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, we have heard about the three meritorious holy sites (tīrthas) that you have described to us here in this sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara."
We wish to hear the greatness of Viśvāmitra; please explain it now, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, the further shore of the ocean and even of the earth can be perceived here, but not the end of the qualities of that sage.
O best of the twice-born, the limit of the wise son of Gādhi is perceived by someone—he who, though a Kṣatriya, attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa. || 4 ||
Even for King Triśaṅku, who had fallen to the status of an outcaste, the gods were visibly manifested as partakers of his sacrificial offerings.
O best of the twice-born, because he had previously commenced the creation out of rivalry with Brahmā, he was then restrained by the gods after they had prostrated before him.
O best of Brahmins, now listen as I describe the majesty of that sacred ford, which destroys all sins. (7)
Thereupon, that high-souled one, with his own hands, dug a pit there, tearing open the surface of the earth on all sides even without a weapon.
Having meditated there, the river Jāhnavī was brought forth from Pātāla; her waters, which are perfectly pure, have arrived in the mortal world.
Furthermore, bathing there is deliciously pleasant and destroys all sins; by him, Bhāskara, the thief of waters, was also installed there.

O best of the twice-born, he who bathes in that auspicious lake on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday during the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, and pays homage to the Sun, is liberated from all leprosy as well as from all sins.
In the northwestern direction from that place, there is a pond born of water, created by Dhanvantari, which destroys all diseases.
There, the noble-minded Dhanvantari first performed austerities; endowed with ascetic power, he paid homage while meditating with a concentrated mind. (13)
Then, after a long time, the Sun-god was pleased with him and said, "I am a granter of boons; choose one, O high-minded one."
Dhanvantari said: O Lord, O best of gods, for that man who performs a bath with devotion in this pool, there shall be a complete destruction of all diseases.

The Blessed Lord said: "O auspicious one, whatever man here, on this excellent day—the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday—shall perform a bath at sunrise with a concentrated mind, he, even if afflicted by disease, shall become free from illness at that very moment. (16)
Free from disease, he will obtain his desired objects; and being free from desire, he will attain liberation. || 117 ||
Having spoken thus, Ravi, the best of gods, vanished; and Dhanvantari, with a joyful soul, then departed for his own abode.
Then, after some time, there was a lord of the earth named Ratnākṣa, the renowned ruler of Ayodhyā, born of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa).
Grateful and generous, always devoted to his own wife, he was a hero of supreme splendor who destroyed all his enemies.
O twice-born ones, due to the ripening of his past karma, that lord of the earth was afflicted with a terrible disease of leprosy, difficult to cure even in the three worlds.
O twice-born ones, there is no medicine in the world that was not employed by him, nor is there any gift that was not given by that high-souled man while he was afflicted with leprosy.
In whatever manner he prepared and administered medicinal herbs, in that very same way his body was severely emaciated by the disease.

Then, O best of the twice-born, having attained dispassion, that king established his son upon the throne and desired to enter the fire, even though he was forbidden by all his wives and trusted servants.
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, having honored the supreme gods, having conversed with his circle of friends, and having instructed his own son; (25)
At that very time, while [the king] was wandering about by chance, a certain pilgrim arrived, possessing a body of divine form.
Then, O twice-born ones, seeing that entire city of the king in such a state of agitation, he was overcome with wonder and questioned a certain man.
The pilgrim said: "O blessed lady, why has this entire great city become so agitated? It is devoid of joy and frequented by children and the elderly whose eyes are filled with tears. (28)
And that king said, "Afflicted by the disease of leprosy and utterly despondent, he will seek to accomplish his end by entering a blazing fire."
Therefore, this entire city has fallen into supreme misery; surely, being permeated by his virtues, it will go to its death.
Having heard that, the kārpaṭika went quickly and spoke to the king: || 31 ||

As if reviving all the deceased people of the king, he said: "O King, do not enter the fire out of this grief born of disease; while this sacred ford (tīrtha), which brings about the destruction of all ailments, still remains."
"O Lord of the Earth, my body was once just like yours; having bathed there, O Master, it has now immediately become like this again. (33)
On the seventh lunar day, falling on a Sunday at the time of sunrise, whatever man on earth afflicted by disease performs a ritual bath there, [is liberated]. (34)
Released from that disease at that very moment, he shall attain perfection; likewise, O best of kings, he shall be liberated from sin just as I am.
The king said: "In which region is such a great sacred site? Tell me quickly. (36)
The pilgrim said: "O King, there is a famous and excellent sacred field called Nāgara upon the surface of the earth; overcome by the disease of leprosy, I went there. (37)
Devoted to pilgrimage for the sake of seeing him, a certain ascetic full of compassion, seeing me there—dejected, afflicted by disease, and deeply distressed—spoke to me as my refuge. (38)
In the northwestern quarter of the god who reclines upon the waters, there is a most meritorious sacred ford (tīrtha) that brings forth the water of Viśvāmitra.
Having gone there, perform your ablutions on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, especially when the month of Māgha has arrived during the bright fortnight.

"By which path you go toward the rising of the sun, that is your leprosy. Having heard this, I arrived there on the seventh lunar day conjoined with the Sun; then, I performed my ablutions in that Śāmbhava spring.
Then, having emerged from that, as soon as I beheld my body, O King, it became such as you have described; this which you have spoken is the truth.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should perform a bath there on the seventh lunar day coinciding with a Sunday, at the time of the sun's rising.
"By which your disease shall perish, as well as even your great sin"—having heard that, the king quickly went forth accompanied by him alone.
When the month of Māgha had arrived, he performed his bath in that manner on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, in the auspicious waters of Viśvāmitra.
Then, at that very moment, he became completely freed from leprosy, assuming a divine form and body like another Kāmadeva.
Then the king, being pleased, gave three crores of gold to that kārpaṭika and spoke these words to him.
"By your grace, I am liberated from this most dreadful disease; therefore, you go to your own home, while I shall remain here with complete contentment. (48)
"Accompanied by my own wife, I shall constantly perform penance, having established my son—who is capable of the duties of kingship—in the kingdom. (49)
Having spoken thus, he dispatched him as well as the others who had assembled to their own homes, while he himself remained right there.
Having established a delightful hermitage together with his wife, O best of the twice-born, he attained supreme perfection in the course of time.
Therefore, this beautiful holy place (tīrtha) in the triple heaven became famous by his name; it removes all diseases and destroys all sins.
There, the Sun-god, the god of gods, was installed by that great-souled one under his own name as the one renowned as Ratnāditya.
Having bathed there on a Sunday falling on the seventh lunar day, he who beholds [the deity] becomes liberated from sin and goes to the world of the Sun.
O best of the twice-born, whatever else occurred there regarding the various fields, that I shall proclaim; listen with well-composed minds.
In that region there was a certain rustic man, aged and afflicted with leprosy; nevertheless, he constantly performed the task of tending cattle. || 56 ||
Once, while he was guarding the cattle there at the foot of the mountain, one animal strayed from the path out of greed for grass.
On the seventh day, on a Sunday, he fell into that waterfall; however, as he was going down, he was not noticed by him at all.
Then, just as he had prepared himself for a meal at home, the owner of that animal arrived, scolding him. (59)
"Why has that animal of mine not arrived at my house? Therefore, bring it here quickly; otherwise, I shall take away your life. (60)
Sūta said: Having heard that, the leper, terrified with fear, went quickly by that very path along which he had wandered upon the earth during the day.
Then, at the end of the night, while darkness still prevailed, he heard from afar the cry of that beast as it had fallen into the great pit.

Then, having gone there and entered that pit, he pulled that animal out with great difficulty from the midst of the water and the most dreadful mire; then, taking it, he went slowly and steadily toward his palace.
Having then entrusted him to him, he went to his own hermitage.
Then, O highly fortunate ones, when he woke up again from sleep and looked at his body in the morning, he saw it entirely free from leprosy.
Filled with supreme splendor, his eyes wide with wonder, he reflected: "What indeed is this? Why has my disease suddenly vanished? (66)
"Surely this is the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha) today at the arrival of night, since I have bathed in the mud for the sake of the animal. (67)
Then, having gone there out of great curiosity, he beheld him who was freed from itching and enveloped in splendor.
Having gone to that place himself and recognized it as the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), he performed penance right there while meditating upon the Sun.
Dwelling in the forest, being properly vigilant day and night, he attained the supreme perfection that is difficult even for the gods to reach.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a ritual bath there. || 71 ||
One should also worship that god Bhāskara, the drawer of water; even today, in this Kali age, a man who bathes there becomes pure.
Whoever worships with devotion at that pool of meritorious water on the seventh lunar day, which falls on a Sunday, is also liberated from sins. (73)
Whoever stands before him and recites the Gāyatrī eight thousand times shall be freed from disease and liberated from all sins.
Whoever, endowed with faith, should give a cow in reference to that [rite], not even one born in his lineage will be seized by disease.
All this regarding the origin of Āditya has been narrated to you by me; by hearing his majesty, a person is liberated from sin.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Ratnāditya," within the "Majesty of the Hāṭakeśvara Region" of the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 212 ||
Sūta said: This greatness of Ratnāditya has been proclaimed to you, which removes all leprosy and destroys all sins. Furthermore, let the great majesty of Ravi be heard likewise. 1.
Formerly, there was a certain Brāhmaṇa who was afflicted by the disease of leprosy.
And by him, O best of the twice-born, the Sun was propitiated while he remained there.
Then, having proceeded to the southeastern quarter, one whose self is purified should fashion an image made of red sandalwood.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Divākara, appearing before his very eyes, was pleased with him and said to him, "I am here as a granter of boons."
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Lord, O God, if you are pleased with me, remove the disease of leprosy, O Master; I have no other purpose, not even for sovereignty over heaven."

The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, having bathed in the auspicious holy pool, perform one hundred and eight circumambulations on a Sunday that falls on the seventh lunar day; then, by offering fruits individually with your hands, you shall be liberated from leprosy."
Even another person here who, having gone to the cow, shall perform this vow, being liberated from all diseases, goes to my world.
The illustrious Sūrya said: Having heard that, the Brāhmaṇa, filled with faith, did exactly so; and he was then liberated from leprosy and attained a divine body.
Then the blessed Sun spoke to him once again when he was free from disease: "O best of Brahmins, what other favor may I do for you? Speak."
He said, "O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, you must remain here forever."
The Blessed Lord said: "From this time forward, my abode shall be in this place; I shall have the name Kuharavāsā."
Then, after some time, O best of the twice-born, a son named Sāmba, endowed with great beauty, was born to Viṣṇu by Jāmbavatī.
O twice-born ones, he causes agitation even in women, including their mothers.
Then, as that best of the Yadus was proceeding along the royal highway, || 13 ||
The women of the city, also filled with contentment, gazed on with great curiosity; abandoning their household chores, they climbed onto the windows.
Eager to behold him whose body was possessed by desire, some women had their limbs only half-anointed, while others had only one eye painted with collyrium.
Others had their hair only half-bound, while others had abandoned their children; some ran about with sandals fastened to only one foot.
And in the second [verse], women with swelling hips ran about wearing sandals; while other women likewise went to the windows. (17)
Overcome with anger, the children and the elders alike cried out in lamentation, their minds distracted by the loosening of the knots of their lower garments.
Other excellent women went to their own windows; he then drew them toward him with the rays of their falling eyes.
A certain passionate woman, upon merely seeing the form of that youth Sāmba—who was like the god Kāmadeva himself—felt her heart sink into the surface of the earth.
Motionless, her limbs tormented by desire, one woman appeared as if she were a painting; another, afflicted by love, released sighs that were like fire.
And beholding him alone, endowed with beauty and youth, they fell from the window onto the surface of the earth, motionless.
Other excellent women engage in conversation with one another: "That loving woman alone is blessed who has embraced his wheel. (23)
When the entire night arising in the month of Māgha has passed, let alone the women, even men may act without restraint. (24)
Stunned by his form, they all spoke thus: "O Atri, we say this: let us serve him, for we are destitute of wealth. (25)

"By which we may behold her face, ever resembling the moon; for by those two ears, the growth of our eyes has undoubtedly been obstructed. Otherwise, we do not know how much further it will grow. (26)
Thus being gazed upon by amorous women and likewise by men, he went forth along the royal highway, longing for the sight of his father.
The sisters, the mothers, and the wives of his brothers who were present—even the women of the brahmins—had fallen into such a state; and so too had his own mothers and especially his sisters. (28)
When another day arrived during the rainy season, at the onset of night, in the dark fortnight when all was shrouded in gloom and nothing could be discerned before one's eyes; (29)
His mother, named Nandinī, afflicted by the arrows of Kāmadeva, assumed the guise of his wife and presented herself at his bed.
Having recognized her as his beloved, he also served that passionate woman with various amorous attentions, performed in ways beyond belief.
Then, because of her, the best of the Yadus felt a doubt: "She who is the daughter of the King of Aṅga is dearer to me than my own life. (32)
She does not know such pleasure as that which was fashioned by her; even courtesans do not know such pleasure in any way whatsoever.
Then, having firmly grasped him by the hand and brought a lamp at that very moment, his mother—who was known as Nandinī—looked upon him.
And then he reproached him, saying: "O wretch, what is this that has been done? It is despised by all the worlds and likewise brings ill repute to men. (35)
She too, overcome with shame and agitated by great fear, vanished at that very moment, pursued by a mighty terror.
O twice-born ones, even though he lamented in distress, Sāmba could not find any sleep; the remainder of that night appeared to him as if it were a hundred years.
Then, when the night had passed and the orb of the sun had risen, that son of Hari arose, overcome with great sorrow.
Having set aside even his necessary duties, he summoned a certain most excellent Brāhmaṇa who was learned in the ordinances of the Dharmaśāstras, and then spoke to him.
In private, endowed with humility and standing with palms joined in reverence, Sāmba said: "If one should become infatuated oneself with one's mother, sister, or daughter... (40)
"Having examined all the treatises on Dharma in their proper order, tell me how his purification may come about according to the ultimate truth."
The Brāhmaṇa said: O child, for the sake of another's wife, an expiation has been ordained; and among all the vessels of Dharma, there are various rules for each of the social classes.
Thus, for these three [women] and for these three [men], the atonement has been fully proclaimed; in this very manner it is prescribed for the sake of purification. (43)

O Yādava, having encountered a delusion caused by a mother, a sister, or even a daughter, wise men must perform a purification out of negligence; for the sake of purification, I know of no other remedy than the *tiṅginī* plant. (44)
O bull among the Yadus, this decision which I have communicated to you regarding all the vessels of the Dharma has been declared; there is no other. 45.
Otherwise, if one who is questioned should prescribe a penance according to his own whim, he would become a sharer in that sin, just like the perpetrator himself. (46)
Sāṃba said: O best of the twice-born, what is the nature of the Tiṅginī and what is its extent? Tell me everything in detail, for I have a need for this. (47)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Yādava, having taken cow-dung powder and filled a pit of your own height, you must lie there upon it until [the time] of the mouth."
And above that, one should apply powder produced from a cow-pen, [covering] as much as the measure of the mouth, while avoiding one's own face. (49)
Then, at the location of the feet, one should kindle the fire so that the cremation of the body occurs gradually. (50)
Remaining there, he should not move his body in any way whatsoever; nor should he cry out, but should meditate solely upon Janārdana.
Then, through the loss of life, purification of the body arises. || 52 ||
I have fully described the true nature of Tiṅginī; this expiation completely destroys even the most heinous sins. (53)
Having heard those words of his, Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, made a firm resolve in his heart regarding the matter arising from the seeker of Tiṅginī.
Then, filled with compassion, he spoke to Vāsudeva in private: "O father, I have been deceived by Nandinī, your wife."
While that wicked woman remained in the darkness having assumed the form of my wife, I, thinking "this is my own wife," consorted with her.
Then, having recognized [her] through her actions and having reproached her, she was dismissed; from that time forward, this disease of leprosy has remained upon my body.
Then I questioned a certain excellent brahmin, a knower of the Dharmaśāstras: "Tell me the prescribed expiation for having violated my mother. (58)
He said, "This is the correct means of accomplishment for my purification by Tiṅginī; as such, I shall accomplish it for the sake of purifying that sin. (59)
"Grant me leave quickly so that I may perform my duty; whatever misdeed I have committed out of childishness should be forgiven by you. (60)
Act in such a way that my mother does not suffer. || 61 ||
Having heard those words of his, which were like the falling of a thunderbolt, Hari, distressed and with eyes filled with tears, then spoke in a faltering voice.
"O son, this deed was not committed by you out of desire, nor was it done through ignorance; therefore, the sin is indeed very slight."
Whatever sin is committed knowingly shall indeed become inexhaustible, if the protector of the earth does not inflict punishment upon it.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, I shall proclaim for you the expiation for the sake of purification, as well as the gift by which leprosy is destroyed. (65)
Thus have been stated, prohibited, and further reconciled, in their entirety, the words of the Sage—both those that are dependent and those that are independent.
Therefore, my son, carry out my word in this matter; it will result in great welfare for you in this world and in the next.
In the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, there is the highly renowned Mārtaṇḍa, established by Viśvāmitra, who destroys all forms of leprosy.
When the seventh lunar day falls on a Sunday in the month of Mādhava, and the asterism presided over by the ancestors (Maghā) occurs during the bright fortnight. || 69 ||
When the rising of the sun has occurred, he who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations with a mind purified by faith [attains the fruit]. (70)
With fruits that are most excellent and of those respective sizes, his leprosy departs immediately; of this there is no doubt. (71)
That man who, being free from disease, performs circumambulations of the Sun, is honored in the world of the Sun for as many yugas as there were circumambulations.
That mortal who, having offered a sacrificial fee on a Sunday, pays obeisance with true devotion, is likewise liberated from diseases.
Therefore, O Great King, propitiate that Sun-god according to this entire ritual procedure which has been described by me to you.
Worship [him] quickly with a mind free from conceptual construction; then, liberated from disease and cleansed of sin, you shall attain a divine body. 75.
Do not give way to despondency arising from the disease of leprosy, for the Lord known as Kuharāśraya resides in that sacred field.
Then, having heard those words, the son of Viṣṇu set forth.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of that god of gods, the wielder of the discus, Sāmba set his mind upon going toward Arbuda.
Then, when an auspicious day arrived, that son of Viṣṇu set forth, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots, and surrounded by an army.
And he was followed for a very long distance by Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, and in an instant by all his mothers with their eyes filled with tears.
By the hero Balabhadra, by the wise Cārudeṣṇa, by Yuyudhāna and Aniruddha, and by the wise Pradyumna; || 81 ||
Then Jāmbavatī, seeing her son heading toward the sacred fords as he departed, began to lament like a female osprey.
"Alas! I am destroyed, I am ruined; for I am truly ill-fated and luckless, since even my only son has fallen into such a state as this. (83)
Then, seeing her weeping, Madhusūdana said to her: "Why will you perform such an inauspicious act for him who has set out on his journey?"

With eyes filled with tears, distressed, and especially with her hair disheveled, she said: "He, now freed from disease and endowed with the fruit of his pilgrimage, having been abandoned by the malady of leprosy, will return once more to your presence. (85)
In the meantime, having descended from his vehicle, Sāmba set out with haste to the place where Jāmbavatī was staying.
Having bowed to her, he stood with a joyful heart and palms joined in reverence; having prostrated, he laughed aloud and spoke these words.
O mother, do not undergo suffering in vain for our sake; I shall indeed return quickly after having completed my pilgrimage to the sacred fords.
Jāmbavatī said: "O child, may all those forest deities protect you in the woods from beasts of prey, from Piśācas, and from all wicked beings on every side, my son. (89)
May Govinda protect your head, and Madhusūdana your throat; may Hṛṣīkeśa protect the region of your arms, and the destroyer of demons (Daityanāśana) your heart.
May the lotus-eyed one protect my belly; may the wielder of the mace protect my waist; may Kṛṣṇa protect the pair of my knees, and may the upholder of the earth protect my feet.
Having thus touched his limbs with her own hand, she embraced him and smelled the crown of his head again and again.
The illustrious woman sent forth that son, having provided him with protection; she then returned, accompanied by the entire retinue of the inner apartments. 93.
With eyes filled with tears, miserable and sighing like a female serpent, so too was the Blessed Viṣṇu together with all the Yādavas.
Having entered the city of Dvārakā and then sent Sāmba away, he, dejected and with eyes filled with tears, proceeded with Balabhadra at his head.
O best of the twice-born, accompanied by his sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen, and others, Sāmba also departed from Dvārakā.
Then, having arrived in due course at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, where the Lord of Yogis is personally established by Ambarīṣa.
Even today Viṣṇu remains there as the destroyer of the sins of living beings; having bathed there and worshipped the Lord, the Master of Yogins, one thereafter— || 98 ||
He gave gifts of various kinds to the Brahmins according to his ability, as well as to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others as well.
Whatever vehicles, garments, or jewels were desired by whomsoever, that son of Hari remained there for three nights with a concentrated mind.
Thereafter, he went to the holy hermitage of Cyavana, where Viṣṇu resides, having been installed by Cyavana.
And on the holy bank of the Sindhu river, which destroys all sins, the Yādava likewise bestowed gifts upon the foremost of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having remained there with self-restraint and endowed with faith, O Sāmba, he performed the desired rites as prescribed by the scriptures and according to the ritual injunctions. || 3 ||
Then, having bathed in the auspicious waters of the Sindhu, he traveled for three nights; thereafter, he proceeded slowly toward Puṣkara and the other sacred sites.
Meditating day and night upon the god who dwells in Puṣkara, that best of the Yadus eventually reached Puṣkara itself.

Having bathed in the meritorious waters of the pool and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, he then took some fruits and went to where the god Viṣṇu was indicated to be stationed.
Then, having worshipped with devotion the God who dwells in the cave, with garments, ointments, incenses, and various kinds of food offerings.
Then, with fruits in hand and endowed with supreme faith, he slowly performed circumambulations while reciting the Sūrya-Gāyatrī.
O best of the twice-born, in whatever manner he performed the circumambulation of that sun, in that very same manner his leprosy subsided.
At that moment, O best of the twice-born, there arose in the mind of the wise Sāmba the realization: "I am liberated from leprosy," free from all doubt.
Then, whatever had arrived there together with him—including elephants, horses, chariots, and precious gems—all that was offered with devotion.
He gave all that, as well as another five villages, to the citizens; then, having installed Sāmbāditya, he set out for his home.
Whatever remained, he offered all of that with devotion to the Sūrya Brahmins after having worshipped the Sun-god.
Having given eight thousand horses, three hundred elephants, six hundred chariots yoked with spirited steeds, and infinite jewels, Sāmba returned home.
He who recites with devotion this unsurpassed narrative of Sāmba, or hears it, in his lineage leprosy shall never arise. (15)
Sūta said: Thus has this entire, supreme account concerning Viśvāmitra been narrated to you; it is the fourth meritorious tīrtha, which brings auspiciousness especially to women. 116.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Sāmbāditya, the Dweller in the Cave," within the Viśvāmitra-māhātmya, in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 213 ||
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, there is another [deity] there as well, established by Viśvāmitra—the Lord of Gaṇas (Gaṇanātha), who bestows all perfections upon men.
Whoever worships on the fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha shall be liberated from all obstacles for the duration of an entire year. || 2 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, tell us now of the origin of Gaṇanātha; how was he born, and what is his celebrated greatness?
Sūta said: And this one was produced by Gaurī herself from the filth of her own body, adorned with the face of an elephant for the sake of sport, using human limbs.
He is endowed with four arms, mounted upon a mouse, holds an axe in his hand, and is pleased by the eating of sweetmeats (modaka).
He is the bestower of all accomplishments in this world, especially for his devotees; formerly, he was [employed] by the Lord in the Tārakāmaya battle.
He waged a fierce battle such as had never been performed by anyone; all the Dānavas were slain, beyond all counting.
Then Śakra, being pleased, spoke to that lord of the battlefield, whose entire body was mangled by wounds and drenched in blood.
O Sugajamukha, for our sake you have waged war, and all the Dānavas, beyond counting, have been slain by you. (9)
Therefore, you shall be worthy of worship even by all the gods, let alone by humans who are constantly overwhelmed by obstacles. (10)
"Those who shall worship you at the commencement of all their undertakings—by my word, may they achieve success in their tasks; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed one then dismissed him with great honor from the presence of Gaurī and Śaṅkara.
This matter was previously asked by the wise Rohitāśva to the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya for the purpose of destroying all the brahmins.
O highly fortunate ones, I shall relate that very matter according to its true nature; listen all of you with concentrated minds to this entire ancient account.
Rohitāśva said: "O Blessed One, all those mortals here, even when they are pure, become beset by obstacles in all their auspicious undertakings. (15)
And in undertakings already begun, especially those born of dharma, obstacles arise by which that task is not accomplished. (16)
Therefore, for the destruction of obstacles, prescribe some vow for me—whether it be a vow, a religious observance, austerity, or even a gift.
By performing this even once here, a human being shall not encounter any obstacle from birth until the end of life for as long as he lives. || 18 ||

Mārkaṇḍeya said: In this regard, I shall proclaim to you that vow which destroys all obstacles, is endowed with every virtue, and annihilates all sins—the very one formerly practiced by Viśvāmitra of purified soul. (19)
The powerful son of Gādhi, renowned as Viśvāmitra, was a high-souled man who maintained a state of enmity toward Vasiṣṭha.
That man of great asceticism was not addressed as "Brāhmaṇa" by Vasiṣṭha in any way for the sake of his Brāhmaṇahood; from that, enmity arose.
Rohitāśva said: Why did the brahmin Vasiṣṭha not say anything at all? For he is the supreme brahmin, as proclaimed even by Brahmā and the other gods themselves. (22)

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Formerly, there was a Kṣatriya king named Viśvāmitra who, while wandering about on a hunt, entered the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha afflicted by hunger and thirst; he was then honored by him.
He had a cow named Nandini who was always a granter of desires; she immediately produced whatever Vasistha desired.
By its power, that king, along with his servants, troops, and vehicles, was then led by him to a state of complete satisfaction with various kinds of sweet foods.

Thinking, "This is a king," he honored him with offerings of water for the feet, food, and other gifts; and he too, having seen that entire power and the origin of the cow, requested her in exchange for wealth consisting of elephants and horses.
At that time, the brahmin did not yield, whether through conciliation, gifts, or even sowing dissension; thereupon, the king indeed employed force.
Then, out of anger, that king drove away that cow.
Then, as she was being led away, she said to Vasiṣṭha: "O Lord, why have I been given by you to this king, that he leads me away with such effort? (29)
Vasiṣṭha said: "O illustrious lady, I did not give you to this king. If he carries you away by force, then act appropriately. (30)
Hearing that, the excellent cow Nandinī, filled with anger, let out a yawn directed toward that army born of the king.
From her mouth, a column of smoke arose thereafter; from that, a most terrible flame; and from that, warriors by the thousands.
Bearing various weapons and fierce like the messengers of Yama, they were Pulindas, Barbaras, Ābhiras, Kirātas, Yavanas, and Śakas. || 33 ||
They said to her: "O auspicious one, tell us for what purpose we have been created."
Nandinī said: "These wicked servants of the king who are forcibly leading me away—let them be slain by your command; I desire nothing else whatsoever. (35)
Then, O great king, that army of Viśvāmitra was slaughtered by them in battle while they were fighting for ten nights.
Viśvāmitra, too, having witnessed that unsurpassed power of Brahman, made a vow there with a loud and melodious voice.
"Then I shall become a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt, since such a wonderful power has arisen even within me. (38)
"Therefore, I shall perform such austerity as is unattainable even by the gods. Having thus established his own son in his own position, he then performed great penance.

For the sake of attaining Brahminhood, he performed a most fierce and exceedingly difficult penance; yet, because of that, he did not attain Brahminhood at all, and fell into a state of supreme embarrassment.
Then, having reached Kailāsa, he properly propitiated Maheśvara, the God of gods, who was accompanied by Gaurī.
"O Lord, having sought refuge on your Kailāsa, the best of mountains, I shall perform penance for the sake of attaining the status of a Brāhmaṇa. (42)
Therefore, may the God of gods grant protection against obstacles for me, so that all this great asceticism I have performed does not come to ruin. (43)
The Blessed One said: "O best of kings, for the sake of purification, perform the worship of the one born from Vināyaka, which must be performed in this rite."
By which your accomplishment arises, born perfectly from the state of Brahmanhood. || 45 ||
Viśvāmitra said: "O best of gods, tell me that; I shall perform it for him accordingly. First, let there be worship of Gaṇeśa for the pacification of all obstacles. (46)
The Blessed Lord said: "In ancient times, this [image] was fashioned by Gaurī using the ointment from her own body; afterwards, it was rendered spotless and assumed the form of a four-armed man."
"For the sake of my sport, this son was fashioned in his childhood state: elephant-faced, of massive body, with a protruding belly and short thighs. (4)
Then I was addressed by her: "O Lord, let this little son of mine be restored to life, so that he may become most worthy of worship in the world. (49)
Then, O King, having been touched by me with the Sṛṣṭisūkta and the Jīvasūkta, he was properly restored to life.
Then, filled with joy, I said to the goddess born of the Himalaya: "Now that the fourth day has arrived, this [vow] has been undertaken by me today. (51)
O highly fortunate one, O Goddess of the gods, by the power of the Jīva-sūkta, this son of yours shall forever be the presiding lord over all my hosts; therefore, he shall be known as Gaṇanāyaka.
O beautiful one, whoever shall worship this with true devotion on the auspicious fourth day while the Jīvasūkta is being recited— || 53 ||
O Goddess, in all his undertakings, all obstacles will go entirely to destruction, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Homage to Laṃbodara, and likewise homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas; to the one who eternally wields the axe, and likewise to the one endowed with speech.
Homage to the one who eats sweetmeats; homage to the one who possesses a single tooth. || 56 ||
Having worshipped with these mantras, one should thereafter offer auspicious modakas as an oblation (naivedya), and then present the water of honor (arghya).
"O Lord, whatever action originating from Śambhu I shall perform, you must always ensure that it remains free from obstacles. (58)
Then, a meal consisting of sweetmeats (modaka) should be offered to the Brahmins according to one's capacity; one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth. (59)
O best of kings, this was previously spoken by me myself, with reference to Gaṇanātha, right in the presence of Gaurī.
Then that goddess, greatly delighted, spoke these words: "From this day forward, whoever among my sons [is appointed] to the office of a Gaṇa..."
Whoever worships correctly according to this rite on the fourth lunar day, all his obstacles will undoubtedly go to destruction.
Whether by remembering or by worshipping [this], whoever shall perform their tasks, those tasks will become unshakable for them; of this there is no doubt.
There is no doubt that, consequently, his prosperity shall remain unshakable.

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, O highly fortunate one, you should duly perform on the fourth lunar day the worship originating from Vināyaka, by which you shall be endowed with your desired object."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard those words of his, King Viśvāmitra performed the worship due to the one born of Gaṇanātha as was appropriate.
He performed extensive penance, free from all obstacles; thereby he attained the status of a Brahmin, which is difficult for even all others to obtain. || 67 ||

Therefore, O highly fortunate one, perform the worship originating from Vināyaka especially when the fourth lunar day has arrived; you will obtain the great enjoyments residing in your heart—of this there is no doubt. (68)
Whoever, having meditated upon whatever desire, worships Gaṇanātha, obtains all of that, just as the word of Maheśvara declares. (69)
One who is sonless obtains a son, one destitute of wealth obtains great wealth, and one conquers enemies in battle by remembering that Gaṇanāyaka.
That woman who has been abandoned by her husband, who is unfortunate and deformed, attains good fortune through the worship of Gaṇanātha.
Whoever constantly recites this or listens to it with a concentrated mind, for that person no obstacle shall ever arise in any of their undertakings.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ritual for Worshipping Gaṇapati in the Context of the Legend of Viśvāmitra," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 214 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, tell us now in detail the procedure for the ritual of the Śrāddha, so that it may become inexhaustible.
At what time should the śrāddha be performed by those devoted to the ancestors? And with what kind of brāhmaṇas and likewise with what materials, O high-minded one? (2)
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, for this very purpose, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya was questioned in former times by Rohitāśva, the son of Hariścandra.
When Hariścandra had gone to heaven and King Rohitāśva was established on the throne, the most excellent sage Mārkaṇḍeya arrived there in the course of his pilgrimage.
He arrived at the holy confluence of the Sarayū for the purpose of bathing; having bathed there and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods according to the prescribed rites, he remained.

He entered that beautiful city of Ayodhyā, whose name is true to its meaning; and Rohitāśva, hearing that the lord of sages had arrived, quickly set out on foot from a great distance to meet him face-to-face.
Then, having bowed his head to him and standing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these sweet words, endowed with humility.

Welcome to you, O best of sages; once again, a very warm welcome, O sage! I am blessed, I have performed meritorious deeds, and I have attained the supreme goal, since my hair has been purified by the dust of your feet. (8)
Having spoken thus and then taking him by the hand as a support, he went to that assembly hall where the great lion-throne was situated.
Then, having seated that sage upon the lion-throne, the best of kings sat upon the surface of the earth, standing with his palms joined in reverence.
Then, standing bowed in humility, he spoke sweetly: "O best of Brahmins, though you are free from desire, what is the reason for your arrival?"
Therefore, tell me the truth; I shall now do for you whatever you desire, O Lord, even that which ought not to be given, since you have come to my home.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "In the course of our pilgrimage, we have arrived here at the holy confluence of the Sarayū; tomorrow morning, I shall depart once again."
"Even those who are free from desire should visit righteous and eminent brahmins; thus it was declared by the brahmins learned in the Purāṇas and possessing insight into the scriptures. (14)
Upon seeing a righteous king, a self-manifested linga (svāyaṃbhuva), and a river flowing to the ocean, one is liberated from the sin committed during that day.
Having spoken thus, that best of sages then made his inquiry, seeing that tiger among kings standing before him, full of humility.
I hope your Vedas have borne fruit; I hope your learning has borne fruit; I hope your wife has borne fruit; I hope your wealth has borne fruit. (17)
Rohitāśva said: How may the Vedas be fruitful? How may sacred learning be fruitful? How may a wife be fruitful? How may wealth be fruitful? (18)

Mārkaṇḍeya said: The Vedas have the Agnihotra sacrifice as their fruit; sacred learning has character and conduct as its fruit; wives have pleasure and sons as their fruit; and wealth has giving and enjoying as its fruit. || 19 ||
Knowing this, O Great King, you ought not to act otherwise.
These four duties have been declared by me to you; they should be performed according to their nature by one who desires both worlds.
Having spoken thus, he then related various stories before him, especially those of the ancient royal sages and the celestial sages.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversation on a certain occasion, O best of the twice-born, King Rohitāśva questioned that most excellent of sages.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony, since many different variations among the twice-born are observed in the performance of the Śrāddha rite. (24)

Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O highly fortunate one, O best of kings, it is true that I have been asked this by you. There are many varieties of Śrāddha, established according to the different Vedic branches (śākhās). (25)
Therefore, I shall state the definitive conclusion regarding this, as it was formerly spoken by Bhartṛyajña, the lord of Ānarta, concerning the correct characteristics of the Śrāddha rite. (26)
Having gone to his own hermitage and approached Bhartṛyajña as he sat comfortably, the king, the lord of Ānarta, prostrated himself and then spoke.
Ānarta said: O Brahmin, tell me now the ritual procedure for the Śrāddha desired by the ancestors, by which my ancestors, gratified by the Śrāddha, may attain satisfaction. (28)

O best of the twice-born, tell me what time is prescribed for the śrāddha, and which substances are required; likewise, tell me of other pure items that are worthy of the śrāddha and should be employed by those desiring the highest satisfaction for the ancestors.
O Brahmin, what kind of brahmins are proclaimed to be worthy of the śrāddha? And what kind are to be avoided? Tell me all of this in detail. (30)
Bhartṛyajña said: O Great King, I shall proclaim to you the unsurpassed ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony, by hearing which even a man may obtain the fruit of performing a Śrāddha.
O King, a wise man must always perform the śrāddha rite at the waning of the moon, provided that he has the eldest son and likewise a lineage.
Just as those afflicted by cold desire fire and clothing, so do the ancestors, tormented by hunger, desire the waning of the moon. (33)
Just as men afflicted by poverty long for wealth, so do the ancestors, emaciated by hunger, long for the waning of the moon.
Just as farmers desire rain for the growth of their crops, so too do they desire the waning of the moon for their own pleasure.
Just as the ruddy goose and his mate long for the sight of the sun, so do the ancestors desire the Śrāddha performed on the new moon day.
Even he who performs the śrāddha with water or even with vegetables on the day of the new moon (darśa), his ancestors attain satisfaction and his sin is destroyed.

When the day of the new moon arrives, the hosts of ancestors, having become like wind, resort to the door of the house and long for the śrāddha of men until the setting of the sun, distressed by hunger and thirst. (38)
Then, when the sun had set, they became hopeless and filled with sorrow; sighing for a long time, they departed while censuring their own kinsman.
Ānarta said: O twice-born one, for what purpose is the śrāddha performed on the day of the new moon? Explain this to me in detail and exactly as it is, with its specific distinctions.
O Brahmin, deceased persons go to a destination produced by their own karma; how then did they come to take refuge with that son? (41)
O Brahmin, this very great doubt resides within our hearts.
Bhartṛyajña said: "O highly fortunate one, this which you have spoken is true: everywhere, deceased human beings go to the destination that is appropriate for their own actions. (43)
However, I shall explain to you how they come to take refuge with one born of the lineage, so that no doubt may remain. (44)
O King, those who die here on this earth go [to that state], and they are not reborn in the mortal world as long as their lineage remains established. (45)
Furthermore, those whose nature is auspicious reside in the abode of the gods, while those men who are evil-natured dwell in the realm of Vaivasvata.
Resorting to another body, they experience the fruit of their own actions—whether auspicious or sinful—which were performed by themselves.
O King, for those dwelling in the world of Yama as well as for those residing in heaven, hunger and thirst arise even more intensely. (48)

O King, as long as three generations from the mother’s side and likewise from the father’s side remain, they—and those beyond them—experience the results of their own good and evil deeds; for them, hunger and thirst never arise at any time.

Even there, O protector of the earth, a fall from that place occurs; due to the extinction of their lineage, they all fall again to the surface of the earth, just like a vessel tied with a fraying rope that is left without support.
For this reason, O lord of men, the wise should always exert effort for the sake of progeny, so that the lineage may endure.
O King, although there are twelve kinds of sons arising from the legitimate son of the body and so forth, not even one of them has been born to me here by the power of fate.
Therefore, O lord of men, the Aśvattha tree should be established with meditative concentration for the protection of the ancestors, and it should be nurtured like a son without any distinction.
O lord of men, as long as that *aśvattha* tree remains—having been planted after the marriage ceremony—the lineage shall endure for as long as a wooden pin (*śamyā*) would remain buried in the earth.
Mortals who give birth to an aśvattha tree, having fallen to the surface of the earth, become liberated from sin and, endowed with auspiciousness, attain an excellent womb.
For this reason, food and likewise water should always be given, O King, with the ancestors in mind; for they are remembered as being composed of those very elements.

O lord of men, he who eats food or drinks water himself without first offering water and grain to the ancestors is a betrayer of his ancestors; even in heaven, neither water nor food shall be obtained by him.
If no [offerings] have been given by mortals born of their lineage, they undergo terrible suffering arising from hunger and thirst; therefore, one should satiate the ancestors.
O King, a man should always worship with his full capacity using milk and various kinds of food, as well as other offerings such as garments, sacrificial gifts, flowers, perfumes, and ointments.

Satisfied by meritorious rites such as the Pitṛmedha and by various kinds of Śrāddhas, those ancestors grant the desired objects that reside in the heart; and, O Great King, the ancestors, when gratified by Śrāddha, bestow the three aims of life.
O King, those wicked men who do not constantly gratify their own ancestors should always be known as mere beasts—two-legged creatures devoid of horns.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Necessity of Performing Śrāddha," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 215 ||
Ānarta said: O twice-born one, there are also many other most meritorious times; why then is the Śrāddha specifically prescribed for the waning of the moon?
Explain all of this to me in detail, O great sage.
Bhartṛyajña said: "O Great King, this is true: there are many times suitable for the śrāddha ceremony which grant satisfaction and contentment to the hosts of ancestors."
The anniversaries of Manu and others, as well as the beginnings of the Yugas, their subsequent transits (saṃkrāntis), Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
In these places, one should perform a faithful offering for the satisfaction of the ancestors; likewise, especially at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in an auspicious, meritorious sanctuary.
When Brahmins worthy of the śrāddha have arrived, or when materials dear to the ancestors are obtained, the wise should always perform the śrāddha, even on a day that is not a festival.
Listen with a focused mind, O King, especially regarding the waning of the moon: the ray named Amā stands at the forefront of the thousand rays of the sun.
By whose own splendor the sun is said to be the illuminator of the three worlds, in him dwells the moon, and therefore she is remembered as Amāvāsyā.

That [offering] is inexhaustible for the performance of religious duties, and especially so for the rites for the ancestors; [the ancestors are] the Agniṣvātta, the Barhiṣad, the Ājyapa, and likewise the Somapa.
O King, the Raśmipās, the Upahūtas, and likewise the other Ayantunas, as well as others known as the Śrāddhabhujs and the Nāndīmukhas, are [invited]. (10)
These are known as the nine classes of Pitṛs born from the gods: the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins.
O best of kings, those ancestors, commanded by Brahmā, satisfy these [other ancestors] while excluding the Nāndīmukha Pitṛs.
Having gratified them, the Lotus-born One then brings about creation.
Other mortals, the ancestors (pitaras), also dwell in the triple heaven; they are seen to be of two kinds: those who are happy and others who are unhappy.
Those members of their own lineage who offer funeral rites (śrāddha) to them in the world of mortals—all of them remain there, highly delighted and joyful like gods. || 15 ||
Those who give nothing at all to their own kinsmen are seen to be afflicted by hunger and thirst and greatly distressed. || 16 ||
Then, after some time, all the Pitṛs, honored by the gods, such as the Agniṣvāttas and others, approached the Lord of the Thirty-three.
O Great King, having been beheld with devotion and honored by the Thousand-eyed One (Indra), as well as by all the other gods, they departed for their own abodes.
O Great King, the world of the ancestors is difficult to attain even for the gods; O King, seeing them set forth, the ancestors born of mortals [were moved]. (19)
O King, those who were afflicted by hunger and thirst, having offered excellent divine hymns and the *pitṛ-sūkta* praises, spoke while assuming a state of wretchedness.
Then, with mantras declared in the Vedas and other supreme hymns that gratify the ancestors, the Pitṛs born of the gods, being greatly delighted, spoke to them.
"We are all pleased with you, O you whose vows are praiseworthy; therefore, speak, so that we may grant whatever resides in your hearts."
The ancestors said: "We are indeed the ancestors known among men who have come here; by virtue of our own deeds, we dwell eternally in heaven together with the gods. (23)
Established in various celestial chariots in every direction, we travel through the desired worlds adorned with banners and flags.
They were frequented by swans and peacocks, enjoyed by throngs of Apsarases, and were being sung to by Gandharvas and praised by Guhyakas.
But as we remain here in conflict with the gods, an exceedingly intense and most dreadful hunger and thirst arise within us. (26)
We consider ourselves to be situated within the heart of that woman; shall we then devour these various birds as well—swans and others with sweet voices—or even the throngs of celestial nymphs? (27)
If someone, overcome by hunger, takes hold of a bird and seizes it in secret for the sake of food, he is not even capable of killing it. || 28 ||
Furthermore, those ageless and immortal birds who dwell in heaven, as well as the enchanting trees in the Nandana and other celestial groves—[all these were brought down]. (29)
"O ancestors, if we may indeed receive those fruits which are seen to have ripened and which are delightful to the mind, then we shall all take them. (30)

Even when pulled with great effort, those [lotus stalks] do not break; yet, even if we, afflicted by thirst, were to drink this water of the river of writing with great exertion, that water would not touch our hands again. (31)
"Neither anyone eating nor even drinking is seen here; therefore, our residence in heaven is indeed terrible and most dreadful. (32)
All these hosts of gods, as well as others such as the Guhyakas, are seen here stationed in their celestial chariots, all with delighted minds.
"Completely freed from hunger and thirst, and enjoying various pleasures, may we all at some time become just like him. (34)
They are entirely free from hunger and thirst and have attained supreme contentment; what then is the cause for this hunger and thirst that arises? (35)
And our sudden affliction shall never perish; therefore act, may you be blessed, so that satisfaction may arise. (36)
"May our lineage be eternal, just like that of the other gods who dwell in heaven; for you, O ancestors, are indeed the deities of those whose souls are purified. (37)
"And we ourselves are among men; therefore, we have come to you for refuge. The fathers said: "This same miserable condition has arisen for us as well. (38)
When the gods, beginning with Śakra, are preoccupied and do not offer us the śrāddha, we shall then come and make our request to all those deities. (39)
Then we attain satisfaction, being satiated by those deities whom those born of your lineage offer with a concentrated mind. (40)
How is it that they all did not reach satisfaction, even though they were fully gratified by those offerings, when their own negligent ancestors could never be satisfied by them in any way? (41)
At that time, all of them would undoubtedly be tormented by hunger and thirst; how much more so those dwelling in hell in the abode of Dharmarāja!
For this indeed has been declared as the cause for you, however it may be, regarding that terrible state arising from hunger and thirst which was described by you. (43)
Therefore, O most excellent ones, if you grant us a share of all that has been offered as *kavya*, we shall indeed perform what is beneficial and auspicious.
Having requested Brahmā and gone to his presence himself, and when they replied, "So be it," he then took them as well.
The divine hosts of ancestors have reached the supreme abode of Brahmā; having placed those Nāndīmukha ancestors at the forefront, Brahmā should offer libations to them.

When the time for creation had arrived, the Lord of the Gods, desiring growth, was then praised by all of them together; having prostrated before that lotus-seated one, all the ancestors stood there filled with humility. (47)
O Indra among kings, Vidhi, addressing those ancestors who were full of humility and preceded their speech with prostrations, spoke to them with soothing and gentle words.
Brahmā said: For what purpose have all you ancestors come into my presence? You are always worthy of worship by me along with the gods.
Likewise, others are also seen by you gathered together with you—those men who stand here possessing very little splendor. (50)
The Pitṛs said: These are indeed human Pitṛs who have attained heaven by their own deeds; yet, situated in the midst of the gods, they are tormented by hunger and thirst. (51)
When our ancestors do not offer the ancestral oblation (kavya) due to negligence, then they do not attain satisfaction; they travel by means of celestial vehicles just as the gods do.
Therefore, our prayer has been made to you for eternal satisfaction; yet we are not capable of granting it, and for that reason we have approached you. (53)
O Lord, may the deities likewise be divided among us.
O Lord of the Gods, without Kavya, this condition would be miserable.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, show us favor along with these [gods], so that there may be eternal satisfaction even for those who remain in their own abodes. (55)
"These will offer us the *kavya* that has been offered by those born of our own lineage; it is because of that, O Lord, that we have arrived in your presence. (56)
And that which is the *kavya* (offering to ancestors) of the gods does not lead to our satisfaction; for that [offering] is devoid of ritual action, and no ritual action exists for them.

Whatever *kavya* (offering for the ancestors) is bestowed upon Brahmins by mortals who have bathed and are wearing clean clothes, that shall become a source of great satisfaction for the ancestors. || 58 ||
"He is the lord of all the gods of the ancestors"—such is the Vedic revelation. One who has bathed has no entitlement to [offerings for] the gods, just as the twice-born have none for the ancestors.
Even nectar given by them would not lead to our satisfaction.
Therefore, act in such a way that those dwelling in heaven may obtain supreme satisfaction from the *kavya* offered by us humans through these [means], as if it were offered directly by them.
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard that and meditated for a very long time, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, then spoke to all those ancestors, O best of kings. (62)

Brahmā said: "In this Tretā Yuga, the designation arising from the offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) has been established; it will prevail through two ages, but it shall not exist in the Kali Yuga."
In whatever measure this decline of the ages shall occur, in that same measure people will become wicked and devoted to other [deities].
If they do not offer those funeral cakes (kavya) to you in any way as prescribed, then a most miserable condition will befall the ancestors.
Therefore, I shall provide a means for the happiness of embodied beings, by which, being fully satisfied, you shall attain supreme contentment.
For his father, his grandfather, and likewise for his great-grandfather and beyond, by means of what is given with devotion to the Brāhmaṇas through specific designation (samuddeśa). || 67 ||
"O ancestors, as long as there shall be supreme satisfaction for all of you, and likewise for my maternal grandfathers and their kin, of this there is no doubt. (68)
When they are satisfied by these three, they shall be satisfied up to my own limit; and whatever means of happiness there may be for your satisfaction, [that shall also be accomplished]. (69)
Listen now, O highly fortunate ones, as I speak of that very food by which one should honor the ancestors through the best of the twice-born.
They shall satisfy [the ancestors] with that very [offering] and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with devotion; by means of that name, eternal satisfaction for you shall come to pass.
Therefore, O ancestors, go contentedly to your own abodes.
Then, O best of kings, having gone together with them in celestial chariots resplendent like the sun, they returned to their own abodes.
Then, O King, after a long period of time had passed, those mortals still did not offer that *śrāddha* which pertains to three generations.
O lord of men, many here constantly offer portions of *kavya* intended for the ancestors, just as was done by them in former times, O King. (75)
O best of kings, a great affliction arising from hunger and thirst arose among those divine ancestors. (76)
Then, having gathered together once more, they all went to Brahmā for refuge; bowing down deeply in great distress, they spoke loudly to the Great-Grandfather: || 77 ||
"O Blessed One, those born of our lineage, having fallen into a state of misery, do not constantly offer us the ancestral rites (śrāddha); therefore, O Lord, we are perishing. (78)
O Lord, devise some means as before, by which even the poor may indeed satisfy their ancestors.
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard those words of theirs, O great king, the Great-Grandfather, filled with compassion, spoke thus to all the hosts of ancestors.
This is true, O highly fortunate ones: people fall into a state of misery day by day, in proportion as the excellent age recedes behind them. (81)
Nevertheless, I shall undoubtedly accomplish your purpose; I will employ a simple means by which you shall find complete satisfaction here.
O Ravi, he who stands at the head of a thousand rays is named Amā; in him dwells the moon, and for that reason the day is known as Amāvāsyā.
On that day, those men who with devotion perform a śrāddha for their ancestors and for themselves shall become well-established.
Endowed with wealth and grain, freed from all enemies, and abandoned by untimely death, they shall undoubtedly [attain this] through my word. 85.
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard those words of his, the ancestors, having obtained the *kavya* offering, became joyful in their minds with delighted inner souls. (86)
Sent by the Lotus-born Brahmā, they departed for their own abodes; and when the day of the new moon arrived, the śrāddha was offered by those born of his own lineage.

Fully satisfied and with contented minds, they remained there for exactly one month. However, as time passed, men on earth fell into a state of distress; consequently, even on this day of Darśa, few indeed perform the Śrāddha for us.
Then all the hosts of ancestors, both those who were divine and those who were human, being once again distressed by hunger and thirst, went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having approached their grandfather together, they prostrated themselves and spoke with great intensity, assuming a state of supreme dejection and speaking with voices choked with tears.
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, you have declared that the month following the waning of the moon is sacred; whatever humans shall perform during it for the sake of pleasing us," (91)
O Grandfather, because of their wretched state, they generally would not do even that; therefore, we suffer extreme affliction arising from hunger and thirst. (92)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, show us favor as you did before; for even now, we who are beset by distress shall be satisfied by you.
Bhartṛyajña said: Then Brahmā, having reflected, spoke to them, filled with compassion: "O ancestors, a simple means for your sake has been devised by me. (94)
O lords of the ancestors, by this you shall attain supreme satisfaction, even if you have not received the *śrāddha* offered on the new moon day for an entire year. (95)
Listen with concentrated minds to how, through my grace, [this occurred] in the fifth fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, when the sun was situated in Virgo.
Furthermore, whatever man offers a śrāddha on the anniversary of the day of death, his ancestors will certainly remain satisfied for the duration of a year. (97)
Knowing this, if men on earth perform the Śrāddha rite during the fortnight of the ancestors (Pretapakṣa), you will undoubtedly become fully satisfied. (98)
O virtuous ones, even for one who does not offer you a śrāddha for as long as a year—even for that single day—[the consequence shall be as follows]. (99)
Even through the gift of mere vegetables, this poor man will attain the status of one who is not to be shunned; likewise, he shall be granted a seat, a bed, food, touch, and conversation.
Those who act together with those who will do so are also the most sinful men; their progeny shall never attain growth at any time.
Neither happiness nor wealth nor grain shall ever be theirs in any way; therefore, O fathers, go quickly and without distraction to your own abodes.
Even when the terrible Kali age has arrived and people have become destitute, human beings will indeed perform at least one Śrāddha ceremony at the end of the year.
By which the entire year may be yours and there may be supreme joy for you. || 104 ||
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard that, the ancestors were delighted and went each to his own abode; even at the end of the year, having obtained the śrāddha, they would not be hungry.
Now, those wicked-souled, pitiable people here who, deluded by Kali, remained fearless and did not offer the Śrāddha even at the end of the year; || 106 ||
Their ancestors, moreover, accompanied by divine forefathers, went to Brahmā for refuge and spoke with distressed minds: || 107 ||
"O Blessed One, even at the end of the year, while the sun is situated in Virgo, those evil-minded ones born in our lineage do not offer the Śrāddha. (108)
O Lord, oppressed by him and overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, we have come to you for refuge; please provide a remedy for that.
O illustrious one, O Lord of the gods, tell us, as before, the easy and supreme means by which, through a single-day Śrāddha, eternal satisfaction may arise for us by your grace. (110)
For even if the extinction of our lineage should occur, our downfall would surely follow. || 111 ||
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard those words of theirs and having meditated for a long time, the Grandfather (Brahmā), overcome with supreme compassion, then spoke respectfully.
Brahmā said: Another means for your gratification has been conceived by me; it is simple, by which your eternal satisfaction shall be complete.
Those who, having reached Gayāśiras, shall offer a śrāddha here to you—even if it be only one—by its power you will attain a divine state.
Even for a person of sinful soul, even for an embodied being who has slain a Brahmin, even for one situated in the Raurava hell or fallen into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Even for one who has entered the state of a preta, if his descendant offers a śrāddha at Gayāśiras, that person shall attain liberation.
Having heard these words of mine, men on earth shall now perform even a single Śrāddha there at Gayāśiras; it will clearly grant you liberation, even for those who are destitute. || 117 ||
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard those words of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), the ancestors, being permitted by him, then departed for their own abodes. (118)
From that time forward, Śrāddha rites were established upon the earth; they are equal to the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and extend as far as three generations of ancestors.
O King, whatever men have gone from before, beginning with Brahmā, toward the other world, for their sake you should act according to your power.
Having granted the desired boon to as many eminent brahmins as that number, he said: "This Śrāddha, which brings happiness to the poor, is one for which no specific deity is invoked. (121)
It grants complete satisfaction to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; therefore, a wise person should perform the śrāddha ceremony.
One who desires to satisfy the ancestors with effort at these times, and especially at Gayā, should do so while longing for both worlds.
If a man does not offer the śrāddha to the ancestors on the day of the new moon, his ancestors, their bodies overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, remain in a state of suffering.
Filled with the desire for their teacher’s favor, they await the fortnight of the departed spirits, just as farmers, unwearied by day or night, await the rain-cloud.
Once the fortnight of the ancestors has passed, as long as the sun has not yet entered the sign of Virgo, the ancestors desire that the śrāddha be offered by their own sons.
Then, O King, even when the sun has entered Libra, some—tormented by hunger and thirst—desire that a śrāddha be offered by those born of their own lineage. (127)
When that time has also passed and the sun has set in the western quarter, the ancestors, becoming despondent and dejected, then depart for their own abode.
For two months, the ancestors of men wait at the door of their house, having become like the wind, afflicted by thirst and emaciated by hunger. (129)
O Lord of the Earth, as long as the sun is situated in Virgo and likewise when it is in Libra, so too, O King, on the day of the new moon, according to the word of Brahmā. (130)
Therefore, O King, one who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors should always perform the śrāddha, especially with water and sesame seeds, according to the word of Brahmā.
Even in the absence of wealth, a wise man should offer the Śrāddha on the day of the new moon; and in its absence, when the Lord of the Day (the Sun) has entered the sign of Virgo.
In the absence of that [opportunity], one should indeed perform a single Śrāddha at Gayā, by which one enjoys the fruit of a Śrāddha offered regularly. || 133 ||
O lord of men, all this that I was asked has been explained to you—namely, by what means this Śrāddha is performed by people who are devoted to their ancestors. (134)
Especially on the new moon day, O King, and during the fortnight of the ancestors (Pretapakṣa).
Whoever should hear this meritorious account of the origin of the Śrāddha, or should recite it, shall be liberated from all defects and obtain the fruit of giving a Śrāddha offering.
That man who recites this origin of the Śrāddha at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, his Śrāddha shall become inexhaustible and free from all defects. (137)
Or if it was performed with improper materials, or even by Brahmins who are unworthy; or if it was not consumed, or devoid of desire, or likewise devoid of mantras. (138)
O best of kings, everything reaches completion through the recitation of this origin of the Śrāddha, as well as through its narration and even its hearing. (139)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of Śrāddha," in the Śrāddhakalpa section of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 216.
Ānarta said: O Lord of Sages, explain today in its entirety that procedure by which the entire śrāddha must be performed; my faith is firmly established. (1)
Bhartṛyajña said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme ritual for the śrāddha, which constantly grants satisfaction to the ancestors and bestows all desires upon men. (2)

One should perform the Śrāddha rites with wealth acquired through one's own labor, and not by means of deceit, theft, fraud, or trickery. One should gather the materials for the Śrāddha with wealth earned through one’s own proper occupation; however, wealth obtained from legitimate gifts is especially distinguished as being worthy of Brāhmaṇas.
A Śrāddha is performed by means of wealth acquired through protection for a king, through agriculture for a Vaiśya, and by means of what is obtained from trade for a Śūdra.
Thus, when a substance endowed with purity has been obtained near the house, one should approach the twice-born who are worthy of the śrāddha on the evening of the preceding day.
Having gone home and become pure, free from desire and anger, he should then invite ascetics, those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), and those engaged in Brahmanical rites.
In their absence, [he should approach] householders who are devoted to the knowledge of Brahman—Brahmins dedicated to the Agnihotra sacrifice and expert in the learning of the Vedas. || 8 ||
Likewise, those who were learned in the Vedas, the elderly, always devoted to the six duties, having many servants and families, though poor, yet endowed with virtues.
O King, those Brahmins who are free from physical defects, liberated from disease, moderate in their diet, and pure—these are proclaimed to be worthy of the śrāddha.
Listen also to those who have been declared unworthy; I shall tell them to you: those with missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those who eat everything, and those who are outcasts. (11)
Those with black teeth, those with protruding teeth, those who sell the Vedas, those who corrupt the Vedas, or even those who are devoid of the Vedic scriptures; || 12 ||
Those afflicted with bad nails, those who are naked twice [at dawn and dusk], those who harm others, those beset by public scandal, as well as atheists and liars. || 13 ||
