Those who live by usury, those who follow improper occupations, those devoid of purity and right conduct, those who are excessively tall, or those who are emaciated, as well as those who are corpulent or excessively hairy—(14).
One who desires honor for the ancestors should exclude those who are hairless at the śrāddha, as well as those who take pleasure in the wives of others and he who is the husband of a vṛṣalī.
A barren woman is indeed called a vṛṣalī, and one whose children have died is also called a vṛṣalī; another vṛṣalī is said to be a maiden who has reached her menses.

A eunuch, a thief, a hypocrite, those who subsist on the food of kings, one born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra), and likewise the son of a woman with the same ancestral rite (ekapravara); || 17 ||

The youngest brother who has previously performed the fire-consecration (adhāna), as well as one who has already married or been initiated before [the eldest], should be abandoned along with his household.
One who abandons his father or mother, one who violates the bed of his teacher, one who forsakes a faultless wife, one who is ungrateful, and one who is a miserly farmer; || 19 ||
One who lives by a craft, one who is negligent, one who lives by trade, and one who makes weapons—one should avoid these at a śrāddha, as well as those whose lineage is unknown.
Henceforth, I shall declare those Brāhmaṇas who are praised for the Śrāddha rite, who were renowned of old as purifiers of the assembly from sins.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa, Trimadhu, and Trisuparṇa rites; one who knows the six Vedāṅgas; one who has completed the ritual bath following the vow of learning (vidyāvratasnāta); and one who recites the Dharmadroṇa. || 22 ||

One who knows the Purāṇas, as well as one who possesses knowledge, should be known as a knower of the Jyeṣṭha-sāman; likewise, one who knows the Atharvaśiras, who attends sacrifices, and who performs good deeds [is also qualified]. || 23 ||
One who washes immediately, one who is pure, a daughter's son, a son-in-law, a sister's son, and one who delights in helping others; || 22 ||
Those who eat refined food, speak refined words, and are always devoted to silent recitation—these Brāhmaṇas should be known as entirely purifiers of the assembly. || 25 ||
All these twice-born men, even those who are censured, when mixed with these [virtuous ones], bring satisfaction to the ancestors upon eating, provided they are born of noble lineage.
Therefore, with every effort, the lineage of the twice-born should be ascertained first; thereafter, character, age, and name, and after that, the giving away of the daughter. (27)

If a man offers a śrāddha feast or gives away his daughter to one who is devoid of learning and virtuous conduct, even if that person knows the Dharma, it is as if he has offered an oblation into a fire without the sacred fires. (28)
Or even as grain sown in saline soil results only in the threshing of chaff, therefore one should employ those endowed with noble family conduct at the śrāddha.
O tiger among kings, having recognized that even those brahmins possessed but little learning, he then took hold of their feet.
Then, with effort, having repeatedly offered salutations with both the left and right hands according to one's ability, [one should offer] pairs [of oblations]. || 31 ||
Then, touching his right knee, he should utter this mantra: "May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come hither. (32)
"Summoned by me with devotion, you too shall partake in the vow. Having thus addressed the twice-born for the sake of the Viśvedevas, [he said this] to the pair.

Then, having performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should consecrate three Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors according to his capacity, one by one separately.
One should invite either one from each of the three [lineages] or just one; this same rule is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇas on the mother’s side as well. || 35 ||
Then, having touched the feet of the twice-born, one who is devoted to the service of the ancestors should utter this with a mind purified by faith: || 36 ||
My father and likewise my grandfather are within your body; let them come together with your own father, and you yourself remain devoted to your vow.
Having thus invited the ancestors as well as the maternal grandfathers, those brahmins, being thus addressed, remained self-restrained in soul.
The sacrificer, with a tranquil mind and endowed with celibacy, having passed that night, the man should rise in the morning. (39)
On that day, one should avoid anger, Vedic study, and despicable acts; one should keep at a distance from oil massage, physical exertion, walking, and riding in vehicles.

Then, when the sun has reached the meridian at the time known as *kutapa*, having bathed and wearing white garments, and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he should perform the *śrāddha* for those invited Brahmins who have arrived satisfied.
In a secluded spot situated within the house, pleasant and sloping toward the south, where the sight of evil-doers and those of cruel deeds does not fall. (42)
If a dog, or a woman in her menses, or an outcaste, or a boar beholds that śrāddha, that śrāddha shall go to futility. (43)
Food that is stale, or that which is offered smeared with oil, or that which contains hair or is otherwise contemptible—that śrāddha shall go to futility. (44)
A śrāddha performed without the ritual divisions, likewise one devoid of silence, and that which is without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—such a śrāddha shall go to futility.
Where the sounds arising from a grinding stone and a mortar persist, or especially those of a winnowing basket, that *śrāddha* shall go to futility. (46)
Where quarreling arises during the performance of the rite, and especially where there is a breach in the row, that śrāddha shall go to futility.
Whatever is performed in the forenoon, at night, or even during the two twilights, as well as in a place that is open to the sky, that śrāddha shall go to futility. (48)
O King, if a Brāhmaṇa or a sacrificer eats or gives a Śrāddha offering without having observed celibacy (brahmacarya), that act shall go to waste.
If husked grain, or grain with its awns, or that which is given as leavings, or ghee and milk that have been half-consumed, are offered, that śrāddha shall go to futility. (50)
O King, listen with a focused mind as I describe those times at which a Śrāddha, when offered, attains imperishability. (51)
O lord of men, I shall also tell you those [rites] taught by Manu and others; listen to them, for they are eternally dear to the ancestors and bring about the destruction of all sins. (52)
In those [tirthas], even a mere drop of water mixed with sesame seeds, when offered to the ancestors with a mind purified by faith, attains imperishability upon the earth. || 53 ||
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth day of Kārttika, as well as the third day of Māgha and likewise that of Bhādrapada. (54)
The new moon day of the month of Tapasya, as well as the eleventh day of Pauṣa; likewise the tenth day of Āṣāḍha and the seventh day of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha, and likewise that of the month of Kārttika and the other [full moon] of Phālguna. (56)
O King, these five full-moon days—from Caitra through Jyeṣṭha—have been declared by me to you as the lunar dates marking the beginnings of the Manvantaras.
Whoever bathes in these waters and offers even water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass, dedicating it to the ancestors, attains the supreme goal.
In this world and in the next, by the grace of the ancestors, what need is there to mention various kinds of food, flavors, garments, and sacrificial fees? (59)
Now listen, O Indra among kings, to the Yugādis, which are dear to the ancestors; by the mere chanting of their names, even the accumulation of sins is destroyed. (60)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, the third day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava, the new moon of Tapas, and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya; 61.

However, for those belonging to the Tretā, Kṛta, and Kali ages, as well as the beginning of the Dvāpara age, there are specific rules regarding bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and especially the libations to the ancestors.
They cause what has been done to become inexhaustible and yield great fruit for virtuous deeds, whenever the sun enters Aries or when it proceeds to Libra.
Then that time, which causes [merit] to be inexhaustible, is called the equinox (viṣuva), O King, when the sun enters Capricorn or Cancer.
Then, the equinox (viṣuva) is specifically distinguished by the designation of its two courses; the sun’s transition into a zodiacal sign is called a saṃkrānti.

The periods beginning with Tretā, preceded by the solar transits (saṃkrānti), are declared in succession to yield great fruit for bathing, giving, recitation, ancestral rites (śrāddha), fire-offerings (homa), and so forth. No obstacle exists during these times; whatever is given is designated as imperishable.
Whatever is given even without faith, even to unworthy recipients by men, or even at an improper time—all that indeed immediately attains imperishability.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Determination of the Substances Suitable for Śrāddha, the Brāhmaṇas, and the Time," in the Śrāddhakalpa section of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 217.
Bhartṛyajña said: O best of kings, this Śrāddha has been described by me in general—how it should be performed by men, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, according to their respective castes.
Henceforth, O King, I shall proclaim what is remembered from my own branch of the Veda, so that there may be fulfillment here for one belonging to one's own country, caste, and birth.
Since faith is the root of the śrāddha, it is therefore proclaimed as "śrāddha"; when that [rite] is performed with that [faith], nothing therein shall go to waste.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, one should perform the śrāddha even if it is undesirable; for that water from the feet of the brahmins which falls upon the ground, O Ruler of the Earth— || 4 ||

Those born into the lineage who have died without sons attain supreme satisfaction, just as the gods do with nectar. As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of a Brahmin, for that long the ancestors drink water from vessels made of lotus leaves.
Furthermore, O Lord of Men, whatever falls upon the ground while the śrāddha is being performed—whether it be flowers, scents, water, food, or even more water—[all that belongs to the ancestors].
By that, O lord of men, those who have attained the state of worms, or even the state of insects, animals, or beasts of prey, reach supreme satisfaction.
Whatever remains as leavings from the washing of the vessels falls upon the ground; by that, those who have fallen into the state of a preta attain supreme satisfaction.
And those born of one’s own lineage who have met death by an untimely demise, as well as women of noble family who died without the funeral rites being performed or who were abandoned; (10)
That which is the portion of the leavings and that which is the scattering upon the darbha grass—by the scattering thus offered, all of them attain satisfaction. (11)
Whatever may be deficient in mantras, or even deficient in timing, or deficient in ritual procedure—that shall all become complete through the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 12 ||
Therefore, a wise person who desires eternal satisfaction for the ancestors and for himself should not perform a Śrāddha ceremony devoid of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā). || 13 ||
A śrāddha ceremony devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) is just like rain falling upon saline soil, or like a dance in the darkness, or like a song for one who is deaf. 14.

Having offered the śrāddha and having partaken of it, one should attain freedom from desire regarding the śrāddha; one should not perform Vedic recitation (svādhyāya), nor should one go to another village. || 15 ||
If one approaches the bed of a woman who has eaten at a śrāddha on that day, his ancestors will consume his semen for that entire month.
If one who has eaten at a śrāddha or the giver of the śrāddha engages in sexual intercourse, his ancestors will undoubtedly subsist on semen for the duration of a year; such is the Vedic revelation.

O King, if a person of little intelligence eats at a śrāddha or performs a śrāddha after having already given one, his ancestors will find their study of the Vedas (svādhyāya) fruitless for the duration of a year; remaining thus deprived of the fruits of the śrāddha, they are tormented by hunger and thirst.
If that lowest of men, having either eaten at a śrāddha or having given a śrāddha, departs for another village, that śrāddha shall go to futility. (19)
A Brahmin must not eat when an invitation has arrived; for if he eats out of delusion, he indeed goes to a downward state.
The sacrificer likewise must not partake of any other meal; all those men who do so certainly go to hell. (21)
If one who has eaten at a śrāddha, or has given a śrāddha, should engage in battle, that fool undoubtedly renders that śrāddha fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon these faults, especially the one who eats at a śrāddha and the sacrificer, O Lord of the Earth. (23)

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Śrāddha," in the Śrāddhakalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 218.
Bhartṛyajña said: O Lord of the Earth, I shall now describe to you the optional Śrāddhas by the performance of which a mortal attains whatever resides in his heart. (1)
O King, for one who desires a woman rich in beauty and adorned with virtue, the first day is appropriate both in this world and in the next.

O King, for one who desires an excellent daughter-in-law who is well-behaved and endowed with beauty, the śrāddha should be performed on the second day of the Pretapakṣa, which is the primary period of the śrāddha rites, O Lord of the Earth. (3)
The wise man who desires horses equal to the speed of the wind in swiftness should perform the Śrāddha on the third day.
He who desires excellent livestock, as well as wealth consisting of both base metals and precious metals, should perform a Śrāddha on the fourth lunar day for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
O lord of men, he who desires beloved sons of virtuous character who adorn the lineage, should always perform the Śrāddha on the fifth lunar day.
O King, a wise man who has departed to the other world and desires the śrāddha offered by his descendants must have that śrāddha performed on the sixth lunar day.
He who desires success in agriculture, whether in the summer or in the autumn, should undoubtedly perform a śrāddha on the seventh lunar day.
O lord of men, he who desires the successful accomplishment of trade arising from commercial dealings should perform a śrāddha on the eighth lunar day.
By performing a śrāddha on the ninth lunar day, one obtains various herds of quadrupeds, as well as good fortune, the destruction of disease, and union with beloved ones.
Whoever performs the śrāddha on the tenth day with a concentrated mind shall always attain his desired success in all undertakings.
On the eleventh day, the man who performs the śrāddha shall obtain wealth, grain, the favor of the king, and whatever else resides in his mind.
And he who performs a Śrāddha on the twelfth day endowed with faith shall obtain excellent sons as well as the cattle he desires. || 13 ||
For that man who desires liberation for himself along with his ancestors, and for one who is childless, the thirteenth lunar day is prescribed for the performance of the Śrāddha rite.
For one who performs [the rite] desiring progeny, there will be the destruction of his lineage; for him, the thirteenth lunar day is not prescribed for the increase of offspring. (15)
O Indra among kings, this is an ancient Vedic injunction regarding the ancestral rites (śrāddha): "May there be born in our lineage one who will offer [us] on the thirteenth day. (16)

One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with honey and clarified butter during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism; specifically, when the thirteenth lunar day coincides with Maghā, one should worship the ancestors with milk-rice.
The ancestors do not desire that year's performance of the Śrāddha rites; the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) has been rejected by one who is terrified of the excellence of his merit.
On that day, Śakra manifested the fear of his son’s death; and for those whose death would be by the sword, or even by an untimely death (apamṛtyu), [he showed it].
And for those who died from calamities, those who met with death by poison, those consumed by fire, and those who met with death by water; || 20 ||
O lord of men, for those killed by snakes or wild beasts, or even by horns or hanging, the Ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed on the fourteenth day.
When that is performed for them, satisfaction arises for those born of that side. || 22 ||
O King, all those desires which were previously described by me to you, one obtains them by performing a śrāddha on the new moon day; of this there is no doubt.
All this regarding the fruit of the optional *śrāddha* has been told to you, O King; having heard which, a human being obtains all his desired objects. (24)

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of Optional Śrāddhas," in the Śrāddhakalpa section of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 219 ||

Ānarta said: "Why does the destruction of one's lineage occur when a *śrāddha* is performed on the thirteenth lunar day? O great sage, explain all of this to me in detail. Bhartṛyajña said: "O King, this is the most meritorious beginning of the Yuga arising at the onset of the Kali age. It should be known as inexhaustible for bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, and likewise for the *śrāddha*. (2)
O King, if the Gajacchāyā occurs on this lunar day, then a Śrāddha performed in conjunction with the Maghā constellation certainly becomes inexhaustible.
He who offers milk mixed with honey on that day, he who offers meat for the sake of the ancestors, and he who offers the vādhrīṇasa bird; || 4 ||
With the meat of a vādhrīṇasa, satisfaction lasts for twelve years; [one should offer] a white, aged goat-lord that drinks thrice [daily], whose senses have declined. || 5 ||

One should know that the vādhriṇasa is likewise the lord of all herds; or one may offer the flesh of a rhinoceros, and satisfaction lasting for twelve years arises—of this there is no doubt; their word is not false to me.
In the Rathantara Kalpa, there was formerly an excellent king named Sitāśva, a native of the Pañcāla country who was devoted to his father.
Perform that śrāddha on the thirteenth day with honey, black pot-herbs, and exclusively with the meat of the rhinoceros, as well as with milk-rice (pāyasa).
He who offers a śrāddha with devotion, dedicated to the Lunar Dynasty (Somavaṃśa), [attains great merit].
Then, after some time, having eaten as much as he desired, he was questioned again by all those brāhmaṇas who were filled with curiosity.
O King, after the funeral rites (śrāddha), seeing him filled with faith and intent on massaging his feet, preceded by prostrations— || 11 ||
The Brahmins said: "O Great King, after performing the Śrāddha, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must then be given to the Brahmins; by that, the Śrāddha reaches the ancestors."
O King, that which was intended for us by you has not yet been bestowed upon us; setting aside base metals and precious goods alike, O King, give it to us without delay. (13)
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard that, the king spoke with a heart full of joy: "I am blessed and I am favored by the Brahmins today; of this there is no doubt. (14)
Those who desire my favor after having eaten at a Śrāddha ceremony for the ancestors, || 1 ||
Therefore, speak, O highly fortunate ones; what shall I give to you?
Or rather, [what is the use of] excellent elephants, intoxicated with rut, born of the Bhadra breed; or even those preeminent steeds, possessing the speed of thought and the wind? (16)
Or rather, what need is there for various places, villages, and cities? For there is nothing whatsoever that should not be given when dedicated to one's ancestors. (17)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "We have no need for horses, nor for jewels, nor for elephants; neither for lands, nor for chief villages, nor for anything else whatsoever. (18)
O Great King, O best of ascetics, since you have been questioned by us for this purpose, therefore grant us the sacrificial fee that destroys all doubt.
Which we all ask, being filled with curiosity. || 20 ||
The king said: "O Vaidikas, the authority to give instruction belongs to the high-souled Brahmins; however, for one of low birth, there is no authority to either bestow or receive [instruction]."
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I am not an omniscient king who would give instruction to you, who are yourselves wise and omniscient. (22)
The Brahmins said: "O lord of the earth, this instruction has arisen from a teacher and his disciple; we request something [from you], so do not be overcome by fear. (23)
And we ask one question, O Lord of the Earth, if you will speak to all these twice-born ones who are filled with curiosity. (24)
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, speak if you know it according to reality; if it is not some most secret matter, we ask you out of curiosity. (25)
The king said: "O Brahmins, if you have any doubt, I shall explain your question without hesitation; if it be a secret, then speak, O you who are free from feverish anxiety. (26)
The Brahmins said: "O King, among these various kinds of food, diverse things to be licked, all these nectars, and likewise drinks..."
Therefore, tell me today why you offer this honey which is censurable, and how it has come to be something unfit for consumption, especially for Brāhmaṇas. (28)
Likewise, O lord of men, when various months have passed, why do you offer nothing but tasteless horse-flesh? (29)
"O Indra among kings, there are purifying vegetables of every kind here, O lord of the earth, which produce a most delicious flavor for the sake of condiments. (30)

"Why do you, endowed with supreme devotion, offer us black potherbs (kālaśāka) along with pungent substances—which are greatly offensive to the palate? Furthermore, one must never, under any circumstances, perform a prohibition regarding [the offering of] food at a śrāddha. (31)

"And that which is left over as remnants must not be discarded; therefore we eat from it. For there must certainly be a reason for this, by which you bestow [this food], so that this accomplishment may remain established. (32)
Therefore, tell us everything, for our curiosity is indeed great: how it is that such a despicable thing as being tasted by a dog was given at a śrāddha? (33)
Just as you, O tiger among kings, bestow [this] with faith. || 34 ||
Having heard those words of the high-souled brahmins, that lord of the earth, filled with shame, spoke with a smile of embarrassment. (35)
O highly fortunate ones, if this secret of ours remains established [in you], I shall speak even that which is not to be told; listen with full concentration. (36)
In a previous birth, I was a sinful hunter; I was a slayer of all living beings and, moreover, a devourer of them. (37)
"O best of the twice-born, at that time I wandered through the forest, devoted to hunting with my bow, seeking lions, tigers, lordly elephants, or śarabhas."
"Once he has come within the range of my arrows, he shall not live at any time. Then, after some time, while wandering upon the surface of the earth..."
O illustrious lady, I have arrived at the hermitage of the great sage Agniveśa; having reached it at midnight, I am afflicted by hunger and thirst.
O best of the twice-born, at that time he remained there, surrounded on all sides by his disciples, expounding the ritual procedure for the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
Agniveśa said: When the moon is in the constellation Maghā (Pitrya) and the sun enters the hand (hasta), that thirteenth lunar day is to be known as the Chāyā, originating from the elephant.
When the moon is situated in Pitrya (Maghā) and the sun is also situated in its rays (Hasta), and the lunar day is that of Vaiśravaṇī (Kṛttikā), that is the shadow of the elephant.
When Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā, swallows the moon at the junctions of the lunar phases, that is to be known as Gajacchāyā; one should perform the Śrāddha rite during it.
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there, even with water and with devotion, his ancestors remain satisfied for twelve years. (45)
When the moon has entered a tree and its shadow faces the east, that is to be known as the "elephant-shadow" (gajacchāyā); what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
That paternal lunar day (tithi) shall undoubtedly be a bestower of merit; on that day, the Śrāddha should be performed with whatever materials have been gathered.
At dawn, however, there is no doubt that it leads to the complete satisfaction of the ancestors, even with vegetables, as well as with inguda, bilva, badara, and cirbhaṭa fruits.
"Whatever food a man eats, his deities eat that same food. Having replied, "So be it," they departed each to their own abode. (49)
All the highly fortunate disciples, headed by Nārāyaṇa, as well as Agniveśya, having taken leave of the best of the twice-born, went to sleep.
And as they were conversing thus at night, I heard it; and I too shall undoubtedly perform the śrāddha ceremony tomorrow morning.
Having slain him, he took his sword and a great quantity of his flesh; likewise, he took honey and especially black pot-herbs (kālaśāka).
Having taken [offerings] from those of my own kind, I shall satisfy those ancestors.
Having thus resolved in my mind, O best of the twice-born, I fell asleep; then, at the clear dawn when the orb of the sun had risen, || 54 ||
"O best of the twice-born, I then gathered many honeycombs, and likewise obtained black pot-herbs according to my desire. (55)
Then, O best of the twice-born, having taken all of that and cooked it at that very moment, I bathed and, with devotion, offered it to my own kinsmen, to my ancestors, and to the hunters.
"O twice-born ones, in this manner I previously gave [offerings] intended for my own ancestors; never at any time have I given anything else to anyone. (57)
Then, after a long time, O twice-born ones, I met my death; by the power of that gift, I entered a royal womb.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the memory of my former births arose within me; and those ancestors were gratified by me with that rhinoceros meat mixed with honey. (59)
"O best of the twice-born, because of this reason I perform the śrāddha ceremony, for it has brought me supreme joy lasting for twelve years."
Abounding with rhinoceros meat, honey, and black potherbs, it was devoid of ritual prescriptions, lacking Brahmins, and bereft of sesame seeds and *darbha* grass.
That Śrāddha was performed by me; this is the fruit that has now come to him, having been properly conducted according to the rules by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
O best of the twice-born, while seated, I perform the śrāddha endowed with faith, provided with darbha grass and sesame seeds, and accompanied by mantras.
I do not know what the fruit will be, nor what shall come to pass at present; therefore, having understood this, you too, O best of the twice-born, [should act accordingly].
O best of the twice-born, when the day of the elephant has arrived and the shadow of the elephant has appeared, you must gratify your own ancestors.
By this, the ancestors shall obtain satisfaction for twelve years, and your own supreme goal shall be attained, just as it has now been achieved by me. (66)
Bhartṛyajña said: Having heard those words of his, all those best of Brahmins were satisfied and offered words of praise to that lord of the earth. (67)
From that time forward, those best of the twice-born, intent on devotion, performed the śrāddha rites on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya.
Satisfied with honey, black pot-herbs, and the meat of a rhinoceros, they attain supreme perfection, mounted upon excellent celestial chariots.
O best of gods, the ancestors, and especially the Pitṛs, together with the deities, vie with one another for power through the influence of that which is offered by one born of their lineage.
O King, having fully understood the purpose of the śrāddha, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and even the two Nāsatyas, conferred with one another regarding the mantra.

"Since no *śrāddha* ceremony takes place on that day upon the surface of the earth, by whose power we all—though pursued by humans intent on performing *śrāddhas*—do not fall into a state of defeat; therefore, we shall curse them. (72)
From this day forward, whoever shall perform a Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day while the thousand-rayed sun is situated in Virgo, his lineage shall suffer extinction. (73)
Thus, by the curse of the gods, this great guest has been consumed by fire.
From that time forward, the supreme Śrāddha is not performed for her; whoever performs it out of negligence shall suffer the destruction of his lineage. (76)
Fearing this, they do not perform [the śrāddha] even under the shadow of an elephant; specifically, this rice-ball has been offered here in the "elephant-shadow" (gajacchāyā).

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gajacchāyā," in the Śrāddhakalpa section of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 220 ||

Bhartṛyajña said: For this reason, O King, on that day no one ever offers a śrāddha for the sake of the ancestors; out of fear of the extinction of their lineage, O King, this truth has been spoken by me. (1)
Even without performing a Śrāddha, milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee should be given to the most eminent Brāhmaṇas on that day for the sake of their satisfaction.
The flesh of the rhinoceros, black potherbs, and the meat derived from the vādhrīṇasa—these are declared to be fit for offering to Brāhmaṇas on all such occasions.
Drinking thrice, with senses diminished, and followed by his entire herd—this is declared to be the vādhrīṇasa, which always grants satisfaction to the ancestors.
Even in his absence, O King, the most excellent rice cooked with milk should be given to the Brahmins on that day for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Even in his absence, water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered, along with Darbha grass, gold, and pieces of gold.
O King, whatever merit arises for a man by performing the fortnightly śrāddha, the entire fruit of that is obtained on that specific day, O King.
O King, one should offer oblations intended for the ancestors with clarified butter, honey, milk-rice (pāyasa), kālaśāka, honey, or the meat of the rhinoceros (khaḍga).

This ancient Vedic revelation states that [the merit] is attained even by what is given without a formal *śrāddha* ceremony; therefore, with every effort, when the lunar mansion of the ancestors has arrived—on the thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada) while the Sun is in the constellation Hasta—one should act accordingly.
O King, even a poor person desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors should offer water mixed with sesame seeds and accompanied by fragments of gold.
Ānarta said: "O Brahmin, since meat is condemned in the scriptures, why then is it used? Tell me everything regarding the śrāddha ceremony."
He who, being merciless, increases his own flesh with the flesh of another, surely goes to hell; this has been declared by the great seers.
And you, O best of the twice-born, describe his power to me, especially regarding the performance of śrāddha; thus, I have this doubt.
Bhartṛyajña said: "This is true, O highly fortunate one: meat is censured by the virtuous. Since it is nevertheless employed in the śrāddha rite, I shall tell you the reason for that. (14)

And when the creation was commenced by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, after he had worshipped the ancestors and the gods led by the Nāndīmukhas, then the sword first appeared, as did the Vādhrīṇasa [goat].
Then all those ancestors, both those who were divine and those born of human origin, accepted [the offering] as if it were their own sacrificial portion.
Then Brahmā said to them: "O Pitṛs, these two have been properly ordained by me for you; accept them as your sacrificial offerings."
From these two, supreme joy shall arise for you; by my word, there is no doubt that these two men are the highest on earth. (18)
Even while killing for your sake, he shall not incur any sin; therefore, one who desires prosperity should give [the gift] with every effort.
The flesh produced from the Khaḍga and Vādhrīṇasa deer provides great satisfaction at a Śrāddha; moreover, those two supreme, divine beings shall go to the heavenly world.
For the giver of the śrāddha, there shall be supreme and very rare spiritual welfare; and for the ancestors, there shall be inexhaustible satisfaction lasting for twelve years.
For this reason, O lord of men, meat is permitted for these two on that specific day; its use on any other occasion has not been prescribed.
Rohitāśva said: O Brahmin, how can a śrāddha that provides satisfaction to the ancestors be performed when the meat of the rhinoceros (vādhrīṇasa) and the rohita fish has not been obtained? (23)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Payasam (milk-rice) mixed with honey should be offered for the satisfaction of the ancestors; by that, indeed, a year-long gratification arises for the ancestors.
O King, the flesh of a goat and that produced from a porpoise are said to bring great satisfaction for a year, excluding the monthly [fasting periods]. (25)
In its absence, O Great King, the flesh of a boar is said to grant satisfaction to the ancestors for ten months; there is no doubt in this matter. (26)
Satisfaction from the flesh of a wild buffalo lasts for nine months; that from a ruru deer lasts for eight months, and that from an ena deer lasts for seven months. (27)
The flesh of the śambara is prescribed for six months, that of the hare for five; four months are said for the śallaka, and three for the tittiri bird.

One may offer the flesh of fish for two months and that of the kapiñjala bird for one month; however, one should never employ the flesh of other animals in rites for the ancestors under any circumstances.
O best of kings, the flesh of these very animals is purifying.
Ānarta said: O best of the twice-born, tell me correctly why these [animals] are considered pure, whose meat is prescribed for the śrāddha; explain that to me. (31)
Bhartṛyajña said: While that Self-born One was creating the world, he himself subsequently created the animals, such as the rhinoceros, the vādhrīṇasa, and others.
O best of kings, after that, others were created according to the measurement of eleven; and Aja was created first, and he likewise attained the state of being fit for sacrifice.
Likewise, O lord of men, these animals were created here first; and by him who was creating the crops, sesame seeds were fashioned first of all. (34)
O King, rice was created for the sake of ancestral rites (śrāddha), as were millet among wild grains, along with wheat, barley, beans, and mung beans.
I shall also describe the wild rice (nīvāra) and the śyāmāka grain in their proper order: they desire satisfaction through meat, yet that meat must be devoid of further meat. (36)

When the various species of flowers were created, the hundred-petaled lotus (śatapatrikā) was created first; therefore, it is always the foremost among them for the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha).

While creating the elements, that Self-Existent One created silver; therefore, it was ordained by Him for use as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in a śrāddha ceremony for the sake of complete satisfaction.
And whatever is given to the twice-born from silver vessels for the ancestors, there is no end to its merit even at the end of a Yuga.
In the absence of silver vessels, one should even recite their names; for, O King, the ancestors are indeed satisfied even by such a recitation.
While creating the flavors, that Self-born One created honey; therefore, it is praised in the Śrāddha ceremony as that which bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors.
A śrāddha that is devoid of honey, even if it is joined with all other flavors and even with sweet foods, does not lead to the satisfaction of the ancestors.
If there should not be even a particle of honey in the śrāddha offering, one should nevertheless utter its name for the satisfaction of the ancestors; for that is how they are pleased. (43)
While that Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was creating vegetables, he first created the kālaśāka; therefore, it bestows satisfaction upon him.

Indeed, while creating time, he first fashioned the *kutapa*; therefore, a wise person who desires eternal satisfaction for the ancestors and happiness for himself should perform the *śrāddha* during the *kutapa* period. (45)
O best of kings, by that Creator, while creating the creepers, the darbha grass was created first; therefore, they are remembered as being worthy for the śrāddha rite.
By that lotus-born creator, while creating the Brāhmaṇas worthy of the Śrāddha rite, the daughters' sons were created first; therefore, they are remembered as being especially worthy of the Śrāddha.
Even if he has abandoned purity, or is deficient or excessive in limbs, one should employ a daughter's son in the Śrāddha for the complete satisfaction of the ancestors.
By him who first released the animals, cows were created; therefore, their milk is recommended for the śrāddha, especially clarified butter.
Therefore, ghee is recommended when given at a śrāddha for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
O best of the twice-born, those who were seen by him first while creating progeny are therefore praised; they always bring satisfaction to the ancestors at a śrāddha ceremony.
While creating the gods, he placed the Viśvedevas at the forefront; therefore, they are to be worshipped first when the rite of Śrāddha has commenced.
Having been properly gratified, they protect that Śrāddha; having been honored previously, they destroy any defects in the Śrāddha.
When these most eminent ones had crept forth, the *phūṛā* Śrāddha was performed by the Grandfather himself; from that, the gods were created. (54)
Because of that, O King, they attained renown throughout all the worlds in ancient times.
This nature of the Śrāddha as a sacrificial session (sattra), which is the supreme secret of the ancestors and which renders what is given inexhaustible, has been proclaimed by me to you. (56)
O best of kings, if anyone recites this while a śrāddha is being performed for brāhmaṇas desiring to eat, that śrāddha shall become inexhaustible.
O King, whoever should hear this endowed with perfect faith shall obtain that merit which belongs to the prescribed śrāddha rite. || 58 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Enumeration of Articles Worthy of Śrāddha Offerings Created by Brahmā at the Time of Creation," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 221.

Bhartṛyajña said: "For those whose death is by weapons, or even by untimely death (apamṛtyu), for those who have died from calamities, and for those who have met a violent end through poison—" || 1 ||
And for those consumed by fire, those who met death in water, those killed by serpents or tigers, and those by horns or even by hanging; || 2 ||
O lord of men, the śrāddha for them should be performed on the fourteenth day; when it is performed for them on that day, their satisfaction for the duration of that fortnight shall be attained.
Ānarta said: Why is the fourteenth day prescribed for the *śrāddha* of those killed by weapons, and not on other days? This is my doubt; please explain it to me. (4)
They do not recommend the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite beyond the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Why is it that [the former] must be performed there? Tell me this in detail.
Why is the *pārvaṇa* rite not performed on that day, especially since it is already the fortnight of the departed (*pretapakṣa*) and the entire *śrāddha* has been completed? (6)
Bhartṛyajña said: O King, in ancient times, during the Bṛhat Kalpa, there was a great Asura named Hiraṇyākṣa, who was powerful, heroic, and a source of terror to all the gods.
Having performed various austerities, especially during the dark fortnight when the month of Nabhasya had arrived, Brahmā was highly pleased by him.
Brahmā said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child; ask for whatever you desire. I shall grant even that which is not to be given; therefore, ask without delay."
Hiraṇyākṣa said: "O Lotus-born One, spirits, ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas, being hungry, constantly beg of me. (10)

When the Śrāddha is performed on the day of the ancestors (Pretapakṣa) while the sun is situated in Virgo, the satisfaction resulting from a year's worth of offerings generally occurs in a single day.
"O Lotus-born One, grant them today the food of truth (tattva); O Grandfather, once they have attained satisfaction through that, they shall remain for a year."
Śrī Brahmā said: Whatever man shall offer a śrāddha to his ancestors on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the departed (pretapakṣa), when the month of Nabhasya has arrived; || 13 ||
By my word, it will happen without doubt for the pretas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and others who have been mentioned by you. (14)
For those who have died by an untimely death and those who have been slain in battles, satisfaction shall be attained when the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is offered by their sons. || 15 ||
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then vanished from sight; Hiraṇyākṣa also, filled with joy, went to his own abode.
And as for the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha that is offered by men on that day to those slain by weapons—I shall explain the reason for that to you.
And those men who, while fighting in battle with a mind free from conceptual construction, are slain by weapons, are not born again as mortals in this world.
Those who are slain with their backs turned, intent on flight, become *preta*s; so said the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Even those who, when being struck, speak out of wretchedness in your presence, or who might feel remorse after being shattered by blows; || 20 ||
Manu Svāyambhuva has declared that even they may become hungry ghosts (preta) in this world; for at times, even among the brave, a wavering of the mind occurs. (21)
Due to their delusion, their own sons should offer the śrāddha there on that day for all embodied beings who have died by an untimely death.
O best of kings, because the state of being a preta arises [from that], that day is specifically proclaimed as worthy of the śrāddha rite.
Since men must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on that day after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, I shall explain the reason for that to you.
O King, if one's own father should ever have fallen into the state of a preta, a śrāddha must be performed on that day for his satisfaction.
On that day, the ancestors beginning with the grandfather (the great-grandfather) are not eligible for the śrāddha anywhere; if one should offer it out of delusion, it is consumed by the Rākṣasas.
O King, by the word of Brahmā, as well as by the bhūtas, pretas, and dānavas, only the ekoddiṣṭa rite is to be performed here, and not the pārvaṇa.
On the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors, when the sun is situated in Virgo, the grandfather does not accept [the offering] together with the father at that time.
Nor did his father, O King, nor likewise his great-grandfather [do so]. || 29 ||
For this reason, O King, the Pārvaṇa rite is not prescribed; for when that day has arrived, the Śrāddha would otherwise become futile.
A Nāgara should perform the Śrāddha rites and vows with Brāhmaṇas born in his own locality; otherwise, those acts would become fruitless. || 31 ||

Whatever Śrāddha is performed by Brahmins born in other places, even if it is certainly complete, it becomes useless when compared with the rites performed by those Nāgaras who are devoted to their duties.

Furthermore, even Nāgara Brahmins who have fallen away from proper conduct are indeed worthy of the Śrāddha; if a kinsman is available, even if he is like a bullock, what is the use of many other Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences? (33)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Determination of the Śrāddha for Those Killed by Weapons on the Fourteenth Day," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Bhartṛyajña said: The Pārvaṇa Śrāddha on the new moon day must be performed with Brāhmaṇas worthy of the Śrāddha; the Śrāddha should never, under any circumstances, be performed in a contrary manner.

If a man performs a *śrāddha* ceremony with those born of adultery, those who have been cast out, and others of such kind, that *śrāddha* will undoubtedly go to waste, even if performed by Brāhmaṇas. (2)
Ānarta said: A very great fear has arisen in me regarding what has been proclaimed here—that a śrāddha performed by those born of adultery or those who have been cast off shall go to futility. (3)
O high-minded one, Manu indeed declared twelve types of sons who always provide the status of a son even to those who are childless.

The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the son bought with money, the son maintained [by adoption], the son accepted [as such], the son received with the bride, and the son of an unmarried girl, O best of men— (5)
Likewise, the other two, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are also proclaimed to be sons.
The disciple was protected from death, as was the aśvattha tree at the edge of the forest; why have these not been mentioned, that you speak in such a manner?

Bhartṛyajña said: "O highly fortunate one, it is true that all of them are sons according to dharma; however, they are declared to belong to the three preceding ages, and do not remove the impurities in the Kali age."

For that purpose, there shall be a lineage among them, limited only to that extent, in age after age, for those worlds abounding in virtuous beings, but not in the Kali age for those of small intellect.
This legal procedure for providing water-stations has been declared for the Kali age alone; since people possess little strength of character, this rule was ordained for that reason. || 10 ||
Listen to the fruit for him who causes a confusion of castes here: from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a son is born who is a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
The one known as the Vāraḍa is remembered as the lowest of all the lowest. || 12 ||
Likewise, from a Kṣatriya [with a Śūdra woman] is born a Sūta; from a Vaiśya, a Māgadha; and from a Śūdra, one is declared an Antyaja. Therefore, these sons are excluded [from the lineage].
O King, for these as well, seven excellent sons were foretold; five [of them] would lead to the destruction of their lineages and the downfall of their ancestors.
The legitimate son, the adopted son, the purchased son, the one reared as a son, the disciple, the one whose life was saved, and likewise the seventh, the *aśvattha* [son]. (15)
For they always protect a man from falling into the terrible hell named Pūn; therefore, they are remembered as "Śobhanāḥ" (the auspicious ones). || 16 ||

The son born of the field (kṣetraja), the son taken with the bride (sahoḍha), the maiden-born son (kānīna), and the kuṇḍa and golaka—these five cause even those ancestors who have reached heaven to fall.
For this reason, the funeral offering (śrāddha) for one born of adultery is in vain.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of Worthy and Unworthy Brāhmaṇas and Others for Śrāddha," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 223 ||

Ānarta said: "O highly fortunate one, O observer of excellent vows, I have heard from you which Brāhmaṇas are worthy of the Śrāddha rite, as well as those sons who are to be avoided, and many other such matters. (1)
Now tell us the ritual preceded by mantras which must always be performed by a householder for the complete satisfaction of the ancestors.
Bhartṛyajña said: Having invited those most excellent Brāhmaṇas for the sake of the Śrāddha and having brought them at the Kutapa hour, one should address them all as follows: || 3 ||
"May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great strength come; may they who are appointed to this śrāddha be attentive. (4)
Having thus worshipped them all and performed a circumambulation, one should place both knees upon the ground and then cause the arghya offering to be presented.

"O Indra among kings, with this mantra and with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sandalwood paste, let these best of the twice-born accept this *argha* offered by me; for the purpose of washing their feet, let them do what is pleasing to me."
Having spoken thus, he should then scatter darbha grass along with unbroken grains (akṣata) upon the smeared surface of the earth, while invoking the Viśvedevas.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should scatter double-folded darbha grass mixed with sesame seeds upon the ground, intending them for one's own ancestors.

In this manner, all rites pertaining to the gods should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya), and those pertaining to the ancestors with the thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), with the exception of the rites for the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
O King, all should be placed facing the east in pairs according to one's ability; likewise, the ancestors on the mother’s side should be placed facing the north.
Either one by one, or even three together, or each separately, one should establish the ancestors with the discus for the complete satisfaction of the forefathers.
One should cause their seats to be offered with the sixth case-ending, using straight darbha grass with unbroken rice grains and water, placed toward the right side.

On the left side, one should scatter double the number of uneven darbha grasses along with sesame seeds; having poured water into the hand, one must by no means place the darbha blades [into the water].
If one who is devoid of wisdom offers a seat made of darbha grass with his hand, the ancestors do not take their place upon that seat.
The invocation should be performed using the second case ending, so that they all come when summoned individually. (15)
If one should ever invoke the ancestors using an incorrect case-ending, those illustrious ones will not arrive, even if they are hungry.
O King, with this mantra, "O Viśvedevas, come hither," their invocation should be performed using unbroken grains (akṣatas) near the head [of the vessel].
Then, with the mantra "uśantastvā," one should invoke the ancestors with sesame seeds; thereafter, O best of kings, one should recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."
With the mantra "śanno devī," accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā," he should likewise pour water into the arghya vessels for the ancestors.

One should cast unbroken grains (akṣata) there with the mantra, "Thou art barley; drive away [evil] from us. Then one should offer sandalwood paste, fragrant flowers, and incense in due order. With a composed mind, one should present the arghya water into hands that hold the pavitra grass.
With the mantra "yā divyā," accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā," one should likewise pour water into the arghya vessels of the ancestors.

"You are sesame, having Soma as your deity, fashioned by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice; mixed with the ancestral offering (svadhā) by the ancients, satisfy these ancestors and these worlds for us, svadhā!"—with these words, he should cast the sesame seeds.
Then, with the mantra beginning "yā divyā," one should cause the *arghya* to be offered; having taken all the *arghya* vessels together into the vessel for the ancestors. (23)
Then, one should place that vessel face-down while reciting the mantra; however, one who desires long life must not look at its water with both eyes.
Then one should take up the items beginning with sandalwood and ending with lamps; thereafter, having taken the cooked food, one should inquire of the brahmins, the best of the twice-born.
"I shall perform a fire-oblation (homa) originating from the ancestors; O sir, let permission be granted to me as I take up the apasavya position. (26)
When they said, "Do so," he then went to the fire-sanctuary; the first oblation was offered with the words: "Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana. (27)
And after that, [one says] "Svadhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors"; then the offered food and the remainder are given to those worthy of the śrāddha.

Then, having given the desired food and touched the vessel, he should perform the silent recitation (saṃjapa). Having taken the thumb of the Brahmin and placed it in the middle of the cooked food, [he should proceed].
Taking the earth as his vessel and reciting the verse dedicated to Viṣṇu, he should likewise not offer salt directly with his own hand.

O King, that *śrāddha* which is given with one's own hand and contains visible salt becomes useless if it is placed upon a vessel while the recipient has already eaten half; therefore, having ascertained that the Brahmins are satisfied, one should then scatter food before them. (31)

May those living beings of my lineage who have been consumed by fire, as well as those who have not been consumed, find satisfaction through what is given upon this earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.
Having offered water once each time, one should mutter the Gāyatrī three times; then, having recited "madhu vātā," one should question the best of the twice-born.
Then, O Indra among kings, being devoted, he should request permission for the remaining food for the sake of feeding his kinsmen, saying, "Are you satisfied? (34)

Afterwards, one should prepare the altar for the ancestors (pitṛvedi) near the remains of the food; however, there should be no leavings of food in the presence of the twice-born who occupy the seats of the ancestral Brahmins.
Then, having prepared the altar for the ancestors sloping toward the south, and having spread darbha grass upon it, he should perform the ritual sprinkling (avanejana).

O King, one should subsequently offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) in due order with the preceding [mantra] ending in the appropriate case-inflection; furthermore, one should again offer water here using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, and indeed, one should offer a thread separately upon each of those rice-balls.
He who constantly applies the thread to the preceding clusters will cause discord among them through its breaking and their mutual conflict. (38)

Then, O King, one should worship all the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) just as one would the best of the twice-born; having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should likewise wash both hands and feet.
Having paid homage to the ancestors, and thereafter having sprinkled [the site] well with water using the left hand, O King of Kings, one should then request the most excellent blessings.

Thereafter, on the sixth day, the inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) should be offered. Taking up the purifiers (pavitra), one should utter "Svadhā" above [the offerings]. When they have replied, "Let there be Svadhā," one should sprinkle [the water] over the funeral cakes (piṇḍa). || 41 ||
Then, taking honey, milk-rice, and water with sesame seeds, he should scatter them over the ancestors while reciting the mantra beginning with "ūrjasva. || 42 ||
Having turned the vessel for the arghya offering face upwards, one should give a sacrificial fee; gold for the deities and likewise silver for the ancestors.

Then, one should offer the water for well-being (svastyudaka) starting with the ancestors while keeping the left hand uppermost; this should not be done by women, nor by children, nor by others, nor by anyone else at all.
And he himself should wash the vessel of the Brahmin invited to the śrāddha. || 45 ||
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, O best of kings, he should pray: "May the ancestors be non-terrible; may our lineage increase. (46)
"May our donors prosper, may our Vedas and our progeny increase, may faith never depart from us, and may we have much to give. (47)
May we have abundant food, may we receive guests, may there be those who solicit us, and may we never have to solicit anyone. (48)

"May these very blessings be fulfilled; may all the gods (Viśvedevas) be pleased thereafter. For the sake of well-being, one should offer water, beginning with the ancestors, while the sacred thread is over the left shoulder. (49)
Then, after reciting the verse "vāje-vāje," he should release [the horse]; having circumambulated it while reciting "āmā vājasya," he should cause it to sit down.
Having performed the massaging of his feet, one should follow him as far as the boundary; then one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) and partake of a meal.
O lord of men, the sun remains visible only as long as it is silent.
Furthermore, if a man performing a *śrāddha* eats after the sun has set, that *śrāddha* becomes fruitless; therefore, one should not eat at night.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Śrāddha," in the Śrāddhakalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 224 ||
Ānarta said: O best among speakers, O high-minded one, please tell me the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite in detail, just as the *pārvaṇa* rite has been described.
Bhartṛyajña said: Listen now to those three [rites] that take place before the collection of the bones; one should perform the Śrāddha at the very place where death occurred. || 2 ||
Then there is the Ekoddiṣṭa; next, the rest stop where it was made on the way; thereafter, the third Śrāddha is prescribed at the place of the funeral pyre.
On the first day, the second day, as well as the fifth, the seventh, the ninth, and the tenth—these are the nine śrāddhas.

Upon reaching the Vaitaraṇī river, the deceased shall obtain satisfaction; the rite is performed for a single individual, devoid of the gods, with a single offering of water (argha) and a single purifying blade of grass (pavitraka).
O best of kings, the rite should be performed without the invocation; likewise, the question regarding satisfaction should be made, and then "svaditam" (it is well-tasted) should be uttered once.

The dismissal of the Brāhmaṇa is performed with the mantra "May you be delighted. One should take two blades of Darbha grass whose tips are neither cut nor split; one should know this as the *pavitra*. This is prescribed for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

In every instance, the father is declared [the recipient]; the father is [the object] in the rite of libation (tarpaṇa), at the time of the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the ancestral rite (pitrya), and when offering the inexhaustible gift (akṣayyodaka) to the father.

In all rites of libation (tarpaṇa) performed for the lineage, the word *gotra* ends in a vowel; in the procedure for the assignment [of offerings], it is used in the dative case as *gotrāya*; and in the offering of the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*), it is used in the genitive case as *gotrasya*.

The form "śarman" is used when performing the rites of *arghya* and so forth; "śarmā" is used in the rite of *tarpaṇa*; "śarmaṇe" is used in the giving of grain; and "śarmaṇaḥ" is used in the procedure for making [the offering] inexhaustible.
In the case of *mātṛ*, *mātre*, likewise *mātuḥ*, *āsane*, *kalpane*, and *akṣaye*; and in the case of *gotra*, *gotrāyai*, *gotrāyāḥ*—these are the nominative and subsequent case endings. (11)
One should likewise pronounce "devi," "devyai," and "devyāḥ" for the mother; the first, fourth, and sixth [case endings] are used for the successful accomplishment of the śrāddha.
If a Śrāddha is performed without the proper case-endings, or conversely, with them misplaced, one should know that it is as if unperformed; it does not reach the ancestors.
Therefore, with every effort, a wise Brāhmaṇa should always perform the ritual for the Śrāddha according to the case-endings as they have been described.
Thereafter, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is established as taking place after one year; however, if an upcoming auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) should occur, one may perform it even before that time.
O King, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, which is for a single deity and not for the three deities, should be performed for the deceased according to the procedure prescribed for the *pārvaṇa* rite.
But it is my considered opinion that this should be done with a single cooking; having taken up the vessel of honorific water (arghapātra) which was prepared for the sake of the deceased. (17)

One should pour that [water] three times into the three vessels for the ancestors; likewise, having divided the rice-ball (piṇḍa) into three parts, one should place them upon the three ancestral rice-balls.

If one brings [the water] with these two mantras, there shall be no state of being a preta thereafter. Then, having performed the *avanejana* (sprinkling) for the ancestors first, in the proper order... (19)
One should again offer all the perfumes, incense, and so forth, reciting [the names] beginning with the ancestors, while omitting the fourth.

Some perform the fourth [offering] for the deceased, and then for their own father; the śrāddha for the father should come first, and the other [for the deceased] afterwards—this is not my opinion. || 21 ||
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* ceremony, except on the anniversary of the death (*kṣayāha*) and on the fourteenth day for those killed by weapons.

Whoever should offer a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa) to a deceased person for whom the sapindikarana has already been performed, one should know that rite to be as if unperformed; such a person becomes a slayer of his ancestors.
But he whose father has passed away while his grandfather is still living should, having pronounced the name of his father, pronounce the name of his great-grandfather.
But the grandfather, having eaten in person, receives the rice-ball (piṇḍa); and on the anniversary of the grandfather's death, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha is prescribed. || 25 ||
If, having somehow abandoned his own progenitor, he does not offer [the funeral cake] to him, then by that unperformed Śrāddha, there is no small amount of fear for him from the ancestors.
On all new moon days (amāvāsyā) and when the father has died, the pārvaṇa rite is prescribed; this is declared to be the case for the middle of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya as well.
As long as the sapinda-relationship has not been completed, one should not perform the śrāddha rite.

When one's father has met his death and the fortnight for Śrāddha rites has arrived, the Śrāddha for the grandfather and others must be performed; however, there is no unification of the funeral rice-balls (naikapiṇḍatā).

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 225 ||
Bhartṛyajña said: Since sapinda-ship is declared to be complete through the ancestral pindas on all sides, as long as that sapinda-ship has not been finalized, the deceased remains a preta. || 1 ||
Even one endowed with righteousness and possessed of ascetic merit [is not exempt]; for this reason, the practice of Sapindikarana has been declared by the sages.
Whichever womb a man may enter elsewhere, he attains satisfaction while residing there from whatever is given by those born of his lineage. (3)
Ānarta said: "O great sage, when one's own ancestors—fathers and grandfathers—are seen in a dream after a long time and they request their own desires, what would happen from that? (4)
Bhartṛyajña said: "Those whose destination has not been determined and who remain in the state of being a *preta*, they all indeed manifest their own selves."
This which I have spoken is the truth for those of my own lineage and no others—namely, how they were born here in this world through their various auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Ānarta said: "In this matter, how should the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite be performed for one who has no son? You ought to tell me that. (7)
Bhartṛyajña said: "O Lord of the Earth, since we do not have a legitimate biological son, how can he become the fourth [son] for our four ancestors?"
Because he departs (vrajati) with great intensity (prakarsena), he is therefore proclaimed as a *preta*; his *sapiṇḍana* rite should be performed by a son, a brother, or a wife.
O Indra among kings, if a fourth [son] is never born, then these eleven sons beginning with the *kṣetraja*, as they have been described, [are recognized]. (10)

O Indra among kings, the wise declare that these substitutes for a son exist so that there may be no omission of rites; for if his subsequent ceremonies are not performed at the proper time, [the lineage perishes].

The Nārāyaṇabali rite, which destroys the state of being a ghost (preta), should be performed for other men who have met with untimely death (apamṛtyu), as well as for those who have committed suicide and for those who have died by the hand of a Brāhmaṇa. || 12 ||
Ānarta said: O high-minded one, how does a person meet with death in this world? (13)
By what action does one go to heaven or even to hell, or to liberation, O illustrious one? Tell me all of this in detail.
Bhartṛyajña said: The righteous, the sinful, and likewise the wise—these three destinies are recorded here. From righteousness heaven is attained, and from sin indeed hell. (15)
"Liberation is attained through knowledge; this truth has been spoken by me. O King, regarding this matter, [I shall speak of] Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, who is yet to come."
O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and best of monarchs, together with Kṛṣṇa, O lord of kings, questioned his grandfather.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Grandfather, how many hells are renowned in the world of Yama? By what sin do living beings go to all of them? (18)
Śrī Bhīṣma said: There are twenty-one hells in the abode of Yama; living beings go to them according to their own past actions. (19)
And two others, variegated and wonderful, stood at the gate in the abode of Yama.
Then Citra painted all the dharmas arising from living beings, while Vicitra, applying supreme effort, painted every sin. (21)
There are always eight messengers of Yama, born from Dharmarāja, who lead men, brought under their control, from the world of mortals [to the realm of the dead]. || 22 ||
Karāla, Vikarāla, Vakranāsa, Mahodara, Saumya, Śānta, Nanda, and Suvākya is remembered as the eighth. || 23 ||
Of these, those four who were previously described as having fierce forms—all of them lead sinful people to the abode of Yama.
Those four others who have been described, possessing bodies of gentle form, lead every righteous person to the abode of Yama.
He was mounted upon a celestial chariot, attended by throngs of apsarases.
And for those who arise from the sinful nature corresponding to their written record, as well as for their servants, no number can be known. (27)
One hundred and eight of those diseases were appointed by Yama to be his assistants here, stationed within the fever and consumption.
Having gone there, those diseases first bring a human being under their control.
Then the messengers of Yama, having gone there, unobserved by all people, seized the vital breath (vāyu) situated at the base of the navel.
Having cast their bodies upon the earth, they travel by the path of Yama; the path of Yama is proclaimed to consist of eighty-six thousand [leagues]. (31)
In that place, O highly fortunate one, the river named Vaitaraṇī is renowned from of old; she is indeed always established there with two currents.
There, O bull of the Bharatas, blood flows in abundance through one stream, and extremely sharp weapons are situated in its midst.
O King, those who indeed bestow a cow upon a Brahmin at the time of death cross over that [ocean of existence] by taking hold of its tail.

Likewise, others [cross] with their own arms that second stream, which is a hundred yojanas wide and situated along the Vaitaraṇī; its flowing water is always accessible to those who possess righteousness.

Those men who are givers of cows, when the time of death has arrived, take hold of the cow's tail and cross that river of vast waters; others, however, who have not given gifts of cows, must cross it by means of their own arms. || 36 ||
Therefore, one who desires a favorable destination for oneself when the time of death has arrived should especially perform the gift of a cow.
Immediately after that, the sinners go by way of the path of evil, while the most righteous, having ascended excellent celestial chariots, proceed by way of the path of dharma.
On the far shore beyond the Vaitaraṇī river, extending five yojanas in length, is the forest named Asipatravana, which inflicts suffering upon the world of the wicked.
There, indeed, are hundreds of sword-leaves made of iron, which cut the bodies of mortals on all sides.
If those wicked-souled ones who have stolen the wealth and the wives of others attain liberation through these nine *śrāddhas*, then [liberation] indeed arises from them. (41)
Beyond that, one should know, is the famous Kūṭaśālmali tree; in it, which is thick with thorns, people hang head downwards.
Those who are betrayers of trust and are always utterly merciless are burned by fire below day and night; however, they attain liberation once the eleventh-day *śrāddha* has been performed.
Therefore, that hell of terrible form is said to be mechanical; there, the slayers of Brahmins and others who are evildoers are tormented. (44)
O King, by means of the Śrāddha performed twelve times and offered to them, they clearly attain liberation from that hell known as Yantra.
Then, glowing iron pillars stand ready; they embrace all those who were devoted to the wives of others.
When the monthly śrāddha has been performed, they shall attain liberation from those [fetters]. || 47 ||

Then, fierce dogs with iron teeth stand ready; they devour those sinful men who eat the flesh from the backs [of living beings]. By performing the Śrāddha on the third fortnight (traipakṣika), they shall obtain liberation from them.
Immediately thereafter, crows with iron beaks stood there; by those whose eyes were filled with passion, other women had been gazed upon. (49)
They repeatedly destroy their eyes as they are born again and again; however, through the śrāddha performed in the second month, liberation is produced.

Then, men who were devoted to backbiting are led through the midst of Śālmalī spikes and other iron thorns; however, by performing the Śrāddha rite for three months, their liberation is brought about.
Then there is the well-known, great, and terrible hell called Raurava; it is ordained for those who slay Brahmins and causes immense suffering. || 52 ||
Those who reside there are repeatedly cut by various weapons; through the performance of the Cāturmāsika Śrāddha, their liberation is brought about.
But another is described as the Kṣāroda hell, which is most terrible; it is ordained for ungrateful people and is always full of intense agony.
Where they are suspended head-downwards with their feet upwards and tormented, their liberation is brought about by the gift of five months' [provisions]. (55)

Beyond that, the hell named Kumbhīpāka should be known as being of a terrible form; there, those who were killers of people and indeed killers of children are seen being thrown into oil and struck with clubs. (56)
Men who betray trust fall into a terrible hell; by making a gift every six months, they are released from that peril.

Likewise, another hell is heard of as being filled with serpents and scorpions; those lowest of men who are hypocrites in this world go there. Through a gift given for seven months, their liberation is brought about. (58)
Likewise, another hell named Saṃvartaka is proclaimed; there [go] those wicked souls who subvert the Vedas and revile the virtuous. (59)
Then their tongues are torn out with tongs made of fire; those who speak falsehood for their own sake have their bodies devoured by dogs.
And for those who speak even for the sake of others, by giving [their own] limbs in their entirety for eight months, their liberation is produced. (61)
Agnikūṭa, Mahāplāva, and the terrible, great Naraka—there indeed do those deluded men go who provide false testimony.
Remaining there, they endure fierce torment and suffer exceedingly; yet, a gift given on the ninth month brings them supreme consolation.
Then there was another [hell] piled all around with iron spikes; and therein were those who set fire to dwellings and those who kill women.
There, afflicted by suffering and being beaten by the servants of Yama, they run about; for them, a gift given during the tenth month serves as liberation from that place.
Then the ground was covered on all sides with heaps of charcoal; those intent on betraying their master wander there in every direction.
A gift given there on the eleventh day leads to liberation; [otherwise, one falls into] a hell of terrible appearance, filled with scorching sand. (67)
Those men who, seeing their master arrive, become intent on flight, they too are cooked there in suffering; for them, the Śrāddha performed during the twelve months reaches [them].
Whatever water or food is given within a year, they enjoy that very thing on their path, provided by their own kinsmen. (69)
Then, after a year has passed, those who have gone into the presence of Dharmarāja encounter the results of their own actions—the auspicious and inauspicious—arising from their own deeds.
Having thus experienced these fifteen hells, those men then attain birth once more in the mortal world.
Those proponents of causal reasoning who take birth in a foreign land attain satisfaction through the constant offering of libations and gifts. (72)
Those who are intent on betraying their masters and those who take birth in an evil kingdom—by the offering of *haṃtakāra*, their satisfaction is produced. (73)
Those men who eat without having first given to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born, are born in a time of famine due to that sin.
When the anniversary of the death occurs and the śrāddha rite is performed, from that satisfaction arises. || 758 ||
Those who create discord between a loving couple by telling lies to one another, their own wives shall become unchaste.

When a single word is spoken [by her], she speaks ten words filled with anger; she is deformed, wandering about, and despised by all the world. Through the merit of those who give their daughters in marriage, happiness shall arise for them and for these women there.
He who creates an obstacle to the giving away of a daughter, or who sells her, shall give birth only to daughters and never to a son alone. (78)
They are born as prostitutes, widows, or likewise unfortunate women; yet, through the attainment of the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage, happiness arises for them.
Those by whom jewels and likewise other scriptures have been stolen are born poor, mute, lame, and sightless; yet for them, happiness arises in this world through the gift of those scriptures. (80)
These hells, which arise within the world of mortals, have been described; by means of these, every action performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is fully known. (81)
Then, through the fruits of his pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthas), his purification comes about. || 82 ||
Bhīṣma said: "O lord of men, all this that I was asked by you has been explained to you, as well as the twenty-one hells and how they are situated. (83)
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, ask whatever doubt remains in your heart.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Torments of the Twenty-one Hells Attained through Various Sins and the Means for Their Prevention," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Hāṭakeśvarakṣetramāhātmya*, within the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira. || 226 ||

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O King, having heard the true nature of the hells, fear has come upon me. How can there be liberation even for those sinners—by means of vows, or observances, or fire-offerings, or by resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites?"
Bhīṣma said: For those men whose bones fall here into the Gaṅgā, the fire of hell shall have no power over them as they stand in its midst.
Those for whose names the Śrāddha rite is performed by their own sons at the Gaṅgā, ascend a celestial chariot and travel above the hells.
O King, those who, having committed a sin, perform the expiation as prescribed, or give gold, shall not go to hell.
The rest, by the attainment of their own karma, experience [its results] as is appropriate; they experience either heaven or even hell, O lord of men.
Those masters who die at the Dhārā-tīrtha while standing before it go to the supreme abode, far removed from all hells.
Whether at Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, or the city of Nāgara; or at Prayāga or Prabhāsa—he who abandons his own body there, even if burdened with great sins, does not behold hell.
He at whose wedding a blue bull is yoked shall not see hell, even if he were a slayer of a Brahmin, by virtue of his own son.
Having undertaken a fast unto death with Janārdana dwelling in his heart, that man who gives up his life does not behold hell.
And those who perform the fast unto death (prāyopaveśana) in the abode of Citreśvara never go to hell at any time. || 10 ||

He who always provides food for the distressed, the blind, the miserable, those exhausted by the road, and those intent on pilgrimage—whether at the proper time or even out of season—that man does not behold hell. (11)
He who gives a water-cow when the sun is situated in Leo, and a sesame-cow when it is in Capricorn, does not behold hell.
By beholding Somanātha at Somagraha and by bathing in the Sarasvatī at the ocean, one shall not go to hell. || 13 ||
