At Sannihitī in Kurukṣetra, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu on a Sunday, he who goes there does not see hell.
He who performs a circumambulation of Tripuṣkara in silence on the full moon day of Kārttika when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation does not behold hell.
But those who behold Caṇḍīśa when the sun has entered Capricorn on a Sunday do not go to hell. (16)
O King, those who rescue a cow from the mud, a Brāhmaṇa woman from slavery, virtuous men from theft, or a twice-born man from execution, do not go to hell.
O lord of men, all this that I was asked has been explained to you: how a man does not go to hell by his own karma, and how even a man who has committed only a slight sin goes to hell. (18)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Means for Dispelling the Torments of Hell," in the Śrāddhakalpa of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira. || 227 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, by seeing the Lord reclining upon the waters, situated at the entrance of the cave for the purpose of sleep, even a sinner is liberated from sin. || 1 ||

Having bathed at that entrance to the cave, which is pure and the refuge of the world, whoever worships with devotion Him who reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa shall obtain liberation from all sins committed from birth until death.
He who worships with devotion the Lord of the Gods while He is in deep sleep during the four months of the rainy season is not born here again.
There, in former times, the highly fortunate sages, having served that Lord and taken earth from his auspicious shrine, [prepared it for their use].

They have attained the supreme abode, that highest station of Viṣṇu; whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, that fruit is produced by his worship during the Cāturmāsya.
Whatever fruit men attain by meeting death while protecting cows, that same fruit is obtained by worshipping the one who reclines upon the waters for four months.

Even one of evil conduct, even one devoted to the wives of others, even a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, or a despised killer of a woman—by worshipping that deity for four months, he is liberated.
The sages said: "O Sūta, regarding that which was spoken by you—that [the Lord] lies upon the waters at the entrance of the cave—how is it so? We have a great doubt concerning this."
It is heard, O Lord, that the divine Madhusūdana always lies upon the Ocean of Milk, the Blessed One having resorted to yogic sleep.
How did that Blessed One lie, stationed at the entrance of the cave? Proclaim this in its entirety, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: "O highly fortunate ones, this is true: in the Ocean of Milk, Madhusūdana lies asleep, having entered into yogic slumber while reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa."
Listen attentively to how the Blessed One himself resided in that field in the form of one reclining upon the waters.
And just as he, having been worshipped there for four months, bestows liberation upon men while residing there, so shall I proclaim. (13)
O twice-born ones, all four months are likewise censurable on this earth for all principal rites, such as sacrifices, marriages, and the like.
Having bowed down to that God of gods, who is beyond attributes yet whose essence is all attributes, I shall proclaim this to you, O best of the twice-born. (15)
To the unmanifest, the immeasurable, who consists of all the gods, to the omniscient lord of poets, and likewise to the self of all beings.
In former times there was a fierce and great Dānava named Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was struck down by Viṣṇu after he had assumed the body of a man-lion (Nārasiṃha).
To him were born two sons, endowed with all auspicious marks: Prahlāda and Andhaka, who were peerless in valor in battle.
When the great asura Hiraṇyakaśipu had departed for the other world, Prahlāda was appointed by his ministers for the sake of consecration.
Then that wise man did not desire the great kingdom of his father and grandfather, even though it had come to him; for that reason, I shall tell you. (20)
The Dānavas always harbor hatred toward the discus-bearing god; however, they never again direct their hatred toward him.
For this reason, all the sons of Diti were abandoned by him; even Viṣṇu, renouncing his own sovereignty, took refuge with him.
Then, by those base Dānavas who were devoted to hatred toward Viṣṇu, Andhaka was established in the kingdom of his father and grandfather.
Andhaka, too, having propitiated the four-faced God of gods, thereafter obtained immortality for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Then Varapuṣṭa also engaged in conflict with Śakra.

Having defeated Śakra in a great battle, the Daitya personally seized the portions of the sacrifice; having gone to Amarāvatī and expelled Śatakratu, he then took possession of heaven together with his own retinue.
And Śakra, having propitiated Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, attends upon him like a servant, accompanied by all the gods.
Then, after a long time, the wielder of the Pināka bow was pleased with him and said to him, "I am a granter of boons; speak, O Śakra, what shall I do?"
Indra said: "O Lord of the Gods, my kingdom, along with its sacrificial shares, has been seized by Andhaka through his prowess; having slain him, quickly restore it to me. (29)
Having heard that from the distressed one, the moon-crested Lord said: "I shall grant you a kingdom encompassing the three worlds."
Then he dispatched a wise messenger named Vīrabhadra, who was a leader of the Gaṇas, saying: "Go and speak thus to that Andhaka."
"By my command, abandon heaven and go to the surface of the earth; rule there over the kingdom that belonged to your father and grandfather. (32)
"Relinquish our sacrificial portions; if not, I shall slay you immediately. Having gone there, he clearly spoke to Andhaka exactly as Śambhu had instructed.
Then the exceedingly powerful Adhaka, possessing great and distinguished intelligence, laughed and spoke to him for the sake of accomplishing his master's purpose.
"Just as a messenger is indeed not to be slain, so I do not kill you; who indeed is this Śaṅkara by name who addresses me in such a manner? (35)
"Does that fool not know me? Or does he perhaps desire death? (36)
Or rather, it is indeed true that he is despondent regarding life itself—constantly afflicted by poverty and deprived of all enjoyments.
For him, playing in the cremation ground, smearing ashes upon his limbs, wearing serpents as ornaments, and having the quarters of the sky as his garment and matted locks for hair; (38)
"What purpose is there for him in living, that he speaks thus to me? Therefore, O messenger, go quickly and deliver my words clearly. (39)
"Abandoning this Kailāsa, perform penance in Vārāṇasī; this place has been granted by me as Kailāsa for my own son. (40)
"O Śaṅkara, there is no doubt that even a wolf is endowed with power; otherwise, I shall take away the life-breaths of you and Indra. (41)
Having heard that and rebuking him again and again, Vīrabhadra, overcome by great anger, returned to Kailāsa.
Then he related those words of the wielder of the Pināka bow, which were especially cruel; thereupon, the wielder of the Pināka became enraged.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Disregard for Śaṅkara’s Command by the Asura Andhaka, Arrogant Due to the Boon Granted by Brahmā," within the Jalaśāyin Episode of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 228 ||
Sūta said: In the meantime, Śambhu, surrounded by all his Gaṇas and by all the gods beginning with Indra, his eyes bloodshot with anger, mounted his bull and went to the city of Amarāvatī. || 1 ||
Andhaka, too, beholding the divine host arrived along with Mahādeva and his attendants, attained the highest satisfaction.
Then, mounting his excellent and auspicious chariot drawn by beautiful white horses, he set forth with his fourfold army for battle.
Then a battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas, as well as with the hosts of deformed appearance, making death the point of no return.

The battle continued for the duration of one thousand years; day by day, it was the gods who suffered destruction there, not the Dānavas. Then, at the end of the thousand years, the moon-crested Lord, filled with rage, raised his trident with his own hand and pierced [the demon].
Although that great asura was himself pierced by that trident, due to the power of Brahmā’s boon, he was not deprived of his life-force.
Then, rising once more, he engaged in battle with the Great-Souled One; and filled with rage, he especially struck down many hosts.
He struck Śaṅkara repeatedly with blows from his mace.
Thus, for the duration of a thousand years, there occurred a fierce battle between Andhaka and the wielder of the Pināka bow, which brought terror to all the worlds.
When that Daitya, though pierced by the trident, did not meet his death, the powerful one rose up again and again and struck blows with his mace.
Likewise, Śaṅkara, having learned that he was exempt from death by virtue of the boon granted by Brahmā and by all the inhabitants of heaven, [acted accordingly].

Then, having pierced him with the tips of his spears and tossed him up into the courtyard of the sky, he held him suspended head-downwards like an umbrella; blood born from his limbs flowed from his body onto the ground.
Until the end of a thousand years, only his skin, bone, and sinew—these three elements—remained; the other four had perished.

Having realized that he was deprived of his strength due to the depletion of his bodily constituents, he then employed the means of conciliation by offering praise together with the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Andhaka said: "I did not know you were a god, O evil-minded one of wicked speech; that which has been done by you is fitting for one endowed with such prowess."
O best of gods, this is appropriate for one blinded by pride, devoid of discernment, intoxicated by his own prowess, and lacking in wisdom. (17)
Having attained prosperity, knowledge, and even sovereignty, one who is ill-behaved and intoxicated by pride does not remain for long, just as I, who am arrogant with pride. (18)
"I am sinful, I am a doer of evil deeds, I am evil-natured, and I am born of sin. Save me, O God, O Lord; be the remover of all sins. (19)
"I am suffering, I am wretched, I am miserable, and I am devoid of power; O Lord, O All-pervading One, you ought to protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (20)
"O Supreme Lord, O Sinless One, I am wicked and filled with sin; for that reason, this thought toward you has arisen in me now. (21)
When the destruction of all evils has occurred, there arises auspicious meditative cultivation.
O Three-eyed Lord, even he who merely recites Your name attains liberation; how much more so one who is devoted to Your worship? (23)
O Lord, for those who are devoid of your worship, their days come and go; those days belong to the dead, not to the living.
May no one be born in that family where Śambhu is not the deity—not even one afflicted with leprosy, or suffering from disease, or lame, or even deaf.
Therefore, O Lord, liberate me; grant me welcome now. O All-pervading One, my inclination toward the Dānavas has departed, and likewise, my kingdom has been abandoned.
Sons, grandsons, and wives have been abandoned along with all my possessions; O best of gods, by this triple truth, I touch your feet. (27)
Having heard those words of his and knowing him to be cleansed of all sin, he slowly lifted him from the stake as he stood there, bowed down in humility.
Then the Lord himself gave him the name Bhṛṅgirīṭi and said, "You shall always be dear to me."
"O son of Mahākāla, you who have the face of an elephant! Stay here, gentle one; through my grace you shall experience happiness and you will not remember your kinsmen. (30)
Having promised "So be it," and having bowed to the moon-crested Lord, he stood together with all his attendants, joined by his reliance upon the Master.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Bhṛṅgīriṭi," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 229 ||
Sūta said: When Andhaka, the best of the Dānavas, had thus attained the status of a Gaṇa, his son named Vṛka was devoid of energy for conquering his enemies.
O best of Brahmins, filled with great fear and accompanied by the surviving Danavas, he entered the interior of the ocean, which was extremely difficult to traverse.
Then Śakra, his soul filled with joy, bowed to the bull-bannered god; having received his command, he entered Amarāvatī.
And he ruled the kingdom happily even throughout the three worlds, O best of the twice-born; furthermore, he received his rightful sacrificial shares upon the surface of the earth.
At that very time, Vṛka, the son of Andhaka, quickly emerged from the ocean and arrived at Jambudvīpa. || 5 ||
Considering the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara to be meritorious and bestowing excellent success, it was there that penance was performed by his father, the evil-minded Andhaka.
Remaining in seclusion, he performed penance so that no one would know of it, meditating with devotion upon the Lotus-born, the foremost of the gods.
For as long as a thousand years, subsisting only on water, that lord of the Daityas performed a second penance while meditating upon the Grandfather (Brahmā).
O best of the twice-born, thereafter he subsisted on air for that length of time, with his senses conquered, touching the surface of the earth only with the tip of his big toe.
And so, O best of the twice-born, when the fifth thousand had arrived, Brahmā attained satisfaction upon seeing his great austerity.
Then, O best of Brahmins, having approached that pit, he said to him: "O wolf, desist from this most terrible austerity!"
Choose a boon—may it be well with you—that which has always resided in your mind.
Vṛka said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then, O Grandfather, make me free from old age and death. (13)
The illustrious Brahmā said: "O child, by my grace you shall become free from old age and death; of this there is no doubt. This which I have spoken is the truth. (14)
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then vanished right there; Vṛka, too, having accomplished his purpose, returned to his father’s home.
Having gone there to the mountain named Raivataka, which was radiant with flowers of every season, he deliberated with his own ministers; then, desiring battle, he mounted Indra’s vehicle.
And Indra, having recognized that Dānava of great strength as being exempt from old age and death through the power of Parameṣṭhin, [acted accordingly].
Abandoning Amarāvatī out of fear, he quickly went to the world of Brahmā accompanied by all the gods. || 18 ||
In the meantime, Vṛka arrived at the abode of the gods, accompanied by his joyful army and retinue. || 19 ||
Then, having received the consecration resulting from the flower-bath from Śukra, he himself established himself in that position of Indra.
Having been consecrated by Śukra to the position of king of the gods, Vṛka established the Daityas in the positions of the deities.
For the sake of providing sacrificial shares to the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Maruts as well, the Brahmins took refuge in the command of Śukra.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Kingdom by Vṛkendra," within the Jalaśāyin Episode of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 230.
Sūta said: Vṛka, having obtained that kingdom produced from the three worlds, then commanded the entire world according to his own will.
In strength, heroism, fortitude, and wrath, that Dānava was a thousand times greater than Andhaka; he was fierce and most terrible.
In the meantime, no mortal on earth performed sacrifice, nor oblation, nor even recitation, having learned that the Daityas had taken possession of the abode of the gods.
Now, he who performs dharma—whether it be a fire-oblation or even recitation—having reached a well-concealed place, does so for the gratification of the immortals.
Then the Daityas residing in heaven, being deprived of their sacrificial shares, fell into great doubt regarding the portions derived from mortals.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, the Dānava dispatched secret spies into the world of mortals and spoke to them skillfully.
Whoever on this earth undertakes or performs for the sake of deities a sacrifice, a fire-oblation, or a gift, he shall undoubtedly be put to death by you at my command.
Then, having heard those words, the exceedingly powerful Dānavas went to the surface of the earth and moved about everywhere in concealment.
Whosoever they saw devoted to muttering prayers or performing fire-sacrifices, or engaged in Vedic study, they slew with sharp swords.
At that very time, O twice-born ones, the best of sages, Sāṃkṛti, remained hidden with his body concealed in that pit where, in former times, Vṛka had previously performed penance.
Then, seeing him stationed within that cave at that time, they rebuked him for his asceticism and spoke with harsh words.
O best of the twice-born, having seen the four-armed image consisting of Vāsudeva standing before him, worshipped with fragrant flowers; || 12 ||

Then, filled with rage, they raised their weapons and struck him; however, when they were unable to kill him as he was enveloped by the splendor of Viṣṇu, all their weapons—even though they were stainless—became blunted.
Then, overcome with embarrassment and filled with despondency, they all reported that news to Vṛka, the lord of the Dānavas.
O highly fortunate one, a certain brāhmaṇa, having placed an image of Viṣṇu before him, performed penance in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Where you performed penance out of fear of all the inhabitants of heaven, and even by stealth, you perform such penance for us as well. (16)
Since all weapons have become blunted against his body, therefore deal with him as is appropriate by means of blows. (17)
Having heard those words of theirs, Vṛka, filled with anger, went to that place where Sāṃkṛti was staying.
Having gone there, he lifted that image of Viṣṇu and, rebuking it again and again, hurled it far outside the pit.
He struck him with a blow of his right foot and said to him, "You deserve to be killed by me, since you [protect] Janārdana, my enemy."
"Because you worship [me] through theft, I shall take away your life. Having spoken thus, that lord of the Daityas struck him with a sword.
Then, O best of the twice-born, although that sword of his was sharp, as it struck his body, it shattered into a hundred pieces.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, that son of Saṅkṛti cursed him.
"O wicked one, since I have been struck by you with kicks of the feet, therefore let your two feet fall instantly upon the surface of the earth! (24)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, as soon as he had spoken those words, his two feet fell upon the surface of the earth like two five-headed serpents.
At that very moment, however, there arose a truly great cry of lamentation from Vṛka’s soldiers and especially from the women.
Then the gods, having recognized that he had fallen into a state of lameness, came to the summit of Mount Meru and struck down his retinue.
The remaining Daityas who survived the slaughter retreated to the depths of Pātāla; Vṛka, too, having become lame, remained steadfastly engaged in penance.
Accompanied by all the women of the inner apartments and filled with pain and grief, Indra then obtained a kingdom from which all thorns had been removed.
And from that point on, religious rites were further established in the netherworld (rasātala).
Then, after a long time, O best of the twice-born, his grandfather, being pleased, arrived there in the middle of the pit and spoke.
"O Vṛka, O child of noble vows, I am pleased with you; choose a boon. I shall surely grant it to you, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (32)
Vṛka said: "O God, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then, O Brahma, grant me a gift of a foot, so that by your grace this lameness of mine may quickly depart."
Having heard that, the Lotus-born One summoned Sāṃkṛti there and spoke to him with conciliatory words: "O best of the twice-born, [this is] regarding this Vṛka. (34)
"By my word, let his lameness depart; therefore, act accordingly."
Sāṃkṛti said: "O Grandfather, O Lord of the gods of gods, never before have I spoken an untruth even in jest; how then can I do such a thing? (36)
Brahmā said: "O best of Daityas, this Vṛka is eternally devoted to me; you are his beloved grandson, and for that reason, I entreat you. (37)
O virtuous sage, I am unable to make your word false.
Sāṃkṛti said: "This Daitya is evil-minded and remains intent on the harm of the gods, especially that of the high-souled Vāsudeva, my city. (39)
Generally, a sinful soul who reviles the twice-born deserves lameness; yet he shall be endowed with great strength and be exempt from old age and death. (40)
"O Lord, if he should obtain your feet—which were formerly bestowed by you—he will destroy the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans. (41)
Therefore, let that form remain as it is; you ought not to perform a transformation, since you, O Lord, must also concern yourself with the welfare of the three worlds.
Brahmā said: When the rainy season has arrived, it is not appropriate to set out on a journey, especially for one desiring victory, except when the onset of cold or heat occurs. (43)
And for that reason, during the four months of the rainy season, he should remain with his feet bound and, being inaccessible to all people, perform his duties with fortitude.
O twice-born one, may that Vṛka, the best of givers, become endowed with feet, by which the welfare of the gods and the twice-born shall be secured.
When this is done, O Brahmin, your word shall not prove false, and the fruit of that asceticism shall not go in vain.
Sūta said: When the high-souled Sāṃkṛti replied, "So be it," two new feet suddenly emerged from his body.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, that fierce Dānava attained the state of a beast and remained within that very pit.
For eight months, he, together with his wife and kinsmen, remained in distress, remembering his great enmity with the gods day and night.
And for another four months, having gone forth filled with rage, he constantly tormented the gods, including Indra, as well as human beings.
He destroys all those places where the Dharma is established. || 51 ||
For four months, she destroys the wives of the gods, as well as all their gardens, cities, and houses. (52)
Then the gods, having approached Janārdana, the God of gods, who dwells eternally in the Ocean of Milk reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa; || 53 ||
Having stayed there in his presence for the four months of the rainy season, they then returned fearlessly to heaven for another eight months.
When that most terrible Daitya had thus become lame, after some time had passed, the King of the Gods, the best of deities, tormented by grief, spoke to Bṛhaspati at the end of the month of Āṣāḍha.
"O Guru, that month has arrived—the terrifying rainy season—in which that Vṛkāsura, who has regained his feet, will come. (56)
Therefore, we must go from here to the Ocean of Milk, the abode of Keśava; one should not remain thus dejected, living as a dependent upon another.
Abandoning their own homes, as well as beds, seats, various vehicles, and whatever else was dear within the house. || 58 ||
Therefore, O best of sages, please tell us some means indeed—whether it be a vow, a religious observance, or a fire sacrifice.
Just as one’s bed is not left empty by one’s own wife, so too is the abandonment of one’s own home not brought about. (60)
"O best of the foremost of the twice-born, I am despondent because of the loss of my own station; for whenever each year arrives, there occurs a displacement from that place. (61)
I shall sleep upon the ground for four months, devoid of a wife, agitated by fear, and devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Having heard those words of him who was afflicted by fear, Bṛhaspati reflected for a very long time and then spoke to the god Śatakratu.
There is a great austerity known as the Aśūnyaśayana vow; perform it with a concentrated mind for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu.
The god Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, who reclines upon the waters in the Ocean of Milk as the source of the universe—he will grant you what is beneficial. 65.
O Vāsava, by its grace, one’s bed shall not become empty, no destruction of the home shall occur, and all enemies shall be destroyed. (66)
Sūta said: When that vow, consisting of the Aśūnyaśayana rite, had been performed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu was pleased and then spoke to the lord of the gods.

Śakra said: "I am pleased; may it be well with you. Choose a boon, O observer of noble vows, for this vow performed during the four months has been fulfilled. Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, request whatever has long resided in your heart. (68)
Indra said: "O Kṛṣṇa, you too know that defeat which is being inflicted upon me here by the lord of the Dānavas, the most wicked-souled Vṛka. (69)
My kingship over the three worlds is established for eight months; for the remaining four months, he comes every year.
Knowing this, O best of gods, show compassion toward me and act in such a way that my sovereignty may be eternal.
Viṣṇu said: "He has been made ageless and immortal by the Lotus-born One; how then can the kingdom be yours while he is still alive? (72)
Nevertheless, O Lord of the Gods, I shall nevertheless act for your benefit.
Having abandoned the Ocean of Milk and gone together with Lakṣmī to the sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara, he then established himself upon that [site].
O Śakra, I shall exert myself and prepare a bed such that he will not move for the duration of four months. (785)
Therefore, O Thousand-eyed One, being oppressed by my weight from that place, you must always perform what is beneficial for you at every rainy season.
Therefore, go now to heaven and rule your kingdom without any thorns; when the rainy season arrives, you need not fear anything arising from it.
O God, whoever shall worship me with true devotion while I am lying there by means of this vow, to him I shall grant his desire. (78)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa dismissed Śatakratu, who was now entirely freed from fear, so that his own kingdom might flourish.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, the omnipresent Lord himself always comes there to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Then, exerting great effort, he made his bed upon Vṛka; once he was crushed by him, he was indeed unable to move.
Then, constantly oppressed by that burden, he was as if dead; this occurred when the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika had arrived.
Viṣṇu makes his rise and goes toward the Ocean of Milk; he too, by the curse of Sāṃkṛti, shall become a wolf and incur lameness.
And thus Hari did not leave his bed for four months out of fear of that evil-minded lord of the Asuras and Dānavas.
In that place, mortals perform all rites, but not those originating from sacrifices; for that Sacrificial Being (Yajñapuruṣa), while asleep, does not partake of the sacrificial portion.
Likewise, all those auspicious sacrifices, beginning with the *ktvā*-affixed rites such as giving gifts, and preceded by the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), are no longer performed. (86)

O twice-born ones, with the exception of the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), all those other rites would be in vain while the Lord of the Universe is asleep.
Whatever vow or religious observance a man performs while the Lord of the gods is asleep, all of that shall become fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, while Janārdana is fast asleep, men should remain established in their vows for the sake of pleasing that deity. 89.
When the eleventh day arrives—the day of Hari’s reclining and awakening—whatever action is performed becomes excellent and imperishable.
What need is there for much speaking here? Whatever vow is performed by men, Hari, standing above the Daityas, attains supreme satisfaction through it.
Thus the Blessed One spoke: "Janārdana was sleeping there; has a fever come upon him, or even great agony? (92)
On that day, whatever food a sinful person eats, [one should avoid it]; therefore, with every effort, when the day of Hari has arrived, [one should observe the fast]. 93.
A wise man should not eat even at another time; how much less so at that place where he sleeps and where he awakens? (94)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, all this that I was asked by you has been narrated—concerning why Janārdana lies within the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Having completely abandoned the Ocean of Milk for four months at all times, O Lord, hear now what the fruit shall be when that [deity] is worshipped.
The man who, established in his vows, worships that Lord for the four months of the rainy season, goes to where that God resides.
What is the use of many gifts given, what use of vows, or what use of fasts—for he who certainly worships the lotus-eyed Lord while He is asleep there? (98)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ekādaśī Vow," within the "Legend of Jalaśāyin" in the "Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Field," in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: While the Lord of the gods, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, was fast asleep, whatever else was to be done—whether a religious observance (niyama) or a vow (vrata)—[should be performed].
"Tell us, is it human sacrifice, or recitation, or charity? Sūta said: O Brahmins, whatever rule there may be when the one whose banner is Garuḍa has fallen asleep..."
"He shall yield infinite fruit," so said the Grandfather (Brahmā). Therefore, by every possible effort, a wise person should [honour] some outsider.

O best of Brahmins, whether it be a restrictive vow, recitation, fire-oblation, Vedic study, or even a religious observance, these must be performed for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus.
The man who passes the four months of the rainy season eating but one meal a day, dedicated to Vāsudeva, shall be born wealthy.
He who takes his meal under the auspices of the lunar mansions while Janārdana is asleep becomes wealthy, endowed with beauty, and possessed of a sound mind.
O best of the twice-born, he who passes the four months of the rainy season by means of alternate-day fasts shall dwell eternally in Vaikuṇṭha.
He who eats only at the sixth meal-time when Janārdana is asleep shall obtain the entire fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
He who, having fasted for three nights, should always spend the four months [of the rainy season] in this way, shall not be born again here in this cycle of existence by any means whatsoever.
Becoming a superior person, he should always spend the four months at dawn and dusk; that man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 10 ||
He who performs the *ayācita* fast while Madhusūdana is asleep shall never suffer separation from his kinsmen.
He who abandons anointing with oil, and especially anointing with ghee, for the four months of the rainy season, shall become a partaker of enjoyments in heaven.
The man who passes even four months in celibacy shall ascend an excellent celestial chariot and dwell in heaven according to his own desire.
He who performs his ablutions for four months, avoiding oil and renouncing honey and meat, shall always be a partaker of liberation.
He who avoids leafy vegetables in Śrāvaṇa, curd in Bhādrapada, milk in the month of Āśvayuja, and meat always in Kārttika; || 18 ||
He shall not be tainted by sin even for what was done during a year; O best of the twice-born, this is the word spoken by Svāyambhuva Manu.
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has ended, Brahmā enters the vegetable; Viṣṇu enters curd in Bhādrapada, and Hara enters milk in Āśvayuja.
All three [types of people] likewise pass away into the state of flesh-eaters during the month of Kārtika; therefore, one should avoid them entirely among the gods.
That mortal who avoids bell-metal while the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa is asleep shall obtain the full fruit of both the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices. || 19 ||
And for that best of Brahmins who eats food free from pungent and salty flavors, all meritorious works of public utility (pūrta) shall likewise always bear fruit. || 20 ||
He who performs a fire sacrifice for four months with sesame seeds and unbroken grains, using Vaiṣṇava mantras ending in "svāhā," is never afflicted by disease.
Whoever, having bathed, stands before Viṣṇu and recites the Pauruṣa Sūkta, his intellect shall increase like the moon, the lord of stars, during the bright fortnight.
He who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of Viṣṇu with fruits in his hand while observing silence is not tainted by sin.
He who, according to his ability, gives sweet food to the foremost of Brāhmaṇas—especially during the month of Kārttika—shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
That learned man who performs the study of the four Vedas within the temple of Viṣṇu during the four months of the rainy season shall always be wise.
And whoever should perform dance, song, and so forth in the house of Viṣṇu, the Apsarases shall perform these before him once he has gone to heaven.
But that Brahmin who provides dancing, singing, and so forth day and night during the four months of the rainy season, shall attain the state of a Gandharva. || 27 ||
O twice-born ones, if all these observances can be performed for four months, or even during a single month of Kārttika, [then they are effective]. (28)
Nevertheless, O best of Brahmins, this must be performed here on the full moon day of Kārttika by Vaiṣṇava men who desire both worlds. (29)
The brāhmaṇa who always avoids bell-metal, meat, razors, honey, eating a second time, and sexual intercourse during the month of Kārtika—[attains great merit].
One shall obtain the fruit of all the aforementioned observances.

Furthermore, O twice-born ones, he who offers a lamp upon the pinnacle of the temple to the deity known as Jalaśāyin during the month of Kārttika shall partake in the fruit of the six previously mentioned observances.
Whatever may be most beloved and whatever may be easily attainable, those seeking auspicious results should undertake a vow regarding that during the Cāturmāsya period.
When a vow has been undertaken, one should indeed give that very thing to a Brāhmaṇa; for he by whom a vow has been performed according to his own capacity shall obtain the fruit from it.
That fool who, during the four months, passes his time without restraint, without vows, or even without the chanting of prayers, is indeed dead though he still breathes. (35)
Just as "crow-barley" is spoken of, or as "wild sesame" grows in the forest—being established by name alone—so too are those men on earth.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, with every effort one should diligently observe even a single minor rule during the month of Kārttika. (37)
O twice-born ones, all this has been narrated to you in detail: the origin of the Cāturmāsya [observances] and the majesty of the vows and restraints.
And whoever should constantly hear this, or even read it with a concentrated mind, shall attain liberation from the sins committed during the four-month period.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for the Cāturmāsya Vow," within the Jalaśāyin Legend of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 232 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, we wish to hear from you the detailed greatness of the Cāturmāsya vows.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, show us compassion now and speak; by drinking the nectar of your words, our faith increases ever further. (2)
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to the greatness arising from the Cāturmāsya vow; I shall relate it to you in full detail.
Having previously heard from the mouth of Brahmā the various rules for religious observances, Nārada again questioned Brahmā with great reverence.
Nārada said: O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, O Brāhmaṇa, although I have heard very many vows from your mouth, I do not attain satiety.
Now I desire to hear about the auspicious Cāturmāsya vow.
Brahmā said: Listen, O divine sage, to me regarding the auspicious Cāturmāsya vow; having heard which, liberation is not difficult for men to attain in the land of Bhārata. (7)
This Blessed One is the bestower of liberation and the cause for crossing over saṃsāra; by the mere remembrance of him, one is released from all sins.
Human birth is difficult to attain in this world, and within that, noble lineage; within that, compassion, and therein, auspicious association with the virtuous. (9)
Where there is no association with the virtuous, nor devotion to Viṣṇu, nor religious vows—especially during Cāturmāsya—one who performs the vow of Viṣṇu is auspicious.
The merit of one who does not observe the vows during the Cāturmāsya period is rendered useless; so too are all holy fords, gifts, and sacred shrines.
When the Cāturmāsya period has arrived, those who remain taking refuge in Viṣṇu possess a life that is truly auspicious, even if their bodies are well-nourished.
When the Cāturmāsya period has arrived, the wise person who bows down to Hari finds his purpose fulfilled; the gods remain granters of boons to him for as long as he lives.
Having attained a human birth, he who turns his back on the Cāturmāsya [vows] is said to have hundreds of sins residing within his body; of this there is no doubt.
Human birth is difficult to obtain in this world, and devotion to Hari is even more difficult to find—especially during the Cāturmāsya period when the Lord Janārdana is asleep.
During the Cāturmāsya period, a person should perform his bath early in the morning; having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, he rejoices in heaven like a god. (16)
Furthermore, he who performs a ritual bath during the Cāturmāsya period shall attain perfection; likewise for one who bathes in a waterfall, a pond, or small wells.

His thousands of sins go to destruction at that very moment. For one who bathes during the Cāturmāsya months—whether at Puṣkara, Prayāga, or anywhere in a great body of water—the measure of his merit is not known.
In the field of Bhāskara on the Revā river, at its eastern confluence with the ocean, he who bathes even for a single day during the Cāturmāsya period incurs no fault.
And he who, with a concentrated mind, bathes in the Narmadā for three days while the Lord of the World is asleep, his sin is shattered into a thousand pieces.
But he who bathes in the Godāvarī at the break of dawn for one fortnight, having shattered the body born of karma, attains the same world as Viṣṇu.
He who bathes with water mixed with sesame seeds, as well as with pure water and water infused with bilva leaves during the Cāturmāsya period, incurs no fault.
Whoever constantly remembers the Gaṅgā while near a vessel of water, that water becomes the water of the Gaṅgā; with it, one should perform the ritual bath.
Even the Gaṅgā, flowing from the big toe of the God of gods, is said to be the destroyer of sins at all times, and especially during the Cāturmāsya.
Since Viṣṇu, when remembered, burns away thousands of sins, therefore the water from his feet, when worn upon the head during the Cāturmāsya period, is auspicious.
During the Cāturmāsya period, Lord Nārāyaṇa resides within the water; bathing there is superior to all holy fords, as it is infused with a portion of Viṣṇu’s splendor.
A tenfold bath should be performed, which has great fruit through the name of Viṣṇu; especially when the God is asleep, a man shall attain divinity. (27)
O Brahmin, whatever auspicious rite consisting of meritorious action is performed without bathing becomes fruitless; the Rākṣasas seize it.
Through bathing one attains truth; bathing is the eternal dharma. Having attained the fruit of liberation through dharma, one never again falls into despair.
Those who know the inner self, those who are meritorious, those who have mastered the Vedāṅgas, and those who bestow all kinds of gifts—they attain purity through bathing [here]. (3)
And for one who has performed his ablutions, Hari remains taking recourse to the body; he becomes the bestower of complete fruit in all ritual activities. || 31 ||
For the destruction of all sins and for the propitiation of the deities, bathing in water during the Cāturmāsya period brings about the eradication of all evil.
One should not bathe at night, nor during the twilight hours except during an eclipse; bathing with hot water at night does not produce purification.
Purification through the sight of the sun is prescribed for all ritual acts; however, during the Cāturmāsya period, purification by water is specifically ordained.
But if one is unable due to physical weakness, O best of Brahmins, one becomes pure by bathing with ashes, or by bathing with mantras, or with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
He who, with a purified soul, performs ablutions before Nārāyaṇa and in sacred fields, holy fords, and rivers—especially during the Cāturmāsya—is truly blessed.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Fruit of Bathing in the Waters of the Gaṅgā," in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Brahmā said: One should perform the libation for the ancestors with a mind endowed with faith; this should be done daily at the conclusion of the bath, and when the deity is concealed, it yields great fruit.
Having offered libations to the ancestors and the deities at the confluence of those two rivers, and having performed rites such as recitation and fire-offerings, one obtains infinite fruit.
Having performed the remembrance of Govinda, auspicious rites should thereafter be carried out; this alone bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors, gods, humans, and others.
One should perform all ritual acts here during this most excellent Cāturmāsya with faith joined to righteousness and purified by mindfulness.

Association with the virtuous, devotion to the twice-born, the propitiation of the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, the gift of cows, the recitation of the Vedas, performing noble deeds, and speaking the truth. || 5 ||
Devotion to cows and devotion to giving are always the means for achieving dharma; when Kṛṣṇa is asleep, even a religious observance (niyama) yields especially great fruit.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, what is the nature of *niyama* (observance), and what is the fruit of *niyama*? Tell me how Hari becomes pleased by means of *niyama*.
Brahmā said: A man possessed of knowledge should exercise restraint over his eyes and other senses in their various activities; from the practice thereof comes great happiness.
This removal of the sixfold group is the supreme subduing of enemies; for this is the root of the inner self and the highest cause of happiness.
There, the qualities of forbearance, truthfulness, and so forth, all of which consist of discernment, abide eternally; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever sense of having fulfilled one's duty arises from performing sacrifices, that belongs only to him who has known this state, and it extends to his ancestors as well.
Even by meditating upon it for a mere moment, the sin arising from hundreds of births is reduced to ashes through the practice of this stainless [mantra] as prescribed.
Day by day, his exhaustion from hunger, thirst, and so forth diminishes; that yogi who is constant in his observances is especially distinguished when Hari is asleep.
If a man, during the Cāturmāsya period, does not remain devotedly engaged in the practice of yoga, then the nectar has slipped from his hand; of this there is no doubt. (14)
For one by whom the mind is restrained, even though it always moves toward all desires, that very mind is indeed the cause for both knowledge and liberation. 15.
An effort must always be made by the wise person to restrain the mind; for when the mind is well-restrained, the attainment of all knowledge is certain. 16.
That mind is to be restrained by forbearance, just as fire is by water; for the wise have declared that through a single forbearance, every rule of conduct is fulfilled.
Truth alone is the supreme dharma; truth alone is the supreme austerity; truth alone is the supreme knowledge; in truth, dharma is established. || 18 ||
Non-violence is the root of Dharma; contemplating it with the mind, one should likewise practice it through action and speech. (19)

The theft of another's property is robbery, which must always be avoided by all human beings; this is especially so during the Cāturmāsya period, with the specific exception of the property of Brahmins and deities.
Furthermore, the wise should always avoid doing what ought not to be done; for he who always conducts himself without deficiency in all his affairs, O Brahmin, [attains success]. (21)
And that yogi is possessed of great wisdom; he thinks, "I am not the one whose intellect is the eye of wisdom. This egoism exists as a poison within the bodies of men.
Therefore, that [state] must always be abandoned, especially while the Lord is asleep; a man should be free from worldly effort, having conquered anger and conquered greed. (23)
Having conquered delusion and pride by means of the enemy in the form of tranquility, his thousands of sins depart from the body in a thousand ways.
Through discernment tranquility is to be grasped, for it is indeed attained through contentment; that lord of sages should restrain envy by means of straightforwardness.
During the Cāturmāsya period, the duty is compassion; it is not the duty of those who harm living beings. At all times and in all acts of giving, one should avoid injury to living beings.
The wise have declared this to be the root of thousands of evils; therefore, compassion toward all beings should be practiced by men with every effort. 27.
Hari eternally dwells in the hearts of all beings; indeed, he who commits injury against living beings is himself defeated.
That dharma in which there is no compassion at all is considered corrupted; without compassion, there is neither wisdom, nor dharma, nor even knowledge itself. (29)
Therefore, the eternal dharma of compassion, which pervades all states of being, should be constantly practiced by men, especially during the Cāturmāsya period. (30)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Rules for the Cāturmāsya Observances," within the Legend of Śeṣaśāyin, in the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada. || 234 ||
Brahmā said: Among all dharmas, they always praise the dharma of giving; especially when Hari is asleep, giving is the cause for attaining the state of Brahman.
"Food is declared to be Brahman; in food the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established. Therefore, a man should always be a giver of food and a giver of water. (2)
The giver of water attains satisfaction, and the giver of food attains imperishable happiness; a gift equal to that of water and food has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again.
Among gifts of jewels, gems, and corals, of silver, gold, and clothing, as well as among all other gifts, the gift of food is preeminent. (4)
The constant giving of food and water, the gift of cows, the recitation of the Vedas, and the fire-oblation during the Cāturmāsya period yield great fruit.
If there is a desire for the state of Vaikuṇṭha or for union with Viṣṇu, one should become a giver of food during Cāturmāsya for the sake of destroying all sins.
"Truly, truly, O divine sage Nārada, I have spoken this to you: throughout thousands of other births, that which was not given does not present itself."
Therefore, all living beings rejoice through the gift of food; even the gods long for one who bestows the gift of food.
Clarified butter mixed with *vajra* should be offered with faith into the vessels; that mortal who performs the gift of *vajra* during the Cāturmāsya is no mere human being.
Providing food for gurus and Brahmins, the gift of ghee, and performing acts of hospitality—those who do not maintain these during the Cāturmāsya period are no longer considered human beings.
The True Dharma, excellent discourse, service to the virtuous, the sight of the holy, worship of Viṣṇu, and delight in giving—these are difficult to find during the four-month periods. (11)
That mortal who, intent upon the ancestors, becomes a giver of food during the Cāturmāsya period, shall have his soul purified of all sins and attain the world of the ancestors.
All the gods, satisfied by the gift of food, grant one's desires; for even an ant, taking food from one's house, goes away [satisfied]. (13)
Indeed, the gift of food—provided it is not forbidden by night or day—is unsurpassed; for while Hari sleeps, even water offered to enemies destroys sin.
The gift of milk, curd, or buttermilk during the Cāturmāsya period yields great fruit; that gift is supreme which is given by one for whom the funeral cake (piṇḍa) was bound at the time of birth.
The giver of vegetables does not see the hellish world of Yama; the giver of clothing shall dwell in the world of Soma until the dissolution of all beings.
When the Lord is asleep, by offering flowers and garments to other images according to one's ability, one's progeny is never diminished.
He who offers sandalwood and agalloch incense during the four-month period becomes a man possessing the form of Viṣṇu, endowed with sons and grandsons. || 18 ||
When the Lord of the World is asleep, one who offers a gift of fruit to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas does not behold the realm of Yama. (19)
He bestows the gift of knowledge, the gift of cows, and the gift of land; for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu in this world, he delivers his ancestors.
Indeed, one who gives jaggery, rock salt, oil, honey, bitter substances, sesame seeds, and rice, dedicating them to the deities, goes to their world.
By giving sesame seeds during the Cāturmāsya period, one shall not become a suckling again; the giver of barley dwells in the imperishable world of Vāsava.
One should offer oblations into the fire and give gifts to the twice-born; cows especially should be well-honored during the Cāturmāsya period.
Whatever meritorious deed has been well-accumulated throughout one's entire life, if it is not given to a worthy recipient when the Cāturmāsya period has passed, [it becomes fruitless]. 24.
But for one who has fallen away from his word, he perishes in an instant; yet for him, his promise increases day by day.
Therefore, one should not merely give a promise, even for the smallest thing; rather, it should be given quickly. A gift increases in value only so long as one does not actually bestow it.
Whatever merit a person in this world might obtain through delusion, even up to ten millionfold, the increase for one who gives during the Cāturmāsya period shall be ten times greater than that.
He shall fall into hell for as long as fourteen Indras endure; therefore, men must always give what has been promised.
It must not be given to anyone else, nor should one who has given it ever let it be lost; he who bestows a bed upon an eminent twice-born during the Cāturmāsya periods [attains great merit]. (29)
By means of the procedure declared in the Vedas, he does not go to the abode of Yama; [he offers] a seat, a water-vessel, and a vessel, specifically a copper vessel.

During the Cāturmāsya period, one should diligently give gifts according to one's wealth to the Brahmins; indeed, all kinds of gifts should be bestowed upon the Brahmins while the Teacher of the World is asleep.
He liberates himself along with his ancestors from sin; the gift of a cow, land, a vessel of sesame seeds, and the unsurpassed gift of a lamp [are meritorious]. (32)
By giving [it] to a twice-born man, he becomes liberated from the three debts.

He is the creator of the universe, the protector of all worlds, the enjoyer of sacrifice, and the bestower of all fruits; it is unto Him that one who is liberated offers gifts, designating Him as the presiding deity among all things.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gifts during the Cāturmāsya," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the "Greatness of the Cāturmāsya" section of the Legend of Śeṣaśāyin, in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 235.

Brahmā said: Viṣṇu is the bestower of desired objects, and the world always has a desire for what is wished for; therefore, with every effort during the four months [of the rainy season], one should renounce that [desire].
For the sake of pleasing Nārāyaṇa, that very [merit] is obtained as inexhaustible; the mortal who possesses faith and performs this shall become a partaker of infinite fruit. || 2 ||
By renouncing bronze vessels, one becomes a lord of the earth on this world; eating from a leaf of the Palāśa tree, one attains absorption into Brahman.
A householder should never eat from a copper vessel; especially during the Cāturmāsya period, he should avoid a copper vessel altogether.
One who eats from arka leaves obtains incomparable fruit; one should especially eat from vaṭa leaves during the Cāturmāsya period.
Wise people should always partake of food using aśvattha leaves; such a king shall become the sole eater of all food throughout the entire circle of the earth.
Likewise, by abandoning salt, a man becomes handsome; by renouncing wheat-based food, he becomes beloved by the people. (7)

One who abstains from vegetables becomes long-lived, and one who observes the Cāturmāsya vow is reborn with great vitality; by renouncing savory juices one becomes possessed of great strength, and by renouncing honey one gains beautiful eyes.

Through the renunciation of mung beans, one attains freedom from enemies; through the renunciation of rajamasha beans, one gains great wealth; and through the renunciation of rice during the Cāturmāsya period, the attainment of horses arises.

By the renunciation of fruit one gains many sons; by the renunciation of oil, a beautiful form; and by the renunciation of turmeric, one becomes wise, while strength and virility are indeed always attained.
By renouncing the meat of the path, one does not see hell; by renouncing the flesh of the pig, one shall attain residence in the world of Brahmā.

Through the renunciation of meat, one gains knowledge; through the renunciation of clarified butter, there is great happiness; by completely abandoning liquor, liberation is not difficult for him to attain. (12)
One becomes powerful by the renunciation of gold; one becomes human by the renunciation of silver. || 69 ||
One who renounces curd and milk shall become a partaker of happiness in Goloka. || 13 ||

Brahmā attained his status through the renunciation of milk-rice; Maheśvara through the swift renunciation [of food]; Kandarpa through the renunciation of cakes; and the one who renounces sweetmeats becomes happy.
One who abandons the householder stage of life and practices external asceticism does not remain in his mother’s womb for four months out of devotion to Hari, like an infant.
By abandoning *marīca* one becomes a king; by abandoning *śuṇṭhī* one becomes a good poet; and by renouncing sugar, one becomes honored by kings. (16)
From the renunciation of molasses comes great prosperity; likewise, from the avoidance of pomegranates and the abandonment of red garments, one becomes beloved by the people. (17)
By renouncing fine silk garments, one shall attain the imperishable heaven; by renouncing food made of black gram and chickpeas, there is no further rebirth.

Black clothing should always be avoided, especially during the Cāturmāsya period; purification from seeing such [black] cloth occurs by beholding the sun, while purification from seeing blue cloth occurs by beholding it.
By the renunciation of sandalwood, one enjoys the world of the Gandharvas; by the renunciation of camphor, one becomes a person of great wealth for as long as life lasts.
By the renunciation of safflower, one shall not see the messenger of Yama; by the renunciation of saffron, a man becomes a favorite of the king.
By renouncing *yakṣakardama* one is glorified in the world of Brahmā; by renouncing flowers one becomes a man of knowledge (*jñānī*), and by renouncing a bed there is great happiness.
One does not suffer separation from one's wife during the Cāturmāsya period; of this there is no doubt. By abandoning false speech, the door to liberation is flung open.
Exposing the vital secrets of others and the immediate accumulation of sin—these, as well as reviling others, one should avoid while the Lord Hari is asleep during the Cāturmāsya period. 24.
Slandering others is a great sin; slandering others is a great fear; slandering others is a great suffering—there is no greater transgression than that. (25)
One incurs a heavy sin merely by censuring [the teaching], just as one becomes a sinner simply by hearing it; there is no greater transgression than that.
By renouncing the grooming of his hair, he is freed from the threefold suffering; he who keeps his nails and hair untrimmed, especially while Hari is asleep.
Day after day, he shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.

By all means, Viṣṇu alone is to be propitiated by the best of yogis and by all castes; one is liberated from terrible bondage by the name of Viṣṇu, and He is especially remembered during the Cāturmāsya.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Renouncing Desired Objects," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna*, in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth *Nāgara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 236.
Nārada said: When should injunctions and prohibitions be observed in the presence of Viṣṇu? Having drunk the nectar of your words, I find no satiety.
Brahmā said: On the day of the Karka Saṃkrānti, having worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion, an offering (arghya) should be presented with auspicious and excellent jambū fruits.
O best of Brahmins, this name of Jambūdvīpa is derived from its fruit; it is [attained] through this mantra by those who are well-restrained in faith and dharma.
If death should befall me anywhere within six months, I have personally offered my very self to Vāsudeva.

With this mantra, the *arghya* offering is presented. Then, when the Cāturmāsya has arrived—the great joy of all the worlds—one should devoutly adopt both the injunctions and prohibitions before Lord Hari.
Injunction is the Vedic ordinance to be performed; prohibition is considered a restrictive rule (niyama). Both injunction and prohibition are indeed Viṣṇu himself.
Therefore, with every effort, Janārdana alone must be served; likewise, the stories of Viṣṇu, the worship of Viṣṇu, meditation on Viṣṇu, and bowing to Viṣṇu [should be practiced].
He who performs everything solely for the pleasure of Hari attains liberation; Viṣṇu is the eternal, true embodiment of the rules governing the social classes and stages of life.

During the Cāturmāsya period, there is especially the destruction of the hardships of birth and other afflictions. Hari alone is to be accepted through the vow; one should perform the vow with the body. This body is to be purified by austerity while the Lord, the treasure-house of penance, is asleep. (29)
Nārada said: O Brahmin, tell me in detail what vow and what austerity have been prescribed, and what deed was performed by me while the Lord was asleep that yielded such great fruit.
Brahmā said: Know that the vow is the vow of Viṣṇu, endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu; and austerity consists in abiding by righteousness, or even the kṛcchra and other such penances. || 11 ||
Listen; I shall first tell you of the greatness of the vow. The vow of celibacy is the essence, the most excellent of all vows. (12)
Celibacy is the essence of austerity; celibacy yields great fruit. One should increase the practice of celibacy in all ritual activities whatsoever. (13)
Through the power of celibacy, fierce austerity proceeds; there is no higher or more excellent means for accomplishing dharma than celibacy.
Especially during the four-month period when the God is asleep, this Great Vow is superior in merit; therefore, O twice-born one, always understand it well. (15)
He who performs this Nārāyaṇa-karma is not defiled; they say there are three hundred and sixty days in a year.
There, the god Nārāyaṇa is worshipped by those who observe vows; "O God, I shall certainly perform such-and-such a hospitable rite," [he said]. 17.
They say that when the God is asleep, performing that vow is superior in merit; it consists of fire-offerings, devotion to Brahmins, faith, and an auspicious mind fixed on righteousness.
Association with the virtuous, worship of Viṣṇu, truthful speech, compassion in the heart, straightforwardness, sweet speech, and constant delight in righteous conduct. (19)

The study of the Vedas, as well as non-stealing, non-violence, modesty, forgiveness, self-restraint, freedom from greed, absence of anger, freedom from delusion, lack of possessiveness, and absence of aversion; || 20 ||
O best among the knowers of Brahman, he whose mental faculty is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa possesses that knowledge which is intent on the practice of hearing; these are the vows by which one abides.
Such a man is declared to be liberated while living; he is never tainted by sins. Indeed, even a vow performed but once always yields great fruit.
During the four months of the rainy season, one should especially observe celibacy and other disciplines; for those men whose four-month period always passes without such vows, [the merit is lost].
The righteous who know the truth have declared that their dharma is in vain; for all castes alike, the practice of vows yields great fruit. (24)
O child, even a very small act performed during the Cāturmāsya bestows happiness; Viṣṇu is seen everywhere by men who are devoted to the service of vows.
When the Cāturmāsya has arrived, one should observe it with great effort.

Worship Viṣṇu, the unborn and radiant one, whose form consists of the twice-born, the sacrificial fire, the sacred fords, and the various divisions of the Vedas; by his grace, you shall stand upon the great tree of liberation and will no longer suffer the heat born from the sun of worldly existence.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Vow," in the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 237.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, O high-minded one, listen in detail to the description of penance, by the mere hearing of which there is the destruction of sins during Cāturmāsya.
The constant worship of Viṣṇu with the sixteen services is indeed penance; therefore, when the Lord of the World is asleep, it is declared to be a great penance. (2)
Indeed, the constant performance of the five sacrifices is itself austerity; and offering that very austerity to Hari during the Cāturmāsya period constitutes great penance.
For a householder, the seasonal sacrifice is indeed always his austerity; during the Cāturmāsya, that great austerity should be practiced for the pleasure of Hari.
Truthfulness and constant austerity are difficult for living beings to find on this earth; yet by performing them while the Lord of the Gods is asleep, one becomes a partaker of infinite fruit.
The constant observance of virtues such as non-violence is austerity; for one of noble intellect, the relinquishing of enmity during the Cāturmāsya period is the highest austerity.
A mortal should indeed perform great austerity and the worship of the five abodes (pañcāyatana), especially during the Cāturmāsya period, for the sake of pleasing Hari.
Nārada said: By whom was this designation "Pañcāyatana" spoken, and how did it come to be? How should the worship be performed? Tell me that in detail and quickly.

Brahmā said: In the morning and midday worship, Ravi (the Sun) is always to be worshipped in the center; at night, Candra (the Moon) should be in the center with auspicious flowers of those respective colors.
In the southeast corner, one should worship Heraṃba for the pacification of all obstacles, especially with red sandalwood and flowers during the Cāturmāsya period.
Occupying the petal of Nairṛta, the Blessed One, the destroyer of the pride of the wicked, always effects the destruction of the enemies of the householder. || 11 ||
The wise man should always worship Viṣṇu, who resides in the southwest corner, with fragrant sandalwood, flowers, and most beautiful food offerings.
The Gotrajā should always be worshipped by the wise in the northwest corner with beautiful and captivating flowers, for the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons. (13)
In the northeast, the Lord Rudra is always worshipped with white flowers for the destruction of untimely death and the removal of all defects.
The greatness of this Pañcāyatana, which cannot be fully described even by Brahmā and the other gods, is indeed worshipped by householders. (15)

This austerity (tapa) should always be performed during the Cāturmāsya period, for it yields great fruit. At all festival times (parvakāla), gifts should be given and austerity practiced constantly; especially during Cāturmāsya, that [merit] becomes infinite.
Purity should always be understood as twofold: external and internal. External purity is achieved through water, while internal purity arises from faith. (17)
The restraint of the senses is the supreme characteristic of austerity; and the withdrawal from the fickleness of the senses during the Cāturmāsya is a great penance.
By constantly restraining the horses of the senses, one prospers in happiness; yet by those very same senses when they go astray, one is cast into hell along with one's life-breaths. 19.
One should subdue the wicked Grāhī, who takes the form of possessiveness (mamatā), by rebuking her; for men, austerity alone always holds greater weight during the Cāturmāsya period.
This desire is the great enemy; one should resolutely conquer it alone. Those great-souled ones who have conquered desire have conquered the entire world.
And this is the root of austerity; indeed, that very thing is the root of austerity: the constant conquest of desire as well as the conquest of volitional intent.
For that alone is supreme knowledge by which desire is produced; they say that very thing is great austerity, the highest fruit of the four-month vow.
Greed should always be abandoned, for sin is rooted in greed; his very conquest of it constitutes his austerity, especially during the Cāturmāsya period. (24)
Delusion and constant lack of discrimination must be avoided with great effort; a man abandoned by them is wise, but one who takes refuge in delusion is not wise. (25)
Arrogance alone is the great enemy residing within the bodies of men; it must always be subdued, especially while the Lord is asleep. (26)
Pride dwells indeed within all beings as a source of fear; by conquering it through forgiveness during the Cāturmāsya, one becomes preeminent in virtues.
The wise man should conquer envy, which is the cause of great sin; by conquering it during the Cāturmāsya, he has conquered the three worlds along with the immortals.
Overcome by egoism, even sages who have conquered their senses abandon the path of dharma and perform actions born of the wrong way. (29)
Having abandoned egoism, one shall attain constant happiness; especially during the Cāturmāsya, there is a great fruit in its renunciation.
For this indeed is the root of austerity: that one should renounce these [objects] from the mind; when all these have been renounced, one becomes composed of the Supreme Brahman. || 31 ||
First, for the sake of purifying the body, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance; this is especially a great austerity during the sleep of the God of gods. (32)
That man who, with devotion, performs a fast on every alternate day during the sleep of Hari shall never go to the abode of Yama.
During the sleep of Hari, a person should always observe the practice of eating only once a day; for him, day after day, he shall obtain the fruit of twelve days. || 34 ||
If a man, during the Cāturmāsya period, is devoted to a diet of vegetables alone, he acquires the merit of thousands of sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
During the four-month period, a man should constantly perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; the merit of that for each single month cannot indeed be described.
When the Lord is asleep, the person of pure intellect who performs the Pārāka penance—or a woman endowed with faith—achieves the destruction of the sins of a hundred births. (37)
He who practices the Kṛcchra penance while the Lord Janārdana is asleep, having shaken off a heap of sins, shall attain the status of an attendant in Vaikuṇṭha. || 38 ||
He who is devoted to the *taptakṛcchra* penance while the Lord Janārdana is asleep shall attain fame or a son, and then go to union with Viṣṇu.
For that embodied being who, during the Cāturmāsya, becomes devoted to a diet of milk alone, thousands of his sins go to destruction. (40)
If a wise man, eating only measured food during the Cāturmāsya period, shakes off all sin, he shall attain the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
A mortal who eats only once a day is not overcome by diseases; and one who abstains from pungent and salty food during the Cāturmāsya period incurs no sin.
Having taken food [only at specific times], he is certainly liberated from great sins during these four months dedicated to Hari; of this there is no doubt. (43)
One who subsists on bulbs and roots, having rescued his ancestors along with himself from the terrible hell, attains the same world as Viṣṇu.
When one subsists on the constant consumption of water during the four months of the rainy season, he undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice day after day. || 45 ||
The man who endures cold and rain during the four months of the rainy season out of devotion to Hari, the Lord of the World grants him his own self. (46)
That which is known as the Mahāpārāka is declared to be a great austerity; by fasting for one month, everything becomes fully accomplished.
But from the day of the Devasvāpini and so forth, until the Pavitra-dvādaśī; and prior to the Pavitra-dvādaśī, until the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī. (48)
This is indeed proclaimed as the second Mahāpārāka; it begins with Śravaṇa-dvādaśī and concludes on Āśvina-dvādaśī. 49.
The wise have proclaimed the third [vow] as the Mahāpārāka; it begins on the twelfth day of the month of Āśvina, which is the auspicious awakening day of the God.
This is indeed proclaimed as the fourth great vow (mahāvrata); whether it be a woman or even a man, [one who observes] even one of these— || 51 ||
The man who performs this with devotion is indeed the eternal Viṣṇu; and this is declared to be the greatest of all austerities.

In this world, that which is performed during the four-month period (Cāturmāsya) is difficult to accomplish and rare to find; it is superior even to a great sacrifice. It is traditionally held that for each day of that [observance], one obtains the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.

This great austerity has been performed by him, which is difficult to attain in the world; this alone is great merit, this alone is great happiness; this alone is the supreme good—the service of the Great Ferryman.
Nārāyaṇa dwells within his body and knowledge arises for him; even if he were a perpetrator of great sins, he becomes liberated while living.
Sins roar only so long, and indeed hells endure only so long, as well as thousands of illusions, as long as there is a month of fasting.
Whoever observes the fast for the four months and remains a guest in another's courtyard shall become free from stain, even having abandoned thousands of murders.
The mortal who causes this to be heard, or who himself constantly recites it—|| 58 ||
Even he, equal to Vācaspati, undoubtedly attains the fruit. || 59 ||

This Purāṇa is supreme and most purifying; by hearing it or reciting it, one becomes a cause for the purification of sins. Having meditated upon that Nārāyaṇa with the mind, one who dies goes to the immortal state, which is superior even to the gods.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Austerity," within the "Greatness of the Cāturmāsya" section of the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, within the "Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Field" of the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 238.
Nārada said: How is the worship performed with the sixteen services? What are those sixteen dispositions that are eternally present during the sleep of Hari? (1)
O Prajāpati, explain this in detail to me as I ask; having obtained your grace, may I become worthy of worship by the world.
Brahmā said: Firm devotion to Viṣṇu should be practiced according to the injunctions of the Vedas and Śāstras. All this has the Veda as its root; the Veda is the eternal Viṣṇu.
The Vedas have the Brahmins as their support, and the Brahmins have the sacrificial fire as their deity; the Brahmin, casting the oblation into the fire, is always worshipping the God in sacrifice.
One who is always devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu sustains the entire world; Nārāyaṇa, when remembered and meditated upon, is the destroyer of afflictions, suffering, and the like.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, Hari resides in the form of water; from that water, foodstuffs are produced for the sake of the satisfaction of the worlds.
That food, produced from a portion of Viṣṇu’s body, is considered to be Brahman itself; having offered that food to Viṣṇu preceded by the ritual invocation (āvāhana), [one should proceed].
He is not overcome by rebirth, old age, afflictions, or formative volitions; the Veda, born of space, existed as one alone in the beginning.
Then, for the sake of prosperity, the Ṛgveda received the designations of Yajurveda and Sāmaveda; the Ṛgveda was previously declared to have a thousand heads, as it were.
This supreme great hymn (*mahāsūkta*) consisting of sixteen verses is composed of Nārāyaṇa; by its mere recitation, even the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) is removed. (10)

First, the wise brahmin should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon his own body according to the injunctions of the Smṛtis; thereafter, he should do so upon an image, and especially upon a Śālagrāma stone.
Then, in due order, one should subsequently perform the invocation and other rites; having invoked the entire form residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Shining with the Kaustubha gem, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, holding a staff in his hand, endowed with a topknot and sacred thread, and clad in yellow garments. || 13 ||
One should meditate upon the Great Renunciant, especially during the Cāturmāsya period—upon Viṣṇu, who consists of such a form and who removes the entire flood of all sins.
And one should invoke him before oneself while established in meditation, O best of the twice-born, with the first Ṛc verse preceded by the syllable Om.
And with the second [syllable], one should mentally visualize a seat together with his attendants; their seats are made of gold. (16)

Through meditations and the yoga of devotion, that [offering] shall become complete; the wise one should perform the offering of water for the feet with the third [verse], and there he should remember the Gaṅgā.

Then an offering of water (arghya) should be made to Viṣṇu with the seven rivers and the seven oceans; thereafter, the act of sipping water (ācamana) should be performed for the Lord of the World with nectar.
The purification of a Brāhmaṇa is declared to be by three sips of water, using water that is in its natural state and free from foam and bubbles. (19)
The twice-born shall be purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; women and Śūdras are purified by water that has merely touched the lips once at the end.
The sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed with a mind endowed with devotion; for Hṛṣīkeśa is to be grasped through devotion, and through devotion He bestows His own self.
Then, one should cause the bathing of the deity to be performed with golden jars containing residual water, scented waters, and all medicinal herbs.
A heap of jewels offered with faith and a mind focused on the waters of sacred fords becomes fruitful; however, that which is given without faith shall be fruitless. (23)
Even water given with faith conduces to infinity; especially during the Cāturmāsya period, a man is purified by faith.

Then, on the sixth day, a bath should be performed, followed by the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). And one should offer two garments along with gold, according to one's devotion and capacity. (25)
The entire world is covered, and Hari is covered with cloth; especially during the Cāturmāsya, the gift of clothing yields great fruit. (26)
Water for rinsing the mouth should again be offered to the ascetic who is the very form of Viṣṇu; and on the seventh day, O lord of sages, the gift of clothing for Viṣṇu should be performed.

Listen now to the nature of that sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from the perspective of spiritual realization (*adhyātma*), which on the eighth day is as radiant with splendor and possesses a touch equal to ten million suns.

When the Brahmin was overcome by anger, [the weapon] shone with a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning; it was produced from the conjunction of the sun, moon, and fire, and was endowed with the three qualities (guṇas). || 29 ||
O best of Brahmins, it is by the power of that heaven consisting of the three Vedas—which takes the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—that a human being is called a twice-born (dvija).
