By birth one is born a Śūdra; by sacramental rites (saṃskāra) one is called twice-born (dvija). [One attains] the power to curse or to bless, as well as anger and graciousness.
And preeminence over the three worlds arises from the Brāhmaṇa alone; there is no kinsman equal to a Brāhmaṇa, and no destination equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa. (32)
There is no one equal to a Brāhmaṇa in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, when the god Janārdana has fallen asleep after the sacred thread has been offered to the Brāhmaṇa.
The entire world has become composed of Brahman; there is no doubt in this matter. On the ninth day, a fine anointing should be performed for the embodiment of the sacrifice (Yajñamūrti).
For by him, through whom Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world, was smeared with the mud of excellent yakṣa-fragrance, this entire world has been nourished and perfumed with glory.
By his splendor, that man becomes like the sun in the world; having attained divinity, the giver of sandalwood rejoices in the worlds beginning with the realm of Brahmā.
Those men who behold Viṣṇu, made beautiful by an application of sandalwood paste, especially during the Cāturmāsya period, do not go to the city of Yama.
On the tenth day, there is worship with flowers as well as worship through devotion; for Lakṣmī always dwells eternally within the flower itself. (381)
No fault whatsoever arises for Lakṣmī, who moves everywhere, just as Viṣṇu, who pervades everything, is not affected by defects. (39)
Likewise, Lakṣmī, who consists of all things, never loses her state of being virtuous (satī) within all images and at all times within all beings.
The worship with flowers is prescribed among humans, gods, and ancestors; by whomsoever Hari alone is worshipped with flowers along with Śrī. (41)
By him indeed the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has been honored; therefore, one should always worship Viṣṇu with very white flowers.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, O Brahmin, if men are always pure and endowed with devotion, and if they perform flower worship properly with devotion; 43.
Whatever desire one may contemplate, its fulfillment shall be uninterrupted; for even if others merely bow down to Viṣṇu, who is honored with flowers. (44)

For them also, the worlds are inexhaustible, and there is an even greater fruit from the Cāturmāsya rites. On the Ekādaśī day, incense should be offered to Hari while he is in the form of a mendicant.
This divine essence of the lord of the forest, rich in fragrance, the most excellent of scents, fit to be smelled by all the gods—may this incense be accepted. (46)
Having recited this mantra, one should daily offer auspicious incense made of agallochum to the Blessed One during the Cāturmāsya; the fruit of this is great.
O best of men, when the God has fallen asleep, [one should offer] pieces of camphor and sandalwood combined with sugar and honey, along with roots of māṃsī.
The gods are pleased by the auspicious incense that captivates the sense of smell; those desiring liberation should perform the offering of lamps on the twelfth day.
The lamp is the foremost among all tasks; it is the lord of lights. The lamp is for the destruction of the mass of darkness; the lamp bestows splendor. (50)

"Therefore, may Janārdana be pleased by the offering of this lamp. This mantra, born of the Purāṇas and joined with a Vedic verse, when employed in its entirety during the offering of a lamp, shall destroy all evil. (51)
Whoever offers a lamp before Hari during the Cāturmāsya period, the heap of his sins is consumed in even a mere moment.
Sins roar and the sinner trembles only so long as the radiant lamp has not been established in the abode of Nārāyaṇa. (53)
Even by the mere sight of the lamp, all success shall accrue to men. || 54 ||
Whatever desire one has in mind when having a lamp offered to Hari, that very desire is accomplished without obstacle, provided the Infinite One is asleep, yielding even greater merit.
Likewise, for the five classes of gods residing in the five abodes, the offering of lamps during the Cāturmāsya period is ordained as yielding great fruit.

Viṣṇu alone is the giver of liberation; when constantly meditated upon, worshipped, and praised, he is satisfied. Whatever is desired and whatever auspicious thing exists in the home, that should be offered by the best of men for the sake of liberation. (57)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Lamp as the Sixteenth Accessory in the Section on the Qualifications for Austerity," within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth *Nāgara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 239.
Brahmā said: For one who performs this lamp-offering to Hari, it shall be superior even to my own lamp; he shall indeed dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, though my own sovereignty was not desired by me. || 1 ||
Nārada said: This lamp, when offered with mantras by men in the temple of Viṣṇu, always yields special fruit; how is it even more so during the Cāturmāsya?
Brahmā said: Viṣṇu is my eternal presiding deity; Viṣṇu is always to be worshipped by me. I meditate upon this Viṣṇu at all times, for He is indeed superior to me.
That lamp is dear to Viṣṇu, always a remover of sins; during the Cāturmāsya period, it especially brings about the fulfillment of all desires.
O son, Viṣṇu is not as satisfied by thousands of sacrifices as he is by a lamp; indeed, he does not grant a boon in the same way through those sacrifices.
By means of a very small expense, the fruit of a lamp for men is infinite; when the festival of Anantaśayana arrives, there is no limit to the measure of merit.
Therefore, one who offers a lamp to Hari with their whole being and endowed with faith is not defiled by sins. (7)
Furthermore, when the offering of lamps is performed with the sixteen services to Hari in the form of a yogi, the entire world is illuminated.
O Brahmin, after the offering of lamps, the presentation of food should be performed on the thirteenth day by those established in the state of liberation who are endowed with devotion.
Having completely renounced the nectar of immortality, even the gods always long for the food of a householder, standing at the very door of his home.
When Hari is asleep, men should especially offer this daily; for the satisfaction of Viṣṇu, he should be honored with offerings of fruit gathered at that specific time.
With betel-leaf vines and auspicious areca nuts, as well as grapes, rose-apples, mangoes, akroḍa fruits, and pomegranates; (12)
One should offer the arghya with great devotion using bījapūra fruits; having taken water from a conch shell, one should place a beautiful fruit upon it. (13)
O best of Brahmins, one should offer this to Keśava with this mantra; furthermore, the water for sipping (ācamana) should be given after the offering of food.
Then one should perform the waving of lights (ārārtika), which destroys all sins; on the fourteenth day, one should pay obeisance to Viṣṇu in the form of an ascetic.

On the fifteenth day, a circumambulation should be performed in all directions together with the twice-born; the fruit that is obtained when water produced from the seven oceans is offered [is attained]. || 16 ||
And by offering water from that [well] to Hari, the beloveds of Viṣṇu attain the entire world of moving and non-moving beings through four circumambulations. || 17 ||
O best of Brahmins, that journey to the holy ford and so forth becomes accomplished; the knower of yoga, most excellent, should contemplate union with the Deity through the sixteenth [digit].
At that time, one should not constantly contemplate the form of Hari as being only the self; because he possesses both a formed and a formless nature, the knower of yoga becomes visible [to him]. 19.
Upon seeing that, all activity arising from the nature of existence and non-existence shall cease; one should contemplate the Self in the midst of the luminaries, possessing the splendor of the sun.
Constantly reflecting within himself, "I am indeed Viṣṇu," he attains a Vaiṣṇava body and becomes a twice-born one liberated while living.
During the Cāturmāsya period, a twice-born man should especially be engaged in yoga; this is declared to be devotion toward Hari, the bestower of the path to liberation. 22.
Īśvara said: O Viṣṇu, this worship of yours, which arises from sixteen means, has been described; by performing it, a twice-born man attains the supreme state. || 1 ||
And thus, through the performance [of this rite], Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas attain supreme liberation; Śūdras have no entitlement to it, nor women ever at any time. (2)
Kārttikeya said: Tell me in detail the dharma of Śūdras and likewise of women; by what means can they attain liberation without the worship of Kṛṣṇa?
Īśvara said: Even by virtuous Śūdras, the investigation of the syllables of the Veda must not be undertaken; it must not be heard nor recited, for one who recites it becomes a partaker of hell.

One should always cause the recitation and listening of the Purāṇas to be performed; however, that which is prescribed in the Smṛtis should be received from a true guru, not through mere recitation or listening.
Skanda said: Who are declared to be the *sacchūdras*? Tell me of them in detail; who are the virtuous (*santaḥ*), who are the *śūdras*, and who are those known by the name *sacchūdras*?
Īśvara said: He whose wife has been wedded according to dharma is declared a true Śūdra; she should be of equal family and appearance, and free from the ten defects.

He who marries according to the Vedic injunctions is proclaimed a true Śūdra; she who is not impotent, free from physical defects, and untainted by major diseases and the like is recommended as a bride.
Blameless, possessing auspicious qualities, free from eye disease, devoid of deafness, not fickle, and sweet-spoken—such is the maiden.
When she has been married by men according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas, being free from the ten defects, she is his wife and his housewife for all time.
He is to be known as a true Śūdra, for he makes the distinction between gods and others; she is proclaimed as the foremost in all meritorious rites. 11.
The Dharma well-practiced by her yields its fruit in full; during the Cāturmāsya period, it is especially superior in merit when performed together with her.

He finds delight in his wife, is pure, and is intent upon nourishing his servants and others; he regularly performs ancestral rites such as the śrāddha, and accomplishes acts of piety such as iṣṭa and pūrta. || 13 ||
The gods are pleased with him through mantras ending in "namaskāra," by the recitation of names, and by auspicious acts such as the five great sacrifices.

One should not abandon the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña): bathing, the libation (tarpaṇa), the fire-oblation (agnihotra) even if performed without mantras, the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), and the honoring of guests. || 15 ||
The five sacrifices (pañcayajña) should indeed be performed by women and Śūdras without mantras; thus, through these five sacrifices, their ancestors and deities are fully satisfied.
Likewise, by her constant service to her husband, all the gods indeed dwell within the body of a devoted wife.
Therefore, when both of them have come together and their views are asked regarding dharma and other matters, the ancestors and deities are satisfied. (18)
And there is always a gathering of all [the deities], beginning with Kārya, at that place; when the Cāturmāsya arrives, they bring about their own welfare through devotion to Viṣṇu. (19)
If a man has taken as his wife one born of the same caste, the first husband shall be entitled to half the share, while the second shall receive nothing at all.

Because she has authority over wealth and purposeful action, she is the upholder of half of dharma; the auspicious or inauspicious karma performed by each of them shall always belong to that respective individual. (21)
O twice-born one, that virtuous woman who follows her deceased husband through excellent asceticism is indeed to be recognized as such; by her, the entire lineage is uplifted. (22)
Whether she was married while still a maiden or even one who had been taken from another caste, she delivers her husband by means of the path of Vaiśvānara.
Just as mud is drawn out from water by righteous men, even so does the virtuous woman who follows her husband rescue him.
If one is born of a different caste or is maintained by another, both of them are considered to be always excluded from religious duties.

Each performs their own respective action and receives the fruit born of that virtuous deed; therefore, whether superior or inferior, those of noble lineage are not distinguished by being born of Śūdras. (26)
That wife who does not increase [her husband's] merit should not be maintained; however, merit performed together with her increases tenfold.
It does not grant infinite satisfaction even through one's sons; furthermore, a maiden who has been purchased for a price is proclaimed to be a slave. (28)

In the case of a true Śūdra who has the right [to perform the rite], that [rite] never occurs at all; for such is the girl who, having been raised by herself, was given to the groom by her father. (29)

Married according to the rites of matrimony, she accomplishes the purposes of the ancestors and the gods; she is endowed with auspicious marks, modest, and possessed of virtues such as discernment, and is truly blessed.
A maiden born of a pure lineage, wedded according to the Dharma and practicing the Dharma, who is truthful in conduct and devoted to her husband, is worthy to give them [the funeral cakes]. (31)
She purifies her entire family, both on the mother’s side and likewise on the father’s side. This indeed has been declared by me to be the supreme rule for virtuous Śūdras.
Born from a lower caste through a Śūdra woman who is inferior in rank, their marriages are of ten kinds, and their offspring likewise become tenfold.
O best of sages, four types of marriage are declared to be the most excellent; the remaining ones have been described by those learned in ancient lore as being for all other classes of people.
The Prājāpatya, Brāhma, Daiva, and Ārṣa are most auspicious; so too are the Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, and Piśācaka. || 35 ||
The Prātibha and the Ghātana—these are said to be the ten types of marriages; indeed, these are proclaimed as the marriages for those of lower castes. || 36 ||

The legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the given son (datta), the made son (kṛtrima), the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna), the cast-off son (apaviddha), the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), and the son born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍhaja). || 37 ||
The bought son and the son of a remarried woman—these ten types of sons are recorded in tradition; though they are inferior even to the legitimate son (aurasa), they too bring auspiciousness to them.
The eighteen base elements of the created beings exist exactly as they are; there is no ritual action according to rule, nor is there even the path of the Smṛtis.
For them, service to Brahmins, meditation on Viṣṇu, worship of Śiva, performing meritorious acts even without mantras, and the giving of gifts should always be practiced.
There is no exhaustion of giving in this world when that which is given is done with faith; a gift given without faith or with impurity is a cause of bitterness. 41.
The dharma prescribed for them, beginning with non-violence, yields great fruit; especially during the Cāturmāsya period, through service to the Lord of the Three Heavens and others.
Likewise, Dharma is practiced by the Sudras through auspicious deeds, non-contentious conduct, meritorious acts of charity, and such things as service to the twice-born. (43)
And subsistence [may be gained] from what arises from truth or falsehood, or from trade and commerce; a moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred as interest.
An increase of one and a quarter [of the fine] is prescribed for Kṣatriyas and the other castes; in this way, there shall never be a bond for the sin.
A mortal who performs the rites for the lords of the gods in the morning, the service of the twice-born at midday, and his own affairs in the afternoon, shall become happy.
Householders should always remain devoted to their duties for as long as they live, delighting in the five great sacrifices and being excellent worshippers of guests and the twice-born.
They were devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, reciters of Vedic mantras, constantly disposed toward giving gifts, and compassionate toward the poor and the afflicted. || 48 ||

By those endowed with virtues such as forbearance and the like, who worship with the twelve-syllable mantra, and who are filled with supreme bliss through the great chanting of the six-syllable mantra; || 49 ||
One should always abide with virtuous offspring, through right conduct, by serving the holy ones, free from envy, and devoid of the affliction of suffering.
Thus, by means of those very acts that attract one to the life of renunciation, the virtuous Śūdras who are devoted to the Dharma should bring satisfaction to all beings according to their means.
Those men who are always devoted to Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other gods, especially during the Cāturmāsya period, sport like gods in heaven forever.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the True Śūdra within the Section on the Excellence of Penance in the Greatness of Cāturmāsya," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the Legend of Śeṣaśāyin, in the Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Region, in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 241 ||
The sages said: Nārada said: "O Grandfather, tell me who the eighteen *prakṛtis* (constituent elements) are; what is their livelihood, and what is their duty? Tell me all this in detail. (1)
Brahmā said: My birth occurred from the interior of the lotus-navel of the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, who had awakened according to the measure of His own time.
Then, after a long time had passed, Keśava, desiring to create various passionate beings, recalled him in his mind.
There, I was born as the four-faced son of Kamalaja; then, entering through the navel-cord into his belly, I looked around.
There, as I ran forward in wonder, contemplating the purpose of creation, there again appeared to me the vision of millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Having emerged once again through the lotus stalk, as soon as I came outside, all that purpose for the sake of creation was forgotten.
Having gone there once more and created the fourfold progeny, he emerged through the navel-stalk with his inner self forgotten.
Then, having become like one who is dull-witted, an incorporeal voice spoke: "Perform penance, O one of great intelligence; this state of dullness is not fitting for you."
Then, for ten thousand years, I engaged in ascetic penance; once more, an imperishable voice born from the sky spoke to me.
Formerly, she manifested through the power of asceticism, taking the form of the Vedas; thereafter, she was commanded by the Blessed One: "Create offspring in many ways."
Resorting to the quality of passion (rajas), I first conceived in my mind a mental creation—a pure emanation of living beings.
From that, indeed, were born the Brāhmaṇas, the lords of sages beginning with Marīci; among them, you were born as the youngest, having reached the further shore of knowledge and the Vedānta.
They are eternally devoted to ritual action and constantly exerted for the sake of creation; whereas the devotee of Viṣṇu is free from worldly activity and is a single-minded servant of Brahman.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, you are my mind-born son; yet, for the sake of preserving the Vedas, I have indeed [bestowed] them upon them in due order.
O Nārada, the first creation was mental, consisting of the twice-born and others; thereafter, I created the physical creation there.
From my mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born; from my arms the Kṣatriyas; the Vaiśyas arose from my thighs; and from my feet the Śūdras came into being. (16)
Through the direct and reverse orders, and by means of sequential application, all those born lower and lower than the Śūdra are produced from the soles of the feet. || 17 ||
All those Prakṛtis are born from a portion of my own body; O Nārada, you should know this, for I shall tell you their names. (19)
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three alone are the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ). [Their duties are] the Vedas, austerity, study, performing sacrifices, and giving gifts.

The livelihood of a Brahmin consists of teaching and likewise from the acceptance of very small gifts; for even if a Brahmin is capable through his ascetic power, he should not engage in accepting large gifts.

Nevertheless, one should never accept [such gifts], because the protection of austerity must always consist of the recitation of the Vedas, the worship of Viṣṇu, meditation on Brahman, and freedom from greed.
Freedom from anger, purity, the essence of forbearance, nobility, devotion to ritual action, and the practice of giving—these are [attained] through virtues such as truthfulness and the like. (22)
He who is always adorned [with these qualities] is called a Brahmin. A Kṣatriya should practice austerity, perform sacrifice, and likewise give gifts. (23)

Their livelihood consists of reciting the Vedas, devotion to Brahmins, and the use of weapons; [they fight] for the sake of women, children, cows, and Brahmins, for the sake of the earth, and in times of danger to their master. || 24 ||
They were made by Brahmā to be the refuge for those who cry out in distress, and those Kṣatriyas who are solely intent on protecting the afflicted. || 25 ||
A Vaiśya who increases wealth, a cattle-herder, a farmer, a seller of juices and other such goods, and one who worships the gods and Brāhmaṇas; || 26 ||
Increasing wealth through legitimate means, performing sacrifices and other ritual acts, giving gifts, and studying—this is declared to be the livelihood of a Vaiśya. (27)
For these very rites, a Śūdra always performs without mantras: the daily Śrāddha dedicated to the six deities, the offering of food (hantakāra), and the libation to the sacred fire.
Devotion to the gods and the twice-born is perfected through prostration; even a Śūdra, having risen at dawn and performed the salutation of their feet, [attains this]. (29)

By reciting these verses consisting of devotion to Viṣṇu, one shall attain the state of Viṣṇu; he who constantly observes the annual vow according to the lunar day, the weekday, and the presiding deity.
A householder who provides food for all living beings is declared to be a Śūdra; indeed, even while performing actions devoid of mantras, he is liberated.
Even a Śūdra who observes the Cāturmāsya vow shall go to the state of Hari; so too shall the artisan, the dancer, the woodworker, and the progenitor (Prajāpati).
The carpenter, the painter, the weaver, the dyer, the cobbler, the spinner, the oil-presser, and the leather-worker. || 33 ||
The butcher, the tanner, the hunter, the fisherman, and the *caṇḍāla* who is born from an outcaste woman—these eighteen are [outcastes] by nature. (34)
The artisan, the goldsmith, the woodworker, the brazier, the arrow-maker, and the potter—these six are excellent by nature. (35)
One who drives donkeys, one who drives camels, and likewise one who drives horses; a cowherd and one who works with bricks—these are the five lowest of the low. (36)
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker, as well as the fisherman, the Meda, and the Bhilla—these seven are remembered as the Antyajas (outcastes). || 37 ||
Whosoever is inferior in caste is the eighteenth man; and among all the constituent elements (prakṛtis), they are superior, middling, and equal.
Three divisions are declared to be known from the determination of the Smṛtis; seven types of artisans are to be known, who are proclaimed as the most excellent. (39)
The goldsmith, the conch-worker, the one who gathers *taṇḍulī* flowers, the betel-seller, the barber, and the jeweler—these are the seven types. (40)
There is no bathing, no oblation to the deities, nor even asceticism and self-restraint; there is no study of the Vedas, no utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and no purification through marriage.
For these castes, the worship of the guru is always prescribed; for Brahmins, however, the constant giving of gifts is the supreme rule. (42)
O great sage, for all castes, for all stages of life, and for all natures, devotion to Viṣṇu is always auspicious. (43)
Thus everything has been told to you, arising from the very nature of things; now hear this highly meritorious narrative of how a Śūdra attained purification.
He of pure intellect who hears or recites this supreme, ancient, and most sacred Purāṇa, being devoted to his duties, shakes off the sins accumulated in the past and goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Eighteen Original Forms," within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: A Śūdra named Paijavana attained purity through the householder’s life; listen to that, O high-minded one, in accordance with the path of dharma. (1)
In former times, it is said, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a Śūdra named Paijavana who was renowned for being devoted to his own duty and a worshiper of Viṣṇu and Brāhmaṇas.
His wealth was always acquired through righteous means; he was ever peaceful, beloved by all people, truthful in speech, and possessed of discernment; and his wife was beautiful. (3)

His wife was a virtuous woman of noble birth from an equal family, wedded according to Vedic rites; she was devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and dedicated to the welfare of the gods and the twice-born.
Born in Kāśī, that young woman was married in Vaijayantī; she was skilled in the practice of dharma and a follower of the Vaiṣṇava vows.
She played with her husband in that manner, being well-disciplined; he too took his pleasure with her at the proper time, like a great elephant with a female elephant.
Through his former merit, that great-souled man attained wealth; he constantly engaged in trade with his own people, dealing in goods from both his own country and foreign lands.
And he causes [benefits] to be performed by means of various kinds of wealth, both belonging to others and his own; in this way, manifold wealth has been produced for that seer of Dharma. (8)
And three sons were born who were devoted to the service of their father; those sons were loyal to their father and free from the pride of wealth and other such things.
Devoted to the words of their fathers, these excellent men were radiant with the practice of their own dharma; they took no pleasure whatsoever in anything other than service to their parents.
Well-connected through their kinship with their father, who perceived both dharma and worldly purpose, his wives performed the worship of their mother and father without restraint.
His residence was endowed with supernatural power and filled with wealth and grain; he too was constantly devoted to righteousness and a worshiper of the gods and guests.
He who never turned his back on anyone who came to his house, giving wealth in the cold season and providing food and water in the heat. (13)
During the rainy season he was a giver of clothing and always a provider of food; he also constructed step-wells, wells, tanks, water-stations, and temples.
Established in the vows of Śiva and Viṣṇu, he performs [these rites] at the appropriate time; for the dharma desired by the social classes, when properly practiced, yields great fruit.
He was always a performer of meritorious works (pūrta-dharma) for others; though he was wealthy, he was never overcome by vices.
He was constantly devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, especially during the Cāturmāsya period.
Once, the sage Gālava was surrounded by many disciples.
Devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, peaceful, established in austerity, and possessing great self-control, he came to the house of the Śūdra Paijavana.
Honoring him with sweet words and services such as rising from his seat and offering a formal welcome, he was once again engaged in ritual hospitality as if he had achieved his life's purpose.
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life has become supreme; today my merit has become fruitful, for virtue has been uplifted by you.
O Sage, my thousands of sins have been consumed by your sight; my entire house has been sanctified by you, a householder. (21)
Pleased by his devotion and relieved of the fatigue of the journey, that tiger among sages spoke to that virtuous Śūdra, who stood with palms joined in reverence.
"Is all well with you, gentle one? Does your mind continue to engage with the Dharma? Are your relatives, wife, children, and others constantly bound to your welfare? (23)
Your devotion to Govinda is constant, as is your inclination toward giving; and in matters of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, your mind possesses great power.
Is the water from Viṣṇu’s feet always worn upon the head or not? And the Gaṅgā-water arising from His feet bestows the fruit of twelve years. (25)
During the Cāturmāsya period, that fruit becomes especially doubled. Devotion to Hari, discourse on Hari, hymns to Hari, and prostration before Hari—[these are the means]. (26)
"Meditation on Hari, worship of Hari, and [worship] while the Lord is asleep—these bring about liberation. To the sage speaking thus, he bowed again and spoke once more.
"According to your view, this has undoubtedly become the fruit of asceticism; nevertheless, I wish to hear your healthy speech. (28)
"The coming of those like you is conducive to all purposes. Thereupon, they both became filled with great joy, their hearts overflowing with delight.
A virtuous Śūdra named Paijavana, being highly esteemed, spoke to the sage: "Please tell me graciously: what is the purpose of your visit? (30)
And what is the connection with visiting holy places when the Cāturmāsya period is near? Gālava spoke thus to that virtuous Śūdra, who was righteous and truthful.
Many months have passed for me while bathing at sacred fords; now that the four-month period has arrived, I shall go to my hermitage.

"On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, I shall observe a vow at home for the sake of pleasing Nārāyaṇa and likewise for my own spiritual welfare. To him, the sage, whose neck was bowed in humility, replied with instructions on dharma.
Paijavana said: O bull among the twice-born, tell me that wisdom born of grace; for there is no eligibility for me in the Veda, nor indeed in the recitation of the essence of the Veda.
Therefore, tell me something from the recitation of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis; for some form resembling the true Self appears to me as having great fruit.
Tell me specifically that which accomplishes liberation during the Cāturmāsya period.
Gālava said: For those men who constantly worship Viṣṇu residing in Śāligrāma, whose surface is always marked with the discus, liberation is not far off.
Whatever auspicious act is performed by one whose mind is fixed upon the Śāligrāma becomes eternally inexhaustible, especially during the Cāturmāsya period. || 38 ||
Wherever there is a Śāligrāma stone and wherever there is a Dvārāvatī stone, liberation is not difficult to attain for one who has obtained the union of both.
On whatever ground the Śāligrāma stone is worshipped by men, it purifies that area for five krośas, even those who are burdened with hundreds of sins.
This is indeed a fiery orb, this auspicious form of Brahman; by the mere sight of it, there is the immediate destruction of all impurities. (41)
O great Śūdra, all holy fords, sacred places of the gods, and all rivers indeed attain the status of being holy fords.
Indeed, by her presence alone, all auspicious rites everywhere attain the status of true ritual action, especially during the Cāturmāsya period.
In whose home the auspicious Śāligrāma stone is worshipped with tender Tulasī leaves, Yama indeed turns his face away from that place.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or even virtuous Śūdras have the right to worship the Śāligrāma, but never others. (45)

The true Śūdra said: O Brahmin, best among the knowers of the Vedas and expert in all the scriptures, it is indeed heard that there is a prohibition against women, Śūdras, and others regarding the Śāligrāma. (46)
How can one such as I perform the ritual for worshipping the Śāligrāma? Please tell me.
Gālava said: O servant, O giver of honor, know that the prohibition applies to wicked Śūdras; for even virtuous women, it is declared that there is no such lack [of eligibility]. (48)
Let there be no doubt in this matter; from doubt one does not obtain the fruit. Those devoted to the worship of the Śāligrāma possess pure bodies and are discerning. (49)
Those who worship during the Cāturmāsya period do not go to the city of Yama, nor do those who wear upon their heads the garland offered to the Śāligrāma.
The thousands of sins of those who offer a lamp before a Śāligrāma stone perish at that very moment. (51)
Their residence in Saurapura never declines at any time. O great Śūdra, those who worship Viṣṇu residing in the Śāligrāma with beautiful flowers even while the Lord Hari is asleep— || 52 ||
Those men who always perform the ceremonial bathing of the Śāligrāma stone with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are no longer subject to the cycle of worldly existence.
He who, having placed within his heart with constant devotion Hari residing in the Śāligrāma—the stainless cause of liberation—meditates upon Him, is a partaker of liberation. 54.
One should place a garland made of Tulasī leaves upon a Śāligrāma stone; especially during the Cāturmāsya period, one shall attain all desires. || 55 ||
A garland made of flowers is not as dear to the Śāligrāma as the goddess Tulasī, who is eternally auspicious and the constant favorite of Viṣṇu. (56)
Tulasī is eternally beloved, especially during the Cāturmāsya period; Śāligrāma is Mahāviṣṇu and Tulasī is Śrī—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, having bathed the Lord Hari, who is present in the Śālagrāma stone, with scented waters and smeared him with sandalwood paste, one should worship Him together with flower clusters.
By performing [worship] with those born from Tulasī, one shall attain all desires; for Brahmā resides in the first leaf, and the Lord Śiva in the second. (59)
In the *Mañjarī*, Lord Viṣṇu is always present as the triad residing in one; therefore, this auspicious *Mañjarī*, joined with its petals, should be accepted by wise people. (60)
Having offered that [merit] with devotion to his guru as the cause for the destruction of rebirth and so forth, and having offered a heap of incense at the Śāligrāma, he becomes intent upon Hari.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, a man is never a denizen of hell; for by seeing a Śāligrāma stone and worshipping it with auspicious flowers, a man [attains liberation]. 62.
One whose soul is purified of all sins attains identity with Hari—he who praises Viṣṇu residing in stone, which originates from the waters of the Gaṇḍakī.
Through the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, he too shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu. O great Śūdra, there are twenty-four varieties of the Śāligrāma stone; listen to them, O high-minded one. (64)
These twenty-four [goddesses] are to be worshipped here in this world; I shall now declare their presiding deity, Viṣṇu, as well as their names.

That very Lord, who is embodied as the twenty-fourth [tattva], is one and the same as the primordial one; he is known by the name Saṃvatsara (the Year), he is the pressing-stone, and he has come as the Primordial God.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Worshipping the Śāligrāma," within the Narrative of Paijavana, in the Section on the Majesty of the Cāturmāsya, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the Narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, in the Majesty of the Hāṭakeśvara Kṣetra, in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 243 ||
Paijavana said: O ascetic, tell me these various distinctions in detail; for by drinking the nectar of your words, my thirst is not at all quenched.
Gālava said: Listen; I shall tell you in detail the various divisions as declared in the Purāṇas, by hearing which a human being is inevitably liberated from all sins.
First Keśava is to be worshipped, second Madhusūdana, third Saṃkarṣaṇa, and after that Dāmodara is remembered.
The fifth is named Vāsudeva, the sixth is designated Pradyumna; the seventh is said to be Viṣṇu, and the eighth is indeed Mādhava.
The ninth is Anantamūrti, the tenth is Puruṣottama; after that is Adhokṣaja, and the twelfth is Janārdana.
The thirteenth is Govinda, the fourteenth is Trivikrama, the fifteenth is Śrīdhara, and the sixteenth is Hṛṣīkeśa.
Nṛsiṃha is the seventeenth, and after that Viśvayoni; Vāmana is proclaimed next, and thereafter Nārāyaṇa is remembered.
Puṇḍarīkākṣa was mentioned first, and after him Upeṃdra; Hari is the twenty-third, and Kṛṣṇa is declared to be the last.
O son of a Śūdra, the various types of Śāligrāma have been described by me to you; likewise, O man of great wealth, these very same varieties of the deity's forms have been declared.
The forms [of the goddess] are indeed always eleven in number according to the lunar days; throughout the year, twenty-four forms are worshipped.
Likewise, there are twenty-four incarnations of the gods; the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, and the half-months known as Pakṣas. || 11 ||
One who worships them daily along with the Lord shall become possessed of devotion; this group of four is declared to be known by the name "Caturviṃśati."
This quartet bestows upon men dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa; the man who hears it with devotion or reads it with a concentrated mind [attains these]. (13)
Hari, the protector of the creation of beings, is pleased with him.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Auspicious Form of the Śāligrāma Stone," within the Cāturmāsya-māhātmya, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 244.

Paijavana said: How did the eternal origin of the universe attain the state of stone within the Śāligrāma stone on the Gaṇḍakī? Tell me that, O brahmin-sage, so that by your grace firm devotion to Hari may arise. For you are indeed like sacred pilgrimage sites, removing sins merely by being seen.
Just as men attain purity by bathing in the nectar of sacred fords, so too has it arisen within me from the nectar of your words; of this there is no doubt. (3)
Gālava said: This meritorious history is recited in the Purāṇas, concerning how that very Blessed One attained the state of being the Śāligrāma.

O sinless one, I shall now tell you how Maheśvara attained the state of being a *liṅga*. Formerly, there was a patriarch named Dakṣa, who was born from the thumb of Brahmā. He had a virtuous daughter, well-endowed with auspicious marks, named Satī; she was then married by Hara, the knower of rites, according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
That man of deluded intellect committed an act of hatred toward Hara during the great sacrifice; because of that intense hatred, Satī became exceedingly enraged.
Then, having approached the sacrificial altar and focused her mind on the internal fire, she became intent on breath control (prāṇāyāma) and performed the renunciation of her body.
Leaving behind her paternal portion and joined with her own portion, she fixed her mind in meditation upon the cool Himalaya.
Wherever the mind goes at the time of death, being subject to the power of its own karma, there an incarnation is born; of this there is no doubt.
For that goddess, being consumed by fire, became the daughter of Himālaya; there, having become Pārvatī, she resorted to severe asceticism. || 11 ||
Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and dedicated to the vows of Hara, the daughter of Himavat fixed her mind upon Maheśvara on the peak of the Himalayas.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Blessed One, Maheśvara, the creator of all beings, arrived at that place in the form of a brahmin.
Having recognized her as pure through asceticism and having tested her through her actions and dispositions, he then assumed a divine form and took Pārvatī by the hand.
"I have been conquered by your ascetic power; what pleasing service may I perform for you? To this, he replied to Maheśāna: "My father and preceptor are my authority. (15)
Being thus addressed, Śaṅkara dispatched the seven ṛṣis; they went there to communicate the agreement with Himavat.
Having offered their petition to Maheśāna, the sages were dismissed and departed. Then, on the appointed day, the gods, headed by Mahendra, [approached] the Lord.
Led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the priests approached the fire; the masters of yoga arrived to see the bull-bannered Lord, who was dressed in the attire of a bridegroom.
Filled with joy and honoring his sense of having fulfilled his purpose, Himavat worshipped [the guest] with auspicious offerings such as madhuparka and other ritual services.
Surrounded by a multitude of twice-born men, he united that maiden with her in marriage according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas and the ritual of taking the hand.
After circumambulating the fire, Girīśa then, being asked about his lineage and other details at the time of the gift, was overcome with shame, O Hara.
At the word of Brahmā, he remained as the remainder of the ritual procedure; at the time of consuming the sacrificial oblation (caru), he manifested as the five-faced one.
Accompanied by all the gods and filled with curiosity, that bridegroom Maheśvara also arrived for the sake of Girijā.
Seeing the nine-faced [form], the people broke into loud laughter and said: "The Vedic revelation has spoken thus; O Śiva, you must remain steadfast! (24)
Though ashamed, she did not abandon him for five births; the dark-eyed woman went only to her husband, who was none other than Hara.
The entire host of gods and mountains was filled with joy; then, when the wedding ceremony was complete, Hara entered the bridal chamber.
Moreover, in the presence of the Gaṇas, that Ambikā could not tolerate it; then, having given him his dowry, he was dismissed by the Mountain.
Honored and treated with hospitality, Viśvakarman went to Mount Mandara; then, in an instant, he [constructed] for him a palace made of jewels.
He fashioned for the God of gods a palace that increased according to his own will, possessing every prosperity, of praiseworthy luster, and adorned with jewels and coral.
It was joined with a thousand pillars, enchanting with jeweled altars, and at its gateway stood the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin.
They appeared with three eyes and tridents in hand, possessing the form of Śaṅkara; all around his garden were thousands of Pārijāta trees.
In that most enchanting house, which increases all desires, the divine wish-fulfilling cow and the celestial jewel were stationed at its threshold.
While he was dwelling together with Pārvatī, Kāma came within the range of his vision; assuming the form of the wind and beholding Śiva, Kāma spoke to Śaṅkara.
Salutations to you who possess all forms; salutations to you whose banner is the bull. Salutations to you, the Lord of the Gaṇas; protect us, O Lord, let there be salutation to you.
The earth touches the world bereft of you as if it were a corpse; nothing whatsoever among the moving and the unmoving is seen without you.
"You are the protector, you are the ordainer, and the cause of the destruction of the world; have mercy, O Mahādeva, and grant me the gift of your body. (36)
Īśvara said: "O sinless one, in that very place on the mountain where you were previously consumed by me in my presence, become once again possessed of your own body."
Having been addressed thus, Kāma then returned to his own body; O Śūdra, he bowed at his feet and became humble with modesty. (38)
Then, filled with great joy, he bowed at the feet of Pārvatī; having obtained their grace, he [departed] from their presence throughout the three worlds.
Possessed of great splendor and endowed with the power of great delusion, he whose bow and arrows are flowers moved about, his hair curled. || 40 ||
With his eyes constantly rolling, he entered their bodies, [honoring them] with divine liquors, divine fragrances, garments, garlands, and the like.
His friends moved about on all sides during the time of their enjoyment; as he thus sported, a hundred years passed by.

Just as a single night seems like an entire age to one whose mind is intent on sexual union, so it was in that interval; the gods, fleeing in fear from Tāraka, went to Brahmā for refuge, and having praised him, they sought his protection. (43)
The gods said: "That Tāraka, who was exceedingly fierce, was granted a boon by you in the past."
Having swiftly conquered Śakra, he enjoys [the world] while being honored by the three realms; you yourself must devise a means for his destruction. (45)
Brahmā said: "He has been granted a boon by me; he shall certainly not be destroyed by me. No one ought to cut down the bitter plant after having nurtured it with their own hand. (46)
Therefore, I shall tell you the means for the slaying of that great-souled one; for he will indeed be born as a son to Maheśāna from Pārvatī. (47)
"Having been so for seven days, he shall slay Tāraka. Having heard these words, [he went] to Mandara, the beauty of the world.
Afflicted by the Daityas and Dānavas, they returned from the world of Brahmā.
There, the attendants (gaṇas) headed by Nandin, bearing tridents, stood with restrained minds, having approached the door of the house.

The gods said: "The gods, their minds deeply afflicted by grief, their splendor utterly destroyed, and having abandoned all their homes and shelters, remained engaged in supreme penance to propitiate the Lord while he was asleep for four months. (51)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gods' Departure for Mount Mandara to Behold Śiva," within the Narrative of Paijavana, in the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* (The Episode of Him Who Lies upon Śeṣa), in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Gālava said: But Śakra and the other lords of the gods, their minds tormented by grief and their mental and physical faculties bewildered by not seeing Īśvara, found no pleasure [in their duties].
Having fashioned images of him who dwells in the hearts of all beings, they propitiated the Lord of the World through austerity, yet they did not attain him.
The god who has matted hair on his head, who holds a trident in his hand and wields the Pināka bow, who carries a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, who possesses ten arms and wears a diadem.
He saw the Lord accompanied by Umā, five-faced and many-armed, with a body as white as camphor, adorned with white sacred ashes.
The Lord was adorned with a sacred thread made of serpents, clad in an elephant hide, and likewise covered by the skin of a black antelope.
There, the gods, having practiced meditation and relying upon the support of trees, undertook the observance of vows and performed supreme austerity.
"The gods were established by means of the six-syllabled mantra of Śiva. The Śūdra said: "How can that practice of vows which was described by you be accomplished? (7)
O Brahmin, speak at length; we are not satiated by these nectars of your words.

Gālava said: Chanting [the names of] the sacred ash, the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the skull-bowl, and likewise the crystal [rosary], as well as the garland of severed heads, the five faces, and the crescent moon upon his head.
Clad in a tiger skin, wearing a loincloth and two earrings, with a pair of bells, a trident, and a sacred thread—such is the nature of his conduct.
"O son of a Śūdra, I have described to you that which is to be characterized by these marks; by this method, all the gods, with Agni at their head, [are to be known]. (11)
They propitiated the bestower of boons by every possible means; and when the Cāturmāsya was completed and the pure month of Kārtika had fully arrived, [they continued their worship].
Seeing the gods who had fulfilled their vows and were purified, Maheśvara, the soul of all beings and the witness of all creatures, being pleased, granted them his favor.
During the Cāturmāsya period, he was gratified by the recitation of the Śatarudrīya according to the prescribed ritual, as well as by meditation and the offering of lamps.
Having perceived that the gods had arrived and were performing worship with sixteenfold offerings toward Hara just as they do for Viṣṇu, out of a spirit of devotion... (15)
The blessed Lord Rudra, being greatly pleased, bestowed upon them auspicious intelligence; then those gods, having consulted together and praised Agni according to his true nature, [proceeded].
They made their faces serene and intent upon the accomplishment of the task; the witness of all actions, possessed of great splendor, assumed the form of a pigeon.
Then he entered into the midst to behold the god Maheśvara; he made various movements with his veils both drawn on and removed.
Seeing him, who possessed a beautiful form, moving with wonderful gait through writhings and glidings, the Blessed One perceived the cause for it there.
Then, being one whose vital energy was drawn upward, he first emitted that seed into it; he held that seed in the mouth of the Fire-god, and she fell outside the house.
When that bird had departed, Pārvatī, her efforts rendered fruitless, became enraged; that Great Goddess then uttered a curse upon all the gods.
"Since my desire has been thwarted by you of wicked intellect, therefore let the inhabitants of heaven quickly turn into stone."
"You shall all become childless and merciless gods. Then, constrained by the curse, they bowed down and sought his grace.
Having entered into great suffering, they spoke again and again: ||| 24 ||
The gods said: You are the mother of all the gods, the eternal witness of all, and always the cause of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the worlds. 25.
You are the form of the true nature of existence, resting upon the great elements; you are Aparṇā, the sustainer of ascetic penances, the supporter of all beings, and the earth.

She is to be propitiated through mantras, the seed of mantras, and the abode of dissolution for the seeds of the universe; she is the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices and other rites, always existing in the form of Svāhā.
Endowed with mantras and yantras within Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, she is eternal in form, of great form, the form of all, and stainless. || 298 ||
Bestowing the highest good upon people afflicted by the three defects, she is Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Mahādevī, and Maheśvarī. (29)

You are the Sovereign of All, the Great Illusion, the bestower of the boon of the seed-syllable of Māyā; you are of excellent form, the most worthy of choice, the giver of boons, and the daughter of the Bestower of Boons.
Those men who always worship you with auspicious bilva leaves—to them you are the perpetual bestower of kingdoms, the granter of desires, and the giver of spiritual perfections.
To those by whom you were especially worshipped with bilva leaves during the Cāturmāsya period, you yourself have become a wish-fulfilling cow for the sake of accomplishing their desires.
Those in this world who always worship [her] together with Maheśvara with great devotion using bilva leaves—for them, there shall be neither suffering nor evil deeds.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya, your worship yields great fruit; from this day forward, those people by whom you have been worshipped with bilva leaves [shall attain the highest reward].
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, you shall bestow upon them unsurpassed knowledge; during the Cāturmāsya, the bilva leaf yields especially great fruit.
Given according to the prescribed rites for the pleasure of Umā and Maheśvara, it becomes inexhaustible; just as Śrī resides in the Tulasī tree, so does Pārvatī reside in the Bilva tree.
You are seen as the universe in embodied form, the bestower of all desired objects; these two, when especially served during the Cāturmāsya period, yield great fruit.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Bestowal of Curses upon Pārvatī, Indra, and Others," within the Paijavana Episode of the Māhātmya of Cāturmāsya, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the Śeṣaśāyyupākhyāna of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Paijavana said: O Sage, O Lord, how did Śrī take the form of Tulasī and Pārvatī reside in the Bilva tree? Tell me this truth in detail.
Gālava said: "In ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, the Dānavas—terrible in form and exceedingly cruel, arrogant in their strength—slew the gods in battle. (2)
And the gods, agitated by fear, went for refuge to Brahmā; preceded by Bṛhaspati, they praised and bowed down to their father.
They all stood with palms joined in reverence, and the Grandfather said to them: "For what reason have you come to our house with such dejected faces?"

"Let the reason be told quickly. [The sages replied: "O you who are joined by the fires, Indra, and the Vasus! O Father, we have been defeated in battle by the Daityas, who perform wondrous deeds. The gods said: [9]
We have all exerted our utmost prowess and have therefore come to you for refuge; protect us, O Lord of the gods, who have approached you for shelter.
Having heard that, the Blessed One Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said: "I am not able to take the side of any person whatsoever."

I shall declare the means before you who are devoted to the True Dharma. Once, a very great dispute arose between the devotees of Śiva and the devotees of Keśava, each desiring to defeat the other. Then, while his own devotees were looking on, the Blessed Lord Rudra [acted].
Establishing oneness with the hosts of Viṣṇu, he assumed a most wonderful form; then, with two halves of his body, he bore the name Hari-Hara.
Hara became half of his body and Viṣṇu the other half; on one side were the marks of Viṣṇu, and on the other side were the marks of Hara.
On one side was Vainateya, and on the other was the bull; on the left was a body with the hue of a cloud, resembling a mass of stones.
At that time, he indeed became white as camphor on his right side; the universe became equal to the union of the two, and the entirety of existence proceeded as a single unity.
Those of divided minds, who had perished by subverting the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti—the heretics and the rationalists—all were filled with wonder.
Abandoning their respective paths, they proceeded along the way to Nirvāṇa; that form, eternally praised, remained on Mandara, the best of mountains. 15.
Even today she remains steadfast, accompanied by the Gaṇas headed by Pramatha; she is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the universe, the infinite seed of all existence.

United with Maheśa and Viṣṇu, she is remembered as the destroyer of sins; she is to be meditated upon by yogis, always worthy of worship, and transcends the qualities that serve as the support for all beings.
Even those seeking liberation, having meditated upon her, go to the supreme state; indeed, by meditating especially during the Cāturmāsya, a mortal becomes non-human.
"The Lord will provide for those who go there. Having said this to them, the Blessed One vanished right then and there.
Those gods, headed by Vahni, also went to Mount Mandara; they wandered here and there, searching for Maheśvara.
Pārvatī resides in the bilva tree and Lakṣmī in the tulasī; in the beginning, the entire universe was first born as consisting of trees.
These trees are most excellent; they all originate from portions of the gods. By the mere touch of them, one is liberated from all sins.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, when the gods beheld the Lord of the Three Worlds, who removes the flood of great sins, by means of that very [rite], || 23 ||
Then a voice arising from the sky spoke to the gods according to the truth: "The Lord of all beings has taken refuge in this tree out of compassion. (24)
When the Cāturmāsya period has arrived, the Aśvattha tree, which bestows compassion upon all beings, should always be served, especially on Saturdays.
By the constant touch of the Aśvattha tree, sin is shattered into a thousand pieces; indeed, those who perform libations with milk mixed with sesame seeds out of devotion [attain the same]. (26)
They shall perform a libation, and thereby their ancestors will attain satisfaction; indeed, by the mere sight of the tree, even great sin is destroyed. (27)

The Pippala tree, when worshipped, meditated upon, seen, or even served—especially during the Cāturmāsya period—leads to the destruction of sins and diseases. An Aśvattha tree that is worshipped and watered brings happiness to all living beings. (28)
Those men who shall proclaim even the name born of the Aśvattha tree—which removes all diseases and carries away the flood of all sins—[shall attain the highest state].
No fear of the realm of Yama arises on their path for those who have caused [the image] to be well-anointed with saffron and sandalwood. (30)

For him, there shall be an absence of the threefold afflictions and he shall attain the status of an attendant in Vaikuṇṭha; [he shall overcome] bad dreams, evil thoughts, and the defeats caused by malignant fevers.
"O Pippala, beloved of Hari, bring about the dissolution of sins! With this mantra, those gods who shall worship the Pippala tree [shall attain their goal]. (32)
Then, among them, Dharmarāja becomes the one who carries out their word; even by his word, Aśvattha is declared to be the bestower of knowledge upon men. (133)
Merely hearing of it removes the sins committed from birth until death; serving the Aśvattha tree brings merit, especially during the Cāturmāsya period. (34)
While the God was asleep, the Lord, the Master, stationed himself in the midst of a tree and remained there as if drinking up all the water on earth.
Water is Viṣṇu, and by its nature as water, Viṣṇu alone is the great essence; therefore, Viṣṇu resides within the tree during the Cāturmāsya, destroying all sins.
Viṣṇu, who has entered all beings, indeed nourishes the world; likewise, he who bows down to Viṣṇu residing in the aśvattha tree shall not go to hell.
That self-restrained man who plants an aśvattha tree upon the earth, his thousands of sins dissolve at that very moment.
The Aśvattha tree is the most sacred among all trees and is endowed with auspiciousness; when planted and meditated upon during the Cāturmāsya period, it bestows liberation and destroys sin. (39)
By placing one's foot upon an *aśvattha* tree, the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) is produced; having needlessly cut it down, one will certainly be cooked in hell. (40)
Viṣṇu is eternally situated at the root, and Keśava is in the trunk; Nārāyaṇa is in the branches, and the Lord Hari is in the leaves.

He who worships the tree during the Cāturmāsya period, especially so, shall undoubtedly attain immortality in the fruit [of liberation], accompanied by all the gods; he is a partaker of liberation. 42.
Therefore, the man who with devotion always serves the Aśvattha tree with every effort destroys the sin produced during that day. (43)

That very Viṣṇu is manifest as the tree itself, whose roots of merit are cultivated by the great-souled ones; taking refuge in whom destroys thousands of sins for men, and who is rich in qualities like a cow of plenty. (44)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Aśvattha Tree," within the Narrative of Paijavana, in the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, during the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 247.
Vāṇī said: Indeed, the Palāśa tree is worshipped in the form of Hari by those who know the ancient lore; for the worship of the Brahma-tree is performed with many ritual offerings. || 1 ||
It is declared to bestow all desires and destroy great sins; there are three leaves on the Palāśa tree, the middle one being consecrated by Viṣṇu.
Brahmā is proclaimed to be on the left and Hara alone on the right; he who always eats from a Palāśa leaf-vessel is the most excellent of men. || 3 ||
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices; especially during the Cāturmāsya period, it bestows liberation upon the one who eats [there].
If those who worship [the deity] constantly with milk or water on Sundays during the Cāturmāsya period, they go to the supreme state.
If it is seen by men who have risen early in the morning, they quickly shake off the hells and go to the supreme state.
The Palāśa tree is the support of all the gods and the means for accomplishing dharma; wherever greed may exist, there this great tree is to be honored.
Just as among all castes the Brahmin is the most eminent, so too, among all trees, the Brahma-tree is the greatest.
At whose root Hara is ever present, at whose trunk the wielder of the trident himself resides, upon whose branches is the Lord Rudra, and within whose flowers is the destroyer of Tripura; || 9 ||
Śiva dwells in the leaves, Gaṇapati likewise in the fruit; the Lord of the Gaṅgā resides in the bark, and the Blessed Lord Bhava in the marrow.
But on all the secondary branches, this entire Lord who is beloved of Hara is present; Hara, white as camphor, is always described exactly as he is.
For thus this highly fortunate one, whose form is that of Brahmā and who is white in color, has been meditated upon for the destruction of enemies and for the complete drying up of sins.
There is no doubt that [the deity] is born for the granting of heart's desires when Thursday arrives, as well as during the Cāturmāsya period. (13)
When worshipped, praised, and meditated upon, he is the destroyer of all suffering. || 14 ||

The hymn of praise to the God is the supreme seed of the gods, which is the embodied Brahman that has attained the state of the Tree of Brahman. This Sthāṇu-form, who is to be constantly served with faith, shall destroy all sins when worshipped during the Cāturmāsya period. || 15 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Palāśa Tree," within the Narrative of Paijavana, in the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 248 ||
Vāṇī said: In whose house the great fruit-bearing Tulasī has been planted by a householder, poverty does not arise there; of this there is no doubt. (1)
Merely by the sight of Tulasī, the heap of sins is dispelled; for the sake of prosperity, Tulasī, the beloved of Hari, arose from drops of nectar.
Drinking the beautiful beverage that removes the sins of living beings, she in whose form Lakṣmī resides and upon whose shoulder the one born from the ocean dwells. (3)
Prosperity (*śrī*) is ever present in its leaves; Lakṣmī herself resides in its branches; Indirā is constantly found in its flowers; and she who was born from the Ocean of Milk dwells in its fruit.
Tulasī, whose form pervades the universe, resides in its dry wood; she dwells in the marrow as Padmavāsā, and in the bark as Haripriyā.
She who possesses all forms, who is the sovereign of all, and who bestows supreme bliss—mortal man who consumes Tulasī does not go to the realm of Yama.
He on whose head Tulasī resides is not tormented by the messengers of Yama; he on whose mouth Tulasī resides is granted the state of Nirvāṇa.
He who holds Tulasī in his hand is freed from the threefold suffering; and Tulasī residing in the heart of living beings grants all desires.
He on whose shoulder Tulasī rests is not smeared by sins; he on whose neck Tulasī hangs is indeed always liberated while living.
The man who always wears a leaf originating from Tulasī attains the success he has meditated upon in his mind; of this there is no doubt.
That man who daily waters the Tulasī plant—which accomplishes all goals for the body and destroys wicked enemies—does not go to the abode of Yama.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, she grants liberation even when merely saluted; for it is known that Nārāyaṇa resides within the water as well as within the trees.
Out of compassion for living beings, Lakṣmī has taken refuge in the tulasī tree; when the Cāturmāsya period arrives, if the tulasī is served [worshipped], [she grants her grace].
For them, thousands of sins constantly dissolve into a thousand parts through the constant remembrance of Govinda and the service of a grove of Tulasī.
If a person, with faith, nurtures the Tulasī plant during the Cāturmāsya period by watering it with milk, that act is exceedingly rare to find. (15)
By the gift of water from the basins for the roots, the entire family is purified; indeed, just as the presence of the auspicious Tulasī causes it to increase eternally. (16)
In such and such a manner, the increase of desire arises for the householder; so it is for the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic as well. (17)
Likewise, if all the *prakṛtis* become devoted to the service of Tulasī with faith, Hari does not cause them any suffering. (18)

The one Hari shines, pervading all trees, his very form permeated by various flavors; and the goddess Kamalā, who destroys suffering and other woes even when constantly remembered, took up residence within the trees.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Tulasī," within the Narrative of Paijavana, in the Section on the Greatness of Cāturmāsya, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the Narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the Sixth Section (Nāga-khaṇḍa) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 249 ||
Vāṇī said: The greatness of the bilva leaf cannot be fully described; for your sake, O Mahendra, I shall speak of it according to its true nature—listen! (1)
The auspicious goddess, daughter of the mountain, having become weary from her stay, a drop of perspiration appeared on the surface of her forehead.
Cast down by Bhavānī, he fell upon the surface of the earth; this great tree was born on Mandara, the best of mountains.
Then the daughter of the mountain, having seen a tree standing in the forest, went there again to sport, her eyes wide with wonder.
She questioned her two companions, Jayā and Vijayā: "Who is this divine great tree that shines in the midst of the forest? It appears with a beautiful form and truly causes great joy. (5)
Jayā said: "O Goddess, this tree born from your body was produced from drops of perspiration; quickly give it a name, for when worshipped, it is the destroyer of sins."
Pārvatī said: "Because this distinguished great tree has pierced through the surface of the earth... (7)
It rose up near me; therefore, let this be a bilva tree. Having approached this tree with devotion, [one should gather] a heap of leaves.
That king who, endowed with faith, shall perform my worship with leaves, will indeed become a sovereign upon the surface of the earth.
Whatever desire one may contemplate, its fulfillment arises for that person who, upon seeing the bilva leaves, shall also exercise faith. (10)

For the sake of worship according to the prescribed rite, I am the giver of wealth; of this there is no doubt. If anyone sets his mind upon consuming the tips of the leaves, thousands of his sins shall spontaneously go to their destruction. (11)
If a person makes the head joined with the tip of a leaf, there shall indeed be no torment of Yama to give him suffering.
Having spoken thus, the delighted Pārvatī departed for her own abode, the goddess accompanied by her female friends and joined by the Gaṇas as well. 13.
Vāṇī said: This bilva tree is excellent, pure, and a destroyer of sins; the goddess Girijā resides at its root—of this there is no doubt. (14)
The goddess Dākṣāyaṇī is in the trunk, Maheśvarī in the branches, the goddess Pārvatī in the leaves, and Kātyāyanī is remembered to be in the fruit. || 15 ||
Gaurī is said to reside in the bark; Aparṇā in the inner bark; Durgā is said to reside in the flower; and Umā in the branches and twigs. (16)
And upon all the thorns, by the command of the Daughter of the Mountain, nine crores of Śaktis are stationed for the purpose of protecting living beings. (17)
They worship her with beautiful leaves and honor that eternal one; whatever desire one may cherish, its fulfillment shall certainly come to pass. || 18 ||

That Maheśvarī, the daughter of the mountain, Maheśvarī of pure form and bestower of liberation upon people, seeing Hara had taken refuge in a Palāśa tree, then assumed the body of a Bilva tree through her own divine play.

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Bilva Tree," within the Narrative of Paijavana, in the Greatness of the Cāturmāsya, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the Narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, in the Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Region, in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 250 ||
Gālava said: Having spoken thus, the auspicious voice from the sky ceased; and those gods of great vows, having witnessed that great marvel, [were amazed]. (1)
And when the Cāturmāsya period arrived, O son of a Śūdra, they worshipped the four trees according to the prescribed rites with a sense of oneness.
Then, when the four-month period was complete, the Lord, whose nature consists of both Hari and Hara, being pleased, assumed a manifest form and spoke to them with affection.
"Go, O lords of the gods, devoted to your great vows; enjoy each your own respective offices, for those Dānavas have been slain by me."
When the two lords of the gods of gods, assuming a single unified form, had spoken thus, the minds of the Gaṇas and the deities then became undivided.
As those two leaders, the subduers of enemies, were thus leading [them], the gods also became free from affliction and joyful in heart due to their lack of discord.
They departed for their own domains with millions of celestial chariots. Galava said: "In that same way, even there, those gods were deluded by the curse of Parvati."
Having praised that Maheśvarī with bilva leaves and worshipped her, he praised her with a gracious countenance, prostrating himself again and again.
Then she, the Mother of the Universe, being thus praised, spoke to the gods: "O best of deities, my curse shall certainly not be in vain."
Nevertheless, I shall show compassion to you who have committed sins; however, O best of gods, you shall not dwell in heaven made of stone.
And having reached the world of mortals, you shall all become bestowers of boons upon the worlds, residing in every manner within idols.
Those boys and girls who have been designated by the taking of hands—you shall become their progeny, without a doubt.
Having spoken thus, that blessed goddess, the bestower of boons upon the gods, addressed both Viṣṇu and Maheśvara in great anger.
Out of fear of her, the gods vanished; they have entered among mortals as images, remaining well-established there while fulfilling the mental aspirations of their devotees. || 14 ||
"Since Maheśāna was not restrained by you even though he was forbidden by Viṣṇu, therefore you too shall become a stone; of this there is no doubt. (15)
Hara, too, having assumed a form made of stone that is censured by the world, shall experience great suffering due to the curse of the Brahmins because of his linga-shape.
Having heard that, Lord Viṣṇu, seeking to appease Pārvatī, bowed down and spoke to Maheśvarī, the wife of Hara.

The illustrious Viṣṇu said: O Great Goddess, you are always the beloved of Mahādeva; for you are the supreme power (śakti) abiding in the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).
Endowed with the three measures (mātrās), you manifest the three qualities (guṇas); you are the mother of Māyā and the others, possessing a form that pervades the universe.
You are praised by the three Vedas, and you appear in the form of a Sādhya, full of passion; you are formless yet possess all forms, and you are the bestower of progeny to the people. || 20 ||
O Sovereign of the Gods, you alone are indeed Phalavelā, Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Oṃkāra, and Vaṣaṭkāra.
O Sustainer of all beings, salutations be to you; salutations be to you, O Auspicious One. Salutations to the passionate one, to the dispassionate one, and to the formidable one, O Blessed One.
Thus praised, she of the bright eyes, with a serene inner soul, spoke these most noble words, yet filled with feigned anger: ||| 23 ||
O Janārdana, this [manifestation] of yours as the Fish cannot be otherwise; for even there you remained, bestowing liberation upon the lords of yogis.
She grants the desires of her devotees, especially during the Cāturmāsya period; she is the river named Gaṇḍakī, the beloved daughter of Brahmā.
Born from the essence of stone, bestowing merit, and possessing great waters—your dwelling shall be in its exceedingly pure water. (26)
Examined by those learned in the Purāṇas according to twenty-four varieties, the Śālagrāma is proclaimed to have gold (jāmbūnada) upon its face.
"You shall become a spherical mass of splendor endowed with glory, possessed of all powers, and the bestower of liberation even upon yogins. (28)
Those men who shall worship you, Viṣṇu, as situated within the stone—to those devotees, you grant the fulfillment of their well-considered desires. || 29 ||
O Lord of Gods, for those humans who, intent on devotion, worship the Lord of Devas present in stone with Tulasī, liberation is not far off.
And whoever shall behold you, Viṣṇu, established in stone and present in an image, with all your limbs marked by the beautiful discus, shall not go to the abode of Yama.
Gālava said: Thus I have told you everything regarding the cause of the Śālagrāma, and how that Blessed Lord Viṣṇu attained the state of stone.
Govinda, having received the great curse, went to his own abode; and Pārvatī, being angry, bowed down to Maheśāna.

Thus, that very Blessed One—the mark of destruction for the entire existence of all beings, past and future alike—He too, Bhava, together with Śrī and the daughter of the Mountain Lord, took up residence among the four trees.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Curse of Viṣṇu," within the Legend of Paijavana, in the Greatness of the Cāturmāsya, in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the Narrative of Śeṣaśāyin, in the Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Field, in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 251 ||
The Śūdra said: This is indeed a great marvel, that the gods, when the Cāturmāsya has arrived, take up residence in all trees, assuming the form of trees themselves. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, who are those gods, and in which places do they dwell? Please explain this to me in detail out of a desire to favor me.
Gālava said: They say that during the Cāturmāsya, water is nectar; by their own will, the deities of the trees drink it as it is held up effortlessly by the gods.
From drinking it, great satisfaction arises; of this there is no doubt. Strength, splendor, luster, physical excellence, and swift prowess [are attained]. (4)
These qualities arise from drinking that which is produced from a portion of Kṛṣṇa; however, by drinking the eternal nectar (nityāmṛta), only a small amount of strength is produced.
They always praise that food; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, for four months, they drink only water.
The ancestors and gods residing in trees, out of a desire for the welfare of living beings, declare that the service of trees is the most excellent practice at all times throughout every month.
Especially when practiced during the four-month period [of the rainy season], these acts bring about happiness; sprinkling trees with water mixed with sesame seeds grants all desires.
Milk-yielding trees, when sprinkled with water mixed with milk, bestow auspiciousness; as well as the fourfold group of trees that was previously described by me.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, it bestows the fruits of all desires; for Brahmā, having taken refuge in the banyan tree, grants boons to living beings.
Taking refuge in the Sāvitrī mantra with sesame seeds as his sacred purifier and white ornaments, the service of sesame seeds is especially fruitful when the Lord is asleep. (11)
Sesame seeds are incomparable purifiers; sesame seeds accomplish the goals of dharma and artha; sesame seeds bestow liberation, and sesame seeds remove sins.
Sesame seeds bestow special fruits; sesame seeds are the destroyers of enemies. Sesame seeds are declared to be foremost among all meritorious things. (13)
They do not call sesame seeds mere grain; they are remembered as "divine grain. Therefore, among all gifts, the gift of sesame seeds is the most excellent. (14)
O son of a Śūdra, by that gift of sesame seeds accompanied by gold, the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa has indeed been accomplished.
The Sāvitrī mantra and sesame seeds are declared to be the accomplishers of all purposes and goals; one should perform libations with sesame seeds, especially during the Cāturmāsya period.
The sight of sesame seeds is meritorious, as are touching them, using them, offering oblations with them, eating them, and likewise applying them as a body rub. || 17 ||
In every respect, this sesame tree destroys sin merely by being seen; when served especially during the Cāturmāsya period, it bestows all happiness.
Mahendra, devoted to the welfare of all beings, remained stationed at Yavamā. The service of Yava is meritorious; likewise are its sight and its touch. (19)
One should perform the libation with barley grains; what is given to the gods becomes inexhaustible. All the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) have taken refuge under the mango tree. (20)
