The Gandharvas [worship] the Malaya tree, the Gaṇanāyakas the Aguru; the Samudras the Vetasa tree, and the Yakṣas the Punnāga. || 21 ||
Likewise, the Nāgas resort to the nāga-tree, the Siddhas to the kaṅkolaka tree, the Guhyakas to the panasa tree, and the Kinnaras to the marica tree. || 22 ||
Kandarpa took refuge in yaṣṭīmadhu and remained there; Vahni (Fire) takes refuge in the great tree raktāñjana and stays there. (23)
Yama [should plant] the Vibhītaka tree, and the Lord of the Nairṛtas, the Bakula; Varuṇa, the Kharjūrī tree, and Māruta, the Pūga tree. || 24 ||
Dhanada [gives] the Akṣoṭaka tree, and the Rudras the Badarī tree; for the Seven Sages there are Mahātāla trees, and Bahula is surrounded by Apsarases.
Surrounded by clouds, dark-hued, and the destroyer of sins, this best of trees is called Jambū because its color is like that of Kṛṣṇa. || 26 ||
Vāsudeva becomes pleased by the gift of its fruits; having taken recourse to a Jambū tree, they provide a meal for the twice-born. (27)
When the Cāturmāsya has arrived and Lord Janārdana is asleep, Hari, being pleased with them, shall bestow the four goals of human existence.
He who, remaining pure, feeds the Brāhmaṇas together with their wives, by him Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī, shall be pleased. (29)
For the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, by clothing [the image] with auspicious garments and ornaments together with his wife, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Whatever fruit is produced by three nights of eating at the *vaṭa* tree and the *śoka* tree, that same fruit is obtained by eating at the *jambū* tree and feeding the twice-born.
On that day, the performer of the rite should observe a single meal; for what more need be said regarding the worship of the Jambū tree? (32)
He is born endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth; of this there is no doubt. Jambū is surrounded by clouds, and Aśoka is like lightning. (33)
The great mountain Laśa was eternally accepted by the Vasus; the Japā tree was [accepted] by the Ādityas, and likewise Madana by the two Aśvins.
With the Viśvedevas and Madhūka, Guggulu with the Piśitāśanas; with Sūrya and Arka, O Lord, and Tripatraka with the pure Soma. || 35 ||
The *khadira* tree [is sacred] to the son of the Earth (Mars), the *apāmārga* to Budha (Mercury), the *aśvattha* to Guru (Jupiter), and likewise the *udumbara* to Śukra (Venus). || 36 ||
The Śamī tree was then accepted by Saturn and by those of the Śūdra caste; Dūrvā grass, suitable for the libations of the ancestors, was accepted by Rāhu.
It is eternally dear to Viṣṇu, especially during the Cāturmāsya period; the sacrificial Darbha grass accepted by Ketu yields great fruit.
Without which virtuous action is never fully accomplished; he who is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of all auspicious things. (39)
For those about to die, he is the form of liberation; he is the great tree standing upon the earth. Within him, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva always dwell eternally.
Even the mere name of those great trees—which grant satisfaction at their roots, their trunks, and likewise their tops—is sufficient; other gods also take refuge in those trees.
For during the four months, there is no doubt that all the wives of the gods take refuge in the creepers during the Cāturmāsya.
Even when merely served, they grant men their desired wishes; therefore, by him who has served the Pippala tree with his whole being— || 43 ||
All trees have been served, especially during the Cāturmāsya period; by him who has served the Tulasī, all creepers have been served.
The entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is nourished when this is practiced during the Cāturmāsya by either a householder or a forest-dweller. (45)
It is practiced by celibate students and ascetics and bestows liberation; one must never cause the cutting down of any of these trees.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, except for the purpose of performing sacrifices and the like; all this that I was asked by you here has been explained in its entirety. (47)
O son of a Śūdra, just as all the gods have attained the state of being trees.
One *aśvattha*, one *picumanda*, one *nyagrodha*, ten *tittiḍī* trees, and three each of *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *āmalakī*—having seen these, one shall not behold hell. (49)

All the gods and those who dwell within the universal tree, the dark streams and those with dark middles and tips—all these become satisfied when that God, the object of universal worship, is served. || 50 ||
The Śūdra said: How was the goddess Pārvatī, who had become enraged and by whose anger the entire world is agitated, appeased by the trident-bearing Lord after she had pronounced a curse? (1)
How did that Blessed Lord Rudra incur the curse of his wife, and having assumed a deformed appearance, how did he again take recourse to his divine body? (2)
Gālava said: Out of great fear of the Goddess, the gods made their forms invisible and remained stationed throughout the entire world of men within [divine] images. || 3 ||
Toward them as well, she, the illustrious Mother of the Universe, the destroyer of sins, who had been praised by Viṣṇu, bestowed her grace with a gracious mind.
And by their power, being constrained by the weight of Pārvatī’s curse, he spoke to Śaṅkara while constantly entreating her: ||| 5 ||
These gods, worthy of universal worship and the bestowers of boons upon the universe, shall become so through my grace when they are propitiated by men with devotion.
"Without you, this deed of mine was performed—a deed censured by the virtuous—on the sacrificial altar at the time of marriage, in the presence of all as witnesses. (7)
The seventh [chapter] concerns the movement of the mandalas and the offering of the hand; and Agni, Varuṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and the deities together with their beloveds.
O Aṅga, accompanied by the gods and Brāhmaṇas from the four directions, you shall perform this divine rite before them in the assembly of people.
Having attained the state of a living being through negligence, how could you commit transgression? Even teachers do not proceed upon the right path, like the common throng of people.
It is heard in the Śruti that in all the worlds, those who are awakened should exercise restraint; even a father must be corrected by his son, and even a teacher himself by his disciple. (11)
A Brāhmaṇa may be disciplined by Kṣatriyas, and likewise a husband by his wife—even one who has gone astray, even if he be the most eminent or a master of the Vedāntas.
Even a person of low status may be instructed; so says the eternal Śruti. The path of the righteous alone is honored everywhere, never the wrong path.
He by whom the Dharma born of his own family has been abandoned becomes fallen; and having died, he reaches hell and is joined with a burden of suffering. || 14 ||
He who abandons the Dharma out of atheism and has come to cause division among his kinsmen should be restrained by all people devoted to the laws of Manu. || 15 ||
O Maheśvara, those people who abandon the duties of their family, the duties toward their kin, and the duties of their country, inevitably fall from their lineage.
One must never abandon the sacred fire, abandon one's vows, abandon the traditional injunctions, or abandon dharma; for by doing so, one indeed becomes an outcaste.
Neither your father, nor your mother, nor your brother, nor even your own kinsmen see any news of you; you have become untouchable, like one who has consumed poison.
Wearing a garland of bones, funeral ashes, and matted hair, clad in rags, fickle, and having abandoned all bounds of decorum—you ought not to stand before me. (19)
"O Lord, you are not one who respects the Brahmins, you are without vows, a mendicant of wicked soul and always deceitful; you do not deserve to converse in my presence. (20)
Thus that queen, weeping with eyes clouded by tears, remained filled with great sorrow even as the Lord of Gods was entreating her.
Once again, the passionate woman, becoming enraged, said to Hara: "I perceive no straightforwardness in your heart; I know it to be eternally hard."
"What was said by the Asura Brahmins appears false to me, since you have directed such a most wicked disposition toward me. (23)
"Since the Brahmins have been deceived, you shall be slain by the Brahmins. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lady said nothing more.
Then Maheśvara, the Lord, with a serene countenance, slowly addressed her with words full of policy and endowed with reason through various forms of courtesy.
Perceiving that her eyes were bright with clarity, Hara then spoke somewhat; his face, which possessed a luster equal to the full moon, became clouded with anger.
"Why do you act thus, O blessed lady? Your words are not at all appropriate; for one should practice compassion toward all beings out of a desire for their welfare. (27)
"O lady of excellent complexion, although you desire that no harm be done to others for the sake of any object, yet this entire world is as dear to you as a son. (28)
O sinless one, you alone are worthy of worship by the world, assuming all forms; if any blameworthy deed has been committed by me, it was indeed for the sake of the gods. (29)
Nevertheless, your son shall be born in this manner, of this there is no doubt; or rather, she is dearer to me than all my own life-breaths.
"I shall act accordingly to fulfill your desires as you wish; becoming cheerful of countenance, O fair-faced one, speak your requests. (31)
Having been addressed thus, the Blessed Lady spoke again to Maheśvara: "If, when the Cāturmāsya has arrived, one is an observer of the great vow (mahāvrata)..."
O Maheśvara, if you perform the Tāṇḍava dance in the presence of the gods after having properly completed your vow of celibacy (brahmacarya), [then I shall grant you the boon].
"If you offer your body for my pleasure and for the sake of Viṣṇu, O lady with a beautiful face, I shall grant you grace instead of a curse. (34)
"Otherwise, my mind does not attain confidence in you. Hearing that, the Blessed One was pleased and replied to her, "So be it. (35)
The Blessed Lady also was delighted, having been chosen for the favor of the curse.

The person who hears this Purāṇa endowed with faith and firmness of mind regarding the realization of non-duality—his life will certainly attain all perfections; O mortals, through truth they attain that state of being heard. (37)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Conciliation of Pārvatī by Śaṅkara," within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth section (*Nāgara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Śūdra said: This speech of yours appears to me as something wonderful, O observer of noble vows, even though it involves great hardship for you as you speak.
Nevertheless, by my good fortune and through my merits, you have come to my home; yet I am not satiated with the nectar of your speech falling from your lotus-like mouth again and again.
This is the narrative of the story of Pibangaurī, filled with extraordinary qualities: how Maheśvara performed his dance surrounded by the gods.
How did it originate during the Cāturmāsya? What vow is said to be observed? How did she bestow her grace, and what indeed was that grace?
O best of the twice-born, explain this in detail to me as I ask; for the Blessed One is honored in the world and acts as a benefactor to me.
"O you of noble vows, being composed and with a serene countenance, speak. Having heard that, Gālava also spoke again, greatly delighted.
Gālava said: O sinless one, I shall relate to you this meritorious history which bestows the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices; listen with a focused mind. (7)
Then, when the Cāturmāsya period had arrived, Hara, filled with devotion and intent upon the vow of celibacy, became joyful of countenance.
He indeed carried out the resolve of the deities and the great sages; then the gods, having assembled, took their place upon Mount Mandara.
Having bowed to Maheśāna, they stood before him with palms joined in reverence; seeing all the gods assembled, Hara spoke to them.
He spoke what was addressed by Pārvatī: "On account of what other task have I been appointed, wherein you are to be my assistants in the performance? || 11 ||
When the Cāturmāsya had arrived, Indra and the other gods became joyful; having offered salutations to the wielder of the trident (Śūlin), they spoke thus.
They returned to their respective abodes in celestial chariots resembling the sun; likewise, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, Maheśvara [arrived].
And she began to dance in order to please Bhavānī. Thereupon, the great sages went to Mandara, the best of mountains. || 14 ||
Nārada, Devala, Vyāsa, Śuka, Dvaipāyana, and others; Aṅgiras, Marīci, and Kardama the Prajāpati. || 15 ||
Kaśyapa, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Bhṛgu; likewise Jamadagni, Uttaṅka, and Rāma the descendant of Bhṛgu. || 16 ||
Agastya, Pulomā, Pulastya, and likewise Pulaha; Pracetas, Kratu, and other great sages as well. || 17 ||
The Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Piśācas, along with the Cāraṇas; the Ādityas, Guhyakas, Sādhyas, Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
All these, including Indra and the others headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, arrived, longing to witness the dance of Maheśa. || 19 ||
Then the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin, likewise presented jewels, ornaments, and garments to the sages and others in due order.
Then, while thousands of musical instruments were being played on all sides and everyone cried out "Victory!", the Blessed One prescribed the vow.
Bhavānī, her heart filled with joy, gazed upon Mahādeva; as did Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Maṅgalāruṇā.
In the midst of her four friends, the fair-faced lady shone resplendently; by virtue of her presence, the world appeared as preeminent in excellence. (23)
The splendor born of her body cannot be described even by the Lord himself, though he is gazed upon by millions of attendants with their various faces.
Surrounded by hosts of Piśācas and Bhūtas, the exceedingly beautiful Nandin, holding a golden staff, shone at the front with the face of a monkey.
The Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Citrasena and others, as well as the Nāgas and the lords of sages, appeared there as if they were depicted in a painting. (26)
Śrīrāga and other Rāgas of great power were his sons; these sons, born from the god Hara, were indeed formless.
Each one had six wives, and for all of them, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was the father; together with those wives, those Rāgas likewise assumed playful bodies.
They appeared suddenly, having been thought of by that Śambhu; I shall tell you their names, so listen, O Mahādhana.
Śrīrāga, the first son of Īśvara, who deludes [the world] and bestows the Supreme Brahman, was placed between their eyebrows. || 30 ||
And from his center, the supreme Gaṇa born of Maheśa emerged; then, the highly illustrious second one, Vasanta, arose from the region of his hips.
And from the wheel, through its purification, there arose Mahādaṃka, the ornament of the universe; he was the third son, yet the fifth [in lineage] among all beings.

He who is called Rāma rejoices within all beings, both stationary and moving, in the form of the inner self (antarātman). 46.

This two-syllabled king of mantras accomplishes all tasks on earth; even the gods sing of Rāma’s name, which is a mine of virtues. (49)
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, you too should always utter the name of Rāma; indeed, he who chants the name of Rāma is liberated from all sins.

Then, with palms joined in reverence and an unperturbed, joyful inner self, he quickly ascended that celestial chariot, crossing over the oceans and rivers.
Beyond Jambūdvīpa, which extends for a hundred thousand yojanas, there is likewise an ocean of salt water twice that size.
Having led them by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun to the Northern Kurus, he reached the island known as Kuśanābha, which is twice the size of the ocean.
That continent is pervaded by divine realms and filled with divine mountains; it is twice the size of Ikṣūda, and the next continent is again twice the size of that one.
Beyond that is the region named Krauñca, which is twice the size of that ocean; beyond even that is the Suroda ocean, twice as large, frequented by yakṣas.
Beyond that is the continent known as Śākadvīpa, twice the size of the former; beyond that is the well-formed ocean in the form of clarified butter (ājya), twice the size of that continent.
It is completely filled with supreme delicacies, where the Siddhas dwell on all sides; and the island twice the size of that is known by the name of the Śālmalī tree.
Twice that size is the ocean there, consisting of the waters of curd-cream (dadhimaṇḍoda); the Sādhyas dwell there constantly, established in great austerity.

Beyond that is the island known by the name Plakṣa, which is twice as large; there the Ocean of Milk is twice its size, where great sages dwell at every turn. These six most divine regions are declared to be the terrestrial heaven. There the ground consists of gold as well as silver.
Having seen it, [he marveled at] the sweet flavors of honey and fruit that grant all desires, where kalpa-trees stand within the houses of both men and women. (48)
They delight in garments and collections of ornaments; these, O best of sages, are the characteristic signs of the continents. 49.
Maheśvara, traveling through the sky by means of his celestial chariot, passed beyond the edge of Plakṣadvīpa, where the Ocean of Milk is twice as wide.
In the midst of that is the very great island, certainly named Śveta; there is the mountain Ramyaka, which has a hundred peaks and immeasurable trees.
Then, upon its peak, a great and divine celestial chariot was established; it was served by trees bearing nectar-like fruits and possessed sands of gold.
In a secluded place, delightful in every way, provided with precious gems, well-enclosed by stone slabs, and free from the presence of others; || 53 ||
The God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, recounted it to Umā; and Kārttikeya also heard that great secret, more secret than the secret.
The yoga of meditation in the form of mantra, known as the twelve-syllabled [mantra]. || 1 ||
It is joined with the syllable Om, complete with its beginning, together with its secret doctrine, and superior even to the Vedas.

Īśvara said: This mantra, joined with three syllables, is itself a single imperishable syllable (*akṣara*). Accompanied by the month of Māgha, it is free from decay, free from deceit, and the purifier of the universe. It is accessible to Viṣṇu, centered in Viṣṇu, and endowed with three mantras; it is served by the entire multitude of cosmic eggs through its fourth digit (*kalā*).
He is to be served by sages free from desire, served by those possessing great knowledge and the like; he pervades from the navel to the head, bestowing unbroken bliss. || 988 ||
The syllable "Oṃ" is your pleasant speech, which destroys great suffering; having first meditated upon that Praṇava, which is the embodiment of knowledge and the refuge of happiness. (59)
Having realized that Brahman is omnipresent, he became intent upon the purification of the body.
Having assumed the lotus posture and performed worship, he whose eye is knowledge— || 60 ||
Having closed his eyes and joined his hands together, the hero should meditate upon the auspicious Śiva within his mind in the form of dhyāna.
Resembling ten million flashes of lightning, with a luster equal to ten million suns, and surpassing a hundred thousand moons in brilliance, that Person illuminated everything.

Having meditated upon that Virāṭ form—which possesses both manifest and unmanifest aspects, which consists of existence and non-existence, and which is the immutable—one shall not become a suckling at the breast again. Even by meditating on it just once during the Cāturmāsya period, there is the total destruction of all sins.
And thus, this form of Murāri is mine; its potency is unfailing and its excellence is boundless.
He who gazes for even a moment upon the Lord, who is capable of destroying the sins arising from hundreds of births; || 64 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Dhyānayoga," in the Cāturmāsya-māhātmya, within the Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the sixth section (Nāgara-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 261.
Pārvatī said: "Having attained the yoga of meditation, may I obtain the yoga of knowledge. O Lord of Gods, act in such a way that I may become immortal. (1)
Īśvara said: || 1 ||
O lady of delicate limbs, this king of mantras known as the twelve-syllabled one has been explained; it is the eternal essence of the Vedas and should be recited. || 2 ||
The Praṇava is the beginning of all the Vedas and the priest for the entire Brahmāṇḍa; it is the foremost in all undertakings and the bestower of all perfections.
The color is white; Madhucchandas is the seer (ṛṣi) and Brahmā is the deity; the Supreme Self is the Gāyatrī, and its application is in all rites. || 4 ||
This seed, consisting of Brahman, contains the entire universe within it. || 1 ||
He is known as the reality of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, the imperishable form of both being and non-being.
The letter Na is yellow in color, the eternal seed-syllable of water; it is the seed of the earth, its meter is *mana*, and it destroys poison through its ritual application.
The syllable *mo* is the seed-mantra of the Earth, joined with Viśvāmitra; it is red in color, possesses great splendor, and is employed as the giver of wealth.
The letter Bha is five-colored, the eternal seed-syllable of water; when joined with Marīci, it is worshipped as the bestower of all enjoyments.
The syllable *ga* has the luster of molten gold and is accompanied by Bharadvāja; it is the seed-syllable of Vāyu, bestowing the primary enjoyment upon those who practice its application.
The letter *va* is white as a jasmine flower, the seed-syllable of the sky, and possessed of great power; when employed with the sage at its head, it bestows liberation. (10)

The letter *ta* is a transformation of lightning; it is known as the great seed-syllable of Soma. It has Aṅgiras as its root and is increased by the vowel *u*; it is devoid of ritual action and is not subject to desire. (11)
The syllable VĀ is smoke-colored, the seed-mantra of the Sun, possessing the speed of thought; it is joined with the sage Pulastya and, when employed, bestows all happiness. (112)

The syllable SUKĀRA is eternal and imperishable, radiant as the hibiscus flower; it is the seed-syllable of the mind, difficult to withstand, residing in Pulaha, and the bestower of desired objects. 13.
The seed-syllable *dekāra* is in the form of a swan and is variegated in color. || 1 ||
The seed of accomplishment, the Great Being, is enjoined to the sacrifice within the ritual.
The letter *vā* is eternally pure; the sacrificer, however, bears the seed. Pracetas is the resort of Śrī, and he bestows liberation upon liberation. || 15 ||

The great seed-syllable of the letter *ya* is tawny-colored; it is the sky-farer (*khecarī*) and the earth-farer (*bhūcarī*), the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*). One should always contemplate it as being on the earth. (16)

In the application of the Bhṛgu-yoga for the exhaustion [of sins], it performs all rites; Gāyatrī is the meter, and this shall be the sequence for the placement upon the body (dehanyāsa) of these [mantras]. || 17 ||
Always assigning the syllable Oṃ, one should assign the syllable A to both feet, the syllable Mo to the secret region, and the syllable Bha to the lotus of the navel.
Having placed the syllable *ga* in the heart, the syllable *va* is situated in the middle of the throat; the syllable *te* is on the right hand, and the syllable *vā* is on the left hand. (19)
One should place the syllable *su* on the mouth and tongue, the syllable *de* on both ears, the syllable *vā* on the pair of eyes, and the syllable *ya* on the head. (20)
The Liṅga-mudrā, the Yoni-mudrā, and likewise the Dhenu-mudrā—this triad indeed constitutes the manifest form of the mantra as its seed-syllable (bīja).
O Goddess, he who joins this together daily is not smeared by sins; this is the twelve-syllable mantra situated upon the tortoise, consisting of the twelve liṅgas. (22)
Indeed, twelve Śālagrāma stones were worshipped; together with them and these manifest forms, they remained in the assembly.

According to their respective colors, by means of meditations accompanied by the seed-syllables (bīja) of the Munis, together with ritual applications (viniyoga) and adorned with Vedic meters (chandas). || 24 ||
O best of sages, for devotees who have honored [the Lord] through meditations and recitations, liberation from the bonds born of karma occurs; of this there is no doubt. (258)
For this yoga, known as the practice of meditation, is indeed difficult to attain; listen with a one-pointed mind as I speak further of the yoga of meditation. (26)
The destruction of sins occurs through the yoga of meditation and not otherwise; this yoga consists of recitation and meditation, and it is undoubtedly the yoga of action (karmayoga). || 27 ||
Arising from the Brahman of Sound through the twelve-syllable Veda, one attains everything through meditation; through meditation, one attains purity. (28)
Through meditation, one attains the supreme Brahman; indeed, yoga is born of meditation. Meditation-yoga with support is that which consists in the vision of Nārāyaṇa.
The second is proclaimed as having all things as its object through the yoga of knowledge; it is formless, immeasurable, the light that is always the body of all.
Resplendent like ten million flashes of lightning, eternally risen and unbroken, it is both partless and yet possessed of all parts, a stainless expanse like the sky.
Its essential nature consists of enjoyment, it is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), incomparable, causing the senses to whirl, embodied, situated in primordial nature (prakṛti), and eternal.
It is both visible and invisible, unborn, the cosmic form (vairāja), eternally radiant, manifold, the source of all, righteous, free from conceptual construction, and without a superior lord.
It is without lineage or obstruction, the cause of hundreds of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), effortless, free from the sense of "mine," devoid of the form of intellect, and stainless.

That form of the Lord is bodiless, free from dualities, and a mere witness; it resembles pure crystal, is devoid of both meditator and object of meditation, is incomparable, and unfathomable—embrace it with your own splendor. (35)
Pārvatī said: "O Lord, tell me how that perfect knowledge, which has the nature of Yoga, is attained; and tell me of Nārāyaṇa, who is formless, and of his abode."
Īśvara said: "The head is the foremost among the limbs; by means of the head, the Great One is supported. (37)
When the Lord is honored with the head, the entire world is honored; yoga is sustained by the head, and strength is borne by the head. (38)
The vital energy is borne upon the head, and life itself resides in the head; for the sun is indeed the head of both the formless and likewise the formed.
The chest is the world of earth (Pṛthivīloka), and the feet are indeed Rasātala; thus, in the form of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), it consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Viṣṇu himself, in the form of Brahmā and as the very foundation of the yoga of knowledge, creates all beings and protects them in every way. (41)
For he, who embodies all the gods, destroys everything; for Viṣṇu’s sovereignty over all months is eternal.
Therefore, by remembering Hari in all months, on all days, and at all times of the day, one is liberated. (43)
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, one is liberated through meditation alone; the service of the Formless is far superior to meditating on the Gaṅgā-tīrtha.

And there is no doubt that the Cāturmāsya is superior to all other gifts; whatever sin has been committed during any month, as well as any auspicious or inauspicious deed during the Cāturmāsya, [is affected by it]. 45.
O Goddess, that shall become inexhaustible; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Therefore, with every effort, the yoga of knowledge is most excellent. (46)
Served in the form of Viṣṇu, he is the bestower of Brahman and liberation; O auspicious one, listen with focused attention to the state of the manifest and the unmanifest.
This should not be told to just anyone, even to one's own son, nor to another who is undisciplined, wicked, fickle-minded, or hypocritical.

The discourse born of Yoga should not be spoken to one who has fallen away from his own words, nor to one who is censurable; however, it may be spoken to one who is constantly devoted, self-controlled, and likewise endowed with virtues such as tranquility.

It should be given even to a Śūdra who is a devotee of Viṣṇu, as well as to a twice-born man; however, it is not taught that the station of Brahman belongs to one who is not a devotee or who is impure.
O you whose wealth is austerity, quickly attain perfection in yoga through devotion to me; know that supreme Nārāyaṇa to be the unmanifest, who is accessible only through knowledge. 51.
Abiding in the form of sound within the heads of all embodied beings, He alone exists as the individual soul (jīva) in the head like the orb of the sun.
Ever-arisen and subtle in form, he is manifested through a physical form; O Goddess, by constant practice, that which is of the nature of the Supreme Self is attained. (53)
Indeed, all the gods dwell within the body of the yogin; likewise, other rivers dwell in the right ear.
Lord Śambhu resides in the heart, and the eternal Brahmā resides in the navel; the earth is at the tips of the soles of the feet, and likewise, water is omnipresent.
Fire, wind, and likewise space are found within the middle of the forehead; and there are five sacred sites (tīrthas) on the right hand—of this there is no doubt. (56)
The sun is declared to be the right eye, and the moon the left; Mars and Mercury are declared to be the two nostrils. (57)
The Guru is in the right ear, and likewise Bhṛgu is in the left ear; Śanaiścara is said to be in the mouth, and Rāhu is proclaimed to be in the anus.
It is said that all the planets reside within the four sense organs; having entered the bodies of yogis, they pervade the fourteen worlds.
O Goddess, [these obstacles] always prevail; therefore, one should constantly practice yoga. Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, the yogi cuts away his sin.
That yogi who, for even a moment, holds his mind upon the crown of his head while closing his ears, is liberated from sins; of this there is no doubt.
I see no difference at all between Viṣṇu, who is devoted to yoga, and even a single yogi who eats but a mouthful of food in one's house.
He shall certainly deliver three lineages along with himself; if he be a Brahmin who is a yogin, he does so even by his mere sight.
O Goddess, he who destroys the heap of sins of all living beings, who performs his duties, is devoted to Brahman, and possesses a share of yoga, is a true Śūdra.
Or even one who is devoted to a true guru shall obtain that formless fruit; he who is a yogi with restricted diet and possesses meditative absorption (samādhi) upon the Supreme Brahman.
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, one becomes absorbed in Hari; just as iron becomes gold through contact with the hand of a perfected being (siddha).
Likewise, by the grace of Hari, a person who has attained a physical form may reach dissolution [in the Absolute], just as water on a path that has fallen into the Gaṅgā is sought even by the gods.
Just as fire always blazes even with mere cow dung, so too does the yogi, when served, bestow all fruits and grant liberation.
For that is always proclaimed by the performers of sacrifice to be the mouth of the deities; in this way, through constant practice, the yogi becomes a vessel for liberation.
O Goddess, this yoga is always practiced by the masters Sanaka and others, who are seekers of liberation and possessors of supreme knowledge; it bestows the perfection of wisdom.
First, the perfection of knowledge always arises for yogins; O Pārvatī, as soon as they have grasped it, they become true yogis.
Then the supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), appear before him; even then, the best of yogis should not set his mind upon them.
Through yoga, the merit arising from all acts of giving and sacrifice comes to be; through yoga, the attainment of all desires occurs, for nothing on earth is unattainable through yoga. (73)
Through yoga, the knot of the heart is not [bound]; through yoga, the enemy of "mine-ness" is not [present]. No one is able to steal the mind of one perfected in yoga. (74)
That very same pure yogi perceives the mind situated in the head, its agitation permanently stilled within the cavity of the tenth door.
For a mortal who covers his ears and investigates the form of sound, that very [sound] is the pinnacle of the Praṇava; that indeed is the eternal Brahman.
That very thing is called the formless (anaṃtarūpa), that itself is the supreme nectar; this resonance in the breath of the nose is the great state of the digestive fire.
This state, which is the abode of the five elements and whose nature is knowledge—by attaining this state, there shall be liberation from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. (78)
For its attainment is difficult to find in this world, as it bestows the perfection of yoga. || 79 ||

Thus the entire universe, both moving and stationary, shines as consisting of Brahman; this state called consciousness is the Lord Viṣṇu himself, the all-pervading. Having known Him—who dwells upon the head, who is most excellent, and supreme among the lords of yoga—the living being casts off the form of illusion born of the world, like a snake its slough.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Jñānayoga," within the "Glorification of the Greatness of Cāturmāsya" in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, under the "Legend of Śeṣaśāyin," in the "Glorification of the Hāṭakeśvara Region" of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 262 ||
Īśvara said: If, having abandoned tāmasa action, one is born amidst actions, then that yogi, consisting of knowledge, becomes the bestower of liberation upon living beings. || 1 ||
When there is a sense of "mine-lessness" regarding the body, when the mind is perfectly pure, and when there is the yoga of devotion toward Hari, then one is no longer bound by karma.
For when the minds of men become peaceful even while performing actions, then the perfection consisting of yoga arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having repeatedly experienced the state of being a guru, the one of great intelligence attains the nature of Viṣṇu while still living and is thereby liberated from the bondage of karma.
Rituals that arise constantly—both the obligatory and the occasional—should not be performed at will, for they only serve to increase suffering and distress.
And know Viṣṇu, O Maheśvarī, to be the lord of all actions; by renouncing everything in him, one is liberated from the entire cycle of worldly existence.
This alone is the supreme knowledge; this alone is the supreme austerity; this alone is the supreme good—that the offering of one's actions is made unto Kṛṣṇa.
For this yoga is indeed stainless; it is declared to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). It is the manifestation of auspiciousness produced by the action of Viṣṇu.
The ancestors, intent on receiving the funeral cakes, continue to wander in saṃsāra as long as no one endowed with devotion is born in their lineage.
O twice-born ones, they roar only so long, and sin roars only so long, as well as those many holy places, until one finds devotion.
He alone is truly possessed of knowledge in this world, for he is the foremost among yogis; he is the performer of great sacrifices, for he is endowed with devotion to Hari.
When the twinkling of the eyes and the blinking of the eyelids cease, yoga is fully attained; for the yogi who has conquered speech, this is proclaimed as the Gomedha sacrifice.
By the constant conquest of the mind, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice; by the constant conquest of conceptual construction, one obtains the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
The constant casting off of the body is proclaimed as the "human sacrifice" (nara-yajña); having slain the animals of the five senses, [one offers them] without fire, with the head and the earrings.
By means of the method of the teacher’s instruction, he attains the state of being Brahman; that yogi, with his food restricted, maintains the three staffs.

He should be known as a true bearer of the triple staff (tridaṇḍin) once the stainless God has been realized—[he] that yogi for whom there is the staff of mind, the staff of action, and the staff of speech. (16)
That yogi is perfected even while living in the form of Brahman; the ignorant one, however, is constantly oppressed by actions that are of the nature of bondage.
For indeed, even while performing actions, the man of knowledge attains liberation, when the state of Brahman is pointed out to him by his teachers. (18)
Then he attains liberation while the body remains alone, until the Supreme Person proceeds toward the attainment of the fruit of Brahman.
To that extent, the existence consisting of karma remains within the tree of Brahman; the sages should always understand its intermediate joints.
The path to liberation is indeed revealed by the twice-born through the synthesis of the Śruti and Smṛti; this liberation is like a city, provided with four gates.
The four gatekeepers there are always Tranquility (śama) and the others; they alone, who bestow liberation, should first be served by human beings. (22)
Tranquility, right inquiry, contentment, and the company of the virtuous—for him by whom these are held in hand, perfection is not far off. (23)
O Goddess, the perfection of yoga is attained by men through devotion to Viṣṇu and the practice of the true dharma; indeed, they know this alone to be sufficient knowledge.
A mortal wandering everywhere among the fields of knowledge for the sake of wisdom obtains pure knowledge instantly from a true guru, like the flame of a lamp. (25)
Whoever contemplates absorption even for a mere moment, his thousands of sins certainly go to destruction at that very instant.
Having abandoned passion and hatred, being free from anger and greed, and seeing with equanimity everywhere—such is the vision of one devoted to Viṣṇu.
The yogi in whose heart compassion for all living beings is firmly established, and who is endowed with purity and right conduct, does not experience suffering. (281)
Free from the layers of illusion, detached from false objects, and devoid of harmful associations—these are the characteristics of one who has attained perfection in yoga. (29)
The conjunction with the fire of possessiveness brings suffering to men; for yogis, the pacification of that which has arisen is the practice of peace.
Then, having extracted the senses, one should restrain them by means of the mind alone; just as iron, when rubbed with iron, attains sharpness. || 31 ||

For the intellect within the body is of two kinds: that which bestows purity is to be received, while that which concerns the objects of worldly existence is to be abandoned; that which pertains to the Supreme Brahman is auspicious.
O Goddess, just as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) bestows both sin and merit, so too [the ritual] performed with focused intent when the auspicious fruit of reality is known, and not otherwise.
The dark [form] and the generative organ, as well as the auspicious one beyond form—these two, located in the heart and in the head, lead to both bondage and liberation. (34)
This imperishable, unmanifest, and immortal whole of yours is proclaimed as the form of forms, the form of Viṣṇu, the embodiment of all forms. (36)
Knowing this, the yogi shall be liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra; a householder attains this through the instruction of the guru, and never otherwise.
When the Guru is pleased in soul, the entire universe becomes gracious to him; and by whomsoever the Guru is satisfied, the ancestors and the deities are likewise gratified.
The instruction of the guru, the sacred image, right reflection, an even mind, and action accompanied by knowledge—these indeed are the characteristics for the attainment of liberation. || 38 ||
Viṣṇu alone is indeed the Lord of Action, for he himself is actionless; and he, whose seed-mantra consists of twelve syllables, is the one who possesses the form of Prāṇa.
The twelve-syllabled wheel destroys all sins, subdues the wicked, and bestows the supreme Brahman. || 40 ||
This very Supreme Brahman, bearing the form of twelve syllables, has been revealed by me to you, O Goddess, as it was indeed [revealed] to Skanda in its pure form. 41.

One should contemplate with faith this essence of the yogis, which is the form of meditation and is to be grasped through devotion; for it is the Enemy of Kaiṭabha who, having burnt away the sins accumulated during four months or ten million births, bestows liberation.
Brahmā said: There, in that city, from the midst of the Ocean of Milk, he emerged at the front of his celestial chariot, oppressed by a burden of splendor.
Making a gesture with his chest and arms, the great fish, who had never been seen before and was free from egoism, approached her presence.
Seeing that fish within the womb of the syllable *huṃ*, Maheśvara paralyzed it with his splendor and spoke these words.
"Who are you, staying within the belly of a fish—whether a god, a yakṣa, or a human? O Lord, tell me how you live while remaining inside my body. (46)
The fish said: "I was cast into the belly of a fish in the ocean born of milk by my mother at her father’s command, [thinking], 'This one does not belong to my lineage.'"
Out of fear for the destruction of his lineage, he brought about the ruin of his own family; the boy born under the Gaṇḍānta yoga was incapable of performing household duties.
"Thus dismissed by my grieving mother, listen, O descendant of the lineage: I was seized even by a fish, and there my time was great. (49)
Through these nectar-like words of yours, the great yoga of knowledge has arisen; by that, you have been fully known by me, both in your embodied form and as that which dwells within the body.
"O Lord of Gods, grant me permission to depart, O Brahman, so that I may be seen by my father and also by Bhavānī. (51)
Hara said: "You are a Brahmin, you possess a beautiful form, and you are worthy of worship as you speak; come out quickly, for you, great fish, have been paralyzed!"
Then, born from his head due to agitation, he was joined with a fish; thereafter, with a deformed face, he emerged outside in an instant.
He was handsome, endowed with a beautiful form, possessed of a fish-like fragrance, equal in luster to the moon, and imbued with a divine scent.
Umā also took that son, who was bowing down, onto her own lap; and Hara, filled with supreme joy, gave him a name as well. (895)
"Since this foremost of yogins was born from the belly of a fish, he shall therefore become renowned in the world as Matsyanātha. (56)

One who has reached the further shore of the yoga of knowledge shall have an indestructible human body; he is free from envy, free from the pairs of opposites, free from desire, and a servant of Brahman.
"And you shall become liberated while living throughout the fourteen worlds. Having been addressed thus, and bowing repeatedly to Maheśāna, he went to Mount Mandara accompanied by Maheśvara.
Brahmā said: Having circumambulated the Goddess and embraced Skanda, he departed.
Then Pārvatī, having attained that unsurpassed knowledge, was delighted; thus she experienced the supreme perfection born from the power of the Praṇava.
Having reached that [state], the Mother of the Worlds, with the water born of the twelve syllables, [purifies] him who hears this account of the origin of Matsyendranātha. (61)
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 62 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of Matsyendranātha," within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, in the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* of the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the sixth *Nāgara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 263 ||
Brahmā said: Kārttikeya, who is dearer to Pārvatī than her own life, was playing nearby, intent on various playful gestures.
Possessing a crimson luster and great majesty, with six faces and marvelous prowess, he sings excessively in some places and dances according to his own will in others.
In some places, upon seeing his mother and father, he was bowed low with humility; and in other places, on the banks of the Gaṅgā, he took on the appearance of one plastering sand.
Searching together with his attendants for various forest trees, he thus sported, and five days passed for him.
Then all the gods, headed by Mahendra, who had fled in terror of Tāraka, praised Śaṅkara with the desire to seize Tāraka.
The gods, together with their hosts, appointed Kumāra as the commander-in-chief on the banks of the Jāhnavī; celestial instruments resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Vahni gave his own power (śakti), and Himavat gave him a vehicle; he was surrounded by tens of millions of hosts born from all the gods.
Having paid homage to the assemblies of sages, he set out for the conflict with his enemies; and in the city of Tāmravatī, the powerful one blew his conch shell.
Then, terrified by the sound of his conch, tens of millions of Daityas and Dānavas from Tāraka’s army fled from that city.
Mounted upon their own vehicles, self-restrained yet proud of their strength, all the gods, empowered by the splendor of Skanda, engaged in battle.
Then he utterly destroyed the Dānava armies; severed by Viṣṇu’s discus, they fell by the thousands upon the earth. || 11 ||
Then, O Sage, hundreds of Dānavas were shattered and slain; at that time, rivers consisting of blood arose in many varieties.
Seeing that army of Dānavas broken, the Lord of the Gods fought in battle; he immediately shattered it in many ways with multitudes of arrows.
Urged by Kṛṣṇa, they fought with their spears and hurled them at Gaṅginī; in an instant, they reduced him, along with his chariot and his charioteer, to ashes.
Then, seeing Tāraka slain, the remaining [demons] went to Pātāla; thereafter, all the hosts of gods praised his prowess.
The celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell; all of them, having achieved victory, were led by Maheśvara.
They consecrated the six-faced one as the commander-in-chief of all the gods; then Pārvatī, her voice faltering with joy, embraced Skanda.
Then, surrounded by her own female companions, she performed auspicious rites; and thus, on the seventh day, the boy shall slay Tāraka.
Having reached Mount Mandara and gladdening his parents, Skanda, overflowing with supreme bliss, spoke everything [to them]. (19)
At the proper time, Śaṅkara reflected upon his marriage; with a gracious soul, he spoke to the son of Gaṅgā, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
O Lord, the time approved for your taking a wife has arrived; perform the rites of marriage, for this is the duty of a man esteemed by all.

"Sport with various enjoyments and celestial chariots that fulfill all desires. Hearing that, the Blessed Lord Skanda spoke these words to his father: "Indeed, I alone am to be seen everywhere among all the hosts; in both visible and invisible objects, what is there for me to grasp, and what is there to abandon? (23)
O Lord of Gods, all women in the entire universe are indeed equal to Pārvatī to me; likewise, I behold all men as being like you.
"You are my guru; protect me from sinking again into hell, for by your grace this knowledge has been known by me in its entirety. (25)
One should cause them to sink once again into the most terrible ocean of saṃsāra; just as one who holds a lamp, having seen the object, would discard the instrument [of illumination].
Likewise, having attained that knowledge, the yogi abandons the cycle of worldly existence, O omniscient Supreme Lord, once he has realized Brahman as all-pervading.
They know him to be a yogi from whom all activities have turned away; for those whose minds are greedy for sense objects, attachment arises even in the forest. (28)
For those who possess equal vision toward all things, liberation is indeed eternal in the home; yet, O Great Lord, knowledge alone is very difficult for human beings to attain. (29)
A wise person should never, under any circumstances, let the knowledge he has attained fall away: "I do not exist; neither do I have a mother, nor a father, nor any kinsman. (30)
Having attained knowledge and reached a state of separation from the worlds, I have obtained this portion as my destiny through fate and by your power; you ought not [to take it]. || 31 ||
There is no doubt that such words were spoken by her who desires liberation; for the Goddess, intent on persistence, spoke thus again and again.
Then, having bowed to his parents, he went to Mount Krauñca; there, in that most meritorious hermitage, he performed supreme austerity.
Having first brought all his senses under control through meditation, he recited the supreme Brahman, the twelve-syllable seed-mantra.

Then, having relinquished the sense of "mine-ness," he attained the yoga of knowledge; when the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* arrived for him without obstacle, [he remained unattached]. (35)
Then their host, becoming enraged, spoke these words: "If you have approached me with such wicked intent... (36)
"Then you shall not overcome those who are as peaceful as we are. Knowing this, Maheśa also [bestowed] that from which the great dawning of knowledge arises.
Even more than I, Skanda, possessing a superior disposition through the yoga of knowledge, his heart filled with wonder, instructed Pārvatī.
And to Umā, who was overcome with grief for her son, Hara [spoke] with the nectar of auspicious words regarding the greatness of Cāturmāsya, which destroys all sins. (39)

Whether it be Maheśvara or the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha (Viṣṇu), when he is dwelt upon in the heart as consisting of meditation, non-dual, and the destroyer of the supreme suffering through the intellect of non-difference, then that very one becomes an exceedingly dear friend.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, this greatness arising from the Cāturmāsya has been recounted to you in detail. What else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Tāraka," within the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Four-Month Vow), in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, within the *Śeṣaśāyy-upākhyāna* (The Narrative of Him Who Lies upon Śeṣa), in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Holy Field of Hāṭakeśvara), in the sixth *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, in the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: "Many vows and observances have been described by you, the number of which is not known when the lotus-eyed Lord is fast asleep."
Indeed, due to the physical incapacity of the body, how can one observe the religious observances? Tell us, O you of delicate limbs, how one may fulfill the vow through gifts instead.
Sūta said: He who is delicate and unable to observe the prescribed restraints should perform there the celebrated Bhīṣmapañcaka.
O best of Brahmins, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one who is composed should rise early in the morning and perform the cleansing of the teeth.
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, one who is devoted to Vāsudeva should observe the restraints (niyamas) mentioned previously for all of them.
On that day, one should observe a fast with devotion; or, if there is physical incapacity, one should give gold according to one's means.
Food fit for oblation should be given to a Brāhmaṇa by men who are devotees of Viṣṇu; in this manner, this supreme vow should be observed for five days.
Hṛṣīkeśa, who assumes the form of the one reclining upon the waters, is to be worshipped with perfumes, incense, food offerings, and also by keeping vigils throughout the night.
Then, when the sixth day has arrived, one should worship the most excellent Brāhmaṇas with devotion, providing them with garments, gold, and sweet food.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should entreat the best of the Brahmins: "By your grace, all my religious observances have been successfully accomplished."
Then they too must say: "May every vow and every observance arising from the four-month period belong entirely to you. (11)

Then, having dismissed those Brahmins, O Indra among kings, he himself should partake of food consisting of all types of nourishment, preceded by the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Whoever performs this vow shall obtain a fruit that bestows great merit; moreover, for one who performs this very vow for five days, intent upon fasting, his fruit shall be a hundredfold.

On the eleventh day, one should perform the worship of Hari with jasmine flowers; on the twelfth day, with bilva leaves; thereafter, on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, with the *śatapatrī* flower, preceded by devotion. (14)

One should worship with the meritorious *bhṛṅgarāja* on the full moon day; on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), Janārdana is to be worshipped with all [these substances]: cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass. (15)
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should cause everyone to consume [these substances] for the purification of the body: agarwood, guggulu, camphor, tagara, and cinnamon bark.
On every single day of the lunar fortnight, one should offer incense throughout; [worship] the Lord who lies upon the waters, the source of the universe, reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa.
"May the Lord accept my *argha* for the sake of attaining success in the Bhīṣma-pañcaka; with this mantra, the *argha* should indeed be offered to the Lord with devotion. (18)
O twice-born ones, having taken water from a conch shell along with flowers, fruits, and sandalwood, one should offer as an oblation milk-rice (paramānna) according to one's capacity.
All this has been narrated to you regarding the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow, as well as the fruit obtained through the observances of these vows.

The sages said: "O highly fortunate one, regarding this vow of Aśūnyaśāyinī which was previously performed by Indra for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) while He was asleep, its fruit has indeed been proclaimed by you. (21)
At what time should it be performed, and by what rite? Therefore, O highly fortunate Sūta, describe the procedure in detail.

Sūta said: When the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa has passed and the second day of the lunar fortnight has arrived, the best of Brahmins should rise in the morning under the asterism presided over by Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā) and avoid conversing with sinners, the fallen, or barbarians.
Then, at the time of midday, having bathed and being pure with washed garments, one should approach the Lord who reclines upon the waters and worship Him with this mantra: || 24 ||
O bearer of the Śrīvatsa, beloved of Śrī, abode of Śrī, Lord of Śrī, imperishable one! May my householder life, which bestows dharma, artha, and kāma, never come to ruin.
May my ancestors not perish, nor may the sacred fires perish; may the deities not perish from me through the separation of husband and wife.
O Kṛṣṇa, just as you are never separated from Lakṣmī, so too, O Lord, may my union with my wife never perish. (27)
O Lord, just as Your bed is always unforsaken by Lakṣmī, so may my bed likewise remain unforsaken in birth after birth. (28)
Having thus made this request, one should then worship the Brahmin according to one's ability, O best of the twice-born, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth. (29)
In this manner, during the months of Bhādrapada, Āśvina, and likewise Kārtika, one should worship Acyuta, the Lord of the World, who reclines upon the waters.
One should consume food that is free from pungent spices, especially avoiding oil; and upon completion, one should then devoutly give [the merit] to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa.
One who gives a bed provided with rice grains and fruits, accompanied by clothing, and likewise gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), shall obtain fruit accordingly.
Thus, for one who properly observes this vow with a concentrated mind, the Teacher of the World, who reclines upon the waters, becomes pleased.
O best of the twice-born, just as Śakra was formerly satisfied, his bed shall never be empty in birth after birth.
Whether committed through ignorance or even with full knowledge, a person shall bring to destruction all sin incurred during the eight months by means of this vow, the Aśūnyaśayana.
If a woman who is childless, one who has given birth only to daughters, or a widow performs this vow with such concentration, the Lord of the World, being pleased with her, bestows purity of body.
In her, no thought arising from evil ever arises; nor does a mind afflicted by desire ever arise in any way whatsoever. (37)
O Brahmins, a maiden who correctly observes this vow obtains a husband of noble birth and endowed with beauty.
He who, being free from desire and composed in mind, performs this vow, shall obtain the fruit of the observances arising from the Cāturmāsya period.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Aśūnyaśayana Vow," within the Jalaśāyin Episode of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: We have heard of the principal holy places (tīrthas) arising within that sacred field, by bathing in which a person properly obtains the fruit of all tīrthas.
O highly fortunate one, please tell us about those principal lingas there, by the sight of which the highest good is attained by all.
Sūta said: And there is a most beautiful linga named Maṅkaṇa, as well as one named Siddheśvara, together with Gautameśvara.

And another, the fourth, is proclaimed as Kapāleśvara; each one undoubtedly bestows the fruit of all the liṅgas, O best of the twice-born, when properly worshipped according to the prescribed rite as described. || 4 ||
In this regard, O best of the twice-born, I shall first proclaim the fruit arising from Maṅkaṇeśvara, pertaining here to the Liṅga conjoined with the syllable 'Ma'.
O twice-born ones, that man who, having reached Śivarātri, remains pure and fasting while performing a vigil during the night; || 6 ||
"The fruit arising from the sight [of the deity], which originates from all the liṅgas, is produced; there is no doubt in this matter," Hara himself said.
The sages said: "O highly fortunate one, at what time does Śivarātri occur? Tell us everything in detail—the procedure for its observance as well as its greatness."
Sūta said: That fourteenth lunar day (tithi) which falls in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha—its night is declared to be the origin of Śivarātri.
In that [tirtha], Hara always manifests within all lingas; he does so especially in all meritorious sites, and this [manifestation] is renowned at Maṅkaṇeśvara.
The sages said: How did Śivarātri originate, and by whom was it established? Why has it become so highly meritorious? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient narrative concerning the dialogue between Bhartṛyajña and King Aśvasena.
Formerly, the lord of Ānarta was known as Aśvasena; he was eternally devoted to dharma and had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. || 13 ||
In former times, Bhartṛyajña was asked this out of curiosity by him, as he observed the Kali age increasing day by day.
Aśvasena said: O virtuous sage, tell me of some vow suited for this Kali age, which requires little effort, yields great merit, and destroys all sins. (15)
O Brahman, mortals were always short-lived even in the ancient Kṛta Yuga; how much more so in the Tretā and Dvāpara, and now that the Kali Yuga has arrived? (16)
Therefore, having abandoned the annual vow, tell me some [vow] that lasts for a single day.
One should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what is to be done in the afternoon; for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or not.
Having heard those words of his, the noble-minded Bhartṛyajña reflected for a long time and, having understood through his divine eye, spoke.
O King, there is a meritorious vow known as Śivarātri; it lasts for a single day, O Great King, and destroys all sins. (20)
In that regard, whatever gift is given, whatever oblation is offered, and likewise whatever mantra is recited—all these attain imperishability when the night vigil is performed. (21)
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth shall obtain wealth; one of short life-span attains long life, and there shall be the complete destruction of enemies. (22)
Whatever desire a mortal contemplates while performing this vow, he shall attain that very thing; one who is free from desire shall attain liberation.
If one should perform a night vigil with even meager wealth, one is liberated from the sins committed during that year; of this there is no doubt. (24)
Whatever signs there may be here, whether stationary or moving, the Lord Hara enters into them during that night.
Therefore, it is called Śivarātri, and by that [name] it is beloved of Hara. He was entreated by all the gods with the desire to bestow grace upon the worlds. (26)

O Blessed One, in this Kali age filled with all manner of sins, come to the earth for one day for the sake of purifying the sins of the year, so that mortals, purified by your worship, may attain sanctity. (27)
Therefore, what is given and offered as an oblation reaches them; however, whatever remains as leavings given by men—all that becomes entirely fruitless.
O Śaṅkara, in this Kali age, nothing at all reaches us, even if it is offered in abundance by impure human beings. (29)
The Blessed Lord said: O Lord of the Gods, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, I shall descend to the surface of the earth at night—not by day—in the Kali age.
And into all the lingas, both mobile and immobile, I shall undoubtedly enter for the sake of purifying the sins of the year. (31)
O best of gods, that man who performs worship to me on that night with these mantras shall become free from sin.

Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta; Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; Oṃ, salutation to Ghora; Oṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa; Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Having thus worshipped the faces with perfumes, flowers, unguents, garments, lamps, and food offerings, one should then present the arghya water. Having worshipped with this mantra and meditated upon me as abiding within the mind. (33)
O Beloved of Gaurī, Lord of Gods, Primordial One of All, Moon-crested One: for the sake of purifying the sins of the year, please accept this arghya from me. (34)
Then one should honor the brahmin with food, clothing, and other gifts; having given him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
And with discourses explaining the Dharma, as well as with lāsya and tāṇḍava dances.
O Lord of the Gods, whoever shall perform this vow here in this manner, it will serve as an expiation for the purification of the sins of a year. (37)
Having heard that, O best of men, all the thirty gods bowed down to the moon-crested Lord and, greatly delighted, returned to their own abodes.
And they dispatched Nārada, the best of sages, across the earth for the sake of always awakening the worlds to the occasion of Śivarātri.
He too, having gone to the surface of the earth, proclaimed everywhere the greatness of Śivarātri as it was spoken by the wielder of the trident.
From that time onwards, Śivarātri was established upon the earth; it is meritorious, bestowing all desires and destroying all sins.
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you an ancient narrative concerning what occurred here in the Naimiṣa forest involving a certain hunter.
There lived a certain hunter who was such by birth alone and not by his actions; his soul was overcome by vices, and he was a stealer of others' wealth. (43)
Never did he observe a vow, nor was any recitation performed by him; he merely seized the wealth of people by resorting to deceit. (44)
Then, after some time had passed, Śivarātri arrived during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, which destroys all sins.
There is a meritorious sacred site there belonging to the trident-bearing God of gods; there, a night vigil was commenced by many people. (46)
O tiger among men, seeing those women adorned with beautiful ornaments, that thief then began to reflect upon the vigil.
If I should encounter any woman adorned with ornaments who has gone out from this palace, I shall seize her. (48)
Then, having killed him and taken his ornaments, I shall depart. || 49 ||
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went into his presence; then, having climbed a karṇikāra tree, he remained there hidden.
He gazed in all directions at the consequences arising from the abduction of the woman, for he was engaged in the act of theft and was especially afflicted by the cold.
Not even a little sleep came to him, nor did the woman depart; then, beneath him, a linga emerged from the earth. Having gone there and taken some leaves, he scattered them over it.
At that very time, however, the sun of sharp rays rose up—bringing unhappiness to unchaste women, thieves, and lustful men. (53)
Then the men and women, devoted to service and tranquil, having prostrated before Maheśvara, went each to their own abode.
And that thief, despondent, emaciated by hunger, and overwhelmed by the cold, descended from that tree and resorted to some means of escape.
Then, after a long time, he passed away; subsequently, he was born in the house of the lord of Daśārṇa, possessing the memory of his former births.
By the power of fasting, even by forceful staying awake, and likewise by the worship of that Liṅga on Śivarātri. || 57 ||
Then, having obtained the great kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather, he caused a beautiful temple for that Liṅga to be constructed.
Year after year, having resorted to the vigil on Śivarātri, one should become intent upon fasting amidst the sounds of songs and musical instruments. (59)

Having worshipped with stories recounting the Dharma and with the sounds of songs, and having offered the *argha* according to the prescribed rite along with the previously mentioned mantras, he gratified the Brahmins with their desired objects and returned to his own abode.
Then, after some time, on the occasion of Śivarātri, sages led by Śāṇḍilya arrived at that temple.
Śāṇḍilya, Bharadvāja, Yavakrīta, Gālava, Pulastya, Pulaha, Gārgya, and many others as well, O King. (62)
That King Bṛhatsena, the son of the lord of Daśārṇa, also arrived to perform the vigil before that Liṅga.
Having worshipped the God and prostrated before the lords of sages, he sat down before him, permitted by those best of the twice-born.
Then, O King, they held many kinds of discourses before him concerning the royal sages of the past, and especially the brahmin-sages.
Then, at the conclusion of that discourse, he was questioned by those exponents of the Veda, whose minds were filled with curiosity and whose eyes were wide open with wonder.
"O King, we all ask you, filled with curiosity: if you, standing in this temple of the deity, will tell us the truth. (67)
The king said: "O best of Brahmins, if I know it, I shall tell you without doubt; having been questioned in the presence of the God, I swear this by my own soul in truth. (68)
The sages said: "Why do you come here from your own country, desiring to perform a vigil, while abandoning various abundant gifts? (69)
"O lord of men, you surely know the reason why this always occurs year after year; if it is not a secret to you, then tell me. (70)
Sūta said: Then, having smiled with embarrassment, he spoke with a heavy heart: "O best of the twice-born, this is indeed a supreme secret, and it is not to be spoken."
Nevertheless, being questioned in the presence of the gods, I shall speak.
Then he related the events arising from his previous life; the thief then spoke of what had indeed occurred on Śivarātri.
In former times, during Śivarātri, he performed the worship of the Lord, as well as the ritual vigil and fasting, with a mind intent on theft. (74)
Endowed with the recollection of their past births, they recounted their various lives exactly as they had occurred; thereafter, all those sages offered various kinds of words of praise.
Having offered blessings to that best of kings, the royal sage, and having kept a vigil during the night, they departed for their own hermitages.
Having worshipped that deity and those best of the twice-born, the king likewise departed for his own city after keeping a vigil throughout the night.
Bhartṛyajña said: O King, thus has Śivarātri arisen upon the surface of the earth, and thus has its greatness been proclaimed to you. (78)
Therefore, O best of kings, he who desires his own prosperity should perform this with every effort, especially in the Kali age. (79)
This was performed by Dilīpa, Nala, and Nahuṣa; by Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, Sagara, and Yuyutsu.
Likewise, by others endowed with specific and perfect faith, all desires—both divine and human—that had been cherished in their hearts were attained. (81)
And likewise by Sāvitrī, by the goddess Śrī, by Sītā, by Arundhatī, by Sarasvatī, by Menā, and by Rambhā as well. || 82 ||
O best of kings, Indrāṇī, Dṛṣadvatī, Svadhā, Svāhā, as well as Rati, Prīti, Prabhāvatī, and Gāyatrī—all of them attained their beloved desires, endowed with supreme good fortune.
And whoever recites this with devotion in the presence of Śiva, he too is liberated from the sins committed during that day; there is no doubt in this matter. (84)
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no god comparable to Hara. There is no austerity superior to Śivarātri; this truth has been spoken by me. (85)
O King, Meru is composed of all jewels, austerity consists of all wonders, and Śivarātri is proclaimed to be composed of all dharmas.
Just as Garuḍa is among birds and the ocean is among rivers, so too is Śivarātri the most excellent among all religious observances.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śivarātri," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Therefore, O great king, this Śivarātri should be observed by a wise man who desires both worlds.
Ānarta said: I have heard in detail the greatness of Maṅkaṇeśvara, which you have proclaimed in connection with Śivarātri.
Now tell me in its entirety, O illustrious one, the origin of Siddheśvara in detail, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Bhartṛyajña said: O lord of the earth, Mahādeva is renowned as Siddheśvara; his origin has already been heard by you from me as I spoke here previously.
Now I shall describe the fruit arising from that gift when he is seen, which results for men in the attainment of the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin). || 5 ||
And there, O King, the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa is praised for one who desires the status of a universal monarch over the entire surface of the earth.
Ānarta said: O great sage, explain to me in full detail that entire procedure for the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa which has been proclaimed.
Bhartṛyajña said: O best of men, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the solstices or equinoxes, or at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
They praise the ritual correctly performed during the waning of the moon by the virtuous Brāhmaṇas who are well-restrained and devoted to their religious observances.
O King, that [gift] should be bestowed after due deliberation upon those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas and are free from fault; it must never be given to just one person alone.

In a pure, level, and auspicious place that slopes toward the northeast, a wise man should have a beautiful pavilion constructed measuring sixteen cubits. In its center, he should have an altar made according to the measurement of four cubits, raised by one cubit according to the hand of the sacrificer.

One should prepare sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring four cubits in each of the four directions, with a length, width, and depth of one cubit. In the northeast, one should place another auspicious altar (vedi), measuring one cubit, rising to the height of a span (ratni); there, one should arrange the deities of the planets (grahas).
Pairs of officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be appointed in the four directions in due order: the Bahvṛcas, the Adhvaryus, the Chandogas, and the Atharvaṇas.

O King, the offering to the deities should be performed by them in silence with great concentration; likewise, they should perform recitation (japa) according to their own capacity using mantras that contain the characteristic marks of those deities.
Two pillars, each one cubit in width and likewise four cubits in height, should be constructed, situated on the south and north sides of the altar.
In the center of that, one should place a very beautiful, firm pillar made of wood—either sandalwood, khadira, bilva, or even aśvattha.
O best of kings, eight trees are auspicious and recommended for the purpose of pillars: the tinduka, the devadāru, the śrīparṇī, or the vaṭa. (19)
One should place the balance, equipped with two pans, in the middle of that; [the officiant] having bathed, wearing white garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents. (20)
Having filled [the area] all around with the world-protectors (lokapālas) in due order, he should thereafter worship the pillars with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
O best of kings, he should proclaim the weighing ceremony and the auspicious day; meanwhile, the patron, with all his own weapons still fastened to his body, [should stand]. || 22 ||
Standing in the western direction, facing eastward and endowed with faith, one should join the palms in reverence and recite this mantra: || 23 ||
The daughter of Brahmā, who is eternally devoted to the supreme truth, belongs to the lineage of Kaśyapa and is renowned by the name Tulā.
O Tula, you whose name is Truth; I shall perform what is most desired and auspicious for myself. Grant me your favor and be present here now.
Then, O best of men, having ascended that [balance], one should first place upon another scale whatever has been gathered according to one's capacity for the purpose of giving.
Gold, silver, or even clothing and whatever else is desired—O King, as long as it is equal to oneself or even greater than oneself. (27)
Then, having approached his chosen deity and taken hold of the sling, he should quickly cast water into the midst of the water for that purpose.
Having descended [into the water] according to the prescribed rites, one should then present everything—along with sesame seeds, gold, and unbroken grains—to the Brāhmaṇas.
Listen now with a focused mind to that fruit which is obtained afterwards.
Whatever sin may have been committed, whether unknowingly or knowingly, a mortal shall destroy it all through the power of this gift. (31)
O best of kings, whatever measure of past sin has been committed, that very same measure goes to destruction through the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.
This preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) has been prescribed for lords whose souls fear physical affliction; it consists indeed of a gift arising from a balance scale.
O King, this was given by Dilīpa, Kārtavīrya, Pṛthu, Purukutsa, and likewise by other monarchs as well. (34)
This gift of the Tulāpuruṣa is meritorious and praiseworthy, bestowing all desires upon men and destroying all calamities. (35)

O best of kings, there shall be no mental anxieties, no physical ailments, no widowhood arising from disease, and no separation from one's kinsmen; this is declared to be the fruit of the Tulāpuruṣa gift.
O best of kings, it is impossible to describe the fruit that arises from the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa when it is bestowed in the Kali age.
O protector of the earth, he who, having reached Dakṣiṇāmūrti in front of the Lord Siddheśvara, makes a gift, obtains a fruit multiplied a thousandfold.
Therefore, having reached the omnipresent Lord Siddheśvara with every effort, a discerning person should perform the Tulāpuruṣa gift.
All holy fords and all sacred shrines are said by the Self-Existent One to be gathered together in one place within the region of Hāṭakeśvara.
Siddheśvara is proclaimed as the foremost of the gods in one place; O best of kings, when he is seen, touched, and worshipped, a mortal obtains all the fruits that have been extolled.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Tulāpuruṣa Gift," within the "Greatness of Śrīsiddheśvara" in the "Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Field," in the sixth section (Nāgara-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 267 ||
Ānarta said: Tell me, by what action among mortals is universal sovereignty over men attained, which crushes all enemies? (1)

Bhartṛyajña said: O lord of men, the status of a ruler of the earth is difficult to attain through all manner of sins; it is attained only by means of austerities, restraints, gifts, and other auspicious vows. || 2 ||

Furthermore, that king who, having become a sovereign, should with faith offer a golden earth before the deity Gautameśvara, will certainly become a universal monarch (cakravartin); thus spoke the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, Hariścandra, Purūravas, Bharata, and Kārtavīrya—these six were universal emperors (cakravartins). || 4 ||

In ancient times, having performed the gift of the earth in the presence of Gautameśvara and having offered a golden representation of the earth, they remained thereafter as sovereign rulers of the entire world.
Ānarta said: "O Blessed One, by what rite should that earth be given? I shall certainly give it away, for my great faith is firmly established."
Bhartṛyajña said: O best of kings, the ground should be made circular with a hundred palas of [gold], or half of that, or according to one's capacity, consisting of twenty-five palas.

O Great King, in the gift of the earth, one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth. It should never be given in a piece smaller than five palas. One should display these seven oceans therein within the enclosure: those produced from salt, sugarcane, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water.
One should delineate the seven oceans and rivers—Jambū, Plakṣa, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, Śālmali, and Puṣkara—in a doubling sequence.
