Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Himavat, Gandhamādana, Vindhya, and Śṛṅgin—one should conceive of these seven as the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). || 11 ||
In the center, one should fashion Meru, and in the cardinal directions, the supporting mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas), as well as the trees Jambu, Nyagrodha, Nīpa, and Plakṣa.
One should represent the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā there as being preeminent; having thus fashioned the entire earth out of gold, O King. (13)
Thereafter, one should have a pavilion constructed just as it was previously planned.
For the worship of the Brahmanas and the household deities, one should prepare sacrificial pits and archways; having performed everything as before, one should construct an altar in the center.
O King, one should establish the earth there with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), using the mantras and signs as prescribed, and then with pure water.
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the five rivers! O Tripuṣkara!"—with these words, and thereafter the Śrīsūkta, the Pāvamāna hymn, and the Haimī hymn; || 17 ||
It is most excellent and supremely delightful, suitable for the rite of bathing.
Having thus bathed [the image] according to the rules, one should cause it to be clothed in various fine garments with the mantra: "yuvā suvāsāḥ. (19)
Having thus recited the mantra "ye bhūtānām," one should then worship; with a concentrated mind, one should offer incense with the mantra "dhūrasi. || 20 ||
Then, one should perform the ārārtika ceremony with the mantra "agnirjyotiḥ"; thereafter, one should arrange the seven types of grain with the mantra "aham asmi."
Having thus performed everything for her, the patron, dressed in white garments, stands before her with palms joined in reverence and should recite these mantras: || 22 ||
By you this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is sustained; I shall bestow my gift upon you, O Earth—be present here.
O Goddess Vasundharā, you are established first even within the bodies of living beings; thereafter, the other elements, such as water and the rest, come into being.
Those who offer you [oblations] obtain you in even greater measure, there is no doubt; they assume a royal form both in this world and in the next. (25)
Having thus offered praise and taken up the water, O King, one should place Vāsudeva in the heart and perform the ritual with this mantra: || 26 ||
By whom that world-creating Earth was raised up from the netherworld (pātāla)—may Janārdana always be pleased with me through the gift of this [earth]. (27)
Having recited this, O best of kings, one should pour that water into the midst of the water, neither upon the ground nor into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa.
Then one should dismiss the Goddess with this mantra, part by part: "She has arrived according to the rule and has been worshipped according to the ritual. (29)
"For our benefit, you may go wherever you please," having then uttered the mantra "usrā veda," O lord of men, she should be distributed and given away to the Brāhmaṇas. (30)
Thus has this entire supreme gift of the earth been described to you; may any king who hears it become a donor in birth after birth.
O King, for that monarch who gives away the earth according to this rite, no loss of his kingdom shall ever occur within his lineage. || 32 ||
Those kings who are seen to be fallen from their kingdoms did not bestow the earth upon Brāhmaṇas of steadfast soul. (33)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the gift of land; and one should never, under any circumstances, take away land given by another.
O Indra among kings, this gift of land is meritorious, praiseworthy, and supreme; even for those who merely hear of it, it destroys the sins of their bodies and so forth. (35)
Let alone the gift of the earth by the lord of the earth; the mere instigation of the donor [to give it] destroys the flood of ignorance. (36)
He shall be handsome, fortunate, and likewise pleasing to behold; free from mental and physical ailments, he will be endowed with sons and grandsons. || 37 ||
By the power of this gift, a mortal is born wise; having thus made the kingdom free of thorns, O Great King, such a person becomes so. (38)
Being delighted, they go to the eternal and painless abode of Viṣṇu; moreover, through the gift of earth, one may even attain the status of a universal emperor.
O best of kings, that which was formerly performed before the god Gautameśvara has been correctly bestowed [as a gift] for as long as one birth remains.
He performs [this merit] for as long as seven future births; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, O King, land should be given there with every effort.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Earth," within the "Greatness of Gautameśvara," in the "Greatness of the Hāṭakeśvara Field," in the Nāgara Khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 268 ||
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, O highly fortunate ones, listen now to the majesty of Kapāleśa, who resides there in that sacred field as the fourth [liṅga].
By merely hearing this, a person here is liberated from sin.
The sages said: "O high-minded one, we have heard the origin of the three previously mentioned lingas, with the exception of Kapāleśvara. By whom was this deity known as Kapāleśvara installed?"
Tell us, what would be the fruit when he is seen and when he is worshipped?
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, this deity was formerly established by Indra under the name Kapāleśvara for the sake of liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

O best of gods, O best of the twice-born, by the power of that [gift], she was liberated; for there is this Vedic revelation: "Sin is released through the gift of a man. Furthermore, any other man who, having worshipped him with great devotion, should offer the personified sin to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa for the sake of purification, shall be freed from the terrible sin arising from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having approached Dakṣiṇāmūrti and gone to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, Bṛhaspati beheld that Śaṅkara and spoke as follows: || 8 ||
He who gives his own body after having fashioned it out of gold is liberated from the sins accumulated in the past; of this there is no doubt.
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, how indeed did the murder of a Brahmin come to pass for the lord of the gods? Tell us all of this, for our curiosity is great. (10)
How did the deity known as Kapāleśvara become established here, and how was the sin of killing a Brahmin destroyed by the power of that Lord of Heaven? (11)
O son of a Sūta, by what rite is that personification of sin to be given away? By which mantras is he to be given, and with what ritual implements?
Tell me, what fruit arises for men from seeing and worshipping [the deity], even without offering their own bodies, through worship alone? (13)
Sūta said: O highly fortunate ones, I shall narrate to you this ancient tale, by hearing which even a man is liberated from sin.

Whether through ignorance or knowledge, by merely beholding this place, one is liberated from the sins committed in other births or arising on that very day; there is no doubt in this, for this truth has been spoken by me. 15.
O best of the twice-born, in ancient times Vṛtra was born as the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, endowed with great heroism from the side of Vibhāvarī, the daughter of Puloman.
Even as a child, he was righteous-souled and beloved by all people; having abandoned his demonic nature, he became devoted to the service of the twice-born.
Having gone to the Puṣkara forest, established in austerity, he gratified the Lord of Gods, the Lotus-born One, by means of supreme meditative concentration.
Brahmā himself, being pleased with him, appeared before his eyes and said, "I am a granter of boons; what task shall I perform for you? (19)
Vṛtra said: "O God, if you are pleased with me, grant me the status of a Brāhmaṇa; having attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa, I shall achieve the supreme state. (20)
"Therefore, nothing whatsoever would be impossible for me through my status as a Brahmin; nor does anything appear to me to be equal to a Brahmin. (21)
There exists no supreme deity higher than the Brahmin; therefore, nothing else—not even sovereignty over the triple heaven—resides within my heart.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was pleased; having himself bestowed the status of a Brāhmaṇa upon him, he then spoke respectfully.
"O Brahmin, you have been ordained by me as my son; now fulfill your desire. Constantly propitiate the Brahmins who are most learned in the Veda. (24)
When the Brahmins are well-pleased, all the deities are gratified; therefore, with every effort, the best of the twice-born should be honored.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by him, Vṛtra then became a Brāhmaṇa, endowed with Brahmanic splendor and devoted to the practice of celibacy.
While that ascetic practice was being maintained, the Dānavas were slain by Indra; thus, the destruction of the lineage of those high-souled Dānavas was brought about. (27)
Then all those Dānavas, having been defeated by the gods, abandoned their own abodes and were filled with misery and grief.
Placing their mother at their head, they approached her presence; and he, seeing his mother accompanied by them, stood together with them.
"Why have the Dānavas, having been defeated, as well as my mother who has become such [as she is], come to me while I am in this state of suffering? What is the purpose of their arrival? (30)
The Dānavas said: "We have been defeated by the gods and have come to you for refuge. Where else can we go? Apart from you, we have no other place of shelter. (31)
Having heard those words of theirs, Vṛtra spoke respectfully: "I shall slay the gods; go there without delay."
And tell me now, O Mother, the purpose of your coming.
The mother said: "O illustrious one, act accordingly and take a wife quickly, if my words arising from you are to be the authority for the increase of our lineage. (34)
This alone is the supreme dharma, this alone is the supreme method: that a son, with a concentrated mind, carries out the word of his mother. (35)
Likewise, for women there is no deity on earth other than their husband; and for a son, it is the same as long as his mother is alive. (36)
And whatever woman, having transgressed [her duty], remains devoted to dharma for her husband—all that becomes fruitless for her; there is no doubt in this matter. || 37 ||
Whatever religious acts a son performs according to his own whim, transgressing the words of his own mother, all of those [acts] belong to her alone. (38)
And they surely become as useless as an oblation poured into ashes, like weeping in the forest or seeds sown in barren soil. (39)
Just as song before a deaf man or dance before one who is blind, so too is any dharma produced by a son that is different from what was performed by his mother’s father. 40.
All this is certain, without a doubt; therefore, O son, I have come to you at the word of my kinsmen and especially because I am afflicted by grief.
Or what is the use of speaking much to you again and again, my son? Listen to how that discharge of debt toward the ancestors is accomplished. (42)
"My child, if you consider me authoritative, then do as I say. Having heard those words of hers, Vṛtra reflected upon them in his mind.
"There is nothing higher than a mother according to the path declared in the Śruti and Smṛti. Having promised "So be it," he brought home his bride.
Tvaṣṭṛ, being pleased with him, then gave him numerous jewels; for him alone there was an endless supply of both base and noble metals, beyond all counting.
Richly endowed with elephants, horses, vehicles, and treasuries, that one of great heroism among the Dānavas was consecrated in his own position, being fully possessed of Brahmanical character.
Then, having heard that Vṛtra had been consecrated in his own kingdom, those asuras and others, the kinsmen of that Vṛtra, were filled with joy.

And the Dānavas who had previously been stationed there arrived—from Pātāla, from mountain fortresses, and even from land fortresses—all having incurred enmity with the gods and being enveloped in great wrath. (48)
Then, encouraged by all the dānavas, that one of great strength set out toward the abode of Mahendra for the destruction of his enemies.
Śakra too, hearing that Vṛtra was approaching with a desire to fight, went forth joyfully to meet him, accompanied by all the gods.
Then a battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas on the vast expanse of Mount Meru, continuing perpetually day and night.
The gods were constantly defeated by the Dānavas; thereupon the Guru said to Śakra, "O Lord of the Gods, do not engage in battle."
This Vṛtra is formidable in battle, endowed with two powers; the four Vedas are before him, and behind him is his bow with an arrow.
Therefore, that most formidable Daitya belongs to you alone in the great battle; for that reason, O Lord of Śacī, enter into an alliance with him.
Therefore, inspire him with confidence and slay that Dānava with your thunderbolt; "the enemy is to be slain by means of the six expedients"—such is the teaching of the scriptures.

Whether eating or lying down, even after giving away your own daughter, having joined her with the gift of a Brahmin, and even after making a solemn oath to your guru—having encountered this world of illusion, conduct yourself accordingly. (56)
Indra said: "If it is so, go yourself and instill confidence in him; by your word, the Dānava will surely gain trust."
Sūta said: Having understood the intention of Śakra, Bṛhaspati set out for the place where the Daitya Vṛtra was stationed, having resolved upon battle.
Vṛtra also, beholding Bṛhaspati who had arrived in person—and being ever devoted to the twice-born—became joyful in heart; bowing down especially with great reverence, he spoke these words: || 59 ||
Vṛtra said: "Welcome to you, O best of the twice-born! Command me, what shall I do? Since Brāhmaṇas are dear to me, therefore speak now. (60)
Bṛhaspati said: "O best of beings, since victory in battle is uncertain due to destiny, therefore, at my word, make an agreement with Mahendra."
"You enjoy the entire earth, and Śakra likewise enjoys the triple heaven; according to this arrangement, you two must always conduct yourselves toward one another."
Vṛtra said: "O Brāhmaṇa, I shall indeed always carry out your word. O noble twice-born one, arrange for my meeting with Śakra right now."
Sūta said: Then the noble-minded Bṛhaspati, having summoned Śakra, brought about a mutual alliance between him and Vṛtra.
Having established a state of mutual enmity and friendship, both those lords of the Daityas and the gods departed from there, highly delighted, and went to their own respective homes.
Then, ever seeking a pretext against Śakra, Vṛtra remained on the watch; yet, despite searching with great effort, he could not find a single vulnerability anywhere.
Even if Purandara should somehow approach his presence, having found some slight vulnerability, he is consumed by his majesty.
Indra said: "I am not able to look at that Daitya in any way whatsoever; since he is pervaded on all sides by splendor, how shall I destroy him?"
Therefore, proclaim some means to me for his destruction, so that I may be able to endure the splendor of that evil-minded one. (69)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his and having meditated for a long time, Bṛhaspati then spoke to Śakra, who stood bowed down with humility.
Bṛhaspati said: O Purandara, lord of the gods, the spiritual splendor of that [child] resides perfectly within his body; therefore, you are not at all able to look upon him.
In that manner, I shall proclaim to you the means arising from his slaughter, by which you shall slay that foremost of Dānavas here.
On the bank of the Prācīsarasvatī, there dwelt a brahmin-sage named Dadhīci, who was a hundred yojanas in height and resided in the Puṣkara forest.
There, constantly performing austerities, he perpetually praised the Grandfather (Brahmā). O Hari, that best of sages became despondent regarding the maintenance of his vital breaths.
He shall be an ancient sage, completely enveloped by old age; go quickly and beg from him his heavy bones.
He will undoubtedly give it to you, even at the cost of his own most beloved life; with her bones, there shall be for you a weapon known as the Vajra.

Therefore, your [weapon] will surely be unfailing, and you shall slay Vṛtra. The splendor of that thunderbolt, augmented by the power of Brahman, will cause the energy born of Vṛtra to be completely pacified.
Sūta said: Having heard that, Śakra, together with all the hosts of gods, went quickly to the Puṣkara forest where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows.
Accompanied by thirty-three crores of sacred fords, he entered the hermitage of Dadhīci, which was there, endowed with wonderful sights.
There, serpents, having attained mutual satisfaction, play with mongooses; likewise, deer sport with lions, and cats with mice.
The crows, together with the owls, were free from mutual enmity through the power of the asceticism of that great-souled Dadhīci. (81)
Dadhīci, too, beholding the gods led by Śakra as they approached, went forward to meet them with a joyful heart and in great haste.
Then, having taken up the water of honor (arghya) and prostrating again and again, he said to Śakra who had arrived: "What task of yours shall I perform? (83)
O Lord of Gods, inform me quickly of him who has arrived at my home.
Indra said: "O best of Brahmins, O virtuous sage, perform the rites of hospitality for me who have come to your home; give me your own bones immediately, without hesitation. (85)
O Lord of Sages, I have come into your presence for this very purpose: the gods have a supreme need for your bones, and through them they shall attain success.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Indra, Dadhīci, filled with satisfaction, then spoke to the thousand-eyed one who was accompanied by all the gods.
"Aha! There is currently no one on earth equal to me, for the Lord of Gods himself has come to my house as a petitioner because of my merit. (88)
Blessed indeed are my bones, O Lord of Gods, which shall always perform your beneficial work for the sake of protecting the inhabitants of heaven. (89)
"Here I am; for your sake, I shall give up my dear life-breaths. O Purandara, take these bones as you wish for the purpose of your own task."
Having spoken thus, that great seer quickly resorted to meditation, drew forth his life-force through the aperture of Brahma, and cast off his body.
O best of the twice-born, at that very moment his body, abandoned by that self, fell lifeless upon the surface of the earth.
At that very time, Śatakratu, having taken up his bones, then spoke respectfully to Viśvakarman: || 93 ||
"With these bones, quickly fashion for me a vajra weapon, by which I may swiftly slay Vṛtra, the foremost of the Dānavas. (94)
Having heard those words of his, Viśvakarman, filled with haste, fashioned the weapon known as the Vajra, which was of a terrible form, according to the specifications.
Then he gave to that wise thousand-eyed one a six-sided, hundred-jointed, formidable object that was slender in the middle. 96.

Then, having perceived through his spies that Vṛtra—who possessed a splendor equal to twelve suns—was established in meditative absorption and intent upon the twilight worship, he took him [with him].
Then, taking his position at the rear, the Lord of the Three Worlds, eager for his destruction, hurled the thunderbolt toward him. (98)
Struck by that thunderbolt, the Dānava was reduced to ashes; yet Śakra, not realizing he had been slain, fled from him out of fear.
In a region devoid of humans, rugged and overgrown with thickets, Śakra then lay hidden; he then perceived the entire world to be filled with Vṛtra.
In the meantime, the gods, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas, beholding him in every direction, approached Śatakratu.
Then, after much difficulty, Śakra was spotted by them hidden in the dense forest, standing terrified among the thickets.
The gods said: "O thousand-eyed one, why are you afraid? This Vṛtra has been slain by you, while being watched by us and by your entire retinue."
"Come from here, O Purandara; let us go toward our home. Now rule the kingdom of the three worlds, which has been cleared of all thorns."
Having heard that, Śatakratu emerged from the midst of the army with his hair standing on end, having heard that Vṛtra, the best of the Dānavas, was slain.
Then, as soon as all the gods beheld that Śatakratu, they saw his body bereft of splendor and filled with a foul odor.
Having seen this, Brahmā, the teacher of the world, spoke to all the gods: "This Śakra is now overwhelmed by the sin of Brahman-slaughter."
Since he, having become a Brahmin, slew Vṛtra through deceit, therefore he must be avoided from afar; otherwise, you will incur sin.
Touching or conversing with one who has killed a Brahmin brings sin upon men; therefore, one should avoid him from afar.
Let alone physical contact with him, or especially conversation; even the mere sight of him, they say, brings all manner of sin upon men. (110)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Brahmā and seeing his own body bereft of luster and enveloped in a foul odor, Śakra [was struck with dismay]. || 111 ||
Then, dejected and with his neck bowed in prostration, he spoke to the Lord of the World: "O God, I am your servant; I have been appointed by you to the position of Indra. (112)
Therefore, O Lord, show me favor; tell me the expiation that destroys the slaughter of a Brahmin, by which purification may arise. (113)
Brahmā said: O slayer of Bala, having bathed in the sixty-eight sacred fords (tīrthas), give away a golden image of yourself known as the "Man of Sin" (pāpapūruṣa).
Having bathed in a sacred ford with its holy waters, he should recite the mantra as prescribed for the high-souled Brāhmaṇa, declaring, "I am a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa. (115)
As soon as you have bathed, wherever that [substance] falls from your hands upon the ground, luster will arise in your body and foul odor will perish.
O Śakra, you must place that skull-bowl at that sacred ford; thereafter, it is to be worshipped in the name of Maheśvara.
Then, with the five mantras of the faces, you must offer your own body made of gold to the best of the twice-born; thereby you shall attain purification. (118)
Having heard those words of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, Śakra took the skull born of Vṛtra and then departed on a pilgrimage.
And that lord of the gods, traveling through sixty-eight sacred fords, arrived in due course at the region of Hāṭakeśvara.
Having bathed in the Viśvāmitra lake, as he was emerging from it, the skull of that self-slaughtered man fell down by itself.
Then he worshipped him with the mantras originating from his mouth—meritorious, all-sin-removing mantras, just as they had been previously declared by Brahmā.
At that very moment, O best of the twice-born, the foul odor vanished from his body, and a great splendor was born from it.
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived together with the gods, having learned that the lord of all the deities was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Śrī Brahmā said: "O best of gods, the fault incurred from the killing of a Brahmin has departed from you; for the purification of the remaining sin, O sir, offer a gift of gold. (125)
This skull which has been worshipped by you in this place was [worshipped] with the five mantras originating from the mouth of Hara, dedicated to Vṛtra.

Then, out of devotion, you shall offer your own body, born of gold, according to the rite accompanied by mantras; thus all your sin, whatever was committed previously, will depart once it has been bestowed upon a Brahmin, O sir. (127)
Thus addressed by Brahmā in the presence of the gods, Śakra then said, "So be it," and immediately gave away his own mass of sin.
O Brahmins, having fashioned one made of gold, he gave it to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa named Vāta who maintained the sacred fires, at the Gartātīrtha.
In the meantime, that Brahmin was censured by the citizens: "Fie, fie upon you, O sinner! Those Vedas which were previously recited by you have been in vain. (130)
"You shall never again have contact with us; for you have accepted alms that arose from a mass of sin. (131)
Then that brahmin born of the Upamanyu lineage, known by the name Vātaka, spoke with his face turned pale.
"O Śakra, since you gave me your own ball of sin, I accepted it as a gift out of courtesy toward you. (133)
O best of gods, while you were looking on, I was not censured for greed; nor was I by all these brahmins who dwell in this city. (134)
Therefore, I shall not accept this gift from you. || 135 ||
If you do not accept it again even though I shall give it to you once more, I will inflict upon you a terrible curse of the Brahmins that brings about total destruction.
Indra said: "If a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches should accept a gift, he would not be tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (137)
Therefore, you have committed no sin; listen here to my words, for you were censured by these Brahmins born in the city. (138)
Among all these [deities], you shall be the foremost in all their rites; and so too shall be those who will be their sons and grandsons, as well as yours.
"O twice-born one, by their command they will all undoubtedly carry out every task, even the smallest, provided it is not devoid of your word."
For them, it will be as fruitless as an oblation poured into ashes; this place shall become renowned by the name Kapālamocana.

O excellent twice-born, those men who, remembering my skull, shall perform a śrāddha ceremony there, will be endowed with liberation; especially during the fortnight of śrāddha, they shall attain the supreme goal.
Having taken wives from families of twice-born men outside the [proper] stations, the Brāhmaṇas born of your lineage shall [be so] by my grace. (143)
"They shall be eligible for all activities in the city. Having spoken thus, the Thousand-eyed One then vanished from sight.
With that wealth acquired through receiving gifts, Vāta also constructed there a temple for the trident-bearing God of gods.
Then Śakra spoke to those Brahmins born in the city: "Whoever, having bathed at Kapālamocana, shall indeed worship the God... (146)
The sin arising from the killing of a Brahmin is undoubtedly destroyed for him; even if he is burdened with a great sin, he shall become free from taint.
Having promised "So be it," he established his own hermitage right there and worshipped Śaṅkara, having invited the Brahmins born in the city.
From that time forward, whatever task arises for them, those Nāgaras who reside there carry it out according to their word. (149)
For this reason, the second one born here is situated in the middle. || 150 ||
All this narrative, which destroys the sins of those men who hear or recite it, concerning the deity Kapāleśvara, has been related to you. (151)
Just as the sin of the high-souled Lord of the Gods was destroyed here, O best of the twice-born, so too was the slaughter of a Brahmin destroyed at that sacred ford.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin and Greatness of Kapālamocaneśvara at Vātakeśvara-kṣetra," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 269 ||
Ānarta said: "Whether out of folly, negligence, desire, or even childishness, that man who commits a sin and does not perform expiation [is lost]."
O best of the twice-born, tell me of that merit which causes the destruction of his sins, by which liberation may be attained immediately, if you are pleased with me, O Lord.
O great sage, tell me the procedure by which I may quickly bestow that mass of sin upon one who is dominated by greed and delusion. || 3 ||
Bhartṛyajña said: One should offer one's own piṇḍa made of gold weighing twenty-five palas.

Having performed the rites during the dark fortnight and bathed according to the prescribed rules, and having first prepared the pavilion and other requirements, he should bathe himself, put on clean garments, and become pure.
Then a man who has committed a sin should worship the essential nature of the earth and the other elements; by doing so, he is indeed liberated from that committed sin, of this there is no doubt.
O lord of men, one should worship that piṇḍa with the names of those twenty-four principles, beginning with earth.

Oṃ, salutation to Earth; Oṃ, salutation to Water; Oṃ, salutation to Fire; Oṃ, salutation to Wind; Oṃ, salutation to Space; Oṃ, salutation to the Nose; Oṃ, salutation to the Tongue; Oṃ, salutation to the Eye; Oṃ, salutation to the Skin; Oṃ, salutation to the Ear; Oṃ, salutation to Smell; Oṃ, salutation to Taste; Oṃ, salutation to Form; Oṃ, salutation to Touch; Oṃ, salutation to Sound; Oṃ, salutation to Speech; Oṃ, salutation to the two Hands; Oṃ, salutation to the two Feet; Oṃ, salutation to the Anus; Oṃ, salutation to the Generative Organ; Oṃ, salutation to the Mind; Oṃ, salutation to the Intellect; Oṃ, salutation to the Consciousness; Oṃ, salutation to the Ego; Oṃ, salutation to the Field-Self (Kṣetrātman); Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Self (Paramātman). One should offer incense with the mantra "dhūrasi," the lamp with "agnirjyotiḥ," and then cause [the deity] to be clothed in garments with the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ. || 8 ||
Then, having brought a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, one should wash his feet and clothe him with garments.
With armlets, bracelets, and ornaments for the fingers.
Having adorned his body, one should then bring forth the image; O Indra among kings, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa with this mantra.
"O twice-born one, this golden self has been given by me to you; whatever sin was previously committed shall become entirely yours. (12)
Thus is the mantra for giving. Then, O King, the Brāhmaṇa should recite this mantra: || 13 ||
"Whatever sin was previously committed by you has indeed been taken up by me in embodied form; therefore, you are now freed from sin. This is the mantra for acceptance. || 14 ||
Having thus given according to the prescribed rule, one should then dismiss the Brahmin; when this has been done, O King, one should then give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Great King, as soon as he attains satisfaction, he removes that sin; once it has been performed, proof of its efficacy appears at that very moment.
The body attains lightness and an increase in vital energy arises; moreover, at night in dreams, one beholds those who remain with contented minds. (17)
Men and women [should worship] with white garments, white garlands, and white unguents; likewise, white-bodied cows, bulls, horses, and various sacred fords (tīrthas). 18.
All this has been told regarding the imposition of the "lump of sin"; by merely hearing it, O Indra among kings, one is liberated from sins.
O King, even elsewhere, a great gift may carry away a mass of sin.
The sin committed during a single lifetime, produced by one's own body, is destroyed a thousandfold at the shrine of the god Kapāleśvara. || 21 ||
O King, the ritual for the altar and the pavilion should be performed exactly as before; however, the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed with the Gāyatrī alone.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Offering the Pinda of Sins," within the context of the *Kapāleśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, the sixth section of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 270 ||
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another group of seven most meritorious liṅgas there, by the mere sight of which, and especially by their worship and adoration, [great merit is attained]. || 1 ||
A mortal is born long-lived and free from all diseases; there, the Great Lord Maheśvara is called Mārkaṇḍeśvara.
Furthermore, Indradyumneśvara is another Hara who removes all sins, and likewise Pāleśvara is the destroyer of all diseases. || 3 ||
Then there is the one known as Ghaṇṭaśiva, who was installed by Ghaṇṭa; and the one named Kalaśeśvara, joined with Vānareśvara. || 4 ||
There, the Lord of the Lords of the Field is called Īśānaśiva; when worshipped with devotion by men, he grants superhuman desires.
All desires cherished by the mind, even while the Kali age prevails.
The sages said: "Who is this one named Mārkaṇḍa by whom the Liṅga was installed? And who was the protector of the earth, Indradyumna? Tell us, O son of Sūta."
Likewise, there was one named Pālaka by whom this Hara was installed; and likewise, he who was known as Ghaṇṭa—into which lineage was he born? (8)
Tell us everything concerning the one known as Kalaśa, who was accompanied by a monkey; O Lord, speak further, for our curiosity remains.
Proclaim further how the highest good is produced for men here, and by which of these best of men the gods were installed in this sacred field.
O son of Sūta, likewise describe in detail their conduct and power, as well as their gifts at the appropriate times and their mantras.
Sūta said: I shall relate to you this ancient narrative, which was told by Bhartṛyajña himself to the lord of Ānarta.
By merely hearing this, a mortal man becomes long-lived; by its power, he never encounters untimely death in any way. (13)
The origin of him who was first celebrated as the one known as Mārkaṇḍeya has been fully narrated to you; it is a destroyer of sins.
O best of sages, I shall now describe Indradyumna, whose lineage and power were honored by all kings. (15)

O best of the twice-born, in former times there was a protector of the earth named Indradyumna; he was a refuge for Brahmins, a protector of virtuous people, a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. (16)
While that knower of Dharma was ruling, there was no famine, nor disease, nor fear caused by thieves for anyone in the world. (17)
Just as the streams of rain, or as the stars in the sky, or as the sands of the Ganges, they are beyond all calculation.
In that same manner, all sacrifices were performed by him with complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), including the Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, Uktha, and Ṣoḍaśin.
O best of the twice-born, there are the Sautrāmaṇī, animal sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya rites, the Vājapeya, the Aśvamedha, and especially the Rājasūya.
Likewise, others performed the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice with minds purified by faith. || 21 ||
By him gifts were given, especially at sacred fords (tīrthas), consisting of sweet foods along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) for the best of the twice-born.
There is no city, nor town, nor sacred ford upon the surface of the earth where his abode in the realm of the thirty gods does not exist. (23)
By him, thousands and hundreds of millions of maidens were bestowed upon Brāhmaṇas who were seekers of wealth. (24)
On the tenth day, during the night, Dundubhi, mounted upon the back of an elephant and with his drums being beaten, wandered throughout the entire city.

"At dawn, the day will belong to Viṣṇu and shall be a destroyer of sins; therefore, a fast must be observed by all, except for the elderly and children. Otherwise, I shall punish anyone who takes food. (26)
Then, by the grace of Viṣṇu, that royal sage Indradyumna went to the world of Brahmā in that very same body.
There, at the end of a thousand kalpas, he was addressed by Brahmā himself: "O Indradyumna, go to the earth; you must not remain here any longer."
Indradyumna said: "O Brahman, why do you swiftly cast me out from my own world? O Lord of Gods, though I am sinless, tell me the reason for this. (29)

The illustrious Brahmā said: Today, the destruction of your fame has occurred upon the surface of the earth; for as long as one's fame remains upon the face of the earth, so long shall that person dwell in heaven.
For this reason, people have caused step-wells, wells, tanks, and temples to be marked with their own names. (31)
Therefore, go to the surface of the earth and establish your own new fame, if you desire to dwell for a long time in this world of mine. (32)
Then, at that very moment, as soon as that lord of kings looked at himself, he found himself arrived upon the surface of the earth toward the city of Kāmpilya.
Then he asked the people: "What is this city known as? What is this country, who is the king here, and what is this town and city? (34)
They said to him: "This supreme place is renowned as Kāmpilya; this region is named Ānarta, and the king here is Pṛthivījaya. (35)
"Who are you, what have you come here for? Tell us, what business do you have? (36)
Indradyumna said: "In former times, there was a protector of the earth named Indradyumna in the city of Rocaka, in the land of Vaijaruka; where is that land and where is that city? (37)
The people said: "O auspicious one, we do not know that city, nor the region, nor the king by the name of Indradyumna about whom you ask. (38)
Indradyumna said: "Is there anyone here who possesses long life and knows that lord of the earth, or his country, or even his city? Tell me that without delay. (39)
The people said: "It is heard that the great sage named Mārkaṇḍeya, who remembers seven kalpas, resides in the Naimiṣa forest; go to him and ask, and you will know."
Then, having gone quickly by way of the sky, he bowed down deeply and questioned that sage who was dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest.
"O excellent sage, has a king named Indradyumna been seen or heard of by you? We have heard that he is long-lived; therefore, we ask you about him. (42)
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O King, within the interval of seven kalpas, neither seen nor heard by me has there been anyone here named Indradyumna; what then can I say to you regarding that?"
Having heard those words of his, that lord of the earth became despondent; having attained a state of supreme detachment, he resolved upon death.
Having brought wood and kindled the fire, King Indradyumna, desiring to enter it, was addressed by him. (45)
And you must not act against me here, for I have become your friend; I shall destroy your death, even if it should be most formidable.
"You are free from disease and you are fortunate; why do you desire death? Tell me the reason for your death, and I shall provide a remedy for it. (47)
Indradyumna said: "I have been told by the inhabitants of Kāmpilyapura that you are long-lived; for that reason, O great sage, I have come here into your presence. (48)
O virtuous sage, if you speak of news concerning Indradyumna, my fame will not be fully recognized; therefore, I shall go to my death. (49)
Sūta said: Having understood his resolve and perceiving that his exertion was in vain, that compassionate lord of sages spoke these words out of courtesy.
"If it is so, do not enter the fire; I shall find that king. I have a supreme friend named Baka Nāḍījaṅgha."
"He is surely our ancient friend and will certainly know that king; therefore come, let us go to his side on the Himalayas."
The sight of the virtuous never, at any time, ever becomes fruitless.
Having spoken thus, the sage and the king, both well-pleased, then set out by way of the sky toward Baka on the Himalayas.
Baka also, seeing that Mārkaṇḍeya had arrived, went forward to meet him and, being pleased, honored him with a welcome.
"I am blessed, I am one who has performed meritorious deeds, since I have met with you! O best among the knowers of Brahman, what hospitality may I offer to you?"
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: You are even longer-lived than I, since you have remained a friend; have you seen or heard of King Indradyumna? (57)
Because of that which was seen by my friend, a cause for death arises otherwise; therefore, I have come to you. (58)
Baka said: "I remember, without a doubt, fourteen kalpas; yet I do not recall even a mention of Indradyumna."
Let the matter of seeing [the Lord] be set aside for now; this which I have spoken is indeed the truth.
Indradyumna said: "Tell us, what is the power of this austerity, of this gift, and of this restraint, by which such a lifespan has been attained even in the state of being a crane? (61)
Baka said: "Due to the greatness of the ghee-blanket of the trident-bearing God of gods, my life has become such as this; my state as a crane arose from the sage's curse. (62)
Formerly, I was a boy in the house of a wise Brāhmaṇa named Pārāśarya in the beautiful city of Camatkārapura. (64)
He was known by the name Viśvarūpa, and by another name he was remembered as Baka; he was exceedingly fickle-minded and was dear to his father.

Then, after some time had passed, O friend, during the transit of the sun into Capricorn, out of extreme fickleness, I took the Jāgeśvara Liṅga—which had been worshipped by my father—and cast it into a jar of ghee.
Then, when the night had passed, I was asked by Janaka: "My son, have you perhaps searched for Jāgeśvara? Therefore, tell me; I shall give you excellent food. (66)
Then, having quickly taken some [food] from that vessel of clarified butter, out of greed for the delicacy, I placed it, soaked in ghee, into my father's hand. (67)
Then, after some time, he met his death; by the power of that [merit], he was subsequently born in a royal palace with the memory of his former life.
In the palace of the lord of Ānarta, I am known by the name Baka; the god Hara was installed by me in Camatkārapura. (69)
O best of Brahmins, by its power, he attained the station of Brahmā.

Then, whatever excellent lingas exist upon the surface of the earth, I indeed cover them with ghee when the sun is situated in Capricorn; likewise, the auspicious linga which was installed by me in Camatkārapura.
Having established his son in the kingdom, he propitiated [the deity] day and night, having appointed servants on all sides provided with wealth and clothing.
Then, after a long time, the blessed Lord Śiva was pleased with me; having approached my presence, he spoke these words.
I am well-pleased, may prosperity be yours, O best of kings, by this gift of a ghee-blanket that is beyond counting. (74)
Therefore, choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—that resides in your heart; I shall grant it even if it be ungivable, were it to be extremely difficult to obtain. (75)
Then I said to Hara: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, O God, make me a Gaṇa; I choose nothing else."
The Blessed Lord said: "Come, O highly fortunate one, to Kailāsa, the best of mountains; together with me, in this very body, become a Gaṇa."

Moreover, whatever other mortal man shall perform this for me at the commencement of night during the transit of the sun into Capricorn, he, having performed it even once with a *kaṃbala*, will surely become one of my attendants.
Furthermore, by fashioning my linga into a symmetrical form, you shall become renowned as Dharmasena, free from all deformity. (79)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One took me from there and, having gone to Mount Kailāsa, bestowed upon me hundreds of millions of attendants.
Then, after some time, while wandering about at will, I went to the Himavat, the great mountain, the best of peaks. (81)
There dwells one named Gālava, who is always established in austerity; his wife is large-eyed and endowed with all auspicious marks.
"O lord of sages, seeing her—whose feet were red like the lotus, whose three parts were deep, whose ankles were hidden, and whose waist was slender—I became possessed by the god of love. (83)
And I thought in my mind: "How can I take her away? Therefore, having become his disciple, I shall practice devotion toward him. (84)
"Having become devoted to service, by that means I shall obtain the beautiful woman. (85)
Then Gālava approached me in the form of a young student, saying: "I am weary of worldly existence; I shall perform great penance. (86)
"O All-pervading Lord, grant me initiation, so that I may become your disciple. (87)
"I shall always bring darbha grass as well as flowers, and I shall always bring sacrificial fuel, fruits, and water. (88)
Knowing me to be endowed with discipline and appearing in the form of a brahmin, he then bestowed initiation upon me according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
Then, having undertaken the initiation, I gratified him and his wife day after day with the prescribed service; yet, even with an impure mind, I remained intent on seeking out their vulnerabilities.
When another day arrived, that high-minded woman, endowed with the nature of women, left the hut at a distance and slept during the night.
Therefore, having assumed a massive form and taking that ascetic woman—who was sleeping soundly and full of trust—I set out facing the south.
Then, having been completely abandoned by me through sleep caused by physical contact, she recognized me as a thief and wept aloud before her disciple.
And she said to her husband, Gālava, the best of sages: "O Lord, this disciple of wicked conduct is carrying me away from here."
Therefore, O illustrious one, protect him before he goes far away. (95)
Hearing that, Gālava said repeatedly, "Stop! Stop!"—"O you of sinful conduct, O evil-souled one, your movement has been paralyzed by me. (96)
From his words, a paralysis of my movement then arose for me, so that I remained perfectly motionless, as if I were merely painted.
Then I was cursed by that high-souled Gālava: "Since I have been deceived by you, O evil-minded one, become a crane! (98)
Then I suddenly saw myself in the form of a crane; yet even in that state as a crane, the memory of my former existence was not lost to me.
Then his wife also performed a bath with her clothes on; her limbs distressed by my touch, she stood ready to utter a curse.
"O wicked one, since while I was asleep and in my menses, you have deceived my husband by assuming the behavior of a crane and taking on another form, therefore become a crane in truth. (101)
Having been thus cursed by those two, he was indeed filled with grief and clung to the feet of the high-souled Gālava. (102)
"I am a follower of the great-souled God of gods, the three-eyed one; renowned as Pālaka, I stand here as the lord of ten million attendants. (103)
Thus, having arrived here on some business of my lord, I fell under the sway of the god of love upon beholding your wife. (104)
O Lord of Sages, having understood this, please forgive my offense; for one who is ill-behaved, even upon attaining prosperity, learning, and sovereignty, [becomes arrogant]. (105)
Just as I, intoxicated with pride, did not remain long in my place, so too have I now approached your presence, having assumed the form of a disciple. || 106 ||
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of recovering this great lady of truth, please show favor to me, who am wretched and prostrate before you.

Since forgiveness is the gift bestowed by ascetics, the voice of cuckoos is their beauty; devotion to one's husband is the beauty of women; learning is the beauty of the ugly, and forgiveness is the beauty of ascetics. (108)
Sūta said: Having heard that piteous speech of his, that sage, a devotee of Maheśvara, recognizing him as being in the position of a kinsman, felt compassion and spoke these words.
The Brahmin Satyavāk resides in the auspicious city of Camatkārapura. || 110 ||
Then, by his instruction, he who is known as Bhartṛyajña will certainly attain the state of a crane through my word; of this there is no doubt. (111)
Then I saw myself having taken refuge in the state of a crane.
Thus, through devotion to Śiva, my long life was secured; and through the greatness of the ghee-blanket, my state as a crane [was ended] despite the sage’s curse. (113)
Indradyumna said: "O bird, it is for this purpose that I have come into your presence—to inquire after Indradyumna’s welfare, for I am resolved upon death. (114)
O bird, she was not recognized by you due to my misfortunes; therefore, I shall serve the blazing fire.
"This was previously vowed by me after resolving it in my mind: as long as Indradyumna remains unrecognized, I must serve the sacred fire. (116)
Therefore, give me your command along with Mārkaṇḍeya, so that I, Baka, whose fame has been ruined, may enter the fire.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Do you know any other man who is superior to yourself in age? I ask this so that, having gone to him, I may perform what is required for the sake of this high-souled one."
"Endowed with supreme faith, he has come here together with me; how then can he abandon his life-breaths while I, his companion, am present? (119)

Furthermore, O bird, there is another appropriate word that I shall say to you: this man, joined with suffering, will prepare the fire; why should I depart for the hermitage without having rescued him? (120)
Sūta said: Having understood their resolve, the crane became deeply distressed and reflected for a very long time: "How might these two find happiness? (121)
Then, seeing that both the king and the sage had brought wood and desired to enter the fire, Baka spoke these words: || 122 ||
"O wise one, do as I say if you wish to live! I have clearly recognized him today—he is King Indradyumna. (123)
Whoever knows my eldest son, who is an expert in all the scriptures, shall take him away as he is resolved upon death. || 124 ||
"Come with me toward Mount Kailāsa, sighing like a serpent and with eyes clouded by tears. (125)
"There is a dear friend of mine, an owl who has lived for a long time; he will surely know him, so do not undergo death in vain. (126)
Then, joined by that great-souled Baka, he arrived at Kailāsa, the best of mountains, together with Mārkaṇḍeya.
Seeing that his most esteemed friend, the crane, had arrived, he approached him joyfully and greeted him with a welcome. (128)
Then, having embraced him who was thus rested again and again, this one named Prākāravarṇana spoke these words.

Welcome to you, O best of the twice-born; O King, a very hearty welcome to you as well. Since you have come today as a friend, tell me the purpose of your arrival and what task you require to be done. (130)
"Who are these two men who have arrived here in my presence along with you—divine in form, highly fortunate, and enveloped in splendor? (131)

Baka said: "This one known as Mārkaṇḍeya is famous here throughout the three worlds; by the grace of Maheśvara, he has attained supreme perfection. This second person is his friend, whom I do not know in truth; he has come into my presence accompanied by that friend Mārkaṇḍeya. (132)
O high-minded one, if you know that king Indradyumna, then tell me the truth by which he may be turned back from death. (135)
"I have known you to be long-lived; therefore, I have come into your presence. (136)
Ulūka said: Twenty-eight kalpas have passed since my birth; I have neither seen nor heard of any king named Indradyumna. (137)

Indradyumna said: "Tell me quickly why you have become an owl; this is a source of curiosity for me, since your lifespan is indeed infinite, yet you have become an owl—fierce and despised by the world. (138)

The owl said: Listen, I shall tell you how my long life was secured; by the grace of Maheśvara and through the worship of bilva leaves, I attained this state of being an owl due to the curse of the high-souled Bhṛgu. (139)

Formerly, O Brahmin, I was a learned man who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge. In the excellent city of Camatkārapura, I was renowned by the name Ghaṇṭaka; I was a celibate student, endowed with self-restraint, and devoted to the worship and adoration of Hara.
Śambhu was always worshipped by me three times a day with one hundred thousand unbroken bilva leaves, consisting of fresh tripatra clusters.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Blessed Lord Hara, being pleased with me, appeared before my eyes and spoke in a voice as deep as a thundercloud: ||| 142 ||
"I am pleased with you, my child; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows, since you have worshipped me at the three times of day with unbroken bilva leaves. (143)
Through the tip of a *bilva* sprout with three leaves, one attains [the desired result]; as much satisfaction is gained by even a single one, so it is not obtained by ten million others.
"May there be welfare for you, O friend; may there be constant auspiciousness even among fragrant flowers. Having thus bowed deeply, he spoke loudly to that moon-crested Lord. 145.
If you are pleased with me, O God, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then, O Lord of the World, make me free from old age and death.
Having promised "So be it," Mahādeva Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, vanished from sight in an instant as he proceeded toward Kailāsa.
Then, having obtained a boon from Maheśvara, I was thoroughly satisfied; filled with joy, I considered myself as one who had accomplished all that was to be done. || 148 ||
At that very time, however, there was Bhārgava, the best of sages, who was proficient in all the scriptures and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches.
He had a virtuous wife, renowned by the name Sudarśanā; she was the daughter of the sage Gālava and was dearer to him than his own life. (150)
He had a daughter who was peerless in beauty upon the earth; she was seen by me suddenly as she was playing according to her own will. (151)
She was slender-waisted, with beautiful hair, lips like the bimba fruit, and long eyes; upon seeing her, I fell under the power of the god of love. (152)
Then I asked: "Whose daughter is this lovely-eyed girl? With every limb so well-proportioned, she shines like a daughter of the gods. (153)
"My friends have told me that she is the daughter of the sage Bhārgava; even now, this lady of lovely smiles remains in the state of maidenhood. (154)
Then, filled with humility and standing with my palms joined in reverence, I went to the descendant of Bhṛgu and requested that maiden from him. || 155 ||
O highly fortunate one, having recognized me as being of his own caste, that son of Bhṛgu also gave his daughter to Virūpa.
Then that maiden, realizing "I have been given by my father according to dharma to one who is deformed," went and spoke these words to her mother: ||| 57 ||
Deeply ashamed and afflicted by extreme grief, she said, "O Mother, look! I have been given in marriage by my father to a deformed man; I have no desire to live. (158)
"Either I shall consume poison or enter the fire. Having heard those words of hers, that twice-born man was restrained by her.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, why was this maiden—so richly endowed with beauty and possessed of all auspicious marks—given by you to one who is deformed? || 160 ||
Having heard these words, Bhārgava, the best of sages, then reproached her, saying: "Fie upon this woman who behaves like a man! (161)
"A maiden has been requested by him, and she is being given to him by me; why then do you forbid me as I am giving away this daughter? (162)
Having spoken thus, he fell asleep together with his wife and daughter. || 163 ||
Then, having arrived at midnight while the daughter of Bhṛgu was asleep, I carried her off and brought her to my own abode during the night while the people were sleeping.
For she had been appointed by me through the power of desire, even though she was unwilling; thereafter, her father, the Brahmin, woke up in the morning. (165)
"Where is that daughter of mine? By whom has she been carried off or lost? Then, he wandered outside near his own grove in search of her.
Followed by many sages along the path of the foot-tracks, he then beheld that maiden, who had performed the auspicious marriage rites.
Weeping there with a loud sound, feeling ashamed and with her face cast downward, that descendant of Bhṛgu, his soul overcome with anger, then spoke to me.
"Since my daughter was married by you according to the rite of a night-stalker, you shall now become a night-stalker as a result of this very act. (169)
Ghaṇṭaka said: "O best of the twice-born, why do you so quickly curse me, who am blameless? This [cow] was given to me by you yourself; therefore, I took her at night."
That evil-minded man who, having previously given away his daughter, later withholds her, goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Then he reflected: "What has been spoken by him is true. Overcome with remorse, he spoke these words: (172)
What you have spoken is true; my word shall not be otherwise. You will assume the form of an owl, of this there is no doubt.
And when the great sage Bhartṛyajña shall arise here, having received his instruction, you will again obtain your own body.
Then I saw myself indeed in the form of Kauśika; nevertheless, my memory of my former existence was not lost.

Then, that daughter of his who had been married by me on that mountain at that time—she too, beholding me in that state and filled with grief, entered the fire, being unwilling to remain a widow. (176)
Thus, O Kauśika of great luster, this state has indeed arisen for me through the curse of Bhārgava, which was uttered by you regarding the maiden. (177)
Because Maheśvara was worshipped with an unbroken bilva leaf, he attained long life; this which I have spoken is the truth. (178)
"Tell me the truth; what service may I perform for you who have come to my home, O illustrious one, even if it be very difficult to accomplish? (179)
Indradyumna said: "I have come into your presence for the sake of attaining knowledge; I was brought here by Nāḍījaṅgha while I was resolved upon death. (180)
If you do not recognize him by his fame and his lineage, then I shall surely enter the blazing fire.
If not, then name some other long-lived person for me; I shall go and ask him whether he knows it or not. (182)
Baka said: "What has been spoken by him today is fitting; therefore, O sir, do that and tell him if you know anyone who is longer-lived than yourself. (183)
If not, then I too shall quickly enter the fire right now, even together with Mārkaṇḍeya, while you look on.
Knowing this, O illustrious one, reflect upon some ancient [place] elsewhere on the surface of the earth, so that you may become a long-lived being. (185)
"Indeed, I have come to your temple with supreme devotion; this man, Mārkaṇḍeya, is especially dear to me. (186)
There are hundreds and thousands of excellent mountains here, in which dwell highly fortunate ascetics who have lived for a long time; otherwise, his life could not possibly be sustained in any way.
"It would be for the supreme benefit of the royal sage Indradyumna, as well as for both of us; therefore, reflect upon this quickly. (188)
Having understood that resolve of the king regarding his own death, that owl, moved by compassion, then spoke these words: || 189 ||
"If it is thus, O illustrious one, that you now desire to die, then come with me to Mount Gandhamādana. (190)
A vulture dwells there, and he is my greatest friend; being long-standing and well-acquainted, he will surely know that king. At my word, he will undoubtedly speak of him without any doubt. (191)
Having heard those words of his, all three—Mārkaṇḍeya and the others—said to him, "O highly fortunate one, do not enter the fire. (192)
"We shall all go there together with you; perhaps he too recognizes King Indradyumna. (193)
Having heard those words of theirs, the king, filled with supreme devotion, set out for Gandhamādana together with all of them.
The king of vultures, seeing them all with palms joined in reverence, beheld the owl before him and, being greatly delighted, went forward to meet him.
Then, with a joyful soul, he said: "Welcome to you, O best of the twice-born! It has been a long time since we last met. And who are these others who are standing here?"
Ulūka said: "This crane Nāḍījaṅgha is known to me as my supreme friend; moreover, Mārkaṇḍa stands as his most intimate companion. (197)
He is renowned throughout the three worlds on earth, remembering seven kalpas; yet I do not know anyone who is even his friend, let alone [his enemy], so quickly.

"Indeed, while dying, he was brought by me into your presence; it has been discovered that this Indradyumna, the lord of men, is alive. Otherwise, he would have quickly entered the blazing fire. (199)
If you know him, then speak of Indradyumna, the lord of the earth; I have come here to question you, for you are as ancient as I am.
The vulture said: "I do not remember a king renowned as Indradyumna; neither have I seen nor heard of such a lord of the earth, Indradyumna. (201)
Having heard those words of his, the king also became deeply dejected; with death firmly resolved upon, he reflected within his mind.
Then, filled with curiosity, he questioned that best of the twice-born: "Tell me, by what action was such a long life as this obtained? (203)
"Therefore, having heard from you about the Fire-god, I shall pay him my respects. (204)
The vulture said: "I was indeed a monkey in the city of Camatkārapura, right there on the slope of Mount Raktaśṛṅga. (205)
In that very place is the great temple of Śambhu, resembling Mount Mandara, known by the name Citreśvara, which destroys all sins.
When spring had arrived there, the people of the city and the countryside came together, and a truly great festival was celebrated.

In a delightful forest near the Liṅga, where trees bore fruit in all seasons, which was beloved by women and enchanting to the people, a beautiful Liṅga was joyfully installed upon a swing made from a tree.
Having performed the worship with *damanaka* flowers and having placed [the deity] upon a well-secured swing, they later returned to their own homes after worshipping the Three-eyed One.
Then, at the onset of night, my heart filled with curiosity, I rocked that most enchanting swing again and again.
While I was thus being shaken on the swing, men arrived at that time; some of them, having struck me with clubs from every direction, terrified me.
Then, having quickly attained death in that very sanctuary, he was reborn in a royal palace, endowed with the memory of his former birth.
The son of Koṭīśvara was renowned by the name Kuśadhvaja; from him, the kingdom of my father and grandfather was obtained by me in due succession. (213)
When ten million years have passed, having gone to the other world by my own karma, I shall swing the illustrious Jāgeśvara according to my desire.

Then, after a long time, Lord Hara was pleased with me by means of the mantras born of the Śiva-siddhānta that had been imparted by my guru; he spoke these words: "I am the bestower of boons upon you. (215)
O Kuśadhvaja, I am well-pleased with your supreme faith; choose a boon—may you be blessed—that has long resided in your heart. (216)
Then, having bowed down, I spoke loudly to that Blessed Lord Hara: || 217 ||
"If you are pleased with me, O God, then make me your own attendant; even sovereignty over the three worlds does not please me now as anything else. (218)
Having been addressed thus by me, that god placed me upon his celestial chariot and suddenly conveyed me to the highly meritorious realm of Śiva.
Then, by the grace of Bhavānī and Hara, I sport there according to my own will, established in the midst of the Gaṇas.
Then, after some time, having ascended his excellent celestial chariot and wandering at will, he arrived right here upon this great mountain.
When the spring season had arrived and the southern wind was blowing, the daughter of Agniveśya was seen standing naked in the midst of the water.
Surrounded by many female companions, sporting according to her desire, that lotus-eyed girl with lips like the *bimba* fruit could yet be grasped within a single fist in the midst of them. (223)
With breasts like bilva fruits, a face like the moon, and endowed with all auspicious marks, I was indeed possessed by the god of love at that very moment.
Then, having descended from that foremost of celestial chariots, she was seized by me by the hand; meanwhile, she uttered piteous cries like a female osprey.
Then those daughters of the lords of sages who were standing there in the water went weeping into the presence of Agniveśya.
"O Brahmin, your daughter is being led away by some celestial traveler, seated upon a magnificent aerial chariot, crying out unrestrainedly. (227)
Having heard that, he then became enraged; looking toward the path of the sky, he set out from his hermitage, rebuking [him] again and again.
Crying out, "Stay! Stay!", he paralyzed it on all sides; by the fierce ascetic power of the brahmin, my celestial chariot was brought to a standstill.
Then, filled with great anger, he said to me: "O sinner, because this girl was now being sported with by you while she was playing... (230)
"O evil-minded one, just as a piece of flesh is seized against one's will by a vulture, so let you become a vulture immediately at my word; of this there is no doubt. (231)
Having been addressed thus by him, I was overwhelmed with shame; having offered my daughter to him and prostrating before him again and again, [I departed]. || 232 ||
Then I spoke to that brahmin Agniveśya, who was great in asceticism: "Your daughter was not recognized by me; you ought not to be angry. (233)
O Lord of Sages, act in such a way that I do not become a vulture.
Then I was told by him: "My word can never be false; therefore, you shall become a vulture. (235)
O base one, when you go to the illustrious Bhartṛyajña for the sake of instruction, it will be by the advice of Ānarta. (236)

And having obtained atonement for that, you shall depart from the state of a vulture. While I was searching for him, he was neither seen nor heard by me; though I became despondent in my condition as a vulture, the end of the curse did not come to me.
The vulture said: "I have explained all this to you—the cause of my state as a vulture, and how my lifespan came to be beyond calculation. (238)
Indradyumna said: Grant me permission quickly; I shall enter the fire, for having attained such detachment, I have no desire at all to live.
Thus addressed by him, he then reflected in his mind: "He has come into my presence accompanied by his friend; therefore, I shall perform a most rare service for him to the best of my ability. (24)
Then, having attained the highest courtesy, he spoke to him with affection: "O sir, do not prepare the fire; first listen to my words. (241)
I shall proclaim to you that which is even more ancient than I.
Whoever shall know him will have no doubt that he is King Indradyumna.
Therefore, come with me to the presence of that Great-Souled One, accompanied by all your followers as well as myself.
Indradyumna said: "O virtuous twice-born one, who is even superior to you in terms of the desire for life? This curiosity of mine is great; therefore, speak, O high-minded one. (244)
The vulture said: "There is a long-lived tortoise named Mantharaka who dwells in Lake Mānasa; he is well-known and will know of Indradyumna."
Having heard those words of his, Mārkaṇḍeya and the other two addressed that best of kings, who was resolved upon death.
"O highly fortunate one, what has been spoken by the wise king of vultures is fitting; we shall all go there where that tortoise is situated. (247)
"Perseverance is the root of prosperity, as all the learned who know the treatises on ethics proclaim; therefore, come, let us go. (248)
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, O best of Brahmins, the king with great difficulty turned back from death and attained supreme detachment.
Then they all set out from Mount Gandhamādana, having directed their course toward the supreme Mānasa lake; and so, traveling through the air, they arrived there in due order.
That beautiful lake Mānasa was frequented by a tortoise who, having emerged from the water, remained there at his pleasure during the summer heat.
And having seen those four and gazed upon them for a very long time, he recognized them all and then vanished into the water.
Then Kauśika spoke to him as he was turning his face away and departing: "O friend, having seen me, you have become averse [to me]. (253)
Even one who has fallen to a low state, upon returning home, becomes most worthy of honor by the virtuous.
Then, O best of the twice-born, standing in the midst of the water with only his head visible above, he replied with humility to that vulture.
I have not turned my face away from you after seeing both of you immediately before; this fifth one among you, who is a great man, now approaches.

Out of fear of that King Indradyumna, I have fled; for in former times, my back was constantly scorched by the sacrificial fire of this king while he was performing sacrifices at Rocaka, that most excellent of cities.
Furthermore, remembering this, a very great fear has arisen within me; it is the great renown of the royal sage Indradyumna that I have taken refuge in. (258)
When these words had been spoken by Kamaṭha, a divine messenger then arrived from heaven at the command of the Supreme Lord.
The divine messenger said: "Come, come, O royal sage, now to the presence of Brahmā. I have been told by Brahmā, O King, that his fame is of many kinds."
When even a small portion [of this] becomes manifest upon the surface of the earth, then King Āneya must be quickly brought here to my world, which is so difficult to attain.
Therefore, come; let us go. Ascend the celestial chariot, for I shall lead you to the presence of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
Indradyumna said: "If these friends of mine—the crane, the owl, and the tortoise—come along with me together with Mārkaṇḍeya," (263)
"I shall come with you to the presence of Brahmā; otherwise I will not come. This which I have spoken is the truth. (264)
The divine messenger said: "All these attendants of Hara have fallen to the earth due to a curse; at the end of the curse, they will undoubtedly go back to the presence of Hara. (265)
Therefore, O King, come, let us depart quickly from here after leaving these behind; for heaven does not please them unless the Lord Maheśvara is released.
Indradyumna said: "If it is so, go; may you be blessed. I shall not go to Triviṣṭapa. I will strive in such a way that I shall become a Gaṇa."
"For one remaining there, the fear of falling will certainly and eternally exist. Having been addressed thus by him, he then took up his celestial chariot.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, the messenger was overcome with great embarrassment; Indradyumna, filled with humility, questioned that tortoise once more.
"Tell us, O tortoise, what was your own deed, since you are so ancient? By what action was this state of being a tortoise attained? Tell me quickly. (270)
The tortoise said: "In former times, while still established in childhood, I was a renowned Brahmin named Śāṇḍilya in the beautiful city of Camatkārapura. (271)
While playing at will in all manner of childhood games, he built a house for Śambhu out of baked bricks; then, having taken the Jāgeśvara Liṅga from there, he installed it within that house.
Then, filled with devotion, I worshipped [the deity] day after day, playing with children and surrounded by them, without the use of mantras. || 273 ||
Then, after some time had passed, when death was imminent, I was indeed born as a Brahmin possessing the memory of my former births in the city of Vaidiśa.
Then, my devotion toward the god Hara increased even further; having gone out daily for alms, I obtained much wealth. (276)
Having constructed a structure merely the size of a palace, a liṅga was installed by me; thereafter, I worshiped the god Paśupati Hara with devotion. || 276 ||
Endowed with the knowledge of Brahman, subsisting on food obtained through alms, and fully committed to celibacy, he should chant the name of Śiva three times a day.
Then, by that power, in another birth I became a sovereign ruler of the earth, endowed with the recollection of my former lives.
Thereafter, O great king, I caused to be built countless palaces for the Three-eyed Lord, resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa. (279)
"O King, such worship as has been described here, arising from many flowers—I perform nothing else here, such as the giving of dharma or other gifts. (280)
Then, after a long time, the moon-crested Lord was pleased with me; thereupon, O royal sage, he spoke, smiling with gentle words: (281)
Jayadatta, I am well-pleased with you, O best of kings! Because of this devotion, speak quickly; what desired thing shall I grant to you? (282)

Then, having prostrated with the eight limbs and offered various kinds of praise, I said to Hara, "O King, make me free from old age and death. Having promised "So be it," he indeed vanished from sight.

The god Aprameyagati is the lord of the fourteen worlds; therefore, endowed with contentment and free from old age and death, I wander upon the surface of the earth at my own will, devoid of enemies. (284)
Then, after a long time had passed, O best of kings, he was tormented by the fire of many desires and remained devoid of devotion to Śiva.
Whichever beautiful woman of another, rich in form and captivating to the mind, I behold, I gaze upon her for a long time and thereafter violate her. (286)
Having abandoned the fear of the King of Dharma (Yama), he has attained the status of a sovereign ruler.
In the meantime, O King, due to my sinful deed, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the entire surface of the earth. || 288 ||
In the meantime, Dharmarāja arrived in the presence of Śiva; immediately thereafter, being deeply distressed, he prostrated himself and spoke aloud.
O Lord, by you, being well-pleased, the protector of the earth Jayadatta was created upon the surface of the earth, exempt from old age and death. || 29 ||
That evil-minded man forcibly destroys the chastity of virtuous women; consequently, all people, out of fear of the king, are excluded from all righteous dharma.
O best of the wise, I have not been born from any inherent nature whatsoever; I tell you the truth: I do not have even a single fear.
Therefore, restrain him quickly before righteousness perishes entirely from the world of mortals through this violation of virtuous women.
Thus addressed, the god, filled with great anger, summoned me as I stood trembling with palms joined in reverence and cursed me. (294)
"Since you have committed a censurable deed through wicked conduct, therefore, consumed by my curse, you shall indeed become a tortoise. (295)
Then, being deeply distressed, I prayed to the Supreme Lord: "O Lord, bring an end to my curse; show mercy toward me. (296)
Then he spoke again: "At the end of the eon known as the sixty, having regained your own body, you shall become one of my attendants."
In the meantime, O lord of the earth, I was born as a tortoise; having reached the waters of the ocean, I remained there, constantly distressed. (298)
Then, after some time had passed, O King, while you were staying upon the earth, you brought the water of the ocean for the purpose of sacrifice. (299)
Having been established upon the surface of the earth and likewise rendered motionless by mantras, hundreds of thousands of sacrifices were then performed over me.

O Great King, although my back was being scorched on all sides by those sacrificial fires while they were being kindled, and though I was burning at that time, my life did not depart because of the grace of Maheśvara. || 301 ||
Only a burning sensation arises, just as from a sin committed in the past; and all of that has undoubtedly been experienced due to the wrath of Hara. (302)
Then, O best of kings, when you had ascended to heaven and the surface of the earth had become a single ocean filled with water, I arrived, floating thereupon, at Lake Mānasa.
Fifty-six kalpas have passed while I remained [in this state]; liberation will come about through four others by virtue of my being in the form of a tortoise. (304)
All this has been explained as the cause of long life: through the propitiation of Hara and the worship of the Lord with many flowers. (305)

"And tell me how Kāmadeva was born as a tortoise out of anger; O illustrious one, tell me what service I may now perform for you who have come to my home—even that which lies in the heart of an enemy. (306)
"For a very long time, my back has been scorched by you with the sacrificial fire; even today, I still see it as if it were standing there blazing."

For this reason, O Lord of the Earth, I have perished upon seeing you; why did you not go to heaven even though the celestial chariot had arrived? It is for this reason that kings practice righteousness. || 308 ||
Indradyumna said: "Even in the abode of heaven, there is constant fear of falling for those in the worlds; therefore, I shall not go there, but I will strive for liberation. (309)
If you will perform the duty for me who have come to your house at this sacrifice, tell me, if you possess such long-standing friendship, what it is.
The tortoise said: "There is a brahmin-sage named Lomaśa who is more ancient than I; it is heard that he has been seen by me, having taken refuge on the bank of a river."
Indradyumna said: "Therefore, come, let us all go quickly ourselves to ask the reason for this long life. (312)
Then those five, having come together, remained in the path of the sky; then they beheld there Lomaśa, who was without any support.

To one who is devoted to the private recitation of sacred texts, self-controlled, and intent upon muttering prayers and performing fire-sacrifices, [he gave shelter] with a mass of grass held in his left hand for the sake of shade.
Indeed, holding a rosary in his right hand, they saw that great-souled one; having circumambulated him, they all sat down and were greeted with a welcome. || 315 ||
Then he asked them: "Who are you, and why have you come here? Tell me with confidence so that I may do everything for you. (316)
The tortoise said: "O virtuous sage, this brahmin-sage named Mārkaṇḍa indeed remembers seven kalpas; he has been brought here by King Indradyumna."

Near this Bakas, however, was the wise Nāḍījaṅgha; having learned that his own life would be long-lasting, and knowing that Indradyumna’s news would take twice as long as his own remaining lifespan, [he remained there]. (318)
Then, when that lord of the earth was not recognized by him, both of them arrived in the presence of this owl.
O excellent twice-born one, twice as many kalpas as that duration have passed for this great-souled king, yet he has not been recognized by him.
Then all three were also brought into the presence of the king of the vultures.
O virtuous twice-born one, fifty-six kalpas have passed for this great-souled king, yet he has not been recognized by him.
All four were likewise brought by him into my presence; and knowing me to be long-lived, O twice-born one, they approached me with a friendly disposition.
"I too recognized him from afar as he approached; for this is surely Indradyumna, whose back was formerly scorched by me. (324)
Having been subdued beneath the earth by that sacrificial fire through mantras, I fled from fear of it, while being held back by vultures and other birds.
Though he entered the water out of affection due to many reproaches, I then said to him once more: "I am not turned away from you. (326)
"Indradyumna, by whose sacrificial fire my back was burnt—meanwhile, a high-minded messenger of the gods arrived before this great-souled one, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot. (327)
This lord of the earth, Kīrti, fell from heaven; immediately after I had spoken, a celestial chariot arrived from the sky.
