"O best of the twice-born, he did not go to heaven without us—excluding Mārkaṇḍeya and including the three who had entered the wombs of animals. (329)
When he questioned me, I further declared my own lifespan: ninety-six kalpas have passed while I have been living.
"I was already asked about this previously; standing here by your side, I am the most ancient one, and you were informed by me. (331)
For this reason, we have all come into your presence; therefore, O King, explain that which he asks of you.
Bhartṛyajña said: Then Lomaśa spoke to him: "O King, ask with confidence; I shall certainly tell you whatever you ask of me. (333)
Indradyumna said: "Why, even though it is the summer season and the sun has reached the meridian, do you not build a beautiful house for the sake of dwelling? Why will you not do so? (334)
Lomaśa said: For whose sake is a house built, since life is impermanent? If the body were eternal, then it would be built for its sake. || 335 ||
Indradyumna said: "Among all people in the worlds, you are heard to be long-lived; for that reason, I have come here with the desire to behold you. (336)
Lomaśa said: "With the arrival of every kalpa, my hair perishes; and when all the hair has ceased to exist, then my destruction will follow."
Behold this body of mine, which is exposed and devoid of hair; for that reason, O high-minded one, I do not build a house.
Indradyumna said: "What deed was performed by you, by which such a life has been sustained? Is this the power of charity, or of austerity, or of religious observance? (339)
Lomaśa said: "In former times, I was a Śūdra overwhelmed by poverty; I used to wander constantly over the surface of the earth for the sake of my belly. (34)
Through great application of ritual action, he reached Hāṭakeśvara; there, emaciated by hunger and afflicted by thirst, he beheld this supreme self-manifested Liṅga, which was then shaken by me.
Having taken this cool and perfectly pure water used for bathing, I then performed worship with these lotuses.
Then, having completed the worship, while I was still on the road, my life-breaths departed as my throat became parched with hunger. || 343 ||
Then, O King, having been born in the house of a Brahmin, I remembered my former births; I remember everything because of my worship of the God of gods.
Thereupon, having fallen into muteness, I did not speak anything at all; my father, filled with great joy, gave me the name Īśāna.
For he had previously been propitiated by Īśāna, who granted him [the boon]; having performed sacrifices and perceived the nature of worldly existence, he attained supreme detachment.

Out of great affection for me, my father would administer medicines, employ spells and incantations, and likewise offer prayers of petition; day and night, he remained untiring in constantly consulting the Brahmins.
Then, O lord of men, laughter arises within my own mind upon seeing the intense attachment to worldly existence of both my father and mother. (348)
Then, O best of kings, when he gradually attained youth, he abandoned those two at night and came here to join me.
Then, with a joyful mind and constant composure, I worship Īśāna with supreme devotion, having bathed him with water. (35)

O best of kings, having adopted the practice of gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*), he maintained his life-sustenance three times a day at the various bathing-places of the Brāhmaṇī, subsisting on wild rice (*nīvāra*), jujube fruits (*badara*), vegetables, cucumbers (*cirbhaṭa*), and fruits and leaves.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, Hara, the sovereign of all gods, having appeared before me, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: || 352 ||
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; choose a boon, O virtuous one! I shall grant it even if it be ungivable, were it even the most difficult to obtain. (353)
Then, having prostrated before him and praised him loudly with various kinds of words, I said: "O Lord, create one who is free from old age and death. (354)
The Blessed One said: Since immortality does not exist anywhere here in this world of mortals, you must therefore establish a limit for your own life.
Then the Blessed One said to me: "O Lord of the Thirty-three, when the end of the eon has arrived, let the destruction of but a single hair of mine occur. (356)
And when the destruction of all my body hairs occurs, O Lord, may I then attain the status of being one of your attendants. (357)
"It shall be so," he said; "therefore, my supreme *liṅga* must always be bathed with this very water produced by the Brāhmaṇī. (398)
O best of the twice-born, you shall be worshiped by Brahmā and the others at the three times of day, and your life shall endure as long as my own reign.
Any other man as well who shall worship me here with devotion and bathe me with true piety will become free from sin.
O best of the twice-born, there shall never be untimely death for him, even when my body has been worshipped but once by Brahmā and the other gods.
He who drinks even once the water originating from the Brahma-tīrtha becomes, at that very moment, a soul purified of all sins.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods then vanished from sight.
But from that time forth, O King, I have remained here, always worshipping this linga with true devotion. (364)
For this reason, my lifespan has become exceedingly vast; it is through the grace of Śaṅkara, and there is no other cause for it here. (365)
Indradyumna said: "I too shall worship this very Liṅga along with you; I will not go elsewhere—such is the firm resolve in my heart. (366)
Lomaśa said: "Do so, O highly fortunate one; you shall obtain what you desire. For a person devoted to Hara, nothing desired is difficult to attain. (367)
"Let Nāḍījaṅgha go home; as for Mārkaṇḍa, the vulture, and the owl, you must stay in my hermitage together with the tortoise. (368)
Then they all said: "O Lord of Men, we shall certainly not return again to our own abode without you; rather, we shall worship this very Linga which has been adored by you. (369)
Having spoken thus, they all remained in the excellent hermitage of Lomaśa and worshipped that very Liṅga at the three times of day.
Having bathed him with the waters of Brāhmaṇīs, they worship him with lotuses and other offerings.
Then, after some time, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived at that place where they were, in the course of his pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Then, having seen Nārada and performed the rites of hospitality, and knowing that he was rested, they questioned him with great humility.
"O great sage, we have all fallen from our [divine] state due to a curse, beginning with Saṃvarta and ending with Kūrma—namely, the four starting with Baka. (374)
He is not recognized anywhere; in what place is he situated? What is his form, what is his measure, what is his conduct, and where does he abide? (375)
Therefore, O illustrious one, if you know where that sage is staying, please tell me; for there is nothing that lies beyond the scope of your knowledge.
Śrī Nārada said: I know that Saṃvarta, the best of sages, thoroughly; he remains in secret conduct, and no one else knows him in any way whatsoever. (377)
That great sage Avadhūta remained constantly in Vārāṇasī; naked, his limbs smeared with filth, he always took refuge in the forest.
For the sake of alms, he would enter that city during the Kutapa period; indeed, he always took his food from certain houses using only his hands as a bowl.
Again, in the evening, he went to yet another forest region; and in that city, there were hundreds and thousands of women of such appearance.
The best of ascetics remain there; I shall describe their characteristics to you, so that by my word you may know him without doubt. (381)
And at the main gate of Vārāṇasī, the corpse must be placed with great care and kept secret, so that no one may know of it. (382)
All the ascetics shall pass by him in great numbers, but Saṃvarta, possessing divine vision, will not bypass Śalya.
But he who performed the withdrawal from that ground where the corpse lay is to be recognized as Saṃvarta; he is to be questioned thereafter.
If he asks, "By whom was I informed of you? then it should be said: "By Nārada; for he indeed knows you always."
If that Nārada asks again, "Where does he stay? [then speak as follows].
Then, having offered [the oblation] to you, he should address the fire-god as he departs.
Having heard those words of Nārada, Lomaśa and all the others, longing for a vision of him, reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Having placed a corpse secretly at the city gate, unobserved by people, they themselves stood at a distance, watching with great care. (389)
Then, at the time of Kutapa, Saṃvarta arrived, possessing the very form that had previously been described by the high-souled Nārada.
Having seen that corpse there with his divine vision, the great sage turned back; though afflicted by hunger and thirst, he did not cross over the thorn at all.
Then, addressing him, they followed after him at that time, crying out, "Stop! Stop! Grant us your favor! (3920)
He too, reviling them and saying, "Turn back! Do not come near me," fled away. (393)
Then, having gone even further, he, overcome by hunger, spoke.
"Tell me quickly by whom I have been commanded; by whom I shall reduce that sinner to ashes in the fire of my curse. (395)
They said: "Indeed, you were pointed out to us by Nārada as being present here; having told us this, he immediately entered the fire. (396)
Saṃvarta said: "I am indeed the one who has now acted against that wicked man, by whom I was directed to adopt this secret conduct of yours. (397)
They said: "O Blessed One, O Great Sage, you have been pointed out to us by Nārada; though we have been searching for a long time, no one else knows you. (398)
O best of Brahmins, having offered that [oblation] to us, he entered the fire; we do not know the cause of that which happened at that very moment.
Saṃvarta said: "I too, being exceedingly enraged, was prepared to utter a curse."
For this very reason, that which is performed by oneself is indeed [the same as] what has been done by him.
Therefore, tell me quickly: for what reason have you all come together?
I shall not remain here for long, nor will I wander toward the city; for I myself shall beg for alms solely for the sake of sustaining my life. (402)
"Let the path be cleared of thorns and let this corpse be removed; otherwise, I shall utter a curse if you do not act accordingly. (403)
Therefore, I must not be mentioned to anyone here; King Marutta is constantly searching for me. (404)
"I will by no means perform a sacrifice for that king, for that lord of the earth has been abandoned by his preceptor, Dhiṣaṇa. (405)
And knowing me to be the son of the Guru, he indeed searches for me from there. || 406 ||
They said: "O excellent sage, all four of us, Baka and the others, have fallen by a curse; indeed, we have attained the state of birds due to the curse of a Brahmin. (407)
We, who were indeed the hosts of Maheśvara and were honored by the three worlds, have been brought to the state of animal birth and have attained supreme detachment. (408)
The end of the curse was ordained by those brahmins to arise from a woman; through your instruction, Baka and the others have therefore sought refuge with you. (409)
Therefore, O illustrious one, O Lord, protect me now from this state of being a bird.
"You are weary from having practiced the state of a bird for a long time; this is the reason, and none other, arising from your association with me. (413)
Saṃvarta said: "If it is so, let us go quickly toward Camatkārapura; Bhartṛyajña, who removes all doubts, is also staying there. (412)
He will indeed grant a most excellent instruction to all of you; by that, you shall attain the resolution of your doubt and [knowledge of] the past exactly as it occurred.
He was formerly Yājñavalkya, who had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures; then, in another birth, he was known as Kātyāyana.
Then, having attained another body, he became the renowned brahmin Vararuci; thereafter, in yet another body, he indeed became the son of a courtesan.
The goddess, the daughter of Brahmā, who is eternally embodied as Speech, was propitiated; yet the goddess herself was not satisfied, perceiving some underlying cause.
But having been born from a Brahmin, upon reaching the end of his body, Sarasvatī herself entered his mouth. (417)
Constantly propitiated in the past, she never deserts him; yet another marvel occurred for that son of a courtesan at the sacrifice. (419)
It reaches the Brahma-sūtra, passes out through the shoulder, and departs. || 419 ||
He alone, and no one else here, removes the doubts of those established in the sacrificial rites of the ancient worlds.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his and having prostrated themselves again and again, they went, urged by Saṃvarta, to where the corpse was.
Having drawn that [image] from there, they all went to Camatkārapura; having seen it stationed there at the sacred site of Vāstusthānapada, they remained there. || 422 ||
Then, having prostrated themselves and remaining humble, they all said: "Indeed, we four alone have been utterly consumed by the curse of a Brahmin."
Three have attained the state of birds, and another the state of a tortoise; these three who stand by our side are the most eminent.
This one has indeed been called Mārkaṇḍeya, and another is Indradyumna; the third is named Lomaśa, renowned as a man of great asceticism. (425)
Now, these three alone are weary of life; you ought to show them favor by granting them instruction.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of theirs, the great sage Bhartṛyajña reflected for a long time and, having understood through his divine eye, spoke.
"Having assembled together, you seven shall each install a linga in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, near the one named Antika. (428)
Then, offer these seven gifts before them; they are known as the "Family Mountains" and are removers of all sins.
Then you shall obtain your desired, divine, and beautiful form, as well as the status of an attendant to the high-souled God of gods, the Three-eyed One.
They said: "O Lord, O Great Sage, proclaim in detail the gift we shall bestow upon them, as well as its measure and the ritual procedure. (431)
Bhartṛyajña said: Meru made of gold should be given, Kailāsa produced from silver, Himādri from cotton, and Gandhamādana from molasses. (432)
Then, according to the prescribed ritual, Suvela should be offered with sesame seeds, Vindhya likewise with sugar, and Śṛṅgin with salt.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his and having established [the image] according to the prescribed rites, || 100 ||
Afterwards, they presented seven lingas as the Kulaparvatas.
In front of Indradyumneśvara, the powerful Indradyumna, abiding by the opinion of Bhartṛyajña, fashioned Mount Meru out of gold.
O best of the twice-born, Kailāsa was given by the wise Mārkaṇḍa to the god Mārkaṇḍeśvara with devotion.
A cotton Himavat mountain was given by Pālaka to the twice-born; furthermore, a mountain known as Gandhamādana made of jaggery was presented before him.
O best of the twice-born, the excellent mountain Suvela was given by Ghaṇṭaka to the god Ghaṇṭakeśvara by Kacchapa.
Likewise, before the deity Kacchapeśvara, a mountain made of sesame seeds and one made of sugar were then offered with devotion. (439)
O best of the twice-born, Śaila [performed this] before his own deity known as Īśāna, and before the Lord of the Monkeys (Vānareśvara).
Then the great mountain named Lavaṇa, known as Śṛṅgin, was offered by the vulture with a heart purified by faith, O illustrious one.
O Brahmins, a marvel occurred there as soon as those excellent mountains were given: their state as birds vanished, and that of the other [the tortoise] likewise vanished.
At that very moment, by his power, all those excellent Brahmins who stood before him became wearers of divine garlands and garments, and were anointed with divine perfumes.
And at that very moment, the celestial chariots of all of them arrived. || 1 ||
Having reached Bhartṛyajña and prostrated before those twice-born ones, they ascended an excellent celestial chariot and arrived at Mount Kailāsa.
All this has been narrated to you—how that group of seven lingas, which destroys all sins, came to be manifested in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Furthermore, anyone else who, endowed with devotion, performs the gift of a mountain for their lineage (kulaparvata-dāna) shall also go to Śiva.
That mortal who, having risen in the morning, beholds those lingas, shall attain liberation even from the sin committed through ignorance. || 447 ||
And whoever bestows these seven mountains here in sequence upon the twice-born in front of their own respective lingas shall go to the third heaven.

Having remained there for another kalpa and having enjoyed the company of excellent apsarases, and after enjoying divine pleasures, when he is born upon earth, he attains the status of a universal monarch and is born as a sovereign ruler of the whole world. || 449 ||
By the gift of one [lamp], the destruction of sin occurs; by two, sons, grandsons, and desired fruits are obtained. (450)
By three [qualities] one becomes a king; by four, a lord of a maṇḍala; and by five, one becomes the sovereign of the land of Bhārata. (451)
The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) declared this: that the lord of Jambudvīpa becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) by means of six [mountains], and one with seven, when they are duly bestowed. || 452 ||
O best of Brahmins, such a man shall always be born as a superior Brahmin in birth after birth; he is never born miserable, poor, or diseased. (453)
Endowed with good fortune and happiness, he shall possess a beautiful body and be rich in jewels; though released from all royal power, he shall be majestic and have conquered his senses.
Therefore, with every effort, especially by rulers of the earth, these mountains should be given, dedicating them to their own chosen deities.
The sages said: "O lord of the earth, regarding that which was stated by you—that in former times the Lord granted to Īśāna a lifespan equal to his own day—"
"Tell us, what shall be the measure of that day? Sūta said: "I shall proclaim to you the measure of the day."
O best of Brahmins, listen clearly as I speak concerning the measurement of time for the devotee of Maheśvara: one-fourth of a *nimeṣa* is a *truṭi*, and two of those constitute a *lava*.
Two *lava*s are said to be one *yava*; fifteen of those are a *kāṣṭhā*. They say thirty *kāṣṭhā*s are a *kalā*, and thirty *kalā*s are considered a *kṣaṇa*.
Sixty kṣaṇas are said to constitute one pala, and sixty of those make one nāḍikā; two nāḍikās are proclaimed to be one muhūrta.
The wise have declared that a day and night consists of thirty muhūrtas; a month consists of thirty days and nights, and they know two months to constitute one season (ṛtu).
Three seasons constitute a solstice, and two solstices constitute a year; this indeed is proclaimed as the year for all human beings.

Those who know the Purāṇas declare that to be a day and night of the gods; the northern course (ayana) is the bright fortnight, which is the day of the gods, while the southern course is their night, during which auspicious deeds are censured.
Just as a sleeping man perceives no enjoyments or the like, so too the gods do not accept their shares of the sacrifice in any way whatsoever.
O best of the twice-born, by this very measure of time, it is proclaimed that [a Manvantara] consists of seventeen lakhs of years.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of twenty-eight thousand years; during that time, the Lord Viṣṇu, who is the preceptor of the world, was white.
The people were liberated from sin, peaceful, self-controlled, and masters of their senses; likewise, they were all long-lived and ever established in austerity.
In whatever manner a man receives his birth, in that same manner he dies; nowhere is death seen by fathers as something arising from their son. (13)
O best of the twice-born, desire, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and envy do not arise among men in that age.
Then, O best of sages, the second age, the Tretā Yuga, was to come; at that time, fierce sin entered Dharma by means of one quarter.
Thereupon the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana assumes a state of passion; and even when a portion of sin has arrived, people become full of rivalry.
Thereafter, for the sake of attaining the path to heaven, they all performed sacrifices, such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, as well as many oblations and similar rites.
Then, by means of their own sacrificial rites, they go to the worlds of the gods, from the root-world up to the fourteenth, reaching as far as the world of Brahmā.
Some are born there with very short lifespans and filled with rivalry; yet even there, my sons, they do not meet death by any means whatsoever.
While the Janaka exists, even minor faults such as desire, anger, and the like are proclaimed to both exist and not exist. (20)
In a single season, the Vaiśyas devoted to agriculture reap seven times the excellent crop that was sown there.
All the cows yield a jar of milk; the buffaloes yield four times that amount, and the camels yield four times as much as those. || 22 ||

Goats and sheep, as well as women, all likewise receive but a quarter [of the merit]. Furthermore, those who are perfected in the study of the Vedas and have renounced the acceptance of gifts become capable of performing acts of both cursing and blessing. || 23 ||

The Kṣatriyas protect the earth according to the duty of their order; there, no thief is seen, nor is there ever a paramour. All the social classes are established in their respective duties and remain devoted to their own specific obligations.
And that [first] is proclaimed to consist of twelve lakhs of years; the second, most excellent yuga consists of nine hundred and sixty thousand [years]. (25)

Lust, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and envy—these six are born there, and jealousy is the seventh. (28)
Then, having associated with one another, those men engage in mutual opposition and do not attain heaven.

Even the four-armed Lord becomes dark-complexioned there; and as long as even a single foot of Dharma remains, so long does he prevail.
Until it eventually meets its destruction, its measure is specified as being exactly four hundred thousand [verses], gradually [increasing] little by little.

And in the twelfth [year], she shall be a maiden united with a husband.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Yugas," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, by a thousand of these [years], a day becomes calculable; on that day, fourteen thousand-eyed beings are born.
The seventh, however, is the thousand-eyed one who currently exists here on the fourteenth day of the seventy-first *saṃvarta* of Brahmā.
The Manus and others likewise exercise sovereignty over the Yugas; beginning with Svāyambhuva, they remain established just as the Śakras do.

When this present cycle of four yugas has passed and only a remnant remains, Bali will become Indra by the grace of Vāsudeva.
By him, the kingdom was promised to him during the eighth Manu period.
In this way, all the other gods, numbering thirty-three crores, shall come into being just as they did in former times.
O Brahmins, eight years have passed since this Brahmā, who is currently established as the creator of the world, was born according to this measurement.
Six months and half a day constitute the first [period], beginning with the bright fortnight; these are measured by the four types of months: solar, civil, lunar, and sidereal.

When Kali departs from all beings on the circle of the earth, it shall be three hundred and sixty-five days; by that [period] less five, the solar year (saura-saṃvatsara) and the civil day (sāvana) shall be completed.
The lunar month is diminished by eleven [days], while the sidereal month is diminished by thirty; likewise, cold, heat, and rain occur according to the solar measurement.
The production of fruits from trees and the excellence of crops likewise [occur]; as do the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices that take place upon the surface of the earth.
Exertions and marriages are determined by the solar reckoning (sāvana), as are all transactions such as usury and those arising from one's profession.
Those [calculations] would be constructed by the lunar month, including the intercalary month; however, the movements of the planets are accomplished by means of the sidereal measure.
There is nothing else whatsoever on the surface of the earth beyond these four measures; by this very standard, gods, daityas, and humans [are measured]. 15.
These excellent Brahmins abide [by this]; this is the ancient Śruti. Whoever, endowed with devotion, should read this which is the measure of the Yuga, [attains the fruit]. || 16 ||
O best of Brahmins, for one who possesses these seven marks, the fear of untimely death shall never arise in any way.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Measurement of the Yugas," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another [liṅga] located there that was established in ancient times by Durvāsas—the liṅga of the Great-Souled Three-Eyed God of gods. || 1 ||

The sages said: Who was this one named Durvāsas? By whom was this Hara installed? At what time, O illustrious one? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said: Formerly, there was a man named Niṃbaśuca in the excellent city of Vaidiśa.
And that certain monastery superintendent, remaining there, worships the Liṅga; whatever he obtains, such as clothing and other things, [he offers]. || 5 ||
He sells [the goods] here and there for the sake of the world of Maheśvara; then he constantly takes gold from them in exchange for their price.
He made no expenditure, being intent solely on accumulation; consequently, O Brahmins, after a long time, the chest of that man devoted to miserliness became unrestrained and filled with gold.
Then, having placed that filled casket in the middle of the earth, he conducts his affairs and never leaves that chamber.
O best of Brahmins, even when engaged in the worship of the gods, he never placed his trust in anyone at any time.
Then, after some time, a certain Brahmin named Duḥśīla, who was a thief of others' wealth, spied upon that [wealth] and reflected: || 10 ||
Then, for the sake of gaining the confidence of that evil-minded one, I shall become his disciple by means of various kinds of humble, pitiable words and flatteries. (11)
And being indolent by day and night, [he thought], "I shall accomplish it without doubt. When another day arrived, he saw him inside that monastery.
Then he approached him who was in the form of a staff, and having prostrated, standing bowed down with humility, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
O Blessed One, today I have indeed heard of your power through your asceticism.
Since there is no other ascetic like this one here on the surface of the earth, I have come from afar, endowed with a spirit of detachment. (15)
Having understood the worthlessness of cyclic existence, which consists of birth, death, and old age, and having realized that human youth here is, in truth, like a dream; (16)
Just as a river born from a mountain is fragile and momentary, so too are sons, wives, and whatever other kinsmen and such there may be. (17)
All these should be fully understood as associations with evil; for the sake of crossing over that ocean of saṃsāra, please speak to me. (18)
O you of noble vows, by your grace, may I today find some means established within your instruction by which I may cross over this cycle of existence.
Having heard those words of his, with the hair on his body standing on end, he reflected: "Who is this devotee of Maheśvara who has arrived here filled with anxiety? || 20 ||
As you say, you are blessed, for such is your resolve, even though you are still in the bloom of youth and remain so very delicate.
He who remains peaceful while still in the prime of youth is said here to be truly tranquil; for when the bodily constituents are wasting away, in whom would peace not arise? (22)
If you should thus possess a firm detachment established toward the cycle of existence, then propitiate Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, who bears the moon upon his crest.
The ocean of existence is not crossed by means of other terrible recitations; this has been correctly understood by me through the study of the scriptures. (24)
Whether he be a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa, a Mleccha, or a man who has committed evil deeds, if he is endowed with the initiation of Śiva and offers even a single flower, [he attains success].
By means of the six-syllabled mantra with devotion upon the linga, he attains that very goal which those who perform sacrifices attain here in this world.
Whoever gives with great devotion a garment, sandals, and a loincloth to one who has received the initiation of Śiva—what need will he have for sacrifices? (27)
Having heard that, the wicked Duḥśīla then grasped his feet; placing his own head upon them, he then spoke these words.
O Lord, by the authority of the Śiva-initiation, grant me grace, so that I may constantly perform service for you with a concentrated mind. (29)
Then that ascetic, O brahmins, reflected in his mind: "This man who has arrived appears to be someone very capable. (30)

"I have no other disciple; therefore, I shall make you one. Then, taking him by the hand, he said: "If it is so, my child, let us make an agreement together, by which I may initiate you this very day."
"You must build a small hut at a distance from this monastery; you must not enter here once the sun has set. (32)
Duḥśīla said: "O best of ascetics, your command alone is my authority. What need have I for a monastery, especially at the confluence of the rivers at night? (33)
That disciple who does not carry out the teacher’s word exactly as it was spoken, his vow is in vain, and after that he goes to hell. (34)
Having heard that, the sage Niṃbaśuca then attained satisfaction and bestowed the initiation of Śiva upon him who was endowed with humility.
From that time forward, he was exceedingly devoted to serving him; intent on his service, he delighted his heart.
Meditating in his mind day after day for the sake of that alone, he perceives no flaw whatsoever, even though he examines it with great effort.
And although he was a devotee of Śiva, he would somehow release that various girdle made of gold from his waist even during meals or the worship of the gods.
Then that immoral man reflected in his own mind: "There is no way at all for me to enter the monastery during the night. (39)
Whatever one bestows at the time of sunset, that becomes a very firm iron bar (parigha) for the evildoer in an instant; what more need I say? (40)
This monastery is firmly constructed of stone and cannot be undermined; because of its height, it cannot be entered by any other various means. (41)
"Shall I administer poison to him? Or shall I slay him with weapons? Or shall I bring about his death even by day through the slaughter of an animal? (42)
As he was reflecting thus, the rainy season arrived; it was during the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun was situated in Cancer.
A certain wealthy man, a devotee of Maheśvara, quickly arrived there; having prostrated himself, he said loudly, "I shall perform the Pavitraka rite. (44)
"O Mistress, if on the fourteenth day you have a command for me, and if you come to my village endowed with grace," (45)
Sūta said: Having heard that, the sage Niṃbaśuca attained satisfaction; saying "So be it," he dispatched him at that very moment.
"I shall come at the proper time accompanied by my own disciple; I will bring about your supreme welfare, my child, of this there is no doubt. (47)
Then, when the time had arrived, having reflected upon the morning rites, that devotee of Śiva set out at the break of day; accompanied by Duḥśīla, his hair stood on end with joy.
Then, as he was proceeding, there stood upon his path the famous and holy river Muralā, which flows toward the ocean.
Having seen her, he spoke these words: "O child, O disciple, I shall perform the worship of the deity together with you; remain steady by the Muralā river."
Having said, "So be it," he remained on that auspicious bank; and he too was always delighted by the virtues of that man who was pure despite [living near] the neem tree.
Recognizing him as a worthy disciple and having attained supreme confidence, he took that [image] which had been concealed and was produced from a measure of gold.
He threw his ragged garment upon the ground near Jāgeśvara, and then went a short distance away for the purpose of voiding excrement.
As long as he remained surrounded by reeds and was out of sight, Duḥśīla took that much [of the garment] and set off quickly toward the northern direction with a joyful heart.
Then he arrived, but he did not see anyone at all who was of immoral conduct; he saw only a patched garment accompanied by Jāgeśvara.
Then, having performed some purification very quickly, he, being deeply dejected, arrived—without even performing the ritual sipping of water—at the place where that ragged garment lay.
Then, realizing that she had been abducted and deprived of even the slightest portion [of her essence], that disciple, overcome by fainting, fell upon the surface of the earth. (57)
Then, regaining consciousness and rising up with great difficulty, he immediately struck his own limbs and his head against a stone.
"Alas! I am slain, I am ruined, I have been robbed by that evil-minded one! What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can I look upon him? (59)
Then, having observed his path, he certainly set out; but due to old age and exhaustion, he turned back and went to the monastery. || 60 ||
Even though he was of immoral character, having taken that amount, he went to another place; there, with that gold, he engaged in various transactions.
Then, having entered the state of a householder and taken a wife, he reached old age, yet remained devoid of progeny.
Then, after some time, a certain Brahmin, devoted to pilgrimage, went to Camatkārapura together with his wife.
Having bathed in all the sacred fords and at the temples of the gods, he beheld while wandering a true sage named Durvāsas.
Devoted to the dance and song of his own deity with true devotion, he saw him, bowed down, and spoke these words: (65)
"By whom was this stainless Liṅga, born of Śaṅkara, established? Why do you dance and sing before it? This conduct of yours is not at all appropriate for sages. (66)
Durvāsas said: "This Liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods was installed by me, because Maheśvara, the God of gods, is fond of dance and song. (67)
I possess no wealth whatsoever with which I might enjoy myself.
In the meantime, one named Cirbhaṭi, a knower of Yoga, arrived; he questioned Durvāsas with these words concerning the Vedānta.
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, enveloped in blind darkness; to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. (70)
Then, having sat down, he gave his decision; and Duḥśīla also understood all of that which was praised by him.
Then, a special devotion toward Hara arose within him; having prostrated before him, he spoke these words aloud: 72.

"O Blessed One, I am a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone and not by my actions. Never have I given food to anyone; rather, having deceived gods and Brahmins, I have seized their wealth while overcome by the vice arising from gambling and prostitutes. (74)
And so, even though I am a Brāhmaṇa, I have made myself a devotee of Śiva as my guru; I have deceived him with many flatteries and have squandered his wealth. (75)
His wealth was even greater and acquired through righteous means; and he, my guru, has come here from the other world. (76)
I am consumed day and night by that very remorse; grant me your grace through the performance of preliminary rites and the giving of gifts.

"I possess abundant wealth, O Lord of Sages, but I have no progeny. Therefore, tell me, O Sage, what is the highest good for that wealth so that, by means of it, I may accomplish everything in this world and the next. (78)
Durvāsas said: "A man who, after committing thousands of sins, subsequently becomes devoted to dharma, may cross the ocean of saṃsāra with great difficulty. (79)
Even if that person whom you have made your Śaiva guru was created by you through unrighteousness, he is nonetheless a guru; of this there is no doubt. (80)

A Brahmin should first be a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), then a householder; thereafter he may be a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and an ascetic (yati), and finally a forest-dweller of the hut-dwelling type (kuṭīcara). || 81 ||
From that one becomes a *bahūdaka*, and from that a *haṃsa*; thereafter, having resorted to this path, one attains liberation. || 82 ||
Furthermore, by you following a wrong path and by that Brahmin as well, who has resorted to the path of Śiva, a great sin has been committed. (83)
Duḥśīla said: "Indeed, Rudra is glorified in all the Vedas as the Lord; why then have you spoken of a fault arising from his initiation? (84)
Durvāsas said: "What you have declared is true; in the Veda, Rudra is celebrated in many ways, as is Vāsudeva, and especially Brahmā. (85)

Furthermore, the initiation of a Brahmin arising from the binding of vows consists of the supreme Gāyatrī as the mantra to be recited; for he is indeed a guru devoted to his vow. He who performs any other initiation, whether Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva, [is not so]. (86)
Even if he were a knower of the six Vedāṅgas, he would not be a Brāhmaṇa here; furthermore, a distinction of marks has arisen in you regarding deceit and such.
There is no doubt that by abandoning your vow, you possess nothing there; therefore, I have properly considered an expiation according to the path of the Smṛtis.
Duḥśīla said: "The wise declare that the friendship of the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together; honoring our state of friendship, I shall say something—listen to that. (89)
"I possess abundant wealth; if it can be accomplished by means of that, then tell me, O illustrious one, how I may do everything. (90)
Durvāsas said: "There is indeed only one means for the destruction of your sin; if you perform it according to my word, you shall become purified. (91)
They praise austerity in the Kṛta age, and knowledge alone in the Tretā; pilgrimage in the Dvāpara, and charity alone in the Kali age.
Now this Kali age prevails, which is of a terrible nature; therefore, give me a black antelope skin for the purification of all sins.
Moreover, you possess a sense of shame arising from the wealth of your guru; for that reason, build a temple for Śaṅkara in his name.
By means of this, you indeed attain freedom from debt to him at that very moment; furthermore, whatever wealth he may acquire elsewhere shall also belong to him.
Always give with a concentrated mind to distinguished Brahmins; especially, always give a vessel of sesame seeds along with gold.
By this, all your sin shall go to destruction from your body; furthermore, I always come here with devotion during the month of Caitra.
"Even though this palace was built by me at a very great distance from Kalpagrāma, I shall go back to that very place; for this is my established vow. (98)
Therefore, you must indeed reflect upon this temple which was built by me; it should always be contemplated here through various acts such as ritual bathing and the like. 99.
Duḥśīla said: "O virtuous sage, I shall do as you say; I will follow your word. (100)
Durvāsas said: When the black antelope skin has been given for the sake of purification from all sins, O twice-born one, offer vessels of sesame seeds for the purification of secret sins.
Sūta said: Having heard those words, that high-souled one then devoutly gave a black antelope skin to a Brāhmaṇa who maintained the sacred fires.
O twice-born ones, according to the instruction of Durvāsas and by the prescribed method, you should always give vessels of sesame seeds to him with constant devotion.
And he bestowed upon him, whose sins had departed, the initiation that brings about liberation; thus, having duly granted the initiation to him whose sins were gone, [he performed the rites]. 104.
Then he spoke sweetly: "Give me my preceptor's fee."
Duḥśīla said: "O Lord, ask quickly for whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) you desire; if I have the power, I shall grant it to you, free from any stinginess regarding wealth. (106)
Durvāsas said: "I shall go to Kalpagrāma now, for the Kali age has arrived; I will not return here until the Kṛta age has indeed come again."
"This palace which has been built by me is indeed half-finished; you must bring it to completion, for this shall be my teacher's fee. (108)

Whatever [performance] such as dance and song there may be, that should be carried out according to one's own ability; likewise, an offering (bali) and other things such as flowers should be presented before him.
Having spoken thus, that lord of sages then departed for Kalpagrāma; and even Duḥśīla acted exactly as he had been instructed.
Sūta said: Thus, as that devoted man performed those duties, he was thereafter celebrated by that name; he who was known as Duḥśīla. || 111 ||
And whoever constantly beholds that deity in the month of Caitra, having performed [this] for a moment, is liberated from the sin accumulated over a year. (112)
Furthermore, whoever performs his entire ceremonial bathing, the sin accumulated over thirty years perishes from that person's body.
Furthermore, whoever performs dance, song, and so forth before him, shall also attain liberation from the sins committed from birth until death.
Sūta said: Even though he was of ill character, having built that temple of Śiva in the name of his preceptor, it became renowned as Nimbeśvara, situated in the southern direction.
He performed this with supreme devotion while recollecting his lotus feet; likewise, his wife, who was known by the name Śākambharī, [did the same].
There, Durgā was installed by her with her own name inscribed upon it; thereafter, only a small remnant of that wealth remained for the two of them.
Having offered it to the deities for the sake of worship and having presented it to the Brahmins, the couple thereafter became eaters of alms. || 4 ||
Then, after some time, Duḥśīla met his death.
O tiger among kings, Śākambharī also, with a mind free from doubt, took that body and entered the fire.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot well-served by excellent apsarases, those two, their hair standing on end with joy, both went to heaven.
O King, whoever recites this supreme narrative born of [the account of] Duḥśīla is liberated from all sins committed through ignorance.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Origin of Nimbeśvara and Śākambharī," in the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 275.
Sūta said: Likewise, O best of Brahmins, there are also eleven other Rudras who dwell here, having been born out of a desire for the welfare of the sages.
By seeing, worshipping, praising, or bowing down to them, a mortal becomes free from sin and liberated from all defects. || 2 ||
The sages said: "Only one Rudra has been heard of, and never a second; he whose beloved wife is Gaurī and who is proclaimed to have Skanda as his son. (3)
"Therefore, we know Rudra alone as the Lord and no other in any way; so, O illustrious one, explain all of these to us in great detail."
Sūta said: "O highly fortunate ones, what you have declared is true: Rudra alone exists; there is no second whatsoever."
Furthermore, O sirs, I shall proclaim how those eleven Rudras were born here; listen with well-composed minds.
In former times, there resided in Vārāṇasī sages of celebrated vows who were eager for the sight of the god Hāṭakeśvara.
Having set out and made an agreement while competing with one another, they said, "I shall see that Lord first, I shall see him first! (8)
He who, having gone there first, does not behold Hara at Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla while standing before everyone else—upon that single person shall fall the sin born of the fatigue of all.
Having spoken thus, they all then set out from Vārāṇasī and thereafter proceeded, running with great speed.

In the meantime, the Lord known as Hāṭakeśvara, perceiving their intention arising from mutual rivalry and noting that they were preceded by great devotion for the sake of seeing him, [appeared]. (11)
While being protected by that small [serpent], at that very moment he emerged from Pātāla through a hole in the city wall for the sake of all those great-souled ones.
Having assumed eleven beautiful forms—bearing tridents, possessing three eyes, and adorned with matted locks—he appeared.
The Lord Śaṅkara stood there equally visible to their sight, wearing a crescent moon and bearing a garland of severed heads.
Then, beholding the bull-bannered Lord standing before them, they knelt upon the earth and offered hymns of praise from every side.
"Alone does this god know that he has come into my sight—the God of gods, Mahādeva, who from the beginning is affectionate toward his devotees. (16)
"Another knows my former birth, O best of ascetics; and the lords of brahmins, having knelt upon the ground, offered hymns of praise. (17)
The ascetics said: Salutations to the God of gods, who consists of all the gods; salutations to the peaceful one, to the subtle one, and salutations to the destroyer of Andhaka. (18)
Salutations be to all the Rudras who always dwell in heaven; they sustain the world with various kinds of winds. (19)
Salutation to all the Rudras who abide in the western quarter and protect all the worlds from the evil-minded Piśācas. 20.
Salutations be to all the Rudras who have taken refuge in the upward direction; they protect all the worlds from the fear of the devouring spirits (bhūtas). || 21 ||
Salutations be to all the Rudras who reside below and above; they always protect all the worlds from the fear of the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
To those innumerable thousands of Rudras who have taken refuge upon the earth—to all of them, as well as to those who protect them from disease, be homage! (23)
Thus praised by those eleven ascetics, all eleven Rudras spoke to those ascetics who were bowed down in devotion.
The Rudras said: "O best of ascetics, I am pleased with you in eleven ways because of your great excess of devotion; therefore, choose whatever you desire. (25)
The ascetics said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with us, and if you grant our desire, then may you always remain right here in these eleven forms."
"In the auspicious field of Hāṭakeśvara, which contains all sacred fords, we dwell while performing our worship. (27)
The Blessed Lord said: "The eleven forms that have been fashioned by me—indeed, with all of these very forms, I shall remain here forever."
But that first form of mine which took refuge on Kailāsa remains forever here on Kailāsa, the best of mountains. (29)
"O best of the twice-born, these forms of ours shall remain right here forever for the welfare of all the worlds. (30)
O twice-born ones, those mortals who, having bathed themselves in the Viśvāmitra lake, worship these images of mine here in due order with your names, shall attain the supreme goal. (31)
O best of the twice-born, what is the use of speaking at great length again and again? Whatever worship is performed for them shall become elevenfold in merit.

Having spoken thus, the Three-eyed Lord vanished on the spot. They too, having established a hermitage there and being endowed with supreme faith, worshipped those forms and attained the highest state.
Furthermore, any other man who worships them with faith goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.
From that time forth, those eleven Rudras were born by number from the God of gods, bearing the body of Maheśvara.
Supremely radiant, endowed with [divine] powers, three-eyed, and holding tridents in their hands—this which I was asked, O best of the twice-born, has all been narrated to you.
The elevenfold [manifestation] is as follows: when Maheśvara was born, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra. || 37 ||
He who worships them with devotion attains the supreme goal; the poor man obtains wealth, and he who is childless shall have sons.

One who is diseased shall be freed from disease, and one who has been defeated shall achieve the destruction of his enemies; by the very propitiation of Him, one shall attain the infinity of all desires. (39)
Furthermore, listen to the fruit obtained by one who is enriched by the initiation of Śiva, who is devoted to the ritual bath of ashes, and who performs the propitiation of that [deity]. (40)
Whatever fruit another mortal might obtain through worship, that same fruit is attained with a single flower by means of the six-syllabled mantra.

He who bears the initiation of Śiva obtains a hundredfold fruit; he who is a Pāśupata obtains a hundredfold more than that from a Śaiva; and so too does he who is a Kālamukha and he who observes the Great Vow (mahāvrata). || 42 ||
And for all those who, bowing with devotion, worship those images, their fruit shall indeed be a hundredfold.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Eleven Rudras," in the *Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*, within the sixth part of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: O great sage, tell us in detail the names of those twice-born ones who have come from Vārāṇasī, and whose eleven-fold Rudra is [worshipped] with supreme devotion; tell us their designations as well.
Sūta said: One among them was a deer-hunter, famous throughout the three worlds; the second was named Sarva; and the third was Nindita.
O best of sages, the fourth is called Mahāyaśas; O best of sages, the fifth is said to be Ajaikapāda.
Ahirbudhnya is the sixth, and Pinākin is the seventh; Paraṃtapa is another, and Dahanas is the ninth.
Īśvara is declared the tenth, and Kapālī is likewise the last; these names by which they are established indeed belong to those Rudras as well, for they were ordained by Hara himself. || 5 ||
The sages said: "Tell us quickly which gifts are commendable for that purpose, and also how the recitation (japa) was previously described by you as being performed."
Sūta said: With that in view, one should give [the gifts] individually to each person; O highly fortunate one, cows should be given visibly, one after another in due order.
To the hunter, a cow manifesting from molasses should be given; to the skull-bearer, one originating from fresh butter should be offered.
A cow arisen from ghee should be given to Ajapāda; a golden cow to Ahirbudhnya; and a cow produced from salt should be offered to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
O best of Brahmins, [the oblations] originating from juices are for Paraṃtapa; those born of food are said to be for Dahana; and those produced from water are for Īśvara.
The Grandfather has declared that the wise man who gives these [gifts] to these great-souled ones shall certainly become a universal monarch (cakravartin). || 11 ||
If they are given even elsewhere, how much more so when in the presence of Bhava? Therefore, with every effort, these should be bestowed with diligence.
If one is unable [to give many], at least one cow should be given with effort; this is the word of Bhartṛyajña regarding all the Rudras. (13)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Giving in the Vicinity of the Eleven Rudras," within the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 277 ||
Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, there are other Sun-gods present there in the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara, who were installed by Yājñavalkya.
He who worships them with devotion, keeping his desired objects in mind on every seventh lunar day, attains them; of this there is no doubt.

The sages said: "Only one sun is seen situated in the vault of the sky; how then are these twelve established in that sacred field? At what time, for what purpose, and by what rite were they so placed, O son of Sūta? (3)
Sūta said: Formerly, there was one named Kṛti, born from Śunaḥśepa.
His son was Śunahputra, the best of sages; his son was Cārāyaṇa, the best of sages. || 5 ||
Then, after some time, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, having been consumed by the curse of Sāvitrī, descended to the surface of the earth.

O Brahmins, when the Gāyatrī has been brought by him for the sacrificial rite, and she remains standing before him at the assembly of all the gods, there shall be no lapse of time as long as he remains firm in his intention to welcome Sāvitrī.
Then, by his command, Gāyatrī was brought as a cowherd girl by Śakra; she was endowed with divine marks.
And having recognized her as the cowherd’s daughter, the Lotus-born One caused her to enter through the mouth of the cow and then drew her out again through the secret passage.
The lineage of the Brahmins and that of the cows are indeed one, though established in two ways: on one side reside the mantras, and on the other side resides the sacrificial oblation.
Having thus made her a Brāhmaṇī woman, the Grandfather (Brahmā), though standing before him, subsequently performed the formal acceptance of her according to the rites prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Then, O best of the twice-born, while she was seated in the wife’s chamber, Sāvitrī arrived, surrounded by the wives of the gods.
Then, beholding her adorned with a girdle, she was overcome with the sorrow of misfortune and consequently cursed Fate.
Sāvitrī said: "Since I, though faultless, have been abandoned by you, O Grandfather, you are indeed my grandfather from this day forward in our union. (14)
"The duty of men should be the taking of another woman as a wife; since you have done this, you shall become a human being. (15)
And he, being especially afflicted by desire, will undoubtedly act according to my word. || 16 ||
Having spoken thus, Sāvitrī left that sacrificial pavilion and, having ascended a mountain peak, thereafter performed great penance.
Due to that curse, the Grandfather (Brahmā) also descended to the surface of the earth in the dwelling of Cārāyaṇa after a long time.
When he reached his youth and remained among men as before, he was likewise tormented by the heat arising from desire.
Then, his mind free from doubt yet proud of his own beauty and fortune, he gazed upon a woman, a maiden, or even an ascetic woman, and took his pleasure with her.
Then, seeing him afflicted by such calamity, the sage Cārāyaṇa himself, out of great indignation, expelled him from his own hermitage.
Abandoned by his father and wandering here and there, he reached the city of Camatkārapura, where Śākalya resided.
By name he was Brāhmaṇaśārdūla, a native of Nāgara who had mastered the Vedas; surrounded by a thousand disciples, he propagated the knowledge of the Vedas.
Then, having bowed deeply to him, he entered into discipleship; and after a long time, he became fully accomplished in the study of the Vedas.
At that very time, the lord of Ānarta himself arrived and remained where Hari himself lies upon the waters.
At that time, he undertook the Cāturmāsya vow in his presence; then, O Brahmins, Śākalya was requested by that king.
"You must constantly perform rites for peace and prosperity in my abode; please grant this favor so that I may remain here as long as I stay. (27)
Having said "So be it," O best of the twice-born, he out of courtesy sent each of his own disciples to that man's residence.
Having performed the rite for peace and having bestowed a blessing upon the king, he received a sacrificial fee from him and returned once more to that brahmin.
Having given that sacrificial fee to Śākalya in his own home, he would always go [to him]; indeed, such was the established practice.
When another day arrived, Yājñavalkya, dismissed by Śākalya, went to the king’s palace for the sake of performing propitiatory rites.
That king had a beautiful and playful consort named Mantharā; and at night, that passionate man enjoyed with her, his lovely beloved.

He was embraced by her with the various amorous gestures (*bhāva*) taught by Vātsyāyana, beginning with the different types of embraces; and he was marked upon his body and his lower lip with diverse patterns such as the peacock’s foot (*mayūrapadaka*), as well as with jewels and corals.
He arrived in the presence of Śākalya for the purpose of study; meanwhile, he was dispatched by him to the king’s palace for the sake of performing propitiatory rites.
O twice-born ones, having been dispatched by him, he went to that royal palace and performed the propitiatory rite according to the prescribed injunctions.

At the conclusion of the rite for peace (śāntika), however, one should take up the water from the ritual jar, which has been prepared with the five limbs and consecrated by the Rudra-mantras themselves.
Taking with him unbroken rice grains and jasmine flowers, he then went to where King Ānarta was staying, engaged in his religious observances. (37)

Having recited the mantra "dyāmālekhi" according to the prescribed rite, including its meter and seer, as soon as he cast it upon his head, he was gazed upon by him [the deity] and cut to pieces with nail-scratches.
Then, with his lower lip thus bitten, the king became dejected.
Seeing him dressed in soiled garments and appearing like a commoner, he laughed loudly and said to him: "O Brahmin, give me a handful of unbroken rice grains. (40)
Seeing this piece of wood situated in the stable, Yājñavalkya, filled with anger, rushed toward it.
Having poured water along with unbroken grains (akṣata) there, O Brahmins, he returned home without accepting the king's customary gift (dakṣiṇā). || 42 ||
In the meantime, various branches adorned with sprouts emerged from all sides of that piece of teak wood.
Having seen that, the king, the lord of Ānarta, was struck with wonder and felt profound remorse, thinking, "Fie upon me for having acted in this way!"
He is surely some divine being who has assumed the form of a Brahmin, by whom such power of this mantra has been established.
"If I accept the water consecrated by his mantra, then I shall undoubtedly become free from old age and death. (46)
O best of the twice-born, as that king reflected thus in wonder, that day became like a hundred years.
When the day had somehow passed for that king, the autumnal night would somehow not come to an end.
Then, having risen at the time of dawn, the lord of the earth summoned Śākalya by means of trustworthy messengers.
Then, standing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke respectfully and humbly: "Tomorrow morning, a disciple of yours who has come into my presence will arrive. (50)
O best of the twice-born, he must still be sent today for the sake of pacification; today, absolute devotion toward him has arisen within me alone.
Having promised "So be it," he went to his own palace and spoke to Yājñavalkya with gentle words for the sake of pacification.
"Go, my child, this very day to the residence of the king; you have been invited by him once again for the sake of performing propitiatory rites. (53)
Yājñavalkya said: "O bull among the twice-born, I will not go to that house for the sake of peace; I was looked upon with disrespect, and no blessing was offered to me. (54)
"Without a doubt, I placed [the fire] upon the wood at his word; therefore, O Guru, send another discerning disciple who, endowed with wisdom, might delight Ānarta."
Śākalya said: "The commands of the king must always be carried out by the people residing in the land, for the sake of providing security and prosperity, as well as for their sole benefit. (56)
O best of the twice-born, that dull-witted person who acts in opposition to kings will never experience happiness in any way.
For those who do not serve kings out of great pride in their birth and other such qualities, begging for alms until death is ordained as their atonement.
While the teacher and the disciple were thus disputing, men sent by the king arrived there once again.
Filled with haste and standing with palms joined in reverence, they said to Śākalya: "Send that disciple away quickly; the king is waiting for him on the road. (60)
When he did not depart even though it was told to him repeatedly, he then dispatched Uddālaka Āruṇi.
To the disciple, who was endowed with discipline and stood with palms joined in reverence, he said: "Go now, my child, at my command to the king's palace."
Having performed the rite of pacification, you should then engage in the study of the scriptures.
Having promised "So be it," he went to that royal palace and performed a rite for peace according to the procedure prescribed by the rules.
Then, taking the water from the jar along with unbroken grains of rice and flowers, he ran to the place where the king was stationed.
The king said: "O twice-born one, grant me consecration by means of the mark of your own mantra upon this wood which stands upright at its tip before you."
Then, having recited an auspicious mantra and personally sprinkled that desired water upon the wood, he departed for his own home.
Upon seeing that wood of such a form, King Ānarta was filled with despondency and overcome with remorse. (68)
Furthermore, at that time, he dispatched another messenger, Vidagdha, who was a learned Brahmin, for the sake of Yājñavalkya and on behalf of Śākalya.
"O best of the twice-born, my bodily sensation is persisting; for the sake of its pacification, quickly dispatch that disciple who was previously gathered. (70)
O best of the twice-born, an insult was committed by me against him yesterday; because of that, a disease suddenly afflicted me even though I did not desire his blessing.
"Therefore, send for me quickly, so that I may attain well-being. Even though he was told this repeatedly, when he still did not go, [the king said: 72.
Then Yājñavalkya spoke respectfully to another disciple; he then sent him, Madhuka Paingya, to that man's house.
He performed that very same rite as had been fashioned by Uddālaka; and a blessing was bestowed upon that Kāṣṭha on behalf of the king.
Having seen that wood of such a form, the king once again dispatched another man for the sake of Yājñavalkya. (79)
Although he was addressed repeatedly, Yājñavalkya would indeed not go; when that happened, he appointed another disciple who possessed many virtues.
Having gone to Pracūḍa and Bhāgavitti as before, he also performed the propitiatory rite just as it had been performed by those two previously.
Then he poured the water of pacification onto that wood with the recitation of mantras; nevertheless, it remained established in that very same form.
Then the king himself, filled with remorse, went to the residence of Śākalya for the sake of [obtaining] Yājñavalkya’s mantra.

Having bowed down to Śākalya, the best of the twice-born, that foremost of brahmins said: "O best of the twice-born, at dawn tomorrow, please direct your disciple to my house for the sake of peace, so that my body may find tranquility. (80)
Then, O best of the twice-born, Śākalya spoke again to Yājñavalkya while King Ānarta was listening.
"O Yājñavalkya, go quickly to the king's palace at my command; O son, perform a propitiatory rite for the destruction of this king's disease."
Yājñavalkya said: "O Teacher, I will not go there; do not speak thus to me. An insult has been offered to me by this king, O Teacher. (83)
Having heard those words of his, he became extremely angry; then, rebuking Yājñavalkya, he spoke further.
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple, there is no wealth on earth that, by giving it, he could become free from his debt. (85)
"Since you have become my disciple yet do not carry out my word, I shall now join you with the curse of Brahmā."
Yājñavalkya said: "If you indeed bestow a curse upon me, O Guru, by means of injustice, then I too shall now bestow a counter-curse upon you. (87)
Even a guru—if he is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, and persisting in a wrong path—is ordained to be abandoned. (88)
Therefore, you have indeed been abandoned by me now; for my teacher does not give such an instruction indiscriminately for the sake of a disciple. (89)
"As many disciples as there are among those who stand here, for that many days I shall carry out your command; otherwise, I shall go far away. (90)
Śākalya said: "If you go elsewhere, then abandon the knowledge which I have taught you, O sinful one! Go away, O wicked disciple! (91)
"Drink this water consecrated by me, which was produced from the razor and the skull; by its power you shall very quickly expel from your belly my own lore, which was previously studied by you."
Having spoken thus and consecrated the water with Atharvan mantras, that best of the twice-born gave it to him to drink for the purpose of inducing vomiting.
Yājñavalkya, having drunk that water consecrated by him, vomited it up along with his food and abandoned that knowledge.
Then, having fallen into a state of delusion, he went to the auspicious Viśvāmitra lake; having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, he became pure and composed in mind.
With devotion, he fashioned those images in the number twelve of the Sun; having then installed them all, he worshipped them with piety.
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Śakra, Varuṇa, and Sāmba; Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Savitṛ as the tenth; Tvaṣṭṛ as the eleventh, and Viṣṇu is called the twelfth. (97)
Thus the wise man established the Sun here in twelve forms; thereafter, he worshipped him constantly with perfumes, flowers, and ointments. (98)
Then, after a long time, the Sun-god appeared before his eyes and spoke these words with affection to the sage Sundara: || 99 ||
"O Yājñavalkya, best of Brahmins, I am well-pleased with you. I shall grant you what you desire; tell me whatever you currently wish for. (100)
Yājñavalkya said: "O Lord, if you grant me a boon, employ me in the recitation of the Vedas, so that I may now become your disciple. (101)
Āditya said: "O best of the twice-born, O twice-born one, I must always perform a circumambulation for the sake of Meru and for the purpose of illuminating the worlds. (102)
Therefore, O twice-born one, how shall I unite you with the recitation of the Vedas?
Therefore, becoming light, stay at my ear and that of my chief horse, by means of my word and my splendor.
"You shall not burn, O illustrious one; staying there, perform your studies. Having promised "So be it," he entered the solar horses.
Then Karṇa studied all four Vedas from his mouth, complete with their limbs (aṅgas), sub-limbs (upāṅgas), and the supplementary treatises (pariśiṣṭas).
Then, when it was completed, he said: "O Lord, pray to me; I shall undoubtedly grant you today the teacher's fee."
Āditya said: "O best of the twice-born, those hymns (sūktas) of mine which are in the Ṛgveda, the sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) in the Yajurveda, and the Sāmans in the third [Veda]," 108.
And all those things declared in the Kalpa should be propagated by you on the surface of the earth in the fourth [age], after providing an excellent exposition.
Those twice-born ones who shall proclaim all of these before me, they all, liberated from sin, shall go to the abode of the gods.
Furthermore, those twice-born ones who, being devoted to me, shall explain [this], they will attain liberation; this which I have spoken is the truth.
Sūta said: Having thus studied the Vedas and having bestowed the teacher’s fee, he returned once more toward Camatkārapura from the presence of the Sun.
Then, approaching Śākalya, he said: "O highly fortunate one, you have previously stood as my guru; request whatever you wish, and I shall grant it as a preceptor's fee."
O best of the twice-born, even if an elder brother, a father, a mother, or likewise a guru should behave with hostility, they must nevertheless be honored by a man; of this there is no doubt. (114)
I have studied all four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs; indeed, I have mastered them all and have fully comprehended their meaning. || 115 ||
"Tell me the truth, O illustrious one; what reward shall I grant you? (116)
Śākalya said: Those secrets of the Vedas which were told to you by the Sun—
"Proclaim to me quickly those [teachings] by which, when explained or recited, there may be the destruction of sin; this shall be my teacher’s fee. (118)
Yājñavalkya said: "Therefore, come with me to where the Suns are established; there I shall proclaim their twelve names to you. (119)
Having heard that, Śākalya, accompanied by his disciples and those twice-born ones, [went] with the disciples who were stationed there and installed by him as forms of the Sun.
Then, standing before him, he recited that exposition of all the Vedāntas exactly as it had been previously taught by Ravi.
And at their conclusion, Yājñavalkya was gratified by Brāhmaṇas who were conversant with the Vedānta and possessed of the fourfold conduct.
"By your grace, we have been declared knowers of Vedānta; being perfected in sacred revelation and study, please accept our preceptor’s fee. (123)

Yājñavalkya said: O twice-born ones, those Brahmins who shall proclaim the praises of these suns of mine before others—by your grace, O Brahmins, may they attain the path to heaven; this, O Brahmins, is my teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā). || 124 ||
Furthermore, those who, endowed with devotion, shall perform this investigation, for them there is that fourth state which is free from old age and death.

The Brahmins said: "In the Kali age, O Brahmins, [people] will be possessed of a state of wretchedness; they will not even have the capacity for recitation, so what need is there to mention exposition? (126)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, recite the Sārasvata among the Vedas, by which even those afflicted by misfortune shall proclaim it.

Yājñavalkya said: "The hymn that begins with 'They yoke the chariot' (rathaṃ yuñjanti), which is characterized by wealth, and the hymn beginning with 'O best of Brāhmaṇas, it is in the Triṣṭubh meter' (triṣṭubhā) are likewise the first. (1293)
The hymn "citraṃ devānām" and likewise another, "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," which is dear to him, were then recited, bringing great joy.
Likewise, those Rigvedic scholars who shall recite the Pāvamāna hymn—indeed, by this very first [hymn] of theirs, they shall go to the supreme goal.
The Sāman-chanters who stand here, pure and steadfast, shall proclaim the twenty-one Sāmans that are beloved by the Ādityas.
But those who, maintaining supreme resolve, shall offer praise to the Sun, they too shall go forth, having pierced through the solar orb.
Those twice-born ones who shall proclaim the *Kṣurikāsaṃpuṭa* as well as the *Sūryakalpa*, together with the *Śāntikalpa*, [shall attain the highest state]. (133)
Even those who recite the Atharvaveda shall attain the supreme goal; even fools, having come together when the day of the Sun has arrived, [shall do so].
O twice-born ones, those who perform prostration endowed with supreme faith shall attain liberation from the sins committed during seven nights.
Sūta said: When those born of the four orders had thus promised, Yājñavalkya was recognized by some among the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, O lord of men, that king was received by the ruler named Ratna for the purpose of hearing all the Vedāntas.
And having fully understood the majesty of the one born from the Sun (Sūryasaṃbhava), O best of the twice-born, he then installed the Sun in that place.
Furthermore, whatever man beholds that [image] on a Sunday is liberated from the sins committed during seven nights; of this there is no doubt. || 139 ||
Thus has all this majesty originating from the Sun been told to you; the man who hears it with devotion shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Whatever fruit is obtained by making a gift during a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or under the asterism of Śravaṇa, one attains that same fruit simply by hearing this supreme majesty.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of Yājñavalkya," within the "Glorious Majesty of Ratnāditya and the Origin of the Twelve Suns" in the "Glorious Majesty of the Holy Hāṭakeśvara Field," in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 278 ||
Sūta said: This entire Purāṇa was formerly spoken by Skanda to Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā; from him, Aṅgiras likewise received it.
From him, the sage Ṛcīka then obtained it; thus it was received through successive lineage throughout all the worlds.
This Skanda Purāṇa was formerly extracted by Kumāra; the man who hears it in the midst of the virtuous is liberated from sin.
This ancient Purāṇa, which bestows long life and brings happiness to all social orders, was composed here by the great-souled Ṣaṇmukha with constant devotion.
Thus has this narrative been told of old; may it be well with you. || 5 ||
If a person hears the majesty of the Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra, no one would be able to calculate the extent of his merit.
He who bestows this greatness of the Dharma upon a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the heavenly world for as long as the number of its syllables.
Just as the streams of rain when it rains, or as the stars in the sky, or as the sands in the Ganges—likewise, no number can be found for them.
Whatever man listens with devotion for even a few days, he becomes successful in all his aims—he who reads this narrative.
One desiring a son obtains sons; one desiring wealth obtains wealth; and a maiden desiring a husband obtains a charming husband.
Relatives who have gone abroad also obtain reunion; indeed, by hearing the Skanda Purāṇa, a man attains his heart's desire.
For those who hear and read it, this bestows all desires upon men; the king conquers the earth and likewise overcomes his enemies. (12)
Having heard this meritorious Purāṇa, one indeed attains a long life; a Brāhmaṇa becomes a knower of the Vedas, and a Kṣatriya obtains a kingdom. (13)
A Vaiśya shall obtain wealth and grain, and a Śūdra shall attain happiness; whoever hears even a single quarter-verse of this [hymn] goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, whoever honors the reciter after hearing this Purāṇa, by him Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra themselves have been worshipped. (15)
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple, there is no wealth on earth that, by giving it, he would become free from his debt. (16)
Therefore, Vyāsa, the instructor of the scriptures, must be fully honored with cows, land, gold, garments, and other such items, as well as with foods that satisfy all desires. (17)
He who, endowed with such devotion, having heard this unsurpassed scripture, honors the instructor, shall attain the state of Śiva. || 18 ||
Merely by hearing the Purāṇas, the sin accumulated over many births comes to rest, and one obtains the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites. || 19 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Listening to the Purāṇas," in the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, within the sixth part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 279 ||
Thus ends the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
